title: It is eating me alive! – A case of intragastric band erosion
clinical_history: A 64-year-old female with a history of gastric band placement since 2012, presents in the last 5 months with worsening cutaneous inflammatory signs and a purulent drainage and redness, surrounding the subcutaneous port, removed 4 months ago. In the ambulatory appointment, the patient was referred for further evaluation with computed tomography.
imaging_findings: CT revealed elevation of the left diaphragm, with the presence of a gastric band positioned at the cardia, below the esophagogastric junction. Signs of erosion and apparent invasion of the gastric wall are observed, with the gastric band partially in the gastric lumen due to the presence of gas foci adjacent to the surgical material. However, there are no evident signs of pneumoperitoneum (Figures 1a and 1b). An abscessed collection surrounding the catheter is also detected along its path to the left lateral abdominal wall, where the subcutaneous port was previously removed (Figures 2a and 2b). An endoscopic study confirmed the imaging findings—the presence of a partially gastric band eroding the gastric wall (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c and 3d).
discussion: Background Gastric banding is a restrictive type of laparoscopic bariatric surgery in which a band is placed around the proximal portion of the stomach [1]. The most common complications are pouch dilatation, band slippage, and port complications [2,3]. However, a new complication from the long-term use of gastric bands has arisen: intragastric band erosion. It develops when there is erosion of the gastric wall by the silicone ring, resulting in its migration to the gastric lumen. This complication is rare, affecting less than 2% of patients and it is a late complication in patients with long use of this device [2]. The pathophysiology is thought to occur due to the high pressures caused by this device, leading to necrosis of the adjacent gastric wall [4,5]. Erosion can also arise from the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and adhesions from the dissection that occurred during band placement [4,5]. Clinical Perspective Intragastric band erosion can be a slow and subtle condition, with half of the patients remaining asymptomatic [6]. Symptoms, when present, may include vague epigastric pain, stop of weight loss, vomiting, haematemesis, port-site infections, or even symptoms of gastric obstruction [7]. In most cases, the erosion is incomplete, but total erosion can occur where the band may migrate and become lodged distally (gastric antrum, duodenum, or even proximal jejunum), leading to mechanical obstruction [2]. Imaging Perspective CT is used to assess the precise location of the band and its relation to the gastric wall, but especially to detect potential complications, such as the presence of perigastric abscesses or pneumoperitoneum [7]. Barium studies can also play a part in the diagnosis as band erosion can be identified by the passage of oral contrast around the intraluminal portion of the band, pathognomonic for this diagnosis. However, no abnormality may be visible in the initial phases [4]. The diagnosis is established and confirmed by endoscopic study [4]. Outcome The appropriate treatment for intragastric band is its removal, by endoscopically assisted approach [8] or by laparoscopic surgery [9]. Take Home Message Intragastric band erosion is a rare and late complication of gastric band use, and its detection is vital, as it is a potentially serious complication. The diagnosis can be made through endoscopic studies and/or barium studies. CT should be considered if there is a suspicion of complications, such as abscess, perforation and peritonitis. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
differential_diagnosis: Gastric perforation Intragastric band erosion Gastric band malposition

title: Coincidental conundrum: Double aortic arch with bronchial foreign body
clinical_history: A 1-year-old male child presented in the emergency with sudden onset dry paroxysmal cough, shortness of breath and a cyanotic spell after ingesting a food particle. There was a history of noisy breathing and recurrent cough since birth. No history of fever or change in voice.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) scan of the chest with virtual bronchoscopy showed a small, well-defined radiopaque shadow (foreign body/corpus alienum), impacted in bronchus intermedius on the right side, causing complete obstruction of the bronchus intermedius with associated complete collapse of the right middle and lower lobes and hyperinflation of right upper lobe (Figures 5 and 6). A complete vascular ring was seen around the trachea and oesophagus at the level of the D3 vertebral body, causing their luminal narrowing (Figures 1a and 1b). The right and left aortic arch fuse with each other and continue inferiorly as descending aorta (Figures 4a and 4b). The right arch was larger as compared to the left arch. Both common carotid arteries and subclavian arteries show separate origins from right and left aortic arches (Figure 2).
discussion: Background Double aortic arch is a rare congenital cardiovascular malformation with a global prevalence of 0.005% to 0.007% and is usually discovered accidentally [1]. It results in a vascular ring that causes tracheal and oesophageal compression and is the most common type of arch abnormality requiring surgery for tracheal and oesophageal compression [2]. A complete vascular ring is formed when both arches are patent. In 73% of cases, the right arch is larger, higher, and located further posteriorly than the left arch, as in this case [3]. The carotid and subclavian arteries originate from each arch and ascend symmetrically, giving rise to the “fourth vessel sign” [4]. Right-sided aortic arches run to the right of the trachea.When the right ductus arteriosus recedes in the fictitious double aortic arch, the dorsal segment of the left arch is interrupted between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, resulting in a right-sided aortic arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery, which is usually asymptomatic [6]. Clinical Perspective Respiratory problems at birth or during infancy should raise the suspicion of a vascular ring. The typical history of a patient with a double aortic arch includes noisy breathing in the first few weeks of life. Neonates may seldom exhibit acute life-threatening events, which are marked by episodes of cyanosis and abrupt apnoea. There may be recurrent episodes of cough and gasping in infancy [3]. Imaging Perspective Both patent arches can be easily identified by the suprasternal view of 2D echocardiography. Patients can have associated congenital heart diseases; hence, 2D echocardiography becomes a crucial investigation in these cases. CT angiography with multi-planar reformats (MPR) and volume reconstructions is one of the best imaging modalities for diagnosis and characterisation of vascular rings [5]. It also gives an illustration of the arterial branching pattern, the position and degree of tracheobronchomalacia, and the cardiac anatomy. But in this case, as the patient presented in emergency with the primary complaint of shortness of breath following foreign body ingestion, a CECT chest was done in which the double aortic arch was an incidental finding. Outcome Dividing the ring to release compression on the oesophagus and trachea is the surgical treatment for a double aortic arch. A pre-operative 2D ECHO was done to rule out any underlying congenital heart disease. The patient underwent rigid bronchoscopy for the removal of the foreign body, and double aortic arch repair surgery to relieve the compression on the trachea and oesophagus. The patient was discharged in a satisfactory condition. Take Home Message High index of suspicion is imperative for rare cardiovascular anomalies presenting with common symptoms. “Satisfaction of search” is a pitfall. Stopping at one diagnosis is never recommended. The keen eye of the radiologist in early diagnosis can turn around patient ’ s quality of life. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Hippocampal sclerosis: A mystery seizure entity
clinical_history: A 16-year-old female patient suffering from medically refractory epilepsy for the last four years presented with focal onset seizure with impaired awareness and lip-smacking. EEG showed bilateral temporal spikes, which failed to localise the seizure origin. Thus, a hybrid PET-MRI was performed to detect and diagnose seizure focus.
imaging_findings: A hybrid FDG PET-MRI of the brain was performed using a dedicated epilepsy MRI protocol. The thin-section-angled coronal sequences at a right angle to the hippocampus’s longitudinal axis were obtained to reduce volume averaging. High-resolution coronal T2 sequence proved most useful in detecting and diagnosing hippocampal sclerosis (HS), aka mesial temporal sclerosis (MTS). MRI shows findings like hippocampal atrophy, loss of internal architecture, dilatation of temporal horn of ipsilateral lateral ventricle, increased hippocampal T2 signal, and atrophy of ipsilateral fornix (Figure 1) on the right side. PET imaging demonstrated temporal lobe hypometabolism on the side of the affected hippocampus, i.e., the right temporal lobe (Figures 2 and 3).
discussion: Background Hippocampal sclerosis (HS), aka mesial temporal sclerosis (MTS), is a condition characterised by the loss of neurons followed by excessive astrogliosis in the CA1 region of the hippocampus and the subiculum [1]. It is one of the most common lesions found in refractory epileptics [2] and is often responsible for medically intractable temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). The exact pathophysiology of this disease is not well understood. It was earlier believed that febrile seizures could be one of the precipitating factors for the development of HS; however, a study done in 2003 showed no association between the two [3]. Clinical Perspective HS is typically characterised by seizures associated with a loss of awareness. These seizures are preceded by symptoms like abdominal discomfort, fear, etc. [4]. HS affects the hippocampus, a vital area for memory, and the amygdala, which is involved in emotions, which could be a possible explanation for all these symptoms. Its diagnosis requires a thorough history, clinical examination, and investigations. These patients are usually evaluated with investigations like video EEG, SPECT, etc., before getting an MRI/PET-MRI. MRI, however, is very sensitive and specific in diagnosing HS [5] and is, therefore, the gold standard for detecting and diagnosing HS. Imaging Perspective HS is assessed by using the epilepsy protocol on the MRI, which makes use of thin coronal slices perpendicular to the hippocampal long axis. The typical features of HS on an MRI include atrophy of the hippocampus, increased intensity on T2-weighted or FLAIR images, and distorted internal architecture of the hippocampus [6]. The real challenge is the diagnosis of bilateral HS, which makes it inoperable, and this is where hybrid PET-MRI can help us by demonstrating bilateral temporal lobe hypometabolism, thus raising the suspicion of bilateral aetiology. Also, it plays a vital role in the early detection of HS, where MRI shows no structural alteration. Hybrid PET-MRI helps differentiate a few temporal lobe pathologies from HS that look similar. For instance, ganglioglioma is hypermetabolic with mild or no enhancement as opposed to hypometabolic focus with no abnormal enhancement in HS. Another example could be PET-MRI helping to differentiate HS from a hypermetabolic metastatic temporal lobe lesion. Outcome Medical management generally yields no results; therefore, in most cases, surgical management is indicated. Laser interstitial thermal therapy is a minimally invasive technique that uses a small laser probe to perform thermal ablation of the affected area. Patients might also undergo other invasive surgeries like resection of the anterior part of the temporal lobe or selectively removing specific parts of the amygdala and the hippocampus. Surgery is contraindicated in bilateral HS. One randomised controlled trial has shown that in TLE, about 58% of patients who underwent surgery experienced better seizure control as compared to 8% of patients receiving medical management [7]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points This study displays the significance of hybrid PET-MRI in the detection and diagnosis of HS. PET-MRI integrates anatomical and metabolic information, which helps us exclude a possible dual aetiology and prevent unnecessary surgery. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Nail–patella syndrome
clinical_history: A 46-year-old male patient, with a known history of human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis C virus coinfection, underwent a computed tomography (CT) to assess liver lesions detected by US, which were later identified as haemangiomas. On physical examination, hypoplastic fingernails were found.
imaging_findings: Incidentally, the CT revealed the presence of bilateral osseous processes projecting from the posterior aspect of the iliac bones (Figures 1a and 1b). Anteroposterior and lateral knee radiographs showed bilateral patellar hypoplasia associated with luxation (Figure 2a), while elbow radiographs demonstrated bilateral radial head hypoplasia with radio-humeral dislocation and abnormal radial curvature (Figure 2b).
discussion: Background Nail–patella syndrome (NPS), also known as Fong disease, is a rare hereditary autosomal dominant disorder caused by LMX1B mutations producing a loss of function of the LMX1B protein. NPS is characterised by a classic tetrad: hypoplastic or absent fingernails, hypoplastic or absent patellae, bilateral iliac prominences (iliac horns), and elbow deformities [1–4]. Iliac horns are pathognomonic for this syndrome [1,2] but are not universally present, occurring in approximately 70–80% of cases [2]. They are bilateral prominences growing from the posterior iliac surfaces, frequently palpable, and named after the bony prominences on the heads of horned animals. Other disorders, such as nephropathy and glaucoma, are associated [1], but renal involvement is the major determinant of the prognosis for NPS [4]. Molecular tests can identify LMX1B gene mutations helping to confirm NPS diagnosis. Clinical Perspective Patients with NPS usually present nonspecific symptoms related to skeletal abnormalities. Cases can range from mild with no functional impact to severe, leading to disability. Our patient presented hypoplastic fingernails and limited supination of the elbows, as well as occasional mild episodes of patellar subluxation. The combined radiological and clinical findings confirmed the diagnosis of NPS. Given the patient’s age, minimal functional limitations, and adaptive behaviours, no immediate intervention was necessary. Imaging Perspective Being typically a syndrome diagnosed incidentally in radiological tests, radiological findings are typical in both conventional radiographs and CT, with the presence of bilateral iliac horns being pathognomonic for this syndrome. Other radiological signs are patellar hypoplasia and hypoplasia of the radial head with associated radio-humeral dislocation. All these findings were observed in our patient. Absence or hypoplasia of the fibula and asymmetric growth of the femoral condyles may also be present. Outcome In this case we present characteristic radiological findings of a rare syndrome that allow a precise diagnosis to be made without the need to perform further complementary tests. Treatment of skeletal abnormalities is usually not necessary as symptoms are usually mild. Nephropathy is the most important associated clinical alteration and determines the prognosis of NPS, being necessary a strict follow-up of the disease due to the possibility of kidney failure. Take Home Message / Teaching Points The characteristic radiological findings allow a diagnosis of nail–patella syndrome to be established. Knowledge of this syndrome is key to detecting associated clinical alterations such as nephropathy and glaucoma. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Adult with testicular yolk sac tumour
clinical_history: A 31-year-old male presented at the urologist with scrotal swelling for 4 weeks. He had no relevant history. Clinically there was a voluminous solid swelling of the right hemiscrotum and retraction of the penis. Blood results showed extremely high alpha-fetoprotein levels >53.000 µg/L.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound showed a large heterogeneous mass in the right hemiscrotum with solid and cystic/necrotic components and vascularisation (Figures 1, 2 and 3). There was no visualisation of normal testicular parenchyma or epididymis on the right. There was a normal left testis and epididymis (not shown). CT showed, besides the large heterogeneous mass in the right hemiscrotum (Figure 4), no metastasis or lymphadenopathies.
discussion: Background Germ cell tumours (GCT) account for 90% of testis tumours, subdivided in 40% seminomas and 50% non-seminomas (yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma, embryonal cell carcinoma, teratoma, mixed GCT). Yolk sac tumours are rare malignant GCT and occur mostly in ovaries and testes. Yolk sac tumours of the testis have a bimodal age distribution, in children younger than 3 and in post-pubertal adults [1]. A radical orchiectomy was performed in this case and showed a pure yolk sac tumour. This is a rare finding in adults, but much more frequent in children. In adults, mixed GCT are much more common. Schiller–Duval bodies on histopathology, also present in this case, are pathognomonic for yolk sac tumours, but are only seen in about 20% of cases [2]. Additionally, almost all cases are positive for alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) on immunohistochemical staining. Clinical Perspective Testicular tumours are the most common non-hematologic malignancy in men between 15–49 years. Patients typically consult with a palpable lump in the testis, a dull ache or heaviness in the scrotum but can also present with sudden scrotal swelling. An elevated serum AFP level is seen in 90% of yolk sac tumours [3]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound is the most used method for the evaluation of the testes. It can be used to differentiate benign and malignant testicular lesions. The majority of paratesticular lesions are benign, unlike intratesticular lesions, which are usually malignant [3]. Compared to seminomas, non-seminomas more frequently invade paratesticular structures (such as epididymis and tunica albuginea in this case). Additionally, non-seminomas more frequently have cystic components and calcifications on ultrasound. It is not possible to further distinguish non-seminomas on ultrasound [4]. Due to embryological descent of the testes, the first site of spread is typically to the para-aortic lymph nodes at the level of the renal vessels. However, metastasis to inguinal and iliac lymph nodes can be present when there is invasion of the scrotal skin. Outcome When there are no lymph nodes of metastasis involved, this cancer is almost always curable. A radical orchiectomy is typically performed and additional chemotherapy can be given to patients after surgery, depending on AFP levels and stage. The degree of AFP serum elevation has a negative prognostic value for yolk sac tumours. The recurrence rate for stage 1 nonseminomas is about 30%, and chemotherapy is successful most of the time [5,6]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: An unexpected mass: Exploring primary cardiac lymphoma
clinical_history: An 81-year-old male with a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department with a one-week onset of orthopnoea and exertional dyspnoea. Laboratory tests demonstrate elevated troponins, the electrocardiogram reveals a third-degree atrioventricular block, and the echocardiogram shows right ventricular thickening and pericardial effusion.
imaging_findings: A PET-CT scan (Figure 1) was carried out revealing a large hypermetabolic myocardial tissue. It extended through the right chambers and around the large vessels, sparing the left ventricle. Additionally, a hypermetabolic nodular image was identified at the left lung base. Therefore, a contrast-enhanced chest CT scan was performed (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c and 2d). It confirmed the presence of an infiltrative hypodense mass in the myocardium. It involved the right atrium, right ventricle, interatrial septum, and atrioventricular groove. The mass caused mural thickening of the right cavities. A cuff encircled the right coronary artery along its course. A moderate pericardial effusion was also observed. Finally, the CT scan confirmed the solid nodule in the posterior segment of the left lower lobe. A CT-guided percutaneous biopsy of the lung nodule was made for histological examination.
discussion: Background Primary cardiac lymphoma is a very rare entity and thus a diagnostic challenge. It is an extranodal lymphoma that derives from lymphoid cells settled in the myocardium. It must be differentiated from secondary cardiac lymphoma, in which myocardial or pericardial involvement is due to regional or distant extension from other sites. Primary cardiac lymphoma represents 1 – 2% of cardiac neoplasms [1]. It is less common than secondary cardiac lymphoma, and both are usually diffuse large B-cell lymphomas [2]. It usually affects people over 60 years of age and its incidence is higher in men [3]. The most part of cardiac lymphomas are idiopathic, although they seem to be related to immunosuppression and Epstein – Barr virus infection. Clinical Perspective The most frequent symptoms are dyspnoea and congestive symptoms. Arrhythmias are also frequent, especially atrioventricular blocks [4]. Imaging Perspective Primary cardiac lymphomas present as homogeneous masses that are hypodense or isodense compared to healthy myocardium. Their behaviour is infiltrative, with a predilection for the right chambers [1]. They usually spread over the epicardial surfaces and involve the aortic root and the coronary trunks [4]. They may also cause lumen-filling defects in cardiac chambers, especially in the right atrium, and even occlude caval openings [4]. Enhancement after contrast administration is minimal [2]. Necrosis areas are very rare [5]. On MRI, lymphomas appear as infiltrative masses with avid and heterogeneous enhancement. Their signal varies from iso to hyperintense on both T1 and T2 sequences, depending on the cellularity of the tumour [4]. Valvular involvement is not common [5]. Pericardial effusion is common [4]. Metastatic spread is possible, being lungs the most frequent site. A biopsy is usually needed to reach a final diagnosis. Outcome Like other B-cell lymphomas, first-line treatment is chemotherapy and rituximab, a monoclonal anti-CD20 antibody. Prognosis varies greatly depending on the type of lymphoma, haemodynamic impact at diagnosis and patient age. Complete remissions are usually achieved although relapses may occur. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Primary cardiac lymphoma is a rare tumour, but it presents some typical radiological features, which, together with clinical information, allow a good diagnostic approach. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Moyamoya disease with internal carotid artery hypoplasia
clinical_history: A 39-year-old male presented with sudden-onset left-sided weakness and mild slurring of speech lasting two days, accompanied by forgetfulness, particularly difficulty in retaining new information. Neurological examination showed left hemiparesis in the left upper and lower extremities, with intact cranial nerve functions.
imaging_findings: MRI revealed acute watershed infarcts in the right centrum semiovale (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c and 1d). Sulcal hyperintensity in the right temporal region (ivy sign) was noted (Figure 1d). CT demonstrated a hypoplastic carotid canal on the left (Figure 2). CT angiography (CTA) showed left internal carotid artery hypoplasia and focal stenosis of bilateral supraclinoid internal carotid arteries ( ICAs) (Figure 3). The left middle cerebral artery ( MCA) was supplied via the posterior circulation, while the left anterior cerebral artery ( ACA) was perfused through the anterior communicating ( ACom) artery. The foetal origin of the left posterior cerebral artery ( PCA) was identified. Digital subtraction angiography ( DSA) confirmed these findings, showing no “puff of smoke” appearance (Figures 4a and 4b) and indicating an absence of collateral formation.
discussion: Background Moyamoya disease (MMD) is a rare cerebrovascular disorder characterised by progressive stenosis and occlusion of arteries at the base of the brain, triggering the formation of abnormal collateral vessels. Unilateral internal carotid artery ( ICA) hypoplasia is a congenital condition with underdeveloped ICA, altering cerebral haemodynamics. The coexistence of these conditions exacerbates ischemic risk through compromised cerebral perfusion and dynamic flow alterations [1]. Clinical Perspective The patient presented with acute neurological symptoms, including weakness and cognitive impairment, indicative of ischemic stroke. Imaging was critical to differentiate this condition from other cerebrovascular disorders. The lack of typical MMD collaterals (“puff of smoke”) added complexity to the diagnostic process. Conveying the haemodynamic instability and risk of recurrent ischemia was essential for therapeutic planning [2]. Imaging Perspective Key imaging findings included hypoplasia of the left ICA, focal stenosis of bilateral supraclinoid ICAs, and watershed infarcts. Diagnostic procedures like MRI and CTA highlighted the ischemic burden and vascular anomalies, while DSA confirmed the findings and ruled out secondary Moyamoya syndromes. The absence of developed collateral vessels further clarified the disease progression [3]. The “puff of smoke” appearance is absent in Moyamoya disease in its early stages, mild cases, or atypical variants. It may also be missed using non-invasive imaging modalities like MRI and MRA. Approximately 20–30% of cases, particularly secondary Moyamoya syndrome, may lack this finding, emphasising the need for thorough angiographic evaluation and clinical correlation. Outcome Management involved medical therapy with antiplatelet agents and neuroprotective drugs to minimise thromboembolic events and optimise cerebral perfusion. Surgical options like direct or indirect bypass were considered based on ischemic severity and individualised risk. Long-term prognosis depends on early intervention and consistent follow-up to monitor disease progression and prevent recurrent strokes [4]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points The coexistence of Moyamoya disease and ICA hypoplasia demands meticulous diagnostic evaluation. Imaging is indispensable in identifying vascular anomalies and ischemic risks. Early intervention, including surgical revascularisation in selected cases, improves patient outcomes. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Pseudoaneurysm of the internal mammary artery caused by angioinvasive aspergillosis
clinical_history: A twenty-nine-year-old male patient on day +90 of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) for acute lymphatic leukaemia was admitted to the hospital due to an episode of frank haemoptysis with haematimetric repercussions. The patient was haemodynamically stable. The medical history of the patient included pulmonary aspergillosis confirmed after fine-needle aspiration.
imaging_findings: ­The patient had undergone a chest X-ray due to fever without a focus on day +28 of HSCT, which showed the presence of a nodule (Figures 1a and 1b). Afterwards, a chest CT was performed, and a nodule on the upper left lobe (ULL) was confirmed. A ground glass opacity surrounding this nodule suggested an angioinvasive aspergillosis (Figure 2a). During the first months of the antifungal treatment, a progressive decrease in size, as well as its perinodular ground-glass component, was evident (Figures 2b, 2c, 2d and 2e). In the fifth follow-up CT scan, the nodule had almost disappeared leading to a linear opacity with a scar-like appearance (Figure 2f). However, in the next control, the nodule had significantly grown, extending to the prevascular mediastinal space and contacting with the anterior chest wall (Figure 2g). Finally, in the CT performed when the patient began with haemoptysis, the mass had encompassed the ipsilateral internal mammary artery, which showed a focal dilatation, findings consistent with a pseudoaneurysm (Figures 2h and 3).
discussion: Aspergillus is a saprophyte fungus with the potential to cause pathogenesis within the respiratory system [1]. Pulmonary aspergillosis can be subdivided into five different categories, including saprophytic aspergillosis, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, aspergilloma, airway-invasive aspergillosis, and angioinvasive aspergillosis [2], being this last category the subtype diagnosed to our patient. Invasive aspergillosis generally affects severely immunocompromised patients (including patients who have recently undergone bone marrow transplantation) [4], and it has a high mortality rate (65–90%) [1]. It can be difficult to suspect this diagnosis, as patients with aspergillosis generally present with nonspecific symptoms, such as fever, chest pain, and cough [1]. Apart from that, as this fungus can invade medium-sized pulmonary arteries, causing haemorrhage [8], patients could also present with haemoptysis [1]. In addition to the clinical picture, imaging findings of this infection are usually nonspecific [8]. It should be borne in mind that in the early stages of this infection, the Aspergillus nodules can be too small to be detected on plain chest radiographs, so it is recommended to perform a chest CT scan if the patient is at risk [1]. The classic CT manifestation of angioinvasive aspergillosis is the halo-sign, which consists of nodules and areas of nodular-shaped consolidation with surrounding ground-glass attenuation, representing pulmonary haemorrhage. The halo sign is nonspecific and could be depicted in other clinical settings [8]. The nodules may cavitate with time, this process reflecting an increased granulocytic response coinciding with bone marrow recovery, eventually resulting on image in the air crescent sign [4]. This way, the patients whose nodules do not cavitate after bone marrow recovery usually have poorer prognosis with higher mortality [1]. Direct invasion into the adjacent chest wall or mediastinal structures may be seen in advanced cases [5], as it occurred to the patient we presented. The internal mammary artery is a branch of the subclavian artery, which travels closely related to the pleura (within the upper intercostal space) and anteriorly to the transversus thoracic muscle [6]. Many causes of disruption of the arterial wall, which could potentially lead to pseudoaneurysm formation, have been documented, including Aspergillus infections [7]. Pseudoaneurysms, unlike true aneurysms, do not involve the three layers of the vessel wall, as they spare the adventitia layer [3]. This way, patients with internal mammary artery pseudoaneurysms may present with various symptoms, including haemoptysis [6]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

final_diagnosis: Pseudoaneurysm caused by pulmonary angioinvasive aspergillosis

title: Bilateral multiple angiomyolipomas
clinical_history: An 80-year-old female patient with a history of arterial hypertension, pancytopenia, and endometrial adenocarcinoma presented to the hospital with general deterioration, tachycardia, and hypotension (75/34 mmHg). On physical examination, the patient had diffuse abdominal pain with signs of peritoneal irritation. The clinical case was focused on sepsis with abdominal origin and a CT scan was requested.
imaging_findings: Axial images from the abdominopelvic CT scan, both without and with intravenous contrast in the venous phase, show bilateral renal structural disruption with significant fat infiltration and multiple solid intraparenchymal lesions. Some of these solid lesions appear hyperdense in the non-contrast study (Figure 1a), suggestive of acute haemorrhagic content (red arrow). After contrast administration (Figure 1b), marked enhancement of renal intraparenchymal solid lesions is visible, with no signs suggestive of active bleeding. Free fluid with a density higher than water is seen in the paracolic gutters and pelvis (Figure 1c), indicative of haemoperitoneum (yellow arrows). A predominance of perirenal fat stranding and paracolic fluid accumulation was also visualised, so it is more likely that the bleeding site was located in the left kidney. Axial, coronal, and sagittal reconstructions of the bilateral renal lesions (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c) show the large size of these lesions and the significant bilateral renal disruption. These findings suggest a diagnosis of bilateral renal angiomyolipomas.
discussion: Renal angiomyolipomas are benign tumours composed of adipose tissue, dysmorphic blood vessels, and smooth muscle. They typically occur sporadically in a single kidney, but bilateral cases are usually associated with tuberous sclerosis, an autosomal dominant genetic disease [1 – 3]. These tumours involve a proliferation of perivascular epithelioid cells, which increases the risk of internal bleeding, especially in lesions larger than 4 cm. Bilateral renal angiomyolipomas are often asymptomatic and, therefore, incidentally detected during imaging studies performed for other reasons. When symptoms are present, they may include abdominal pain, haematuria, or a palpable mass [4]. Spontaneous bleeding is a serious complication, particularly in patients with large tumours. Imaging is critical for identifying these lesions, assessing their size and risk of complications, and distinguishing them from other kidney tumours. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are essential tools for diagnosing angiomyolipomas. CT is the study of choice, showing masses with fat density (< -20 Hounsfield units), which is characteristic. MRI confirms the presence of fat density and can guide in differentiating between benign and malignant tumours without using radiation [5,6]. Spontaneous kidney bleeding is called Wunderlich syndrome, a rare entity with fewer than 500 cases reported in the literature. Angiomyolipoma is the most common cause of this condition according to the literature. The clinical manifestations are grouped into Lenk triad (severe abdominal pain, enlargement of the side and haemorrhagic shock) [7]. In our patient, the severe pancytopenia (31,000 platelets) could facilitate spontaneous retroperitoneal bleeding. Treatment depends on size and symptoms. Tumours smaller than 4 cm generally only require surveillance, while larger or symptomatic tumours may necessitate selective embolisation or partial nephrectomy to reduce the risk of bleeding [8,9]. Early identification and monitoring via imaging help prevent complications and guide treatment. Another useful treatment option is medical therapy with everolimus, especially in patients with tuberous sclerosis [10]. In our patient, bilateral renal angiomyolipomas were an unusually late finding, as these tumours are typically diagnosed earlier, often incidentally, due to symptoms or because they are associated with tuberous sclerosis. This case highlights the importance of early detection and monitoring of renal angiomyolipomas, especially in older patients or those presenting with atypical symptoms, as a delayed diagnosis can lead to severe complications. Despite initial imaging, the patient’s condition rapidly deteriorated, developing haemodynamic instability within hours of the CT scan and ultimately passing away two days after admission. The autopsy confirmed retroperitoneal bleeding as the cause of death. This case reinforces the critical role of timely imaging in detecting and managing these lesions to prevent fatal outcomes, emphasising the need for a proactive approach, particularly in high-risk cases. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Gastric haemangioma, an uncommon lesion
clinical_history: A 71-year-old female with a history of previous surgeries, including the resection of a pancreatic cystic lesion and lysis of abdominal adhesions due to an episode of intestinal subocclusion, presented to the emergency department with abdominal pain and vomiting. Blood tests revealed no significant abnormalities.
imaging_findings: Abdominal ultrasound revealed a heterogeneous, hyperechoic solid mass with cystic areas and vascularisation on colour Doppler imaging, likely originating from the gastric wall ( Figures 1a and 1b ). Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) in the venous phase demonstrated a lobulated, hypodense tumour in the gastrohepatic ligament, measuring up to 15 x 9 cm. This was associated with hypodense thickening of the lesser curvature of the stomach and multiple foci of fat interspersed among the soft tissue parts of the lesion. A cluster of irregularly shaped calcifications located in the caudal aspect of the lesion was also noted (Figures 2a and 2b). Given the suspicion of a gastrointestinal stroma tumour, an ultrasound-guided percutaneous biopsy was performed. Histopathological analysis revealed mature adipose tissue and dilated blood vessels lined by endothelial cells without atypia. Areas of fibrosis and old haemorrhage were also observed (Figure 3). These findings were consistent with the diagnosis of a benign vascular tumour, specifically a capillary gastric haemangioma.
discussion: Background Gastrointestinal haemangiomas are benign vascular tumours that can occur throughout the gastrointestinal tract, with the small intestine being the most frequent site. However, gastric haemangiomas are exceedingly rare, with only a few cases documented in the literature. These tumours may occur as solitary or multiple lesions and are sometimes associated with congenital conditions such as Osler–Weber–Rendu disease and Maffucci syndrome [1]. Histologically, haemangiomas are classified into capillary, cavernous, and mixed types. The cavernous subtype consists of larger blood vessels and large, blood-filled spaces (caverns), whereas the capillary type comprises smaller vessels (capillaries), both surrounded by endothelial cells [2]. Cavernous haemangiomas carry a higher risk of rupture, leading to significant gastrointestinal bleeding. Most haemangiomas present as pedunculated, intraluminal, and polypoid masses. However, some demonstrate an infiltrative submucosal growth pattern [1]. Clinical Perspective Many haemangiomas are discovered incidentally during imaging for unrelated conditions. They have a nonspecific clinical presentation. Nevertheless, the most common symptom is acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Some patients may present with only abdominal pain or anaemia due to chronic, occult bleeding. Bleeding can range from slow and insidious to massive and life-threatening, often mimicking other emergencies such as peptic ulcers, with emergency endoscopy often performed for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. Imaging Perspective CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are the preferred diagnostic modalities, as they provide detailed information on lesion characteristics and their relationship with adjacent structures, aiding in the assessment of surgical resectability [3]. CT and MRI typically reveal a vascular enhancement pattern characteristic of haemangiomas. The presence of phleboliths within a gastric mass is highly suggestive of haemangioma but is not always observed. Differential diagnoses include gastric masses or submucosal pathologies such as gastrointestinal stromal tumours, carcinomas, metastatic lesions, and varicose vessels [1,3]. Outcome In symptomatic cases, the treatment of choice is complete surgical resection, with no reported post-surgical recurrences. Depending on the size and location of the lesion, wedge resection, subtotal or total gastrectomy may be performed [2]. In this patient, surgical intervention was not pursued due to the resolution of abdominal pain and the absence of additional symptoms, such as gastrointestinal bleeding. Long-term follow-up was chosen instead. Endoscopic resection is rarely performed due to the submucosal location of these tumours and the associated high risk of bleeding [4]. Take Home Message / Teaching points These tumours can pose preoperative diagnostic challenges, as biopsies are often avoided due to their submucosal location and risk of bleeding. Imaging studies play a pivotal role in suggesting the diagnosis and avoiding biopsy, demonstrating the characteristic imaging appearance of progressive enhancement and the presence of phleboliths. Awareness of gastric haemangiomas is essential, as surgery is the preferred approach in symptomatic cases.

title: Fat-containing lymph nodes: An imaging clue to diagnose Whipple’s disease
clinical_history: A 51-year-old female patient, a farmer, presented with two years history of abdominal pain, vomits, diarrhoea, asthenia, weight loss (12%), and arthralgias. Laboratory findings showed iron deficiency anaemia , increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, mild leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, C-reactive protein 6 mg/dL (normal value < 0.5 mg/dL) and hypoalbuminemia 2.5 g/dL.
imaging_findings: Abdominal-pelvic computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed cystadenocarcinoma of the right ovary with suspicion of lymph node metastases and the patient was referred to our oncology institute. The exams were re-assessed and the malignant ovarian tumour was excluded, as the MRI was highly suggestive of cystadenofibroma (Figure 1). In addition, the CT demonstrated low-attenuation lymph nodes (fatty infiltration) in the left supraclavicular region, mediastinum, retroperitoneum and mesentery (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, 2d, 3a, and 3b). Furthermore, prominent jejunal folds were seen on T2-weighted images (Figure 4).
discussion: Background Whipple’s disease is a rare systemic disorder caused by the gram-positive bacterium Tropheryma whipplei . This condition primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract but can involve multiple organ systems. Most cases have been reported in North America and Europe [1], with a notable prevalence in caucasian males, particularly those in outdoor professions, suggesting a potential link to oral transmission related to soil and animal contact [2,3]. The disorder exhibits a male predominance, occurring with a ratio of 4:1 compared to females. The association with the HLA-B27 haplotype suggests a genetic predisposition, although the detailed pathogenesis of the disease remains unclear [1]. Clinical Perspective Patients with Whipple’s disease typically present with gastrointestinal symptoms that resemble other malabsorption syndromes. Common manifestations include significant weight loss, diarrhoea, arthralgias, fever, and abdominal pain. Occult gastrointestinal bleeding is prevalent, occurring in up to 80% of cases. Physical examination often reveals peripheral lymphadenopathy in approximately 50% of patients [1,3]. Laboratory findings often reveal anaemia (usually microcytic or normocytic), relative lymphopenia and increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate; markers of malabsorption are usually found, such as decreased total lymphocytes count, low serum albumin, prealbumin, and transferrin. Imaging Perspective Imaging studies display nonspecific changes, including the thickening of small bowel folds and enlarged abdominal lymph nodes with very low attenuation [3,4]. Outcome The hallmark pathological feature of Whipple’s disease is the massive infiltration of periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) -positive granules in foamy macrophages within the lamina propria of the small intestine, particularly in the duodenum [3]. In the case described, a duodenal biopsy was performed during endoscopy, and the specimen showed the described characteristics, confirming the diagnosis. Additionally, the search for RNA of Tropheryma whipplei by real-time polymerase chain reaction was positive. If left untreated, Whipple’s disease can be fatal. Fortunately, the clinical response to appropriate antibiotic therapy is generally prompt. Initial treatment usually involves a two-week induction therapy with bactericidal antibiotics that can penetrate the blood-brain barrier, such as intravenous cephalosporins (e.g., ceftriaxone) or β-lactams (e.g., meropenem). This is followed by long-term treatment using trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for at least 12 months [3,4]. Take Home Message In conclusion, early recognition and treatment of Whipple’s disease are crucial to prevent severe complications and increase the chances of recovery. Regular monitoring through clinical examination is essential to evaluate the patient’s response to therapy and ensure optimal outcomes. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Ischiorectal liposarcoma
clinical_history: A 40-year-old man with lower abdominal pain received a CT abdomen/pelvis in the emergency department to rule out appendicitis. An incidental fat attenuation mass was present in the right ischiorectal fossa. Five years later, the patient presented again with pelvic pain and received a CT pelvis.
imaging_findings: The initial CT study identified a right ischiorectal fossa fat attenuation mass displacing the anal canal towards the left without enhancing soft tissue, fluid or calcifications (Figures 1a and 1b). There was a thin capsule surrounding the mass. When the patient presented again five years later, a CT pelvis showed that the mass had significantly enlarged (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). It contained two well-defined cystic compartments with homogeneous fluid attenuation (15 HU) and an irregular enhancing soft tissue rim in the posterosuperior compartment. An MR pelvis done shortly thereafter recapitulated these findings but revealed that the apparently homogeneous central collection on CT contained a mix of fluid and soft tissue, with both thin and thick septations (Figures 3a, 3b, 4a, and 4b). Additionally, the entire mass had a thick, irregular rim of enhancement.
discussion: Background Ischiorectal fossa lesions can be classified as congenital, inflammatory/infectious, traumatic, and neoplastic. Clinical history is important, particularly in the case of inflammatory/infectious and traumatic lesions. The mass’ original presentation as a fatty lesion and the development of fluid and soft tissue components narrow the differential diagnoses. Imaging Perspective The original fatty composition of the mass suggests a lipoma. Benign lipomas can have septations, in which case they may appear identical to malignant, well-differentiated liposarcomas on imaging [1]. However, the interval enlargement and development of soft tissue components suggest liposarcoma and virtually excludes a benign lipoma. Additionally, well-differentiated liposarcoma is considered less likely due to the high soft tissue content and degree of growth. Alternatively, an extragonadal germ cell tumour (sacrococcygeal teratoma) could be considered [2,3]. Likewise, a dermoid cyst would appear similarly, given the fatty appearance of its sebum and the heterogeneous composition [4]. Due to the fatty appearance of the mass, other neoplasms were not considered. These include a retrorectal tailgut cyst, a perineal epidermoid cyst, and an anterior sacral meningocele, as neither lesion typically contains fat [5]. The interval appearance of fluid and soft tissue attenuation collections in the fatty mass, however, did lead to a potential differential diagnosis of a perirectal abscess. Outcome A biopsy confirmed an ischiorectal liposarcoma. This is an extremely rare diagnosis, with several case reports and single institution reports [6–9]. The most recent WHO classification of soft tissue tumours identifies 5 subtypes of liposarcoma: well-differentiated, dedifferentiated, myxoid, pleomorphic, and myxoid pleomorphic [10]. Dedifferentiation can occur in any type of liposarcoma, which can be seen with increasing soft tissue within the mass (with a minimum suggested nodular growth of 1 cm) [11]. The case discussed in this report likely represents a myxoid liposarcoma, given its high water content. Radiologic-pathologic correlation could help confirm the tumour subtype. Liposarcoma is treated with surgical resection, with neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy considered on a case-by-case basis. For patients with fatty tumours of the internal trunk (mediastinum, abdomen, or pelvis), sarcoma cancer centre referral, core needle biopsy, and regular follow-up are recommended, regardless of size [12]. Teaching Points Ischiorectal neoplasms are rare, and fat narrows the differential to lipoma, liposarcoma, and germ cell tumour. Lipoma and well-differentiated liposarcoma can be difficult to distinguish on imaging. Soft tissue growth within a fatty lesion suggests a liposarcoma which is not well-differentiated. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Unilateral axillary lymphadenopathy, a rare presentation of toxoplasmosis
clinical_history: A 43-year-old woman presented with complaints of a lump in the left axilla. She had no clinically significant background. History of breast cancer in her family was positive for her mother, at 49 years old. Physical examination revealed axillary adenomegalies of elastic consistency, mobile and slightly painful to touch.
imaging_findings: We started the evaluation with bilateral mammography, and breast and axillary ultrasound. Mammographic projections revealed dense breast tissue (ACR category C) with no concerning features, such as focal asymmetries, nodular densities or grouped microcalcifications (Figure 1). Complementary ultrasound evaluation did not reveal suspicious breast lesions. However, ultrasound evaluation of the left axilla revealed several lymphadenopathies with cortical thickness >3 mm, reduction of the fatty hilum, round shape and/or lobulated cortex and hypoechoic texture (Figures 2a and 2b). Lymph nodes on the right axilla were considered normal (not shown). A left lymph node core biopsy was performed on the lymph node with the highest cortical thickening (Figures 2c and 2d). As the mammographic study was limited by dense breast tissue, we directly performed a contrast-enhanced mammogram (CEM) to search for occult breast neoplasia. No hypervascular lesions were noted (Figure 3). Histopathologic examination suggested the diagnosis of toxoplasmosis (Figures 4a and 4b), which was further confirmed by serologic tests.
discussion: Toxoplasma gondii , an intracellular protozoan parasite with worldwide distribution, is responsible for the infectious disease named toxoplasmosis. Transmission from animals to humans occurs when infectious oocysts present in cat faeces contaminate raw meat/water. When Toxoplasma gondii oocysts invade the intestinal epithelium, they disseminate and encyst in any nucleated cell. The combination of oocysts proliferation with the host’s immune response may cause clinical manifestations. Even so, most immunocompetent hosts with primary infection are asymptomatic (80 – 90% of cases). When symptoms do occur, they typically are self-limited and develop 5 to 23 days after exposure to the parasite. Isolated cervical or occipital lymphadenopathy is the most common symptom, followed by constitutional symptoms [1,2]. Axillary lymphadenopathy is a rare form of presentation [3 – 5], resulting in a rare presumed diagnosis without proceeding to microbiopsy or cytology. After the anatomopathological suggestion of toxoplasmic lymphadenopathy, the diagnosis must be confirmed by serological tests [4,6]. The most common cause of unilateral axillary adenopathy is upper limb infection/injury, as systemic illness — such as autoimmune/granulomatous diseases, metastases or lymphoproliferative disease — commonly presents with more generalised involvement [5,7]. Another possible cause in female patients is breast malignancy, which further obligates imaging workup with at least mammography and breast ultrasound [8]. This is particularly relevant when features of malignancy are present on physical examination (firm, hard, tender, fixed or matted nodes). Sonographic assessment of lymph nodes implies a systematic evaluation of different morphological parameters — such as shape and cortical morphologic features — , and hilum/cortex vascularisation on Doppler ultrasound. Focal hypoechoic cortical lobulation or round shape with an absence of the fatty hilum (hypoechoic node) are worrisome features and mandate further cytological or histological studies. This is explained as metastatic deposits are arrested by immune cells in the periphery of a node, causing focal enlargement of the cortex. As a focal metastatic deposit enlarges, replacement of the fatty hilum is established, leading to the commonly described round hypoechoic node. A lymph node with an imperceptible cortex, a thin 3-mm or less cortex, or a diffuse symmetric cortical thickening of more than 3 mm, is considered benign. Generalised lobulated cortical thickening is regarded as a likely benign node and does not demand pathological characterisation. A peripheral nonhilar blood flow is considered a suspicious feature of malignancy [8 – 10]. In our case, mammography, breast ultrasound and even CEM were innocent. Although rare, the possibility of facing a malignant entity with lymphatic unilateral presentation — occult breast tumour, lymphoma or metastases — forced the biopsy. Even so, we believe that if a proper clinical history had been collected in the first place — regarding recent contact with cats, alimentary habits, history of systemic symptoms — , we could have reassured the patient that we were probably facing a benign pathology. In conclusion, many different benign and malignant pathologies can be responsible for axillary adenopathies. Collecting clinical data can help prevent unnecessary imaging workup and/or biopsy. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Pylephlebitis and pancreatic parenchymal varices: A rare complication of hepatic abscess
clinical_history: A 37-year-old man presented to our department of surgery with complains of high-grade fever, chills, vomiting and abdominal pain in epigastric region for the last 7 days. Laboratory investigations revealed a raised total leukocyte count (TLC) (of 18,500 cells/μL) with increased absolute neutrophil count (80%), and mildly deranged alkaline phosphate levels (200 IU/L).
imaging_findings: Initial abdominal ultrasonography (USG) revealed hepatomegaly with a large left lobe liver abscess (350 cc) and signs of impending rupture. Mild prominence of intrahepatic bile ducts (Figures 1a and 1b) and a few intrahepatic veno-venous collaterals (measuring ~2 mm in diameter) were also noted between the branch of the middle and right hepatic vein (Figures 2a, 2b and 6). Doppler study showed echogenic content with absent colour flow at the porto-splenic confluence, suggesting thrombosis, along with collateral vessel formation at the porta hepatis, likely indicative of cavernous transformation (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, 3d, 4a and 4b). Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) scan of the abdomen confirmed the abscess and thrombosis, additionally revealing pinpoint narrowing of the inferior vena cava (IVC) with a small segment thrombus (Figures 5a, 5b, 5c, 5d and 5e). Notably, pancreatic parenchymal varices were observed (involving the head, and body of the pancreas) draining directly into the splenic vein (Figures 3e and 4c). Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) was also performed (Figures 7 and 8), revealing prominent intrahepatic bile ducts in the left lobe of the liver and non-visualisation of the biliary channels distal to the common hepatic duct (CHD) consistent with biliary obstruction.
discussion: In our patient, blood culture revealed Escherichia coli ( E. coli ), which was also isolated from the hepatic abscess aspirate, confirming the source of infection. Hepatic abscess (HA) occurs due to infiltration of liver parenchyma by bacterial, parasitic and rarely fungal infections [1]. Hepatic abscess can also lead to venous thrombosis, which has often been attributed to the mechanical compression of vascular structures and the presence of localised inflammation [1 – 11]. Inferior vena cava (IVC) thrombosis and portal vein thrombosis due to infective aetiology are rare complications of liver abscesses described in case reports [2 – 16]. The close anatomical relationship between the hepatic vasculature and the IVC makes it vulnerable to secondary thrombosis in the presence of an infectious hepatic abscess. Thrombosis of the IVC in this patient is likely attributable to a combination of factors including localised inflammation and a hypercoagulable state induced by sepsis, as probable contributors. Additionally, septic emboli originating from the abscess may have exacerbated the thrombotic process. Pylephlebitis, an infective suppurative thrombophlebitis of the portal vein, is an uncommon condition with an incidence ranging from 0.37 to 2.7 cases per 100,000 person-years [12]. Hepatic abscess can be formed secondary to pylephlebitis or vice versa [13]. The most reported symptoms at admission are fever (75.5%) and abdominal pain (66.4%), with diverticulitis (26.5%) and acute appendicitis (22%) being the leading causes [12,14 – 16]. It can lead to severe complications like bowel infarction needing resection (single case report), portal hypertension with development of varices (up to 11.1%) and mortality of the patient (8.7% to 19%) [12,14 – 16]. Portal hypertension, defined as an increase in the pressure within the portal venous system, commonly results from obstruction of blood flow through the liver due to cirrhosis or thrombosis of the portal vein [17,18]. This increased pressure leads to the development of collateral pathways, including varices, to decompress the portal system [17,18]. These varices can form complex networks and are often associated with significant non-vascular abnormalities, including portal biliopathy, a condition characterised by biliary obstruction due to variceal compression of the bile ducts [19 – 21]. Pancreatic parenchymal varices are an extremely rare manifestation of portal hypertension, described in only 2 case reports and one case series [22 – 24]. The common hepatic bile duct (CHD) stenosis observed in this patient is likely secondary to external compression by the adjacent hepatic abscess and associated inflammatory changes. Additionally, ischemic insult caused by portal vein thrombosis and increased venous pressure due to pylephlebitis could have exacerbated the biliary obstruction. Compression-related biliary stenosis is a recognised complication of hepatic abscess and is often managed through drainage of the abscess, followed by endoscopic stenting to restore bile flow [19 – 21]. The dual involvement of the portal and systemic venous systems (pylephlebitis and IVC thrombosis) strongly suggests that the hepatic abscess was the initiating pathology, with pylephlebitis and pancreatic parenchymal varices being secondary sequelae. The abscess, located in the left lobe of the liver, likely caused localised inflammation and compression of adjacent vascular structures, including both the portal vein and IVC. This is consistent with the pathophysiology of abscess-induced thrombosis, wherein inflammatory mediators and hypercoagulable states promote venous thrombosis in adjacent vessels. This interpretation is further supported by the absence of any primary mesenteric venous infection or systemic prothrombotic condition. Diagnosis of HA is primarily reliant on imaging techniques such as sonography or CT scans [1]. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) is the preferred method for diagnosing hepatic abscesses, boasting a sensitivity of up to 97% [1,11]. This imaging technique is effective in detecting potential perforations, ruptured liver abscesses, ascites, pleural effusions and other rarely occurring complications like venous thrombosis [1,2 – 16]. When a liver abscess is observed in the caudate lobe or near a vascular channel, it is important to carefully examine for vascular complications, including abscess extension. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) can be useful in completing the work-up searching for biliary obstruction as a possible complication of HA [1,20]. Patient management includes antibiotic management with percutaneous drain placement for liver abscesses to limit the systemic effects of sepsis [1,12 – 16,25,26]. This is followed by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) guided plastic stent placement for biliary stenosis [1,20,21,27]. Finally, anticoagulation therapy for pylephlebitis and IVC thrombosis will be initiated [1,12 – 16]. Regular imaging follow-up is also necessary for understanding the progression of the disease. Teaching Points / Take-Home Message Hepatic abscesses may lead to rare complications like IVC thrombosis and pancreatic parenchymal varices. Cross-sectional imaging is essential for detecting such complications as some pathologies can be missed on ultrasound; IVC thrombosis in this case was first detected on CECT abdomen. Prompt multidisciplinary management, including image-guided percutaneous drainage, antibiotics, and anticoagulation, is critical. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Tumefactive demyelinating with open ring sign
clinical_history: A 55-year-old female presented with status epilepticus and focal seizures in the left arm, with progressive behavioural disturbance, and altered sensorium over 4 weeks duration. The patient is HBsAg positive; otherwise, all laboratory findings were within the normal limits. Neurological and other systemic examinations were within the normal limits and no cranial nerve palsy was detected.
imaging_findings: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain with contrast was done to find the aetiology behind it, and it revealed a lesion in the supratentorial compartment, centred within the deep white matter in the right frontal cortex. A cerebrospinal fluid (C SF) culture was done, and it showed an oligoclonal band suggestive of intrathecal IgG antibody synthesis. Patient was started on salmeterol and clinicians finds significant improvement in seizures.
discussion: Background Tumefactive demyelinating lesion is a special type of neuroinflammatory disease that can affect patients with or without a conclusive neurological condition, most often multiple sclerosis. Numerous studies indicate a rare occurrence of tumefactive demyelinating lesions, which primarily afflict people in their second and third decades of life and occur in 1 – 2 cases per 1000 cases of multiple sclerosis. Other primary demyelinating diseases like acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) and acute haemorrhagic leukoencephalitis also manifest as tumefactive demyelinating lesions. Clinical Perspective Some tumefactive demyelinating lesions are asymptomatic and are incidentally detected on MRI. S ymptomatic lesions present acutely and vary on the basis of size, location and mass effect of the lesion over surrounding structures. Hemiparesis being the most common presentation, they can also present with motor dysfunction, sensory dysfunction, cognitive and cerebellar symptoms like apraxia, aphasia, seizures and impaired visual field defect. Imaging Perspective MRI is the best imaging modality for tumefactive demyelinating lesions. Diagnostic ambiguity still exists, but some traditional MRI findings of tumefactive demyelinating lesions have been added. Tumefactive demyelination is an uncommon but important manifestation of multiple immune-mediated neurologic diseases that can be difficult to diagnose. Tumour-like demyelinating lesions and brain tumours can be distinguished by MRI pooled sensitivity and specificity, which have been reported to be 89% and 94%, respectively [1,4]. The frontal and parietal lobes are where tumefactive demyelinating lesions most frequently occur. Tumour-causing demyelinating lesions fall into four categories: ring-like, megacystic, infiltrative, and balo-like. The imaging characteristics of tumefactive demyelination are [1]: Large lesion with little mass effect and oedema : Tumefactive demyelinating lesions typically have a limited shape and cause vasogenic oedema or minimal mass effect; typically, they involve the supratentorial compartment and are centred inside the white matrix. Ring-like or open-ring enhancement : The enhancing portion of the ring is believed to represent the leading edge of demyelination and thus favours the white matter side of the lesion. Centrally dilated vein within the lesion : Cha et al. noted a dilated vascular structure running centrally within several of the studied tumefactive demyelinating lesions; the presence of a central vein within the white matter lesion, called the “central vein sign” , is a specific biomarker of perivenous inflammatory demyelination; these veins represent dilated veins draining toward distended subependymal veins. Rapid resolution after steroid therapy : The majority of tumefactive demyelinating lesions will respond well to corticosteroid therapy, with the lesions on follow-up imaging showing a significant reduction in size. The most commonly reported MRI feature of tumefactive demyelination, among the previously mentioned features, is an open ring enhancement. This feature shows an incomplete portion of the ring abutting the cortex’s grey matter, with the enhancing component of the ring facing the lesion ’s white matter and pertaining to an advancing front of demyelination [2,3]. Another typical feature is a high apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC). A more persistent inflammatory response is shown by the non-enhancing core in the centre.

final_diagnosis: Tumefactive demyelination with open ring sign

title: Incidental but indispensable finding: Persistent left superior vena cava
clinical_history: A 73-year-old female with chronic cough was admitted to our hospital with complaints of breathlessness for 1 week. The jugular venous pressure was elevated, bilateral pitting pedal oedema was present, and a long systolic murmur was heard in the tricuspid area. A 2D echocardiogram showed dilated right atrium (RA) and right ventricle (RV), severe tricuspid regurgitation/pulmonary arterial hypertension ( TR/PAH), and RV dysfunction. ECG showed a right bundle branch block. The patient was referred to our department for a CT pulmonary angiogram.
imaging_findings: CT pulmonary angiogram showed a thrombus in the right pulmonary artery (Figure 1) and its branches, and a focal thrombi in the left descending pulmonary artery and its branches. Incidentally, we noted variant anatomy in the venous system of the thorax. The right brachiocephalic vein, formed by the union of the right internal jugular vein and right subclavian vein, was seen continuing as superior vena cava. The left brachiocephalic vein was absent (Figure 2). A persistent left superior vena cava (Figures 3, 4, 5 and 6 ) was noted draining into the right atrium through the coronary sinus (Figures 3 and 4). Features of right heart failure were noted: right atrium and right ventricle were dilated, and there was reflux of contrast into dilated intrahepatic inferior vena cava and hepatic veins.
discussion: Background and Imaging Perspective Persistent left superior vena cava (PLSVC) is a rare but most common anomaly of the venous system of the thorax. Prevalence in general population varies from 0.2 to 3%. In congenital heart disease patients, the prevalence varies from 1.3 to 11% [1]. SVC develops from the cardinal system of veins, which is one of the three primitive venous systems, along with the umbilical and vitelline systems. There are symmetrical (right and left) pairs of anterior and posterior cardinal veins. Anterior cardinal veins drain the cranial aspect, and posterior cardinal veins drain the caudal aspect of the embryo. These join to form the right and left common cardinal veins, which drain into the ipsilateral horns of the sinus venosus and then to the heart (Figure 7). SVC (Figure 8) develops by forming bridging anastomosis between the right and left anterior cardinal veins. Bridging anastomosis develops into the left brachiocephalic vein (BCV). Then, there is an obliteration of the caudal part of the left anterior cardinal vein, forming the ligament of Marshall. The left sinus venosus and left common cardinal vein form the coronary sinus. The proximal right anterior, right common cardinal vein and right sinus venosus form the normal SVC. Failure of regression of the left anterior cardinal vein and adjacent part of the left common cardinal vein results in PLSVC (Figure 9). Various hypotheses have been postulated regarding the development of PLSVC. One of these is the “low left atrial pressure theory”, which states that low pressure in the left atrium, due to other anomalies, fails to compress the coronary sinus and left cardinal vein, leading to the formation of PLSVC [1,2]. In 90% of cases, PLSVC is associated with a normal SVC on the right, known as double SVC (DSVC). If SVC does not develop on the right in the presence of a PLSVC, it is called isolated PLSVC (IPLSVC) and is associated with cardiac anomalies and cardiac situs disorders. Single ventricle, atrial and ventricular septal defects, tetralogy of Fallot have been reported as most common associated cardiac anomalies [3–5]. Other associations include the right-sided arcus aorta, coarctation of the aorta, and heterotaxy [6]. Clinical Perspective Although PLSVC is asymptomatic and detected incidentally, there is some clinical significance. Dilated coronary sinus associated with PLSVC can compress the atrioventricular node and the bundle of His and cause arrhythmias. It can complicate mitral valve surgery [7]. PLSVC detection is important before invasive procedures like central venous catheter insertion, cardiac resynchronisation therapy or pacemaker implantation [1,2]. Detection of PLSVC is also important before some cardiac surgeries like venous rerouting procedures, surgeries with cavo-pulmonary anastomosis and transplantation surgeries [1]. Teaching Points PLSVC is usually insignificant and asymptomatic, but it can cause significant problems in a few clinical scenarios. Therefore, its detection is important and should be reported in radiology reports even if detected incidentally.

title: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy: When images say everything
clinical_history: A 7-year-old boy with a history of neonatal distress at term birth, with no evident pre-existing cause at screening, was referred to the radiology department for language delay, cerebellar syndrome, and gait disorders. Physical examination, blood tests, and initial brain CT were unremarkable. A subsequent brain MRI was performed.
imaging_findings: Brain MRI revealed bilateral enlargement of the peri-rolandic cortex, indicating chronic lesions with T2WI and FLAIR hyperintensity. The lesions extended along the external capsule as an evident FLAIR hyperintensity on coronal images, suggesting a severe hypoxic-ischemic event. No other abnormalities were noted.
discussion: Background Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) remains a significant cause of neonatal mortality worldwide. Despite advancements, up to 23% of affected neonates die, and 25% experience permanent neurological deficits [1]. While clinical criteria can guide diagnosis, MRI is essential for definitive evaluation, especially in cases of atypical presentation or discordant clinical findings. MRI can identify specific patterns of injury, assess disease progression, and predict long-term outcomes. Clinical Perspective Preterm neonates are more vulnerable to HIE than full-term infants. Brain damage can occur within a few minutes of a hypoxic-ischemic event. Clinical diagnosis is based on evidence of foetal distress, proven acidosis, low Apgar score, need for resuscitation, neurological signs of encephalopathy, and multiorgan dysfunction, without evidence of infection, congenital malformations, or metabolic disorders. Imaging Perspective MRI is the gold standard for diagnosing HIE, with findings differing between preterm and full-term neonates, given variations in the arterial supply. The injury pattern is influenced by brain maturity and the severity of hypoperfusion. In the acute phase, DWI shows restricted diffusion, that typically pseudo-normalises by the end of the first week [2]. In term newborns with profound acute hypoxia, the “basal ganglia-thalamus pattern” is predominant, correlating with motor impairment. T1 hyperintensity of grey matter begins on the 2nd day of life, and persists for months, while T2WI hyperintensity (oedema) appears by the 3rd day. Chronic HIE is characterised by atrophy and T2 hyperintensity. In contrast, full-term infants suffering prolonged partial or mild-to-moderate asphyxia exhibit a watershed pattern affecting the parieto-occipital and posterior temporal lobes, leading to atrophy known as ulegyria [3]. Spectroscopy MRI (SRM) in the basal ganglia can reveal decreased N-acetylaspartate (NAA) and increased lactate levels, with increased lactate-to-creatinine and lactate-to-NAA ratios indicating a worse neurological outcome. MRI also helps rule out other causes of encephalopathy, including haemorrhage, perinatal stroke, neoplasms, and congenital malformations. Outcome The pattern of lesions, particularly the involvement of basal ganglia, cortical lesions, abnormal DWI, and SRM findings, is associated with poor prognosis and persistent neurological impairment. Marked EEG abnormalities are also linked to a worse prognosis. While mild HIE in term infants often resolves, 25% develop significant neurologic sequelae. Early identification and prompt management in paediatric intensive care units are crucial for optimal outcomes [2]. Take Home Message Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is a clinical-radiological spectrum of brain injury following perinatal ischemia. Early diagnosis is crucial for optimal management and prognosis. MRI is essential for diagnosis, assessing injury severity, and predicting outcomes. Informed consent has been obtained from the legal representative of the patient for the anonymous publication of the content.
differential_diagnosis: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy Hypoglycemic encephalopathy Perinatal stroke Seizure
