title: Giant mediastinal mature teratoma in a child
clinical_history: A two-year-old male infant with a recent history of bronchopneumonia, which did not course with fever or elevated inflammatory parameters, was referred to our hospital with a history of new-onset orthopnoea, right hemithorax hypophonesis and basal crackles.
imaging_findings: A chest radiograph (CXR) was first performed, which showed a right-sided hemithorax opacity with dense structures within it and a slight left mediastinal shift (Figure 1). A chest ultrasound (Figure 2) was next carried out to discern the presence of pleural effusion, demonstrating the presence of a heterogeneous mass occupying the right hemithorax with anechoic and hyperechoic and pleural effusion with debris. Given these findings, a thorax CT (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, 3d and 3e) was performed, confirming a voluminous heterogeneous anterior mediastinal mass which occupied the right hemithorax with soft tissue, bone and fat densities compatible with a mature teratoma. Tumour markers (CEA, alfa fetoprotein and b-HCG) were negative . In order to plan the surgery, an MRI and 3D CT reconstruction were also achieved (Figures 4a, 4b, 4c, 5a, 5b and 5c). The patient had complete surgical excision (Figure 6) with no complications and an uneventful postoperative period with resolution of his symptoms .
discussion: Mediastinal mature teratomas are the third most frequent type of tumour found in the paediatric mediastinum, after lymphoma and neurogenic tumours. These tumours develop in the mediastinum as a result of migration of foetal germ cell precursors along germinal ridges, moving from the yolk sac to paired structures along the midline [1]. Mediastinal mature teratomas tend to appear at two distinct age ranges: around two years old, as depicted in our case, and during adolescence [1]. The clinical presentation can vary widely based on the variable size of the tumour and the mass effect it causes on nearby structures, including stridor, cough, shortness of breath, and haemoptysis [2]. Mass effect can lead to atelectasis and post-obstructive pneumonia [2]. Such as in our case, persistent non-infectious respiratory symptoms in infants should prompt consideration of a mediastinal mass. Additional signs may include chest pain, orthopnoea, superior vena cava syndrome, or vague symptoms like weight loss. On the other hand, some patients are asymptomatic, with up to 60% being identified through routine CXR. A sharply defined lesion on CXR should raise suspicion of a mediastinal teratoma [1–3]. Cross-sectional imaging is crucial for both diagnosis and surgical planning. Most mediastinal mature teratomas appear as solid, lobulated and encapsulated masses arising from the prevascular space. Calcifications are seen in 25% of cases, and the combination of fat, cystic components and calcifications in an anterior mediastinal mass is suggestive of this diagnosis. Additionally, the presence of a fat-fluid level or teeth within the mass is pathognomonic of a mature teratoma, as depicted in our case [2–4]. A well-defined staging system exists for teratomas arising in gonadal structures; however, because of their infrequency, no specific staging systems have yet been described for primary germ cell tumours of the mediastinum. Mature teratomas are composed of ectodermal, mesodermal, and/or endodermal germ cell elements, and two of three germ cell layers are required to make this diagnosis [1]. Prevascular tumours include mediastinal teratoma, thymic lesions, lymphoma and vascular anomalies, with solid masses typically representing either mediastinal mature teratoma or lymphoma. A diffuse nodular enlargement of the thymus with mass effect on nearby structures suggests lymphoma [1,2]. There is still limited data on mediastinal teratomas. As it is a rare tumour, there is not any specific work-up and treatment guidelines. As shown in several reports, early referral and treatment show good prognosis [2 – 4]. The preferred treatment is complete surgical excision, achieved by carefully separating the tumour from surrounding tissues, which may pose some difficulties such as the proximity to vital structures and the possibility of adhesions. However, it is still feasible to achieve complete excision, which provides a curative approach with minimal complications [2–4]. Patients who undergo resection of benign mature teratomas can be observed for a short period of time (3 – 6 months) postoperatively while wound healing and progression of patient activity are monitored [5 ]. All patient information has been fully anonymised in the manuscript and associated files.

title: Turf toe with hallux varus
clinical_history: A male patient presented to an orthopaedic consult with pain and deformity in the hallux after suffering a trauma to the foot several months prior. He delayed seeking medical attention. After observing a deformity of the great toe of the foot, radiography and MRI were ordered.
imaging_findings: The radiography of the foot revealed a varus deformity of the great toe with partial medial subluxation of the first metatarsophalangeal joint (Figure 1). MRI showed a non-acute tear of the plantar plate of the first metatarsophalangeal joint (Figure 2), accompanied by injury to the lateral capsular structures and collateral ligaments (Figures 3a and 3b), with oedema and thickening of lateral metatarsosesamoid ligament, probably by associated partial tear (Figures 4a and 4b). The adductor hallucis remained intact and the sesamoids were not proximally retracted due to the integrity of the sesamoid phalangeal ligaments, specifically the lateral one (Figure 5). On the medial side, the collateral sesamoid phalangeal ligament was normal, and both sesamoids showed no oedema-like changes (Figure 5). The extensor tendons and sagittal bands of the great toe remained normal (Figure 3a). Regarding the metatarsophalangeal joint, imaging showed chondral irregularity of the articular surfaces, mostly on the base of the proximal phalanx, due to either post-traumatic changes or early degenerative manifestations (Figure 2).
discussion: Turf toe refers to an injury of the first metatarsophalangeal joint (MTPJ), with a hyperextension mechanism, often occurring during athletic activities, with a higher prevalence of these injuries in football players competing on artificial surfaces with softer soled shoes, allowing greater speed and traction [1]. It involves spraining the plantar structures of the greater toe, leading to a spectrum of injuries, from mild sprains to complete tears [2]. Unlike the lesser MTPJs, the first MTPJ lacks a single dominating fibrocartilaginous capsular thickening. Rather, the sesamoids are invested by the fibrocartilaginous pad at the plantar first MTPJ, which is inseparable from the musculotendinous structures, paired metatarsosesamoid ligaments (MTSLs), sesamoid phalangeal ligaments (SPLs), and plantar capsule. These work together to form the plantar plate complex, a functional unit [2]. In the current case, the trauma led to a disruption of the lateral capsular and collateral complex, as well as a partial lesion to the lateral metatarsosesamoid ligament, contributing to the development of hallux varus, where the proximal phalanx of the great toe deviates medially. Patients often exhibit pain, oedema, and instability at the MTPJ at the time of the injury, albeit delayed presentation can mask early signs of damage. In these situations, imaging is essential since a physical examination might not be enough to determine the full extent of the injury. MRI is particularly useful for assessing soft tissue injuries, such as plantar plate and collateral ligament tears [3], which were present in this case. Radiographs can confirm deformities, such as hallux varus, as seen here. From an imaging perspective, diagnostic pearls include evaluating for plantar plate integrity, sesamoid positioning, and morphology of the capsule and its ligamentous attachments on MRI [3]. These findings help confirm the extent of joint instability and deformity. A common grading system proposed by Anderson [4] classifies turf toe injury into three different grades, ranging from stretching of and partial tears of the plantar complex to complete tears, each with their commonly associated signs and symptoms. While these lesions occur due to a mechanism of hyperextension of the first MTPJ, hyperflexion injuries sustained during sports such as beach volleyball are termed “sand toe” and are associated with dorsal capsular injury of the first MTPJ [5]. Treatment typically involves conservative management with immobilisation, but in cases with significant deformity or instability, surgical intervention may be necessary [6]. Early imaging is crucial in guiding treatment and predicting outcomes since untreated or misdiagnosed turf toe can result in lasting deformities like hallux varus with degenerative changes [1, 6 ].

title: Filarial dance: Radiological insights
clinical_history: A 71-year-old lady reported to the emergency with a history of a fall and was referred for CT brain. Retrospective history revealed recurrent swelling and itching over the left temporal region for the last 6 months.
imaging_findings: No trauma-related abnormality was seen on CT. However, a thick-walled cystic lesion was noted in the subcutaneous plane on the left temporal region of the scalp (Figure 1). Ultrasound of the lesion showed a cyst with actively mobile, tubular serpiginous structures, having echogenic walls showing a “filarial dance” sign (Figures 2 and 3).
discussion: Background Dirofilariasis is a zoonotic condition occurring when humans serve as accidental hosts to Dirofilaria immitis , Dirofilaria repens , and Dirofilaria tenuis . Dirofilaria immitis is the commonest Dirofilaria globally [1]. Dogs serve as the definitive host for the parasite, with the mosquito acting as the intermediate host. Microfilariae present in the dog’s peripheral blood are ingested by the mosquito, where they develop into infective larvae that can then be transmitted to incidental hosts, such as humans. The infection is endemic in continents like Asia, Africa, and Europe. In Asia, this infection is commonly caused by Dirofilaria repens and is seen in Sri Lanka and southern states of India [2]. The initial cases of human ocular and subcutaneous dirofilariasis in India were recorded in the state of Kerala, occurring in 1976 and 2004, respectively [3]. Clinical Perspective Of the 782 cases documented worldwide, one-third were orbital lesions. The majority of reported cases involved exposed regions of the head and neck, accessible to mosquitoes [4]. Occasionally, the parasite has been detected in deeper locations, including peritoneum, omentum, breast, and liver. Many infected subjects are asymptomatic, and a strong clinical suspicion is essential for making a diagnosis. Subcutaneous nodules are the most common initial symptom, but those can be indicative of various conditions like lipoma, fibroma, foreign body granuloma, soft tissue sarcoma, metastasis, and other parasitic infections, including onchocerciasis or cysticercosis. Serologic tests are unreliable due to the worms ’ lack of reproduction in the human body, causing insufficient parasitic burden [5]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound, with its real-time imaging capabilities, can definitively diagnose the presence of the parasite if it is alive — visualised as a motile, folded tubular structure exhibiting parallel echogenic stripes within a cyst. Even when the worm is dead or non-motile but maintains structural integrity, ultrasound remains the definitive diagnostic modality, with no alternative differentials [6]. CT findings are non-specific and may show heterogeneous soft tissue mass with peripheral enhancement, simulating an abscess. Outcome Surgical removal of the worm is the definitive treatment. However, antiparasitic treatment with ivermectin and diethylcarbamazine may be advised if secondary lesions are suspected in deeper parts such as the chest or abdomen [7]. Usually, clinical symptoms will disappear after the parasite is removed. Our patient was treated conservatively with diethylcarbamazine (tablets) and showed symptomatic improvement. Take Home Message Ultrasonography is a useful non-invasive diagnostic tool in making a reliable diagnosis of subcutaneous dirofilariasis, and identifying live adult worms. Specific imaging findings for dirofilariasis can be observed using ultrasound, and other possible differential diagnoses can also be excluded. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
differential_diagnosis: Dirofilariasis Epidermal inclusion cyst Cysticercosis Foreign body granuloma

title: A case of spondylocostal dysostosis
clinical_history: A one-year-old full-term-born male child, born to non-consanguineous parents, presents with complaints of thoracic deformity. No history of previous surgeries.
imaging_findings: The AP chest radiograph (Figure 1) demonstrated the absence of ribs in the right mid-zone, with fusion of multiple adjacent ribs. Fusion of multiple ribs was also noted on the left side. The image showed evidence of dextroscoliosis. Further evaluation with computed tomography revealed bifid ribs with segmental fusion and widening at multiple levels bilaterally (Videos and Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, 3, 4, and 5). Fusion of posterior vertebral elements was observed at multiple levels, and dextroscoliosis was noted involving the thoracic spine. Posterior vertebral arch defects were identified involving the L5 vertebra and all sacral vertebrae (Figures 2b and 2c). Mild volume loss of the right hemithorax was noted. The pulmonary parenchyma, bronchial, and vascular markings appeared normal bilaterally.
discussion: Spondylocostal dysostosis (SCD), commonly referred to as Jarcho – Levin syndrome, is a rare genetic growth disorder that was first identified by Saul Jarcho and Paul Levin in 1938 [ 1 ]. Patients typically exhibit multiple vertebral anomalies across different levels of the spine, such as hemivertebrae, butterfly vertebrae, and fused hypoplastic vertebrae [2]. A common characteristic is the presence of congenital rib malformations, which may be fused, absent, or excessively developed. Patients may show defects in the neural arches of the vertebrae, potentially resulting in conditions like spina bifida or other neural tube defects. These abnormalities can lead to neurological deficits and complicate the overall clinical presentation. As a result of these abnormalities, affected individuals have a higher risk of developing thoracic insufficiency syndrome, which can ultimately result in early neonatal death. However, despite these severe complications, around 50% of cases may survive into adulthood [3]. For over fifty years, there has been uncertainty about the differences between two phenotypically similar syndromes that lead to thoracic insufficiency, i.e., spondylocostal dysostosis (SCD), also referred to as Jarcho – Levin syndrome, and spondylothoracic dysostosis (STD), also known as Lavy – Moseley syndrome: Spondylocostal dysostosis (SCD) is linked to mild to moderate respiratory insufficiency, occurs in various ethnic groups, and has been associated with genes like DLL3, which is related to the Notch pathway. In contrast, spondylothoracic dysostosis (STD) is connected to more severe respiratory issues, is primarily found in Puerto Rican populations, and is thought to be associated with the MESP2 gene, which is also part of the Notch pathway [4].
differential_diagnosis: Spondylocostal dysostosis (Jarcho–Levin syndrome) Spondylothoracic dysostosis (Lavy–Moseley syndrome)

title: Hydatid cyst mimicking liver metastasis in a cancer patient
clinical_history: A 55-year-old female patient was admitted to our oncology centre with follicular lymphoma. She had a seven-kilogram weight loss over one year, loss of appetite, and fever of unknown origin. There is no significant medical history, and physical examination revealed only cervical lymphadenopathy. The patient’s blood workup revealed a slight increase in C-reactive protein (1.2 mg/dL) and creatine kinase (151 U/L), with no other abnormal laboratory findings.
imaging_findings: Computed tomography detected a large lesion, measuring 7.5 x 5 centimetres, heterogeneous, with fluid densities and lobulated margins in the superior segments of the right hepatic lobe (Figure 1). Due to the patient’s clinical context, an ultrasound-guided biopsy was performed, which revealed an unrepresentative fragment of liver tissue, encompassing a fibro-hyalinised nodule. An abdominal magnetic resonance (MR) was performed to characterise the hepatic lesion further (Figures 2, 3a, 3b, and 4). The MR revealed a heterogeneous, complex cystic lesion with a thin wall, hypointense on T2-weighted images, and hyperintense on T1-weighted images, located within the right liver lobe. The lesion exhibited radiating septa towards the periphery, appearing as low-signal intensity on T2-weighted images and high-signal intensity on T1-weighted images. These septa delineated multiple smaller cysts, hypointense on T1 and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, occupying almost the entire lesion. After contrast administration, the lesion did not exhibit restricted diffusion and no significant enhancement of the soft tissue component.
discussion: Background Hydatid disease is a zoonotic infection, endemic in the Mediterranean region, caused by the Echinococcus granulosus tapeworms [1]. The infection manifests with cysts formation in different organs, particularly the liver and the lungs in 90% of the cases [1]. Humans can become incidental intermediate hosts by consuming food contaminated with Echinococcus eggs or through direct contact with a definitive host, typically a domestic dog [1]. Clinical Perspective The early stage of primary infection is asymptomatic [1,2]. Hepatic cysts can cause upper abdominal pain or discomfort, hepatomegaly, and cholestasis [1,2 ]. Cysts might rupture into the peritoneal cavity, leading to anaphylaxis, or into the biliary tree, causing cholangitis [3]. Imaging Perspective The right lobe is the most affected portion of the liver. Imaging findings in hepatic hydatid disease vary with the cyst growth stage, including whether it is unilocular, contains daughter cysts, and the extent of calcification [4]. On CT, hydatid cysts typically appear as well-defined, fluid-filled lesions with thin walls (Figure 1). They may contain internal daughter cysts separated by a hydatid matrix, creating the characteristic spoke-wheel pattern. Calcification of the wall is present in 50% of cases [4]. On MR, hydatid cysts typically display low signal intensity on T1-weighted sequences, although the intensity may vary depending on the concentration of proteinaceous materials and cellular debris [4]. On T2-weighted images, the cysts typically exhibit high signal intensity, facilitating the identification of daughter cysts (Figures 2, 3a, 3b, and 4) [4]. Outcome Serological tests revealed positive Echinococcus granulosus IgG antibodies, indirect immunofluorescence (1:640), and a positive western blot, combined with imaging findings, suggested active infection. The patient started treatment with albendazole for two months and underwent a partial laparoscopic cystectomy. Over the follow-up period, the patient showed no signs of cyst recurrence. Liver function tests remained stable, and imaging studies confirmed the absence of residual cysts. Surgery, particularly with a laparoscopic approach, remains essential for hydatid disease, offering similar outcomes to open surgery [2]. The PAIR technique—puncture, aspiration, ethanol or hypertonic saline injection, and re-aspiration—is also an option for active disease or recurrence post-surgery in selected cases [2]. In our case, differentiating between metastatic lesion and hydatid disease was crucial due to their different treatments and prognosis. Take Home Message Evaluation of complex cystic liver lesions in patients with malignancy should consider infectious aetiologies as differential diagnoses. MR is important in differentiating complex cystic liver lesions when CT or ultrasound findings are inconclusive. T2-weighted imaging is the most specific sequence, allowing the visualisation of daughter cysts within the main cyst, as they appear hyperintense due to high fluid content. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Hepatic hydatid disease (type IIb) Cystic/necrotic liver metastasis Hepatic abscess Biliary cystadenoma/cystadenocarcinoma

title: SELSTOC – A sternal “do not touch” lesion
clinical_history: A 17-month-old boy presented with a 3-day history of sternal swelling and pain. No fever or any other symptoms. There was no history of trauma. Physical examination revealed a 2 cm swelling in the manubriosternal region. Inflammatory parameters were normal except for a slightly elevated value for C-reactive protein.
imaging_findings: The chest radiograph revealed a presternal soft tissue swelling without calcifications and with no evidence of bony anomalies at the sternum, such as bone erosions or a periosteal reaction (Figure 1). A CT scan showed a fusiform soft tissue density lesion, centred on the manubriosternal joint, involving both superficial and deep planes of the synchondrosis, with subcutaneous and mediastinal extension, measuring 46 x 27 x 37 mm. No significant irregularity of the bony surfaces at the manubriosternal synchondrosis is visible. However, a separation between the manubrial and sternal ossification centres is evident , accompanied by densification of the adjacent subcutaneous tissue (Figures 2a and 2b). Ultrasound revealed a hypoechoic and heterogeneous, dumbbell-shaped lesion centred on the manubriosternal synchondrosis. This lesion crosses the synchondrosis, extending superficially into the subcutaneous tissue and deeply to the depth of the chest wall/anterior mediastinum. Colour Doppler ultrasound demonstrated no internal vascularisation. Additionally, there is a thickening of the soft tissues surrounding the manubriosternal joint (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c]. Bone scintigraphy showed no significant abnormalities.
discussion: Rapidly growing sternal and parasternal masses are rare in the paediatric population but can be concerning due to the potential suspicion of malignancy [1]. In 2010, Winkel et al. described SELSTOC (self-limiting sternal tumour of childhood) as asymptomatic, self-limiting, and typically self-involuting tumours, that arise from an exaggerated immune response to an aseptic inflammatory process, with no history of trauma. The aetiology of these acute sternal lesions of non-neoplastic and non-infectious origin remains uncertain [2,3]. Clinically, SELSTOC presents as a firm mass, generally 1–4.5 cm in diameter, located in presternal or parasternal regions. Occasionally, there may be red or blue discolouration, local tenderness, or mild fever. Laboratory findings are typically unremarkable, though mild elevations in C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) may occur [1]. Radiologically, SELSTOC shows no aggressive features. Ultrasound is the preferred imaging modality and often reveals a characteristic “dumbbell-shape”, with presternal and retrosternal components, and connected by a narrow neck between the segments of the sternum or between the sternum and the adjacent rib cartilage. These lesions appear well-defined, hypoechoic relative to surrounding subcutaneous fat, and may be bordered by reactive fluid. They show no internal vascularisation and demonstrate no invasion of adjacent bone or muscle, nor any connection to the skin. In contrast to malignant sternal masses, which exhibit invasive growth and destruction of adjacent tissues, SELSTOC remains localised and gradually diminishes [2,4]. Diagnosis is established by observing spontaneous reduction in size over a few weeks or until complete resolution, generally within an 18-month period. So, ultrasound follow-up is recommended to monitor for shrinkage [1,3]. CT and MRI do not play a significant role in the diagnosis of this entity. On MRI, restricted diffusion has been reported in some cases, so this finding should not be misinterpreted as indicative of malignancy or abscess [1,4]. The differential diagnoses include malignant sternal lesions, which typically exhibit aggressive signs of destruction, invasion of neighbouring structures, and a tendency to increase in size, unlike SELSTOC. Osteomyelitis is another consideration; however, SELSTOC does not align clinically or radiologically. Notably, it lacks periosteal reaction, cortical erosion or destruction, increased fatty marrow density, and other signs consistent with osteomyelitis [3,4] . The absence of aggressive behaviour and the characteristic appearance on ultrasound support the “wait-and-see” approach, which was implemented in this case . On a follow-up ultrasound examination conducted two weeks later, a reduction of the lesion size was observed, and demonstrated complete resolution at the six-month follow-up. In summary, SELSTOC should be suspected in infants and children presenting with a rapidly growing, sternum-adjacent mass, particularly when accompanied by characteristic ultrasound findings, lack of systemic symptoms, and an otherwise normal physical examination. This profile supports a conservative “wait-and-see” approach, as SELSTOC represents a “do not touch” lesion in paediatric practice [1,2]. Written informed patient’s family consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Right internal carotid artery agenesis with basilar aneurysm
clinical_history: A 60-year-old female presented to the emergency department with a sudden onset of severe headache and transient loss of consciousness. She reported dizziness and blackout without trauma. Her medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and chronic tobacco use. Neurological examination showed no focal deficits, but she complained of persistent headaches and nausea.
imaging_findings: An axial non-contrast CT revealed a linear hyperdensity in the left basifrontal lobe, consistent with acute haemorrhage (Figure 1). On MRI, the T1-weighted image showed a linear hyperintensity in the left basifrontal lobe corresponding to haemorrhage (Figure 2a), while the FLAIR sequence demonstrated hypointensity correlating with T1 hyperintensity, surrounded by hyperintense oedema (Figure 2b). Axial SWI images displayed multiple blooming foci indicative of blood products, confirmed by filtered phase imaging and evidence of intra-ventricular extension (Figures 3a and 3b). Diffusion-weighted imaging indicated diffusion restriction with low ADC values, suggesting cytotoxic oedema (Figures 4a and 4b). Time-of-flight (TOF) magnetic resonance angiography revealed non-visualisation of the right internal carotid artery from the C1 segment, collateral flow to the right middle cerebral artery (MCA) from the anterior communicating artery, a hypoplastic right posterior communicating artery (PCOM), a basilar top aneurysm, and a suspected ruptured aneurysm from the A1 segment of the left anterior cerebral artery (ACA) (Figure 5). CT angiography confirmed the absence of the right internal carotid artery (ICA) and identified a fusiform aneurysm at the top of the basilar artery (Figures 6a, 6b, 6c and 7).
discussion: Background & Pathophysiology Agenesis of the internal carotid artery (ICA) is a rare congenital anomaly with an estimated prevalence of less than 0.01%. This condition arises from failure in embryonic development between the 4th and 6th gestational weeks. Agenesis can be unilateral or bilateral, with bilateral cases being rare and often incompatible with life. The absence of the ICA leads to compensatory collateral circulation through the circle of Willis, primarily involving anterior and posterior communicating arteries. However, altered haemodynamics can predispose patients to aneurysm formation due to increased stress on collateral vessels [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Patients with ICA agenesis may remain asymptomatic due to robust collateral circulation but can present acutely if an associated aneurysm ruptures. In this case, subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) and intraparenchymal haemorrhage were directly related to rupture of an A1 segment left anterior cerebral artery aneurysm, likely exacerbated by chronic hypoxia from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and tobacco use [3,4]. Imaging Perspective This case underscores advanced imaging’s critical role in diagnosing complex vascular anomalies. Non-contrast CT serves as the initial modality for evaluating acute haemorrhage, while MRI, including DWI and TOF-MRA, provides detailed insights into vascular anatomy and pathology. CT angiography confirmed the absence of the right ICA and identified aneurysmal dilation at the basilar artery apex [5,6]. Management & Outcome Given the acute presentation with SAH and identified basilar aneurysm, treatment options included endovascular coiling versus surgical clipping. Due to complex anatomy, endovascular coiling was chosen as a safer approach. The patient underwent successful coiling with stabilisation of her neurological status and gradual improvement in headaches [7]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Congenital agenesis of the ICA is a rare vascular anomaly associated with significant cerebrovascular complications. Multimodal imaging is essential for accurate diagnosis and guiding therapeutic decisions. Maintain a high suspicion for vascular anomalies in patients with unexplained SAH. A multidisciplinary approach is crucial for optimising patient outcomes.

final_diagnosis: Right internal carotid artery agenesis with fusiform basilar aneurysm

title: Rhomboid fossa of the clavicle
clinical_history: An otherwise healthy 22-year-old man presents with acute respiratory symptoms and has an emergency CT scan performed, which reveals an incidental finding.
imaging_findings: No abnormalities are evident on a PA radiograph of the chest (Figure 1). The CT reveals no thoracic abnormalities except for two bilateral cortical defects of the undersurface of the sternal extremity of each clavicle, being slightly larger on the left side (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). An MRI is additionally performed, revealing no evidence of a pathological fracture, soft tissue mass or bone marrow oedema (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c).
discussion: Background The sternoclavicular joint is stabilised by several ligaments, with the costoclavicular ligament being the main stabilising force. It attaches the first rib to the inferior surface of the sternal end of the clavicle. The clavicular insertion usually has a rough small eminence known as the “impression for the costoclavicular ligament” [1]. It may present as a roughened eminence or as a depression of variable depth [2,3]. In the latter case, it may be known as a rhomboid fossa. Clinical Perspective This variant has been reported [4,5] to be more often unilateral and to occur predominantly in younger males, with the largest fossae being reported in males aged 20 to 30 years. Another study [4] reported a significant association with the dominant hand side, supporting a mechanical stress aetiology. To our knowledge, no clinical symptoms have been associated with this anatomical variant. The clinical history is essential to consider other differential diagnoses, especially if the patient is older, symptomatic and/or has a history of malignancy. Imaging Perspective The rhomboid fossa presents as an elliptical or circular, well-defined cortical defect with smooth margins and variable depth, located on the inferior surface of the sternal end of the clavicle [4,5]. It is not associated with aggressive features such as intra-lesional soft tissue, periosteal reaction or pathological fractures. Concerning imaging technique, it may escape detection in conventional radiography, especially when it presents with a shallower depth. CT allows easy detection and is the modality of choice to characterise this variant. MRI allows for easier detection of soft tissue and bone marrow oedema. The differential diagnoses of this lesion are limited, considering its characteristic features and lack of worrisome stigmata. The clavicle is a rare site for malignant tumours [6,7], with plasmacytoma, Ewing sarcoma and osteosarcoma being most frequently reported. Benign lesions that may mimic a rhomboid fossa are varied [8] and may include osteomyelitis, eosinophilic granuloma, aneurysmal bone cyst and giant cell tumours, with the first being accompanied by fever and pain, whereas the last three may present as enlarging swellings with intra-lesional soft tissue. Outcome It is a benign anatomical variant with no recommended treatment. Take Home Message The rhomboid fossa variant should be suspected in an asymptomatic young male who presents with an oval, well-defined, and non-aggressive cortical defect of the inferior aspect of the sternal end of the clavicle. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: OEIS (omphalocele, exstrophy, imperforate anus, and spinal dysraphism) with concomitant malformations
clinical_history: A newborn with ambiguous genitalia and multiple congenital anomalies was admitted in March 2023. Born preterm at 34 weeks, the infant faced respiratory distress, electrolyte imbalances, and sepsis.
imaging_findings: The patient presented with extensive congenital anomalies, including an omphalocele with liver and bowel herniating through a membrane-covered defect, bladder exstrophy, and imperforate anus. Spinal imaging revealed fusion defects in the lower thoracic and lumbar vertebrae, with an associated cystic mass with dystrophic neural elements. Cranial imaging showed a low-lying torcular Herophili, ventriculomegaly, fullness of the foramen magnum, and possible aqueductal stenosis. Other imaging findings included ectopic kidneys (one partially thoracic and another pelvic), midgut malrotation, sacral agenesis, rib synostosis, pubic symphysis diastasis, ambiguous genitalia, and other musculoskeletal abnormalities, highlighting extensive multi-system involvement. Due to the patient’s medical instability and eventual demise, as well as lack of resources, further imaging could not assess other abnormalities including undescended testes and detailed evaluation of the urinary system. These structural abnormalities posed considerable diagnostic and management challenges.
discussion: OEIS (omphalocele, cloacal exstrophy, imperforate anus, and spinal dysraphism) was originally coined by Carey et al. in 1978 to describe a complex congenital anomaly that may arise very early during embryonic development [1] . It is estimated to have a worldwide incidence of 1 in 200,000 to 400,000 live births [2] . As of writing, there are no reported cases in our country’s scientific literature. In an ideal setting, these findings would be seen during a congenital anomaly scan in prenatal ultrasound. The complexity of the case requires a multidisciplinary team to determine the subsequent management [3] . In our case, only a cranial and abdominal CT was done due to the patient’s medical instability and lack of resources. Given such limitations, the most important in OEIS is to diagnose omphalocele and exstrophy as these are management-changing [3] . The liver and some bowel loops are within the omphalocele [4] . Cloacal exstrophy was seen on the CT scan (Figure 3). Imperforate anus is clinically diagnosed and is the least important in OEIS as it is the most convenient to treat [2] . Spinal dysraphism is necessary in the diagnosis of OEIS complex, and was seen as posterior spinal fusion defects in the lower thoracic and lumbar vertebrae with an exophytic cystic mass continuous with the spinal canal and herniation of string-like soft tissues. An MRI could have been useful in evaluating the spine for other segmentation anomalies [5] . Other concomitant malformations that were seen included ambiguous genitalia, which would have been better evaluated with MRI [5,6] . Chiari II malformation was also diagnosed, with only one case reported in literature with OEIS association [5,7–10] . Renal ectopia and intestinal malrotation are also rare associations in OEIS, with only 4 and 13 cases, respectively, reported in the literature [1,7,9,10] . OEIS cases provide insights into the early developmental abnormalities [1,9] . This is the first reported case in our country’s scientific literature; prenatal management, prognostication, and family counselling should be emphasised as there are no reported cases of surviving infancy [2,3,5,8–10] . In this case, the CT scan was able to provide us with an abundance of information for the evaluation of our patient, emphasising the role we have as experts in diagnostic imaging: to provide the best service we can to our patients by prioritising the imaging studies that will give us the most useful information. However, despite medical care and imaging, our patient condition worsened, ultimately resulting in their demise. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Acromioclavicular cyst secondary to massive rotator cuff tear
clinical_history: An 85-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with a rapidly growing mass on her left shoulder (Figure 1), with no history of trauma. On physical examination, the mass was hard and non-mobile.
imaging_findings: A shoulder X-ray and ultrasound scan were performed in order to rule out malignancy. The X-ray (Figure 2) shows a rounded, homogeneous soft-tissue density mass on the left shoulder, located just above the acromioclavicular joint (ACJ). Additionally, the humeral head is seen cranially displaced, with subsequent narrowing of the subacromial space. Osseous degenerative change can be seen in both the humeral head and the ACJ. On the US exam (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c), the images show a supraclavicular fluid collection, predominantly anechogenic but heterogeneous, that appears to be erupting superiorly from the acromioclavicular (AC) interval. No Doppler signal is detected. On interrogation of the rotator cuff, the exam shows the absence of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus tendons over the humeral head, as well as bony contour irregularity.
discussion: With the presumptive diagnosis of an acromioclavicular cyst secondary to a chronic massive rotator cuff tear, a percutaneous drainage was performed for symptom relief. After cytological analysis, no malignancy was detected, with cellularity (macrophages and lymphocytes on a proteinaceous background) consistent with the diagnosis of a cyst. Acromioclavicular joint (ACJ) cysts are fluid-filled sacs that form adjacent to the ACJ, often due to underlying degenerative joint disease or rotator cuff tears. These cysts typically result from the extrusion of synovial fluid through a disrupted ACJ joint capsule, leading to pseudocyst formation [1]. Patients typically present with a visible or palpable swelling over the AC joint, along with discomfort or localised pain. The main clinical problem arises from differentiating these cysts from other soft tissue masses [1]. Imaging is crucial to confirm the presence of a cyst and to assess any underlying joint pathology. It is important to convey whether there is evidence of severe AC joint degeneration, rotator cuff damage, or communication between the joint and the cyst. Ultrasound is typically the first-line imaging modality, allowing visualisation of the cyst and surrounding structures. Key findings include a well-defined, anechoic or hypoechoic mass near the AC joint, although this may not always be the case, as some cysts may show a heterogeneous appearance due to bleeding, infection, or proteinaceous content, as was our case. Ultrasound may also show communication between the joint and the cyst, which confirms its synovial origin (a feature known as “geyser sign” [2] (Figure 3). The absence of internal Doppler signals (Figure 3a) can also be key in ruling out an underlying solid mass. Besides, a fast growing pace (as in the case presented), makes malignancy more unlikely. MRI is also valuable, particularly when assessing for concurrent rotator cuff tears or AC joint degeneration. X-ray can also be helpful to define the relation of the mass to bony structures and can provide indirect rotator cuff information, with humeral head cranial displacement and subacromial space narrowing often seen in massive cuff tears [3] (Figure 1). Biopsy is rarely necessary for diagnosis. The treatment of AC joint cysts is typically conservative, focusing on alleviating symptoms by draining the cyst. Recurrence is common unless underlying joint pathology is addressed. In cases where the cyst is large, surgical options may be considered, which often involve resecting the cyst and repairing the joint. The prognosis depends on the severity of the underlying joint condition. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: A rare cause of persistent baby teeth
clinical_history: An 18-year-old female presented to the maxillofacial surgeon with persistent primary teeth and a palpable left pre-auricular mass, which she first noticed two years prior. No other symptoms were present.
imaging_findings: An orthopantomogram showed a large exophytic sclerotic bone lesion in the left mandible ramus, persistent primary teeth, caries, and multiple smaller sclerotic bone lesions interspersed in the mandible, some with cortical expansion (Figure 1). A CT scan of the maxillofacial region confirmed the presence of a dense ivory-like exophytic lesion growing out of the left mandibular ramus (Figure 2), compatible with an osteoma, and multiple well-delineated lesions of mature bone between the roots of the teeth compatible with hypercementosis. During clinical examination, a mass was palpated on the forehead leading to a CT scan of the skull, revealing multiple small, sessile sclerotic lesions protruding from the outer table (Figure 3), also consistent with osteomas.
discussion: Background Gardner’s syndrome, a subtype of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the APC gene. Its incidence is around 1/7,000 to 1/30,000 [1] and is characterised by numerous colorectal polyps and various extracolonic manifestations. These polyps have a high likelihood of progressing to colorectal cancer, typically in the fourth decade of life. Extracolonic manifestations include dental anomalies, osteomas (in up to 80% of patients), congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE), and soft tissue tumours like desmoid tumours, epidermoid cysts, papillary thyroid cancer, hepatoblastoma and pancreatic cancer [2]. Dental involvement, such as odontomas, unerupted teeth, impacted teeth, or supernumerary teeth, and hypercementosis is present in 30 – 75% of FAP patients [2,3]. Genetic testing confirmed a variant in the APC gene in our case, confirming the diagnosis of Gardner ’s syndrome. Clinical Perspective The initial diagnosis is usually straightforward, as patients will have a familial history of FAP. Dental, maxillofacial, and skin abnormalities are quite common and can be the first symptoms in a young adolescent. The colorectal polyps are often asymptomatic, but screening in patients with confirmed or suspected Gardner ’s syndrome is necessary because of their high cancer risk [1,2,4]. In childhood, an ultrasound of the liver to screen for hepatoblastoma can be considered. Evaluation for pancreatic cancer, biliary neoplasms, or desmoid tumours is usually only performed if symptoms occur. Imaging Perspective Osteomas can be diagnosed on X-ray or CT and appear as very dense sessile or exophytic bone lesions, consisting of mature lamellar bone. Multiple osteomas should always raise the suspicion of Gardner ’s syndrome, especially in adolescent patients or in patients with associated dental abnormalities like in our case. Ultrasound is useful to screen for hepatoblastoma in children, and CT of the abdomen is useful when there is suspicion of abdominal desmoid tumours, pancreatic cancer, or biliary neoplasm. Outcome Treatment typically involves an individual approach with screening for FAP-associated tumours. An annual colonoscopy starting at the age of twelve years old is recommended, and eventually, a preventive proctocolectomy is often performed [1,4]. Furthermore, screening of the upper gastrointestinal tract, the retina (for CHRPE), and the thyroid gland is recommended. Despite follow-up, patients still have an 80% risk of developing colorectal carcinoma before the age of 60 [1]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Persisting baby teeth can be a manifestation of Gardner ’s syndrome, especially when associated with osteomas. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Third or fourth branchial cleft cyst simulating a retropharyngeal abscess
clinical_history: A nine-year-old female child presented with fever, restriction of neck movements and posterior bulging of the mucosa of the posterior oropharyngeal/hypopharyngeal wall lateralised to the left side on nasopharyngolaryngoscopy. Piriform sinuses were inspected and did not show any irregularities.
imaging_findings: A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck revealed a well-defined oval fluid collection, with rim enhancement, in the retropharyngeal space, measuring 2 x 2 x 1 cm (ap/axial/cc) ( a rrows in Figures 1 and 2). Retropharyngeal space oedema was also present, from the skull base to the hypopharynx level ( small arrow in Figure 2 ). Additionally, a thin well-defined rim- enhancing fistulous tract could be identified, running from the inferior left border of the retropharyngeal collection to the upper pole of the left thyroid lobe (arrows on Figure 3).
discussion: Background Third and fourth branchial cleft cysts are rare congenital defects. They are located on the left side in most cases (80%) [1,2]. They can present as a cyst or as a sinus, with an external sinus tract opening in the lower lateral neck below the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle or an internal opening, usually located in the pyriform sinus. Clinical Perspective These cysts can present in childhood and may present as neck masses, occasionally mistaken for neck abscesses or even suppurative thyroiditis in the case of fourth branchial cleft cysts when infection is present [3]. This case illustrates how an infected cyst located in the retropharynx, slightly lateralised to the left side, may simulate a retropharyngeal abscess. Imaging Perspective Differential diagnoses include a retropharyngeal abscess, an atypically located third or fourth infected branchial cleft cyst, suppurative thyroiditis , necrotic adenopathy, and schwannoma. The well-defined oval fluid collection, with rim enhancement with a fistulous tract to the upper pole of the left thyroid lateral lobe, suggests a branchial cleft cyst anomaly. Third branchial cleft cysts tend to present as cysts/abscesses in the posterior triangle of the neck (although may also occur along the lower anterior neck), whereas fourth branchial cleft cysts may present in relation to the thyroid gland. If they form a sinus, the sinus tract will drain into the pyriform sinus [1]. The d ifferentiation between third and fourth branchial cleft cysts relies classically on their location in relation to the superior laryngeal nerve, with third branchial cleft cysts classically coursing superior to it and fourth branchial cleft cysts inferior to it [1–4]. Both can pass through or terminate in the upper thyroid lobes [5]. The proximity of the third and fourth branchial arches makes distinguishing these abnormalities radiologically difficult, and the separation can only be done intraoperatively. This case highlights this diagnostic difficulty, and because the treatment was incision and drainage (transorally) rather than excision through a transcervical approach, its location in relation to the superior laryngeal nerve was not determined. Therefore the diagnosis of third or fourth branchial cleft cyst remained. Outcome Treatment of third and fourth branchial cleft cysts rely classically on surgical excision of the cyst (with or without hemithyroidectomy) and the entire course of the fistulous tract to avoid recurrences. More recently, some authors have increasingly advocated for endoscopic treatment, with cauterisation of the sinus tract opening in the pyriform sinus, as a minimally invasive technique with fewer complications and costs [5–8]. Fluoroscopic fistulography or CT fistulography may be used to delineate the course of a branchial cleft sinus or fistula. This can be used in surgical planning and in avoiding potential complications. In this case, as it was an acute setting, incision and drainage was performed along with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, which resulted in successful treatment. A neck MRI was done after the discharge, and no cyst was identified. The patient remains in follow-up by the otolaryngology department, as recurrence is possible. Take Home Message / Teaching Points The proximity of the third and fourth branchial cleft cysts leads to difficulty distinguishing these abnormalities and the definitive diagnosis can only be done intraoperatively by determining the relationship of the cyst and tract with the superior laryngeal nerve. Third and fourth branchial cleft cysts are very rare anomalies and should be considered in the differential diagnoses of a lower neck mass, especially when presenting in children.

title: Endometriosis and its rare complication, malignant transformation
clinical_history: A 41-year-old female came to the gynaecology outpatient department with a history of painful menstruation, lower abdomen pain, dyspareunia and secondary infertility. There was no history of fever, vaginal discharge, recent surgery or previous obstetric surgery. Pelvic examination revealed cervical motion tenderness with no abnormality in external genital organs or perineum.
imaging_findings: A transvaginal ultrasound revealed focal adenomyosis, a simple right ovary cyst and a complex cyst in the left adnexa. Contrast-enhanced MRl confirmed a well-defined, oblong-shaped, multi-loculated cystic lesion in the left adnexa, having T1FS hyperintense signals (Figure 1a) and heterointense signals on T2W images with fluid-fluid level (T2 shading) (Figures 1b and 1c). The left ovary was not visualised separately. A heterogeneously enhancing, eccentric nodule having T1 isointense and T2 intermediate signal intensity (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d) with hyperintense signal on DWI and hypointense signal on corresponding ADC maps was also seen in the lesion (Figures 3a and 3b). The possibility of a malignant transformation in tubo-ovarian endometriosis was suggested. Ultrasound findings indicating focal adenomyosis and a simple right ovary cyst were also confirmed on MRI. The patient was operated, and the histopathological examination confirmed low-grade endometrioid adenocarcinoma (malignant transformation) in left tubo-ovarian endometriosis (Figure 4a). Secondary carcinomatous deposits in lymph nodes were also seen (Figure 4b).
discussion: Endometriosis is a common, chronic condition, which is prevalent in 5%–15% of reproductive age females. It is characterised by the presence of endometrial glands and stroma at ectopic location [1]. While endometriosis can affect any organ, common sites include ovaries, fallopian tubes and other pelvic organs/ligaments. Multiple theories are proposed to explain the pathophysiology, but none of them is established. The clinical symptoms and severity of the disease depend on the site of ectopic tissue rather than the disease load. Usual complaints are chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia and infertility [2]. Ultrasound findings of typical endometriosis include well-defined cystic lesions with homogeneous low-level echoes [3]. Even though the malignant transformation is rare according to literature (less than 1%), endometrioma should be carefully evaluated to rule out any malignant focus/nodule [4]. Some of the mimickers also need to be ruled out, like intra-cystic clots, which may appear like mural nodules despite clots not showing internal vascularity [5]. Also, cyclic hormone-related changes in ectopic endometrium should not be confused with malignant transformations [5]. On MRI, typical endometriosis shows T2 shading and absence of internal enhancement on post-contrast images. The malignant changes in endometriosis are suggested by the presence of enhancing solid nodules/components, diffusion restriction on DWI and ADC maps in solid nodules, and unusual increase in size, or disappearance, of T2 shading [6]. The histological criteria for diagnosing endometriosis-associated malignancies (EAMs) include the presence of endometriosis tissue near the site of the tumour, the tumour having endometrial tissue, exclusion of metastasis, and a histological transition from benign to malignant change [7]. Ovaries are the site of approximately 80% of EAMs, while one-fifth of the malignancies are extra-ovarian [7]. Histological subtypes of malignant ovarian endometrioma include endometrioid (the most common), clear cell, mucinous, low-grade serous and high-grade serous carcinomas. Most of the tumours are histologically low-grade. Extra ovarian malignancies associated with endometriosis are commonly endometrioid or clear cell carcinomas and rarely include endometrial stromal sarcomas, adenosarcomas, and carcinosarcomas. Surgical excision is the mainstay of treatment in malignant endometriosis. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Even though the malignant transformation of endometrioma is rare, radiologists should always look for the features which may suggest malignant transformation. Malignant transformation can be differentiated from benign endometriosis, as benign endometriosis will not show enhancing and restricting solid nodules. Haemorrhagic cysts are usually T1 hyperintense with absence of typical T2 shading or enhancing solid components. A patient with a tubo-ovarian abscess will have a fever with a cystic lesion showing internal diffusion restriction on MRI and absence of internal enhancement. Written informed consent was obtained and the identity of the patient is kept confidential throughout the manuscript and related documents.
differential_diagnosis: Benign endometriosis Malignant transformation in endometriosis Haemorrhagic cyst Tubo-ovarian abscess Cystic neoplasm

title: Parotitis after surgery: A radiological case study
clinical_history: We present the case of a 62-year-old man with a distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma treated with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy who developed rapid swelling in the left preauricular region within hours after Ivor Lewis oesophagectomy. CT was performed to rule out active bleeding and postoperative haematoma.
imaging_findings: CT showed diffuse enlargement of the left parotid gland with increased heterogeneous uptake of contrast material, fat stranding in the left parotid space, and thickening of the adjacent superficial layer of the deep cervical fascia (Figures 1 and 3). Oedema and fat stranding extended slightly into the soft tissues of the ipsilateral buccal and masticator spaces, and the sternocleidomastoid muscle was enlarged (Figures 2 and 4). There was no involvement of deeper compartments. No haematomas or signs of active bleeding were observed.
discussion: Background Acute postoperative parotitis, also known as “anaesthesia mumps”, is a rare complication consisting of swelling of the parotid glands after surgical or endoscopic procedures [1]. It has been reported following various surgeries, including orthopaedic, obstetric and gynaecological, neurosurgical, and spinal procedures [2]. The aetiology and pathogenesis remain unclear; possible mechanisms include stasis of glandular secretions, blockage of Stensen’s duct by direct compression, and retrograde airflow due to increased oral cavity pressure [3]. Other factors that have been implicated include trauma, infection, dehydration, and hypersensitivity reactions (drug allergies), as well as the use of anticholinergics, vasopressors, and muscle relaxants [4]. Clinical Perspective Acute postoperative parotitis typically presents as unilateral or bilateral parotid gland swelling, usually developing during surgery or, more commonly, within a few hours after procedures requiring general anaesthesia [4]. Although nearly always benign, it poses a clinical challenge due to its sudden onset and potential to mimic more serious conditions, such as postsurgical infection or haematoma. Imaging, particularly CT, is often necessary to differentiate acute postoperative parotitis from other complications, such as abscesses, haematomas, or salivary gland tumours. Radiology reports should confirm the diagnosis, rule out severe complications, and provide guidance on the clinical course, which typically resolves without intervention. This information helps reassure patients and supports appropriate management. Imaging Perspective Findings in acute postoperative parotitis are indistinguishable from acute parotitis due to other causes. The clinical context—acute onset of parotid enlargement following procedures requiring general anaesthesia—and imaging findings consistent with acute parotitis are crucial for the diagnosis. Outcome Acute postoperative parotitis is typically benign and self-limiting, resolving within a few days without sequelae. In rare cases, it can produce severe symptoms requiring emergency intervention [2]. Special attention should be given to endotracheal tube management and rehydration therapy. When acute postoperative parotitis leads to airway obstruction, timely patient notification and appropriate treatment are essential. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Acute postoperative parotitis is a rare, typically benign condition with unilateral or bilateral parotid swelling after general anaesthesia. Presentation includes sudden-onset parotid swelling during or shortly after surgery. Imaging (especially CT) is crucial to distinguish it from abscesses, haematomas, and other severe complications. The course is usually self-limiting, resolving in a few days without sequelae; management is conservative . Severe cases are rare but may require emergency intervention if airway obstruction occurs. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Acute postoperative parotitis Haematoma and active bleeding Postsurgical infection (e.g., abscess) Viral parotitis (mumps) Bacterial sialadenitis

title: Paranasal sinuses obstructive mucoceles
clinical_history: Female patient, 76 years old, with progressive ptosis and strabismus of the left eye. Relevant clinical history included basal cell carcinoma of the right hemiface with right orbital and maxillary invasion, resected 10 years previously.
imaging_findings: CT scan shows expansion and complete opacification of the nasal cavities, ethmoidal cells, sphenoid sinus, and frontal sinuses with bony reabsorption and externalisation of the expansile lesions into the extraconal compartment of both orbits, deviating and shaping the right superior rectus and left medial rectus muscles (Figures 1a and 1b). Bone window reveals extensive erosive changes and bony dehiscence in the papyraceous laminae and roofs of the orbits (Figures 1c and 1d). MRI images show predominantly high T1 and T2 signal content (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c) that does not suppress with fat saturation (Figures 2d and 2e) in keeping with protein-rich content fluid and areas of mild T2 hypointensity due to dehydrated secretions. Post-gadolinium images show no contrast enhancement within the expansile lesions (Figures 2f and 2g). The post-operative CT shows the removal of the previous mucoceles with a resolution of the mass effect upon the orbital cavities. There is still inflammatory mucosal thickening of the paranasal sinuses which remain partially aerated. (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c).
discussion: Background Paranasal sinus mucoceles are benign, slow-growing, expansive pseudocystic formations lined with epithelium containing aseptic mucus [1–3]. These cystic masses result from sinus ostia obstruction, leading to mucus accumulation and enlargement, which causes sinus bony wall expansion. The incidence of mucoceles is increasing, particularly secondary mucoceles, often linked to previous sinus surgery or facial trauma [2]. Clinical Perspective Despite their benign nature, mucoceles can cause local morbidity due to their mass effect on neighbouring structures [1]. Symptoms vary depending on the affected sinus, classified as rhinological, neurologic, or most frequently ophthalmologic, with optic neuropathy being the greatest concern. Poorer outcomes are related to posterior ethmoid and sphenoidal mucoceles or delayed treatment of mucopyoceles [5]. Radiological evaluation, particularly CT scans, is crucial for diagnosis, providing detailed anatomical information and aiding in surgical planning [2]. Imaging Perspective CT findings typically reveal an expansile, homogeneous lesion without air within the sinus, with convex margins. The density of mucoceles varies depending on hydration levels [2]. CT is the most effective technique for assessing the impact of mucoceles on bony walls. MRI is the most effective method for illustrating the relationship between the mucocele and surrounding structures, particularly since mucoceles may result from neoplastic obstruction of the sinus outflow tracts, and MRI excels at revealing any associated tumoural lesions [2]. On MRI, the signal intensity of mucoceles is variable depending on the degree of water and protein content. As water content decreases and protein concentration increases, there is a progressive increase of T1-weighted and a progressive decrease of T2-weighted signal intensities [1,4]. Characteristically, there is no internal enhancement, which helps differentiate these lesions from soft tissue tumours. Diffusion-weighted images might be misleading since retained secretions may show restricted diffusion [2,4,5]. Histopathology In our case (Figures 4a and 4b), histopathology showed mucosa covered by respiratory-type epithelium with slight chronic inflammatory and reparative changes and foci of recent haemorrhage; bone showed no pathological alterations. There was no evidence of dysplasia or invasive neoplastic tissue. Outcome The therapeutic strategy for mucoceles depends on lesion location and extent, as determined by imaging. Surgical excision is the primary treatment, using either external or endonasal endoscopic approaches. Early intervention is crucial to prevent visual compromise, especially in cases of mucopyocele [2]. Take Home Message Sinonasal mucoceles are pseudocystic lesions that develop gradually. CT scan is the primary diagnostic tool used to confirm clinical or endoscopic suspicion of a mucocele. Although benign, they can behave aggressively toward adjacent structures. MRI is recommended when there is diagnostic uncertainty between a mucocele and other tumoural or inflammatory lesions, or when there is intraorbital, intracranial extension, or sphenoidal involvement [2]. title: Extrapulmonary cystic manifestation of angioinvasive pulmonary aspergillosis
clinical_history: A 37-year-old lady came to the hospital with a complaint of a non-irritating cough, which was managed as an allergic cough and she was discharged with medication. However, she was brought back to the hospital with exertional dyspnoea, abdominal swelling and mild pitting bipedal oedema. This time, she was admitted for a comprehensive diagnostic workup. In the last 10 years, she had been treated for pulmonary aspergillosis and hypothyroidism.
imaging_findings: High-resolution chest CT showed bilateral ground glass opacities, fibrosis and asymmetric cylindrical bronchiectasis. The left upper lobe bronchus was severely ectatic, leading to a large peripheral cavity (positive feeding bronchus sign) (Figure 1a). In the hila, there were multiple well-defined mattered cystic lesions compressing and narrowing the diameter of the right interlobar pulmonary artery and the left lower lobe pulmonary artery (Figures 1b, 1c, and 1d). There was no evidence of pulmonary embolism. An echocardiogram scan showed that the right cardiac chambers were dilated with impaired right ventricular function and right ventricular hypertrophy. There was also evidence of severe tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary arterial hypertension.
discussion: Background Pulmonary aspergilloses constitute a group of mycotic diseases with a wide spectrum of clinical syndromes often dependent on the host's immune status or previous history of bronchopulmonary disease. There are three classifications of the disease, namely, invasive aspergillosis, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and chronic aspergillosis [1]. Clinical Perspective Invasive aspergillosis typically afflicts patients who are immunocompromised patients, while chronic pulmonary aspergillosis afflicts patients who have had a history of parenchymal lung disease such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or previous mycobacterial lung disease. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis afflicts patients with bronchial asthma or cystic fibrosis, mainly due to an allergic response to aspergillus [1]. Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis has been associated with high mortality rates, and it can be airway-invasive or angioinvasive [1]. Imaging Perspective There are no specific radiological features associated with angioinvasive aspergillus infection. Typical radiological patterns may include nodules with or without ground-glass opacities, masses, consolidation, wedge-shaped infarcts and pleural effusions. In the advanced stage of the disease, cavitary formation is prevalent [2]. In this case report, the unusual feature of cystic lesions in the perihilar regions was a rare finding in angioinvasive pulmonary aspergillosis. CT findings are vital for guiding further invasive diagnostic procedures such as flexible bronchoscopy with alveolar lavage and/or CT-guided biopsy, which are helpful in narrowing the diagnosis through microbiological and histological diagnosis [2]. Outcome In our case, based on clinical, radiological and histopathology, the diagnosis of systemic fungal infection (aspergillosis) was made. Initially, the patient improved and was scheduled for a discharge. However, she suddenly changed her condition with the onset of cough, restlessness, and severe haematemesis after a session of chest physiotherapy. Resuscitation attempts were unsuccessful, and she succumbed. The autopsy report revealed marked parenchymal and airway fibrosis with extensive haemorrhage and fungal elements with hyphae branching at acute angles (Figures 2a and 2b). In the hila, there were multiple cystic lesions of varying sizes. Some of the cysts contained a clear fluid with a white capsule while others contained serous fluid and were adherent to blood vessels and airways. Take Home Message / Teaching Points The identification of a “feeding bronchus sign” can aid in the diagnosis of peripheral lesions through a guided bronchoscopy. CT pulmonary angiogram has a better sensitivity and specificity in the diagnosis of angioinvasive pulmonary aspergillosis. A combination of clinical, radiological, and pathological diagnoses can narrow down the diagnosis of the disease. title: May–Thurner syndrome with phlegmasia cerulea dolens
clinical_history: A 54-year-old female with no past medical history presented with sudden onset left groin pain, spreading down the left lower limb. The entire limb was cold, with blue discolouration and swelling. The patient had full loss of sensation and power below the knee. Peripheral pulses were absent up to and including the femoral artery.
imaging_findings: CT angiogram of the lower limbs showed a gradual filling defect in the left distal superficial femoral artery in a markedly swollen lower limb (Figure 1). The CT also demonstrated dilatation of the left external iliac vein, internal iliac vein, femoral vein, popliteal vein and great saphenous vein. Hence, a CT portal venous phase of the lower limbs was performed, showing a unilateral filling defect from the left common iliac vein down to her crural veins in keeping with an extensive thrombosis or more specifically, phlegmasia cerulea dolens (PCD) ( Figures 2a and 2b). In addition, this second CT demonstrated good contrast opacification of the arteries and confirmed that no arterial occlusion was present (Figure 3). The arterial filling defect seen on the initial CT angiogram was due to arterial insufficiency caused by PCD. The CT portal venous phase also shows compression of the left common iliac vein against the lumbar vertebra by the overlying right common iliac artery, demonstrating May – Thurner Syndrome (Figure 4).
discussion: Background Phlegmasia cerulea dolens (PCD) is a severe form of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) characterised by significant venous obstruction, leading to limb cyanosis, pain, and swelling [1]. PCD often results in venous gangrene (40–60% of cases), and the mortality rate has been reported as 20–40%, with 20–50% of patients requiring amputation [2]. Additionally, the left leg is more commonly affected than the right [2]. May–Thurner syndrome (MTS) is caused by extrinsic compression of the left common iliac vein against the lumbar vertebra by the overlying right common iliac artery. This anatomical variant increases susceptibility to extensive DVT and, in severe cases, PCD [3]. Clinical Perspective PCD presents as a clinical triad of limb pain, swelling, and cyanosis [2]. Massive oedema develops quickly, creating a firm and tense limb, and arterial insufficiency leads to diminishing peripheral pulses [2]. Imaging is essential to differentiate PCD from other vascular emergencies and to confirm any underlying aetiologies, such as MTS. A bedside ultrasound was initially performed on this patient by the emergency physician, but the findings were mistaken for an arterial embolism as the vessels were not correctly identified. This error occurred because the vein was non-compressible due to the thrombosis, and the artery appeared collapsible and non-pulsatile due to arterial insufficiency. For this reason, a CT angiogram was performed first, prior to the CT venogram. This highlights the importance of urgent formal imaging to establish a correct diagnosis and expedite urgent treatment. Imaging Perspective First-line imaging for PCD typically involves venous duplex ultrasonography due to its availability and low risk to the patient [4]. However, computed tomography venogram is an alternative study, which is beneficial for visualising a proximal thrombus in the iliac veins or inferior vena cava, as well as identifying anatomical abnormalities of pelvic vessels. Additionally, venography is useful in patients who would be candidates for catheter-based interventional management, as it can establish the nature and extent of the thrombus, thereby guiding treatment [4]. Outcomes Typically, therapeutic options for PCD include [4]: Supportive measures such as elevation of the affected limb. Definitive management includes any combination of the following, depending on severity: Anticoagulation with intravenous heparin. Percutaneous mechanical thrombectomy . Catheter-directed thrombolysis. This patient had all the above management options. In addition, a repeat venogram four days later demonstrated residual stenosis of the left common iliac vein secondary to MTS and therefore stenting was performed to prevent recurrence. A full malignancy and haematological work up was negative and lifelong rivaroxaban was commenced to lower future risk of thrombotic events. The patient was discharged with no complications. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Non-mammary breast metastasis originating from retroperitoneal sarcoma
clinical_history: A 56-year-old woman with a known history of retroperitoneal sarcoma, who was receiving radiotherapy, was referred for evaluation of newly palpable lumps in her left breast and left axillary region.
imaging_findings: A diagnostic bilateral mammogram (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d; previous mammogram is not available for comparison) shows two circumscribed masses in the left breast upper-outer quadrant. On the ultrasound of the left breast and axilla (Figures 2a and 2b), there are two adjacent hypo-echoic masses with circumscribed borders in the left breast at 2 o’clock; m oreover, there is a similar mass in the left axillary region. The abdominal CT scan with contrast (Figures 3a and 3b) shows a large heterogeneously enhancing mass in the retroperitoneal space with left kidney invasion and aortic wall encasement. The histopathologic exam reveals highly atypical spindle cells with large pleomorphic hyperchromatic nuclei and high nucleo/cytoplasmic ratio (Figure 4).
discussion: Background Despite primary breast cancer being the most common female malignancy, metastases to the breast from non-mammary malignancies are rare and contribute up to 2% of all breast malignancies [1 – 4]. Metastasis originating from contralateral breast carcinoma is the most common source of metastases to the breast. Metastases from non-mammary origins include malignant melanoma, lymphoma, lung cancer, ovarian carcinoma, soft tissue sarcoma, and gastrointestinal and genitourinary tumours to their prevalence [4 – 6]. The most accepted explanation for the fact that breast tissue is the rare site for receiving metastases is the dominant presence of fibrous tissue and relatively poor blood supply [6]. Clinical Perspective Metastatic breast lesions are dominantly present with a solitary palpable breast mass. However, multiple masses and diffuse infiltrative disease are the less frequent presentations. About 25% of patients experience bilateral breast metastatic lesions. Moreover, axillary lymph nodes are frequently involved [5]. It is usually not associated with skin or nipple retraction; even presentation with pain, tenderness, and nipple discharge is unusual [6]. Imaging Perspective Breast metastases from non-mammary malignancies have two known pathways for spread: haematogenous and lymphatic. Each type of metastasis to the breast has known radiological features, but the features are not specific to the metastases. At mammography, metastases to the breast commonly present as a solitary non-calcified mass. The other presentations include multiple masses, calcified masses, and axillary adenopathies. Microcalcifications are rare, but if present, it is the result of psammoma bodies in some ovarian cancers, rarely thyroid or mucin-producing gastrointestinal cancers. Unlike primary breast malignancies, speculations, architectural distortion, and skin retraction are rare, predominantly due to a lack of desmoplastic reaction. However, carcinoid metastases manifest with infiltrating growth patterns mimicking invasive breast cancer [7]. Lymphatic spread may appear as axillary lymphadenopathy. In cases of lymphatic obstruction, it can result in breast oedema, asymmetries, and skin thickening, mimicking inflammatory breast cancer [7]. Typical ultrasound features depend on the metastatic pathway. Ultrasound features in haematogenous metastases include single or multiple, round to oval-shaped, well-circumscribed hypoechoic masses without speculations or architectural distortion, commonly in subcutaneous rather than parenchymal breast tissue. Typical US features of lymphatic metastases, in cases of the lymphatic block, include diffusely and heterogeneously increased echogenicities in subcutaneous fat and glandular tissue with a thickened trabecular pattern and secondary skin thickening [8]. Prognosis Metastases to the breast from non-mammary origins have a poor prognosis. The main indicators of prognosis are the biological characteristics of the primary tumour and the presence of metastases to other organ systems. Teaching points It is essential to consider non-mammary metastases to the breast in patients with a history of known malignancy and a recently palpable lump. It is also essential to differentiate a primary breast carcinoma from a metastasis as treatments differ for these clinical situations. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
