title: Unusual liver masses in a neonate: CEUS study with MRI and pathologic correlation
clinical_history: A 2-day-old male presented with non-bilious emesis and a left thigh cutaneous lesion. The patient was found to have pyloric atresia requiring gastroduodenostomy; this procedure led to intestinal malrotation, and the appendix was removed prophylactically. During surgery, the cutaneous lesion was also biopsied. The patient was transiently jaundiced following surgery; this resolved spontaneously, but a liver ultrasound was requested as part of the workup of this.
imaging_findings: Liver US showed a normal biliary tree and 2 hypoechoic liver lesions: the larger a 6 mm lesion in segment IVb (lesion 1). Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) was performed to further characterise. Three lesions were examined with 4 boluses of ultrasound (Total vol. 1.1mL, Optison, GE Healthcare Inc., using a Phillips EPIQ machine). Lesion 1 had increased in size (seg. IVb, now 32 mm) (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d); Lesions 2 (seg. II, 7 mm) (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d) and 3 were also seen (seg. I,10 mm) (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d). To further characterise, a liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast was performed. Lesion 1 (34 mm) was T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense, infiltrative, rectangular area with capsular retraction (Figures 4a, 4b and 4c). Lesions 2 (Figure 4d) and 3 were T1 hypointense with central T2 hyperintensity relative to the liver. No lesions showed enhancement, macroscopic fat, or diffusion restriction.
discussion: Background Infantile myofibromatosis is a rare (1:150,000 – 400,000) disorder of myofibroblasts; it can be divided into three subtypes: 1) Solitary, a single cutaneous nodule (75% of cases); 2) Multicentric, involving skin, muscle and bone (25% of cases); 3) Generalised, included within the multicentric type but with visceral involvement. This accounts for up to 1/3 of multicentric disease (10 %– 15% of overall cases) [1] . The solitary form occurs more often in males, and the multi-centric form in females [2] . Clinical Perspective Patients present with solitary or multiple cutaneous lesions, plus visceral lesions in the generalised subtype; imaging is imperative to ensure visceral lesions are identified given the different prognoses of multicentric compared to generalised disease. On biopsy, lesions can show a spectrum of findings, from myopericytoma (myoid spindled cells around multiple small blood vessels) to myofibroma (biphasic tumour with mitotic cellular zones and surrounding hyalinisation). Fifty per cent of the solitary and 90% of multiple forms are genetic with several associated mutations, including mutations in platelet-derived growth factor receptors [2]. In this case, histology demonstrated appendiceal myofibroblastic proliferation and multilobulated proliferation of cutaneous perivascular cells, suggestive of myofibroma. Genetic testing revealed PDGFRB heterozygosity. Furthermore, the patient’s mother had similar cutaneous lesions removed as a child at the same hospital; a review of her tissue showed the same genetic mutation. These imaging, pathological, and genetic findings suggested a diagnosis of generalised familial myofibromatosis. Imaging Perspective Imaging appearances are organ-specific. Bone lesions on radiograph and CT are lytic with peripheral sclerosis. Soft tissue lesions are iso or hypo-attenuating to muscle on CT and T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense on MRI, and may show peripheral enhancement [3] . On ultrasound, hepatic lesions can be hyperechoic with an anechoic centre, but appearances vary [3] . CEUS findings have not been described in the literature. CEUS uses microbubbles, similar in size to red blood cells, that remain intravascular, allowing real-time observation of vascular enhancement. The variable CEUS appearances reflect the array of pathological findings in this syndrome, with greater arterial enhancement correlating to areas of vascularity and non-enhancement to areas of hyalinisation. CEUS — with dynamic arterial-phase imaging and an intravascular contrast agent — is better able to capture the features of this tumour than CT or MRI, where contrast is distributed in the interstitium, and the early arterial enhancement of these lesions is not appreciated due to the higher temporal resolution of CEUS. Outcome While the solitary form often spontaneously regresses within 12 – 18 months, the generalised form has a high mortality: 33 %– 76% [4] . In the generalised form, visceral tumours can affect organ function and require low-dose chemotherapy. In one study, children given low-dose chemotherapy had a 95% five-year overall survival [5] . Surgical resection and immunotherapy with sunitinib, a PDGFR inhibitor, can also be considered in the context of treatment failure or toxicity [6] . Take Home Message / Teaching Points Infantile myofibromatosis is a rare but at times fatal disease that has a wide-ranging clinical and radiological presentation. It should be included in the differential diagnoses for multiple liver lesions, and CEUS features may vary between lesions within the same organ, as depicted here. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Intrasubstance humeral avulsion of glenohumeral ligament injury revealed through MR arthrography
clinical_history: A 19-year-old male presented to the orthopaedic surgeon with complaints of recurrent left shoulder pain. The patient practices combat sports and associates the complaints with a recent fall during training. A shoulder magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was conducted, followed by MRI arthrography (MRA) due to inconsistent findings.
imaging_findings: MRI revealed oedematous changes in the inferior glenohumeral joint capsule, with increased signal intensity on the fat-saturated proton-density (PDFS) sequence, suggestive of an inferior glenohumeral ligament ( IGHL) lesion (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c). Additionally, there was an increased signal intensity in the superior labrum, which may indicate a labral lesion. However, this finding was considered non-specific due to the absence of intra-articular fluid or contrast (Figure 1a). Subsequent MRA revealed an intrasubstance full-thickness rupture of the anterior band of the IGHL with contrast extravasation (Figures 2a and 2b). This finding was not documented on the previous conventional MRI, which only indicated capsular oedema. Additionally, the axillary pouch changed from its normal U-shape to a J-shape on fat-saturated T2-weighted sequences (Figures 3a and 3b), indicating IGHL laxity and loss of its stabilising function . MRA also identified a superior labrum from anterior to posterior ( SLAP) lesion (Figures 2c, 2d, and 3c), which was not clearly visible on MRI due to lack of fluid joint distention.
discussion: Background Humeral avulsion of glenohumeral ligament (HAGL) injuries are an uncommon cause of shoulder instability characterised by disruption of IGHL, predominantly documented in young athlete male patients [1,2]. Clinical Perspective The IGHL complex comprises an anterior and posterior band with an interposed axillary pouch. Its primary function is to restrain anterior and posterior translation of the humeral head [1,2]. HAGL lesions can be categorised according to the involvement of the anterior or posterior band and the presence or absence of bony avulsion [2]. Anterior band involvement is more common, with a reported frequency of 93% [2]. The IGHL lesion may occur at three anatomical sites: glenoid insertion (40%), intrasubstance (35%), and humeral neck insertion (25%) [1,2]. In our case, the patient had an anterior full-thickness intrasubstance HAGL lesion of the IGHL, without bony avulsion. Imaging Perspective Typical MRI features of HAGL injuries include an increased signal intensity and thickening of the IGHL and inferior capsule, contrast extravasation or joint effusion along the humeral neck, and a distinctive J-shaped axillary pouch ( “J” sign ) due to the avulsion of the IGHL [1,2,4]. Additionally, many HAGL cases are associated with humeral head osteochondral lesions, labral injuries, and rotator cuff lesions, with the subscapularis tendon being the most commonly affected structure [1,2,4]. Although arthroscopy remains the method of choice for assessing shoulder instability, MRI is essential to guide both arthroscopic and preoperative evaluation of shoulder instability. These injuries are often challenging to diagnose and, without a high index of clinical suspicion, can be easily overlooked [2,3]. In our case, conventional MRI detected oedematous changes suggestive of IGHL injury, but the capsuloligamentous tear was only confirmed after distension of the joint capsule with contrast material. These findings align with the literature, indicating that MRA could increase sensitivity in detecting labroligamentous injuries of the glenohumeral joint, including HAGL injuries, when compared to conventional MRI alone [3, 5]. Additionally, fat-saturated T1-weighted abduction external rotation MRI sequence (ABER) can help in detecting anterior and posterior labral tears, especially when routine MRI axial images do not clearly identify a lesion [5]. Outcome The patient underwent arthroscopy and surgery, which confirmed an IGHL tear that was repaired. The SLAP lesion and an anteroinferior Bankart lesion were also identified and repaired with tenotomy of the long head of the biceps tendon and labrum fixation. Take Home Message In conclusion, this case emphasises the valuable contribution of MR arthrography imaging to diagnostic approaches in assessing shoulder instability. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Portal vein non-bifurcation
clinical_history: A 19-year-old male reported to the hepatology outpatient department as a voluntary liver donor. The general physical and systemic examination was unremarkable. Initial baseline laboratory investigations were normal. Ultrasound abdomen revealed no significant pathology. Later, he underwent contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) with intravenous contrast administration as per liver donation protocol.
imaging_findings: On contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen in the portal venous phase, the liver showed a smooth surface. Portal venous non-bifurcation anatomy was observed. The m ain portal vein continued as a single right lobar intra-hepatic portal vein without division at porta hepatis. After giving origin to a branch for segments VI and VII, it then gave off the segment VIII branch and arched anteriorly towards the left lobe with decreasing calibre, and continued as the left portal vein, giving segmental branches to the left hepatic lobe ( Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c). The main portal vein calibre was normal at porta hepatis and measures about 14 mm in diameter. The calibre of the left portal vein was 8 mm. There were three main hepatic veins draining into the inferior vena cava (IVC) ( Figures 2a and 2b) . Variant hepatic arterial anatomy was seen where the right hepatic artery originated directly from the celiac axis, and the left hepatic artery was replaced from the left gastric artery ( Figure 3) .
discussion: The absence of portal vein bifurcation is a very rare anomaly and accounts for 0.03 – 2% of all hepatic vasculature anomalies [1]. The aberrations in normal anastomotic patterns and the involution of vitelline veins during the formation of the portal vein lead to anomalies in the bifurcation of the portal vein [2]. Additional congenital portal vein variations encompass complete or partial portal vein agenesis, atypical portal vein branching patterns, and arteriovenous malformations [3]. In adults, the portal vein typically spans around 8 cm in length, with a normal diameter ranging from 7 to 13 mm and drains blood from the gastrointestinal organs, spleen, pancreas and gall bladder into the liver. The portal vein originates posterior to the pancreatic neck, formed by the confluence of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. It then ascends alongside the free edge of the lesser omentum, entering the liver through the porta hepatis [4]. At the porta hepatis, it splits into the right portal vein and left portal vein. The right portal vein enters the right hepatic lobe and divides into the right anterior and posterior branches, supplying their respective segments. The left portal vein supplies segments of the left hepatic lobe [5]. Between the 4th and 10th week of gestation, the portal vein develops from the vitelline and umbilical veins. Three anastomotic channels connect the proximal segments of the right and left vitelline veins, located on either side of the developing duodenum. The cranial and caudal anastomotic channels lie ventrally, whereas the mid-anastomotic channel runs dorsally to the developing duodenum. The main portal vein originates from the dorsal anastomotic channel, where it incorporates the left vitelline vein between the entry points of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins [5,6]. It also includes a segment of the right vitelline vein located between the dorsal and cranial ventral anastomoses. The right branch of the portal vein forms from the portion of the right vitelline vein beyond the cranial ventral anastomosis. In contrast, the left branch of the portal vein arises from both the cranial ventral anastomosis and the segment of the left vitelline vein located distally to it [5,6]. The remaining segments of the vitelline vein and the caudal ventral anastomotic channel undergo regression [6]. The portal vein non-bifurcation or the absence of the left portal vein can result from the failure of anastomosis between the caudal segment of the right vitelline vein and the left umbilical vein [2]. Understanding the diverse portal vein anatomies ( Figure 4) and branching pattern is crucial for medical practitioners, particularly surgeons and interventional radiologists, in procedures like liver transplantation, lobar hepatectomy, vascular interventions such as transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt, as portal vein variations necessitate tailored interventional strategies to mitigate post-procedural complications. Awareness of portal vein anomalies is essential for effective and safe surgical and radiological interventions. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Paediatric brain metastasis from pelvic rhabdomyosarcoma mimicking encephalitis
clinical_history: A 12-year-old girl with pleomorphic pelvic rhabdomyosarcoma (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d), diagnosed one year ago, was admitted to the paediatric emergency department with dysarthria, agitation, right arm numbness, eye deviation, and a focal seizure. She had undergone surgery and radiotherapy six months ago, and her chemotherapy was ongoing. A PET-CT performed 40 days prior showed no metabolic activity in the tumour region and no evidence of metastasis. On examination, she had stable vital signs, transient fever, no meningeal sign, alongside neurologic findings of dysarthria and left-sided weakness.
imaging_findings: Initial head CT and MR revealed cerebral sulcal effacement and cortical diffusion restriction in the left parietotemporal lobe. A subsequent MR scan showed a millimetric cystic lesion with vascularised walls, perilesional vasogenic oedema, and overlying leptomeningeal enhancement (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d ). These findings suggested cerebritis or a possible abscess. Blood tests revealed elevated C-reactive protein (11.3 mg/L), with normal complete blood count and cerebrospinal fluid parameters. The latter was negative for infectious or malignant cells, including Toxoplasma gondii . She was hospitalised and treated empirically with antibiotics and antivirals despite inconclusive infection markers. Her symptoms improved, but a follow-up MR study after two weeks revealed significant progression, including worsening diffusion restriction, meningeal enhancement, cortical thickening, a 5 mm subfalcine shift, and compression of the left lateral ventricle (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c). Brain metastasis was suspected and confirmed on biopsy via left frontoparietal craniotomy.
discussion: The diagnosis of brain metastasis in paediatric rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is challenging in case of atypical presentations; therefore, MR could guide appropriate management strategies. To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of cerebral metastasis from rhabdomyosarcoma resembling encephalitis in the literature. The most comprehensive studies on brain metastasis of RMS were conducted by Moreira et al. [3] and De et al. [1], involving 59 and 23 patients, respectively. These studies found leptomeningeal enhancement to be the most common pattern. However, lesions may also present as haemorrhagic or non-haemorrhagic parenchymal masses [5–7]. Importantly, imaging features of cerebral abscesses can overlap with those of primary or secondary neoplasms. Accompanying cortical gyriform diffusion restriction, commonly seen in infections, can further complicate the differentiation. While clinical and laboratory parameters, along with the response to treatment, can aid in diagnosis, these features may overlap. In our case, initial imaging with CT and MR revealed sulcal effacement and cortical diffusion restriction in the left parietal lobe, findings often associated with encephalitis. A subsequent MR examination demonstrated a cystic lesion with high signal intensity on the wall after contrast injection, perilesional vasogenic oedema, and leptomeningeal enhancement. These features pointed towards an infectious aetiology. Although in oncology, a metastatic lesion is typically the top differential in a patient with cancer rather than infection, the patient’s symptoms improved after being treated empirically with antibiotics and antivirals. Due to this, the diagnosis of an infectious aetiology became stronger. A follow-up study performed 2 weeks later revealed increased cortical swelling with associated high cellularity, meningeal enhancement, and subfalcine shift. Therefore, a biopsy was carried out; this was consistent with infiltrative neoplastic tissue. This case underscores the importance of considering metastatic disease in oncological patients presenting with neurological symptoms but not associated signs of infection. Diffusion restriction on MR is indicative of high cellularity within a lesion, as seen in cancer due to densely packed neoplastic cells restricting water molecule movement, leading to hyperintensity on DWI and hypointensity on apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps, spectroscopy and perfusion, which are valuable techniques for differentiating infectious from neoplastic lesions. However, these were not acquired in our patient due to her clinical improvement after starting antibiotherapy. Additionally, PET-CT was not repeated as it had been performed 40 days earlier and was negative for metastases, with no activity observed in the primary tumour [8,9]. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity and the necessity of comprehensive radiological assessments in children with aggressive extracranial cancer and unusual neurological manifestations. Early recognition of atypical brain metastases can lead to timely diagnosis, tailored treatment plans, and potentially improved outcomes.
differential_diagnosis: Encephalitis Cerebral abscess Primary brain tumour Brain metastasis from rhabdomyosarcoma

title: Incidental discovery of multiple pulmonary arteriovenous malformations during oncological staging
clinical_history: A 67-year-old female patient diagnosed with a malignant renal mass underwent a CT examination for cancer staging. Her general symptoms were interpreted at that time within the oncological context.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced CT examination of the thoracic, abdominal and pelvic regions was performed. Multiple images with tissular densities, mostly located peripherally, were identified in both lung areas. The described images ranged in size from a few millimetres (Figures 1a and 1b) to around 22x15 mm (Figures 2a and 2b), and enhanced during the arterial phase similarly to pulmonary vascular structures (Figures 3 and 4), with feeding vessels from lobar arteries and drainage into lobar veins (Figures 5a, 5b, 6a, and 6b).
discussion: Background Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVMs) are direct atypical connections between arterial and venous pulmonary circulations, resulting in right-to-left shunts with high flow. These malformations are commonly part of congenital syndromes, like hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) [1]. Secondary conditions (e.g., surgery for congenital heart disease or hepatopulmonary syndrome) are rare causes of PAVMs [2]. Clinical Perspective Although about 50% of individuals with PAVMs are asymptomatic [3], these malformations can present with clinical symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnoea and hypoxemia. Even asymptomatic patients carry an important risk for complications like brain abscess and stroke due to intrapulmonary shunting [2], or loco-regional events, such as arteriovenous malformation (AVM) rupture, leading to haemoptysis or haemothorax [1] . More than one in four patients will experience a paradoxical embolic stroke, abscess, or myocardial infarction, and life-threatening haemorrhage affects one in one hundred pregnant women [4]. Imaging Perspective CT has become the gold standard for identifying PAVMs. However, transthoracic contrast echocardiography (TTCE) is often preferred for initial screening because it does not involve radiation. Despite this advantage, TTCE is operator-dependent. Therefore, if an adequate level of expertise in TTCE is not available, CT is recommended as the definitive imaging exam due to its reliability and accuracy [2,4]. Paying close attention to the vascular anatomy of the lesions is crucial for diagnostic accuracy. To differentiate PAVMs from similar-looking conditions, it is essential to identify their components: the feeding artery, the draining vein and the vascular nidus between them, with the draining vein generally being the larger vessel. Occasionally, telangiectatic PAVMs appear as ground-glass opacities, though these are often found alongside more typical PAVMs [5]. Outcome Screening for PAVMs should be conducted in all patients aged 16 and above who have a confirmed or suspected diagnosis of HHT. CT scans should only be repeated when there is a clinical suspicion of an enlargement of PAVMs, indicated by symptoms, other medical findings, or specific clinical situations, such as post-pregnancy [4]. Endovascular management is currently the first-line treatment for PAVMs, surpassing surgical options due to its lower risk of complications. The goal is to exclude AVMs from pulmonary circulation, selecting the embolic agents and specific technique based on pre-treatment imaging [6]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVMs) are often associated with hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) or other hereditary syndromes that involve vascular abnormalities. While many patients are asymptomatic, even in those cases, PAVMs can lead to serious complications, including stroke, brain abscess or AVM rupture. CT is the gold standard for diagnostic imaging, while endovascular management represents the first-line treatment. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Neurogenic heterotopic ossification
clinical_history: A 39-year-old man presented to the emergency department with tibial and fibular fractures and a traumatic brain injury (TBI) after a motor vehicle accident.
imaging_findings: Imaging studies obtained after the trauma revealed a comminuted wedge fracture of the tibial diaphysis with mild displacement and angulation, along with an overlapping fibular fracture (Figure 1), and multifocal subarachnoid haemorrhage in the right frontoparietal and left parietal regions on brain CT (Figure 2). Six months after the initial injury, during which the patient remained bedridden without any new trauma history, shoulder X-rays and CT scans were performed due to complaints of shoulder pain (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c). The imaging revealed extensive bilateral heterotopic ossification in the lower glenohumeral joint, indicating mature ossification.
discussion: Background Heterotopic ossification (HO) is a disorder characterised by new bone formation outside of normal skeletal locations and surrounding paralysed joints [2]. This condition can be categorised into two main types: acquired (the most prevalent type and the primary focus of this presentation), and congenital diseases [4]. HO can result from various causes, such as trauma, surgical interventions, burns, and neurological or rheumatologic diseases, with patients having traumatic brain injury (TBI) and elbow fractures or dislocations being 15 times more likely to develop HO than those without TBI [1,3,4]. 8-20% of TBIs go on to develop neurogenic HO around major joints, with the most frequently affected areas being the hip and thigh [1]. The pathophysiology is not fully understood, but a neurohumoral response is believed to be involved [3]. Clinical Perspective Clinical findings typically arise 3 to 12 weeks after the triggering event [4] and may include pain, decreased joint mobility, and inflammatory signs [1]. Notably, serum alkaline phosphatase levels significantly increase within the first six to 12 weeks after injury in affected patients [1]. Imaging Perspective Plain radiographs and computed tomography (CT) are the gold standard methods due to their ability to detect immature bone formation. However, calcifications are only detectable around three to six weeks after symptom onset [1]. In the acute phase of HO, due to inflammation, MRI reveals nonspecific findings, including isointense or hyperintense areas on T1 and T2 sequences. As calcification progresses, signal voids appear at the periphery on all MRI sequences. When mature, more specific signs emerge — such as a hyperintense cancellous fat mass surrounded by hypointense cortical bone — aiding in diagnosis [4]. Three-phase bone scintigraphy is a highly sensitive method that detects early changes, making it an important tool for monitoring and therapeutic planning [4]. Outcome Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs ( NSAIDs), bisphosphonates, and localised low radiation may, prophylactically, benefit high-risk patients, while established HO treatment includes physiotherapy for joint mobility and surgical excision [4,5]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Heterotopic ossification (HO) is characterised by the formation of bone in soft tissues, particularly around major joints, with the hip being the most commonly affected joint, often resulting from various causes, the most common being trauma to the central nervous system. The presentation can vary significantly, ranging from no radiological findings to complete joint ankylosis, and the exact pathogenesis of the disease is still unclear. Early diagnosis is challenging due to non-specific imaging changes that may be mistaken for other conditions. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Tensor fascia latae pseudotumour in a setting of abductor tendinopathy
clinical_history: A 68-year-old woman presents to the radiology department with pain in her right hip and knee. She reports that the pain began approximately 12 months ago, with a marked worsening over the past six months. She now presents with a palpable mass on the lateral aspect of her right thigh. There is no evident history of trauma.
imaging_findings: On MRI, gross asymmetry is seen in the tensor fascia latae musculature. The right tensor fascia latae is markedly hypertrophic in comparison with the contralateral side, measuring 61 mm vs 34 mm in diameter in the axial plane (Figures 1a and 1b). Tendinopathy of the right gluteus medius and minimus is best visualised in the proton density (PD) fat sat sequence, in which a high signal is seen, corresponding to the insertion in the greater trochanter (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). No histopathological samples were taken based on benign characteristics on imaging.
discussion: Background Tensor fascia latae pseudotumours are a benign compensatory reaction to the loss of function in the lateral hip abductors [1,3]. A similar presentation can be seen in patients suffering from lumbosacral radiculopathy [2]. The tensor fascia latae plays a supporting and stabilising role in the hip joint, as well as aiding in external rotation. The tensor fascia latae is part of the main group of hip joint abductors, together with the gluteus medius and minimus, having the capacity to compensate for loss of function in the main abductors [1,4]. Clinical Perspective A thorough physical examination, correlated with the clinical findings, is crucial in cases where a palpable tumour and pain arise without a history of trauma. In this patient’s case, the palpable mass was identified as compensatory hypertrophy of the tensor fascia latae, secondary to underlying tendinopathy of the hip abductors. An astute clinician can thus guide the diagnostic process towards the correct conclusion, avoiding unnecessary alarm regarding malignancy. This approach spares the patient unnecessary distress and the potential risks associated with unwarranted biopsies or surgical interventions [5]. Imaging Perspective Soft tissue differentiation and proper visualisation of tendinopathy are most optimally seen with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), as is shown in this case. Ultrasound as a modality can also be used for the direct visualisation of tendinopathy, with the biggest limitation being the experience level of the examiner. It is also possible to utilise computed tomography (CT) imaging, though somewhat suboptimally, as CT does not allow for direct visualisation of tendinopathy, but rather via indirect signs such as structural changes over time [5]. Take Home Message As presented in this case, the diagnosis of tensor fascia lata pseudotumour, caused by chronic tendinopathy of gluteal abductors can be confirmed with available diagnostic imaging and physical examination. A careful physical examination and referral to the right imaging modality made it possible to confirm the diagnosis quickly and without the need for invasive procedures. This allowed treatment to begin promptly, helping to reduce the patient’s stress. Due to the severity of the tendinopathy, surgical tendon re-insertion was performed, and the patient is now following a physiotherapy programme. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Superior sinus venous atrial septal defect
clinical_history: A 1-year-old boy without relevant medical history presented to the paediatrician with failure to thrive and shortness of breath. Clinical evaluation revealed a pulmonary flow murmur without further abnormalities.
imaging_findings: First, a transthoracic cardiac ultrasound was performed (Figure 1). This showed a large atrial septal defect of 13 millimetres near the confluence with the junction of the superior vena cava (SVC) and the right atrium. Because of the strong association with associated partial anomalous pulmonary venous return (PAPVR), a contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT*) was executed. This confirmed the presence of a superior sinus venosus atrial septal defect (SVASD) (Figures 2 and 3) and PAPVR, in which the right superior pulmonary vein culminates in the supracardiac segment of the SVC (Figure 4). There is evidence of significant right heart strain with moderate dilatation of the right atrium (RA) and right ventricle (RV), secondary to left-right shunting (Figure 5). The lung window shows mild diffuse pulmonary oedema (Figure 6). * CT scanner details: Siemens Force; 128-slice; administered contrast, 22ml Iomeron; ECG-gated, trigger on ascending aorta; total radiation dose for this study, 0.15 mSV.
discussion: Background Sinus venosus atrial septal defects (SVASDs) are a rare type of congenital heart defect, accounting for 5%–10% of all atrial septal defects (ASDs) [1]. These defects are found posteriorly in the posterior part of the interatrial septum. They are frequently associated with partial anomalous pulmonary venous return (PAPVR) from the right lung. SVASDs cause an atrial left-to-right shunt because the pressure in the left atrium is higher than in the right atrium [2,3]. The often-coexisting PAPVR, present in approximately 90% of cases, leads to further shunting. This additional shunting can cause the development of Eisenmenger physiology to occur sooner than it would with an isolated atrial septal defect [4]. Clinical Perspective The clinical features of SVASD can be variable, often dependent on the size of the defect and the presence of associated anomalies, such as PAPVR. When the defect is minor, patients can remain asymptomatic. If the defect is significant, symptoms may include tiring quickly, tachypnoea, shortness of breath, failure to thrive, recurrent respiratory infections, and abnormal heart rhythms. Auscultation may reveal a pulmonary flow murmur. Imaging Perspective The diagnosis of SVASD is primarily achieved through echocardiography, which provides detailed visualisation of the atrial septum. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is often the first-line diagnostic tool, but transoesophageal echocardiography (TEE) offers superior resolution. Advanced imaging techniques, including cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) and CECT, also play a role in comprehensively evaluating SVASD. These modalities offer detailed anatomical information, enabling precise visualisation of the defect and the anatomy of the pulmonary veins. CMR is particularly valuable in assessing the haemodynamic impact of the defect and planning surgical intervention [5 ]. In our case, cardiac MRI was not performed but this can be useful to evaluate the flow velocity and volume over the septal defect. Outcome Surgical intervention remains the definitive treatment for SVASD. The goal is to close the defect and reroute any anomalous pulmonary veins to the left atrium. The surgical approach typically involves using a patch to close the defect and creating a baffle to redirect blood flow appropriately [6]. Percutaneous closure of the defect using a device presents significant technical challenges due to insufficient rim and the necessity of rerouting the abnormal pulmonary veins [7]. In our patient, early surgical repair with the Warden method was performed. This includes transecting and re-anastomosing the superior vena cava to the right atrial appendage and baffling of the anomalous pulmonary veins through the atrial septal defect [8]. Take Home Message / Teaching Point The sinus venosus atrial septal defect is a rare congenital heart defect characterised by an opening in the atrial septum located near the junction of the vena cava and the right atrium. It is often associated with p artial anomalous pulmonary venous return, in which pulmonary veins drain into the right atrium or systemic veins instead of the left atrium. Look for radiological signs that are consequences of these anomalies, such as right ventricular volume overload and pulmonary hypertension. All patient data and related files have been completely anonymised throughout the manuscript.

title: Fibrous hamartoma of infancy
clinical_history: A 4-month-old male infant presented with a palpable mass on his arm. The parents noticed it since he was a month and a half old. Clinical examination showed a painless mass without signs of inflammation.
imaging_findings: On ultrasound (US), the mass was poorly defined and hyperechoic compared to muscle, located in the subcutaneous tissue. The lesion exhibited a serpentine pattern of hypoechoic bands with a hyperechoic border [1] (Figure 1a). It showed low vascularity on colour Doppler (Figure 1b). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a non-encapsulated soft tissue mass in the subcutaneous tissue of the arm, resting on the fascia without involving the underlying muscle. T1 and T1 fat-saturated images showed isointense tissue relative to muscle, with interspersed fatty foci (Figures 2a and 2b). No enhancement was noted after gadolinium injection (Figure 2c).
discussion: Fibrous hamartoma of infancy (FHI) is a benign fibrous tumour of the subcutaneous tissue. It affects children under 2 years old. Up to 20% of cases can be congenital. There is a male predominance of 2:1 [2]. The majority of the lesions are located above the waist, particularly in the axilla. Fibrous hamartoma of infancy was recently reclassified by the WHO as a neoplastic condition after the identification of recurrent mutations involving EGFR exon 20 insertions/duplications in the lesion [3,4]. From a histological perspective, fibrous hamartoma of infancy presents as a poorly defined, superficial soft-tissue mass with three distinctive components: mature fibrous connective tissue, mature adipose tissue and an immature mesenchymal component [5]. The imaging characteristics of fibrous hamartoma of infancy are nonspecific, reflecting the varying proportions of the diverse histological elements. On ultrasound, FHI typically presents as a heterogeneous hyperechoic mass with a “serpentine pattern”. The masses usually show an ill-defined or lobulated margin, with minimal vascularity on Doppler ultrasound [1,9]. On MRI, fibrous hamartoma of infancy is often poorly defined, and the appearance varies depending on the amounts of fat relative to fibrous and mesenchymal tissue. The three different tissue types seen at histology contribute to the MRI appearance. The presence of fat strands interspersed in the fibrous tissue helps to suggest the diagnosis preoperatively [5–9]. Fibrous hamartoma of infancy is a benign tumour, although it can be locally aggressive. The treatment of choice is surgical excision [2]. In our case, surgical resection followed by pathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of fibrous hamartoma of infancy . The surgery was performed at a specialised centre, as required in these cases. The surgeons found a soft tissue mass lying on the muscle in contact with the hypodermis, without involvement of the fascia or the adjacent muscle. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease in the Achilles tendon
clinical_history: 81-year-old woman who was presumed to be suffering from polymyalgia rheumatica and was receiving 2.5mg/week of ledertrexate. The patient suffered from chondrocalcinosis of the wrist joints, bilateral arthritis in her hands and repeated bouts of plurifocal synovitis in her wrists and metacarpophalangeal joints. The patient presented for an ultrasound due to Achilles tendon pain due to suspected bilateral Achilles tendonitis.
imaging_findings: Multiple hyperechogenic elongated deposits with acoustic shadowing are located within the central part of the right Achilles tendon and following its long axis (Figures 1 and 2), as well as in the left Achilles tendon (Figures 3 and 4). The Achilles tendons are thickened and hypoechogenic. The findings were identical in both Achilles tendons.
discussion: Background Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD) is a common pathology, affecting 4–7% of the adult population in Europe and the USA, but can take diverse clinical forms [1]. The disease may affect single or multiple articulations and may or may not be accompanied by an inflammatory syndrome [1,2]. It may be hereditary or sporadic, with age being the major risk factor [1,2]. Chondrocalcinosis is a common finding in CPPD, though it may also cause geodes, osteophytes and severe joint destruction [1]. In around a quarter of cases, there may be calcifications in the tendons, most often found in the gastrocnemius; though, the tendons of the quadriceps, triceps or, as in this case, the Achilles tendon, have also been reported [1]. Clinical Perspective Patients with CPPD will oftentimes have a confusing presentation, ranging from asymptomatic to acutely painful, waxing and waning over several months [3]. When affecting the Achilles tendon, the patients may experience differing levels of pain, signs of Achilles tendon enthesopathy and deep retrocalcaneal bursitis [4]. Intra-tendinous calcifications may be an unexpected finding in an exam performed to rule out tendinitis, and thus may help reorientate the diagnosis towards CPPD due to its specificity as an indirect sign of the pathology [5]. Imaging Perspective When examining a tendon with calcium pyrophosphate deposits using ultrasound, the deposits will appear as multiple hyperechogenic elongated/linear formations with acoustic shadowing along the long axis of the tendon [2]. Ultrasound is particularly useful as it may be able to demonstrate calcifications too small for conventional radiography to detect [5]. Power Doppler may also be used to demonstrate hypervascularisation in the context of inflammation. Conventional radiography will demonstrate intra-tendinous calcifications in the long axis of the tendon [1]. The role of MRI is limited due to its insensitivity with regard to calcifications [1]. A differential diagnosis for intra-tendinous deposits is hydroxyapatite deposits, though their shapes differ from those of CPPD in that they are more homogeneous, rounded and hypoechoic [5]. Outcome The demonstration of this sensitive and specific finding for CPPD may help reorientate a patient’s therapy in the context of non-specific symptoms of a hitherto unknown CPPD. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Multiple linear hyperechogenic bands along the axis of the Achilles tendon are calcifications, a finding which is sensitive and specific to calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD). All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement in malignant mitral valve prolapse
clinical_history: A 45-year-old athlete with chest discomfort and palpitations presented to the cardiologist. Electrocardiogram showed low-density ventricular extrasystoles at rest, which increased in density with stress. Echocardiography revealed mild mitral regurgitation and mild left ventricular hypertrophy with a basal septal thickness of 12 mm.
imaging_findings: Cardiac magnetic resonance was performed on a 3 Tesla MRI scanner. Steady-state free precession (SSFP) sequences identify billowing of both mitral leaflets, with mitral valve prolapse (MVP) of the posterior leaflet (5 mm), mitral annular disjunction (6 mm) and “curling” (Figures 1a and 1b; yellow arrow). Mitral regurgitation was not significant. Biventricular function was normal. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) was present in the subendocardial–intramyocardial layer of the basal inferolateral wall, suggesting replacement fibrosis (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d; white arrows). Native T1 mapping in the same region was elevated: 1360 ms (local normal range 1150–1250 ms), confirming myocardial fibrosis (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d; yellow arrow). Cardiac CT ruled out significant stenosis in the circumflex artery and posterolateral artery (Figure 3; circumflex artery: yellow arrow).
discussion: Background Mitral valve prolapse ( MVP) is a common valvulopathy, affecting 2.4% of the general population [1]. It is defined by the systolic displacement of one or both mitral leaflets into the left atrium [2]. Although typically benign, a malignant phenotype can lead to life-threatening arrhythmias. Malignant phenotype is suggested by clinical characteristics (such as palpitations or syncope), electrocardiographic abnormalities (like T-wave abnormalities or premature ventricular contractions), and imaging findings (e.g., myxomatous changes in the mitral valve, severity of mitral regurgitation, curling and longitudinal strain alterations) [3]. Evidence suggests that LGE in the context of MVP is associated with major adverse cardiac events [3]. LGE can present in various patterns, with subendocardial LGE being the rarest (7%). Other LGE patterns associated with MVP include midwall (more common, up to 65%), patchy (28%), and papillary muscle LGE [4] . LGE in MVP indicates an arrhythmogenic substrate and appears related to mechanical forces on the subvalvular apparatus affecting the subendocardial layer, although its cause is not yet fully understood [2 – 4]. Clinical Perspective When a subendocardial LGE pattern is observed, distinguishing it from ischemic aetiology is critical due to different treatment approaches and prognoses. If MVP is present, a non-ischemic aetiology should be suspected. In cases where it is unclear if subendocardial fibrosis is related to MVP, evaluating the circumflex or posterolateral artery for significant stenosis may be useful. Imaging Perspective Differentiating between ischemic and MVP-related replacement fibrosis based solely on subendocardial LGE can be challenging. If LGE presents with a patchy or mid-wall pattern, distinguishing it from ischemic aetiology becomes easier, as ischemic aetiology typically affects the subendocardial layer. In such cases, differentiating from other aetiologies, such as myocarditis or non-specific LGE, can be more challenging; however, if MVP is present, it is likely the cause of the LGE. In our case, with subendocardial – intramyocardial LGE pattern, a non-ischemic aetiology was further suspected due to the greater extent of mid-wall LGE compared to subendocardial LGE. Furthermore, myocardial segmental hyperdynamic movement and hypertrophy with curling are important factors to consider, as ischemic pathology would be associated with myocardial thinning and hypokinesis. Myocardial thickness at the basal septum measured 12 mm, which was not considered clinically relevant in this context and was clearly below the 15 mm threshold used as a diagnostic criterion for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Take Home Message / Teaching Points LGE in MVP indicates replacement fibrosis and is associated with major adverse cardiac events. Though it can present in various patterns, recognising subendocardial LGE is important, as its differential diagnosis includes ischemic LGE. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Acute pelvic pain and fever post-miscarriage – An unusual cause
clinical_history: A 39-year-old with multiple uterus leiomyomas at 12 weeks of gestation presented to the emergency department with metrorrhagia and sudden onset of lower abdominal pain. An ultrasound confirmed a spontaneous abortion. Within 36 hours, she developed a fever and maintained pelvic pain; because of that, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed.
imaging_findings: Admission gynaecological ultrasound (not shown) revealed multiple uterine leiomyomas with a regular endometrium minimal intracavitary fluid, confirming the spontaneous abortion. An extra-ovary cystic lesion was visualised with heterogeneous content. MRI (Figure 1) showed multiple pelvic masses with heterogeneous T2 signal intensity with a hypointense rim corresponding to a high signal intensity on T1W, with no central enhancement. The uterus shows a normal signal intensity and enhancement with no signs of endometritis/pyometritis. There was minimal distension of the endometrial cavity with haematometra without signs of retained products of conception. There was no evidence of complex free fluid in the pouch of Douglas nor pelvic collections. The cystic lesion corresponded to the left haematosalpinx. The diagnosis of necrotic/apoplectic leiomyomas was made based on imaging findings along with the history of recent pregnancy.
discussion: Acute pelvic pain and fever after a miscarriage more frequently occur because of an infection due to retained products of conception that can become a nidus for bacterial growth [1]. On the other hand, uterine leiomyomas are the most common gynaecologic neoplasms, particularly during the reproductive years, and tend to grow under the influence of oestrogen and progesterone [2–5]. Despite their high prevalence, many leiomyomas are asymptomatic, with only 20–50% causing clinically significant symptoms that require medical attention [4]. In pregnancy, leiomyoma-related complications occur in 10–20% of cases [6]. The WHO (2020) classified the different smooth muscle tumours of the uterus, including leiomyomas subtypes and degenerations [2]. Apoplectic leiomyoma, or red degeneration, is a rare condition more frequently associated with pregnancy or hormonal stimulation [2,4–7]. Occur due to ischemic necrosis caused by venous thrombosis or vascular disruption that leads to coagulative necrosis [2,4,6,7]. Patients typically present with acute pelvic or abdominal pain, sometimes accompanied by low-grade fever, leucocytosis, or nausea [2,4,6,8]. Imaging is essential to distinguish complications of leiomyomas from other acute conditions. Although ultrasound is usually the first modality of choice in suspected gynaecological pathologies, MRI is superior for assessing pelvic masses as it can provide detailed tissue characterisation [2,7–9]. While ultrasound may show a heterogeneous or hypoechoic mass with cystic spaces, MRI provides a definitive diagnosis by precisely identifying haemorrhagic and necrotic changes within the fibroid: high signal intensity on T1W due to thrombosed peripheral vessels; the signal intensity on T2W can have different appearances depending on the stage of haemorrhage; in postcontrast sequences, there is lack of contrast enhancement, particularly within the central portion of the lesion due to loss of blood supply, helping to differentiate apoplectic leiomyoma from malignancies like sarcomas [2,5–7]. These imaging appearances mimic uterine postembolisation findings [4]. Additionally, a pyomyoma is not only a possible leiomyoma-related complication more frequent in pregnancy but also can result from an apoplectic leiomyoma that becomes infected [8,10]. As apoplectic leiomyomas, they show a peripheral rim hyperintense on T1W [8,11]. However, in postcontrast sequences, the peripheral rim is better delineated and enhanced, and the values on the ADC map in the centre of the lesion are lower because of the high cellularity related to purulent material [5,8,11]. The lesion may also present intralesional gas, better depicted on tomography-computed images [7,11]. Most cases of apoplectic leiomyomas are treated conservatively with pain control, although radiological findings of severe necrosis or complications may prompt surgical intervention, such as myomectomy or hysterectomy [ 6]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Rare fistulated gallstone presenting as gastric mass on imaging
clinical_history: An 84-year-old Caucasian male presented with dyspepsia, weight loss, and macrocytic anaemia. The patient had a history of multiple comorbidities, including implantable cardiac defibrillator placement, pulmonary embolus, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), right inguinal hernia repair, and osteoarthritis.
imaging_findings: Initial investigations, including oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy (OGD), revealed a large submucosal/extrinsic mass in the distal antrum, prompting further evaluation with a CT scan. A CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous (IV) contrast and oral contrast ( 750 ml of water given 1 hour before the scan, followed by a 2.8 g sachet of carbex with 10 ml of carbex solution immediately before the scan on the CT table) was performed. Imaging demonstrated a 3 cm x 2.5 cm x 2 cm calcified lesion within the pre-pyloric antrum wall, adjacent to a collapsed gallbladder, suggestive of cholecystogastric fistulation with gallstone migration (Figures 1, 2, and 3). A repeat OGD confirmed the presence of a gallstone embedded within the pre-pyloric gastric wall (Figure 4), with a small fistula opening through which the gallstone was seen. Endoscopic intervention with the insertion of a guidewire through the fistula followed by balloon dilatation of the fistula opening was performed (Figure 5). During the procedure, the decision was made against breaking down the gallstone due to its size as well as lack of available space in the relevant area.
discussion: Background Gallstone ileus, characterised by the obstruction of the intestinal lumen due to the impaction of gallstones, is a well-documented condition in medical literature [1–3]. However, the presence of a gallstone embedded within the stomach antrum wall, mimicking a gastric mass, is an exceedingly rare occurrence [4]. This case report aims to document the unique presentation of a fistulated gallstone within the pre-pyloric antrum wall, presenting as dyspepsia and weight loss, and to discuss its diagnosis and management in the context of existing literature. Clinical Perspective Gallstone ileus occurs in 0.15% to 1.5% of cases involving cholelithiasis and accounts for less than 0.1% of all intestinal obstruction cases [5]. In most cases (75%–83%), the gallstone passes from the gallbladder into the duodenum; however, it may also pass into the colon or stomach [5]. Diagnosis of this condition is often delayed due to the vague and often intermittent nature of the symptoms [5]. Additionally, the “tumbling phenomenon”, whereby the stone moves through different sections of the gastrointestinal tract, may also increase diagnostic testing difficulty in such presentations [6]. In the aforementioned case, the patient presented with dyspepsia and weight loss; however, patients may also present with nausea, vomiting, constipation and abdominal distension [6]. Risk factors for developing gallstones and subsequent gallstone ileus include multiple comorbidities and older age [5], both of which are relevant to this patient. Potential differential diagnoses for calcified gastric lesions include gastrointestinal stromal tumours [7] and gastric bezoars [8]. However, the former is characterised by irregular morphology, larger size, and punctate calcification [7]. Gastric bezoars, consisting of ingested foreign material, appear mottled due to trapped air, and are often mobile [8]. Imaging Perspective Contrast-enhanced CT has been shown to be the optimal form of imaging when investigating potential gallstone ileus, with high sensitivity (93%), specificity (100%) and accuracy (99%) [9]. It can also aid treatment planning by providing an estimated measurement for the size of the ectopic gallstone [9]. Plain abdominal radiographs can also aid diagnosis, showing a sign known as “Rigler’s triad” in 40% to 70% of cases, manifesting as partial or complete intestinal obstruction, pneumobilia, and an ectopic calcified gallstone [6]. Other useful imaging techniques include abdominal ultrasonography and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy [5]. Outcome The treatment of gallstone ileus may be surgical or endoscopic, with the decision depending largely on the location of the stone [5]. In this case, an endoscopic approach was opted for due to its proximal position in the gastric antrum. Due to the size of the gallstone, it was not possible to create a fistula to retrieve it, and as the patient remained asymptomatic following the procedure, the decision was made to continue monitoring rather than re-attempting intervention. Take Home Message This case presents a rare manifestation of gallstone pathology, with the presence of a fistulated gallstone within the stomach antrum wall mimicking a gastric mass. To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of its kind, highlighting the importance of considering atypical presentations of gallstone-related complications in patients presenting with dyspepsia and weight loss [10]. The successful management of this case underscores the necessity of a multidisciplinary approach, involving gastroenterologists, surgeons, and radiologists, in the diagnosis and treatment of complex gallstone pathologies. Further research and case documentation are warranted to better understand the clinical spectrum and optimal management strategies for such rare presentations.

title: CBCT-guided trans-anastomotic ureteral stent placement in a kidney transplant recipient
clinical_history: A 63-year-old male, who had a renal transplantation from a cadaveric donor 3 months earlier due to diffuse mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis.
imaging_findings: In view of worsening renal function indices and hyperpyrexia, the patient underwent an ultrasound which highlighted grade III hydro-nephrosis. The patient was admitted to our hospital to undergo a unilateral percutaneous nephrostomy procedure that was performed under fluoroscopy guidance and intravenous deep sedation. Because the graft was in the right iliac fossa , t he patient was supine. The antegrade pyelography revealed a stricture at the ureteral-bladder anastomosis and a tortuosity of the ureter , causing an occlusive narrowing of the ureter that prevented the contrast medium from passing into the bladder. Despite several attempts through multiple angles of the C-arm, from 18° cranial (CRA) to 34° caudal (CAU) and from 52° right (RAO) to 19° left (LAO) angulations, the ureteric bud cannot be visualised (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d). After a failed attempt to overcome the ureteral narrowing, an 8.5 Fr nephrostomy drainage was placed in the renal pelvis. The second attempt was scheduled for 2 weeks later.
discussion: CBCT (Cone-Beam Computed Tomography) Methods Under fluoroscopy guidance, the existing nephrostomy catheter 8.5 Fr was removed over a 0.035 Rosen J-tipped guidewire, and a 7F introducer sheet was placed in the renal pelvis. Manual contrast injection showed no changes from the previous procedure. Given the challenges in determining the C-arm working angle , being a recognised tool to assist interventional radiologists [1], a CBCT acquisition was performed. During CBCT acquisition, given the patient’s sedation and to minimise beam hardening artefact, the left arm was hyper-abducted (at least 135°) using the radiolucent swivel arm board, while the patient's right arm remained adducted. Despite the right arm position, the “wide gantry bore” enabled the area of interest to be positioned in the system's isocentre during CBCT. The contrast medium, isosmolar and isotonic contrast medium (Iodixanol, Visipaque ® 320, and GE Healthcare) diluted 50:50 with saline, was injected manually through the 7F introducer sheath and a 40°/sec acquisition was performed in at least 5 sec over a 210° arc with a maximum source to detector distance (SDD, 129.5 cm) and normal image detail. The AutoExposition Control system chose technical parameters, the temporal resolution was 50 frames/sec, and the acquisition time was 5 sec. CBCT Findings 3D images were reconstructed on a workstation (Advantage Workstation 4.7, GE Healthcare) and displayed across volume rendering (VR), axial, sagittal and coronal views; the axial-reconstructed and VR images revealed an unusual C-arm angulation (LAO 90°) necessary to visualise the ureteric bud (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). Through the LAO 90° projection, the ureter was easily accessed using a 0.038-inch j-tip hydrophilic guidewire (Radifocus™ Guide Wire M Standard Type, Terumo) and a 5F hydrophilic catheter (Radifocus™ Angiographic Catheter, Terumo) was advanced into the bladder (Figure 3); it was exchanged for a super-stiff guidewire (Amplatz Super Stiff, Boston Scientific), and the severe ureteric stricture was dilated using a 5mm balloon (ATB ADVANCE PTA Dilatation Catheter, Cook Medical). Then, a 6F-26cm trans-anastomotic double-pigtail ureteral stent (Percuflex Plus, Boston Scientific) was placed over the guidewire, and the safety kit of the stent was removed. A final fluoroscopic image was stored to verify the correct stent position (Figures 4a and 4b). Background Urological complications, including ureteral stenosis (US), occur in 2% – 15% of kidney transplant recipients, with graft ureter stenosis affecting 0.5% – 6.3% of cases, commonly arises from ischemia, inflammation, or infection, and may occur especially in the first 3 months after kidney transplantation [2 – 5]. Complications commonly arise where the donor ureter is anastomosed to the recipient 's urinary bladder [6] and, because of its strong correlation with a survival rate of the transplanted kidney [7], a delay in diagnosis and treatment may result in the deterioration of graft function and even graft loss [8,9]. Imaging Perspective It is well known that CBCT increases radiation exposure in abdominal procedures compared to fluoroscopy, especially when multiple CBCT scans are performed [10 – 11]. However, in our experience, the ability of CBCT to accurately detect the correct projection can result in a reduction in overall radiation exposure. In fact, considering the significant difficulties encountered and the need for multiple fluoroscopic acquisitions, a comparison of the cumulative radiation exposure from fluoroscopy performed prior to CBCT with that from CBCT itself revealed that fluoroscopy resulted in higher patient exposure (fluoroscopy: DAP 27.6 Gycm² and Kair 0.24 Gy, CBCT: DAP 19.6 Gycm² and Kair 0.05 Gy). Additionally, the exposure time was notably shorter for CBCT than for fluoroscopy (Fluoroscopy Time 1.7 seconds vs. 82.8 seconds), which also translated to a faster determination of the correct projection. So, although CBCT should be used sparingly due to its potential to increase patient radiation dose, its advantages in procedural guidance, including faster and more accurate determination of C-arm angulation [12] and the real-time intraoperative availability of high-quality 3D images [13] , are significant and should also be considered during the planning phase of non-vascular complex procedures, such as ureteral stenting. The integration of this imaging technique could play a pivotal role in ensuring procedural success, enhancing execution efficiency, and reducing the need for multiple fluoroscopic acquisitions. Take Home Message The CBCT scan offers precise treatment planning capabilities that can significantly enhance patient care also in cases where the ureteral bud or the ureteral anastomosis cannot be easily visualised. It emerged as an essential tool also in non-vascular interventional radiology procedures. Placement of the ureteral stent and completion of the interventional procedure was accepted as technical success. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Leukaemic infiltration of the optic nerves (LON)
clinical_history: The patient is a 62-year-old woman with recurrent acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) B, PH+, without central nervous system (CNS) involvement, treated with chemotherapy and imatinib and second-line therapy with blinatumomab and ponatinib with disease remission. One year later, she presents with headache and impaired colour vision, worse on the left side.
imaging_findings: Neuro-ophthalmology investigations revealed dyschromatopsia with abnormal Ishihara colour plates test, a slight decrease of visual acuity on the left, decreased peripheral vision, optic disc swelling with no retinal haemorrhages, and a bilateral (p100) delayed response on evoked potentials. C erebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed an inflammatory pattern with no neoplastic cells on flow cytometry. EEG was normal. Bone marrow biopsy showed no morphological, imunophenotypical, or mollecular (BCR-ABL1/ABL1) evidence of recurrent disease. MRI of the brain and orbits demonstrates irregular thickening of the intraorbital segment of the optic nerve sheath on the right side and, on the left side, thinner subarachnoid space, blurred optic nerve-CSF interface and a T2W hyperintensity of the optic nerve (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c). After gadolinium administration, there is bilateral enhancement of the optic nerve sheath (Figures 2a and 2b) and restricted diffusion (Figures 3a nad 3b). The remaining segments of the optic pathway were unremarkable and no mass lesions were found in the orbit or intracranial compartments. Particularly, there were no signs of leptomeningeal involvement. Presumptive diagnosis: Leukaemic infiltration of the optic nerve.
discussion: Isolated leukaemic infiltration of the optic nerve is rare as the initial presentation of disease recurrence, particularly in the absence of CNS or bone marrow involvement. It is thought to result from inadequate penetration of antileukaemic drugs in the optic nerve sheath, which acts as a pharmacologic sanctuary unaffected by systemic and even intrathecal chemotherapy. Infiltration of the perineural space by leukaemic cells obstructs the CSF flow, precluding cytotoxic drugs from being delivered [ 1]. It is most often seen in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia , followed by acute myeloid leukaemia , chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, and chronic myelogenous leukaemia . Over 50% of patients have concomitant leptomeningeal involvement with a positive CSF, and in 43% of patients, imaging studies (CT/MRI) are negative [2]. Early diagnosis is crucial for adequate treatment and to improve visual outcomes. In fact, leukaemic infiltration of the optic nerve is a neuro-oncology emergency, with a variety of ophthalmologic complications if not urgently treated, namely central retinal artery or vein occlusion, neovascular glaucoma, retinal detachment and ultimately loss of vision [ 2] . Clinical presentation is unspecific and the differential diagnosis is wide, including inflammatory, infectious, ischemic and toxic conditions secondary to radiation, chemo and immunotherapies. The diagnosis becomes even more challenging in the absence of CSF and/or bone marrow involvement. MR imaging can be of help by showing CSF obliteration in the optic sheath, perineural enhancement wrapping around the optic nerve and restricted diffusion on DWI reflecting hypercellularity in the perineural space [ 1] . Whereas restricted diffusion can be seen in acute ischemic optic neuropathy, it affects the optic nerve proper, is not associated with perineural enhancement, and clinical presentation is usually revealing. Perineural empyema/abscess can also restrict on DWI, but the contrast enhancement is peripheral to the area of restricted diffusion. Optic neuritis, the main differential diagnosis, affects the optic nerve proper and is featured on MRI by increased T2 signal intensity and enhancement of the optic nerve itself, without restricted diffusion. Optic perineuritis, either idiopathic or secondary to infectious or autoimmune diseases, does not show restricted diffusion on MRI [ 3] . For undetermined cases in patients with progressive vision loss, optic nerve biopsy should be weighted in a multidisciplinary setting [ 4] and if leukaemic infiltration is confirmed, urgent treatment with corticosteroids, radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy should be offered. Even when offered optimal treatment, the prognosis is dismal, with most patients quickly developing recurrent CNS and systemic disease and/or therapy-related complications [ 5] . Unfortunately, our patient deceased after 3 months with systemic and CNS recurrent disease.

title: White cord syndrome: The unknown complication after cervical decompressive surgery
clinical_history: A 63-year-old woman diagnosed with recurrent meningioma located in the foramen magnum consulted for headache and paraesthesia of the upper limbs. It was decided to perform decompressive surgery and, in the immediate postoperative period, she presented tetraplegia with preservation of consciousness and requirement of mechanical ventilation.
imaging_findings: The preoperative MRI showed an extra-axial expansive lesion located in the foramen magnum, measuring 3.9 x 2.1 cm, and producing a mass effect on the bulb and spinal cord, displacing them posteriorly and to the left. It also compromised the V4 segment of the right vertebral artery (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d). The MRI on day +2 after the surgery showed signs of tumour persistence of the partially removed lesion (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c) and signal alteration in the bulb and upper spinal cord, with hyperintensity in T2/FLAIR sequences (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c) and hypointensity in T1. Diffusion sequences showed signs of mixed oedema (vasogenic-cytotoxic), all in relation to ischemic-oedematous phenomena (Figures 4a to 4i).
discussion: White cord syndrome (WCS) is an extremely rare acute spinal cord injury that occurs following decompressive surgery, causing unexplained neurological deficits [1,2]. The first reported case, by Chin et al. in 2013, was a 59-year-old male patient who underwent anterior cervical decompression for a C5 – C6 cervical disc disease and developed postoperative tetraplegia [3]. The pathophysiology is complex and is thought to reflect the mechanisms of parenchymal ischemia/reperfusion secondary to rapid spinal cord decompression after chronic compression associated with spinal oedema. The decompression leads to sudden expansion and reperfusion of the chronically compressed segment exposing it to excess blood flow that can lead to injury to the blood-brain barrier, triggering a cascade of free radical-mediated injury resulting in spinal cord dysfunction [1,2,4 – 6]. Symptoms usually appear when surgery is completed and the patient is sent back to his/her unit. It is characterised by a sudden motor weakness that, in most reported cases, resolves with the return to normal function, but in some patients, the symptoms persist without improvement [6,7]. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, and postoperative MRI is the best way to document intrinsic spinal cord changes. Radiological findings are characterised by focal or diffuse hyperintensity of the spinal cord on T2-weighted sequences, which may persist for more than 6 weeks [1,4,7]. On T1-weighted images, these lesions appear hypointense, with no enhancement after gadolinium administration [8]. There is no published literature regarding the value of diffusion-weighted MRI in this pathology. However, since there is an ischemic and oedema mechanism in the pathophysiology, it could help to corroborate the diagnosis. In addition, MRI allows to rule out other postoperative causes (e.g., extramedullary haematoma, new/residual extrinsic spinal cord compression) that may require additional treatment [1]. There is no protocol for the treatment of this pathology. Options include admission to intensive care units for neurological monitoring, elevation of mean arterial pressure (i.e., an average of 85 – 95 mmHG) to perfuse a compromised/ischemic cord, and administration of steroids (as they reduce oxidative stress), along with rehabilitative physical therapy [1,4,7,8]. Our patient, after the acute episode and her stabilisation, was referred to a hospital specialising in spinal cord injuries for motor and respiratory rehabilitation. She died 2 years later from urinary sepsis. Since very few cases of WCS are described in the literature, treating physicians should be aware of this rare but serious complication and, so, early recognition and timely treatment of this pathology are important. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Central cord syndrome White cord syndrome Compressive myelopathy Epidural haematoma

title: Subacute combined degeneration from recreational nitrous oxide
clinical_history: A 26-year-old male with progressive paraesthesia in four limbs for the last 15 days. The patient acknowledges nitrous oxide abuse as a recreational drug. Neurological examination shows vibratory sensitivity deficit , proprioceptive impairment in lower limbs, and difficulty with tandem gait. There are no motor deficits.
imaging_findings: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the cervical (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d) and thoracic (Figures 2a and 2b) spine was performed using T1 and T2-weighted sequences in sagittal and axial planes. An extensive area of T2 hyperintensity was found restricted to the posterior columns of the spinal cord bilaterally and symmetrically at two locations: in the cervical spine extending from C1 to C6 and at the lower thoracic spine , sparing the conus medullaris [1].
discussion: Background Nitrous oxide (N 2 O) is an inorganic gas used as an inhaled anaesthetic in paediatrics and odontology. It has become a recreational drug owing to its euphoric effect and its use is widespread among young people. The route of administration is by inhalation from cartridges commonly known as “whippets”. Nitrous oxide oxidises cobalamin (the active form of vitamin B12, essential for the stability of myelin sheaths ), resulting in a functional vitamin deficit as opposed to an actual vitamin B12 deficiency due to malnutrition or malabsorption [2]. The most vulnerable nerve fibres are the posterior columns of the spinal cord, which provide proprioceptive and vibratory sensations ; t he corticospinal tracts and peripheral nerves are more rarely affected . Thus, vitamin B12 deficiency affects the nervous system, leading to a condition known as subacute combined degeneratio n [2,3]. Clinical Perspective Subacute combined degeneration (SCD) initially presents with paraesthesia in the extremities and loss of vibratory sensation (hypopallesthesia). Proprioceptive deficits can cause ataxia, instability, gait disturbances, and hyporeflexia. Furthermore, there may be motor deficits with pyramidalism or polyneuropathy. Finally, symptoms of dementia may appear in the advanced stage, though it is exceptional to reach this level [3]. Imaging Perspective On MRI, SCD presents with T2 hyperintensity confined to the posterior columns of the spinal cord , forming the inverted V sign in the axial plane [4]. The injury usually starts in the cervical and upper dorsal segments [4]. There is typically no enhancement after contrast administration. The final diagnosis is achieved by combining the clinical, analytical, and imaging information. MRI is used to confirm clinical suspicion and determine the extent and response to treatment [4,5]. Outcome Treatment consists of monthly intramuscular vitamin B12 supplementation and strict cessation of nitrous oxide consumption. Despite this, up to 50% of patients may have residual symptoms, usually paraesthesia [5]. Take Home Message / Teaching Point Nitrous oxide abuse is common in our society, especially in young people. Subacute combined degeneration should be suspected in any patient with compatible neurological symptoms and nitrous oxide abuse. Early diagnosis is important to start treatment as soon as possible and prevent potential neurological aftermaths. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

final_diagnosis: Subacute combined degeneration secondary to abuse of nitrous oxide
