title: Light bulb in the pelvis – Rare case of pelvic paraganglioma
clinical_history: A 24-year-old lady presented to the emergency department with accelerated hypertension. She had a history of recurrent episodes of sudden onset palpitations, headache and giddiness for the past two years, with uncontrolled hypertension despite being on multiple antihypertensive medications. Her blood investigations revealed elevated serum normetanephrine (1990 pg/mL).
imaging_findings: Trans-abdominal ultrasound (Figures 1a and 1b) showed a well-defined heterogeneously hyperechoic lesion in the right adnexa, seen separate from the right ovary, measuring approximately 4.7 x 5 x 4.8 cm, and with high internal vascularity. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis (Figures 2a, 2b, 3a, and 3b) showed a hyperdense mass (average HU of 29) with intense heterogeneous arterial enhancement and few central non-enhancing areas suggestive of necrosis. It was located in the right adnexa and paracervical region, abutting the uterus (which was displaced to the left). It was abutting the posterior urinary bladder wall anteriorly and the rectum posteriorly with no invasion of the right ureter, iliac vessels and lateral pelvic side wall. On MRI of the pelvis, the lesion was deep to the lateral pelvic fascia on the right, heterogeneously iso to hyperintense on T1WI (Figures 4b and 5), heterogeneously hyperintense on T2WI ( “light bulb sign” ) (Figure 4a), with areas of restricted diffusion on DWI and maintained fat planes with the adjacent structures (Figures 6a and 6b). On 68Ga-DOTATATE scan, there was intense homogeneous SSTR (somatostatin receptor) expression in a large well-defined soft tissue density mass in the right adnexa and paracervical region with maximum standardised uptake value (SUV max) of 20.19 (Figure 7).
discussion: Background Paragangliomas can be sympathetic or parasympathetic in origin. Functional sympathetic paragangliomas secrete excess catecholamines and are hormonally active. They can be extra-adrenal or adrenal (pheochromocytoma) in location. The abdomen (retroperitoneal paraganglia or organ of Zuckerkandl) is the primary site of origin for extra-adrenal sympathetic paragangliomas, while the pelvis and thorax are rare sites. First reported in 1902, paraganglioma can present as a pelvic retroperitoneal mass, and approximately 135 cases have been reported since then [1]. Here we present a rare case of pelvic paraganglioma. Although they can develop at any age, paragangliomas typically occur in the fourth or fifth decades of life without any sex predilection [2]. More than 90% of paragangliomas are parasympathetic paragangliomas, which are hormone-silent, chromaffin-negative tumours. They are typically found in the head and neck areas, along vascular structures. These are slow-growing tumours and may or may not have compressive symptoms [2]. Parasympathetic paragangliomas are less likely to be malignant whereas more likely to be familial and multifocal [3]. Clinical Perspective Sweating, palpitations, and headaches are the most typical clinical manifestations associated with hypersecretion of catecholamines, as in our patient. The typical biochemical work-up involves the measurement of plasma-free metanephrines and/or 24-hour urinary excretion of fractionated metanephrines. Biopsies of paragangliomas can cause bleeding due to their hypervascular nature and are hence avoided. 15%–35% of extra-adrenal sympathetic paragangliomas are malignant, with lung, bone, liver, and lymph nodes being the most common sites of metastases. Benign and malignant paragangliomas have overlapping features on imaging as well as on histopathology. The presence of metastases on imaging, along with other features such as irregular margins, infiltration of adjacent structures, and vascular invasion, are signs which suggest malignancy [3,4]. Our patient did not have any of these features on imaging. While the majority of paragangliomas are solitary, they can sometimes be multicentric and hereditary (in about 10% of cases). Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN IIA and IIB) and neuroectodermal syndromes (tuberous sclerosis, neurofibromatosis, and von Hippel–Lindau disease) are linked to these familial tumours. Paragangliomas can also arise as a component of the Carney triad [5,6]. Our patient had a positive genetic workup for NF1; however, there were no clinical features. Imaging Perspective Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas typically present as a mass on CT with an unenhanced density greater than 10 Hounsfield units (HU), avid contrast enhancement, and delayed washout. There may be haemorrhage, necrosis, calcifications, and cystic changes within the tumour. On MRI, they are heterogeneous and show T2 prolongation and strong post-contrast enhancement, which results in the “light bulb sign” [5–8]. SSTR imaging (68Ga-DOTATATE) helps in identifying metastatic or multifocal disease, especially in patients with hereditary paragangliomas, which aids in planning surgical or systemic treatment [9]. Outcome To reduce the risk of intra-operative bleeding, the patient underwent a preoperative embolisation followed by a laparotomy and excision of the lesion (Figure 8). The blood loss during surgery was not significant, and she did not require any blood transfusion. The blood pressure returned to the normal range postoperatively. She was tapered off antihypertensive medications and was stable on discharge. She was advised to have annual follow-ups with imaging and biochemical screening in view of the risk of recurrence.

title: An unexpected cause of breast pain: Mondor’s disease
clinical_history: A 29-year-old healthy woman presented with a 4-day history of right breast pain and periareolar bruising associated with a 1-day periareolar indurated tumefaction. She denied any other symptoms, trauma, or regular medication use. Physical examination revealed a 2-cm indurated, painful cord-like structure in the periareolar region associated with bruising and petechial lesions.
imaging_findings: Ultrasonography of the right breast revealed a subcutaneous, non-compressible, tubular hypoechoic structure with low-level internal echoes along an extension of approximately 28 mm (Figures 1 and 2). No blood flow was detected on colour or spectral Doppler studies (Figure 3). Furthermore, the adjacent soft tissues showed increased echogenicity. No other anomalies were seen in the right breast. Ultrasound scans of the left breast and axillary regions yielded no significant findings.
discussion: Background Mondor’s disease (MD) is a rare, benign condition with an incidence rate of 0.085–0.96%. It affects both genders, with women being three times more affected, particularly between the ages of thirty and sixty [1–8]. This condition involves superficial thrombophlebitis and can impact various venous drainage systems. The most commonly affected vein is the thoracoepigastric vein, which produces a fibrotic cord in the lateral thoracoabdominal region, followed by the lateral thoracic vein, which presents along the side of the chest wall, occasionally extending towards the axilla—known as axillary web syndrome—, and the superior epigastric vein, resulting in a palpable cord in the inferior outer quadrant of the breast. Additionally, penile MD has been described as involving the superficial dorsal vein of the penis [2,5,8,9]. Although the pathophysiology of MD is not fully understood, the proposed model integrates Virchow’s triad and results from inflammation and clot formation in superficial veins, which can cause the vessel to adhere to the skin, forming a characteristic cord-like structure [1–5]. Most cases of MD (45%) are idiopathic; however, they may also be secondary to various aetiopathogenic factors, such as trauma, excessive physical exercise, breast surgery (including mammoplasty and breast biopsy), the use of tight or highly compressible surgical bras, as well as cancer, smoking, infections, thrombophilic disorders, vasculitis, and the intake of oral combined hormonal contraception. Recently, cases have been reported in relation to COVID-19 [9], likely due to hypercoagulability and systemic inflammation. Axillary web syndrome has been reported after axillary lymph node dissection and sentinel lymph node biopsy [5]. Penile MD may be associated with neoplasms, excessive sexual activity or trauma [3,4]. Clinical Perspective Symptoms include sudden chest pain and a palpable, tender, erythematous cord-like structure along the affected vein [1–7]. Additional symptoms may occur in secondary MD, such as high-grade fever, malaise and extensive bruising [3,6,10]. The diagnosis is generally based on medical history and physical examination [3–7]. In atypical cases—such as when no cord-like structure is present, or other symptoms associated with secondary MD, such as fever, are evident—ultrasound imaging can confirm the diagnosis. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound typically shows a subcutaneous, non-compressible tubular anechoic or hypoechoic structure with a beaded appearance, with no blood flow on colour or spectral Doppler [1–7]. Sometimes, low-level internal echoes may be present, representing a thrombus. The surrounding soft tissues may be hyperechoic due to the inflammatory response. Mammography is primarily helpful in determining aetiology rather than confirming the diagnosis since underlying breast cancer has been reported in up to 12.7%, emphasising the importance of evaluating for malignancy in unexplained MD cases [4,7]. Mammographic findings may be inconclusive or reveal a linear density [1,5]. The appearance of MD on mammography can resemble various conditions, leading to misdiagnosis. Such conditions include dilated ducts and subdermal cysts, especially in retroareolar MD. Tumour invasion into the venous system, scarring from surgery or radiation, and fat necrosis may create similar linear or cord-like structures. Furthermore, axillary lymphadenopathy can be confused with venous cords in the axilla [11]. MD is recognised as a “special case” in the BI-RADS classification, and its findings are classified as BI-RADS 2 (Benign) [12]. Other imaging modalities are normally not indicated [5]. Outcome Mondor’s disease is usually self-limiting, with spontaneous resolution in 4–8 weeks [1,3–5]. Biopsy is generally not recommended; however, it should be considered in highly suspicious cases of malignancy, vasculitis, and recurrence [1–7]. Treatment focuses on symptom relief, using local heat and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [1,2,4,5]. Systemic anticoagulation is typically discouraged, but it might be considered for patients with hypercoagulable conditions [2,4,5]. In cases of secondary MD, it is crucial to address the primary disease, as MD itself is not life-threatening, but the underlying diseases may pose a risk of fatal outcomes [3]. Clinicians should be aware of MD to provide appropriate reassurance and avoid unnecessary investigations [4–6]. In this case, the patient presented with a painful, cord-like structure in the breast, and MD was confirmed by ultrasound. The history of bruising and petechial lesions might suggest secondary MD. The patient was discharged with symptomatic treatment and scheduled for follow-up in 3 months. At the follow-up appointment, the patient showed no breast abnormalities on physical examination and reported a complete resolution of symptoms one month after the initial assessment. The immune and coagulation studies showed no abnormalities. Take Home Message Mondor’s disease is a rare, self-limiting superficial thrombophlebitis, often idiopathic but sometimes secondary to conditions like hypercoagulative states or trauma. It presents as a painful, cord-like structure, typically diagnosed through clinical history and examination, resolving spontaneously within 4–8 weeks. Ultrasound may help in atypical cases. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Widening of the intercondylar notch in neurofibromatosis type 1
clinical_history: A 50-year-old female with a known history of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) presented with atraumatic pain and weakness of the left leg. She had previously had a focal neurofibroma excised from the left thigh. MRI imaging of the left femur and knee was performed to identify a cause for the pain.
imaging_findings: MRI scan of the left knee (Figures 1, 2, and 3) demonstrated diffuse T2 bright and iso-hypotense T1 tissue infiltrating the subcutaneous and intermuscular planes at the posterior aspect of the knee and reaching the periosteal surface of the distal femur, causing bone dysplasia with widening of the posterior intercondylar notch. CT imaging also demonstrated the marked widening of the intercondylar notch (Figures 4 and 5).
discussion: Background The intercondylar notch is a depression in the distal femur between the medial and lateral condyles; it provides attachments for the cruciate and meniscofemoral ligaments [1]. A widening of the intercondylar notch can be caused by haemophilic arthropathy, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculous arthropathy, and psoriatic arthropathy [2]. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a mutation in the NF-1 gene located on chromosome 17. NF1 commonly manifests with the presence of café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas [3]. To our knowledge, there is no literature describing a widening of the intercondylar notch in NF1. This report suggests the potential for such an association. Clinical and Imaging Perspective Approximately 59.6% of individuals with NF1 develop some form of malignancy in their lifetime [4]. In our institution, we regularly perform MRI whole-body surveillance for patients with complex NF1. We have observed different types of neurogenic lesions in this population, including focal neurofibroma, diffuse neurofibromatosis tissue, plexiform neurofibroma and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour ( MPNST): Localised focal neurofibromas are well-circumscribed spherical or ovoid lesions, which demonstrate typical targets comprising central T2 hypointensity due to collagen, and peripheral T2 hyperintensity due to myxoid material [5]. Diffuse neurofibromatosis tissue appears as infiltrating T2 hyperintense tissue. This can be interspersed with fatty tissue and often demonstrates prominent feeding vessels. Diffuse neurofibromatosis tissue can spread across tissue planes and also extend along the periosteal surface causing bone remodelling. It is very rare for diffuse neurofibromatosis tissue to transform into malignancy, and hence, excision is generally not required unless there is impaired function or significant psychological impact [6]. Plexiform neurofibromas are a conglomeration of individual neurofibromas causing a “bag of worms” appearance. Given the multiplicity of lesions within the plexiform, there are higher chances of malignant transformation. The diagnosis of MPNST is challenging but suggested by rapid growth (volume doubling time of one year or less), central necrotic change with loss of target appearance, peri-lesional oedema, irregular margins and invasion of neighbouring structures. Bone dysplasia in NF1 is seen in typical sites such as the sphenoid wing and distal third of the tibia with pseudoarthrosis. The pathogenesis of bone dysplasia in NF1 is attributed to NF tissue propagating along the periosteum, causing bone remodelling or mesodermal dysplasia (in the absence of any macroscopic lesion) [7]. Regarding potential differential diagnoses for this appearance, there were no low T2 signal nodular elements to indicate hemosiderin deposition to suggest this being pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS). PVNS would also not tend to extend outside the joint capsule. There was also no T1 hyperintensity to indicate fatty tissue to suggest this being lipoma arborescens. Intra-articular tumours are extremely rare, the most common potential soft tissue tumour around the knee would be a synovial sarcoma, which would not tend to have intra-articular extension as per this case. We have provided a companion case from our complex NF1 service, shown in Figures 6a and 6b, with almost identical appearances with widening of the intercondylar notch due to infiltrative neurofibromatosis tissue. Outcome Given the patient’s history of NF1 and symptoms, a biopsy was performed to rule out potential malignancy. Histology showed a tumour of haphazard arrangements of bland spindle cells within a loose collagenous stroma. There was no significant atypia and no necrosis. Mitoses are inconspicuous. Immunohistochemistry showed strong positivity for S100 and SOX10. There was reticular staining for CD34 throughout and p16 was positive. MIB1 is very low. Appearances were of a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumour consistent with neurofibroma. No evidence of malignancy in the sampled material. The lesion was stable on sequential MRI scans over a 10-year period, indicating a benign process. Take Home Message / Teaching Points NF1 patients may develop diffuse neurofibromatosis tissue, which has a very low risk of malignant transformation. NF1 can cause bone dysplasia with or without adjacent local or diffuse neurofibromas Widening of the intercondylar notch may be caused by intra-articular neurofibromatosis tissue of the knee joint; further cases are necessary to prove this hypothesis. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Calcinosis in limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis
clinical_history: A 62-year-old woman with a 10-year history of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis presented with insidious pain and swelling of the left thumb’s fingertip. Physical examination revealed sclerodactyly and a tender nodule on the distal phalanx of the first finger.
imaging_findings: Radiographic imaging of the left hand (Figures 1a and 1b) and thumb (Figure 2) revealed a well-defined calcification in the soft tissue overlying the distal phalanx of the left first finger, measuring approximately 1.5 cm. Periarticular osteopenia was also observed, particularly evident at the thumb (Figure 1b). Cortical thinning and blurring of the margins were noted in the proximal interphalangeal joint of the ring finger (Figure 1a). No other significant findings were identified.
discussion: Background Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is an immune-mediated disorder characterised by skin and connective tissue fibrosis and vascular dysfunction [1–2]. Calcinosis is a common manifestation in limited SSc and often develops years after the initial diagnosis of SSc [2–4]. Its pathophysiology is unclear, but digital vasculopathy appears to contribute to its development [2,3]. Clinical Perspective Calcinosis may significantly affect patients’ quality of life due to pain, skin ulceration and potential infection [3]. Early detection is crucial for timely decision-making on optimal management [2–3]. Imaging Perspective Radiography is the preferred diagnostic tool for confirming calcinosis, as it efficiently identifies calcified deposits in soft tissues [3–4]. Outcome Treatment of calcinosis in SSc remains challenging [2–3]. Therapeutic options include symptomatic management and preventive measures against ulceration and infection [3]. In severe cases, surgical excision is considered [2–3] . Teaching Points Radiographic imaging allows the identification of calcinosis in systemic sclerosis ( SSc). Calcinosis is a common manifestation of SSc and can impact the quality of life. Management of calcinosis remains challenging, with treatment primarily focused on symptom relief and prevention of complications.

title: Mandibular brown tumour
clinical_history: A 53-year-old male patient presented with a lump in his left jaw, with noted enlargement in 2 months. There were no associated symptoms or relevant clinical history. Physical examination disclosed an expansile lesion in the left mandibular region and excluded palpable lymph nodes.
imaging_findings: Non-enhanced computed tomography (CT) dental scan showed an expansile lytic lesion centred to the angle and ascending ramus of the left mandible, measuring 4 cm at its largest axis, with well-defined, multilobulated borders and ground-glass ossified matrix (Figures 1a and 1b). The final report included osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma as diagnostic hypotheses and the patient was referred to our tertiary hospital. Contrast-enhanced cervical CT performed at our hospital better depicted that the lesion did not invade adjacent structures (Figure 2) and enabled evaluation of the infra-hyoid neck. A solid, hypodense, 3.5 cm mass was identified posterior to the right thyroid lobe (Figure 3) and a provisional diagnosis of parathyroid adenoma was proposed. On ultrasound, the referred nodule was well-defined and hypoechoic (Figures 4a and 4b). Laboratory findings revealed elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) (301pg/mL) and elevated calcium levels (13mg/dL). Parathyroid scintigraphy with technetium-99m methoxy-isobutyl-isonitrile ( Tc-99m MIBI) was performed and an adenoma of the right inferior parathyroid was confirmed (Figures 5a and 5b).
discussion: Background Brown tumours, also known as osteitis fibrosa, cystica generalisata or von Recklinghausen’s disease of bone, are osteolytic giant-cell lesions originating from increased osteoclasts activity in the setting of hyperparathyroidism (HPT) [1,2]. The radiological hallmarks of HPT are diffuse bony demineralisation and subperiosteal and subligamentous bone resorption. These bony changes of HPT are identical in primary, secondary and tertiary HPT. The earliest bony changes of HPT occur in the hands, skull and alveolar bone of the jaws, with loss of the lamina dura that surrounds the tooth socket. Other classic HPT features are localised lytic bone lesions (brown tumours) and metastatic calcification of soft tissues [3]. The incidence of brown tumours is reported to be 3–4.5% in primary HPT and 1.5–1.7% in secondary HPT [1,4]. These lesions are more commonly observed in women than men (3:1 ratio), typically appearing between the fifth and sixth decades of life but with a wide age distribution [2,5,6]. Work-up for primary HPT in children and young adults should always include investigation of hereditary disorders, such as multiple endocrine neoplasia and hyperparathyroidism with jaw tumour syndromes, as well as non-syndromic disorders [7]. Clinical Perspective The name “brown tumour” comes from its brownish appearance on biopsy, caused by high vascularity, haemorrhage, and hemosiderin deposits [3]. Brown tumours can manifest as solitary or multiple lesions, with a preference for the mandible, ribs, clavicle and pelvis, and rarely seen in the skull or associated with the nasal/paranasal sinuses [4,5]. Clinically, they appear as slow-growing, palpable bony swelling that may cause bone pain or pathological fractures [5]. Imaging Perspective On radiographic imaging, brown tumours are seen as well-defined, lucent, and expansile lytic lesions. The cortical bone may be thinned or fractured, and other radiographic signs of HPT are often present [1,4]. CT scans reveal multilocular osteolytic lesions with ground-glass opacities that may disrupt the cortex. Unlike bone cysts, these lesions enhance with contrast media [1]. Magnetic resonance imaging findings vary depending on the composition of the tissue within the lesion [4]. The similarity in radiologic appearance between brown tumours and other bone tumours makes the diagnosis challenging [4]. A definitive diagnosis relies on identifying elevated serum calcium and PTH levels [2]. Bone biopsy may be required, keeping in mind that brown tumours share histological features with other giant cell lesions, including the presence of mononuclear spindle cells and multinucleated osteoclasts [5,6]. For this reason, a histological diagnosis of a giant cell tumour following bone biopsy requires adequate work-up for HPT. Outcome The primary approach to managing brown tumours is treating the underlying HPT. These lesions often regress following parathyroidectomy or appropriate medical treatment for the endocrine disorder. Surgical removal of the tumour may be necessary if it is located in a critical anatomical location, causes neurological symptoms, or does not regress following parathyroidectomy [4,6]. In the case described, the diagnosis of a brown tumour in the left mandible was confidently established, as the patient had primary HPT caused by a confirmed parathyroid adenoma, and the bone lesion exhibited compatible radiological features. After surgical removal of the parathyroid adenoma, calcium and PTH levels normalised. Follow-up CT imaging 6 months later showed significant improvement of the brown jaw tumour, with increased sclerosis, although the mandibular region remained expanded (Figures 6a, 6b, 6c, and 6d). All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Large intracranial hydatid cyst
clinical_history: A 4-year-old female presented with complaints of headache for the last 2 months, imbalance while walking since 2 days, and intermittent vomiting since 1 day. On physical examination, the patient had left-sided facial weakness with ipsilateral deviation of the mouth for 1 month. The patient had no history of convulsions, fever or trauma. Birth history was unremarkable with no history of neonatal intensive care unit admission.
imaging_findings: MRI brain revealed a well-defined, biloculated intra-axial cystic lesion with smooth enhancing margins in the left frontal, gangliocapsular, and anterior temporal regions, associated with adjacent T2/FLAIR hyperintensity indicating oedema (Figures 1, 2, 3, and 4). The lesion appeared hypointense on T1WI, hyperintense on T2WI, and fully suppressed on FLAIR, without DWI restriction or SWI blooming (Figures 2, 3, 4, 5a, and 5b). No solid component was identified. The lesion caused significant mass effect, including a 9 mm midline shift to the right, compression of the left lateral ventricle, and contralateral ventricular dilatation. It displaced the falx medially and compressed the genu and body of the corpus callosum, left thalamus, left cerebral peduncle, and the temporal horn of the left lateral ventricle. It also displaced the left anterior cerebral artery to the right and the left middle cerebral artery posteriorly (Figures 5a and 5b). Differentials included cerebral hydatid, neuroglial cyst, and arachnoid cyst. A pre-operative chest X-ray revealed a large cystic lesion in the right upper lung field (Figure 6), suggesting synchronous cerebral hydatid.
discussion: Background Hydatid disease, a zoonotic infection caused by tapeworms, is most commonly associated with Echinococcus granulosus in humans [1]. Cerebral hydatid cysts (CHCs) are exceptionally rare, comprising only 2% of all intracranial space-occupying lesions, even in endemic regions [2]. These cysts are more frequently observed in children than in adults and are typically found in the supratentorial region, especially within the middle cerebral artery territory, with the parietal lobe being the most commonly affected area [3]. Clinical Perspective Small cysts are often asymptomatic, while larger cysts can lead to symptoms such as headache, vomiting, seizures, hemiparesis, signs of raised intracranial pressure, and even coma, depending on their location [4]. Imaging Perspective CT and MRI serve as the primary imaging tools for diagnosing cystic lesions. Among these, MRI is preferred due to its superior ability to visualise the cyst wall, pinpoint the exact location, detect superimposed infections, evaluate cyst contents, and aid in surgical planning while excluding other potential diagnoses [5]. On MRI, CHCs typically present as round or oval, well-defined cystic lesions that are isointense to cerebrospinal fluid on T1WI and T2WI. They exhibit hypointense walls on T2WI, without associated perilesional oedema or contrast enhancement, classifying them as simple or uncomplicated CHCs. In contrast, complicated intracranial hydatid cysts exhibit distinct imaging features, due to secondary changes such as rupture, infection, or degeneration. On T2WI, these cysts often show heterogeneous signal intensity resulting from altered cyst content, such as proteinaceous material, debris, or blood. The cyst wall may appear thickened with irregular margins and show contrast enhancement, indicative of inflammation or vascularisation. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) frequently reveals restricted diffusion, reflecting secondary infection or rupture. Additionally, floating membranes or internal septations may be visible within the cyst cavity on T2 or FLAIR sequences. Surrounding vasogenic oedema is a common finding, signifying an inflammatory response to the complicated cyst [6]. Calcification of the cyst wall is a rare finding. Outcome The main treatment for intracranial hydatid cysts is surgical removal, aiming for complete and radical excision. A major surgical complication is cyst rupture, which can result in subarachnoid dissemination, severe anaphylactic reactions, and an increased risk of recurrence. Albendazole is advised in cases of intraoperative cyst rupture or recurrence [7]. In our case, the patient underwent surgical excision of the lesion and was kept on follow-up. Take Home Message Although hydatid cysts are benign lesions, timely diagnosis and appropriate management are crucial to reducing mortality and morbidity.

title: Unusual bends in faulty bones
clinical_history: A 6-year-old boy presented with deformity of the left forearm (Figure 1a) for three months. Three years back he sustained an injury while playing and had accidentally hit the door. The boy had multiple cafe au lait spots on the back and cutaneous neurofibroma in his left knee (figures 1b and 1c).
imaging_findings: A radiograph of the left forearm done three years back (Figure 2) showed a small expansile lytic lesion with ground glass matrix and cortical thinning in the diaphysis of the left radius. The margins were sclerosed with a narrow zone of transition and no periosteal reaction. The current radiograph (Figure 3) revealed enlargement of previously seen lesions with multiple lytic and ground glass areas. There was a malunited fracture in the distal meta-diaphyseal end of the left ulna. On MRI, the lesion measured 2.4 x 2 x 5.1 cm. It was T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense with lobulated margins, and T1/T2 hypointense internal septations (Figures 4a and 4b). The lesion showed intense enhancement with a type 2 curve in the perfusion study (Figures 4c and 4d). A diagnosis of fibrous dysplasia (FD) in the radius and pseudoarthrosis in the distal ulna was made in a child with neurofibromatosis type 1.
discussion: Background Pseudoarthrosis is typically described as the creation of a joint-like structure by fibrous hamartoma due to the unsuccessful healing between two bony ends, located away from the actual joints [1,2]. It is exemplified by anterolateral bending and non-union fracture in the diaphysis of long bones [3]. Pseudoarthrosis is associated with Jaffe–Campanacci syndrome, osteogenesis imperfecta, ankylosing spondylitis, the end stage of inflammatory arthritides, neurofibromatosis type 1, and FD [1–3]. Neurofibromatosis type 1 is the most common phacomatosis. Both mesodermal dysplasia and external pressure from the neurofibromas lead to various skeletal presentations [4]. Various skeletal findings in neurofibromatosis include non-dystrophic or dystrophic scoliosis, kyphosis, sphenoid dysplasia, dural ectasia, posterior vertebral body scalloping, thinning of the vertebral lamina and pedicles, ribs narrowing, and pseudoarthrosis [4]. Imaging Perspective On a radiograph, FD shows ground glass opacity or radiolucency in the diaphysis with the widening of the medullary canal, endosteal scalloping, and cortical thinning. Shepherd crook deformity or bending of the affected bone is common. On CT, the lesion has an HU of 60–140 with better osseous delineation than the radiographs [5]. The lesion is T2 variable intense, T1 hypointense, and shows avid contrast enhancement [6,7]. Both non-ossifying fibroma (NOF) and FD are seen in neurofibromatosis and are morphologically similar; however, NOF is lytic, eccentric, and located at the metaphysis of long bones. MRI is useful from a surgical point of view to assess the line of resection and subtle soft tissue changes, and to look for non-enhancing cystic areas. Outcome Various treatment strategies include bracing, resection of the lesion, and bridging with vascularised tibial/fibular bone graft, Illizarov technique, and amputation. The continuous growth of the immature skeleton coupled with inherent mesodermal dysplasia hinders the normal healing process, and thus, the surgical results are not satisfactory [3]. A systematic review undertaken by Siebelt M et al. concluded that fibular bone graft had better outcomes for forearm pseudoarthrosis [8]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points In a child with cafe au lait spots and bony deformity, one should suspect benign bone conditions like fibrous dysplasia (FD). Diagnosis can be made on the radiograph itself; however, an MRI is necessary for surgical planning. Although pseudoarthrosis is more common in the tibial bone, few works of literature have reported pseudoarthrosis in the forearm in neurofibromatosis [9–13], but the involvement of radius with FD and pseudoarthrosis of the ulna in a neurofibromatosis type 1 was unique in our case. The pseudoarthrosis in the distal ulna was a sequelae of an untreated trauma in the past that had aggravated due to mesodermal dysplasia in this case. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
differential_diagnosis: Fibrous dysplasia and pseudoarthrosis in neurofibromatosis type 1 Non-ossifying fibroma
final_diagnosis: Fibrous dysplasia and pseudoarthrosis in neurofibromatosis type 1

title: Caudal regression syndrome and associated urinary system malformations
clinical_history: A 22-year-old male patient with a congenital pelvic deformity has been complaining of urinary incontinence. On examination, atrophic gluteal muscles could be seen. His past medical history was remarkable of frequent urinary infections.
imaging_findings: In voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) images, the coccyx and distal part of the sacrum were not visualised, suggesting caudal regression syndrome (Figure 1a). Evidence of vesicoureteral reflux is seen bilaterally, more prominent on the left side (grade 3 vesicoureteral reflux ( VUR)) and grade 1 on the right side (Figure 1b). Both ureters are inserted into the prostatic segment of the urethra along with the segmental urethral dilatation (Figure 1c). In coronal and sagittal T2W magnetic resonance urography (MRU) images, distal segments of the sacrum and coccyx are absent, suggesting caudal regression syndrome (Figures 2a and 2b). The conus medullaris terminates normally at the L1 level (Figure 2b). In addition, the right kidney is not visualised, and the left kidney shows compensatory hypertrophy (Figure 2a). Coronal T2W MR images show both ureters are terminated at the dilated prostatic segment of the urethra (ectopic right side ureteral insertion in Figures 3a and 3b, and left side insertion in Figure 3c).
discussion: Background Caudal regression syndrome (CRS) is defined by different varieties of structural impairments in the caudal spinal part of the body. This condition happens approximately in 1–2 per 100,000 live births. It is associated with a wide range of multisystemic anomalies [1]. Its precise aetiology is not known, but maternal diabetes is thought to be associated with this syndrome [2]. Clinical Perspective Individuals with CRS can have other pathologies in different parts of their body, such as deformities in the lower extremities, spinal abnormalities, renal maldevelopment, ectopic kidneys, abnormal bladder function (neurogenic), and undeveloped anogenital organs [3]. According to a study assessing 21 patients with CRS, the occurrence of neurogenic bladder, bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, and hypoplastic uterus (Müllerian agenesis type I) was in seventeen (81%), five (23.8%) and one (4.8%) patient respectively. Moreover, in nine patients (42.9%) diagnosed with an imperforated anus, eight (38.1%) had anorectal stenosis, and one (4.8%) had anal stenosis [4]. Another study reported a patient with CRS for the first time who also had vaginal atresia (in distal parts of the genital system), presenting with periodical lower stomach pain [5]. In another study, the most common urologic disorders found in the CRS population were neurogenic bladder (60%), kidney agenesis (13%–20%), and reduced renal function (8%–12%) [6]. Additionally, CRS patients complaining of back pain and bowel incontinence should be investigated for possible tethered cord syndrome (with the help of radiologic findings) [7]. Imaging Perspective CRS can be divided into two main groups. In group 1, there is an abrupt spinal cord termination together with a club-shaped cord ending. Group 2 has a less severe presentation, and the sacrum is partially well-preserved. Group 1 patients often have major morbidities, including lower limb deformities, and bladder and bowel dysfunctions [9]. Inappropriate crown-rump length, a protrusion of the lower part of spine and an exceeded nuchal translucency may be the first signs of CRS in ultrasonography images [4,8]. MRI is considered as a pivotal imaging modality in demonstrating of the vertebra-spinal anomalies and associated concomitant defects, such as urinary, genital, anorectal, and spinal cord anomalies [4]. Due to a high incidence of neurogenic bladder (60%) in affected patients with CRS, all of them should be investigated for bladder function and urinary tract obstruction [6]. Outcome Being familiar with such co-existing anomalies can lead to a well-organised screening program in the affected population, which can detect the respective pathologies before causing further damage, and also can help with rectifying the associated defects [4]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points The occurrence of the other related pathologies is not constantly connected with the severity of the vertebral column malformation; hence, medical team members should check for possible coexisting abnormalities. Two of the most prevalent co-morbidities are genitourinary and anorectal impairments, which should be assessed in all caudal regression syndrome cases. MRI is a vastly helpful imaging modality in determining such concomitant pathologies and also has an important role in distinguishing defects without obvious outward signs.

title: Boerhaave syndrome associated with pneumomediastinum extending to the neck
clinical_history: A 58-year-old male with worsening nausea for the past 72 hours presented to the emergency department with severe chest pain radiating to the back in the context of 4 recent episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis. He was afebrile, diaphoretic, and mildly tachycardic. Cardiac workup, complete blood count, and electrolytes were normal.
imaging_findings: A chest X-ray followed by contrast-enhanced chest CT were performed. The X-ray demonstrated pneumomediastinum extending into the neck and a tiny left apical pneumothorax. Notably, left pleural effusion with atelectasis and consolidation were also seen (Figure 1a). The coronal CT images were closely correlated to the X-ray findings, clearly showing the pneumomediastinum extending superiorly towards the neck soft tissues. A pneumothorax at the left lower lung base, not previously seen on X-ray, is also demonstrated on coronal CT view (Figure 1b). The axial chest CT image on lung window showed evidence of pneumomediastinum with air around the oesophagus. Left pneumothorax and bilateral pleural effusions are also seen (Figure 2). On the soft tissue window, a thickened distal oesophagus was seen; however, no clear site of perforation was appreciated. Bilateral complex attenuating pleural effusions were also observed but there was no obvious contrast extravasation (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Boerhaave syndrome refers to spontaneous transmural perforation of the oesophagus secondary to a sudden increase in pressure inside the oesophageal lumen. Epidemiologically, this condition has a higher prevalence in males, with the greatest incidence seen in middle-aged men. Risk factors include excessive alcohol use, overeating, weightlifting, compressed air injury, childbirth, abdominal trauma, defecation, and epileptic seizures. Alcohol use and overeating are the most important risk factors as they increase the risk of forceful vomiting [1]. The most common site of perforation involves the posterolateral lower third of the oesophagus above the gastroesophageal junction, as this area has a lower density of longitudinal muscle fibres. Since this region abuts the left pleura, the left pleural cavity is most commonly affected [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Classically, patients present with Mackler’s triad of vomiting, subcutaneous emphysema, and lower thoracic pain [3]. However, this triad presents in only 50% of the cases [4]. Instead, the presentation can greatly vary, ranging from dysphagia, neck pain, abdominal pain, chest pain, fever, sepsis, dyspnoea, and haematemesis. Given the clinical variability, imaging is needed to conclusively identify an oesophageal rupture [5,6]. Imaging Perspective Chest X-ray remains one of the first-line investigations for acute onset of chest pain, a common finding in Boerhaave syndrome. However, X-ray findings can be non-specific, ranging from pleural effusions, pneumothorax, atelectasis, and airspace infiltrates, and may not be immediately suggestive of an oesophageal rupture. As such, CT remains the preferred diagnostic modality. In addition to the aforementioned X-ray findings, CT provides key diagnostic clues, including paraoesophageal and paraaortic air collections, oesophageal wall thickening, pneumomediastinum, mediastinal fluid collections, and oesophagopleural fistulae [5]. Imaging can help guide the location of the perforation, the degree of contamination of gastric contents into the pleural cavity or mediastinum and identify any oesophagopleural fistulae. This information, combined with the patient’s haemodynamic stability, dictate the treatment approach. Thoracotomy, thoracoscopy, and endoscopy are used for primary repair of the tear and to drain any extravasated content [7]. Outcome The patient in this case underwent an esophagogastroduodenoscopy to localise the perforation and a thoracotomy was later performed for primary repair of this posterolateral oesophageal wall tear seen 2 cm above the squamocolumnar junction. They made a full recovery. Take Home Message / Teaching Points It is important to consider spontaneous oesophageal rupture in the differential diagnosis of sudden onset chest pain, especially after forceful vomiting. CT chest is the recommended imaging modality to evaluate signs of Boerhaave syndrome. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Concurrent emphysematous osteomyelitis and pyelonephritis: A rare, life-threatening condition
clinical_history: A 56-year-old diabetic woman with irresectable low-grade serous carcinoma (undergoing induction chemotherapy) presented to the emergency department with two weeks of lower back pain radiating to both lower limbs. Symptoms of urinary retention and constipation emerged a week earlier when marked neutrophilic leukocytosis was identified during a routine oncology follow-up.
imaging_findings: A lumbar spine CT revealed pre-sacral and posterior paravertebral emphysema, with intracanal gas extending into the intervertebral spaces (L4–L5, L5–S1) and vertebral bodies (L4, L5), consistent with the pumice stone sign (Figures 1a and 1b). Gas was also observed in the renal pelvis and left ureter (Figure 1b, arrow). An abdominal CT scan showed an enlarged left kidney with perinephric inflammatory fat stranding, multiple hypodense lesions scattered in the renal parenchyma, and areas of parenchymal hyperenhancement after contrast administration. Gas was also depicted within the renal pelvis and the rest of the collecting system. These findings were compatible with emphysematous pyelonephritis (Figures 2a and 2b). Lumbar MRI revealed gas within the vertebral bodies (L4, L5), more pronounced in L5 and adjacent intervertebral discs. Prevertebral and paravertebral tissue oedema and thickening, with gadolinium enhancement, extended into the foramina and spinal canal. Bilateral psoas muscle involvement further indicated a severe infectious/inflammatory process, accompanied by extensive intracanal gas formation (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d).
discussion: Background Osteomyelitis is a bone infection that affect s the marrow, cortical bone, and surrounding tissues. It may result from haematogenous spread, direct inoculation or contiguous extension from adjacent infections. Gas-forming osteomyelitis, a rare subtype, is typically caused by anaerobic or facultative anaerobic bacteria and, thus, frequently linked to malignancy, diabetes, or trauma [1–3]. The pathophysiology involves bacterial colonisation, inflammatory bone destruction, and gas production, leading to soft tissue invasion and systemic complications [4]. Concurrent presentations of emphysematous osteomyelitis and pyelonephritis are extraordinarily rare, with only five cases reported in the literature [2,5–8]. Clinical Perspective It typically presents with localised pain, swelling, erythema, and systemic signs of infection such as fever or elevated inflammatory markers. In this case, the patient exhibited a 287.4 mg/dL reactive protein level on admission. Gas-forming osteomyelitis may present with crepitus or subcutaneous emphysema, which can provide additional diagnostic clues. However, this condition is often challenging to diagnose, particularly in immunocompromised or diabetic patients, where symptoms may be nonspecific [3]. Conveying findings such as bone gas, potential abscesses, and adjacent structure involvement is crucial to guide the physician towar ds appropriate interventions while excluding alternative diagnoses, such as trauma or malignancy [4]. Imaging Perspective Imaging plays a vital role in diagnosis, offering insights that clinical examination alone cannot provide. Key findings include bone gas formation and destruction, as well as the involvement of adjacent soft tissues [9]. In this case, the CT demonstrated mild dilation of the left ureteropelvic system, intrapelvic and bladder gas, and gas extending into the paravertebral soft tissues, lumbar vertebrae, and spinal canal. MRI confirmed the extent of inflammation, with gadolinium enhancement of pre and paravertebral tissues and psoas muscles. These findings indicated an emphysematous infectious/inflammatory process originating in the left reno-collecting system, spreading to the axial skeleton. Outcome Empirical antibiotic therapy with meropenem and vancomycin was initiated in the context of septic shock. Urgent surgery addressed severe spinal cord compression, including laminectomy, flavectomy, partial discectomy, and posterior epidural empyema drainage (Figures 4a, 4b, 4c, and 4d), followed by arthrodesis and posterior fixation for stabilisation (Figures 6a, 6b, and 6c). Four days post-admission, antibiotics were adjusted to ceftriaxone after Klebsiella pneumoniae isolation from blood, urine, and intraoperative samples. An 81-day vancomycin course was completed due to purulent wound drainage (Figures 5a and 5b). Assisted ambulation at 11 months was regained after intensive rehabilitation. Prompt treatment is critical to minimise irreversible neurological deficits [1,10,11]. This case highlights the importance of imaging in diagnosing infections, guiding surgery, and enabling tailored treatments, emphasising multidisciplinary care for optimal outcomes. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Enterovesical fistula Retroperitoneal trauma Post-surgical changes Osteonecrosis Emphysematous osteomyelitis & emphysematous pyelonephritis Secondary invasion of retroperitoneal or vertebral structures

title: Double trouble: Simultaneous Achilles rupture and tennis leg
clinical_history: Case 1 is a 54-year-old female who experienced right ankle pain after an injury, leading to the clinical suspicion of Achilles tendon rupture, and was evaluated by radiograph and MRI after 1 week. Case 2 is a 62-year-old male who reported calf pain, raising concerns for deep vein thrombosis, further evaluated with ultrasound. He noted a trivial trauma occurred 10 days prior.
imaging_findings: In Case 1, the lateral ankle radiograph revealed increased soft tissue thickness around the Achilles tendon with small calcification (Figure 1). MRI indicated significant disruption (95%) of the distal 5.5 cm of the tendon, cystic areas, and signs of haemorrhage (Figures 2a, 2b, 3a, 3b, and 4). Extensive oedema in the posterior lower leg muscles led to a screening of the leg that identified a 2.8 x 1.6 x 5.4 cm collection in the intermuscular fascial plane, causing indentation on the soleus. The plantaris tendon was partially torn, while the soleus and medial gastrocnemius exhibited grade 1 strain without fibre discontinuity (Figures 5a and 5b). In Case 2, the ultrasound showed a bulky distal 6.0 cm Achilles tendon with altered echotexture, multiple calcific foci, and a high-grade partial thickness tear (Figures 6a, 6b, and 6c). An anechoic collection measuring 3.3 x 1.2 x 8.6 cm was observed in the intermuscular fascial plane, between the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles, with no increased vascularity noted on the Doppler study (Figures 7a and 7b).
discussion: Both patients had co-existent high-grade near full-thickness tears involving the distal Achilles tendon and showing features of background calcific tendinitis and tennis leg. Ultrasound is an inexpensive and widely available diagnostic tool for accurately diagnosing both tennis leg and Achilles rupture. Although MR imaging is not mandatory for diagnosis, it is more sensitive, subtle findings can be picked up, and provides greater detail of information. Tennis leg is most often a sports-associated injury incurred during an extension of the knee and forced dorsiflexion of the ankle [1]. In a study conducted by Delgado et al. [1], patients diagnosed to have tennis leg had the following spectrum of imaging findings: partial rupture of the medial head of the gastrocnemius (66.7%), collection between the medial head of the gastrocnemius and soleus without muscle injury (21.3%), plantaris tendon rupture (1.4%), partial rupture of the soleus (0.7 %). Rohilla et al. suggested that injury to any muscle in the posterior superficial compartment, including the gastrocnemius, soleus, or plantaris, can cause comparable symptoms, commonly known as “tennis leg”. However, the extent of these symptoms can vary in severity. When the plantaris muscle or tendon is ruptured in isolation, the symptoms are typically milder than those associated with a rupture or strain of the gastrocnemius or soleus muscles, leading to a quicker recovery in terms of mobility [2]. Conservative management with RICE (rest, ice application, compression of the affected part, and elevation), analgesics and physiotherapy are recommended. USG-guided steroid/analgesic injections, as well as evacuation of haematoma, may be done in cases complicated by compartment syndrome [3]. Achilles tendon ruptures in older patients may occur at sites of chronic degeneration during routine activitie s [4]. Both our patients had the rare association of calcific Achilles tendinopathy with high-grade tear along with features of tennis leg. They were managed conservatively as one patient had no significant functional impairment on follow-up, and the other was a poorly controlled diabetic and, hence, surgical Achilles repair was deferred.

title: Giant pituitary macroadenoma with cavernous sinus invasion
clinical_history: A 50-year-old female patient presented with headache, visual disturbances, and bitemporal hemianopia. Hormonal assays indicated abnormal levels of serum prolactin and growth hormone.
imaging_findings: The patient’s MRI brain showed a large lobulated sellar lesion (Figure 1) on post-contrast sagittal images, showing suprasellar extension and anteriorly extending into both sphenoid sinuses and ethmoid sinuses. Axial T2 image (Figure 2) shows the lesion to be predominantly involving the left cavernous sinus and encasing the left internal carotid artery, and seen extending into the left orbital apex and left frontal and temporal lobes. FLAIR coronal image (Figure 3) shows compression of adjacent brain parenchyma, lateral ventricle, and brainstem. In the post-contrast axial image (Figure 4), the lesion was seen extending into the right cavernous sinus with suprasellar extension into both frontal lobes and sphenoid sinuses.
discussion: Background Pituitary lesions can lead to significant hormonal imbalances and should be addressed promptly. Pituitary tumours make up approximately 16.8% of all brain tumours from 2012 to 2016, followed by meningiomas and glioblastomas, according to the CBTRUS (Central Brain Tumour Registry of the United States) [1]. Clinical Perspective The most common tumour of the anterior pituitary is pituitary adenoma. Pituitary lesions smaller than 10 mm in size are called microadenomas, whereas lesions larger than 10 mm are called macroadenomas. Some giant macroadenomas can be 4 cm or larger [2]. Macroadenomas can result in mass effect by causing compression on optic chiasma or can result in suprasellar extension. Giant pituitary tumours can result in cavernous sinus invasion. Pituitary tumours are prone to infarction or haemorrhage, a condition known as pituitary apoplexy, which can cause headaches, loss of vision, ophthalmoplegia, and hormonal disturbances. Risk factors include pregnancy, hypertension, hypotension, and anticoagulant therapy [3]. Imaging Perspective MRI is the preferred modality for diagnosing pituitary and parasellar tumours. To assess the extent of invasion into sellar and parasellar areas, both Hardy and Knosp devised classification systems. Hardy's system evaluates osseous sellar margin destruction. Knosp's classification assesses cavernous sinus invasion and internal carotid artery encasement, with five grades: Grade 0 (normal), Grade 1 (extension to medial 50% of cavernous internal carotid artery (ICA)), Grade 2 (extension to lateral 50% of cavernous ICA), Grade 3 (extension beyond lateral margins of ICA), and Grade 4 (complete encasement of cavernous ICA) [4]. Outcome Treatment options for pituitary macroadenomas include medical therapy for hypersecretory tumours (e.g., dopamine agonists like bromocriptine for prolactin-secreting tumours), radiotherapy to reduce hormone production and prevent recurrence, and surgical intervention. Minimally invasive transsphenoidal surgery is effective for treating approximately 95% of pituitary tumours.

title: Fluoroscopic findings of duodenum inversum
clinical_history: A 3-year-old female with poor feeding toleration, aspirating all consistencies of food, with failure to thrive, was planned for gastrostomy tube placement, and an upper gastrointestinal study was requested for the anatomic assessment.
imaging_findings: A fluoroscopic upper gastrointestinal study was done by injection of barium via the indwelling enteric tube. The stomach exhibited a normal appearance and was normally emptied through a normal pylorus, duodenal bulb, and descending duodenum (Figure 1). After an initial descent of the duodenum, the third part of the duodenum did not cross the midline as expected. Instead, it ascends on the right side of the spine posterior and parallel to the descending duodenum up to the level of the duodenal bulb and then completes its transverse course and reaches the left upper abdomen (Figures 2 and 3).
discussion: Duodenum inversum, also known as inverted duodenum or duodenum reflexum, is an uncommon congenital anatomical variation that alters the path of the duodenum. In this variant anatomy , the third part of the duodenum folds backwards over the second part and crosses the midline higher up than usual. However, the duodenojejunal junction stays in its usual anatomical position [1,2]. Typical results from an upper gastrointestinal series show contrast flowing from the second part of the duodenum back into the first part and then into the bulb, along with a delay in movement through the duodenum, and a quick passage of contrast through the third part of the duodenum [2]. This is unlike the redundant duodenum, where the descending duodenum is longer and redundant; however, it crosses the midline at the expected level. The duodenum inversum is believed to occur because the dorsal mesentery persists, allowing the duodenum to remain mobile. Most individuals with this condition do not show symptoms or experience vague symptoms like epigastric pain, nausea, or bloating [3]. Being familiar with this variant anatomy is important so that it is not mistaken as malrotation, which can lead to unnecessary surgical intervention. Although we do not see the duodenum crossing the midline at the expected level, the duodenojejunal junction’s position on the spine’s left side at the level of the duodenal bulb rules out intestinal malrotation. The patient subsequently underwent a gastrostomy procedure.
differential_diagnosis: Duodenum inversum Redundant duodenum Intestinal malrotation

title: Rasmussen aneurysm: Acute haemoptysis in post-tuberculosis patient
clinical_history: A 64-year-old man with a prior history of pulmonary tuberculosis presents with an acute onset of significant haemoptysis. He mentions experiencing weight loss, tiredness, and intermittent fever. His medical history is unremarkable, except for tuberculosis, which was treated a decade ago. A chest X-ray performed recently demonstrated cavitary abnormalities.
imaging_findings: CT angiography provided the main findings, consisting of a localised aneurysm of a pulmonary artery branch located near a tuberculous cavity (Figures 2a and 2b), representing the aneurysm. Hyperdense opacity with surrounding haematoma indicates active bleeding, while multiple air locules within the opacity are characteristic of a tuberculous cavity (Figures 1a and 1b), distinguishing it from other pulmonary lesions. Centrilobular ground-glass nodules may be observed around the haematoma, suggesting endobronchial dissemination of blood (Figure 4). Post-contrast imaging reveals focal enhancement of the aneurysm, aiding in precise assessment of its size, shape, and location (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c).
discussion: Background Rasmussen aneurysm is defined as an inflammatory pseudoaneurysmal dilatation of a pulmonary artery branch situated adjacent to or within a tuberculous cavity (Figures 1a, 1b, 3a, 3b, and 3c). This entity arises during the reparative phase of tuberculosis as a consequence of a progressive degradation of the arterial wall. Histopathologically, the adventitial and medial layers are replaced by granulation tissue, which subsequently transitions into fibrin, resulting in thinning of the arterial wall, segmental pseudoaneurysm formation, and potential rupture. These aneurysms predominantly localise to the upper lobes and exhibit a peripheral distribution pattern [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Rasmussen aneurysm can cause life-threatening haemoptysis. Patients commonly present with haemoptysis as a clinical manifestation during the progression of the disease, ranging from blood-streaked sputum to massive haemorrhage [2]. However, haemorrhage is often treated through conservative treatment and interventional radiological procedures [3]. Imaging Perspective Computed tomography angiography (CTA) is the imaging modality of choice for Rasmussen aneurysms, offering high-resolution visualisation of vascular and pulmonary structures. In our case, imaging reveals a well-circumscribed aneurysm originating from the branches of the pulmonary artery (Figures 2a, 2b, and 5). Pulmonary angiography may show the aneurysm arising from the pulmonary artery branches with active bleeding. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) can be used to confirm the diagnosis and guide embolisation. The final diagnosis is made by correlating clinical and radiological findings [2,4]. Outcome Therapeutic strategies for managing Rasmussen aneurysm include conservative management and radiological interventions such as bronchial artery embolisation (BAE) in patients presenting with bronchopulmonary artery shunting and surgical excision [5]. Direct embolisation of the aneurysm through the pulmonary artery provides effective haemorrhage control in cases where the aneurysm is not connected to bronchial or systemic arteries. For peripheral aneurysms, transthoracic percutaneous embolisation has been reported as a viable alternative to endovascular techniques. Surgical resection is reserved for select cases, particularly those with adequate pulmonary reserve and recurrent, life-threatening haemoptysis refractory to other treatments. The majority of patients experience rapid clinical improvement following embolisation or conservative therapy [3,4]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Rasmussen aneurysm represents an uncommon yet potentially life-threatening complication of tuberculosis. Clinicians must maintain a high degree of suspicion in patients presenting with haemoptysis and a prior history of tuberculosis. Computed tomography angiography is the diagnostic modality of choice for diagnosis. Transarterial embolisation is considered the first-line treatment, providing effective haemorrhage control and improved clinical outcomes. Despite these measures, the prognosis remains unfavourable in many cases, even with aggressive surgical intervention. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Spontaneous extra-pleural haematoma in an anticoagulated patient
clinical_history: An 81-year-old male patient on anticoagulation therapy, with a history of hip fracture and acute renal insufficiency, underwent a standard chest X-ray as part of the preoperative evaluation for a total hip replacement. He was asymptomatic on the respiratory level, with no dyspnoea or chest pain.
imaging_findings: The initial X-ray revealed a likely pleural right peripheral opacity with smooth borders and no acute angles (Figure 1). A CT scan was then performed, demonstrating an extra-pleural collection measuring 30 × 72 × 87 mm (AP × TR × CC). The collection was spontaneously hyperdense, suggesting the presence of blood or fluid with a high protein content. Additionally, the “extra-pleural fat sign” was observed, confirming an extra-pleural process rather than a pleural or lung lesion (Figures 2 and 3). In the presence of renal insufficiency and an extra-pleural mass, contrast injection was not performed. Consequently, a mass with potential bleeding could not be definitively ruled out, and an MRI was conducted. T1-weighted MRI images showed the extra-pleural collection appearing hyperintense due to the presence of blood products (Figure 4). In T2-weighted images, the lesion was mildly hyperintense, consistent with the presence of subacute haemorrhage or an organised haematoma (Figure 5). On diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), a hyperintense signal with ADC restriction was observed (Figures 6a and 6b). After gadolinium injection, a peripheral enhancement of the lesion’s capsule was observed, with no enhancement observed within the lesion itself (Figure 7). This supports the primary haemorrhagic nature of the lesion rather than an inflammatory or neoplastic process. Non-contrast CT and MRI scans of the thorax were performed using T1, T2, DWI, and T1 fat-saturated gadolinium sequences in a Philips Ingenia 1.5T high-field MRI scanner and a Philips Incisive 32-slice CT scanner.
discussion: An extra-pleural haematoma (EPH) is a rare condition characterised by the accumulation of blood in the space outside the pleura, typically resulting from trauma, anticoagulation therapy, or surgical procedures [1]. Although these haematomas can occur in various clinical settings, they remain infrequent, particularly in the absence of trauma. The clinical presentation of extra-pleural haematomas is often subtle, with patients experiencing non-specific symptoms such as chest pain or respiratory distress. The recognition of extra-pleural haematomas can be difficult due to their resemblance to other pleural and lung pathologies. They typically present as well-defined, hyperdense collections on CT scans, which are often associated with an extra-pleural fat layer. This fat layer helps to differentiate them from interpleural processes such as effusions or lung tumours, which are more commonly seen in clinical practice [2]. On MRI, the haematoma typically appears hyperintense on T1-weighted images due to the presence of blood products. In T2-weighted images, it may show varying intensities, often appearing hypointense when the haemorrhage is organised or older. Haematomas typically show hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with restricted ADC values in the subacute stage. This occurs due to the intracellular presence of methaemoglobin, which limits water mobility and causes diffusion restriction. The absence of enhancement after fat-saturated gadolinium administration, further supports the diagnosis of a haematoma, distinguishing it from neoplastic or inflammatory processes. While CT scans remain the gold standard for detecting extra-pleural haematomas, MRI should be recommended for evaluating these cases. It not only provides complementary information on the age of the haemorrhage and its organisation but also plays a crucial role in ruling out underlying pathological processes, which can help guide treatment decisions and reduce the need for unnecessary biopsies.

title: Elevated lipase in a patient with melanoma treated with nivolumab
clinical_history: A 55-year-old male, with skin melanoma (IIIc), on adjuvant immunotherapy with nivolumab since 6 months, previously without comorbidities, presented with >5-fold increase in serum lipase and an onset of diabetes . Nivolumab was suspended till lipase decreased. After the reintroduction of nivolumab, another elevation of lipase and abdominal pain were noted.
imaging_findings: Computed tomography showed diffuse pancreatic parenchymal enlargement, heterogeneity (Figure 1), and slightly increased peripancreatic fat attenuation. There were no radiological signs of cholelithiasis or cholecystitis. Additionally, diffuse colon and rectal wall thickening and hyperenhancement were reported (Figure 2), as well as a triangular enhancement defect in the left kidney (Figure 3). At the second onset of symptoms, MRI was performed, demonstrating pancreatic volume increase, with signal alterations on T2-weighted images, especially in the pancreatic head, and diffuse restricted diffusion (Figures 4a, 4b, 5, 6a, and 6b). Additionally, mildly expressed peripancreatic and mesenteric fat stranding was noted. No pancreatic duct or biliary tree dilatation was observed. There were no fluid collections, free abdominal fluid or adenopathy.
discussion: Background Acute pancreatitis, a potentially life-threatening disease, is diagnosed based on radiological and clinical features, including >3-fold elevation of lipase or amylase above limit levels [1]. Nivolumab is a human monoclonal antibody, acting as a programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) inhibitor, that was proven beneficial for the treatment of melanoma and other malignancies [2]. The capacity of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) to alter pro and anti-inflammatory balance is used to boost anti-cancer response, though, with an associated risk of adverse events (AEs) [2], such as immune-related pancreatitis, defined as pancreatic inflammation with no other documented cause [3,4]. It is a T-cell-mediated process, yet the exact mechanism remains undetermined [5]. It is more often observed when: using cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA-4) than PD-1 agents; when combining CTLA-4 and PD-1 agents than in monotherapy; and, finally, in melanoma than in other oncologic diseases [5]. Clinical Perspective At first, the patient presented with acute inflammation, resembling interstitial oedematous pancreatitis. Symptoms worsened following the reintroduction of nivolumab, suggesting a recurrent or chronic process, as observed by Kramer et al. [6]. After the final discontinuation of Nivolumab, symptoms and morphological changes resolved (Figures 7, 8a, and 8b), except for diabetes, requiring insulin therapy. Adverse events, regardless of ICIs effectiveness in tumour treatment, may result in cessation of therapy, leading to patient’s death [5], as in the demonstrated case, where melanoma progressed with multiple metastases. Imaging Perspective When immune-related pancreatitis is suspected, radiological studies should be performed, even if they may not reveal any changes, to exclude other causes of pancreatic inflammation , such as choledocholithiasis . Oncology specialists recommend using ultrasonography, CT and MRI, followed, if needed, by endosonography with biopsies [3]. ICI-related pancreatitis presents: parenchymal heterogeneity, volume increase, hypoenhancement, peripancreatic fat stranding, compatible with interstitial oedematous pancreatitis [6] , or any finding known from other types of pancreatitis [7] . Additionally, intestinal wall thickening, hyperenhancement, vasa recta engorgement, bowel distension, and attenuation or signal changes in renal parenchyma may be noted, revealing colitis/enterocolitis or renal involvement [7–9]. Outcome American and European societies recommend cessation of ICIs therapy in severe acute immune-related pancreatitis [3,10]. There are limited data concerning pharmacotherapy. Positive results were obtained with corticosteroids [5]. Immunosuppressants and biologics were applied in management of challenging ICI-related pancreatitis [5,6]. Teaching points When a patient treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) presents with clinical and/or radiological signs of pancreatic inflammation, immune-related pancreatitis should be investigated. ICI-related pancreatitis is a diagnosis of exclusion. A temporary or permanent treatment discontinuation has to be considered, depending on clinical and radiological data. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Splenic tail
clinical_history: A 46-year-old male patient presented to our department for routine follow-up imaging after left radical orchiectomy 19 years earlier due to a testicular germ cell tumour, and with retroperitoneal recurrence 11 years after surgery. He had a previous history of left orchidopexy during childhood to repair cryptorchidism.
imaging_findings: In this patient, who underwent a left radical orchiectomy for a testicular germ cell tumour, the abdominal-pelvic computed tomography (CT) revealed tubular-shaped splenic tissue along the left paracolic gutter, representing a retroperitoneal splenic cord connecting the spleen to the remaining mesonephric structure in the left lower quadrant (Figures 1a to 1i). Additionally, this condition was associated with congenital absence of lower limbs (Figure 2). Retrospectively, the described abdominal features were considered stable compared to the oldest examination available in our database, which was performed at the time of the retroperitoneal recurrence (Figures 3a to 3f).
discussion: Splenogonadal fusion (SGF) is a rare congenital malformation characterised by an abnormal connection between the spleen and a gonad or other mesonephric derivative. It can be continuous (the spleen and the gonad are linked by a cord of splenic tissue or fibrous band – 55% of the cases) or discontinuous (splenic tissue is present in the gonad but without connection to the orthotopic spleen) [1]. SGF is much more common in males (95%) and occurs almost exclusively on the left side (98%) [2]. Half of the reported cases present at less than 10 years of age, and 82% of the cases occur in patients younger than 30 [3]. The cause of SGF remains unclear, but it is thought that the inappropriate fusion occurs between the fifth and sixth weeks of gestation, before gonadal descent [2]. Congenital anomalies are present in 26% of cases of SGF. The most commonly associated abnormality is cryptorchidism (31%) [2]. Other associated congenital anomalies are micrognathia, cleft palate, facial muscle agenesis, cardiac defects, thoracopagus, osteogenesis imperfecta, anorectal abnormalities, limb defects, and spina bifida [1–3]. SGF is often an incidental diagnosis while exploring the inguinal region for cryptorchidism or hernia [1]. Sometimes it presents as a scrotal mass, which can mimic a testicular neoplasm and may lead to unnecessary orchiectomy [2,3]. On ultrasound, SGF may appear as a homogeneous, hypoechoic, extratesticular solid mass (overlapping features with testicular malignancies). On colour, Doppler may show a central feeding vessel with a branching pattern, different from the “criss-cross” pattern typically seen in malignant tumours. However, any pattern of vascularity within a scrotal mass is potentially suspicious [2]. CT also has diagnostic value for SGF: a homogeneously enhancing, noncalcified, soft-tissue mass with similar density to the spleen may suggest SGF in the appropriate clinical context [2]. The most accurate preoperative imaging is technetium-99m scintigraphy, which demonstrates uptake in splenic tissue. Increased fixation of the radioactive tracer within the scrotum may indicate the diagnosis of SGF if there is strong clinical suspicion [2,3]. Radiologists must be familiar with this entity and its imaging characteristics, as SGF is a rare cause of testicular swelling or mass. Recognising it can, in some cases, help avoid unnecessary radical orchiectomy. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Non-ischemic cerebral enhancing (NICE) lesions
clinical_history: Five days after an uncomplicated embolisation of an asymptomatic, growing right middle cerebral artery (MCA) aneurysm, a 56-year-old woman comes to the ER due to headache, a seizure and fluctuant left upper extremity weakness and left campimetric defects. A Todd’s paralysis is suspected, and the patient is admitted for a workup.
imaging_findings: Initially, a brain CT is performed, which shows no significant abnormalities apart from the embolisation material (Figure 1). Then a brain MRI is performed, including the following sequences: DWI (Figures 2a and 2b), SWI (Figure 3), T2, FLAIR (Figure 4), 3D TOF and pre and post-gadolinium T1 (Figures 5a and 5b). The MRI discloses multiple round lesions varying in size in the right hemisphere. The lesions are spontaneously T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense, the largest ones showing a small, central T2 hypointensity. Post-gadolinium enhancement is demonstrated in all the lesions. No restricted diffusion or susceptibility artefacts are present. Follow-up imaging after 6 months (Figures 6, 7, 8a, and 8b) shows overall improvement with resolution of the enhancing foci. However, T2 hyperintensity is still present, and central punctate susceptibility artefacts have appeared, interpreted as microhaemorrhagic foci.
discussion: Background & Clinical Perspective Non-ischemic cerebral enhancing (NICE) lesions are a rare complication of neuroendovascular therapy. They consist of granulomatous reactions to small foreign body particles that are embolised from devices used during the procedure (a PVP catheter coating appears to be responsible), with vascular involvement, and may cause micro to macrohaemorrhagic complications [1,2]. Patients usually suffer headaches and focal neurologic symptoms, including both seizures and deficits (campimetric defects, paresis, etc.) that develop days to weeks (7 weeks on average [3]) after an often uncomplicated endovascular procedure. An incidence of about 0.6–1% has been reported [2,4]. Imaging Perspective MRI is the modality of choice. Typical findings consist of multiple, patchy, round-shaped lesions, variable in size (often punctate), commonly affecting the territory irrigated by the artery that has been subject to endovascular treatment. White matter, grey matter and leptomeninges may be affected. Lesions are typically T2 hyperintense with a central iso or hypointense component. They are characteristically T1 hypointense with marked punctiform or ring-like gadolinium enhancement. DWI signal is variable. Some lesions may show low SWI signal intensity as a result of haemorrhage. NICE lesions may sometimes be distributed in a way that mimics watershed infarcts (although, most frequently, there are lesions outside watershed areas). However, NICE lesions often show no or mild restriction to diffusion and contrast uptake, unlike acute infarcts. Subacute infarcts may show enhancement. Nonetheless, a punctate or ring-like enhancement is more suggestive of NICE lesions. A round T2 hyperintensity with a central T2 hypointensity also suggests NICE lesions. The clinical scenario is also very helpful. Brain CT scans could show no abnormalities (as in this case) or disclose small hypodense areas [1–4]. Outcome Management consists mainly of corticosteroids to tackle the inflammatory response. Antiplatelet medication is often adjusted to prevent haemorrhagic complications [2]. Radiological and clinical evolution is heterogeneous and unpredictable, with a variable degree of improvement or stability being the most common outcome. Few patients recover completely, while a progression of symptoms has also been reported [2–4]. This patient was discharged after a week, upon clinical improvement. Six months later, her paresis had resolved, and she was independent, although moderate memory impairment and speech difficulties were present. Teaching Points NICE lesions should be suspected upon headache, malaise and/or focal neurologic symptoms appearing days or weeks after a neuroendovascular procedure, regardless of no immediate complications having taken place. Untreated lesions could lead to severe neurologic dysfunction. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Non-ischemic cerebral enhancing (NICE) lesions Subacute cerebral infarcts Cerebral microabscesses Brain metastases
