title: Pro-B cell lymphoblastic leukaemia presenting with multiorgan metastasis in a child
clinical_history: A 2-year-old female was admitted to the emergency department due to a 2-week history of constipation, drooling, and left eye strabismus due to oculomotor nerve paralysis. Further physical examination without clinically significant findings. Initial laboratory tests upon admission showed white blood count (WBC), neutrophils, and lymphocytes within normal ranges.
imaging_findings: An initial contrast-enhanced CT scan of the brain (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d) showed a lesion that extended to cranial structures and temporal lobes, involving deep neck spaces. An initial contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominal CT scan (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d) showed pleural thickening, subpleural nodules, pancreatic lesions with dilated pancreatic duct calibre, bilateral renal cortical lesions, and a right paraspinal lesion invading the spinal canal at L2–L3 with nerve roots involvement, suggestive of metastasis. Pelvic lymphadenopathies were identified. A 2-month follow-up contrast-enhanced MRI (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d) revealed a smaller lesion compared to the previous CT, with decreased intracranial and cerebral extension and a reduced cerebral and cerebellar volume. The 2-month follow-up contrast-enhanced thoracoabdominal CT scan (Figures 4a, 4b, 4c, and 4d) showed no pleural thickening areas or subpleural nodules. The pancreas with a size reduction of the focal lesions. The pancreatic duct calibre was preserved, and the kidneys had no infiltrative lesions. Generalised reduction of pelvic lymphadenopathy. The paraspinal lesion was not visible. A not previously identified generalised fatty infiltration was shown.
discussion: Metastatic manifestations in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL), especially those involving extensive soft tissue and bone structures, as in this case, are rare and atypical. Different leukaemia subtypes show organ-specific metastasis, including involvement of bone marrow, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, central nervous system, pancreas, skin, and testes, with peak prevalence between 2 and 5 years of age [1,2]. During the patient’s first admission, the otorhinolaryngology service performed a cranial biopsy, which reported an irregular macroscopic pink lesion on the aspirate. A bone marrow aspiration was drawn, obtaining lymphoid-looking blasts. This case report highlights an unusual presentation of metastatic ALL in a two-year-old female patient diagnosed upon admission with pro-B type CD9+, CD10 neg, CD19+, CD22+, CD24+, CD38+, CD81+, CD79acy+ subjected to induction chemotherapy. Translocations panel detected T(1;19), which is assigned to a high-risk group due to poor outcome association, and a higher risk of relapse than other children [3]. The primary imaging findings demonstrated a significant response to chemotherapy, which consisted of vincristine (4 induction doses at 1.5 mg/m²), doxorubicin (2 induction doses at 25 mg/m²), and Oncaspar® (pegaspargase) (2,500 IU/m²), subsequently adding cyclophosphamide. Studies indicated a reduction in the number and extent of lesions. Two months after the initial imaging, a follow-up MRI was performed, and the cranial lesion was reduced, with decreased infiltration of craniofacial structures. However, bone involvement persisted in areas such as the left mandibular condyle, right mandibular ramus, clivus, and left sphenoid wing, likely reflecting a partial therapeutic response two months after treatment onset. This patient’s course is consistent with prior studies that report some efficacy of chemotherapy in reducing leukaemic infiltrates [4]. Fatty liver disease observed in this patient may be due to the use of chemotherapeutic agents [5]. Health-promotion initiatives [6] and combining targeted therapies with chemotherapy could reduce adverse effects such as liver damage while improving outcomes [7]. The decision to perform a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen was based on clinical urgency, anaesthesiology service availability and acquisition time. CT provided a fast and comprehensive evaluation of the abdominal organs, enabling timely detection of potential complications [8]. Additionally, a low-dose CT protocol was employed to adhere to ALARA principles while ensuring diagnostic accuracy [9]. As teaching points, we discussed unusual metastasis sites due to acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL), like the pancreas, which can complicate diagnosis and treatment. We addressed the issue of chemotherapy-related hepatotoxicity and other organ toxicities and underlined the need for close monitoring and potential modifications to treatment plans. We also stressed the importance of follow-up imaging (e.g., MRI) to assess treatment response and identify potential relapses or disease progression. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Uncovering the unexpected: An intercostal nerve schwannoma
clinical_history: In an ambulatory appointment, a 29-year-old female patient presented with chronic and persistent cough. No smoking history was referred, and the physical examination was unremarkable. An ambulatory chest x-ray was performed in our institution and further evaluation with computed tomography (CT), followed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), was later requested.
imaging_findings: The chest x-ray (Figures 1a and 1b) revealed an opacity, with rounded and well-defined borders, localised in the posterior and medial regions of the right middle lung field. Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT /Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d) revealed in the right paravertebral region, next to the posteromedial aspect of the 7 th and 8 th costal arches, a large nodular lesion, with 47 x 49 x 41 mm (L x AP x T), ovoid with regular and well-defined borders, heterogeneous and with marked peripheral contrast uptake. It is localised in an extrapulmonary topography , as it is centred on the chest wall and shows obtuse angles with the thoracic wall, and it is near proximity to nerve structures. There were no signs of invasion of adjacent structures, particularly bone structures. The contrast-enhanced thoracic MRI images (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, 3d, and 3e) confirmed the localisation and nature of the mass, further characterising it as a soft tissue lesion showing heterogeneity of signal in the T2-weighted sequences, with areas of interstitial hyperintensity and markedly heterogeneous uptake after contrast administration.
discussion: Background Neurogenic tumours can originate from various neural crest tissues, including peripheral nerves and sheaths [1]. Schwannomas, also named neurilemomas, are benign tumours that arise from Schwann cells, which are responsible for the myelin sheath that covers peripheral nerves [2]. These lesions can involve the spinal nerve roots, sympathetic chain, or peripheral nerves [3]. These tumours typically occur in the head and neck as well as involving nerves in the flexor surfaces of the upper and lower extremities. They can also occur in the posterior mediastinum [4]. Schwannomas can develop at any age but are most commonly seen in individuals between 20 and 50 years old, affecting both genders equally [3,5]. Clinical Perspective Patients may be asymptomatic or present with a variety of symptoms, often related to the compression of adjacent structures: localised pain (depending on the nerve root compressed), neurological symptoms (such as weakness, numbness, or paraesthesia may occur if the tumour compresses spinal nerves), and even respiratory symptoms, for instance, cough and even dyspnoea from the compressive effect on the airway [3]. Imaging Perspective Thoracic schwannomas can be visualised using several imaging modalities. A chest x-ray shows a well-defined nodular area of increased density in the mediastinum, requiring further evaluation using a section technique. CT is used to assess to location and nature of the lesion. Schwannomas present as well-defined masses. On non-enhanced CT, these lesions typically show attenuation slightly less than or equal to the density of muscle and punctate calcifications may be seen occasionally. The presence of low-attenuation areas in larger lesions is frequently observed and indicates hypocellularity and/or cystic degeneration. With contrast administration, they tend to exhibit most frequently heterogeneous with peripheral contrast enhancement. On MRI-weighted images, low signal intensity is observed on T1-weighted images, with high signal intensity on T2-weighted due to most frequently to cystic degeneration. After contrast administration, a heterogeneous pattern of contrast uptake is seen. In larger lesions, erosion without destruction of adjacent bone structures can be visualised, indicating the benignity of this entity [6,3,7]. The final diagnosis is established by histological evaluation, after biopsy or surgical removal. [4] Outcome The appropriate treatment is surgical excision. The prognosis is very good, as these tumours are benign and malignant transformation is very uncommon [6]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Schwannomas are benign tumours, typically solitary and a slow-growing lesion. Their detection is crucial to prevent complications, as these benign tumours can grow to reach considerable dimensions and compress nearby structures, leading to symptoms. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Cystic adventitial disease of the popliteal artery
clinical_history: A 51-year-old female patient without significant medical history presented at the Department of Vascular Surgery to rule out deep vein thrombosis (DVT). The patient complained of right-sided paraesthesia and claudication. No pulsations were felt distal to the popliteal artery.
imaging_findings: Doppler-ultrasound (US) of the right knee was performed (Figure 1). DVT was ruled out. US showed a sharply delineated hypo-echogenic lesion in close relationship with the popliteal artery. There was a narrowing of the arterial lumen with flow acceleration indicative of significant stenosis. Computed tomography angiography (CTA) (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c) showed a non-enhancing hypodense lesion, ca. 27 Hounsfield Units (HU), in keeping with a cyst in the wall of the popliteal artery. The cyst causes significant narrowing of the arterial lumen over a segment of approximately 6 cm. Based on the imaging findings, the diagnosis of cystic adventitial disease (CAD) of the popliteal artery was made, which was confirmed during surgery (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c).
discussion: CAD is a rare vascular pathology characterised by cyst formation in the adventitia of the vessel wall due to accumulation of mucinous material with secondary stenosis of the lumen. CAD was first described by Atkins and Key, predominantly affecting peripheral vessels. Most cases occur in arteries, with venous involvement being rare [1–3]. Various theories exist on the cause of CAD, but none are universally accepted. The first hypothesis is that recurrent popliteal artery trauma leads to cyst formation. Another theory suggests that pluripotent mesenchymal cells in the adventitia form cysts during embryogenesis. Finally, the synovial herniation theory suggests joint capsule damage allowing extrusion of synovial fluid into the adjacent vessel wall, leading to cyst formation [2,3]. CAD typically affects healthy middle-aged individuals, with a male/female ratio of 15:1. Intermittent claudication with approximately 20 minutes recovery time is the characteristic clinical presentation. Neurovascular examination at rest is usually normal. However, passive flexion of the knee may elicit diminished distal pulses, which is called Ishikawa’s sign [2–4]. Imaging is required for diagnosis and differential diagnosis. Doppler-US is the preferred first-line diagnostic method, showing the lesion as a hypo or anechogenic, well-defined cyst in the wall of the affected vessel, most often the popliteal artery. Narrowing of the vessel lumen with increased velocity on duplex and absent flow in the cyst is seen [3,4]. Both CT and MRI may reveal additional information regarding the size, morphology and location of the cysts in the wall of the vessel, as well as possible communication with the adjacent joint. The cyst is hypodense on CT and hypointense and hyperintense on T1 and T2-weighted images (WI), respectively. CT and MRI angiography visualise the luminal stenosis with a typical “hourglass shape”, referring to the morphology of the blood vessel narrowing with a narrow middle and wider end. Contrast enhancement is not typically seen within the cyst, but there may be mild enhancement of the surrounding arterial wall in case of associated inflammation [3,4]. Conservative management should be considered first, as spontaneous resolution is possible. However, progressive disease is the rule. Historically, surgical removal was preferred with graft interposition of the diseased segment. This offers the best long-term patency and was also performed in our case. Image-guided percutaneous aspiration is less invasive with faster recovery but with variable clinical outcomes. Endovascular procedures like angioplasty and stenting have shown disappointing outcomes [2,3]. For our patient, neuropathic complaints unfortunately persisted following surgery; in contrast, vascular flow demonstrated significant recovery.

title: Partial agenesis of the pericardium
clinical_history: A 78-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a two-week history of a persistent, non-productive cough. A chest X-ray revealed a left-sided pleural effusion. There was no evidence of fever, weight loss or night sweats. A non-enhanced chest CT scan was performed to complete the study and clarify the findings.
imaging_findings: The heart demonstrates horizontalisation and leftward deviation, with infero-posterior displacement of the apex (Figures 1 and 2). A thin pericardial line is evident over the right cardiac chambers, delineated by the presence of epicardial and pericardial fat. The identification of a pericardial recess posterior to the ascending aorta (Figure 3) further supports the presence of a complete right-sided pericardium. In contrast, the left cardiac chambers demonstrate direct apposition of the epicardium to the pulmonary parenchyma without intervening epicardial or pericardial fat (Figure 1). Lung tissue was identified in atypical locations, including between the aorta and pulmonary artery, typically occupied by the superior pericardial recess, and between the diaphragm and the left heart (Figures 4 and 5). Lateral displacement of the left atrial appendage (Figure 6) was also noted. These findings are characteristic of the absence of the left-sided pericardium. No inflammatory changes in the lung parenchyma or left pleural effusion were observed.
discussion: The pericardium typically provides structural support, friction reduction and protection for the heart, effectively isolating it from surrounding structures such as the mediastinum and lungs [1]. Typically, the pericardium is identified on computed tomography (CT) by its distinct delineation from the adjacent myocardium, facilitated by the presence of epicardial and pericardial fat layers. However, direct visualisation can be challenging, especially in younger individuals with reduced fat deposition [2]. Congenital absence of the pericardium (CAP) is a rare congenital cardiac anomaly characterised by the complete or partial absence of the pericardial sac. Variations of CAP include absence of the entire pericardium, unilateral absence (right or left) or a partial defect resembling a foramen. In nearly 80% of cases, the left-sided pericardium is partially or completely absent, while involvement of the right-sided pericardium is uncommon [1,2]. CAP is commonly discovered incidentally during cardiac or thoracic imaging performed for unrelated reasons or unexpectedly during surgical procedures. Although often asymptomatic, individuals with CAP may experience a variety of symptoms, which are frequently nonspecific. These include atypical chest pain, shortness of breath, and palpitations, with chest pain being the most commonly reported symptom [3]. Generally, patients with complete absence of the entire or just the left-sided pericardium do not require intervention [2,3]. Due to the low incidence of CAP, many clinicians and imaging specialists may lack familiarity with this condition, potentially leading to diagnostic oversights in thoracic and cardiac imaging studies.

title: Multi-organ complications of Lemierre’s syndrome
clinical_history: A 29-year-old man presented to the emergency department with fevers, right infraorbital swelling, diplopia and seizures, preceded by one week of dental and throat pain despite multiple courses of antibiotics from various dentists. Maxillofacial surgeons reviewed and requested contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) head and neck.
imaging_findings: Initial CT neck with contrast demonstrated an upper 4th tooth periapical lucency and abscess with parotid oedema. There was extensive thrombophlebitis of the right internal jugular vein and its branches with parapharyngeal inflammatory stranding and mild effacement of the right fossa of Rosenmüller; however, no retropharyngeal abscess or airway compromise. Solid nodules were partially visualised within the lung apices and subsequently characterised with a dedicated CT thorax, demonstrating extensive cavitating lung nodules in keeping with septic emboli and the diagnosis of Lemierre's syndrome. Contrast MRI, performed for confusion and 6th cranial nerve palsy, highlighted enhancement of the right abducens nerve, extension of the thrombophlebilitis to involve cavernous sinus bilaterally, and a T2/FLAIR signal abnormality within the medial right temporal lobe with peripheral ring enhancement in keeping with abscess. An MRI one week later demonstrated new borderzone infarcts with a subsequent CT angiogram highlighting an incidental right main pulmonary trunk embolism.
discussion: Background Lemierre’s syndrome is characteristically defined by a recent history of oropharyngeal infection, internal jugular vein (IJV) thrombosis and metastatic septic emboli [1,2]. Fusobacterium necrophorum is a gram-negative bacterium very responsive to beta-lactams and the most implicated organism in Lemierre’s syndrome. While the disease is rare, with a low mortality rate, it is associated with several life-threatening and altering complications. Clinical Perspective Patients typically report a primary infection of the oropharynx involving tonsils or peritonsillar tissue. Approximately two weeks later, there is a local invasion of surrounding tissue resulting in IJV thrombophlebitis. Clinical sequelae often occur around this time due to metastatic septic emboli [1]. In this case, the patient presented with twelve days of dental pain followed by fevers, worsening throat pain, right periorbital swelling and diplopia secondary to abducens nerve palsy. CECT head and neck revealed right upper tooth periapical abscess, periodontitis, right parotitis with right jugular vein and retromandibular vein thrombophlebitis. Although Lemierre’s is commonly associated with F. necrophorum [1], Candida albicans was grown from the patient’s sputum, and he tested positive for Epstein–Barr virus (EBV). Existing literature acknowledges a relationship between F. necrophorum and EBV, but this relationship is not yet understood [1]. Patients can become systemically unwell, requiring organ support in addition to management with broad-spectrum antimicrobials and anticoagulation; however, the efficacy of anticoagulation is still unclear [1]. This patient was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit for intravenous vasopressors due to vasospasm, likely secondary to bilateral narrowing of cavernous internal carotid arteries. Imaging Perspective This case highlights the importance of satisfaction of search and review areas, which, in this case, features the difficult assessment of the cavernous sinus as well as ensuring to review the edge of film on a CT angiogram to diagnose a large central pulmonary embolus. CECT neck is the gold standard diagnostic tool for Lemierre’s, as it allows for radiological diagnosis of the IJV and associated complications such as abscesses. Radiologists can advise further imaging to investigate neurological complications and look for further septic metastases and transthoracic echocardiography to rule out infective endocarditis. Outcome Despite the severity of the patient’s illness, he was discharged close to his functional baseline after an admission of 25 days, which included two weeks in intensive care. His positive outcome was likely due to the prompt request for imaging from the maxillofacial surgeons which led to a radiological diagnosis of Lemierre’s within hours of presenting.

title: Split cord malformation – A congenital finding in a geriatric patient
clinical_history: An 84-year-old woman presented with intermittent lower limb pain, sensory disturbances, and gait/balance difficulties over 1.5 years, worsening over six months. She was wheelchair-bound at presentation. The patient reported longstanding rectal incontinence but denied back pain.
imaging_findings: Initial clinical suspicion pointed to anterior spinal cord syndrome at Th11, prompting an MRI of the spine that revealed an unexpected type 2 split cord malformation (SCM), a rare congenital anomaly typically diagnosed in childhood. MRI is the modality of choice for SCM evaluation. MRI showed a sagittal cleft on the spinal cord at the level of Th8. The two hemicords appear to be ventrally attached (Figure 2) without a clear demarcation border between them (Figure 3). The scanning is otherwise unremarkable, save for age-related foraminal stenosis.
discussion: Split cord malformations (SCM) are rare spinal dysraphisms originating from embryogenic disturbances [1]. While commonly diagnosed in children, adult-onset cases occur, often due to progressive neurological compromise [5]. Distinguishing type 1 from type 2 SCMs relies on identifying the number of dural tubes: Type 1 has two separate tubes, while type 2 has a single tube containing both hemicords [1]. Type 2 SCM, characterised by two hemicords within a single dural sac, is typically milder but can still lead to significant deficits. In some cases, the fibrous septum dividing the hemicords is not visible on imaging but is confirmed surgically [1,5]. SCM may coexist with other spinal anomalies, such as tethered cord, hydromyelia, and vertebral defects [2,3]. In rare cases, vertebral abnormalities, including hemivertebrae and scoliosis, may be present, complicating diagnosis [4]. In elderly patients, SCM may remain undiagnosed for decades due to non-specific symptoms, reinforcing the importance of MRI in patients with unexplained progressive neurological deficits [2,4]. SCM in adults is poorly understood, with limited data on its progression. Vaja et al. reviewed 16 patients, including 3 adults, and found pain, lower limb weakness, gait abnormalities, and bladder dysfunction as common presentations [3]. Zaleska-Dorobisz et al. reported a case diagnosed at age 78, after decades of unrecognised symptoms, demonstrating how SCM can be overlooked in older patients, even with progressive deficits [4]. Surgical untethering is the treatment of choice for symptomatic cases, improving pain, motor function, and sphincter control [2]. However, in elderly patients, conservative management may be considered based on symptom severity and surgical risks. Take Home Message This case highlights a rare late presentation of type 2 SCM in an 84-year-old woman with progressive neurological symptoms. MRI confirmed the diagnosis, reinforcing the need to consider congenital malformations in elderly patients with unexplained deficits. SCM may remain undiagnosed for decades, as seen in prior reports, making imaging and thorough physical exams essential for earlier recognition. Surgical intervention remains the standard treatment for symptomatic cases, though management should be individualised [2,3]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Lipomatosis of the median nerve
clinical_history: A 45-year-old right-hand dominant female patient presented with a painless lump at the palmar aspect of the left wrist and hand. The lump had gradually increased in size over 4 years. She experiences mild weakness and loss of sensory sensation in the 1st to 4th fingers. The patient denied any history of trauma. On examination, the lump was soft to the touch with a positive Tinel’s sign.
imaging_findings: An ultrasound was performed, followed by regional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). These depict long segment expansion of the left median nerve from the middle of the forearm to the wrist and palmar side of the hand. The nerve fascicles are thickened and encased in fibro-fatty soft tissue (Figures 1a and 1b). On T1 and T2-weighted MRI images, hypointense thickened nerve fascicles enveloped by hyperintense fat exhibit a “coaxial cable” appearance on axial images and a “spaghetti string” appearance on sagittal and coronal images (Figures 1a, 1b, and 2), implying lipomatosis of the median nerve.
discussion: Background Lipomatosis of the nerve, also known as fibro-lipomatous hamartoma (FLH), is a peripheral nerve mass caused by mature adipocyte proliferation combined with fibroblastic tissue interspersed in twisted, enlarged nerve bundles [1]. It is a rare cause of carpal tunnel syndrome in children [2]. The most commonly affected nerve is the median nerve (>80% of cases). The other less commonly involved nerves are brachial plexus, ulnar, sciatic, peroneal, etc [3]. It is more frequently present in peripheral nerves of the upper limb than in the lower limb [4]. Its pathogenesis is unclear. Some believe it to be congenital, whereas some believe it to be acquired due to chronic irritation of the nerve [2,3]. The clinical presentation is variable and depends on its rate of growth and degree of compression of the nerve. If associated with nerve compression, it presents as a painful lesion. It could present as macrodactyly if it involves digital branches [5]. It is most commonly seen under ten years of age [6]. Imaging Perspective Usually, a soft, painless mass is seen on examination, which can be located using palpation. This is not enough for diagnosis and differentiating it from other similar pathologies [2]. Imaging gives us valuable insight and helps us in narrowing down the differential diagnosis. Often, radiographs are normal or can show non-specific findings such as soft-tissue thickening [8]. Ultrasound and MRI are the most crucial imaging tools for diagnosis. A distinctive hypoechoic coaxial nerve fibre cabling covered in an echogenic fatty substratum is seen on ultrasound. No intra-lesional vascularity is noted on Doppler imaging [6–9]. MRI demonstrates hyperintense signal on T1/T2 sequences with a signal drop on fat-suppression sequence [8]. The fibrous component of the lesion displays T2 hypointense signal. On axial images, a co-axial cable-like appearance is noted. MRI imaging feature of spaghetti-like appearance on coronal images is pathognomic for this benign neoplasm [10,11]. Outcome In view of its benign nature, a conservative approach is recommended for asymptomatic cases [12,13]. If the patient is experiencing pain due to carpal tunnel syndrome, carpal tunnel release followed by nerve biopsy is the recommended treatment. Prognosis has been mixed, with a high complication rate after excision in the form of loss of nerve function [3]. Take Home Message Lipomatosis of the median nerve is a rare benign tumour involving the median nerve most frequently [10]. Ultrasound and MRI imaging play a pivotal role in diagnosis and follow-up [8,10,11]. Conservative treatment is preferred for asymptomatic cases [10]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Widespread gastrointestinal contrast following enteral potassium binder administration
clinical_history: A 74-year-old man with a history of bilateral urolithiasis was admitted to the hospital with a severe acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia secondary to urosepsis. He received intravenous antibiotics and medical management for hyperkalaemia, including intravenous insulin and oral sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) prior to initiation of haemodialysis.
imaging_findings: A renal tract ultrasound demonstrated right-sided hydronephrosis. A ureteric stent was fluoroscopically placed for obstructed pyelonephritis, after which the patient became febrile, hypotensive, and delirious. An abdominal x-ray was performed to check the stent position. The abdominal x-ray (Figures 1a and 1b) shows bilateral urolithiasis, a right-sided retrograde ureteric stent, a right-sided femoral venous catheter and a urinary catheter. There is also contrast material throughout the colon and rectum. This was concerning for iatrogenic puncture of the gastrointestinal tract during fluoroscopic ureteric stent placement. A non-contrast CT was performed. The CT images of the abdomen (Figures 2a, 2b, 3a, 3b, 4a, and 4b) confirm the presence of dense radiopaque material in the large bowel. It also shows a right-sided renal subcapsular haematoma. There is no intraperitoneal contrast, free fluid, or gas to suggest gastrointestinal perforation.
discussion: The presence of contrast throughout the gastrointestinal tract in this patient was highly concerning for iatrogenic perforation of the bowel during stent placement, which may have required significant surgery. In this case, the CT thankfully excluded perforation. When contrast is seen in the gastrointestinal tract it is important to consider complications of previous fluoroscopic procedures, but also ingestion of radiopaque material. To our knowledge, the patient had not undergone any procedure involving oral contrast ingestion. A comprehensive review of the patient’s medication was undertaken. Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) is a novel medication approved for medical management of hyperkalaemia [1], reducing serum potassium levels by 0.46 to 1.1 mEq/L over 48 hours [2]. Radiopacity of SZC has been demonstrated by a group who performed a CT scan on a plastic bag containing SZC and demonstrated that the ex-vivo SZC had similar absorption of Hounsfield units compared to those measured from contrast material with the gastrointestinal tract on a CT scan from a patient who had recently ingested SZC [3]. Radiopacity of SZC is known and is included in the product characteristics [4], but in our experience, this is not widely known by clinicians prescribing this medicine. Take Home Message / Teaching Points SZC (Lokelma®) is a novel medication entering widespread use in patients with hyperkalaemia. Its use must be noted when requesting, performing or interpreting scans in this patient group. When contrast is noted in the bowel or other unexplained places, a comprehensive review of the patient’s medication is vital. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
differential_diagnosis: Haemorrhage as a result of stent placement Gastrointestinal perforation Ingestion of sodium zirconium cyclosilicate Ingestion of radiopaque medication (calcium carbonate, amiodarone, or ferrous sulphate) [5,6]

title: Duplex collecting system with ectopic ureter
clinical_history: A 62-year-old woman with a history of right supernumerary kidney nephrectomy presented with two days of left lumbar pain radiating to the groin, recurrent pyelonephritis, and mild haematuria. Vital signs were stable, with left flank tenderness. Labs showed elevated CRP (8.11 mg/dL), leukocytosis (17.4 x10⁹/L), and bacteriuria. Urinalysis revealed haemoglobin +++, leukocytes ++, and multi-sensitive E. coli on culture.
imaging_findings: A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan was performed. The imaging revealed a right kidney of normal size and morphology, with cortical irregularity in the upper pole and surgical clips in the renal hilum (Figure 1), consistent with a previous nephrectomy of a supernumerary kidney. The left kidney was of normal size and morphology. Adjacent to the medial aspect of the upper pole, a solid lesion with punctate calcifications was noted (Figures 2a and 2b), giving rise to a second ureter (Figures 3a and 3b), likely associated with an atrophic supernumerary kidney. The non-functioning ureter appeared to drain into the urethra, with no identifiable outlet at the bladder level (Figures 4a and 4b). There was dilation of the distal third of the non-functioning ureter, measuring up to 18 mm in transverse diameter, with wall thickening and enhancement, suggestive of ureteritis (Figures 5a, 5b and 5c).
discussion: Background The ureters transport urine from the kidneys to the bladder, typically inserting at the vesical trigone. While renal anomalies are common, ureteral ectopia is rare. Clinical presentation varies: in males, it is often asymptomatic; in females, it may cause recurrent urinary tract infections and incontinence. The collecting system begins forming in the fourth week of gestation, with the ureteral bud evolving into the renal system. Ectopia is frequently associated with a duplex collecting system, where two ureteral buds or a bifurcated bud result in dual systems [1]. Ectopic ureters insert beyond the vesical trigone and occur in 1 in 1900 cases, predominantly in females (5:1) [2]. A supernumerary kidney (SK) arises from abnormal nephrogenic cord division during the fifth to seventh weeks of gestation. SKs are often asymptomatic but can cause complications such as pain, incontinence, pyelonephritis, and calculi [3]. Most ectopic ureters are linked to duplex systems, often with dysplastic upper poles. Surgical management aims to preserve renal function, restore continence, and prevent infections [4]. Clinical Perspective In males, ectopic ureters insert above the external sphincter, avoiding incontinence. Common sites include the bladder, prostatic urethra, seminal vesicles, or epididymis. In females, they may bypass the sphincter, causing incontinence, with insertions in the urethra, vagina, or uterus [5]. Symptoms in both sexes include urinary obstruction, infections, and dysplasia of the duplex system’s upper pole. A non-functional ectopic ureter in a duplex system may explain recurrent urinary infections, lumbar pain, and poor drainage, as observed in this case [6]. Imaging Perspective The patient’s history of right supernumerary kidney nephrectomy and Uro-CT findings, including cortical defects, calcifications, and a duplicated system, confirmed the diagnosis. Delayed-phase imaging demonstrated ureteral functionality, while thickened ureteral walls suggested infection [7]. Outcome A 62-year-old patient with recurrent infections had an ectopic ureter draining from an atrophic SK into the posterior urethra. Imaging revealed poor drainage and inflammation, consistent with the observed symptoms of haematuria and bacteriuria. Surgical resection of the non-functional ureter was indicated to prevent further infections and preserve renal function. Teaching Points Imaging, particularly abdominal CT, is essential in diagnosing congenital anomalies like ectopic ureters. Ectopic ureters, though rare, can have significant clinical implications, especially in females. A multidisciplinary approach combining imaging, history, and surgical intervention ensures effective management. Awareness of congenital anomalies aids in early diagnosis and prevents complications such as pyelonephritis or chronic kidney disease.

title: The hidden loop: Uncovering a lateral meniscus enigma
clinical_history: A 42-year-old male athlete presented with significant knee discomfort and episodes of locking after a rapid directional change during a football match. Physical assessment revealed tenderness along the joint line and a restricted range of motion. The Lachman test was negative, although meniscal tests showed a lesion of the lateral meniscus.
imaging_findings: Left knee magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a bucket-handle tear of the lateral meniscus. The sagittal proton density-weighted sequence showed a displaced meniscal fragment in the intercondylar notch, resulting in a classic “double posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) sign” and “double delta sign” (Figure 1). The “flipped meniscus sign” (Figure 2), “absent bow tie sign”, and “ghost meniscus sign” (Figure 3) were also present, supporting the diagnosis. No tears, sprains, or surrounding oedema of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) were observed. Coronal T2-weighted images showed decreased body volume and high signal of the meniscus body, with the residual lateral meniscus being displaced into the intercondylar notch (Figure 4), which corroborates the diagnosis. Axial sequences confirmed the lateral meniscal tear, with the displaced meniscal fragment well seen in the intercondylar notch. It also shows high within the lateral meniscus body (Figure 5). There was no associated oedema, bone contusion, or other abnormal findings. These collective imaging features, in the absence of significant knee joint effusion, support the diagnosis of an isolated bucket-handle tear of the lateral meniscus, with no associated ACL injury.
discussion: Background Bucket-handle tears of the lateral meniscus are a distinct type of meniscal injury characterised by a vertical longitudinal tear with the displacement of a meniscal fragment into the intercondylar notch, resembling the handle of a bucket [1]. These tears are relatively uncommon, representing 10%–30% of all meniscal tears, with a higher prevalence in the medial meniscus compared to the lateral meniscus [2,3]. Lateral bucket-handle tears are particularly rare, occurring approximately seven times less frequently than their medial counterparts [4]. The incidence of these injuries is notably higher in younger individuals, often associated with trauma, although spontaneous cases have been reported in children [5]. These tears frequently occur in conjunction with ACL injuries, complicating clinical evaluation and influencing treatment strategies [6]. The relationship between bucket-handle tears and ACL injuries underscores the need for careful assessment to determine the best surgical and long-term management. However, lateral bucket-handle tears may also present as isolated injuries, a pattern that differs from the more common medial tears, which are typically associated with ACL ruptures [2]. Clinical Perspective The clinical significance of these injuries is substantial, as they often manifest with mechanical symptoms such as knee locking, clicking, and instability. If left untreated, these tears can lead to the early onset of osteoarthritis due to compromised joint biomechanics. The lateral meniscus plays a vital role in load distribution, joint stabilisation, and shock absorption, making the timely recognition and management of these injuries critical. Imaging Perspective MRI is essential for diagnosing bucket-handle tears, although its sensitivity can vary significantly, ranging between 84% and 93% [7]. Several characteristic MRI signs, such as the “absent bow tie” sign, “double PCL” sign, and “flipped meniscus” sign, aid in identifying these injuries [7,8]. However, diagnosing lateral meniscus bucket-handle tears can be challenging due to the complex anatomy of the lateral meniscus and its proximity to structures like the popliteal hiatus and the lateral inferior geniculate artery. Outcome Surgical intervention is generally indicated for bucket-handle tears to restore joint mechanics and prevent long-term degenerative changes. Repair techniques are preferred over meniscectomy whenever possible to preserve the functional role of the meniscus. Early and accurate diagnosis facilitated by MRI and supported by clinical correlation ensures the best outcomes. Radiologists play a pivotal role in identifying these injuries and providing detailed evaluations to guide surgical planning. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
differential_diagnosis: Bucket-handle tear of the lateral meniscus Intra-articular loose body Displaced flap tear of meniscus
final_diagnosis: Bucket-handle tear of the lateral meniscus

title: Bilateral choroidal detachment with recurrent posterior scleritis secondary to sarcoidosis
clinical_history: A 75-year-old female presented with a four-day history of sudden onset frontal headache, vomiting, ophthalmalgia, photophobia and blurred vision. Her past medical history included migraines, right-sided phacoemulsion and an intraocular lens implant six years ago. Fundoscopy demonstrated choroidal folds and effusions. Laboratory blood workup revealed only elevated serum ACE levels.
imaging_findings: Initial computerised tomography (CT) head imaging and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head were unremarkable. Specifically, CT did not identify any orbital pathology. MRI of the orbits revealed bilateral effusions in the suprachoroidal space, with low signal intensity on T1 sequences (Figure 1) and high-intensity signal on T2 sequences (Figure 2). Findings were more pronounced on the right side. Effusions extended anteriorly past the ora serrata. Contrast-enhanced sequences with fat suppression visualised choroidal and scleral enhancement (Figure 3). There was no evidence of intraocular mass or retinal detachment. A subsequent high-resolution CT chest scan revealed biapical scarring, mild bronchial wall thickening and subtle fissure nodularity in the upper zones (Figure 4) and a 10 mm subcarinal lymph node (Figure 5). Thoracic imaging findings were non-specific and equivocal for sarcoidosis.
discussion: Background Choroidal detachment (CD) describes the separation of the choroid from the sclera arising from fluid accumulation within the suprachoroidal space. Although CD is typically a complication following trabeculectomy, it can be secondary to trauma and inflammation, including scleritis and neoplasms [1,2]. Posterior scleritis (PS) describes scleral inflammation posterior to the insertion of the rectus muscles accounting for 6% of cases of scleritis. Most patients present with unilateral symptoms. Bilateral choroidal detachment is a rare and unusual presentation [3,4]. Clinical Perspective Clinical presentation in conjunction with fundoscopy can reveal PS as a differential diagnosis, and tonometry can aid in excluding acute glaucoma, which may be clinically similar. PS is associated with systemic inflammatory conditions, including vasculitis, rheumatoid arthritis and sarcoidosis, requiring comprehensive immunology screening to obtain a diagnosis [5]. Imaging Perspective MRI of the orbits have higher sensitivity compared to CT in visualising suprachoroidal space effusions. B-scan ultrasonography has higher sensitivity in distinguishing between choroidal effusions and retinal detachment and remains the most useful confirmatory investigation to diagnose retinal and choroidal detachment [6,7], although ocular ultrasound is most often performed by ophthalmologists. Radiologists should also be able to differentiate between choroidal detachment and retinal detachment on cross-sectional imaging, which may appear similar on first inspection. In choroidal detachment, there is extension past the ora serrata anteriorly and posteriorly, and there is divergence at the optic disc. The reverse is true for retinal detachment. Outcome Although our patient’s symptoms improved with prednisolone, she had multiple relapsing episodes of PS and CD following the completion of courses of oral steroids. With equivocal radiological findings of sarcoidosis, pulmonary physicians eventually diagnosed our patient with isolated extra-pulmonary sarcoidosis with posterior scleritis. Sarcoidosis is a multi-systemic non-caseating granulomatous disorder of unknown aetiology, typically affecting adults aged between 30 and 50, with most patients eliciting pulmonary involvement [8]. Ophthalmic sarcoidosis can develop in the absence of any notable systemic involvement although posterior scleritis is a rare and unusual manifestation [9,10]. Take Home Message Physicians should consider choroidal detachment in patients presenting with visual disturbances, which can be demonstrated on fundoscopy and confirmed with MRI. In instances of posterior scleritis, physicians should be aware of multi-systemic inflammatory diseases to ensure patients get prompt and appropriate management. Our patient had multiple relapses of PS whilst off steroids prior to her diagnosis of sarcoidosis. Other differentials include IgG4-related disease, ruled out by serum IgG4 levels and histopathology, and Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada (VKH) syndrome, excluded based on the absence of bilateral panuveitis and characteristic skin or neurological findings [11]. Teaching Points Physicians should be aware of choroidal detachment in patients presenting with ophthalmalgia. Radiologists should be able to differentiate between choroidal and retinal detachment on cross-sectional imaging. Bilateral posterior scleritis can be secondary to sarcoidosis with minimal respiratory involvement. Ocular sarcoidosis is a diagnostic challenge, and physicians should have a low threshold for suspicion Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
differential_diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematous Choroidal detachment and posterior scleritis Acute glaucoma Sarcoidosis IgG4 related disease Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome

title: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria
clinical_history: A 73-year-old woman presented with abdominal pain, mild jaundice and dark urine for 3 days. Initial blood tests revealed anaemia and elevation of serum creatinine, total bilirubin, and lactate dehydrogenase. Further analytical evaluation excluded autoimmune and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemias. Flow cytometry analysis of peripheral blood showed a deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins. Abdominal ultrasound did not reveal any significant findings, so an abdominal magnetic resonance (MRI) was subsequently conducted.
imaging_findings: MRI excluded acute biliary pathology but revealed abnormal bilateral renal cortical hypointensity on both T2 (Figure 1) and T1-weighted (Figure 2) sequences. In gradient-recalled echo (GRE) imaging, the renal cortex demonstrated a relative increase in signal intensity on the out-of-phase sequence (Figure 3) compared to the in-phase sequence (Figure 2). Reduced cortical enhancement was observed after intravenous contrast administration (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c). The spleen and liver showed no significant parenchymal signal abnormalities (Figure 5). Isolated renal haemosiderosis was presumed. Abdominal ultrasound and computed tomography did not reveal significant abnormalities.
discussion: Background Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) is a rare, nonmalignant clonal haematological disorder characterised by a deficiency of GPI-linked complement regulators on the membranes of haematopoietic cells, rendering them susceptible to complement-mediated damage [1,2]. Haemosiderin accumulation resulting from intravascular haemolysis occurs exclusively in the kidneys and is common in PNH [3]. Clinical Perspective PNH presents with symptoms such as fatigue, jaundice, dark urine (particularly in the morning), and abdominal pain. Hallmark features of the disease include intravascular haemolysis, an increased tendency for thrombosis, and bone marrow failure, which contribute to significant morbidity and mortality [1,4]. Renal dysfunction often manifests as acute kidney injury or chronic kidney disease [5]. Imaging Perspective In renal cortical haemosiderosis, signal intensity changes are attributed to the superparamagnetic properties of haemosiderin. On T1-weighted imaging, the renal cortex appears hypointense due to T1 shortening, while the medulla retains its normal signal, leading to reversed cortex-medulla differentiation. On T2-weighted imaging, the cortex also appears hypointense as haemosiderin significantly reduces T2 relaxation time. In gradient-recalled echo (GRE) imaging, differences between in-phase (IP) and out-of-phase (OOP) sequences are notable: the cortex appears darker on IP due to longer echo times amplifying T2* effects, while it appears relatively brighter on OOP as shorter echo times reduce these effects [3]. Although renal haemosiderosis is a hallmark of PNH, it can also be observed in other haemolytic anaemias. However, unlike most haemolytic anaemias (e.g., sickle cell disease, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, and hereditary spherocytosis), PNH involves minimal contribution from the reticuloendothelial system to red blood cell destruction. Consequently, liver and spleen signal intensity remains normal in PNH unless transfusion-related iron overload or vascular thrombosis is present [3,6]. Outcome Treatment for PNH depends on symptom severity. Mild cases may require only folic acid or iron supplements. Anticoagulation is essential for thrombosis prevention in high-risk patients. Severe cases benefit from eculizumab, an anticomplement agent that reduces haemolysis and improves quality of life. Bone marrow transplantation offers a potential cure for severe or refractory cases [1,2]. Take Home Message PNH is a rare, acquired cause of intravascular haemolysis. Although renal involvement is uncommon, it can lead to chronic kidney failure due to cortical haemosiderin deposits and microvascular thrombosis. The diagnosis of PNH is challenging due to nonspecific clinical manifestations, but MRI can aid in narrowing the differential diagnosis by identifying the characteristic pattern of isolated renal haemosiderosis.

title: Radiopathological features of tumoral calcinosis
clinical_history: A 13-year-old boy presented with pain over the left hip for the last 3 years and a gradually enlarging mass for the last 2 years. Upon physical examination, the left hip range of motion was reduced. Lab tests showed normal calcium, high serum phosphorous of 7.07 Eq/dL, and normal parathormone levels.
imaging_findings: A radiograph of the left hip demonstrated multilobulated periarticular calcifications (Figure 1). MRI (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, 3d, and 3e) showed a well-defined, lobulated lesion affecting the glutei, vastus lateralis, and obturator externus muscles. Multiple fluid-calcium levels, termed the “sedimentation sign”, were noted, with calcifications appearing hypointense on both T1 and T2-weighted sequences, and fluid appearing hypointense on T1-weighted and hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences. These lesions exhibited heterogeneous contrast enhancement. CT imaging revealed a multilobulated calcific mass without bone or joint involvement (Figures 2a and 2b). Histopathological examination (Figures 4a and 4b) confirmed the diagnosis of tumoral calcinosis, revealing fibro-collagenous tissue with granular calcifications arranged in lobules with surrounding multinucleated giant cells, foamy macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.
discussion: Background Tumoral calcinosis is characterised by periarticular mass with calcium deposits. It is commonly seen around the region of the hips, shoulders, and elbows [1]. After analysing 122 cases of tumoral calcinosis, in 1996, Smack et al. [2] proposed the following pathogenesis-based classification: Primary normophosphatemic tumoral calcinosis : Patients with normal serum phosphate, serum calcium, and no evidence of disorders associated with soft tissue calcification. Primary hyperphosphatemic tumoral calcinosis : Patients with elevated serum phosphate, normal serum calcium and no evidence of disorders associated with soft tissue calcification. Secondary tumoral calcinosis : Patients with concomitant diseases that can lead to soft tissue calcifications such as chronic renal failure, pseudoxanthoma elasticum, malignancy, sarcoidosis, primary hyperparathyroidism, scleroderma, hypervitaminosis D, and milk-alkali syndrome. Pathogenesis Three major hypotheses have been suggested [3]: (a) Repetitive trauma resulting in dysfunctional reparative processes; (b) Periarticular forces dissecting histiocytic aggregates that initiate osteoclastic activity; (c) Haemorrhage due to microtrauma inducing an amplification of the reparative response. Clinical Perspective The most common site of involvement is the lateral hip. However, elbow, shoulder, hand, Achilles tendon, and others may also be involved. Clinical presentation is variable, from no involvement to massive, severe, and incapacitating lesions. Calcifications typically begin during the first two decades of life and can limit joint mobility, impeding physical activities [4]. Imaging Perspective Amorphous, multilobulated, and rim-like calcifications in a peri-articular location are seen on plain radiographs. On computed tomography, fluid-fluid levels in cystic loculi are seen, resulting from calcium layering resulting in the “sedimentation sign”. However, the lesion may appear homogeneous, indicating reduced activity during the quiescent phase. There is an absence of osseous damage or erosion by neighbouring soft-tissue mass. On magnetic resonance imaging, T2-weighted sequences display an inhomogeneous hyperintense signal. Two common patterns are observed: a nodular pattern with alternating areas of hyperintensity and signal void, or a diffuse hypointense signal. On T1-weighted sequences, the lesions appear hypointense and inhomogeneous. The hypointense signal on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted images is due to the calcific nature of the deposits, and the foci of T2 hyperintensity suggest the presence of inflammation [3,5,6]. Histopathology Features Under light microscopy, the H&E-stained tissue section from the mass typically reveals several cystic cavities with calcified regions encircled by palisaded histiocytes and a large number of foreign body-type giant cells [3,6,7]. Management and Prognosis Management should be tailored according to the lesion’s type, stage, size, proximity to vital structures, and the patient’s symptoms [5]. For primary tumoral calcinosis, early surgical excision is typically the standard approach [8], although the high recurrence rate often necessitates repeated surgeries [9,10]. In cases associated with hyperphosphatemia, medical management involving phosphate depletion, achieved through dietary modifications, phosphate-binding agents, and potentially acetazolamide to increase phosphate excretion, can be effective [9,11–14]. Medical treatment is generally preferred during the active stage of the disease, while surgical intervention may be more successful during the quiescent stage when encapsulation has occurred [15]. For patients with secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism who do not respond to medical therapy, subtotal or total parathyroidectomy can be beneficial [16–18]. In cases with end-stage renal disease, renal transplantation may be considered when other treatments are ineffective [5]. The prognosis of tumoral calcinosis largely depends on early detection, effective management of underlying metabolic disturbances, and a strategic combination of surgical and medical therapies [15,19].
differential_diagnosis: Soft tissue sarcoma Myositis ossificans CPPD disease Hydroxyapatite deposition disease Hyperparathyroidism Primary hyperphosphatemic tumoral calcinosis Synovial osteochrondromatosis

title: SMART syndrome – A stroke-mimic
clinical_history: A 45-year-old male with a history of glioblastoma, submitted to surgical resection followed by Stupp protocol 11 years ago, and organic psychosis, with therapeutic noncompliance and multiple hospitalisations in recent years, presented to the emergency department with acute onset gait disturbance, right-sided muscle weakness, numbness and behavioural changes.
imaging_findings: A head CT performed upon admission revealed a status post left parietal craniotomy, with a cortico-subcortical temporoparietal surgical site exhibiting gliosis, stable when compared to previous imaging. No new hypodensities suggestive of stroke were observed, and CT angiography excluded arterial occlusion. Subsequent brain MRI T1-weighted post-contrast images demonstrated de novo cortical gyriform enhancement in the previously treated surgical site, specifically in the temporoparietal region, with extension into the occipital, insular and remaining temporal lobe. Perfusion arterial spin labelling (ASL) study indicated increased cerebral blood flow (CBF) in the affected area. Importantly, there were no signs of acute stroke nor tumour progression, as evidenced by the absence of restricted diffusion, an extension of the high T2 FLAIR signal or nodular enhancement.
discussion: Stroke-like migraine attacks after radiation therapy (SMART) syndrome is a rare, delayed complication following cerebral radiation, typically manifesting years after treatment, with onset ranging from a few years to up to 30 years, with a mean of 10 years [1]. It can occur following radiation therapy for primary brain tumours or metastases, most commonly in patients receiving doses above 50 Gy, though it may also develop with lower doses. The pathophysiology of SMART syndrome remains poorly understood. Brain biopsies usually show no specific abnormalities [2]. It is believed to be multifactorial, starting with radiation-induced mitochondrial dysfunction leading to neuronal damage and blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption. This can cause neuronal hyperexcitability and cortical spreading depression, a wave of neuronal depolarisation that suppresses spontaneous electrical activity. Disruption of the BBB, and cerebral oedema, similar to posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), are also thought to contribute [3,5]. Clinically, SMART syndrome presents with stroke-like symptoms, including aphasia, hemianopsia, vision loss, hemiparesis, and hemiparesthesia. Some patients experience migraine-like headaches (with or without aura), seizures, and encephalopathy of varying severity. A history of post-radiotherapy migraine, with or without aura, is also common [4]. The condition is typically self-limited, with symptoms resolving within weeks to a few months, although persistent neurological deficits and imaging sequelae may occur [2]. On head CT, regions of hypodensity may be seen with minimal mass effect, and laminar necrosis with or without cortical calcifications can appear as sequelae. Brain MRI typically shows gyriform cortical and leptomeningeal enhancement, cortical thickening, and increased signal intensity on T2 and T2-FLAIR, with mild mass effect and occasional diffusion restriction. These changes are typically confined to previously irradiated areas. T1-weighted imaging may show high signal intensity in the cortex, suggesting reparative processes, and perfusion studies can demonstrate altered cerebral blood flow. Diagnostic criteria for SMART syndrome include: a history of cranial, craniospinal, or whole-brain radiation therapy, without evidence of recurrent neoplasm; a triad of prolonged, reversible symptoms such as headache, seizures, and hemiparesis; characteristic MRI findings; and the exclusion of other pathologies [4]. SMART syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion and should only be diagnosed in the appropriate clinical context. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Low-grade central osteosarcoma of the humerus
clinical_history: 26-year-old female with no relevant past medical history presented with a two-year history of worsening pain at the right proximal humerus and associated weakness.
imaging_findings: X-ray of the right shoulder (Figures 1a and 1b) showed an expansile lucent proximal humeral meta-diaphysis lesion with well-defined medial and craniocaudal margins, narrow zone of transition, mild lateral endosteal scalloping and subtle medial periosteal reaction. CT of the right shoulder (Figures 2a and 2b) showed a predominantly fat-density soft tissue mass and an extensive area of full-thickness cortical loss anteriorly with focal permeation of the posterior cortex of the meta-diaphysis. Subsequent MRI (Figures 3, 4a, 4b, 4c, and 4d) confirmed a 4.8 cm maximum diameter predominantly fat-signal lesion within the proximal humerus with mildly enhancing internal curvilinear soft tissue stranding and more nodular soft tissue superiorly with speckled intra-lesional fat and extensive full thickness cortical loss and medial cortical permeation with secondary stress fracture. Mildly enhancing mild peri-lesional marrow and cortical oedema were also noted. There was no extra-osseous invasion. Nuclear medicine whole-body scan revealed avid uptake at the right proximal humerus with no other disease.
discussion: Background Low-grade central osteosarcoma (LGCO) is a subtype of osteosarcoma that accounts for less than 2% of this tumour type [1]. It is slow-growing and usually affects the metaphysis and meta-diaphysis of long bones, particularly the femur and tibia, and rarely the small bones of hands and feet, or the mandible [1–3]. It is more common in young adults, peaking in the 3 rd decade. Clinical Perspective LGCO often presents with non-specific symptoms such as pain and swelling lasting from weeks to years [4]. Due to a close resemblance with fibrous dysplasia, the diagnosis is usually based on clinical, imaging and histological features [5]. As in this case, several biopsies are often required before the diagnosis of LGCO is reached due to the similarities of histopathology and immunohistochemistry in LGCO and benign fibro-osseous pathologies and the usually minimal cytological atypia and low mitotic activity [2]. Treatment usually involves surgery with or without chemo-radiotherapy depending on the tumour extent and resection margins. LGCO can recur with an increasing risk of higher-grade disease at each recurrence. Imaging Perspective X-ray features in this case, demonstrate an expansile lucent lesion of a long bone with a mild endosteal scalloping and subtle periosteal reaction. Differential diagnoses for these appearances include giant cell tumour, aneurysmal bone cyst, metastasis, and, rarely, an infection such as osteomyelitis. In literature, LGCO has variable x-ray appearances but has most commonly lytic appearance with thin and incomplete trabecula, mixed lytic and sclerotic appearance and, least commonly, diffuse sclerotic appearance. Cases have also been described resembling benign lesions such as aneurysmal bone cyst or chondromyxoid fibroma. Other described x-ray appearances include predominantly lytic lesion with varying amounts of thick and coarse trabeculation resembling low-grade fibro-osseous lesions such as fibrous dysplasia or fibrous cortical defect/non-ossifying fibroma [2,5]. CT/MRI features in this case, demonstrate a fat-density soft tissue mass, extensive area of full-thickness cortical loss and permeation, as well as enhancing peri-lesional marrow and cortical oedema. Differential diagnoses would include liposarcoma, intraosseous lipoma, metastasis, and occasionally fibrous dysplasia. In literature, MRI appearance often resembles other fibro-osseous lesions with heterogeneous T1 and fluid-sensitive signal and presence of intra-lesional fat. Hide et al. described heterogeneous low T1-weighted signal and high T2-weighted signal with cystic foci and fluid-fluid levels on MRI [8]. Enhancement is usually heterogeneous and mild, but Wakabayashi et al. suggested considerable contrast enhancement of solid components on T1 [9]. Regardless of the modality, cortical permeation, periosteal reaction, or extra-osseous soft tissue invasion/extension are best appreciated on MRI and CT and are seen in most cases of LGCO [2,5–7]. Identification of such features allows better targeted sampling during image-guided biopsy reducing the risk of falsely reassuring histopathology and sub-optimal management. Histopathological Perspective Microscopic Description Sections show a moderately cellular tumour infiltrating the soft tissue. It is composed of mildly atypical spindled to ovoid cells in a fibrous stroma with foci of woven bone deposition. Numerous interspersed mast cells are seen. Also included is a fragment of cortical bone that appears to be permeated by the tumour. In this area, there are features of fracture callus. Occasional normal mitoses are identified. No necrosis is seen. Histological Opinion Section opinion, bone humerus: the features are in keeping with a low-grade central osteosarcoma. Outcome LGCO carries an overall 5-year survival rate of approximately 90%. Reduced survival is associated with increasing size, distant spread, and performance status [4]. Good quality imaging improves the chances of imaging diagnosis of LGCO, better planning of image-guided biopsy and better surgical planning allowing en-bloc resection to reduce risk of recurrent disease and subsequent high-grade transformation and metastasis. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: A cervical polypoid mass – What we should think about
clinical_history: A 50-year-old woman was referred to our hospital with a complaint of abdominal distension and irregular menstrual bleeding for 2 months. She had no significant past medical history. The pelvic examination revealed a large polypoid mass protruding into the vagina.
imaging_findings: Transvaginal ultrasonography (not shown) demonstrated a solid and heterogenous cervical mass. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, 1d, 1e, 1f, 1g, and 1h) revealed a large mass in the endometrial cavity originating from the uterine fundus protruding into the cervix. The mass was predominantly solid with high signal intensity on T2-weighted images (T2WI) with heterogeneous contrast enhancement. It was not possible to identify the ovaries. Extrauterine large solid and cystic/necrotic lesions were also documented. Computed tomography (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c) confirmed the presence of a voluminous pelvic mass. There was minimal pelvic ascites with no lymphadenopathy. The possibility of a uterine sarcoma was made based mainly on the large size of the polypoid mass with a high signal on T2WI with aggressive behaviour and possible metastasis to the peritoneum/ovaries. The final diagnosis of uterine adenosarcoma with sarcomatous component was made on histopathological evaluation after hysterectomy. The para-uterine masses represented peritoneal metastases with ovaries with no pathologic features.
discussion: Background Accounting for 8% of all uterine sarcomas, uterine adenosarcoma is a mixed epithelial-mesenchymal tumour composed of benign glandular epithelium and malignant mesenchymal (stromal) elements [1–7]. The stromal component drives the malignancy, usually with low-grade features with low malignant potential [1,3,6,7]. However, high-grade variants such as adenosarcoma with sarcomatous overgrowth (SO), in which the sarcomatous component constitutes more than 25% of the tumour, have a worse prognosis [2–4,7,8]. Adenosarcoma typically originates in the endometrium but may also occur in the uterine cervix and extrauterine pelvic locations such as the fallopian tube and ovaries [1,3,4,6]. It primarily affects postmenopausal women with no significant difference in ethnicity [3,6]. Risk factors are not yet well established, but endometriosis, previous pelvic irradiation and treatment with oestrogen-modulating agents (such as tamoxifen) may represent an additional risk factor for adenosarcoma [3,5,6]. Clinical Perspective Clinically, patients often present with abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pain, or abdominal distension [1,3,6]. On pelvic examination, a protruding polypoid lesion may be observed through the cervix [3,4,6]. Imaging Perspective Imaging is essential to distinguishing adenosarcoma from benign uterine pathologies (like fibroids or polyps), mainly if low-grade, and to guide preoperative staging [3,8]. Transvaginal ultrasound may be an initial tool, but MRI is preferred due to its superior soft-tissue resolution. MRI characteristically reveals a large polypoid mass that arises in the uterine fundus and protrudes through the external cervical os, with heterogeneous high signal intensity on T2WI with small cystic components corresponding more likely to glandular epithelial components or necrosis. Malignant stromal components enhance more prominently on contrast imaging than benign epithelial elements. Haemorrhagic necrosis shows high signal intensity on T1-weighted images (T1WI) and is particularly common if SO is present. When it is a low-grade tumour, it characteristically shows slightly higher ADC values than other carcinomas and uterine sarcoma subtypes [1–4,7,8]. The most common site of extrauterine spread is locally within the pelvis, with rare lymph node involvement and distant metastases, even in cases of recurrent disease [2]. In the literature, ovarian metastases were not found in patients with uterine adenosarcoma [4]. Outcome Definitive diagnosis often requires hysteroscopy and biopsy, but surgical excision is essential [2,6]. The standard treatment is total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy [2,5,6]. Lymphadenectomy is reserved for cases with suspected nodal involvement [4,6]. High-risk cases, including those with SO or extrauterine spread, may benefit from adjuvant radiotherapy or chemotherapy [4–6]. The prognosis is generally favourable for localised, low-grade adenosarcomas [2,4–6]. However, recurrence is common and increases with SO, deep myometrial invasion and extrauterine spread [2,4,5,7]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Pyometrocolpos in infancy: An early presentation of imperforate hymen
clinical_history: A 3-month-old girl was brought to casualty with a history of intermittent fever for 1 month, abdominal distension, and straining while passing urine and stools for 4 days. On examination, a soft, tender, non-mobile midline mass was palpated in the suprapubic region.
imaging_findings: Transabdominal greyscale ultrasound revealed a large, well-defined cystic lesion in the pelvis with dense mobile echoes (Figure 1). The mass was seen posterior to the bladder and anterior to the rectum and was extending into the abdominal cavity up to the umbilicus. The cystic structure was in continuity with the stretched uterine cavity (Figure 2). Suprapubic probe tenderness was positive. There was no evidence of any solid component or calcifications within. Both the ovaries were seen separately from this lesion. Bilateral kidneys showed mild hydronephrosis. Bowel loops were normal in course, calibre, and peristalsis and were displaced to the periphery. On transperineal ultrasound examination, there was a thin membrane of 1 mm thickness at the vaginal orifice (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Imperforate hymen is a congenital anomaly that occurs due to failure of resorption of hymen epithelial cells resulting in non-canalisation of the vaginal plate [1]. It usually coexists with other urogenital anomalies [2]. Pyometrocolpos is a cystic dilatation of the uterine cavity and vagina via accumulation of pus due to secondary infection of the obstructed cervicovaginal secretions [3]. Clinical Perspective Imperforate hymen usually presents at the time of menarche, with the patient complaining of cyclical abdominal pain and primary amenorrhoea [4]. It is rarely diagnosed in infancy. In these cases, under the effect of maternal oestrogens via breastfeeding, there are excessive cervicovaginal secretions that fail to drain per vagina and, in turn, provide the perfect nidus for bacterial growth resulting in pyometrocolpos [5]. They are also often associated with a history of urinary tract infections [6]. In newborns, the hymen is often thick and redundant (under the effect of maternal oestrogens), expanding to become crescentic as age advances [7,8]. Thus, it can easily be missed in the absence of a thorough physical examination to rule out the same in relevant clinical settings. Our case is atypical because of the very early age of presentation, the absence of effect of maternal hormones through feed due to maternal mortality, no history of urinary tract infection or any other associated urogenital anomalies. Imaging Perspective As the clinical presentation of pyometrocolpos is nonspecific and examination findings are similar to an abdominal mass, ultrasound plays an important role in diagnosing this condition. Ultrasound not only helps in diagnosing this condition without the risk of radiation exposure, but it also helps to rule out other congenital urogenital anomalies often associated with it. In cases of large pyometrocolpos, it is useful to rule out complications like bladder outlet obstruction and large bowel obstruction [9]. Outcome Hymenectomy and drainage of pus is the simple curative treatment for this condition, and the patient shows good recovery with a return of normal leucocyte count within a few days [10,11]. Our patient underwent hymenectomy with drainage of pus (Figure 4) and hymenoplasty. Take Home Message Our case highlights the importance of considering pyometrocolpos as an important differential while evaluating newborn females with acute tender abdominopelvic mass and the usefulness of pelvic ultrasound in diagnosing the same. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Rib sarcoma synovial in pregnancy
clinical_history: A 32-year-old female patient, in her 25th week of pregnancy, presented with a mass in the left breast for 4 months. She visited the hospital due to dyspnoea, a non-productive cough, and chest pain; symptoms started one month prior. She denied other symptoms and reported no significant medical history.
imaging_findings: CT contrast-enhanced abdominal images in the venous phase, acquired in an oblique coronal plane (Figure 1a), reveal a mass originating from the fourth left costal arch. The mass invades the thoracic wall, elevates the pectoral muscle, and displaces the left mammary gland. In the axial plane (Figure 1b), the mass is observed in contact with the pulmonary artery trunk and the pericardium, without evidence of heart infiltration. In the sagittal plane (Figure 1c), the erosion of the fourth left costal arch is observed. A 3D reconstruction video (Figure 2) provides a clearer visualisation of the relationship between the mass, the major vessels, and the heart. It is evident that the mass does not compress or collapse the mediastinal structures. In the intraoperative image (Figure 3), the tumour is seen in contact with the pericardium. A biopsy revealed a spindle cell malignant mesenchymal neoplasm with morphological and immunophenotypic features consistent with a diagnosis of monophasic synovial sarcoma.
discussion: Background Synovial sarcoma is a rare malignant neoplasm derived from mesenchymal cells. It predominantly occurs in young adults and can develop in various parts of the body, accounting for 5% to 10% of soft tissue sarcomas [1]. Most patients are between 15 and 40 years old, with no significant gender predilection. The most common site of presentation is the lower limbs (80%–95% of cases). In this case, the tumour originated in a costal arch, a presentation that represents less than 1% of all synovial sarcomas [2]. Clinical Perspective These tumours typically present as masses with slow, indolent growth, and symptoms vary depending on the site of involvement [3]. When located in the thoracic region, as in this case, patients may present with dyspnoea, cough, haemoptysis, and chest pain. Synovial sarcoma has the potential to metastasise distantly. Imaging Perspective Imaging studies are particularly useful for assessing the tumour’s extent, dimensions, and involvement of adjacent structures. On ultrasound, synovial sarcomas may appear as hypoechoic, rounded, or lobulated masses, sometimes showing internal flow on colour Doppler. This appearance can mimic benign tumours. However, some synovial sarcomas exhibit more heterogeneous echotexture [4]. On CT scans, these tumours typically appear as well-circumscribed lesions that displace adjacent structures without invading them, and they generally lack evidence of local metastases [5]. Contrast-enhanced MRI reveals heterogeneous enhancement due to necrosis and internal haemorrhage. The lesions are isointense to thoracic muscles on T1-weighted images and may show heterogeneity on T2-weighted images, reflecting haemorrhage, necrosis, and cyst formation. Diffusion restriction may also be observed on ADC maps. The principal differential diagnosis includes sarcomas originating from the intercostal muscles. However, these can be differentiated by the bone remodelling seen in tumours arising from the costal arches. Other potential differentials, such as lung tumours and mesotheliomas, typically do not exhibit aggressive thoracic wall modifications. Outcome The initial treatment for synovial sarcoma is surgical resection, often preceded by chemotherapy and radiotherapy to reduce tumour size and improve surgical outcomes. Take-Home Message / Teaching Points CT imaging is particularly important for the diagnosis, staging, and prognosis of synovial sarcoma. This type of tumour typically displaces adjacent organs without easily invading or infiltrating them. In this case, displacement of the left breast and pectoral muscle was evident. Synovial sarcomas often present as highly heterogeneous lesions due to their tendency to develop necrosis. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Synovial sarcoma of the intercostal muscles Synovial sarcoma originating from a costal arch Metastasis to the thoracic wall Chondrosarcoma Osteosarcoma Enchondroma Neurofibroma/Schwannoma
