title: Hidradenitis suppurativa
clinical_history: A 41-year-old woman presented with worsening perineal pain and pustular skin lesions. Examination revealed extensive erythematous and pustular lesions in the perineal and perianal regions, with rope-like dermal thickening and induration. Multiple fistulous openings with purulent and haemoserous discharge were noted.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound of the perineal and perianal regions revealed dermal and hypodermal band-like structures indicative of fistulas/tunnels, with multiple dermal collections around hair follicles containing hyperechoic hair fragments (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c). Some hypodermal fluid collections were connected to the epidermis via sinus tracts (Figure 1d). Power Doppler showed increased vascularity, suggesting active inflammation (Figure 1e). MRI demonstrated skin thickening at the perineum and labia majora, hypertrophic scarring, and deep subcutaneous fistulas/tunnels extending into the ischioanal space and perianal region (Figures 2a and 2b), with left adductor muscle involvement suggestive of myositis (Figure 2c). The tunnels exhibited post-contrast rim enhancement, indicating active inflammation, but no fistulas communicating with the anal canal lumen were identified. After immunomodulatory therapy, significant lesion reduction was observed, with resolution of the fistulas and myositis. Residual skin thickening and scarring were noted, with minimal post-gadolinium enhancement, indicating minor active inflammation (Figures 3a and 3b).
discussion: Background Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic inflammatory disorder characterised by deep-seated nodules, abscesses, fistulas, sinus tracts, and scarring, typically affecting the axillae, inguinal area, sub-mammary folds, and perianal regions. This disfiguring condition causes significant pain and reduced quality of life. HS is thought to result from follicular hyperkeratosis within the pilosebaceous apocrine unit, though its exact mechanism remains unclear [1]. Clinical Perspective The diagnosis of HS requires three criteria: the presence of typical lesions, involvement of characteristic locations, and chronicity. Chronicity is defined as at least two recurrences within six months. Patients often report pain, malodour, burning, and itching. While the role of bacteria and infections in HS remains debated, they likely contribute to its chronicity [2]. Imaging Perspective Imaging in HS is essential for identifying the type and extent of anatomic abnormalities, monitoring treatment progress, and performing presurgical mapping of lesions [3]. The sonographic diagnosis of HS is based on identifying key findings, including widened hair follicles, dermal alterations, pseudocysts, fluid collections, and fistulas (tunnels). The presence of three or more of these findings confirms the diagnosis. Colour Doppler imaging aids in assessing and monitoring vascular patterns in and around lesions, providing insights into disease activity and progression [3,4]. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the preferred imaging modality for assessing the extent of HS and identifying complications. It is also valuable in differentiating HS from Crohn’s disease, one of its main differential diagnoses [5]. Anogenital HS manifestations are more frequently described in MRI literature. The MRI protocol for HS should include T2-weighted sequences with fat suppression or short tau inversion recovery (STIR) images to differentiate fluid retention from fat. Inflammatory phenomena are best highlighted by T1 sequences with gadolinium contrast injection. In T2, abscesses appear hyperintense, while T1 with gadolinium enhances the distinction between fluid collections, fibrous scars, necrotic, and inflammatory tissue, improving fistula pathway visualisation [5,6]. Although fistulas in the anoperineal region are more frequent in Crohn’s disease, they tend to communicate with the anal tract and often display higher complexity in comparison with HS [5]. Outcome HS significantly affects patients’ quality of life, making prompt treatment essential to reduce its burden. Available medications are limited and mostly off-label, with surgical interventions often required for remission. Immunomodulatory therapies targeting specific cytokines may offer an effective option for controlling the condition [2]. Take-Home Message Imaging techniques are crucial in the management of hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), and dermatologists should recommend their use. Ultrasonography is effective for monitoring lesions, tracking treatment progress, and staging the disease. MRI, with its high soft-tissue resolution, is particularly useful for assessing deep-seated disease manifestations. It provides a detailed characterisation of the complex anatomy of the anal canal, making it especially valuable in cases of perianal HS.

title: Unusually restricted
clinical_history: A middle-aged patient presented with what were initially suspected to be new-onset migraines but then developed auditory and visual hallucinations and complex paranoid beliefs. They became confused and intermittently incoherent with deteriorating coordination, becoming unsteady and sustaining several falls. The clinical picture was further complicated by the onset of myoclonus and a rapidly progressive cognitive decline, which raised suspicion for a neurodegenerative condition.
imaging_findings: The patient initially underwent a CT which showed only generalised cerebral atrophy. They then had further investigations with an MRI, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and corresponding apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) images. This revealed widespread restricted diffusion involving almost the entire cortex except the superior temporal gyrus and also affecting the caudate bilaterally and the left lentiform nuclei. Fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) imaging showed a more subtle high signal in these areas. Other than some small and non-specific foci of high signal in the deep white matter, there were no further positive findings.
discussion: Background Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) is a rare, rapidly progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by cognitive decline, movement abnormalities, and behavioural changes. It is caused by the accumulation of abnormally folded prion proteins in the brain tissue leading to neuronal destruction and brain tissue degeneration. There are three types of CJD: sporadic, genetic and acquired [1]. Sporadic CJD accounts for the majority of cases, with a peak incidence in the sixth and seventh decades of life. Genetic CJD is linked to mutations in the prion protein gene (PRNP), while acquired forms result from transmission via contaminated medical instruments, blood products, or through prion-infected tissue (e.g., variant CJD). Clinical Perspective & Evolution Patients typically present with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, ataxia, visual disturbances other neurological signs such as speech and movement abnormalities. The condition progresses quickly, often within months, with patients experiencing profound cognitive and motor decline. Due to the varied clinical manifestations, CJD can initially be mistaken for other neurodegenerative disorders, such as Alzheimer’s disease, frontotemporal dementia, or psychiatric illnesses. As the disease progresses, patients may develop cortical blindness, muscle rigidity, and difficulty with swallowing. Early diagnosis is difficult but critical, as it facilitates prompt infection control measures, appropriate clinical management, and palliative care [2]. Imaging Perspective & Laboratory Diagnosis MRI of the brain is a crucial diagnostic tool in the evaluation of suspected CJD. The classic MRI findings include “cortical ribboning”, which refers to the gyriform restricted diffusion seen in the cortex, alongside abnormal findings in the basal ganglia. These abnormalities, including the characteristic diffusion restriction in the basal ganglia and cortex, are highly suggestive of CJD. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is particularly valuable, as it has a high sensitivity for detecting these changes in the early stages of the disease, before other findings become apparent on conventional MRI sequences. Studies have proposed diagnostic algorithms based on DWI findings, and they are often used in conjunction with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis to confirm the diagnosis [3,4]. Sometimes the diagnosis will only be confirmed post-mortem. In addition to imaging findings, laboratory tests play a critical role in confirming the diagnosis of CJD. CSF analysis can reveal the presence of 14-3-3 protein, a marker of neuronal injury, which is highly suggestive of CJD, although it is not definitive. The RT-QuIC (Real-Time Quaking Induced Conversion) assay has emerged as a highly sensitive and specific test for detecting prion proteins in CSF, offering a more accurate means of diagnosing CJD. In some cases, genetic testing for mutations in the PRNP gene may be performed, particularly if the patient has a family history or there is suspicion of genetic CJD [7–9]. Outcome Supportive care is the mainstay management strategy for CJD, and there is currently no curative therapy. The prognosis is poor, with most patients succumbing to the disease within a year of symptom onset. In this case, the patient unfortunately passed away shortly after diagnosis. The rapid deterioration emphasised the importance of imaging and laboratory diagnostics in reaching a timely diagnosis. Early recognition allowed for the exclusion of other treatable conditions and facilitated appropriate palliative care planning [5]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) is a rare but devastating and incurable neurodegenerative disorder. Early diagnosis is crucial for appropriate management, infection control, and palliative care particularly. MRI using DWI is the imaging modality of choice for detecting characteristic changes in the brain [6]. Laboratory tests, such as CSF analysis (14-3-3 protein and RT-QuIC), and genetic testing for PRNP mutations, further aid in confirming the diagnosis and distinguishing CJD from other conditions with similar presentations. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files. The patient unfortunately died shortly after imaging, and it was not possible to seek consent. In view of the rarity of the disease, fewer demographic details than would usually be included have been offered to preserve their anonymity.

title: Morel-Lavallée lesion in a patient with previous myxoid liposarcoma
clinical_history: A 52-year-old male presented to the outpatient clinic with swelling over the right greater trochanteric region, which progressively grew after a fall four months before. He had a previous history of neoadjuvant radiotherapy followed by resection of a soft tissue sarcoma in the left thigh seven years before.
imaging_findings: On the preoperative MRI performed seven years before (Figures 1, 2a, 2b, and 2c), an intramuscular lobulated mass was seen in the left tensor fascia lata, extending into the subcutis. The mass showed areas of high signal on T1WI (Figure 2a), which became hypo-intense after fat suppression (Figure 2b). The mass was heterogeneous, predominantly hyperintense on T2WI (Figure 2b) and showed internal areas of heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium contrast (Figure 2c). The current MR study revealed a thick-walled, well-defined lesion superficial to the right tensor fascia lata, with heterogeneous high signal on T1WI (Figures 3a and 3b) and T2WI (Figures 4a and 4b), persisting after fat suppression. Multiple internal fluid-fluid levels were present. While post-contrast T1WI sequences (Figure 5) showed intralesional heterogeneous high signal, the dynamic subtraction sequence (Figure 6), only showed a thick peripheral enhancing rim. Therefore, the pseudoenhancement seen on the static sequences was due to a haemorrhage-related high native T1WI signal.
discussion: Background Morel-Lavallée lesions (MLL) occur after trauma with closed degloving injury, causing a fluid collection from continuous capillary drainage into the space between the subcutis and fascia. They often occur at the peritrochanteric region or proximal thigh [1,2]. On the other hand, myxoid liposarcoma (MLS) is a malignant tumour containing small round cells and lipoblasts, set in a myxoid stroma with branching capillaries [3]. Clinical Perspective MLL usually present as a progressive soft tissue swelling weeks to years after trauma, potentially mimicking a soft tissue sarcoma [1]. In this case, a previous history of MLS confounded the clinical picture. Given MLS’s propensity to metastasise to unusual sites such as bone, muscle and (retro)peritoneum, clinicians must be suspicious of new swellings [4]. Imaging Perspective Since MLL may clinically mimic other lesions, a history of trauma is important to aid the diagnosis. On MRI, MLL usually appear as well-defined deep subcutaneous collections at the proximal thigh or peritrochanteric area, superficial to the fascia, surrounded by a hypointense pseudocapsule. Internal signal intensity may vary, depending on chronicity and internal composition. On T1WI, there may be hyperintensity in the acute phase due to haemorrhage, and hypointensity in chronic phases from haemosiderin deposition [1]. On T2WI, MLL usually show heterogeneous high signal, often with septations and fluid-fluid levels [5]. Post-contrast, peripheral rim enhancement may be present [6]. In this case, subtraction images were helpful in distinguishing true enhancement from pseudoenhancement. As for MLS, they appear on MRI as well-defined lobulated masses, with hyperintense T2WI signal, potentially mistaken for cysts if not carefully evaluated. T1WI shows an intermediate to low signal, sometimes with small high-signal areas of fat (nodular or septae), making fat-saturated sequences essential. After contrast, they show typical cloud-like enhancement, distinguishing them from cysts. Therefore, cystic-appearing lesions in atypical locations should raise suspicion and prompt contrast administration [7]. Since MLS show T2WI hyperintensity and have a propensity for extra-pulmonary metastases, they are best staged by whole-body MRI [4,8]. Outcome MLL have a good prognosis if small and treated early with compression, aspiration or sclerodesis. More chronic lesions usually have a pseudocapsule predisposing to recurrence, and open surgery may be needed [9]. Take-Home Message Myxoid liposarcomas (MLS) are malignant tumours which may mimic cystic lesions on imaging if not carefully evaluated. Morel-Lavallée lesions (MLL) can clinically mimic soft tissue tumours. History of adequate trauma and a typical location point towards the correct diagnosis. Static or dynamic subtraction images after gadolinium contrast may help to differentiate MLL from soft tissue tumours. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Incidental cerebellar calcified pseudoneoplasm of the neuraxis: A rare finding
clinical_history: A 63-year-old female, with a history of anterior cervical diskectomy and fusion, had a CT head and cervical spine in 2007 for unrelated symptoms. Incidentally, imaging identified a heavily calcified lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere. The patient remained asymptomatic and, therefore, opted for regular follow-up imaging as opposed to surgical management.
imaging_findings: The CT brain demonstrated a 2.5 cm (maximal diameter), highly calcified intra-axial lesion with no surrounding oedema or mass effect, within the right cerebellar fossa (Figures 1 and 2). The MRI demonstrated the same lesion within the right cerebellar hemisphere, measuring 2.5 cm (maximal axial measurement). The lesion abutted the inferior tentorial surface; however, a broad base against it was not exhibited. There was no notable mass effect or surrounding oedema. On T1 (Figure 3) and T2 (Figure 4) weighted images, the lesion displayed a low signal intensity. Additionally, blooming artefacts were observed on gradient imaging (Figure 5). During the 17-year follow-up period, the patient exhibited no symptoms. Biennially, MRI heads revealed no change in the lesion size or associated mass effect.
discussion: Background Calcified pseudoneoplasm of the neuraxis (CAPNON) represents a rare category of benign fibro-osseous, calcified lesions of unknown aetiology [1,2]. They develop within the central nervous system (CNS), both intra and extra-axially [3]. CAPNON has been theorised to be secondary to a reactive rather than neoplastic process [2]. Clinical Perspective CAPNON most commonly presents as compressive symptoms of adjacent structures contingent upon its localisation within the CNS. Intracranially, the manifestation of CAPNON may include seizures, headaches, dizziness, sensory or motor symptoms [4]. Conversely, spinal CAPNON often presents with localised back pain. However, CAPNON diagnosed incidentally is the rarest within the literature [5]. Imaging Perspective CT findings of CAPNON include a solid, markedly calcified lesion of the parenchyma or leptomeninges [2–4]. The top differentials include calcified cavernoma or calcified meningioma [2]. MRI findings are more characteristic and offer the opportunity to discern between the differentials. On MRI, CAPNON demonstrates a well-defined lesion with hypointense signals in T1 and T2 sequences. The presence of rim enhancement, but minimal to no associated oedema, is commonly described [2,3]. Contrastingly, cavernomas may have higher signal intensity on T2 sequences representing cystic spaces and demonstrate a popcorn appearance [2]. Calcified meningiomas are broad-based extra-axial lesions frequently associated with a dura tail, with possible vasogenic oedema, and T2 signal intensity varying depending on their subtype [3,6]. CAPNON is easier to diagnose on MRI. In cases where the lesion is surgically resected, histology demonstrates fibrous stroma and chondromyxoid matrix of a heavily calcified mass [2,3]. Outcome In symptomatic individuals, complete surgical resection of the CAPNON is the gold standard treatment of the consequential mass effect [3,4,6]. Chemotherapy or radiotherapy is not required due to CAPNONs benign nature [4]. Most cases of surgically resected CAPNON occur via craniotomy; however, there has been one reported case of an endoscopically resected CAPNON located at the anterior skull base [4,7]. This highlights the critical role of imaging in surgical management planning. In our case, the patient remained asymptomatic, and therefore, with no interval change of the CAPNON, surgical resection was not deemed beneficial. Take Home Message / Teaching Points CAPNON is a rare differential for a calcified mass on CT. Nevertheless, it is important to be aware of this finding as the approach to managing this benign lesion differs significantly from that for malignant differentials. In the case of our asymptomatic patient, a radiologist’s confidence in identifying the calcified lesion as CAPNON, a benign lesion, and not a malignant pathology saves the patient unnecessary invasive investigations and treatments. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
differential_diagnosis: Calcified meningioma Calcified cavernoma Calcified pseudoneoplasm of the neuraxis Oligodendrogliomas Choroid plexus papilloma

title: Cerebrospinal fluid pseudocyst causing ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction
clinical_history: A 20-year-old male with a history of traumatic brain injury as an infant with subsequent hydrocephalus status post ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt. Shunt revision was done 2 years back. Elevated blood pressure was noted in the outpatient department and referred to emergency.
imaging_findings: CT head demonstrated ventriculomegaly (Figure 1a) compared to the baseline CT one year back (Figure 1b). The shunt series, including anteroposterior radiographs of the skull, neck, chest, and abdomen, showed a left-sided VP shunt coursing along the neck and chest with the peritoneal part coiled within the right upper quadrant. A large globular density was noted in the right upper quadrant overlying the liver shadow. Prior abandoned shunt is also visualised (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). The right upper quadrant ultrasound showed a fluid collection displacing the liver posteriorly (Figure 3). CT abdomen demonstrated a subcapsular collection of fluid with scalloping of the liver parenchyma. The distal shunt coiled and terminated within the cyst (Figures 4a and 4b).
discussion: Shunt placement that drains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the obstructed ventricular system in the brain to the peritoneal cavity is a common treatment for hydrocephalus. However, shunt malfunction is common. The incidence of ventriculoperitoneal shunt failure ranges from 25% to 40% at 1 year and 63% to 70% at 10 years [1]. A high index of suspicion should be made for shunt malfunction when there are clinical findings of increased intracranial pressure, including headache, nausea, vomiting, blurring of vision, increased blood pressure, altered mental status, and abnormal gait [2]. Unenhanced CT is the first choice to evaluate the ventricular size. Comparison with previous baseline CT will be beneficial. In our institution, a series of radiographs (frontal and lateral, including head and neck, and frontal of chest and abdomen) are obtained to include the entire course of the shunt to exclude kinking and discontinuity of the radiopaque portion of the shunt. The most common cause of proximal obstruction is occlusion of the ventricular catheter tip by ingrowth of choroid plexus and particulate debris or blood products in the shunt valve, whereas pseudocyst formation, catheter migration, and erosion into soft tissue are the common causes of distal obstruction [3]. CSF pseudocyst is the most common cause of distal VP shunt obstruction. It is a loculated collection of the CSF around the terminal end of the VP shunt due to adhesions and omental migration. When the tip pierces the hepatic capsule, it can collect in the subcapsular location, as in our case. The stable location of the tip in serial radiographs with globular density overlying, which displaces the bowel loops, is indicative of a pseudocyst and can be confirmed by ultrasound or CT [4]. The pseudocysts are treated with externalisation of the catheter tip and drainage of the pseudocyst. Laparoscopic pseudocyst drainage and externalisation of the tube to the peritoneal cavity was done in our case, and it resolved the symptoms.
differential_diagnosis: Hepatic subcapsular cerebrospinal fluid pseudocyst Localised ascites Peritoneal cerebrospinal fluid pseudocyst

title: Nodular fasciitis of the breast: Two cases
clinical_history: The first patient, a 63-year-old woman, presented a painless left sternal lump over 3 weeks. Clinical examination revealed a subcentimetre mobile nodule. An ultrasound was requested. The second patient, a 55-year-old man, presented a 1 cm left breast lump over 6 months. The gynaecologist ordered additional radiological exams.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound images of the woman’s breast (Figure 1a) demonstrated a 4 mm (Figure 1b) parasternal nodule in the upper inner quadrant (UIQ) with indistinct margins. Vascularity was absent (Figure 1c). The lesion was classified as BI-RADS 4A, and a core biopsy was recommended (Figure 1d). Previous mammograms were BI-RADS 1 with type C breast pattern (Figure 1e). In the second case, oblique mammographies with the tomosynthesis technique were performed. A skin marker was placed in the area of interest (Figure 2a). Images showed a poorly defined UIQ nodule almost overlapping the pectoral muscle. On ultrasound, an apparently subcutaneous nodule of 15 mm was present, heterogeneous in appearance and with poorly defined edges. Hyperechoic halo and acoustic shadow can both be seen (Figure 2b). A core biopsy was performed in a single act. The histopathological report concluded in both cases nodular fasciitis. Immunochemistry tests revealed smooth muscle actin 1A4+ in case number one. In the second case, despite actin being negative, a FISH study was performed showing the rearrangement of the USP6 gene located in the chromosomal region 17p13.2.
discussion: Background Nodular fasciitis (NF) is a benign fibrous neoplasm that usually affects young and middle-aged individuals [1–5]. It was described in 1955 by Konwaler as a subcutaneous pseudosarcomatous fibromatosis [1]. Clinical Perspective Most frequently, it appears in the superficial or deep fascia of the soft tissue, predominantly in the upper extremities and trunk [2,3]. The aetiology is still unknown, and breast involvement is rare, with only a few cases reported [1,4,5]. Breast NF presents as a painless and unilateral rapidly growing nodule that does not associate with axillary lymph nodes or skin retraction [1–3,5]. This entity is often mistaken because its clinical and radiological characteristics are similar to breast cancer [4,5]. Imaging Perspective Mammographic appearance is an irregular or spiculated nodule with poorly defined margins [1,3,5]. Calcifications are generally not detected [1,2]. On ultrasound (US), it can be detected as an infiltrative mass: a hypoechoic nodule with irregular margins [1,3–5]. Hyperechoic halo, acoustic shadow or perilesional invasion can be present [1,2]. Vascularity is usually absent [1–3,5]. For a definitive diagnosis, it is necessary to perform a US-guided core biopsy [1–3,5]. Positiveness for smooth muscle actin or vimentin is necessary [1,3]. In the absence of these, the rearrangement of the USP6 gene can be studied in the chromosomal region 17p13.2, which is also diagnostic [3]. Moreover, on histopathological examination, a fibroblastic proliferation with a myxoid component, microbleeds and inflammatory areas is frequently seen [3,5]. Outcome Vacuum-assisted excision can be used for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes [1]. Conservative management is also possible while surgical excision is performed in equivocal cases [1,3,5]. Recurrences have been described in 2% of cases [3]. The prognosis of NF is good [1]. In our cases, the first one has undergone conservative treatment, while the second is waiting for surgery. Take Home Message / Teaching Points NF of the breast is a rare entity that mimics breast cancer clinically, radiologically and histopathologically. It must be remembered that it has a rapid, painless growth, that can be performed a vacuum excision and that the differential diagnosis must be made with a tumour of breast origin and sarcoma. The most important feature creating a suspicion of this entity was that, in both cases, the location of the nodules was uncommon, almost in the subcutaneous cellular tissue or deep in the fascia.

title: Mucinous adenocarcinoma of the prostate
clinical_history: A 74-year-old man, who had suffered acute urinary retention 2 months ago and had been wearing a urinary catheter ever since, came to the urology consultation. The examination revealed an enlarged, painless prostate with normal consistency. His PSA level was elevated (95.20 ng/ml), so an MRI of the prostate was ordered.
imaging_findings: MRI showed a voluminous prostate (218 cm 3 ) with a lobulated, multilocular mass encompassing almost the entire prostate, with multiple septa and extensive structural changes without clear differentiation between the transitional and peripheral zones. The mass showed a heterogeneous T2 hyperintense sign with some hypointense areas (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 2a). The multicystic prostatic mass showed no restricted diffusion (Figures 2b and 2c) and no enhancement of the cystic part of the lesion, but enhancement of the internal septum (arrows) in dynamic contrast enhancement (DCE) (Figures 2e and 2f). In the left peripheral zone, there was a more solid part (asterisk) with low T2 signal intensity (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 2a), which showed restricted diffusion (Figures 2b and 2c) and marked enhancement in the DCE (Figures 2e and 2f), raising suspicion of malignancy. There was no clear distinction between the mass and the anterior part of the rectum (Figure 1b, orange arrow). No lymph node involvement was detected. The core biopsy (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d) revealed a mucinous adenocarcinoma in all 12 samples [Gleason 8 (4 + 4)].
discussion: Background Mucinous adenocarcinoma of the prostate (MAP) is a rare variant of adenocarcinoma of the prostate characterised by excessive mucin production by cancer cells. It is recognised when more than 25% of the tumour consists of glands with extraluminal mucin [1–3]. The 2005 International Society of Urological Pathology consensus on Gleason grading classifies MAP with a Gleason score of 8 (4 + 4), indicating a high-risk tumour [1,3–5]. MRI plays a crucial role in the diagnosis of MAP as it provides detailed imaging, which, in combination with clinical data, helps to differentiate MAP from other prostate pathologies and to make an accurate differential diagnosis [3,6,7]. Clinical Perspective MAP may resemble other types of prostate cancer, remain asymptomatic for years and be discovered incidentally by an elevated PSA level. When symptoms do occur, they are similar to other types of prostate cancer. They are often non-specific and include urinary retention, dysuria, stranguria, perineal discomfort, nocturia, haematuria and weight loss [6,7]. MRI is crucial for an accurate diagnosis as it can show clear imaging features of MAP. Due to its rarity, diagnosis is sometimes complicated by the possibility of biopsy errors. Radiologists need to sensitise pathologists and clinicians to this situation [1,6,8]. Imaging Perspective MRI plays a crucial role in the identification of MAP, as the MRI findings are very different from those of a common adenocarcinoma of the prostate [8,9]. The distinct mucinous areas show unique signalling features on MRI that help to differentiate this subtype from conventional prostate carcinomas. On T2-WI, the lesion typically appears hyperintense due to the high water content of the mucin, in contrast to conventional adenocarcinomas. DCE may show heterogeneous early enhancement patterns and DWI may show less restricted diffusion compared to typical prostate carcinomas. Transrectal ultrasound can detect hypoechoic areas but is less specific than MRI. CT can be used for staging or exclusion of metastases but is less useful for initial assessment. Imaging findings should be correlated with an elevated PSA level and biopsy results to confirm the diagnosis [6,8,9]. Outcome Outcomes of MAP depend largely on early detection, proper grading and treatment strategies. Age and the presence of distant metastases are associated with a poorer outcome [8]. Treatment often follows the protocols for prostate cancer, including surgery, radiotherapy and systemic therapies. Prognosis is not significantly worse than that of conventional acinar adenocarcinoma and is influenced by general factors such as Gleason score, tumour stage and choice of treatment [8,9]. Cancer-specific survival and overall survival are generally comparable when the stage and type of treatment are taken into account. This highlights the importance of collaboration between radiologists, pathologists and clinicians for accurate diagnosis and personalised treatment planning [6,8]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Congenital lobar overinflation associated with supracardiac total anomalous pulmonary venous connection
clinical_history: A 2-year and 11-month-old female toddler presented with a 6-month history of progressive cough, fast breathing, and tiredness. On examination, the patient was tachycardic and tachypneic, and had an oxygen saturation of 87% (breathing room air). Auscultation revealed a harsh systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.
imaging_findings: Initial chest radiography revealed a hyperlucent and overinflated right upper lobe with no mediastinal displacement (Figure 1). There is increased density of both lung bases. 53 days after the chest radiograph, a lung-window chest computed tomography (CT) revealed a hypoattenuating right upper lobe with a significant decrease in pulmonary vascularity (Figure 2a). On the mediastinal window, aberrant drainage of the right and left pulmonary veins into the superior vena cava was visualised (Figures 2b, 2c, and 2d). The vessels merged into a common vessel before draining to the superior vena cava. The main pulmonary artery is enlarged (2.3 cm at its bifurcation), pointing to an underlying pulmonary hypertension. Given the aforementioned diagnoses, an open surgical repair is planned. The child is receiving oral spironolactone (6.25 mg/day) and furosemide (10 mg/day) as a temporary measure.
discussion: Congenital lobar overinflation (CLO) is an uncommon respiratory condition that selectively expands one or multiple segments of the lung and occurs between 1 in 20,000 to 30,000 live births, and most cases manifest during the first year of life [1]. Respiratory distress can occur at birth or shortly thereafter due to the mass effect of the hyperxpanded lung, which can occasionally be excessive enough to cause mediastinal displacement [1,2]. Air trapping results from intrinsic causes such as cartilaginous defects, bronchial stenosis, or extrinsic causes such as vascular rings/slings [3]. The third most common pattern, right upper lobe involvement, occurs at a rate of 21% [4]. A concomitant congenital heart disease is a rare but important complication to search for. Congenital heart defects occur in 12–14% of patients with CLO. Left to right shunt lesions, mainly ventricular septal defects, are the most common [5]. An abnormal pulmonary venous return happens when the pulmonary veins drain to the right side of the heart in whole or in part. This makes oxygenation poor, and babies can show cyanosis at birth [6]. A right-to-left shunt such as a patent foramen ovale or, less commonly, an atrial septal defect is required for survival. Kamath et al. reported 1 case of aberrant pulmonary venous connection with associated CLO, which underwent successful staged surgical repair [7]. A chest radiograph is generally the initial imaging modality for respiratory distress at birth and can show persistent overinflation of a segment or lobe, which in severe cases causes mediastinal shift [2]. Documenting a pleural line, beyond which no lung markings will be visible, can differentiate a hypolucent lung region with mediastinal shift from pneumothorax [2,3]. CT is required to confirm CLO. Attenuated vasculature is an important clue to differentiate CLO from its mimickers. Post-contrast studies can also diagnose associated cardiac abnormalities [1]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

final_diagnosis: Congenital lobar overinflation associated with supracardiac total anomalous pulmonary venous connection

title: Bifid pancreas
clinical_history: A 67-year-old man presented for a gastroenterology consultation for a follow-up of colorectal cancer. He was asymptomatic, and his medical history was otherwise unremarkable. An abdominopelvic computed tomography (CT) was requested.
imaging_findings: Portal venous phase contrast-enhanced CT (Figures 1a and 1b 1) and magnetic resonance with T2-weighted images (Figures 2a and 2b) showed a mass-like image adjacent to the dorsal edge of the pancreatic body, continuous with pancreatic parenchyma, with lobulated contours and homogeneous soft tissue attenuation/signal intensity similar to that of the pancreatic parenchyma. A thin, bifurcated central line of hyperintensity is depicted in the axial T2-weighted image (Figures 2a and 2b), consistent with the bifurcated main pancreatic duct. These findings were consistent with bifid pancreas.
discussion: The pancreas can present with various anatomical abnormalities. Bifid pancreas, also known as “fishtail pancreas”, is a rare developmental anatomic branching anomaly of the main pancreatic duct [1]. Anatomical variants of the pancreatic duct system can be classified as: (a) migration variants, like ectopic and annular pancreas; (b) fusion variants, like pancreas divisum; (c) number or form variants, which include bifid pancreas [2]. In pancreatic development, the ventral anlage initially consists of two lobes, each with its own duct. One lobe grows into the pancreatic head, while the other regresses to form the uncinate process. If regression fails, a bifid pancreas can result, creating an abnormal branching of the main pancreatic duct and forming dorsal and ventral tails [3]. There have been only a few cases reported on bifid pancreas. While its clinical significance remains unclear, cases of acute pancreatitis confined to one tail [4] and chronic pancreatitis with calcifications in the ventral bud have been documented [1]. Misinterpreting this variant as a pathological condition, such as a neoplasm, is a concern. Therefore, it is essential for radiologists to recognise and understand this anatomical variation. Most cases are detected incidentally [1,5]. On CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, bifid pancreas manifests as a bifurcation of the pancreatic parenchyma, with cranioventral and dorsocaudal buds [4]. Some reports describe it as a pseudomass on CT scan [1]. Kikuchi et al. published a case of a bifid tail of the pancreas presenting as a gastric submucosal tumour [6]. The similar parenchyma attenuation, as well as the identification of the main pancreatic duct bifurcation, where magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) may be particularly useful, should help in differential diagnoses between a duct branching anomaly and a mass lesion, such as an exophytic pancreatic neoplasm, a peripancreatic adenopathy or a mass from a neighbouring organ. Bifurcated main pancreatic duct is another ductal anomaly that very closely resembles bifid pancreas, but it is not always indicative that the pancreatic parenchyma is also bifid [4]. Although bifid pancreas is a benign anomaly that usually does not require any specific therapy [1], surgeons must be aware when surgeries are performed on bifid pancreas due to the possibility that there are two pancreatic ducts that need to be reconstructed [5]. Similarly, due to potential mistake of interpretation with some kind of disease as stated below, namely neoplasms, it is important that radiologists are made aware of this variant.
differential_diagnosis: Bifid pancreas Pancreatic neoplasm Peripancreatic adenopathy or neoplasm

title: Bone amyloidosis: A rare case in a young adult
clinical_history: A 26-year-old male presented with progressively worsening pain in his right leg, along with increasing thigh swelling and leg shortening. Four years prior, he had sustained a right femur fracture, which was managed conservatively. Initial investigations revealed elevated blood paraprotein levels, with IgG lambda measuring 53 g/L (normal range 0.057–0.263 g/L).
imaging_findings: The radiograph (Figure 1a) shows a bizarre expansile lesion in the right proximal femoral shaft, characterised by multiple distinct lucencies and thickened intervening septa. A pathological fracture is also evident. Computed tomography (CT) (Figures 1b, 1c, and 1d) reveals an extensive expansile lesion filled with abnormal soft tissue (Figure 1d). The lesion contains thickened, remodelled septa (Figure 1c), and the outer cortex appears irregular and extremely thin in most areas. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figures 2a and 2b) of the right femur demonstrates a 10 cm expansile lesion in the proximal femoral shaft. The lesion has regions with high T1 signal intensity, consistent with haemorrhage (Figure 2d), and areas showing fluid-fluid levels (Figures 2a and 2c). A subsequent PET-CT scan revealed high uptake in the lesion, with no evidence of additional disease sites (Figure 3). The histological examination showed amyloid deposition, identified by the Congo red staining of amorphous material, which exhibited apple-green birefringence under high-intensity cross-polarised light (Figures 4a and 4b).
discussion: Background Amyloidosis is a condition where the deposition of insoluble misfolded proteins occurs in the extracellular space. Localised amyloidosis involves the accumulation of fibrillary proteins restricted to a single organ, while in the systemic form, multiple organs or sites are affected [1]. In contemporary practice, classification is primarily based on the chemical analysis of amyloid proteins and their associated clinical entities [2]. Primary amyloidosis is characterised by the absence of detectable plasma cell dyscrasia or abnormal serum proteins, while secondary amyloidosis is associated with a systemic disease, characterised by prolonged cellular breakdown [3]. With over 40 subtypes described, light chain amyloidosis (AL) is the most common form associated with bone involvement [4,5]. Although rare, bone amyloidosis can be linked to plasma cell disorders and monoclonal light chains, where abnormal extracellular deposition of AL amyloid fibrils occurs in various tissues, including the bone [6,7]. Clinical Perspective Infiltration of bone by amyloid typically manifests clinically with symptoms such as pain, pathological fractures, and neurological symptoms, particularly when the spine is affected. However, bone amyloidosis often shows nonspecific imaging findings, mimicking other skeletal pathologies and complicating diagnosis [3,5]. Imaging Perspective Radiographically, lytic lesions, bone destruction, and pathological fractures, with or without associated calcification, can be observed. In some cases, focal amyloid deposits, referred to as amyloidomas, can present as mass-like lesions that mimic neoplasms. They may also induce osteopenia with associated cortical thinning or erosion, often rendering them indistinguishable from other bone lesions such as multiple myeloma [5]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is particularly valuable for detecting early marrow infiltration and soft tissue involvement [5], showing low to intermediate T1 signal and low T2 signal, due to T2 shortening at amyloid deposition sites. This T2 shortening helps distinguish amyloidomas from chondrosarcomas, and myelomatous lesions, which show higher T2 signals. Gadolinium enhancement is frequently seen [8]. Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography helps in detection, localisation, and treatment response assessment, while histology and immunohistochemistry are essential for definitive diagnosis [5]. Regarding treatment, chemotherapy, immunomodulatory agents, and in some cases, autologous stem cell transplantation are options for patients with AL amyloidosis [1]. Radiation therapy may also be warranted in cases of localised amyloid light chain amyloidosis [1]. Take Home Message Bone amyloidosis, although rare, should be considered in patients with plasma cell dyscrasias presenting with skeletal complaints as seen in our case. Recognising its imaging features alongside its clinical and laboratory findings is vital for diagnosis and proper treatment and to prevent severe complications like fractures and deformities. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Aneurysmal bone cyst Myeloma Fibrous dysplasia Bone amyloidosis Post-traumatic granulation tissue Tuberculosis (unknown if patient has tuberculosis)

title: Cecal volvulus: A rare presentation of intestinal obstruction
clinical_history: A 47-year-old female patient presented at the Emergency Department with severe acute abdominal pain associated with nausea and vomiting. She also referred cessation of flatus and bowel movements for 4 days. Past medical history is unremarkable. On physical exam, the abdomen was distended and tender with no rebound or guarding.
imaging_findings: A plain erect abdominal radiograph revealed the presence of an air-distended large bowel loop in the left upper quadrant consistent with the inverted cecum, and multiple fluid levels (Figure 1). An abdominal contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) was later performed, with coronal and sagittal reconstructions (Figures 2, 3a, 3b, 4a, 4b, and 5). On CT images, there was a markedly distended large bowel loop in the left upper quadrant with air-fluid level, measuring a maximum calliper of 7.5 cm, adjacent to a small blind-ending tubular structure compatible with the ileocecal appendix, consistent with the inverted cecum. A clockwise whirl sign composed of spiralled loops of collapsed cecum and ileum, with twisting of central fatty mesentery with enhancing distended vessels, was present (Figures 4a and 4b). The gradual tapering of the obstructed cecum at the site of the whirl resulted in a stenosis, with the appearance of a bird’s beak (Figure 5). There was also dilation of small bowel loops, filled with fluid. There were no signs of bowel perforation, as well as no signs of pneumatosis intestinalis or other signs of vascular compromise.
discussion: The patient underwent urgent laparoscopy and the presumed diagnosis of closed loop obstruction due to cecal volvulus was confirmed. Background Cecal volvulus is a twisting of the cecum around its own mesentery and accounts for nearly 1% of all intestinal obstructions [1]. It is often associated with an anatomical variation like abnormal peritoneal fixation, which allows greater mobility of the proximal colon. This condition can be triggered by factors such as adhesions, scarring or an abdominal mass that acts as a pivot point. Complications include closed-loop bowel obstruction with compromised blood flow, potentially resulting in gangrene, perforation and even death [2]. Clinical Perspective Cecal volvulus generally occurs in patients between 30–60 years old and accounts for 11% of all intestinal volvulus [3]. Patients with cecal volvulus typically experience cramping abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and obstipation [4]. Imaging Perspective Historically, cecal volvulus has been identified using conventional X-ray films. Key radiographic features include a round, air-distended loop of the bowel with haustral markings directed towards the left upper quadrant, sometimes resembling the “coffee bean” sign, similar to the classic radiographic sign of sigmoid volvulus [3]. Although barium enema has shown high sensitivity for detecting cecal volvulus [4], it is rarely used due to the infrequent clinical suspicion of large bowel obstruction or volvulus. Nowadays, computed tomography (CT) is generally used for patients with gastrointestinal or abdominal symptoms. Several studies have detailed CT findings in cecal volvulus, including the “whirl sign” [5] and “ileocecal twist”. Other stated signs include the “bird beak” sign, convergent crossing transition points (“X-marks-the-spot sign”) and mesenteric fat invagination (“split-wall sign”), both described in studies on sigmoid volvulus [6]. Other causes of bowel obstruction include ileus paralyticus or simple mechanical obstruction (cases in which a bowel segment is obstructed only at one point), which configure cases of simple bowel obstruction, associated with a lower risk of complications and allowing a more conservative approach. On the other hand, a closed-loop obstruction, such as cecal volvulus, immediately requires a surgical approach because of its high morbidity and the risk of death in case of a late diagnosis. In the colon, ischemic complications only occur on the volvulus. Simple mechanical colon obstructions more often present a risk of diastatic perforation [7]. Outcome The success rate for reduction in cecal volvulus with colonoscopy is significantly lower than that for sigmoid volvulus, and over half of cecal volvulus cases experience recurrence. For uncomplicated cases, surgical options such as cecopexy are available, offering low morbidity rates (0–8%) and a minimal risk of volvulus recurrence. However, in cases involving gangrene or perforation, surgical resection becomes essential to avoid recurrence and is associated with low morbidity and mortality [3]. Take Home Message Cecal volvulus is a critical abdominal condition requiring surgical intervention, potentially manifesting as an acute abdomen. It is essential for radiologists to recognise its imaging features across various modalities to provide an accurate diagnosis and support clinicians and surgeons in patient management.

title: Rare association of synchronous primary digestive cancers
clinical_history: A 78-year-old male patient with a history of alcoholism and smoking was referred to the otorhinolaryngology department for dysphagia. Clinical examination revealed a painless 4 cm thickening lesion of the uvula. Cervical palpation revealed no adenopathy. A biopsy of the lesion was performed.
imaging_findings: CT scan revealed the presence of a uvula tumour (Figure 1), a suspicious hepatic lesion and a solid cystic lesion in the body of the pancreas. MRI showed a pancreatic body lesion, measuring 22 mm, with cystic and tissue components, intensely enhanced after contrast injection (Figure 2), and a 55 mm heterogeneous hepatic mass, of the segment IV, intensely enhanced after contrast injection (Figure 3). There was no dilatation of the pancreatic or biliary ducts. We performed an FDG PET-CT, which demonstrated an intensely hypermetabolic uvula (SUVmax at 9.2), with moderate hypermetabolism of the adenopathies (SUVmax at 2.5) and the liver lesion (SUVmax at 5.4) (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c).
discussion: Background Synchronous multiple primary cancers are defined as two or more cancers occurring in the same individual, diagnosed simultaneously or within 6 months. Their frequency ranges from 2–17% [2]. Primary squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the uvula is rare, accounting for less than 1% of oropharyngeal SCCs [3]. Multiple primary cancers are often influenced by factors such as genetic susceptibility, unhealthy lifestyle, and low immunity. Cancers of the upper digestive tract and oral cavity are associated with alcohol and smoking [4]. Genetic mutations, such as in the P53 tumour suppressor gene, may also contribute to the development of multiple cancers [5], but we did not carry out this search because it was not available at our centre. Clinical Perspective Dysphagia is a common symptom in oesophageal and oropharyngeal cancers, whereas neuroendocrine tumours of the pancreas may remain asymptomatic, especially when small [6]. In this case, dysphagia was the symptom that led to the diagnosis of the uvula lesion, with other tumours identified during extension screening. An upper endoscopy was performed as part of the extension assessment, which revealed a bourgeoning lesion of the oesophagus located 22 cm from the dental arches, measuring 15 mm (Figure 5), and which was not seen on PET-CT. Biopsy of the uvula and oesophagus lesion revealed a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, whereas biopsy of the pancreatic lesion revealed the presence of a grade 3 well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour (NET). Imaging Perspective Uvula cancer is typically suggested during clinical examination, with imaging used to check for lymph node involvement or metastasis. Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours are hypervascular on CT and MRI, showing hypo-attenuation on non-contrast scans, hyper-attenuation on arterial scans, and iso-attenuation on portal scans [7]. Imaging in this case revealed oesophageal, pancreatic, and hepatic lesions. Echo-endoscopic biopsy confirmed the pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, and liver biopsy verified its secondary location. Outcome Synchronous tumours are commonly seen in SCC of the respiratory system and oesophagus, particularly with alcohol consumption and smoking. However, the combination with a pancreatic NET is unusual. The patient underwent uvula resection with lymph node removal, followed by oesophageal tumour resection. Histology of surgical specimens confirmed squamous cell carcinoma of the uvula and oesophagus, while adenopathy was non-specific. The endoscopic resection had R1 margins, requiring adjunctive radiotherapy. The NET is currently being treated medically. Take-Home Message The coexistence of two squamous cell carcinomas is much more frequent than with a different type. This should be considered in cases of an atypical metastatic spread of the primary tumour, a high tumour burden in relation to the degree of tumour markers, or differential SUVmax values seen on hybrid imaging. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Incarcerated adult femoral hernia containing right fallopian tube
clinical_history: A 38-year-old woman consulted the emergency department for a lump in the right groin that had been evolving for months, which in the last two days has increased in size and has become painful on palpation in the last 24 hours. She also reported pain in the right iliac fossa of recent onset. She reported normal bowel function and denied nausea, anorexia or urinary symptoms. Physical examination revealed a painful mass, 2x3 cm in the right groin, irreducible and non-pulsatile. She was afebrile, with 74 bpm and a blood pressure of 132/86 mmHg. Blood analysis showed no relevant alterations.
imaging_findings: A CECT was performed, showing a right crural hernia with herniation of a small amount of fat and with a liquid collection inside (Figures 1, 2, and 3). The hernial neck measures approximately 7 mm, through which part of the fallopian tube appears to be introduced (Figures 1, 2, 3, and 4), also tracking the ovary, which is located anterior to the uterus (Figures 2, 4, and 5). No periovarian fat hyperdensity, pelvic ascites, or other indirect signs of torsion were observed. No herniation of bowel loops was observed. There is a right adnexal lesion compatible with the known ovarian dermoid cyst, 3x3.8 cm axial diameters, and a right ovarian follicle of 2.4 cm (Figures 4 and 5).
discussion: Background Femoral hernias represent a small percentage of all groin hernias, less than 8% in reported series. This type of hernia occurs mainly in women, is more frequent in the elderly, and typically affects the right side. Femoral hernias occur when intra-abdominal contents, mainly omentum and small bowel, pass through the femoral ring into the femoral canal [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Under normal conditions, there is no embryological connection between both structures. The femoral ring is located higher than the adnexa, making the herniation of a fallopian tube in a femoral hernia extremely rare. The incidence of this pathology is higher in childhood due to the greater proximity of the adnexal structures to the femoral canal and also in women due to the greater width of the femoral ring compared to men [3]. In adulthood, the development of femoral hernias is believed to be influenced by several factors, such as conditions that increase intra-abdominal pressure and acquired weakness in the abdominal and pelvic walls, as occurs in obesity, or multiparity [2]. Due to their narrow opening and the strong ligaments that constitute their anatomical boundaries, these hernias present a higher risk of incarceration and strangulation, thus requiring urgent surgical intervention [3]. Imaging Perspective Diagnosis of femoral hernias is primarily made by physical examination. However, in certain cases, imaging techniques such as abdominal ultrasound, CT scans, or MRI can be valuable, especially due to the wide range of potential contents within the hernia [1]. Typically, on axial CT, femoral hernias present with a narrow, funnel-shaped neck appearing below the inguinal ligament, between the lacunar ligament and the femoral vein (medial to lateral). This vein may often appear indented and compressed due to the presence of the hernial sac, which can result in the swelling of collateral veins further down. Coronal images can also be quite helpful, as they often show the hernia within the fat-filled space between the inguinal ligament, the common femoral vein and the adductor longus muscle [4]. Outcome Female adnexa are particularly sensitive to ischemia, which can result in an infarcted ovary or fallopian tube, making early diagnosis and surgical intervention crucial for a favourable outcome. During surgery, if the fallopian tube is viable, it should be repositioned in the pelvic cavity, whereas if there are signs of established ischemia or significant pathological changes, the affected structure should be removed. Our patient underwent urgent surgery; during the operation, the hernia sac was opened, revealing a strangulated right femoral hernia containing a viable fallopian tube (Figure 6). The hernia contents were carefully reduced, the sac was removed, and the defect was repaired with a polypropylene mesh. I hereby declare that I have obtained the patient’s consent for the writing and publication of this case report.

title: Dorsal wrist swelling: Carpal boss with associated synovial cyst
clinical_history: A 60-year-old female presented at the orthopaedic clinic due to a swelling on the dorsal aspect of her left hand. The swelling had developed over the past year, increasing in size recently. No significant trauma was recalled. The patient reported no significant pain or functional limitations.
imaging_findings: The X-ray demonstrated a subtle bony prominence around the metacarpophalangeal joints, visible only in the lateral projection (Figure 1a). No abnormalities were identified in the frontal projection (Figure 1b). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a bony prominence between the trapezoid and third metacarpal, with associated degenerative changes in the quadrangular trapezoid–capitate–metacarpal joint (Figures 2a, 2b, 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d). A lobulated cystic mass was noted on the dorsal aspect of the wrist (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d), located between the extensor tendons, and it appeared to communicate with the carpometacarpal joint of the third metacarpal and the capitate bone. The findings are consistent with a carpal boss (CB) associated with a dorsal synovial cyst. No additional significant abnormalities were observed.
discussion: The carpal boss (CB), first identified by Fiolle in 1931, is a bony prominence typically located on the dorsal aspect of the quadrangular joint, commonly at the base of the second or third metacarpal [1]. This osseous protuberance frequently fuses with the base of the second or third metacarpal, the capitate, or the trapezoid [2]. Although its aetiology remains uncertain, it has been associated with degenerative osteophyte formation and trauma, including fractures of the metacarpal base, avulsions of the dorsal carpometacarpal ligaments, or bone overgrowth from chronic traction on the extensor tendons [1,2]. Carpometacarpal coalition and an accessory ossicle, such as the os styloideum , are other causes reported in the literature [1,2]. The presence of a CB can disrupt nearby joint biomechanics [1,2]. This condition is often asymptomatic, although patients may experience localised swelling and discomfort at the affected carpometacarpal joint [2,4]. Symptoms may arise from extensor tendon tendinopathy (extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis) or secondary osteoarthritis [1,2]. Additionally, a synovial cyst may form in approximately 30% of carpal boss cases and become inflamed [1,2]. Differential diagnoses may include synovial cysts, exostoses, subcutaneous calcifications, and, more rarely, bone or soft tissue tumours [2,4]. X-ray and CT scans provide valuable information on osseous structures, and a modified lateral wrist view with hand flexion, 30° to 40° supination, and 20° to 30° ulnar deviation (known as the “carpal boss view”) can aid in visualising dorsal bony overgrowth [4]. Although this X-ray view may suffice for diagnosis, advanced imaging such as CT or MRI often provides additional detail. MRI is particularly beneficial for identifying bone marrow oedema, which has been associated with symptomatic cases, and provides excellent delineation of adjacent soft tissue pathology [2,3]. In our case, MRI revealed a bony overgrowth bridge with degenerative changes around the quadrangular joint, along with an associated synovial cyst. Treatment for symptomatic CB generally starts conservatively, using non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, activity modification, and splint immobilisation. Surgical intervention, including excision, may be required for persistent cases [4]. In conclusion, CB should be considered in the differential diagnosis of dorsal wrist swellings. Accurate imaging is essential for definitive diagnosis and effective management, with MRI proving valuable for detailed assessment of the complex anatomy surrounding the quadrangular joint. Understanding the anatomical relationships and characteristic imaging findings may contribute to optimal treatment outcomes, reducing the risk of chronic pain and functional impairment. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Duodenal laceration with biliary leak following motorcycle crash
clinical_history: A 30-year-old man was admitted following a motorcycle accident involving a frontal collision with a car. The patient was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit, sedated and ventilated, with a nasogastric tube and peritoneal drainage.
imaging_findings: Initial imaging included an enhanced abdominopelvic CT scan that identified hepatic parenchymal disruption in segment VI with capsular rupture and moderate free fluid (Figure 1). Persistent yellow peritoneal drainage raised suspicion of biliary tract injury. A follow-up CT, ten days after, revealed increased intra-abdominal fluid, loculations and enhancing peritoneal leaflets, suggestive of peritonitis and considering the hypothesis of a biliary leak. It is noted that pneumoperitoneum was not evident (Figure 2). A gadoxetate disodium-enhanced MR cholangiogram showed pre-existing haemorrhage in the initial phases (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c), but delayed imaging (7 hours) revealed minimal contrast in the hepatorenal recess and a fistulous tract from the lateral wall of the second duodenum (Figures 3d, 3e, and 3f). Methylene blue injected via a nasogastric tube reinforced the suspicion of a hollow viscus perforation, having been identified in the peritoneal drainage. In hindsight, and with the knowledge of the hepatobiliary sequence, the linear tract was identified (Figure 4). However, due to the subtle nature of the findings, it only became evident to the radiology team after the MR dynamic study.
discussion: Background Duodenal lacerations are rare in blunt abdominal trauma due to the retroperitoneal location and fixation by the ligament of Treitz [1]. These injuries can be associated with biliary leaks, peritonitis, and secondary complications [2]. Clinical Perspective Symptoms are often nonspecific, including abdominal pain [1,2]. Diagnosis requires a high index of clinical suspicion and detailed imaging studies [1,2]. Imaging Perspective Gadoxetate disodium-enhanced MR cholangiography plays a significant role in diagnosing biliary tract injuries, enabling visualisation of contrast excretion through biliary ducts in the hepatobiliary phase [3,4]. Unlike extracellular contrast agents, gadoxetate disodium is hepatobiliary-specific, actively taken up by functional hepatocytes via organic anion-transporting polypeptides (OATP1), with 50% excreted into bile ducts [3,4]. This dual pathway provides detailed visualisation of the liver and biliary system, especially valuable in trauma settings [3,4]. In this case, gadoxetate disodium was fundamental in identifying a biliary leak secondary to a duodenal laceration. Initial imaging during the hepatobiliary phase at 20 minutes post-injection revealed no clear evidence of active biliary contrast extravasation, temporarily excluding a biliary leak. However, a couple of hours-delayed imaging demonstrated minimal contrast extravasation into the hepatorenal recess, allowing the detection of a subtle fistulous tract from the lateral wall of the second part of the duodenum. The finding was key in diagnosing the biliary leak, particularly in the absence of other classic signs of hollow viscus laceration, such as pneumoperitoneum. Delayed phase imaging allowed identification of laceration also on precontrast T2 weighted imaging, since the findings were very subtle. Outcome The patient underwent surgical intervention, which confirmed a 3 cm laceration in the lateral wall of the second part of the duodenum. Teaching Points Complexity of duodenal lacerations : Duodenal lacerations are rare in blunt abdominal trauma. Their retroperitoneal location and anatomical fixation make them challenging to diagnose [1]. Association with biliary leaks : Duodenal lacerations may be accompanied by secondary biliary leaks due to their proximity to the bile duct system [1,3]. Awareness of this association can guide imaging protocols and improve diagnostic accuracy in trauma settings [3]. Gadoxetate disodium as a diagnostic tool for biliary leaks : Gadoxetate disodium-enhanced MR cholangiography is highly effective for detecting biliary tract injuries, leveraging its selective uptake and biliary excretion properties to visualise biliary leaks [3]. Value of the hepatobiliary phase : Allows for detailed evaluation of bile duct integrity and potential leaks [3]. Retrospective analysis : Subtle findings may be overlooked in the acute setting. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Bilateral infected endometriomas on emergency CT
clinical_history: A 50-year-old woman arrived at the emergency room with intense acute pelvic abdominal pain and a mild fever (37.5°C). She had a history of stage IV endometriosis. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis (22.7x10^9/L) and high CRP levels (31.98 mg/dL).
imaging_findings: An emergency abdominal contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) was requested, revealing a bilaterally multilocular complex adnexal mass with a multilayer appearance and thickened walls. The larger cyst measured 10 cm on the left side and 5 cm on the right side (Figures 1a and 1b). Bilateral tubo-ovarian abscesses were suspected on CECT, with noted adherences between the multilocular masses, uterus, and sigmoid colon. Due to the patient’s history and the presence of large multilocular masses in stage IV endometriosis, laparoscopic evaluation was performed, confirming the CT diagnosis of bilateral purulent endometriomas (Figure 2) and the adherences. Surgical management included extensive resection of ovarian tissue with drainage of the endometriotic cysts (Figure 2). Postoperative care involved a recommendation for subsequent therapy with GnRH agonists to further manage the condition, along with the placement of two peritoneal drainages. The excised ovarian tissue was sent for histological examination, and the drained fluid underwent culture studies. Both the blood culture and bacterial sample within the endometrioma tested positive for Proteus mirabilis bacteria. Antibiotic therapy with piperacillin/tazobactam was initiated for 10 days. Pathological examination confirmed the presence of abscesses within the endometriotic cysts.
discussion: Infected endometrioma (IE) is a rare cause of acute abdomen and is considered a gynaecologic and surgical emergency. Severe endometriosis can lead to complications such as tubo-ovarian abscess in 2.3% of cases [1]. Various risk factors contribute to secondary infection complications within endometriomas, including a compromised local immune system, haematogenous and lymphatic spread infections, pelvic inflammatory disease, intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD), transcutaneous oocyte retrieval, and endometrioma aspiration [1–4]. Endometriomas create pathways for bacterial growth, increasing the risk of developing an abscess within the ovary [1–4]. The most commonly reported bacteria in IE is E. coli , while the presence of Proteus mirabilis strains in both blood culture and endometrioma suggests a urinary tract infection [1,4]. Diagnosing IE can be challenging due to nonspecific symptoms, but it is crucial to identify this complication promptly, as conservative treatment is often ineffective. CECT is the recommended imaging modality in the emergency setting, although diagnosing IE through CT can be difficult [3]. Blood infection caused by Proteus mirabilis strains is relatively rare, and IE caused by Proteus bacteria is typically under-reported [4,5]. CECT features may not always be specific, but a diagnosis of IE may be indicated by a multilayer appearance of the cyst with thickened enhanced walls resembling the “double target sign” seen in liver abscesses [1–3]. A multimodality approach, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), can also aid in characterising IE and providing a differential diagnosis [2]. Management of IE is typically performed through laparoscopic emergency surgery due to the increased risk of peritonitis, pelvic adhesion, and sepsis [1-4]. Diagnosing IE can be difficult as it may present similarly to a neoplastic ovarian mass. However, a thorough clinical history of severe endometriosis, combined with laboratory values, can aid in making an accurate diagnosis through imaging.

title: Critical illness-associated cerebral microbleeds
clinical_history: Our patient is a 64-year-old male admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) due to a prolonged cardiac arrest, who was on mechanical circulatory support with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). He was COVID-19-negative and presented with an encephalopathic syndrome.
imaging_findings: A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed, and the susceptibility-weighted imaging sequence (SWI), revealed multiple small hypointense foci consistent with cerebral microbleeds (CBMs). These lesions were diffusely distributed across the subcortical white matter, splenium of the corpus callosum and posterior fossa, affecting the brainstem (midbrain and pons), as well as both cerebellar hemispheres. The cortex and periventricular regions were spared (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c). In addition, we found small watershed infarctions (Figures 2a and 2b).
discussion: Background Cerebral microbleeds represent focal deposits of haemosiderin-laden macrophages, which confer these lesions’ paramagnetic properties. They are commonly associated with chronic arterial hypertension, cerebral amyloid angiopathy and diffuse axonal injury, among other aetiologies [1]. Critical illness-associated cerebral microbleeds is a term encompassing many underlying causes, and it is mainly seen in ICU patients. Its pathophysiology in hypoxic-ischemic states is multifactorial, including endothelial dysfunction, blood-brain barrier disruption, and oxidative stress [2]. Clinical Perspective The knowledge of this condition is essential, particularly in the context of ECMO, which requires systemic anticoagulation and thereby increases bleeding risk. As a result, these patients have a potential risk for intracranial haemorrhages with a negative impact on the neurologic outcome [3]. Imaging Perspective Extensive involvement of the corpus callosum is a hallmark of this entity. Moreover, hypoxemia history is a common finding in the patient profile [2]. Therefore, a combination of clinical and radiological findings suggests that critical illness-associated cerebral microbleeds are different from other microbleed phenomena. Outcome Although CBMs’ clinical significance is not fully understood, they may serve as imaging biomarkers for the severity of brain injury and potential long-term cognitive outcomes. In the end, our patient had a poor neurological evolution and persistent multiorgan failure, so palliative sedation was provided. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Critical illness-associate cerebral microbleeds is an entity which should be considered when imaging reveals a specific distribution of CBM with involvement of subcortical white matter and corpus callosum, but sparing the cortex, deep and periventricular white matter, basal ganglia and thalami. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Hourglass bladder deformity
clinical_history: A 26-year-old male with severe haemophilia A presented to the emergency department with a month-long history of haematuria, dysuria, and lower abdominal pain. The patient is an active smoker and reported a weight loss of 20 kg over the last year. The patient admitted recreational use of ketamine.
imaging_findings: Initial ultrasound imaging revealed a low bladder volume with symmetrical bladder wall thickening (Figure 1a) and bilateral hydronephrosis. CT intravenous urography (IVU) demonstrated mucosal enhancement and confirmed symmetrical bladder wall thickening, forming the classic “hourglass bladder deformity” (Figures 1b and 1c). Additionally, ureteral wall thickening, proximal urinary tract dilation, and hydronephrosis were observed (Figure 2).
discussion: Background Ketamine-induced cystitis (KIC) is a condition caused by prolonged ketamine use, characterised by inflammation of the bladder wall. The pathophysiology involves several mechanisms: ketamine and its metabolites are directly toxic to the urothelium, leading to an inflammatory cascade that damages bladder tissue [1]. Chronic inflammation can alter blood flow to the bladder, leading to ischemia and fibrosis, which reduces bladder capacity and elasticity. Finally, ketamine may disrupt neural pathways regulating bladder function, exacerbating symptoms [2]. Clinical Perspective Patients with KIC often experience symptoms such as increased urinary frequency, urgency, dysuria, haematuria and suprapubic pain, significantly affecting quality of life [3]. KIC poses clinical challenges, including chronic pain, functional impairment and potential complications like bladder fibrosis and progressive renal dysfunction [3]. Imaging, including ultrasound, CT and MRI, is essential for assessing bladder morphology, excluding other conditions, and guiding treatment. Imaging Perspective Imaging is essential for diagnosing KIC and evaluating urinary tract involvement. Ultrasound can show localised bladder wall thickening, calcifications and hydronephrosis [4]. CT is useful to determine the extent of urinary tract damage and is important to exclude upper urinary tract malignancy in the setting of haematuria. Imaging findings on CT include enhancement of the bladder mucosa, diffuse or localised thickening of the bladder wall and reduced bladder volume causing the typical “hourglass bladder deformity”; other potential causes for this sign are chronic inflammation leading to fibrosis, malignancy, tuberculosis and post-radiation changes [4]. Upper urinary tract involvement includes hydronephrosis and ureteral wall thickening. The diagnosis of ketamine-induced uropathy is challenging due to its symptom overlap with conditions such as urinary tract infections, interstitial cystitis and bladder pain syndrome. Therefore, thorough imaging and clinical evaluation are crucial for accurate diagnosis and management [4]. Outcome Managing ketamine-induced cystitis requires prompt treatment to alleviate lower urinary tract symptoms and prevent upper urinary tract damage [2]. Cessation of ketamine use is the cornerstone of treatment, especially in the early stages, as it allows the urinary tract to recover. Pharmacological treatments like non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, anticholinergics and botox instillation can also help if combined with ketamine cessation. In severe cases, surgical interventions such as ureteral re-implantation or bladder reconstruction may be necessary [2]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points The “hourglass bladder deformity”, a result of diffuse or localised thickening of the bladder wall and reduced bladder volume, should raise suspicion of ketamine-induced uropathy. Patients may not readily disclose ketamine abuse, and clinical symptoms are often nonspecific. Therefore, one must remain vigilant and consider KIC when imaging findings suggest this deformity. title: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix–Saguenay
clinical_history: A 27-year-old male with progressive imbalance while walking and generalised tonic-clonic seizures from 5 years of age. No significant family history. Neurological examination revealed lower limb spasticity, brisk reflexes, extensor plantar reflex, features of ataxia, impaired pain, and touch sensations. Ophthalmic and fundus examinations were normal.
imaging_findings: MRI brain revealed the atrophy of the superior cerebellar vermis and the atrophy of the superior cerebellar cortex. The inferior vermis and the inferior cerebellar cortex are spared (Figures 2 and 3). T2/FLAIR linear hypointense stripes in the pons at the level of superior and middle cerebellar peduncle giving a tigroid/striped appearance (Figures 1a and 1b). Atrophy of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord is seen (Figure 3). Mildly atrophic pre-central and post-central gyri (Figure 4) with the thinned-out body of corpus callosum (Figure 2) also seen.
discussion: Background Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix–Saguenay (ARSACS) is a rare autosomal recessive spastic ataxia, initially identified in the region of Charlevoix–Saguenay, province of Quebec, Canada [1,9]. It is also reported in other parts of the world [3,4,8,10]. A few cases are also reported from India [3,4], but the prevalence has not been calculated yet. It is caused by a mutation in the SACS gene located on chromosome 13q12.12 [1,2]. SACS gene codes for the protein sacsin [10] which is expressed in cerebellar Purkinje cells and motor neurons [3]. Clinical Perspective It is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that typically presents in infancy; however, childhood [4] onset and teenage onset presentations are reported [3,5,8]. It is characterised by degeneration of Purkinje cells and spinocerebellar connections [6], commonly leading to gait ataxia, spasticity, cerebellar atrophy, and peripheral neuropathy [1,3,6,10]. Ataxia, spasticity, and polyneuropathy are considered a clinical triad [1,10]. Imaging Perspective MRI is the modality of imaging. MRI findings include atrophy of the superior cerebellar vermis with sparing of the inferior cerebellar vermis, T2/FLAIR hypointensities in the pons forming a characteristic tigroid or striped appearance, cervical cord atrophy, T2WI hyperintense rim around the thalamus, mid corpus callosum thinning, and bilateral parietal cortex atrophy [3,4,7,8,10]. Hypermyelination of optic disc nerve fibres [8], inferior vermis atrophy, and cerebellar hemisphere atrophy are other known infrequent findings [1]. Diagnosis of ARSACS is by clinical and imaging findings [1]. Definitive diagnosis needs molecular genetic testing [1,5]. Outcome It is slowly progressing, and patients become wheelchairs dependent by the third or fourth decade of life [10]. The disease is incurable [6]. The imaging gives insight considering the diagnosis. Supportive therapies like physiotherapy and anti-spasticity drugs can help to postpone the disabilities [11]. Early imaging and diagnosis can help in family screening and patient counselling. Even though it is a rare disease, multiple cases have been reported from different parts of the world during the last decade due to advances in imaging techniques and the availability of molecular genetic tests. Written informed consent for publication has been obtained from the patient relatives.
