title: Pleural splenosis: A diagnostic challenge in a benign condition
clinical_history: A 44-year-old woman with a history of controlled asthma and splenectomy following a gunshot wound 30 years prior presented with a dry cough, occasionally producing yellow-green sputum. She reported intermittent moderate dyspnoea and wheezing on auscultation, with symptoms gradually worsening over the past 30 days.
imaging_findings: Chest computed tomography (CCT) revealed solid nodules with homogeneous attenuation and enhancement (Figure 1), smooth borders, no calcifications (Figure 2), and no distortion of the adjacent lung parenchyma within the left pleural space (Figure 3). The nodules were randomly distributed along the longitudinal axis and measured up to 5.9 cm at the base of the hemithorax (Figure 4). A previous splenectomy was confirmed by the absence of the spleen in the abdominal cavity (Figure 5).
discussion: Splenosis is a rare, benign condition defined as the heterotopic autotransplantation of splenic tissue fragments, commonly occurring after abdominal trauma or surgical manipulation [1]. Splenic tissue implants typically occur in the abdominal and pelvic cavities, with thoracic involvement being rarer [2,3], where the blood supply is derived from the surrounding tissues [3]. This condition is often an incidental finding in asymptomatic patients, although symptoms such as pleurisy and haemoptysis may occur [3]. The mean delay in diagnosis is 18.8 years after splenic trauma [2]. In this case, the diagnosis occurred 30 years after splenectomy. The main clinical clue was a history of splenic trauma with diaphragmatic rupture. On CCT, splenosis is identified as homogeneous, non-calcified pleural lesions that may exhibit a tiger-stripe enhancement pattern and range in size from a few millimetres to several centimetres. Most cases present with multiple lesions [3]. There are anecdotal reports of mediastinal and subcutaneous involvement in the thorax, the latter related to chest tube placement [3]. The patient, in this case, had no history of malignancy, significantly reducing the likelihood of mesothelioma and metastases in the differential diagnosis. Furthermore, there was no laboratory evidence favouring an infectious process. In this context, the most likely alternative diagnoses included solitary fibrous tumour, which is commonly a single lesion, and intrathoracic extramedullary haematopoiesis, which is typically associated with an underlying condition, despite its rarity. As noted, patients with thoracic splenosis are usually asymptomatic, and definitive diagnosis is challenging without knowledge of prior splenic injury [4]. The gold standard for confirming splenosis is 99mTc-labeled heat-denatured red blood cells (HDRBC) scintigraphy, which was not performed in this case due to the patient’s decision to follow up after clinical and imaging findings suggested a benign condition. This decision highlights the importance of shared decision-making in cases where malignancy is not strongly suspected. Medical intervention is generally unnecessary for splenosis, with surgical treatment reserved for symptomatic patients or when malignancy cannot be excluded. Follow-up may be warranted for patients whose clinical history lacks definitive information, particularly in cases involving trauma with diaphragmatic rupture. Take Home Message Although pleural splenosis is a challenging diagnosis, and thoracic involvement is uncommon, a detailed patient history is crucial to maintaining a high index of suspicion. Diagnostic tools such as 99mTc-labeled DRBC scintigraphy may help confirm the diagnosis, particularly in complex cases where malignancy cannot be excluded.
differential_diagnosis: Mesothelioma Metastases (lung adenocarcinoma, melanoma, thymoma, or gastrointestinal) Tuberculosis Pleural splenosis Solitary fibrous tumour Intrathoracic extramedullary haematopoiesis

title: Rare cause of pulmonary thromboembolism
clinical_history: A 20-year-old woman presented with progressive shortness of breath and chest pain for 3 days. She was diagnosed with thrombosis involving the left popliteal vein to the common femoral vein with the possibility of a slow-flow vascular malformation of the left popliteal region. She was referred to our institute for further management.
imaging_findings: USG (ultrasonogram) : Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) involving the left popliteal vein (Figure 3a), superficial and common femoral veins (Figure 3b) with heteroechoic lesion around the popliteal vessels (Figure 3c). CTLL angiogram (computed tomography lower limb) : A lobulated heterogeneously enhancing lesion (Figure 4a) in the distal left thigh and proximal leg (intramuscular and intermuscular plane), extending into the popliteal vein (Figure 4b), superficial femoral, common femoral and common iliac veins (Figure 4c). CTPA (computed tomography pulmonary angiogram) : Eccentric filling defect involving the main and right pulmonary arteries (Figure 1a), extending to the right interlobar artery (Figure 1b), right basal trunk (Figure 1c), and segmental branches of the right upper lobe and left basal trunk [1]. Thrombus noted in the right atrium and ventricle. Multiple cavitary consolidations involving bilateral lower lobe segments (Figure 2). PET-CT (positron emission tomography – computed tomography) : High-grade metabolic activity in the left popliteal and thigh lesion (Figure 5b) and in the deep venous tumour thrombus (Figure 5a), bilateral pulmonary arteries (Figure 6b), right atrium (Figure 6a) and ventricle.
discussion: Background Synovial sarcoma is a rare soft tissue tumour due to translocation t (X, 18) resulting in SYT1–SSX fusion genes [1]. It is commonly seen in young adults. It is seen in the extremities [4]. The name was coined due to the presence of tissue resembling synovial tissue and its presence near joints [2]. Inferior vena cava leiomyosarcoma is a common vascular neoplasm. The other entities include intimal sarcoma of the pulmonary artery, angiosarcoma, hemangioblastoma, epitheliod hemangioendothelioma and lymphoma [4]. Clinical Perspective Synovial sarcomas of the extremities often present with pain and swelling of the affected extremity. They can also present with acute breathlessness due to deep venous thrombosis and resultant pulmonary thromboembolism. Doppler USG can be used to differentiate a bland thrombus from vascular lesions since intravascular synovial sarcoma is complicated by deep vein thrombosis [2]. DVT can be managed conservatively, but synovial sarcoma requires wide surgical excision and radiotherapy combined with chemotherapy [3,4]. Imaging Perspective Doppler USG detects arterial flow, which is used to differentiate the vascular tumour from a bland thrombus. CECT can be used to differentiate the tumour from a bland thrombus. It also helps in delineating the extension of the lesion. PET-CT can detect the activity of the vascular lesion and its invasion into pulmonary vessels [1]. It can also be used in the follow-up of the patient to assess the treatment response. Biopsy of the lesion can be done via image guidance. Outcome Biopsy was done. The histopathological specimen demonstrated monophasic spindle cells in a hypercellular fascicular architecture with little intervening stroma (Figure 7). Six cycles of chemotherapy with Adriamycin®, ifosfamide and mesna were given. Now she is on maintenance therapy with pazopanib. Post-chemotherapy PET-CT showed a significant decrease in metabolic activity in the popliteal lesion and its extension, and a complete resolution of metabolic activity in bilateral pulmonary arteries, right atrium and right ventricle (Figure 8). Take Home Message / Teaching Points In a patient with DVT with pulmonary embolism, radiologists play a pivotal role in differentiating the bland thrombus from a neoplastic vascular lesion in aiding the surgeon in better patient management [1]. This case emphasises how critical it is to rule out malignancy in patients who appear with unusual clinical characteristics and an unexplained pulmonary embolism. A young patient presenting with unexplained thromboembolism and swelling of a lower extremity with characteristic arterial Doppler signal within the thrombus should elicit a diagnosis of intravascular tumour [2].

title: Pancreatic lymphoepithelial cyst
clinical_history: A 50-year-old patient is referred from the primary care due to epigastric pain radiating to the left flank, accompanied by asthenia and episodes of postprandial nausea, as well as signs of panniculitis in both lower limbs. Blood tests revealed elevated CA 19-9 levels (135.5 U/mL).
imaging_findings: A contrast-enhanced CT scan was performed, revealing a hypodense lesion with cystic appearance in contact with the anteroinferior margin of the pancreatic tail, with areas of higher density inside it, which are suggestive of septations (Figures 1a and 1b). A contrast-enhanced MRI was conducted to further characterise the lesion. It showed a heterogeneous tumour with an atypical cystic appearance, related to higher signal intensity on T1-weighted and lower intensity on T2-weighted images, when compared to free water and the presence of small cystic rounded areas with higher intensity on T2-weighted images (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). Some small foci of signal drop on out-of-phase T1-weighted sequences compared with in-phase T1-weighted sequences were observed inside the lesion (Figures 3a and 3b). Additionally, areas of diffusion restriction were noted within the lesion (Figures 3c and 3d) and contrast-enhancing septations (Figure 3e). There was no visible communication with the main pancreatic duct.
discussion: Background Lymphoepithelial cysts are very rare benign pancreatic lesions of uncertain origin [4]. They are true pancreatic cysts which are filled with keratinised material, lined by squamous epithelium, and surrounded by lymphoid tissue and are most frequently located in the head of the gland and are more common in men, typically appearing from middle age to old age [1–3]. Differentiating these cysts from other pancreatic cystic lesions can be challenging [1–3]. Clinical Perspective Patients typically remain asymptomatic [2–4], with an incidental diagnosis on imaging studies that were conducted for unrelated reasons. Some patients may also present with abdominal pain [2] and elevated CA 19.9 levels [1,3], indicating malignant pancreatic pathology and prompting diagnostic evaluation. Performing imaging tests in both scenarios is crucial to delineate lesion characteristics and guide appropriate clinical management. Imaging Perspective In most cases, contrast-enhanced CT and MRI with contrast are performed after incidentally discovering a cystic lesion or when imaging is conducted due to suspicion of pancreatic neoplasia [2]. CT scans typically show a cystic lesion with heterogeneous content originating from the pancreatic gland [4]. With these findings, the evaluation is typically completed with MRI; although the lesions typically show the characteristic features of cystic lesions, there are often additional characteristics that help us refine our diagnosis. These lesions often show heterogeneous hypointense signal intensity on T1-weighted sequences and heterogeneous hyperintense signal on T2-weighted sequences [2]. Areas of restricted diffusion and regions where signal intensity decreases on out-of-phase T1-weighted sequences compared to in-phase sequences are observed. This phenomenon is attributed to the presence of keratin within the cyst [2,4]. However, the definitive diagnosis is typically based on anatomopathological examination [1,2]. Outcome A core needle biopsy of the pancreatic lesion provided inconclusive results for diagnosis. Subsequently, a distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy were performed due to suspicion of malignancy, leading to the final diagnosis. No signs of recurrence were observed in subsequent follow-up examinations. Take Home Message Identifying the aetiology of a pancreatic cystic lesion through imaging techniques is challenging. The crucial aspect involves assessing the risk of malignancy and carefully evaluating the potential benefits of invasive procedures to obtain histopathological samples in each case.

title: Vertebral artery dissection associated with fibromuscular dysplasia and acute dysphagia
clinical_history: A 40-year-old woman presented with acute confusion and severe swallowing difficulties. Initially suspected of stress-induced psychosis, she exhibited vomiting, anorexia, and weight loss. Due to ongoing symptoms and abnormal pulmonary imaging, a neurological evaluation was initiated to assess potential central causes of dysphagia.
imaging_findings: CT imaging revealed bilateral ground-glass opacities in the lungs, primarily in the peribronchovascular and basal regions (Figures 1a and 1b). Swallowing X-ray demonstrated severe dysfunction with stasis of contrast material in the pharynx and valleculae (Figures 2a, 2b, 3a, and 3b) and aspiration (Figure 4). MRI showed a small infarction in the left medulla oblongata, consistent with partial Wallenberg syndrome (Figures 5a, 5b, and 5c). A hyperintense T1 signal in the left vertebral artery suggested dissection (Figures 6a and 6b), which was confirmed by CT angiography (Figure 7). Additional findings included bilateral irregularities in the vertebral and carotid arteries, indicative of underlying fibromuscular dysplasia (Figures 8a, 8b, and 8c).
discussion: Background Vertebral artery dissection (VAD) is a rare but serious cause of stroke in young adults. Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) is a non-inflammatory, non-atherosclerotic vascular disease that leads to arterial wall abnormalities, predisposing affected individuals to stenosis, aneurysms, and dissections. FMD is a known predisposing factor for spontaneous dissection, occurring in 15% of cases, predominantly in women [1,2]. Clinical Perspective In this case, the patient’s symptoms initially mimicked psychogenic disorders, leading to an initial misdiagnosis. However, the development of acute dysphagia prompted further neurological imaging, which identified an underlying vascular pathology. Wallenberg syndrome, also known as lateral medullary syndrome, occurs due to infarction in the posterior circulation, particularly affecting the lateral medulla. Classic symptoms include dysphagia, hoarseness, vertigo, nystagmus, and ipsilateral facial numbness. In this patient, the presentation was partial, with dysphagia as the predominant symptom, highlighting the variability of clinical manifestations in VAD-related infarcts. Imaging Perspective Ground-glass opacities on the chest CT, combined with clinical dysphagia, led to the diagnosis of severe swallowing dysfunction and aspiration on a swallowing X-ray. An MRI of the brain revealed a hyperintense lesion in the posterior lateral left medulla oblongata on FLAIR imaging, with restricted diffusion and ADC reduction, confirming a subacute infarction. This infarct location affects the nuclei of cranial nerves IX and X, explaining the patient’s dysphagia and its associated risks. T1-weighted imaging revealed a hyperintense signal within the left vertebral artery, raising suspicion for arterial dissection. CT angiography confirmed this by demonstrating high-grade stenosis and an irregular luminal contour in the affected artery. Additionally, bilateral luminal irregularities in the vertebral and carotid arteries were noted, suggesting the presence of underlying FMD. Outcome Imaging findings confirmed the presence of a vertebral artery dissection and an associated infarction, which manifested as a partial Wallenberg syndrome. The identification of bilateral arterial irregularities suggested an underlying systemic vascular pathology, ultimately leading to the diagnosis of FMD. This case underscores the critical role of imaging in diagnosing complex neurovascular conditions and preventing misdiagnosis in patients with atypical stroke presentations. Take Home Message Consider vertebral artery dissection in patients presenting with unexplained neurological symptoms, particularly those with acute dysphagia. Fibromuscular dysplasia is an important risk factor for spontaneous arterial dissections and should be considered in young stroke patients with luminal irregularities. Imaging, particularly MRI and CT angiography, is essential for differentiating vascular from psychogenic causes in patients with atypical neurological presentations. Early and accurate imaging assessment can prevent misdiagnosis and facilitate appropriate long-term management in patients with underlying vascular pathology.

title: Palpable mass associated with brachiocephalic arteriovenous fistula
clinical_history: 68-year-old male, a known case of chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage V on dialysis, complaints of swelling in the left forearm and difficulty in cannulation. The patient had a history of left brachiocephalic arteriovenous fistula formation with a polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) brachiocephalic graft. Local examination showed dilated tortuous swellings on the left forearm reaching up to the cubital fossa.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound examination showed a relatively well-defined, predominantly hypoechoic lesion with a cystic component within, showing multiple septations and communication to the underlying vessel. Colour Doppler examination showed a typical “to-and-fro” pattern of flow (yin-yang sign) within the lesion and vessel with turbulent flow adjacent to the lesion. Communication with flow was noted between the lesion and the adjacent vessel.
discussion: Background An anastomotic pseudoaneurysm is a false aneurysm that occurs at the site of a vascular anastomosis. It is characterised by the disruption of the vessel wall with blood leaking into the surrounding tissue, creating a pulsating haematoma [1]. The polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) or Teflon graft is a synthetic vascular graft commonly used in bypass surgeries to restore blood flow, often in cases of severe arterial occlusive disease. In the context of a PTFE bypass graft, this complication is rare but significant [2]. Clinical Perspective Patients typically present with a pulsatile mass, localised pain, or signs of graft infection. There may also be symptoms of distal ischemia if the pseudoaneurysm causes significant blood flow disruption [3]. Imaging is crucial in diagnosing this condition as physical examination alone is insufficient to determine the extent and nature of the pseudoaneurysm. It helps differentiate between true aneurysms, haematomas, and other complications such as graft thrombosis or infection [4]. Imaging Perspective Diagnostic imaging plays a pivotal role in the assessment. Ultrasound : This can be the first imaging modality due to its accessibility and ability to visualise blood flow and pseudoaneurysm characteristics. It shows a pulsatile mass with characteristic “to-and-fro” flow on colour Doppler imaging [2]. CT angiography (CTA) : Provides detailed vascular anatomic information, including the size, location, and extent of the pseudoaneurysm, the relationship of the pseudoaneurysm with adjacent structures, and helps assess for any complications. MR angiography (MRA) : Useful in patients with contraindications to iodinated contrast, providing similar information to CTA. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) : The gold standard for vascular imaging, used particularly when endovascular intervention is being considered [5]. These imaging techniques are essential in pre-surgical planning, determining the size and extent of the pseudoaneurysm, and assessing for potential endo-leaks or graft integrity. Outcome Therapeutic options include surgical repair or endovascular interventions. Surgical options might involve resection of the pseudoaneurysm and revision of the anastomosis or graft replacement. Endovascular approaches may include the use of stent grafts to exclude the pseudoaneurysm, and thrombin injection with or without balloon protection [4]. The thrombin induces rapid clot formation, effectively sealing the sac, while the balloon prevents the migration of the thrombus into the arterial system. Prognosis largely depends on the promptness of diagnosis and intervention. Imaging not only aids in diagnosis but also in monitoring post-intervention for potential recurrence or complications, significantly impacting therapy planning and patient management. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Anastomotic pseudoaneurysms are serious complications of PTFE grafts, necessitating prompt diagnosis and intervention. Imaging modalities such as colour Doppler ultrasound, CTA, and MRA are crucial for accurate diagnosis and surgical planning. Prompt diagnosis with adequate imaging and therapy planning is pivotal in a better prognosis. Regular imaging follow-up is essential for monitoring post-intervention outcomes.
differential_diagnosis: True aneurysm Anastomotic pseudoaneurysm (PTFE brachiocephalic bypass graft) Haematoma Arteriovenous malformation Infection (mycotic aneurysm) Abscess Seroma Lymphocele Neoplasm

title: Growing breast myoid hamartoma in pregnancy
clinical_history: A 27-year-old pregnant woman at 12 weeks of gestation presented with a growing, painless mass in her left breast. The patient had no significant past medical history or family history of breast cancer. Clinical examination revealed a firm, mobile, non-tender mass in the retro-areolar region of the left breast.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound imaging at 12 weeks gestation showed a well-circumscribed lobulated heterogeneous mass with predominantly isoechoic echogenicity containing hyperechoic areas. No increased vascularity on colour Doppler ultrasound was noted. These features could suggest a benign mass with lactational changes (e.g., fibroadenoma, hamartoma, or galactocele) (BI-RADS category 3) (Figures 1a and 1b). At 24 weeks, the lesion grew to 100×53×114 mm (Figures 2a and 2b). At 38 weeks of gestation, the mass was occupying the whole breast. The increased vascularity on colour Doppler ultrasound is most likely due to breast engorgement during pregnancy (Figure 3). A core needle biopsy confirmed the lesion as benign with no evidence of malignancy (Figure 4).
discussion: Background Breast lesions during pregnancy present unique diagnostic and management challenges due to hormonal changes, particularly elevated levels of oestrogen and progesterone. These changes can influence the growth of both benign and malignant breast lesions. Imaging and treatment decisions must balance the safety of the mother and foetus while ensuring accurate diagnosis and effective management. Common lesions encountered during pregnancy include fibroadenomas, phyllodes tumours, and, less commonly, malignancies [1,2]. Clinical Perspective The patient presented with a growing, painless breast mass during pregnancy, a scenario requiring careful evaluation. While most breast lesions in pregnancy are benign, such as fibroadenomas or hamartomas, the potential for malignancy cannot be overlooked. The increasing size of the lesion during gestation raised concerns about its behaviour, necessitating thorough imaging and histopathological evaluation. Mammography is generally avoided due to high breast density and radiation concerns, making ultrasound the preferred modality in this population [3]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound findings are crucial for characterising breast lesions during pregnancy. In this case, the lesion appeared as a lobulated heterogeneous mass with predominantly isoechoic echogenicity containing hyperechoic areas, which initially suggested benign entities like fibroadenomas or phyllodes tumours. However, the lesion’s rapid growth warranted additional diagnostic measures to exclude malignancy. The biopsy revealed a spindle cell stroma and the presence of smooth muscle bundles, pointing towards a rare diagnosis consistent with hamartomatous changes, but with features distinguishing it from more common benign tumours [1,2]. Outcome Management of this lesion required a multidisciplinary approach. Given its benign nature, as confirmed by biopsy, and the absence of symptoms or malignant features, conservative management was chosen. This involved regular ultrasound monitoring throughout the pregnancy. Postpartum imaging showed a 20% regression in size, supporting the decision to avoid surgical intervention during pregnancy. The final diagnosis highlighted a unique presentation of a lesion rarely seen in pregnant women, with hormonal influences playing a likely role in its progression [2,3]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Hormonal changes during pregnancy can lead to rapid growth of breast lesions, both benign and malignant. Ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice during pregnancy and can effectively guide further management. Core needle biopsy is indispensable for confirming the diagnosis and excluding malignancy in rapidly growing lesions. Conservative management is feasible for asymptomatic cases, with surgery reserved for postpartum or symptomatic lesions.
differential_diagnosis: Fibroadenoma Galactocele Phyllodes tumour Leiomyosarcoma Adenomyoepithelioma Myoid hamartoma of the breast (MHB) Breast carcinoma

title: Inflammatory cerebral amyloid angiopathy
clinical_history: A 76-year-old male patient with a prior diagnosis of cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) was referred to the emergency department from a nursing home due to progressive clinical deterioration over the past 24 hours. The patient presented decreased consciousness. No fever or recent trauma was reported. An urgent CT scan was requested (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, 3d, and 4).
imaging_findings: Non-contrast CT performed four years earlier at the onset of CAA (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d) showed an isolated convexity subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) in the right frontal sulcus without trauma, in a patient with mild cognitive impairment. In the MRI one month after SAH, susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) sequence (Figure 2), significant superficial haemosiderosis and multiple supra and infratentorial microhaemorrhages are observed as hypointense areas with a “blooming” effect. Urgent CT (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 4) demonstrated an intraparenchymal haematoma in the right basal ganglia, a smaller left frontal haemorrhage, and extensive hypodensity in the left supratentorial white matter suggestive of cerebral oedema. In the MRI, two weeks after the acute event and corticosteroid treatment, hyperintensities in white matter on T2-weighted (Figures 5a, 5b, and 5c) and FLAIR (Figures 5d and 5e) sequences are observed, without diffusion restriction (Figures 5f and 5g), corresponding to vasogenic oedema with improvement compared to the previous CT (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, 3d, and 4). CT one month after the acute event (Figures 6a, 6b, 6c, 6d and 7) showed near-complete resolution of cerebral oedema, confirming the response to corticosteroid treatment.
discussion: Inflammatory cerebral amyloid angiopathy (ICAA) is a rare variant of CAA, characterised by a perivascular inflammatory response secondary to β-amyloid deposition in cortical and leptomeningeal vessels. Its unilateral form is even more uncommon and can mimic other conditions such as primary central nervous system vasculitis, tumours or inflammatory diseases [1–3]. CAA typically presents with recurrent lobar haemorrhages, cortical microbleeds, superficial siderosis, and progressive cognitive decline like Alzheimer’s disease [3,4]. ICAA, in contrast, involves an inflammatory perivascular response to β-amyloid deposition, leading to vasogenic oedema and subacute neurological deficits [1,2,5]. However, in our patient, clinical evaluation of the inflammatory process was limited due to preexisting dementia and the presence of a basal ganglia haematoma. Cranial CT is essential for the initial assessment, particularly in emergency settings. It allows for the rapid detection of lobar and deep haemorrhages (such as the basal ganglia haematoma in this case, as seen in Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, 3d, and 4), as well as white matter oedema, which, when correlated with a history of CAA, can suggest an inflammatory response [6]. CT also helps rule out mass lesions or hydrocephalus and is widely available. MRI remains the gold standard for a more detailed characterisation of the inflammatory process and differentiation from other entities. FLAIR and T2-weighted sequences show hyperintensities in white matter due to vasogenic oedema. SWI sequences are useful for detecting cortical microbleeds and focal superficial siderosis (Figures 5a, 5b, 5c, 5d, 5e, 5f, and 5g), hallmark findings of CAA [4,5,7]. Treatment is primarily based on corticosteroids [7,8]. In our patient, the radiological diagnosis of probable CAA [6], according to the modified Boston criteria (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, 1d, and 2), along with imaging features suggestive of ICAA [7,8] associated with a basal ganglia haematoma, guided the decision to initiate corticosteroid therapy. As demonstrated by MRI two weeks later (Figures 5a, 5b, 5c, 5d, 5e, 5f, and 5g) and CT one month after diagnosis (Figures 6a, 6b, 6c, 6d, and 7), there was a clear corticosteroid response in ICAA. Clinically, the patient also showed improvement, although with residual deficits from the basal ganglia haemorrhage. Unfortunately, the patient developed bilateral pneumonia one month after the last CT and subsequently passed away. In conclusion, in ICAA, the combination of clinical and imaging findings is crucial for diagnosis, particularly in patients with progressive neurological deterioration and unexplained vasogenic oedema. CT plays a fundamental role in the initial evaluation, enabling rapid detection of haemorrhages and oedema, while MRI provides better differentiation of inflammatory causes. The presence of microhaemorrhages and superficial haemosiderosis on SWI sequences suggests underlying CAA. Although biopsy remains the gold standard for confirmation, in clinical practice, a favourable response to corticosteroid therapy can support the diagnosis [7,8]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Inflammatory cerebral amyloid angiopathy Primary vasculitis of the central nervous system Subacute infarction Diffuse glioma Autoimmune encephalitis

title: Lipoblastoma: An approach to imaging-based diagnosis
clinical_history: A 3-year-old male was brought by the parents to the paediatrics outpatient department when they noticed a rapidly increasing swelling in the right gluteal region of the child. The child did not complain of any pain or fever. A local examination of the swelling site revealed a firm and palpable lesion. The skin over the swelling was normal.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound revealed a large, circumscribed, echogenic lesion in the right gluteal region with internal vascularity on colour Doppler. A fat-containing lesion was suspected, and MRI was advised for further characterization. MRI confirmed a well-defined, lobulated, septated, soft tissue lesion in the intermuscular plane of the right gluteal and upper thigh region with predominantly hyperintense signals on T1W images with few hypointense areas and septa hyperintense signals on T2W images with few T2 hypointense septa and suppression of signals on fat-saturated images, confirming the fatty component within the lesion. On gadolinium-enhanced images, the lesion showed mild heterogeneous enhancement along with thick enhancing septa. The patient underwent surgical excision of the lesion. Histopathology revealed low mitosis with areas of myxoid changes, the presence of multiple mature and immature adipocytes and monovacuolated and multivacuolated lipoblasts cells in different stages of development within the lesion. The final diagnosis was made as the classic subtype of lipoblastoma.
discussion: Lipoblastoma is a very rare, fat-containing, benign, mesenchymal tumour of infancy and children less than 3 years. Although it may affect both genders, male predominance is seen [1,5]. Lipoblastomas are almost exclusive to infancy and young children, and only a few case reports of lipoblastoma in adults are published in the literature [2]. The usual sites of involvement are extremities, head, neck, and trunk; however, they can rarely involve the pleural membrane, pericardium and parotid gland [3]. The tumour is soft in consistency and is rapidly growing in nature, although it can be slow-growing, and is usually painless. The tumour has the potential for local invasion and rapid growth, yet they carry an excellent prognosis if they are resected completely. No report of malignant transformation or metastases have been reported to date; however, the lesion may show relapse/recurrence, especially after incomplete resection [4]. Presenting symptoms depend on the site of the lesion [5]. Lipoblastomas are usually well-defined, encapsulated lesions; however, when they exhibit infiltrative features, the term lipoblastomatosis is preferred [6]. On ultrasound, a typical lipoblastoma is seen as a hyperechoic mass, which extends along the fascial planes with little or no mass effect on adjacent structures. On CT scan, it shows a typical fat density lesion with heterogeneous enhancement. Calcification is never seen in lipoblastomas [6]. On MRI, the mass/lesion shows heterogeneous enhancement with multiple enhancing septa and signal intensity consistent with fat (T1 bright and T2 intermediate with signal suppression on fat saturation images). On histopathology, lipoblastomas have various subtypes, and the predominant cell type favours the diagnosis of one subtype. The subtypes include classic, myxoid, lipoma-like and hibernoma-like. The classic subtype (as in our case) usually contains spindle and stellate mesenchymal cells, adipocyte, monovacuolated and multivacuolated lipoblasts, and intercellular mucin [6]. Lipoblastomas have an excellent prognosis when early surgical excision is done. Reaching the diagnosis Lipoma could be a possibility, but lipoma is rare in children and the presence of fatty and non-fatty tissue in the same lesion makes typical lipoma a less likely possibility. Also, with thick enhancing septa, lipoma is less likely. The age of the patient and possible myxoid component and thick enhancing septa favour the malignant pathology more than the benign. Liposarcoma and lipoblastoma are very close differentials, and histopathology is usually required to differentiate them. However, the age in our case favours lipoblastoma over liposarcoma. Teratoma would have calcific foci, osseous components, as well as tissue of other germ cell layers. Rhabdomyosarcomas are common in childhood, but the large amount of fatty component in our case makes it less likely. Written informed consent was taken from parents of patient and the identity of the patient is kept confidential throughout the manuscript and related documents.
differential_diagnosis: Lipoma Lipoblastoma Liposarcoma Teratoma Rhabdomyosarcoma

title: An unusual case of multiple cystic lesions
clinical_history: A 41-year-old male presents with a history of microscopic haematuria, a palpable right flank mass, and recurrent headaches. A CT scan was performed, followed by a brain MRI to rule out tumoural pathology. The patient had no significant medical history.
imaging_findings: In the abdominal CT scan, multiple bilateral renal cystic lesions with septum formation were observed. The right kidney had multiple, irregular, heterogeneous lesions with significant enhancement post-contrast, and hypodense central areas related to necrosis, the biggest located in the superior pole. Similar characteristics were noted in the left kidney lesions (Figure 1). Also, multiple simple pancreatic cysts and splenic vein dilation were observed, along with pancreaticosplenic collaterals. There is a lesion in the splenic hilum that enhances and follows contrast in different phases, suggestive of a splenic hamartoma (Figure 2). The brain MRI revealed multiple heterogeneous lesions with a cystic and a solid component in the posterior fossa, showing avid and homogeneous enhancement of the solid portion, and causing vasogenic oedema and mass effect on the pons (Figures 3a, 3b, and 4).
discussion: Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) syndrome is an autosomal-dominant hereditary disease caused by mutations in the VHL gene. This condition is characterised by the development of multiple benign and malignant tumours in various organs, such as brain haemangioblastomas, pancreatic cysts, clear renal cell carcinomas (RCC), renal cysts, pheochromocytomas, and paragangliomas [2]. The clinical manifestations of VHL depend on the affected organs. For example, renal cell carcinomas, or larger cysts may present as palpable tumours, and pheochromocytomas can cause secondary hypertension [3,4]. Central nervous system haemangioblastomas are the predominant tumours with the cerebellum being the most frequent site, as demonstrated in our patient. Notably, these tumours exhibit multifocality in up to 79% of cases [4,5], as in the case of our patient (Figure 2). Richard et al. [6] proposed four types based on their appearance: Type 1: Simple cyst without an observable nodule. Type 2: Cyst with a mural nodule. Type 3: Solid tumour. Type 4: Solid tumour with internal cysts. Typically, these tumours are classified as WHO grade 1. Type 2 is the most frequent, and it presents as follows: the cystic portion generally follows the fluid signal on different sequences, and the mural nodule tends to be isointense on T1 and hypointense on T2. After gadolinium administration, the solid portion (nodule) shows enhancement, while the cystic portion does not enhance [4,5]. Other tumours can appear in the abdomen, such as multicentric renal cysts and RCC, which may coexist as simple cysts, complex cysts, and cystic RCCs, generally tending to be bilateral, as observed in our patient (Figures 1 and 2). For the evaluation of these tumours, renal protocol CT should be used. Typically, they present as heterogeneous with early avid enhancement and rapid washout, often associated with central necrosis when there is rapid growth [4,5] (Figures 1 and 2). For pancreatic tumours, the most common are pancreatic cysts (Figure 2), which tend to be multiple and asymptomatic, behaving like simple cysts across different imaging modalities. It is important to rule out the presence of serous cystadenoma, which tends to be multilocular with septa. Tumours smaller than 3 cm tend to be homogeneous with rapid washout [7]. In our patient, the renal tumour was surgically resected, and histopathological analysis confirmed clear cell renal carcinoma. Molecular genetic testing was performed, identifying a pathogenic variant in the VHL gene and confirming the diagnosis. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
clinical_history: A 19-year-old woman, recently undergoing ovarian stimulation for oocyte donation, was admitted with a 7-day history of abdominal pain, progressive distention, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea. Her vital signs showed hypotension (88/56 mmHg) and tachycardia (125 bpm). Laboratory analysis revealed haemoconcentration and hypoalbuminemia. Both blood and urine pregnancy tests were negative.
imaging_findings: A plain abdominal X-ray showed an abnormal arrangement of the small bowel loops in the upper abdomen, suggesting the presence of a pelvic mass (Figure 1). Abdominal ultrasound (US) demonstrated bilateral ovarian enlargement with multiple anechoic follicles and a moderate amount of free intraperitoneal fluid (Figures 2a and 2b). Given the laboratory findings of haemoconcentration and hypercoagulability, along with a markedly elevated D-dimer, a thoracoabdominal computed tomography (CT) scan was performed. Contrast-enhanced CT ruled out acute thromboembolic events and confirmed severe bilateral ovarian enlargement (>12 cm) with multiple follicles, which displaced the colon and small bowel loops, as well as the presence of ascites. The CT also showed bilateral pleural effusions (Figures 3a and 3b). The set of imaging, clinical and laboratory findings was compatible with severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS). The patient was subsequently hospitalised for medical treatment and symptom control.
discussion: Background OHSS is an iatrogenic complication of assisted reproductive therapy and a potentially life-threatening emergency. It represents an exaggerated response to ovulation induction or ovarian stimulation, which typically occurs during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle or in early pregnancy, frequently following hormonal treatment with luteinising hormone or human chorionic gonadotropin [1,2]. Pathophysiologically, angiogenic vasoactive substances are secreted by the ovaries, leading to increased capillary permeability and an accumulation of fluid in the extravascular space. The condition is characterised by bilateral ovarian enlargement due to multiple follicular cysts, along with anasarca, including soft tissue oedema, ascites and pleural effusion, and haemoconcentration [2]. The modified Golan classification categorises OHSS into mild (grades 1 and 2), moderate (grade 3) and severe (grades 4 and 5) based on clinical symptoms, imaging, and laboratory findings. Moderate cases are defined by the presence of ascites, while severe cases are characterised by ascites, pleural effusion, and/or an ovarian size greater than 12 cm, as in our case [1]. Clinical Perspective The most common clinical presentation includes rapid weight gain, abdominal distention and pain, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Dehydration can lead to hypovolemia, resulting in hypotension and oliguria. In the most severe cases, thromboembolic events may occur due to haemoconcentration [3]. Imaging Perspective The defining finding of OHSS is consistent across all imaging tests: symmetrical, bilateral enlargement of both ovaries with multiple cystic lesions (enlarged follicles), which may be associated with ascites and pleural effusion [1–3]. Radiologists provide essential information to classify the degree of severity of OHSS by evaluating the presence of ascites, pleural effusion, and ovarian size. Abdominal US is the preferred initial imaging modality. In severe cases, particularly with haemoconcentration and coagulation abnormalities, CT is useful to rule out acute thromboembolic complications. Imaging studies also allow quantifying the degree of ascites, especially in cases that require repeated paracentesis [1]. Outcome Mild OHSS is usually treated with medical observation. In severe cases, the most critically ill patients may present with thromboembolic complications, pericardial effusion, arrhythmias, and anuria, requiring medical treatment, such as anticoagulant therapy, and close monitoring. In some cases, ovarian rupture may occur, requiring oophorectomy via laparotomy. Likewise, massive ascites can lead to abdominal compartment syndrome, necessitating evacuative paracentesis [1]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is a rare and potentially life-threatening complication of assisted reproduction therapies. Radiologists play an essential role in its diagnosis, classification of severity, and monitoring of the course of the disease. It is important to recognise its imaging features and differentiate it from ovarian cystic neoplasms. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Pneumothorax secondary to scalp angiosarcoma metastasis
clinical_history: A 68-year-old male presents with an ulcerated crusty lesion on the scalp that has been growing rapidly for 4 months. The lesion was resected with clear margins. Five months later, he returned with sudden dyspnoea, haemoptysis, and areas of bone exposure and scant granulation tissue on the scalp.
imaging_findings: In the selected images, a subcutaneous mass can be seen on the high convexity of the skull (Figures 1a and 1b), occupying a large portion of the scalp, with diffuse enhancement during the contrast-enhanced CT scan, a finding that corresponds to angiosarcoma. In the chest CT on the same date, no significant changes were observed in the pulmonary parenchyma (Figure 2). Six months after the first CT, multiple cystic lesions were noted throughout the pulmonary parenchyma, with peripheral ground-glass halos suggesting alveolar haemorrhage (Figure 3b). The largest of these is located in the left upper lobe, with a continuity defect in its walls, associated with a large ipsilateral pneumothorax (Figure 3c). Given the clinical context, these findings raise the possibility of cystic metastases leading to spontaneous pneumothorax.
discussion: Angiosarcomas are malignant neoplasms with endothelial differentiation, characterised by irregular neoangiogenesis and numerous anastomoses. It is a highly invasive tumour, with a high rate of lymph node dissemination and metastases usually present at the time of diagnosis, resulting in a very limited prognosis [1,2]. The cutaneous version of angiosarcoma is its most common form: about 60% of angiosarcomas originate from the skin of the head and neck, typically in older adults in sun-exposed areas [3,4]. Despite its uncertain aetiology in most cases, instances have been reported of its association with radiotherapy for breast cancer [5], pre-existing haemangiomas, or arteriovenous malformations in areas of trauma or previous surgery. Patients typically present with a painful lesion of rapid growth, bluish or purplish in colour, resembling a bruise, on the scalp or face, with indistinct borders due to rapid dermal spread and a high incidence of multiple neoplastic foci (multicentricity) [1]. Like other types of sarcomas, the lungs are the primary site of metastasis, most commonly presenting as solid nodules, indistinguishable from other types of pulmonary metastases. The second most common presentation are multiple gradually increasing cysts, especially associated with haemopneumothorax. Such findings have been proposed as diagnostic for secondary lesions in previous studies [7,8]. Among the differential diagnoses for the thoracic condition of this patient, bullae, pulmonary cysts, and pneumatoceles stand out. However, these diagnoses become less likely as they were not evidenced in the initial chest CT, as well as due to the more infiltrative characteristics present in this case, including their association with alveolar haemorrhage and necrosis. As stated, the mentioned patient progressed in less than 6 months with the emergence of cystic pulmonary lesions, alveolar haemorrhage, pneumothorax, and an extensive area of necrosis observed during surgery, findings that are compatible with metastatic spread from the primary cutaneous focus of angiosarcoma. The patient passed away 4 months later due to progressive deterioration of his respiratory pattern, despite the treatment employed.

title: Partial segmental thrombosis of the corpus cavernosum
clinical_history: A 33-year-old male with a history of erectile dysfunction (on sildenafil 100 mg) and left varicocele presented to the emergency department with a several-day history of left perineal pain after starting a new prescription of tadalafil 5 mg. He denied trauma. Examination revealed left corporal body induration and a varicocele.
imaging_findings: An axial CT pelvis with IV contrast (Figure 1a) demonstrated asymmetric enlargement and hypoattenuation of the proximal segment of the left corpus cavernosum, concerning for thrombosis. Absence of the right seminal vesicle and a left-sided varicocele were also noted (Figure 1b). The finding of right seminal vesicle agenesis, which is often associated with renal anomalies, prompted further evaluation with a CT abdomen with IV contrast, which revealed right renal agenesis with compensatory left renal hypertrophy (Figure 2). A penile ultrasound was attempted to further evaluate the corpus cavernosal findings but was ultimately nondiagnostic, as the patient could not tolerate the examination due to pain. MRI of the pelvis with contrast confirmed partial segmental thrombosis of the left corpus cavernosum (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d). Additionally, a fibrous septum at the crural-cavernosal junction was present bilaterally (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d), which has been associated with impaired crural venous outflow and thrombosis.
discussion: Background Partial segmental thrombosis of the corpus cavernosum (PSTCC) is a rare condition involving thrombus formation within the proximal corpus cavernosum, primarily affecting young men [1,2]. Although the definitive aetiology of corpus cavernosal thrombosis is unknown, reported risk factors include perineal compression or trauma, malignancy, haematologic disorders, cycling [1], and the use of phosphodiesterase inhibitors [3,4]. The pathophysiology is thought to involve disruption at the crural-cavernosal junction, where a fibrous septum acts as a mechanical barrier, leading to venous stasis and localised thrombus formation [2,5]. Clinical Perspective Patients with PSTCC commonly present with localised penile pain, a palpable mass, and/or erectile dysfunction. Physical exams are often significant for tenderness, swelling, and rigidity of the proximal corpus cavernosum. Although rare, timely diagnosis is crucial to avoid complications such as persistent pain and impaired erectile function [2]. Imaging is essential to establish a definitive diagnosis and distinguish PSTCC from other penile pathologies. Imaging Perspective Imaging modalities, including ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are essential for diagnosing PSTCC and ruling out other penile conditions. CT and ultrasound are commonly used first due to their widespread availability. Greyscale ultrasound often shows increased prominence and heterogeneity of the thrombosed corpus cavernosum, while Doppler ultrasound reveals absent blood flow within the thrombus and possible collateral vessels [2]. MRI confirms the diagnosis, showing increased volume of the thrombosed segment, hyperintensity on T1, hypointensity on T2 weighted imaging, and no enhancement post-contrast. The fibrous septum at the crural-cavernosal junction demonstrates low-signal intensity on all MRI sequences. Outcome Conservative management, including anticoagulation and anti-inflammatory medications, is preferred. Follow-up imaging may help assess thrombus resolution and identify any persistent structural issues [6]. Our patient’s symptoms improved with enoxaparin, and sildenafil 20 mg daily was prescribed to prevent scarring. Despite a family history of hypercoagulability, genetic and hypercoagulability tests were negative. We suspect our patient is anatomically predisposed to PSTCC due to asymmetric increased vascular pressure on the left, caused by the congenital absence of the right kidney and seminal vesicle, along with a fibrous septum at the crural-cavernosal junction. Take-Home Message / Teaching Points PSTCC is a rare but diagnosable condition that should be considered in patients with penile pain and a palpable mass. MRI is the gold standard for definitive diagnosis. Symptoms typically resolve with conservative treatment, including systemic anticoagulation.

title: Bone marrow oedema syndrome of the knee
clinical_history: A 42-year-old male driver presented with insidious onset pain and effusion of the right knee for 3 weeks. The patient had a similar history the previous year, which resolved after taking nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The knee range of motion was terminally painful. There was no history of trauma, arthritis or comorbidities.
imaging_findings: Radiographs of the right knee revealed normal bone density without fracture or erosion. MRI of the right knee revealed patchy areas in the epimetaphyseal region of both the femoral condyles, showing hyperintense signals on proton density fat-suppressed (PDFS) images (Figure 1) and correlating hypointense signals on T1W images (Figure 2), suggestive of marrow oedema. Mild knee joint effusion was noted without synovial thickening, erosions or low signal lines. The ligaments and menisci were normal. The tibial condyles, fibula and patella showed normal marrow signal intensity. The articular cartilage, posteromedial and posterolateral corners of the knee joint were normal.
discussion: Background Bone marrow oedema syndrome is a transient, mostly self-limiting entity presenting as joint pain, which usually affects middle-aged males [1] or pregnant females. The condition is defined by clinical features like pain and decreased joint mobility with no clear cause and no signs of infection or trauma with typical bone marrow oedema features on MRI [2]. The hip is the most common site, though the knee, ankle and feet can be rarely affected. Ischemic insult is hypothesised as the cause for this oedema, but this is based on the studies of the hip joint [3,4]. Another theory suggests that the condition is a type of atraumatic complex regional pain syndrome [5]. Other proposed associations are with reduced bone mineral density, vitamin D deficiency, cirrhosis and type IV hyperlipoproteinemia [6,7]. Clinical features may mimic inflammatory arthritis, but absent synovitis and erosions on imaging help in the differentiation. The symptoms peak in 1–2 months, with complete resolution in 3–9 months [7]. Imaging Perspective MRI is the imaging modality of choice for the diagnosis. The marrow oedema usually starts from the medial condyle of the femur with progression to the lateral condyle, affecting both the epiphysis and metaphysis. On T2 fat-suppressed images and PDFS images, there will be hyperintense signals in the affected areas [8]. The T1W images will show correlating hypointense signals. There will be an associated increase in interstitial fluid, presenting as knee joint effusion or soft tissue oedema. Lack of very low signal intensity serpiginous areas, “double line” sign and “rim” sign helps to rule out osteonecrosis [9], although subchondral insufficiency fractures may be present as low signal intensity lines. Lack of cortical disruption and soft tissue extension with a maintained contour of the condyles helps to rule out neoplasm. X-ray and CT can detect osteoporosis and subchondral fractures, which may be present in the late phases of the disease. The clinical findings, the self-limiting nature and the bone oedema pattern on imaging in the absence of trauma favour the diagnosis of the condition. Outcome The patient improved symptomatically with conservative treatment using protected weight bearing and NSAIDs. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Bone marrow oedema syndrome can rarely affect the knee and should be considered as a possibility in transient atraumatic knee pain. It is a diagnosis of exclusion made using clinical-radiological features. MRI is the diagnostic modality of choice to rule out the other common pathologies.

title: Skull base chondrosarcoma presenting with multiple peripheral nerves paralysis
clinical_history: A 24-year-old woman presented to an otorhinolaryngology consultation with a 2-month history of dysphonia and a 2-year history of gradual right hearing loss. No other symptoms were reported. Right vocal cord paralysis was noted at flexible nasofibrolaryngoscopy. A CT of the neck and chest was requested for further evaluation.
imaging_findings: CT demonstrated signs of right vocal cord paralysis, right tongue haemiatrophy, and atrophy of the right trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles (Figure 1). A lytic lesion in the right skull base was noted, only partially covered, given the undirected protocol. There were no other relevant findings. A brain and skull base CT and MRI were requested for further evaluation. CT showed a lytic lesion centred at the petroclival synchondrosis, with extensive destruction of the clivus and petrous temporal bone, showing calcified areas and involvement of the foramen jugular and carotid canal (Figure 2). At MRI, the lesion showed marked T2WI hyperintensity, T1WI hypointensity, and heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c). There was no restriction to the diffusion of water molecules, with high ADC values (Figures 4a and 4b). The lesion infiltrated the right cavernous sinus, right Meckel’s cave, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, and the hypoglossal canal (Figures 5a, 5b, 6a, and 6b).
discussion: Background Skull base chondrosarcomas are rare malignant tumours arising from hyaline cartilage remnants, comprising 0.15% of all intracranial neoplasms [1,2]. Clinical Perspective These tumours typically present between the fourth and sixth decades of life [2]. They are slow-growing but locally aggressive [2,3]. Most skull-base chondrosarcomas occur in the middle fossa, specifically at petroclival or petrosphenoidal synchondroses [2]. Symptoms reflect their location, resulting from direct compression of critical neurovascular structures [2]. In this case, a complete neurological examination confirmed paralysis of the cranial nerves VI, IX, X, XI and XII. Imaging Perspective These tumours exhibit a destructive, lytic appearance on CT with calcifications in a characteristic “rings and arcs” pattern, indicative of hyaline cartilage nodules mineralisation [1]. MRI demonstrates low to intermediate signal intensity on T1WI, high signal intensity on T2WI, and moderate to avid enhancement; however, variability exists based on mineralisation extent [1,4–6]. Skull base chondrosarcomas typically occur in a paramedian location but may be midline in 10%–30% of cases [1]. It can be difficult to differentiate from chordoma, a midline mass involving the clivus with extensive bone destruction and coarse calcifications representing sequestered normal bone. Both have similar T1WI and T2WI signal intensities and similar contrast enhancement patterns, but chordoma typically shows a honeycomb pattern of enhancement and a more heterogeneous T2WI signal compared to non-mineralised chondrosarcoma [7,8]. Also, chondrosarcoma shows higher ADC values [5–7]. Given the patient’s age, Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) and haematological conditions were considered. LCH is more common in younger patients. Skull base plasmacytoma and lymphoma demonstrate low to intermediate signal on T2WI and show restricted diffusion [7,8]. When chondrosarcomas affect the jugular foramen, paraganglioma and schwannoma must be considered. Paragangliomas show permeative osseous erosion with a “salt and pepper” appearance on T1WI, while schwannomas demonstrate smooth osseous remodelling and avid enhancement with cystic change [7,8]. Other differentials include giant cell tumour, with a typical T2WI hypointensity [7,8]. Outcome Surgery remains the preferred treatment, often with adjuvant radiotherapy [9–11]. After a multidisciplinary team meeting, and given the tumour’s aggressiveness, surgery was performed without a prior biopsy. Through a contralateral transsphenoidal approach, the lesion was only partially resected due to technical difficulties related to its anatomical complexity. Pathology confirmed a grade II conventional chondrosarcoma. The patient became asymptomatic, and a watchful waiting approach was adopted, with an MRI evaluation every 3 months (Figures 7a and 7b). Take Home Message Direct inspection of the skull base is difficult. Symptoms are nonspecific and usually related to the compression of neurovascular structures. Imaging characteristics along with demographics and lesion location are crucial in the diagnostic framework. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Acute vasitis: An important non-surgical differential of acute groin pain
clinical_history: A 65-year-old male presented with 2 days of severe right-sided lower abdominal pain. He was pyrexial with a raised neutrophil count (9.2x10^9/L) and CRP (55mg/L). Examination revealed right inguinal swelling and tenderness. Due to the high suspicion of incarcerated inguinal hernia, a CT abdomen and pelvis was requested.
imaging_findings: A portal venous phase CT abdomen and pelvis found a thickened and hyper-enhancing right spermatic cord, with the supra-scrotal vas deferens measuring up to 5mm. Further inflammation was seen within the inguinal canal, and a small reactive hydrocele was noted. A unilaterally enlarged right seminal vesicle was identified, however, there was no abscess. On the assumption that these findings were due to infection, oral ciprofloxacin was commenced, with temperatures and pain settling within the first 24 hours. The patient has not had any subsequent presentations. A right inguinal hernia repair was also performed during the inpatient stay with antibiotic cover to reduce the risk of infection. There were no complications.
discussion: The vas deferens is a muscular tube that transports sperm from the epididymis to the urethra. It forms the posterior portion of the spermatic cord, entering the abdomen via the deep inguinal ring [1]. Acute vasitis refers to inflammation of the vas deferens occurring from ascending lower urinary tract pathogens. This typically results in a non-specific presentation of lower abdominal pain with or without inguinal swelling and systemic infection [2–4]. Potential complications include a seminal vesicle abscess. In the literature, acute vasitis is often described as rare [3–6]. However, it is likely underdiagnosed because of similarities in presentation to other diagnoses, including epididymo-orchitis and incarcerated inguinal hernias, as seen in previous case reports [3–7]. Further cases have shown that vasitis is a common intra-operative diagnosis, indicating that with history and examination alone, vasitis is often indistinguishable from these better-known differentials [7]. Imaging is, therefore, vital in diagnosing acute vasitis. Ultrasonography (US) is an accessible first-line investigation and can exclude epididymo-orchitis. On US, the inflamed vas deferens appears heterogeneously hypoechoic with a thickened wall [8]. Colour Doppler may identify hyperaemia in the wall [11]. However, sonography is poor at excluding an incarcerated inguinal hernia, with incarceration displaying non-specific signs of hypervascularity and free fluid, diminishing its diagnostic role in this case [9]. Computed tomography (CT) is often the imaging modality of choice to confirm acute vasitis. The spermatic cord is seen as enhancing and thickened with oedematous changes and surrounding fat stranding. There may be an associated reactive hydrocele or seminal vesicle abscess [7,8]. Fat stranding and a thickened spermatic cord can be misinterpreted as an incarcerated hernia [10]. However, coronal images should establish no traceable bowel loop entering into the inguinal canal. In contrast to an incarcerated hernia, in vasitis there will be asymmetric thickening and enhancement of the spermatic cord. MRI is advantageous as it provides better visualisation of pelvic soft tissues, enabling the reader to trace the vas deferens. MRI is particularly favourable in younger patients as it minimises the risks from ionising radiation [7,8,10]. A clinical history suggestive of urinary tract symptoms, along with a positive urine culture, are both helpful in making the diagnosis. Once diagnosed, acute vasitis can be treated with antibiotics targeting gram-negative bacteria [2]. This case, alongside previous cases, demonstrates the importance of proactively checking the spermatic cord and inguinal regions on CT, to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary surgical intervention. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: A rare congenital disorder of metabolism: Homocystinuria
clinical_history: A 14-year-old male presented to the paediatric department with a history of headache, which was severe and diffuse in nature and associated with 2–3 episodes of non-projectile vomiting. There was no associated history of blurring of vision, loss of consciousness, seizure, trauma, fever, pain abdomen or loose stool. On examination, he had an emaciated appearance with microcephaly and hyperextensible joints. The patient had developmental delay since infancy, which he gradually gained at >3 years of age. He had an episode of seizure at 6 years of age, and his EEG revealed generalised epileptiform discharges. He was started on valproate, which was stopped in 2020. He continued to have multiple episodes of headache and vomiting during this period. He presented with bilateral papilledema in September 2021.
imaging_findings: MRI brain revealed T2 hyperintensities (Figures 1a and 1b) involving bilateral subcortical, deep, periventricular and cerebellar white matter with sparing of the perirolandic white matter. These areas show restriction of diffusion (Figures 2a and 2b) and do not show blooming on gradient echo (GRE) images. There is a prominence of bilateral optic nerves with tortuosity and optic nerve sheath dilatation (Figures 3a and 3b) with mild subluxation of both lenses (Figure 4). There is a relative increase in choline creatinine peak with preserved N-acetylaspartate (NAA) in TE 135 ms (Figure 5). Imaging done 3 months later revealed a mild reduction in global white matter hyperintensity (Figure 6). The next imaging, done 2 years later, revealed a significant reduction in the white matter hyperintensities and restriction of diffusion involving the white matter (Figure 7).
discussion: Background Homocystinuria is a rare congenital disorder of metabolism, inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion with a deficiency of the enzyme cystathionine-β-synthase whereby the metabolism of homocysteine to methionine is affected. This is because of the mutation of the CBS gene on chromosome 21q22.3, with incidents varying in different studies from 1/100,000 to 1/200,000. Patients with homocystinuria have elevated plasma levels of homocysteine and, usually, methionine. Only homocysteine appears in the urine (it is not present in the urine of normal subjects) [1]. Clinical Perspective Clinical manifestation has a wide spectrum of severity depending upon the individual with multi-system involvement. Four main organs can be involved [2]: Eyes : Ectopia lentis and/or severe myopia. Skeleton : Excessive height and length of the limbs (marfanoid habitus), osteoporosis and bone deformities, such as pectus excavatum or pectus carinatum, genu valgum and scoliosis. Central nervous system : Developmental delay/intellectual disability, seizures, psychiatric and behavioural problems, and extrapyramidal signs. Vascular system : Thromboembolism Imaging Perspective There are no specific radiographical features for homocystinuria. Although not specific, an MRI brain may show [3]: Multiple cortical-subcortical infarctions in the cerebellar and cerebral hemispheres of varying ages. Diffuse white matter signal intensity abnormalities may be present secondary to demyelination. Occlusive vessel or dural sinus disease on MR angiography or venography. Lens dislocation. Outcome This case emphasises the role of radiological investigations, especially MR scans, in the early diagnosis and evaluation of progression of the disease. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Patients suspected with homocystinuria should be evaluated by relevant specialists to confirm the diagnosis, detect genetic basis, manage the clinical manifestations and provide necessary counselling. With an early diagnosis and serial imaging for the progression of the disease, the severity of the long term sequalae of the disease can be reduced.

title: Intracranial tuberculoma masquerading as a neoplastic lesion
clinical_history: A 51-year-old male patient presented with right-sided limb weakness and slurred speech for a month. No vomiting/seizures/syncope was reported.
imaging_findings: MRI showed a well-defined lesion in the left periventricular region, measuring 1.8 x 1.5 x 1.6 cm (AP x ML x CC) with significant perifocal oedema (Figure 1). The lesion was T2 hetero-intense (Figure 1) with a T2 hypointense and T1 hyperintense rim (Figure 2), showing diffusion restriction (Figure 4). Associated mass effects noted were midline shift to the right, left uncal herniation, and effacement of the left lateral ventricle (Figure 6). Extensive vasogenic oedema was noted involving the left gangliocapsular region, left frontotemporal lobe, left hemi-midbrain, and left hemi-pons (Figure 1). On post-contrast images, the lesion showed heterogenous enhancement with involvement of the left lateral ventricular margin (Figure 3). Tractography showed interruption of white matter tracts in the region of the lesion (Figure 5a). The region of perilesional oedema showed only deviation of the left internal capsule and left superior longitudinal fasciculus tracts (Figure 5a), explaining the patient’s symptoms. Fractional anisotropy was decreased (Figure 5b) while mean diffusivity was increased (Figure 5c) within the lesion and in the region of perilesional oedema. The patient then underwent left FP craniotomy and excision of the lesion.
discussion: Background Tuberculosis (TB) is a significant public health concern, with global incidence rates rising between 2022 and 2023 [1]. Central nervous system (CNS) tuberculosis, the most severe form, accounts for 1–5% of total TB cases and has high mortality and disability rates [2,3]. Predisposing factors include HIV, malnutrition, immunosuppressant use, and measles infection [4,5]. It manifests most commonly as meningitis followed by tuberculomas and cerebral abscesses [6,7]. Clinical Perspective Tuberculomas, which make up 5–30% of intracranial mass lesions in developing countries, often cause non-specific symptoms like headaches, seizures, focal neurological deficits, and papilloedema [8,9]. They can be solitary or multiple, often occurring in the brain, spinal cord, or extra-axially [10]. As tuberculomas are reversible with anti-tuberculous medication, they need to be distinguished from other intracranial space-occupying lesions [11]. Imaging Perspective Tuberculomas can be difficult to differentiate from other parenchymal lesions due to their varied features on CT and MRI [11,12]. They typically appear as iso or hyperdense lesions with homogeneous or ring enhancement and irregular walls on CT. The target sign, noted in 1/3 of the cases, is the presence of central calcification with surrounding hypodensity [13]. On MRI, they have varying findings depending on the stage of the lesion. Non-caseating tuberculomas appear T2 hyperintense and T1 hypointense, with homogeneous contrast enhancement. Caseating tuberculomas with a solid centre show central T2 hypointensity due to granulation tissue. Caseating tuberculomas with central liquefaction show central T2 hyperintensity and T1 hypointensity with post-contrast ring enhancement [14,15]. Atypical MRI findings can lead to delayed diagnosis of tuberculomas and subsequent increased expenditure for investigating other diagnoses [16]. A study by Khan et al. [17] observed three major patterns of white matter involvement by tuberculomas on DTI (diffusion tensor imaging): interruption and deviation, exclusive interruption, and exclusive deviation. No infiltration of perilesional white matter fibres was seen in any of the lesions in contrast to high-grade gliomas. The study also reported decreased FA (fractional anisotropy) values and increased ADC (apparent diffusion coefficient) values in the tuberculoma centre and perilesional white matter [17]. Outcome Tuberculomas are treated with anti-tuberculous drugs, systemic dexamethasone or TNF (tumour necrosis factor) antagonists, and surgery for larger lesions or deteriorating clinical status [18–21]. Prompt administration of anti-tuberculous therapy results in a resolution of over 85% of cases [22]. Take Home Message In conclusion, understanding DTI features of intracranial tuberculomas is crucial due to their potential to aid in distinguishing them from neoplasms, which they often mimic. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Vallecular lipoma: A rare cause of dysarthria
clinical_history: A 65-year-old female presented with dysarthria and mild dysphagia over six months. No significant weight loss or constitutional symptoms were reported. There was no history of thyroid disease or a family history of malignant disorders. She had no complaints of neck swelling or ear symptoms.
imaging_findings: CT of the neck revealed a well-defined, fat-density lesion with a smooth margin in the vallecula, predominantly on the right side, attached to the lingual surface of the epiglottis. The lesion had a mean HU value of -100.9. It caused mild oropharyngeal narrowing without significant obstruction. No calcifications, cystic changes, or contrast enhancement were observed. There were no signs of invasion into adjacent structures or other indicators of malignancy. The nasopharynx and laryngopharynx were normal, and no cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. Ultrasound (US) examination revealed an ill-defined hyperechoic lesion in the vallecular region. Based on the imaging findings a diagnosis of vallecular lipoma was proposed.
discussion: Background Lipomas are benign tumours of mature adipose tissue. Approximately 13% of all lipomas occur in the head and neck region. However, oral cavity and oropharynx lipomas comprise only 1–4% of all benign lesions in these locations [1]. Vallecular lipomas are extremely rare and often present as slow-growing masses. Their aetiology remains unclear but may involve aberrant adipose tissue proliferation or metaplasia. Clinical Perspective Patients with vallecular lipomas may present with symptoms such as dysarthria, dysphagia, dysphonia, altered voice quality, or a sensation of a foreign body in the throat due to the mass effect. Asymptomatic cases are typically incidental findings during imaging or endoscopy. Accurate diagnosis is essential to rule out malignant lesions or differential diagnoses such as laryngoceles or mucous retention cysts. Though benign, the location of these lesions makes them prone to life-threatening complications such as airway obstruction [2]. Imaging Perspective While US may be used in some settings, CT is typically the preferred initial imaging modality for patients presenting with dysphagia or dysarthria, particularly in the absence of a palpable neck mass. Hyperechoic fat lesions, such as vallecular lipomas, may mimic other entities like a lingual thyroid. However, CT is sufficient for diagnosing and planning treatment in homogeneous fatty lesions with well-defined borders and no suspicious features. Features such as internal septa, nodular components, or enhancement should raise suspicion for other entities such as liposarcoma. MRI should be reserved for complex lesions, infiltrative features, or uncertainty about the involvement of adjacent structures. In our case, CT findings clearly indicated a benign fatty lesion, obviating the need for MRI. Differential Diagnosis Atypical and spindle cell lipoma, lipoblastoma, ectopic thymolipoma, teratoma, dermoid cyst, and epidermoid cyst. Imaging clues can help distinguish these entities. Atypical lipomas may demonstrate septations or nodular features, while lipoblastomas are often seen in younger patients. Teratomas and dermoid cysts contain calcification or hair-like structures indicating the presence of mature skin elements. Epidermoid cysts usually contain internal debris with a characteristic onion skin appearance and, on MRI, show restricted diffusivity of water molecules. Outcome Surgical excision is the treatment of choice, particularly in symptomatic cases, and offers an excellent prognosis [3]. In this case, the patient underwent endoscopic resection of the lesion without complications. Histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of vallecular lipoma. Take-Home Message / Teaching Points Vallecular lipomas, though rare, should be included in the differential diagnosis of upper airway masses. US features should be interpreted cautiously, considering potential mimicry by other entities like lingual thyroid. CT is sufficient for diagnosing and planning treatment for simple cases. MRI should be reserved for complex lesions or suspicious imaging findings.
