title: Typical imaging findings in spindle cell lipoma (SCL)
clinical_history: A 46-year-old man with a previous history of right nephrectomy due to complicated chronic hydronephrosis from urolithiasis was referred to our institution due to a painless, progressively enlarging swelling on the back. On examination, a palpable and mobile swelling was seen in the back on the right at the thoracolumbar level.
imaging_findings: MRI revealed a well-defined, round, soft tissue mass on the right side of the back at the thoracolumbar level. It was entirely subcutaneous, superficial to the deep fascia covering the latissimus dorsi and erector spinae muscles (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 2). The mass contained large areas of high signal on T1-weighted imaging (WI), which became hypointense after fat suppression, consistent with fat. It also showed well-defined non-lipomatous areas, hypointense on T1WI, hyperintense on T2WI, and which showed intense homogeneous enhancement after contrast, suggesting the presence of myxoid components (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c). No diffusion restriction was present (Figures 3a and 3b). A contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis was performed as part of the workup since the differential diagnosis included myxoid liposarcoma. It showed intralesional areas of fat and non-adipose tissue (Figure 4). No metastases were observed. In a prior study performed eight years earlier, no subcutaneous lesions were present (Figure 5).
discussion: Background Spindle cell lipomas (SCL) are uncommon benign tumours containing mature adipocytes and collagen-forming spindle cells, usually set in a fibromyxoid stroma. Subtypes include fat-poor, myxoid, angiomatous, and plexiform, among others [1]. Clinical Perspective SCLs typically affect middle-aged men (M:F > 9:1), often presenting as single, slowly growing, painless subcutaneous masses in the posterior neck, back or shoulder [1,2]. Although SCLs may mimic other lesions on imaging, such as liposarcoma, due to the presence of adipose and non-adipose components, the typical location in a middle-aged man should suggest the diagnosis of SCL [3]. Myxoid and dedifferentiated liposarcoma may also present as subcutaneous masses but are more common in the deep tissues of the extremities and retroperitoneum, respectively [1]. In this case, the typical location and demographic favoured SCL over liposarcoma. However, since myxoid liposarcoma was considered, a CT was performed to assess for metastases. A later biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of SCL. Imaging Perspective On CT and MRI, SCLs typically appear as well-circumscribed subcutaneous lesions with macroscopic fat and soft tissue components, representing adipocytic and collagen-forming spindle cells, respectively [4,5]. Adipose components are easily identifiable on CT and MRI with fat suppression sequences. However, the percentage of fat varies and may even be absent in fat-poor SCL [1,5]. Non-adipose components are hyperdense relative to fat on CT, and on MRI show variable intermediate to high signal on T2WI [5]. On pathology, the proportion of myxoid stroma varies, being especially abundant in the myxoid subtype [1]. This can probably explain why the T2WI signal varies and why SCLs of the myxoid subtype are often misdiagnosed as myxoid liposarcomas [6,7]. Intense enhancement of the non-adipose components after contrast is common [3,5,6]. The key diagnostic clue on imaging is the presence of a well-defined subcutaneous soft tissue mass with fatty and non-fatty components in the typical location in a middle-aged man [1–3]. The final diagnosis of SCL requires histopathology [4]. In post-nephrectomy patients, renal cell carcinoma metastases should always be considered, as they can appear in almost any location [8]. However, in this case, no prior history of malignancy supported this diagnosis. Outcome SCLs are benign lesions, and complete excision is usually curative [1]. Teaching Points Spindle cell lipomas are rare benign lipomatous tumours, often confused with malignancy. A well-defined, heterogeneous subcutaneous mass with areas of macroscopic fat in a middle-aged man’s posterior neck, back or shoulder strongly suggests SCL. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Gastric outlet obstruction post intragastric balloon insertion
clinical_history: A 63-year-old lady with a 3-day history of vomiting, constipation and midline tenderness following uncomplicated insertion of an intragastric balloon (IGB) 11 days prior for weight loss. Past medical history included appendicectomy and a self-deflating IGB 5 years previously for weight loss which passed without complication after 3 months. Biochemical assessment demonstrated metabolic alkalosis secondary to vomiting.
imaging_findings: A contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis was performed, which demonstrated a 12 cm hypoattenuating focus within the distal body of the stomach and pylorus with proximal dilation of the gastric body with fluid (Figure 1). The pyloric sphincter is effaced by the gastric balloon forming a tight seal (Figure 2). There is no small bowel dilatation to suggest a more distal small bowel obstruction, and there is no evidence of free air or fluid surrounding the stomach to suggest perforation (Figure 3).
discussion: Background With an obesity epidemic engulfing the Western World over the last number of decades, there has been increasing use of IGBs for weight control in those in which more invasive bariatric surgery is not feasible or appropriate and other lifestyle measures have failed [1]. IGBs can be swallowed or endoscopically placed within the stomach and the balloon inflated with saline [1,2]. They act by simulating the feeling of satiety and subsequently reducing calorific intake. Due to their minimally invasive nature, the risks involved are often less than those of invasive bariatric surgery with most patients experiencing minor nausea, vomiting and dyspepsia, which is usually transient over the first 7 to 10 days. However, a number of serious complications have been reported, including visceral perforation, gastric erosion, pancreatitis, bowel obstruction and gastric outlet obstruction, with the potential for significant morbidity and mortality [1,3–6]. Gastric outlet obstruction occurs when the balloon migrates into the pylorus and occludes passage into the duodenum with a handful of cases reported in the literature [6–9]. Clinical Perspective In the context of the recent IGB insertion, the differential focused on the complications of the recent procedure and allowed for appropriate initial management, investigation and intervention. Metabolic alkalosis and electrolyte abnormalities can be clinically catastrophic, and hence, prompt diagnosis and management are imperative for patient safety. Imaging Perspective The role of imaging was to confirm the diagnosis of obstruction secondary to the intragastric balloon and to exclude, where reasonable, other serious complications, in particular, the presence of gastric perforation or acute pancreatitis, allowing for appropriate management. Outcome The patient’s stomach was initially decompressed with a nasogastric tube to alleviate any vomiting. IV fluids and electrolyte replacement were administered to correct the underlying metabolic alkalosis with ongoing biochemical monitoring. The next day the patient underwent an endoscopy where the balloon was punctured and retrieved. Assessment of the stomach demonstrated minor gastritis for which proton pump inhibitors were started. After 24 hours of monitoring for complications, the patient was safely discharged home. Take Home Message / Teaching Points As the frequency of weight loss interventions such as intragastric balloons increases, so will the number of complications. Awareness of these devices and their complications is paramount in allowing early recognition and safe management. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Young female with herpes simplex encephalitis mimicking limbic encephalitis
clinical_history: A 40-year-old female patient presented with complaints of fever, altered sensorium and convulsions with a short history of 2 days. Her vitals were normal. She was further advised for an MRI brain non-contrast study for further evaluation.
imaging_findings: In this patient, the MRI brain non-contrast study was performed, and it revealed T2 hyperintense signal abnormality with FLAIR hyperintense signal changes involving bilateral medial temporal lobes. No abnormal post-contrast neuro-parenchymal or leptomeningeal enhancement was noted.
discussion: Discussion Herpes simplex (HSV) encephalitis is a common cause of encephalitis in adults, most frequently by the HSV-1 variant, with approximately 90% predilection, and the rest 10% by HSV-2 [1]. Early diagnosis improves the prognosis; however, it warrants certain imaging challenges. Poor prognostic factors include delayed diagnosis resulting in delayed management and extremes of age group involved [3]. Clinical presentation includes fever, focal seizures, altered sensorium and neurological deficits. In neonates, systemic and non-neurological features can be present [2]. Imaging Perspective MRI imaging is advised in clinically suspected cases and helps in prompt diagnosis. The radiological features involve abnormal hyperintense signal changes on T2 and FLAIR in bilateral temporal lobes and insular cortices [4]. On post-contrast images, no significant enhancement is seen. The involvement could be asymmetrical as well. In children, there can be extra-limbic involvement with gliosis [5]. Early detection on MRI imaging aids in improving prognosis drastically with early institution of treatment in the form of antiviral and antiepileptics [6]. Outcome HSV encephalitis and limbic encephalitis were considered possible differential diagnoses. A cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) study was performed, which revealed pleocytosis and elevated protein. Clinicopathological findings with radiological findings were suggestive of HSV encephalitis. A PCR text of the CSF can be further performed to confirm the diagnosis. In our case, antiviral was started earlier based on clinical findings and CSF pleocytosis, without waiting for the PCR study of the CSF. Take Home Message A short clinical history with sudden onset fever and seizures along with CSF findings of pleocytosis and elevated protein along with PCR study of CSF are confirmatory of herpes simplex encephalitis. Limbic encephalitis is a possible close differential diagnosis. HSV encephalitis can be managed promptly with the prognosis depending on early diagnosis with the help of imaging. Differential diagnosis should be considered and co-related with clinicopathological findings.

title: Septo-optic dysplasia plus syndrome with bilateral perirolandic and perisylvian polymicrogyria
clinical_history: A 21-year-old female presented with weakness in her right upper and lower limbs, absent vision in the left eye, reduced vision in the right eye since infancy, and neonatal seizures with no history of neurodevelopmental delay or anosmia. Examination showed diminished muscle strength, hyperreflexia in right-sided limbs, with extensor plantar response.
imaging_findings: MRI brain was performed with the following protocol: T1WI axial, T2WI in axial, sagittal and coronal planes, T2 FLAIR (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery), SWI (susceptibility weighted imaging), DWI (diffusion-weighted imaging), T1 MPRAGE (magnetisation-prepared rapid gradient echo), TIRM (turbo inversion recovery magnitude) coronal, DIR (double inversion recovery) sagittal, and 3D CISS (constructive interference in steady state). MRI revealed absent septum pellucidum giving the appearance of “mono-ventricle” to bilateral lateral ventricles. “Box-like” or “squared-off” frontal horns of lateral ventricles pointing inferiorly (Figures 1a and 1b). Hypoplasia of splenium of the corpus callosum, bilateral optic nerves (left > right) and optic chiasma was noted (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d). The pituitary gland and stalk (infundibulum) appeared normal (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d). The left frontoparietal lobe showed closed-lip schizencephaly, explaining the right-sided weakness (Figures 3a and 3b). Bilateral perirolandic and perisylvian polymicrogyria were also seen (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c). Septo-optic dysplasia plus was diagnosed based on the characteristic midline abnormalities and cortical malformations.
discussion: Septo-optic dysplasia (SOD), also known as de Morsier syndrome, is a rare congenital brain malformation thought to be a part of the holoprosencephaly spectrum. It is a triad of midline defects involving septum pellucidum and/or corpus callosum, hypoplastic/dysplastic optic nerve and hypothalamic-hypophyseal endocrine dysfunction [1]. Any two features of the classic triad are required for the diagnosis [1,2]. SOD-plus terminology is used in the setting of associated cortical malformations like schizencephaly [3]. Most cases are sporadic due to genetic abnormality or in-utero injuries like vascular disruption (proximal anterior cerebral artery), viral infections and exposure to valproic acid [4,5]. SOD presents with reduced visual acuity (bilateral in 80%), nystagmus, endocrinal abnormalities like neonatal hypoglycemia, hypoglycemic seizures, growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism and rarely precocious puberty, central diabetes insipidus and adrenal insufficiency. In SOD-plus, the optic apparatus is less severely affected and neurological manifestations like developmental delay, seizures or motor deficits are distinguishing features [4,6,7]. Dysmorphic midline abnormalities may be seen [4]. Schizencephaly is the most consistently associated cortical malformation [3]; others include polymicrogyria, focal cortical dysplasia (FCD) and grey matter heterotopia [8,9]. FCD results in drug-resistant epilepsy [10]. MRI brain is the imaging modality of choice. It confirms the diagnosis and explains the neurological symptoms with prognostic information. CT demonstrates absent septum pellucidum, small optic apparatus and small bony optic foramina. MRI findings include midline anomalies like absent/hypoplastic septum pellucidum, corpus callosum, fornix and hypoplastic optic nerve (usually bilateral)/optic chiasma. Pituitary abnormalities like hypoplasia of the pituitary stalk or anterior pituitary, and ectopic neurohypophysis predict endocrine abnormalities. “Box-like” or “squared-off” lateral ventricular frontal horns pointing inferiorly are seen on coronal images. On sagittal images, the low position of the fornix gives an “empty” appearance to the lateral ventricles. Other findings are hypoplastic olfactory tract/bulb, incomplete hippocampal rotation, persistent cavum septum pellucidum, cerebellar hypoplasia and encephalocele [8,11]. Schizencephaly is the dysplastic grey matter-lined cleft extending from the pia mater to the ependyma of the ventricle. It can be “closed-lip” with apposed cleft walls, nipple-like outpouching at the ependymal surface or open-lip wherein cerebrospinal fluid separates cleft walls. Polymicrogyria is a thickened, overfolded cortex with a nodular surface. Early diagnosis helps prompt a multidisciplinary team of endocrinologists, ophthalmologists, and neurologists addressing hormonal imbalance, visual impairment, autism, and obesity. There is no cure for SOD-plus. The constellation of symptoms and their severity dictates the highly variable prognosis [12]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Simultaneous lacrimal and parotid gland lymphoma
clinical_history: A 57-year-old woman presents with a left preauricular lump of two weeks’ evolution. Physical examination reveals a soft, mobile 1 cm left preauricular lump upon superficial palpation. An MRI and a fine-needle aspiration biopsy was requested for further evaluation.
imaging_findings: Facial MRI revealed a small lesion in the superficial lobe of the left parotid gland, located cranial to the Stensen duct, and anterior and lateral to the facial nerve, showing mild heterogeneity and peripheral enhancement after contrast injection. It exhibited a very low apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) value on the ADC map (0.4 to 0.5x10^-3 mm 2 /second) and a type III TIC (time-intensity curve), suggesting radiological aggressiveness (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, 1d, and 1e). Additionally, a marked enlargement of the left lacrimal gland was observed, with similar radiological findings on diffusion and dynamic gadolinium-enhancement sequences, indicative of an infiltrative process (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, 2d, and 2e). The low ADC values on both lesions gave the clue to diagnose a possible concomitant lymphoproliferative process, and this finding is key to the diagnosis [1].
discussion: Background Around 25% of extranodal lymphomas develop in the head and neck, mainly in the parotid glands, tonsils, and pharynx [2]. Orbital lymphomas are rare, accounting for 1–2% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas and 8% of extranodal cases, yet they are the most common primary orbital tumours in adults over 60 years [1]. Clinical Perspective Parotid lymphoma typically presents as a painless, progressively enlarging solitary mass, with systemic B symptoms being uncommon [4]. Orbital non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) frequently involves the lacrimal gland, manifesting as painless, progressive proptosis or orbital swelling [5]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound (US) and computed tomography (CT) findings are often nonspecific. Both benign and malignant lesions may appear similar, though irregular borders, heterogeneous enhancement, lymphadenopathy, or invasion suggest malignancy. However, the absence of these features does not rule out lymphoma [6,7]. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) has proven useful for diagnosing lymphomas. These tumours exhibit high cellularity, leading to restricted diffusion, high signal intensity on DWI, and low ADC values [8–10]. Conventional MRI typically shows low T1 signal intensity, variable T2 signal intensity, and strong gadolinium enhancement [6]. Positron emission tomography (PET) is valuable in identifying extranodal involvement. In this case, both glands showed intense glucose uptake with no additional significant findings. The differential diagnoses include IgG4-related disease, lymphoid hyperplasia, and granulomatous diseases. IgG4 disease and lymphoid hyperplasia have higher ADC values, progressive enhancement, and fibrosis (T2 hypointense in IgG4 disease). Granulomatous diseases exhibit variable T2 signal, nodular or rim enhancement, and mild to moderate diffusion restriction. Treatment and Outcome Definitive diagnosis is based on histopathological evaluation with immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining [3]. Tissue sampling can be performed via fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB), core needle biopsy (CNB), or excisional biopsy, such as superficial parotidectomy. In this case, FNAB suggested lymphoid neoplasia, and parotidectomy confirmed follicular lymphoma grade II. MRI revealed similar lacrimal gland involvement, leading to a stage II classification according to the Ann Arbor system. Stage I and II lymphomas are commonly treated with radiotherapy. However, in cases where secondary toxicity is a concern, alternatives like watchful waiting or rituximab monotherapy are considered [11]. In this case, the patient received rituximab and showed favourable progress. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Pony ride under pressure: A case of atypical compartment syndrome
clinical_history: A 36-year-old woman presented with permanent pain of increasing intensity in her right leg that had been evolving for 24 hours. The pain appeared immediately following a horse ride in an improperly adjusted stirrup and was not relieved by paracetamol, ketoprofen and morphine. No significant medical history.
imaging_findings: MRI of the legs showed a swollen appearance of the right anterolateral compartment muscles with: Fat-suppressed coronal T2-weighted (Figure 1) and axial PD-SPIR (Figure 2) emphasised the acute involvement of the lateral compartment of the leg through a noticeable bulging of the compartment muscles, which is clearly visible in the axial view when compared to the healthy contralateral side. Additional loss of fascicular architecture is seen. Diffuse hyperintensity of the compartment indicates muscular oedema. Sagittal T1-weighted sequence showed slight spontaneous high signal intensity within the involved muscles (Figure 3). After injection, the fat-suppressed axial T1-weighted sequence (Figure 4) showed focal defects of enhancement within the proximal portion of the muscles, indicating areas of ischemia. No other causes of acute pain, including a stress fracture, deep vein thrombosis or focal muscular strain, were identified on the examination. The diagnosis of acute compartment syndrome was confirmed by MRI.
discussion: Background Compartment syndrome is defined by an increase in intracompartmental pressure (ICP) above 30 mmHg [1]. Any situation that raises ICP can cause this condition, potentially leading to ischemia or necrosis. Most cases result from a neighbouring bone fracture, the anterior compartment of the leg being the most common location [1]. In 25% of cases, the cause is non-traumatic, often leading to diagnostic delays [1]. Among other favouring activities, horse riding has been reported in the literature [2] due to repeated ankle dorsiflexion that is known to increase ICP in the lateral compartment of the leg [3]. Hip and knee flexion may also contribute due to a reduced venous outflow [3]. Clinical Perspective Acute compartment syndrome (ACS) is a surgical emergency that can result in neurological deficits, rhabdomyolysis, infection, amputation and even death. The typical initial presentation shows tension localised to the muscle compartment with disproportionate pain. Neurovascular signs include paresthesia, hypoesthesia, motor dysfunction, pulselessness, and are often the result of late-stage tissue damage. Atraumatic ACS represents a diagnostic challenge for the clinician, and the contribution of MRI can be of considerable help. Imaging Perspective The T1 sequence shows a bulging and hypertrophic appearance of the muscle compartment due to pathophysiological hyperpressure. Spontaneous hyperintensity within the pathological muscle compartment is suggestive of interstitial bleeding [4]. Low oedematous changes within the subcutaneous tissue rule out the presence of cellulitis. T2 or STIR sequences show a diffuse hyperintensity of the muscle group, suggesting oedema. Although this diffuse compartment involvement is not totally specific to ACS, it rules out the differential diagnosis of focal muscle tear. Oedema is also visible in delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), which combines pain and muscle swelling after unusual exertion. It should be emphasised that there is no muscle ischaemia or necrosis in DOMS, which is by definition reversible [4]. After contrast injection, there is usually significant diffuse enhancement of the affected muscle in ACS [4]. When present, unenhanced focal areas should be reported as they suggest an advanced ischemic process, progressing towards muscle necrosis [4]. The presence of such areas rules out the diagnosis of DOMS. Outcome Early fasciotomy (i.e., in less than 6 hours) is the main treatment option to ensure functional recovery, which imaging should not delay [1]. When the diagnosis has been delayed, as in most cases of atraumatic ACS, it is still recommended to carry out a surgical exploration to remove the nerve compression and hope for a chance of recovery [2]. MRI can help the surgeon to selectively choose the appropriate fascia to incise and assess the extent of necrosis [5]. In our case, the patient underwent decompressive fasciotomy, but no ICP was reported. Take Home Message / Teaching Points A detailed history and knowledge about atraumatic acute compartment syndrome (ACS) are key to ensuring rapid intervention. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Morgagni–Larrey hernia in an adult
clinical_history: A 24-year-old female with a history of bronchitis and cough underwent a chest x-ray and subsequent transthoracic echocardiography at an external facility.
imaging_findings: The chest x-ray at an external facility revealed cardiomegaly, while the subsequent transthoracic echocardiography suggested dextrocardia. Upon presentation to our facility for further evaluation, an electrocardiogram demonstrated a significant baseline artefact, likely indicating normal sinus rhythm. Additionally, a chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a large left-sided Morgagni–Larrey diaphragmatic hernia encompassing most of the transverse colon and omentum, extending through a substantial subxiphoid orifice measuring approximately 4.3 x 5.2 cm (Figures 1 and 2). This anatomical anomaly induced cardiomediastinal displacement to the right due to mass effect, with a portion of the stomach antrum, displaced superiorly into the anterior mediastinal defect (Figures 3 and 4). Unfortunately, the radiographic scan done in the outside facility cannot be obtained but the scout image from the CT scan shows what is thought to be cardiomegaly (Figure 5).
discussion: Background Morgagni–Larrey hernia represents one of the four classifications of diaphragmatic hernias. Morgagni and Larrey hernias are both types of anterior diaphragmatic hernias resulting from congenital defects in the diaphragm. Specifically, they occur due to incomplete fusion between the pars sternalis and pars costalis of the hemidiaphragms. The differentiation between the two is primarily based on their anatomical location: Morgagni hernia typically occurs on the right side of the diaphragm, and Larrey hernia occurs on the left side of the diaphragm. Despite this distinction, both hernias share similar embryological origins and clinical presentations. They are collectively referred to as anterior diaphragmatic hernias of Morgagni–Larrey [1]. The other categories encompass a Bochdalek hernia, characterised by a defect in the posterolateral region, a hiatal hernia, involving the oesophageal hiatus, and a paraoesophageal hernia, situated adjacent to the oesophageal hiatus [2]. The classical Bochdalek hernia constitutes approximately 80% of all congenital diaphragmatic hernias, while Morgagni hernia makes up about 3-4% of diaphragmatic hernias in both children and adults. In Morgagni–Larrey hernia, the defect tends to be small, and symptoms typically arise due to the size and contents of the hernia. The herniated contents commonly include segments of the omentum and colon, although the stomach, liver, and small intestines may also be involved. Morgagni hernias are predominantly located on the right side, occurring in approximately 90% of cases, with left-sided Morgagni–Larrey hernias accounting for 8% and bilateral hernias for 2% [2]. Although left-sided and bilateral hernias occur, Morgagni hernias occur on the right side due to the pericardial attachments to the diaphragm that provide protection and support to the left side [2]. Imaging Perspective Chest X-ray stands as the predominant imaging tool for diagnosing this variant of diaphragmatic hernias, yet initial diagnostic imaging may yield negative results in numerous patients. Notable findings such as a bowel gas pattern, the presence of air-fluid level in the thoracic cavity, or lucency in the chest with a deviation of the heart and mediastinum may be apparent, further complicating and challenging the conclusive diagnosis [4]. CT scans play a crucial role in providing additional characterisation of anterior mediastinal masses initially detected on chest radiographs, thereby assisting in preoperative diagnosis and surgical planning. A CT scan can be used to diagnose a Morgagni–Larrey hernia radiographically, which is characterised by the presence of a sizable pericardiac fat density along with linear densities resembling omental blood vessels and an unusual elevation of the transverse colon. Additionally, CT imaging aids in distinguishing a cardiophrenic mass from cardiac structures and enables the identification of bowel loops within the thoracic cavity [5]. Outcome Once the diagnosis is established, elective surgical intervention for foramen of Morgagni is recommended irrespective of age, aiming to mitigate the risk of potential emergent complications like incarceration and strangulation. Various approaches, including transabdominal and transthoracic techniques, either through open surgery or endoscopy, have been employed for this purpose [6]. title: Emphysematous pyelonephritis. Ultrasound, X-ray, and CT findings
clinical_history: A 59-year-old male with no significant medical history presented with right flank pain and urinary symptoms that began 24 hours earlier. On arrival, high glucose levels (290 mg/dL) and abnormal urine sediment were noted. The patient exhibited hypotension and rapid renal impairment, prompting an urgent abdominal X-ray and subsequent ultrasound.
imaging_findings: An abdominal ultrasound reveals an enlarged right kidney with dirty echogenic foci and reverberation artefact in the renal calyces and parenchyma (Figure 1), raising suspicion for emphysematous pyelonephritis, and prompting an urgent abdominal CT scan. The CT scan indicates several gas bubbles in the renal parenchyma and collecting system, extending into the proximal ureter (Figures 2a and 2b). Moderate inflammatory changes are noted in the perinephric fat, but there is no evidence of collections, free abdominal fluid, or ectopic gas outside the Gerota’s fascia. No signs of nephrolithiasis are identified. The left kidney appears normal. An abdominal x-ray is reviewed (Figure 3), revealing clear evidence of right renal enlargement and emphysema that were initially overlooked.
discussion: Background Emphysematous pyelonephritis is a life-threatening infection with mortality rates as high as 90% [1]. Prompt imaging diagnosis is of utmost importance since rapid medical treatment may significantly reduce mortality and avoid a nephrectomy. Gas formation within renal parenchyma occurs due to the fermentation of glucose and lactate by bacteria, such as E. coli (49%–67%), Klebsiella (20%–24%), Proteus (5%–18%), Enterococcus (14%), and Pseudomonas (5%) [1], all of which find a convenient spot in the renal parenchyma to grow. Clinical Perspective The main risk factors include poorly controlled diabetes, obstructive uropathy, and hypertension. It is important to maintain a high clinical suspicion when assessing a poorly controlled diabetic patient presenting with flank pain, fever, nausea, and suspected urinary tract infection. Once the diagnosis of emphysematous pyelonephritis is established, prompt starting of antibiotic therapy and close clinical monitoring is crucial. While older publications recommended early nephrectomy, current guidelines advocate a more conservative approach, using third or fourth-generation cephalosporins or carbapenems and performing percutaneous drainage of collections when necessary [2]. Percutaneous drainage has been shown to preserve renal function in the affected kidney in up to 70% of patients [2], and nephrectomy is now reserved for cases that do not respond adequately to conservative management. Imaging Perspective The affected kidney may appear enlarged on ultrasound, with small hyperechoic gas bubbles inside, casting a characteristic “dirty” acoustic shadow. It is essential to describe whether the gas is confined to the renal parenchyma or extends beyond the kidney into the perinephric fat. Additionally, perinephric collections that could be drained percutaneously should be noted. If there is uncertainty or the extent of the lesions cannot be accurately assessed, an abdominal CT scan should be performed. On CT imaging, the renal parenchyma often appears enlarged and heterogeneous, and hypodense abscesses containing fluid and gas may be seen. Gas bubbles should be evident on CT. Conventional abdominal X-ray can only detect approximately 30% of cases of renal emphysema [1]. Outcome Our patient underwent retrograde placement of a double J stent and received third-generation intravenous cephalosporins for 14 days, resulting in adequate recovery. Previously unknown type 2 diabetes mellitus was diagnosed, and insulin treatment was initiated. A control CT was performed on day 15, which showed gas bubble resolution, leading to the stent’s removal and the patient’s discharge. Take Home Message When performing abdominal ultrasounds in septic patients with urinary tract infections, particularly in poorly controlled diabetics, a high clinical suspicion for emphysematous pyelonephritis should be maintained. If intraparenchymal gas is detected, a confident diagnosis can be made. Therefore, prompt antibiotic treatment must be initiated, and percutaneous drainage should be considered. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Primary hyperparathyroidism with fibrous dysplasia
clinical_history: A 20-year-old woman came to the emergency department with complaints of multiple bone pains. She reported fractures of the right forearm and the right leg three years ago, occurring without any significant trauma. Laboratory findings revealed elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP > 1400) and parathyroid hormone (720 pg/ml), serum calcium level was 10.8 mg/dl, and serum creatinine level was 0.9. There was no skin lesion.
imaging_findings: Skeletal Survey (Radiograph of the skull, dorso-lumbar spine and both upper and lower extremities) The shafts of the long bones showed ground glass opacities with expansion of the medullary cavity and thinning of the cortex. There were multiple lytic lesions in the shaft of the long bones, and a few of them showed a sclerotic rim. There were areas of sclerosis in the metaphysis of the long bones (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d). The dorsal lumbar spine showed reduced bone density with endplate sclerosis, consistent with a rugger-jersey spine (Figure 2b). Multiple lytic lesions were seen in the scapula, ribs, clavicle, multiple vertebral bodies, pelvic bones and metacarpals on both sides (Figures 2a and 2c). There was subperiosteal resorption on the radial aspect of the head of the second proximal phalanx (Figure 3). Skull radiograph showed a widening of the diploic spaces with multiple well-defined, variable-sized sclerotic lesions (Figure 4). CT Brain The CT brain revealed a widening of diploic spaces with multiple well-defined sclerotic and ground glass density lesions (Figures 5a, 5b, and 5c). USG Neck In the US of the neck, there was a well-defined heterogeneously hypoechoic lesion posterior to the right lobe of the thyroid (Figure 6). CT Parathyroid Protocol A hypodense enhancing lesion posterior to the right lobe of the thyroid was detected, suggestive of parathyroid adenoma (Figures 7a, 7b, 8a, 8b, 9a, 9b, 9c).
discussion: Fibrous dysplasia (FD) arises from GNAS1 gene mutations on chromosome 20, activating Gsα and causing abnormal osteoblastic proliferation and maturation [1–3]. It affects single (monostotic) or multiple (polyostotic) bones, often the femur, tibia, ribs, or skull [4]. Polyostotic cases may include McCune–Albright syndrome, characterised by polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait spots, and early puberty, as well as other endocrinopathies or Mazabraud’s syndrome associated with soft tissue myxomas [5–7]. Hyperparathyroidism, characterised by excessive parathyroid hormone, can be classified as: Primary : Due to adenoma, hyperplasia, or cancer. Secondary : Due to chronic hypocalcemia caused by vitamin D deficiency or renal osteodystrophy. Tertiary : Due to an autonomous adenoma after prolonged hyperstimulation in renal insufficiency. FD and hyperparathyroidism share similar mechanisms. Both are generated by the intracellular downstream effect of activation of the parathyroid hormone (PTH) G protein-coupled receptor of osteogenic cells. In hyperparathyroidism, these receptors are overstimulated by excessive amounts of PTH, whereas they are constitutively active due to Gsα mutations in patients with FD [8]. The resulting activation of AMP-protein kinase A signalling leads to an increase in osteoclastogenesis and subsequent bone resorption in both FD and hyperparathyroidism [9]. Indeed, both conditions are characterised by elevated levels of bone turnover markers. While there is evidence to suggest that mutant cells in FD lesions are more sensitive to PTH, interestingly, elevated serum PTH does not seem to impact unaffected bone in FD patients [10]. The bone lesions of FD can be classified as cystic, sclerotic and mixed. Lesions of FD are often seen as eccentrically located smooth and homogeneous areas of ground glass matrix in the medullary bone. Craniofacial FD typically presents as dense, sclerotic lesions that result in cortical thinning due to the expansion of fibro-osseous masses within the bone. A periosteal reaction is generally absent unless associated with a pathological fracture. While endosteal scalloping may occur, the outer cortical contour remains smooth. The lesion may exhibit expansile remodelling caused by the growing fibro-osseous mass. A thickened layer of sclerotic bone, known as the “rind sign”, is often observed. Additionally, small cartilage islands within FD lesions may ossify, appearing as dense punctate or flocculent calcifications. When these enchondromas are present within an FD lesion, it is termed fibrocartilaginous dysplasia, a condition most commonly found in the proximal femur [11]. The radiological features of hyperparathyroidism include subperiosteal, subchondral, and subligamentous bone resorption, along with findings such as the “salt-and-pepper” skull, brown tumours, acro-osteolysis, rugger-jersey spine, and osteopenia. Subperiosteal bone resorption occurs due to increased bone turnover caused by the dysregulated effects of parathyroid hormone (PTH) on calcium homeostasis in bone [12]. Elevated PTH levels promote the expression of nuclear factor-κβ ligand (RANKL), which binds to RANK receptors on osteoclast precursors, indirectly enhancing bone resorption through osteoclast activation [13,14]. These bone changes are most frequently seen in the radial margins of the proximal and middle phalanges of the second and third fingers [15]. The “salt-and-pepper” skull is a distinguishing feature of hyperparathyroidism, characterised by diffuse lytic areas interspersed with normal bone in the calvarium, creating a granular appearance [16]. Lytic lesions, resulting from localised bone loss, are referred to as brown tumours in hyperparathyroidism. In cases of prolonged disease, clusters of osteolytic, cyst-like lesions known as osteitis fibrosa cystica may develop. Common locations for brown tumours include the pelvis, mandibles, ribs, long bones, hands, and vertebrae [17]. Ehrig and Wilson reported two cases of monostotic FD and primary hyperparathyroidism [18]. Rosen and Palmer reviewed 350 cases of hyperparathyroidism over 20 years, and identified five patients with facial bone lesions; histology revealed FD in two cases and non-ossifying fibromas in the other three [19]. Turcu and Clarke described 10 patients showing the coexistence of FD and primary hyperparathyroidism, most with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia [1]. Although such coexistence has been reported, no syndromic or genetic association has been identified, and these cases are considered coincidental. Teaching Points Fibrous dysplasia (FD) and primary hyperparathyroidism can coexist, though rarely. Awareness of this coexistence is crucial to avoid misdiagnosis.

title: Neurocysticercosis impersonating a cerebrovascular episode
clinical_history: A 60-year-old female presented to the casualty with an episode of loss of consciousness for a period of thirty minutes. After regaining consciousness, the patient lost power in all four limbs and was unable to walk without assistance.
imaging_findings: On NCCT (non-contrast computed tomography) brain, multiple small hypodense cystic lesions were noted, many showing scolex inside depicted by the hyperdense eccentric dot within and surrounding oedema (Figures 1a and 1b). A few of them were seen with calcifications inside, suggesting calcified scolices, thus describing the different stages of the disease. A sub-centimetric calcified lesion was seen in the intermuscular plane between the left semispinalis capitis and trapezius muscle (Figures 1a and 1b). On MRI correlation, multiple well-defined sub-centimetric hyperintense lesions were noted in bilateral cerebral hemispheres. Internal eccentric scolex was noted; however, no evidence of mass effect was seen (Figures 2a and 2b). On X-ray examination, multiple calcified lesions were seen in the intermuscular plane along bilateral proximal lower limbs, suggesting disseminated disease and rice grain calcifications (Figure 3). Further ultrasonographic evaluation depicted a non-compressible, hypoechoic cystic lesion with a central calcification in the gracilis muscle along the medial compartment of the thigh (Figure 4).
discussion: Neurocysticercosis is a neurological manifestation of a parasitic infection caused by larvae of a tapeworm known as Taenia solium [1]. The larval cysts, ingested through contaminated pork, undergo excystation within the intestine to produce gravid proglottids. Upon traversing through the intestines, they release a hexacanth embryo, which may breach the intestinal wall to enter the bloodstream. Consecutively, the embryo may spread to other organs and tissues, developing into a cysticercoid leading to disseminated cysticercosis. Cysticercosis can give rise to various manifestations ranging from backache in cases of spinal involvement [1], restricted ocular movement, cluster headache [2], reduced visual acuity, and vision loss in ophthalmic involvement to muscular pain and pseudohypertrophy [3] in the muscles. Neurocysticercosis may manifest as recurrent seizures, hemiparesis, intracranial hypertension (secondary to hydrocephalus), or leptomeningeal fibrosis [4]. In this case, a 60-year-old normotensive and euglycemic female came with episodic loss of consciousness and headache since morning. There was no history of any head trauma, deviation of angle of mouth, seizure, or fever. The patient had a similar episode one year back for which she was hospitalised. There was no other significant history. A classical appearance of multiple cerebrospinal fluid density cystic lesions with a central dot sign and the presence/absence of surrounding oedema should point towards the diagnosis of cysticercosis. Radiological diagnosis depends upon the number and location of the lesions, the stage of infection, and the associated complications [5]. The cysts can involve the brain parenchyma, subarachnoid spaces, ventricles, peripheral muscles, and, in severe cases, the spinal cord. The cerebrospinal fluid examination may help in the initial diagnosis of cases of intraventricular or subarachnoid infections [6]. Neurocysticercosis is one of the most common helminthic infestations affecting the central nervous system in humans and is a leading cause of acquired epilepsy [7]. As no specific clinical symptoms exist, imaging plays a vital role in diagnosing the disease. Metastases show multiple moderate-size ring-enhancing lesions with extensive surrounding oedema. Tubercular granulomas can be suspected in patients with classical history and lobulated, ring-enhancing lesions on imaging with calcification larger than those in neurocysticercosis. Tuberculomas also show a lipid-lactate peak on MR spectroscopy [8]. Cerebral abscesses show a double-rim sign with true restriction diffusion and signs of cerebritis and ventriculitis. Toxoplasmosis may be suspected in an immuno-compromised patient with lesions of size 1 to 3 cm predominantly involving the basal ganglia, thalami and corticomedullary junction [9] with chunky calcification. Knowledge of these imaging findings can help the physician in early diagnosis, appropriate treatment decisions, and the follow-up of patients with cysticercosis. The treatment options include anti-helminthic drugs to kill viable parasites, antiepileptic drugs, and steroids to treat neurological and inflammatory symptoms. The prognosis is good if the disease is detected in the early course. Neurocysticercosis is one of the few diseases that could potentially be prevented, controlled, and eliminated; hence, it becomes crucial to diagnose the condition early for better patient outcomes [10]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained from the patient.

title: Metastatic disease to the breast from small lung cell carcinoma
clinical_history: A 31-year-old female with a history of small cell lung cancer undergoing chemotherapy and radiotherapy presented with a painless palpable mass in the right breast.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound and tomosynthesis were obtained to evaluate breast symptomatology. Ultrasound images of the breast demonstrate bilateral oval hypoechoic masses with increased internal and in-rim vascularity on colour Doppler evaluation and a hard elastographic pattern, score 4 according to the Tsukuba scoring system (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, 3a, 3b, 3c, 4a, 4b, and 4c). Tomosynthesis of the right breast in a lateral-medial oblique view demonstrates a round mass with obscured margins in the posterior third of the upper right quadrants (Figure 2). Right lateral-medial oblique tomosynthesis reveals an isodense oval mass with circumscribed margins in the lower quadrants (Figure 5). Findings were classified as BI-RADS 4b. An ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy was performed, and histopathologic examination was consistent with metastatic carcinoma of immunotype compatible with an origin in the respiratory tract (Figures 6a, 6b, and 6c).
discussion: Background Metastatic disease to the breast is rare, with a prevalence ranging from 0.1% to 6.6% [1–3]. Lung adenocarcinoma, ovarian papillary serous carcinoma, and melanoma are the most common primary carcinomas that metastasise to the breast [4]. However, other types of lung cancer, including small cell carcinoma, can also metastasise to the breast [5]. Clinical Perspective The most common presentation is a firm, painless, palpable mass in the breast [2]. The most common location is in the upper outer quadrant (50%) due to the abundance of vascularity, lymphatic drainage, and glandular tissue [3]. Its appearance may occur at the same time as the clinical manifestation of the primary tumour (synchronous) or years after the diagnosis of primary cancer (metachronous) [6]. Imaging Perspective Mammographic findings include single or multiple round or oval, high-density masses with circumscribed margins [3,7]. Less frequently, the margins may be microlobulated or indistinct. Typically, there is no associated desmoplastic reaction, architectural distortion, or microcalcifications, except in some cases with ovarian metastatic cancer due to the presence of psammomatous bodies [3,7,8]. Typical ultrasound features include single or multiple, round to oval-shaped, well-circumscribed or microlobulated hypoechoic masses without spiculations, architectural distortion, posterior acoustic shadow, calcifications, and skin or nipple changes (9,10). Doppler ultrasound evaluation of metastatic masses can demonstrate increased internal and rim vascularity, a key to distinguishing metastases from other conditions [3,7,8,10]. Strain elastography can be useful in diagnosing malignancy, with scores of 4 or 5 according to the Tsukuba score system [11]. Histopathology is the gold standard for diagnosing metastatic disease in the breast. An ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy can help distinguish it from primary breast disease or other benign conditions, such as fibroadenomas or phyllodes tumours [2]. Outcome Therapeutic options for metastatic disease to the breast consist of systemic therapy, whether chemotherapy or radiotherapy, as indicated by the primary malignancy [12]. Surgical resection is reserved for isolated metastases, with long-term survival reported occasionally. The prognosis of metastases to the breast remains poor. The survival rate varies from 2 to 13.9 months [4,13]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Metastatic disease to the breast is rare. Secondary breast masses should be included in the differential diagnosis of multiple breast masses with a benign appearance, especially if there is a primary tumour elsewhere in the body. Clinical history and radiologic features should be considered in differentiating a secondary mass from primary breast cancer or other benign pathologies. The gold standard for the diagnosis is histopathology. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Fibroadenoma Phyllodes tumour Primary breast carcinoma Primary or secondary lymphoma Metastatic carcinoma of immunotype (compatible with an origin in the respiratory tract)
final_diagnosis: Metastatic carcinoma of immunotype (compatible with an origin in the respiratory tract)

title: Incidental presacral myelolipoma
clinical_history: A 67-year-old female with a history of hypertension, lower back pain from multiple older compression fractures and long-term hyponatraemia was referred for a thoracic and abdominal CT scan with contrast to rule out malignancy. The present case reports an incidental finding with no correlation to the abovementioned symptoms.
imaging_findings: Initial contrast CT showed a local, rounded, well-defined mass measuring 30 mm x 52 mm x 41 mm (AP x CC x TR), with a low-density fat component, a soft tissue component and no cortical erosion, destruction or scalloping (Figures 1, 2, and 3). In close proximity to the mass, a marginally enlarged lymph node was located cranially to the left of the mass (Figure 3). MRI with T1-weighted (T1W) (Figure 4) and STIR (Figure 5) images showed the presacral mass to have a high heterogeneous signal, but with a fat signal, and the mass to be well defined and with high probability of being encapsulated. Additionally, T1-fat saturation weighted sequence without and with contrast (Figures 6, 7, and 8) showed the mass to be of high fat content, showing discrete linear strands of contrast enhancement in the mass, but no nodular enhancement. MRI also confirmed no presence of bone marrow oedema.
discussion: Background Myelolipoma is a benign, often asymptomatic tumour that consists of fatty tissue and haematopoietic cells [1]. It mostly occurs in the adrenal glands, but has been reported extra-adrenally in some rare cases, with the most common location being the retroperitoneum, especially the presacral space [2]. Clinical Perspective Due to myelolipomas often being asymptomatic tumours they are most often discovered incidentally on imaging studies due to other reasons [1]. Because of the complex anatomy of the presacral space there is a wide variety of possible presacral masses, with different origins, to consider when approaching findings on imaging studies [3]. For instance, the higher fat content of the myelolipoma makes them easily mistaken for liposarcomas [1–2] or hibernomas [1]). Myelolipomas are usually treated conservatively unless they are symptomatic or there is haemorrhage inside the tumour [4]. It has been argued that myelolipomas larger than 4 cm should be considered for surgical removal due to becoming symptomatic within 3 years [5]. Imaging Perspective CT imaging will show a heterogeneous mass with hypoattenuation consisting mainly of fatty tissue, but the encapsulating borders are not clearly defined, citing the need for complementary MRI [6]. MR imaging will show high signal intensity in T1W with fat signal [3]. Additionally, MR imaging will show no abnormalities in the bone marrow [6]. Furthermore, both on CT and MRI, it should be noted that one distinct feature of a presacral myelolipoma is the position in the midline as well as no destruction of the adjacent bone, with these characteristics making it more distinguishable from, e.g., liposarcoma—the most common retroperitoneal, fat containing malignancy [6]. Lastly, it should be noted that differentiating myelolipomas from other retroperitoneal fat-containing masses solely on radiological imaging findings is a very challenging task and therefore warrants biopsy to confirm the diagnosis. Outcome In the present case, the treatment offered, after CT-guided biopsy verified myelolipoma, was a conservative regimen with no intervention or follow-up, due to being a benign tumour with no risk of mortality. Although presacral myelolipomas are rare occurrences, the present case report further underlines that they should be considered in the differential diagnosis in other cases of fat-containing lesions in the retroperitoneum, especially in the presacral space.

title: Distinguishing features of cochlear incomplete partition type III
clinical_history: A 2-year-old male with moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss.
imaging_findings: The cochlea demonstrates an absent modiolus, while the interscalar septa remain intact, creating a characteristic “corkscrew” appearance. The cochlear aperture is enlarged, the modiolus is absent, and a widened internal auditory canal is absent (Figures 1 and 2).
discussion: Auditory screening is now included in the standard post-natal care for early diagnosis of hearing loss. Early therapy is essential for language development. CT and MRI are necessary to identify morphological causes of hearing disorders and to clarify the possibility of hearing-improving ear surgery or cochlear implantation [1]. Incomplete partition type III (IP-3) is a rare congenital inner ear anomaly characterised by malformation of the bony labyrinth, particularly affecting the cochlea. This condition is associated with mutations in the POU3F4 gene, which is located on the X chromosome and predominantly affects males. Hence, it is also called X-linked sensorineural hearing loss [2]. The hallmark imaging finding on a CT scan is the absence of the bony modiolus (the bony structure that normally supports the cochlear nerve and the interscalar septa) and of the septum between the base of the cochlea and the internal auditory canal, along with a widened internal auditory canal. The interscalar septa are present. Cochlear implantation is the primary treatment for sensorineural hearing loss associated with IP-3. Due to the lack of modiolus and hence abnormal communication between the subarachnoid space, as the surgeon enters the cochlea during the cochlear implantation, persistent, profuse leakage of cerebrospinal fluid is encountered, and this phenomenon is called gusher syndrome. The risk of gusher syndrome necessitates specialised surgical expertise [3]. Cochlear implantation was later successfully performed on the right side of our patient. An incomplete partition is a group of inner ear malformations in which the external aspect and dimensions of the cochlea are preserved; however, the internal architecture of the cochlea is disorganised to a variable degree. This group may represent up to 40% of inner ear malformations [2]. Incomplete partition type I (IP-1) : The cochlea lacks both the modiolus and the interscalar septum, resulting in no internal partitions. This condition is accompanied by a dilated vestibule, creating a characteristic “figure 8” appearance. Incomplete partition type II (IP-2) : The cochlea shows a cyst-like appearance at its apex due to an incomplete interscalar septum in the middle and apical turns. However, the modiolus and interscalar septum in the basal turn remain intact. This condition is accompanied by an enlarged vestibular aqueduct and was historically known as Mondini malformation. Incomplete partition type III (IP-3) : The cochlea exhibits a “corkscrew” appearance due to the complete absence of the modiolus, while the interscalar septum remains intact. This condition is also associated with a widened internal auditory canal. Take Home Message Attention to the modiolus, interscalar septum, associated dilatation of the vestibule, vestibular aqueduct, and internal auditory canal can help us to differentiate different types of cochlear incomplete partition correctly. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Metastatic melanoma in the gallbladder
clinical_history: A female patient in her 50s with a known diagnosis of melanoma of the pectoral region underwent a follow-up PET/CT.
imaging_findings: The PET/CT revealed suspicious lung nodules and left axillary lymphadenopathy, and an area of abnormal uptake in the gallbladder (Figure 1). Subsequent CT showed an endoluminal polypoid lesion with heterogeneous arterial enhancement. There was no evidence of invasion into the adjacent hepatic parenchyma or extension to the surrounding fat (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c).
discussion: Background Melanoma is a form of skin cancer that invades locally and spreads through the lymphatic system and bloodstream to distant organs. Haematogeneous dissemination can lead to a wide range of unpredictable imaging findings, mimicking other malignancies or benign conditions [1]. Common metastatic sites include the liver, lungs, and brain [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Melanoma neoplastic cells may disseminate to the gallbladder via the bloodstream or as mucosal implants from bile via the liver. Isolated gallbladder metastasis (GM) is rarely described and usually occurs in the setting of widespread metastatic disease. These lesions are usually asymptomatic and primarily detected at follow-up imaging or autopsy [2]. Malignant melanoma is the leading cause of metastatic tumours in the gallbladder, representing over 50% of all metastases in this location [3]. The most common clinical manifestation of gallbladder melanoma is abdominal pain secondary to cholecystitis, resulting from cystic duct obstruction. Other sources of metastases to the gallbladder include breast cancer, renal cell carcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma [3]. Imaging Perspective Gallbladder metastases are typically diagnosed using multiple imaging modalities. In over 90% of cases, they are diagnosed at a late stage, often accompanied by metastases to other organs, reflecting the terminal phase of the malignancy. On ultrasound, metastatic melanoma of the gallbladder typically appears as one or more hyperechoic masses exceeding 1 cm in size and attached to the gallbladder wall. On CT, it can present as a polypoid hypervascular lesion or as focal, irregular thickening of the wall. While most metastatic lesions originate from peritoneal spread and involve the serosal surface, some may appear as intraluminal polypoid masses [2,3]. Gallbladder metastases are generally larger than 1 cm and firmly attached to the gallbladder wall. When the biliary tree is affected, intraluminal masses and bile duct dilation may also be observed [3]. On MRI, metastatic melanoma lesions typically demonstrate hyperintensity on T1-weighted native sequences due to the presence of melanin, which serves as a key imaging feature aiding diagnosis. However, this characteristic can also be observed in haemorrhagic metastases, such as those from renal cell carcinoma. Melanoma and renal cell carcinoma metastases will also both avidly enhance in the arterial phase, with washout in delayed phases [4]. Additionally, they appear hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences and exhibit diffusion restriction, further distinguishing them from other gallbladder pathologies [1]. Outcome The surgical approach is controversial. Some studies prefer open surgery to minimally invasive techniques to minimise port site recurrence. Moreover, because GM is usually intraluminal and lymphadenectomy of the hepato-duodenal ligament is not recommended, laparoscopic cholecystectomy appears to be appropriate [2]. In our case, laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed. Pathology revealed a sessile polypoid lesion with no wall infiltration. Microscopy confirmed a polypoid, mucosa-confined malignant melanocytic neoplasm. Due to systemic involvement, the patient underwent chemotherapy and showed a marked reduction in pulmonary and axillary lesions, with no new lesions over two years. Take Home Message Melanoma metastases should be considered when a de novo lesion appears in a patient with a history of melanoma. Gallbladder melanoma should be considered when a hypervascular polypoid lesion is present on the gallbladder.

title: Liver abscess in an adolescent with Schistosoma mansoni
clinical_history: A 12-year-old Malagasy boy consulted for a fever that had been evolving for two months, with a notion of trauma and pain in the right upper quadrant as well as chronic diarrhoea. A parasitological examination of the stool found eggs of Schistosoma mansoni . An ultrasound and a CT scan were then ordered.
imaging_findings: On ultrasound (Figure 1), there were multiple confluent hypoechoic nodular formations, some of which have peripheral hyperechoic walls in segment VII of the liver. On CT scan (Figures 2 and 3), the formation corresponds to multiple hypodense fluid collections with thick peripheral enhancing walls with peri-lesional oedema in segment VII of the liver. There was an extracapsular extension into the hepato-renal space. The liver was enlarged, measuring 187 mm in the midclavicular line. The spleen was also increased in size, measuring 160 mm in height. The rest of the examination was considered normal.
discussion: Background Schistosomiasis is an endemic disease of Madagascar [1]. It is caused by a trematode of the genus Schistosoma . It is transmitted by swimming in infected water. In Madagascar, there are Schistosoma haematobium and Schistosoma mansoni , the latter is responsible for intestinal schistosomiasis. Children are especially at risk when swimming [1]. It has been shown in the literature that Schistosoma infection is a risk factor for pyogenic abscess in the liver [2]. Schistosomiasis hepatic manifestations are a chronic result of the granulomatous reaction to Schistosoma eggs within small portal venules with peripheral periportal fibrosis, liver cirrhosis, and portal hypertension. This can be complicated by abscess formation [3]. Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia is the most common underlying cause of abscess formation and is frequently isolated from concomitant pyogenic liver abscesses. Staphylococcus aureus enters through breaches in the skin, may lead to bacteraemia in vulnerable host, leading to hepatic colonisation [2]. Clinical Perspective Schistosomiasis may present acutely as a febrile illness or more commonly in chronic form. Chronic lesions are characterised by chronic inflammation and fibrosis, leading, for example, to cirrhosis in hepatic involvement [3]. Intestinal schistosomiasis causes abdominal pain, diarrhoea and blood in the urine. It is associated with hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. A pyogenic abscess causes febrile abdominal pain. Imaging Perspective On ultrasound, liver abscesses are not well demarcated, and they can be heterogeneously hypoechoic with internal echoes or hyperechoic. There is no central perfusion on colour Doppler. On CT scan, pyogenic liver abscesses correspond to a lesion with a hypodense centre and a peripheral enhancing wall. The characteristic sign is called the double target sign, in which there is a hypodense centre, hyperdense rim and a surrounding hypodense perilesional oedema [4]. On MRI, the centre is T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense, and restricted on diffusion. The periphery tends to be hyperintense on all signals [5]. Outcome A bacteriological analysis and a culture of this collection were carried out, in which we found the germ Staphylococcus aureus . The outcome is variable depending on the time of the onset of the treatment and the presence of complications (hepatic vein thrombosis, portal vein thrombosis, rupture, sepsis, thrombosis, inferior vena cava thrombosis). The treatment is essentially a percutaneous drainage of the abscess associated with antibiotic therapy and antiparasitic drugs. Take Home Message Although the combination of schistosomiasis and pyogenic hepatic abscess is rare, clinicians should consider this entity in patients from endemic areas who present with imaging findings consistent with hepatic abscess formation. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Telangiectatic osteosarcoma of the sacrum
clinical_history: A 13-year-old boy was brought by his parents with complaints of pain and swelling in the right hip and right iliac fossa since three months. He had difficulty in walking since one month. On examination, there is swelling and tenderness at the right hip.
imaging_findings: A pelvic radiograph revealed a soft tissue opacity in the right iliac fossa, erosion of the right sacroiliac (SI) joint and the right sacral ala, with the right hip joint abducted and externally rotated (Figure 1). CT demonstrated a heterogeneously hypodense lesion originating from the right sacrum, with a large exophytic pelvic component and soft tissue extension into the right SI joint (Figures 2a and 2b), displacing bowel loops and the bladder to the left (Figures 3a and 3b). MRI revealed a T1/T2 heterogeneously hyperintense soft tissue lesion from the right sacrum with an exophytic pelvic component and multiple cystic areas suggesting blood degradation products (Figures 4a and 4b). There were diffusion-restricted areas (Figures 5a and 5b), extension into the S1 and S2 neural foramina with nerve root encasement (Figure 6), and heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement (Figure 7).
discussion: Telangiectatic osteosarcoma (TOS) is a rare variant of osteosarcoma, representing 0.4–12% of cases [1]. It commonly occurs during the pubertal growth spurt, with the p53 gene inactivation playing a key role. Common symptoms include localised pain, swelling, and sometimes pathological fractures or joint effusions, with metastases at diagnosis in some cases [2,3]. Radiologically, TOS typically manifests as a lytic, destructive lesion in the metaphyseal regions of long bones such as the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus. It can also affect the pelvis, skull, and ribs [2–4]. Radiographs reveal geographic bone destruction, cortical disruption, and soft tissue invasion, indicative of aggressive growth [2,3,5]. CT imaging demonstrates low-attenuation areas suggestive of haemorrhagic components, cortical irregularities, and a soft tissue mass [5,6]. MRI findings include heterogeneous low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images due to cystic and haemorrhagic components, with fluid-fluid levels observed in 74% of cases [3,7]. Histologically, TOS is characterised by blood-filled or empty cystic spaces separated by thick septa containing atypical cells, with nodular or solid components enhancing on imaging [3,5]. While TOS can mimic aneurysmal bone cysts (ABCs) or giant cell tumours, the presence of osteoid matrix production confirms the diagnosis [2,8]. Core-needle biopsies may yield insufficient samples due to the tumour’s cystic nature, risking false negatives [6,7]. Diagnostic criteria include cystic spaces lined by high-grade atypical cells [8]. Unlike benign ABCs, which feature reactive vascular processes and non-malignant stromal cells, TOS shows malignant cells within the septa [9]. Central giant cell granulomas and tumours lack the large sinusoidal spaces seen in ABCs and TOS. Sacral TOS poses additional challenges due to the sacrum’s anatomy, making surgical excision difficult and increasing the risk of misdiagnosis [7,10]. The expansive growth often leads to cortical destruction and soft tissue invasion, complicating treatment. Management involves a multimodal approach, with neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgical resection. However, achieving negative surgical margins is difficult, particularly in the sacrum, due to the tumour’s proximity to critical structures [5,10]. Misdiagnosis of TOS as ABC may delay treatment, adversely affecting outcomes. Take Home Message Telangiectatic osteosarcoma of the sacrum presents unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenges, considering its proximity to bowel and pelvic organs. Misdiagnosis of TOS as ABC may lead to diagnostic delay and poor treatment outcomes.

title: Breast fibromatosis associated with breast implants
clinical_history: An asymptomatic 72-year-old woman with a history of breast implant placement more than 20 years ago attended her breast screening examination.
imaging_findings: The mammogram shows subglandular breast implants with folds in the left prosthetic envelope and increased density anterior to the left implant (Figure 1). Ultrasound revealed periprosthetic fluid corresponding with the dense area seen on the mammogram, along with a solid hypoechoic mass with fusiform shape, indistinct margins, and internal vascularity on colour Doppler, located in the anterior subcapsular region (Figures 2a and 2b). MRI confirmed bilateral pre-pectoral single lumen silicone implants and periprosthetic fluid on the left side. No rupture signs were detected in the left implant. A mass beneath the left prosthetic capsule showed intermediate signal on T1-weighted sequences and high heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted sequences with low-signal intensity bands (“band sign”). In a sagittal image, the “tail sign” was identified emerging from the inferior portion of the lesion. The contrast-enhanced study showed early enhancement with washout in delayed phases (type III kinetic curve) (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, 3d, and 3e). Fine needle aspiration of the periprosthetic fluid and core needle biopsy of the mass confirmed breast fibromatosis (Figure 4) and inflammatory fluid without malignancy.
discussion: Background Breast fibromatosis, a rare benign entity classified under extra-abdominal desmoid tumours, accounts for 0.2% of all breast tumours [1,2]. It can arise from breast parenchyma, muscle-aponeurotic layers, muscle tissue, or the capsule formed after breast implant placement, with more cases linked to silicone implants than saline ones, likely due to their higher prevalence [3,4]. This condition typically appears 2–3 years after implant placement and is associated with family history, trauma, or surgery [1,4]. The exact cause of implant-associated fibromatosis is unclear, though evidence suggests dysplastic wound healing may play a role, with mutations in the APC gene and beta-catenin disrupting the Wnt signalling pathway and promoting abnormal cell proliferation [1,5]. Imaging Perspective Radiologically, fibromatosis can present with distinctive features like intramuscular invasion (Staghorn sign), linear extension to the fascia (fascial tail sign), or hypointense bands on T2-weighted MRI sequences [6]. On mammography, it appears as a dense mass with defined or irregular borders, without microcalcifications. Ultrasound typically shows a hypoechoic irregular mass with or without internal vascularity, while MRI displays an intermediate signal on T1 and a heterogeneous signal on T2, with variable contrast enhancement. When associated with breast implants, capsular thickening or a subcapsular mass may be seen [4–7]. Differential diagnoses include invasive ductal carcinoma (which has more irregular borders, possible microcalcifications, and metastatic potential), lobular carcinoma (which can be multifocal and bilateral), fibroadenoma (which typically has well-defined borders), and low-grade fibrosarcoma (which behaves more aggressively with greater vascularity and irregular margins) [8,9]. Implant-related conditions to differentiate from include anaplastic large cell lymphoma (which appears 1–5 years post-implant and is usually associated with periprosthetic seroma and lymph node involvement), and granulomas (which present as solid masses with heterogeneous enhancement) [3,4,9]. Outcome Despite being benign and the lack of metastatic potential, fibromatosis can show aggressive growth and invasiveness, making wide local excision with negative margins the treatment of choice [1,5,6]. However, recurrence rates remain high, especially with positive margins, and medical treatments like interferons, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, cytotoxic agents, and chemotherapy have shown mixed results in controlling recurrences [3,4,9–11]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Breast fibromatosis is a rare benign tumour, often associated with silicone breast implants, appearing 2–3 years after implant placement. Radiologically, it can show signs like intramuscular invasion and linear extension to the fascia, and it must be differentiated from other breast conditions such as invasive carcinoma and fibroadenoma. Treatment involves wide local excision with negative margins, although recurrence is common, especially with positive margins. Medical treatments, such as interferons and chemotherapy, have shown mixed results in managing recurrences. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: A rare cause of cerebral calcifications: Fahr’s disease
clinical_history: A 68-year-old male presented to the medical OPD with complaints of ataxia, multiple episodes of falls while walking, and bed wetting for a one-year duration, with gradually progressive symptoms. On examination, the patient had shuffling gait, tremors, and cogwheel rigidity. Nerve conduction studies, parathyroid hormone assay and calcium studies were within normal limits.
imaging_findings: Non-contrast CT head revealed bilaterally symmetrical hyperdense areas in bilateral basal ganglia, thalami, subcortical white matter, red nucleus, dentate nucleus and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c). MRI brain revealed bilaterally symmetrical areas that were hyperintense on T1WI, hypointense on T2WI, and showing blooming on gradient echo sequences (GRE) images in the bilateral basal ganglia, thalami (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c), bilateral red nuclei (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c), bilateral dentate nuclei and cerebellar hemispheres (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c), and subcortical white matter (Figures 5a, 5b, and 5c). These areas did not show restriction of diffusion on DWI images. There were discrete and confluent areas of T2 and FLAIR hyperintensities in periventricular and deep white matter of bilateral frontoparietal lobes, showing no restriction of diffusion.
discussion: Background Fahr’s disease, also called familial idiopathic basal ganglia calcification, primary cerebral ferrocalcinosis, primary familial brain calcification, and striatopallidodentate calcinosis, is a neurodegenerative disorder affecting the microvasculature of the brain, leading to diverse neuropsychiatric symptoms. It has autosomal dominant inheritance. The disease was first described by German neurologist Karl Theodor Fahr in 1930 [1]. The age of onset of this disease is in the third and fourth decades of life [2]. Clinical Perspective The criteria for diagnosis [3] on clinical examination are as follows: Progressive neurologic dysfunction, including movement disorder with or without neuropsychiatric manifestations. Absence of a mitochondrial or metabolic disease. Absence of infectious, toxic, and/or traumatic causes. Family history consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. Neuropsychiatric symptoms include dementia, delirium, confusion, hallucinations, psychosis, mood disorders, panic attacks, irritability and aggression. Somatic symptoms include Parkinson-like movement disorder, seizure, headache, stroke and syncope [2,4]. Imaging Perspective The typical imaging findings in Fahr’s disease include bilaterally symmetrical hyperdense areas involving the basal ganglia, thalami, red nuclei, dentate nuclei, subcortical white matter and centrum semiovale, representing calcifications. The areas of calcifications appear hyperintense on T1WI; however, the T1 signal diminishes at higher concentrations. On T2WI, the appearance may be hypointense or hyperintense, according to the difference in the composition of the calcium deposits and the presence of other mineral deposits such as zinc, manganese and iron in the same areas. The calcifications are seen as areas of blooming on GRE sequences on MRI (or susceptibility artefacts on SWI images), and these sequences show higher sensitivity in detection as compared to other sequences. FDG-PET may show reduced uptake involving the bilateral basal ganglia, and also the temporal and parietal cortices [5]. The criteria for diagnosis [3] on neuroimaging include bilateral basal ganglia calcifications. The pattern of calcification guides the diagnosis [6] and differentiates it from physiological calcifications or other erosive causes. CT is more sensitive than MRI for evaluation in Fahr’s disease. Imaging of the skeletal system is also done to look for secondary causes. Outcome This case emphasises the role of radiological investigations, especially CT and MRI scans, in the diagnosis of Fahr’s disease, which is important in differentiating it from other neuropsychiatric disorders with similar manifestations, and in deciding the management protocol. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Fahr’s disease should be suspected in patients in whom basal ganglia calcifications are noted and with associated clinical symptoms. These patients should be evaluated by relevant specialists to confirm the diagnosis, rule out secondary causes, detect genetic basis, manage the clinical manifestations and provide necessary genetic counselling.
