title: Biventricular endomyocardial fibrosis in an early middle-aged woman
clinical_history: A 34-year-old female patient presented with exertional dyspnoea, weakness, abdominal pain, and lower limb swelling persisting for a month. There was no history of fever. Initial ultrasound investigation revealed mild ascites, multiple small abdominal lymphadenopathies and minimal pericardial effusion. Laboratory results showed haemoglobin of 12.2g/dL, platelet count of 105×109/L and white blood cell count of 3.32×10 9 /L. A 12-lead ECG revealed prolonged P waves, abnormal Q waves, poor R wave progression, and T wave abnormalities (Figure 1).
imaging_findings: Echocardiography revealed mild pericardial effusion, grade II diastolic dysfunction, right ventricle with segmental aneurysmal dilation and apical retraction, mild mitral regurgitation, and hyperechoic mass at the left ventricular apex, indicative of fibrofatty tissue deposition. While the right ventricle (RV) showed localised enlargement due to aneurysm formation, the overall restrictive physiology remained evident (Figures 2a and 2b). No thrombus was detected on echocardiography and cardiac MRI. Chest X-ray showed an enlarged cardiac silhouette and elevated diaphragms. The patient was referred for a cardiac MRI in our department. Cardiac MRI, done with cine imaging, perfusion, and early and late gadolinium-enhanced (LGE) PSIR sequences on MAGNETOM Vida 3T scanner revealed ascites, pericardial effusion, enlarged right atrium, retraction of the RV apex (RV apical notch), RV aneurysm, obliteration of the left ventricular (LV) apex on True FISP (true fast imaging with steady-state free precession) cine imaging (Figure 3). The LV end-diastolic volume was 69 mL, and the end-systolic volume was 28 mL. Similarly, the RV end-diastolic volume measured 70 mL, with an end-systolic volume of 39 mL, indicating relatively small chamber volumes. LGE imaging demonstrated subendocardial fibrosis with fat infiltration at both the LV and RV apices, resulting in a V-shaped enhancement pattern in each ventricle (Figures 4a, 4b, 4c, and 4d).
discussion: Background Endomyocardial fibrosis (EMF) is a form of restrictive cardiomyopathy, predominantly affecting young populations in Africa and Kerala (India) with a prevalence of 15–20% [1]. Despite its identification over 70 years ago, the exact mechanisms of EMF remain unclear [2]. Malnutrition, parasitic infections, systemic non-infectious diseases, and genetic factors are reported associations [2]. Eosinophilia from parasitic infections may trigger the immune response during the disease’s early stages, and a cassava-rich, low-protein diet in genetically predisposed individuals may also contribute [2]. Clinical Perspective EMF presents with left ventricular filling restriction, atrial enlargement, subendocardial fibrosis, thrombus formation, and valve regurgitation. The disease progresses in three phases: (1) necrosis and acute carditis, (2) a subacute phase with thrombi, and (3) fibrosis leading to restrictive cardiac patterns and valvular dysfunction [3]. Mocumbi et al. proposed diagnostic criteria, including endomyocardial plaques, thrombi, right ventricular apex retraction, atrioventricular valve dysfunction, and atrial enlargement [4]. They categorised EMF into three types based on ventricular involvement: biventricular, right-sided, and left-sided. The classification depended on whether the pathological changes affected both ventricles equally, were predominantly confined to the right ventricle, or were mainly limited to the left ventricle. Additionally, a severity assessment system was established, considering both structural alterations and functional impairments. The total score ranged from 0 to 35, with cases scoring 8 or below classified as mild, those between 8 and 15 as moderate, and scores above 15 as severe. In the present study, the total score was 14, in the absence of any thrombus, indicating the moderate severity of the disease. Histologically, fibrosis is marked by increased cardiac fibroblasts, promoting collagen production beneath the normal endocardial lining [5]. Early diagnosis is crucial due to the high mortality risk associated with fibrosis. Imaging Perspective In the present case, right atrial enlargement, RV apical notch, LV apex obliteration, and biventricular EMF with single V sign on LGE distinguished it from amyloidosis and Ebstein’s anomaly. Echocardiography is useful for initial diagnosis, detecting mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, atrial enlargement, and fibrous plaques. However, it lacks the resolution to differentiate EMF from other cardiomyopathies in patients with poor acoustic windows [6]. Cardiac MRI provides superior structural and functional insights. Cardiac MRI confirmed the presence of a fibrofatty mass at the LV apex, which was seen as a region of signal heterogeneity on cine imaging and demonstrated LGE, suggesting fibrosis. No perfusion defect was seen in the first-pass cardiac MRI (CMRI) perfusion, which helps differentiate this from an ischemic aetiology. Distribution of fibrosis was characteristic of EMF, with involvement of both ventricular apices rather than a coronary artery territory. This finding correlated with the echocardiographic observation of fibrofatty deposition. LGE imaging demonstrated subendocardial fibrosis with fat infiltration, differentiating it from thrombus. The pattern of enhancement, along with associated structural changes, supported the diagnosis of biventricular EMF. RV and LV ejection fractions were 53% and 64%, respectively, with grade I diastolic dysfunction. Left and right atrial volumes were 67.15 mL/m² and 144.16 mL/m², respectively. LGE demonstrated subendocardial enhancement with a single V sign at both ventricles’ apices (Figures 4a, 4b, 4c, and 4d). The double V sign in EMF shows three layers: normal myocardium, thickened enhanced endomyocardium, and thrombus (with/without calcifications). Thrombus appears as a perfusion defect on first-pass CMRI. However, in some cases, the single V sign is observed with subendocardial enhancement at the apex, without thrombus and not limited to any coronary territory described in literature and was evident in the present study [7]. The single V sign observed in the LGE images is a characteristic feature of biventricular EMF, defined by subendocardial fibrosis at both the LV and RV apices, resulting in a V-shaped enhancement pattern in each ventricle. This sign is indicative of the apical fibrotic changes and retraction seen in EMF, distinguishing it from other restrictive cardiomyopathies. The presence of the single V sign in both ventricles is a key diagnostic feature and supports the diagnosis of EMF in this case, as supported by previous literature [7]. Mitral regurgitation, attributed to fibrofatty mass deposition, was quantified at 17 mL by planimetry and 19 mL by 4D flow. Left atrial enhancement suggests fibrosis, which can contribute to functional mitral regurgitation by causing annular dilation, impaired atrial contractility, and altered haemodynamics. In EMF, extension of fibrosis from the apex to the posterior mitral leaflet may further restrict leaflet motion, exacerbating mitral regurgitation. In this case, the absence of significant LV dilation and the preserved ejection fraction suggest that the regurgitation is more related to localised myocardial involvement rather than global ventricular remodelling. While the fibrofatty mass itself may not directly involve the mitral valve, associated atrial and ventricular remodelling can indirectly lead to mitral regurgitation. Mitral and tricuspid regurgitation correlate with a poor prognosis, with mortality rates reaching 75% in advanced cases despite pharmacological treatment [8]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Endomyocardial fibrosis (EMF) presents with left ventricular restriction, atrial enlargement, fibrosis, thrombus, and valve regurgitation, with symptoms like dyspnoea and weakness. Cardiac MRI reveals anatomical details, including right atrial enlargement, ventricular apex retraction, and fibrosis with characteristic patterns, such as the V sign with late gadolinium enhancement. The double V sign in EMF shows three layers: normal myocardium, thickened enhanced endomyocardium, and thrombus. Thrombus appears as a perfusion defect on first-pass cardiac MRI. In some cases, a single V sign is observed with subendocardial enhancement at the apex, without thrombus and not limited to any coronary territory. While echocardiography is a first-line diagnostic tool, cardiac MRI offers tissue characterisation, allowing for visualisation of myocardial fibrosis pattern and cardiac morphology. Cardiac MRI distinguishes EMF from conditions like hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, amyloidosis, and Ebstein’s anomaly, with scoring systems aiding diagnosis.

title: Hypothetical traumatic midbrain cleft
clinical_history: A 3-year-old male child presented with restricted eye movements (down and out left eye) and progressive weakness in the right limbs for the last 2 years. The patient had a history of penetrating trauma by a long piece of metal involving the region just above the right upper eyelid prior to this. The piece was then pulled out and wound sealed without any significant ocular injury. Examination revealed signs of left third nerve palsy and a decrease in motor function in the right limbs.
imaging_findings: An MRI brain was done for further evaluation. It revealed a linear T1 hypotense (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c) and T2 hyperintense cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cleft showing suppression on FLAIR sequence (Figures 2a and 2b) involving the ventral midbrain on the left side with transection of the left crus cerebri and probable involvement of the course of the left oculomotor nerve. No diffusion restriction/GRE blooming seen.
discussion: Midbrain cleft formation secondary to brain trauma is an exceedingly rare phenomenon. Symptoms can be due to injury to rostral midbrain nuclei and tracts. Few cases have been reported. One case involved a 28-year-old man who sustained a severe closed head injury after being struck by a large truck, leading to the development of a subdural haematoma (SDH) that required evacuation. Following hemicraniectomy, the man had new-onset bulbar symptoms, facial and oculomotor weakness, and ataxia. CT scan showed a lesion in the midbrain (cystic in nature) originating from the aqueduct. The autopsy later confirmed the presence of the cleft [1]. Another case [2,3] involved a 41-year-old man who fell due to an intoxicated state, resulting in an acute SDH involving the right cerebral convexity with adjacent contusions. A midline shift of 9 mm was noted, which required craniectomy for decompression. Ten months later, after recovering enough to return to work, the patient experienced diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia and no sensation in the left hand. A cleft was noted involving the superior aspect of the fourth ventricle during imaging, which was seen extending towards the right and rostrally through the midbrain and thalamus. The aqueduct seemed patent on cisternography. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed, which showed normal CSF pressure and halted clefts enlargement, preventing further progression. Paralysis of the bilateral superior recti, the ipsilateral medial rectus, the inferior rectus and the inferior oblique is noted in lesions involving the oculomotor nucleus [4]. Ipsilateral pupillary dilatation may be seen if there is injury to the Edinger–Westphal nucleus. Lesion of the red nucleus or its cerebellar projections may lead to tremors or ataxia. The interstitial nucleus of Cajal is responsible for the vertical gaze of the eyeballs; damage may cause downbeat nystagmus [5]. An increase in CSF pressure and a decrease in parenchymal elasticity could lead to CSF flow-related damage and resultant cleft formation. Increase in CSF pressure waves could also result from acute blockade of the ventriculoperitoneal shunt or due to chronic coughs [6] and Valsalva manoeuvre. Extensive contusions during trauma can cause resultant gliosis [7], which may lead to loss of elasticity of the cerebral aqueduct. Similar loss of elasticity may be implicated in our case. Gliosis also reduces brain compliance, which, as described by Bateman [8], is the plasticity of the brain to deform and allow ventricular enlargement with increasing CSF pressure. However, we could not demonstrate diffuse axonal injury changes in our case as the patient presented to us around 22 months post-injury. To our knowledge, this represents the first reported CSF cleft through the midbrain after penetrating trauma near the eyelid region. To conclude, we report this rare case of traumatic brainstem transection cleft with its clinical-radiological features, with relevant clinical anatomy and physiology.

title: Polyostotic melorheostosis: A rare form of mesenchymal dysplasia
clinical_history: A 25-year-old male patient with no significant past medical background is referred for left knee pain since the age of 10, associated with knee swelling. Since then, he has always maintained complaints but lived a normal life. Plain radiograph, CT scan and MR were ordered for further investigation.
imaging_findings: On plain film (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d), there are periosteal and endosteal cortical thickening associated with extra-cortical bone formation along the anterior aspect of the left tibia and the medial aspect of the left femur. Areas of central medullary hyperostosis can be observed in the inferior third of the femoral diaphysis and in the femoral head. The lesions have an appearance that resembles “flowing candle wax”. CT scan (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, 2d, and 2e) allows for further acknowledgement of the changes described above. MR performed on a 1.5T MR scanner (T1 and STIR sequences in axial and coronal planes; Figures 3a and 3b) depict extensive changes with very low signal on all imaging sequences, mainly involving the left femur and tibia, with diffuse thickening of the bone cortex giving the bone surface a wavy appearance, as well as multiple intramedullary foci showing marked hypointensity, indicating a strong component of bone sclerosis. The lesions show eccentric growth, extending from the diaphysis to the epiphysis, and exceeding the cortical surface.
discussion: Background Melorheostosis, or Leri’s disease, is a rare type of mesenchymal dysplasia characterised as a benign sclerosing bone dysplasia, most commonly presenting in late adolescence. The name originates from the Greek words “melos” (limb), “rhein” (flowing) and “ostosis” (bone formation). Although it can affect any bone, it typically involves the long bones of the lower limbs and can manifest at any age. The condition may appear as polyostotic or monostotic, occasionally affecting both sides [1], and tends to have a sclerotomal distribution. The exact cause of melorheostosis is unknown. It can coexist with other benign or malignant bone conditions, such as osteosarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, or Buschke–Ollendorff syndrome [2]. Imaging Perspective On radiographs, melorheostosis is characterised by flowing cortical hyperostosis along one side of the long bone shaft, often compared to “wax dripping down a candle”. These hyperdense areas appear segmentally and spread distally from one bone to another [3]. CT scans show cortical and medullary hyperostosis as high-attenuation areas, while MR reveals low signal intensity on all imaging sequences, with endosteal involvement sometimes encroaching on the marrow space. Although para-articular soft-tissue masses are well documented, their imaging characteristics are not extensively explored. CT highlights the degree of mineralisation, confirming these masses are usually not connected to the underlying bone. MR reveals a heterogeneous signal pattern due to mineralised zones, fat and fibrovascular tissue [4]. Differential Diagnoses Other diseases that course with periosteal and endosteal cortical thickening should be considered in the diagnostic work-up, such as hereditary sclerosing bone dysplasias (e.g., progressive diaphyseal dysplasia, hereditary multiple diaphyseal sclerosis) or overlap syndromes, whereas acquired syndromes with increased bone density may simulate sclerosing bone dysplasias, such as Erdheim–Chester disease [5]. Progressive diaphyseal dysplasia (PDD) and hereditary multiple diaphyseal sclerosis (HMDS) are diseases of intramembranous ossification. The metaphysis and epiphysis are typically not involved, since these regions are formed by endochondral ossification, presenting a sharp demarcation of normal bone in these regions (as opposed to melorheostosis, which presents disturbances in both endochondral and intramembranous ossification). The distribution of osseous involvement in HMDS differs from that in PDD (bilateral and symmetric cortical thickening involving both the periosteal and endosteal surfaces of long bones) in that there is either unilateral or asymmetric and asynchronous bilateral involvement of long bones, typically the tibia or femur [5]. Erdheim–Chester disease is a rare, multisystem, non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis of unknown cause. The osseous involvement typically affects the appendicular skeleton, with the lower extremities being involved more often, and presents with cortical thickening, narrowing of the medullary cavity and loss of the corticomedullary junction. It typically has a bilateral and symmetric distribution involving the diaphysis and metaphyses, with sparing of the epiphyses, differing from melorheostosis [5]. Outcome Melorheostosis may remain asymptomatic for long periods. However, it can cause pain and deformities, leading to significant functional limitations. The disease progresses chronically, with alternating periods of exacerbation and remission, advancing more rapidly in children than in adults. Clinically, patients may present with limb deformity, joint stiffness, pain and restricted movement due to contractures or fibrosis. Complications like limb shortening or lengthening, or angular deformities are also common [6]. There is no definitive treatment for melorheostosis. Management options include both non-surgical and surgical approaches to relieve symptoms. Take Home Message Though benign, melorheostosis can lead to considerable morbidity. Radiologists must be familiar with its diverse clinical and imaging features to support accurate diagnosis and effective management, aiding surgeons in planning further treatment.

title: Radiological manifestations of congenital hypothyroidism in a 19-year-old male
clinical_history: A 19-year-old male presented with short stature, mental retardation, breathlessness, and abdominal distension. He also exhibited coarse facial features, periorbital oedema, hypotonia, bradycardia, and features of congestive heart failure (Figure 1). Biochemical workup revealed primary-type hypothyroidism with low levels of thyroid hormones and high levels of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). X-rays and ultrasound (USG) were performed for further workup
imaging_findings: The X-ray findings revealed significant skeletal abnormalities consistent with congenital hypothyroidism. The spine shows bullet-shaped vertebral bodies with flattening and increased intervertebral disc spaces (Figure 2). The bilateral knees showed generalised osteopenia, stippled epiphyses, widened metaphyseal ends, and absent patellar ossification with a bone age of less than 3-4 years (Figures 3 and 4). Skull X-rays highlighted Wormian bones, incomplete suture fusion, an enlarged sella turcica, and hypoplastic paranasal sinuses (Figures 5 and 6). Wrist X-rays demonstrate three ossified carpal bones, non-visualised distal ulna epiphysis, and partially ossified metaphysis (Figure 7). Chest X-rays reveal a narrow thoracic cavity, stippled humeral epiphyses and cardiomegaly (Figure 8), while pelvic X-rays show a narrowed pelvis with coxa vara and stippled femoral epiphyses (Figure 9). USG of the neck confirmed the absence of the thyroid gland in the neck, submandibular, and sublingual regions. USG of abdomen and thorax revealed cardiomegaly, hepatomegaly with dilated inferior vena cava and hepatic veins (suggestive of congestive hepatomegaly), ascites and right-sided pleural effusion. The diagnosis was made based on the ultrasonographic findings combined with clinical and biochemical evidence suggestive of congenital hypothyroidism. While thyroid scintigraphy is indeed the gold standard for differentiating between ectopic thyroid tissue and true agenesis, it was not performed in this case.
discussion: Congenital hypothyroidism (CH) is a condition resulting from the absence, malformation, or dysfunction of the thyroid gland at birth, leading to inadequate thyroid hormone production. It affects growth, metabolism, and neurodevelopment. The condition is primarily caused by thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis or ectopy) or dyshormonogenesis, which impairs hormone synthesis. Untreated cases result in delayed skeletal maturation, growth failure, and neurocognitive deficits [1]. Symptoms may include short stature, mental retardation, coarse facial features, hypotonia, constipation, delayed bone age, and poor growth. Late diagnosis leads to irreversible complications like severe growth, mental retardation and even heart failure. Imaging is crucial to detect delayed skeletal maturation, epiphyseal stippling, and absent thyroid tissue [2,4]. The absence of thyroid hormone from birth results in growth arrest, delayed bone maturation, and short stature. Ossification centres develop abnormally, exhibiting an irregular, mottled pattern with multiple foci that merge, creating a porous or fragmented appearance referred to as stippled epiphyseal dysgenesis. This condition is most commonly observed in large cartilaginous centres, such as the femoral head, humeral head, and tarsal navicular bone [3]. X-rays reveal delayed bone age, stippled epiphyses, and skeletal abnormalities, while ultrasound suggests thyroid gland absence, establishing the diagnosis with thyroid function tests [4]. Thyroid ectopia or absence can be further confirmed by nuclear medicine scans. Radiologists must convey findings to confirm hypothyroidism and exclude differential diagnoses like growth hormone deficiency and skeletal dysplasias: Growth hormone deficiency presents with delayed bone age proportional to the patient’s height age. Bones are smaller but maintain normal shape and structure without significant metaphyseal abnormalities. Epiphyseal development is typically normal but smaller in size due to delayed growth. Radiographic findings in growth hormone deficiency generally lack the structural abnormalities seen in CH, showing only reduced bone size consistent with overall growth delay. Skeletal dysplasias exhibit structural bone deformities rather than just delayed growth. Radiographs often show abnormal epiphyseal and metaphyseal morphology, including irregularly shaped and dysplastic epiphyses, metaphyseal flaring or irregularities, and abnormal vertebral bodies (e.g., platyspondyly, kyphosis). These changes are usually permanent, progressive, and unresponsive to hormonal therapies. Unlike congenital hypothyroidism, skeletal dysplasias demonstrate characteristic malformations that are diagnostic of specific dysplasia types [5]. Early thyroid hormone replacement therapy is crucial for treating congenital hypothyroidism. Early detection through imaging techniques allows for timely treatment, leading to normal growth and development, while delayed diagnosis can result in permanent impairments [6].

title: Left-sided gallbladder: A rare anatomic variant
clinical_history: A 46-year-old male presented with recurrent left lower abdominal pain for 6 months, resulting in multiple emergency department visits. Physical examination was unremarkable, with stable vital signs and normal laboratory tests. Despite normal findings, the patient continued to experience pain and was referred to general surgery for further investigation.
imaging_findings: An ultrasound, abdominopelvic contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were performed, all of which were normal. Incidentally, a left-sided gallbladder (LSG) was observed, defined as a gallbladder located on the left side of the ligamentum teres, without situs inversus (Figures 1, 2 and 3). No evidence of gallstones or other hepatobiliary pathologies was found. Additionally, the patient exhibited a portal vein anomaly of the trifurcation type (Figure 4), where the left portal vein, along with the anterior and posterior branches of the right portal vein, all arise directly from the main portal vein.
discussion: The gallbladder typically resides between hepatic segments IV and V. LSG is a rare anomaly, occurring in 0.2–1.1% of cases [1], where the gallbladder is positioned on the left side of the ligamentum teres (round ligament). LSG can be categorised into three types: situs inversus, ectopic left-sided gallbladder (true left-sided gallbladder), or right-sided ligamentum teres [2–4]. True LSG may arise through two mechanisms: (a) migration of the gallbladder to the left lobe, where the cystic duct remains in its normal position and crosses the common duct from right to left before joining the common hepatic duct on the right [5]; or (b) direct budding from the left side of the liver, where the cystic duct joins the common duct or left hepatic duct from the left side, and the gallbladder is located under the left liver lobe (segment III) [5,6]. In contrast, LSG associated with right-sided round ligaments is typically found in segment IVb and is often accompanied by anomalies of intrahepatic portal veins and biliary branches [7]. Portal vein anomalies, significant in surgeries such as hepatectomy, split liver transplantation, or living donor liver hepatectomy, can be classified into three types: trifurcation, bifurcation, or undetermined patterns [8]. In our case, the patient presented with an LSG caused by a right-sided ligamentum teres and a portal vein trifurcation, where the left portal vein, as well as the anterior and posterior branches of the right portal vein, arise directly from the main portal vein. The primary diagnostic clue for LSG on imaging (US, CT, MRI) is a gallbladder located on the left side of the ligamentum teres. Among imaging techniques, CT is the most effective for identifying anatomical variations of portal veins associated with this anomaly. Other modalities, such as angiography, CT angiography, or MRI, provide additional details regarding vascular and biliary anomalies, assisting with preoperative planning [9]. Patients with LSG typically do not require specific treatment or surgery. However, identifying this anatomical variant is crucial for surgical planning, especially for procedures like left hepatectomy for tumours, laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and split or living donor liver transplantation [10]. Recognising LSG during routine imaging ensures accurate preoperative preparation. Although imaging aids in diagnosing LSG, some cases may only be detected intraoperatively, requiring modifications to the surgical approach. This can be challenging even for experienced surgeons. Studies indicate that LSG is associated with an increased risk of bile duct injury (up to 7.3%) due to anomalies in biliary ducts, portal veins, and other structures [11]. In conclusion, LSG is a rare anatomical variant often discovered only during surgery. Greater awareness of LSG and its associated abnormalities, combined with accurate imaging, can improve surgical outcomes and reduce complications.

title: Low phospholipid-associated cholelithiasis causing post-cholecystectomy biliary colic
clinical_history: A 36-year-old non-obese female with a history of cholecystectomy in the last four months presents to the emergency department with clinical signs including right upper quadrant pain, generalised jaundice, and a fever of 38.5°C. Liver function tests reveal hepatic cytolysis and cholestasis (elevated AST/ALT and ALP). An abdominal ultrasound was requested.
imaging_findings: Abdominal ultrasound with a low-frequency probe reveals the presence of multiple hyperechoic formations within the intrahepatic bile ducts, causing posterior acoustic shadowing (Figure 1) and resulting in dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts (Figures 2 and 3). The common bile duct was clear. The presence of jaundice and fever raised concerns about an associated cholangitis, prompting the indication for hepatobiliary MRI. The MRI reveals more pronounced dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts, particularly in the left lobe of the liver, containing multiple signal-void formations consistent with the previously described biliary calculi (Figures 4 and 5). Additionally, T1-weighted sequences post-gadolinium demonstrate subtle thickening and enhancement of the intrahepatic bile duct walls along with peribiliary hepatic infiltration, secondary to the inflammation of the liver adjacent to biliary ducts caused by potential cholangitis (Figure 6).
discussion: Low phospholipid-associated cholelithiasis (LPAC) syndrome, also known as genetic cholesterolemic lithiasis, is a rare bile duct calculus condition described in 2001. It constitutes about 5% of symptomatic lithiasis cases and is characterised by a low concentration of phospholipids rather than excess cholesterol in the bile. Typically affecting young, non-overweight women, it often results from a mutation in the ABCB4 gene, causing disrupted bile metabolism and intrabiliary microlithiasis. Diagnosis involves criteria like age under 40, biliary pain recurrence post-cholecystectomy, and specific ultrasound findings [1,2]. Imaging plays a central role in the diagnosis of this condition. An ultrasound, performed as the initial imaging modality, allows for the detection of revealing signs in approximately 80 to 85% of patients. This includes visualising intraparenchymal hyperechoic foci with posterior acoustic shadowing, intrahepatic bile duct calculi, and sometimes intraparenchymal sludge. However, the detection of small microlithiasis may be limited. Doppler ultrasound highlights the colour comet-tail artefacts known as “twinkling artefacts”, which are signs of microlithiasis; contrary to pneumobilia, they are not mobile. However, CT and MRI are utilised to rule out differential diagnoses like primary sclerosing cholangitis, recurrent pyogenic cholangiohepatitis, Caroli disease, and residual common bile duct lithiasis. They may also detect complications such as cholangitis, pancreatitis, hepatic abscess, and cholangiocarcinoma. Yet, both techniques present certain limitations, especially for the detection of microlithiasis <3 mm, impacted ampullary stones, and cholesterol-based stones, which are invisible on CT scan [1]. In cases where T1 in-phase and out-of-phase imaging is available, this is a helpful tool in distinguishing between stones and pneumobilia. This technique was not used in our case but has been reported to improve diagnostic accuracy in certain settings. Distinguishing classical gallbladder lithiasis from LPAC syndrome involves age at onset, sex ratio, and imaging findings. Classical lithiasis usually appears after 50, with a 1.5:1 female-to-male ratio, displaying isolated gallbladder lithiasis on imaging. Conversely, LPAC syndrome affects younger individuals, often with a 3:1 female-to-male ratio, and exhibits intrahepatic lithiasis and comet-tail artefacts on ultrasound. Recurrent pyogenic cholangitis (RPC) has distinct pathophysiological and imaging features. From a pathological standpoint, it is often associated with hepatobiliary infestation by Clonorchis sinensis (liver fluke) or Ascaris lumbricoides , which promote stone formation and biliary strictures. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) typically reveals characteristic intra- and extrahepatic biliary dilatation with multilevel strictures, intraductal pigmented calculi, and segmental liver atrophy, particularly in the left hepatic lobe. Key imaging signs include reduced arborisation of peripheral ducts, known as the “arrowhead sign”, and multiple biliary strictures. In our case, the combination of age younger than 40 years, a history of cholecystectomy, and the presence of intrahepatic calculi without biliary duct strictures led us to consider the diagnosis of LPAC syndrome. Treatment primarily employs ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) for cholesterol solubilisation, yielding symptom relief in most cases. Interventional radiology offers percutaneous biliary drainage and endoscopic recanalisation for complex cases, while surgery is reserved for complications or UDCA failure. In summary, LPAC syndrome is underdiagnosed, characterised by recurrent biliary pain, particularly in young individuals with ABCB4 mutations. The detection rate of LPAC syndrome signs in ultrasound can vary widely, from 5% (inexperienced radiologist) to 90% (expert radiologist), according to a non-published study (LPANGH study) [2]. CT and MRI are useful for ruling out differential diagnoses and detecting complications. Understanding the distinctive features of LPAC syndrome is crucial for accurate diagnosis and appropriate management [1–4]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: MRI of the bend: Peyronie’s disease
clinical_history: A 54-year-old man with a long-term history of diabetes presented to the urology department with complaints of penile deviation during erection for the past two months. Physical examination revealed superficial indurations along the superior midline aspect of the penis.
imaging_findings: MRI in the flaccid state was preferred due to patient discomfort and embarrassment, as well as the sufficient visibility of plaques without the need for an erection. It was performed in the supine position using a surface coil, revealing plaques in the midportion of the superior tunica albuginea (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d). The plaques were longitudinally oriented, of varied sizes, and ranged from focal to extensive. They appeared isointense on T1-weighted and were better visualised as hyperintense areas on T2-weighted images using the periodically rotated overlapping parallel lines with enhanced reconstruction (PROPELLER) technique. This technique is particularly suited for Peyronie’s disease due to its motion correction, high-resolution soft tissue contrast, and artefact reduction, ensuring clear visualisation of plaques and fibrosis without the need for an erection. After gadolinium injection, the plaques exhibited diffuse enhancement, consistent with florid inflammation.
discussion: Background Peyronie’s disease (PD) is a chronic fibrotic condition affecting the penis. Histopathologically, the disease is characterised by a focal inflammatory reaction, fibrotic plaque formation, and, occasionally, calcifications. Effective treatment requires assessing whether the disease is predominantly in an inflammatory or fibrotic stage to determine the feasibility of conservative management [1]. Clinical Perspective Peyronie’s disease accounts for less than 1% of urological diseases and is typically diagnosed between the 4th and 6th decades [1]. Repetitive trauma, hormonal imbalances, and metabolic disease contribute to its pathophysiology. Common complaints include penile curvature, painful erections, reduced penile length, and erectile dysfunction. Physical examination often reveals well-demarcated, palpable plaques on the tunica albuginea. The underlying mechanism of the disease is a vasculitis in the connective tissue at the interface between the corpus cavernosum and tunica albuginea. Early stages are characterised by lymphoplasmacytic cellular infiltration, which progresses to fibrosis and sclerosis in advanced stages. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound is the primary imaging modality for identifying the localisation and extent of plaques, which may affect the dorsal, ventral, lateral aspects of the penis, or the septum, with or without involvement of adjacent structures. Commonly reported findings include hyperechogenic plaques that may be calcified and stable (with posterior acoustic shadow) or non-calcified (without posterior acoustic shadow). Hypoechoic/isoechoic plaques, indicative of early-stage oedema, are better visualised during a prostaglandin E1-induced erection. Less common findings include focal defects of the tunica albuginea and an “hourglass deformity” involving the entire penis circumference. Dynamic US evaluation also allows the assessment of erectile function and curvature angle. However, US cannot reliably differentiate between active inflammatory and quiescent stages of the disease. MRI provides detailed anatomical visualisation, including inflamed plaques. T2-weighted images are superior for identifying indurations, though these may also be visualised on T1-weighted images. Gadolinium injection is essential for detecting florid inflammation, which appears as enhancement around or within the plaques [2]. Outcome Plaque size and calcification are the primary parameters used to assess therapeutic response. In the early inflammatory stages, conservative management is typically employed, including low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy, phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, hyaluronic acid, and collagenase derived from Clostridium histolyticum . In chronic fibrotic stages with severe shortening and sexual dysfunction, surgical correction remains the only viable option [3]. Take Home Message Peyronie’s disease is a chronic fibrotic condition, primarily presenting as penile curvature and painful erections. Ultrasound enables the evaluation of plaques morphology, volume, and erectile function, while MRI provides insights into their inflammatory or fibrotic nature, guiding subsequent management. Informed consent has been obtained from the patient to the anonymous publication of the content.

title: Swallowing the diagnosis: A rare case of oesophageal leiomyoma
clinical_history: A 47-year-old woman presented with epigastric pain and uneasiness since six months. She had no difficulty in swallowing or regurgitation of food. She had no respiratory complaints. An ultrasonography of the abdomen was unremarkable. The patient was subjected to an erect chest radiograph for routine evaluation.
imaging_findings: Erect frontal chest radiograph showed a well-defined, lobulated, homogeneous, soft tissue opacity (green arrow) in the left lower hemithorax, obscuring the medial aspect of the left dome of the diaphragm. It was seen as continuous with an ill-defined, left paravertebral soft tissue opacity (pink arrow). There was no silhouetting of the left heart border (Figure 1). A barium (95% w/v) oesophagogram showed unobstructed passage of barium through the thoracic soft tissue opacity. The retrocardiac oesophagus was tortuous and deviated to the left with a normal gastro-oesophageal junction (Figure 2). An unenhanced CT of the chest was performed with oral contrast, followed by intravenous contrast-enhanced CT with oral contrast in the same sitting. Axial unenhanced images showed circumferential, homogeneous thickening of the lower oesophageal wall with patency of the lumen showing orally administered water-soluble contrast. There were a few tiny foci of calcification within the wall (pink arrow on Figure 3). Sagittal venous phase images showed homogeneous enhancement of the thickened oesophageal wall without areas of necrosis (blue arrow) or evidence of invasion into surrounding structures (Figure 4). Coronal unenhanced images in the lung window showed surrounding atelectasis without signs of lung parenchymal involvement (Figure 5).
discussion: Oesophageal lesions present with dysphagia to solids or liquids when there is narrowing of the lumen or may be detected incidentally on chest CT performed for pulmonary indications when the lesion involves the oesophageal wall without luminal compromise. Oesophageal tumours can be classified into benign and malignant, with the clinically symptomatic lesions generally being larger in size and malignant in nature [1]. Benign circumferential thickening of the oesophagus occurs in oesophagitis with the aetiology being infective, caustic injury or radiation therapy, and manifests as homogeneous thickening of > 3–5 mm or in strictures due to gastro-oesophageal reflux disease [2]. Benign tumours of the oesophageal wall, like schwannoma, granular cell tumour and leiomyomas, generally present as focal, eccentric thickening of the oesophageal wall [2]. Single and double contrast oesophagograms can detect extra-luminal pathologies as filling defects in the oesophageal outline and luminal pathologies as irregularities in the mucosa. They are usually performed first to understand the need for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. Oesophageal leiomyomas occur in the middle and distal thirds of the oesophagus as intramural, homogeneous, smoothly marginated masses causing filling defects on oesophagograms. They may show calcific foci, which are relatively specific to leiomyomas compared to gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GISTs) and lymphomas [1]. However, they may occasionally present as circumferential masses. In a retrospective study by Yang et al. [3], two of the twelve patients with biopsy-proven oesophageal leiomyomas had circumferential thickening of the oesophageal wall. Oesophageal leiomyomas are usually less than 3 cm in size and are characterised as giant leiomyomas when greater than 5 cm in size, which is rare, as in our case. When presenting as focal, intramural masses, leiomyomas are difficult to differentiate radiologically from other entities like neurofibromas, haemangiomas and fibromas [4]. When presenting as circumferential thickening, a rare differential diagnosis is lymphoma, which usually manifests as direct extension from the stomach. It can show enlarged mucosal folds, polypoid lesions or submucosal nodules as well [1]. Another differential is GIST, which presents as an eccentric, exophytic lesion with haematemesis due to mucosal ulceration. It shows moderate enhancement, greater than that of leiomyomas and rarely shows calcific foci [5]. Malignant oesophageal neoplasms, on the other hand, usually present in a late stage with dysphagia due to stricture formation. They produce asymmetric or symmetric, heterogeneously enhancing thickening of the oesophageal wall with irregular mucosal contours and proximal shelfing on barium oesophagograms [6]. In our case, a CT chest was performed for characterisation of the suspicious lesion seen on the radiograph following barium oesophagogram. The lesion was seen continuing with the oesophageal lumen. Subsequently, the patient was subjected to an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, which revealed a homogeneous submucosal bulge in the oesophagus with intact mucosa (Figure 6). In order to rule out a malignant lesion like lymphoma, she underwent an endoscopic biopsy. The histopathology revealed spindle-shaped cells with bland cytology in sweeping fascicles, positive for SMA on immunohistochemistry, and suggestive of a benign smooth muscle tumour. Since our patient had no dysphagia, she is being followed up on an outpatient basis and being treated conservatively with daily oral proton pump inhibitors without surgical intervention. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient after ensuring that the patient's details would not be revealed in any way.

title: Split dual left anterior descending coronary artery (LAD)
clinical_history: An 82-year-old female with hypertension and dyslipidemia had a scheduled cardiovascular check-up, but no significant symptoms.
imaging_findings: Coronary CT angiogram (CCTA) shows two left anterior descending arteries (LAD) arteries, both originating from the left coronary system (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, 1d, and 1e). A short LAD originates from the LAD proper and terminates proximal to the anterior interventricular sulcus (AIVS) (red arrow). A long LAD originates from LAD proper and courses on the left ventricle side of the proximal AIVS (yellow arrow).
discussion: Dual left anterior descending artery (LAD) is when two LADs supply the heart. Incidence varies from 0.68% to 6% in different case series [1], though CT angiography may suggest a higher prevalence [3,4] reported a prevalence of 1% in their study. The two LADs are typically referred to as “short LAD” and “long LAD”. The initial classification described four types based on the origin and course of short and long LADs [4]. Over time, the initial classification has expanded, with up to thirteen variants being described based on variations in origin and course [3]. The new classification system is based on three main groups, which are split based on how the LADs run (e.g., anterior/epicardial, septal/intramyocardial, inter-arterial, retro-aortic) [1]: Group I – “Split” dual LAD : Both LADs come entirely from the left coronary sinus; the common LAD bifurcates into short LAD and long LAD. Group II – “True” dual LAD : The left coronary artery has a dual origin from the left coronary sinus and the right coronary sinus. Group III – “Anomalous” dual LAD : The left heart arteries originate entirely from the right coronary sinus. Dual LAD rarely causes blood flow problems. Missing the short LAD during surgery can lead to incomplete blood flow. Anomalies with a pre-pulmonic course are more likely to be injured during median sternotomy [3]. CCTA are the best way to see your heart arteries. Sometimes, it may miss it if the long LAD comes from the other side sinus [3]. Outcome Since our patient had no symptoms, a follow-up was advised, and no medication was needed. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Dual LAD, though rare, is important to know about. The novel classification system [1] offers a systematic approach to categorising these variations, which can aid in diagnosis and treatment planning. CCTA plays a critical role in identifying and characterising dual LAD, particularly in cases where the long LAD has an anomalous origin or course. Awareness of this anomaly and its potential clinical implications is essential for cardiologists, radiologists, and cardiac surgeons.

title: Osteochondromas of the scapula: An unusual location
clinical_history: A 24-year-old male patient complains of long-lasting chest pain, which worsens in the prone position and interferes with sleep. He denies any dyspnoea, palpitations, or a history of trauma. His medical history includes anxiety and a surgical procedure to remove multiple bone tumours from his lower limbs six years ago.
imaging_findings: A computed tomography (CT) scan was performed on the chest, revealing two lesions on the left scapula: one on the ventral surface in the subscapular fossa and another on the dorsal surface in the infraspinatus fossa (Figures 1 and 2). Both lesions presented calcium density and were found to have continuity with the adjacent bone, assuming a pedunculated conformation with anterior and posterior protrusion. These well-defined lesions did not show destruction of the cortical bone, irregular calcifications, or periosteal reaction of the underlying bone.
discussion: Chest wall lesions are relatively rare and can be benign or malignant, originating in soft tissue, bone, or vascular tissue. The radiologist must differentiate between benign lesions, which can be diagnosed through imaging alone (referred to as “do not touch lesions”), and those requiring histological examination [5,6]. In this case, two bone lesions were detected on the scapula, displaying continuity with the underlying bone and lacking signs of malignancy. These indicative features support the diagnosis of osteochondromas. The presence of numerous bone tumours in the lower limbs further supports the diagnosis. Osteochondromas can be multiple and appear in various locations, in this case, suggesting the potential presence of an underlying syndrome. Osteochondroma, or bone exostosis, is the most common benign bone tumour, representing 10–30% of all primary bone tumours, typically affecting men under 30 years of age [1,4]. It is characterised as a “do not touch lesion” that originates from a defect of the growth plate, in which cartilage fragments relocate to an ectopic location. These lesions ossify and maintain corticomedullary continuity with the underlying bone tissue. Generally, they present a thin cartilage cap and have the potential to grow until late puberty [1,2,4]. These lesions can be sessile or pedunculated, solitary or multiple, and typically involve the metaphysis of long bones, such as the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus. Rarely, osteochondromas can occur in the distal extremities, pelvis, spine, and scapula, accounting for 3–5% of cases in the latter location [2]. While it is typically asymptomatic, osteochondroma can be associated with chronic pain, oedema, bursa formation, pathological fractures, and vascular or neurological compromise [1,2]. Osteochondromas have a risk of malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma, especially when multiple or associated with syndromes such as Trevor’s disease or hereditary multiple exostoses. Potential predictors include pain, bone erosion, irregular calcifications, post-puberty size increase, and thickening of the cartilage cap exceeding 2 cm in adults and 3 cm in children [3–5]. The diagnosis is usually achieved through conventional radiography or computed tomography, identifying a calcium opacity/density structure in a characteristic location that maintains corticomedullary continuity with the underlying bone [5], without exhibiting signs of malignancy. Evaluating the thickness of the cartilage cap is crucial for predicting the risk of malignancy and is best assessed using ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging. Asymptomatic lesions typically do not require treatment; however, symptomatic or visually deforming lesions may undergo surgical resection, generally yielding a positive prognosis.

title: Twisted fate – A rare case of isolated tubal torsion with haematosalpinx
clinical_history: A 30‐year‐old woman (P1L1) presented with a two‐day history of acute pelvic pain and vomiting. There was no history of fever or vaginal bleeding. Her menstrual cycles were regular, but often accompanied by mild dysmenorrhea. No history of tubal ligation. The patient’s medical history was unremarkable, and a urinary pregnancy test was negative.
imaging_findings: Transvaginal sonography (TVS) revealed a convoluted, heterogeneously echogenic mass in the pouch of Douglas (POD), predominantly towards the right, showing significant surrounding inflammation. At its distal end was a well-defined, hypoechoic cystic lesion measuring approximately 3×4 cm, exhibiting peripheral mucosal infoldings with a classic cog-wheel pattern, strongly indicating tubal origin. The cyst contained homogeneous low-level internal echoes, raising suspicion for a haematosalpinx. Doppler imaging demonstrated a twisted vascular pedicle with a near-classic whirlpool pattern, along with pronounced adnexal hyperaemia. The right ovary maintained its normal anatomical position, morphology and good stromal vascularity, however, with mild periovarian hyperaemia. A small volume of echogenic free fluid was present in the POD. The left ovary, adnexa, uterus and cervix appeared unremarkable, while the endometrium exhibited features of hyperplasia.
discussion: Background Isolated tubal torsion (ITT) is a rare gynaecological emergency where the fallopian tube twists in isolation without ovarian involvement. Its incidence is approximately 1 in 1.5 million women, making it an uncommon cause of acute pelvic pain [1,2]. Contributing factors include hydrosalpinx, haematosalpinx, paraovarian cysts and adhesions [3,4]. The torsion disrupts venous and lymphatic drainage, progressing to ischemia, infarction, and necrosis if untreated [5]. Haematosalpinx may result from tubal torsion, further complicating its clinical course [6]. Clinical Perspective ITT typically presents as acute, unilateral lower abdominal pain that may be sharp, cramp-like, or radiate to the groin or thigh. Additional symptoms, including nausea and vomiting, mimicking other abdominal emergencies such as ovarian torsion, ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, or renal colic, may lead to frequent misdiagnosis [1,3]. In adolescent and reproductive-aged women, paraovarian cysts and hydrosalpinx are common predisposing factors, while ITT is extremely rare in postmenopausal women [2,4]. Due to its nonspecific clinical presentation, imaging is crucial in differentiating ITT from other causes of acute abdomen [5]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound (US) is the primary diagnostic tool for ITT. Key findings include an elongated, dilated, fluid-filled fallopian tube with a thickened wall or an echogenic convoluted tube associated with a distal mass (e.g., paraovarian cyst, hydrosalpinx, haematosalpinx), essentially with a spared normal ovary. Colour Doppler may reveal absent or reduced blood flow; however, normal vascularity does not exclude torsion due to the tube’s dual arterial supply [3]. A “whirlpool sign” on Doppler, indicating a twisted vascular pedicle, is a hallmark feature [6]. When US is inconclusive, CT or MRI can help by identifying a twisted tubular structure, peritubal oedema, or haematosalpinx [2,5]. Laparoscopy remains the gold standard for diagnosis and treatment [1]. Outcome Management depends on ischemic severity. Early detorsion may restore blood flow and preserve fertility [4]. However, in cases of necrosis, salpingectomy is necessary [2,5]. Our patient underwent immediate right salpingectomy, which revealed a partially twisted fallopian tube with haematosalpinx at the fimbrial end showing patchy tubal necrosis, while the right ovary remained normal and was preserved. Take Home Message Isolated tubal torsion (ITT) is a rare but critical differential diagnosis in acute pelvic pain. A high index of suspicion is essential, particularly in patients with risk factors like hydrosalpinx or adnexal cysts. Ultrasonography, Doppler, and advanced imaging, when necessary, facilitate early diagnosis. Laparoscopy remains the definitive tool, with prompt intervention vital for fertility preservation and complication prevention. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Bilateral frontal oligodendroglioma
clinical_history: A previously healthy 53-year-old female patient presented to the emergency department with an episode of dysarthria followed by a decrease in the level of consciousness, without sphincter involvement. Physical examination upon admission was unremarkable, with no signs of neurological focal deficits.
imaging_findings: Non-enhanced CT shows two hypodense frontal lesions involving the cortex and the subcortical white matter with minimal surrounding oedema (Figure 1). The right lesion presents with a gyriform coarse calcification, and there is no enhancement after intravenous contrast administration (Figure 2). The left lesion produces light bone remodelling. On MRI, the lesions exhibit heterogeneous signal intensity and ill-defined margins, predominantly showing hyperintensity on T2/FLAIR sequences without communication between them through the corpus callosum (Figures 3a and 3b), and areas of hypointensity on susceptibility-weighted imaging consistent with coarse calcifications on the right side and bleeding on the left side (Figures 4a and 4b). There is no significant diffusion restriction (Figures 5a and 5b). Following contrast administration, only minimal linear enhancement is observed on both lesions (Figure 6). A perfusion study was carried out showing an increase in the cerebral blood volume (Figures 7a and 7b), and spectroscopy reveals a decrease in the N-acetylaspartate (N-Ace) peak, no elevation of lactate (LL) and an increased choline (Ch) level (Figures 8a and 8b).
discussion: Background Oligodendrogliomas (OG) rank as the third most prevalent type of glioma, with a higher incidence in adults. These tumours frequently affect the cortical grey matter, with a predilection for the frontal lobes. When a lesion in the frontal lobe crosses the corpus callosum, it can produce a characteristic “butterfly glioma” appearance [1]. Their occurrence in the infratentorial region is uncommon. From a genetic standpoint, OG exhibit distinctive mutations that distinguish them from other gliomas. A key genetic feature is the co-deletion of chromosome arms 1p and 19q, a hallmark alteration that correlates with improved prognosis and enhanced chemotherapy responsiveness. Another essential genetic marker for diagnosing OG is a mutation in either IDH1 or IDH2 [2]. According to the 2021 WHO Classification of CNS tumours, OG are categorised as either grade 2 (low-grade) or grade 3 (previously termed anaplastic OG) [3]. Clinical Perspective The clinical presentation of OG is typically nonspecific, with headaches being a common initial symptom. Seizures are also frequently observed and may be the primary manifestation. Additionally, some patients exhibit focal neurological deficits, which depend on the exact tumour location [2]. Imaging Perspective MRI and CT scans are essential and complementary tools in the initial assessment of OG. On non-contrast CT, OG generally appear hypodense, though variations in density are frequently observed. Coarse calcifications are present in up to 90% of cases, and a cortical gyriform pattern of mineralisation is a distinctive feature suggestive of OG [1]. On MRI, OG tend to have a signal intensity lower than that of grey matter on T1-weighted sequences. In contrast, T2-weighted images show a hyperintense lesion with marked heterogeneity. Although cystic degeneration, haemorrhage, and peritumoural oedema may be present, they are not common findings. Following intravenous contrast administration, OG usually do not exhibit significant enhancement, though in some cases, mild patchy or multifocal enhancement with a dot-like or lacy pattern can be observed [1,4]. Diffusion restriction is not a typical feature of OG; in some instances, facilitated diffusion is observed, appearing as hyperintensity on apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps [4]. MR perfusion imaging does not reliably differentiate OG grades, as some low-grade OG exhibit increased relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV). MR spectroscopy provides insight into regional neurochemical variations and metabolite concentrations, typically revealing moderately elevated choline levels with reduced N-acetylaspartate and no lactate peak. Outcome Treatment of oligodendrogliomas is multifactorial, consisting of surgical, chemotherapy and radiation therapy methods. Each treatment should be approached on a case-by-case basis [1]. In the presented case, after a multidisciplinary team meeting the patient underwent surgery of the two lesions with macroscopic free margins. The histology report confirmed that both tumours were grade-2 oligodendrogliomas with codeletion 1p/19q and mutation of the IDH gene. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Male breast haemangioma: A rare entity
clinical_history: A 58-year-old male, a former smoker with anxiety disorder, presented with a one-year history of a palpable nodule in the right breast. Mammography and ultrasonography revealed a suspicious mass in the right breast and an incidental finding of a small nodule in the left breast.
imaging_findings: Right Breast Mammography of the right breast demonstrated a high-density mass with irregular shape, spiculated margins, and associated nipple retraction in the retroareolar region (Figures 1a and 1b), corresponding to the palpable lesion. Ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic, irregularly shaped lesion with spiculated margins and posterior acoustic shadowing, measuring approximately 29 x 21 mm (Figure 2a). These imaging findings are highly suggestive of malignancy, classified as BI-RADS 5. Left Breast Mammography of the left breast revealed a lobulated nodule of intermediate density in the upper outer quadrant, without calcifications (Figure 1a). On ultrasonography, this lesion appeared oval, hyperechoic, well-circumscribed, with lobulated margins and no posterior acoustic shadowing, measuring 8 mm (Figure 2b), classified as BI-RADS 4a. On the staging CT, the nodule demonstrated avid and homogeneous contrast enhancement, consistent with a benign vascular lesion (Figures 3a and 3b). No axillary lymphadenopathy or distant metastatic disease was observed.
discussion: Background Haemangiomas are rare benign vascular tumours of the breast, extremely uncommon in males, with few reported cases [1,2]. Vascular tumours of the breast are predominantly seen in women, with angiosarcoma accounting for over 65% of cases [1–3]. Haemangiomas consist of dilated vascular channels lined by endothelial cells without atypia [3]. They can be classified into capillary, cavernous, venous, and perilobular types, with cavernous and capillary being the most frequent [3–5]. Despite their benign nature, they must be distinguished from angiosarcomas due to overlapping imaging features [3,4]. Clinical Perspective Male breast nodules often prompt concern for malignancy. Imaging is crucial in evaluating such lesions to differentiate benign from malignant causes. Typically asymptomatic, haemangiomas are often identified as incidental findings or palpable nodules. In this case, the right breast nodule showed malignant features, while the left breast lesion was identified incidentally and demonstrated benign characteristics. Proper imaging and biopsy are key to guiding management and avoiding unnecessary interventions [3,4]. Imaging Perspective On mammography, breast haemangiomas are often seen as well-circumscribed, oval or lobulated masses, similar in density to fibroglandular tissue, occasionally with calcifications [3,5]. On ultrasonography, findings are variable, with haemangiomas presenting as hypoechoic, isoechoic, or hyperechoic lesions, often with smooth or lobulated margins and no posterior acoustic shadowing [6,7]. In this case, the incidental left breast lesion was a hyperechoic, well-circumscribed nodule consistent with a benign vascular lesion. Colour Doppler may reveal vascularity, although benign lesions may also appear hypovascular due to slow flow or thrombosis [8]. Histopathological analysis remains the definitive diagnostic method [1]. Outcome In our case, the imaging features suggested malignancy in the right breast lesion, while the left breast lesion demonstrated characteristics of a benign vascular lesion. Both lesions underwent ultrasound-guided core biopsy, confirming invasive carcinoma (grade 2) in the right breast and haemangioma in the left breast. The malignant lesion in the right breast, confirmed histologically as an invasive carcinoma (T4bN0M0), was treated with surgery and adjuvant therapies. The incidental haemangioma in the left breast required no treatment beyond imaging follow-up, consistent with current recommendations for benign vascular lesions confirmed by biopsy. Debate exists regarding the malignant transformation of haemangiomas to angiosarcomas, with some authors doubting its occurrence [1,2,8]. Imaging follow-up is generally sufficient for benign lesions without clinical suspicion of malignancy [3,4,8]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Breast haemangiomas, though rare, should be considered in the differential diagnosis of male breast lesions, particularly when imaging reveals benign features. Mammographic and US features can help differentiate benign vascular lesions from malignancies. Imaging findings of haemangiomas are often nonspecific, necessitating histopathological analysis for definitive diagnosis. Conservative management with imaging follow-up is often sufficient for confirmed benign haemangiomas.

title: Restrictive allograft syndrome (RAS): A form of chronic lung allograft dysfunction
clinical_history: A 56-year-old male with a bilateral lung transplant for 6 years develops dyspnoea and a decline in lung function. Follow-up high-resolution CT (HRCT) is performed and shows a worsening of pulmonary pathology.
imaging_findings: CT imaging (Figures 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5) shows volume loss of both lungs, bronchiectasis, pleural and subpleural reticulations (predominant in the apices of the upper lobes). These findings are compatible with restrictive allograft syndrome.
discussion: Background Restrictive allograft syndrome (RAS) is a form of chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) characterised by irreversible upper lobe fibrosis and a restrictive physiologic profile, with a significant decline in forced expiratory volume (FEV1) (≤ 80% of baseline) and total lung capacity (TLC) (< 90% of baseline). RAS is associated with a grim prognosis, with median survival significantly lower than that of bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS), respectively 1.5 years and 3 years. RAS has a prevalence of 25–35% of all CLAD over time [1–3]. Clinical Perspective Patients typically present with progressive respiratory symptoms, including dyspnoea and cough, often leading to a decline in pulmonary function. The clinical problem is significant due to the rapid progression and poor prognosis associated with RAS. Imaging is crucial for differentiating RAS from other forms of CLAD and for identifying the extent and pattern of lung involvement [2–4]. Imaging Perspective Key imaging findings in RAS include upper lobe reticulations, ground-glass opacities, and pleural or subpleural fibrosis. HRCT is particularly useful for identifying these features and differentiating RAS from BOS. CT scans are recommended at the onset of CLAD to define the phenotype and as baseline imaging. The final diagnosis is made through a combination of clinical presentation, pulmonary function tests, and imaging findings, often supplemented by biopsy if necessary [1,3–5]. Outcome Therapeutic options for RAS are limited and include immunosuppressive therapy, which is primarily focused on managing symptoms and slowing disease progression. Imaging plays a critical role in therapy planning by helping to monitor disease progression and response to treatment [1,2,4,6]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Restrictive allograft syndrome (RAS) is a severe form of CLAD with distinct imaging and clinical features that necessitate early and accurate diagnosis. Imaging, particularly HRCT, is essential for differentiating RAS from other forms of CLAD and guiding treatment decisions. Understanding the imaging characteristics and clinical implications of RAS can significantly impact patient management and outcomes post-lung transplantation. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Solitary bone plasmacytoma
clinical_history: A 66-year-old man with no significant medical history develops back pain after a running session. After starting physiotherapy, the complaints became acutely worse and did not disappear during the night. No other B-symptoms were present.
imaging_findings: Computer tomography (CT) of the thoracic spine showed a moth-eaten osteolytic aspect of the 7th thoracic vertebral body with a pathological wedge-shaped compression fracture. There is an associated homogeneously enhancing extensive paravertebral and epidural soft tissue component (approximately 56 x 65 x 47 mm) with encasement of the azygos vein. MRI demonstrated diffuse T1 hypointense, STIR hyperintense (compared to the disci) bone marrow infiltration of the 7th vertebral body with paravertebral and epidural mass extension. The mass showed homogeneous contrast enhancement with marked diffusion restriction (ADC value of 710 μm²/sec). A compressive myelopathy developed based on the epidural component. Encasement of the azygos vein is seen, as well as intercostal arteries traversing through the mass without invasion. There were no signs of invasion of the disci or other vertebrae. Additional CT thorax and abdomen, PET-CT, and whole body MRI showed no other lesions or adenopathies.
discussion: Background A plasmacytoma is part of a spectrum of plasma cell dyscrasias, which are mature B-cell malignancies [1,2]. Less than 5% are classified as solitary plasmacytomas. These can be divided into solitary bone plasmacytoma (SBP) or solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma. Both subtypes are more common in men and occur at a median age of 55 years [1,2]. The tumour cells accumulate in a single location by definition, without causing anaemia, hypercalcaemia or renal impairment. When one or more of these complications are present, then the disease has developed into multiple myeloma [3]. On average, progression to multiple myeloma takes 10 years to develop [4]. The lesion usually involves the axial skeleton or flat bones. The distal appendicular skeleton is rarely affected [3]. Clinical Perspective Patients initially often present with pain in the affected region or with a pathological fracture. When the vertebrae are affected, neurological symptoms may be present as well due to spinal cord compression [3]. Imaging Perspective The tumour is osteolytic on classic radiography or CT. The typical appearance is described as a “mini brain”: thickened radially arranged cortical bands resembling cortical sulci. A soft tissue component surrounding the bone can be seen [5]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the most accurate imaging modality to assess the bone marrow involvement. The tumour is homogeneous hypo to isointense on T1WI and hyperintense on T2WI. Bright homogeneous enhancement is seen after intravenous gadolinium contrast [3,5]. The mean apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) value in diffusion weighted imaging lays around 750–770 μm²/sec [6–8]. It is a 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose avid lesion on positron emission tomography. This is particularly useful in treatment response assessment [4]. Homogeneous signal characteristics and encasement of vascular structures instead of invasion helps to differentiate it from metastasis which are usually heterogeneous and invasive [5]. Mean ADC value in metastases is around 1184–1214 μm²/sec, which is significantly higher than in SBP [7,8]. Outcome Recommended therapy is local external radiation therapy up to 50 Gy. Response rates range from 80–90%. The median overall survival is 10 years. The majority of patients will eventually progress to multiple myeloma [4]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Think of solitary bone plasmacytoma (SBP) in a solitary pathological fracture. Homogeneous signals and ADC values can help to differentiate it from metastasis. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Desmoid fibromatosis of the knee
clinical_history: A 54-year-old female patient, with no relevant previous history, presented to the outpatient clinic complaining of a progressively growing swelling at the left popliteal fossa, with associated limited knee flexion and local pain. At clinical examination, a firm and non-mobile swelling was evident at the popliteal region on the left.
imaging_findings: MRI showed a subfascial soft tissue mass mainly composed of tissue isointense to the muscle on T1-weighted (T1) sequences, hyperintense on T2-weighted fat-suppressed (T2FS) sequences and which, after contrast with fat suppression (T1 Gd), showed intense and fast enhancement, as well as “feathery” margins (flame sign). These areas were mixed with areas of very low signal on T1 and T2FS, which did not enhance after contrast (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 2). Some diffusion restriction was seen in the more enhancing areas (Figures 3a and 3b). The extra-articular mass extended into the subcutis, as well as into the muscle bellies of the biceps femoris and medial gastrocnemius. The mass also encased the peroneal nerve (Figure 4), following its trajectory until the level of the fibular head (Figures 5a and 5b). Reactive oedema along the deep fascia of the lower leg was also present.
discussion: Background Desmoid fibromatosis (DF), also known as desmoid-type fibromatosis, aggressive fibromatosis, or desmoid tumour, is a rare type of benign soft tissue tumour of the deep compartments known for infiltrative growth and locally aggressive features. DF most commonly occurs in the extremities, followed by the abdominal wall, retroperitoneum, abdominal cavity and chest wall. It often follows trauma, surgery, or pregnancy and may occur associated with Gardner syndrome [1]. Clinical Perspective DF usually present as a growing, painless, non-mobile mass in the deep compartments. In the limbs, manifestations may include chronic pain, contracture, or decreased range of motion, depending on size and involvement of surrounding structures [1,2]. Imaging Perspective MRI is the best tool to determine DF’s location and extension and to monitor size and signal characteristics during follow-up [2]. These lesions tend to be locally aggressive, extending along fascial planes and displaying feathery, flame-like margins (flame sign). Involvement of neurovascular structures or invasion of other tissues can be present and should be documented [3]. The final diagnosis of DF is made with histopathology, which shows areas of myxoid matrix and cellular stroma interspersed with areas of collagenous tissue, correlating well with the tumour’s appearance on MRI [3,4]. Cellular areas display high T2 signal and intense enhancement after gadolinium contrast, while collagenous areas show hypointensity on all sequences and no enhancement. Highly cellular areas may show diffusion restriction, whereas areas with low cellularity and fibrous content may show higher ADC values [3,5]. The proportion of cellular to collagenous content may vary and can be a sign of tumour vitality, ranging from predominantly cellular lesions (more likely to show progression) to predominantly collagenous lesions with almost no enhancing tissue (less likely to progress) [6]. Outcome Despite its aggressive behaviour, DF is a benign tumour that does not metastasise and may even spontaneously regress [1,7]. As resected lesions tend to locally recur, there has been a shift towards non-surgical options, which can include watchful waiting, treatment with systemic therapy (nirogacestat, tyrosine kinase inhibitors or cytotoxic chemotherapy) or radiation [1,8,9]. Teaching Points Desmoid fibromatosis (DF) is a rare, locally aggressive soft tissue tumour that does not metastasise. MRI is the best method to assess location, size, extension, and to monitor during follow-up. Imaging features follow tumour histology, with cellular areas showing high T2 signal and enhancement, and collagenous areas showing no enhancement and low signal on all sequences. title: Complicated enchondroma managed with curettage and bone grafting
clinical_history: A 65-year-old lady presented with complaints of pain and swelling in the left-hand middle finger following minor trauma. She has been having on-and-off dull aching pain. She sought treatment in a local hospital with buddy strapping. The blood investigation showed mildly elevated CRP (5.8 mg/dl) and ESR (50 mm/hr) but normal serum creatinine, calcium, phosphorus and alkaline phosphatase.
imaging_findings: X-ray showed a well-defined central expansile lytic lesion with scalloped margins involving the base of the 3rd proximal phalanx of the left hand with few specks of calcifications, and pathological fractures involving medial and lateral walls of the 3rd proximal phalanx (Figure 1a). Computed tomography showed similar findings to X-ray (Figure 1b). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the hand showed a well-defined expansile lytic lesion which was T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense, and showed no diffusion restriction with scalloping and fracture involving medial and lateral walls, causing splaying of sagittal bands on both sides (Figures 1c, 1d, 1e, 1f, and 1g).
discussion: Background Enchondromas on the hands are the most common site of the benign cartilaginous tumour, constituting 35% of cases of enchondromas [1]. A retrospective assessment of histology confirming benign tumours of the hand between 1992 and 2015, noted that 76% of the cases were enchondromas, of which 14% of the cases had atypical presentation and 2.2% showed recurrence [4]. The most common areas involved were the proximal phalanx (48%), metacarpals (20%), middle phalanx (17%), and distal phalanx (15%). Clinical Perspective While the majority of the cases are asymptomatic, they may complain of nonspecific complaints that could be missed. Attention to the symptom may be given following trauma, pain or swelling, that may lead to incidental diagnosis on radiologic evaluation. Pathological fractures may be noted in 40–60% of the cases [2]. The role of biopsy is limited in cartilaginous tumours compared to bony tumours due to morphological heterogenicity, sampling error and focal high grade areas; thus radiology has a higher role in evaluation [3]. Imaging Perspective Imaging surveillance of enchondroma may vary based on the location and calcification of the tumour. Enchondromas are usually seen in small tubular bones of the hands and feet. X-ray may show a well-circumscribed lytic lesion with expanded cortex and a narrow zone of transition. Calcification, if present, may present as fine, punctate or arc-like. No periosteal reaction or soft tissue involvement is seen. CT is usually not required for diagnosis; however, it can show a non-aggressive expansile lytic lesion with a narrow zone of transition with or without endosteal scalloping and rings and arcs of calcifications within (which is suggestive of chondroid matrix). MRI shows T1 intermediate to hypointense signal intensity and T2 hyperintense signal with rings and arcs of low signal intensity, which show enhancement after contrast administration. Management There are no recommended guidelines on the management of enchondromas. Asymptomatic enchondromas are followed through regular check-ups. A study on the cost-effectiveness of radiological evaluation of enchondromas noted that since there is a low risk of malignancy and enchondroma growth, patients with asymptomatic stable enchondromas should be reviewed every 6 months [5], thereby limiting the overutilisation of advanced imaging studies. Radiological imaging also plays an important role in the follow-up of these cases for recurrence [6]. Finally, there is a debate regarding the timing of surgical intervention, with Zhou et al. recommending early surgical interventions in pathological fractures in enchondroma for better results [7]. However, a higher rate of complications was noted in early interventions compared to delayed interventions. Outcome The patient was counselled and underwent curettage with cancellous bone grafting and K-wire fixation (Figures 2a and 2b). The curettage bone was sent for histopathological examination. The fragment showed a hypocellular tumour with abundant hyaline cartilage matrix, with tumour cells embedded in lacunar spaces and dispersed evenly with degenerative changes, suggestive of enchondroma. No nuclear atypia or mitotic activity were noted, and adjacent fibroadipose tissue was uninvolved (Figures 3a and 3b). Take Home Message / Teaching Points Enchondroma should be considered as a differential diagnosis in cases with vague finger pain aggravated following trauma, as it is commonly noted as an incidental radiological diagnosis. Early surgical curettage with bone grafting provides a favourable outcome in the management of pathological fractures in enchondroma.
