title: Beyond the mainstream: Understanding the accessory lobe of liver
clinical_history: A 13-year-old male presented with pain in the right hypochondrium and loss of appetite for 1 month. There was no history of fever. The patient has a history of a successfully treated abdominal tuberculosis, for which he had taken anti-tubercular treatment for 1 year.
imaging_findings: An ultrasound was performed, which showed a well-defined round to oval isoechoic lesion in segment IV of the liver, without any significant internal vascularity. A contrast CT scan was further requested, which demonstrated a well-defined round to oval lesion, measuring ~6 x 4.2 x 5.1 cm, well demarcated from the rest of the liver with the same attenuation as that of the normal liver tissue. It was located inferior to segment IV (Figures 1a and 1b) with arterial supply from a branch of the left hepatic artery (Figure 2) and venous drainage into a branch of the middle hepatic vein. It was seen to cause mild dilatation of central and peripheral intrahepatic bile ducts in the left lobe due to compression (Figure 3). The liver was otherwise normal in size with maintained segmental morphology and normal hepatic veins. The left branch of the portal vein was attenuated in calibre; however, it showed normal contrast opacification (Figure 4). Physiological areas of altered attenuation were also noted in the right lobe of the liver.
discussion: Background Accessory liver lobes (ALLs) are anatomical variations of the liver related to excessive development of normal liver parenchyma [1,2]. They either arise as a direct continuation of the liver or are attached to the liver via a stalk [3]. Their genesis is thought to be the result of an error in the development of the endodermal caudal foregut and segmentation of the hepatic bud during the third week of gestation [1,4]. It is believed that the increase in intra-abdominal pressure during intrauterine life, caused by the developing tunica muscularis recti along with simultaneous liver enlargement, leads to the formation of ALLs. Another theory proposes the development of ALL by pull caused by the weight of the intra-abdominal liver on a portion of the developing liver entrapped in the septum transversum [3]. Though congenital, accessory liver lobes have also been reported in the adult population [4,5]. Clinical Perspective ALLs are found both in the paediatric and adult population and are generally asymptomatic and of little clinical significance, with an estimated incidence of 0.5–1% [6,7]. They are often incidentally detected at the time of imaging, laparoscopy or autopsy [4]. There are, however, instances of ALLs being diagnosed in the setting of acute torsion, especially in pedunculated forms, which are then resected surgically [8,9]. Resection is also mandated in the event of development of concurrent focal nodular hyperplasia, adenomas and hepatocellular carcinoma [3,10]. Cases of ALLs simulating a mass in the right upper quadrant and presenting with symptoms of pain, vomiting, constipation, or bloating have also been reported [4,5]. Besides torsion, other complications include traumatic rupture and infarction [3]. Imaging Perspective The diagnosis of an ALL is commonly made on CT scan, where it is seen as a soft tissue attenuation lesion isodense to the liver [3]. However, in cases of doubt or in paediatric patients where radiation dose needs to be minimised, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may be performed using hepatobiliary contrast agents [3]. They may be sessile or pedunculated, the pedicle containing vessels and biliary ducts in the latter [2]. The best-known example is that of a Riedel’s lobe, which represents hypertrophy of segments V and VI of the liver [2]. Another example of an ALL is an elongated left lobe, which is an extension of the left lobe of the liver beyond the stomach [3]. In our case, based on the imaging findings, the differentials included an accessory lobe of liver, an ectopic liver lobe and focal nodular hyperplasia. Since it had the same attenuation and enhancement pattern as that of the normal liver parenchyma, the possibility of focal nodular hyperplasia was ruled out, and since it was in direct continuity with the remaining liver parenchyma, an ectopic lobe was also ruled out, and we arrived at a diagnosis of accessory liver lobe. Outcome Laparoscopy is indicated in cases of pedunculated forms or in the event of complications [5]. Large lobes may also lead to compression of adjacent organs. Rarely, they may also lead to diaphragmatic defects and hepatic dysfunction [3]. Associations with congenital biliary atresia, congenital diaphragmatic defects, and hepatic cavernous haemangiomas have also been reported [3]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Accessory liver lobes (ALLs) are rare morphological variants often detected incidentally on imaging or in the setting of acute complications. Differentiating them from malignancies and predicting the possibilities of complications is essential while evaluating such cases. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Uncommon cause of acute abdomen: Lesser omental infarction
clinical_history: A 65-year-old female presented with a 3-day history of upper abdominal pain and nausea without vomiting, bowel changes, or systemic symptoms. Examination revealed epigastric tenderness without peritoneal signs. Laboratory results showed mild elevated CRP (16 mg/L) and WCC (11.9 x 10⁹/L), with normal liver functions and amylase levels.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed ill-defined fat stranding in the lesser omentum, located near the lesser curvature of the stomach. This fat stranding was not associated with a well-defined mass. The stomach and pancreas appeared normal on imaging, except for a small hiatus hernia identified incidentally. There was no evidence of free intraperitoneal gas, bowel wall thickening, or signs of bowel obstruction. No other abnormalities were observed in the abdominal and pelvic structures, and no additional masses or lesions were noted.
discussion: Background Intraperitoneal focal fat infarction (IFFI) is a self-limiting acute abdominal condition caused by necrosis and inflammation of peritoneal fat due to vascular compromise [1]. The term IFFI encompasses conditions involving infarction or torsion of structures like the greater omentum, lesser omentum, epiploic appendages, or the falciform ligament, which share similar clinical features, imaging findings, treatment strategies, and prognosis [2]. The omentum, divided into greater and lesser sections, is a fold of the peritoneum surrounding the stomach and other abdominal organs. The greater omentum connects the greater curve of the stomach to the transverse colon and is relatively prone to torsion due to its large size and mobility [3]. Omental infarction (OI) arises from either primary or secondary causes. Primary causes are typically linked to vascular events, while secondary causes may result from trauma or surgical interventions [4]. Clinical Perspective OI can present with various clinical manifestations depending on the affected side. For example, greater OI typically presents with acute right iliac fossa pain, as the right section is most affected, while lesser OI often causes epigastric pain, mimicking pancreatitis or peptic ulcer [5,6]. Because the clinical findings may be nonspecific, accurate imaging diagnosis is crucial to avoid unnecessary workups and surgical interventions. Imaging Perspective On ultrasonography, lesser OI appears as a solid, noncompressible, painful hyperechoic mass usually found in the epigastric area between the left hepatic lobe and the stomach, mimicking pancreatic lesions. On CT imaging, the diagnostic gold standard, OI typically presents as fat thickening with surrounding inflammation [7]. Hyperattenuating streaks, often indicative of fibrous bands or dilated thrombosed vessels, are other common findings. The CT provides specific and consistent findings and rules out differential diagnoses safely. Outcome Our patient displayed typical clinical and imaging findings, leading to an accurate diagnosis and successful management with conservative measures, such as simple analgesics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Despite the absence of histopathological confirmation, the diagnosis of lesser OI seems definitive, supported by complete symptom resolution after conservative treatment. Imaging follow-up was not conducted. Take Home Message IFFI is a less recognised but self-limiting cause of acute abdominal pain that can mimic more serious intra-abdominal conditions. Conservative management is typically sufficient and results in complete symptoms resolution, often with no follow-ups required. Accurate diagnosis, via CT imaging, is essential to differentiate IFFI from other surgical emergencies and to avoid unnecessary invasive interventions, as seen in our patient and other case studies [8]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
clinical_history: A 19-year-old woman, recently undergoing ovarian stimulation for oocyte donation, was admitted with a 7-day history of abdominal pain, progressive distention, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea. Her vital signs showed hypotension (88/56 mmHg) and tachycardia (125 bpm). Laboratory analysis revealed haemoconcentration and hypoalbuminemia. Both blood and urine pregnancy tests were negative.
imaging_findings: A plain abdominal X-ray showed an abnormal arrangement of the small bowel loops in the upper abdomen, suggesting the presence of a pelvic mass (Figure 1). Abdominal ultrasound (US) demonstrated bilateral ovarian enlargement with multiple anechoic follicles and a moderate amount of free intraperitoneal fluid (Figures 2a and 2b). Given the laboratory findings of haemoconcentration and hypercoagulability, along with a markedly elevated D-dimer, a thoracoabdominal computed tomography (CT) scan was performed. Contrast-enhanced CT ruled out acute thromboembolic events and confirmed severe bilateral ovarian enlargement (>12 cm) with multiple follicles, which displaced the colon and small bowel loops, as well as the presence of ascites. The CT also showed bilateral pleural effusions (Figures 3a and 3b). The set of imaging, clinical and laboratory findings was compatible with severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS). The patient was subsequently hospitalised for medical treatment and symptom control.
discussion: Background OHSS is an iatrogenic complication of assisted reproductive therapy and a potentially life-threatening emergency. It represents an exaggerated response to ovulation induction or ovarian stimulation, which typically occurs during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle or in early pregnancy, frequently following hormonal treatment with luteinising hormone or human chorionic gonadotropin [1,2]. Pathophysiologically, angiogenic vasoactive substances are secreted by the ovaries, leading to increased capillary permeability and an accumulation of fluid in the extravascular space. The condition is characterised by bilateral ovarian enlargement due to multiple follicular cysts, along with anasarca, including soft tissue oedema, ascites and pleural effusion, and haemoconcentration [2]. The modified Golan classification categorises OHSS into mild (grades 1 and 2), moderate (grade 3) and severe (grades 4 and 5) based on clinical symptoms, imaging, and laboratory findings. Moderate cases are defined by the presence of ascites, while severe cases are characterised by ascites, pleural effusion, and/or an ovarian size greater than 12 cm, as in our case [1]. Clinical Perspective The most common clinical presentation includes rapid weight gain, abdominal distention and pain, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Dehydration can lead to hypovolemia, resulting in hypotension and oliguria. In the most severe cases, thromboembolic events may occur due to haemoconcentration [3]. Imaging Perspective The defining finding of OHSS is consistent across all imaging tests: symmetrical, bilateral enlargement of both ovaries with multiple cystic lesions (enlarged follicles), which may be associated with ascites and pleural effusion [1–3]. Radiologists provide essential information to classify the degree of severity of OHSS by evaluating the presence of ascites, pleural effusion, and ovarian size. Abdominal US is the preferred initial imaging modality. In severe cases, particularly with haemoconcentration and coagulation abnormalities, CT is useful to rule out acute thromboembolic complications. Imaging studies also allow quantifying the degree of ascites, especially in cases that require repeated paracentesis [1]. Outcome Mild OHSS is usually treated with medical observation. In severe cases, the most critically ill patients may present with thromboembolic complications, pericardial effusion, arrhythmias, and anuria, requiring medical treatment, such as anticoagulant therapy, and close monitoring. In some cases, ovarian rupture may occur, requiring oophorectomy via laparotomy. Likewise, massive ascites can lead to abdominal compartment syndrome, necessitating evacuative paracentesis [1]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is a rare and potentially life-threatening complication of assisted reproduction therapies. Radiologists play an essential role in its diagnosis, classification of severity, and monitoring of the course of the disease. It is important to recognise its imaging features and differentiate it from ovarian cystic neoplasms. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Thrombosis of the corpus cavernosum with associated membrane
clinical_history: A 37-year-old male presented with history of two weeks of painful swelling at the base of the penis, radiating towards the left gluteal region; it was not associated with sexual intercourse or erectile loss. On physical examination, swelling was noted at the left base of the penis.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound of the penis shaft with grey scale (Figure 1a) and colour Doppler (Figure 1b) images show an endoluminal echogenic, non-compressible thrombus with increased volume of the left cavernous body associated with absent vascular flow, confirmed with colour Doppler. MRI images show fusiform distension of the proximal portion of the left cavernous body from the penile root, with compression of the contralateral cavernous body. This segment demonstrated mild hyperintensity on T1 (Figure 3), and isointensity with discretely hypointense areas on T2 (Figure 2), without diffusion restriction (Figure 4) nor enhancement after the administration of paramagnetic contrast in the dynamic study (Figure 5). Follow-up imaging after treatment shows resolution of the thrombotic findings. However, a hypointense band on T2 in the left cavernous body persisted (Figure 6), compatible with the presence of a membrane. The location of the membrane corresponded with the side affected by thrombosis.
discussion: Partial thrombosis of the cavernous bodies is a rare condition with an uncertain aetiology. It is more common in young men with coagulation disorders, as well as in patients exposed to repeated microtrauma, such as cyclists and strenuous intercourse, and those with a history of cancer [1–3]. Although the pathogenesis of thrombosis is not completely understood, the presence of a transverse membrane, which acts as a blood flow barrier creating separate venous drainages (the proximal third uses the cavernous and internal pudendal veins, and the distal third uses dorsal veins) has been suggested as a possible triggering factor for thrombosis formation [1,4]. Compression manoeuvres, including microtrauma, harm the proximal drainage, resulting in blood stasis and thrombus formation due to disrupted venous outflow. In our case, a membrane was observed on the same side as the thrombosis, supporting this hypothesis [1,4]. There are other similar case studies that report the presence of membranes and cavernous body thrombosis. Histologically, these membranes consist of fibrous tissue, with either congenital or post-traumatic aetiology [1,3]. The most frequent clinical presentation is a painful perineal mass, which may be associated with erectile dysfunction. The condition is usually unilateral, although bilateral thrombosis cases have been documented [1,2]. The most useful imaging techniques for diagnosis include ultrasound and MRI. Ultrasound is typically the first technique used, allowing visualisation of segmental enlargement of the cavernous body at the perineal level, associated with the absence of Doppler flow. MRI is the technique of choice to confirm the findings, showing an increase in cavernous body size that compresses the contralateral side, with altered signal intensity on T1 and T2 sequences, as well as absence of contrast enhancement in the dynamic study [2]. This clinical and radiological presentation does not constitute a urological surgical emergency, and the treatment is conservative, based on anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy. There is no consensus on the specific anticoagulant treatment, with possible options including low molecular weight heparins, vitamin K antagonists, and antiplatelet agents [2]. Our patient progressed well with anticoagulant treatment, and follow-up MRI after several months showed complete clinical and radiological resolution of the condition. However, the membrane persisted on the follow-up images, suggesting it might have been a triggering factor for the thrombosis.

final_diagnosis: Partial segmental thrombosis of the cavernous body

title: Parosteal lipoma of the right iliac wing
clinical_history: Incidental finding in the right iliac bone of a 68-year-old male patient with lung cancer who was undergoing a routine follow-up.
imaging_findings: The patient had lung cancer, and during a follow-up oncology CT scan, we incidentally discovered a painless mass in his right pelvic wing. CT of the pelvis shows a well-defined lesion in the right pelvis protruding into the iliac muscle with dense calcifications and a rim of fatty tissue that confirms its lipomatous nature (Figures 1a and 1b). On bone window, the calcified nature of the lesion can be clearly seen as an excrescence from the right iliac wing, causing a mild periosteal reaction on the adjacent bone cortex (Figure 2). The scout view of the CT is also helpful in observing the lesion, its close relation to the right iliac wing, with clumped calcifications and fatty tissue in the periphery (Figure 3).
discussion: Parosteal lipomas are rare benign adipose tumours, accounting for 0.3% of all lipomas [1] and are closely associated with the periosteum. While MRI is valuable for evaluating soft tissue characteristics and assessing neurovascular involvement, CT imaging plays a critical role in identifying bone-related changes and confirming the presence of adipose tissue, which is key to the diagnosis of parosteal lipoma. On CT, parosteal lipomas typically appear as well-circumscribed masses with fat attenuation values between -50 and -150 Hounsfield units. These fat-density lesions are distinguishable from the surrounding soft tissue, making CT an important tool in identifying the lipomatous nature of the mass [1]. Parosteal lipomas are intimately attached to the periosteum of the bone, and CT may show bone remodelling such as cortical thickening, scalloping or periosteal reaction. These changes are typically due to chronic pressure from the tumour rather than invasive growth, which helps to differentiate them from malignant lesions [2]. CT also shows internal calcifications or ossifications within the tumour, especially near the bone interface. These findings are important in differentiating parosteal lipoma from other soft tissue tumours. Bony changes may include exostosis (bony outgrowth) or hypertrophic bone formation at the site of attachment [3,4]. CT is effective in visualising the relationship of the mass to adjacent structures, including neurovascular bundles and joints. This is essential for preoperative planning, especially in cases where the lipoma may be compressing surrounding tissues [5]. The main differential diagnoses include osteochondroma, liposarcoma, and Nora lesion (bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation, or BPOP). Imaging, particularly MRI and CT, is crucial for their differentiation [4]. Osteochondroma typically presents as a bone outgrowth with a continuous marrow and cortical connection to the underlying bone, often with a cartilaginous cap seen on MRI. Liposarcoma, particularly well-differentiated types, can mimic parosteal lipoma, but often demonstrates thicker septations, nodular enhancement, and less defined fat content on MRI. Nora lesions are aggressive-appearing, heterotopic bone formations with an irregular bone-cartilage-fibrous tissue mixture, typically without marrow continuity, distinguishing them from osteochondromas. In summary, parosteal lipomas appear on CT as well-defined fat masses in close association with the periosteum. Secondary bone changes such as cortical thickening, calcifications or ossifications can be seen on CT and, if MRI is available, together they can provide a comprehensive diagnostic approach.
differential_diagnosis: Parosteal lipoma Osteochondroma Liposarcoma Nora lesion / Bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation (BPOP)

title: Laryngeal metastasis of lung adenocarcinoma
clinical_history: An 82-year-old woman presented with a left anterior cervical mass. Physical examination showed a firm lump in the anterior cervical space. Relevant medical history included adenocarcinoma of the lung diagnosed two years prior to the present episode, treated with surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy, hysterectomy for uterine fibroids and hypercholesterolemia.
imaging_findings: Neck ultrasound with colour Doppler showed an ill-defined lesion involving the left lamina of the thyroid cartilage with some peripheral vascularisation (Figure 1). Further evaluation by neck CT depicted an expansive solid lesion arising from the left lamina of the thyroid cartilage, containing calcified components (Figure 2) and a necrotic core (Figure 3). The lesion showed extralaryngeal extension to the extrinsic (sternohyoid and thyrohyoid) muscles of the larynx. There was also enlargement of the left cricothyroid space and obliteration of the paraglottic fat. Lesion characterisation by ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology revealed epithelioid cells with cytological atypia, isolated and in small aggregates. These cells expressed AE1/AE3 and TTF1, compatible with the clinical hypothesis of metastasis from a primary lung neoplasm. The patient subsequently underwent a head CT, which showed no evidence of central nervous system spread; and an 18F-FDG PET/CT for restaging, which revealed disease progression to the lung parenchyma, pleura and bone.
discussion: Adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer [1]. It is also the leading cause of cancer-related death in the European Union [2]. Metastasis to the larynx is uncommon [3] and can occur via haematogenous or lymphatic spread [4], the latter through retrograde lymphatic drainage from the thoracic duct. Clinical presentation may range from hoarseness, dysphagia, and dysphonia to the patient being asymptomatic [4,5]. Laryngoscopy is essential for mucosal inspection. A tissue biopsy is often required to confirm the diagnosis, with histological examination revealing the characteristic glandular structures of lung adenocarcinoma, including mucin-producing cells. CT or MRI of the neck assists in evaluating the laryngeal lesion and surrounding tissues. In the case of a mucosal bulge with normal overlying mucosa, submucosal lesions should be considered in the differential diagnosis. Those centred at the laryngeal cartilages include primary cartilaginous and bone tumours and metastases. In our case, the hypothesis of chondrosarcoma of the larynx was deemed less likely, as calcifications, when present, tend to show a ring-like or “popcorn” pattern (chondroid matrix) [6] and approximately two-thirds of laryngeal chondrosarcomas originate in the cricoid cartilage [7,8]. The hypothesis of primary squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx was considered unlikely, given that the lesion was centred to the cartilage with no evidence of mucosal changes, both on endoscopy and imaging. Locally advanced squamous cell carcinomas of the larynx may cause thyroid cartilage invasion and extralaryngeal spread, but usually do not cause cartilage expansion. Management of laryngeal metastasis from lung adenocarcinoma depends on the overall stage of the disease, the patient’s general health, and the response of the primary tumour to treatment. Treatment options include systemic therapy, radiation therapy, and surgical resection [5]. Prognosis is heavily dependent on the extent of metastatic spread, the response to systemic therapy, and the patient’s overall performance status. Laryngeal metastasis from lung adenocarcinoma, although rare, is significant due to its potential impact on patient management. Early recognition through clinical evaluation and appropriate imaging is crucial for distinguishing this condition from other laryngeal disorders. Treatment must be tailored to the individual patient. In our case of an older patient, showing multi-metastatic disease, and no evidence of dyspnoea or respiratory insufficiency, it was decided to initiate treatment with osimertinib. Clinically, the hoarseness and cervical mass have been improving, and a 4-month follow-up CT scan is scheduled to evaluate treatment response.
differential_diagnosis: Laryngeal metastasis of lung adenocarcinoma Laryngeal chondrosarcoma Squamous cell carcinoma

title: Meconium periorchitis
clinical_history: Patient, 2 days old, born at 39 weeks of gestation from a controlled and uneventful pregnancy. At birth, notable observations included the violaceous discolouration of the scrotal skin, bilateral scrotal swelling, and difficulty in locating the testes in the scrotal sacs and inguinal canals (Figure 1).
imaging_findings: In the postnatal testicular ultrasound (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d), both scrotal sacs were occupied by heterogeneously echogenic lesions with poorly defined borders and multiple internal calcifications. These were not considered masses due to the unclear borders. Moderate increased vascularisation was noted on Doppler study. The abdominal ultrasound showed no calcifications, cysts, or free fluid. The testes and epididymides were difficult to visualise but appeared morphologically normal in the upper poles of both scrotal sacs. To complete the study, a simple X-ray of the abdomen and scrotum was performed, revealing multiple coarse, diffuse, bilateral intrascrotal calcifications, with no intra-abdominal abnormalities observed (Figure 2). MRI (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c) identified solid lesions occupying both scrotal sacs, hyperintense on T2 sequences with hypointense microcalcifications on T2. Both testes were of normal size and morphology and located within the scrotal sacs. No inguinal hernias were identified.
discussion: Background Meconium periorchitis consists of a sterile chemical inflammatory reaction and subsequent calcification of the peritesticular tissue, due to the passage of meconium into the scrotal bag, through the vaginal process [1]. It occurs after intestinal perforation during foetal life [2]. It is generally a benign, self-limiting process. Knowledge and clinical suspicion of this entity are essential, as they avoid possible unnecessary orchiectomies [3]. To date, fewer than 100 cases have been described in the available global literature [5–8]. Clinical Perspective Meconium periorchitis was first described ultrasonographically by Wax et al. in 2007. Its clinical presentation consists of a characteristic “triad”: a scrotal mass with internal calcifications, the appearance of hydrocele, usually bilateral, and the absence of vascularisation on colour Doppler study [4]. The fluid is reabsorbed, and the residual calcifications do not alter the testicular parenchyma. The absence of vascularisation on colour Doppler study was not detected in our patient, in whom increased Doppler vascularisation was observed, which is explained by the fact that sterile meconium in the scrotum induces a local inflammatory response [5]. Imaging Perspective Diagnosis has been made using simple radiography and/or ultrasound. However, we have not found references to the use of MRI in the literature. In our case, MRI was very useful as the main differential diagnosis in question was bilateral testicular tumour, and MRI helped determine that it was meconium periorchitis. Therefore, we suggest using MRI in cases of diagnostic uncertainty to reach a final diagnosis. The MRI provided critical diagnostic clarity, confirming the condition as meconium periorchitis rather than a bilateral testicular tumour. Outcome In our case, the paediatric surgery service at our hospital decided on a conservative management approach, and we do not have histological confirmation. An ultrasound was done weeks later, showing a spontaneous improvement of the testicular mass (Figures 5a and 5b). All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Imaging features in connective tissue disorder-associated usual interstitial pneumonia
clinical_history: A 68-year-old former smoker with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hypothyroidism consulted for progressive exertional dyspnoea. Pulmonary function tests showed a restrictive pattern and reduced diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO).
imaging_findings: High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest with axial (Figures 1a and 1b), coronal (Figure 1c), and sagittal (Figure 1d) reconstructions demonstrated findings consistent with an interstitial lung disease. Bilateral involvement with a clear apicobasal gradient with extensive subpleural reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, and predominant honeycombing in the lower lobes was observed. Exuberant honeycombing was present, involving nearly the entire fibrotic pulmonary parenchyma (Figure 1b). A sharp and abrupt transition between normal and fibrotic lung parenchyma was noted in the craniocaudal direction (arrows in Figures 1c and 1d). The small areas of fibrosis of the upper lobes were limited to the anterior segments (arrowheads in Figures 1a and 1d). No evidence of superimposed infection or ground-glass opacities was revealed. No suspicious pulmonary nodules, masses, or mediastinal lymphadenopathy were identified. Mild dilation of the pulmonary arteries and a cardiac pacemaker were noted. No pleural or pericardial effusion was present.
discussion: Background The radiological pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) may have an unknown cause in cases of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) or can be secondary to systemic connective tissue disorders (CTD) [1,2]. Clinical Perspective In patients with UIP, it is important to differentiate those secondary to CTD from those with IPF. This distinction is of significant prognostic and therapeutic value, as secondary pulmonary involvement may benefit from treatment of the systemic disease to attempt to prevent progression [1–3]. Imaging Perspective There are findings in chest CT studies that can help distinguish cases of UIP in IPF from those of UIP associated with CTD. Exuberant honeycombing refers to the presence of honeycombing in more than 70% of the lung parenchyma with fibrosis. The “straight edge” sign is defined as a narrow and abrupt transition zone between normal pulmonary parenchyma and fibrotic parenchyma in the craniocaudal direction. The “anterior upper lobe” sign is described when fibrotic involvement of the upper lobes is concentrated and limited to their anterior segments, associated with more extensive fibrosis in the bases [3,4]. Outcome Exuberant honeycombing, the “straight edge” sign, and the “anterior upper lobe” sign are more frequently observed in patients with CTD compared to patients with IPF, with the “straight edge” sign being the most specific of the three [3]. Teaching Points The presence of any of the three signs described, or their combination, on a chest CT with a UIP pattern should suggest the possibility of a CTD as the cause of the pulmonary injury and recommend a comprehensive rheumatological evaluation [2,3]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: The enigma of heterotopic bone formation
clinical_history: A 13-year-old male child presented with an acute onset of pain and swelling in the right side of the anterior chest region for 3 weeks. No history of trauma or any other complaints were reported. The initial work-up showed normal blood parameters. The patient underwent computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thorax for evaluation.
imaging_findings: On CT (Figures 1a and 1b), the right pectoralis muscles appear bulky with soft tissue lesion having peripheral ossifications with sparing of the centre. The underlying bone appears normal. No features of invasion of the adjacent structures are noted. On MRI (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, 2d, and 2e), the right pectoralis major muscle appears bulky with diffuse inflammation, oedema and postcontrast enhancement. A focal, ill-defined, slightly lobulated, T2/IR (inversion recovery) heterointense intramuscular soft tissue mass lesion with heterogeneous enhancement is seen in the lateral part of right pectoralis major muscle, measuring about 5.5 x 4.5 x 4 cm (CC x TR x AP). Peripheral nodular and curvilinear T2 hypointensities with blooming in gradient images are seen in the lesion. Based on these imaging features, the possibility of myositis ossificans was given.
discussion: Background Myositis ossificans (MO), also known as heterotopic bone formation, is a pseudo-inflammatory condition originating from skeletal muscle, characterised by metaplastic, non-malignant bone tumour formation. MO typically follows trauma, often affecting large muscles in the lower limbs. Non-traumatic cases present diagnostic challenges, leading to misdiagnosis in many patients without a trauma history. MO progresses through three phases, i.e., early (<4 weeks), intermediate (4–8 weeks), and mature (>8 weeks), displaying the “zone phenomenon” with ossifications that are peripheral and centripetal [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Patients often experience prolonged muscle pain, paraesthesias, and weakness due to mechanical irritation from the ossification process. Symptoms improve as lesions mature, with few or no symptoms later [1,3]. Imaging Perspective Radiography is limited in the evaluation of MO, especially in areas with complex anatomy such as the chest wall or spine. CT is excellent for assessing mineralisation and osseous involvement [1,3,4]. The imaging and clinical findings of MO vary depending on the stage of development. During the early phase, MO displays non-specific MRI features, appearing isointense to muscle on T1, hyperintense on T2/STIR sequences, and enhancing following contrast administration. In the intermediate stage, predominantly peripheral calcifications of varying thickness appear, which are coarse, flocculent, or scattered central calcifications. A rim of low signal intensity on the edge suggests calcification, and central low signal foci (soft tissue) are observed in all MR imaging sequences. Enhanced MR images show variable enhancement patterns with reduced surrounding oedema. As the lesion advances, it calcifies from the outer edge inward, a process known as the “zone phenomenon” [3,5]. During the mature stage, MRI reveals a clearly defined, densely calcified lesion displaying low signal intensity and lacking surrounding oedema. Key imaging features of MO include the absence of adjacent tissue invasion and the retention of viable muscle fibres within the lesion, which are typically affected in tumour cases [1,3,5]. In the early phase, differentiating MO from soft-tissue sarcoma is challenging due to overlapping imaging features. However, in the mature stage, diagnosis becomes clearer, characterised by a peripheral rim of calcification. MO may exhibit a striated appearance on T2 and STIR sequences, along with perilesional muscle oedema, features that are generally not observed in sarcomas. A comprehensive medical history, including details of trauma or prolonged immobilisation, is essential for accurate diagnosis [6]. Outcome Treatment for MO is challenging due to its multistep progression, and many cases need no intervention. For symptomatic patients experiencing mild pain or those unsuitable for surgery, conservative management with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs is recommended. Surgical resection is considered if MO persists [1]. Teaching Points Myositis ossificans (MO) manifests as painful muscle swelling, progressing through early, intermediate, and mature phases over 8+ weeks. Diagnosis relies on trauma history, clinical symptoms, and imaging findings depicting the “zone phenomenon”. While often trauma-related, MO can occur spontaneously and may initially mimic malignancy.

title: Cerebral microbleeds in a critically ill patient
clinical_history: A 47-year-old woman with ultra-refractory stenosing ileocolic Crohn’s disease, multiple treatment failures, and prior intestinal resections was readmitted with a disease flare. She deteriorated, requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission, where she developed sepsis, respiratory failure with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and encephalopathy.
imaging_findings: A computed tomography (CT) scan performed on admission revealed an expansive intraparenchymal lesion in the knee of the corpus callosum, with poorly defined margins and a heterogeneous appearance, with areas of high density suggesting intralesional haemorrhage (Figure 1a). Moderate adjacent vasogenic oedema was noted, with no enhancement after intravenous contrast administration (Figure 1b), raising the possibility of an intraparenchymal haematoma. A brain MRI confirmed the lesion, which appeared hyperintense on both T1 and T2/FLAIR sequences (Figures 2 and 3), with diffusion restriction and marked hypointensity on the SWI sequence, indicative of haemosiderin remnants. No intralesional enhancement was observed. Additionally, the SWAN sequence demonstrated numerous foci of chronic microbleeds in the juxtacortical white matter (Figure 5a), corpus callosum (Figure 5b), internal capsules (Figure 5c), pons, and both middle cerebellar peduncles (Figure 5d). Diffuse hyperintensity was also observed on T2/FLAIR, relatively symmetric in the bilateral frontoparietal white matter, without diffusion restriction or underlying pathological enhancement, suggestive of a probable post-hypoxic leukoencephalopathy component (Figure 4).
discussion: Cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) or microhaemorrhages are increasingly detected due to the widespread use of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). They appear as hypointense foci on T2*-weighted sequences or susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) and consist of haemosiderin deposits. CMBs are common in normal ageing and various conditions, including Alzheimer’s disease, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, hypertensive encephalopathy, diffuse axonal injury, and others [1,2]. The distribution of microhaemorrhages will help us interpret the findings and associate them with specific pathologies. It is well known that microhaemorrhages in the basal ganglia and thalamus are associated with chronic hypertensive encephalopathy, while lobar corticosubcortical microhaemorrhages, predominantly in the parieto-occipital regions, are linked to cerebral amyloid angiopathy [1]. Recent studies have highlighted the presence of cerebral microbleeds in critically ill patients, exhibiting a distinctive distribution pattern. This pattern shows extensive microbleeds, diffusely involving the juxtacortical white matter and corpus callosum but sparing the cortex, deep and periventricular white matter, basal ganglia, and thalami [1,3]. The involvement of the internal and external capsules, middle cerebellar peduncles, and brainstem has been reported and is also observed in our case [1]. The exact mechanism underlying their development remains unknown; however, it has been hypothesised that they may result from subacute microvascular inflammatory processes, pyogenic vasculitis, endothelial dysfunction and/or microemboli [2]. Common factors in these patient populations include the presence of respiratory failure or sepsis, possibly causing hypoxemia-induced microangiopathy or sepsis-related coagulopathy [3]. Cerebral microbleeds have been correlated with the severity of the patient’s condition and are associated with an increased risk of both ischemic and haemorrhagic stroke [2]. During hospitalisation, the patient in our case experienced neurological deterioration, progressing to a vegetative state. Imaging studies revealed not only characteristic microbleeds associated with critical illness but also an intraparenchymal haemorrhage centred in the genu of the corpus callosum. Subsequently, after improvement of the underlying conditions that led to this severe state, the patient showed significant neurological recovery, regaining consciousness and cooperation. She was eventually discharged in stable condition.
differential_diagnosis: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy Chronic hypertensive encephalopathy Central nervous system vasculitis Cerebral microbleeds in a critically ill patient Cerebral fat embolism Diffuse axonal injury

title: Overshunting-associated myelopathy
clinical_history: A young male presents with ataxic gait, numbness in lower limbs, and difficulty in standing and walking. To evaluate further, MR brain and MR spine screening was done, which suggests compensated hydrocephalus. Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting was done to treat this. After VP shunting, he presents with headache, with symmetrical weakness in the upper limbs and lower limbs.
imaging_findings: Pre-shunt There is prominence of the midline cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) space in between the lower parts of the bilateral cerebellar hemispheres inferior to the vermis, displacing the vermis mildly upward and the communication to the 4th ventricle—this may represent a Blake’s pouch cyst, an incidental finding as seen in Figure 1. There is moderate dilatation of both supra and infratentorial ventricular systems without obvious periventricular ooze, i.e., the possibility of compensated hydrocephalus as seen in Figure 3. There is evidence of engorgement of the epidural venous plexus causing mass effect over the cord, as seen in Figures 4a and 4b. Post-shunting There is evidence of enlargement of the ventral epidural space showing enhancement in the cervical spine and proximal dorsal spine up to the D2 level, with extension cranially till the foramen magnum with prominent flow voids, likely engorged epidural veins within it, causing cord compression as seen in Figure 5. There is evidence of an enlarged pituitary gland (mid sagittal height of 12.7 mm) as seen in Figure 6. There is evidence of a round dural venous sinus as seen in Figure 7. Given these findings, the possibility of excessive CSF diversion needs consideration.
discussion: Background Overshunting-associated myelopathy (OSAM) is an infrequent complication of ventricular shunt placement. It is caused by intracranial hypotension and compensatory engorgement of the epidural venous plexus secondary to CSF shunting [1]. Its pathophysiology is explained by the Monro–Kellie hypothesis. The Monro–Kellie hypothesis suggests that the sum of the total volume of brain, cerebrospinal fluid and intracranial blood is constant [2]. Hence, the levels of all fluids (CSF and blood) are expected to be stable and compensatory increase intracranial venous blood volume for CSF depletion, the blood directly flows into the valveless plexiform venous network [3,4]. In our case, the patient underwent shunt ligation and subsequently, symptoms improved. Clinical Perspective Common symptoms of CSF overdrainage include headache, nausea, vomiting, weakness in bilateral upper limbs and lower limbs, neck pain radiating to the head and arms, sensory loss, and postural headache. To identify this issue as soon as possible and to offer appropriate and prompt care [4–7]. Imaging Perspective Brain MR findings associated with intracranial hypotension show diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement and venous engorgement of the spinal cord venous plexus. There may be compression of cervical nerve roots [4]. Outcome Chronic CSF overdrainage can lead to cervical myelopathy due to spinal cord compression by dilated vertebral veins/epidural venous plexus [8]. Awareness of this reversible condition can prevent unnecessary treatment delays and improve outcomes significantly. Take Home Message / Teaching Points A high index of suspicion is necessary for the diagnosis of overshunting-associated myelopathy since patients may mistakenly seek out or be referred to an orthopaedic, delaying the onset of treatment. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Epipericardial fat necrosis: An unusual cause of acute chest pain
clinical_history: A 35-year-old man, non-smoker, presented to the emergency department of our institution with a three-day history of left pleuritic chest pain, exacerbated by deep breathing and accompanied by diaphoresis and nausea. The laboratory findings and electrocardiogram (ECG) were normal, and his past medical history was unremarkable.
imaging_findings: On chest radiographs (Figures 1a and 1b), a small ill-defined opacity was perceived in left anterior juxtacardiac topography, associated with a small left-sided pleural effusion. A thoracic computed tomography (CT) was acquired for better characterisation (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d) and showed an encapsulated ovoid fatty lesion in the left anterior mediastinum with surrounding soft tissue stranding. The left-sided pleural effusion was confirmed, and a small-volume pericardial effusion was also perceived.
discussion: Background Epipericardial fat necrosis (EFN) is a rare, self-limiting, benign inflammatory condition first described in 1957 by Jackson et al. [1]. Although its aetiology and pathophysiology are not yet completely understood, it shares pathologic features with fat necroses found in other locations, such as in epiploic appendagitis and omental infarction [2]. The main hypotheses include ischemia from spontaneous torsion of the vascular pedicle or capillary rupture with haemorrhagic necrosis due to increased intrathoracic pressure related to the Valsalva manoeuvre [3,4]. Clinical Perspective EFN usually presents as a new-onset acute chest pain in otherwise young healthy patients [5]. The pain is typically pleuritic, left-sided, moderate to severe, and may be exacerbated by deep breathing and coughing, thus resembling other urgent conditions such as pulmonary embolism, acute aortic or coronary syndromes, or acute pericarditis [6,7]. Physical examination is often unremarkable, but tachycardia, diaphoresis and pericardial friction rub may be present [7,8]. Laboratory tests and ECG are usually normal [8]. As clinical and laboratory findings are nonspecific, imaging studies are crucial for the diagnosis. Imaging Perspective Chest radiograph may be normal in the first 48–72 hours, after which a paracardial opacity ipsilateral to the chest pain, may be present [8]. On CT, the preferred modality for diagnosis, EFN appears as a well-defined, oval-shaped fatty lesion anterior to the pericardium with surrounding inflammatory changes, such as soft-tissue stranding and thickening of the adjacent pericardium, findings resembling epiploic appendagitis [3]. Pleural and pericardial effusion may occur [9]. Although not usually necessary for the diagnosis, similar findings can be found on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), with the lesion showing high signal intensity on T2-weighted images and a slight peripheral rim of gadolinium enhancement, characteristic of an active disease [10]. Differential diagnoses should include other fat-containing mediastinal lesions, such as pericardial lipoma, pericardial liposarcoma, thymolipoma, and diaphragmatic hernias [5]. Pericardial lipomas present as well-defined, homogeneous fat-attenuation masses, while thymolipomas are typically large, asymptomatic, and contain interspersed soft-tissue components. Pericardial liposarcomas, though rare, may exhibit heterogeneous soft-tissue elements and invasion of adjacent structures [11]. The presence of pericardial thickening, inflammatory stranding, and acute chest pain favours EFN over these entities. Outcome Conservative treatment with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs is the mainstay of management, as this condition is self-limiting. A follow-up chest CT scan is recommended in 4 to 8 weeks to confirm resolution and definitively exclude malignancy [8,12]. In our case, the patient was re-evaluated in an internal medicine consultation 3 months after the initial emergency department admission, where complete resolution of symptoms was confirmed. Given the absence of any persistent or recurrent complaints, follow-up imaging was not requested. Teaching Points EFN is a rare, still underdiagnosed benign cause of acute chest pain, often mimicking more serious cardiac or pulmonary pathologies. Although its symptoms can be concerning, the condition is self-limiting and typically requires only conservative management. Accurate diagnosis relies heavily on recognising specific radiological findings, underscoring the importance of radiologists being aware of this entity and its subtle imaging features, to prevent misdiagnosis and unnecessary interventions. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Gastrosplenic fistula: A rare complication of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
clinical_history: A 65-year-old male presents with septic shock and acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Past medical history is significant for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (diagnosed September 2024), hypertension, type 2 diabetes, aortic ectasia, hepatitis C, cirrhosis, and a left pleural effusion.
imaging_findings: A non-contrast CT with oral contrast (due to impaired kidney function) was performed and demonstrated a necrotic mass with gas foci in the region of the spleen with high-density material in the dependent portion of the mass (Figure 1). There is also a large defect in the gastric wall near the junction of the body and fundus, with the tip of the indwelling enteric tube exiting the gastric lumen into the splenic abscess. On 3D reconstruction, the feeding tube is noted to pass through the defect into the abscess (Figure 2). The feeding tube is seen through a fistula with extraluminal contrast on abdominal radiograph (Figure 3). CT with intravenous (IV) contrast (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c) shows irregular gastric fundus thickening with a large heterogenous mass extending into the spleen, and there is extensive retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy involving the left psoas muscle. PET-CT (Figures 5a and 5b) shows an intensely hypermetabolic necrotic mass with central gas and fluid collection in the splenic fossa with intense peripheral hypermetabolism to max SUV 25.5 and extensive intensely hypermetabolic retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.
discussion: Background Gastrosplenic fistula (GSF) is a rare pathological connection between the stomach and the spleen, most often caused by splenic or gastric lymphoma [1]. Other causes of GSF include gastric adenocarcinoma, splenic abscesses, peptic ulcers, post-gastric sleeve resection, and post-chemotherapy treatment. While the pathophysiology is not completely understood, the leading theory suggests that a GSF may develop following rapid necrosis of lymphoma cells in the gastric wall and splenic capsule following chemotherapy or occurring spontaneously [2]. Clinical Perspective GSF often presents as nonspecific left upper quadrant abdominal pain [3]. Other symptoms may include constitutional symptoms or an upper gastrointestinal bleed, though it may also present asymptomatically [1,4]. The nonspecific symptoms at presentation, along with its rarity, make diagnosis challenging, with delays potentially leading to fatal complications such as catastrophic gastrointestinal bleeding or diaphragm involvement [2,5]. As clinical findings alone are insufficient to diagnose GSF, CT imaging is used to help aid diagnosis, evaluate underlying pathologies, including lymphoma, and identify potential complications such as abscesses and bleeding [5]. Imaging Perspective Endoscopies are often used initially to evaluate causes for upper gastrointestinal bleed and may demonstrate an ulcer in the fundus or greater curvature of the stomach [3,5]. Endoscopy can be beneficial to confirm the presence of GSF, but should be used in addition to CT. CT with contrast is the imaging modality of choice as it can generally identify a fistulous tract between the stomach and spleen [6]. Another supporting finding on CT is air in the spleen, although this finding may also occur in a splenic abscess. In addition, CT may be used to identify complications of GSF as well as evaluate the extent of lymphoma involvement [5,6]. Outcome Pathology results from core biopsy sections were consistent with a large B-cell lymphoma of germinal centre type, with atypical cells positive for PAX-5, CD20, BCL-6, and BCL-2. Management of GSF depends on the underlying cause and involves a multi-disciplinary approach. Chemotherapy is used for management of underlying lymphoma, and most cases typically involve resection of the spleen and stomach [2,3]. CT is used to determine the extent of GSF involvement and guide surgical intervention. Prognosis is variable, but patients who are unable to have surgery tend to have poor outcomes. A massive upper gastrointestinal bleed is a feared complication of GSF [7]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Gastrosplenic fistula (GSF) is a rare and potentially fatal complication to look out for in patients with a gastric or splenic lymphoma. A CT showing air in the spleen or a fistulous tract between the stomach and spleen may be suspicious for a GSF. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Testicular torsion in the setting of bell-clapper deformity
clinical_history: A 12-year-old boy presented to the emergency department two hours after the onset of acute and intense left testicular pain. On physical examination, the left testicle was slightly oedematous and markedly painful to palpation. Given these findings, a scrotal ultrasound was requested.
imaging_findings: The scrotal ultrasound revealed both testicles in the scrotal sac, with normal dimensions, morphology and echotexture (Figure 1). Above the left testicle, in the scrotal sac, there was a small nodule clinically visible, palpable and intensely painful on ultrasound evaluation. On ultrasound, this nodule revealed to be a twist of the left spermatic cord—the whirlpool sign (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). A hydrocele surrounding the left testicle and the distal segment of the homolateral spermatic cord was also observed (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). The colour Doppler signal was preserved bilaterally; however, the left testicle presented a tardus-parvus waveform on spectral Doppler imaging (Figures 3a and 3b). Based on these findings, the diagnosis of partial torsion of the left testicle in the setting of bell-clapper deformity was suggested.
discussion: Bell-clapper deformity results from a congenital anomaly of the tunica vaginalis, which, instead of attaching to the posterolateral aspect of the testicles, attaches higher to the spermatic cord, enveloping the testis, epididymis and distal spermatic cord, allowing the testicle to rotate freely within the scrotum and predisposing it to torsion [1–3]. Patients with bell-clapper deformity are typically asymptomatic until torsion occurs. Testicular torsion presents with acute onset of severe scrotal pain and swelling, often accompanied by nausea and vomiting. The testicle may have a higher and horizontal position, and the cremasteric reflex may be absent [2–8]. Bell-clapper deformity may present with an atypical horizontal/oblique testicular position, a redundant spermatic cord segment in the scrotal sac, an incomplete epididymal attachment to the testicle, or a hydrocele completely encircling the testicle, epididymis and distal spermatic cord [1]. In the early stages of torsion, the testicle may have a normal echotexture, denoting viability. As the torsion persists, it becomes enlarged and hypoechoic due to oedema. Without prompt treatment, the ischemia progresses, and the testicle may infarct and develop haemorrhage and necrosis, presenting with a heterogeneous echotexture [2,3,7–9]. Doppler ultrasonography is the imaging modality of choice, providing real-time assessment of scrotal structures and blood flow. Doppler imaging demonstrates perfusion changes even in the early stages of testicular torsion. Colour Doppler can show reduced/absent arterial and venous flow (complete torsion) or compromise only of the venous flow (partial torsion). In early or partial torsion in progression, spectral Doppler may demonstrate reversed/absent diastolic flow, increased resistive index, and then tardus-parvus or monophasic waveforms, while the colour Doppler signal is still patent. Power Doppler has higher sensitivity to detect slow blood flow when the colour Doppler signal is absent [2,5,8,10–15]. The whirlpool sign of the twisted spermatic cord is a key feature, confirming the diagnosis even if the testicle has a normal grayscale appearance and the testicular blood flow is preserved [2,8,12–14]. Secondary findings such as thickening of scrotal skin and hydrocele may be present [8,9]. Immediate surgical intervention is required to untwist the spermatic cord and restore blood flow. The best outcomes occur when surgery is performed within six hours of symptom onset [2,10,16]. If the testicle is viable, an orchiopexy is performed to prevent torsion recurrence. Given the high likelihood of the bell-clapper deformity being bilateral [3,12], prophylactic orchiopexy of the contralateral testicle is recommended. Cases of testicular infarction require orchiectomy. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Trochlear dysplasia – A developmental cause of patellar instability
clinical_history: A 45-year-old female patient was referred to the radiology department in view of a history of recurrent patellar dislocation and knee joint pain aggravated for the last 20 days. No history of trauma.
imaging_findings: The trochlear groove appears shallow with a sulcal angle measuring 165 degrees (>150 degrees is considered abnormal) (Figure 1). The lateral trochlear inclination angle measures 9 degrees (<11 degrees is considered abnormal) (Figure 2). A trochlear facet asymmetry is seen with a ratio measuring 34% (<40% is considered abnormal) (Figure 3). The trochlear depth measures 2.5 mm (<3 mm is considered abnormal) (Figure 4). Proton density/Fat saturation (PD/FS) hyperintensity is seen in the medial patellar retinaculum with partial disruption of the fibres (<50% thickness), suggestive of a low-grade partial thickness tear. A mild lateral subluxation of the patella is seen. Grade IV chondromalacic changes (Outerbridge staging) are seen in the lateral articular surface of the patella at the patellofemoral joint space (Figure 5).
discussion: Trochlear dysplasia is one of the most common developmental/anatomical causes of patellar instability. Other anatomical causes include quadriceps dysplasia, patella alta, and increased tibial tuberosity–trochlear groove distance [1]. The patients commonly present with complaints of acute primary patellar dislocation. Chronic patellar instability presents with recurrent patellar dislocation and knee joint pain due to arthritis [2,3]. The aim of imaging is to find the underlying cause of patellar instability, whether anatomical or due to medial patellofemoral ligament injury secondary to twisting knee motions. Imaging is important as it depicts the secondary damage caused to the bone, cartilage, and ligaments due to patellar instability. This will ultimately guide orthopaedic surgeons to customise treatment plans for the patients [4]. Various measurements are taken on axial T2-weighted MRI images that help us to diagnose trochlear dysplasia mentioned as follows: Trochlear sulcal angle . It is measured at the trochlear groove between the medial and lateral trochlear facets. The normal angle is less than 145–150 degrees [5]. Lateral trochlear inclination angle . It is measured at the most superior section, showing trochlear cartilage on axial images. The normal angle is more than 11 degrees [6]. Trochlear facet asymmetry . It is the ratio of the length of the medial femoral facet to the lateral femoral facet that is calculated at 3 cm above the tibiofemoral groove. The normal value is more than 40% [7]. Trochlear depth . It is measured at the same level as the trochlear facet asymmetry. The normal value is more than 3 mm [7]. Other ancillary findings include medial patelofemoral ligament injury, lateral condylar defects, and osteochondral defects in the patella. The Dejour classification gives 4 grades of trochlear dysplasia [8]: Type A – Normal trochlear morphology with shallow trochlear groove. Type B – Markedly flattened trochlea. Type C – Asymmetric trochlear facets with the medial facet being hypoplastic. Type D – Cliff pattern of trochlear facet; Vertical link between the medial and lateral facets. Mild trochlear dysplasias (Dejour type A and B) are managed conservatively, while advanced trochlear dysplasias (Dejour type C and D)rochlear dysplasias are managed surgically [9,10]. MRI imaging is crucial in determining the cause, severity, and treatment planning for patellofemoral instability.

title: Primary mediastinal choriocarcinoma with lung metastases
clinical_history: A 32-year-old man with erectile dysfunction and bilateral gynaecomastia showed elevated prolactin (21.3 µg/L), testosterone (1348 ng/dL total testosterone) and human chorionic gonadotropin (38.3 U/L) levels. Further work-up showed normal breast ultrasound and scrotum ultrasound.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced CT shows a lobulated mass in the anterior mediastinum (Figures 1, 2, and 3), with antero-posterior, latero-lateral and caudo-cranial diameters of approximately 67 x 78 x 75 mm. The mass has hyperdense walls with calcifications and a hypodense centre, possibly reflecting central necrosis. There is an abutment of the superior vena cava, the ascending aorta, the brachiocephalic vein and the pericardium (Figures 1, 2, 3, and 4). There is moderate pericardial fluid (Figures 2 and 5). There are multiple nodular lung lesions bilaterally, compatible with lung metastases (Figure 6). A sample of one of the lung nodules was obtained via surgery. Pathology showed a primary germ cell tumour (choriocarcinoma). Chemotherapy (bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin) was started. An interim evaluation was done with fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET). There was a weak FDG signal in the wall of the mediastinal mass (Figure 7) and in the lung metastasis (Figure 8). Excision of the mediastinal tumour and bilateral lung metastases was performed after 3 cycles of chemotherapy.
discussion: Background Primary mediastinal choriocarcinoma (PCC) is a rare germ cell tumour characterised by the presence of trophoblastic cells and elevated serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels. It often presents with aggressive behaviour and can metastasise rapidly, complicating diagnosis and treatment [1–4]. Clinical Perspective Patients typically present with respiratory symptoms such as cough, haemoptysis, and shortness of breath, often leading to misdiagnosis as lung cancer. Imaging is crucial for identifying the extent of the disease and guiding further diagnostic procedures. It is essential to communicate the need for serum hCG testing (elevated in 96.4% of patients with choriocarcinomas [5]) to the requesting physician when mediastinal masses are suspected [3]. Imaging Perspective Key imaging findings include large mediastinal masses and pulmonary nodules. Chest CT scans are particularly useful for assessing the extent of the disease. The final diagnosis is often confirmed through immunohistochemical staining of biopsy samples, which can distinguish PCC from other malignancies [2]. Outcome Therapeutic options include systemic chemotherapy regimens (bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin), which can improve symptoms and reduce tumour burden. The prognosis is generally poor, especially in advanced cases, but early diagnosis and treatment can improve outcomes. Imaging plays a vital role in therapy planning by monitoring treatment response [2]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Early recognition of primary mediastinal choriocarcinoma (PCC) as a differential diagnosis in young males with mediastinal masses is critical. Elevated serum hCG levels should prompt further investigation, including imaging and biopsy, to facilitate timely intervention [2]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Shedding light on mixed sclerosing bone dysplasias
clinical_history: A 43-year-old female patient presented with complaints of right knee pain for one month and hemi-hypertrophy of the right lower limb since birth. No history of trauma. The patient was evaluated with X-ray of both lower limbs, computed tomography (CT), followed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the knee.
imaging_findings: X-rays of knee, leg and foot (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c), CT (Figures 2a and 2b) and MRI (Figures 3a and 3b) show variable bone sclerosing spectrum with shared features of osteopoikilosis, osteopathia striata and melorheostosis seen in right lower limb bones involving the right femur and tibia, right fibula, multiple tarsal bones, metatarsal and phalanges.
discussion: Background Sclerosing bone dysplasias encompass a range of skeletal abnormalities with diverse clinical, radiologic, and genetic features. Mixed sclerosing bone dysplasia is a rare disorder, with an estimated prevalence of less than 1 in 1 million. These are classified as hereditary or non-hereditary. Hereditary dysplasias include intramedullary osteosclerosis, melorheostosis, and overlap syndromes. They arise from osteoblast or osteoclast dysregulation, leading to abnormal bone accumulation. Examples include osteopetrosis, pyknodysostosis, osteopoikilosis, osteopathia striata, progressive diaphyseal dysplasia, hereditary multiple diaphyseal sclerosis, and hyperostosis corticalis generalisata [1,2]. During the 7th week of embryogenesis, endochondral ossification begins with the formation of primary spongiosa. It undergoes resorption and transforms into secondary spongiosa, remodelled by osteoclasts to form the medullary cavity and trabeculae. Failure of secondary spongiosa resorption can lead to striated trabecular bone (osteopathia striata) or focal densities (osteopoikilosis) [1,3]. Overlap syndromes, such as the combination of osteopoikilosis, osteopathia striata, and melorheostosis, demonstrate features of multiple sclerosing bone dysplasias. The most prevalent one combines osteopoikilosis, osteopathia striata and melorheostosis. Clinical Perspective Bone lesions are usually asymptomatic and incidentally found on radiographs. When melorheostosis presents clinically, joint contracture or pain, especially in adults, is the most common symptom. Imaging Perspective Radiographs and CT are commonly used to evaluate bony sclerosis. Osteopoikilosis, an autosomal-dominant disorder, presents as compact lamellar bone deposits in the spongiosa, resembling enostoses or bone islands. It commonly affects the tarsal, carpal, pelvic bones, and meta-epiphyseal regions of the long bones [1,4,5]. Osteopathia striata (Voorhoeve disease), previously thought to be autosomal dominant, is now considered X-linked dominant. It appears in rapidly growing areas, such as the femur, with striations parallel to the bone’s long axis. Imaging shows dense linear striations in the diaphysis and metaphysis, and fan-shaped striations in the iliac bones [3,6]. Melorheostosis (Leri disease) has no familial predisposition. It manifests in a sclerotome distribution, often monostotic or monomelic, affecting long limb bones. Imaging reveals periosteal and endosteal sclerosis with a “dripping candle wax” appearance [2,6]. Amongst the differential diagnoses, Paget’s disease is polyostotic, causing osseous sclerosis, coarse trabecular thickening, and bone enlargement, mainly in the axial skeleton. Myelofibrosis shows diffuse sclerosis affecting the medullary cavity. Sickle cell disease leads to bone infarcts, avascular necrosis, and “fish-mouth” vertebrae. Erdheim–Chester disease affects diaphyses and metaphyses, sparing epiphyses, and radiotracer uptake is seen in osteoblastic metastasis [1]. Outcome Most cases are asymptomatic with a good prognosis. Melorheostosis progresses slowly in adults and faster in children. Conservative treatments are often effective. Severe cases may require surgical interventions like tendon release, osteotomies, or even amputation. Teaching Points Accurate diagnosis of sclerosing bone dysplasias requires knowledge of their radiologic features, distribution, and clinical presentation. Melorheostosis presents as monostotic or monomelic sclerosis in long bones with a “dripping candle wax” radiographic appearance. title: Retroperitoneal metastasising leiomyoma mimicking malignancy – A sheep in wolf clothing
clinical_history: A 44-year-old premenopausal woman presented with dysmenorrhea. Ultrasound (USG) revealed a bulky uterus with multiple fibroids. She subsequently underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy combined with a left salpingo-oophorectomy and right salpingectomy. Six months post-surgery, she presented with abdominal fullness and difficulty breathing.
imaging_findings: A chest CT scan revealed numerous parenchymal and subpleural nodules of varying sizes, randomly distributed in both lungs (Figures 1a and 1b). No intralesional calcifications noted. A contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen identified a large, heterogeneously enhancing mass with both solid and cystic components in the left para-aortic region, the aortocaval and left external iliac regions, exerting a mass effect on nearby visceral structures without signs of direct invasion (Figures 2a and 2b). A USG-guided Tru-cut biopsy was performed on the left para-aortic solid-cystic mass and sent for histopathological examination (Figure 3). On follow-up FDG-PET/CT, the retroperitoneal masses showed no significant fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake (Figures 4a and 4b).
discussion: Background The term “benign metastasising leiomyoma” (BML) was first introduced by P. Steiner in 1939 to describe well-defined lung nodules in women with a history of hysterectomy for uterine leiomyoma [1]. Although metastasis to the retroperitoneum and spine is rare, such cases have been documented. The exact mechanism remains unclear, but it is hypothesised that smooth muscle cells may enter pelvic venous channels during surgical trauma, enabling metastasis to distant sites [2]. Clinical Perspective Most patients remain asymptomatic. However, a history of hysterectomy for uterine leiomyoma can be a significant indicator [3]. In symptomatic cases, patients might experience chest pain, shortness of breath, cough, or, rarely, haemoptysis. Imaging Perspective There is no definitive imaging hallmark for BML, but the most common finding is well-defined pulmonary nodules scattered throughout both lungs. These nodules typically lack calcification and do not show significant post-contrast enhancement. Pleural or endobronchial involvement has not been reported. In retroperitoneal metastases of leiomyoma, imaging often reveals nodal masses exerting mass effect on surrounding structures without direct invasion. Larger masses may demonstrate necrotic changes. This case is particularly rare, as it presents both pulmonary and retroperitoneal disseminating leiomyomas in the same patient. On FDG-PET, the lesions are non-FDG avid, implicating their benign nature [4]. Outcome Most uterine and benign metastatic leiomyomas express hormone receptors, making hormone-based treatments a viable option [3]. There is clinical evidence of regression in metastatic leiomyoma cases following menopause or post-pregnancy [5]. Medical castration using GnRH agonists has shown promising results for treating BML. Nevertheless, surgical resection remains the standard treatment for cases unresponsive to medical therapy [6,7]. In our case, the patient initially received hormonal therapy to reduce the tumour size. However, a follow-up PET scan, conducted six months later, revealed an increase in the necrotic component of the non-FDG avid left para-aortic mass (Figures 4a and 4b). Due to worsening symptoms caused by the mass effect on abdominal organs, the multidisciplinary team decided to proceed with surgical removal of the abdominal masses. A surgical roadmap was developed to guide the procedure (Figure 5). Intraoperative findings and postoperative specimens were correlated with preoperative CT images (Figures 6a, 6b, and 6c). Histopathology of the specimen revealed interlacing fascicles of spindle-shaped and epithelioid cells within an oedematous stroma. The cells exhibited indistinct borders, elongated nuclei, dispersed chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli (Figures 7a and 7b). Teaching Points Benign metastasising leiomyoma should be considered a differential diagnosis in women with retroperitoneal masses and a prior history of surgery for uterine fibroids, as these lesions may spread through pelvic venous channels. Radiologists are pivotal in early detection, preoperative evaluation, surgical guidance, and postoperative follow-up. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
