title: Chronic abdominal pain revealing a rare case of mesenteric teratoma
clinical_history: A 49-year-old healthy female with well-controlled hypertension has experienced mild, intermittent abdominal pain for 2 years. She reports no weight loss or blood in stools. Previous treatments with analgesics and antispasmodics were ineffective, and diagnostic tests were normal. Her primary care physician has ordered an abdominal ultrasound and CT scan to rule out underlying pathology before treating her for functional colopathy.
imaging_findings: The ultrasound showed an intra-peritoneal mesenteric well-circumscribed lesion, a round cystic mass located within the right quadrant. It exhibits anechoic to hypoechoic fluid content, consistent with fat-rich material. Within the cyst, multiple echogenic, mobile, round structures are visualised, corresponding to the “floating balls” sign. These intralesional structures demonstrate posterior acoustic shadowing or variable echogenicity, suggesting sebaceous content or fat globules. Echogenic foci with posterior shadowing are also noted along the cyst wall and within the lesion, compatible with internal calcifications. The cyst wall is thin and regular, with no evidence of vascularity on colour Doppler imaging. Upon CT examination, an intra-peritoneal mesenteric cystic lesion is identified, measuring 72 x 64 x 70 mm. It appears round, well-defined, with a thin wall, and a low-attenuating content with a measured density of -140 Hounsfield Units (HU). Within this lesion, small round structures with higher attenuation than the surrounding liquid (-40 HU) are observed, realising the “floating balls” sign. Additionally, small calcifications are present both in the cyst wall and within the cyst itself (Figures 1a and 1b). It is noteworthy that the patient’s ovaries showed no abnormalities. The diagnosis of mesenteric dermoid cyst was established.
discussion: Background A dermoid cyst, also known as a mature teratoma, is a tumour originating from totipotent embryonic cells. The term “teratoma”, meaning “monster” in Greek, was introduced by Rudolph Virchow in 1869 due to the tumour’s inclusion of differentiated tissues like hair or bone [1]. Teratomas, aside from occurring in the gonads and sacrococcygeal region, are most commonly found in the mediastinum, particularly the anterior mediastinum. Other frequent sites include the central nervous system, lungs, abdomen (including mesenteric and retroperitoneal areas), head and neck (especially the cervical region), and urinary tract (such as the kidneys or bladder). They most commonly occur in early childhood, with mature mesenteric teratomas in adults being extremely rare [1,2]. While mature teratomas are generally benign, distinguishing them from immature, malignant teratomas is crucial, though malignant transformation in mesenteric teratomas is exceptionally rare. While mature cystic teratomas (MCTs) in general exhibit a malignant transformation rate of approximately 1% to 3%, specific data on mesenteric teratomas are limited due to their rarity. Some reports suggest that the incidence of malignancy in mesenteric cysts, which include mesenteric teratomas, is less than 3% [2]. Clinical Perspective Symptoms are nonspecific and typically result from the tumour’s compressive effects. Patients may experience dull abdominal pain and a sense of heaviness when the tumour enlarges significantly. Physical examinations are often unremarkable unless the mass is large enough to be palpable [2]. Imaging Perspective Diagnosis relies heavily on imaging, with certain features being pathognomonic. Ultrasound reveals a well-defined cystic lesion displacing nearby organs, with internal characteristics such as [3]: Fluid-fluid level (fat over water-rich fluid). Rokitansky nodule (dense, echogenic nodule with shadowing). Hair (intertwined hyperechoic lines). Bony structures. Dense intracystic formations causing a “floating balls” sign. “Tip of the iceberg” sign, i.e., attenuating cyst filled with sebaceous material and hair. CT scan provides detailed differentiation of structures, identifying cystic lesions with lipid and calcification components, Rokitansky nodules, and sebaceous material “balls”. While the presence of fatty and bony elements strongly suggests a teratoma, histological confirmation is needed for predominantly solid masses [3,4]. On MRI, a mesenteric teratoma typically appears as a heterogeneous mass with fatty components (hyperintense on T1 and T2), cystic regions (hyperintense on T2 and hypointense on T1), and calcifications (hypointense on both T1 and T2). No significant enhancement is typically seen in the cystic areas, but if there are solid components, these may show some degree of enhancement after gadolinium administration. The imaging characteristics correlate with the presence of different tissue types, aiding in the diagnosis [4–6]. Outcome Our patient underwent surgery outside our institution. The operative and histopathological reports describe a cystic lesion embedded in the mesentery, with histology confirming a mature teratoma. Surgical removal is recommended due to potential malignancy risks. The approach depends on tumour size, location, and surgical preference. In our case, surgery performed outside the institution revealed a mesenteric cystic lesion, confirmed as a mature teratoma via histopathology [5,6]. Surgical excision and histological examination are essential in the management of mesenteric teratomas to confirm the diagnosis and rule out malignancy. Complete surgical removal also reduces the risk of recurrence and guides further management if malignancy is present [5,6] Take Home Message Many mesenteric teratomas remain asymptomatic and are discovered incidentally during imaging for unrelated issues. Histological confirmation is essential for predominantly solid lesions where imaging may not conclusively differentiate benign from malignant. Besides malignancy, large teratomas can cause complications like torsion, rupture, or infection. Management often requires collaboration between radiologists, surgeons, and pathologists for optimal patient outcomes. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Paravesical hernia – An unusual cause for closed-loop obstruction
clinical_history: A 65-year-old male presented with abdominal distension and pain of 10 days’ duration. No vomiting or obstipation was seen.
imaging_findings: A contrast-enhanced CT (computed tomography) scan of the abdomen was performed. Small bowel loops appeared dilated with multiple air-fluid levels (Figures 1, 2a, and 2b). A transition zone was found on the right side of the urinary bladder. A closed-loop obstruction was found with distal ileal loops as content, causing indentation of the right superolateral wall of the urinary bladder (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c). A few dilated loops show a small bowel faeces sign (luminal contents resembling colonic faecal matter with gas bubbles). The hernial sac was filled with a minimal amount of fluid. There was no abnormal enhancement of the small bowel loops within the hernial sac. No thickening of the bowel walls was noted. Large bowel loops were collapsed. The cecum appeared normal.
discussion: Background Internal hernia is a rare cause of small bowel obstruction. It presents with nonspecific clinical manifestations [1]. The paravesical type of internal hernia is an extremely rare cause. In a patient presenting with small bowel obstruction without a history of previous surgery and located in the vicinity of the urinary bladder, paravesical hernia should be included in the differentials. The supravesical fossa lies between the median and medial umbilical ligaments and the transverse vesical fold [2]. Supravesical hernia can be classified into internal and external types [3]. These hernias can be prevesical, paravesical, or even intravesical. Clinical Perspective Internal supravesical hernia usually occurs in elderly males in their sixth decade. It is usually nonspecific and may present with features of small bowel obstruction due to the narrow neck. So, early preoperative diagnosis is challenging. If left untreated, it can lead to complications like ischemia and gangrene. Imaging Perspective As clinical diagnosis is challenging, CT (computed tomography) plays an important role in diagnosis. Imaging findings include dilated small bowel loops with a transition zone in the paravesical location with or without indentation of the bladder [4]. Plain radiography and USG (ultrasound) may show features of small bowel obstruction, but will not aid in the diagnosis of the aetiology of small bowel obstruction. CT helps identify the hernia, specific location, and transition zone, as well as the severity of obstruction and early identification of complications. Management Timely surgical intervention is needed to reduce the hernia and prevent the complications of ischemia and gangrene. Surgical closure of the hernial orifice is required to prevent recurrence. Resection of the sac is not required. This can be done laparoscopically or via laparotomy. Reduction of the obstruction and closure of the defect are the primary aims of surgical intervention. Outcome In our case, a diagnosis of right paravesical hernia causing closed-loop obstruction was given. During the laparoscopic approach, a defect was identified between the medial umbilical ligament and median umbilical ligament (Figures 4a and 4b). Obstructed bowel loops were reduced, which were not gangrenous. The defect was closed with continuous sutures with non-absorbable material (Figure 4c). Take Home Message / Learning Points An elderly male presenting with pain and vomiting, with a CT scan showing clumped small bowel loops near the urinary bladder, should prompt the diagnosis of paravesical internal hernia.

title: Secondary arteriobiliary fistula
clinical_history: An 83-year-old man with suspected cholangiocellular carcinoma upon previous contrast-enhanced computed imaging (CT), presented to the emergency department with an acute onset of upper abdominal pain in the right upper quadrant (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d). Eleven days prior, two biliary drainages had been placed after locoregional therapy with endoscopic microablation. Subsequently, a dual-phase contrast-enhanced CT imaging was performed for further evaluation.
imaging_findings: Upon axial contrast-enhanced CT imaging, the stomach and duodenum were seen to be distended and with mixed hypo- and hyperdense contents, suggestive of an intraluminal haematoma (star and triangle in Figure 2a, and star in Figure 2b). Two biliary drainages from the duodenum to the left and right main hepatic ducts were seen in place (Figure 2a, and arrow in Figure 2c). Compared to the axial contrast-enhanced CT imaging done approximately two weeks priorly, a progression of the intrahepatic mass can be detected (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d). Upon detailed review, a 9 mm pseudoaneurysm of the right hepatic artery bulging towards the biliary ducts was seen at the kissing point of the bile drainages (arrow in Figure 2d). There was no contrast media pooling detectable in the abdomen or duodenum. In conclusion, these findings highly suggest the presence of an arteriobiliary fistula with recent bleeding.
discussion: Background The occurrence of arteriobiliary fistulas in the framework of hepatic artery pseudoaneurysms is extremely rare [1,2]. In this pathology, the biliary system gets connected to the intra- or extrahepatic arterial vasculature, causing bleeding into the bile ducts and the duodenum. This does generally not occur spontaneously but is mainly associated with diagnostic or therapeutic interventions like transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) or endoscopic biliary procedures followed by blunt abdominal trauma [3,4]. Notably, considering the occurrence of hepatic artery pseudoaneurysms, the right hepatic artery is affected in >90% of cases [4]. Imaging Perspective This case highlights the importance of the assessment of foreign bodies and the combination of different diagnostic clues. First of all, the filling of the stomach and duodenum is abnormal. Especially when considering the mixed density contents with HU of 50–70, a haematoma has to be suspected. Secondly, the intrahepatic bile ducts were seen progressively dilated, and the intrahepatic mass showed clear progression compared to two weeks prior, which is highly unlikely to be due to a tumour progression in this short term, and thus, must have another reason, in this case, biliary haemorrhage (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d). Thirdly, the patient has undergone multiple endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) procedures with recent endoscopic microablation and placement of two bile duct drainages, which must lead to a close assessment, including the comparison to prior studies. Outcome and Discussion Following the suspicion of this diagnosis, a nasogastric tube was placed, which surfaced blood, further confirming the presence of the arteriobiliary fistula. Laboratory assessment showed a relevant drop in haemoglobin levels from 12 g/dl at admission to 7 g/dl after CT imaging. After in-depth interdisciplinary discussions with surgeons, internal medicine doctors, and the patient, the decision was made for emergency stenting of the right hepatic artery to cover the fistula and avoid life-threatening haemorrhage, albeit a palliative situation. This treatment approach was done in accordance with the practice guidelines of the Society of Vascular Surgery, suggesting repair of symptomatic hepatic artery pseudoaneurysms in an endovascular-first approach [5]. The indication for treatment was evident given the localisation and size of the pseudoaneurysm as well as the presence of arteriobiliary fistula [4,5]. Stentgraft placement was considered the most feasible option, as it allowed for exclusion of the aneurysm and fistula while preserving the right hepatic artery [5]. In the given framework, coil- or liquid-embolic-agent embolisation were considered not feasible. The procedure was completed successfully, and no further episodes of bleeding occurred (Figures 3a and 3b). One month after the procedure, the patient succumbed to the sequelae of the underlying cholangiocellular carcinoma. Written informed consent for publication has been obtained from the patient.

title: Carcinoma arising from anal fistula
clinical_history: A 62-year-old male with anal swelling and bleeding of years of evolution. Physical examination revealed a mass of approximately 20 cm in perianal region, with several fistulous tracts covering anal and perianal area with purulent secretion.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced CT showed a voluminous low-density gluteal mass with areas of internal enhancement (Figures 1a and 1b). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a multiloculated, cauliflower-like 21 x 16 x 11cm gluteal mass. It extended through both ischioanal fossae and fistulised to the anal canal with two posterior tracts (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). The lesion was hypointense with respect to the muscle in T1-weighted sequences and showed high signal intensity in T2, compatible with abundant myxoid-mucinous content. Contrast-enhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted MR imaging showed linear and papillary mesh-like enhancing areas (Figure 2d).
discussion: Background Carcinoma arising from the anal fistula is an uncommon tumor of the anal canal, accounting for less than 5% of anal tumors [1]. It has been suggested that chronic inflammatory pathology can predispose regular epithelium within a perianal fistula to malignant transformation. There are three primary pathological subtypes of carcinoma associated with anal fistula: adenocarcinoma, mucinous adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. Among them, mucinous adenocarcinoma is the most frequently occurring histological type [2]. Clinical Perspective Common presenting symptoms typically consist of perianal pain, pruritus, mucinous discharge and abscess formation, often accompanied by an ulcerative lesion or a palpable mass in the perianal area [3]. The early detection of a carcinoma developing from an anal fistula is quite challenging, either due to its nonspecific clinical symptoms or its extremely slow growth rate [2]. Imaging Perspective On different imaging modalities, such as CT and MRI, carcinoma arising from anal fistula presents in most cases as a multiloculated or cauliflower-like mass with internal septa. The presence of a fistulous tract connecting the mass to the anal canal is a distinguishing feature of it. On T2-weighted MR images, mucinous adenocarcinoma has a hyperintense signal. In the postcontrast sequences, however, it presents a progressively mesh-like and septal enhancement [4]. Outcome The histopathological diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of extracellular mucinous lakes surrounded by well-differentiated, dilated, and tortuous glands [5]. In our case, the biopsy histology reported an infiltrating malignant neoplasm forming large mucinous lacunae, some of them lined by a mucosecretory columnar epithelium associated with fibroinflammatory stroma with granulation tissue, corresponding to a mucinous adenocarcinoma of intestinal type arising from anal fistula (Figure 3). Lateral colostomy was performed and treated with palliative chemotherapy. Although the literature has few studies on carcinoma arising from anal fistula, most reviewed reports suggest that radical surgical excision is the preferred treatment, with abdominoperineal resection being the procedure of choice. However, the effectiveness of neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemoradiotherapy remains uncertain [6]. Long-term survival rates remain poor for patients with locally advanced-stage disease [7].

title: Postoperative elongation of the xiphoid process
clinical_history: A 63-year-old male had undergone curative surgery for gastric cancer. Due to subsequent gastroenteric anastomosis dysfunction and hepatic haemorrhage, he underwent three upper abdominal laparotomies before being discharged in good condition. A year later, he presented with respiratory-synchronous pain in the region of the xiphoid process, i.e., xiphodynia.
imaging_findings: A CT scan of the abdomen was performed following the final surgery. The xiphoid process measured 5 cm in length (Figures 1a and 1b), and two stapler lines were visible, one vertical and one horizontal, corresponding to the abdominal incisions from the laparotomies. Approximately one year later, a CT scan of the thorax revealed significant elongation of the xiphoid process, which had doubled in length (Figures 2a and 2b), notably within a relatively short period of time. The elongation exhibited an irregular contour with a distal protrusion extending to the left (Figure 3), corresponding to the course of the vertical stapler line (Figure 1a). The structure of the elongation resembled that of normal trabecular bone, with a thin layer of dense cortex surrounding the central, lesser dense bone, in direct and smooth continuation of the original bone, leading to an appearance of an elongation rather than that of ectopic bone tissue.
discussion: We believe the elongation of the xiphoid process to be an example of heterotopic ossification (HO) triggered by the previous laparotomies. HO is defined as ectopic bone formation in soft tissues [1]. While HO is relatively common after orthopaedic surgery, its incidence following abdominal surgery is rare. Though a retrospective study found CT-based evidence of HO in 25% of patients following abdominal laparotomy [2], this incidence is hardly in line with clinical experience and contrasts with the broader literature, consisting predominantly of sporadic case reports. These include several instances of heterotopic ossification in midline incisions [3], including near the xiphoid process [4], but a distinct postoperative elongation of the xiphoid process is rare. To our knowledge, this has been reported only four times [5–8], twice following abdominal surgery [6,8]. HO can be genetic or acquired [1]. Various theories have been proposed regarding the mechanism behind acquired HO. There is a general consensus that a trigger is necessary to initiate ossification, such as a surgical midline incision. Other examples include chest compressions, burn injuries, as well as repeated external mechanical microtrauma in a carpenter and a surfer [9]. One theory, as to how such triggers initiate HO, suggests that periosteal cells released from adjacent bone, such as the xiphoid process, become implanted in the scar tissue in which they ossify. Another theory claims that trauma triggers differentiation of local stromal mesenchymal stem cells to osteoblasts [3]. This theory is more widely favoured, as it explains how HO can occur far from other bone tissue, e.g., the mesentery [10]. Enomoto et al. [7] proposed that a case of postoperative elongation of the xiphoid process occurred due to distraction osteogenesis, a method of bone lengthening used in orthopaedic surgery. They suggested that the xiphoid process was fractured during surgery, subsequently pulled caudally by the abdominal muscles and later reconnected to the sternum. Due to the direct elongation of the xiphoid process, this case intuitively supports the latter theory. Regardless of the cause of HO, there is consensus that treatment is only indicated in symptomatic cases, in which HO should be surgically excised [1,8]. In our case, the patient experienced discomfort due to the elongated xiphoid process and has been referred for surgical assessment. Take Home Message Postoperative xiphoid elongation due to heterotopic ossification is a rare condition, which can cause respiratory-synchronous pain and abdominal discomfort. The underlying mechanism is unclear and treatment is surgical excision. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

final_diagnosis: Postoperative elongation of the xiphoid process

title: Paediatric/adolescent gestational trophoblastic disease – Complete hydatidiform mole (molar pregnancy)
clinical_history: 17-year-old female presents to the emergency department with a 2-week history of markedly elevated beta-hCG levels, brown vaginal discharge, and back pain. The patient reports an uterus growing in size and can now be palpated at the level of the umbilicus. The patient has a history of irregular menses.
imaging_findings: Transabdominal sagittal (Figure 1a) and coronal (Figure 2b) uterine ultrasound shows a diffusely enlarged uterus containing a heterogeneous, avascular, solid and cystic mass with multiple small cystic spaces (“bunch of grapes” appearance). Contrast-enhanced pelvic CT in sagittal (Figure 2a) and coronal (Figure 2b) projections shows a diffusely enlarged uterus containing cystic and solid mass-like components.
discussion: Background Gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) is a spectrum of malignant and benign gestational tumours including complete or partial hydatidiform mole (HM), invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumour and epithelial trophoblastic tumour [1]. Under the umbrella of GTD, a complete hydatidiform mole (CHM) is the uninhibited proliferation of trophoblastic tissue (both cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast) coupled with vesicular swelling of associated placental villi and absence of a foetus. Risk factors for complete hydatidiform moles include very young or advanced reproductive age or multiple grand multiparas [1,2]. The rate of recurrence in subsequent pregnancies is 1.2–1.4% and a consequent 10-fold greater risk of repeated HM compared to women with no history of HM [2]. Clinical Perspective Patients typically present with a vague history of vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain, and, potentially, a positive pregnancy test. Imaging is necessary to rule out uterine pregnancy complications, ectopic pregnancy, and other complications. If complete hydatidiform moles are left untreated, the risk of progression to trophoblastic malignancy is between 5% and 15% of patients [3]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound is typically the first imaging exam for workup consistent with this presentation. A hydatidiform mole will reveal the absence of foetal structures, diffuse hydropic villi commonly described as a “snowstorm” appearance or a “bunch of grapes” [4]. MRI can provide further characterisation of the uterus and its contents. CT has a limited role, but sometimes it can be used in emergency setting or when pregnancy is not yet known [5]. Outcome Successful dilatation and curettage with suction was performed by gynaecological oncology specialists, followed by two consecutive rounds of actinomycin-D therapy. Beta-hCG levels consistently declined upon treatment to near normal levels. The patient is receiving routine follow-up for potential pulmonary metastasis. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Early detection and intervention of a complete hydatidiform mole (CHM) can cease the progression to systemic malignancy and rupture complications. CHM in adolescents has greater risk for multiple recurrences and continuous monitoring for distant malignancy is vital.

title: A case of primary hepatic adenosarcoma
clinical_history: A 53-year-old male patient presented to our outpatient clinic with persistent dull pain in the right upper abdomen. Physical examination revealed a flat and soft abdomen with mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant.
imaging_findings: The patient had complete imaging data, including CT, MR, and PET-CT. All imaging examinations showed a mass in segment VII/VIII of the liver. Unenhanced CT scan showed that the lesion was low-density, with a CT value of about 23 HU, linear calcification at the edge, and mild shrinkage of the liver capsule. After enhancement, the lesion did not enhance, and the surrounding liver parenchyma was mildly enhanced in the arterial phase (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d). The mass contains mixed low signal on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images and T2-weighted fat-suppressed images (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d). Coronal T2-weighted fat-suppressed images and coronal venous-phase T1-weighted fat-suppressed images showed that the intrahepatic bile duct beside the mass is dilated and connected to the lesion; the edge of the lesion and the adjacent bile duct showed mild enhancement (Figures 3a and 3b). Diffusion-weighted image (DWI, b = 800 mm2/s) showed a slightly higher signal (Figure 4a). The ADC map does not show restricted diffusion (Figure 4b). Similar to the CT-enhanced images, on T1-weighted enhanced arterial phase images, it can also be seen that the liver parenchyma around the lesion is slightly enhanced (Figure 4c). PET-CT showed a slight increase in FDG metabolism (Figures 5a, 5b, 5c, and 5d).
discussion: Adenosarcoma is a rare tumour that usually occurs in the female reproductive system [1,2]. When it occurs in the uterus, it is called Müllerian duct adenosarcoma, which typically has a low degree of malignancy [3]. Adenosarcoma is characterised by both benign epithelial and malignant stromal components. Some scholars classify adenosarcoma as a kind of sarcoma, being the rarest form of uterine sarcoma, accounting for only 0.2% of all uterine malignant tumours [3]. Adenosarcoma can also be secondary to other sites, such as the liver, colon/rectum, breast, and retroperitoneum [4,5], usually secondary to endometriosis at these sites. Primary adenosarcoma in the liver is extremely rare [6], with only four cases reported in the literature with imaging data. Primary hepatic adenosarcoma typically lacks a clear background of liver cirrhosis or elevated AFP or CA199 levels, making preoperative diagnosis challenging. Diagnosis currently relies on pathological and immunohistochemical analysis. The treatment of primary hepatic adenosarcoma mainly relies on early radical surgery, and chemotherapy (doxorubicin + vincristine + dacarbazine) [2] or radiotherapy [6] can be received after surgery. In our case, the patient underwent partial hepatectomy. Postoperative pathology confirmed the presence of a malignant tumour in the right anterior lobe of the liver, and a soft mass could be seen in the dilated bile duct. The microscopic examination showed well-differentiated bile duct glands interspersed with short spindle cells. The spindle cells surrounded the glands, exhibited a high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, and demonstrated nuclear division. Focal interstitial myxoid degeneration and chronic inflammatory cell infiltration were observed around the tumour. The small bile ducts were disordered, with an increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and severe atypical hyperplasia (Figures 6a and 6b). Immunohistochemical analysis indicated that the epithelial components were CK positive and Ki-67 was highly expressed. Based on existing literature and this case, the imaging features of hepatic adenosarcoma are as follows: a hepatic cystic mass, low density on CT, mixed low signal on T1-weighted images, and mixed high signal on T2-weighted images and T2-weighted fat-suppressed images. Enhancement characteristics suggest a hypovascular tumour with slight enhancement at the lesion’s edge and some solid components; this may be caused by the high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio in the tumour and the inflammatory infiltration around the tumour. There may be dilation of the adjacent intrahepatic bile duct and potential invasion into the adjacent intrahepatic bile duct.
differential_diagnosis: Hepatic cholangiocarcinoma Primary hepatic adenosarcoma Undifferentiated carcinoma (also known as sarcomatoid carcinoma) Hepatic fibroadenoma

title: Peritoneal hydatidosis: A rare form of hydatid disease
clinical_history: We report a case of a 16-year-old patient living in a rural environment. The symptomatology goes back to 3 months with diffuse abdominal pain, distension, and with vomiting and fever 3 days before his admission to the ER. Clinical examination revealed a slight dullness of the flanks and hypogastrium.
imaging_findings: An abdominal ultrasound was performed and revealed multiple hepatic, splenic and peritoneal cystic lesions with large intraperitoneal effusion (Figure 1). Abdominal and pelvic CT scan in axial, sagittal and coronal sections showed multiple cystic lesions adherent to the peritoneal leaflets, falciform ligament, great omentum and mesentery (Figures 2 and 4). The largest cyst is located in the left iliac fossa, measuring 55.5 x 42 mm, containing some calcifications (Figure 3), and with a large intraperitoneal effusion. The CT scan also revealed hepatic and splenic cystic lesions.
discussion: Background Hydatid disease remains prevalent in Mediterranean countries, with the liver and lungs being the most commonly affected organs [1]. It is a disease of young adults and infants [2]. Peritoneal involvement is less frequent, accounting for approximately 13% of all abdominal cases [1]. Peritoneal hydatidosis may be primary or secondary. The primary form is exceptional, and occurs either by haematogenous or heterotopic migration of a hydatid cyst, usually in the liver, which has ruptured its adventitia or retained its membrane intact. The secondary form, which is the most frequent, is often due to fissure or rupture of a hepatic hydatid cyst, or more exceptionally, of a splenic hydatid cyst [4]. In our case, it is probably a secondary form due to the presence of hepatic and splenic cysts. Clinical Perspective Peritoneal echinococcosis is clinically polymorphic due to the extreme diversity of hydatid cyst locations. Abdominal pain may be diffuse, violent, or may be attenuated and persisting. Palpation of an abdominal mass may be present. Partial or complete intestinal obstruction may be seen, due to bowel compression by hydatid cysts. Biological tests can show high levels of eosinophils and a positive hydatid serology [4]. Imaging Perspective Imaging is a crucial step in the diagnosis. A variety of imaging techniques are nowadays useful, allowing a positive and topographic diagnosis, and contributing to therapeutic management and monitoring of treated patients: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality used for the diagnosis and detection of hydatid disease in its abdominal locations, with a reliability of more than 90% in most series reported in the literature [2]. It is a rapid, accessible and affordable imaging examination that can reveal useful imaging features. Abdominal CT allows a much more precise diagnosis. It confirms the diagnosis and allows a mapping of the different locations, which is extremely useful for surgical planning [2]. Magnetic resonance imaging is not usually used in the diagnosis of peritoneal hydatidosis, especially in urgent situations. Outcome The treatment remains, above all, surgical. Medical treatment is associated pre- and postoperatively to avoid recurrences, which can be frequent in secondary to non-sterilised cysts [2]. Our patient underwent a splenectomy with extensive peritoneal lavage, followed by antiparasitic medical treatment. Teaching Points Despite its rarity, the diagnosis of peritoneal hydatidosis should be considered, especially in endemic contexts. Clinical findings, positive hydatid serology and imaging findings are the mainstays of a positive diagnosis of this entity.

title: Atypically presenting Burkitt lymphoma with postpartum ovarian enlargement
clinical_history: A 32-year-old, 12-week postpartum female presented with an incidental finding of bilaterally enlarged ovaries on ultrasound. The patient was asymptomatic at the time of presentation, with no associated abdominal pain, fever, or systemic symptoms. There was no significant personal or family history of malignancy or other chronic illnesses.
imaging_findings: On the initial ultrasound, both ovaries were massively enlarged (right 444 cm³, left 120 cm³) and displayed a heterogeneous echo texture with hypervascularity. No significant free fluid or adnexal torsion was noted. On contrast-enhanced whole-body MRI, bilateral ovarian masses exhibited scattered bulky lesions with significant diffusion restriction and contrast enhancement, without signs of necrosis or haemorrhage (Figure 1). Additional bulky lesions were identified in the breasts, mesentery, intestinal serosa, peritoneum, and the wall of the terminal ileum. PET-CT demonstrated intense fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake (SUV max. 14 g/ml) in the same regions identified on MRI, confirming metabolic activity consistent with malignancy (Figure 2). Breast imaging (ultrasound and mammography) revealed numerous sharply circumscribed, hypervascular, hypoechoic masses in both breasts (Figure 3). The biggest lesion measured 140 cm³. Mammography confirmed these findings, identifying well-defined, radiodense masses without calcifications or architectural distortion (Figures 4a and 4b). Taking account of all the imaging features together, these lesions were categorised as BIRADS 5.
discussion: Background Burkitt lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterised by rapid proliferation and extranodal involvement. It is classified into three clinical variants: endemic, sporadic, and immunodeficiency-associated [1]. The sporadic form, seen in this case, commonly involves the gastrointestinal tract and abdomen but rarely presents with postpartum ovarian enlargement or breast involvement. Primary ovarian Burkitt lymphoma accounts for 0.5% of non-Hodgkin lymphoma and 1.5% of ovarian cancers, while primary breast Burkitt lymphoma accounts for <1% of non-Hodgkin lymphoma and 0.04–1% of breast malignancies [3,4]. Clinical Perspective Burkitt lymphoma typically presents with rapidly enlarging masses, systemic symptoms such as fever, night sweats, or weight loss, and gastrointestinal complaints [1]. Hormonal changes in the postpartum period can cause benign breast lumps like galactocele (due to elevated prolactin) or even ovarian masses like functional cysts of luteomas of pregnancy (due to fluctuating oestrogen and progesterone). The asymptomatic postpartum presentation in this case underscores the importance of imaging in identifying atypical manifestations of Burkitt lymphoma. Early recognition is critical due to the rapid progression of this malignancy and the need for immediate treatment. Imaging Perspective This case highlights the diagnostic utility of multimodal imaging: Ultrasound identified the ovarian involvement, prompting further evaluation. MRI provided detailed anatomical information and confirmed the presence of widespread bulky lesions with diffusion restriction. PET-CT played a pivotal role in confirming the metabolic activity of the lesions and staging the disease. Breast imaging further established the presence of multifocal disease in the breasts. Key imaging findings include: Bilaterally enlarged ovaries with heterogeneous signal intensity and diffusion restriction. Multisystem involvement, including breast and gastrointestinal tract lesions. Intense FDG uptake on PET-CT. Outcome The patient underwent biopsy of the ovarian and breast lesions, which confirmed Burkitt lymphoma. Following the diagnosis, she was referred to oncology for aggressive chemotherapy based on the CODOX-M/IVAC protocol [1,2]. Early initiation of therapy is crucial in Burkitt lymphoma, given its high proliferation index. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Atypical presentations of aggressive malignancies, such as postpartum ovarian enlargement, necessitate a high index of suspicion and comprehensive imaging. Multimodal imaging is indispensable for diagnosis, staging, and guiding biopsy in cases of suspected lymphoproliferative disorders. Early recognition and treatment are essential to improve prognosis in aggressive diseases like Burkitt lymphoma. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Metastatic disease Primary ovarian malignancy Burkitt lymphoma Other aggressive lymphoma

title: Oesophageal mucocele post corrosive stricture surgery presenting as mediastinal mass
clinical_history: A 45-year-old presented with dysphagia and post-prandial vomiting since one month. She had a history of accidental corrosive ingestion 20 years back, for which she was managed surgically (an elective retrosternal oesophageal bypass surgery using a gastric pull-through procedure was performed). She underwent bougie dilatation of the esophagogastric anastomosis for similar presenting symptoms.
imaging_findings: Frontal chest radiograph showed a fairly well-defined, round soft tissue opacity in the retrocardiac region with a broad base towards the mediastinum (Figure 1). There were no calcifications or cavitation within the opacity. The lateral border of the descending thoracic aorta was obscured by the lesion. On esophagogram, the neo-oesophagus (pulled up stomach) was seen in the right paramedian retrosternal region (Figures 2a and 2b). There was no opacification of the native oesophagus. Unenhanced chest CT showed passage of oral contrast through the neo-oesophagus into the stomach. There was a well-defined fluid-filled elongated cystic lesion (max. diameter of 6.8 cm) in the posterior mediastinum, posterior to the heart and anterior to the descending thoracic aorta. It was communicating with the narrowed proximal and mid native oesophagus (Figures 3a and 3b).
discussion: Surgical isolation of the oesophagus is done in cases of atresia, trachea-oesophageal fistula, oesophageal strictures (peptic, corrosive), malignancy, or perforation [1]. A surgical neo-oesophagus is created in the substernal region by using either the stomach, the colon, or rarely, the jejunum as a conduit [2]. The native oesophagus is left in situ, unless there is severe esophagitis [3]. However, excision of the diseased oesophagus is considered when feasible, especially in the absence of factors such as previous perforation, mediastinitis, dense adhesions, or fistula formation. Additionally, excision of the native oesophagus is beneficial according to certain schools of thought, given the risk of development of cicatricial carcinoma at the site of chronic stricture. A mucocele of the oesophagus is a rare complication of oesophageal isolation where there is continuous secretion of mucus by the chronically irritated native oesophagus [3]. The rarity of this complication is secondary to the fact that usually the mucosa is almost completely destroyed by recurrent chronic inflammation and scarring [4]. The size of the mucocele depends on the intraluminal pressure. Usually, the mucus glands undergo atrophy under high pressure, which serves as a checkpoint for further increase in size [5]. The mucocele is usually asymptomatic and is often discovered incidentally. However, it is brought to attention mostly by virtue of its size, which causes mass effects on the adjacent structures. Other complications include secondary infection, development of a fistula, or perforation. Radiological investigations play a key role in the diagnosis of a mucocele. Although not specific, a radiograph shows a well-defined posterior mediastinal opacity. Air-fluid levels are absent [2]. Even on barium studies, the excluded segment of the oesophagus does not fill with barium. CT and MRI help in characterisation and diagnosis, especially in the given clinical context. On CT, the lesion shows fluid density and owing to its multiplanar reconstruction, the relation with the excluded oesophagus is established. The lesion is hyperintense on T2 and hypointense on T1-weighted MRI sequences. Hyperintensity on T1 sequences suggests a proteinaceous nature of the content. When there is superadded infection, there is increased attenuation of the contents with peripheral enhancement and adjacent fat stranding. On MRI, there is a diffusion restriction of the infected contents. Imaging differentials include common posterior mediastinal cystic lesions such as foregut duplication cyst (oesophageal, bronchogenic or neurenteric), post-operative collection, and intrathoracic pancreatic pseudocyst. Surgical history clinches the diagnosis along with the relation to the native oesophagus. Mucoceles usually develop within weeks or a few months after the surgery. However, in our case, the patient presented after many years, thus stressing the point that the pathology could be elusive, and radiology plays a key role in the diagnosis [6]. The common complications in cases of gastric conduit include anastomotic leak and stricture, which are demonstrated on conventional imaging such as esophagogram [7]. When symptomatic, the management of a mucocele includes surgical resection. A CT-guided percutaneous drainage is a temporary solution [4]. There is also a risk of the development of carcinoma, which supports the idea of mucocele resection. Oesophageal bypass should be reserved for patients with a limited lifespan or contraindications for esophagectomy [8].

title: Abdominopelvic actinomycosis masquerading peritoneal carcinomatosis
clinical_history: A 46-year-old woman was admitted with fever, night sweats, weight loss and abdominal pain for several months. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the lower quadrants. Past history included HIV infection under antiretroviral therapy, with viral load undetectable. The laboratory tests showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia and elevation of C-reactive protein.
imaging_findings: Abdominal and pelvic (suprapubic) ultrasound (US) revealed an intramural uterine leiomyoma and an intrauterine device (IUD) well placed in the endometrial cavity. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) revealed multiple areas of nodular thickening in the root of the mesentery and throughout the peritoneum (Figures 1 and 2). There are also signs of invasion of the abdominal wall. Small volume of ascites was identified in the parietocolic gutters and in the rectouterine pouch (Figures 3, 4, and 5).
discussion: Background Actinomycosis is a rare but severe chronic bacterial infection caused by Actinomyces spp., most commonly Actinomyces israelii . Actinomycetes are commensal inhabitants of the oral cavity and gastrointestinal tract, causing infection when they breach the mucous membranes [1]. Pelvic actinomycosis is included in the spectrum of pelvic inflammatory diseases, and the main risk factors are IUD, previous surgeries and trauma. Abdominal extension occurs by contiguous spread [2]. Clinical Perspective Clinical presentation is nonspecific, usually indolent abdominal pain, weight loss, fever, abnormal vaginal discharge, bowel obstruction or hydronephrosis. A palpable mass may be present [3,4]. Imaging Perspective US is usually the first-line imaging modality, but CT and/or magnetic resonance play important roles in the evaluation of the disease extent. The most common imaging finding is a complex adnexal mass with heterogeneous contrast enhancement, associated or not with bowel wall thickening. Involvement of multiple anatomical compartments violating anatomical boundaries is typical, as in our case, and the contiguous spread of the infection leads to extensive inflammatory fat infiltration. Characteristically, there is minimal or no ascites, which may be a clue. Tubo-ovarian abscesses may occur in severe cases [1,3,5]. These imaging findings overlap with other gynaecological and non-gynaecological conditions, including intestinal lymphoma and Crohn’s disease, particularly when there is bowel wall thickening. The presence of caseating lymphadenopathy is highly suggestive of peritoneal tuberculosis. Locally advanced ovarian cancer may be suspected in the presence of a complex adnexal mass with an infiltrative and aggressive pattern of spread. Peritoneal carcinomatosis manifests as fluid accumulation within the peritoneal cavity and soft-tissue infiltration of the various peritoneal ligaments and mesenteries. There are several distribution patterns, the mass-like pattern is the most similar to actinomycosis. One should be aware that the distribution of peritoneal carcinosis is clearly related to ascitic fluid dynamics, which is a game changer in differentiating these two entities [3,5–7]. The diagnosis of actinomycosis is confirmed with microbiology, with the identification of the bacteria. Outcome In our case, the clinical and imaging findings raised suspicion of peritoneal carcinomatosis, so a core biopsy of the abdominal wall mass was performed. The histopathological examination revealed inflammatory changes caused by Actinomyces israelii . Prompt treatment with intravenous penicillin G is essential to prevent complications that ultimately may lead to infertility. For more severe cases, combined medical and surgical treatment may be required [2]. Removal of the IUD is also mandatory. Take Home Message Pelvic actinomycosis is a challenging diagnosis. This condition should be included in the differential diagnosis of an adnexal/pelvic mass, specifically when an IUD is present and/or when the mass has aggressive imaging features. An inconclusive biopsy should also raise suspicion for this diagnosis. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Peritoneal carcinomatosis Peritoneal tuberculosis Abdominopelvic actinomycosis Primary ovarian cancer

title: Slipping rib syndrome: An unrecognised cause of chest pain
clinical_history: A 39-year-old male, with no prior relevant medical history, presents with atraumatic intermittent sharp pain in the lower segment of the right anterior thoracic wall. The symptoms began two months earlier when the patient started exercising (CrossFit), mostly triggered by training (especially abdominal crunches) whilst being asymptomatic in normal daily activities.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound imaging of the costochondral region of the patient showed a normal arrangement of ribs and rib cartilage while the patient was in a supine position (Figure 1). No abnormalities in bone or cartilage contours, nor any soft tissue lesions were identified. Dynamic ultrasound of the symptomatic area, performed while the patient replicated the movement that elicits pain (abdominal crunches), revealed hypermobility of the 9th rib cartilage, which moved upwards and became pinned beneath the 8th rib cartilage (Figures 2 and 3). This triggered the pain, with a popping sensation associated. When the patient returned to the supine position, the 9th rib returned to its normal position (Figure 4).
discussion: Background Slipping rib syndrome (SRS) is a rarely diagnosed condition, characterised by hypermobility of one or more “false” ribs (8–10th) [1–3], allowing the lower rib cartilage to become pinned beneath the upper rib of the affected segment, which in turn leads to friction/irritation of the intercostal nerve, straining of the intercostal muscles, and overall tissue inflammation [1]. It was first described in 1919 by Edgar Ferdinand Cyriax and is also known as the Cyriax syndrome. Few cases have been reported in the literature, with some studies suggesting a higher prevalence among women [3]. Both direct trauma and indirect mechanisms—such as forceful respiratory movements or strenuous pushing/lifting actions—are considered primary aetiological factors in the development of this syndrome [1]. Clinical Perspective Due to the nonspecific localisation of pain, the relative rarity of the condition, and a general lack of awareness among physicians, the diagnosis of SRS may be delayed by years [1]. It is often misdiagnosed as psychogenic pain [1], which leads to nontherapeutic procedures and medications [2]. The diagnosis of SRS is primarily clinical and can be supported by physical examination, notably through the hooking manoeuvre, first described in 1977 [5]. Patients typically present with sharp, intermittent pain that transitions into a dull, aching discomfort after the inferior rib returns to its normal position. The pain may follow a dermatomal distribution within the affected intercostal space, originating anteriorly and radiating posteriorly [2]. Patients often report a clicking or popping sensation in the affected area. Pain in the costochondral region is commonly triggered by sudden or jerking movements, such as sneezing, coughing, bending forward, or chest rotation. These provocative manoeuvres, or a combination thereof, are frequently encountered in sports and recognised as common triggers for SRS [4]. Imaging Perspective Imaging can play a role in the diagnostic process. Chest radiographs are usually unremarkable, and computed tomography often fails to detect any abnormality, as the supine position generally alleviates symptoms [1]. However, dynamic ultrasound performed while the patient replicates the movement/position that provokes pain—such as coughing or performing abdominal crunches—may demonstrate slipping of the affected costochondral area. Outcome Treatment includes conservative/medical therapies (decreased activity, physical therapy, oral/topical NSAIDs), minimally invasive procedures (nerve block), surgery [2], or a combination of these. Take Home Message SRS is a rare condition characterised by hypermobility of the false ribs. Radiologists should be familiar with its clinical presentation and imaging findings to facilitate accurate diagnosis and ensure appropriate patient management. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Tietze syndrome Costochondritis Rib fracture Slipping rib syndrome Pleuritic pain Sternalis syndrome

title: Sphenoid sinus mycetoma: A rare cause of chronic headache
clinical_history: A 71-year-old female presented with progressively worsening holocranial headache over 3 years, occasionally accompanied by photophobia and phonophobia, sometimes waking her at night, and refractory to mild analgesics. She denied visual symptoms, sinus surgery, or head trauma. Ear, nose, and throat (ENT) examination was unremarkable.
imaging_findings: CT of the paranasal sinuses revealed complete opacification of the left sphenoid sinus by a hyperattenuating lesion, with moderate expansion and smooth thinning and remodelling of its osseous walls (Figure 1a). Calcifications were present within the lesion (Figures 1b and 3). A focal dehiscence of the sinus roof in close proximity to the anterior cranial fossa floor and sclerosis of the posterior and lateral walls of the sinus were seen (Figure 1b and 1c). On MRI, the lesion was iso to mildly hypointense on T1-W (Figure 2a) and markedly hypointense on T2-W (Figure 2b). Restricted diffusion was observed in the right sphenoid sinus on DWI/ADC (Figure 4a). Post-contrast T1-W imaging revealed a smooth peripheral rim of enhancement (Figure 5). Additionally, a thin dural enhancement was noted contiguous to the erosion of the sinus roof. The adjacent brain parenchyma appeared normal, with no signs of oedema or infiltration.
discussion: Background Mycetoma, also known as fungal ball, represents the most prevalent form of non-invasive fungal rhinosinusitis in immunocompetent individuals and is primarily associated with impaired mucociliary clearance, which facilitates fungal proliferation, particularly by Aspergillus fumigatus [1,2]. While it most commonly involves the maxillary sinus, the sphenoid sinus is affected in 10–25% of cases [3]. Clinical Perspective Mycetomas are frequently asymptomatic and are often identified incidentally during radiologic evaluation. When symptomatic, they most commonly present with headache, typically localised to the territory of the first branch of the trigeminal nerve, retro-orbital pressure and visual disturbances, which are primarily attributed to optic nerve compression or inflammation [4]. Imaging is essential for diagnosis, assessing disease extension, and planning surgery to avoid complications. Imaging Perspective Initial imaging suggested a sphenoid sinus mucocele, characterised by a well-defined expansile lesion with bone remodelling and hypointensity on both T1-W and T2-W imaging—a feature often seen in mucoceles containing proteinaceous or dehydrated material. However, surgical exploration revealed dense fungal debris within the sphenoid sinus. This prompted a retrospective review of the imaging, which revealed additional features supporting the diagnosis of a mycetoma. These included the presence of calcifications—corroborated by susceptibility-weighted imaging on MRI—, heterogeneity in density and signal within the lesion, and bony sclerosis of the lateral and posterior walls of the sphenoid sinus on CT. The smooth, thin linear dural enhancement without parenchymal involvement may suggest reactive pachymeningeal enhancement secondary to chronic inflammatory changes associated with the adjacent dehiscent sinus roof. While these findings may raise concern for potential extrasinus extension, as seen in invasive fungal rhinosinusitis, the absence of typical features such as destructive bone erosion, soft tissue invasion or aggressive imaging characteristics, support the interpretation of the bony dehiscence as a result of chronic pressure-induced bone remodelling. Outcome In this case, the patient underwent a type III left sphenoidal sinusotomy via endoscopic sinus surgery, which revealed the sinus filled with yellow, tenacious debris mixed with necrotic material (Figure 6). Microbiological analysis confirmed the presence of Aspergillus fumigatus . Recurrence is not expected since adequate sinus ventilation and drainage were achieved. Imaging is crucial in surgical planning as it identifies dissection limits, anatomical variations and critical structures, ensuring a safer removal of the lesion. Take Home Message Mycetomas should be considered in the differential diagnosis of sphenoid sinus lesions, namely when mucoceles exhibit atypical features. Lesions exhibiting T2-W hypointensity and magnetic susceptibility artefacts suggestive of calcification are suggestive of a mycetoma. Endoscopic sinus surgery ensures mycetoma treatment with low recurrence risk. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
differential_diagnosis: Sphenoid sinus mycetoma Isolated chronic rhinosinusitis Sphenoid sinus mucocele Invasive fungal rhinosinusitis

title: Kaposi sarcoma of the palate
clinical_history: A 48-year-old male smoker presented with a 3-month history of painful oral erythematous lesions, aggravated by feeding and cold water, and weight loss. Examination revealed two ulcerative violaceous lesions on the left anterior hard palate and the right posterior hard palate. No palpable cervical lymph nodes or other mucocutaneous lesions were seen.
imaging_findings: With a presumptive diagnosis of squamous cell cancer (SCC), the patient underwent a biopsy of the larger lesion and a computed tomography (CT) of the oral cavity and soft tissues of the neck, which revealed a 25 mm, ill-defined, hyperenhancing lesion with bone erosion on the left hard palate, protruding into the nasal fossa (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d), and a 10 mm hyperenhancing lesion on the right posterior hard palate with periodontal osteolysis of the adjacent molar teeth, teeth loosening, and alveolar bone destruction (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d). Palatine canals and pterygopalatine fossa were unremarkable. There was hypertrophy of the palatine tonsils and nasopharynx lymphoid tissue, and multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes without necrosis or calcifications, the largest at level IIIB bilaterally, with approximately 22 mm in maximum diameter. The biopsy showed subepithelial vascular proliferation CD34+, spindle cells with low to moderate atypia expressing human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8), and slit-like vascular spaces compatible with Kaposi sarcoma (KS). Laboratory testing disclosed human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) 1 infection with a CD4 count of 24 cells/μl.
discussion: Background Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)-associated KS is a rare angioproliferative malignant neoplasm [1] and the most common HIV-associated neoplasm [2,3]. It accounts for 90% of HIV-related neoplasms in patients with AIDS [2], although rarer since the introduction of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) [2,3]. It is well established that HHV8 contributes to the development of KS [1–4] and can be transmitted sexually, via blood and saliva [3]. Clinical Perspective KS predominantly involves the mucocutaneous regions [1,2] but can be disseminated, affecting multiple systems [2,3]. Oral cavity KS occurs in up to 65% of patients with AIDS-associated KS [3], and the most commonly affected sites are the palate, gingiva, and tongue [3,5]. Clinically, it presents as painful, purplish exophytic, often ulcerated, and multicentric lesions [1,5] that are soft on palpation and may haemorrhage after minor trauma [1]. Imaging Perspective Imaging aids in diagnosing, staging, and follow-up [1]. Key imaging features include multicentricity, vivid contrast enhancement, and adjacent bone erosion [3]. In the jaws, periodontal osteolysis with teeth loosening is common [1,3,5] and raises diagnostic problems with other HIV-associated conditions, such as bacillary angiomatosis and necrotising ulcerative periodontitis [5]. The presence of other signs of HIV infection, such as lymphoid tissue hyperplasia of the Waldeyer’s ring, enlarged cervical lymph nodes, and lymphoepithelial parotid cysts, may raise a higher degree of suspicion. When HIV infection is not known, the diagnosis can be challenging, and lesions are often mistaken for other common conditions such as SCC, minor salivary gland tumours, and vascular tumours [5] or malformations [4]. Biopsy is mandatory to confirm the diagnosis, which shows typical spindled endothelial cells with minimal to moderate atypia bordering slit-like vascular spaces [1] and immunohistochemical identification of HHV8 [1]. Outcome Treatment depends on prognostic factors, dividing patients into low-risk and high-risk [3]. HAART is the first-line treatment for low-risk patients; however, after its introduction, practitioners must remain vigilant for potentially fatal exacerbations of KS due to immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) [3]. Chemotherapy is used for aggressive disseminated disease and non-responsive/recurrent disease [3]. Antiangiogenic drugs may also be used for disease control [3]. Excision is reserved for bulky lesions with functional or cosmetic impact [3]. Radiation therapy should be used with caution as it has been associated with toxic mucosal reactions [3]. Kaposi sarcoma (KS) in AIDS patients is associated with a poor prognosis [3]. However, the course of the disease can vary significantly [1], from a slow, inactive condition to a rapidly advancing illness, resulting in death [2]. In our patient, as the disease was localised and the prognostic index was favourable, it was decided to start only HAART. The oral lesions disappeared almost completely after 6 months, and the patient is doing well, with a CD4 count of 83 cells/μl. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Retroperitoneal ganglioneuroblastoma presenting with enuresis and hypogastric pain
clinical_history: A 9-year-old child presented with a complaint of intermittent lower abdominal pain and nocturnal enuresis for two months. There were no gastrointestinal issues, weight loss, asthenia, or lower urinary tract symptoms. The patient had no significant past medical history. During the physical examination, a palpable mass with a hard consistency and non-mobile nature was detected on the left flank. Laboratory studies were normal, including urine catecholamine levels. Tumour markers, including hCG, AFP, and CEA, were also assessed and found to be within normal ranges.
imaging_findings: Abdominal ultrasound revealed a solid mass inferior to the left kidney and anterior to the psoas muscle (Figure 1a). The mass was vascularised (Figure 1b), had smooth edges, was slightly heterogeneous, predominantly isoechogenic, with some echogenic foci inside, and measured 5 x 5 x 11 cm in the axial, anteroposterior, and longitudinal axes (Figure 1c). Further MRI studies (Figures 2a and 2b) showed a retroperitoneal mass inferior to the left kidney and between the left psoas and quadratus lumborum muscles. While there was no evidence of invasion into adjacent structures, it did result in anterior shifting of the psoas muscle. The lesion exhibited an intermediate and heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted images and a low signal on T1-weighted images (Figure 3), with no restriction on the diffusion study (Figures 4a and 4b). The dynamic study (Figures 5a, 5b, 5c, and 5d) presented heterogeneous and progressive uptake by the contrast product, being more evident in the later phase.
discussion: Primary retroperitoneal solid tumours are uncommon and, as a recent study revealed, around 70% of paediatric primary retroperitoneal malignant tumours were of neurogenic origin [1]. In our case, a percutaneous biopsy was initially performed, and histological analysis revealed a peripheral neuroblastic tumour with a predominance of ganglioneuromatous elements, with the final diagnosis to be confirmed on the surgical specimen. Then, the tumour was surgically resected, and the final histological diagnosis was ganglioneuroblastoma-intermixed (GNBI). Peripheral neurogenic tumours are embryonal tumours that originate from primitive neural crest cells in the neuroectoderm [4] and are histologically divided into four main categories: neuroblastoma, ganglioneuroblastoma-nodular, ganglioneuroblastoma-intermixed, and ganglioneuroma [2,5]. GNBI is considered a transitional tumour composed of ganglionic cells at different levels of development, and for this reason, its biological behaviour is intermediate between neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroma. This rare tumour affects older children rather than infants and neonates, who are more commonly diagnosed with neuroblastoma. GNBI occurs in locations where sympathetic nervous system cells are present, with the most common sites being the adrenal medulla, extra-adrenal retroperitoneum, and posterior mediastinum. Diagnosing this tumour in the early stages can be challenging due to the nonspecific nature or absence of symptoms [5]. When symptoms do occur, abdominal pain is the most common, caused by local effects from the primary tumour or metastatic disease [3]. In our case, the child experienced enuresis, likely due to the compressive effect on the bladder or nerve bundles. Pain in the hypogastric region can also be attributed to the tumour’s size and its compressive effect on adjacent structures. Multimodality imaging is necessary for the diagnosis, staging, response assessment, and follow-up of GNBI [5]. Generally, GNBIs have a regular shape with well-defined margins that can cause pressure displacement of surrounding large vessels and structures. In the US, GNBI tumours typically appear as a heterogeneous and predominantly echogenic mass, with anechoic areas indicating necrosis or haemorrhage, and echogenic foci suggesting calcifications. Doppler ultrasound can assess blood flow in vessels surrounded by tissue [3]. At MR imaging, ganglioneuroblastoma usually appears as a heterogeneous mass, with variable enhancement, demonstrating relatively low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) offers valuable insights into tumour differentiation, with ganglioneuroblastomas exhibiting higher apparent diffusion coefficient values compared to poorly differentiated neuroblastomas [5]. CT scans and nuclear medicine tests are also important to evaluate metastatic disease, as the staging significantly influences the outcome of these patients. In our case, the child underwent both a chest CT and an MIBG (meta-iodobenzylguanidine) scan (Figure 6), which revealed no evidence of metastasis. Molecular analysis of the tumour revealed a pathogenic variant in the PTEN gene. Additionally, the MYCN status was evaluated and found to be negative, which supports a less aggressive tumour phenotype [2]. Early radical surgery is the best treatment for retroperitoneal ganglioneuroblastoma. The prognosis depends on the ratio of neuroblasts to ganglion cells in histology. Older age and larger tumour size are associated with poorer outcomes [4].

title: Traumatic brachial plexopathy
clinical_history: A 47-year-old man presented with a history of weakness in the right arm since a few weeks. There was a history of a road traffic accident two months back.
imaging_findings: MRI of the brachial plexus showed a pre-fixed plexus with supply from the C4 nerve root. There was diffuse oedema in the C4–C6 nerve roots with thickening of the C5 and C6 nerve roots and the superior trunk (Figures 1a, 1b, and 2c). The nerve roots were hyperintense on T2 sequences and bulky as compared to the contralateral side (Figures 2a and 2b). There was oedematous thickening of the right axillary nerve throughout its course with subacute denervation oedema in the deltoid and the teres minor muscles (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c). Subacute denervation with grade I fatty infiltration is also noted in the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles.
discussion: Adult onset brachial plexopathy can be either traumatic or non-traumatic. Non traumatic causes include infections, inflammation, neoplasm, radiotherapy, etc. MRI offers an excellent insight into the anatomy as well as the pathologies affecting the brachial plexus. Brachial plexus is formed by the postganglionic ventral nerve roots from C5–T1. The pre- and postganglionic segments are labelled with respect to the dorsal root ganglion. They are further subdivided into five roots, three trunks, six divisions and three cords. The major terminal nerves (musculocutaneous, median, radial and ulnar nerves) are branches of the cords. When the C4 root is included, it is termed as pre-fixed, whereas when T2 is included, it is post-fixed [1]. Understanding the important anatomical landmarks is mandatory to localise the affected segment. Roots are assessed at the level of the foramen with the first rib as a landmark for C8 and T1 roots. The trunks are assessed in the interscalene triangle above the first rib along the subclavian artery. The divisions are beyond the lateral margin of the first rib and posterior to the clavicle. The cords are located adjacent to the coracoid process and adjacent to the axillary artery. The terminal nerves are at the four corners surrounding the axillary artery [2]. Nerve conduction study serves as an adjunct to MRI in cases of traumatic plexopathies. Seddon proposed a functional classification for nerve injuries as neuropraxia, axonotmesis and neurotmesis. The nerve rootlets are best appreciated on MR myelography. The arachnoid mater stops at the level of the foramina, while only the dura mater extends beyond. Hence, any cerebrospinal fluid containing lesion is either an arachnoid diverticulum or post-traumatic pseudomeningocele (seen in 80% of avulsions) [3]. Rootlet contrast enhancement and muscle signal intensity alteration (T2, T1 hyperintensity with contrast enhancement) are indirect markers of nerve injury. Paravertebral muscle changes suggest preganglionic involvement. Postganglionic pathologies are identified as nerve thickening and hyperintensity with denervation oedema. These changes are better evaluated on STIR sequences. In acute denervation, the muscle is hyperintense on T2 with maintained bulk, while in subacute denervation, there is varied T2 hyperintensity with a mild increase in signal on T1. In chronic denervation, there is fatty atrophy of the muscle [4]. Management depends on the nature of involvement, such as pre vs post ganglionic injury, and encompasses a multidisciplinary approach, including surgical repair and physiotherapy. Commonly used nerve grafts are sural, medial pectoral, phrenic and the spinal accessory nerve [5].

title: Adult communicating hydrocoele presenting as intermittent inguinal swelling
clinical_history: A 25-year-old male patient presents with complaints of an intermittently appearing right inguinal lump. The swelling is described as painless, usually induced by heavy exercise, and manually reducible. His general practitioner suspects an inguinal hernia, and the patient is referred to our hospital for an ultrasound.
imaging_findings: Initially, at ultrasound, a normal right inguinal canal is seen, with no herniation at rest or inducible by Valsalva manoeuvre. We asked the patient to stand up and repeat the Valsalva manoeuvre, but still no herniation or swelling was perceived (Figure 1). Given the suggestive clinical history, the patient was asked to move around until the swelling could be noticed. After this, an infiltrating anechogenic fluid was seen in and surrounding the inguinal canal, disappearing after applying some pressure (Figure 2). Subsequent abdominal ultrasound excluded ascites or major intra-abdominal anomalies. Scrotal ultrasound was performed next, showing a bilateral hydrocele without any further intrascrotal anomaly (Figures 3a and 3b). The right-sided hydrocele was confirmed to increase after reduction of the inguinal fluid, confirming our suspicion of communication through a patent processus vaginalis.
discussion: Background The processus vaginalis embryologically forms as a peritoneal evagination through the internal inguinal ring during the third month of foetal life, through which the testicles descend. The inguinal portion subsequently obliterates, with the distal portion persisting as the tunica vaginalis. Closure usually happens within the first 6 months after birth, patency rates gradually decline until age 3–5. Usually, the left side closes before the right side. Patency-related pathology is thus usually seen in the paediatric population [1]. Clinical Perspective Failure of normal closure can result in inguinal herniation, isolated cord hydrocele or communicating hydrocele, also termed congenital hydrocele. Infants usually present with groin swelling exacerbated by raised intra-abdominal swelling (e.g., crying or straining). Congenital hydroceles will usually spontaneously resolve before the age of 2 [2]. Examples of symptomatic patent processus vaginalis in the adult population are rare. Imaging Perspective Typically, communicating hydrocele is diagnosed clinically in the paediatric population. However, for atypical presentations such as inguinal swelling in an adult patient, as in this case, ultrasound can help confirm the diagnosis. Ultrasound will show anechoic fluid that may communicate with the peritoneum and extend into the scrotum [3]. A hydrocele of the spermatic cord is a variant where fluid is present within a segment of a patent processus vaginalis with obliterated processus distally. A scrotal hydrocele will only show fluid surrounding the testis without proximal communication. It is important to perform the ultrasound also in a standing position, preferably with a Valsalva manoeuvre, to confirm the diagnosis. Outcome Surgery is usually curative, with plication being the procedure of choice. In the paediatric population, watchful waiting will usually result in spontaneous closure by the age of 1, while in the adult population, surgical options are selected based on the underlying cause, but with an excellent prognosis [2]. Take Home Message When encountering unexpected findings on ultrasound, it is often important to take a step back and hypothesise possible underlying causes. As in this case, the clinical suggestion of inguinal herniation with discordant findings of inguinal fluid should prompt an additional search of either abdominal or scrotal causes. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Moyamoya disease: An unusual blood vessel condition
clinical_history: A 25-year-old female presents to the emergency department with disorientation. No neurological focality is observed. The patient has a history of migraine and blurred vision in the past year. No other relevant medical background.
imaging_findings: CT shows loss of grey-white matter differentiation in the left parietal lobe and hypointensity in the white matter (Figures 1a and 1b), which indicates a stroke lesion in the left parietal lobe. In CT with contrast (Figures 2a and 2b), stenosis of the right middle cerebral artery (arrow), a filiform course of the left middle cerebral artery and extensive collateral circulation in the region are seen (arrowheads). Angiogram of the left cerebral circulation (Figures 3a and 3b) confirms the presence of significant vascular collateralisation around the circle of Willis (arrows), giving the classic “puff of smoke” appearance. An irregular vascular course with multiple stenoses is also observed. The angiogram of the contralateral side (Figures 3c and 3d) shows similar findings. FLAIR-weighted (Figure 4a) and T1 post-contrast (Figure 4b) images show cortical hyperintensity and cortical enhancement, respectively, in the left parietal region (arrows).
discussion: Background Moyamoya disease is an idiopathic vasculopathy that causes stenosis in the intracranial internal carotid arteries and the proximal branches of the cerebral arteries [1]. The incidence is higher in individuals of Asian descent and in females. It has two incidence peaks: in childhood and between 30 and 40 years old [1–3]. Clinical Perspective The stenoses lead to the formation of multiple collaterals around the circle of Willis, the cortical surface, the leptomeninges, and branches of the external carotid artery through the dura. This explains the clinical presentation: on one hand, stroke due to the stenosis itself, and on the other, symptoms resulting from the collaterals, mainly haemorrhages due to vessel fragility, or both. Some individuals experience headaches due to the contact of collaterals with nerve endings in the dura [1,2]. Moyamoya syndrome is the presence of this vascular pattern caused by an underlying pathology [2]. Some of these entities are listed below in the differential diagnosis list. Imaging Perspective The main finding is the presence of multiple stenoses or occlusions in the major intracranial arteries, along with numerous collateral vessels, giving the classic “puff of smoke” appearance. The findings can be observed with any imaging technique. However, despite multiple advances in non-invasive imaging modalities, angiography remains the gold standard [3,4]. Collaterals may be high-flow, manifesting as tortuous flow voids on T1 and T2-weighted sequences. However, low-flow pial collaterals may also be present. This manifests as cortical enhancement on T1-weighted sequences after intravenous contrast administration and as hyperintensity on T2/FLAIR sequences, leading to the classic “ivy sign” [3–5]. In case of microbleeds, blooming artefacts can be observed on susceptibility-weighted sequences. Outcome The prognosis of the disease is variable and depends on its severity. The Suzuki grading system is based on radiological findings and allows for the determination of severity, thus providing prognostic value [2]. The treatment of these patients is complex. Medical management is primarily based on antithrombotic and antiplatelet agents; however, the risk-benefit ratio must be carefully considered due to the risk of haemorrhage. Surgical revascularisation has been considered for the management of recurrent strokes and cerebral haemodynamic impairment [6]. Follow-up Our patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for monitoring. Tests to identify secondary causes were negative. The patient was discharged with mixed aphasia, and close follow-up was recommended. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
