title: Classic MRI findings in a case of Japanese encephalitis
clinical_history: A 28-year-old previously healthy female presented to the emergency department with high-grade fever, chills, and rigors for three days, followed by a sudden onset of confusion, disorientation, and generalised tonic-clonic seizures. There was no recent travel or vaccination history, but she resides in an area with reported endemic activity of Japanese encephalitis (Amritsar, Punjab, India). No focal neurological deficits were noted on initial examination.
imaging_findings: On MRI, T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences demonstrated hyperintense signals involving the bilateral thalami, caudate nuclei, pons, midbrain, and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) showed corresponding areas of restricted diffusion, indicative of acute or subacute pathology. Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) revealed patchy focal blooming within the thalami, suggestive of haemorrhagic components. The basilar artery flow void was preserved on T2-weighted images. MR venography showed no evidence of thrombosis in the internal cerebral veins or the straight sinus.
discussion: Background Japanese encephalitis (JE) is a mosquito-borne flavivirus infection endemic to parts of Asia. It is the most common cause of viral encephalitis in Southeast Asia and the Western Pacific. While several flaviviruses can cause encephalitis, Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is notable for producing especially severe neurological complications [1]. Once in the central nervous system, JEV triggers inflammation, neuronal injury, and oedema, particularly involving deep grey matter structures such as the thalami and basal ganglia. Clinical Perspective Patients typically present with an acute febrile illness that may progress to altered mental status, seizures, and focal neurological deficits [2]. Imaging is essential for early diagnosis and to differentiate JE from other causes of encephalitis and acute febrile encephalopathy. Radiologists play a key role by identifying hallmark imaging features suggestive of JE, guiding serological testing and timely supportive care. Imaging Perspective MRI is the imaging modality of choice in suspected cases of JE. Classic findings include bilateral symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the thalami, especially the pulvinar region. Additional involvement of the midbrain, basal ganglia, cerebellum, and cerebral cortex may also be observed. Restricted diffusion is often present in the acute phase, as demonstrated in this case. Haemorrhagic changes may occur and were evident in our patient on SWI [3]. Outcome Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein levels. JE-specific IgM antibodies were detected in the CSF via ELISA, confirming the diagnosis. The patient received supportive treatment, including antiepileptics and intensive care management. Neurological recovery was partial, with residual cognitive deficits noted at discharge. Take Home Message / Teaching Points In patients presenting with acute febrile encephalopathy and bilateral thalamic involvement on MRI, Japanese encephalitis (JE) should be a key consideration, particularly in endemic regions. Early recognition through imaging facilitates appropriate diagnostic testing, management, and prognostication. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Hepatopulmonary hydatid disease complicated with bronchopleural fistula and hydropneumothorax
clinical_history: A 19-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department with acute left-sided pleuritic chest pain, productive cough with whitish sputum, and dyspnoea. The patient reported recent pruritic skin lesions treated with corticosteroids and frequent contact with domestic animals. On examination, the patient was febrile and pulmonary auscultation revealed abolished breath sounds in the left lower lung field. Laboratory workup showed leukocytosis (11500/mm 3 ) with mild eosinophilia (7%).
imaging_findings: Chest X-ray demonstrated a left lower lobe cavitating lesion with air-fluid level (Figures 1b and 1c, arrows) and evidence of pleural effusion (Figure 1b, arrowhead). Contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed a cystic cavitating lesion (Figure 2a, arrow) complicated with hydropneumothorax (Figure 2a, star) in the likely context of an underlying bronchopleural fistula. Note the presence of the “water lily” sign (Figures 2b and 4) secondary to the presence of collapsed and folded endocyst membranes floating freely within the fluid-filled pericystic cavity, following gravity, and resembling water lily petals on the surface of a pond. Incidentally, a second cystic lesion was identified in the liver (Figure 5). The overall imaging findings were consistent with hepatopulmonary hydatidosis, which was serologically confirmed.
discussion: Hydatid disease, also known as echinococcosis, is a parasitic zoonosis resulting from the infection of Echinococcus tapeworm species (mainly E. granulosus and E. alveolaris/multilocularis ), endemic in Mediterranean countries and regions where livestock raising is common. The liver is the most frequently affected organ, followed by the lungs [1]. CT imaging is the modality of choice, allowing detection of cysts, internal membranes, wall calcifications, diaphragmatic defects when transdiaphragmatic spread into the pleural cavity is suspected, and complications such as rupture, infection or communication with the bronchial tree [2]. Based on their morphology and internal architecture, hydatid cysts are classified into four categories [3]: Type I: simple cyst. Type II: cyst with daughter cyst(s) and matrix. Type III: calcified cyst (dead cyst). Type IV: complicated cyst. In our case, the patient had a type IV pulmonary hydatid cyst in the left lower lobe complicated with bronchopleural fistula and subsequent hydropneumothorax. Incidentally, a second cystic lesion was found in the liver corresponding to a type I hydatid cyst. The treatment of hydatid disease ranges from the administration of antihelminthic agents (albendazole, mebendazole), surgical excision, or watchful waiting for inactive cysts. Regarding medical treatment, the outcomes were improved when surgery and antihelminthic therapy were combined [4]. In this case, serological testing was positive for Echinococcus granulosus and the patient was referred for medical treatment and surgical resection of the cystic lesions.

title: A cervical rib with pseudoarthrosis with the underlying first rib
clinical_history: A 19-year-old female presented with a 2-week history of painless swelling in the right side of her neck, which was preceded by intentional weight loss that was thought to have caused the swelling to become more prominent. On examination, a non-tender lump was noted in the right supraclavicular region.
imaging_findings: A plain radiographic series of the region of interest was initially performed, given that the palpable abnormality felt bony in nature. This showed an extra cervical rib on the right side, with an apparent pseudoarthrosis with the underlying first rib (Figures 1a, 1b, and 2). A CT scan was done during the same visit, and the mentioned finding was confirmed (Figures 3a, 3b, and 4).
discussion: Background Cervical ribs are a rare occurrence and are defined as accessory ribs originating from the 7th cervical vertebra [1]. They have a slight female predominance, and the majority are bilateral [7]. An even rarer occurrence is when a pseudoarthrosis forms between a cervical rib and the ipsilateral first thoracic rib. It results in the formation of either a bone bridge or a fibrous band, and is reported to be associated with mutations in Hox genes [2,3]. Clinical Perspective Cervical ribs with or without pseudoarthrosis often exist without causing any symptoms. The typical finding on examination is a hard, smooth, immobile and non-tender swelling in the posterior triangle or supraclavicular area of the neck [4]. They are a cause of thoracic outlet syndrome, which may present after years of no symptoms with neurovascular compromise of the ipsilateral upper limb. Evidence of this includes arm numbness or tingling, pain or ache in the neck, fatigue with use and arm swelling or a change in colour [2,3]. Imaging Perspective X-ray imaging demonstrates the presence of the cervical rib, while further evaluation with CT can confirm pseudoarthrosis between the ribs. X-ray is a useful initial assessment for the presence of a cervical rib. CT bone imaging can clearly demonstrate the articulation between a cervical rib and the ipsilateral thoracic rib by showing evidence of bony protrusions or exocytosis of the ribs. Concerning the differentials, in our case, osteophyte formation associated with cervical spondylosis was not seen on imaging, and was unlikely given the age of the patient. In addition, no aggressive features were demonstrated to suggest malignancy. Outcome Cases which do not cause any symptoms do not require intervention and can be left alone. However, when complicated by thoracic outlet syndrome, management is required. Conservative measures for milder cases include physiotherapy, occupational therapy and analgesia. In patients with symptoms that are non-resolving or that are severe, surgical resection of the rib and decompression scalenectomy are necessary [5,6]. Imaging with CT can accurately assess the extent and position of the pseudoarthrosis of the cervical rib. Take Home Message / Teaching Points A cervical rib pseudo-articulating with the underlying first rib, even though a rare entity, should be considered whenever an imaging specialist is faced with a supraclavicular lump that feels bony in nature. The patient may have been initially referred for ultrasound, in which case the cervical rib can be followed backwards towards the lower cervical spine, possibly also visualising the pseudoarticulation. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Bilateral ovarian lesions – What we should think about
clinical_history: A 53-year-old woman with a past medical history of rectal adenocarcinoma treated with mucosectomy 6 years ago presented with a 2-month history of abdominal distension and pain. Recent colonoscopy and endoscopy revealed no changes. She had minor anaemia and the CA-125 was elevated (3x the normal) with a normal CA of 19.9.
imaging_findings: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figures 1 and 2) revealed bulky, heterogeneous, large, multiloculated cystic lesions of probable ovarian origin with signal intensities on T1 and T2-weighted images, suggesting mucin content. Moreover, there were some irregular septa with contrast enhancement and restriction on diffusion-weighted sequences, with no solid component. There were neither ascites nor peritoneal nodules. Additionally, a suspicious peripheral hepatic lesion invading the diaphragm was documented. A percutaneous computed tomography-guided biopsy was performed (Figure 3), demonstrating probable pancreatic or biliary duct cell origin but not excluding metastatic lesion from a primary ovarian tumour. The diagnosis of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, presented initially as a bilateral ovarian tumour, was made in the analysis of the surgical specimen.
discussion: Bilateral malignant tumours involving the ovaries could be a primary, more frequently serous carcinoma, or metastasis [1]. The diagnosis is challenging because of the overlapping clinical and imaging features, mainly when ovarian metastases are the first sign of an undiagnosed primary cancer [1,2]. Ovarian metastases account for 3–5% of all ovarian malignancies, most of which originate from the digestive tract [1,3]. The most well-known ovarian metastasis is the Krukenberg tumour, resulting from a mucin-producing tumour, usually gastric or colonic adenocarcinoma, with cholangiocarcinoma being an infrequent cause [2–5]. The primary route for ovarian metastasis from intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is peritoneal spread [4,5]. On the other hand, ovarian cancer typically spreads along the peritoneum, so perihepatic and subdiaphragmatic implants are not uncommon. In both conditions, patients present nonspecific symptoms such as pelvic pain, abdominal distension, or weight loss. Despite the significant overlap of serum CA 19-9 level between primary and metastatic ovarian tumours, a high value in cases of bilateral ovarian masses should significantly raise the clinical suspicion of the metastatic tumour to the ovary, which was not the case [5]. CA-125 is nonspecific [5]. Imaging could also aid in distinguishing these two entities as it could find other locations for a primary malignancy. Ultrasound is usually the first modality of choice in suspected gynaecological pathologies, but MRI is superior for assessing pelvic masses as it can provide detailed tissue characterisation. Computed tomography is not recommended for the initial evaluation to study adnexal masses, although it is helpful to look for concomitant primary malignancy and stage when it is documented. Metastases to the ovary are more likely small, bilateral and predominantly solid and may have cystic areas as they occur with the most frequent bilateral ovarian tumours [1,6,7]. On the other hand, metastasis from colon cancer and appendiceal cancer can appear as multicystic ovarian tumours [7]. Bilateral predominant multiloculated cystic ovarian masses with a stained-glass appearance on MRI (represented by locules with different signals on T1WI and T2WI depending on the degree of mucin concentration) raise the suspicion of a mucinous nature [6,7]. Moreover, the cyst wall, septa thickness, and internal solid components or nodules demonstrated at contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging and DWI/ADC map sequences suggest malignancy over borderline and cystadenoma mucinous tumours [6,7]. As the preoperative differentiation between metastasis and primary ovarian tumours is essential in selecting the most appropriate treatment, radiologists should contemplate this diagnosis in patients with ovarian masses of unknown origin. title: Paraneoplastic anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor-related encephalitis
clinical_history: A 33-year-old female presented to the emergency department due to recurrent daily episodes of misperceptions (metamorphopsia, dysmetropsia), spontaneously self-limiting, evocative of Todd’s syndrome. No fever, headache, recent infections or vaccinations, or psychiatric history were reported. An electroencephalogram (EEG) showed a well-organised background with a slow right temporal focus, without seizures.
imaging_findings: An initial brain CT scan was inconclusive, while MRI showed a subcortical white matter lesion in the right temporoparietal area, characterised by T2/FLAIR digitiform hyperintensity (Figure 1a), no reduced diffusivity, with curvilinear gadolinium-enhancing lesions along perivascular spaces (Figures 1b and 1c). The perfusion study (Diffuse correlation spectroscopy, or DCS, technique) did not indicate increased rCBV values (Figure 1d). These findings steered towards an inflammatory process. An angiography was performed, which ruled out vasculitis and other vascular conditions. Systemic screening through CT and FDG-PET revealed the presence of a cephalopancreatic hypervascular lesion (Figure 2), attributable to a neuroendocrine tumour (pNET), confirmed by ultrasound endoscopic biopsy. PET showed hypometabolism of the temporal and occipital regions bilaterally, while the right temporoparietal lesion showed mild uptake (Figures 3a and 3b). Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination showed mild pleocytosis, type 2 oligoclonal banding, negative aquaporin 4 (AQP-4) and MOG antibody, while NMDAR antibody tested positive, suggestive of autoimmune encephalitis.
discussion: Background Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) encephalitis is currently the most common type of autoimmune encephalitis, mediated by antibodies against the NMDAR's GluN1 subunit. It is known that it can be the manifestation of a paraneoplastic process in about a quarter of cases. Above all, it is associated with ovarian teratomas, but other underlying neoplasms are also described [1]. Clinical Perspective NMDAR encephalitis is characterised by a wide spectrum of neuropsychiatric symptoms, usually starting with mental status changes, as acute psychosis, and progressing with dyskinesias, autonomic dysfunction, decreased consciousness and hypoventilation during the course of the disease [2]. Imaging Perspective The diagnostic approach is based on the 2016 Graus et al. criteria [3], reviewed in 2023 [4]. It uses a combination of conventional clinical neurological assessment and standard diagnostic tests (CSF studies, EEG), which generally do not involve MRI [3,4]. Although MRI shows significant findings in only up to half of the cases, especially in the early stages, it is essential to find features of encephalitis and exclude features of demyelination (in particular acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)) and other mimics (e.g., inherited mitochondrial and metabolic disorders) [5]. Brain MRI abnormalities, such as transient cortical signal changes and variable enhancement, differ widely, with no distinctive signs and localisation of the disease, limbic and extralimbic. Recent studies suggest that FDG-PET might be more sensitive than MRI in detecting abnormalities of anti-NMDAR encephalitis [6]. Typical FDG-PET findings in anti-NMDAR encephalitis include a characteristic anteroposterior glucose metabolism gradient, with frontotemporal hypermetabolism and occipital hypometabolism, although it demonstrates marked variability [7]. The integration of FDG-PET into the diagnostic workflow enhances the detection of subtle encephalitic changes. It is important to be aware that NMDAR encephalitis can occur synchronously or overlap with other demyelinating disorders in 4% of cases, especially with myelinating oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD), a rare clinical-radiological phenotype with seizures (FLAMES) or anti-AQP-4-related syndromes [8,9]. There are only a few case reports describing the association between this autoimmune encephalitis and neuroendocrine tumours in various districts, testifying to the significance of this case [10]. Outcome NMDAR encephalitis has a relatively good prognosis and usually responds well to first-line immunotherapy (e.g., intravenous methylprednisolone (IVMP), intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), and plasma exchange (PLEX)) if administered early. In our case, after treatment, the MR follow-up showed a remarkable reduction in pathologic findings (Figure 4). Take Home Message Autoimmune encephalitis requires a prompt clinical diagnostic framework in order to administer immunotherapy in a timely manner, improving patient outcomes and anticipating the long turnaround time of antibody results [11]. Cerebrospinal fluid testing, brain electrical activity studies and integrated imaging (MRI and FDG-PET) coordinate the clinical assessment. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Organic foreign body in the left main bronchus
clinical_history: A 7-month-old boy choked while eating corn but recovered after first aid. He experiences intermittent dyspnoea, stridor during respiration, and excessive crying.
imaging_findings: In chest computed tomography (CT), soft tissue with attenuated density is observed at the distal end of the left main bronchus, measuring approximately 5 x 3 mm (Figures 1a and 1b). Also observed is a unilateral hyperinflation of the left lung resulting from partial obstruction of the left main bronchus by a foreign body, “ball valve” imaging (Figures 2a and 2b). The virtual airway map revealed a discontinuity at the distal end of the left main bronchus (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Infants and young children frequently aspirate small food particles, with vegetable material being the most common cause of foreign body aspiration. Male children exhibit greater involvement than female children regarding incidences and mobility [1]. Clinical Perspective The initial signs of bronchial foreign bodies in children leading to lower airway obstruction consist of coughing, choking, sudden difficulty breathing, and the start of wheezing. Following this, a symptom-free period might occur, potentially making diagnosis more difficult [2]. A quiescent phase is frequently observed, lasting up to 1 week before complications such as pneumonia or atelectasis arise [3]. In cases with delayed presentation (≥ 30 days), foreign bodies are often obscured by granulation tissue and chronic inflammation, leading to higher false-negative rates during bronchoscopy; in one study, 25% of patients presented more than 1 month after aspiration, and late-stage cases commonly present with a cough producing mucus, fever, or repeated instances of pneumonia [3]. The right main bronchus exhibits a larger diameter, a smaller angle of divergence from the tracheal axis, and a greater airflow compared to the left bronchus. This anatomical configuration accounts for the higher incidence of foreign bodies in the right bronchial tree (53.7%) as opposed to the left (38.2%). Imaging Perspective Organic food items possess a radiolucent nature, making them challenging to detect on conventional X-ray imaging [4]. The false negative of a foreign body may be overlooked in 30% of cases [1,4]. A chest X-ray is normal in 40–60% of confirmed cases [3,5,6], with a reported sensitivity of 60–68% and specificity of 66–67% [5]. Indirect signs, such as air trapping, are considered more reliable but necessitate expiratory or decubitus views [3,8]. Chest CT/virtual bronchoscopy is the most effective modality for identifying impacted foreign bodies in the airway lumen, utilising thin slices and high-resolution contrast [1]. It offers a sensitivity of 85–100% and specificity of 50–100% [5,9], and also effectively detects radiolucent foreign bodies and complications such as bronchiectasis [10]. Bronchial foreign bodies are often misdiagnosed as asthma, bronchiolitis, or recurrent pneumonia [8,12]. Key steps to rule out alternatives include obtaining a history detailing a choking episode, present in 75–90% of cases [6], and persistent cough or wheeze unresponsive to bronchodilators [11,12]. Imaging is also crucial; repeated X-rays or CT scans are recommended if initial imaging is normal, but suspicion remains [8,13], and virtual bronchoscopy can help localise foreign bodies preoperatively [9]. Ultimately, bronchoscopy is required for a definitive diagnosis, particularly when imaging is negative but clinical suspicion is high [6,13]. Outcome Our patient underwent a flexible bronchoscopy for the removal of an organic foreign body. Notable improvement was observed after the procedure, with discharge occurring the following day. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Infants and young children, particularly males, frequently aspirate small vegetable food particles. Initial symptoms like coughing and choking may be followed by a symptom-free period; delayed presentation (≥ 30 days) is associated with chronic symptoms, granulation tissue, and higher false negatives. Due to anatomical differences, foreign bodies are more common in the right bronchus; organic items are radiolucent, leading to high rates of normal chest X-rays. Diagnosis relies on history (choking episode), imaging (CT/virtual bronchoscopy is effective with 85–100% sensitivity), and definitive bronchoscopy, especially to help rule out alternative respiratory conditions.

title: Diagnosis of nodular pulmonary amyloidosis by core needle biopsy
clinical_history: An 88-year-old patient presented with an incidental lung mass. A computed tomography-guided biopsy and a bronchoscopy were performed, but the results were inconclusive. Given the size and characteristics of the lesion, radiotherapy was considered. The patient was asymptomatic and exhibited a normal clinical examination. The third biopsy yielded diagnostic results.
imaging_findings: Conventional chest X-ray shows an enlarged right pulmonary hilum and magnification of the cardiac silhouette due to the superimposed right lower lobe mass (silhouette sign) (Figure 1). Computed tomography (CT) with a soft tissue window shows a right lower lobe mass with an approximate diameter of 38 x 36 x 66 mm, with ill-defined borders and calcifications within (Figure 2). The pulmonary window shows atelectasis adjacent to the mass, as well as bronchial contact without complete collapse (Figure 4). PET/CT (positron emission tomography) shows FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) fixation in the lesion, suggesting malignancy (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Amyloidosis is a rare systemic disease caused by extracellular deposition of insoluble proteins. Its aetiology and prevalence are uncertain. Primary (AL) amyloidosis is the most common form, with an annual incidence of 6–12 cases per million people [1]. Amyloidosis can affect any organ individually or in combination [2]. Amyloidosis deposition in the lungs is very infrequent. It is important to note that lung involvement is more commonly observed in the localised form [3]. Classic radiological signs of tracheobronchial and pulmonary disease include nodular and irregular narrowing of the tracheal lumen, airway wall thickening, nodules, and calcified amyloid deposits. The most common clinical manifestations are dyspnoea or cough, haemoptysis, and recurrent pneumonia [3]. Clinical Perspective Pulmonary amyloidosis is usually asymptomatic, but when it presents with dyspnoea, it is important to differentiate it from transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR), the incidence of which is increasing. The diagnosis differs from that of pulmonary amyloidosis; in ATTR, cardiac scintigraphy is essential [4]. Pulmonary lesions can easily be confused with malignant masses, both on CT and PET/CT, especially when they are hypermetabolic. In our patient, due to the uptake and size of the lesion, chemotherapy and radiotherapy were even considered [5]. A complete clinical history, including medical, family, occupational history, exposure to toxic agents, alcoholism and smoking, as well as a complete physical examination, is important to make a good differential diagnosis with lung cancer, interstitial lung diseases, fungal diseases and diseases associated with exposure [3]. Imaging Perspective Diagnostic tests include conventional chest X-ray, which may show calcified or non-calcified pulmonary nodules, bronchial thickening, and even airway opacification. Chest CT shows lesions in the form of nodules or parenchymal pulmonary masses, subpleural, and tracheal. PET/CT may or may not show FDG uptake in the lesions [5], which is a major problem in guiding the diagnosis. The definitive diagnosis is made using pathological anatomy with Congo red staining; the biopsy sample can be obtained by flexible bronchoscopy, CT-guided biopsy, or ultrasound. Outcome Management depends on whether there are symptoms or not. It is usually conservative through radiological follow-up, as is the case with our patient, although the clinical picture due to its compressive mass effect may require surgical, medical or ablative treatment [6]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Pulmonary amyloidosis presents a diagnostic dilemma—a nonspecific clinical and radiological presentation, which can mimic other lung diseases, complicating the clinical approach. Its radiological and metabolic presentation can resemble malignant lesions. This requires the patient to undergo interventional diagnostic procedures, including repeat procedures and recommending aggressive treatments, as in the case presented. It should always be considered as a diagnostic option. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Lipoma of the tibialis anterior tendon sheath
clinical_history: A 68-year-old male presented with a gradually enlarging swelling over the anterior aspect of the right ankle, first noticed two years earlier. He reported no pain, trauma, functional limitation, or gait disturbance. On examination, a ~5 cm, well-circumscribed, mobile, and non-tender soft tissue mass was observed, not adherent to deep planes and without skin changes or signs of inflammation.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound demonstrated a well-circumscribed soft tissue mass measuring 33 × 28 × 14 mm (L × AP × T) within the subcutaneous tissue, completely enveloping the tibialis anterior tendon. The lesion exhibited a heterogeneous echotexture, predominantly iso-echoic relative to the surrounding fat (Figures 1 and 2). Subsequent MRI revealed a fusiform, encapsulated mass located within the subcutaneous plane, anterior to the aponeurosis, and circumferentially enveloping the tibialis anterior tendon (Figure 3). The lesion appeared hyperintense on T1-weighted sequences with multiple internal hypointense septations (Figure 3), showed high-signal intensity on T2-weighted gradient-echo sequences (Figure 4), and demonstrated marked hypointensity on fat-suppressed proton density-weighted images (Figures 5 and 6). Across all sequences, the signal characteristics closely resembled those of subcutaneous adipose tissue, consistent with a lipomatous composition.
discussion: Lipomas are benign mesenchymal neoplasms composed of mature adipocytes, most commonly found in subcutaneous tissue, but they may also develop in deeper locations such as skeletal muscle, near bone, or in association with tendon sheaths [1]. The latter presentation is rare, especially in the foot and ankle, with few cases documented [2,3]. When arising adjacent to tendons or within joints, these lesions are sometimes referred to as synovial lipomas, as they originate in the sublining of the synovial layer [4]. They have been most frequently described in the knee, particularly the infrapatellar fat pad and suprapatellar pouch, but have also been reported in the wrist, hand, hip, lumbar facet joints, and ankle [5]. Although typically asymptomatic, as in our case, they may cause pain, mechanical symptoms, or even neurologic deficits. In rare cases, they have been associated with tendon rupture [5]. Histologically, they are indistinguishable from conventional lipomas, consisting of mature adipose tissue enclosed by a thin fibrous capsule and lined by synovium [5]. Imaging features are also typical of adipose lesions: high signal on T1 and T2-weighted MRI, with signal loss on fat-saturated sequences. In our case, the lesion presented these classic features and circumferentially enveloped the tibialis anterior tendon. The terminology used to describe adipose lesions involving the synovium can be confusing, and a clear distinction is necessary between synovial lipomatosis, lipoma arborescens, and synovial lipoma, as described by Oesman et al. [4]. Lipoma arborescens is a benign lesion with frond-like synovial proliferation and subsynovial adipocyte infiltration, usually affecting the knee. Synovial lipomatosis is often used more broadly for diffuse synovial fat infiltration, with or without villous features. Synovial lipoma, in contrast, is a localised, encapsulated mass covered by synovium, without villous morphology [4]. Similar cases of tendon sheath lipomas have been described. Gurich and Pappas [2] reported one in the fourth extensor compartment of the hand, while Woo and Lui [3] described one involving the tibialis anterior tendon. Although lipomas are benign and carry an excellent prognosis, their surgical management depends on location and depth. Superficial lipomas are generally easy to excise with a very low recurrence rate. In contrast, deep-seated lipomas, particularly those involving tendon sheaths, are more technically challenging due to their proximity to neurovascular structures or fascial compartments. As a result, they carry a slightly higher risk of local recurrence. Nevertheless, the overall recurrence rate remains low, estimated at less than 5% [1].

title: A case of OHVIRA / Herlyn–Werner–Wunderlich syndrome
clinical_history: A 13-year-old female came with complaints of a slowly growing suprapubic mass since a few months and lower abdominal discomfort. She was further advised to undergo ultrasound imaging and subsequently CT abdomen for renal anomaly, and MRI pelvis for further evaluation.
imaging_findings: MRI pelvis reveals a large tubular T1 hyperintense structure in the pelvis on the right side, consisting of haemorrhagic contents in an enlarged hourglass-shaped right uterine horn and cervix. The left uterine horn appears unremarkable. CT abdomen (Figures 1 and 2) reveals an empty right renal fossa with a cross-fused kidney seen on the left. No obvious free fluid or adnexal lesion is seen.
discussion: Background OHVIRA (obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral renal anomaly) syndrome is a Müllerian anomaly comprising a triad of uterine didelphys, obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral renal anomaly, also known as Herlyn–Werner–Wunderlich (HWW) syndrome. The incidence of Müllerian duct anomalies ranges from 0.8 to 4%, and the incidence of OHVIRA syndrome is estimated to be 1/20,000 in the general population [1]. Clinical Perspective Patients usually present with cyclical dysmenorrhea, pelvic lump or pelvic pain [2]. Sometimes, late presentation can also occur secondary to a small communication between the duplicated cervix, allowing flow of blood through it. The anomaly is secondary to defects in Müllerian and Wolffian ducts, with fusion defects in Müllerian ducts around the gestational age of 8 to 9 weeks, resulting in uterine and vaginal anomalies, and of Wolffian ducts in ipsilateral renal anomaly [3]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound and MRI pelvis are the modalities of choice for diagnosis, with the former being the first line of investigation [4]. Transabdominal ultrasound usually reveals an ipsilateral absent or dysplastic kidney with a large cystic lesion with internal echoes in the pelvis. There can be displacement of the uterus [5]. MRI pelvis usually reveals a large T1 hyperintense and T2 hypointense tubular structure, i.e., a dilated uterine horn in the uterine didelphys secondary to haematocolpos and haematometra with separate visualisation of displaced normal cervix and vagina. Blind hemivagina and cervical atresia can also be seen. Management Early diagnosis aids in early management [5]. Treatment usually involves drainage of the collection with resection of the transverse vaginal septum followed by vaginal remodelling. Complications Prolonged vaginal obstruction can result in rupture, adhesions, infertility issues and endometriosis. Take Home Message OHVIRA syndrome is a rare Müllerian duct anomaly which usually presents with a patient’s menarche. A correct and early diagnosis helps in prompt management, restoring fertility and relieving symptoms.

title: Wilson’s disease neurological manifestations: MRI correlation
clinical_history: A 14-year-old male presented with progressive dysarthria, ataxia, gait disturbance, headache, dizziness, and a history of recurrent falls. Physical examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly without convulsions or neck rigidity. Liver enzymes were within normal limits.
imaging_findings: MRI of the patient revealed symmetrical abnormal T2WI and FLAIR hyperintensities in bilateral thalamus (with sparing of medial thalamic nuclei), bilateral caudate, putamen, claustrum, midbrain (with sparing of red nucleus and substantia nigra—“face of the giant panda” sign), pons and dorsal brainstem (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, 2, and 3). No evidence of blooming on FFE images or restriction on DWI and ADC maps. Abnormal T1WI hyperintensity noted within the globus pallidus (Figure 4). USG of the abdomen revealed altered echotexture of the liver with hepatosplenomegaly, consistent with chronic liver parenchymal disease /(Figure 5).
discussion: Background Wilson’s disease (WD) is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired biliary copper excretion and accumulation of copper in various organs, especially the liver, brain, and cornea [1,2]. The global prevalence is estimated at approximately 1 in 30,000, with clinical onset typically occurring between the first and third decades of life [1]. Clinical Perspective Neurological manifestations commonly emerge in the second decade, aligning with the presentation in our patient [2,5]. Classic neurological features include dysarthria, tremor, dystonia, and ataxia [5]. Hepatic involvement in WD can vary widely, from asymptomatic hepatomegaly to overt cirrhosis [2]. Interestingly, our patient exhibited hepatosplenomegaly despite normal liver enzymes—an observation consistent with literature noting that clinical findings can precede biochemical abnormalities in WD [1,2]. Imaging Perspective MRI is the most sensitive modality for detecting neuroparenchymal changes in Wilson’s disease [4]. Typical findings include symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities involving the basal ganglia, thalamus, brainstem, and cerebellum [4,5]. The “face of the giant panda” sign in the midbrain and the “face of the miniature panda” in the pons are characteristic but not universally present [4]. In our case, symmetrical involvement of the caudate nucleus, putamen, and thalami (with sparing of the medial nuclei), as well as brainstem structures, supports a diagnosis of toxic metabolic encephalopathy associated with Wilson’s disease [4,5]. Additionally, T1 hyperintensity in the globus pallidus likely reflects secondary hepatocerebral degeneration, possibly due to manganese deposition [4]. Abdominal USG revealed hepatosplenomegaly and altered liver echotexture, consistent with chronic hepatic involvement secondary to copper overload. Urinary copper levels of the patient were elevated. Outcome Management involves copper chelation using agents such as D-penicillamine or trientine, and zinc therapy to inhibit intestinal copper absorption [2,3]. With timely diagnosis and intervention, neurological manifestations may improve or stabilise, though irreversible damage can occur in advanced cases [3,5]. Liver transplantation remains an option in patients with fulminant hepatic failure or decompensated cirrhosis [2]. Take Home Message Imaging plays a vital role not only in initial diagnosis but also in monitoring disease progression and treatment response. Serial MRI may show regression of signal abnormalities with successful therapy [4,5].

title: Breast cancer metastasis to the stomach: A rare form of presentation
clinical_history: A 52-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with abdominal pain. The patient had a history of a complicated appendectomy several years prior. Surgeons requested a contrast-enhanced CT scan to clarify the diagnosis.
imaging_findings: The contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed dilated small bowel loops with an apparent calibre change in the lower quadrant of the abdomen (Figure 1). As no masses or bowel thickening were identified, the diagnosis was consistent with an incomplete small bowel obstruction, likely due to abdominal adhesions—a diagnosis of exclusion. The patient had a history of a complicated appendectomy several years prior. Additionally, the gastric wall showed thickened gastric folds (Figure 2). Subsequent gastroscopy confirmed the thickened folds, and biopsies were obtained (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c). Histopathological examination revealed atrophic gastritis and tumoural cells positive for GATA 3, mammaglobin, and oestrogen receptors. Both conventional (Figures 4a and 4b) and contrast-enhanced mammography (Figures 5a and 5b) demonstrated bilateral diffuse masses with non-mass enhancement. Palpable areas were biopsied in the lower inner quadrant of the right breast—4 o’clock—(Figure 6a) and the junction of the outer quadrants of the left breast—9 o’clock—(Figure 6b). No axillary lymphadenopathy was detected (Figures 6c and 6d).
discussion: Background Gastric metastases from breast cancer are extremely rare, with a reported prevalence rate lower than 5% [1–5]. The common metastatic sites for breast cancer are bone, lungs, liver, and brain [1–5]. Gastrointestinal involvement, particularly gastric metastasis, is uncommon. When it occurs, breast cancer—especially invasive lobular carcinoma—is the most frequent primary tumour to metastasise to the stomach [1–5]. Lung cancer is the second most frequent, likely due to its high overall prevalence [3]. Clinical Perspective Abdominal pain is the most common presenting symptom [1–5], followed by anorexia, dysphagia, nausea, vomiting and early satiety—symptoms that often mimic those of primary gastric cancer [1–5]. Imaging Perspective The most frequent radiologic pattern of gastric metastasis is linitis plastica [1,2,4,5]. Imaging and endoscopic findings are typically nonspecific [1,2], making histopathological analysis of endoscopic biopsies essential for diagnosis [1–5]. Middle-aged women are most commonly affected [1–5]. Outcome Although average survival following the diagnosis of gastric metastasis is approximately 7–14 months [1,2,4], survival can be extended up to 44 months in selected cases where the primary tumour is controlled and a gastric resection is feasible [1,2,4]. However, gastric involvement often occurs as part of widespread metastatic disease [1–5], making systemic treatment, such as chemotherapy and hormonal blockade, the mainstay of therapy [1–5]. In our case, histopathology confirmed bilateral grade 2 invasive carcinoma of no special type (NST), positive for hormone receptors. Additional immunochemistry showed positivity for E-cadherin and CK 19, ruling out lobular carcinoma. Chemotherapy with ribociclib and letrozole was initiated. Regarding the incomplete bowel obstruction, the patient was managed conservatively with bowel rest, leading to clinical resolution. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Gastric metastasis from previously undiagnosed breast cancer poses a significant diagnostic challenge. It is usually accompanied by other distant metastases, which was not the case in our patient. Given the isolated gastric involvement, immunohistochemistry played a crucial role in differentiating primary gastric cancer from metastatic lesions. Systemic treatment remains the preferred therapeutic approach.

title: Endometriosis of the canal of Nuck
clinical_history: A 26-year-old female presents with a one-year history of right groin fullness and pain beginning the first two days of menstrual bleeding and lasting for two weeks. Movement and touch exacerbate the pain. Prior medical history is unremarkable. Physical exam reveals tenderness in the right groin.
imaging_findings: Superficial ultrasound of the right groin showed a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass with internal vascularity in the right inguinal canal measuring up to 2.4 cm (Figures 1 and 2). MRI of the pelvis, with and without contrast, confirmed an ill-defined mass in the right inguinal region, specifically within the canal of Nuck. The lesion appeared as a T1 isointense, heterogeneously T2 hyperintense enhancing mass, most consistent with endometriosis given the patient’s history of cyclical pain (Figures 3, 4, 5, and 6).
discussion: Background Endometriosis is the growth of extrauterine endometrial tissue, commonly within the ovaries or surrounding pelvic structures. The exact mechanism is unclear, but retrograde menstruation of endometrial progenitor cells may play a role [1]. Rarely, endometrial tissue grows in extrapelvic locations such as the thoracic cavity or the canal of Nuck [1,2]. Endometriosis of the canal of Nuck may present as a painful inguinal mass enlarging during menstruation [3]. Clinical Perspective Symptoms of endometriosis include intermenstrual bleeding and pain during periods, intercourse, urination, and defecation. Depending on the tissue location, symptoms may deviate from the typical presentation [4]. Endometriosis of the thoracic cavity may result in chest pain or shortness of breath [5]. Extrauterine endometrial tissue is often hormonally responsive, and symptoms may vary depending on the menstrual cycle phase [4,6]. Imaging Perspective Laparoscopic exploration is the gold standard for diagnosis; however, imaging is helpful in identifying the presence of endometrial tissue in atypical locations [3,7]. MRI is favourable, as it provides high contrast resolution, lacks ionising radiation, and can detect haemorrhagic lesions with high sensitivity. Within the canal of Nuck, endometrial tissue can be seen in proximity to or directly affecting the round ligament [3]. T1 and T2-weighted sequences show different signal intensities depending on the composition of endometrial tissue [3,8]. In lesions with solid components, T1-weighted images show isointense or hyperintense signals compared to muscle, and T2-weighted images show hypointense or hyperintense signals [8]. Lesions with adhesions appear as low signal intensities with obliteration of organ interfaces [9]. Endometriomas present with the “T2 shading sign”, seen as T2 shortening in lesions that appear hyperintense in T1-weighted imaging [10]. Outcome While there is no cure for endometriosis, treatment provides symptomatic relief [11]. Both pharmacologic or surgical methods can be considered. Imaging plays a key role in the early detection of endometriosis, ensuring that treatment is begun sooner, and also directs surgical planning [3,11]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Imaging findings can guide the types of treatments a patient may receive. Patients with mild findings may use drugs suppressing ovulation or menstruation. The presence of the “T2 shading sign” suggests decreased responsiveness to hormonal therapy. These patients may require surgical management. Imaging performed prior to surgery characterises the disease burden, allowing for minimally invasive surgery to be performed [10,12]. title: Imaging features in connective tissue disorder-associated usual interstitial pneumonia
clinical_history: A 68-year-old former smoker with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hypothyroidism consulted for progressive exertional dyspnoea. Pulmonary function tests showed a restrictive pattern and reduced diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO).
imaging_findings: High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest with axial (Figures 1a and 1b), coronal (Figure 1c), and sagittal (Figure 1d) reconstructions demonstrated findings consistent with an interstitial lung disease. Bilateral involvement with a clear apicobasal gradient with extensive subpleural reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, and predominant honeycombing in the lower lobes was observed. Exuberant honeycombing was present, involving nearly the entire fibrotic pulmonary parenchyma (Figure 1b). A sharp and abrupt transition between normal and fibrotic lung parenchyma was noted in the craniocaudal direction (arrows in Figures 1c and 1d). The small areas of fibrosis of the upper lobes were limited to the anterior segments (arrowheads in Figures 1a and 1d). No evidence of superimposed infection or ground-glass opacities was revealed. No suspicious pulmonary nodules, masses, or mediastinal lymphadenopathy were identified. Mild dilation of the pulmonary arteries and a cardiac pacemaker were noted. No pleural or pericardial effusion was present.
discussion: Background The radiological pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) may have an unknown cause in cases of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) or can be secondary to systemic connective tissue disorders (CTD) [1,2]. Clinical Perspective In patients with UIP, it is important to differentiate those secondary to CTD from those with IPF. This distinction is of significant prognostic and therapeutic value, as secondary pulmonary involvement may benefit from treatment of the systemic disease to attempt to prevent progression [1–3]. Imaging Perspective There are findings in chest CT studies that can help distinguish cases of UIP in IPF from those of UIP associated with CTD. Exuberant honeycombing refers to the presence of honeycombing in more than 70% of the lung parenchyma with fibrosis. The “straight edge” sign is defined as a narrow and abrupt transition zone between normal pulmonary parenchyma and fibrotic parenchyma in the craniocaudal direction. The “anterior upper lobe” sign is described when fibrotic involvement of the upper lobes is concentrated and limited to their anterior segments, associated with more extensive fibrosis in the bases [3,4]. Outcome Exuberant honeycombing, the “straight edge” sign, and the “anterior upper lobe” sign are more frequently observed in patients with CTD compared to patients with IPF, with the “straight edge” sign being the most specific of the three [3]. Teaching Points The presence of any of the three signs described, or their combination, on a chest CT with a UIP pattern should suggest the possibility of a CTD as the cause of the pulmonary injury and recommend a comprehensive rheumatological evaluation [2,3]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Solitary fibrous tumour of the pelvis
clinical_history: A 75-year-old woman had unintended weight loss and anaemia for several months. There was no history of bowel or urinary changes, and an endoscopy was negative. A CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was performed to evaluate for malignancy.
imaging_findings: A CT of the abdomen and pelvis was performed in a portal venous phase (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c). An ovoid, heterogeneous soft tissue mass with smooth, well-defined margins was present in the left upper mesorectal space, mildly displacing the rectum to the right. It measured 61 x 58 x 45 mm and did not contain cystic spaces or macroscopic fat. The mass did not herniate through the sciatic notch and did not appear along the expected path of a nerve or vasculature. Upon administration of IV contrast, the mass was hypervascular on the portal venous phase. There was free fluid in the pelvis, representing simple ascites, without evidence of complexity or active bleeding. No MRI was performed since the patient was lost to follow-up after her initial CT scan and biopsy.
discussion: Clinical Perspective Pelvic soft tissue masses are rare, and often present with symptoms of mass effect such as pain, fullness, and urinary or bowel symptoms [1,2]. They can herniate outside of the pelvis or compress the iliac vasculature, leading to iliac vein thrombosis [6]. Pelvic soft tissue masses can be characterised by visceral involvement, anatomic location, and intrinsic characteristics [1,2]. These features narrow the differential diagnosis. Imaging Perspective The patient’s mass was solid, without cystic areas or fat. It was unclear whether the rectum was involved; if originating from the rectum, it could be a large exophytic gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST), but if not, it could be an extraperitoneal mass in the mesorectal space. Due to the imaging findings (exophytic, hyper-enhancing, no rectal thickening) and negative endoscopy, rectal adenocarcinoma was unlikely. The hypervascular nature favoured a solitary fibrous tumour (SFT), with leiomyosarcoma, dedifferentiated liposarcoma, and rectal GIST on the differential [3]. Other possible diagnoses include angiomyolipoma, fibroma, fibrosarcoma, desmoid tumour, haemangioma, and angiosarcoma, though the lack of fat or cystic components makes these unlikely [3]. The lack of fat also removed consideration of extragonadal dermoid cyst, lipoma, and well-differentiated liposarcoma [4]. Biopsy confirmed SFT of the pelvis. SFT can be classified as low-aggressive, high-aggressive, or dedifferentiated, based on factors like age, size, mitotic count, and tumour necrosis [5]. Malignancy is suggested based on size >5 cm (as in this case), haemorrhage, necrosis, and pleomorphic nuclei [2,4]. Based on its small size, low mitotic count, and lack of necrosis, the patient’s SFT had a low predicted metastatic risk. However, haematogenous metastasis can occur even in benign-appearing masses [2]. SFT is the second most common pelvic soft tissue sarcoma, following leiomyosarcoma, and is similar in prevalence to either dedifferentiated or well-differentiated liposarcoma [6]. Outcome There is no standard approach to treatment and follow-up for SFT of the pelvis [2]. Due to the vascularity of the mass, they may be embolised to reduce bleeding prior to biopsy or en bloc excision [2]. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy are not generally offered [2]. Surgery alone is sufficient to manage low-risk SFT; however, high-risk tumours can recur or metastasise [7]. Recurrence may be delayed, so follow-up annually for 10–20 years is preferred, and MRI is the ideal imaging modality due to its superior soft-tissue contrast [7,8]. Teaching Points Pelvic masses should be characterised by visceral involvement and anatomic space. Solitary fibrous tumours (SFT) are hypervascular and can bleed post-biopsy. Describe the involvement of nearby structures to help surgical planning. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Preoperative diagnosis of vesico-appendiceal fistula in a diabetes patient
clinical_history: A 62-year-old woman with a 17-year history of diabetes mellitus presented to our institution with a 3-month history of progressive lower urinary tract symptoms, including urinary frequency, urgency, dysuria, and gross haematuria. Notably absent was acute right lower quadrant abdominal pain. After hospitalisation, it was found that there were pneumaturia and faeces-like changes in the urine (Figure 1).
imaging_findings: Transabdominal ultrasonography showed a gas-like strong echo and irregular hyperechoic stone-like mass with posterior shadowing in the bladder (Figure 2a). To exclude gynaecological diseases, a transvaginal ultrasound was performed. The right lateral wall of the bladder and the adjacent bowel were connected through a fistula. The fistula tract was about 3.8 cm long and 0.58 cm wide, characterised as a central hyperechoic and peripheral hypoechoic tract on sonogram (Figure 2b). These ultrasound findings supported the diagnosis of vesico-enteric fistula, but the specific part of the intestine could not be clarified. A computed tomography (CT) scan showed a small air-fluid level at the top of the bladder (Figure 3a). A tubular tract could be seen protruding from the right lateral wall of the bladder up to the neighbouring thickened bowel and this is filled with contrast-opacified urine (Figure 3b). A diagnosis of fistulous communication between the bladder and bowel was suggested following the findings on the excretory-phase CT scan. CT coronal scan showed faecal stones in the bladder (Figure 3c). Cystoscopy showed an oedematous right lateral wall of the bladder associated with inflammatory changes. It also revealed a fistulous tract opening with a diameter of 1 cm, with pus moss and yellow floc attached to the bladder mucosal surface. The yellow floc is the stone-like mass seen on the ultrasound. The cystoscope could be inserted via a sinus tract opening in the right lateral bladder wall, where the distal tip exhibited bifurcation. Despite attempts, the endoscope could only advance 2 cm beyond the entry point, with further progression prevented by this structural anomaly.
discussion: Background Vesico-appendiceal fistula (VAF) constitutes less than 5% of all vesico-enteric fistulas (VEF) [1]. VAF is a rare complication of appendicitis and malignancy. Harrison Cripps first depicted VAF in the medical literature over a century ago [2]. Some researchers have shown that the incidence of VAF is 0.2% to 0.3%. Such fistulas occur most commonly in patients between 10 and 40 years old [1]. Clinical Perspective We suspect that long-standing diabetes might have potentially predisposed the patient to the development of VAF following appendicitis. In addition, bladder stones are also present in this patient, the formation of which is often caused by urinary retention, urinary tract infection, foreign bodies, or metabolic abnormalities. And when fistulas are present, stone formation may be indirectly promoted through infection, foreign body introduction, and inflammatory responses. The typical clinical features of VAF are faecaluria, pneumaturia and recurrent urinary tract infections. The most common organisms cultured in urine are Escherichia coli and Klebsiella [3]. VAF is often misdiagnosed as VEF and difficult to diagnose preoperatively [4]. VAF is usually reported in individual cases and lacks specific clinical manifestations. Cystoscopy and CT scan are the most valuable methods to confirm the diagnosis of VAF. There are few reports on the ultrasound manifestations of this disease in the literature. Imaging Perspective The direct sign of ultrasonic diagnosis of VAF is the ultrasonic visualisation of the channel between bladder and appendix. The indirect signs include strong echoes of gas or faecal matter within the bladder, and clinical manifestations such as pneumaturia or faecaluria. On CT scan, the most common sign in the diagnosis of VAF is an air-fluid level in the bladder, followed by local thickening of the bladder wall or bladder mass. Imaging of the urinary tract using CT urogram, or abdominal CT, performed with positive GI luminal contrast, can aid in delineating fistulous communication between the bladder and the bowel. CT can also help to rule out bowel or bladder tumours. Cystoscopy reveals non-specific findings for smaller fistulas, such as congestion and oedema of the bladder mucosa, papillary projections, effervescence of bubbles, turbid urine, and visible faecal debris. Cystoscopy can confirm the diagnosis of VAF when a fistula in the bladder is found to be connected to the appendix. Outcome Surgery is the best treatment for VAF, including appendectomy and partial cystectomy [5]. In our case, the tip of the appendix was found to be tightly adhered to the bladder during the operation. Thus, the part of the bladder wall adhered to the tip of the appendix was removed after the appendix was cut at the base of the appendix. Exploration during resection can reveal communication between the appendix and the bladder. In this case, the existence of a fistula was confirmed by a variety of imaging methods before surgery. The patient was cured after the surgical treatment (Figures 4a, 4b, 5a, and 5b) and recovered well after a 5-month follow-up. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Vesico-appendiceal fistula (VAF) is a rare entity and is often discovered incidentally. Imaging plays a crucial role in diagnosing and managing VAF, particularly in patients with pneumaturia and faeces-like changes in the urine. Imaging or cystoscopy evidence of a fistula between the bladder and the appendix indicates a diagnosis of VAF. Air in the bladder is also an important indirect sign of VAF.

title: A case of unicentric Castleman disease in the abdomen
clinical_history: A 34-year-old male with one week of sudden-onset fever, abdominal pain, cervicalgia, myalgia, palpitations and shortness of breath. Recent history of travel to Africa for 1 month, and medications for malaria prophylaxis and pre-exposure prophylaxis for HIV. On examination, he had a fever of 38,2°C, tachycardia and right lower quadrant abdominal tenderness. Initial workup was non-contributory, with normal CBC, BMP, chest x-ray, and abdomen ultrasound. With wide differentials, including endemic, infectious and neoplastic conditions, CT of the head, neck and chest was performed and was unrevealing. Serology and lumbar puncture were also performed and were unremarkable.
imaging_findings: A contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis was performed, and revealed a 3.7 x 3.1 x 5.1 cm, avidly enhancing paraduodenal mass with central calcification (Figures 1a and 1b), presumed to be an enlarged lymph node. Adjacent organs, including the bowel, were unremarkable. There was no lymphadenopathy elsewhere. An endoscopic ultrasound was done (Figures 2a and 2b) to obtain an aspiration biopsy that revealed B-cell follicles with no evidence of malignancy. After discussion, the patient opted for watchful waiting. A follow-up CT done after 4 months demonstrated no significant change in size or appearance of the mass. This was subsequently excised, and histopathology revealed the final diagnosis.
discussion: Diagnosis Histopathological analysis of the excised mass (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, 3d, 3e, and 3f) revealed an encapsulated lymph node with architectural distortion, multiple follicles with atretic germinal centres, thickened mantle zones with lymphocytes arranged in a concentric lamellar array, and hyalinised venules in interfollicular area—characteristic of hyaline vascular variant of Castleman disease (HVCD). The immunohistochemistry profile demonstrated the expression of CD20 (B-cell marker) in the germinal centres, CD3 (T-cell marker) in the paracortical zone and CD21 (follicular dendritic cell marker) in germinal centres, expanding towards the hyperplastic mantle zone, characteristic of HVCD. Due to a single site of involvement, a final diagnosis of unicentric Castleman disease (UCD) was made. Background Castleman disease (CD) is a rare lymphoproliferative disorder divided into unicentric and multicentric subtypes, based on the sites of involvement and course of disease. UCD is usually an incidental finding, seen in all ages with a peak in the fourth decade, and presenting as a single enlarged lymph node or nodal region [1]. Most patients are asymptomatic, whereas large lesions can present with mass effect on adjacent structures. Imaging Perspective CT is the preferred modality as it allows for a more holistic evaluation of the surrounding structures. On unenhanced CT images, UCD is seen as a homogeneous mass, isodense to skeletal muscle, most commonly involving a single mediastinal compartment [2]. Usually non-invasive, it can sometimes invade adjacent structures. Homogeneous, intense contrast enhancement is considered characteristic, reflecting lesion hypervascularity [2]. Heterogeneous enhancement due to internal necrosis or fibrosis and discrete, coarse or arborising patterns of calcification may be seen in a small fraction of patients [2]. FDG-PET can help identify a metabolically active node that can be targeted for biopsy. On ultrasound imaging, the masses appear as well-defined, homogeneously hypoechoic lesions with increased through transmission. There is variable internal colour flow reported and these lesions can mimic cysts. MRI can be used to delineate the tissue margins in invasive lesions, with the CD mass typically being T1 hypo-to-isointense and T2 iso-to-hyperintense relative to skeletal muscle and showing intense post-contrast enhancement [2]. Pathology The pathological diagnosis of CD typically involves excisional biopsy, given the heterogeneous nodal involvement and the small size of the needle biopsy specimen. Two reported pathological subtypes of CD include hyaline vascular (HV) and plasma cell (PC) types. Unicentric Castleman disease (UCD) is usually HV type, while multicentric Castleman disease (MCD) usually has a mixed or PC-predominant pattern. The HV subtype of CD is characterised by the proliferation of distinctive lymphoid follicles throughout the nodal structure. The follicular mantle is expanded and demonstrates an “onion-skin” concentric ring of lymphoid cells. Germinal centres are small and involuted with depletion of B cells and often with prominent, sometimes dysplastic follicular dendritic cells. Additional findings can include capsular fibrosis, sometimes with associated broad fibrous bands disrupting the background lymph node architecture. The plasma cell subtype (PC) is characterised by sheets of plasma cells in the interfollicular zone, which may also show scattered eosinophil and mast cell infiltrates. The specimen in the PC subtype also frequently shows follicular hyperplasia with a sharply defined mantle zone and generally hypocellular germinal centres. Outcome UCD can be treated with excision, which is curative in the majority of patients, relapse being a rare phenomenon. If resection is not possible, treatment aims to alleviate symptoms, which usually arise due to mass effect on surrounding structures [3]. There is no consensus in the literature on the management of UCD that is unresectable. It is important to acknowledge that MCD, in contrast, is a systemic disease, which can present with multifocal lymph node enlargement, anasarca, splenomegaly and systemic signs such as fevers, weight loss and night sweats (this is not discussed in this case report) [4]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Spontaneous pneumothorax secondary to a fistulised rheumatoid nodule
clinical_history: A 67-year-old woman with a longstanding history of rheumatoid factor-positive rheumatoid arthritis (RA) was being treated with subcutaneous methotrexate 10 mg. She went to the emergency department due to sudden dyspnoea and left chest pain.
imaging_findings: Chest X-ray showed a moderate left pneumothorax and a cavitated lesion in the subpleural region of the left upper lobe (LUL) (Figure 1a), which was present on a prior chest X-ray (Figure 1b). After a chest tube was placed (Figure 1c), the pneumothorax did not fully resolve, and symptoms persisted, prompting a CT scan. CT reported a left pneumothorax. The tube was correctly positioned. A cavitated nodule located in the LUL with communication to the pleural cavity was shown in axial (Figure 2a) and coronal planes (Figure 2b). Other broad-based nodules in the pleural surface were identified (Figure 2c). The rest of the parenchyma presented a slight thickening of the interlobular septa with a diffuse bilateral distribution, probably related to RA-associated interstitial lung disease. A subsequent revaluation, after reviewing the patient’s radiological history, concluded that the image of a cavitated nodule (Figures 2a and 2b) corresponded to the lesion visible in the previous X-ray (Figure 1b), and proposed the differential diagnosis between cavitated lung neoplasia, rheumatoid nodule and other cavitary lesions such as tuberculosis.
discussion: Clinical Perspective & Imaging Perspective Pneumothorax can be an urgent condition requiring prompt treatment and is classified into primary, secondary, and traumatic types. Primary pneumothorax occurs spontaneously without significant lung disease, while secondary pneumothorax is linked to conditions like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, tuberculosis, cancer, cystic fibrosis, and autoimmune diseases (such as rheumatoid arthritis). Common symptoms include chest pain, shortness of breath, tachypnoea, and hypoxemia. Diagnosis involves a chest X-ray and sometimes a CT scan to identify underlying conditions [1]. Rheumatoid arthritis is a collagen vascular disease that affects 1–2% of the population [2], being the most common form of chronic inflammatory arthritis [3]. It occurs more frequently in 25-year-old to 50-year-old women [2,4]. Nearly 50% of patients experience extraarticular involvement. Pleural disease (thickening or effusion) is the most common thoracic manifestation, while cricoarytenoid arthritis and bronchiectasis are typical for large airway involvement. About 5% of patients show clinically significant interstitial lung disease, with patterns including usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP), cryptogenic organising pneumonia, and follicular bronchiolitis [2]. Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules occur in < 1% of patients [3], more frequently in men, smokers with subcutaneous nodules, high rheumatoid factor titers and longstanding disease [2,5]. They may be single or multiple [5], typically well-defined [4] with a 0.5–5.0 cm diameter [2], located along the interlobular septa or subpleural regions of upper and middle lung zones [5] and can calcify. Histopathologically, they are identical to the subcutaneous nodules [2,4], showing central fibrinoid necrosis, palisading mononuclear cells and vasculitis [5]. They are usually asymptomatic unless they cavitate or rupture (50%) [4], leading to complications like infection, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax, which can be further complicated by bronchopleural fistula [2,4,5]. Oucome & Treatment Treatment for pneumothorax varies based on size and symptoms. Small pneumothoraces (< 50% of hemithorax) without breathlessness or lung disease are managed conservatively. Secondary small pneumothoraces (< 1 cm) with minimal symptoms also receive conservative treatment. For large primary pneumothoraces or those with breathlessness, needle aspiration may be used. However, chest tubes are the most definitive treatment, especially for large secondary pneumothoraces (> 50%), as in our case, or tension pneumothorax [1]. Pleurodesis is considered the final solution. It has been reported that patients with secondary pneumothorax and bronchopulmonary fistula required long-term care and were resistant to repeat talc pleurodesis [3]. Surgical treatment can be necessary to control the fistula, as in our patient, where a wedge resection was performed (Figure 3a) due to the persistent pneumothorax and suspicion of malignancy. However, malignancy or infection were less likely in this case because of the long-term course and the absence of clinical and laboratory data of infection. Finally, on the one hand, the macroscopic histopathological examination showed a lesion with central necrosis and pleural breach (Figure 3a) that corresponded to the cavitation and fistulisation seen on CT. On the other hand, microscopic examination of the lesion revealed a central area of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by a palisade of epithelioid histiocytes, fibrosis, and inflammatory cells, compatible with a rheumatoid nodule fistulised to the visceral pleura (Figure 3b). All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Linitis plastica in diffuse stomach carcinoma
clinical_history: A 40-year-old woman presented to the gastroenterologist with postprandial fullness and nausea persisting for one year, along with a 4 kg weight loss. She had no abdominal pain and reported normal faeces. Blood tests were normal.
imaging_findings: On ultrasound (Figure 1), a suspicion of a thickened stomach wall was raised. CT (Figures 2a and 2b) confirmed diffuse wall thickening and hyperaemic inner lining of the stomach with a small lumen. Lymphadenopathies were identified in the gastrohepatic and gastrocolic ligaments. No peritoneal metastases were observed on CT, but the lack of significant intra-abdominal fat limited definitive exclusion. During gastroscopy Figure 3), insufflation of the stomach was difficult, but no focal tumoral process was noted. Initial MRI (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c) showed diffusion restriction of the stomach lining. Additionally, multiple subtle peritoneal, mesenteric, and serosal lesions were identified, which were confirmed via diagnostic laparoscopy. Follow-up MRI (Figures 5a and 5b) showed disease progression with increased wall thickening of the stomach in the antrum, pylorus, and duodenal bulb, as well as the development of bilateral ovarian lesions.
discussion: Background There is no clear consensus whether the term linitis plastica describes the rigid leather bottle-like appearance of the stomach, or if it should be reserved for cases of infiltrative adenocarcinoma [1,2]. The term has been used in describing certain rectal cancers and scirrhous metastases to the gastrointestinal tract [3,4]. “Linitis” refers to the microscopic appearance of bands of filaments resembling linen, and “plastica” means inelastic [5]. The most common cause of linitis plastica is the diffuse type gastric adenocarcinoma, a rare phenotype of gastric cancer, characterised by diffuse growth of malignant cells with signet ring features [6]. It is believed that the diffuse infiltration of cancer cells causes extensive submucosal fibrosis and wall thickening, resulting in wall stiffening [7]. Clinical Perspective Linitis plastica is often difficult to diagnose due to its rare nature and nonspecific symptoms, such as vague epigastric discomfort and weight loss [1]. Mostly, the disease is already in an advanced stage at the time of diagnosis, limiting curative treatment options [1]. Additional diagnostic challenges arise due to the lack of distinct luminal lesions and because standard biopsy techniques may yield false-negative results due to the disease’s submucosal nature [8]. Multiple deep biopsies or laparoscopic exploration are often required for definitive diagnosis [8]. Imaging Perspective The primary imaging modalities for suspected linitis plastica are endoscopic ultrasound and CT [8]. MRI has a higher sensitivity for the detection of peritoneal metastatic disease compared to CT [9,10]. A barium meal study typically shows a narrowed lumen with loss of mucosal folds, but lacks sensitivity [2]. If linitis plastica is used as a descriptive term for diffuse wall thickening and a small lumen on imaging, differential diagnoses include infiltrative adenocarcinoma of the stomach, metastases of lung or breast cancer, lymphoma, inflammation, diffuse scarring (e.g., ingestion of corrosives) and Ménétrier disease [11]. Outcome Linitis plastica is associated with rapid progression and a poor prognosis due to its late-stage diagnosis and frequent peritoneal dissemination. Reported median survival ranges from 5 to 17 months, with a 5-year survival rate between 4% and 29%, even after “curative resection”. Advanced-stage disease (stage IV), no surgical resection, and lack of chemotherapy administration were associated with decreased survival [12]. In our case, the biopsies showed diffuse type adenocarcinoma, and peritoneal metastases were present at the time of diagnosis. Two years after diagnosis, there was peritoneal metastatic disease progression under chemotherapy (e.g., Krukenberg tumours). All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Gallbladder agenesis with primary common bile duct calculi
clinical_history: A 41-year-old female presented with a one-month history of recurrent right upper abdominal pain and vomiting, with a history of similar symptoms recurring over the past two years. Examination revealed mild tenderness without jaundice or guarding. Labs showed mildly elevated bilirubin (1.31 mg/dl total, 0.9 mg/dl direct) and alkaline phosphatase (331 IU/L), with near-normal transaminases (SGOT 31 IU/L, SGPT 49 IU/L).
imaging_findings: The patient underwent an MRI abdomen, which revealed two filling defects, one measuring ~ 2.3 x 1.4 cm (Figures 1 and 3) in the common hepatic duct, and the other ~ 1.5 x 1.1 cm in the common bile duct (CBD) (Figures 2 and 4), with the CBD measuring ~ 1.7 cm in maximum diameter. The gallbladder was not visualised in the gallblader fossa. MRI findings excluded both ectopic gallbladder and chronic cholecystitis as differential diagnoses. No ectopic gallbladder was identified, with the absence of cystic structures in the intrahepatic, retrohepatic, retroduodenal, falciform ligament, and lesser omentum regions (Figures 1, 2 and 5). Additionally, there was no evidence of a contracted or fibrosed gallbladder adjacent to the duodenum, nor any features suggestive of chronic inflammation such as mural thickening, pericholecystic fat stranding, or surrounding inflammatory changes. Coronal sections confirmed the absence of the gallbladder and depicted the primary calculi within the common hepatic duct and common bile duct (Figures 3, 4, 6 and 9). Additional sequences—T2 HASTEIRM FS axial (Figure 5),T2 TRUFI coronal (Figure 6), T2 HASTE axial (Figure 7), T2 HASTE FS coronal (Figure 8), and T2 TSE 3D coronal (Figure 9)—consistently demonstrated gallbladder agenesis and primary common bile duct stones.
discussion: Gallbladder agenesis is a rare condition where the gallbladder fails to develop during the fifth week of gestation. This results from failure of the cystic bud to develop in utero, without extrahepatic biliary atresia [1,2]. First described by Lemery in 1701, gallbladder agenesis has an incidence ranging from 0.01% to 0.06% [3]. Gallbladder agenesis is an uncommon congenital anomaly that poses significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges due to its propensity to mimic other hepatobiliary conditions. This condition, marked by the absence of the gallbladder and cystic duct, is often misinterpreted on transabdominal ultrasonography as cholecystitis with gas-filled bowel loops, periportal tissues mimicking a contracted gallbladder with stones, cystic duct obstruction or as a scleroatrophic gallbladder [4]. Accurate preoperative identification is essential to avoid unnecessary surgical interventions. Gallbladder agenesis can be classified into three distinct categories. Category 1 involves multiple fetal anomalies associated with perinatal death due to non-biliary abnormalities [5]. Category 2 consists of asymptomatic individuals in whom the anomaly is discovered incidentally during autopsy or surgery for unrelated conditions [5]. Category 3 includes symptomatic individuals who present with hepatobiliary disease symptoms and undergo surgery, only for the absence of the gallbladder to be discovered intraoperatively [5]. In our case, gallbladder agenesis was isolated, with no associated congenital anomalies identified on clinical examination or imaging. Based on this classification, our patient falls into Category 3. The absence of the gallbladder increases the likelihood of CBD stones, with 25–50% of individuals with gallbladder agenesis developing choledocholithiasis [6]. In the general population, it is estimated that 5–20% of patients with gallbladder disease are found to have CBD stones during cholecystectomy [7]. The elevated prevalence of biliary stones in gallbladder agenesis is thought to be related to biliary dyskinesia, which is similar to post-cholecystectomy syndrome [8]. Retrograde hypertonic contractions of the sphincter of Oddi can lead to biliary stasis, ductal dilatation, and stone formation [8]. In our case, the patient underwent CBD exploration and choledocholithotomy with T-tube drainage. This intervention not only facilitated the removal of the obstructing calculi but also confirmed the diagnosis intraoperatively by revealing a complete absence of the gallbladder and cystic duct. For confirmed cases of gallbladder agenesis with choledocholithiasis, magnetic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) remains the primary non-invasive diagnostic modality, and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) remains the primary therapeutic modality [1,3]. Standard treatment for CBD stone removal includes endoscopic sphincterotomy, papillary balloon dilation, and basket or balloon extraction [9–11]. However, approximately 10–15% of cases fail to respond to these methods due to factors such as altered anatomy, impacted or large stones, or intrahepatic stone locations [9–11]. Advanced therapeutic techniques, including mechanical lithotripsy, electrohydraulic lithotripsy (EHL), laser lithotripsy, and extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL), have proven effective in managing refractory cases [9–11]. In cases where ERCP fails, surgical options such as choledocholithotomy with T-tube drainage or primary closure of the CBD with biliary drainage tube placement may be considered [5,9–11].
