title: Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome: Association with a unique constellation of anomalies
clinical_history: A 22-year-old unmarried female presented with primary amenorrhea and a new-onset right inguinal swelling associated with episodic pain for the past 6 months. On clinical examination, the swelling was non-compressible. Secondary sexual characteristics were present and appropriately developed.
imaging_findings: Initial abdominal ultrasound revealed agenesis of the uterus, right pelvic ectopic kidney in a suprapubic location, and a right inguinal hernia containing cystic structures. Further evaluation with pelvic MRI confirmed the absence of the uterus and upper two-thirds of the vagina (Figures 1a and 1b), consistent with Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser (MRKH) syndrome. A right canal of Nuck hernia was noted, with the right ovary and a dilated fallopian tube (hydrosalpinx) within the hernial sac (Figures 2a and 2b). The left ovary was normal. The right renal fossa was empty, and a pelvic kidney was visualised in the suprapubic region (Figures 3a and 3b). Incidentally, an MRI of the upper abdomen demonstrated the absence of the body and tail of the pancreas, consistent with dorsal pancreatic agenesis (Figure 4).
discussion: Background MRKH syndrome represents a class of Müllerian anomalies characterised by the congenital absence of the uterus and upper vagina, typically diagnosed during the evaluation of primary amenorrhea [1]. A lack of Müllerian duct development between the fifth and sixth weeks of gestation causes it. The syndrome affects 1 per 4500 female births and can be classified into two types: type-1 (isolated uterovaginal agenesis) and type-2 (with associated anomalies which include renal, skeletal, vertebral anomalies, hearing defects, and, rarely, cardiac anomalies) [2]. This case demonstrates a rare constellation of findings in a patient with MRKH syndrome, including a canal of Nuck hernia containing ovary and hydrosalpinx, ectopic (pelvic) kidney, and dorsal pancreatic agenesis. To our knowledge, the simultaneous occurrence of MRKH with hydrosalpinx within a canal of Nuck hernia and dorsal pancreatic agenesis has not been reported in the literature, making this a unique and noteworthy combination. Imaging Perspective In females presenting with primary amenorrhea and normal secondary sexual characteristics, imaging plays a pivotal role in diagnosis. MRI is especially helpful in diagnosing complex Müllerian anomalies and associated anomalies, which are likely to impact further management and fertility counselling. Although 3D ultrasound is effective for evaluating uterine anomalies, MRI has an edge in detecting complex cases and systemic associations. Diagnosis of MRKH syndrome is straightforward on MRI. However, special caution should be taken to avoid missing other relevant pelvic and extrapelvic findings. Ovaries and fallopian tubes are normal in most cases; however, there can be undescended ovaries or they may be abnormally placed in the canal of Nuck hernia, as in this case. It is pertinent to know the status of the ovaries, as these patients can have biological children through in vitro fertilisation and surrogacy only if their ovaries are normal. Outcome Herniated ovaries are at risk of undergoing infarction due to vascular compromise. Undescended ovaries may undergo torsion. Surgical exploration confirmed a right canal of Nuck hernia with a viable ovary and dilated fallopian tube (hydrosalpinx) due to constriction at the hernial neck. Hernial contents were reduced, and hernioplasty was performed. Vaginoplasty was also performed using the McIndoe technique with a skin graft. The patient was counselled that following vaginoplasty, she will be able to engage in sexual activity but will not be able to conceive or become pregnant. Take Home Message Multisystem congenital anomalies may coexist in MRKH syndrome. Comprehensive MRI evaluation is crucial for diagnosis and guiding endocrine, surgical, and fertility decisions. Awareness of such rare associations aids in accurate diagnosis, prevents unnecessary interventions, and facilitates timely, multidisciplinary care. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Intrahepatic splenosis mimicking a malignant lesion
clinical_history: A 62-year-old male patient presented to the emergency room with visual disturbances and right-hand weakness. He had a medical history of alcoholism, tobacco use, hyperlipidaemia, and traumatic splenectomy, and was hospitalised due to an ischemic stroke. He underwent routine diagnostics, where, from laboratory tests, only hyperlipidaemia was clinically significant.
imaging_findings: Routine abdominal ultrasound revealed an asymptomatic, well-defined, homogeneous, hypoechogenic mass measuring 46 x 36 mm in the 8th liver segment (Figure 1). On abdominal multidetector computerised tomography (MDCT), the mass was ill-defined and isodense to the surrounding liver parenchyma on unenhanced scans (Figure 2a). Following intravenous contrast, the lesion demonstrated increased attenuation (Figure 2b), whereas, in the latter phases, it was isodense with the surrounding liver parenchyma (Figure 2c). Other findings included two splenunculi, one near the lesser curvature of the stomach (Figure 2d) and one in the left subphrenic region (Figure 2e). Contrast abdominal MR scans confirmed a well-defined, slightly T2-hyperintense mass measuring 43 x 30 mm (Figure 3a). The mass showed poor uniform post-contrast enhancement in the arterial phase (Figure 3b), following washout in later phases (Figure 3c). The mass showed significant restricted diffusion on DWI (Figure 3d) and low ADC values (Figure 3e).
discussion: Background Splenosis is a common, acquired condition of ectopic spleen tissue defined as the autoimplantation of viable splenic tissue following splenic surgery or trauma [1,2]. Usually, these are multiple sessile lesions in the abdominal and pelvic cavities, but splenosis rarely occurs intrahepatically or even intrathoracically and subcutaneously [2]. Clinical Perspective Splenosis is benign and mostly asymptomatic, but radiological findings may mimic malignant lesions, leading to unnecessary invasive procedures if malignancy cannot be excluded [1,3,4]. Imaging Perspective The diagnosis of intrahepatic splenosis can be suspected based on the “triad” presented by Toh et al. (2020) [1]: History of splenectomy or abdominal trauma; Absence of risk factors for liver malignancy; Typical imaging pattern on contrast-enhanced imaging. The suggested patterns include increased contrast uptake in the arterial phase with isodensity in the portal venous phase and homogenous hypodensity in the delayed phase [1]. A heterogeneous “zebra” enhancement pattern in the arterial phase is also typical for spleen tissue. On native MRI scans, hypointensity in T1 and hyperintensity in T2-weighted scans should typically be seen. The lesion should have a hypointense rim surrounding the lesion on T1-weighted imaging. After contrast administration, in the arterial phase, heterogeneous or arciform enhancement is expected, followed by homogeneous enhancement in the delayed phase [1]. A Tc-99 sulfur colloid scan and Tc-99m heat-damaged RBC scintigraphy can help establish the diagnosis [2,5], as can percutaneous biopsy or contrast-enhanced ultrasound, leaving surgical resection reserved for when it is not possible to exclude malignancy [1]. Outcome In our case, the patient had a history of abdominal trauma. Still, he has a history of alcoholism, which is a risk factor for malignancy, and the radiological appearance was atypical. On abdominal MR, it did not present with the expected post-contrast appearance, and it did not show a characteristic rim surrounding the lesion on T1-weighted imaging. Moreover, it showed restricted diffusion and low ADC values, suggesting malignancy. Due to the atypical presentation and inaccessible localisation, biopsy was not feasible; hence, surgical resection was performed. During the operation, a similar lesion, not visible on MRI scans, measuring a few millimetres in diameter, in the 7th liver segment, was found and resected; both were sent for histological analysis. The patient recovered well from the operation, and histological analysis revealed preserved white and red pulp architecture, suggesting the accessory spleen, splenosis or spleen autoimplantation. Take Home Message Considering splenosis in differential diagnoses can prevent unnecessary interventions when malignancy is excluded. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Microvascular obstruction in acute myocardial infarction
clinical_history: The patient is a 54-year-old male with no significant medical history who presented to the emergency department with generalised weakness, nausea, and mild thoracic pain persisting for 4 days. Clinical examination was unremarkable. However, electrocardiography (ECG) demonstrated diffuse ST-segment elevation in leads V1–V6. Laboratory tests revealed markedly elevated serum troponin levels.
imaging_findings: An urgent coronary angiography was performed due to suspected myocardial infarction, revealing an occlusive thrombus in the proximal left anterior descending artery (LAD), with distal collateral circulation from the right coronary artery (RCA) (Figures 1a and 1b). Because of the late presentation and the presence of collaterals, recanalisation was not performed. Subsequently, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) was conducted to assess further management. CMR performed two days after presentation demonstrated an extensive anteroseptal infarction with akinesia, a left ventricular (LV) end-diastolic volume of 248 ml, an LV stroke volume of 78 ml, and an ejection fraction (EF) of 31%. T1 mapping revealed elevated values in the infarcted region, suggesting diffuse oedema consistent with the acute phase (Figure 2). Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging, acquired 10 minutes post-contrast administration, identified a transmural infarction with a central subendocardial zone of microvascular obstruction (Figures 3a and 3b).
discussion: Background Microvascular obstruction (MVO) is a complication of myocardial infarction (AMI), characterised by impaired perfusion at the microvascular level, even after epicardial coronary artery reperfusion. It occurs as a result of endothelial dysfunction, capillary damage, and distal embolisation of thrombotic material [1]. MVO is a critical determinant of myocardial injury and has been associated with worse outcomes, including larger infarct size, adverse left ventricular remodelling, and increased mortality [2]. The pathophysiology involves ischemia-reperfusion injury, inflammation, and intramural haemorrhage, all contributing to a non-reflow phenomenon that limits myocardial recovery even after successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) [3]. Clinical Perspective Patients with AMI and MVO often present with persistent chest pain and signs of heart failure despite successful restoration of epicardial blood flow. MVO is a key clinical problem as it affects myocardial salvage and long-term prognosis. Traditional markers, such as ST-segment resolution and biochemical markers, are insufficient for detecting MVO, necessitating advanced imaging techniques [4]. Imaging plays a crucial role in evaluating the extent of myocardial injury, differentiating viable from nonviable myocardium, and guiding clinical management. Imaging Perspective Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with LGE is the gold standard for diagnosing MVO. It typically appears as a hypoenhancing region within an area of infarcted myocardium 10–15 minutes after contrast administration. T1 and T2 mapping can provide additional information on myocardial oedema and haemorrhage, which are common in severe MVO cases. Myocardial contrast echocardiography (MCE) and positron emission tomography (PET) may also be useful but are less commonly employed [5]. The final diagnosis is made by integrating clinical findings with imaging evidence of persistent perfusion defects in the infarcted myocardium. Outcome MVO is associated with poor prognosis, including increased risk of heart failure, adverse LV remodelling, and higher mortality rates [6]. Therapeutic options include pharmacological agents such as vasodilators, anti-inflammatory drugs, and mechanical interventions like intracoronary thrombectomy and cardioprotective strategies during PCI [7]. The presence of MVO significantly influences therapeutic decision-making, emphasising the importance of early and accurate imaging assessment [8]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Microvascular obstruction (MVO) is a critical determinant of adverse outcomes in AMI. Advanced imaging, particularly CMR, is essential for detection and risk stratification. All patient data and related files have been completely anonymised throughout the manuscript.

title: An unusual cervical mass
clinical_history: A 75-year-old male patient with a history of non-metastatic urothelial carcinoma and prostate cancer, both successfully treated surgically two years ago. During follow-up, a palpable, hard, and fixed cervical mass was detected. No history of neck trauma or radiation.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound showed a 6 cm solid and heterogeneous left mass with internal calcifications and intralesional vascularisation, not arising from the thyroid gland (Figures 1a and 1b). This mass was displacing and compressing the left internal jugular vein, which was still permeable (Figures 1c, 1d, and 1e). Findings were consistent with a calcified adenopathy. A subsequent non-contrast CT due to renal impairment revealed a solid left supraclavicular mass, with a heterogeneous density, irregular outlines, and thick calcifications. Thickening of the lateral-cervical ipsilateral musculature was also observed (Figures 2a and 2b). There was a pathological adenopathy with calcifications at the Va cervical level (Figure 2c). A core needle biopsy was performed, and histology reported infiltration of spindle-shaped, pleomorphic, and atypical cells, followed by the formation of an osteoid matrix and chondroid tissue (Figures 3a and 3b).
discussion: Background Extraskeletal osteosarcoma (EOS) is a rare mesenchymal malignant neoplasm arising outside the bone and occurs within the soft tissue or organs [1]. It constitutes 1% of all tissue sarcomas and 4–5% of osteosarcomas. It is slightly more common in males and develops in individuals over 50. The most frequent locations are the thighs, followed by the buttocks, upper extremities, abdominal cavity and retroperitoneum [1–3]. Pathophysiology A widely accepted theory proposes that muscle fibroblasts undergo metaplasia into osteoblasts or chondroblasts, which can develop into osteosarcoma when stimulated by external or internal factors. A history of trauma or radiation has been associated, with 4–13% of cases being secondary to radiation therapy [2,3]. Clinical Perspective The most common clinical presentation is the progressive growth of a hard mass, painful or not [1–3]. The hardness depends on the bone quantity of the tumour [1]. Imaging Perspective Plain radiographs may show increased soft tissue density; mineralisation is seen in only 50% of cases [3]. CT reveals a soft tissue mass not arising from adjacent bone structures, often showing cystic degeneration, necrosis and heterogeneous calcification or ossification. The calcification or bone distribution is heterogeneous, found in the central region and/or along the periphery of the mass. CT is useful to assess matrix mineralisation and distinguish EOS from myositis ossificans, where mineralisation proceeds from the periphery to the centre. EOS typically shows central deposition [1,3]. On MRI, the mass appears isointense to muscle on T1WI and isointense or slightly hyperintense in T2WI due to oedema. Low-signal fibrous septa may be seen [1–3]. The presence of haemorrhage is not uncommon and can appear as hyperintense foci on T1WI and T2WI (methaemoglobin), or as hypointense foci on T2WI (haemosiderin deposition) [2,3]. The mass could have a well-circumscribed appearance and a complete or incomplete capsule of tumour cells, fibrous tissue and inflammatory components. MRI is also useful to assess local invasion [2]. Both in CT and MRI, there will be a marked or mild enhancement in the parenchyma, depending on the degree of necrosis [1,3]. Imaging manifestations are non-specific, and the non-visualisation of mineralisation does not exclude the diagnosis of EOS [2]. This is why the final diagnosis was provided by percutaneous core needle biopsy. Histologically, the tumour shows proliferation of spindle cells, along with bone or osteoid tissue and cartilage. The spindle cells directly produce the osteoid tissue, which tends to be concentrated in the central region of the tumour, distinguishing it from myositis ossificans. The osteoid matrix can appear in a delicate and lace-like branching pattern and, less frequently, in broad sheets [1,2]. Outcome Treatment includes amputation or wide surgical resection and adjuvant chemotherapy [1,2], with radiotherapy in some cases [2]. Our patient received palliative care after a chest CT revealed multiple pulmonary metastases, classifying the disease as stage IV. Prognosis is poor due to the frequent local recurrences and metastasis to the lungs and bones. Size is the best prognosis factor; lesions less than 5 cm have a better outcome [2]. Our patient died a few months after the diagnosis. Take Home Message Extraskeletal osteosarcoma (EOS) is a rare condition that is challenging to differentiate from other entities. Nevertheless, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of masses that do not originate from bone structures that present thick and lumpy mineralisation in imaging tests. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Polyethylene spacer dislocation in a total knee arthroplasty
clinical_history: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department (ED) after feeling a “pop” in his knee while ascending stairs. He reports knee pain, instability, and swelling. Anteroposterior (AP) and lateral knee radiographs are obtained.
imaging_findings: Knee radiographs show a left total knee arthroplasty with an anteromedial dislocation of the polyethylene spacer, associated mild valgus angulation of the knee and mild lateral tibiofemoral subluxation, large knee joint effusion, and an ossific fragment along the medial margin of the proximal tibia measuring 1.5 cm. This favours old trauma or postsurgical, though comparison with any available prior radiographs would be recommended. Old fracture deformity of the distal femoral shaft and vascular calcifications were noted.
discussion: Background The fixed-bearing type prostheses for total knee arthroplasties involve a radiolucent polyethylene spacer between the tibial and femoral components, much like articular cartilage. Complete dislocation of the polyethylene spacer is a rare potential complication of this type of knee arthroplasty, typically associated with trauma or wear [1,2]. Other potential causes include improper surgical placement or failure of the prosthetic locking mechanism [1]. Treatment is typically surgical revision of the prosthesis [1]. Clinical Perspective Symptoms of polyethylene spacer dislocation can include varus–valgus joint instability, limited range of motion, audible noises (metal-on-metal motion), mechanical symptoms, and pain [1–3]. A frequent complication of dislocation is damage to the tibial baseplate or the femoral articular surface of the prosthesis [2,3]. Soft-tissue complications can also occur and will vary depending on the direction of the dislocation [2]. Anterior dislocation can result in patellar tendon injury [3]. Posterior displacement has been reported to cause compression of the popliteal artery and amputation secondary to ischemia [4,5]. As such, dislocation of the polyethylene spacer should be considered in the differential diagnosis of a painful or mechanically unstable total knee arthroplasty. Imaging Perspective Because of the radiolucent properties of the polyethylene inserts, many manufacturers include radio-opaque markers [5,6]. This allows radiographs to be used to establish baseline imaging immediately after a total knee arthroplasty as well as for follow-up imaging [6]. Further imaging can be obtained with MRI, in which the polyethylene insert is expected to appear as a low-signal-intensity structure on all pulse sequences [2,5]. Teaching Points Fixed-bearing prostheses for knee arthroplasties involve a radiolucent polyethylene spacer between the tibial and femoral components. Dislocation of the polyethylene spacer is a potential complication of total knee arthroplasty and should be considered in the differential diagnosis of a painful or mechanically unstable total knee arthroplasty. The most common cause of dislocation is trauma, but nontraumatic dislocation may be caused by improper surgical placement of the spacer or failure of the prosthetic locking mechanism. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Stone-containing caliceal diverticulum
clinical_history: A 56-year-old man presented with a one-month history of intermittent dull right-sided flank pain.
imaging_findings: Computed tomography urography revealed a well-defined, rounded structure at the level of the mid calyces of the right kidney (Figure 1a). On non-contrast images (soft tissue window), the lesion appeared as a calcified mass measuring approximately 1.6 x 1.7 x 2.2 cm (Figure 1b). On bone window images, the lesion was seen to consist of numerous tiny calcifications rather than a single solid mass (Figure 1c). Localised cortical thinning was noted (Figure 2), likely due to chronic pressure or adjacent parenchymal remodelling. Excretory-phase images demonstrated a fluid-contrast level within the lesion, indicating layering of contrast material (Figures 3a and 3b). Communication with adjacent middle minor calyces was evident (Figure 4), confirming the diagnosis of a calyceal diverticulum containing multiple calcifications.
discussion: Background A calyceal diverticulum (CD) is a cystic cavity formed by the protrusion of a calyx into the renal parenchyma. It maintains communication with the collecting system through a narrow channel referred to as an infundibulum or neck, and is usually lined by transitional epithelium, similar to the rest of the urinary tract [1,2]. The exact aetiology of CD remains unclear. The prevailing hypothesis suggests a congenital origin. Acquired cases may occur secondary to infection, cyst rupture, vesicoureteral reflux, or obstructive urolithiasis [2,3]. CD is relatively uncommon, detected in 0.2–4.5% of the general population, more frequently affecting females (2:1), most often located in the upper pole (48.9%), with bilateral involvement in approximately 3% of cases [3,4]. CD is divided into two types. Type I is more common, typically located in the upper pole and communicating with a minor calyx. Type II is less frequent, larger in size, and communicates directly with the renal pelvis or a major calyx, usually in the interpolar region [5]. Clinical Perspective In most patients, CD is asymptomatic. If symptoms do occur, they may include dull flank pain, urinary frequency, recurrent urinary tract infections or haematuria. In some cases, renal colic may develop due to stone formation within the diverticulum, a common complication due to urinary stasis [4,5]. Imaging Perspective Although CD is radiolucent and not visible on plain radiographs, it can appear as a meniscus-shaped density when containing milk of calcium, with this density changing based on patient positioning, such as upright, supine, or decubitus views. On ultrasound, the diverticulum may mimic a simple renal cyst but can contain echogenic foci suggestive of milk of calcium or stones. On non-contrast CT and in the nephrographic phase of contrast-enhanced CT, the diverticulum appears as a simple cyst. The diagnosis is confirmed only in the excretory phase when the cyst fills with contrast material, indicating communication with the collecting system, and shows contrast layering inside. Although intravenous urography is less commonly used today, it remains a reliable method for demonstrating the narrow communication between the diverticulum and the calyx by visualising contrast entry in delayed images [3,6]. Outcome In asymptomatic patients, conservative observation is often sufficient. Management of symptomatic CD with stones includes shockwave lithotripsy, ureteroscopy or percutaneous nephrostolithotomy [2,4]. Take Home Message In summary, calyceal diverticulum is a benign, typically congenital renal lesion that may become clinically relevant when complicated by infection or stone formation. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Saw-tooth cardiomyopathy
clinical_history: A 29-year-old female patient presented to the cardiology department with episodes of numbness in both her upper and lower extremities, which spontaneously resolved after 30 minutes. She also reported episodes of chest pain that she attributed to stress. Heart auscultation was normal. ECG showed diffuse ST-elevations.
imaging_findings: Echocardiography (ECG) demonstrated severe systolic heart failure, with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 30%. The exam showed basal hypokinesia and preserved apical contractility, along with irregularities in the lining of the left ventricular myocardium (Figure 1). A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) scan revealed no coronary abnormalities but confirmed the irregularities in the left ventricle wall (Figure 2). Subsequently, a cardiac MRI was performed, which revealed moderate left ventricle dilation and irregularities in the ventricle wall, including protrusions of myocardial bridges, multiple crypts, and thinning of the inferolateral apex with diffuse dyskinesia (Figures 3 and 4). Severe left ventricular dysfunction was confirmed, with an LVEF of 20% and a global longitudinal strain (GLS) of -7.85%, as well as ventricular dyssynchrony. A non-ischemic fibrosis region was also present in the interventricular septum and the posterior hinge point. The right ventricle appeared to be normal in morphology and function.
discussion: Background Saw-tooth cardiomyopathy (STC) is a rare form of cardiomyopathy that primarily affects the left ventricle, particularly the apex and middle segments of the lateral and inferior walls [1]. Few cases have been documented in the literature involving both adults and children, including a case of a two-month-old infant, suggesting that this condition may have early and possibly prenatal origins [2]. The exact pathophysiology of STC is not fully understood, and no pathogenic genetic mutations have been identified to date [3]. Clinical Perspective The range of clinical symptoms varies widely, from asymptomatic cases to symptoms such as dyspnoea, chest pain, or even severe left ventricular dysfunction and heart failure [4]. Abnormalities on the ECG, such as left bundle branch block, have been reported; however, the ECG can also appear normal [5]. Imaging Perspective Due to the presenting symptoms, the initial imaging is typically an echocardiogram, which can reveal abnormalities in the left ventricle wall and potential dysfunction. The subsequent step should ideally be a cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement imaging, which can confirm or exclude STC. This imaging technique illustrates a distinct “saw-tooth” appearance of the left ventricle wall, characterised by multiple band-like projections of compacted myocardium, particularly at the apex and middle segments of the inferior and lateral walls, accompanied by myocardial thinning in the crypts. Late gadolinium enhancement usually does not show evidence of fibrosis or ischemia. Cine sequences can be employed to identify and quantify functional abnormalities. Outcome The most common complications and reasons for hospitalisation are left ventricular failure or left bundle branch block. Management and prognosis are closely related to the extent of ventricular dysfunction, and treatment typically includes standard heart failure therapies. Follow-up is recommended, and with appropriate treatment, recovery of cardiac function and symptomatic improvement can be achieved. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Saw-tooth cardiomyopathy (STC) is a rare type of left ventricular cardiomyopathy that can result in left ventricular dysfunction. It has a distinctive appearance in imaging, most clearly seen in cardiac MRI. Therefore, it is essential to recognise this condition and distinguish it from left ventricular noncompaction.

title: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis with total ureteral involvement
clinical_history: A 29-year-old male with a history of recurrent urolithiasis presented with persistent abdominal pain and unexplained fever. Blood tests revealed elevated inflammatory markers and impaired renal function.
imaging_findings: On the CT scan, the left kidney is markedly enlarged, and multiple kidney calculi, including a staghorn calculus, are identified within the calyces and renal pelvis (Figures 1a and 2a). Diffuse thinning of the renal cortex and non-homogeneous, poorly differentiated renal parenchyma, replaced by multiple hypodense fluid-filled cavities (mean attenuation ~ +11 HU) (Figure 1b), with rim enhancement (Figure 3), consistent with the “bear paw sign”, associated with minimal air-fluid levels. Fat-density areas (mean attenuation ~ -60 HU) within and adjacent to the fluid collections (xanthomas) are seen (Figure 1c). The renal pelvis and calyces are dilated. The perirenal fat stranding and thickening of both Gerota’s and Zuckerkandl’s fasciae are noted, indicating stage II–III inflammatory extension. The entire ureter shows diffuse wall thickening with fat stranding and linear calcifications in the mid-ureter (Figure 2b). On the delayed urographic phase, there is no contrast excretion, confirming impaired left kidney function (Figure 4a and 4b).
discussion: Background Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP) is a rare type of chronic pyelonephritis, associated with staghorn calculus (80%) and urinary infection, leading to renal and extra-renal inflammation [1–4]. Clinical Perspective XGP is usually unilateral, diffuse, with a left-sided predominance [5,6]. The estimated incidence in the general population is about 0.0014%, and 0.6–1.0% among patients with chronic pyelonephritis. Peak incidence is at 50–70 years, with a 2:1 female-to-male ratio [7,4]. Other risk factors include renal malignancies, diabetes, and rheumatoid arthritis [1,7]. Chronic inflammation and macrophage infiltration replace normal renal tissue with xanthoma cells, possibly driven by vimentin expression [1]. Patients with XGP typically address flank or abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, fever, and weight loss. A palpable renal mass may be detected. Laboratory findings include leukocytosis, anaemia, and positive urine culture for P. mirabilis or E. coli [4,6,7]. XGP is known as “the great imitator” due to its ability to mimic other conditions, particularly renal malignancy [1,6]. Imaging Perspective Radiograph findings can include nephrolithiasis, enlarged renal outline and psoas sign [6]. Computed tomography (CT) is the gold standard for XGP staging. It is classified into three stages: stage I (nephric), stage II (perinephric), and stage III (paranephric) according to Malek and Elder (1978) [1,5]. The most specific CT feature is the axial “bear paw sign” (72% of cases). It results from dilated calyces filled with hypodense fluid collections (-10 to +30 HU) surrounded by rim-enhancing residual renal parenchyma, centred around a paradoxically contracted renal pelvis. The presence of a staghorn calculus is common but not essential for diagnosis [1,6]. Areas of fat-density (-20 to -100 HU) are called xanthomas (5.56%), located within or adjacent to fluid collections [5]. Contralateral compensatory hypertrophy can be seen [1]. Delayed imaging typically shows minimal contrast excretion, indicating impaired renal function [6]. The stage II signs include perinephric fat enhancement with thickening of the Gerota’s fascia [1,5]. Stage III disease involves extension beyond the perinephric space. Complications may include abscesses and fistulas [8,9]. Ureteral involvement is a rare finding, presenting as irregular wall thickening with surrounding fat stranding. The definitive diagnosis is made by histopathology [6]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Bronchogenic cyst of the retropharyngeal space
clinical_history: A 64-year-old man with a history of smoking and occasional alcohol use presented with a foreign body sensation and odynophagia. Clinical examination showed a bulge on the right lateral pharyngeal wall with normal mucosa and palatine tonsil. Neurological exam and lab tests, particularly white blood cell count, SR and RCP, were unremarkable.
imaging_findings: The patient underwent an MR scan showing a 20 x 35 x 43.5 mm cystic mass in the right retropharyngeal space (RPS) (Figures 1a and 1b), bulging the prevertebral muscles and impinging on the oropharynx, with leftward deviation and reduced airway patency. The mass was spontaneously hyperintense to muscle on T1W images (Figure 2), hyperintense on T2W images, with a thin septation on T2 FS images (Figure 3). There was no restricted diffusion on the ADC map (Figure 4), and no enhancement was noted on subtracted T1W images before and after gadolinium administration (Figures 5a and 5b). There was no oedema in the surrounding tissues, and no abnormalities were seen in the pharynx, larynx, oesophagus, thyroid, or cervical lymph nodes. A comparison with an MR scan from 20 years ago showed the lesion was already present but smaller (10 x 20 x 35 mm) (Figure 6). At that time, the MRI was performed for unrelated reasons, and the incidental retropharyngeal lesion was interpreted as a presumed vascular malformation. Since the patient was asymptomatic, follow-up observation and monitoring was implemented, but the patient was lost to follow-up after a few years.
discussion: Retropharyngeal lesions have a narrow differential diagnosis, including infections, metastatic lymphadenopathy, lymphoproliferative diseases, mesenchymal tumours (e.g., vasculo-lymphatic malformations, neurogenic tumours, sarcomas), and, more commonly, invasion from adjacent neoplasms from the pharynx, oesophagus, thyroid, or sinonasal epithelium. In our case, the absence of contrast enhancement, smooth contour of the lesion and slow growth over 20 years ruled out a lymph node metastasis, lymphoproliferative disease and a sarcoma, and the absence of restricted diffusion ruled out a suppurative lymphadenopathy and retropharyngeal abscess. Although no neurologic deficits were noted, namely Horner’s syndrome, a cystic/haemorrhagic neurogenic tumour could not be completely excluded. The presence of spontaneous hyperintensity on T1W images can reflect fat (excluded in this case on the basis of the FS T1W and T2W images), high protein content, melanin or haemorrhage. With a presumed diagnosis of a benign cystic lesion, atypical branchial cyst, foregut duplication cyst or an ectopic parathyroid cyst, the patient underwent transoral surgery with dissection of the capsule of the retropharyngeal mass. The patient recovered uneventfully. Histopathology revealed a retropharyngeal bronchogenic cyst (Figure 7). Among retropharyngeal cystic lesions, atypical branchial cysts and foregut duplication cysts, either bronchogenic or oesophageal, are the most frequent. Bronchogenic cysts (BC) are congenital abnormalities secondary to abnormal budding of the ventral foregut, lined by ciliated columnar or cuboidal cells and surrounded by tissue resembling normal bronchus [1–3]. The majority of these cysts (70%) occur in the mediastinum [2,4], comprising 10–15% of all mediastinal tumours and 50–60% of cystic lesions in the mediastinum [3]. Other locations are rare, including the skin, left ventricle, adrenal glands and neck [5]. In the neck, there are only a few cases reported, with a predilection for the paediatric male population [6]. Patients with large BC may clinically present with respiratory distress, recurrent infections, and gastrointestinal or cardiac symptoms, although small lesions are commonly asymptomatic [7]. Since lesions in the RPS are not accessible clinically, cross-sectional imaging (CT, MRI and/or PET-CT) is essential for their evaluation to help differentiate between benign and malignant lesions. BC and branchial cysts are well-circumscribed lesions characterised by a Hounsfield unit measurement close to water (<20 HU, unless infected) and exhibiting thin walls on CT scan. On MRI signal intensity varies based on their protein concentration but is typically hyperintense on T2WI [3,7]. In cases of superinfection, cysts may develop thicker walls, show mural enhancement, and display signs of surrounding inflammation [7]. Surgery remains the treatment of choice for symptomatic patients. Complete removal is important as the presence of any cystic remnants increases the likelihood of recurrence [7,8]. Carcinomas arising from foregut duplication cysts have been described in the literature, highlighting the importance of full surgical excision and regular clinical and radiological follow-ups to monitor recurrence [8–10]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Acute Marchiafava–Bignami disease
clinical_history: A 36-year-old male with chronic alcohol use presented with a sudden loss of consciousness. He had no history of seizures, fever, or vomiting. Blood tests were normal. Vitamin B12 and folate levels were not measured.
imaging_findings: Brain MRI showed: Symmetrical T2 and FLAIR hyperintensities in corpus callosum (Figures 1a, 1b, 2a, 2b, 3a, 3b, 4a, 4b, and 5) with T1 hypointensities (Figures 1c, 2c, 3c, 4c, and 4d). Diffusion restriction on DWI with low ADC values (Figures 1d, 1e, 2d, 2e, 3d, 3e, 4d, and 4e). Additional involvement of the bilateral fronto-parieto-temporal cortex and corticospinal tracts involving the posterior limb of the internal capsule and midbrain. No post-contrast enhancement (Figures 6a and 6b).
discussion: Background Marchiafava–Bignami disease (MBD) is associated with chronic alcohol abuse and thiamine deficiency, causing corpus callosum demyelination and necrosis [1,2]. It primarily affects malnourished alcoholics [3]. Clinical Perspective MBD presents acutely (confusion, seizures, coma) or chronically (cognitive decline) [4]. Imaging is crucial for diagnosis due to overlap with other encephalopathies [5,6]. Imaging Perspective On CT scans, abnormalities in the corpus callosum often go undetected unless the lesion is significantly large or involves a subacute haemorrhage. During the acute phase, there is typically low attenuation and symmetrical swelling of the corpus callosum. In the subacute stage, the swelling tends to decrease, while the chronic phase is characterised by diffuse atrophy of the structure [8]. MRI findings are more sensitive and commonly reveal areas within the corpus callosum that are hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2 and FLAIR sequences, often accompanied by diffusion restriction. These abnormalities can extend to involve the genu and adjacent white matter [5,6]. Mass effect is usually absent. In the acute setting, contrast enhancement may be present, whereas in chronic cases, the lesions may evolve into centrally located cavities, with preservation of the dorsal and ventral layers of the corpus callosum—a pattern often referred to as the “sandwich sign” [7]. Outcome Poor prognosis when there is cortical involvement. Despite treatment, the patient usually dies within 10 days [6]. Take Home Message Suspect Marchiafava–Bignami disease (MBD) in alcoholic patients with acute neurological symptoms [1,3]. MRI (especially DWI and ADC) is diagnostic [5,6]. The “sandwich sign” is characteristic [7]. Cortical involvement worsens the prognosis [6].

title: The mysterious membrane: A case of duodenal web
clinical_history: A four-year-old girl presented with complaints of bilious vomiting containing food particles after meals for two years. The patient was predominantly on a liquid diet as her symptoms worsened with the intake of solids. On examination, the abdomen was soft and distended with visible peristalsis.
imaging_findings: The frontal chest radiograph (Figure 1) showed dilatation of the stomach and proximal duodenum. There is the presence of air in the distal bowel loops. Both the lungs and cardiophrenic angles are normal. The cardiac silhouette is normal. The barium meal (Figures 2a and 2b) showed the swallowing mechanism to be normal. The passage of barium through the oesophagus to the stomach is smooth and unobstructed. The oesophageal mucosal pattern is normal. It shows no extrinsic mass effect or intrinsic filling defect. There is no gastro-oesophageal reflux or hiatus hernia. There is dilatation of the stomach and of the D1 and D2 segments of the duodenum (Figure 2a). The passage of barium from the stomach into the proximal duodenum is delayed momentarily. There is a short segment of circumferential narrowing at the D2 segment of the duodenum with transverse filling defect and resultant delayed passage of barium into the D3 and D4 segments (Figure 2b). The above findings are suggestive of a duodenal web at the D2. Intraoperative findings (Figure 3) confirmed the diagnosis of duodenal web.
discussion: Background & Clinical Perspective A duodenal web is characterised by a partial membrane in the duodenal lumen, leading to partial or intermittent complete obstruction. It is commonly identified during the neonatal period. Nonetheless, the clinical presentation, timing of diagnosis, and radiological findings vary depending on the diameter of the web’s aperture. When the obstruction is partial, symptoms usually present during the second or third year of life. There is no gender predisposition. Most duodenal webs (approximately 85%–90%) are in the first and second segments of the duodenum. However, about 20% and 10% are found in the third and fourth parts, respectively [1]. Duodenal webs may coexist with congenital conditions such as Down syndrome, hypospadias, foregut duplication cysts, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, inguinal hernia, cleft lip, and intestinal malrotation. During embryological development, the duodenal lumen becomes temporarily occluded between the 5th and 12th weeks of gestation due to epithelial cell proliferation. Recanalisation occurs through a process of vacuolation. A failure of this process can result in congenital duodenal atresia [2]. The aperture size of the web influences the severity of obstruction, the age at which symptoms appear, and the corresponding imaging features. In the early stages, symptoms may include feeding intolerance and vomiting. Later in childhood or adolescence, patients may present with nausea, abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, and occasionally acute pancreatitis. Imaging Perspective The initial imaging modality is abdominal radiography, which may show dilated bowel loops depending on the location and severity of the obstruction. The presence of gas in the distal loops may indicate a partial obstruction. Ultrasonography has limited utility but may show dilated loops with content and help localise the web. Upper gastrointestinal barium studies are useful for visualising the duodenal contour and help identify narrowing or obstructions caused by a web. A duodenal web often appears as a transverse filling defect or narrowed region in the duodenum on barium imaging. Fluoroscopic evaluation during an upper gastrointestinal contrast study demonstrated the characteristic “windsock sign”, indicating a mucosal outpouching of a fenestrated duodenal web projecting into the distal duodenum. Computed tomography scan is beneficial for confirming these findings, although it is less preferred considering the younger age group. Management & Outcome Surgical intervention remains the gold standard for symptomatic duodenal webs. The primary surgical approach involves duodenotomy with excision of the web [3]. Endoscopic management includes balloon dilation or radial incision and cutting [4]. The role of interventional radiology remains underutilised, despite its minimally invasive nature and potential to obviate the need for surgical intervention. Minimally invasive image-guided techniques have shown promise in the management of membranous duodenal stenosis, potentially eliminating the need for surgical intervention. Fluoroscopically guided balloon dilatation has been reported as a safe and effective treatment option, with initial case series demonstrating successful outcomes in children without requiring subsequent surgery [5]. Similarly, image-guided approaches have been described as novel and effective methods for managing both congenital and acquired duodenal strictures, offering a less invasive alternative to traditional operative procedures [6]. In addition, endoscopic intervention by paediatric gastroenterologists has also shown promise; gastroscopic resection of the duodenal membrane was successfully performed in a series of six children, avoiding surgical intervention [7]. Take Home Message Partial duodenal obstruction from a congenital web typically manifests during the second or third year of life. Symptoms such as recurrent vomiting, abdominal distension, weight loss and constipation should raise a clinical suspicion. Due to the subtle signs of partial obstruction, diagnosis can be challenging for general practitioners. Abdominal radiographs and computed tomography scans are instrumental in establishing a diagnosis, and surgical treatment is usually effective. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Unilateral cochlear hypoplasia and cochlear nerve aplasia
clinical_history: A sixteen-year-old male patient presented with congenital deafness on the left side and normal hearing on the right side. There was a family history of deafness and hearing loss on the father’s side. He experienced relatively few difficulties in daily life. Audiometry showed near-total deafness on the left side and normal thresholds on the right.
imaging_findings: A 3T MR study of the temporal bones was performed. The thin, heavily T2-weighted images revealed a bud-like, cystic cochlea on the left side with absent normal turns, modiolus and interscalar septa (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c and 6). Additionally, there was no identifiable left cochlear nerve, and apart from the facial nerve, there was only one other nerve, smaller in calibre compared to the facial nerve, in the internal auditory canal, consistent with a hypoplastic vestibulocochlear nerve and cochlear nerve aplasia (Figures 3a, 4a, 4b, 4c, 4d, 4e, and 4f). The vestibular nerve did not bifurcate into a superior and inferior branch. The left inner ear canal was small in calibre as well, progressively narrowing from medial to lateral. The left vestibule appeared mildly globose (Figure 2). The left lateral semicircular canal exhibited focal signal loss, which could either be a true abnormality or an artefact. The inner ear structures and inner ear canal on the right side were normally developed (Figures 1a, 1b, 3b, 5a, 5b, 5c, 5d, 5e, and 5f).
discussion: Background Bony inner ear malformations contribute to about 20% of congenital sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) [1]. Classification systems, like the Sennaroğlu classification, assist clinicians in diagnosing and managing these anomalies. Cochlear hypoplasia (CH), one such anomaly in which the cochlea is underdeveloped, shows smaller dimensions and various internal abnormalities [2,3]. Clinical Perspective Hearing loss in CH can range from mild to profound and tends to be stable, though in some cases it may worsen. The severity and type of hearing loss—whether conductive, mixed, or sensorineural—can vary. These diverse patterns complicate the identification of CH, as no specific audiological feature is unique to it [2]. Imaging Perspective CT imaging is essential for evaluating bony structures in CH, while MRI with T2-weighted sequences is required to assess the cochlear nerve. In CH, the cochlea and vestibule can be identified as separate structures. CH type I presents with a severely deformed, bud-like cochlea, lacking a modiolus or interscalar septum. In the other CH subtypes progress, the malformation becomes less pronounced, which can make diagnosis more difficult [2]. Facial nerve abnormalities are common, and displacement of segments like the labyrinthine portion may occur, especially in syndromic cases such as CHARGE syndrome. Accurate imaging is key for planning cochlear implantation or other surgeries, as cochlear size and facial nerve positioning may require a different electrode and tailored surgical approach, respectively [3,4]. Outcome For those with mild to moderate hearing loss, hearing aids are typically effective in terms of hearing rehabilitation. However, cochlear implantation is often required for patients with severe to profound hearing loss, especially if the cochlear nerve is normal. In cases of cochlear nerve hypoplasia, cochlear implants may still be feasible. In cochlear nerve aplasia, auditory brainstem implantation is currently the only hearing rehabilitation option. Additionally, patients with conductive or mixed hearing loss (due to concomitant stapedial fixation) may benefit from stapedotomy [3]. In our case, no treatment was done, because of the late presentation and few complaints in daily life. Take Home Message The diversity in inner ear malformations, including cochlear hypoplasia (CH), necessitates accurate classification for optimal diagnosis, as different types of inner ear malformation have different management implications. Understanding the clinical, radiological, and audiological features of CH helps determine the best interventions, improving hearing outcomes and quality of life. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Mandibular manifestation of infantile cortical hyperostosis (Caffey disease)
clinical_history: A 6-month-old infant presented with a history of on-and-off soft tissue swelling over the left cheek since 2 months (Figure 1). No history of trauma. Full-term normal delivery.
imaging_findings: Head and neck CT with bone reconstruction showed cortical irregularity with sclerosis, solid periosteal reaction, increase in cortical width and density, seen along the angle and ramus of the left hemimandible (Figures 2a and 2b). On MRI, the corresponding area showed mild STIR hyperintensity (Figure 3) and T1 hypointensity (Figure 4). No evidence of any significant diffusion restriction was seen in this region (Figures 5a and 5b). Surrounding oedematous changes were seen in the left masticator muscles and infratemporal fossa. No focal discrete collection or solid component was seen.
discussion: Background Infantile cortical hyperostosis, or Caffey disease, is a rare, self-limiting disease presenting with clinical features of fever, irritability, and on-and-off soft tissue swelling. This disease has two forms: the mild infantile form and the severe prenatal form. It can have both sporadic and familial transmission with autosomal dominant and recessive patterns. A mutation in the COL1A1 gene (type 1 collagen) is associated with Caffey disease; there is no sex or racial predilection [1,2]. Imaging Perspective On imaging, Caffey disease is characterised by subperiosteal reaction and new bone formation involving the diaphysis of the long bones and mandible. The disease most commonly affects flat bones like the mandible (70–80%) and clavicles. Among the long bones, the ulnae are most commonly affected. On radiograph, subperiosteal cortical hyperostosis under the region of soft tissue swelling is seen in Caffey disease. Radiograph is not the diagnostic imaging because it is important to rule out other imaging differentials [3]. CT findings include cortical hyperostosis and the presence of radiolucent areas within the bone. MRI shows periostitis and soft tissue oedema. MRI gives detailed information about the soft-tissue reactions and marrow oedema, appearing T2 and STIR hyperintense, and T1 hypointense. MRI helps to differentiate infantile cortical hyperostosis from osteomyelitis, which presents with lytic areas of bone destruction, irregular or interrupted periosteal reaction and soft tissue abscess in some cases. MRI also helps in differentiating Caffey disease from bone tumours such as Ewing sarcoma, which is an important differential diagnosis of Caffey disease [4]. Outcome As noted above, Caffey disease is self-limiting and resolves spontaneously. Symptomatic treatment consists of NSAIDs. Late complications include mandibular asymmetry and undergrowth, as well as disease recurrence in childhood. Take Home Message A high index of suspicion and awareness of the existence of this condition is necessary, and it is important to differentiate it from other differentials like osteomyelitis. A detailed history, clinical examination, basic laboratory studies and radiograph are sufficient enough to make a diagnosis in most cases, and MRI can help to exclude the important differential diagnoses.

title: Clawed life – A case of familial split hand/foot malformation
clinical_history: A 2-year-old male child was brought by his 34-year-old mother with complaints of abdominal pain and recurrent vomiting. The child was clinically stable, and the abdominal ultrasound was normal. However, we incidentally discovered that both the mother and the son had physical impairments in their bilateral upper and lower limbs.
imaging_findings: The child had a classical median cleft with rudimentary bilateral thumbs with loss of opposition movement (Figure 1). A frontal radiograph revealed a bilateral median cleft, and the right hand’s proximal phalanges of the middle and index fingers fused, resulting in syndactyly. An additional middle phalanx was observed in the right thumb. Bilaterally, the thumb and index finger were displaced toward each other (Figures 2a and 2b). The radiography of the child’s feet depicted the absence of three of his metatarsals (Figure 2c). The X-ray of the infant’s skull showed multiple convolutions, suggesting a copper-beaten appearance (Figure 3). Interestingly, his 34-year-old mother, too, suffered from a similar deformity. On clinical inspection, both her right and left hands showed the presence of only three fingers (Figure 4a). A hypoplastic index finger was seen in the left hand. Bilateral feet showed only two toes with possible syndactyly (Figure 4b).
discussion: Background Split hand/split foot malformation (SHFM), also described as lobster-claw deformity, is a congenital limb deformity most commonly affecting the median rays of the hand and foot. Both sporadic (non-familial) and familial cases have been previously documented [1]. The disorder manifests as various phenotypes, ranging from a slight shortening of the third digit to its total absence, as well as bidactyly, monodactyly, and syndactyly [2]. The patient may have hypoplasia and/or a total lack of the phalanges, metacarpals, and metatarsals [3]. Every 1 in 90,000 people is thought to be affected by split hands and feet deformity [4]. Clinical Perspective A developing limb bud consists of two layers of cells: highly proliferating central mesenchymal cells surrounded by a layer of ectodermal cells. The limb bud development is initiated by the signalling molecules that specialised cell groups produce: the apical ectodermal ridge (AER), the progress zone (PZ), and the zone of polarising activity (ZPA) [5]. The interplay between these three cell groups regulates the pattern of limb development in three dimensions: anteroposterior, proximodistal, and dorsoventral [5]. The failure to maintain the AER leads to the development of SHFM. Apart from genetic factors, environmental factors like apoptosis in the AER can also lead to SHFM [5]. The literature mentions six types of basic SHFM, ranging from SHFM1 to SHFM6, and one additional SHFM/SHFLD (split hand/split foot malformation and long-bone deficiency) type [5]. The final confirmation can be given by the genetic makeup of the patient. The likely SHFM type in this case can be SHFM1 (7q21) or SHFM3 (10q24), both typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. This can be supported by bilateral, symmetric limb involvement in both mother and child, isolated limb deformities without syndromic features, and the absence of long bone abnormalities. As we were unable to perform the genetic testing on the patient, we were unable to classify the condition definitively [5]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasonography can be used to diagnose SHFM antenatally [6]. Antenatal diagnosis in the first trimester with amniocentesis can detect the anomaly, preventing this outcome. Outcome Regarding the cleft hand, Adrian Flatt remarked, “A functional triumph but a social disaster” [2]. There have been very few reported cases of surgical intervention in such patients. The primary aim of the surgery in SFHM is to improve the unsettling appearance. Post-surgery, one ray might still be missing, but with good closure of the cleft and the achievement of parallelism of the long fingers, the physical appearance of the hand can be improved. All things considered, the course of treatment may be lengthy and does not guarantee complete limb function. Genetic counselling for parents before planning a pregnancy is one of the most effective ways to diagnose and prevent SHFM. Counselling may be recommended for affected persons, including lifestyle management, physiotherapy sessions, and occupational therapy for improving motor skills and range of motion. Take Home Message Median cleft hand or split hand foot malformation is a complex, rare malformation that needs multidisciplinary management. Prosthetics used with reconstructive surgery can enhance prognosis and improve quality of life.

title: Neuroacanthocytosis syndrome (chorea-acanthocytosis)
clinical_history: A 33-year-old female presents with a 6-year history of abnormal involuntary movements of all limbs, face, and lips, which initially started as increased fidgeting and finger flicking. Cognitive decline began a year later, with memory loss, disorientation, and difficulty dressing and eating, and now is fully dependent for activities of daily living.
imaging_findings: A contrast-enhanced MRI (CEMRI) of the brain was performed with 1.5T with sequences of T1WI inversion recovery 3D, T2WI axial and coronal, 3D FLAIR, SWI, DWI, and MR spectroscopy (MRS). MRI revealed atrophy of the head of the caudate bilaterally (Figures 1 and 2) with decreased FH:CC ratio of 1.18 (frontal horn width to intercaudate distance ratio) (Figure 5) and increased CC:IT ratio of 0.25 (intercaudate distance to inner table width ratio) (Figure 6). Volume loss of the putamen and globus pallidus was noted bilaterally. An enlargement of the bilateral frontal horns of the lateral ventricles, giving a box-like configuration, is noted. There is evidence of T2/FLAIR hyperintensities (Figures 3 and 4) seen in the involved region with mild grade II mineralisation seen in globi pallidi, extending to bilateral posterolateral putamen and also in the substantia nigra. Mild prominence of sulci and ventricles with grey matter volume loss is suggestive of mild cerebral volume loss. MRS shows choline peak and mild NAA (N-acetyl aspartate) loss in the basal ganglia (Figures 7a, 7b, 7c, and 7d).
discussion: Background Neuroacanthocytosis (NA) refers to a group of rare hereditary neurodegenerative disorders characterised by the presence of acanthocytes in peripheral blood and progressive dysfunction of the basal ganglia [1]. The most common subtype, chorea-acanthocytosis (ChAc), results from biallelic mutations in the VPS13A gene, leading to a deficiency of chorein, a family of bridge-like lipid transfer proteins [2,3]. The clinical and imaging presentation frequently overlaps with Huntington’s disease (HD), often complicating the diagnostic process. Clinical Perspective Huntington’s disease is the most common condition thought of in patients with chorea and a positive family history. Neuroacanthocytosis, although rare, should also be considered. Points leading to the favour of NA are the presence of lower face dystonia (HD mainly involves the forehead), feeding dystonia, and characteristic head drops [7]. Imaging Perspective MRI plays a key role in differentiating NA from HD. In HD, the earliest and most prominent finding is atrophy of the caudate nuclei, with relative sparing of the putamen and globus pallidus in early stages [5]. In contrast, NA often demonstrates more extensive and symmetric involvement of the caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus [4,6]. T2 and FLAIR hyperintensities in these regions are common in NA, reflecting gliosis. A particularly distinguishing feature is the mineralisation of the basal ganglia, best seen on T2/SWI sequences, which is rare in HD and serves as a key radiological differentiator. In our case, MRS revealed decreased NAA and elevated choline in the basal ganglia, consistent with neuronal loss and metabolic stress. Outcome There is currently no curative therapy for NA. Management is supportive and includes pharmacologic treatment of movement disorders and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Early recognition through imaging is critical for initiating genetic counselling, preventing misdiagnosis, and avoiding unnecessary testing. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Neuroacanthocytosis (NA) should be suspected in patients with movement disorders and basal ganglia mineralisation, especially when imaging shows combined atrophy of the caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus. T2/SWI sequences and MRS can provide crucial diagnostic information, helping distinguish neuroacanthocytosis from Huntington’s disease.

title: Unilateral right pulmonary artery agenesis with collateral circulation
clinical_history: A 37-year-old male presents at the emergency room with haemoptysis. Otherwise, there were no significant findings and no medical history.
imaging_findings: Chest X-ray shows an asymmetry in the hilar vascularisation, with absence of a normal vascular right hilum (Figure 1). Computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) with dual energy (DE) is performed. The right pulmonary artery is absent (Figures 2, 3, and 5). There is a large collateral circulation of the right lung by the bronchial arteries, which can be seen as enlarged in the mediastinum and right hilar region (Figure 4). The right lung shows a slight volume loss, and there is a minor shift of the cardiomediastinum to the right (Figure 6). Dual energy perfusion maps reveal asymmetric hypoperfusion of the right lung, compatible with secondary oligemia due to the agenesis of the right pulmonary artery (Figures 7 and 8). Ventilation-perfusion scintigraphy reconfirms the asymmetric hypoperfusion of the right lung (perfusion of 95.4% left lung and 4.6% right lung) (Figure 9), while there is a slightly asymmetric ventilation (64.9% left lung and 35.1% right lung) (Figure 10).
discussion: Background Unilateral absence of the pulmonary artery (UAPA) is a rare congenital anomaly (estimated at 1 in 200,000 young adults [1]) that can lead to various respiratory symptoms, including haemoptysis. This condition often presents diagnostic and therapeutic challenges, particularly in adult patients [2]. Clinical Perspective Adult patients with UAPA may present with respiratory symptoms such as dyspnoea (41.5%), recurrent infections (35.4%), or haemoptysis (41.5%) [2]. Some patients may have severe pulmonary hypertension or a heart anomaly associated [3]. However, some individuals remain asymptomatic (15.4–30%) [2,3]. The differential diagnoses of haemoptysis are wide and have to be made with tuberculosis, other respiratory infections, malignant lesions, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, and vascular anomalies [4]. Imaging is crucial to confirm the diagnosis of UAPA and to assess the extent of collateral circulation and any associated complications [1]. Imaging Perspective Chest CT and CT angiography are essential for visualising the absence of the pulmonary artery and identifying collateral vessels. The development of collateral circulation may involve arteries such as the bronchial, intercostal, subdiaphragmatic, subclavian, or coronary arteries. This collateral circulation may be visible in the lung as thickened interlobular septae. Imaging can reveal compensatory hypertrophy of the contralateral lung and any associated bronchiectasis or vascular abnormalities. A combination of imaging modalities, including chest X-ray, CT and echocardiography, helps in making a definitive diagnosis and planning treatment [1,5,6]. Outcome Therapeutic options for managing haemoptysis due to UAPA include selective embolisation, lobectomy, or pneumonectomy. The prognosis varies depending on the severity of symptoms and lung function. However, surgical intervention, particularly pneumonectomy, has shown favourable outcomes in preventing recurrent haemoptysis [1–3]. Imaging significantly impacts therapy planning by providing essential information on vascular anatomy and lung perfusion, guiding the choice of surgical intervention [7]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Adult patients with unilateral absence of the pulmonary artery (UAPA) may present with vague respiratory symptoms, giving a wide differential diagnosis. Understanding the clinical and imaging aspects of UAPA is crucial for effective diagnosis and management, highlighting the importance of a comprehensive approach in patients with haemoptysis. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: A berry in the tongue – An unusual location of haemangioma
clinical_history: 8-year-old female with swelling in the dorsal aspect of the tongue on the left side, present since birth, with slight enlargement in the past 6 months. No history of fever, breathing difficulties, or bleeding tendency. On physical examination, it showed a bluish swelling in the anterior tongue measuring 1.5 x 1 cm, and it was a soft, non-tender mass on palpation (Figure 1).
imaging_findings: Ultrasound of the dorsal aspect of the tongue showed a well-circumscribed hypoechoic lesion with smooth margins in the anterior aspect of the tongue on the left side. No evidence of calcifications (phleboliths) or cystic areas. No surrounding induration was seen. Colour Doppler studies showed mild internal vascularity (Figure 2). MRI showed a well-defined T2 intensely hyperintense (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c), and iso to slightly hyperintense signal in T1-weighted images (Figure 5) in the anterior aspect of the tongue on the left side. No blooming artefacts on the gradient echo sequences (GRE) images (Figure 4). No evidence of true diffusion restriction. Homogeneous contrast enhancement on post-contrast T1 images was seen (Figure 6). Delayed post-contrast images are not available due to patient motion artefacts.
discussion: Background Vascular lesions in the oral cavity are relatively uncommon, including lymphangiomas, haemangiomas, and arteriovenous malformations. Haemangiomas are vascular developmental disorders marked by a phase of rapid growth followed by a gradual yet certain regression [1]. Clinical Perspective Congenital haemangiomas are seen at birth. Infantile haemangiomas present during the first week of life. Most of them grow during the first 6 months and involute by the age of 5. Haemangiomas are developmental vascular abnormalities, and nearly half of these lesions occur in the head and neck region [2]. Haemangioma is considered a hamartomatous lesion, but it is rarely seen in the oral cavity. The most common sites are the buccal mucosa, palate, tongue, and the angle of the mandible, in that order. Possible complications include bleeding tendency, pain, difficulty in chewing, speaking difficulties, and mass effect and macroglossia in case of large lesions. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound with Doppler study is the initial modality of choice to characterise the lesion and to evaluate the vascularity of the lesion. In USG, haemangiomas appear as a well-defined hypoechoic lesion with or without calcifications with internal vascularity (as seen in Figure 2). CT and MRI can be used to demonstrate the extent and depth of the lesion, feeding vessels, and mass effect in case of large lesions. CECT may demonstrate intense contrast enhancement, whereas unenhanced CT may show calcifications. The final diagnosis is made by contrast MRI, which shows a homogeneous pattern of enhancement. Outcome Patients require special care because they are prone to injury, bleeding, and ulceration. Significant haemangiomas can also lead to swallowing difficulties and breathing problems. Most of them are asymptomatic and managed conservatively, which was done in our case. If symptoms like haemorrhage, dyspnoea and dysphagia persist, treatment is needed. Different treatment modalities are available, such as intralesional corticosteroids, sclerosing agents, embolisation, resection, and laser photocoagulation [3]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Tongue haemangiomas can be easily confused with vascular malignancy or melanoma owing to their rare occurrence in the oral cavity [4]. Imaging modalities like USG, colour Doppler studies and MRI of the oral cavity can be used to arrive at a proper diagnosis.

title: The great mimicker: Vertebral lymphoma presenting as Guillain–Barré syndrome
clinical_history: A 5-year-old female presented with a 2-week history of progressive bilateral lower limb weakness (power 3/5) and hyporeflexia, without sensory deficits, bowel or bladder involvement, or systemic symptoms. Upper limbs were unaffected. No recent infections, vaccinations, or trauma were reported.
imaging_findings: MRI of the whole spine revealed altered signal intensity involving the D4 vertebra, with widening of the right neural foramen. A well-defined, lobulated mass of altered signal intensity was noted arising from the vertebra and extending into the extradural extramedullary location of the spinal canal via the widened right D4 neural foramen. It extended longitudinally from D3 to D5 vertebral body levels and measured approximately 8 × 12 × 8 mm (Figure 1). The mass circumferentially encased the spinal cord, causing displacement and compression of the dural sac toward the left (Figure 2). This resulted in T2/FLAIR hyperintensity within the spinal cord at the level of compression, suggestive of cord oedema or myelomalacia. The D4 vertebral body appeared hyperintense on STIR and hypointense on T1WI as compared to other vertebrae (Figures 4 and 3b). The extradural extramedullary mass lesion appeared hyperintense on STIR and isointense on T1WI as compared to the spinal cord (Figures 4 and 3b). The D4 vertebral body and the mass lesion both showed diffusion restriction and post-contrast enhancement (Figures 3a, 3b, 5a and 5b), suggesting vertebral marrow involvement and supporting a vertebral origin for the lesion. Based on the imaging findings, the possibility of a vertebral body lymphoma with extradural extension was raised.
discussion: Primary vertebral lymphoma presenting in the epidural space accounts for 0.1% to 6.5% of all lymphomas [1]. These tumours typically arise from bone marrow of the vertebrae with potential for extension into epidural space, causing spinal cord compression [2]. The presenting symptoms of spinal lymphoma in children are often nonspecific, leading to diagnostic delays. As in this case, the clinical presentation of the patient led the clinician to provisionally diagnose it as Guillain–Barré syndrome. However, the absence of preceding viral illness, the pattern of weakness progression, and normal cerebrospinal fluid findings prompted further neuroimaging. The critical finding that pointed toward vertebral lymphoma in this case was the diffusion restriction within the D4 vertebral body, in addition to the soft tissue component. This pattern strongly suggested a primary vertebral marrow origin of the tumour with subsequent extradural extension, rather than a spinal lesion secondarily invading the bone. MRI characteristics of vertebral lymphoma include isointense signal on T1 and T2 sequences, homogeneous enhancement, and importantly, diffusion restriction within both the soft tissue and osseous components [3,4]. The vertebral involvement pattern in lymphoma typically shows preservation of disc spaces and vertebral height despite marrow infiltration, unlike in infections, which often destroy disc spaces. The transforaminal extension seen in this case is also characteristic of lymphoma’s infiltrative nature [3,4]. Several other entities may mimic spinal lymphoma in children: Neuroblastoma typically demonstrates heterogeneous enhancement, calcifications (30–50% of cases), and shows higher T2 signal intensity than lymphoma [5]. Ewing sarcoma more commonly demonstrates osseous destruction with large soft tissue mass [6]. Spinal tuberculosis (Pott’s disease) characteristically involves disc spaces with vertebral body destruction and paraspinal abscesses with thin peripheral enhancement [5]. Primitive neuroectodermal tumours (PNETs) usually appear as heterogeneously enhancing masses with cystic/necrotic components, unlike the homogeneous appearance of lymphomas [6]. Early detection of spinal lymphoma is essential, as prompt initiation of chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy can prevent permanent neurological deficits. Surgical intervention is typically limited to diagnostic biopsy and emergent decompression in cases of severe cord compression. The presence of vertebral body involvement, as identified through diffusion restriction, impacts treatment planning by confirming the origin of the tumour and guiding appropriate systemic therapy [3]. In our case, surgical excision was performed to decompress the dural sac. The histopathologic evaluation suggested diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
differential_diagnosis: Neuroblastoma with spinal extension Primary vertebral lymphoma with extradural extension Ewing sarcoma Spinal tuberculosis Primitive neuroectodermal tumour (PNET)
final_diagnosis: Primary vertebral lymphoma with extradural extension

title: Child with resected medulloblastoma presenting with insidious hip pain
clinical_history: A 6-year-old child with a diagnosis of Gorlin syndrome, so far manifested by medulloblastoma resected two years ago, and disease-free in subsequent follow-ups until now, presented with insidious hip pain. Given her medical history, a pelvic CT was performed.
imaging_findings: Brain MRI, performed 2 years previously, at the time of medulloblastoma diagnosis, revealed a mottled intraparenchymal mass in the posterior fossa with heterogeneous enhancement and hydrocephalus (Figures 1a and 1b). Actual pelvic CT showed extensive osteolytic involvement with a soft tissue component affecting all included bony structures (vertebral bodies, pelvic girdle, and femurs), with severe destruction of the pelvis and both femoral heads (Figures 2a and 2b). Given the presence of lytic metastases, a subsequent whole-body CT with intravenous contrast in the portal phase was performed, revealing retroperitoneal adenopathic conglomerates (Figure 3) and a single hepatic metastasis (Figure 4).
discussion: Background Medulloblastoma is the most frequent malignant brain tumour in children, with peak incidence at ages 3–4 and 8–9 years. In adults, it is uncommon, comprising only 0.4–1% of primary brain tumours. Typically, it arises as a midline mass in the fourth ventricle, leading to obstructive hydrocephalus and increased intracranial pressure. Leptomeningeal dissemination occurs in approximately 33% of cases at diagnosis. Extraneural metastases (ENM) are rare but may involve bones, bone marrow, lymph nodes, lungs, and liver [1–3]. Molecular classification divides medulloblastomas into four subgroups: WNT-activated, SHH-activated, Group 3, and Group 4 [4]. Additionally, they are associated with hereditary syndromes such as Cowden, Gardner, and Gorlin syndromes [5]. Clinical Perspective Due to their highly cellular nature, medulloblastomas grow rapidly, leading to an acute clinical presentation. Symptoms typically develop over weeks and are dominated by signs of intracranial hypertension secondary to hydrocephalus [4]. MRI is the imaging modality of choice, though CT scans are often the first study performed in emergency settings. In our case, the patient initially presented with headache and ataxia, which prompted a brain MRI (Figures 1a and 1b), which revealed the tumour mass in the posterior fossa and signs of hydrocephalus. Imaging Perspective Most medulloblastomas (94%) originate in the cerebellum, with 75% located in the vermis. Tumours in other locations are more frequent in older children and adults [1]. MRI features: T1-weighted : Hypointense relative to grey matter. T1 with contrast : Heterogeneous enhancement in most cases. T2/FLAIR : Hyperintense with variable heterogeneity due to necrosis, cysts, or calcifications. DWI and ADC : Marked restricted diffusion due to high cellularity. MR spectroscopy : Elevated choline and taurine, reduced NAA. Given the high risk of cerebrospinal fluid dissemination, complete neuraxis imaging is recommended to assess leptomeningeal spread. If ENM is suspected, whole-body CT or PET-CT should be considered. Histopathological analysis after surgical resection confirms the diagnosis. Outcome Management includes surgical resection, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy. Prognosis depends on the extent of resection, presence of metastases at diagnosis, and molecular and histological characteristics. Current long-term survival rates range from 70% to 80%. However, the development of ENM significantly worsens the prognosis [1,3,4]. Our patient underwent surgical resection of the tumour mass, and follow-up MRIs of the entire neuraxis showed no evidence of disease. However, two years later, after the diagnosis of ENM, she received chemotherapy and radiotherapy for two months. Treatment was discontinued due to disease progression, as new metastatic lesions appeared. Therapeutic efforts were subsequently limited, and the patient passed away five months later. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Medulloblastoma should be considered in the differential diagnosis of posterior fossa tumours, especially in children. Extraneural metastases (ENM) are rare, with lytic bone metastases being the most common. Their presence is associated with a poor prognosis. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
