title: Chondroblastoma with secondary aneurysmal bone cyst changes in patella
clinical_history: A 25-year-old male presented with a one-month history of progressive, dull aching pain localised to the anterior right knee, exacerbated by activity (particularly stair climbing and squatting) and partially relieved with rest. He reported no history of trauma, fever, night sweats, or constitutional symptoms. On examination, there was absence of swelling over the knee joint.
imaging_findings: Radiograph of the right patella revealed a well-defined, eccentric lytic lesion with non-sclerotic margins, endosteal scalloping and cortical thinning (Figure 1). MRI demonstrated a solitary, oval, expansile, and geographical lytic lesion (28 x 20 x 33 mm) in the right patella, with internal septations, blood fluid levels and a narrow zone of transition. There was a soft tissue component (13 x 14 x 15 mm) on the superomedial aspect (Figure 2). The soft tissue component appeared hyperintense on proton density fat-saturated (PDFS) sequence, hypointense on T1-weighted images and showed homogeneous post-contrast enhancement (Figures 5a and 5b). No periosteal reaction, skip lesions, or significant soft tissue invasion was observed. CT of the right patella showed absence of any matrix calcification within the lesion (Figure 6). Based on imaging findings, the differential diagnosis included giant cell tumour (GCT) with secondary aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) changes and chondroblastoma with secondary ABC changes.
discussion: Chondroblastoma is a rare benign bone tumour, typically affecting the epiphyses of long bones in adolescents and young adults (10–25 years of age) [1]. It accounts for less than 1% of all primary bone tumours. Patellar involvement is uncommon. Secondary aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) changes may occur, resulting in fluid-fluid levels on imaging [2]. Patients usually present with localised pain and swelling. Chondroblastoma often occurs in skeletally immature patients but can rarely be seen in adults. Imaging is crucial for diagnosis, surgical planning, and to differentiate from other lytic lesions such as giant cell tumour (GCT) and primary ABC. On plain radiographs, chondroblastoma typically appears as geographic radiolucent bone lesions with a narrow zone of transition and may show internal “fluffy” calcifications in about half of the cases. Additional features include endosteal scalloping and cortical thinning. A periosteal reaction, particularly in a meta-diaphyseal location, may be seen, and up to one-third of patients can exhibit joint effusion [3,4]. On MRI, chondroblastoma typically exhibits lobular internal architecture, with a thin hypointense sclerotic rim visible on both T1 and T2-weighted images. Surrounding bone marrow and soft tissue oedema is often present. In some cases, fluid-fluid levels may be observed, particularly in the presence of secondary aneurysmal bone cyst changes [5]. It is important to distinguish between primary ABC, which typically lacks solid components and appears as a purely cystic lesion with fluid-fluid levels, and secondary ABC changes, which are often associated with an underlying tumour such as chondroblastoma or GCT and may present with enhancing solid components or septations [6]. The presence of a lytic, septated lesion with blood-fluid levels in the patella of a young adult raises suspicion for GCT or chondroblastoma with secondary ABC changes. In our case, the patient’s skeletal maturity made GCT more likely than chondroblastoma. Osteomyelitis was considered less likely due to the absence of systemic signs such as fever and the lack of aggressive imaging features such as cortical destruction or periosteal elevation. Our patient underwent curettage and bone grafting. Histopathological examination revealed sheets of mononuclear cells exhibiting oval to elongated nuclei with characteristic longitudinal nuclear grooves (“coffee bean” appearance), along with the presence of distinctive “chicken wire” calcification and scattered multinucleated giant cells, findings consistent with chondroblastoma exhibiting secondary aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) changes. Following curettage, chondroblastoma has a recurrence rate of approximately 10–20%, necessitating regular follow-up imaging to monitor for residual or recurrent disease [1].

title: An unusual case of recurring pneumonia in a toddler
clinical_history: A 2-year-old toddler with a history of recurrent pneumonia, a SpO2 of 96%, and diminished breath sounds at the left lung base was admitted for further evaluation. Despite multiple symptomatic treatments, no imaging studies had been performed previously. Therefore, a chest X-ray was requested to further evaluate the patient.
imaging_findings: The X-ray revealed hyperexpansion of the left lung with consolidation in the left base and thickening of the bronchial walls in the right lung, without areas of consolidation (Figure 1). With clinical suspicion of a pulmonary malformation, a contrast-enhanced CT was performed. The CT images showed hyperexpansion of the left lung with hypodense material located approximately 18 mm from the carina (Figure 2). The bronchial tree was slightly ectatic, without bronchial wall thickening, and there was linear atelectasis at the level of the lingula and the base (Figure 3a). There was a rightward shift of the cardio-mediastinum. The right lung was relatively compressed, with posterior hypoventilation phenomena. The large bronchi on the right were normally patent, but there was hilar vascular congestion (Figures 3b and 3c). A bronchoscopy was performed for the removal of the foreign body. A few days later, an X-ray (Figure 4) showed regular expansion of both lungs.
discussion: Congenital syndromes involving the broncho-pulmonary system, such as lung agenesis-hypoplasia complex, congenital pulmonary airway malformations, congenital lobar overinflation, and scimitar syndrome, can present with varying degrees of lung opacification or hypoplasia in the affected hemithorax. These conditions often lead to a mediastinal shift and overinflation of the contralateral hemithorax [1]. Although many of these congenital syndromes are typically rare, they are usually diagnosed in childhood. Diagnosis in adulthood is extremely uncommon, likely occurring only in mild cases or when other associated abnormalities are absent [2]. In our case, a CT scan initially suggested the possibility of lung agenesis or hypoplasia, but these were quickly ruled out. The right lung appeared underinflated, and the vascular structures were so congested that an arteriovenous malformation was considered [3]. However, the presence of obstruction in the left bronchus by hypodense material led to the identification of the left lung as the pathological one. This finding supported a diagnosis of a “check valve” mechanism, which was causing hyperexpansion of the left lung, compression of the right lung, congestion of the vascular structures, and a rightward shift of the mediastinum. The “check valve” mechanism allows air to enter the bronchus around the foreign body but prevents its exit, leading to overinflation of the affected lung. Due to the delayed diagnosis, our patient child experienced recurrent episodes of pneumonia over several months. Consequently, linear atelectasis and consolidation developed in the left lung. Foreign body aspiration is a common issue in children, necessitating prompt recognition and early treatment to prevent serious and potentially fatal outcomes. Accidental inhalation of both organic and inorganic foreign bodies remains a significant cause of childhood morbidity and mortality [4]. Foreign bodies typically lodge in the right tracheobronchial tree due to the wider and steeper anatomy of the right main bronchus. However, in this particular case, the left bronchus was involved. As stated by Pugmire et al [5]: “Foreign-body aspiration can manifest with nonspecific symptoms and the correct diagnosis can be delayed. Delayed foreign-body removal increases the risk of complications, including pneumonia, atelectasis, and bronchomalacia, so careful attention should be paid to lung inflation in cases where there is a history of non-specific or prolonged respiratory complaints”. Bronchoscopy remains the gold standard for diagnosing foreign bodies in the tracheobronchial tree and offers the advantage of enabling their removal [6]. In our case, after successfully retrieving the foreign body, which was identified as a tangerine seed, a follow-up X-ray confirmed normal expansion of both lungs, with only a small area of consolidation at the left base. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Mammary tuberculosis
clinical_history: A 56-year-old woman presented with a painless right breast lump, present for three months. She also reported easy fatigability, ptosis, and exertional dyspnoea for one year. She was diagnosed with myasthenia gravis, and was started on immunosuppressants five months ago. There was no history of tuberculosis (TB) or contact with TB patients.
imaging_findings: High-resolution CT of the thorax showed a well-defined soft tissue density in the anterior superior mediastinum. CT-guided biopsy revealed polygonal epithelial cells with interspersed lymphocytes, suggestive of thymoma type B1. Only non-contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax was performed (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c) due to contraindication to iodinated contrast in myasthenia gravis. An elliptical pleural-based hyperdense lesion with peripheral calcification and central fluid density was noted along the lateral right hemithorax, suggestive of empyema. A lobulated soft tissue lesion was seen in the lower inner quadrant of the right breast, extending into the underlying pectoral muscle. Ultrasound correlation was advised. Ultrasound of the right breast (Figures 2a, 2b, and 3) revealed an irregular, heterogeneously hypoechoic lesion with posterior enhancement, oriented parallel to the parenchyma from 3 to 5 o’clock position, 2 cm from the nipple–areola complex. No internal vascularity or calcification was seen. The lesion extended into the pectoralis muscle and appeared soft on elastography. It was categorised as BIRADS 4A. Fine-needle aspiration cytology was advised (Figures 4a and 4b).
discussion: Mammary tuberculosis is a rare clinical entity that often mimics breast carcinoma or benign/malignant abscesses. It is usually unilateral and should be considered in immunocompromised states such as HIV infection, diabetes, or iatrogenic immunosuppression [1]. Lactating women are at higher risk due to increased vascularity and dilated ducts, which are more prone to trauma and infection [2]. Tuberculosis may reach the breast via haematogenous spread, lymphatics, direct extension from the chest wall or axillary lymph nodes, or via inoculation through injured skin or ducts [3–5]. The most common presentation is a breast lump, typically located in the central or upper outer quadrant. It may mimic carcinoma—being hard, irregular, and fixed to the skin, muscle, or chest wall [5,6]. Secondary signs may include inflammation, abscess formation, skin ulceration, and diffuse mastitis. Based on clinical and imaging features, mammary tuberculosis can be classified into three forms: nodular, diffuse, and sclerosing. The nodular form is well-circumscribed and slow-growing, presenting as an oval mass on mammography and mimicking carcinoma. The diffuse form shows multiple lesions with sinus tract formation and resembles inflammatory breast cancer. The sclerosing form is seen in elderly women, marked by dense fibrosis and minimal caseation [2,7,8]. Imaging plays a key role in assessment. On ultrasonography, 60% of cases present as hypoechoic masses; sinus tracts or fistulae may be detected [3,6]. Mammography has limited value in young women due to dense breast tissue, but may reveal findings indistinguishable from carcinoma in older patients. CT and MRI can help evaluate the extent of disease beyond the breast. The gold standard for diagnosis remains microbiological confirmation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis via Ziehl–Neelsen staining or culture. Fine-needle aspiration cytology may not always detect the bacilli, but the presence of epithelioid cell granulomas and caseous necrosis is highly suggestive and often sufficient for diagnosis. Differential diagnoses include breast carcinoma, fat necrosis, plasma cell mastitis, periareolar abscess, idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, actinomycosis, and blastomycosis [3,9–12]. The mainstay of treatment is standard four-drug anti-tubercular therapy (ATT). Surgery is usually limited to diagnostic biopsy, drainage of abscesses, or excision of residual lesions unresponsive to medical therapy. Simple mastectomy is reserved for extensive, refractory cases, typically without axillary dissection [7,8,10,13]. Conclusion Given the known association between thymoma and extrathymic malignancies, as well as the increased risk of secondary malignancies in thymoma patients, any painless, slow-growing breast lump in such individuals warrants suspicion of malignancy. However, tuberculous mastitis, though rare, should also be considered, especially in patients on immunosuppressive therapy, which predisposes them to reactivation of latent or new tuberculosis, including extrapulmonary forms. Take Home Message Mammary tuberculosis, though rare, should be considered in the differential diagnosis of breast lumps, especially in immunocompromised patients, to ensure timely initiation of anti-tubercular therapy and avoid misdiagnosis as carcinoma.

title: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy
clinical_history: A 7-year-old male presented with progressive cognitive deterioration, visual dysfunction, behavioural disturbances, and declining academic performance over several months. This clinical progression raised suspicion for a neurodegenerative disorder.
imaging_findings: Brain MRI demonstrated characteristic features of cerebral X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. T2 and FLAIR (Figures 1a, 1b, 2a, 2b, 3a, 3b, 4a, 4b, and 5) show hyperintensities in parieto-occipital white matter, corticospinal tracts (internal capsules, peduncles, pons), middle cerebellar peduncles, and corpus callosum splenium. T1 (Figures 1c, 2c, 3c, and 4c) shows hypointensities in affected areas, with spared subcortical U-fibres. DWI and ADC sequences (Figures 6a and 6b) show periventricular hyperintensity (DWI) with low ADC, suggesting restricted diffusion. Peripheral contrast enhancement (Figures 7a and 7b) indicates active demyelination/inflammation.
discussion: Pathophysiology X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD) is an X-linked peroxisomal disorder caused by mutations in the ABCD1 gene. These mutations impair peroxisomal β-oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs), resulting in their accumulation in neural tissue, adrenal cortex, and testes. This accumulation leads to inflammatory demyelination, adrenal insufficiency, and hypogonadism [1,2]. Clinical Presentation The childhood cerebral form of X-ALD, the most severe phenotype, typically presents between 4 and 10 years of age. Early features include behavioural changes, cognitive regression, and declining academic performance. Rapid progression follows, leading to visual impairment, seizures, spastic paresis, and a vegetative state if untreated [1,3]. Neuroimaging Hallmarks On CT, it may reveal symmetrical hypodensities in the parieto-occipital white matter. Disease progression can involve the frontal lobes, midbrain, pons, corpus callosum, and internal/external capsules. Peripheral contrast enhancement suggests active demyelination [8]. On MRI, T2/FLAIR-weighted images show symmetric posterior white matter hyperintensities (parieto-occipital > frontal), often with contrast-enhancing margins [3,4]. Advanced cases may exhibit signal abnormalities in the brainstem, internal capsules, and subthalamic tracts [4]. On MR spectroscopy, it shows reduced N-acetylaspartate (NAA) and elevated lactate levels, reflecting axonal damage and metabolic stress [5]. Outcome and Management Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) remains the only proven therapy to halt disease progression when administered early. MRI-based Loes scoring aids in assessing eligibility [6]. Lorenzo’s oil may delay the onset in asymptomatic individuals but does not benefit those with established disease [1,7]. A multidisciplinary approach is essential for supportive care, including neurology, endocrinology, and rehabilitation. Corticosteroid therapy is indicated for adrenal insufficiency [1,3]. Take-Home Message Consider X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD) in boys aged 4–10 years with cognitive decline and parieto-occipital white matter lesions. MRI is crucial for early diagnosis and treatment planning. Timely haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can significantly alter the disease course. Genetic screening is vital for family counselling.

title: Hirayama disease
clinical_history: A 21-year-old Caucasian man, an amateur drummer, presents with a two-year history of progressive weakness of the left distal hand. There is no associated pain or sensory loss. Past medical and family history are unremarkable. There is no history of preceding trauma.
imaging_findings: On MRI performed with the neck in the neutral position, T2 and T1-weighted sagittal images (Figures 1 and 2, respectively) reveal mild spinal cord atrophy at the C5–C7 level. On T2 axial images (Figure 3), atrophy of the left anterior horn is clearly visible. In the flexed position (Figure 4), there is an anterior shift of the posterior wall of the cervical dural sac at the C3–Th3 level. A crescent-shaped epidural venous plexus appears in the posterior epidural space, showing high signal intensity on both T1 and T2-weighted sequences and is accompanied by flow voids.
discussion: Background Hirayama disease is a rare, progressive neurological disorder that primarily affects young males, typically between the ages of 15 and 25 years, with a higher prevalence in Asian populations [1]. The condition is characterised by distal upper limb muscle weakness and atrophy, usually presenting unilaterally or in a predominantly asymmetric pattern. Typically, there are no pyramidal signs or sensory disturbances [2,3]. Chronic microcirculatory alterations within the territory of the anterior spinal artery, induced by repeated or sustained neck flexion, are believed to lead to necrosis of the anterior horn cells in the lower cervical spinal cord, constituting the proposed etiopathogenesis [4]. Clinical Perspective The clinical challenge in Hirayama disease is its gradual, asymmetric muscle weakness, which is often misdiagnosed as other neuromuscular disorders. Early recognition is vital, as conservative treatment can stabilise the condition. When requesting imaging, it is important to convey the suspicion of Hirayama disease to ensure the use of appropriate imaging techniques, particularly dynamic studies. Typically, Hirayama disease presents with distal weakness and muscle wasting in one or both upper extremities, an insidious onset with progression over 1 month to 5 years, coarse tremors in the fingers, cold paralysis, and the absence of sensory loss. Atypical presentations may include positive pyramidal signs, proximal upper extremity muscle atrophy, prolonged progression, and sensory deficits [3]. Imaging Perspective MRI, particularly dynamic flexion imaging, is crucial for diagnosing Hirayama disease. In the neutral position, findings may include intramedullary high signal intensity in the anterior horn cells on T2-weighted imaging, asymmetric lower cervical spinal cord atrophy, along with straight alignment or kyphosis of the cervical spine [3]. In the flexed position, hallmark findings include anterior displacement of the posterior dural sac, accompanied by a prominent posterior epidural venous plexus. This venous plexus appears as a crescent-shaped, uniformly enhancing lesion with flow voids in the posterior epidural space [2]. Outcome Hirayama disease typically progresses over 1 month to 5 years, followed by a plateau. About 70% of patients have mild, persistent disabilities. Conservative treatment with a cervical collar limits neck flexion and halts progression until the growth spurt is completed, while physiotherapy helps strengthen muscles. In severe cases, surgery, such as cervical discectomy or duraplasty, may be required [1–3]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Delayed detection of infraorbital foreign body using CT and US
clinical_history: A 5-year-old child was admitted to the ER because of a punctiform cut of the medial side of the right inferior eyelid, with concomitant oedema, erythema, and localised pain during finger pressure, combined with the inability to complete opening of the eyelid, after an accidental fall occurred 12 days before.
imaging_findings: At the admission, the patient brought a former non-contrast CT scan performed 10 days before, which showed well-circumscribed, hypoattenuating spots, with the appearance of infraorbital air, deeply inside the medial side of the right orbit (Figures 1a and 1b), with associated mild exophthalmos and inflammatory changes of the fat tissue nearby, adjacent to the ocular bulb. The extraocular muscles appeared intact. US examination showed a diffuse hyperechogenicity of the infraorbital fat tissue, characterised by a strong colour-Doppler signal, an indicator of intense vascularisation due to inflammation, but the most remarkable finding was an anechoic image with regular borders, spindle-shaped (Figures 2a and 2b). A new CT examination was performed. It confirmed the inflammatory signs within the orbital fat tissue and the presence of a linear-shaped area alongside the ocular bulb and the muscles. It had a higher/equal density than the soft tissue surrounding, with sharp and well-defined borders (Figures 3a and 3b). These findings are highly suspected for foreign bodies.
discussion: Background Orbital trauma is a common clinical scenario, often associated with foreign bodies (FB), which are found mainly within the orbit in the superior, medial and inferior compartments [4]. Approximately 1/6 of cases of penetrating orbital trauma are associated with FBs [1]. These kinds of injuries are more common in children than in adults (ca. 45% vs 25%, respectively) [3]. Clinical Perspective FBs require urgent removal, owing to their reactive nature and the high risk for infection. As an organic matter, wood is an optimal substrate for developing a nidus for bacteria, eventually leading to inflammation or, at worst, abscess formation with fistula, osteomyelitis and intracranial complications. Identifying and localising an infraorbital FB is often a challenging radiological issue; the real difficulty, which may lead to a delayed diagnosis, is that patients may have subtle signs of trauma, such as conjunctival lid lacerations or other intraocular injuries, with hidden entry wounds [2]. Imaging Perspective A missed FB on imaging may lead to a delay in primary surgical intervention. Plain radiography is a widely available modality, but it is not enough for evaluating orbital soft tissue injuries. X-rays are often unable to detect non-metallic FB, so they are inappropriate for a diagnosis. Although non-invasive and inexpensive, US examination is highly operator-dependent, even if it allows a quite complete evaluation of the orbit. Computed tomography (CT) is the first-line imaging method for exploring ocular trauma, especially in patients with a suspected infraorbital FB [10]. On the other hand, characterising wood on CT imaging is difficult due to its radiolucency and low density, which can be mistaken for air in the setting of traumatic orbital emphysema [5]. In the acute stage, it appears as a hypodense linear or cylindrical well-demarcated focus, surrounded by hyperdense inflammatory tissue. Therefore, some FBs may be overlooked on CT or appear only as free orbital air without proper windowing and post-processing reconstructions: a wide window width (WW) and multiplanar reconstructions are recommended. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is seldom used as an initial imaging technique in emergency departments. In addition, its use is strictly contraindicated in foreign bodies with unknown origin, even if MRI is more accurate in distinguishing the fragment from the surrounding tissue’s inflammatory reaction [4]. Outcome In our case, surgical removal of the FB, a wood splinter, and infection prophylaxis led to a good outcome (Figure 4). Take Home Message / Teaching Points Fundamental points in the clinical and imaging evaluation of infraorbital FBs include location, size, number and composition, all of which can affect prognosis and surgical approach, followed by a careful history regarding the mechanism of injury and materials involved. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Bilateral adrenal pheochromocytomas presenting as haemorrhagic stroke in a young adult
clinical_history: A 21-year-old male presented to the emergency department with a sudden onset of altered sensorium and left-sided weakness. Blood pressure on arrival was 240/130 mmHg.
imaging_findings: Non-contrast CT of the brain revealed a large right-sided intracerebral haematoma with midline shift and uncal herniation (Figure 1). Emergency decompressive craniectomy was performed (Figure 2). Subsequent evaluation with contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d) revealed bilateral well-defined, enhancing adrenal masses (4.2 × 3.8 cm on the right and 2.9 × 2.5 cm on the left), showing arterial-phase hyperenhancement and washout on delayed phase. No calcification or fat was noted. MRI of the abdomen showed corresponding bilateral adrenal masses that were hyperintense on T2-weighted images (Figures 4a and 4b). No evidence of local invasion or metastatic disease was seen. These imaging features, along with biochemical correlation, supported the diagnosis of bilateral pheochromocytomas.
discussion: Background Pheochromocytomas are rare catecholamine-secreting tumours arising from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. They account for less than 0.2% of hypertension cases but can lead to devastating cardiovascular and neurological complications if undiagnosed [1]. Bilateral involvement, as seen in this patient, occurs in about 10% of sporadic cases and more commonly in familial syndromes such as MEN type 2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2), VHL (Von Hippel–Lindau), and NF-1 (neurofibromatosis type I) [2]. Clinical Perspective This young male presented with a haemorrhagic stroke—an uncommon but recognised manifestation of undiagnosed pheochromocytoma. Sudden catecholamine surges from these tumours can trigger hypertensive emergencies, precipitating cerebrovascular events. Early suspicion is essential, especially in young patients with refractory or paroxysmal hypertension. Imaging Perspective Contrast-enhanced CT is often the first imaging modality to reveal adrenal lesions during the workup for secondary hypertension. The classic imaging appearance includes a hypervascular mass with avid arterial-phase enhancement and venous washout. MRI is complementary due to its high sensitivity in detecting T2-hyperintense pheochromocytomas (the “light-bulb sign”). A study validated the diagnostic utility of MRI features in differentiating pheochromocytomas from other adrenal tumours with positive biochemical results [3]. Moreover, recent studies demonstrate that integrated CT–MRI models enhance diagnostic confidence in distinguishing pheochromocytomas from adenomas [4]. In this case, bilateral adrenal masses with characteristic enhancement patterns and positive urinary catecholamines guided the diagnosis. Outcome Following neurosurgical stabilisation, the patient was started on alpha-blockade followed by beta-blockade. Planned adrenalectomy was deferred until adequate haemodynamic control was achieved. Bilateral adrenalectomy mandates lifelong steroid replacement. Imaging played a central role in establishing the diagnosis, guiding medical stabilisation, and surgical planning. Take-Home Message / Teaching Points Always consider secondary causes of hypertension in young patients with haemorrhagic stroke. Bilateral adrenal pheochromocytomas are rare but life-threatening if undiagnosed. Imaging provides crucial diagnostic and therapeutic guidance, especially in acute settings. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

final_diagnosis: Bilateral adrenal pheochromocytomas with hypertensive haemorrhagic stroke

title: Dextrocardia with situs inversus totalis in a 72-year-old male
clinical_history: One male patient aged 72 years complained of one-week chest pain and three-day exertional dyspnoea. There was no past history of cardiovascular, respiratory, or gastrointestinal disease.
imaging_findings: Chest X-ray demonstrated dextrocardia with gastric bubble on the right and thereby suggested situs inversus totalis. ECG demonstrated inverted P waves in leads I and aVL. CT thorax and abdomen established complete mirror-image organ position of thoracic and abdominal organs: heart positioned on the right, liver on the left, and spleen/stomach on the right. There were no vascular anomalies or acute pathology. The lungs were normal without effusion or consolidation.
discussion: Background Situs describes the position of the thoracic and abdominal organs. Situs solitus refers to the normal arrangement, situs inversus refers to a complete mirror-image reversal, and situs ambiguus (or heterotaxy) denotes an abnormal arrangement that does not fit either of the previous categories and often accompanies congenital heart disease. Heterotaxy syndromes include right and left isomerism, which are associated with complex cardiac and splenic abnormalities [1]. Clinical Perspective Patients with situs inversus totalis are frequently asymptomatic. However, when symptoms such as chest pain or dyspnoea arise, accurate clinical assessment becomes essential. Our patient presented with symptoms suspicious of a cardiac origin. Given the unusual anatomical findings on examination (right-sided apex beat and heart sounds), imaging was pursued to clarify the diagnosis. Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is a genetic disorder that affects ciliary motility and may occur in patients with situs inversus. When situs inversus is combined with chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis, it is termed Kartagener syndrome. Although our patient did not report chronic respiratory symptoms or exhibit radiographic features of bronchiectasis, awareness of this association is clinically relevant, especially in paediatric or younger patients. Imaging Perspective Initial chest radiography suggested dextrocardia with situs inversus. ECG findings further supported this. CT thorax and abdomen provided a definitive diagnosis by showing a complete mirror-image arrangement of thoracic and abdominal structures. Such imaging is crucial to avoid misinterpretation and mismanagement, particularly in emergencies or surgical planning. Although no vascular anomalies were noted in this patient, situs inversus may be associated with variations such as a left-sided inferior vena cava (IVC), azygos continuation of the IVC, or interrupted IVC. Recognising such anomalies is vital during interventional procedures or vascular imaging [2,3]. Clinical Significance Recognition of situs inversus totalis is vital in clinical and emergency settings to prevent misdiagnosis, especially in interpreting symptoms of conditions such as myocardial infarction or appendicitis, where organ location is reversed. Proper identification also guides appropriate surgical planning. Situs inversus totalis needs to be identified for correct diagnosis and surgical management since the reversed organ positioning may make interpretations of usual conditions (e.g., appendicitis, cardiac event) more complex. The arrangement seen in Figure 3 is a characteristic feature of situs inversus with dextrocardia, a rare condition that may be linked to syndromes like Kartagener syndrome. Recognition of this anatomic variation is important for clinical assessments and interventional procedures. Such reversed organ positioning should be identified preoperatively and during diagnostic investigations to avoid misinterpretation of pathology. Situs inversus may be isolated or a component of syndromic conditions like Kartagener syndrome. Outcome No acute cardiac or respiratory pathology was identified in our case. The patient was managed conservatively with analgesics and bronchodilators. He was educated about his condition and advised to carry a medical alert card for future emergencies. No surgical or invasive procedures were required. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Situs inversus totalis is often discovered incidentally. Awareness of such anatomical variants is essential for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning. Imaging plays a pivotal role in confirming the diagnosis and excluding associated anomalies. Patients should be informed about their condition, especially in preparation for emergencies or interventions.

title: Peripheral nerve traumatic neuroma
clinical_history: A 15-year-old girl underwent a foot ultrasound three months following a sharp penetrating trauma (stepping on an open ring binder), which caused skin penetration, with subsequent hypoesthesia and numbness of the hallux. She experienced persistent pressure-sensitivity at the scar site, with radiating symptoms to the great toe upon localised pressure.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound examination with a 26 MHz hockey stick transducer revealed a spindle-shaped hypoechoic thickening of the digital nerve branch of the medial plantar nerve to the hallux (the medial proper plantar digital nerve to great toe/nervus digitalis plantaris propri medialis halluci) with a maximum diameter of 2.2 millimetres in which the normal fibrillar pattern was altered (Figures 1a and 2). The spindle-shaped thickening was contiguous with a hypoechoic scar trajectory extending toward the dermis, likely representing the fibrotic path of the penetrating injury (Figure 1a). The proximal and distal parts of the nerve were normal (Figures 1b and 1c). Based on these findings, the diagnosis of traumatic neuroma was made.
discussion: Background Traumatic neuromas frequently develop as a consequence of nerve injury or surgical intervention. They result from aberrant nerve formation and connective tissue proliferation, which occurs during attempted reinnervation of a partially or completely disrupted nerve [1]. Clinical Perspective These lesions are broadly classified into terminal neuromas, typically associated with complete nerve transections such as those following limb amputations, and neuromas-in-continuity or spindle neuromas, which manifest as spindle-shaped swellings along partially or totally transected nerves. In contrast, spindle neuromas can also result from chronic repetitive blunt trauma, which contributes to perineural fibrosis, observed in conditions such as Morton’s neuroma or bowler’s thumb [1]. Patients with traumatic neuromas frequently present with localised pain at the neuroma site and paraesthesia in its dermatome [1]. Different clinical nerve injury classifications are used to describe the severity of nerve damage. Two of these classification systems are the Seddon [2] and Sunderland classifications [3]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasonography is a fast, cost-effective imaging modality with good spatial resolution, offering a dynamic assessment of the nerve. High-resolution nerve imaging is best achieved using a high-frequency linear transducer such as the “hockey stick” probe [4]. In addition to nerve damage itself, chronic muscle denervation changes, such as atrophy and fatty infiltration, can be detected. However, ultrasonography has limitations in visualising deeper nerves and in identifying early muscle denervation changes, for which magnetic resonance imaging is superior [1]. In addition, ultrasound is used for perineural (nerve block) injections, aiding in diagnosis and treatment [4]. Outcome Management strategies include surgical excision or neurolysis to alleviate symptoms. Nonoperative approaches consist of different types of anti-neuropathic drugs, including membrane-stabilising agents (gabapentin and pregabalin being the primary treatment resulting in a decrease of neurotransmitter release), antidepressants and anticonvulsants, opioids and muscle relaxants. Other non-operative strategies include physiotherapy, nerve block injections (steroid drugs, alcohol, local anaesthetics), ultrasound-guided radiofrequency ablation or ultrasound-guided cryotherapy, shockwave therapy, and electrical stimulation [1]. In this case, the patient underwent ultrasound-guided injection of the neuroma using Depo-Medrol ® 40 mg/mL and Marcaine ® in a 1:1 ratio. Follow-up two weeks post-injection showed marked clinical improvement with no pain during routine daily activities, although some persisting discomfort during prolonged physical exertion. The orthopaedic specialist prescribed an insole to reduce localised pressure. Teaching point High-resolution ultrasound serves as an optimal first-line imaging technique to detect traumatic peripheral nerve neuromas due to its accessibility, real-time capability, and diagnostic accuracy. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Testicular cancer patient with a palpable axillary lump. Recurrence?
clinical_history: A 20-year-old man with a history of mixed non-seminomatous germ cell tumour with focal invasion of the vascular tunic (pT1N2M0, S2 – Stage IIIB) underwent radical orchiectomy, adjuvant chemotherapy, and retroperitoneal lymphadenectomy, remaining under surveillance with serum markers and body CT scans. An axillary swelling was noticed on physical examination, and a chest CT scan was ordered.
imaging_findings: In the left axillary region, an oblong structure measuring approximately 60 mm in longitudinal extension is identified, isodense to the muscular planes. This image extends from the lateral border of the latissimus dorsi muscle to the pectoralis major muscle.
discussion: Background The Langer’s axillary arch, or axillopectoral muscle, is one of the most common musculoskeletal anatomical variants in the axillary region, with an estimated prevalence of 8%, although some references mention up to 14% of the population [1,2]. This variant can be classified as a “complete arch” when it extends from the latissimus dorsi to the pectoralis major, or as an “incomplete arch” when the insertion is in another muscle, such as the biceps brachii, for example [3]. Clinical Perspective The Langer’s axillary arch can be completely asymptomatic and is often an incidental finding on tomographic exams. Some patients may report a palpable nodule in the ipsilateral axillary region. Due to its location and relation to nervous, vascular, and lymphatic structures of the axillary region, knowledge of the anatomy of this area is crucial for surgical planning, particularly in axillary dissection for breast cancer [2,3]. Depending on its location and size, the axillary arch may cause deep venous thrombosis in the upper limbs due to compression of the vascular bundle and possibly thoracic outlet syndrome [1,4]. Imaging Perspective As some axillary arches may be palpable, their imaging recognition is essential to avoid unnecessary procedures, such as biopsies [5]. Ultrasound evaluation may show an isoecogenic structure relative to the muscular planes. It is not always possible to identify the proximal and distal insertions. MRI and tomography scans may be useful for evaluation of the extension of the structure, excluding other causes for axillary lumps and also better defining the relationship between the axillopectoral muscle and adjacent neurovascular structures [1]. Outcome In the presence of symptoms such as deep venous thrombosis or hyperabduction syndrome, the axillary arch should be resected [5]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points This is a common but under-recognised anatomical variant. Its radiological identification is crucial, especially before any intervention in the axillary region, notably before axillary dissection in breast cancer. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Müller–Weiss syndrome
clinical_history: A 23-year-old female presented with acute pain and swelling in her left ankle following a fall down the stairs. Clinical examination showed severe bilateral pes planus and mild hindfoot varus.
imaging_findings: Radiographic evaluation demonstrated flattening and contour irregularity of the middle and lateral thirds of the navicular bone, accompanied by sclerotic bone remodelling (Figure 1a). A step-off deformity was noted at the dorsal aspect between the navicular and cuneiform bones on the lateral view, along with flattening of the talar dome (Figure 1b). MRI confirmed these findings, revealing deformity and flattening of the central and lateral portions of the navicular bone, with bone marrow oedema predominantly in the central and dorsal regions. In addition, fragmentation of the central navicular bone was observed (Figures 2a, 2b, 3a, 3b, and 4).
discussion: Background Müller-Weiss syndrome is a rare disorder characterised by osteonecrosis of the navicular bone, leading to midfoot deformity. It predominantly affects adults aged 40 to 60 years, with a higher prevalence in women, and is often bilateral [1]. The cause remains unclear, but chronic mechanical stress on the navicular, combined with its limited blood supply, is considered the primary contributor. The navicular bone receives blood from branches of the dorsalis pedis and medial plantar arteries, but the central portion has significantly reduced vascularisation, making it more vulnerable to ischemia (Figure 5) [2]. Clinical Perspective Patients usually present with chronic pain in the midfoot and hindfoot. Swelling and tenderness are often noted along the dorsomedial aspect of the foot. A key clinical sign is paradoxical pes planovarus, where the foot appears to have a flattened arch (pes planus) but also tilts inward (varus), creating a seemingly contradictory presentation. This deformity alters foot mechanics, increasing stress on other joints, which may lead to anterior knee pain due to tibial rotation and altered patellar tracking. Subtalar joint stiffness and limited mobility may also be observed in later stages [2]. Imaging Perspective Radiological assessment is essential for diagnosis and staging. Weight-bearing X-rays are the first-line imaging modality as they allow visualisation of load-dependent changes in foot alignment and reveal dynamic deformities that are not apparent on non-weight-bearing images [2]. Early signs include a downward tilt of the arch, signalling early misalignment. As the disease progresses, the navicular bone collapses and fragments, leading to a comma or hourglass shape. The talus shifts upward and outward (dorsolateral subluxation), causing the heel to tilt inward (hindfoot varus). Advanced cases show total collapse of the navicular, with direct articulation between the talus and cuneiforms, often accompanied by arthritis [1]. MRI is valuable for detecting early signs, such as bone marrow oedema, though this finding is non-specific and can also be seen in other conditions such as stress fractures or reactive changes [3]. CT provides visualisation of bone structure and precise 3D reconstructions. This is crucial for preoperative planning, allowing accurate assessment of bone deformity, joint congruency, and the extent of fragmentation, vital for surgical decision-making [4]. Outcome In the early stages, conservative management with orthotics and physical therapy can relieve symptoms and reduce deformity progression. If symptoms persist or worsen, surgery may be necessary. Talonaviculocuneiform arthrodesis, a procedure to fuse the bones, helps stabilise the foot, correct deformities, and reduce pain [5].

title: Appendiceal endometriosis presenting as acute appendicitis
clinical_history: A 22-year-old woman presented at the general practitioner with acute abdominal pain in the right upper quadrant (RUQ), general malaise and nausea during her menstruation. Clinical examination found pressure soreness in the RUQ and a positive Murphy’s sign. Blood tests revealed leukocytosis and an elevated CRP level.
imaging_findings: The CT (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d) showed an abnormally enlarged appendix of 13 mm, which was in contact with the parietal peritoneum. Signs of inflammation were present, e.g., hyperaemia, as well as six locoregional lymph nodes of up to 7 mm. The appendix was described as atypical, and the existence of underlying lesions was suggested. Additionally, an unsuspicious adnexal cyst of 15 mm was described on the right side. The initial preferred diagnosis on CT was acute appendicitis with the possibility of an underlying tumour, and the patient was referred to the emergency department of the hospital. Histopathological examination of the resected specimen (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d) found ulcerations of the mucosa, and neutrophils were reported throughout the appendiceal lumen and wall. The serosa was covered in a suppurative and fibrinous exudate. Furthermore, the presence of endometrial glands and stroma throughout the inflamed appendix was confirmed through immunohistochemistry. Thus, the final diagnosis was an acute appendicitis caused by appendiceal endometriosis.
discussion: Background Appendiceal endometriosis (AE) is the presence of endometrial epithelium and stroma in the appendiceal wall, which occurs in 0.4% of the general population. The prevalence of appendiceal complications is higher in women suffering known endometriosis at 1.7% and even higher in cases of deep infiltrating endometriosis at 2.5–44%. AE may cause or mimic acute appendicitis in up to 2.5% of all acute appendiceal cases. Despite its relevance, given that 6–10% of women of reproductive age suffer from endometriosis, the pathophysiology remains uncertain [1,2]. Clinical Perspective AE often goes unnoticed by patients and caregivers, as the symptomatology can be nonspecific and subtle. It can, however, be the cause of cyclical abdominal pain among other acute and chronic abdominal affections, such as acute appendicitis (AA), chronic appendicitis, gastrointestinal bleeds, neoplasms, intussusception, or intestinal perforations. Although extremely rare, endometriotic implants can potentially lead to mucocele formation due to chronic obstruction of the appendiceal lumen, requiring thorough preoperative evaluation [1,3–5]. Imaging Perspective Abdominal CT has a high sensitivity (88–100%) and specificity (91–99%) for AA [6]. Typical characteristics include an increased diameter of the appendix, wall thickening, and hyperaemia. Preoperative diagnosis of AE is difficult, if not impossible, as there is no characteristic imaging pattern. However, atypical presentation can be detected on CT scans, as shown in Figures 1a and 1b, and the possibility of AE in young women must be kept in mind. The final diagnosis is made based on histopathological examination of the specimen [1,2]. Outcome Laparoscopic surgery is the standard treatment for AA, while it functions as the main diagnostic and, possibly, therapeutic treatment for endometriosis [2]. An appendectomy will relieve the acute episode of AA, but cyclical abdominal pains may persist or occur postoperatively if other lesions are present. It may be beneficial to evaluate the entire abdominal cavity when given the chance in patients presenting with AA due to AE and a previously unknown history of endometriosis [1]. In fact, opportunistic appendectomy could pose multiple advantages, and the possibility must be considered when women with endometriosis undergo laparoscopic abdominal surgery. This may positively affect the outcome, as endometriosis can have a significant impact on the intra and interindividual aspects of one’s quality of life [4]. Take Home Message Appendiceal endometriosis should be considered as a possible differential diagnosis for women of reproductive age with (lower) right abdominal pain, if clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings are not typical for acute appendicitis. Vague, atypical and/or nonspecific cyclical abdominal complaints can be linked to endometriosis in biological women of reproductive age. Examine the entire abdominal cavity during laparoscopic surgery in women with a history or suspicion of endometriosis. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Rock spleen in sickle cell disease: A report of two cases
clinical_history: Case 1 A 28-year-old patient with known homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS) presented with chronic fatigue, diffuse abdominal pain, and hip joint discomfort exacerbated by walking. Case 2 A 34-year-old patient with a known history of sickle cell disease underwent CT for left upper quadrant abdominal pain and chronic fatigue.
imaging_findings: Case 1 Abdominal CT scan (Figures 1a and 1b) revealed a markedly reduced spleen size, with the parenchyma completely replaced by dense, coarse calcifications. The spleen had irregular but preserved contours. Post-contrast CT images did not show any enhancement within the splenic parenchyma. There was no perisplenic collection or lymphadenopathy. Bone window CT images through the pelvis revealed bilateral femoral head avascular necrosis (AVN), with subchondral collapse and cortical irregularities (Figures 2a and 2b). Case 2 Abdominal CT scan (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d) demonstrated a severely atrophied spleen appearing as a densely calcified structure in the left upper quadrant. The calcifications are confluent and coarse, with no visible soft tissue component. Post-contrast images showed no contrast enhancement, and no other abdominal or bony abnormalities were identified.
discussion: Background Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an inherited haemoglobinopathy characterised by red cell sickling due to haemoglobin S polymerisation in hypoxic conditions, leading to recurrent vascular occlusion and tissue infarction [1]. The spleen, particularly susceptible to repeated infarcts, progressively undergoes fibrosis, calcification, and ultimately, autosplenectomy or “rock spleen”, resulting in complete functional loss of splenic tissue [2,3]. Clinical Perspective In SCD, functional asplenia usually develops in childhood. This greatly increases the risk of serious bacterial infections, especially from Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae . Preventive measures like vaccinations and antibiotic prophylaxis are essential [3,4]. Autosplenectomy itself rarely needs direct treatment. However, abdominal imaging is important during episodes of abdominal pain, suspected splenic sequestration, or trauma. Imaging Perspective Chronic autosplenectomy, or “rock spleen”, presents on CT as a shrunken spleen with diffuse, extensive calcifications and no enhancement, confirming the loss of functional splenic tissue [5]. Additional characteristic imaging findings in SCD patients include skeletal changes (bone infarcts, vertebral endplate sclerosis), hepatobiliary manifestations (gallstones, hepatic iron overload), renal complications (papillary necrosis), and pulmonary alterations (pulmonary hypertension, acute chest syndrome). Outcome Chronic autosplenectomy generally does not need any therapeutic intervention. Management mainly involves preventive measures to reduce infection risk through immunisation, patient education, and rapid treatment of suspected infections. Radiologic confirmation of autosplenectomy reinforces the importance of preventive care. The prognosis primarily depends on effective SCD management. Notably, autosplenectomy eliminates the risk of acute splenic sequestration episodes, improving overall patient stability [3,4]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Sickle cell disease (SCD) commonly leads to autosplenectomy through repeated infarction. A “rock spleen” represents the end stage: a small, heavily calcified, non-enhancing spleen on CT. Coexistent bone findings, like femoral head avascular necrosis, are also common and should be carefully evaluated.

final_diagnosis: Autosplenectomy (rock spleen) secondary to sickle cell disease

title: An unusual cause of limb pain in the emergency department
clinical_history: A 35-year-old female with an unremarkable past medical history presented to the emergency department complaining of pain and swelling of the right thigh in the last 4 days. On physical examination, it was possible to palpate a firm, consistent mass. There was no history of trauma.
imaging_findings: An ultrasound of the right leg was performed and showed the presence of a heterogeneous solid highly vascularised mass located superficial to the femoral vessels (Figures 1a and 1b). A CT scan with intravenous contrast was requested and confirmed the presence of a large heterogeneous lobulated solid mass with avid enhancement located in the medial muscular compartment of the thigh (Figures 2a and 2b). No lymph node enlargement was seen. MRI was performed and confirmed a mass with an intermediate signal on T1-weighted images and a heterogeneous high-signal on T2-weighted images (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 4). The lesion showed avid gadolinium-enhancement and a central necrotic area, and was located in close juxtaposition with the superficial femoral neurovascular bundle, which remained intact. A biopsy was performed and histopathological analysis showed mesenchymal proliferation of fusiform cells (CD 34+, STAT6+, and SOX 10-) with ecstatic and branched vessels in keeping with solitary fibrous tumour.
discussion: Background Solitary fibrous tumours (SFTs) are uncommon soft tissue neoplasms accounting for less than 2% of all soft-tissue tumours with an age-adjusted yearly incidence of 1 new case per million people [1]. The most common location of these tumours is the thoracic cavity, and it was only in 1991 that the first series of extra-thoracic tumours was published [3]. However, they can occur at almost every anatomic location, and SFTs of the soft tissues of the trunk and extremities constitute only 10% of these already rare neoplasms [4]. These tumours occur equally in both genders and are not associated with known risk factors [1,5]. These are fibroblastic/myofibroblastic tumours and are the result of somatic mutations that result in overexpression of the NAB2-STAT6 fusion proteins [6]. Clinical Perspective Although the majority of SFTs are benign, 10% to 20% can have aggressive behaviour and be locally invasive or present with metastasis [5]. Some authors report the occurrence of metastasis in up to 35–45% in large series [2]. For these reasons, all these patients must be monitored as the prognosis is unpredictable. Some authors report that extrapleural location, increased tumour size and mitotic activity, infiltrative margins, nuclear pleomorphism, and necrosis may be associated with more aggressive clinical behaviour [3,7]. These tumours are often asymptomatic and present as incidental findings. However, patients may also present symptoms due to the mass effect or related to paraneoplastic syndromes. Imaging Perspective The imaging findings vary and lack specificity. However, a highly vascular and well-defined (oval/round) contrast-enhancing lesion exhibiting homogeneous low-to-intermediate signal intensity on T1-weighted MRI and low signal on T2-weighted MRI should raise suspicion. The low signal on T2-weighted MRI is due to collagen content, but can be variable and heterogeneous. On ultrasound, these tumours are usually hypoechoic, although sometimes there are cystic and necrotic areas. The final diagnosis is made through a biopsy and immunohistochemical testing. Outcome Surgical excision is the gold standard therapy for localised SFTs. Individuals with inoperable or metastatic disease face a poorer prognosis. However, new targeted therapies have been developed, such as drugs with antiangiogenic activity, with promising results [5]. Take Home Message Solitary fibrous tumours (SFTs) are uncommon neoplasms of mesenchymal origin that can mimic other soft tissue neoplasms, therefore often representing a diagnostic challenge. Less than 10% of these tumours arise in the soft tissues of the trunk and extremities. Accurate diagnosis and surgical planning are essential for the success of therapy. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Persistent abdominal pain in an elderly patient: A diagnostic imaging challenge
clinical_history: An 81-year-old man was referred with a four-month history of persistent right upper quadrant pain radiating to the back. Liver function tests were normal, and he denied fever or pruritus. His medical history included pacemaker implantation, malaria, appendicectomy, arterial hypertension, and orthopaedic surgeries. No alcohol abuse or smoking was reported.
imaging_findings: The patient first underwent abdominal ultrasound and contrast-enhanced CT scan (Figures 1a and 1b), which revealed consistent findings: gallbladder hydrops with thin walls, moderate dilatation of the intrahepatic right bile ducts, and an ill-defined 1.5 cm soft-tissue lesion at the junction of the cystic duct and the common bile duct. Gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI (Figures 2a and 2b) with magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) (Figures 3a and 3b) confirmed tissue infiltration at the junction of the right anterior segmental duct and common bile duct, explaining the dilatation of the right anterior bile ducts. Endoscopic ultrasound and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) (Figure 4) were subsequently performed to perform biopsies and to place a plastic biliary stent.
discussion: Background Intraductal papillary neoplasm of the bile duct (IPNB), introduced in the 2010 WHO classification of precursor lesions for cholangiocarcinoma, is an intraluminal lesion of intra and extrahepatic bile ducts characterised by epithelial proliferation around a fibrovascular stalk, with varying degrees of dysplasia [1]. IPNB is more common in Asia due to hepatolithiasis and clonorchiasis as major risk factors [2], while in Western countries, choledochal cysts and primary sclerosing cholangitis are common predisposing conditions [3]. Although considered the biliary counterpart of pancreatic intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN), IPNB shows a higher incidence of invasive carcinoma (72% vs. 21%) and lower mucin production (30% vs. nearly always). Both lesions share four histological subtypes: the aggressive pancreato-biliary subtype is more frequent in IPNB, while the indolent intestinal subtype is more frequent in IPMN. The gastric subtype, observed in our patient, is the least common, occurring in 6–10% of cases [4]. Clinical Perspective IPNB diagnosis is challenging due to variable clinical presentation, ranging from asymptomatic to nonspecific symptoms. Common presentations include right upper quadrant pain (as in our case), recurrent cholangitis, or obstructive jaundice from mucin-induced bile flow obstruction with cholestatic laboratory abnormalities [2]. Imaging Perspective Imaging with MRI, CT, or ERCP plays a key role. Four radiological patterns are described, based on tumour location, morphology, and bile duct dilatation. When the tumour component predominates, an intraductal mass with proximal-only or proximal-distal ductal dilatation is observed. In contrast, predominant mucin production may result in severe ductal dilatation without a visible mass, or focal aneurysmal dilatation presenting as a cystic lesion. The most frequent pattern is a polypoid lesion causing proximal-distal ductal dilation due to both mucin production and mechanical obstruction [5]. Although histopathology is required for definitive diagnosis, some worrisome features may suggest an IPNB associated with invasive carcinoma: visible intraductal mass, size ≥2.5 cm, multifocality, bile duct wall thickening, and adjacent organ invasion [6]. DWI may enhance lesion conspicuity, and ADC values ≤1.0×10 -3 mm 2 /s are associated with a higher likelihood of invasiveness [7]. Outcome Given its malignant potential and risk of biliary obstruction, surgery is the standard treatment, often including regional lymphadenectomy [8]. Prognosis depends on invasiveness, lesion number, and resection margins and is generally better than cholangiocarcinoma. Accurate preoperative staging is critical, as undetected lesions are a common cause of recurrence [4]. Our patient underwent surgical resection (Figure 5). A single regional node was removed with no involvement at histopathology (Figures 6a, 6b, and 6c). At 6-month follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic and liver function tests were normal. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Fibroadenoma in a 12-year-old male without hormonal alteration
clinical_history: A 12-year-old boy without significant previous medical history presented in the ultrasound department for evaluation of a palpable lump noticed since the last two weeks in the left breast. The lump was non-tender and showed no changes in the overlying skin. There was no history of medication use. The hormonal profile and routine CBC profile were normal.
imaging_findings: Focused high-resolution ultrasound of both breasts and each axilla was performed using a high-frequency linear probe. The ultrasound identified a well-defined, well-encapsulated, hypoechoic lesion with smooth margins (Figure 1). It measured 3.8 x 2 x 3 cm in size and involved the left breast at the 12 o’clock periareolar region. The lesion was oriented parallel to the tissue planes (Figure 3). A single gentle lobulation was seen in this lesion. No significant vascularity was displayed on the colour Doppler study (Figure 2). The right breast was normal, and both axillae were normal.
discussion: Background Fibroadenomas are the most common benign breast mass in females [1]. Fibroadenomas rarely occur in the male breast; approximately only 17 cases of fibroadenoma have been reported in males, most of which were reportedly derived from gynecomastia [2]. Fibroadenomas are rare in the male breast owing to the absence of glandular lobules. The few cases described mostly developed due to oestrogen stimulation [3]. Fibroadenoma in the male breast is a rare clinical finding and is typically linked with gynecomastia and imbalances in serum sex hormone levels. A presentation lacking these associations, as observed in our case, is exceptionally uncommon [2]. Historically, some pathologists questioned the existence of fibroadenoma in males, suggesting that reported cases might actually represent nodular areas of gynecomastia [1], but Agrawal et al. [5], in his case series, presented patients who did not have any causative factors theorised up till now and were concluded to be idiopathic in aetiology. Imaging perspective Sonographic features of male fibroadenoma are similar to those of fibroadenomas in the female breast. On ultrasound, the lesion appears as an oval, hypoechoic formation that is circumscribed, with well-defined margins and, in some cases, macrolobulations. Examination with colour Doppler shows vascularisation, which generally consists of one or two vessels that penetrate the parenchyma of the lesion and have harmonically distributed terminal branches [4]. Outcome Ultrasound and FNAC (fine needle aspiration cytology) are diagnostic tools used to reach a conclusion. Surgical excision is confirmatory, and excision could help reduce complex emotional distress and improve the quality of a patient’s life (QOL). The surgical management depends on the coexisting concurrent disease and the patient’s emotional state [1]. In our case, after surgical excision, the patient remained stable, with no recurrence of disease up to the date of publication of this report. Take Home Message Fibroadenoma of the male breast is a rare yet confirmed pathology that definitely should be on your radar when diagnosing breast lumps in males. What makes our case particularly fascinating is that it defies expectations by presenting without any prior or current hormonal imbalance. It is an intriguing reminder that medical mysteries often come with surprises!

title: The eye-of-the-tiger sign: Hallmark of pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration
clinical_history: An 11-year-old girl with normal hearing and cognition had severe dysarthria and language delay since birth. Neurological exam showed no motor deficits but significant expressive impairment. Given the persistent speech delay, a brain MRI was requested for further evaluation.
imaging_findings: Brain MRI images demonstrated the eye-of-the-tiger sign. There is marked hypointensity of the globus pallidus on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences secondary to iron deposition, containing minimal dot-like hyperintensities (vacuolisation), associated with comma-shaped high-signal intensity in the antero-medial part of the globus pallidus, likely due to gliosis (Figures 1 and 2). There is also marked hypointensity on both T2*EG and DWI (diffusion-weighted images) sequences due to susceptibility effects (Figures 3 and 4).
discussion: Background Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN), formerly known as Hallervorden–Spatz syndrome (HSS), is a subtype of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA). It is caused by mutations in the PANK2 gene and is characterised by progressive extrapyramidal symptoms, including dystonia, rigidity, and speech impairment. Clinical Perspective PKAN typically presents in childhood or early adolescence with progressive movement disorders, including dystonia, parkinsonism, and speech difficulties. As the disease advances, patients may develop cognitive impairment and motor disability. Given the overlap of clinical features with other neurodegenerative disorders, imaging plays a crucial role in distinguishing PKAN from other conditions. Early identification through MRI can guide genetic testing, confirm the diagnosis, and help in patient management. Imaging Perspective The hallmark radiologic feature of PKAN is the eye-of-the-tiger sign, a distinctive MRI finding reflecting a combination of iron deposition, gliosis, neuronal loss, and vacuolisation [1]. While traditionally linked to PKAN, studies have reported the presence of this sign in other extrapyramidal disorders, such as progressive supranuclear palsy and cortical-basal ganglionic degeneration, highlighting its diagnostic significance in neurodegenerative conditions [1]. MRI is the gold standard for diagnosing PKAN. The eye-of-the-tiger sign, seen on T2-weighted imaging, consists of bilateral hypointensity of the globus pallidus due to iron deposition and central hyperintensity within the hypointense globus pallidus, attributed to vacuolisation and gliosis. This finding is highly specific for PKAN and aids in differentiating it from other neurodegenerative diseases. However, it is important to note that similar imaging appearances may occasionally be seen as incidental findings on 3T MRI in asymptomatic individuals. This reinforces the need to correlate imaging findings with clinical presentation in order to avoid overdiagnosis in atypical cases. The relationship between iron accumulation and vacuolisation in the medial globus pallidus appears to be dynamic. Baumeister et al. observed the disappearance of the eye-of-the-tiger sign in a patient over time, suggesting that progressive iron deposition may overshadow the hyperintense region as vacuolated tissue is resorbed [2]. Moreover, while PANK2 mutations are commonly associated with PKAN and the presence of the eye-of-the-tiger sign, cases have been reported where this characteristic MRI finding exists in patients without PANK2 mutations, reinforcing the genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity of the disease [2]. Outcome There is no curative treatment for PKAN, but symptomatic management includes botulinum toxin injections for dystonia, deep brain stimulation, and supportive therapies. Iron-chelating agents are being investigated but have not yet proven effective in halting disease progression. MRI findings can assist in therapy planning, particularly in assessing disease severity and monitoring progression.

title: Paradoxical tuberculoma post-antitubercular therapy
clinical_history: A 4-month-old male child from a tuberculosis (TB) endemic region presented with complaints of poor feeding, loss of weight for a month, and a low-grade, evening fever without any associated rash or chills for 15 days. The patient also had jerky movements of the right upper and lower limbs without any other signs of seizure disorder. The patient showed positive Kernig’s (pain and resistance to knee extension on flexing the patient’s hip and knee to 90 degrees and then attempting to extend the knee) [1] and Brudziński’s signs (in a patient with supine position, positive Brudziński’s is involuntary flexion of the hips and knees when the patient’s neck is passively flexed) [2].
imaging_findings: As the patient showed positive Kernig’s and Brudziński’s signs, meningeal TB was suspected. However, the chest radiograph was normal. On MRI, subtle T2 FLAIR (fluid attenuation inversion recovery) hyperintense minimally enhancing foci were seen in the bilateral cerebral cortex, caudate nucleus, thalami, and right hemipons with diffusion restriction and without blooming on gradient echo (GRE) sequences (Figures 1a and 1b). Subtle areas of leptomeningeal enhancement along the bilateral frontoparietal region were also seen. Mild communicating hydrocephalus was seen. A follow-up scan was advised after 4 months of antituberculosis treatment (ATT), as the patient had reduced activity, drowsiness, and episodes of seizure. On follow-up MRI, multiple conglomerated T2 hyperintense T1 fat-sat ring-enhancing lesions were seen in bilateral gangliocapsular and periventricular regions with leptomeningeal enhancement and hydrocephalus (Figures 2a and 2b). Mild surrounding cerebral oedema was also noted.
discussion: Patients with tuberculous meningitis who exhibit initial improvement after ATT might experience a paradoxical reaction, which is defined as the development of new tuberculous lesions or the worsening of pre-existing ones either clinically or radiologically [3,4]. A drug-resistant state or treatment failure may be incorrectly suggested by the clinical or radiological deterioration linked to such a reaction, and it may even lead to the search for a different diagnosis [3]. These lesions are usually identified incidentally during regular follow-up CT scans or when new neurologic symptoms appear while receiving ATT [5]. Although paradoxical tuberculomas are thought to develop in patients with immunological reconstitution, neither age nor immunosuppression has been proven to be associated with their emergence [5]. In our patient, a follow-up sputum examination after one and three months of beginning the ATT was negative, suggestive of successful treatment. This helped us to rule out disease progression, development of drug-resistant TB, and failure of treatment. Within 14–270 days of beginning treatment, patients with tuberculous meningitis have been known to experience such reactions, which commonly manifest as intracranial tuberculomas, mimicking an intracranial space-occupying lesion [5]. Drug resistance, irregular medication use, or failure of medications to cross the blood-brain barrier do not constitute the reason for this condition. The host’s immunological response to ATT, i.e., exaggerated inflammatory response during antituberculosis treatment delivery, along with immunological reconstitution and increased exposure to antigens, is the principal cause of paradoxical responses and is frequently observed during the intense phase of the treatment [5]. A variety of mycobacterial proteins cause hypersensitivity in infected hosts. Tuberculostatic medications destroy mycobacterial structures and release bacilli, which cause inflammation and focal swelling [5]. These cause a delayed type of hypersensitivity reaction. Clinically, the patient may present with fever, headache, altered sensorium, decreased vision, and seizures post-initiation of ATT [3]. Radiologically, patients may show meningeal inflammation, arachnoiditis, hydrocephalus, and infarcts. The occurrence has been associated with a younger age at the time of initial diagnosis, although it does not vary by length of treatment. Although it may be documented years later, post-treatment paradoxical reactions (PR) primarily develop in the first six months following the conclusion of TB therapy [6]. These are greater and more severe in people with HIV on highly active antiretroviral treatment (HAART) [7]. 9.8% of TB-affected children in research by Gellago et al. developed a PR, which was shown to be in line with findings from prior research [4]. It is essential to be aware of paradoxical reactions in tuberculous meningitis because they can result in incorrect conclusions (such as an inaccurate diagnosis, treatment failure, mycobacterial drug resistance, drug toxicity, or the existence of a malignancy) [3]. A paradoxical response may not always indicate a failure of treatment [3]. Hence, ATT does not need to be altered or stopped. These patients likely need to be monitored for years. According to a few previous studies, a better outcome may arise from early detection, immunomodulatory drugs, and systemic corticosteroid treatment [3,5].
