title: Ultrasonographic features of Caroli syndrome
clinical_history: An eight-month-old female child presented with jaundice and abdominal distension. Clinical examination revealed icterus, a distended stomach, and prominent superficial veins. Laboratory reports showed elevated serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase and serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase levels with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound (USG) showed grossly coarsened echotexture of liver with multiple tiny communicating and non-communicating cystic lesions (Figures 1a and 1c). A slightly irregular liver outline was also noted (Figure 1c), indicating liver cirrhosis. Figure 1b shows a large intrahepatic cyst near the porta hepatis containing echogenic debris in dependent location, measuring 2.2 x 1.1 cm (indicating Caroli disease). Many sections also showed ill-defined hypoechoic nodules in the liver, indicative of dysplastic nodules (Figure 1d). The gallbladder was distended, showing an elongated gallbladder neck with a thickened wall (2.4 mm) and increased pericholecystic echogenicity (Figure 2a). Mild dilatation of the cystic duct was also noted (Figure 2b). Another section showed both liver and right kidney in profile with increased renal parenchymal echotexture (Figure 3). Colour Doppler assessment showed absent colour flow in cystic structures, suggesting cystic lesions to be biliary dilatations (Figures 4a and 4b). A splenomegaly of 8 cm with a dilated (10 mm) splenic vein was noted (Figure 6).
discussion: Congenital hepatic fibrosis (CHF) is predominantly an autosomal recessive condition; however, 56% of cases are reported to be sporadic [1]. CHF is characterised by malfunctions of the renal and hepatobiliary systems. Portal hypertension results from ductal plate malformations, periportal fibrosis, and secondary biliary strictures [2]. The course of the disease can range from mild hepatobiliary manifestations to full-blown liver cirrhosis. Most cases are diagnosed during adolescence or early adulthood [1]. Patients primarily present with manifestations of portal hypertension, such as splenomegaly and bleeding varices. However, clinical presentations can be nonspecific, making diagnosis challenging [3]. Other hepatic vascular malformations associated with CHF include cavernous transformation of the portal vein and hyperplasia and hypertrophy of hepatic artery branches within the portal tracts [4]. Several conditions may coexist with CHF, including biliary cysts, Caroli disease, choledochal cysts, Von Meyenburg complex, autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, renal dysplasia, nephronophthisis, and medullary sponge kidney. Todani classification of choledochal cysts: Type I: Fusiform or cystic dilatation of the extrahepatic bile duct (most common). Type II: True diverticulum from the common bile duct. Type III: Choledochocele, i.e., cystic dilatation of the intraduodenal portion of the common bile duct. Type IVa: Multiple cysts involving both intra and extrahepatic bile ducts. Type IVb: Multiple cysts involving only the extrahepatic bile ducts. Type V: Intrahepatic cysts only (Caroli disease). ARPKD (autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease) is almost always associated with CHF. The combined form of Caroli disease and CHF is termed Caroli syndrome [1]. Renal disease is predominant in neonates and infants, whereas liver-related complications are more common in older children and adults. The genetic cause of both CHF and ARPKD has been identified as mutations in the PKHD1 gene on chromosome 6p21.1-p12 [5]. On imaging, altered parenchymal echotexture and inhomogeneity are suggestive of CHF. The medial segment of the left lobe of the liver often remains normal or may undergo hypertrophy, unlike viral and alcoholic cirrhosis. Augmented arterialisation of the liver manifests as an enlarged hepatic artery. Fibrosis appears as periportal thickening, and biliary dilatations present as communicating tubular cystic structures. Parenchymal cysts are a hallmark of renal involvement, leading to altered renal echotexture. Ultrasonography remains the primary imaging modality for evaluation. Colour Doppler helps assess vascular patency, portal and splenic vein dilatations, collateral vascularisation, and flow direction in cases of portal hypertension. This is the preferred modality in paediatric cases requiring long-term follow-up. Serial ultrasound examinations are valuable for monitoring disease progression and complications, such as worsening fibrosis, increasing biliary dilatation, and development of portal hypertension features. Its non-invasive nature, lack of ionising radiation, and wide availability make USG an ideal tool for regular surveillance in both children and adults with CHF and associated disorders [8,9]. MRI and MRCP (magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography) play a pivotal role in the detailed assessment of the hepatobiliary system in CHF and its associated anomalies. MRCP, utilising heavily T2-weighted sequences, provides a non-invasive and high-resolution visualisation of fluid-filled biliary ducts and cysts. It is especially useful in confirming the diagnosis of Caroli disease and choledochal cysts by demonstrating intrahepatic biliary dilatations and the characteristic “central dot sign”. Additionally, MRI enables superior soft tissue contrast, accurate mapping of fibrosis, detection of regenerative and dysplastic nodules, and evaluation of renal involvement in ARPKD. Contrast-enhanced MRI sequences also assist in identifying complications such as cholangitis, portal vein thrombosis, and cavernous transformation, which may not be clearly evident on USG or CT [6]. While biopsy remains the gold standard for diagnosis, imaging findings can often enable a non-invasive diagnosis [7]. Take-Home Message Congenital hepatic fibrosis (CHF) presents with characteristic imaging features, often obviating the need for liver biopsy. Practising radiologists should be aware of this uncommon condition to facilitate prompt diagnosis and treatment.

title: Breast tumefaction in a newborn
clinical_history: A 19-day-old female newborn was brought to our hospital because of left breast tumefaction for 2 days, with localised erythema and irritability. No fluctuance or nipple discharge was noted. No fever was present. The white blood cell count was elevated. The delivery was eutocic (40 weeks and 2 days) and unremarkable.
imaging_findings: The right breast was unremarkable (Figure 1a). The breast bud is hypoechoic relative to subcutaneous fat. The left lower quadrant’s mammary tissue was poorly marginated and more echogenic than the contralateral side (Figure 1b), with increased Doppler colour flow in the lower quadrants (Figure 2a). In the inferior aspect of the quadrants, an avascular area without colour flow was noted, measuring 4 x 3 x 3 mm, with through-transmission and surrounding hyperaemia (Figure 2b). The subcutaneous tissue was thick and hyperechoic.
discussion: Background Neonatal mastitis is defined by breast inflammation with or without abscess, occurring in the first 2 months of life [1]. It is a rare condition (1–2 cases per year in large centres) [1,2]. The proposed physiological mechanism involves maternal hormonal stimulation of the neonatal breast, allowing skin and mucous membrane pathogens to reach breast tissue through the nipple and mammary ducts [3]. The predominant agent is Staphylococcus aureus [1]. Clinical Perspective The infection is limited to the breast in most cases. Rarely, cellulitis, fasciitis, brain abscess and generalised sepsis can ensue [1,4–6], underscoring the importance of prompt treatment not only to prevent complications but also to prevent compromise of breast development [1]. Fever occurs in less than 50% of the patients and leucocytosis in less than 75% [1,2]. Imaging Perspective The uninvolved breast bud is hypoechoic relative to subcutaneous fat. The involved breast is poorly marginated and more echogenic than the contralateral side. Surrounding subcutaneous fat is thicker and more echogenic. Both the involved breast bud and subcutaneous fat have increased colour Doppler flow [7]. Abscess formation rate varies from 40 to 70% [1,7,8]. They usually present as hypoechoic (sometimes hyperechoic) avascular areas with surrounding hyperaemia and slightly increased through-transmission. The diagnosis is typically clinical, with a fraction of patients undergoing US examination. US is then reserved for abscess suspicion (when fluctuance is dubious or if there is delayed response to antibiotics) or if the diagnosis of mastitis is in question. Typically, a complete sepsis work-up is done. Breast discharge should be Gram-stained and cultured to direct the antibiotic therapy [7]. Outcome Therapeutic options range from oral or intravenous antibiotics to aspiration or incision and drainage of an abscess [1,2,7,8]. Most newborns improve within 24–48 hours of antibiotic therapy [8,9,10]. In our case, the newborn was admitted and started on empiric intravenous flucloxacillin. After 2 days, and with improvement of symptoms, the route of administration was switched to oral. The newborn was discharged on day 4 and continued on antibiotics until day 7, and is doing well. Long-term consequences of neonatal mastitis are unknown, with reported cases of breast atrophy at the drainage site [11]. Teaching Points Early diagnosis is key to preventing local complications or sepsis. US is paramount to confirm the diagnosis of mastitis and in abscess detection. Findings include increased echogenicity of the breast bud and hyperaemia. Breast abscesses manifest as hypoechoic (sometimes hyperechoic) avascular areas with surrounding hyperaemia. Written informed consent was obtained from the mother.

title: Post-operative hepatic artery pseudoaneurysm with haemobilia: From diagnosis to intervention
clinical_history: A 61-year-old man, who underwent cholecystectomy with choledocho-duodenostomy for an endoscopically non-retrievable, impacted common bile duct stone, developed sudden onset abdominal pain, a fall in haemoglobin by 4 g/dL, and a rise in the bilirubin levels, two days after the surgery.
imaging_findings: Pre-contrast CT abdomen (Figure 1a) showed a dilated common bile duct with hyperdense content of blood attenuation. The arterial (Figure 1b and 1c) and venous (Figure 1d) phases of the CT abdomen revealed an outpouching of size 7 x 5 mm from the right hepatic artery, which matched the blood pool. There was no evidence of an active leak or blush. On the coronal reformatted image (Figure 1e), the common bile duct was dilated throughout its course and measured up to 24 mm at the porta. It showed intrahepatic biliary radicle dilatation and pneumobilia. Under digital subtraction angiography (DSA) guidance, a selective celiac artery cannulation was performed using a 4F Simmons 1 catheter and Glidewire® via the right common femoral artery cannulation. A small pseudoaneurysm (Figure 2a) was seen arising from the right hepatic artery just distal to the gastroduodenal artery. Super-selective cannulation using a microcatheter was achieved, and embolisation of the right hepatic artery was performed with multiple Nester® coils (Figure 2b). Post-embolisation angiogram revealed no leak or blush, and the right hepatic artery was successfully embolised (Figure 2C).
discussion: Background and Clinical Perspective Haemobilia is caused by numerous conditions, like post-procedural vessel or duct injury done for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes, blunt trauma to the abdomen, biliary obstruction due to gallstones, pancreaticobiliary inflammation, telangiectasia, or hepato-biliary tumours [1–5]. 50% of the cases are iatrogenic, and therefore, a high index of suspicion should be kept in a patient who has had a recent hepato-biliary intervention [5]. In a study conducted by Sandblom in 1973, traumatic cases were more prevalent than iatrogenic cases [3]. However, in 2001, Green et al. reported 65% of haemobilia cases due to iatrogenic causes [6]. The previous dictum of “do no harm” in medical practice has now changed into a more aggressive approach, which leads to iatrogenic complications [3]. Various diagnostic and therapeutic procedures performed that lead to haemobilia are percutaneous procedures like liver biopsy, transhepatic cholangiography (PTC), transhepatic biliary drainage (PTBD), and transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPSS) [1,4,5]. The risk of haemobilia was greater with PTBD (2.6%) than with PTC (0.7%) [7]. Haemobilia due to transhepatic drainage was seen in 5% of cases, while it was 1% in patients who underwent liver biopsy. Bleeding was an unusual complication of TIPSS surgery, thermal ablation, and hepatobiliary surgeries, accounting for less than 1% incidence for each [5]. The post-endoscopy-related haemobilia incidence was significant (1–2%) [5]. Blunt trauma to the liver is usually from a stabbing, gunshot wound, or a motor vehicle accident. It is the most common cause of haemobilia in the paediatric population [1]. In laparoscopic surgeries, accidental injury to the bile ducts can result in bile leakage, which in turn causes vascular irritation and pseudoaneurysm formation [1]. Stone erodes the bile duct wall and causes necrotic erosion of adjacent vessels. Inflammation in the bile duct has been known to cause pseudoaneurysms of the cystic artery [1]. In malignancies like hepatocellular carcinoma, there is an invasion of the bile ducts by tumour cells, causing haemobilia [1,2]. Imaging Perspective The initial modality for screening haemobilia is non-contrast CT. It helps to detect high-density attenuation of blood within the biliary system. However, it has poor specificity in localising the cause of the bleeding. CT angiography (non-invasive) and catheter angiography are the gold standard to localise and characterise the bleeding source and treat the same [5]. Extravasation of contrast into the biliary tree and the presence of a fistula or an aneurysm on DSA are consistent with the diagnosis of haemobilia [4]. Management and Outcome The two most important aspects in managing haemobilia are first to achieve haemostasis and next to maintain the patency of the biliary duct [1,2]. The latter is done to avoid blood clot formation in the biliary tract, leading to cholecystitis, cholangitis, or pancreatitis [2]. The Society for Vascular Surgery’s clinical practice guidelines recommend an endovascular first approach for hepatic artery aneurysm to maintain arterial flow for hepatic [8]. Arterial embolisation is currently the standard practice with a success rate of 80–100% and is recommended in cases of intrahepatic artery aneurysm [1,8]. Aneurysmal coiling is done from the distal to the proximal part of the vessel to avoid refilling via collaterals. Due to dual liver blood supply, hepatic artery coiling is a feasible option; however, it is avoided in patients with shock, liver transplant recipients, or portal vein thrombosis [1]. Patency of the portal vein is therefore a prerequisite to prevent ischemic damage to the liver in patients with liver transplants or cirrhosis [5]. Other complications as a result of hepatic artery embolisation are gall bladder infarction, necrosis of hepatic parenchyma with subsequent abscess formation [1]. To prevent these complications, hepatic artery stenting is a better alternative, which not only takes care of aneurysm but also maintains luminal patency and thus the integrity of the hepatic artery [1]. Partial hepatectomy or ligation of a bleeding vessel is the last surgical measure when everything fails [5]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Right ovarian vein drainage into the portal vein
clinical_history: A 60-year-old woman with alcoholic liver disease presented with worsening jaundice, bilious vomiting, dark urine and new acute back pain. Blood tests showed coagulopathy and hyperbilirubinaemia. Due to concern for retroperitoneal bleeding, a contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis was performed.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis revealed acute vertebral compression fractures at L1, L2, L4, and in the lower thoracic spine, likely responsible for the pain. There was no evidence of retroperitoneal haemorrhage. Incidentally, as seen in all figures, the right ovarian vein was seen coursing superiorly, draining anomalously into the portal vein, which was moderately dilated in the upper abdomen. The portal vein appeared patent, with no evidence of thrombosis or collateral formation at the confluence site. The liver showed periportal oedema with an irregular contour, consistent with cirrhosis. Features of pelvic congestion syndrome were also noted.
discussion: Background The ovarian veins usually follow a predictable pattern: the right drains into the inferior vena cava, while the left drains into the left renal vein. Variations are more commonly reported on the left side, including duplication or alternative drainage into the renal, iliac, or lumbar veins [1–3]. These are often incidental findings during surgery, dissection, or imaging. In contrast, right-sided ovarian vein variants are rarer, and direct drainage into the portal vein is exceptionally uncommon and not previously described in the literature. A direct ovarian–portal connection suggests a congenital anomaly, possibly due to aberrant embryologic development of the venous system during weeks 4–8 of gestation [4]. Abnormal persistence or regression of embryonic venous channels, particularly the vitelline and subcardinal veins, may account for this atypical venous configuration [4]. Clinical Perspective The anomalous drainage of the right ovarian vein into the portal vein was incidentally detected and was not responsible for her presenting symptoms. The morphology and course of the vessel suggest a congenital venous variant rather than an acquired shunt, as it appeared smooth, solitary, and without surrounding varices. However, in the context of end-stage liver disease, portal hypertension may have amplified or unmasked this anomaly by increasing portal flow or pressure. Imaging Perspective Contrast-enhanced CT with venous-phase imaging was used in this patient, which incidentally was the correct method for identifying vessel abnormalities. The right ovarian vein was first visualised from its pelvic origin and then traced in both axial and coronal planes to confirm the point of drainage. Outcome Although no specific treatment was required for the ovarian vein drainage, the patient was transferred to a tertiary liver centre for further evaluation of end-stage liver disease and was subsequently listed for, and underwent, liver transplantation. The vascular anomaly was not the cause of her symptoms, but its identification was relevant in the context of preoperative imaging and surgical planning. Take Home Message / Teaching Points The right ovarian vein typically drains into the inferior vena cava; drainage into the portal vein is exceptionally rare. Most described ovarian vein variants involve the left side and terminate in systemic venous structures. Multiphase contrast-enhanced CT is the key modality for identifying ovarian vein variants. Accurate anatomical tracking in multiple planes is essential to confirm unusual drainage patterns. Such findings may be incidental, but are important in the context of preoperative or transplant planning. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Kaposi sarcoma: Disseminated involvement in an HIV-positive patient
clinical_history: A 36-year-old male, HIV-1 positive since age 22 with no follow-up for 4 years, presented with progressive dyspnoea, cough, thoracic pain, and fatigue. Initially treated for presumed community-acquired pneumonia with partial symptom improvement, but later experienced worsening respiratory symptoms. Denied fever or night sweats.
imaging_findings: Chest X-ray revealed mediastinal widening, likely due to a mass, accompanied by ill-defined lower lung opacities and bilateral pleural effusion, more pronounced on the right (Figure 1). Thoracic CT demonstrated a large anterior mediastinal mass (10.8 × 5.3 × 7.6 cm), heterogeneously enhancing with cystic areas and displacement of adjacent vascular structures without invasion, likely representing a conglomerate of necrotic hypervascular lymph nodes (Figure 2). Additional mediastinal adenopathies were noted. Pulmonary findings included bilateral “flame-shaped” peribronchovascular opacities (Figure 3a), patchy ground-glass opacities, and interlobular septal thickening (Figure 3b). Bilateral pleural effusion was also evident. Systemic hypervascular adenopathies involved the axillary, mesenteric, and inguinal regions bilaterally (short diameter up to 1.7 cm) (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c). Abdominal imaging revealed cutaneous millimetric nodules in the thoracic and abdominal walls (Figure 5), hepatomegaly (17.9 cm in craniocaudal length), and gastric wall thickening (Figures 6a and 6b).
discussion: Background Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade vascular tumour caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), classified into classic, endemic, iatrogenic, and AIDS-related forms. AIDS-related KS, the most aggressive variant, often presents with disseminated cutaneous and visceral involvement in immunocompromised individuals. Thoracic and abdominal involvement are common, and imaging is key for assessing disease extent [1,2]. Clinical Perspective This patient presented with respiratory symptoms, systemic lymphadenopathies, and an anterior mediastinal mass, a constellation of findings that raised suspicion for an AIDS-related malignancy or opportunistic infection. Imaging was crucial to assess the extent of disease, identify characteristic features, and guide further diagnostic and therapeutic steps. Findings such as hypervascular lymphadenopathies, pleural effusion, and “flame-shaped” pulmonary opacities strongly suggested Kaposi sarcoma [1,2]. Differential diagnoses based on imaging include several conditions that may mimic disseminated Kaposi sarcoma. AIDS-related lymphoma is a common cause of anterior mediastinal masses in immunocompromised patients and often presents with well-defined, bulky lymphadenopathy. Although central necrosis is uncommon in lymphoma, it can occasionally occur in high-grade subtypes due to rapid tumour growth [1]. Opportunistic infections such as atypical pneumonia (e.g., Pneumocystis jirovecii ), mycobacterial infections (e.g., tuberculosis), and fungal infections (e.g., Aspergillus ) are frequent in HIV patients and may cause bilateral pulmonary opacities and systemic symptoms. These infections may also result in necrotic mediastinal lymphadenopathy, which helps distinguish them from the hypervascular nodes seen in KS [1,2]. Lymphangitic carcinomatosis is an important consideration for interlobular septal thickening and patchy ground-glass opacities, although it is less common in this patient population [1]. Multicentric Castleman disease, associated with HHV-8 and HIV, should be considered when hypervascular lymphadenopathy is present [2]. Pulmonary oedema can cause interlobular septal thickening, but it was unlikely in this case, given the clinical context. Sarcoidosis can show perilymphatic nodules predominantly along the peribronchovascular bundles, subpleural regions, and interlobular septa, potentially mimicking the distribution of pulmonary KS [1]. Imaging Perspective Imaging played a critical role in narrowing these broad differentials, highlighting features highly suggestive of KS, guiding the biopsy approach, and supporting a prompt and accurate diagnosis [1,4]. CT demonstrated classic AIDS-related KS features, including bilateral “flame-shaped” peribronchovascular opacities, interlobular septal thickening, and hypervascular lymphadenopathies in mediastinal, axillary, mesenteric, and inguinal regions [1,2]. Gastric wall thickening, although not histologically confirmed, may represent visceral involvement of KS, a known manifestation in disseminated disease [3,4]. Cutaneous nodules detected on CT correlated with violaceous cutaneous lesions observed during physical examination, further supporting the diagnosis of disseminated KS [1]. These imaging findings strongly suggested disseminated KS, with the combination of hypervascular lymphadenopathies and characteristic pulmonary findings serving as key diagnostic clues [1,2]. Accurate diagnosis requires integrating imaging, clinical context, and histopathological confirmation [1–4]. In our case, the final diagnosis was established histopathologically through a CT-guided biopsy of the mediastinal mass. Histopathological analysis remains the gold standard for diagnosing KS, confirming the imaging findings [1]. Outcome The patient initiated antiretroviral therapy (ART) and systemic chemotherapy for KS, achieving partial improvement. Imaging was crucial in staging the disease, guiding the biopsy, and identifying multifocal involvement. Prognosis depends on visceral involvement and immune reconstitution achieved with ART. Therapeutic options include ART, systemic chemotherapy, and radiotherapy for localised lesions. Early imaging is essential for treatment planning and monitoring response [1,3,4]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points AIDS-related Karposi sarcoma (KS) frequently involves thoracic and abdominal organs, presenting with characteristic imaging findings. Bilateral “flame-shaped” pulmonary opacities and hypervascular lymphadenopathy are hallmark imaging features. Imaging plays a critical role in diagnosing disseminated KS, staging disease, and guiding biopsy and therapy planning.

title: CT-guided embolisation for first run angiography-negative gastrointestinal bleeding
clinical_history: A 67-year-old male patient was admitted with a complicated pneumonia. During the hospitalisation, after the introduction of enoxaparin 40 mg, haematochezia developed, associated with hypotension and tachycardia, as well as a decline in haemoglobin levels (from 10.6 g/dL to 7.4 g/dL) requiring 2 units of red blood cells. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed and was unremarkable.
imaging_findings: After an initial angio-CT revealed active bleeding from the distal ileum (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d), the patient was taken to the angio-hybrid suite. Right femoral artery vascular access was obtained with a 5F sheath. No active extravasation of contrast was noted in the first run 2D-angiography of the superior mesenteric artery (Figure 2a). Abdominal and pelvic CT with administration of contrast in the 5F catheter positioned in the superior mesenteric artery confirmed active extravasation (Figure 2b). Embolisation was done with the aid of the syngo Embolisation Guidance package software of the Nexaris Angio-CT (Siemens Healthineers), which permits overlaying of CT-arteriograms on live fluoroscopy visuals, with instantaneous roadmaps (Figure 2c). When the target vessel was selected with the microcatheter, angiography confirmed active bleeding (that was occult in the initial angiography) (Figure 3a). Injection of 0.6 mL of ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) was performed (Figure 3b). Final angiography confirmed exclusion of the bleeding (Figure 3c).
discussion: Background Small bowel gastrointestinal bleeding occurs between the ligament of Treitz and the ileocecal valve, accounting for 5%–10% of gastrointestinal bleeding events [1]. In patients above 40 years, the most common causes are angioectasia and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug therapy [2]. Angio-CT is the preferred imaging modality if there is brisk overt bleeding with haemodynamic instability [3], with a sensitivity as high as 0.3 mL/min [4]. Clinical and Imaging Perspectives If the patient is haemodynamically unstable, with confirmed active bleeding detected on angio-CT, transfer to the angio suite is preconised, to permit prompt embolisation if extravasation of contrast is confirmed on catheter angiography [3]. However, the sensitivity of catheter angiography in the detection of acute gastrointestinal bleeding averages 60% [5]. If a first-run angiography from the superior mesenteric artery is negative, angio-CT from a catheter positioned in the superior mesenteric artery, in a hybrid suite, with dedicated embolisation guiding software, can guide the way to the culprit vessel, as shown in our case. After superselective catheterisation of the culprit vessel with a microcatheter and another angiography run, active extravasation/pseudoaneurysm may finally become visible in angiography. The use of software guidance also spares fluoroscopy time and radiation exposure. Provocative mesenteric angiography (e.g., with heparin or vasodilators) is also another preconised alternative when the initial angiography run is negative, with mean positivity rates of 49% [3,6]. Outcome Endovascular treatment options were embolisation with Gelfoam ® , coils, polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), EVOH or glue. Surgical segmental resection was also an option, albeit invasive in a fragile patient. Embolisation with EVOH was pursued. Gelfoam ® , coils and PVA are not so permanent as EVOH and glue. Glue in the mesenteric territory could be unpredictable and with higher risks of non-target embolisation [7]. Our patient had melena the day after the procedure, probably because of digested blood products, but did not suffer from new episodes of gastrointestinal bleeding. After 2 weeks, lactic acidosis developed, and a CT was performed (Figures 4a and 4b), revealing segmental distal ileal branch dilation and adjacent fat stranding. A segmental enterectomy was performed, and the resected segment corresponded to the embolised territory. This was a complication due to proximal embolisation. A more selective embolisation of the culprit vessel or the use of coils could have prevented this, allowing for collaterals to prevent small-bowel ischemia. However, coils have a higher chance of rebleeding, and a more selective catheterisation was not feasible due to the risk of dissection of a very small and tortuous vessel. We opted for the sacrifice of proximal vessels in the emergency setting. Unfortunately, the patient passed away 3 months after the procedure with septic shock and multiorgan failure. The prolonged hospital stay, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and middle and posterior cerebral artery stroke further debilitated his status. Teaching Points Software-guided CTA (computed tomography angiography) with the catheter/microcatheter positioned in the respective distal branch of the mesenteric artery can be of great value when initial DSA (digital subtraction angiography) is negative in patients with acute gastrointestinal bleeding. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: LBSL in a young female patient
clinical_history: An 18-year-old female who recently migrated with her family due to war presented with longstanding, progressive motor impairment of unclear origin. She was referred by an outpatient neurologist after multiple sclerosis had been excluded. No previous medical records were available from her country of origin. According to her mother, she developed normally in her early infancy, walking independently. Around 17–18 months, shortly after vaccination (possibly MMR), she developed dragging of one leg, recurrent fevers, and loss of motor milestones. A verbal diagnosis of post-viral encephalitis was given at the time. Her condition fluctuated, but cognition remained intact. She developed progressive gait decline during her childhood. Wheelchair use began at age 15, and she is now fully dependent for transfers, though she eats and writes independently. Clinical and neurological examination revealed esophoria, mild tongue deviation, weak facial muscles, hypotrophic upper extremities with reduced fine motor control, joint hypermobility, increased tone and reflexes with bilateral positive Trömner signs, and severe leg-dominant spastic tetraparesis. Given the unclear clinical presentation, brain and spinal MRI were performed.
imaging_findings: Brain MRI revealed symmetrical T2 (Figures 1) and FLAIR (Figures 2) hyperintensities in the supratentorial white matter (excluding U-fibres), splenium of the corpus callosum, posterior limb of the internal capsule, pons along trigeminal pathways, inferior cerebellar peduncles, and pyramidal tracts of the medulla oblongata. DWI (Figures 3) showed restricted diffusion with low ADC (Figures 4). No contrast enhancement was observed (Figures 5). MR spectroscopy (Figures 6) revealed a lactate peak at the level of the abnormal white matter. Spinal MRI (Figures 7 and 8) displayed longitudinal signal abnormalities predominantly involving the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts throughout the entire cord. Findings suggested a metabolic leukodystrophy. Diagnosis was confirmed by genetic testing.
discussion: Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and lactate elevation (LBSL) is a rare autosomal recessive leukodystrophy caused by mutations in the DARS2 gene, located on the long arm of chromosome 1 [1,2]. LBSL was first described by Marjo S. van der Knaap, a Dutch paediatric neurologist, and her international colleagues in 2002 [3]. It manifests with slowly progressive pyramidal, cerebellar, and dorsal column dysfunction. Typical symptoms include spastic paraparesis, gait disturbances, and proprioceptive loss, while cognitive function often remains preserved [1]. This patient exhibited a classic clinical trajectory, including early developmental regression, progressive spastic tetraparesis (leg-dominant), and wheelchair dependence before the age of 18. MRI showed hallmark features of LBSL: symmetrical involvement of the cerebral white matter (with U-fibre sparing), corpus callosum, internal capsule, trigeminal tract, cerebellar peduncles, and corticospinal tracts [3]. These findings, coupled with restricted diffusion and lactate peak, supported the diagnosis. Although a lactate peak in the abnormal white matter on MR spectroscopy is typically associated with the condition—and even reflected in its name—this feature does not necessarily have to be present [4]. Genetic testing revealed compound heterozygous variants in DARS2 , confirming LBSL [1]. While no curative therapy exists, supportive management includes physiotherapy and periodic imaging follow-up [1,4]. Take Home Message MRI findings are helpful for the early recognition of LBSL. Diagnostic confirmation relies on genetic testing. Supportive management is crucial for preserving function and quality of life. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Giant serous cystadenoma of the pancreas: An uncommon presentation
clinical_history: A 73-year-old female patient underwent follow-up at our institution for 14 years due to a pancreatic head lesion. The lesion was monitored at six-month intervals through ultrasound, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging, revealing sustained growth throughout the surveillance period. However, the patient remained asymptomatic, and laboratory tests were unremarkable.
imaging_findings: Cross-sectional imaging of the upper abdomen, namely computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), revealed a multicystic lesion in the pancreatic head, with lobulated margins, enhancing internal septations (Figures 1, 2, and 3) and a central fibrotic scar with stellate calcifications (Figures 1a–1h). On ultrasound, the lesion depicts multiple hypoechoic/anechoic cysts and hyperechoic septations (Figure 4). Over time, the lesion’s enlargement led to gradual dilatation of both the bile ducts and the main pancreatic duct. In the most recent magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) (Figures 2a–2i), the pancreatic lesion measured approximately 97 x 86 x 126 mm (length x width x anteroposterior axis). The common bile duct had a calibre of 15 mm, and the main pancreatic duct had a maximum calibre of 7 mm. The pancreatic parenchyma was atrophic.
discussion: The overall imaging findings are consistent with a giant serous cystadenoma (SCA) of the pancreas. SCA is a benign cystic pancreatic neoplasm, mainly affecting women, typically over the sixth decade of life—the “grandmother lesion” of the pancreas [1]. Most patients are asymptomatic, with SCA discovered incidentally on imaging for unrelated conditions. However, larger tumours may compress surrounding structures and manifest clinically with abdominal pain, jaundice (compression of the common bile duct), pancreatitis (obstruction of pancreatic ducts), weight loss or early satiety (compression of the stomach) [1–3]. Giant SCA is an uncommon presentation occurring when it exceeds 10 cm in diameter [4]. Imaging is important for characterising SCAs based on morphology, distinguishing them from other cystic lesions, identifying atypical presentations and complications, and guiding appropriate treatment. MRI/MRCP better evaluates cyst morphology and the pancreatic ductal system, while CT can show additional information, such as calcifications [3,5]. Microcystic SCA is the most common type, consisting of a well-circumscribed, multilobulated lesion with multiple (> 6) small cysts (< 2 cm) separated by thin septa, often centred around a fibrous stellate scar, which may have calcifications. Macrocystic SCA has fewer (< 6) but larger cysts (≥ 2 cm) and does not have a central scar [2,6]. SCAs do not communicate with the main pancreatic duct [2]. Pancreatic SCAs may have atypical presentations, such as haemorrhage and invasion of adjacent structures, which can mimic malignant neoplasms. These require careful imaging evaluation, and histological characterisation may be necessary. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) may be helpful for further characterisation. Fine needle aspiration may be performed during EUS to evaluate cyst fluid and help distinguish SCAs from mucinous cystic tumours [1,7]. Although SCAs are typically considered benign, there are rare cases of malignant transformation of these lesions, particularly giant SCAs, suggesting a possible correlation between tumour size and malignant potential [3,4,6]. Some imaging features of SCA may overlap with other pancreatic lesions. Differential diagnoses include mucinous cystic neoplasms, which typically have a smooth external contour and a thick enhancing capsule; malignant subtypes may display wall irregularity, thick septations, mural nodules, papillary projections and wall or septal calcifications [2,3,7]. Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) manifests as a focal or diffuse dilation of the main duct (main-duct IPMN), as a cystic lesion communicating with the main duct (side-branch IPMN) or both. Solid pancreatic pseudopapillary neoplasms are encapsulated lesions, often with cystic and solid components and may show internal areas of haemorrhage [1,2]. Pseudocysts are often unilocular fluid collections with a smooth and thin enhancing capsule, occurring in a setting of pancreatitis [2]. As SCAs are benign, most asymptomatic patients can be managed with regular imaging follow-up. Surgery is indicated for lesions with rapid growth (annual growth > 4 mm), large and symptomatic tumours and when the cystic nature of the lesion is uncertain [4,6–8]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Right internal auditory canal duplication with bilateral vestibular dysplasia
clinical_history: A 3-year-old female presented with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) noted since birth. There was no history of perinatal infections, trauma, or family history of hearing impairment. Developmental milestones were otherwise normal.
imaging_findings: High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the temporal bones revealed duplication of the right internal auditory canal (IAC), separated by a bony septum into a wider superior and a narrowed inferior canals. The superior canal continued into the facial nerve canal, while the inferior canal communicated with the bony cochlea and vestibule (Figures 1, 2, and 3). Imaging revealed dilated and dysplastic vestibule and lateral semicircular canal on both sides (Figure 4). The superior and posterior semicircular canals appeared normal. Additionally, the left internal auditory canal (IAC) was normal in both morphology and calibre.
discussion: Duplication of the internal auditory canal (DIAC) is a rare congenital anomaly, with fewer than 50 cases reported worldwide [1]. It is characterised by a bony septum dividing the IAC into two distinct canals, typically with the superior division transmitting the facial nerve and the inferior division the cochlear nerve [2]. This anomaly is most commonly identified during evaluation for congenital sensorineural hearing loss in children. The present case is notable for the combination of right-sided DIAC with bilateral vestibular and lateral semicircular canal dysplasia, representing a complex congenital inner ear malformation spectrum which are less commonly reported but recognised inner ear malformations [3]. Lateral semicircular canal dysplasia results from abnormal embryological development and may contribute to vestibular dysfunction [4]. The exact embryological cause of DIAC is unclear but likely stems from abnormal development of the otic capsule and IAC in early gestation. Normally, the IAC transmits the facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves through a single bony canal. In DIAC, a bony septum divides the canal into two, often associated with aplasia or hypoplasia of the vestibulocochlear nerve, contributing to sensorineural hearing loss. This may result from disrupted nerve development due to abnormal bony formation or vice versa, reflecting developmental arrest of the otic placode or neural crest. DIAC frequently coexists with other inner ear anomalies, such as dysplastic vestibules and semicircular canals, suggesting a broader embryological defect from a common timing of insult during otic development. High-resolution CT remains the imaging modality of choice for detailed delineation of bony inner ear anatomy in such cases, aiding diagnosis and management planning [2]. Early and accurate diagnosis is crucial for counselling regarding prognosis and cochlear implantation candidacy.

title: Cervical agenesis with endometrioma presenting as primary amenorrhea
clinical_history: A 45-year-old female presented with a longstanding history of primary amenorrhea and cyclical lower abdominal pain since adolescence. The pain occurs every month, typically lasting 3–5 days, and is described as crampy and localised to the lower abdomen and pelvis.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound examination done on a Samsung RS80A ultrasound machine showed a bulky uterine body with hypoechoic endometrial collection (Figure 1). A heterogeneously hypoechoic lesion with internal echogenic debris was noted in the right adnexa, arising from the right ovary (Figure 2). The left ovary appears normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed using a 1.5 Tesla GE MR machine. T2-weighted sagittal and axial images of the MRI pelvis show the presence of the fundus and body of the uterus, which is oriented in the right lateral position in the pelvic cavity, with the absence of the cervix (Figure 3). However, the vagina is visualised. T1 hyperintense and T2 mildly hypointense endometrial collection is noted within the endometrial cavity (Figures 3 and 4). A well-defined T1 hyperintense and predominantly T2 hypointense (T2 shading sign) cystic lesion with a thin wall is noted in the right adnexa, arising from the right ovary (Figures 5 and 6). Minimal pelvic ascites is noted.
discussion: Background Cervical agenesis is a rare congenital Müllerian anomaly, representing approximately 3% of all Müllerian duct anomalies and occurring in about 1 in 80,000–100,000 women [1]. It results from the failure of canalisation or fusion of the Müllerian ducts during embryogenesis, resulting in absent cervical tissue. Retrograde menstruation typically leads to the early onset of complications like endometriomas. Endometrioma, also known as “chocolate cyst”, is a form of endometriosis where ectopic endometrial tissue forms a cystic mass in the ovary [2]. Clinical Perspective Patients with cervical agenesis typically present during adolescence with primary amenorrhea and cyclical abdominal or pelvic pain, owing to obstructed menstrual flow and haematometra or haematosalpinx. In rare cases like this one, diagnosis is delayed until adulthood. Longstanding obstruction can result in retrograde menstruation, increasing the risk for endometriosis and endometrioma formation [3]. Imaging plays a pivotal role in diagnosing this anomaly, especially when physical examination reveals a blind vaginal pouch and no cervical os. The radiologist must alert the referring physician of the anatomical abnormality, associated complications, and guide surgical planning. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound may suggest haematometra and a pelvic cystic lesion, but MRI is the modality of choice for accurate delineation of Müllerian anomalies and associated complications [4]. In our patient, MRI confirmed complete cervical agenesis with haematometra and a right-sided ovarian endometrioma. Key imaging findings are a distended uterus with T1 hyperintense endometrial collection and a well-defined ovarian lesion with characteristic T1 hyperintensity and T2 hypointensity, consistent with an endometrioma. MRI enables comprehensive evaluation of uterovaginal anatomy, guides the differential diagnosis, and therapeutic planning. Outcome Treatment options depend on symptom severity and anatomic feasibility. While uterovaginal canalisation may be considered in select cases, hysterectomy is often the definitive treatment in women with a noncommunicating uterus and significant symptoms, especially when fertility is no longer desired [5]. Imaging findings directly influence surgical decisions by assessing anatomical variants and identifying associated pathology. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Cervical agenesis should be suspected in women with primary amenorrhoea and cyclic pain. MRI is essential for the precise characterisation of Müllerian anomalies. Delayed diagnosis may lead to complications such as endometriosis or endometrioma. Early identification aids in tailored surgical planning and symptom relief.

title: A rare case of clear cell soft tissue sarcoma of the knee
clinical_history: A 78-year-old female presented to the surgery outpatient department with complaints of painless swelling, posterior to the left knee, for 20 years, with a recent onset of pain (since 3 months) after getting hit by an animal at the site of swelling. On examination, the swelling was firm and lobulated with no overlying skin changes. There was a history of weight loss and loss of appetite. No other comorbidities. No family history of malignancy.
imaging_findings: A plain lateral radiograph of the knee demonstrated a soft tissue lesion seen on the posterior aspect of the knee (Figure 1). Soft tissue ultrasound (US) demonstrated a large lobulated and irregularly shaped heterogeneously hypoechoic mass lesion with internal vascularity, seen posterior to the left knee (Figure 2 ). A few central hypoechoic necrotic/cystic areas were also seen. The mass was also seen displacing the popliteal vessels superficially. MRI (with contrast) findings revealed a large T1 heterointense lobulated mass lesion in the popliteal fossa with patchy areas of T1 hyperintensity (Figure 3). It also showed heterointense signal on T2W images (Figure 4). The lesion also showed patchy areas of diffusion restriction on DWI and ADC (Figures 5a and 5b) and heterogeneous enhancement on post-contrast study (Figure 6). It was seen displacing and causing near-complete encasement of the popliteal neurovascular bundle. There was no obvious involvement/infiltration of the overlying skin.
discussion: Background Soft tissue sarcomas are rare mesenchymal tumours, of which clear cell soft tissue sarcoma is rarest, accounting for less than 1% of all. These sarcomas usually involve tendons or aponeurosis of distal extremities [1,2], followed by upper extremities and rarely involve neck and trunk [3]. Younger age group people are affected more, with a slight female predilection [4]. As these tumours are aggressive and morphologically appear similar to melanomas, early diagnosis and early treatment provide better clinical outcomes [5]. The only way to differentiate between the two is chromosomal translocation of t(12:22)(q13:q12) which affects the EWSR1-ATF1 gene [6,7]; this translocation has not been described in melanosomes. Clinical Perspective These are usually slow-growing and mostly painless tumours [8], with a tendency to metastasise to lungs and regional lymph nodes, and characteristic local recurrence even after treatment [2]. Adverse prognostic factors are tumour size > 5 cm, lymph node metastasis, recurrence, and necrosis [2,9]. As these tumours have a tendency to metastasise quickly, close follow-up is necessary [10] to avoid a missed or delayed diagnosis. Imaging Perspective MRI helps in characterising the tumour, its extent, staging and preoperative assessment [11]. T1 hyperintense signals are also seen in melanomas, making this a strong differential. However, less involvement of the skin can be of help. One needs to look for parameters like age, size, location, necrosis, calcification, skin lesions, necrosis, and invasion into adjacent tissues while making the diagnosis of clear cell sarcoma. Outcome In this case, histopathological examination showed cellular nests of clear cells (due to glycogen) with eosinophilic cytoplasm, separated by fibrous bands with prominent nucleoli and vesicular chromatin (Figure 7a). Areas of necrosis with melanin pigment deposits were also seen with pigment-laden macrophages (Figure 7b). Focal areas of atypical mitosis were also seen. Immunohistochemistry was positive for HMB-45 (Figure 8a), S-100 (Figure 8b), Melan-A, BCL-2 and Ki-67. Negative staining for CK and CD-34 was also observed. Teaching Points Clear cell soft tissue sarcoma is the rarest of all soft tissue sarcomas. When evaluating soft tissue tumours of limbs, clear cell sarcoma with melanocytic differentiation should be considered a strong differential, especially when MRI shows hyperintense signals on T1W images compared to the muscle.

final_diagnosis: Clear cell soft tissue sarcoma with melanocytic differentiation

title: Contrast-enhanced mammography findings in lymphocytic mastopathy
clinical_history: A 49-year-old premenopausal woman presented to the gynaecologist with complaints of a painful right breast lump, which had started two weeks before. She had no known history of significant medical conditions. The physician ordered a bilateral mammography (Figure 1) and a breast ultrasound (Figure 2).
imaging_findings: A mediolateral oblique tomosynthesis view of the right breast revealed a 7 cm asymmetry in the upper outer quadrant (UOQ) (Figure 1). Ultrasound showed a hypoechoic palpable mass (Figure 2) with indistinct margins and no vascularity. No suspicious axillary lymph nodes were shown. The breast lesion was assigned a BI-RADS 4C category, and a US-guided vacuum-assisted biopsy (10G) was performed. The diagnostic workup was completed with contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM) after the biopsy (Figures 3a and 3b), which demonstrated a 7 cm non-mass enhancement in the UOQ of the right breast. Histopathological examination revealed no evidence of malignancy. The tissue showed features consistent with sclerosing lymphocytic mastitis, including a dense lymphocytic infiltrate, collagenised stroma, and a thickened basal membrane. The findings were reviewed in a multidisciplinary team with pathologists, gynaecologists and radiologists. Although the initial imaging findings were highly suspicious for malignancy (BI-RADS 4C), retrospective analysis revealed that the clinical and imaging features were concordant with the pathological diagnosis. Upon further review of the patient’s history, there was no evidence of diabetes or autoimmune disease. However, laboratory tests showed chronic hyperglycaemia, with HbA1c values between 5.8% and 6.1%. She was referred to an endocrinologist and underwent an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), which revealed glucose levels of 89 mg/dl at 0 minutes and 183 mg/dl at 120 minutes. Her BMI was 30.85 kg/m2. Based on these findings, a conservative approach was adopted, with dietary intervention aimed at glycaemic control. At the six-month clinical follow-up, she reported no pain or palpable lump in the breast. OGTT values had improved to 83 mg/dl at 0 minutes and 137 mg/dl at 120 minutes, with an HbA1c of 5.4%. Follow-up breast imaging one year after biopsy showed complete resolution of the focal asymmetry (Figure 4).
discussion: Background Lymphocytic mastitis is an uncommon fibroinflammatory breast lesion with an unclear aetiology [1–3]. It is more frequently observed in patients with poorly controlled long-standing type 1 diabetes (also known as diabetic mastopathy) [1–4]. Exogenous insulin administration may trigger inflammatory reactions in the breast [1,3]. Alternatively, the secondary autoimmune effects of the accumulation of glucose in the extracellular connective tissue are thought to induce an immune response [4] that could be a possible mechanism to explain the association of lymphocytic mastitis with type 2 diabetes, as reported herein. However, this illness has also been described in association with other autoimmune or endocrine disorders, and in patients without any such comorbidities [2–4]. Clinical Perspective This condition more commonly affects premenopausal women between 30 and 50 years of age [1,3,4], and is rarely observed in men with gynecomastia [1,3]. Clinically, it presents as one or more asymptomatic, firm breast masses, varying in size and location [1–4]. A predilection for the subareolar region has been reported [3,4]. Inflammatory signs at breast physical examination are usually absent [3,4]. Imaging Perspective The most common mammographic finding of lymphocytic mastitis is asymmetry underlying a palpable mass, generally between 3 and 6 cm in diameter [1,3,6]. Lymphocytic mastitis at mammography may disclose no findings, being distinctive for the absence of masses, calcifications and spiculated lesions [1,3,5,6]. Ultrasound often shows hypoechoic areas with irregular margins and marked posterior acoustic shadowing, caused by fibrosis. This prominent shadowing is characteristic and often more pronounced than that seen in neoplastic lesions. Although it is more commonly associated with malignancy, it can also be observed in benign lesions with a high degree of fibrosis [1,3,6]. Although MRI findings are not specific for lymphocytic mastitis, they may aid in establishing the diagnosis and confirming the benign nature of the lesion [5]. At MRI, lymphocytic mastitis most often demonstrates gradual and persistent non-mass enhancement, but it has no specific MRI pattern, and it may disclose no findings [3–6]. To our knowledge, contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM) findings of lymphocytic mastitis have not been previously reported. We present the first documented case showing this entity as a non-mass enhancement on CEM. Our findings correlate well with previously reported MRI-based studies [5,6]. Outcome Core needle biopsy is the preferred diagnostic method [1–4]. Clinical and imaging findings of lymphocytic mastitis are nonspecific, often overlapping breast cancer features. Therefore, this diagnosis requires histological proof with core needle biopsy, multidisciplinary correlation, and clinical and imaging follow-up. Excisional biopsy should be reserved for cases with reasonable doubt and suspicion of malignancy, especially considering the high recurrence rates reported after surgical excision [1,3]. A conservative, observational approach is initially recommended to avoid unnecessary surgery [1,3]. Follow-up should include annual clinical review and imaging with mammography and/or ultrasound [1]. Marking the biopsy site with a clip can help to confirm adequate biopsy sampling and facilitate future monitoring. Following an excision, recurrence rates can be as high as 32% [3]. There is no evidence to suggest that lymphocytic mastitis increases the risk of the development of breast cancer [3]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Diagnosing lymphocytic mastopathy can be challenging due to its similarities with breast carcinoma [1,3]. The diagnosis is particularly difficult in patients without type 1 diabetes or autoimmune diseases. Multidisciplinary integration of clinical and multimodal imaging findings is of paramount importance to avoid repeated biopsies and unnecessary excisional procedures. Follow-up with imaging—including mammography and ultrasound, CEM, or MRI—is important, as lymphocytic mastitis may be a self-limited disease, as demonstrated in our report. However, recurrence in the same or the contralateral breast is possible, highlighting the need for continued surveillance.

title: Rare case of post-COVID fungal osteomyelitis of the patella
clinical_history: A 30‐year‐old man presented with two months of right knee pain and swelling. He had recovered from COVID‑19 pneumonia three months earlier after receiving systemic steroids. During his stay in the hospital, the patient has received dexamethasone injection 8 mg/day through the intravenous route for 10 days with gradual tapering over the next 2 weeks. No evidence of diabetes mellitus or other systemic comorbidities. Localised tenderness over the patella was noted; there were no systemic symptoms or history of trauma.
imaging_findings: Radiographs of the knee in anteroposterior, lateral, and skyline views revealed superficial sclerosis of the patella, along with a subtle erosion at its inferior pole (Figures 1a and 1b). There were no signs of fracture or significant soft tissue injury. Given the clinical context and radiographic findings, infection was suspected, and an MRI was recommended. On MRI, the patellar inferior pole appeared hypointense on T1 images (Figures 2a and 2b) and hyperintense on proton density (PD) fat-saturated sequences (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c). Diffusion-weighted images (DWI) also indicated restriction (Figures 4a and 4b). The subchondral bone and articular cartilage remained largely intact, although a mild effusion was present. Post-contrast images showed thickening and enhancement of the synovium (Figures 5a and 5b). Osteomyelitis of the patella was considered likely.
discussion: Background Isolated fungal osteomyelitis of the patella in adults is an extremely rare entity, with only a handful of cases reported in the literature. Immunosuppression plays a central role in its development, with steroid therapy being a well-recognised risk factor for mucormycosis of the bone [1,2]. In addition, the post-COVID-19 era has seen a noticeable rise in fungal infections [3]: “ Glucocorticoid‐induced immunosuppression, hyperglycaemia and lymphopenia predispose to the pathogenesis of mucormycosis. The rampant use of glucocorticoids in patients with COVID‐19 has undoubtedly contributed to the upsurge in the number of cases of COVID-19-associated mucormycosis ” [4]. Other risk factors include trauma, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, and intravenous drug abuse [5–7]. Clinical Perspective Clinically, the presentation is variable; however, swelling and tenderness localised over the patella remain the most consistent findings. Notably, the range of knee motion is often relatively preserved, in contrast to septic arthritis, and systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise may be absent [8]. Imaging Perspective Radiographic imaging may reveal superficial patellar sclerosis and subtle focal erosions, yet these findings are nonspecific. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the modality of choice due to its high sensitivity in detecting early bone marrow oedema, synovial thickening, and joint effusion. However, differentiating fungal osteomyelitis from tubercular or pyogenic forms based solely on imaging is challenging. For instance, while Shah et al. [9] noted that the absence of marginal sclerosis may point toward tuberculosis, some cases can demonstrate marginal sclerosis. In contrast, pyogenic osteomyelitis usually presents with an acute onset, marked systemic symptoms, and imaging features such as focal bone lysis, prepatellar abscess formation, and draining sinus in advanced cases. Other imaging modalities, such as ultrasonography (USG), provide rapid assessment of periosteal reactions, cortical irregularities, soft tissue abscesses, and joint effusions, with colour Doppler detecting areas of increased vascularity. Computed tomography (CT) is particularly useful for identifying sequestra, involucrum, cloaca, or intraosseous gas, and it serves as an excellent guide for needle biopsies. Bone scans, though not routinely used, offer a viable alternative when MRI is contraindicated or when there is a suspicion of multifocal osteomyelitis. Outcome Early diagnosis of fungal osteomyelitis relies on a high index of suspicion, especially in patients with subtle clinical findings. Laboratory confirmation through pus aspirate and culture is critical for identifying the causative organism. Treatment typically involves antifungal therapy—often amphotericin B—with surgical debridement considered when necessary. In our case, subsequent joint aspiration revealed aseptate, broad fungal hyphae consistent with Mucor species (Figure 6). The patient was started on antifungal treatment (isavuconazole, capsule 100 mg, three times a day for the initial two days and then followed by a single daily dose for the next 1 week) while being carefully observed. Clinical improvement was noted over the following weeks, and without any complications, the patient was discharged from the hospital. Teaching Points Isolated fungal osteomyelitis of the patella in adults is exceedingly rare and can present subtly. MRI is invaluable for detecting early changes, though distinguishing fungal osteomyelitis from tubercular or pyogenic variants may require further clinical and laboratory correlation. Prompt diagnosis and targeted antifungal treatment are essential to reduce morbidity and prevent complications. An infectious disease specialist’s opinion should be sought as early as possible, particularly when fungal osteomyelitis is suspected, for early diagnosis and treatment. Take Home Message In patients with a history of COVID‑19 and steroid use, a high index of suspicion for atypical pathogens in osteomyelitis should be considered. MRI is invaluable for detecting subtle patellar changes and guiding targeted diagnostic aspiration, thereby influencing therapeutic management. Written informed consent for publication was obtained from the patient’s relative.

title: Lentiform fork sign on CT: A rare imaging correlation
clinical_history: A 60-year-old female with a known history of chronic kidney disease, on monthly haemodialysis and type 2 diabetes mellitus, presented with confusion and lethargy for the past 2 days. There was no history of trauma, fever, or seizures. On examination, the patient was disoriented but exhibited no focal neurological deficits.
imaging_findings: Non-contrast CT (Figure 1) shows bilateral symmetric hypodensity in the lentiform nuclei, with surrounding more hypodense internal and external capsules forming the “lentiform fork sign”. There is a sub-centimetric-sized subcortical calcification in the right parietal lobe. MRI brain T2-weighted (Figure 2) shows bilateral symmetric hyperintensity in the thalamus, lentiform nuclei, particularly in the putamen and globus pallidus, with marked symmetrical hyperintensity of the internal, external capsules and internal and external medullary laminae. MRI FLAIR axial section (Figure 3) through the basal ganglia shows symmetric hyperintensity in the external capsule, internal capsule and internal and external medullary laminae on both sides. There is also hyperintensity in bilateral thalamus, putamen and globus pallidi.
discussion: The “lentiform fork sign” is a characteristic MRI feature of the basal ganglia, frequently observed in the setting of acute metabolic acidosis. It has been observed in several metabolic conditions such as uremic encephalopathy, diabetes mellitus, and intoxication from substances like menthol and ethylene glycol. This imaging sign is thought to arise due to the high metabolic demands of the basal ganglia, rendering them susceptible to hypoxic, toxic, and metabolic insults [1]. Uremic encephalopathy is a metabolic disorder that occurs due to the accumulation of neurotoxic substances in patients with inadequately managed acute or chronic kidney disease. Clinically, uremic encephalopathy can manifest with a wide range of symptoms, from mild cognitive deficits to deep coma. Although MRI is considered the gold standard for identifying uremic encephalopathy-related changes, especially in the basal ganglia, computed tomography (CT) may also detect characteristic abnormalities in more advanced stages. The lentiform fork sign is primarily thought to result from metabolic acidosis, which plays a central role in its pathogenesis [2], which leads to disruption of the blood-brain barrier. The distinctive imaging appearance is believed to result from varying metabolic susceptibilities between neurons of the basal ganglia and astrocytes in the surrounding white matter [3]. On T2-weighted and FLAIR MRI sequences, the white matter encircling the basal ganglia, including the internal and external capsules, appears hyperintense, forming the characteristic “fork” configuration. The hyperintense external capsule represents the fork’s prongs, while the internal capsule and adjacent internal and external laminae constitute the stem of the fork [4]. Identifying this imaging pattern is crucial even on CT scans, especially in resource-limited settings or when MRI is contraindicated. In the case of our patient, the detection of the lentiform fork sign on non-contrast CT prompted urgent initiation of dialysis, which was followed by clinical improvement. While traditionally described on MRI, this sign may also be appreciated on CT in advanced cases of uremic encephalopathy. Early recognition of this rare but significant radiologic finding can aid prompt diagnosis and management, particularly where MRI access is limited. Timely correction of metabolic acidosis through dialysis remains a cornerstone of treatment. Uremic encephalopathy has a good prognosis with early dialysis or transplantation, as symptoms are usually reversible. Delayed treatment can lead to severe complications or death. Prompt management is crucial. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: A rare case of antenatally diagnosed Goldston syndrome
clinical_history: A 24-year-old gravida 2 para 1 female presented for an obstetric anomaly scan, which showed a single live intrauterine pregnancy corresponding to 21 weeks of gestation. The patient has a previous history of abortion due to skeletal dysplasia 2 years ago. There was no history of consanguinity and no relevant positive family history of any neurological or renal disorders in any of the family members.
imaging_findings: Anomaly scan showed enlarged retrocerebellar space with aplastic vermis and bilateral dilated ventricles (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c). The maximum width of lateral ventricles was 12.9 mm and 10.7 mm on the right and left side, respectively. Bilateral kidneys were enlarged with multiple cysts and loss of corticomedullary differentiation, and the urinary bladder was not distended (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). In view of the central nervous system (CNS) abnormality characteristic of Dandy–Walker malformation (DWM) and the presence of cystic renal dysplasia, a provisional diagnosis of Goldston syndrome was made. Foetal MRI was advised for detailed assessment of the CNS and confirmation of the diagnosis. The foetal MRI showed enlarged retrocerebellar space with aplastic vermis and bilateral dilated ventricles; both kidneys were also found to be enlarged (Figures 3a and 3b). In view of these findings, the diagnosis of Goldston syndrome was confirmed. Following this, the patient chose to undergo medical termination of pregnancy. After termination, a foetal autopsy was performed, which confirmed the antenatal imaging findings (Figures 4a and 4b).
discussion: Background Goldston syndrome (GS) is an extremely rare congenital disorder which is characterised by the presence of Dandy–Walker malformation (DWM) and bilateral cystic renal dysplasia [1]. The first reported case of GS in intrauterine life was reported by Gloeb et al. [2]. It was diagnosed by ultrasound at the 17th week of gestation, and the authors suggested that GS might be considered a part of the spectrum of Meckel–Gruber syndrome [2]. The second reported case of GS in intrauterine life was at the 28th week of gestation, with DWM, cystic dysplastic kidneys, structural cerebellar anomalies and other associated anomalies, which included large fontanelle, low-set ears, hypertelorism and retrognathia [3]. DWM on antenatal scan should prompt a search for other extracranial malformations, particularly in genitourinary, cardiac and skeletal systems, to rule out syndromes like Goldston, Meckel–Gruber, and Miranda, which may be incompatible with life. There are some case reports which also reported the association of Goldston syndrome with hepatic fibrosis [4]. Imaging Perspective In our case, the ultrasound findings of an enlarged retrocerebellar space with vermian agenesis and bilateral multicystic kidneys pointed towards the probable diagnosis of GS. These findings are consistent with those reported by authors such as Gupta et al., who described similar prenatal imaging features in a foetus diagnosed with GS at 22 weeks of gestation [5]. MRI findings confirmed the absence of the cerebellar vermis and the presence of ventriculomegaly. MRI’s superior soft-tissue contrast enhances the visualisation of posterior fossa structures, thereby facilitating an accurate diagnosis [6]. Avcu S. reported similar findings in their case study, where foetal MRI confirmed the sonographic diagnosis of DWM associated with polycystic kidneys [7]. In this case, in addition to the usual findings of absence of the cerebellar vermis and the presence of ventriculomegaly, the foetus also had hydrocephalus. The differential diagnosis of GS includes other ciliopathies such as Meckel–Gruber syndrome [8] and Joubert syndrome [9], which also present with cerebellar and renal anomalies. However, in our case, there was no occipital encephalocele or polydactyly that helped us distinguish it from Meckel–Gruber syndrome. Outcome Prognosis in GS is often poor. It may be useful, in suspected cases, to perform an antenatal microarray sequencing, karyotyping and foetal MRI, and to involve a neonatal team to manage parental expectations of the poor predicted outcome. Survival beyond the postnatal period depends on the severity of the condition. A multidisciplinary approach, including palliative care, should be established early in the baby’s life [10]. Conclusion This case reinforces the importance of detailed prenatal imaging in diagnosing rare syndromic conditions like Goldston syndrome (GS). Further research into the genetic underpinnings of GS is necessary to enhance understanding and management of this rare entity.

title: Imaging evolution of a rare case of cystic pulmonary tuberculosis
clinical_history: A nine-year-old boy, previously healthy, presented with fever, cough, dyspnoea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Eighteen days after hospital admission, he had the first spontaneous bilateral pneumothorax, needing drainage, intensive care unit admission, and mechanical ventilation. After 3 months, even with remaining lung lesions and pneumothorax, he could be discharged for outpatient follow-up.
imaging_findings: The initial imaging exam was a chest radiograph (X-ray) showing a bilateral diffuse micronodular acinar infiltrate (Figures 1a and 1b). A computed tomography (CT) was performed, which revealed a diffuse micronodular pattern and random distribution throughout the lung parenchyma, suggestive of an inflammatory/infectious process (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). The patient experienced several pneumothoraces, all of which were drained. Up to three chest tubes were placed simultaneously (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, 3d, 3e, and 3f). A second contrast-enhanced chest CT revealed confluent cystic lesions, prevailing on the upper lobes and posterior regions (Figures 4a, 4b, 4c, 4d, 4e, and 4f). A few weeks later, another contrast-enhanced chest CT showed the same findings, but with larger pneumothoraces on both sides, despite the presence of three thoracic drains (Figures 5a, 5b, 5c, 5d, and 5e). Pneumomediastinum was noted. Before hospital discharge, the patient underwent a new contrast-enhanced chest CT. The lung abnormalities persisted, but the patient was able to tolerate them even after the chest tubes were removed (Figures 6a, 6b, and 6c). Eight months later, a follow-up chest CT revealed almost complete recovery of the pulmonary abnormalities, with sequelae changes and discreet cystic lesions, and with favourable evolution of the imaging findings over the eleven-month follow-up period (Figures 7a, 7b, and 7c).
discussion: Background Tuberculosis is a disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis . It is more prevalent in developing countries and mainly affects immunosuppressed patients. Nowadays, the vaccine against severe types of tuberculosis is part of the national vaccination program in some countries, decreasing its incidence [1]. Cystic pulmonary tuberculosis is a severe and extremely rare form of tuberculosis. There are only a few cases published. This condition is characterised by multiple lung cysts, predominating in the upper and middle lobes. Cysts tend to converge and can be associated with centrilobular nodules and reticular opacities, which have an infectious aetiology. This form of tuberculosis is classified as a cystic pulmonary disease, which can have other aetiologies, including malignant, lymphoproliferative, interstitial, congenital and infectious causes [2–8]. The pathophysiology is not established. The proposed hypotheses include: bronchiolar oedema and narrowing of the lumen, causing obstruction of the bronchioles, decreasing pulmonary drainage and leading to cysts formation; bronchiectasis due to bronchiolar wall involvement in granulomatous infection, containing caseous material, and leading to fibrosis and cysts formation; and the most accepted hypothesis, which is obstruction of the bronchiolar check valve associated with caseous necrosis, resulting in air leakage into the interstice, forming cysts [2–8]. Clinical Perspective The symptoms are similar to other pulmonary tuberculosis, presenting with a long clinical evolution and fever, dyspnoea, weight loss, night sweats, cough, and asthenia [2–8]. Imaging Perspective Chest radiograph is usually the first imaging exam, but findings are nonspecific, such as bilateral pulmonary infiltrate, nodules and consolidation. Initially, chest computed tomography (CT) may reveal interstitial nodules, tree-in-bud pattern, consolidation with lymph node enlargement, cavitation, bronchial parietal thickening and pleural effusion. As for cystic tuberculosis, chest CT shows cysts in the upper and middle zones, with centrilobular nodules and opacities around. The lesions are large, irregular and coalescent, leading to recurrent pneumothoraces [2,5,8]. Outcome Treatment is the same as for other forms of tuberculosis, with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. The duration of the treatment depends on the affected organs, and the prognosis is usually good [2]. When treatment is effective, and it is in most cases, the infection is healed, and the cystic lesions disappear, leaving only fibrosis. Some cases are irreversible, without pulmonary improvement and progress to bullous lung lesions. In those cases, mortality results from disease aggressiveness and delay in diagnosis [2,3,6]. Management In our case, after the initial chest imaging studies (radiography and CT), the differential diagnoses of miliary tuberculosis and pneumocystosis were considered. Accordingly, serological tests and the interferon gamma release assay (IGRA) were requested for diagnostic confirmation. IgM serologies for cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, and herpes virus were negative, as were tests for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis. During the investigation, the patient developed acute respiratory failure and altered level of consciousness, leading to his transfer to the intensive care unit, where he received non-invasive ventilatory support, antibiotic therapy with levofloxacin and amikacin, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sampling. Subsequently, the rapid test for Mycobacterium in the CSF was positive, as was the IGRA test, confirming the diagnoses of pulmonary tuberculosis and neurotuberculosis, despite negative acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smears from both sputum and tracheal aspirate. Antibiotics were discontinued, and treatment with prednisolone and a standard anti-tuberculosis regimen comprising rifampicin, isoniazid, and pyrazinamide was initiated (ethambutol was added 43 days later, when the patient reached 10 years of age), to be administered for two months. Upon completion of this intensive phase, treatment was continued with rifampicin and isoniazid for a further ten months. During the subsequent two-month hospital stay, the patient developed confluent pulmonary cystic lesions and multiple pneumothoraces, which required chest drainage and further worsened respiratory failure. At one point, he needed three simultaneous chest drains with continuous suction. Given this clinical scenario, Langerhans cell histiocytosis was suspected; however, the diagnosis was clinically ruled out. With treatment, the patient maintained adequate oxygen saturation on room air and was able to continue management at home, despite persistent pulmonary cystic lesions and pneumothorax. At the outpatient follow-up eight months later, the patient showed near-complete recovery of the pulmonary parenchyma and a marked improvement in overall clinical condition. Take Home Message Although tuberculosis is no longer prevalent in developed countries, it remains endemic in less-developed countries. Cystic pulmonary tuberculosis is a rare condition, and it is important to raise awareness of it, as treatment is effective and associated with a good prognosis and quality of life.
