title: Dancing megasperm: A rare sonographic sign
clinical_history: A 59-year-old man who had undergone a bilateral vasectomy 20 years earlier underwent a scrotal ultrasound due to mild right testicular discomfort. There was no history of trauma or associated symptoms, and no relevant physical examination or laboratory findings. He had no history of travel outside Europe.
imaging_findings: An ultrasound scan using a high-frequency linear transducer (Figures 1a, 1b, and 2) revealed multiple tiny hyperechoic foci within the left epididymal body, measuring less than 1 mm and exhibiting continuous oscillatory movement. The right epididymis had a homogeneous echotexture and normal, symmetric vascularisation using Doppler ultrasound. No abnormal findings were observed in the remaining scrotal ultrasound, including the right testicle and epididymis.
discussion: Multiple mobile, punctate, hyperechoic foci within the epididymis may be indicative of: Dancing megasperm : secondary to epididymal obstruction [1–2], mainly in patients with a history of vasectomy [1,3], where they are thought to represent clumps of agglutinated spermatozoa (“megasperm”) trapped within dilated ducts [1–3]. Filariasis dance sign : secondary to Wuchereria bancrofti infection (scrotal filariasis), where they may represent microfilariae or “filarial worm nests” within obstructed and dilated lymphatic channels [1,4–5]. The imaging findings are indistinguishable between them, highlighting the importance of the patient’s medical history in differentiating between these two conditions. It is particularly important to assess a history of prior vasectomy, travel to filarial-endemic areas or prior filarial infection. While scrotal filariasis requires treatment, dancing megasperm is an incidental sonographic finding which poses no clinical concern [5]. In dancing megasperm, the visualised mobility is likely caused by the phenomenon of acoustic streaming, whereby movement within a fluid is induced by high-intensity sound waves [1–2]. This sign is most often associated with a history of prior vasectomy, but it could also occur as a result of epididymal obstruction due to other causes, such as previous orchiepididymitis or scrotal surgery [1–3]. In a study searching for the dancing megasperm sign in patients undergoing a scrotal ultrasound, Frates et al. [3] found it in 0.3% of patients in the non-vasectomy group and 12% of patients in the vasectomy group. The time since vasectomy in the latter group ranged from 13 to 34 years. It is important to be aware of this sonographic sign and its possible causes, as well as its differential diagnoses, in order to avoid unnecessary investigations. In this clinical case, a diagnosis of dancing megasperm was made based on the patient’s history of vasectomy and the absence of laboratory findings or prior travel to a filarial-endemic area, and no further investigation was performed. The testicular discomfort was transitory and had resolved with analgesic therapy in the follow-up consultation.
differential_diagnosis: Scrotal filariasis Dancing megasperm Epididymitis

title: Segmental schwannomatosis of the brachial plexus
clinical_history: A 54-year-old man known to have hypertension and type 2 diabetes experienced paraesthesia in his left hand and distal part of his left forearm for several months. On examination, multiple well-defined skin nodules were found, globally distributed, along with reduced sensation distally in the left upper limb.
imaging_findings: MRI of the brachial plexus with intravenous contrast showed multiple well-marginated lesions with heterogeneous signal in the infraclavicular part of the left brachial plexus, including the trunks and divisions (Figures 1, 2a, 2b, and 3), extending into the axilla and proximal parts of the upper arm, suggestive of neurofibromas. MRI of the spine and brain showed no abnormalities, including vestibular schwannoma, and the patient was diagnosed with schwannomatosis.
discussion: Background Schwannomatosis is a rare, benign disorder characterised by widespread schwannomas that rarely affect the brachial plexus. To our knowledge, this is the first case reported in our country. Schwannomas are benign, slow-growing, and well-encapsulated tumours arising from the nerve sheaths of peripheral nerves [2]. Schwannomatosis most commonly presents between the ages of 30 and 60 [3]. The estimated incidence is about 1 in 70,000, with 80–85% of cases occurring sporadically [1]. Clinical Perspective The disease shares a phenotypic overlap with neurofibromatosis (NF) 2, in which patients also develop schwannomas, particularly affecting the vestibular nerve [4]. Typical symptoms include multiple painless, well-defined tumours with focal neurological deficits and pain secondary to nerve compression [2]. Diagnostic evaluation should include a thorough clinical examination, relevant imaging studies, histopathological analysis, and genetic testing. Differential diagnoses include neurofibromas, lipomas, lymphomas, lymph nodes or lymph node metastases, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours and ganglion cysts [2]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound, CT, MRI, and nerve conduction studies each have a role in diagnostic imaging of schwannomatosis; however, MRI is considered the most valuable modality [3]. On MRI, schwannomas typically appear hypointense or isointense on T1, hyperintense on T2 and STIR sequences, and show strong contrast enhancement [3]. Outcome In this case, genetic testing for five NF1-related genes showed normal results. Due to progressive symptoms, three nodules were surgically removed from around the left elbow. Pathological examination identified two schwannomas and one lipoma. A mutation analysis for NF-related disorders was performed on DNA from one of the resected schwannomas, which did not confirm an NF2 diagnosis. The goal of treatment for schwannomatosis is to preserve neurological function while managing symptoms [1]. Surgery should be considered for significant symptoms, clearly correlating to specific schwannomas. Some cases have suggested a beneficial effect of bevacizumab in patients with schwannomatosis [1]. Take Home Message While schwannomatosis involving the brachial plexus is rare, it should be considered as a differential diagnosis in patients presenting with relevant neurological symptoms.
differential_diagnosis: Neurofibromas Brachial plexus schwannomas Lymphoma Brachial plexopathy Metastases

title: Probable incidental osteolipoma of the tuber cinereum
clinical_history: A 55-year-old man, smoker, with a 1–2 month history of abdominal pain and cough. He was recently diagnosed with small cell lung cancer. The patient exhibited no neurological symptoms.
imaging_findings: A non-contrast and contrast-enhanced head CT was performed as a staging study. The CT scan revealed no signs suggestive of intracranial dissemination of the underlying disease. However, an incidental lesion was identified at the hypothalamic level, characterised by two distinct tissue densities: a predominantly calcified peripheral component, and a central fatty component with mean attenuation of -80 Hounsfield units (HU) (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d). Subsequently, a cranial MRI was performed that also did not show signs of intracranial dissemination. The suprasellar lesion observed on CT appeared as a well-defined hyperintense lesion on T1-weighted images with signal suppression on FLAIR sequences, indicating the presence of fat (Figures 2a and 2b). Additionally, there was prominent blooming on VEN BOLD, attributed to calcification (Figure 3). The lesion originated from the tuber cinereum and measured approximately 8 mm. No evidence of diffusion restriction (ADC/DWI) or contrast enhancement was observed (Figures 4a and 4b). A follow-up CT three months later demonstrated no changes (figures 5a and 5b). Based on the location and imaging characteristics, a diagnosis of osteolipoma of the tuber cinereum was established.
discussion: Background Osteolipomas of the tuber cinereum are very rare, benign and usually asymptomatic lesions discovered incidentally. They are traditionally considered a type of meningeal lipomas [1] located at the region of the tuber cinereum, from where they can project into the suprasellar or interpeduncular cisterns. Imaging Perspective The peculiar architectural arrangement of a central core of mature adipose tissue and a peripheral rim of bone helps to distinguish these lesions from other kinds of lipomas [2]. The coexistence of fat and bone within a lesion at the tuberculum sellae is characteristic, and can be seen on imaging, so the diagnosis can be established on a radiologic ground. On CT imaging, osteolipomas present as lesions with a combination of fat and calcified components. The central fatty component appears hypodense with attenuation values ranging from -50 to -100 HU, while the peripheral calcified component appears hyperdense. MRI further characterises these lesions. The fatty component is hyperintense on T1-weighted images and demonstrates signal suppression on fat-suppressed sequences, confirming the presence of mature fat. The calcified component appears hypodense on most sequences and exhibits blooming on T2*/SWI sequences. Typically, these lesions show minimal or no enhancement after contrast administration, aiding in their differentiation from other tumours. Outcome The clinical course is generally indolent, and these lesions can usually be managed conservatively without surgical intervention. Take Home Message Osteolipomas should be included in the radiologic differential diagnosis for hypothalamic masses that exhibit fat signal intensity and calcification [3]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
differential_diagnosis: Simple lipoma Osteolipoma of the tuber cinereum Teratoma Dermoid cysts Craniopharyngiomas

title: Ectopic gallbladder with empyema
clinical_history: An 82-year-old female patient presented with a history of right upper quadrant pain for 1 month, which got aggravated with fever for 5 days. She was referred from the department of general surgery with clinical suspicion of acute cholecystitis. No history of prior surgery. No other medical comorbidity. Laboratory blood tests revealed a raised total leucocyte count.
imaging_findings: On USG (ultrasound), a well-defined isoechoic collection measuring approximately 420 cc with a thick echogenic rim was noted in subcapsular location along segment VIII of the liver, showing posterior acoustic enhancement (Figure 1). The gallbladder could not be visualised. On CECT (contrast-enhanced computed tomography) abdomen, the gallbladder is not visualised in the gallbladder fossa and is seen located anterosuperiorly to the right lobe of the liver in the right subdiaphragmatic region (Figure 2a). It was overdistended with an oedematous wall showing heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement and minimal pericholecystic inflammatory changes in the form of pericholecystic fat stranding and minimal non-enhancing pericholecystic fluid collection. A tiny focus of air is noted in the gallbladder lumen (Figure 2b). No evidence of radiodense calculus or obvious breach of the gallbladder wall. A limited MRCP (magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography) study—the study was incomplete due to patient-related factors—revealed the cystic duct in communication with the ectopic gallbladder (Figures 3a and 3b).
discussion: Background The gallbladder’s migration arrest results in an uncommon congenital variant called ectopic gallbladder, where it is situated distant from its normal anatomical location. Commonly involved ectopic locations include regions below the left lobe of the liver, intrahepatic and retroperitoneum [1]. The liver parenchyma can be seen encasing the gallbladder in the case of an intrahepatic gallbladder [2]. Clinical Perspective The patient presented with clinical features of right upper quadrant pain with fever and raised total leukocyte count, and was clinically suspected to be a case of acute cholecystitis. Imaging Perspective A provisional diagnosis of liver abscess was made on ultrasound, but the CECT abdomen was helpful in better characterising the lesion and in precisely providing the anatomical location of the ectopic gallbladder. The CT was also superior in detecting the presence of air foci within the gallbladder. A limited MRCP study was helpful in establishing the communication of the cystic duct with the ectopic gallbladder. Therefore, it is critical to understand that the likelihood of an ectopic position must be taken into account when the gallbladder is not visible in its typical location [3]. Significant difficulties can arise from ectopic gallbladders, such as a higher chance of co-existing cholelithiasis [4] because of biliary stasis, the possibility of twisting if the gallbladder is hanging on a mesentery, or even herniation via the foramen of Winslow. Outcome Our patient underwent open abdominal surgery, and it was confirmed that the cystic lesion was indeed an ectopic gallbladder. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Appropriate surgical planning and pre-operative imaging evaluation are crucial. Technical difficulties may arise during cholecystectomy or any other biliary procedure when the gallbladder is in an aberrant location. With insufficient clinical history, it could be mistaken for gallbladder agenesis or post-cholecystectomy condition [5]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Disseminated peritoneal leiomyomatosis in a hysterectomised patient
clinical_history: A 38-year-old woman with a history of multiple surgeries for recurrent uterine leiomyomas, including hysterectomy and left adnexectomy, underwent pelvic ultrasound, which revealed a pelvic mass. Further evaluation with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed. Tumour markers, including CEA, CA125, and CA19-9, were within normal limits.
imaging_findings: MRI showed a well-circumscribed solid mass that appeared mildly hypointense on T2-weighted imaging (T2WI) (Figure 1a) and iso to hypointense on T1-weighted imaging (T1WI) (Figures 1c and 2a), demonstrating intense and heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement (Figure 2b). Smaller nodules were seen posterior to the primary mass, along the anterior abdominal wall, and near the bladder dome, corresponding to the expected location of the urachal insertion (Figures 1b, 1c, 2b, 2c, and 3). They were more T2-hypointense and enhanced homogeneously. The primary lesion closely abutted the right ovary and moulded the adjacent external iliac vein, which remained patent. No evidence of restricted diffusion was observed. There were no signs of ascites or peritoneal thickening. Considering the imaging features and the patient’s fibroid history, disseminated peritoneal leiomyomatosis was deemed most likely.
discussion: Background Disseminated peritoneal leiomyomatosis (DPL) is a rare benign condition characterised by the presence of multiple leiomyomatous nodules scattered throughout the peritoneal cavity, often mimicking peritoneal carcinomatosis. It predominantly affects women of reproductive age. Although the exact pathogenesis remains unclear, two main theories have been proposed. The iatrogenic theory suggests that surgical procedures—particularly those involving morcellation—may lead to the peritoneal dissemination of leiomyoma cells [1]. Alternatively, the hormonal theory posits that hormonal stimulation may induce metaplastic transformation of submesothelial stem cells into smooth muscle cells [1]. Clinical Perspective Most DPL cases are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally. When symptoms are present, they are usually nonspecific and may include abdominal discomfort, bloating, or manifestations related to mass effect. Clinical diagnosis can be challenging, especially in individuals with a history of uterine leiomyomas or prior hysterectomy, as the presentation may mimic malignant peritoneal disease or metastatic implants [1]. Imaging Perspective MRI is the preferred modality for characterising lesions in DPL. DPL nodules typically appear iso to hypointense on T1-weighted images and demonstrate variable signal intensity on T2-weighted sequences, often with low signal due to their fibrous composition. Post-contrast imaging usually reveals enhancement. In this case, both the primary mass and associated nodules exhibited classic imaging characteristics of leiomyomatous tissue. In our case, their distribution and morphology—particularly in the setting of leiomyoma recurrence following hysterectomy (Figure 3)—were highly suggestive of DPL. Diagnostic evaluation of DPL may involve ultrasound, CT, MRI, and histopathological analysis. Although histopathological confirmation was not obtained in this case, the diagnosis of DPL was considered highly probable based on characteristic imaging features, long-term lesion stability, the patient's clinical history, and the absence of laboratory or radiological signs indicative of malignancy. A follow-up computed tomography (CT) scan (Figures 4a and 4b) performed two years later showed no change in the size or appearance of the lesions, reinforcing the presumptive diagnosis. Outcome DPL is a benign condition with a low risk of malignant transformation. Management strategies depend on symptom severity, lesion burden, and fertility considerations, and may include hormonal therapy, surgical debulking, or expectant observation. Imaging is essential not only for establishing the diagnosis but also for distinguishing DPL from peritoneal carcinomatosis or metastatic disease, thereby helping to prevent unnecessary invasive interventions. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Disseminated peritoneal leiomyomatosis (DPL) should be considered in women with a history of recurrent uterine leiomyomas, particularly following surgical intervention, when imaging reveals multiple peritoneal nodules demonstrating low T2 signal intensity and post-contrast enhancement. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Mandibular manifestation of infantile cortical hyperostosis (Caffey disease)
clinical_history: A 6-month-old infant presented with a history of on-and-off soft tissue swelling over the left cheek since 2 months (Figure 1). No history of trauma. Full-term normal delivery.
imaging_findings: Head and neck CT with bone reconstruction showed cortical irregularity with sclerosis, solid periosteal reaction, increase in cortical width and density, seen along the angle and ramus of the left hemimandible (Figures 2a and 2b). On MRI, the corresponding area showed mild STIR hyperintensity (Figure 3) and T1 hypointensity (Figure 4). No evidence of any significant diffusion restriction was seen in this region (Figures 5a and 5b). Surrounding oedematous changes were seen in the left masticator muscles and infratemporal fossa. No focal discrete collection or solid component was seen.
discussion: Background Infantile cortical hyperostosis, or Caffey disease, is a rare, self-limiting disease presenting with clinical features of fever, irritability, and on-and-off soft tissue swelling. This disease has two forms: the mild infantile form and the severe prenatal form. It can have both sporadic and familial transmission with autosomal dominant and recessive patterns. A mutation in the COL1A1 gene (type 1 collagen) is associated with Caffey disease; there is no sex or racial predilection [1,2]. Imaging Perspective On imaging, Caffey disease is characterised by subperiosteal reaction and new bone formation involving the diaphysis of the long bones and mandible. The disease most commonly affects flat bones like the mandible (70–80%) and clavicles. Among the long bones, the ulnae are most commonly affected. On radiograph, subperiosteal cortical hyperostosis under the region of soft tissue swelling is seen in Caffey disease. Radiograph is not the diagnostic imaging because it is important to rule out other imaging differentials [3]. CT findings include cortical hyperostosis and the presence of radiolucent areas within the bone. MRI shows periostitis and soft tissue oedema. MRI gives detailed information about the soft-tissue reactions and marrow oedema, appearing T2 and STIR hyperintense, and T1 hypointense. MRI helps to differentiate infantile cortical hyperostosis from osteomyelitis, which presents with lytic areas of bone destruction, irregular or interrupted periosteal reaction and soft tissue abscess in some cases. MRI also helps in differentiating Caffey disease from bone tumours such as Ewing sarcoma, which is an important differential diagnosis of Caffey disease [4]. Outcome As noted above, Caffey disease is self-limiting and resolves spontaneously. Symptomatic treatment consists of NSAIDs. Late complications include mandibular asymmetry and undergrowth, as well as disease recurrence in childhood. Take Home Message A high index of suspicion and awareness of the existence of this condition is necessary, and it is important to differentiate it from other differentials like osteomyelitis. A detailed history, clinical examination, basic laboratory studies and radiograph are sufficient enough to make a diagnosis in most cases, and MRI can help to exclude the important differential diagnoses.

title: Oesophageal-vulvar syndrome: A rare syndromic association of dual-site leiomyomatosis
clinical_history: A 22-year-old female presented with dysphagia for 9 years and gradually increasing vulval swelling for 5 years. Clinical examination revealed a firm, non-tender, lobulated mass (~8x8 cm) involving bilateral labia with intact overlying skin. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a bulge in the mid and lower oesophagus with intact mucosa and luminal narrowing.
imaging_findings: MRI thorax showed a long segment bulky circumferential wall thickening of the lower thoracic oesophagus extending till the gastric cardia (Figure 1c), with T1 isointense (Figure 1a) and T2 mildly hyperintense appearance (Figure 1b) compared to the skeletal muscle. It shows mild homogeneous enhancement without necrotic areas (Figure 1d), a very smooth outline and a clear plane with the aorta, cardia and thoracic spine. MRI pelvis showed a large, lobulated, well-circumscribed mass (~9x7 cm) involving the clitoral region and bilateral labia majora. It appears T1 isointense (Figure 2b) and T2 hyperintense compared to that of skeletal muscle (Figures 2a and 2d), it shows diffusion restriction (Figures 2e and 2f) and a marked homogeneous contrast enhancement (Figure 2c). The mass was seen overhanging the urethral orifice and vaginal introitus without causing urinary outflow obstruction. Non-contrast PET-CT showed FDG-avid soft tissue lesions corresponding to the oesophageal wall thickening (SUV max = 9.2) (Figures 1e and 1f) and vulval mass (SUV max = 9.8) (Figures 2g and 2h). There were no calcifications, intralesional fat, or cystic areas within the lesions.
discussion: Background Although encapsulated oesophageal leiomyomas are common, its diffuse counterpart, i.e., diffuse oesophageal leiomyomatosis, is a rare hamartomatous disorder characterised by proliferation of oesophageal smooth muscle cells. It can occur in isolation or in association with visceral leiomyomatosis [1]. Pelvic leiomyomas are benign smooth muscle tumours that can rarely be found in extrauterine locations. Vulval leiomyomas are believed to originate from smooth muscle cells of the round ligament, erectile tissue, or vessel walls [2,3]. Coexistence of oesophageal leiomyomatosis with genital or vulvar leiomyoma is termed oesophageal-vulvar syndrome [4,5]. This rare syndrome affects young females, with only 14 cases documented in the literature. First described in 1953 by Whalen and Astedt, it was reported in a mother and daughter [4,6], suggesting a possible hereditary component. This syndrome has also been associated with X-linked Alport syndrome in about 5% of cases [6]. Clinical Perspective Hypertrophied oesophageal smooth muscle in diffuse oesophageal leiomyomatosis can encroach into the oesophageal lumen, causing dysphagia. It can mimic oesophageal neuromotor disorders until cross-sectional imaging demonstrates the hypertrophied oesophageal wall [1]. Vulval leiomyoma presents as a slow-growing, painless, firm vulval mass, and can be mistaken for Bartholin’s cyst during clinical examination; imaging can help differentiate between these two solid vs cystic conditions [7]. The co-existence of both lesions poses diagnostic challenges. Imaging Perspective Barium swallow in oesophageal leiomyomatosis may demonstrate the level of oesophageal obstruction and can mimic other oesophageal motility disorders [1] as opposed to its localised counterpart—oesophageal leiomyoma—which is seen a focal filling defect projecting into the luminal contrast column, showing slightly obtuse angle with the adjacent oesophageal wall and overlying smooth mucosal surface. Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI demonstrate diffusely thickened and homogeneously enhancing oesophageal wall without encasement of adjacent structures or lymphadenopathy [1]. MRI is the investigation of choice for the evaluation of pelvic soft tissue masses. Vulval leiomyomas appear as well-circumscribed lesions with T1 and T2 signal intensities reflecting the smooth muscle composition, and show variable degrees of post-contrast enhancement [3]. MRI helps in accurate delineation of surrounding structures and thereby helps in surgical planning and vulval reconstruction. Leiomyomas usually demonstrate low or absent FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) uptake on PET-CT. However, larger lesions may exhibit variable uptake that can mimic aggressive malignancies, limiting the diagnostic utility of PET-CT in such cases [8]. FDG PET-CT findings, specifically in the diffuse form—leiomyomatosis—have not been documented in the literature. Outcome Our patient underwent oesophagogastrectomy and complete excision of the vulval mass with vulval reconstruction. Histopathological examination of the resected specimens and immunohistochemistry (IHC) confirmed spindle cell neoplasm of the oesophagus (leiomyomatosis in view of the diffuse circumferential morphology) and vulval leiomyoma. Post-operative recovery was uneventful, and the patient remains under surveillance with no complaints after 1 year. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Diffuse oesophageal leiomyomatosis and vulval leiomyoma are uncommon benign lesions of mesenchymal smooth muscle origin and can rarely present together in the same patient, when they are termed oesophageal-vulvar syndrome. MRI provides diagnostic clues, hinting at a benign nature and helps in surgical planning. Histopathology confirms the diagnosis. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Spinal epidural abscess
clinical_history: A 42-year-old male presented to the emergency department with weakness and paraesthesia in the lower limbs, back pain, and fever. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed an increased white blood cell count (predominantly polymorphonuclear) and protein. He had a history of gonococcal urethritis and syphilis and a recent influenza B respiratory infection.
imaging_findings: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows a longitudinally extensive posterior extradural extramedullary collection from T2 to T9 of heterogeneous appearance with isointense and hyperintense areas in T1-weighted sequence (Figure 1) and high signal intensity on T2-weighted and STIR sequences (Figure 2). It causes a compressive effect on the spinal cord with anterior thecal sac displacement (Figure 3). There is increased STIR and T2 cord signal in the compressed segment, suggestive of compressive myelopathy (Figure 2). The contrast-enhanced T1-weighted sequence shows diffuse meningeal spinal enhancement (Figures 4, 5a and 5b). The magnetic field strength of the MRI scanner used was 3T.
discussion: Background Spinal epidural abscess is a rare entity with high morbidity. Incidence is increasing due to the growing number of susceptible populations [1]. The main associated risk factors are immunosuppression, intravenous drug use or spinal procedures [1,2]. Extradural spinal infections are caused by bacterial or fungal pathogens. Staphylococcus aureus is the most commonly responsible organism, causing about half of infections [3]. Pathogens reach the epidural space through three mechanisms: haematogenous spread from a distant source, direct invasion, or spinal surgical procedures [1–3]. Clinical Perspective Spinal epidural abscess has a non-specific clinical presentation that makes it difficult to diagnose. The classic symptoms are spine back pain, fever and neurological focality. However, this triad is present in only 10–30% of cases [1,2]. Abnormal laboratory results, such as elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, are common but nonspecific [3]. Imaging Perspective MRI is the modality of choice due to its high sensitivity and specificity [3]. Differentiating epidural from intradural lesions can be difficult. Epidural lesions cause effacement of the epidural fat, displacement of the dura, and compression of the spinal cord [3,5]. Epidural abscesses present a hypointense signal on T1 and a hyperintense signal on T2 and STIR. Intramedullary hyperintense T2 signal of the compressed segment indicates probable acute spinal oedema and ischemia. Post-contrast T1-weighted images allow assessment of the stage of infection: the phlegmonous stage shows homogeneous enhancement, whereas the mature abscess has a non-enhancing core surrounded by a rim enhancement. Extensive abscesses may show diffuse dural enhancement. Diffusion-weighted imaging is useful for characterising spinal collections, as abscesses typically show restricted diffusion. CT has a limited role, mainly used to assess bone involvement and for preoperative planning [3–6]. The differential diagnosis includes epidural haematoma, postoperative seroma, or disc herniation, which typically show minimal or no contrast enhancement and do not show restricted diffusion. Spinal metastases may show irregular enhancement and tissue invasion. Clinical presentation is essential to guide an accurate diagnosis [5,6]. Outcome Immediate treatment is necessary due to high morbidity and mortality. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics are recommended. Patients with neurological deficits should undergo immediate surgical decompression. Non-surgical treatment may be considered in patients without neurological symptoms or with multiple comorbidities [1–3,5]. The patient in our case underwent emergency drainage of the collection. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus was the microorganism responsible for the infection. Take Home Message Spinal epidural abscess is a difficult entity to diagnose and requires a multidisciplinary evaluation. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential to reduce morbidity and mortality. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Genetically proven primary ciliary dyskinesia
clinical_history: A 14-year-old boy presented with a chronic history of rhinosinusitis and productive cough for years. There were no associated symptoms of haemoptysis, fever, or weight loss. On examination, he had mild basal crepitations. Otherwise, no dysmorphic features or dextrocardia. No palpable organomegaly or lymphadenopathy. History of paternal aunt infertility was reported.
imaging_findings: Initial chest radiograph showed mild right lower zone faint opacification with no dextrocardia (Figure 1). The high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) revealed mild bilateral lower lobe predominant bronchiectasis with bronchial wall thickening and mucoid impaction as well as centrilobular nodules (Figures 2a and 2b). The rest of the lung parenchyma was well aerated. No situs inversus or dextrocardia was seen. No mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Paranasal sinuses (PNS) CT revealed near complete opacification of the paranasal sinuses with frothy secretions as well as associated pharyngitis and left-sided otomastoiditis (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is a rare autosomal recessive disease, causing dysfunction of the motile cilia. This, in turn, leads to multi-system involvement primarily affecting the respiratory system, paranasal sinuses and reproductive organs [1]. Modern gene sequencing has led to a rise in diagnoses, with an estimated prevalence of 1:7500 people affected [2]. Clinical Perspective The most characteristic clinical manifestation of PCD is a productive (wet) cough, which develops in infancy and gradually progresses into adulthood. Other features include the development of rhinosinusitis as well as fertility issues. Laterality is present in 50% of cases, including situs inversus totalis or dextrocardia [1]. Imaging Perspective On HRCT, the development of bronchiectasis with upper lobe sparing is the hallmark feature [1]. Other imaging findings include bronchial wall thickening with mucoid impaction and centrilobular nodules [3]. It is important to exclude the presence or absence of laterality, as it can be seen in 50% of cases and is associated with Kartagener’s syndrome [1,3]. Another associated entity is Young’s syndrome, which represents a triad of rhinosinusitis, azoospermia leading to reduced fertility, and bronchiectasis [4]. The absence of laterality can delay recognition, as seen in our case. Thus, raising the possibility of the diagnosis based on the imaging findings is crucial to prompt further evaluation and ensure early diagnosis. The current diagnostic algorithms include initial assessment by measurement of nasal nitric oxide. Further evaluation includes high-speed video microscopy of nasal mucosal brushing or transmission electron microscopy. Genetic testing, if available, is performed to confirm the diagnosis, which is being increasingly adopted in clinical practice [2]. Outcome and Management Our patient underwent whole exome sequencing (WES), revealing a pathological DNAH5 gene (Figure 4), which is the most commonly implicated gene [1]. Management is usually targeted for symptomatic relief with improvement of mucociliary clearance and early intervention of airway infections [2]. Early recognition with a low threshold for clinical suspicion in conjunction with the CT findings, even in the absence of laterality, plays a pivotal role in early recognition and timely diagnosis and management. title: T1 bright spots – A case of neurocutaneous melanosis
clinical_history: A 2-day-old female neonate born through normal vaginal delivery to non-consanguineous marriage was found to have dark pigmentation in the groin, perineum, lower back, upper and lower extremities, including hands, with hair growth in these areas (Figure 1). No other abnormalities on clinical examination and blood workup. This finding raised suspicion of phacomatosis, prompting a brain MRI to assess for neuroparenchymal abnormalities.
imaging_findings: Multifocal punctate T1 hyperintense foci scattered in bilateral cerebral cortices, left amygdala and left cerebellar hemisphere (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). These did not show restricted diffusion or blooming on SWI. No signal changes were seen on T2 (Figure 3). No leptomeningeal T1 hyperintensities were seen. Post-contrast images showed no leptomeningeal or neuroparenchymal enhancement.
discussion: Background Congenital cutaneous melanocytic naevi and central nervous system (CNS) melanocytic lesions are hallmarks of neurocutaneous melanosis (NCM), a rare non-inheritable phacomatosis [1]. It is a neurocristopathy caused by aberrant migration of damaged neural crest cells affecting both the skin and the central nervous system, which are ectoderm descendants [2]. CNS lesions can be leptomeningeal or parenchymal. It was described in 1861 by Rokitansky [3]. Clinical Perspective Characteristic cutaneous findings raise clinical suspicion of phacomatosis, and MRI is crucial to determine central nervous system involvement. Usually, these patients present at the hospital following a seizure or headaches related to hydrocephalus. Neurological symptoms usually manifest before the age of 1 and are usually variable depending on the location of involvement. Usual presentations include seizures, hydrocephalus, weakness, aphasia, etc. Hydrocephalus can be related to Dandy–Walker malformation, which has a close association with NCM. Another reason is cerebrospinal fluid flow obstruction caused by these lesions. The occurrence of haemorrhages secondary to intraparenchymal lesions has been reported [4]. Spinal cord involvement could cause weakness, paraesthesia, bowel or bladder incontinence [5]. Later, these patients are prone to develop mental disturbances at puberty [6]. Imaging Perspective The role of CT remains limited, except for acute presentation or in the absence of MRI. Otherwise, MRI remains the first choice. On CT, hydrocephalus or posterior fossa malformations may be seen. MRI remains the investigation of choice, with intraparenchymal lesions appearing hyperintense on T1. They may not be apparent on T2. Variable diffusion and susceptibility characteristics, as in cases of haemorrhage, can be confounding. Associated posterior fossa malformations like vermian hypoplasia, Dandy–Walker malformations, etc., can also be identified on conventional sequences. Post-gadolinium sequences help in identifying meningeal involvement, seen as leptomeningeal enhancement. Outcome The prognosis of NCM is grim, with the majority of symptomatic patients dying within 3 years of initial presentation, from overgrowth of benign melanocytic cells or malignant transformation [1]. NCM associated with large bathing trunk naevi or Dandy–Walker malformations are reported to have a higher rate of malignant transformation, with the risk estimated at approximately 2.5% to 5% and is highest during the first 5 to 10 years of life [7]. Management remains symptomatic, with few recommending removing the cutaneous lesions to circumvent malignant transformation, which has an incidence of 5–15% [1]. There have also been reports of the incidence of malignant melanoma in these patients who undergo immunosuppressive therapy [8]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points MRI of the neuraxis is a must to look for CNS involvement and predict prognosis. T1 bright lesions in the brain? Think of melanin, especially in locations not typical for ischaemia or haemorrhage. These patients require regular follow-up to look for malignant transformation. However, there are no established clear guidelines for this due to the rarity of this condition. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Clawed life – A case of familial split hand/foot malformation
clinical_history: A 2-year-old male child was brought by his 34-year-old mother with complaints of abdominal pain and recurrent vomiting. The child was clinically stable, and the abdominal ultrasound was normal. However, we incidentally discovered that both the mother and the son had physical impairments in their bilateral upper and lower limbs.
imaging_findings: The child had a classical median cleft with rudimentary bilateral thumbs with loss of opposition movement (Figure 1). A frontal radiograph revealed a bilateral median cleft, and the right hand’s proximal phalanges of the middle and index fingers fused, resulting in syndactyly. An additional middle phalanx was observed in the right thumb. Bilaterally, the thumb and index finger were displaced toward each other (Figures 2a and 2b). The radiography of the child’s feet depicted the absence of three of his metatarsals (Figure 2c). The X-ray of the infant’s skull showed multiple convolutions, suggesting a copper-beaten appearance (Figure 3). Interestingly, his 34-year-old mother, too, suffered from a similar deformity. On clinical inspection, both her right and left hands showed the presence of only three fingers (Figure 4a). A hypoplastic index finger was seen in the left hand. Bilateral feet showed only two toes with possible syndactyly (Figure 4b).
discussion: Background Split hand/split foot malformation (SHFM), also described as lobster-claw deformity, is a congenital limb deformity most commonly affecting the median rays of the hand and foot. Both sporadic (non-familial) and familial cases have been previously documented [1]. The disorder manifests as various phenotypes, ranging from a slight shortening of the third digit to its total absence, as well as bidactyly, monodactyly, and syndactyly [2]. The patient may have hypoplasia and/or a total lack of the phalanges, metacarpals, and metatarsals [3]. Every 1 in 90,000 people is thought to be affected by split hands and feet deformity [4]. Clinical Perspective A developing limb bud consists of two layers of cells: highly proliferating central mesenchymal cells surrounded by a layer of ectodermal cells. The limb bud development is initiated by the signalling molecules that specialised cell groups produce: the apical ectodermal ridge (AER), the progress zone (PZ), and the zone of polarising activity (ZPA) [5]. The interplay between these three cell groups regulates the pattern of limb development in three dimensions: anteroposterior, proximodistal, and dorsoventral [5]. The failure to maintain the AER leads to the development of SHFM. Apart from genetic factors, environmental factors like apoptosis in the AER can also lead to SHFM [5]. The literature mentions six types of basic SHFM, ranging from SHFM1 to SHFM6, and one additional SHFM/SHFLD (split hand/split foot malformation and long-bone deficiency) type [5]. The final confirmation can be given by the genetic makeup of the patient. The likely SHFM type in this case can be SHFM1 (7q21) or SHFM3 (10q24), both typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. This can be supported by bilateral, symmetric limb involvement in both mother and child, isolated limb deformities without syndromic features, and the absence of long bone abnormalities. As we were unable to perform the genetic testing on the patient, we were unable to classify the condition definitively [5]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasonography can be used to diagnose SHFM antenatally [6]. Antenatal diagnosis in the first trimester with amniocentesis can detect the anomaly, preventing this outcome. Outcome Regarding the cleft hand, Adrian Flatt remarked, “A functional triumph but a social disaster” [2]. There have been very few reported cases of surgical intervention in such patients. The primary aim of the surgery in SFHM is to improve the unsettling appearance. Post-surgery, one ray might still be missing, but with good closure of the cleft and the achievement of parallelism of the long fingers, the physical appearance of the hand can be improved. All things considered, the course of treatment may be lengthy and does not guarantee complete limb function. Genetic counselling for parents before planning a pregnancy is one of the most effective ways to diagnose and prevent SHFM. Counselling may be recommended for affected persons, including lifestyle management, physiotherapy sessions, and occupational therapy for improving motor skills and range of motion. Take Home Message Median cleft hand or split hand foot malformation is a complex, rare malformation that needs multidisciplinary management. Prosthetics used with reconstructive surgery can enhance prognosis and improve quality of life.

title: IgG4-related breast disease
clinical_history: A 74-year-old woman presented for a breast ultrasound, clinically indicated due to the presence of a solitary, mildly palpable nodular area near the scar of a previous breast resection performed several years earlier for a benign condition (intraductal papilloma). She denied any relevant associated symptoms.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound examination revealed, in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, a superficial hypoechoic lesion measuring approximately 20 mm in diameter, with well-defined, lobulated margins (Figure 1a) and minimal internal vascularity on colour Doppler (Figure 1b), located adjacent to the previous surgical scar. No other significant or suspicious findings were noted in either breast. Bilateral axillary lymph nodes appeared mildly hyperplastic, but with preserved echo structure. In view of the imaging findings and clinical context, an ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy of the lesion was performed. Histological analysis of the breast tissue revealed extensive stromal fibrosis with a nodular infiltrate of small B and T lymphocytes and a moderate number of CD138-positive plasma cells, which showed polyclonal expression for kappa and lambda light chains. Eosinophilic granulocytes were also present. Immunohistochemistry showed over 50 IgG4-positive plasma cells per high-power field (HPF) in multiple fields, raising suspicion for IgG4-related disease, especially when considered together with clinical and laboratory findings. No carcinoma was found, and the lesion was classified as B2 (benign). The patient underwent ultrasound (Figures 2a and 2b) and mammographic (Figures 3a and 3b) follow-up at 6 months, which confirmed the presence of the vascularised hypoechoic lesion with well-defined, lobulated margins. She was subsequently referred for a specialised rheumatologic consultation.
discussion: Background IgG4-related breast disease (IgG4-BD), also known as IgG4-related sclerosing mastitis, is a rare and under-recognised form of IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD), a multisystemic immune-mediated condition [1]. It was first characterised in 2003 [2]. Breast involvement is extremely uncommon, with only 48 cases reported in the literature to date [3]. Clinical Perspective Clinically, IgG4-BD often presents incidentally and mimics malignancy in the guise of painless, solitary masses, often discovered on routine imaging [4]. Systemic symptoms are unusual. Features like axillary lymphadenopathy or nipple retraction have been reported but are uncommon. Concomitant involvement of classically affected IgG4-RD organs (i.e., pancreas, salivary or lacrimal glands) does not occur in all cases, therefore making isolated IgG4-BD challenging to diagnose [3]. Imaging Perspective Imaging with mammography, ultrasound and MRI often show ill-defined, non-calcified lesions, with specific features which are suspicious for malignancy. PET-FDG (Positron emission tomography – fluorodeoxyglucose) imaging, when available, may show uptake in involved regions [3]. Histopathology is the gold standard for diagnosing IgG4-BD, typically revealing dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, numerous IgG4-positive plasma cells, and high IgG4 + IgG + cell ratios [4,5]. However, typical IgG4-RD features—storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis—are often absent in breast cases, suggesting a need to adapt current diagnostic criteria for this specific manifestation. Additionally, while serum IgG4 levels are often elevated, they may be normal and must be interpreted together within the overall clinical picture [3]. Outcome Treatment for IgG4-BD is not standardised, but current guidelines recommend treating both symptomatic and asymptomatic patients. Corticosteroids are the first-line therapy, showing excellent response and low relapse rates. Rituximab and other immunomodulators appear promising but are not yet widely used [6]. Conclusion In conclusion, IgG4-related breast disease (IgG4-BD) is a rare but important differential diagnosis for suspicious breast lumps that mimic malignancy but are benign on biopsy. Greater awareness among clinicians and pathologists is crucial to prevent misdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment. Future diagnostic criteria for IgG4-related disease should consider organ-specific histological differences, especially for breast, to enhance diagnostic accuracy and management. Take Home Message IgG4-related breast disease is a rare, benign condition that can closely mimic breast malignancy on imaging. Accurate diagnosis relies on histopathological evaluation and awareness of this under-recognised entity to avoid unnecessary surgical intervention and guide appropriate therapy. title: Oesophagogastric anastomotic leak
clinical_history: A 77-year-old man with gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma undergoes a McKeown oesophagectomy. No fluoroscopy was performed after surgery as a baseline examination. Seven days after the surgery, he presents with a fever and an increase in inflammatory markers, and undergoes a CT scan.
imaging_findings: Non-enhanced CT reconstruction demonstrates the cervical oesophagogastric anastomosis, associated with hyperdense material consistent with surgical material, with an air-fluid level collection observed in the right upper paramediastinal region adjacent to the surgical material (Figure 1). Images acquired following the oral administration of a diluted, non-ionic contrast agent demonstrate contrast medium extravasation (Figures 2 and 3), which is consistent with a cervical oesophagogastric anastomotic leak. Additionally, there is a perianastomotic collection (Figures 4 and 5).
discussion: Background Surgical management of oesophageal and oesophagogastric junction tumours depends on tumour characteristics, lymphadenectomy extent, conduit choice, patient status, and surgeon’s preference [1]. The stomach is the preferred conduit, though the colon or jejunum may be used [1]. The McKeown oesophagectomy employs three incisions, combining transhiatal and transthoracic approaches for total transthoracic resection with thoracic lymphadenectomy and cervical anastomosis. Pulmonary complications are the most common postoperative issues [2], while anastomotic leaks—occurring in up to 44%—pose the greatest risk, contributing to 40% of postoperative mortality [3]. Risk factors include conduit ischaemia, neoadjuvant therapy, and comorbidities [4]. Cervical anastomoses are more leak-prone due to increased conduit length and tension [1], though confined neck anatomy limits contamination and morbidity [5]. Clinical Perspective Oesophageal anastomotic leaks usually occur within 10 days [1] and may present with fever, tachycardia, and local or systemic signs of infection. Complications include mediastinal abscesses, mediastinitis, respiratory failure and potentially multi-organ failure [6]. Imaging Perspective A contrast oesophagogram may diagnose anastomotic leaks, but has a 57% false-negative rate, especially with cervical anastomosis [7]. CT with diluted water-soluble oral contrast is the preferred imaging modality [8]. Dilution varies with contrast concentration [8]. At our hospital, we use iomeprol 350 mg iodine/mL diluted at a 1:3 contrast-to-water ratio. A pre-contrast scan improves detection of surgical materials. Oral contrast should be ingested immediately before acquisition. Contrast leakage and mediastinal gas are highly specific for leaks [8]. Assessment without oral contrast may be limited by postoperative mediastinal air and fat stranding [9]. If doubtful, fluoroscopy with undiluted water-soluble contrast or endoscopy can be performed [7, 8]. Differential diagnosis includes abscesses—gas-containing collections near the anastomosis. A defect near surgical material confirms a leak. Haematomas appear hyperdense without contrast extravasation or defect. Outcome Cervical leaks are managed by draining the neck wound and performing dressings [10]. Endoscopic stenting may be considered. Thoracic leaks often require re-exploration [11]. All patients require haemodynamic monitoring and adequate drainage. A nasogastric tube may prevent further contamination. Endoscopy assesses conduit viability. Prompt systemic antibiotics are essential if a leak is suspected [12]. Our patient was managed conservatively with intravenous antibiotics and endoscopic sponge placement, which was later removed. Take Home Message Anastomotic leak following oesophagectomy is a critical complication that radiologists must be aware of. CT with water-soluble oral contrast is the most reliable imaging modality for its detection.

title: The hidden kidney: Thoracic ectopic kidney through a diaphragmatic defect
clinical_history: A 46-year-old male with systemic hypertension presented with prolonged upper abdominal discomfort and dyspepsia. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including renal function and electrolytes, were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography was performed, followed by a computed tomography scan for further evaluation of the findings.
imaging_findings: In the ultrasound (USG), the left kidney could not be visualised in the left renal fossa. The right kidney was normal in size and echogenicity. Further scanning localised the left kidney above the left hemidiaphragm, suggesting thoracic ectopy (Figure 1). The chest X-ray showed a well-defined radio-opaque lesion in the left lower zone not obliterating the cardiac silhouette (Figure 2). Computed Tomography (CT) revealed a posterolateral diaphragmatic defect on the left side, consistent with Bochdalek hernia (Figures 3a and 3b). The left kidney, retroperitoneal fat, tail of the pancreas, and renal vessels herniated into the thoracic cavity. The kidney appeared normal in size, attenuation, and parenchymal structure with no evidence of hydronephrosis or structural abnormalities.
discussion: Background A thoracic ectopic kidney is a rare anomaly caused by the abnormal migration of the kidney during embryogenesis. It accounts for less than 5% of all ectopic kidneys and is commonly associated with congenital diaphragmatic defects such as Bochdalek hernia [1,2]. During normal development, the kidneys ascend from the pelvis to their retroperitoneal position by the 8th week of gestation. Failure to arrest this migration can result in the kidney passing through a diaphragmatic defect into the thoracic cavity. Bochdalek hernias arise from incomplete closure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane during foetal development and are the most common defects associated with ectopic thoracic kidneys. These hernias are often diagnosed in neonates, but may remain asymptomatic until adulthood, as in this case [1,3]. Clinical Perspective Thoracic ectopic kidneys are often asymptomatic and are incidentally detected on imaging. However, complications such as hydronephrosis, urinary obstruction, nephrolithiasis or recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) may occur due to anatomical abnormalities. The ureter in thoracic kidneys is elongated to accommodate the increased distance to the bladder, which predisposes the kidney to urinary obstruction and vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). In turn, VUR increases the risk of UTIs and renal damage. When associated with a congenital diaphragmatic defect, such as a Bochdalek hernia, there is also the risk of herniated abdominal contents causing thoracic compression or, rarely, visceral strangulation. In this case, the patient’s dyspepsia was unrelated to the ectopic kidney, and imaging ruled out complications such as obstruction, VUR, or hydronephrosis [4]. While thoracic ectopic kidneys primarily involve renal malposition and malrotation, they may also be associated with other congenital anomalies of the renal tract. Though rare, thoracic ectopia can coexist with collecting system abnormalities such as duplex ureters or ureter duplication, as part of the broader spectrum of congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract. Renal ectopia is also linked to ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction and vesicoureteral reflux, likely due to aberrant ureteral length and insertion angles. While these associations are more common in pelvic ectopia, vigilance is warranted for collecting system anomalies even in thoracic cases. A “true thoracic kidney” is an extremely rare form of renal ectopia, accounting for less than 0.01% of all ectopic kidneys, in which the kidney ascends into the thoracic cavity through a closed diaphragm, without any associated diaphragmatic defect such as a Bochdalek hernia [6]. In contrast, the present case involved herniation of the kidney through a congenital diaphragmatic defect, classifying it as a secondary thoracic ectopia. Imaging Perspective Imaging is critical for the diagnosis of thoracic ectopic kidneys, particularly for the evaluation of associated complications. Ultrasound is an effective initial tool for detecting the absence of a kidney in its normal location, whereas CT or MRI is essential for confirming the ectopic position and identifying associated abnormalities. In this case, CT imaging confirmed herniation of the kidney along with retroperitoneal fat, tail of the pancreas, and renal vessels through a left-sided Bochdalek hernia. The normal size and structure of the kidney, with no evidence of hydronephrosis, indicates preserved renal function [2]. Outcome Our patient remained asymptomatic, with a thoracic ectopic kidney and Bochdalek hernia, and had normal renal morphology and function on imaging. In the absence of complications such as hydronephrosis, vesicoureteral reflux, or recurrent infections, routine imaging follow-up was deemed unnecessary. Instead, the patient was counselled on potential warning symptoms, including flank pain, urinary tract infections, or changes in urinary patterns, which would warrant prompt clinical reassessment. Teaching Points A thoracic ectopic kidney is a rare anomaly that is often discovered incidentally during imaging for unrelated conditions. Associated complications included hydronephrosis, urinary obstruction, and vesicoureteral reflux due to elongated ureters. Imaging, especially CT or MRI, is essential for diagnosing thoracic ectopic kidneys and evaluating their associated risks. Conservative management is appropriate for asymptomatic patients with normal kidney function; however, regular follow-up is necessary. Surgical intervention may be required in symptomatic cases with significant complications to restore normal drainage and prevent renal damage.

title: A painful journey: Intra-abdominal pathology caused by a migrated foreign body
clinical_history: A 22-year-old man with a history of epilepsy presented to the emergency department with a four-hour history of right lower quadrant abdominal pain and fever. Blood tests revealed leukocytosis and elevated C-reactive protein levels.
imaging_findings: A computed tomography (CT) scan (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c) revealed concentric mural thickening and mucosal enhancement of a segment of the distal ileum. Additionally, a 5 cm linear hyperdense structure was visualised at the ileocecal valve, extending beyond the intestinal wall. An exploratory laparotomy revealed a microperforation of the distal ileum, and a primary closure of the mural defect was performed. However, no foreign body was identified. Two months later, the same patient presented to the emergency department complaining of hypogastric pain and proctalgia. Another CT scan (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c) showed concentric mural thickening of the rectum with hyperenhancement of the mucosa. Within the rectal lumen, a linear hyperdense structure was observed, likely corresponding to the previously described image and suggestive of a migrated foreign body.
discussion: Background Foreign body (FB) ingestion is a common occurrence, though it is an infrequent cause of acute abdomen [1–4]. Severe complications, such as gastrointestinal obstruction or perforation, may arise. This condition typically affects children, individuals with psychiatric disorders, dementia, or risk-taking behaviours [4]. Clinical Perspective Symptoms vary from nonspecific abdominal pain to signs of peritonitis, which can often be prevented with prompt diagnosis and management [1,2,4]. Perforations are most commonly caused by sharp, elongated objects (e.g., fish bones, chicken bones, or toothpicks) and typically occur in areas of luminal narrowing or angulation, such as the terminal ileum or rectosigmoid junction [1,2,4]. Imaging Perspective Imaging plays a crucial role in the localisation of foreign bodies. Plain radiography is useful for detecting radiopaque objects, while computed tomography (CT) can identify radiolucent objects and assess potential complications [1,2]. Key findings on CT include the identification of the foreign body, intestinal wall thickening, mesenteric fat stranding, and pneumoperitoneum [1,4]. Mucosal trauma-related lesions are associated with intestinal ischaemia and can manifest as pneumatosis on imaging [1,4]. Endoscopy enables direct visualisation and retrieval of the object and is the method of choice in many cases [1,3]. Outcome Timely intervention significantly improves patient outcomes. Most FBs (80–90%) pass through the gastrointestinal tract without causing harm, permitting conservative management [1]. Around 10–20% require endoscopic intervention, especially when the FB is in the oesophagus or stomach [1,3]. Less than 1% necessitate surgery, typically in cases of bleeding, peritonitis, abscess, or fistula [1–3]. Surgical procedures may involve resection of the affected intestinal segment [1,2]. While perforations generally occur within 7–10 days of ingestion [1,4], some cases report FBs embedded in the intestinal mucosa for up to 9–10 months, underscoring the importance of imaging and early intervention regardless of clinical symptoms or negative radiographic findings [3]. In our case, rectal exploration under sedation enabled the removal of the foreign body, which was subsequently identified as a toothpick. Teaching points Diagnosing foreign body (FB) ingestion requires a high degree of suspicion, a detailed medical history, and a thorough physical examination, given the significant variability and nonspecific nature of clinical presentations. Imaging techniques, particularly computed tomography (CT), are essential for determining the location and characteristics of the object, as well as associated complications. Management of foreign body ingestion depends on the type and location of the object. Surgical removal is sometimes necessary to prevent secondary complications, which are not uncommon. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Epithelioid osteoblastoma of the thoracic spine
clinical_history: A previously well 12-year-old male presented to the accident and emergency department of a regional paediatric hospital with a 2-week history of worsening bilateral lower limb paraesthesia in the form of loss of fine touch, vibration and proprioception from the level of T5 distally, signifying mass effect on the dorsal columns with sparing of pain and temperature sensation. He also had reduced motor function of the lower limbs with clonus and brisk reflexes.
imaging_findings: MRI brain was normal. MRI of the whole spine (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, 1d, and 1e) demonstrated a large solitary solid cystic lesion, centred over the spinous process and the lamina of T5 bilaterally, more extensive on the right. The solid lesion is iso/mildly hypointense to bone, with areas of T1 and T2 hypointense signal, suggestive of calcifications. The solid component measured 3.4 x 3.7 x 4.4 cm (transverse x anteroposterior x craniocaudal) and demonstrated avid enhancement. The mass is expansile with cortical expansion and trabecular replacement. It extends into the spinal canal, causing severe canal stenosis and cord compression. There was evidence of bone marrow oedema within the body of T5. No other intra or extramedullary lesions were identified. A follow-up CT thorax, abdomen and pelvis (Figures 2a and 2b) with bony reformats demonstrated an expansile lytic lesion with cortical expansion involving the posterior elements of T5. There was no bony destruction. There are areas of calcification seen within the internal osseous matrix. No other bony lesions were identified, and no abnormality of note was found in the thorax, abdomen or pelvis.
discussion: Diagnosis Due to the locally aggressive nature of this lesion on MR and the broad list of differential diagnoses based on imaging findings, the clinical team proceeded to perform a percutaneous biopsy of the lesion before a definite plan was in place. Our differential diagnoses based on imaging findings included epithelioid osteoblastoma, fibrous dysplasia, giant cell tumour, osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma in addition to metastatic bony disease. Histopathological assessment was in keeping with an osteoblastoma, in this case, of the thoracic spine. Background According to the World Health Organization (WHO) Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone, 5th Edition (2020), osteoblastoma is defined as a benign bone-forming neoplasm characterised by the production of trabeculae of woven bone lined by prominent osteoblasts within a vascularised stroma [1]. It is a rare benign bone-forming tumour accounting for less than 1% of all bony tumours [2]. It typically affects the spine and long bones and is more common in adolescents and young adults, with a slight male predominance [1,2]. Common sites include the posterior elements of the spine, long bones and occasionally the skull or jaw [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Symptomatology ranges from pain to neurological symptoms if there is spinal involvement causing radiculopathy [2]. Osteoblastoma typically presents as a lytic bone lesion larger than 2 cm with well-defined borders and lacks permeation into the surrounding bone [2]. Histologically, osteoblastomas consist of interlacing trabeculae of woven bone surrounded by plump osteoblasts and a richly vascularised fibrous stroma [1]. Imaging Perspective In a study looking at 35 patients with spinal osteoblastomas, Liu et al. were able to summarise the rationale for using multimodality imaging to further evaluate these lesions [3]. Computerised tomography is thought to be useful in localising the nidus and demonstrating calcifications [3]. It is also useful for visualising the internal matrix and assessing for cortical expansion and/or cortical destruction [3]. MRI has an additional diagnostic value through assessing the nidus, extra-osseous involvement, bone marrow oedema and soft tissue oedema. MRI should be performed prior to biopsy in vertebral bone lesions to minimise post-procedural artefacts caused by haemorrhage or biopsy tract, to preserve diagnostic quality and to facilitate more accurate anatomical and pathological evaluation. Outcome In our case, the patient underwent resection of the posterior elements of T5 with posterior instrumented orthopaedic fusion. He had an excellent recovery and was discharged on day 4 postoperatively. Both CT and MRI imaging played a crucial role in delineating this and narrowing down the list of differential diagnoses. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Osteoblastoma Fibrous dysplasia Telangiectatic osteosarcoma Giant cell tumour Ewing sarcoma

title: Epidermoid cyst of the quadrigeminal cistern in a paediatric patient
clinical_history: A 10-year-old boy, previously asymptomatic, presented with paroxysmal episodes of paraesthesia affecting all four limbs. Neurological examination revealed no motor weakness, cranial nerve deficits, or cerebellar dysfunction.
imaging_findings: An MRI of the brain was performed based on clinical suspicion, revealing a small lesion, measuring 18 x 13 mm axially, in the quadrigeminal plate cistern (Figure 1). The lesion exhibited radiological features consistent with an epidermoid cyst, i.e., hyperintense on T2 (Figures 1 and 2), hypointense on T1 (Figure 3), and with marked restricted diffusion (Figures 4 and 5). There was a mild mass effect on the tectal plate, but no obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct and no hydrocephalus.
discussion: Background Epidermoid cysts of the quadrigeminal cistern are rare, benign intracranial tumours. These slow-growing lesions are most commonly found in the cerebellopontine angle (40%), fourth ventricle (5–18%), and approximately 30% in the subarachnoid spaces of the basal cisterns [1,2]. These are believed to arise between the third and fifth weeks of gestation due to abnormal gastrulation, resulting in the entrapment of ectodermal remnants within the developing neuroectoderm. These remnants accumulate desquamated epithelium and keratin, leading to the formation of epidermoid cysts [1,3]. These lesions constitute 0.5–1.8% of all primary intracranial tumours and predominantly occur between the third and fifth decades of life, with a low incidence in paediatric populations [4,5]. A retrospective study by Nair et al. [1] reviewed 15 cases of large quadrigeminal cistern epidermoid cysts in patients aged 14–45 years. Before our case, no previous studies had documented epidermoid cysts of the quadrigeminal cistern presenting with all four limbs paraesthesia in a paediatric patient. Additionally, the absence of hydrocephalus in our case further distinguishes it from the typical presentation. Clinical Perspective Most intracranial epidermoid cysts present with neurological symptoms such as seizures, weakness, and headaches [6]. Quadrigeminal cistern epidermoid cysts are often associated with hydrocephalus. Due to their location near critical neuroanatomical structures, the quadrigeminal cistern epidermoid cysts can present with a variety of neurological symptoms, including headaches, hydrocephalus, ataxia, and oculomotor disturbances [1,7]. Imaging Perspective On CT, epidermoid cysts are low in density due to their contents—primarily cellular debris and high cholesterol levels. Contrast enhancement is typically absent. On MRI, epidermoid cysts often resemble arachnoid cysts or enlarged cerebrospinal fluid spaces, making differentiation challenging. They may exhibit heterogeneity on FLAIR, producing a characteristic “dirty cerebrospinal fluid” appearance. DWI and ADC mapping demonstrate restricted diffusion, a key feature that allows for definitive diagnosis. Outcome Surgical excision remains the treatment of choice. Long-term follow-up is essential to monitor for recurrence or delayed complications. Our case was discussed at a multidisciplinary neurosurgical meeting, and a conservative approach was recommended due to the significant risk of surgery, benign nature of the lesion and absence of related symptomatology, including mass effect or hydrocephalus. This has been under surveillance for 5 years and remains unchanged. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Intracranial epidermoid cysts are rare in the paediatric population, often presenting with nonspecific symptoms. Early identification is crucial for appropriate management. This case underscores the importance of considering epidermoid cysts in the differentials for paediatric intracranial masses and tailoring management to the individual patient’s clinical course. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Epidermoid cyst Arachnoid cyst Dermoid cyst Neurocysticercosis

title: Mycetoma foot with classic “dot-in-circle” sign
clinical_history: A 59-year-old male agricultural worker from a rural area, with a long history of barefoot fieldwork, presented with a long-standing history of swelling over the plantar surface of the left foot, now progressing to involve the dorsal surface and with a history of a discharging sinus. The patient denies any history of trauma.
imaging_findings: A clinical image of the plantar (Figure 1a) and dorsal surface (Figure 1b) of the left foot shows multiple soft and firm nodules that were nontender, along with no discharging sinus at present. X-ray of the left foot (Figure 2) and lateral views show soft-tissue density over the lateral aspect of the left foot with cortical remodelling of the diaphysis of the 4th metatarsal. Ultrasound shows multiple cystic lesions, with a few of them showing tiny echogenic grains in the dependent portion (dot in a circle) (arrow in Figure 3). On T2W sagittal (Figure 4a), soft tissue mass shows conglomerates of small (2–5 mm), rounded, hyperintense lesions with few of them showing central low-signal intensity dots and peripheral low-signal intensity rim around these hyperintense areas, representing a “dot-in-circle” sign. A few cystic areas are noted within this mass, which contains T2 hypointense foci—likely spores. On post-contrast T1 fat-saturated (FS) coronal image (Figure 4b), the involved region of soft tissue shows rim enhancement around the granulation tissue along with minimal enhancement of the central dot. There is sparing of the underlying bones and tendons. No evidence of marrow oedema noted.
discussion: Background Mycetoma is a chronic granulomatous disease that primarily infects the subcutaneous tissue and is prevalent in tropical regions, mainly in Africa, Mexico, and India. It can be caused by fungi (Eumycetes) or bacteria (Actinomycetes) [1]. This case is unusual in that the patient is 59 years old, slightly older than the typical demographic affected by mycetoma, which predominantly includes young adult males in endemic regions. Clinical Perspective Common clinical features include swelling, draining sinuses, and the presence of granules in the discharge. It is known to occur in farmers who walk barefoot, leading to minor trauma that allows pathogens to enter and form discharging granulomas, and can progress to severe deformity and disability if not treated [2]. Imaging Perspective Early radiographs might appear normal, but as the disease progresses, they can reveal soft tissue swelling, periosteal reactions, and lytic bone lesions with sclerotic borders. Ultrasound adds diagnostic value by revealing the hallmark “dot-in-circle” sign even before bone involvement is detectable. It is a fast, accessible, and cost-effective modality, especially useful for initial evaluation and for guiding aspiration or biopsy [2]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the most sensitive modality for diagnosing mycetoma, with the “dot-in-circle” sign being a hallmark feature. MRI plays a pivotal role in assessing mycetoma foot, primarily due to its superior soft tissue contrast and ability to depict deep structures without the use of ionising radiation. Characteristic MRI features include hyperintense signal changes in the affected soft tissues and the formation of well-defined lesions that may exhibit peripheral oedema or necrosis. Moreover, MRI can elucidate the extent of bone involvement and associated complications, guiding surgical planning and therapeutic interventions. While the presence of the “dot-in-circle” sign on MRI is highly suggestive of mycetoma, current literature indicates that imaging alone cannot reliably differentiate between bacterial (actinomycetoma) and fungal (eumycetoma) aetiologies [5,6]. This reinforces the importance of correlating radiologic findings with clinical, microbiological, and histological data for accurate diagnosis and management. Outcome A biopsy was performed to confirm the diagnosis, which showed fungal hyphae in deep subcutaneous tissue by periodic acid Schiff (PAS) stain (Figure 5a) and Grocott methenamine silver stain (Figure 5b). Antifungal agents (itraconazole or voriconazole) for eumycetoma and antibiotics (trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole) for actinomycetoma are the mainstays of treatment. Long-term therapy (6–12 months) is often required [3]. Surgical debridement or amputation is reserved for advanced cases with extensive tissue destruction. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent disability [4]. Supportive care, including pain management and wound care, also plays a vital role in promoting healing and improving patient quality of life.
differential_diagnosis: Mycetoma foot Chronic bacterial osteomyelitis Tuberculosis
