title: Xanthogranulomatous and emphysematous pyelonephritis in a bifid ureter system
clinical_history: A 46-year-old female presented to the emergency department with a fever, anorexia, constipation, abdominal pain in the left flank and iliac fossa, and vomiting for the past two days. Painkillers had not provided relief. Laboratory findings showed signs of a urinary tract infection, including leukocytosis, elevated CRP levels, pyuria, and haematuria.
imaging_findings: Due to clinical suspicion of pyelonephritis, a multiphase CT scan was performed. CT images revealed a left kidney with a bifid urinary system, a staghorn calculus, an enlarged upper pole, a distended calyceal system, and dispersed air bubbles around the calculus and within the renal cortex (Figure 1). The contrast-enhanced CT images best displayed the hypoattenuating cortex of the upper pole, along with dilated, fluid-filled calyces protruding into the cortex, still surrounded by a thin rim of parenchyma resembling the paw of a bear (“bear paw sign”) (Figure 2). The inflammatory process extended beyond the renal parenchyma into the peri and pararenal spaces, with perirenal fat stranding, thickening of the anterior renal fascia, and multiple reactive subcentimetric para-aortic lymph nodes supporting the tentative diagnosis of emphysematous and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (Figures 3a, 3b, and 4). A follow-up CT performed two weeks later showed a complete regression of the gas bubbles and resolution of perirenal inflammatory signs (Figure 5).
discussion: Background Bifid ureter is an anatomical variant resulting from a complete or incomplete duplication of the urinary tract, with a prevalence of approximately 5% [1]. In our case, there was an incomplete duplication of the upper part of the left urinary system, with fusion occurring in the distal ureter. No associated obstruction was observed. Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP) is a severe, destructive granulomatous process secondary to chronic renal infections associated with obstructive uropathy. It results in the replacement of renal parenchyma by fibrofatty inflammatory tissue composed of lipid-laden epithelioid macrophages (xanthoma cells) [2–4]. The infectious and destructive process may remain confined to the renal parenchyma or extend to adjacent perirenal and visceral spaces, as described in the Malek classification [4]. XGP is generally unilateral and affects the entire kidney. However, in 10–17% of cases, a focal form may occur, either in a normal kidney or in a duplex urinary system, as in our case. Calyceal stones and hydronephrosis are commonly present. XGP can occur at any age but is most common in middle-aged to elderly patients, with a twofold higher prevalence in women [2–4]. Emphysematous pyelonephritis (EP) is a life-threatening necrotising infection that can lead to sepsis and multiorgan failure. It is characterised by the presence of gas bubbles within and around the kidney. EP also shows a female predominance and is associated with high morbidity and mortality rates [2,3,5]. Both XGP and EP typically present unilaterally and are commonly caused by Proteus mirabilis and Escherichia coli . These infections are more frequent in women and patients with diabetes [2,3,5]. Clinical Perspective Clinical symptoms are often vague and include general malaise, weight loss, and fever. However, flank pain, haematuria, and laboratory findings frequently indicate a urinary tract infection [4,5]. Imaging Perspective CT has become the diagnostic modality of choice for both XGP and EP, which have their distinct imaging features. In XGP, characteristic findings include renal enlargement, staghorn calculi, and fluid-filled, dilated calyces producing the classic bear paw sign. Inflammatory extension to the perirenal space may also be seen, with fat stranding, thickened fascia, lymphadenopathy, and perinephric fluid, contributing to staging via the Malek classification. Rare complications include fistula formation and psoas abscesses [2–4]. In EP, hallmark findings include gas bubbles within or around the kidney, intrarenal or perirenal fluid collections, and parenchymal destruction. Abscesses may also be present [2,3,5]. Outcome After the diagnosis of focal xanthogranulomatous and emphysematous pyelonephritis in a bifid ureter, our patient was initially treated with analgesics and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Although surgical intervention, such as drainage or partial/total nephrectomy, is typically recommended, she was managed with DJ stenting and discharged after four days. A follow-up CT and elective partial heminephrectomy were scheduled for two weeks later (Figure 5).

title: Neuro-Behçet’s disease: Always challenging
clinical_history: A man in his mid-20s with a 2–3 week history of intermittent severe headache, photophobia, nausea and vomiting, presented with generalised seizures. Treatment for meningoencephalitis was given, and the patient improved. Two months later, he developed sudden bilateral lower limb weakness and pins and needles sensation below the waist.
imaging_findings: MRI showed diffuse cortical and subcortical white matter T2 hyperintensity involving the hippocampi and parahippocampal gyri bilaterally and cortical signal abnormality in the left superior frontal lobe (Figures 1a and 1b). Two weeks later, an MRI (not shown) showed near complete resolution of the abnormal signal intensities. No abnormalities were seen in the cervicothoracic spine. MRI whole spine two months later showed extensive increased signal of the central cord spanning from C2 to T8 vertebrae with cord expansion (Figures 2a and 2b), and areas of ring-enhancing foci within the cord at C2 (Figures 2c and d). There were also confluent and continuous lesions involving the medial aspect of the right temporal lobe, optic tract, corticospinal tract and hypothalamus. This extends into the right cerebral peduncle and the pyramids of the right pons (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Behçet’s disease is a multisystemic and chronic inflammatory vasculitis of unknown aetiology, affecting vessels of different sizes and in various organs. The mean age of presentation is 20–30 years, and it is most prevalent in the Middle East, Mediterranean, and East Asia. Males are affected 2–5 times more than females. Associations include HLA-B51 [1]. Clinical Perspective The diagnosis requires fulfilment of several criteria (one or more points for each: ocular lesions, genital/oral aphthosis, skin lesions, neurological and vascular manifestations, positive pathergy test); there is no single diagnostic test. The likelihood of diagnosis increases with a higher score. Central nervous system (CNS) manifestations (headaches, sensory disturbances, dysarthria, cerebellar signs and personality changes) affect 4–49% of patients and are usually preceded by ulcerative lesions [2]. This patient had no history of ocular lesions or aphthosis, and CNS imaging was necessary due to neurological symptoms. Imaging Perspective MRI of the brain and spinal cord are crucial for identifying the inflammation and extent of the lesions. Neuro-Behçet’s has a wide variety of manifestations, such as focal or multifocal lesions, meningoencephalitis, and cerebral vein thrombosis. Parenchymal lesions usually involve the mesodiencephalic junction (thalamus, midbrain and internal capsule—cascade sign), pons (2nd most common), basal ganglia (bilateral in a third of cases), subcortical white matter and spinal cord (less common), often as longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis [3]. Lesions are hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2 with vasogenic oedema, isointense to slightly hyperintense on DWI, and typically demonstrate patchy contrast enhancement. Lumbar punctures with cerebrospinal fluid analysis and blood tests are important to identify or exclude underlying autoimmune conditions or infection. The diagnosis is made with a combination of the clinical score associated with blood tests, and excluding other conditions. This patient had various negative antibody tests, such as aquaporin-4 IgG-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders (AQP4-NMOSD) and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease (MOGAD). Oral ulcers were then searched and found and a positive HLA-B51. Outcome Treatment aims to manage symptoms and prevent complications, as there is no cure. Medications include immunosuppressants, corticosteroids and biological therapies, tailored to the individual and severity of symptoms. The disease affects multiple organs [4], which requires multidisciplinary care. It may progress, resolve (with therapy or spontaneously) or recur. Imaging plays a decisive role in identifying CNS areas affected, helping to exclude other diagnoses, and to monitor treatment outcome. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Neuro-Behçet’s disease has a varied clinical presentation, which overlaps with several other CNS diseases. Raising this possibility with clinicians will aid in searching for the aphthous lesions and supporting blood tests, further helping to suggest the diagnosis. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Plexiform neurofibroma – A rare case of neurofibromatosis 1 with abdominal manifestations
clinical_history: A 15-year-old female presented with a two-year history of progressively enlarging, painful swellings on both sides of the neck, along with a recent onset of abdominal pain of one week’s duration. Examination revealed multiple palpable swellings in the axillary, cervical and inguinal regions as well as café-au-lait spots over the extremities and trunk.
imaging_findings: Ultrasonography of the neck revealed multiple oval and spindle-shaped hypoechoic lesions in the bilateral posterior triangle (Figures 1a and 1b) and the anterior neck region. Similar subcutaneous lesions were noted in bilateral level 4 regions (Figures 1c and 1d), abutting carotid vessels. The contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) abdomen revealed heterogeneously enhancing oval-shaped lesions abutting the duodenojejunal flexure (Figures 2a and 2b) and a similar enhancing oblong lesion in the pelvis, posterior to the rectum at L5–S1 level (Figures 3a,3b, and 3c). Multiple hypodense, hypoenhancing nodules were imaged in the mesentery encasing the inferior mesenteric artery from its origin (Figures 4a and 4b), and extending into the pelvis and bilateral retroperitoneum. Similar nodular lesions were seen extending from the neural foramina of the lumbar spine, extending along the course of nerve roots into sciatica foramina and along the sciatic nerve (Figures 5a, 5b, and 5c). A few small nodules were also noted adjacent to bilateral femoral vessels (Figures 6a and 6b). Multiple variable-sized hypodense subcutaneous nodules were noted diffusely scattered in the abdominal wall.
discussion: Peripheral nerve sheath tumours comprise nearly 5% of benign soft tissue tumours, and plexiform neurofibroma is a rare subtype of benign neurofibroma that occurs exclusively in neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) [1]. Neurofibromatoses are autosomal dominant inherited neurocutaneous disorders secondary to mutations in the NF gene. NF1 is a multisystem genetic disorder with neurocutaneous, ophthalmic, pulmonary, abdominopelvic and musculoskeletal manifestations.NF1 is diagnosed based on clinical criteria and the presence of at least 2 diagnostic criteria (café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, axillary or inguinal freckling, optic glioma, and distinct osseous lesions) in an individual who does not have a parent diagnosed with NF1 and one of these features in individuals with a parent already diagnosed with NF1 [2]. They typically present with localised lesions and rarely as a plexiform variant. This case illustrates various imaging manifestations across multiple organ systems, notably abdominopelvic and neurological manifestations. Intra-abdominal neoplasms associated with NF1 can be categorised based on their cellular origin into neurogenic, neuroendocrine, embryonic and interstitial cells of Cajal neoplasms [3]. They most commonly manifest in the retroperitoneum and pelvis along the distribution of the lumbosacral plexus, but can also involve any portion of the gastrointestinal tract or mesentery. In this particular case, multiple nodular lesions were observed in the mesentery, pelvis, bilateral retroperitoneum and neural foramina. Solitary and multifocal gastrointestinal stromal tumours can occur in NF1, often manifesting in the small bowel [4]. Our case also demonstrates a similar heterogeneous enhancing oval lesion abutting the duodenojejunal flexure. Beyond cutaneous involvement, NF1 also affects the spinal cord and spinal nerve roots, which can provide important diagnostic clues as demonstrated in our case [5]. Hence, a multidisciplinary approach is essential for the diagnosis and management of NF1, with good clinical and radiological correlation. One of the key concerns with plexiform neurofibromas is their potential to undergo malignant transformation into malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours. Whole-body MRI has emerged as an essential tool for NF1 surveillance. Imaging features suggestive of malignant transformation include an enlarging mass, peripheral enhancement, perilesional oedema, and increased tumour heterogeneity. MRI of the brain and spine is recommended for patients with unexplained or progressive symptoms for surveillance. In this case, the final diagnosis was confirmed based on an excision biopsy of the cervical mass, which revealed benign spindle cell tumour morphology consistent with neurofibroma. The abdominal pain, possibly due to mass effect from the lesions, was effectively managed with analgesics. Symptomatic improvement was noted, and the patient was discharged following a detailed discussion of potential complications and the possible need for surgical intervention. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Beyond benign appearances: Telangiectatic osteosarcoma masquerading as a benign lesion
clinical_history: A 38-year-old man presented in 2014 with right knee pain. X-ray showed a well-defined lytic lesion of benign appearance in the proximal tibia. Bone scan and SPECT-CT suggested benign features but recommended MRI. Lost to follow-up, the patient returned in 2022 with knee pain and functional impairment after minor trauma, prompting further evaluation.
imaging_findings: The initial knee X-ray in 2014 (Figures 1a and 1b) showed a posterior-eccentric, well-defined, sclerosed lytic lesion with posterior cortical insufflation in the proximal tibial epiphysis/metaphysis, suggesting a likely benign Bone-RADS 1 lesion in actual guidelines (Figure 2) [1,2]. Bone scintigraphy and SPECT-CT in 2014 (Figures 3 and 4) identified diffuse hyperaemia and radiotracer uptake at the level of the proximal right tibia around a lytic bone lesion with posterior cortical insufflation. A benign process was suggested as the first possibility. However, due to the low specificity of the study, MRI was still recommended, but the patient did not return for follow-up. Additionally, the lesion presented heterogeneous/lucent content, which was not mentioned in the report, which in current guidelines would reclassify the lesion as Bone-RADS 4 and would be referred for oncology or biopsy [3]. The patient returned in 2022 with worsening knee pain. CT (Figure 5) revealed a heterogeneous epimetaphyseal lesion with cystic areas, amorphous calcifications, cortical erosions and extension into surrounding soft tissues. MRI (Figures 6a, 6b, 6c, 7a, 7b, 8, 9a, 9b, and 9c) of the same lesion demonstrated multiple fluid-fluid levels with haemorrhagic/proteinaceous component, probable haemorrhagic foci, enhancing solid nodules, cortical breach, and muscle infiltration. Findings were consistent with aggressive telangiectatic osteosarcoma. Biopsy confirmed a high-grade osteosarcoma.
discussion: Background Telangiectatic osteosarcoma (TO) is a rare, aggressive, high-grade malignant tumour that accounts for 1.2–12% of all osteosarcomas and primarily affects children, teenagers, and young adults, with a male predominance [4,5]. It is distinguished by the presence of large haemorrhagic or necrotic cavities, giving it a radiological and histopathological appearance similar to aneurysmal bone cyst and giant cell tumour [5]. It most commonly appears in the metaphysis of long bones, particularly in the knee, with the distal femur being the most common region, followed by the tibia [6–8]. Clinical Perspective TO’s clinical symptoms are identical to those of conventional osteosarcoma. The most prevalent signs and symptoms include local discomfort and/or soft tissue mass as well as pathological fractures [6–8]. Imaging Perspective TO can be diagnosed using a variety of imaging modalities [4,7,9]: Plain radiographs : Osteolytic tumour with asymmetric extension and an aggressive growth pattern, including cortical destruction and limited peripheral sclerosis. Pathologic fractures are also common. Computed tomography (CT) : Soft-tissue mass, some osteoid matrix mineralisation, fluid levels, and thick peripheral and nodular septal enhancement (viable high-grade sarcomatous tissue). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) : Soft tissue mass with haemorrhage and fluid-fluid levels are seen in most cases (74%). Typically, aneurysmal bone cyst presents as a less aggressive lesion with no soft tissue mass and lower tumour sizes [4,7,9]. Because of these radiological parallels with other benign entities, image-guided core needle biopsy is almost always utilised to confirm diagnosis. However, it is crucial to note that TO is not always well sampled due to its lytic and cystic character, which can lead to misdiagnosis [10]. Outcome Previously, the prognosis and clinical outcome of TO were considered to be poor. Since the introduction of chemotherapy, the prognosis has significantly improved, with around a 60% survival rate at 10 years. Most patients can be cured with neoadjuvant chemotherapy plus surgery [8]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Telangiectatic osteosarcoma (TO) is a rare and aggressive variant of osteosarcoma which can pose diagnostic difficulties with other benign lesions, mainly with an aneurysmal bone cyst. Distinguishing between these two entities is critical because their therapy and prognosis differ greatly. By combining clinical, imaging and pathology tests, we can reduce the number of misdiagnosed patients. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Aneurysmal bone cyst Unicameral bone cyst Telangiectatic osteosarcoma Giant cell tumour Non-ossifying fibroma

title: Primary leptomeningeal anaplastic T-cell lymphoma, anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) positive
clinical_history: 27-year-old male with a 3-month history of 15 kg weight loss and new-onset focal to generalised tonic seizure. Neurological exam showed right hemiparesis and cranial nerve VII palsy.
imaging_findings: Focal leptomeningeal thickening with a nodular appearance extending along the Sylvian fissure and superior temporal sulcus, demonstrating heterogeneous enhancement following intravenous gadolinium administration, accompanied by white matter oedema in the left cerebral hemisphere. A craniectomy with biopsy was performed, which revealed an anaplastic T-cell lymphoma, CD30 positive and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) positive.
discussion: Background Anaplastic T-cell lymphoma accounts for 2% of adult non-Hodgkin lymphomas, predominantly affecting lymph nodes. Central nervous system (CNS) involvement is extremely rare [1], and at the time of this review, very few cases have been found in the literature [2]. Its histopathological and molecular features include CD30 expression and classification based on the presence or absence of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) gene [3]. In fact, ALK expression is considered a favourable prognostic marker [4]. Clinical Perspective The typical clinical presentation includes lymphadenopathy, weight loss, and fever. However, primary CNS involvement leads to atypical symptoms such as seizures, hemiparesis, visual impairment, and cranial nerve palsies [5]. However, the clinical picture is similar to that presented by infectious meningitis, carcinomatous leptomeningitis, or neurosarcoidosis [6]. Imaging Perspective Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging is the modality of choice. Findings include leptomeningeal enhancement in up to 74% of patients, often extending to the cerebral convexities and involving cranial nerves [7], such as leptomeningeal thickening with nodules’ enhancement or diffuse swelling, and, in general, oedema of the underlying basal white matter [8]. Cerebral blood volume (CBV) map in dynamic susceptibility testing can show an increase in relative CBV in areas of lymphoma [4], while tractography, as shown in this case, allows for assessment of adjacent white matter tract displacement and is useful for surgical planning [9]. Definitive diagnosis is made through biopsy, revealing pleomorphic cells with eccentric, horseshoe-shaped nuclei and eosinophilic perinuclear regions, which express CD30 and often ALK [10]. Outcome Therapeutic options include ALK inhibitors, low-dose methotrexate, and multi-agent chemotherapy. ALK-positive status is generally associated with a better prognosis compared to ALK-negative anaplastic large-cell lymphoma. Early imaging plays a critical role in guiding biopsy and treatment planning, particularly in rare primary CNS presentations. In this case, imaging directly impacted the clinical decision to proceed with biopsy and initiate targeted therapy [11]. In patients with ALK-positive disease, ALK inhibitors such as lorlatinib have shown promising results, even in relapsed or refractory disease [1]. Early and timely detection through imaging and biopsy is essential for proper and timely diagnosis and treatment. This case highlights the importance of considering anaplastic T-cell lymphoma in the differential diagnosis, especially in young patients with atypical neurological symptoms and leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI. Teaching Points Primary leptomeningeal anaplastic large-cell lymphoma is an extremely rare but important differential in cases of atypical CNS symptoms and leptomeningeal enhancement. MRI with contrast is essential for initial assessment, but not diagnostic. Histopathological confirmation with immunohistochemistry (CD30, ALK) is required. Targeted therapies based on ALK status can lead to favourable outcomes. Consider lymphoma in the differential diagnosis of leptomeningeal disease, especially in young adults with progressive neurological symptoms.

title: Benign surprise: Retropancreatic benign teratoma – A clinical conundrum
clinical_history: An 11-year-old child presented with a pricking type of upper abdominal pain on and off for 6 months. No history of fever, vomiting, or loss of appetite. No previous history of similar complaints. On examination, tenderness is present over the epigastric and left lumbar region. Routine laboratory investigations were normal.
imaging_findings: On ultrasound, a relatively well-defined heteroechoic lesion with a hyperechoic rim is noted in the retropancreatic area, with a focal exophytic hypoechoic area in the anterior aspect of the lesion (Figure 1). No obvious internal vascularity on colour Doppler. On contrast-enhanced (CE) CT, a ~ 6.8 x 7 x 8.1 cm well-defined, smoothly marginated, heterodense soft tissue density lesion (predominantly fat component in the posterior aspect with few small solid components and calcific focus in the anterior aspect) is noted in the retropancreatic region (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). Regarding relations and mass effect, the lesion, superiorly, abuts the coeliac trunk and inferiorly displaces the third part of the duodenum. Anteriorly, it displaces the body and tail of the pancreas, abuts the splenic artery and mildly compresses the splenic vein. Posteriorly, abuts the left renal vein. Medially, there is a widening of the duodenal C loop, and laterally, a displacement of adjacent bowel loops. There is no obvious evidence of infiltration with the structures mentioned above or vascular complications (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d).
discussion: Background Teratomas are non-seminomatous germ cell tumours containing elements from two or more embryonic germ layers. Primary retroperitoneal tumours originate within retroperitoneal tissues, while secondary tumours spread to the retroperitoneum from other primary sites [8]. Primary retroperitoneal teratomas are rare neoplasms composed of tissue from all three germ cell layers—ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm—and can contain a wide variety of tissue types [1,2]. Unlike secondary tumours, they arise independently in the retroperitoneal space without originating from adjacent organs. These tumours account for approximately 1–11% of retroperitoneal neoplasms and are most frequently diagnosed in neonates and young adults, with 43–55% presenting within the first year of life, and less than 10–20% occur in individuals over 30 years of age [3]. Retroperitoneal teratomas are typically found near the upper pole of the kidney, showing a slight preference for the left side [7]. Retropancreatic localisation, however, is extremely rare [7]. Clinical Perspective Patients may present with abdominal pain, distension, nausea, vomiting, or compressive symptoms, but in most cases, it is asymptomatic. Imaging Perspective Radiological imaging is the primary modality for diagnosing retroperitoneal teratomas. A plain abdominal radiograph may reveal a soft tissue mass with calcifications, which appear either along the margins or scattered within the lesion; such calcifications are present in 50–60% of cases and can aid in the diagnosis [2], as observed in our case. Cross-sectional imaging, such as CT or MRI, is more definitive, allowing differentiation of the lesion’s components—including fat, sebaceous material, soft tissue, and calcifications [4,5]. Non-contrast CT is preferred for retroperitoneal teratomas due to its ability to detect fat, calcifications, and cystic components, which are characteristic of these tumours [4]. MRI sequences, particularly T1-weighted imaging with fat suppression, effectively delineate fat, calcifications, and cystic components in retroperitoneal teratomas. These sequences enhance tissue differentiation, aiding in the assessment of tumour composition and adjacent structures. Additionally, MRI’s superior soft tissue contrast and multiplanar imaging capabilities provide comprehensive anatomical details, facilitating accurate diagnosis and surgical planning [8]. Additionally, serum tumour markers such as CA19-9, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) may be elevated in retroperitoneal teratomas, providing supplementary diagnostic information [3]. Outcome The primary treatment for retroperitoneal teratomas is surgical excision. Our patient underwent exploratory laparotomy with complete resection (Figures 4a and 4b). Histopathology showed a benign teratoma with cystic areas lined by squamous epithelium and adnexal structures, and solid areas with smooth muscle, cartilage, and haematopoietic tissue (Figures 5a, 5b, and 5c). No immature elements were seen. Postoperative recovery was uneventful.

title: Uterine artery embolisation for caesarean scar ectopic pregnancy
clinical_history: A 41-year-old female patient, gravida 5, para 3, who had undergone a caesarean delivery 12 years ago, presented with 7 weeks of amenorrhea and mild vaginal bleeding. Serum beta-hCG was elevated to 87.407 mIU/mL.
imaging_findings: Initial transvaginal ultrasound revealed a gestational sac with a hydropic yolk sac located at the isthmic-cervical junction in the anterior uterine wall, without embryonic cardiac activity, consistent with caesarean scar implantation, and marked vascularisation on colour Doppler study (Figures 1a and 1b). Superselective catheterisation of the left and right uterine arteries allowed for precise visualisation of uterine microvascularisation, followed by embolisation using permanent microspheres in the segmental branches, which led to a marked reduction in vascular supply to the gestational site (Figures 2a, 2b, 3a, and 3b). Follow-up pelvic ultrasound demonstrated complete resolution, with no visible gestational sac and absence of free fluid, confirming procedural success and effective haemostasis (Figure 4).
discussion: Caesarean scar ectopic pregnancy is a rare but increasingly reported condition, correlating with the global rise in caesarean deliveries. It carries significant risks, including massive haemorrhage and uterine rupture. Management strategies depend on gestational age, clinical presentation, and the patient’s reproductive goals. Therapeutic options include expectant management, systemic or local methotrexate administration, surgical intervention, or endovascular procedures [1,2]. In this case, following a multidisciplinary evaluation, endovascular embolisation was chosen to avoid emergency surgery and preserve uterine integrity. Under spinal anaesthesia and fluoroscopic guidance, selective catheterisation of the uterine arteries was performed using a microcatheter. Methotrexate (10 mL) was infused intra-arterially, followed by embolisation with 300–500-micron permanent microspheres and absorbable haemostatic gelatin sponge (Gelfoam ® ). Immediate cessation of blood flow to the gestational site was observed, with preservation of the main arterial trunks. The procedure was uneventful, and the patient was discharged three days later without complications and a decreasing serum beta-hCG of 12.347 mIU/mL, almost eight times lower than the level at admission [3]. The combined therapy of arterial embolisation with methotrexate has demonstrated superiority over embolisation as a single treatment for ectopic pregnancy, especially in challenging or atypically located cases, due to its synergistic action, which optimises the resolution of trophoblastic tissue. Embolisation promotes vascular occlusion and ischemia, while methotrexate exerts its cytotoxic effect. This combination not only increases clinical success rates but can also reduce the need for more invasive surgeries, preserving fertility and minimising haemorrhagic complications by concentrating the medication at the target site and promoting more efficient reabsorption of the gestational mass [3]. This case underscores the critical role of early diagnosis and multidisciplinary coordination in managing caesarean scar ectopic pregnancies. Superselective uterine artery embolisation proved to be a safe and effective minimally invasive treatment, allowing for rapid haemostasis, preservation of fertility, and avoidance of more invasive surgical approaches. Interventional radiology continues to be a cornerstone in the management of complex obstetric cases [4,5]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: CT angiography findings in atypical acute presentation of Leriche syndrome
clinical_history: A 62-year-old male presented to the emergency department with a three-day history of dyspnoea, epigastric discomfort, dizziness, and transient central chest pain. His medical history included left femoral bypass, arterial ulcers, asthma, and anxiety. Clinical examination revealed clamminess, laboured respiration, mild epigastric tenderness, tachycardia, and normotension. Serum troponin was elevated at 119 ng/L.
imaging_findings: CT angiography (CTA) of the thoracoabdominal aorta was performed to exclude aortic dissection. Sagittal reconstructions (Figure 1) demonstrated advanced atherosclerotic disease with complete occlusion of the abdominal aorta distal to the renal arteries, secondary to a calcified atheromatous plaque. Coronal images (Figure 2) confirmed extension of the occlusion into both common iliac arteries. Axial views (Figure 3) revealed occlusion of a previously placed femoral–femoral crossover graft. Further axial and coronal reconstructions (Figures 4a, 4b, 4c, and 4d) demonstrated extensive collateralisation within the pelvic vasculature. Bilateral internal iliac artery occlusion was also observed (Figure 5). No radiological evidence of aortic dissection was identified. Overall, the findings were consistent with chronic aortoiliac occlusive disease, in keeping with Leriche syndrome.
discussion: Background Leriche syndrome, also known as aortoiliac occlusive disease (AOD), is a chronic vascular condition characterised by progressive atherosclerotic plaque formation at or near the aortic bifurcation. This process ultimately leads to occlusion of the distal abdominal aorta, the iliac arteries, or both. Over time, collateral circulation develops to compensate for the resulting reduction in distal perfusion. These collateral pathways commonly involve the internal iliac, inferior epigastric, and thoracoabdominal arteries [1]. Clinical Perspective Clinically, Leriche syndrome is classically associated with a triad of bilateral claudication, erectile dysfunction, and diminished or absent femoral pulses. However, many patients—particularly those with well-developed collateral circulation—may present atypically or remain asymptomatic [2]. In this case, the patient presented with elevated troponin levels and nonspecific symptoms, prompting imaging to exclude acute cardiac pathology, such as aortic dissection. CT angiography played a crucial role in redirecting the diagnosis toward a chronic vascular aetiology. Imaging Perspective CT angiography is the preferred diagnostic modality due to its rapid acquisition, high spatial resolution, and ability to delineate the extent of disease and visualise collateral networks [3,4]. In this case, imaging revealed complete occlusion of the abdominal aorta and bilateral common iliac arteries, occlusion of a femoral-femoral bypass graft, and extensive collateralisation within the pelvic vasculature. These findings were consistent with chronic aortoiliac occlusion and excluded acute dissection [3,4]. Furthermore, CT angiography findings informed long-term management by detailing vascular anatomy relevant for surgical planning, including the adequacy of collateral perfusion. Outcome As the patient exhibited no signs of critical limb ischaemia, conservative management with dual antiplatelet therapy and statins was initiated. He was referred for outpatient vascular follow-up, and lifestyle modifications were advised. The imaging findings were instrumental in avoiding unnecessary cardiac interventions and contributed to appropriate risk stratification and ongoing surveillance. Take Home Message In summary, Leriche syndrome may present atypically, particularly in patients with robust collateral circulation. CT angiography is not only essential for accurate diagnosis and exclusion of acute vascular emergencies but also plays a central role in guiding management decisions and long-term follow-up strategies. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Diffuse uterine leiomyomatosis: A rare discovery
clinical_history: A 45-year-old woman presented with a progressively enlarging abdominal mass in the hypogastric region, first noticed two years ago. She had no digestive or gynaecological symptoms. Examination revealed a firm, mobile, non-tender mass in the pelvis extending to the right flank and below the right costal margin. Haemoglobin was low (10.4 g/dL) and Ca125 was elevated (60 U/mL), while other tumour markers were normal.
imaging_findings: A contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT scan reveals significant uterine enlargement, with multiple myomatous formations, and a smaller one exhibiting peripheral dystrophic calcification, consistent with diffuse uterine myomatosis (Figures 1a, 1b, and 2). Additionally, a solid, hypervascular nodule is noted in the left vulvar region, suggestive of a leiomyoma of the distal left round ligament (Figure 3). This is associated with a right retroperitoneal cystic mass originating from the right adnexal region and extending upwards through the retroperitoneum to the posterior aspect of the duodenum, suggestive of secondary lymphatic malformation (Figures 4a, 4b and 4c). The whole-body PET/CT shows that the uterus is significantly enlarged and exhibits multiple myomatous formations with a heterogeneous distribution of the radiopharmaceutical. Areas of increased FDG uptake warrant further targeted evaluation to determine their nature. No evidence of metabolically active distant tumour disease is identified (Figures 5a, 5b, and 5c).
discussion: Background Diffuse uterine leiomyomatosis (DUL) is a rare condition characterised by the diffuse replacement of normal uterine parenchyma with numerous leiomyomas, resulting in a symmetrically enlarged uterus [1,2]. Affecting mainly women in later reproductive years, DUL typically presents with menorrhagia and infertility and is more common among African American women and those with a family history of leiomyomas [3]. Hysterectomy remains the standard treatment. However, for women wishing to preserve fertility, conservative options like myomectomy and uterine artery embolisation have shown favourable outcomes [1,4]. Accurate diagnosis and treatment planning rely on MRI and a multidisciplinary team including radiologists, gynaecologists, and surgeons [3,4]. Clinical Perspective DUL symptoms mimic those of common fibroids—heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pain, abdominal enlargement, and pressure—complicating preoperative diagnosis [5]. Although elevated Ca125 levels are typically associated with malignancy, they can also occur in benign fibroids. In the context of a large pelvic mass, these findings raise malignancy concerns and underscore the need for CT or MRI [2–4]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound is usually the initial diagnostic tool, but CT and MRI are preferred for their detailed imaging and superior soft tissue contrast [4]. MRI is critical for preoperative mapping and for distinguishing DUL from diffuse adenomyosis and endometrial stromal sarcoma, given that DUL leiomyomas have indistinct, merging margins [1,3]. The radiological findings of diffuse uterine leiomyomatosis (DUL) on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) include a symmetrical enlargement of the uterus, multiple ill-defined myomatous nodules, diffuse thickening of the myometrium, and a “globular uterus” appearance. Additionally, on MRI, the nodules may exhibit signal variations depending on their tissue composition. These findings are crucial for early diagnosis and preoperative assessment [1,2,5]. The imaging findings, together with the clinical picture, supported a benign aetiology and helped rule out malignancies such as lymphoma or uterine sarcoma. In this case, imaging plays a critical role in characterising a large pelvic mass and differentiating between benign and malignant aetiologies [3,4]. Outcome Surgical intervention—hysterectomy with retroperitoneal mass resection—is recommended to alleviate symptoms and confirm benignity. Although the prognosis post-resection is excellent, fertility preservation is uncommon in advanced cases, making long-term follow-up essential [1,2,4]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Diffuse uterine leiomyomatosis (DUL) typically affects women in the later reproductive years, presenting with a progressive abdominal mass and anaemia. CT and MRI are vital for differential diagnosis and treatment planning. PET/CT can help rule out malignancy by showing no metabolically active distant disease. Coordinated multidisciplinary management is key for optimal diagnosis and treatment.

title: Vanishing fingers in a patient with chronic cough
clinical_history: A 72-year-old woman was seen in a rheumatology and respiratory clinic with chronic productive cough, mild joint stiffness in her hands, and itchy eyes. She also had long-standing hip and knee pain indicative of osteoarthritis. Her medical history includes hypertension, psoriasis, diverticulosis, and mild dust mite sensitisation. She is an ex-smoker.
imaging_findings: X-ray of the hands (Figure 1) revealed the absence of the left first, third, and fourth distal phalanges, and the right first, second, third, and fourth distal phalanges. Severe degenerative changes at the second distal interphalangeal joints, with early gullwing deformities. All of the small joints exhibit increased sclerosis and narrowing. X-ray of the feet (Figure 2) was also performed, which did not show any signs of acro-osteolysis. Pulmonary function tests were not available. High-resolution chest CT (Figures 3a, 3b, 4a, 4b, and 4c) showed basal predominant ground glass changes with minor peripheral reticulation and associated traction bronchiectasis, suggesting probable non-specific interstitial pattern (NSIP) of interstitial lung disease (ILD). She was diagnosed with acro-osteolysis (AO) of the hands and interstitial lung disease, likely secondary to psoriatic arthritis.
discussion: Background Acro-osteolysis (AO) is a rare condition identified by resorption of the distal phalanges of the fingers and/or toes and is associated with a wide range of conditions. Rheumatologic diseases, including scleroderma, mixed connective tissue disease, psoriatic arthritis, and rheumatoid vasculitis, often lead to AO through chronic inflammation and vascular compromise. Endocrine disorders, particularly hyperparathyroidism, increase bone resorption in distal extremities. Environmental factors like polyvinyl chloride (PVC) exposure can impair vascular integrity and contribute to bone damage. Trauma, including thermal injuries and stress fractures, can directly damage bone [1–4]. Neurological conditions such as syringomyelia and leprosy cause AO through sensory loss and repetitive injury. Congenital syndromes, including Rothmund–Thomson syndrome and progeria, predispose individuals to AO. Additionally, idiopathic or familial cases, neoplastic conditions, and infections may cause phalangeal resorption. Dermatologic conditions, like epidermolysis bullosa and Sézary syndrome, lead to AO due to chronic skin-bone interaction [3–5]. Clinical Perspective AO presents with subtle changes in the hands and feet, such as joint pain, stiffness, or mild deformities. As the condition progresses, symptoms like synovitis, dactylitis, skin thickening, and joint deformities may appear. Systemic features vary depending on the underlying condition and may include respiratory symptoms, joint pain, fever, ocular involvement, and skin changes. In cases of malignancy, symptoms like weight loss, jaundice, and night sweats may also be present [3,4,6]. Imaging Perspective Plain radiography remains the gold standard for diagnosing AO, revealing characteristic bone resorption. Initial investigations should include a full blood count, coagulation profile, liver and renal function tests, and inflammatory markers like CRP and ESR. For autoimmune causes, an autoimmune profile, including ANA, ANCA, ENA, dsDNA, rheumatoid factor, and anti-CCP antibodies, is recommended. Additional tests, such as parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels, ACE levels, synovial fluid analysis, HbA1c, chest CT, or spine MRI, may be warranted based on the suspected underlying condition [3,4]. Outcome The patient was diagnosed with psoriatic arthritis and offered methotrexate to treat both the joints and the interstitial lung disease. She refused this and is currently under surveillance. Teaching Points AO may serve as an early marker for specific rheumatological conditions or signal worsening of an underlying disease. Plain radiography is the primary diagnostic tool for AO, with additional imaging used to assess associated conditions. Due to its association with diverse aetiologies, AO evaluation requires a thorough systemic assessment, including targeted autoimmune and metabolic testing. Written informed consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Interrupted pituitary stalk syndrome with absence of the septum pellucidum
clinical_history: A 15-year-old male patient presents with neuropsychomotor developmental delay, pan-hypopituitarism, and epilepsy, diagnosed at age 5. He was hospitalised for 90 days after birth due to jaundice, cyanosis, and seizures. Referred for hormone therapy optimisation, he showed developmental delay and convergent strabismus, prompting a brain MRI for initial evaluation.
imaging_findings: In the skull acquisitions (Figures 1a and 1b), points of hyperintensity were identified along the midline in the parasagittal (ectopic) location, along the floor of the third ventricle without the pituitary stalk (especially visible in Figure 1a), findings consistent with ectopic neurohypophysis and hypoplastic anterior pituitary. The anterior horns with a quadrangular appearance and the absence of the septum pellucidum can be observed (Figure 2), which supports the diagnosis of a midline malformation.
discussion: The findings from the brain MRI, combined with the clinical history of pan-hypopituitarism and neuropsychomotor delay, suggest the diagnosis of interrupted pituitary stalk syndrome due to ectopic neurohypophysis and the absence of the septum pellucidum. Ectopic neurohypophysis is diagnosed when it is located outside its usual position, typically along the infundibulum or at the median eminence. It is a rare disorder that presents with growth hormone deficiency and may be associated with other malformations, including midline malformations such as the absence of the septum pellucidum [1,2]. The association between interrupted pituitary stalk syndrome and midline malformations such as the absence of septum pellucidum may have several causes, including mutations in the HESX1 and LHX4 genes, which are important in the development of pituitary and midline structures. Mutations like this are associated with various phenotypes, including the one presented by our patient [3,4]. Agenesis of the septum pellucidum can be total or partial, and can be caused by developmental malformation or secondary to hydrocephalus. The development may be associated with other malformations such as schizencephaly, holoprosencephaly, ectopic hypophysis, and agenesis of callosal [5,6]. Disruptive events may contribute significantly to midline cerebral malformations. Perinatal insults, particularly foetal hypoxia, haemorrhage, placental insufficiency, maternal exposure to vasoactive substances such as cocaine, and congenital infections, including cytomegalovirus (CMV), have been implicated in the pathogenesis of such anomalies. These disruptive processes can interfere with the normal development of the septum pellucidum, leading to presentations ranging from isolated abnormalities to complex associated malformations such as septo-optic dysplasia and polymicrogyria [7,8]. Clinical manifestations vary by mental retardation, motor deficit, ophthalmology such as blindness, endocrine (hypopituitarism) and neurological manifestations, such as epilepsy, as seen in the case. Because of those manifestations, studies suggest imaging, ophthalmologic and endocrine investigations for early diagnosis and management of other malformations and diseases [5,6,9]. Looking at differential diagnosis, imaging has protagonism in most of them, as holoprosencephaly, septo-optic dysplasia and schizencephaly. These can be excluded by neuroanatomic observation in MRI studies [6,9]. The prognosis is highly variable depending on the phenotype presented. As there is no cure, the treatment of these patients is purely symptomatic. Therefore, it is crucial to identify changes early in order to initiate timely hormonal treatment, ensuring proper development. Many of the diagnosed patients reported in previous studies required tertiary neonatal intensive care units [9]. In the presented case, optimisation of hormone replacement therapy and control of the symptoms related to the condition were carried out.

title: Post-colonoscopy complication beyond pneumoperitoneum
clinical_history: A 53-year-old female presented with left-sided abdominal pain and associated left shoulder pain. A few hours preceding the episode, the patient underwent a colonoscopy. On examination, the abdomen was tender to palpation throughout. Initial blood tests revealed no abnormality. Repeat blood tests revealed a drop in haemoglobin (Hb) levels.
imaging_findings: Abdominal and thorax plain film revealed no abnormal findings (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c). CT abdomen-pelvis post-contrast in the venous phase ruled out pneumoperitoneum and revealed a large perisplenic haematoma with haemoperitoneum (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, 3a, and 3b). Furthermore, active bleeding was visualised in the venous phase (Figures 2b, 2c and 3b), more centrally located on the surface of the spleen, without a clearly identifiable bleeding arterial source. There was no observed splenic laceration or involvement of the splenic hilum. In conclusion, imaging reveals a perisplenic haematoma secondary to active bleeding; therefore, a grade III splenic rupture according to the AAST (The American Association for the Surgery of Trauma). This prompted the patient to undergo an emergency splenic embolisation. Angiography confirmed active bleeding with the likely source being the accessory splenic artery (Figure 4a). Both the accessory splenic artery and the superior polar artery were embolised, bringing active bleeding to a halt (Figure 4b).
discussion: As with many invasive medical procedures, colonoscopy may be associated with a spectrum of post-procedural adverse events, ranging in severity from mild discomfort to life-threatening complications. Commonly reported symptoms include abdominal discomfort and bloating. However, more serious complications, though rare, may include gastrointestinal perforation and bleeding, post-polypectomy syndrome, air embolism, and splenic injury [1,2]. Imaging helps identify features that contribute to including and excluding differentials. For example, intestinal perforation is usually identified by the presence of extraluminal air [3]. Furthermore, post-polypectomy syndrome—also known as post-polypectomy coagulation syndrome and resulting from electrocoagulation injury during a colonoscopic polypectomy—typically presents on computed tomography (CT), with mural thickening with a stratified enhancement pattern, a mural defect containing fluid and surrounding fat stranding, all in the absence of extraluminal air [4]. Splenic injury, although an infrequent complication of colonoscopy, represents a serious and potentially fatal outcome, with reported mortality rates of up to 4.5% [5]. The estimated incidence is less than 0.0005%, though this figure may be underestimated due to the non-specific clinical presentation and frequent misdiagnosis [6]. The proposed mechanisms of splenic injury involve either direct trauma during the passage of the colonoscope through the splenic flexure or excessive traction on the splenocolic ligament, potentially resulting in rupture of the splenic capsule. Splenic injuries are typically classified as parenchymal, subcapsular, or involving intraperitoneal extension [5]. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen is highly sensitive and specific for detecting splenic injury, with sensitivity and specificity ranging from 96% to 100%. CT findings may include splenic lacerations, subcapsular or intraparenchymal haematomas, and evidence of active haemorrhage [7]. The AAST grading scale is commonly employed to assess the severity of splenic injury and guide appropriate clinical management [7]. Recognition of the full spectrum of post-colonoscopy complications is essential for timely diagnosis and effective treatment. CT imaging plays a pivotal role in the evaluation of these complications, particularly in cases of suspected splenic injury.

title: Iliopsoas hibernoma
clinical_history: A 43-year-old female patient presented to the emergency department with acute cholecystitis. During imaging work-up, an incidental iliopsoas mass was detected on CT. MRI was subsequently performed for further characterisation.
imaging_findings: CT shows a well-defined, complex iliopsoas mass containing fat and soft-tissue components, demonstrating heterogeneous enhancement and prominent internal vessels (Figures 1a and 1b). MRI reveals an encapsulated lesion with high T1 signal intensity, slightly lower than subcutaneous fat, and heterogeneously high T2 signal intensity, with only partial fat suppression (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, 2d, 2e, and 2f). It exhibits relatively homogeneous hypervascular enhancement with curvilinear branching septations, with no restricted diffusion.
discussion: Background Hibernomas are rare benign tumours originating from brown adipose tissue, accounting for less than 1% of all lipomatous tumours. They typically affect adults, usually between 20 and 50 years of age, with a slight male predominance. Common locations include the thigh, shoulder, back, and neck, whereas involvement of the iliopsoas muscle, as presented in this case, is extremely rare [1]. Clinical Perspective These lesions are frequently asymptomatic and discovered incidentally during imaging studies performed for unrelated conditions. Given their benign nature, accurate imaging characterisation is essential to avoid unnecessary aggressive management and patient anxiety. Thus, it is crucial to highlight imaging features suggesting benignity to guide clinical decision-making appropriately [2]. Imaging Perspective CT typically shows a well-circumscribed lesion containing fat and soft-tissue densities, often along with prominent enhancing vessels indicative of its hypervascularity. MRI is the gold standard, demonstrating lesions with high signal intensity on T1-weighted images, slightly lower than subcutaneous fat, and heterogeneously high signal intensity on T2-weighted images, with incomplete fat suppression. Prominent intratumoural vessels manifest as curvilinear structures on T2-weighted sequences, distinguishing hibernomas from other lipomatous lesions [3,4]. Hibernomas typically present a smooth, well-defined capsule without signs of infiltration or invasion into adjacent structures. Features suggestive of malignancy—irregular margins, infiltrative growth, nodular non-fatty areas, marked size progression, restricted diffusion—are generally absent. However, occasional complexity and heterogeneity (e.g., cystic areas, incomplete fat suppression, intense enhancement) can overlap with malignant lipomatous tumours; hence, histopathological confirmation is generally reserved for cases with atypical imaging features or relevant clinical symptoms [4,5]. Outcome Management hinges on the correlation of imaging and clinical data. Lesions that display textbook imaging features and are asymptomatic can be safely managed with conservative imaging follow-up, sparing the patient invasive procedures. When atypical features or symptoms raise concern for well-differentiated liposarcoma, core-needle biopsy is recommended; the specimen typically demonstrates multivacuolated brown fat cells with strong UCP1 immunoreactivity, confirming hibernoma and ruling out malignancy [5]. Surgical excision is reserved for equivocal, symptomatic or enlarging masses, or when definitive treatment is preferred; when performed, complete resection is curative and recurrences are exceedingly rare, resulting in an excellent prognosis [6,7]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Hibernomas are benign, hypervascular, lipomatous tumours originating from brown adipose tissue. Characteristic imaging features include encapsulation, heterogeneous fatty content, and prominent intralesional vessels, especially evident on MRI. Definitive diagnosis typically requires histopathological examination, but conservative follow-up is appropriate when imaging features are unequivocally benign.

title: Bilateral pelvic cystic masses: Not always ovarian in origin
clinical_history: A 68-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of progressive abdominal distension and vague pelvic discomfort. Physical examination revealed a palpable midline abdominal mass. Routine laboratory investigations were unremarkable. Abdominopelvic CT was performed for further evaluation.
imaging_findings: Unenhanced abdominopelvic CT demonstrated two large, well-defined, predominantly cystic pelvic masses (Figure 1). The right-sided lesion (22 × 15 × 19 cm), centred in the cul-de-sac and extending into the right iliac fossa, was intraperitoneal, displacing small-bowel loops superiorly and the uterus postero-leftward while preserving a fat plane with the right psoas muscle (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). The left-sided mass (15 × 17 × 15 cm) occupied the left flank/iliac fossa, had a slightly irregular thick wall, and abutted the left psoas muscle, kidney, aorta and iliac vessels without an intervening fat plane, displacing ileo-jejunal loops anteromedially—features consistent with a retroperitoneal origin (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c). Compression of the left ureter produced moderate pelvicalyceal and proximal ureteral dilatation (Figure 4). A morphologically normal left ovary was identified caudal to the mass (Figure 5), whereas the right ovary was obscured. No ascites, peritoneal implants or pathological lymph nodes were present.
discussion: Background and Clinical Perspective Most bilateral pelvic cystic masses are presumed adnexal. In this patient, only the right lesion was an ovarian serous cystadenoma—a benign intraperitoneal epithelial tumour that typically appears as a thin-walled uni or multilocular water-attenuation cyst [1]. The left mass proved to be an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour (IMT), a rare mesenchymal neoplasm with intermediate malignant potential and ~ 25% local-recurrence rate, preferentially arising in the retroperitoneum [2]. Because both entities present with nonspecific abdominal distension or discomfort, imaging must establish the compartment of origin before surgery. Gynaecologic teams manage intraperitoneal adnexal disease, whereas retroperitoneal tumours often require vascular or urologic expertise; misclassification risks incomplete resection or unsuspected vascular/ureteric injury. Imaging Pearls Normal-ovary sign – visualisation of a morphologically normal left ovary caudal to the left-flank mass immediately excluded an adnexal origin for that lesion. Intraperitoneal/ovarian (right) mass – cul-de-sac epicentre, preserved fat planes with psoas/kidneys/vessels; may show an ovarian “claw” sign [1,3]. Retroperitoneal (left) mass – obtuse angles with posterior parietes, loss of psoas fat stripe, encasement of proximal ureter causing ipsilateral ureterohydronephrosis, direct contact with aorta/kidney, and anterior displacement of ileo-jejunal loops with a clean cleavage plane—the “embedded-organ” sign [4]. Morphology – IMT exhibited a thicker, irregular wall and heterogeneous soft-tissue stranding; when contrast is given, enhancement is usually peripheral or heterogeneous [3]. The serous cystadenoma remained uniformly cystic with a thin wall. Outcome Histology confirmed ciliated serous epithelium in the ovarian cyst and ALK-positive myofibroblastic proliferation in the retroperitoneal mass [2,5]. Both lesions were resected en bloc. Serous cystadenoma is cured by oophorectomy. IMT prognosis is excellent after complete excision, yet imaging follow-up is advised because 15–25 % recur. ALK inhibitors (e.g., crizotinib) are an option in unresectable or metastatic disease [5]. Our patient remained disease-free at 24-month surveillance, and the left hydronephrosis has resolved [6]. Take Home Message “Bilateral” pelvic masses may occupy different compartments—trace fat planes and seek a normal ovary. Loss of retroperitoneal fat planes, ureterohydronephrosis and fixation to psoas/kidney strongly suggest a retroperitoneal origin, even on unenhanced CT. Accurate localisation prevents surgical surprises and ensures referral to the appropriate subspecialty team.

title: Thyroid tissue where? A rare case of struma ovarii
clinical_history: A 52-year-old female with a history of right mastectomy underwent a routine abdominopelvic CT angiogram to identify any suitable perforators for her elective right deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) flap breast reconstruction. The patient’s CA125 and thyroid function tests were normal.
imaging_findings: Arterial phase computed tomography (CT) identified an incidental 7.5 × 5 cm bilobed lesion in the midline and left posterior pelvis. The medial locule had fluid attenuation, while the lateral component contained hyperattenuating material (hyperdense fluid or solid material) (Figure 1). Transvaginal ultrasound confirmed a biloculated cystic lesion from the left adnexa into the pouch of Douglas. It contained simple anechoic fluid surrounding echogenic material with scattered echogenic foci, some showing comet-tail artefacts consistent with colloid (Figure 2). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a biloculated lesion with thin, minimally enhancing walls and septation, and a tiny avidly enhancing solid focus at the posterior septation. The medial locule had a simple fluid signal with dependent debris, and the lateral locule showed low T2 and mildly high T1 signal, suggesting viscous colloid (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d). Limited surgical excision was performed. Histology revealed macro and microfollicles containing colloid, consistent with struma ovarii.
discussion: Background Struma ovarii is a rare ovarian teratoma composed entirely or predominantly (>50%) of mature thyroid tissue [1,2]. While typically benign, malignant transformation occurs in about 5% of cases [3]. Functionally, it can mimic thyroid tissue and occasionally cause hyperthyroidism. It arises from totipotent germ cells capable of differentiating into thyroid tissue [4]. Clinical Perspective Patients often present with nonspecific symptoms such as abdominal pain, a palpable mass, or distension. Rarely, signs of hyperthyroidism, such as tachycardia or weight loss, may appear if the thyroid tissue is hyperfunctional [1]. It accounts for 0.3–1% of all ovarian tumours and 2–3% of mature cystic teratomas [2]. Imaging Perspective Imaging plays a key role in identifying the mass and suggesting a benign origin. Early radiological suspicion can prevent unnecessary oncologic surgery, particularly when clinical suspicion is low [2]. Struma ovarii poses a diagnostic challenge due to its variable imaging features. Unlike typical teratomas, it lacks macroscopic fat. It often appears as a multicystic mass, with or without solid components. On ultrasound, it may be solid, cystic, or mixed; echogenic foci with comet-tail artefacts may represent colloid but are subtle and often overlooked [2]. A proposed ultrasound feature is a smooth, vascular, echogenic solid component known as “struma pearls”, though this is nonspecific [5]. Non-contrast CT may show a multicystic, hyperattenuating mass with wall enhancement [2]. MRI offers better characterisation, revealing multiloculated cystic lesions with solid areas that vary in T1 and T2 signal intensity depending on colloid content. Post-contrast enhancement of solid components may mimic malignancy. Iodine-123 planar or single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) may show increased uptake due to functioning thyroid tissue [4]. Definitive diagnosis requires histopathology from surgical excision. Outcome Most cases are benign and managed with surgical resection of the affected ovary. Malignant cases may require thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine therapy. Prognosis is excellent for benign tumours with low recurrence after surgery [3]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Struma ovarii is a rare ovarian germ cell tumour predominantly made of thyroid tissue. Characteristic imaging features should raise radiologic suspicion. Multimodal imaging, clinical correlation, and multidisciplinary input are key to accurate diagnosis and appropriate management. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files. Special thanks to Dr Rebecca Wiles and colleagues at the Liverpool Women's Hospital regional Gynae-Oncology multidisciplinary team for reviewing this case and sharing their expert opinion regarding imaging and management.

title: Unmasking Morquio syndrome: The not-so-subtle subtleties on imaging
clinical_history: An 8-year-old boy presented with an insidious onset of right palmar contracture without any history of trauma. Clinical examination revealed short stature, prominent frontal bossing, and hepatosplenomegaly, while cognitive function remained intact. Laboratory investigations excluded endocrine pathology. Subsequent imaging was undertaken to assess for nutritional bone disease, with a focus on rickets.
imaging_findings: Skeletal survey revealed multiple subtle yet characteristic abnormalities. Radiographs of the wrists (Figure 1) demonstrated mild metaphyseal flaring of the distal radius and ulna bilaterally, along with bullet-shaped 2nd and 3rd proximal metacarpal bases. There was a marked delay in carpal bone ossification, with small, reduced carpal bones for the patient’s age. Lateral radiograph of the dorso-lumbar spine (Figure 2) revealed multilevel vertebra plana, with central anterior beaking. Cervical spine CT demonstrated a J-shaped sella (Figure 3a) and fracture of odontoid (Figures 3b and 3c), indicating cervical spine instability. Pelvic radiograph showed flared iliac bones with characteristic inferior constriction, giving the near classic “wineglass” appearance (Figure 4a). The acetabular cavities were enlarged and shallow, with subtly dysplastic femoral epiphyses. Radiographs of the knees revealed metaphyseal flaring of the distal femora and proximal tibiae with minor genu valgum (Figure 4b). Chest and abdomen radiograph showed subtle anterior broadening of the ribs (Figures 5a and 5b). Collectively, these findings suggested a diagnosis within the spectrum of mucopolysaccharidoses, with features most consistent with Morquio syndrome (MPS IV), ruling out nutritional rickets.
discussion: Background Morquio syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type IV or MPS IV) is a rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase (GALNS), which impairs the degradation of keratan sulfate and chondroitin-6-sulfate. The resultant accumulation of glycosaminoglycans leads to progressive systemic involvement, with predominant skeletal manifestations [1,2]. First described in 1929 by Morquio and Brailsford, its incidence ranges from 1 in 75,000 to 1 in 450,000 live births depending on ethnicity [2,3]. Clinical Perspective The disorder typically manifests in early childhood, often between 1 and 3 years of age [2]. Classic phenotypic features include short stature, pectus carinatum, kyphoscoliosis, genu valgum, hypermobile joints, and coarse facial features. Despite the extensive somatic involvement, intelligence is preserved, distinguishing Morquio syndrome from other types of mucopolysaccharidoses [2,4]. Odontoid hypoplasia and ligamentous laxity predispose to atlantoaxial instability, which may result in cervical cord compression and myelopathy [3,5]. Other systemic findings include hepatosplenomegaly, recurrent respiratory infections, obstructive sleep apnoea, valvular heart disease, corneal clouding, and characteristic dental anomalies such as enamel hypoplasia and caries [4,5]. In contrast to classical cases with overt phenotypic features, our patient exhibited a relatively subtle presentation. The facial characteristics were not prominently coarse, and the diagnosis was not suspected clinically until imaging findings raised the possibility. This underscores the importance of radiological vigilance even in seemingly routine investigations such as wrist X-rays for short stature or suspected rickets. Imaging Perspective Radiography plays a pivotal role in early diagnosis. Skeletal survey typically reveals platyspondyly with central anterior beaking, J-shaped sella, and odontoid hypoplasia-posing risk for atlantoaxial instability [1,5]. Wrist radiographs may show bullet-shaped proximal metacarpals and delayed carpal ossification, while the pelvis classically demonstrates flared iliac wings with inferior constriction creating the characteristic “wineglass” appearance and shallow acetabula [1,5]. Lower limb radiographs reveal metaphyseal flaring and valgus deformity of distal femora and proximal tibiae [1,3]. These features collectively reflect dysostosis multiplex and guide diagnostic confidence. Outcome Although morbidity in Morquio syndrome commonly results from cervical myelopathy, respiratory complications, and valvular heart disease, our case was detected early during work-up for isolated palmar contracture. The diagnosis was supported by positive urinary glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) and confirmed via enzyme assay showing GALNS deficiency. The patient was managed conservatively, with the contracture addressed and no active intervention required. He was advised to have regular follow-ups to monitor for emerging skeletal or systemic complications. Genetic testing was not performed due to financial constraints, but the enzyme assay confirming GALNS deficiency was considered diagnostic. Take Home Message Morquio syndrome (MPS IV) is a rare lysosomal storage disorder characterised by preserved cognition and distinctive skeletal abnormalities. Radiological recognition of subtle yet typical features is crucial for early detection, with the diagnosis confirmed by enzyme assays. Timely, multidisciplinary management improves prognosis and functional outcomes. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Haematometrocolpos in an 11-year-old girl with intermittent hypogastric pain
clinical_history: An 11-year-old premenarche girl presented with a 3-week history of intermittent hypogastric pain, not being able to sleep for more than two hours at a time for the last 5 days. Clinical examination revealed a palpable pelvic mass and suprapubic tenderness. The patient had no other relevant findings on physical examination. Blood and urine tests were all within normal limits.
imaging_findings: A transabdominal pelvic ultrasound was performed and revealed a significant distension of the vagina, measuring 6.8 x 8.3 x 15.3 cm, with echogenic material occupying its lumen (approximately 450 ml). The distension extended to the uterus, which showed hyperechogenic material inside its lumen. Both annexes were of normal appearance. There was no evidence of acute appendicitis, hydronephrosis or other significant findings.
discussion: Background Haematocolpos refers to the accumulation of menstrual blood in the vaginal canal, usually due to an imperforate hymen. The term haematometrocolpos is used when uterine distention is also present [1]. The incidence of haematocolpos associated with an imperforate hymen is approximately 0.14% [2]. Similar features may be observed in various Müllerian duct anomalies (MDAs), such as a low transverse vaginal septum. However, unlike a vaginal septum, an imperforate hymen is not a true MDA but rather a pathological persistence of the hymenal membrane [3]. Clinical Perspective Most infants remain asymptomatic and undiagnosed until menarche, when they present with cyclic pelvic pain and primary amenorrhea. Up to 46–58% of the cases also present urinary retention. On physical examination, the vaginal opening reveals a bulging, bluish membrane that is transilluminable. After the obstruction is relieved, patients generally experience normal fertility and favourable obstetric outcomes [2,4]. Imaging Perspective A transabdominal pelvic ultrasound shows a distended vagina filled with fluid containing low-level internal echoes, consistent with blood. The uterus may appear mildly enlarged, with fluid in the endometrial cavity suggestive of early haematometra. These findings are consistent with haematocolpos caused by an imperforate hymen [1,2,5]. Ultrasound is the preferred initial imaging modality in adolescent patients due to its availability, safety, and ability to evaluate pelvic anatomy. MRI may be considered when the diagnosis is uncertain or if complex Müllerian anomalies are suspected [3]. Outcome The diagnosis is usually confirmed surgically via hymenotomy, which allows the drainage of the retained blood. The patient usually recovers well after the procedure and reports normal menstruation at follow-up. Early imaging-based diagnosis is essential for prompt treatment and for preventing complications such as endometriosis, chronic pelvic pain, or reproductive sequelae. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Haematocolpos should be considered in girls with primary amenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, and urinary symptoms. Ultrasound is usually sufficient for diagnosis, revealing a fluid-filled, echogenic, distended vagina. Early recognition ensures prompt surgical treatment and reduces long-term complications. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Mixed malignant ovarian germ cell tumour
clinical_history: A 23-year-old woman presented with two weeks of abdominal distension, pelvic pain and urinary frequency. Emergency thoraco-abdominal computed tomography (CT) was performed, followed shortly by dedicated pelvic MRI for loco-regional characterisation.
imaging_findings: Initial contrast-enhanced pelvic CT (Figures 1a and 1b) demonstrated a 17 × 16 × 12 cm, predominantly solid, left retro-uterine mass with heterogeneous enhancement on the left ovary, anterior displacement of the uterus, and compression of both distal ureters, resulting in moderate bilateral hydroureteronephrosis. No macroscopic fat, calcification or pathological lymph-node enlargement was identified. Subsequent pelvic MRI (Figures 2a and 2b) showed mainly solid tissue with intermediate T2 signal (Figures 2a and 2b) and avid post-gadolinium enhancement (Figure 3), containing scattered cystic-necrotic foci. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) showed marked hyperintensity of the solid components with low ADC values, consistent with high cellularity (Figures 4a and 4b). The tumour–uterus interface was smooth, and the right ovary appeared normal, displaced anteriorly. Ascites was minimal and confined to the pouch of Douglas. No peritoneal implants or pathological lymphadenopathy were identified on either CT or MRI.
discussion: Background Malignant ovarian germ cell tumours (OGCTs) comprise less than 5% of ovarian cancers and predominate in adolescents [1,2]. Mixed OGCTs contain two or more malignant subtypes, while embryonal carcinoma, yolk-sac tumour, choriocarcinoma and immature teratoma are recognised components [3]. Clinical Perspective Rapid growth produces pelvic pain, distension, or acute abdomen. Serum β-hCG, AFP, and LDH profiles suggest underlying components and enable surveillance. Early recognition is vital because platinum-based chemotherapy renders cure rates higher than 90% [1]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound detects an adnexal mass, but CT and MRI stage the disease. Mixed OGCTs are usually huge (> 15 cm), predominantly solid, and highly heterogeneous; cystic, haemorrhagic, necrotic or fatty foci mirror their composite histology [2]. MRI best delineates tissue composition, capsular integrity, bowel/uterine interface and ureteric encasement, guiding fertility-sparing surgery. A complete CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is essential for staging because it assesses retroperitoneal lymph nodes, hepatic involvement and potential pulmonary metastases—findings that become particularly relevant when a choriocarcinomatous component is present. Outcome Standard treatment is unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with full staging, followed by platinum-based chemotherapy (BEP). Fertility can be preserved in most stage I–II cases. Our patient underwent fertility-sparing resection. She remains disease-free under surveillance. Take-Home Message / Teaching Points Large, heterogeneous solid ovarian masses in young women strongly suggest malignant ovarian germ cell tumour (OGCT). MRI characterises composite tissue elements and local extent, crucial for conservative surgery. Whole-body CT is mandatory for nodal and distant staging. Mixed OGCTs are aggressive yet highly curable with timely multidisciplinary therapy. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
