title: Swapping artefact mimicking iliac bone lesion: A diagnostic MRI pitfall
clinical_history: A 29-year-old patient with a history of chronic hip pain and previous spinal fusion surgery for Bertolotti's syndrome presented with persistent discomfort despite surgical treatment (Figure 1). Due to ongoing symptoms, an MRI of the sacroiliac joints was performed to evaluate for any potential underlying pathology.
imaging_findings: MRI using the Dixon technique demonstrated in the axial sequence (Figures 2a and 2b) a well-defined, geographic high-signal lesion in the right iliac bone on the water-only images, which could easily be mistaken for bone marrow oedema or an infiltrative process. However, the lesion was not visible on other sequences, including T1-weighted and STIR images (Figures 3a and 3b), where true marrow pathology would typically be expected. This discrepancy suggested that the observed signal alteration was due to a fat–water swapping artefact rather than a real osseous abnormality.
discussion: The Dixon method, also known as chemical shift-encoded imaging, is an advanced MRI technique that provides fat suppression and has become an alternative to traditional fat-saturated and STIR sequences in musculoskeletal imaging [1]. This technique is based on the acquisition of in and out-of-phase images, from which water-only and/or fat-only images are generated through post-processing calculation [1,2]. However, Dixon sequences are susceptible to fat–water swapping artefacts, which can lead to diagnostic pitfalls [3,4]. In this case, MRI using the Dixon technique showed in the axial sequence a well-defined, geographic high-signal lesion in the right iliac bone, which might be easily misinterpreted as bone marrow oedema or an infiltrative process. However, the “lesion” was not visible on other sequences, including T1-weighted and STIR images, where true marrow pathology would typically be expected. This discrepancy suggested that the observed signal alteration was caused by a fat–water swapping artefact rather than a real bone abnormality. Fat–water swapping artefacts occur due to the inherent ambiguity in differentiating fat and water signals in the presence of field heterogeneity [4]. In this case, the patient’s history of spinal fusion surgery likely contributed to local magnetic field inhomogeneity, exacerbating the risk of misregistration errors, resulting in the fat signal being assigned to the water image and the water signal being assigned to the fat image. Such artefacts are common in regions near metallic implants, where magnetic susceptibility variations interfere with accurate fat–water separation. Recognising fat–water swapping artefacts is crucial to prevent misdiagnosis [5,6]. One key strategy is to correlate findings across the other sequences, ensuring that suspected abnormalities are consistently visible on T1-weighted, STIR, or fat-saturated images. Additionally, reviewing the in-phase and out-of-phase source images can help confirm whether the signal changes are real or artefact-related. In clinical practice, incorporating non-Dixon fat-suppressed acquisitions or using multi-point Dixon techniques can further mitigate the risk of these artefacts. In conclusion, this case emphasises the importance of recognising swapping artefacts when interpreting Dixon sequence MRI. The presence of a geographic high-signal lesion on water-only images, without correlation on the other sequences, should be carefully evaluated to avoid unnecessary concern for bone pathology. Being aware of this artefact helps to ensure the right diagnosis and optimal patient management. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Glioneuronal tumour of the posterior fossa in a young male
clinical_history: A 25-year-old male presented with headache and giddiness for 3–4 months. He previously experienced diplopia for one month, which resolved following a right-sided medium-pressure ventriculoperitoneal shunt surgery 1 year ago.
imaging_findings: MRI revealed a predominantly cystic lesion with minimal solid components, measuring approximately 24 × 33 × 73 mm, centred in the lower fourth ventricle. It appeared T1 hypointense (Figure 3a) and heterogeneously T2 hyperintense, with multiple fluid-intensity cystic areas (Figure 1a). The solid areas demonstrated minimal post-contrast enhancement (Figure 3b), while the cystic portions remained non-enhancing. Mild diffusion restriction on diffusion weighted imaging–apparent diffusion coefficient (DWI–ADC) sequences (Figures 4a and 4b), and blooming foci were noted on fast field echo sequences, with corresponding PHASE hyperintensities, suggesting haemosiderin deposition (Figures 5a and 5b). CT screening showed tiny calcific foci. The lesion caused anterior displacement of the posterior pons (Figure 1a), medulla, and upper cervical cord, and abutted the cerebellar hemispheres, vermis, and both middle and inferior cerebellar peduncles. Posteroinferiorly, it extended into the cisterna magna via the foramen of Magendie and into the spinal canal up to 28 mm below McRae’s line. Lateral extension into both cerebellopontine angles was noted via the foramina of Luschka, with associated mild upstream hydrocephalus (Figures 1b and 2a).
discussion: Background Rosette-forming glioneuronal tumours (RGNTs) are rare, typically benign (WHO grade I) neoplasms, characterised by a biphasic histological architecture composed of both glial and neuronal elements. These tumours predominantly affect young adults, with a mean age of approximately 30 years, and exhibit a predilection for the posterior fossa, especially the fourth ventricle [1]. Histologically, the presence of neurocytic rosettes and perivascular pseudorosettes distinguishes RGNTs from other glioneuronal tumours. Although generally considered indolent, RGNTs have occasionally demonstrated aggressive behaviour, including malignant transformation and cerebrospinal fluid dissemination, underscoring the importance of early diagnosis and close follow-up [3]. Clinical Perspective Clinically, patients often present with nonspecific symptoms such as headache, nausea, vomiting, and gait disturbances, primarily resulting from obstructive hydrocephalus due to mass effect on cerebrospinal fluid pathways. In this case, the patient exhibited headache, giddiness, and transient diplopia prior to surgical intervention. Imaging Perspective Imaging plays a pivotal role in diagnosis and management by localising the lesion, evaluating its extent, and assisting in preoperative planning. MRI is the modality of choice, with RGNTs typically appearing as well-demarcated, solid-cystic lesions with T1 hypointensity and T2 hyperintensity [1,2]. Minimal post-contrast enhancement is commonly seen in solid components, while cystic regions remain non-enhancing. Some cases show the so-called “green bell pepper sign”, indicating peripheral enhancement with central low signal [1]. CT imaging may supplement MRI findings by detecting calcifications within the lesion and assessing bony structures. Outcome Definitive diagnosis relies on histopathological confirmation, as in this patient, where surgical resection revealed classic features of RGNT, including neurocytic rosettes and perivascular pseudorosettes. Gross total resection is typically curative, with a favourable prognosis and low recurrence risk [2]. In this case, the patient underwent successful surgical removal of the tumour, with resolution of preoperative symptoms and histopathological confirmation of RGNT. Timely imaging and surgical intervention are critical in managing RGNTs effectively and avoiding long-term neurological complications. Take Home Message / Teaching Points RGNTs (Rosette-forming glioneuronal tumours) are rare, benign tumours that primarily affect young adults and are commonly located in the fourth ventricle. Clinical symptoms are often nonspecific and result from increased intracranial pressure due to obstructive hydrocephalus. Imaging features, including the “green bell pepper sign”, can aid in diagnosis but are not pathognomonic. Surgical resection is the treatment of choice, with a generally favourable prognosis. Awareness of RGNT’s radiological and histopathological characteristics is essential for accurate diagnosis and management.

title: Sudden cardiac arrest revealing subarachnoid haemorrhage and brain death
clinical_history: A 50-year-old female was found unresponsive at home, experiencing pulseless electrical arrest. Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) was achieved after cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). She had no preceding trauma, headache, or cardiac disease history. Minor self-resolving chest pain episodes at rest were reported two weeks earlier. Post-resuscitation, examination revealed fixed dilated pupils and absent brainstem reflexes.
imaging_findings: Non-contrast CT head (Figure 1) demonstrated moderate-to-large volume subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH), centred at the Circle of Willis, with intraventricular extension into the occipital horns and fourth ventricle. There was basal cisternal partial effacement, mild cerebellar tonsillar descent, and no midline shift noted. CT angiography (CTA) with 60 ml iohexol intravenous injection captured both arterial and late venous phases revealing total absence of intracranial arterial opacification involving bilateral internal carotid and vertebral arteries, with preserved filling of external carotid branches (Figure 2). Findings fulfilled the strict 10-point CTA scale for cerebral circulatory arrest, i.e., brain death (Figure 3) [1]. No calvarial fractures or mass lesions were identified. Visualised upper thorax demonstrated non-specific lung ground-glass opacities and rib fractures attributed to CPR. Overall, imaging confirmed diffuse cerebral injury secondary to SAH with associated cerebral circulatory arrest, consistent with brain death.
discussion: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is a life-threatening emergency, classically presenting with sudden-onset severe headache. However, in rare cases, SAH may trigger abrupt cardiac arrest through neurogenic mechanisms, mediated by a massive catecholamine surge leading to myocardial dysfunction and arrhythmias [2,3]. This patient presented without prior neurologic symptoms, and initial cardiac arrest diverted suspicion away from a primary neurological cause. However, coma, fixed pupils and absent brainstem reflexes persisted after ROSC, prompting urgent neuroimaging. Non-contrast CT revealed diffuse basal SAH with intraventricular extension, loss of grey-white differentiation and 3.8 mm tonsillar herniation—surrogates of critically elevated intracranial pressure and global ischaemia. Multiphasic CT angiography (CTA) performed with a 60 ml iohexol bolus captured arterial (20 s) and late venous (~ 60 s) phases. The CTA study demonstrated the classic imaging signature of brain death, fulfilling the validated 10-point CTA scale for cerebral circulatory arrest by Frampas and Sawicki, i.e., complete non-opacification of intracranial internal carotid arteries, vertebrobasilar axis, bilateral A3, M4, P2 segments and the deep venous system, while external carotid branches opacified normally, confirming optimal contrast timing and cerebral circulatory arrest [1,4,5]. Among these criteria, absent deep venous filling is regarded as the earliest and most sensitive CTA marker, with 98–100 % sensitivity when a late phase is acquired [5,6]. Ancillary imaging is indicated when clinical determination of death is limited by sedatives, hypothermia or inability to perform apnoea testing. Compared with radionuclide or catheter angiography, CTA is rapid, widely available and non-invasive, and current evidence shows no detrimental effect of iodinated contrast on transplantable organs [5,6]. False negatives have been described after decompressive craniectomy or large skull defects; neither was present in this case. Despite maximal neurocritical care—including targeted temperature management and vasoactive support—the imaging and neurological findings were irreversible in our patient. Following multidisciplinary discussion, life-sustaining measures were withdrawn. This case underscores two teaching points: When coma persists after ROSC, early CT/CTA can simultaneously identify the aetiology and, when criteria are met, provide definitive confirmation of brain death. Catastrophic intracranial haemorrhage should remain on the differential for sudden cardiac arrest of unclear origin. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Hepatic arteriovenous malformations in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
clinical_history: A 55-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with long-standing recurrent epistaxis and progressive fatigue. Physical examination revealed mucocutaneous telangiectasias on the nasal mucosa and tongue, as well as mild hepatomegaly. Laboratory tests showed iron-deficiency anaemia and mildly altered liver function tests, with cholestasis but no hyperbilirubinemia.
imaging_findings: Colour-Doppler abdominal ultrasound revealed multiple dilated arterial vessels in both liver lobes, corresponding to branches of the hepatic artery, with one vessel forming a direct communication with the main portal vein (Figures 1a and 1b). Subsequent contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated diffuse dilatation of intrahepatic arterial branches and early filling of the dilated hepatic veins during arterial phase, suggestive of arteriovenous shunting, and multiple small hypervascular nodules consistent with hepatic telangiectasias. Mild intrahepatic biliary duct dilatation was also noted, likely due to extrinsic compression by dilated vessels (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). Further evaluation with MRI confirmed the presence of intrahepatic arteriovenous malformations. Post-contrast T1-weighted Dixon sequences and MR angiography provided superior characterisation of the vascular anomalies, ruling out portal vein thrombosis and parenchymal changes typical of chronic liver disease (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), also known as Rendu–Osler–Weber disease, is an autosomal dominant vascular disorder characterised by the development of mucocutaneous telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) in various organs. Hepatic involvement is common and may remain asymptomatic or lead to complications such as high-output cardiac failure, portal hypertension, or biliary disease in the form of ischemic bile duct necrosis and sepsis [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Diagnosis of HHT is based on the Curaçao criteria: spontaneous and recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias at characteristic sites (lips, oral cavity, fingers, nose), visceral AVMs (pulmonary, cerebral, hepatic), and a first-degree relative with HHT. Meeting three or more criteria confirms the diagnosis. In this case, the patient presented with long-standing epistaxis, visible mucosal telangiectasias, and hepatic vascular anomalies on imaging—fulfilling at least three criteria. Although there was no known family history, the diagnosis was clinically well supported [2]. Imaging Perspective Imaging plays a pivotal role in detecting, characterising, and monitoring hepatic involvement in HHT. Ultrasound, particularly with Doppler, is often the first-line modality. It may show dilated hepatic arteries, early venous filling due to shunting, and turbulent flow. It is useful for screening and follow-up. Contrast-enhanced CT offers better spatial resolution and can reveal hypertrophied hepatic arteries, early enhancement of the hepatic and portal veins, and small hypervascular nodules consistent with telangiectasias. It is also helpful to assess for biliary compression and exclude mass lesions. MRI is the modality of choice for detailed vascular characterisation. T1-weighted sequences with fat suppression (e.g., Dixon) and post-contrast imaging can identify telangiectatic foci and define abnormal vascular channels. MR angiography is valuable for mapping AVMs, visualising feeding arteries and draining veins, and evaluating shunt severity. MRI also allows exclusion of cirrhosis, Budd–Chiari syndrome, or hepatic neoplasms through analysis of parenchymal signal, architecture, and vascular anatomy [1,3]. Outcome Due to the absence of cardiac overload, portal hypertension, or biliary complications, conservative management was chosen. Clinical and imaging follow-up was recommended to monitor disease progression and assess for future complications requiring intervention or multidisciplinary management. Take Home Message Multimodal imaging, especially MRI and CT, is essential for the accurate diagnosis and management of hepatic vascular involvement in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT). It also aids in excluding other hepatic pathologies and tracking disease progression [1–3].

title: Primary bone lymphoma
clinical_history: A previously healthy 3-year-old boy presented with recurrent atraumatic pain and refusal to walk for several weeks. The right proximal lower leg was swollen, and mobilisation was painful. Laboratory analysis at admission showed increased white blood cell count of 12.6 x 10³/mm³ and C-reactive protein of 20.2 mg/l.
imaging_findings: Radiography showed an irregularly moth-eaten mixed osteolytic-sclerotic lesion with a wide zone of transition in the proximal tibial diaphysis. The cortex was permeated with a transverse pathological fracture, interrupted lamellar periosteal reaction, and soft tissue swelling (Figures 1a and 1b). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed extensive bone marrow replacement in the proximal tibia with adjacent soft tissue mass showing heterogeneous contrast enhancement, cortical permeation, bone destruction with focal cortical breakthrough (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d). Bone marrow changes were hypointense on T1-weighted images (WI) and heterogeneous hyperintense on STIR and fat-suppressed PD images. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography–computed tomography (FDG PET–CT) scan showed markedly increased uptake in the proximal right tibia, adjacent soft tissue, and right popliteal, inguinal, iliac and retroperitoneal lymph nodes (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c). Other distant metastases were absent.
discussion: Background Primary bone lymphoma (PBL) is a subtype of lymphoma primarily originating from the bone. It may either present as a solitary lesion, with or without involvement of regional lymph nodes, or affect multiple bones without nodal or visceral disease [1]. PBL comprises about 3% of all malignant bone tumours and 4–5% of all extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHL). PBL is mostly seen in adults in their fourth or fifth decade [2]. Skeletal involvement in malignant lymphoma in the paediatric population is uncommon. The majority of PBLs are non-Hodgkin lymphomas [1]. Clinical Perspective PBL may arise in any part of the skeleton. In the appendicular skeleton, the metadiaphysis of femur, tibia and humerus are most often involved [3]. Pain and swelling of the involved site are two of the most common clinical manifestations of PBL. Other less common presentations include inability to bear weight due to a pathological fracture and systemic “B-type” symptoms including fever, weight loss and night sweats. Laboratory results are usually unremarkable. Imaging Perspective Imaging features are nonspecific. Radiography may be unremarkable or may show a lytic, sclerotic or mixed lesion, lamellated or discontinuous periosteal reaction, cortical destruction, pathological fracture, and soft tissue mass. A lytic destructive lesion with a moth-eaten and/or permeative wide zone of transition is most common [4]. CT scan may be used for lesion detection in anatomic complex areas and is valuable for guiding percutaneous biopsy [2,4]. MRI is the method of choice for local staging and evaluation of bone and soft tissue involvement. Bone marrow involvement is hypointense on T1-WI, and of intermediate to high signal intensity on T2-WI and short tau inversion recovery (STIR) depending on the cellular density. The lesion enhances after gadolinium contrast administration [2]. FDG PET–CT is useful in staging and restaging PBL. Whole-body MRI including diffusion-weighted imaging may also be used. Outcome A solitary osseous lesion corresponds to stage I. In stage II, there is a solitary bony lesion with regional lymph nodes, whereas distal nodal involvement is seen in stage III disease. Multifocal bone disease is classified as stage IV [5]. The prognosis is directly correlated to the stage of disease and the age of the patient, with a better prognosis for the lower stage, and in children when compared to adults. Histopathological examination with immunohistochemical and molecular techniques is mandatory for final diagnosis [1,4]. Distinguishing osseous NHL from other bone tumours is important because the former has a better prognosis and different treatment. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Neurosarcoidosis presenting with longitudinally extensive myelitis and the spinal “trident sign”
clinical_history: A 66-year-old woman developed progressive neck pain, headache, and ascending lower-limb paraesthesia over 3 months that culminated in sudden bilateral leg weakness and ataxia. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed lymphocytic pleocytosis with hyperproteinorrachia, and a 2024 mediastinal node biopsy revealed non-necrotising granulomas. Her history includes uterine ablation (2006) and sinus surgery (1995).
imaging_findings: Sagittal T2-weighted MRI of the spine (Figure 1) revealed diffuse hyperintensity and swelling from C2 to T10 with a sharp transition at T11. Post-gadolinium T1 images (Figure 2) showed confluent dorsal subpial and central canal enhancement, producing the axial “trident sign”. There was patchy nodular enhancement involving the posterior and circumferential pial surfaces. The conus was spared. Brain MRI demonstrated two punctate cortical–subcortical enhancing foci without mass effect (Figures 3a and 3b). CT chest (Figures 4a and 4b) confirmed bulky right paratracheal and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Compared with prior studies (December 2020), cord swelling and enhancement were mildly reduced after steroid therapy.
discussion: Sarcoidosis is an uncommon multisystem granulomatous disorder, with an annual incidence of roughly 0.001–0.015% of the general population [1]. Clinically apparent neurosarcoidosis develops in only ≈ 5–10% of those patients, and in up to 50% it is the first disease manifestation [2]. Spinal involvement is the rarest form (< 1% of all sarcoidosis) and typically presents as longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis with dominant dorsal subpial and pial enhancement—the “trident” pattern seen in our patient [2–4]. The axial “trident sign” combines crescentic dorsal subpial enhancement with a linear central canal component, resembling a three-pronged spear. First described by Zhang et al. in 2016 [2], the sign is highly suggestive of spinal sarcoidosis and helps distinguish it from other causes of longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM) such as neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, MOG (myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein) antibody disease, lymphoma and paraneoplastic myelitis [7,8]. However, its sensitivity is limited, and absence does not exclude the diagnosis [6]. Our patient fulfilled the 2018 Neurosarcoidosis Consortium Consensus Group diagnostic criteria for probable neurosarcoidosis, namely, a compatible neurologic syndrome, histologic confirmation of systemic sarcoidosis outside the nervous system, and reasonable exclusion of alternative disorders [5]. Differential diagnoses were considered and ruled out: neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (serum AQP4 and MOG antibodies negative), infectious myelitis (CSF cultures and fungal/TB studies negative; CSF/serum ACE normal), and intramedullary metastasis (two punctate cortical–subcortical enhancing foci ≤ 2 mm, non mass like, with no primary malignancy). Prolonged immunosuppression is essential. About half of patients relapse when prednisone falls below 20 mg, so a steroid-sparing agent—methotrexate, mycophenolate, or infliximab—should be added early [2,5]. In our patient, paraparesis flared within days of the first 5 mg taper; stability was achieved only after mycophenolate mofetil was introduced, allowing stepwise prednisone reduction together with focused physiotherapy and bladder follow-up. Because the spinal “trident sign” is highly specific, its appearance on the index MRI of this unexplained longitudinal myelopathy immediately pivoted the differential toward sarcoidosis, prompted mediastinal node biopsy, and delivered timely immunotherapy, interventions that likely averted permanent cord damage [9,10]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Regarding a case of pyogenic spondylodiscitis
clinical_history: A 56-year-old patient with a history of type 2 diabetes, arterial hypertension, and knee osteoarthritis treated with intra-articular steroids was admitted due to fever of unknown origin. The patient reported lumbar pain for the past week, with no associated symptoms.
imaging_findings: Non-contrast and contrast-enhanced CT of the skull, thorax and abdomen was performed to identify a possible infectious focus. The key findings included heterogeneous density in both psoas muscles due to the presence of gas bubbles, with no collections detected following contrast administration (Figures 1a and 1b). In addition to the gas identified in the psoas muscles, gas bubbles were observed within the L3 vertebral body. Unenhanced and contrast-enhanced lumbar spine MRI was performed. The axial T2-weighted image (Figure 2a) shows an enlarged left psoas muscle due to multiple round collections with increased signal intensity. A similar collection is observed in the ipsilateral paraspinal muscle and the right psoas muscle. In the axial post-contrast T1-weighted sequence (Figure 2b), the described lesions, which exhibit enhancement after contrast administration, are also seen (marked with blue stars). Sagittal T1-weighted images pre (Figure 2c) and post-contrast (Figure 2d) demonstrate heterogeneous very subtle enhancement of the L2, L3, L4, and L5 vertebral bodies, as well as the intervertebral discs. The sagittal views demonstrate lesions in the psoas and paraspinal muscles, with hyperintense signal on T2-weighted (Figure 2e) and STIR (Figure 2f) sequences at the level of the L2, L3, L4, and L5 vertebral bodies.
discussion: Background Spondylodiscitis is an infection affecting the intervertebral discs and adjacent vertebral bodies. The majority of cases are of bacterial origin, with Staphylococcus being the primary causative agent. Tuberculous and fungal aetiologies may also be identified, particularly in immunocompromised patients. The infection is more frequently observed in older adults and is commonly disseminated haematogenously [1,2]. In adults, intervertebral discs are avascular, predisposing them to ischaemia and infarction of the vertebral endplates, particularly along the anterior margin, leading to bone destruction and disc involvement [1,2]. Clinical Perspective The lumbosacral region is affected in 55% of cases, with infection confined to a single level in 65% of patients. Complications include neurological impairment, abscess formation, and spinal instability. Severe, stabbing lower back pain is reported in 93% of cases. Blood cultures are positive in 30–78% of patients. In cases with negative blood cultures, CT-guided percutaneous biopsy is recommended to confirm the diagnosis and identify the causative microorganism [1,3]. Imaging Perspective Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is considered the most sensitive modality for early diagnosis (< 2–3 weeks after symptom onset), with a sensitivity of 97% and specificity of 93%. Key diagnostic findings in pyogenic spondylodiscitis include: Paraspinal or epidural oedema, appearing as hypointensity on T1-weighted images and hyperintensity on T2-weighted images, with enhancement of the intervertebral disc space [1,3]. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is useful for distinguishing infection from degenerative changes. The claw sign, a sharply defined paired linear hyperintense signal, is characteristic of Modic type 1 changes, whereas spondylodiscitis typically presents with diffuse signal abnormalities [2,3,6]. CT is valuable for detecting early bony changes, although it may appear normal within the first three weeks. As the disease progresses, vertebral endplate erosions, reactive sclerosis, osteopenia, intradiscal hypodensity, and soft tissue swelling obscuring adjacent fat planes may be visualised. Intravenous contrast administration improves the detection of abscesses within the psoas muscle or epidural space, as well as the identification of gas inclusions, which suggest an infectious process but may also be observed in degenerative discitis [2,4,5]. Image-guided percutaneous biopsy is considered a key tool for confirming the diagnosis and identifying the causative microorganism [4,5]. Outcome Conservative treatment is effective in 70% of pyogenic infections, while surgical intervention may be required in more than 50% of cases. The overall cure rate is 91%, with 24% of patients experiencing residual disability and a mortality rate of 8% [3,5]. Take Home Message A combination of MRI and CT provides essential imaging features that allow for accurate diagnosis, differentiation of infectious from degenerative changes, and timely management to prevent complications [1,4,5]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: An uncommon branchial cleft anomaly
clinical_history: A 42-year-old lady presented with a gradually progressive, painless, cystic swelling in the left infra-auricular region for the last 12 months. No other swellings were noted in the neck. There was no prior history of ear discharge or parotitis. Clinical examination showed no evidence of skin changes or facial nerve palsy.
imaging_findings: Ultrasonography reveals a cystic lesion with internal echoes within the substance of the left parotid gland with a beak-like projection on its deeper aspect (Figure 1). CT scan demonstrates a well-defined, homogeneous, smoothly marginated, non-enhancing lesion (density of 35 HU before and 36 HU after contrast administration) located in the left parotid gland, causing thinning and outward displacement of the residual gland parenchyma (Figure 2). MRI reveals a T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense, and STIR hyperintense, intra-parotid lesion occupying superficial and deep lobes of the parotid with a small blind-ending tract projecting anteromedially into the parapharyngeal space. No fistulous tracts to the external auditory canal were noted. There was no evidence of fat stranding or enlarged lymph nodes (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c).
discussion: Background Defects in complete fusion or involution of the branchial arches during embryological development can give rise to the formation of epithelial cystic remnants of these structures, called branchial cleft cysts [1,2]. First branchial cleft cysts comprise only 7% of all branchial cleft cysts [3]. They are related to the parotid gland or the external auditory canal. Second branchial cleft cysts are the most common, usually related to the sternocleidomastoid or the carotid sheath. Third and fourth branchial cleft cysts are quite rare and are related to the thyroid gland and pyriform sinuses, respectively [4]. There are three types of first branchial cleft cysts, based on their location [5]: Type I: Inferoposteromedial to the pinna. Type II: Between the angle of the mandible and the external auditory canal. Type III: Related to the parotid gland. First branchial cleft cysts extending medial to the facial nerve are exceedingly rare, with only a few cases described in the literature [6]. Clinical Perspective Usually manifest during the second decade of life as a cystic swelling around the parotid region. Discharging sinus/fistula, otorrhoea, recurrent parotid abscesses, facial palsy are few other clinical presentations. Imaging Perspective They are well-circumscribed cystic masses usually seen in relation to the parotid gland. Ultrasonography is usually the first line of investigation which shows thin-walled, anechoic, cystic lesion with or without internal debris. Computed tomography shows a thin-walled, well-defined, non-enhancing, fluid density lesion. MRI is the investigation of choice as it can not only accurately characterise the lesion, but also best establish anatomical relations of the lesion with the deeper structures and neurovascular bundles. USG-guided FNAC (fine-needle aspiration cytology) can be used to characterise the lesion and classify it accordingly. In addition, any surrounding inflammatory/granulomatous changes, cellular atypia or mitotic figures can be detected using FNAC. Outcome Based on the imaging findings, differential diagnoses of first branchial cleft cyst, lymphoepithelial cyst, Warthin’s tumour or sialocele were proposed in our case. A USG-guided FNAC was performed with an inconclusive result. Considering the benign features of the lesion, the patient underwent surgical excision. Histopathology revealed a mucoid cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium along with a few cartilaginous elements, confirming the diagnosis of first branchial cleft cyst (left) type III with parapharyngeal extension. Surgical excision is the mainstay of management. Challenges include complete excision along with the tract and preserving the integrity of the seventh cranial nerve [7]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Hodgkin lymphoma presenting as persistent cough in a young female
clinical_history: A 29-year-old female patient presented to the Emergency Department with a persistent dry cough for 2 months in the absence of any fever, chills or weight loss. At presentation, vitals were within normal limits and physical examination was significant only for reduced breath sounds on the left side.
imaging_findings: Initial chest x-rays reveal abnormalities of the mediastinal contours, with increased tissue density found most significantly in the left mediastinal region. On frontal radiograph (Figure 1a), pulmonary vessels can be seen through the mass, known as the hilum overlay sign, suggesting the mass is located anterior or posterior to the hilum. Lateral radiograph (Figure 1b) demonstrates opacification of the anterior mediastinum. The hila, including the main bronchi, remain clearly visualised and the doughnut sign is absent. Together, these features help to localise the mass to the anterior mediastinum and exclude hilar or middle mediastinal origin. Subsequent non-contrast CT imaging (Figure 2) confirms a left, large, homogeneous lobulated mass in the anterior mediastinum with posterior displacement of the left main bronchus. Further investigation with PET–CT (Figure 3) revealed avid FDG uptake in the anterior mediastinal and supraclavicular regions. The patient then underwent CT-guided biopsy of the anterior mediastinal mass and was diagnosed with nodular sclerosing Hodgkin disease.
discussion: Background Hodgkin lymphoma, also known as Hodgkin disease, is a type of lymphoma characterised by the presence of Reed–Sternberg cells [1]. It is a malignant neoplasm derived from B-lymphocytes. Hodgkin lymphoma presents in a bimodal distribution, most commonly affecting young adults around the third decade of life and older individuals greater than 60 years of age [2]. Hodgkin lymphoma can be subdivided into classical Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) and nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL (NLPHL). HL accounts for around 95% of cases and consists of multiple subtypes, including nodular sclerosing, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich and lymphocyte-depleted [2]. NLPHL is rarer and typically follows a more indolent course. The pathogenesis of this disease is not entirely understood, but the Epstein–Barr virus, detected in nearly half of HL patients [3], and genetic factors, evidenced by the increased risk of occurrence among monozygotic versus dizygotic twins of patients with Hodgkin lymphoma [4], contribute to the development of HL. Clinical Perspective Patients with Hodgkin lymphoma commonly present with painless lymphadenopathy. However, approximately one-third of patients may also report B-symptoms such as weight loss, fevers, and night sweats [1,5]. Mediastinal involvement may result in chest pain, cough, or dyspnoea. Although HL primarily spreads through contiguous lymph node regions, extra-nodal involvement can occur in the lungs, liver, spleen, or bone marrow, especially in advanced stages [5]. Imaging Perspective Historically, imaging of Hodgkin lymphoma involved chest radiographs and lymphangiography, often followed by diagnostic laparotomy with splenectomy to assess abdominal and splenic involvement [6]. The rise of CT eliminated the need for diagnostic laparotomy by enabling the visualisation of lymph nodes and solid organs [6]. The implementation of MRI further enhanced the ability of clinicians to assess tissue and bone involvement. Today, although initial imaging may initially involve plain radiographs and CT, [F-18]2-fluoro-2-deoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET–CT) has become the gold standard for staging, assessing tumour burden and treatment response [6]. This is due to its ability to leverage the high metabolic activity of Hodgkin lymphoma, allowing for the direct visualisation of regions with increased uptake [6]. Ultimately, definitive diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma requires sampling of the lesion with subsequent cytological and immunohistochemical analysis. Outcome Prognosis depends on multiple factors, including patient age, tumour burden, and tumour subtype [1]. Treatment is dictated by staging. HL is staged using the Ann Arbor system, classifying disease from stage 1 (single nodal region) to stage 4 (disseminated extranodal involvement), with an “a” or “b” suffix denoting the absence or presence of B-symptoms [3]. This patient was diagnosed with stage 2a nodular sclerosing HL. Generally, localised radiotherapy may be appropriate for stage 2a and below, while chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy may be required for stage 2b and above [1]. This patient commenced chemotherapy and will undergo follow-up FGD PET–CT scans for response assessment. Five-year survival rates for early-stage HL among adolescents and young adults exceed 90% [7]. Take Home Message Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) may present with isolated respiratory symptoms in young adults. CT is essential for identifying mediastinal involvement and guiding biopsy. PET–CT is critical for diagnosis, staging and assessing treatment response.

title: A rare case of intraventricular haemangioblastoma
clinical_history: A 34-year-old patient undergoes a scheduled MRI study due to a one-year history of migraine-like headaches, accompanied by visual disturbances, paraesthesias in the right upper limb, and instability before and during the pain.
imaging_findings: The MRI reveals a lesion located in the right temporal horn of the lateral ventricle, with a prominent cystic component and a solid nodule that appears hypointense on T1-weighted images (Figures 1a and 1b) and hyperintense on T2-weighted images (Figure 2). This solid, heterogeneous nodule shows intense enhancement following gadolinium administration (Figures 1c, 1d, and 1e) and areas of microcystic architecture, without evidence of subependymal spread. Extensive T2-FLAIR hyperintensity is observed throughout the surrounding white matter, consistent with vasogenic oedema. The mass exerts a moderate compressive effect on the ventricular system, causing a slight midline shift (Figure 2). Notably, the lesion displays prominent draining veins, reflecting its hypervascular nature (Figures 3a and 3b). No diffusion restriction is identified on DWI sequences (Figure 4). Perfusion imaging confirms a highly vascularised tumour (Figure 5a, 5b, 5c). Magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrates a prominent lipid and lactate peak, likely indicative of necrotic components (Figure 6).
discussion: Background Haemangioblastomas (HBs) are rare, benign, and highly vascularised mesenchymal neoplasms of the central nervous system (CNS), classified as WHO grade I tumours [1]. They account for approximately 1.5–2.5% of all intracranial tumours and up to 12% of posterior fossa neoplasms, most frequently arising in the cerebellum of adults between the third and fifth decades of life. Around 60–75% of cases are sporadic, while the remainder are associated with Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease, an autosomal dominant genetic syndrome [2]. Although most commonly found in the posterior fossa, HBs can also occur in the spinal cord, brainstem, and, less frequently, in supratentorial regions (4–13%). Their presence in the lateral ventricles is exceedingly rare [3]. Clinical Perspective The clinical presentation is primarily determined by tumour size and location. Due to the very limited number of reported cases, the specific clinical behaviour of this entity remains unclear [5]. However, some symptoms have been consistently described, including headache, dizziness, and even visual disturbances, some of which are similar to those observed in infratentorial cases. These symptoms are usually related to mass effect, surrounding oedema, or growth of the cystic component. Lesions within the lateral ventricle may need to grow larger to produce symptoms, due to the available space in this anatomical compartment [2–5]. Imaging Perspective Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the preferred imaging modality due to its superior anatomical resolution. A characteristic finding is a vividly enhancing mural nodule within a well-defined cyst. On T1-weighted sequences, the nodule typically appears hypo to isointense, and the cyst fluid resembles cerebrospinal fluid. Post-contrast T1 images show intense enhancement of the mural nodule, with no enhancement of the cyst wall. On T2-weighted images, the nodule appears hyperintense, and flow voids caused by dilated peripheral vessels are often seen. MR perfusion usually demonstrates high relative cerebral blood volume, and MR spectroscopy may show a prominent lipid peak and reduced N-acetyl aspartate (NAA), helpful for differential diagnosis [2,6]. Outcome Complete surgical resection is the treatment of choice and is usually curative, given the tumour’s benign nature. In patients with VHL, close follow-up is essential due to the risk of new lesions. Imaging is crucial for early detection of recurrence [6,8]. Take Home Message Although benign, haemangioblastomas can have significant clinical consequences. MRI plays a key role in diagnosis, particularly in atypical locations, allowing for timely and effective management.

title: Cavernous haemangioma mimicking malignancy in patient with deep inferior epigastric perforator flap reconstruction
clinical_history: A 62-year-old female patient presented with a palpable self-reported lump for approximately a month in the upper-inner quadrant of the left breast. Five years ago, she was diagnosed with an extensive left ductal carcinoma in situ (TisN0M0), which led to a mastectomy. The reconstructed breast was assessed through clinical examinations, whereas imaging surveillance was limited to the contralateral breast. Three years later (i.e., two years ago), she underwent a unilateral bipedicled deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) flap reconstruction of the left breast.
imaging_findings: In 2025, the patient detected a palpable lump in the left reconstructed breast. An ultrasound (US) examination revealed a suspicious unifocal mass with irregular shape and ill-defined margins. A core needle biopsy was performed under US guidance, confirming the diagnosis of malignancy: invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (NST), grade 2, with positive oestrogen and progesterone receptors and negative human epidermal growth factor 2 (ER+PR+HER2-). Following the confirmed malignancy, the patient was referred for a breast MRI to further evaluate the extent of disease. The MRI highlighted the recurrent mass (Figure 1a, 1b, and 1c). A separate 6 mm lesion cranial to the recurrence showed some benign features (oval shape, well-defined margins, T2 hyperintensity) but was considered suspicious due to avid contrast enhancement (although type 1 kinetics), the clinical context, and its unexpected location in a DIEP flap. A second-look ultrasound demonstrated the recurrent mass but failed to clearly identify the additional lesion (Figures 1d and 1e), prompting further investigation with contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM). On low-energy CEM images, an oval opacity with circumscribed margins and without microcalcifications was observed (Figures 2a and 2b). On recombined images, the mass exhibited homogeneous enhancement (Figures 2c and 2d), displaying high conspicuity. No additional associated features were noted. A tomosynthesis-guided biopsy was subsequently performed (Figure 2e). Histopathology revealed a cavernous haemangioma (CH) (Figure 3). The breast recurrent cancer was not covered in the mammography field of view due to its deep-seated location. A retrospective review of the abdominal MRI performed three years earlier (prior to the DIEP flap reconstruction) identified the CH as a well-defined, subcutaneous abdominal mass, hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging, with the characteristic avid “light-bulb” post-contrast enhancement (Figures 4a and 4b).
discussion: The deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) flap is an advanced autologous breast reconstruction technique, most commonly performed post-mastectomy, and in selected cases following breast-conserving surgery, to optimise aesthetic outcomes and restore breast symmetry. This method involves harvesting skin, fat, and blood vessels from the lower abdomen while preserving the rectus abdominis muscle, thereby maintaining abdominal wall strength and reducing donor-site morbidity. The harvested tissue is then microsurgically transplanted to the chest to reconstruct the breast, offering a natural appearance. While normal (single-pedicled) and bipedicled DIEP flaps are the most common types—distinguished mainly by the number of abdominal vascular pedicles used (one versus two) and thus the amount of available tissue and complexity—other variants like stacked, extended, or hybrid DIEP flaps exist to meet specific surgical requirements and patient needs [1,2]. Despite its advantages, the DIEP flap procedure can be associated with flap-related complications [2–4]. Early postoperative issues include seroma, haematoma, infection, and arterial thrombosis. Late complications may include fat necrosis, resulting from inadequate blood supply to the transplanted fat tissue, which can form firm lumps that mimic malignancy. Regarding breast cancer recurrence, studies indicate that DIEP flap reconstruction does not increase recurrence risk compared to mastectomy alone [5,6]. The incidence of local recurrence ranges from 2% to 7%, depending on the initial cancer stage and tumour biology, with patients presenting with high-grade tumours and positive nodal involvement facing a higher risk of local recurrence [7]. Our case highlights a key limitation of CEM and conventional mammography: restricted field of view. While the CH was readily visualised, the recurrent mass was not captured, due to its deep-seated location. This emphasises that the importance of clinical examination and careful correlation between clinical findings and imaging modality capabilities is essential to avoid missed diagnoses. To date, no studies have characterised the imaging appearance of CH within DIEP-reconstructed breasts. CHs are rare, benign vascular tumours not commonly associated with breast reconstruction procedures, including DIEP flap surgeries. These lesions can either be transferred inadvertently from the donor abdominal tissue or develop independently within the reconstructed breast. Independent development may be stimulated by factors such as surgical trauma, enhanced angiogenesis resulting from flap perfusion, or post-radiation effects in irradiated patients. Although the transfer of a pre-existing CH from abdominal tissue during DIEP reconstruction is theoretically plausible, it remains exceedingly uncommon. Breast haemangiomas typically present as circumscribed masses across mammography, ultrasound, and MRI. Phleboliths may be visible on mammography, while MRI characteristically shows T2 hyperintensity and progressive, persistent enhancement. The characterisation of additional MR-detected lesions, particularly small, centimetric findings, poses a diagnostic challenge, especially in patients who have undergone oncoplastic surgery. In patients with DIEP flap reconstruction, cavernous haemangioma should be considered as a potential benign differential diagnosis. Definitive diagnosis often requires further imaging assessment and biopsy. Take Home Message Prospective imaging-based diagnosis of breast cavernous haemangiomas remains challenging and often requires biopsy confirmation. Careful review of preoperative abdominal MRI or CT can aid in identifying pre-existing haemangiomas, potentially avoiding unnecessary biopsy when evaluating lesions in DIEP-reconstructed breasts. Cavernous haemangioma may be transferred from the abdominal wall into the reconstructed breast. The risk of breast cancer recurrence is primarily determined by the initial tumour stage and biological characteristics, rather than DIEP flap reconstruction. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: CT findings of restrictive allograft syndrome after lung transplantation
clinical_history: A 66-year-old female with a history of bilateral lung transplantation for terminal chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presented with progressive exertional dyspnoea and increasing oxygen dependence. She had recently recovered from influenza A with bacterial superinfection and was known to have persistent fungal colonisation.
imaging_findings: Chest CT, 2 years after transplantation (Figure 1a), showed normal post-transplant findings and a known cavitary lesion in the left upper lobe. On follow-up CT (Figure 1b), half a year after the previous CT, i.e., 2.5 years after transplantation, new-onset diffuse cylindrical bronchiectasis and bilateral perihilar ground-glass opacities appeared. Additional findings included subpleural reticulations, upper lobe consolidations (Figures 2 and 3), and mild reactive mediastinal lymphadenopathy. The cavitary lesion appeared more flattened and spiculated. There was mild airtrapping. These findings are highly suggestive of chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD), specifically the restrictive allograft syndrome (RAS) phenotype with overlapping features of acute fibrinous and organising pneumonia (AFOP).
discussion: Chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) is the principal cause of late graft failure after lung transplantation, with two widely recognised phenotypes: bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS) and restrictive allograft syndrome (RAS) [1,2]. RAS, although less common, is more aggressive and characterised by restrictive lung physiology along with upper-lobe predominant fibrosis, ground-glass opacities, and traction bronchiectasis. Serial high-resolution CTs (HRCT), at two and at two and a half years post-transplant in this case, demonstrated a transition from mild air trapping in the basal lungs to RAS-congruent features overlapping with acute fibrinous organising pneumonia (AFOP): diffuse ground-glass opacities, subpleural fibrosis, traction bronchiectasis, and upper-lobe volume loss. Notably, these imaging features raised suspicion for pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis (PPFE), a fibrosing process increasingly recognised as part of the RAS spectrum in transplanted lungs. PPFE typically presents on CT with dense subpleural fibrosis and pleural thickening in the upper lobes, marked volume loss, and traction bronchiectasis. Histopathological analysis in RAS patients frequently reveals fibroelastic proliferation in subpleural regions, confirming PPFE as a frequent correlate of RAS [3]. Restrictive chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) is increasingly recognised as a heterogeneous entity encompassing several fibrotic and inflammatory patterns. Histopathologically, it includes PPFE and AFOP as part of the RAS spectrum. PPFE is characterised by dense subpleural fibroelastosis and pleural thickening, while AFOP is defined by intra-alveolar fibrin balls and organising pneumonia without hyaline membrane formation. In our patient, several features on serial CT imaging and clinical evolution support these diagnoses: PPFE features include dense subpleural reticulations and upper-lobe volume loss with traction bronchiectasis. AFOP features include the appearance of diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities and consolidations without evidence of infection, which correlate with inflammatory processes seen in AFOP. These overlapping imaging findings highlight the complex nature of restrictive CLAD phenotypes and emphasise the importance of integrating imaging, clinical data, and, where available, histopathology for accurate phenotypic classification. Clinical trajectories of PPFE in lung transplant recipients can vary significantly. Some patients exhibit gradual decline (slow progressors), while others deteriorate rapidly to respiratory failure. This variable tempo has important prognostic implications. In advanced and refractory cases of RAS/PPFE, re-transplantation may be considered for selected candidates who meet eligibility criteria and lack contraindications. In the current patient, pulmonary function tests revealed a restrictive pattern, i.e., reduced FVC (forced vital capacity), stable low FEV1 (forced expiratory volume, 1 second), with persistent oxygen dependence. Persistent BAL (bronchoalveolar lavage) galactomannan positivity mandated prolonged dual antifungal therapy (isavuconazole and terbinafine). Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy was performed to assess disease aetiology. Despite maximal medical management, the patient’s respiratory and functional status warranted initiation of palliative oxygen support, psychological care, and a scheduled 6-minute walk test (6MWT) to inform ongoing management. This case underscores the diagnostic importance of combining clinical, functional, and serial CT data to distinguish between BOS and RAS, and in identifying overlapping or progressive fibrotic processes such as AFOP and PPFE. Recognising PPFE—and differentiating between slow and fast progressors—can inform prognosis, therapeutic intensity, and candidacy for re-transplantation. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Restrictive allograft syndrome (RAS) is an aggressive chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) phenotype with distinct imaging features, particularly upper-lobe fibrosis and bronchiectasis. Serial CT imaging is valuable in differentiating between CLAD phenotypes and identifying overlap syndromes like acute fibrinous organising pneumonia(AFOP). Progressive oxygen dependency in CLAD should prompt multidisciplinary management, including supportive and palliative care.

title: Breast schwannoma: A rare diagnosis behind a painful palpable mass
clinical_history: A 53-year-old woman with no relevant personal or family medical history presented with a palpable, firm, and painful mass in the medial aspect of the right breast, first noticed approximately one month earlier. The mass had progressively increased in size and remained painful. It was located at the 3 o’clock position, 10 cm from the nipple, and palpated as a superficial subcutaneous lesion. There were no skin changes, nipple discharge, or systemic symptoms. Diagnostic image workup was performed.
imaging_findings: A superficial sub-centimetre oval, circumscribed, isodense mass was identified in the lower inner quadrant of the right breast (Figures 1a and 1b). A thin radiolucent halo was also observed surrounding the lesion, suggestive of a capsule. No suspicious calcifications, architectural distortion or skin changes were observed. Targeted ultrasound (Figures 2a and 2b) demonstrated an oval, circumscribed, parallel-oriented, hypoechoic mass with small cystic areas and posterior acoustic enhancement. The lesion measured 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.4 cm and was located in the subcutaneous tissue, immediately beneath the dermis, with no visible connection to the skin. No internal vascularity, adjacent inflammatory changes, or abnormal intramammary or axillary lymph nodes were observed.
discussion: Diagnosis Despite its benign appearance, the lesion was classified as BI-RADS 4 due to new pain, recent growth, and the absence of prior studies for comparison. An ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy was performed and revealed spindle cell proliferation in fascicles, with Antoni A and B areas. Immunohistochemistry showed diffuse S-100 and Sox10 positivity, confirming a benign schwannoma. Background Schwannomas are benign tumours derived from Schwann cells of the peripheral nerve sheath. They most commonly occur in the head, neck, and extremities, while breast localisation is rare, accounting for less than 0.2% of all breast tumours and approximately 2.6% of all schwannomas [1,2]. Although most are benign, there have been isolated reports of malignant transformation [2,3]. These tumours may be associated with neurofibromatosis type II, but the majority are sporadic, as in this case [3,4]. Schwannomas in the chest typically arise in the posterior mediastinum; in this patient, however, the mass was intramammary [4]. Schwannomas tend to occur as solitary, well-encapsulated masses, with sizes ranging from 0.7 to 11 cm [1,5]. Clinical Perspective Breast schwannomas are typically slow-growing, painless, and mobile lesions [1,2,4]. Pain or tenderness may occur with superficial nerve involvement or superficial location [2,6]. Although uncommon, a short-term increase in size has been reported, and this case is an example of it [4,6]. This growth pattern does not necessarily indicate malignancy but may prompt further evaluation. These lesions are often categorised as BI-RADS 4a, with a low likelihood of malignancy. Although malignant transformation is rare, histological confirmation is recommended [2]. Imaging Perspective On mammography, most schwannomas appear as well-circumscribed masses. In some cases, they may be mammographically occult or present as ill-defined soft tissue densities [2,3]. A thin radiolucent halo was observed surrounding the lesion on tomosynthesis. This “halo sign” is commonly associated with benign breast lesions, such as cysts and fibroadenomas, and may support the benign nature of a superficial, well-circumscribed mass [7]. However, it has not been routinely reported in published cases of breast schwannoma, likely due to the rarity of this tumour type [1,2,4]. On ultrasound, they are generally described as well-circumscribed hypoechoic lesions. Additional features suggestive of a schwannoma include the “target sign” (hyperechoic centre with hypoechoic periphery), posterior acoustic enhancement, and peripheral nerve continuity [1,3]. However, these features may also be seen in other peripheral nerve sheath tumours such as neurofibromas [3]. The mass in this case demonstrated cystic areas, a finding also reported in previous cases [3,4]. Doppler ultrasound was acquired but not documented, likely due to the absence of appreciable vascularisation. In the literature, schwannomas are most often hypovascular, though occasional cases report peripheral vascularity [2,4,6]. MRI was not performed in this case, as the lesion was superficial, palpable, and showed benign features on conventional imaging. MRI is generally not performed in such cases, but in previously reported instances where it was conducted, schwannomas typically appeared as well-circumscribed, T2-hyperintense lesions with heterogeneous contrast enhancement [2,4]. Although most cases present benign imaging features, atypical characteristics, such as irregular margins, heterogeneous echotexture, or increased vascularity, have also been described [3,4,6]. Differential diagnosis of a superficial, well-circumscribed breast mass includes several benign and indeterminate entities. Epidermal inclusion cysts are subcutaneous, avascular lesions that may appear hypoechoic with posterior enhancement, mimicking schwannomas, but often present with a visible skin tract or punctum. Fibroadenomas are often considered in the differential diagnosis of oval, circumscribed breast lesions [1,5], particularly in younger women, but are typically located deeper within the breast parenchyma. Phyllodes tumours can appear oval and circumscribed but tend to be larger, with lobulated margins and a more rapid growth rate [3]. Neurofibromas may have overlapping features but are frequently multiple or associated with neurofibromatosis [3]. Spindle cell lesions, including benign and malignant tumours, are histologically diverse and cannot be reliably differentiated by imaging alone, reinforcing the importance of biopsy in indeterminate cases [3]. Outcome Histological analysis confirmed a benign schwannoma with characteristic morphology and immunoprofile. Surgical consultation was recommended due to persistent symptoms. Prognosis is excellent after excision, and recurrence is rare. There is minimal risk of malignant transformation, except in the context of neurofibromatosis type 1, which was not present in this case [3,5]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Breast schwannomas are rare benign tumours that may mimic more common entities. Imaging findings are typically benign, but biopsy is often needed for definitive diagnosis. Benign schwannoma should be considered in palpable, painful BI-RADS 4a lesions. S-100 and Sox10 positivity, combined with Antoni A/B architecture, confirm the diagnosis. Management is surgical for symptomatic cases; otherwise, conservative follow-up may suffice.

title: Acute hemichorea in a patient with diabetes mellitus: Diabetic striatopathy
clinical_history: A 66-year-old male patient presents with episodes of involuntary jerky movements of the left arm, left leg and left mouth corner since 3 days, in combination with a broad-based gait pattern. The patient is known to have diabetes mellitus type 2. Blood tests showed elevated blood glucose levels of 236 mg/dL and HbA1c of 10.8%.
imaging_findings: On initial non-contrast CT evaluation (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c), there was no evidence of intracranial haemorrhage. There were no detectable zones of hypodensity, which could suggest cerebral oedema or tissue loss. Subtle increased attenuation of the lentiform nucleus and head of the caudate nucleus on the right side was noticed, best appreciated on the coronal images (Figure 1b). MRI showed corresponding spontaneous T1 hyperintensity in the right lentiform nucleus as well as in the head of the caudate nucleus with sparing of the anterior limb of the internal capsule (Figure 2a). No other obvious changes were seen on other sequences (Figures 2b, 2c, 2d, 2e, and 2f). There were no susceptibility artefacts on T2* imaging (Figure 2f), which, in combination with the CT findings, allowed to rule out acute haemorrhage. The combination of clinical, biochemical and imaging findings suggested the diagnosis of hyperglycaemia-induced haemichorea-haemiballismus syndrome, otherwise known as diabetic striatopathy. Follow-up MRI (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, 3d, 3e, and 3f), 5 months later, showed resolution of the T1 hyperintensity in the head of the caudate nucleus and diminished T1 hyperintensity at the level of the right lentiform nucleus (Figure 3a).
discussion: Background Hyperglycaemia-induced haemichorea-haemiballismus syndrome, also known as diabetic striatopathy (DS), is a rare neurological complication of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, associated with non-ketotic hyperglycaemia and elevated HbA1c levels. Its prevalence is estimated to be 1 in 100,000 patients [1]. Clinical Perspective Patients typically present with an acute onset of involuntary movements (haemichorea-haemiballismus) affecting one side of the body. Limbs as well as facial muscles can be affected. Prodromal symptoms such as headache, gait imbalance or confusion have been reported. The movements can be abrupt or continuous, often worsen with stress, but subside during sleep [2,3]. Imaging Perspective Imaging is critical for the diagnosis of DS. Non-contrast enhanced CT imaging typically shows hyperdensity in the contralateral basal ganglia, most often in the putamen and caudate nucleus. These findings can be subtle, as demonstrated in our case. MRI imaging shows spontaneous T1 hyperintensity in the corresponding regions. Increased susceptibility and high diffusion signal on b1000 sequences can be seen in the affected regions. Although unilateral changes are typical, a few cases with bilateral involvement of the basal ganglia have been reported. The underlying pathophysiology is thought to involve severe hyperglycaemia as well as compromised vascular supply to the striatum. The syndrome is seen in diabetic patients and can be associated with coexisting carotid and cerebral artery stenosis [2]. Outcome The prognosis in patients with DS is generally favourable. With prompt glycaemic control, the involuntary haemichorea-haemiballismus movements completely resolve within seven days in most patients. The mean period of complete radiologic reversal on CT and MRI was documented to be around 60 and 180 days, respectively, according to Chatterjee et al. [4]. Discernible changes on CT and MRI were, respectively, seen after 24 and 120 days. About a quarter of patients only partially recover, and about 20% were seen to recur even after initial resolution of the basal ganglia anomalies. This illustrates the importance of both clinical and neuroradiological follow-up [5]. Our patient clinically improved over the next few months. Nevertheless, choreatic movements in the left hand persevered until his most recent neurological follow-up consult 6 months after initial presentation. Take Home Message Diabetic striatopathy (hyperglycaemia-induced haemichorea-haemiballismus syndrome) is a rare neurological complication characterised by acute-onset unilateral hyperkinetic movement disorder that is associated with poorly controlled diabetes. On neuroimaging, hyperdensity in the basal ganglia is seen on CT with associated spontaneous T1 hyperintense signal alterations. Prognosis is favourable with prompt glycaemia control. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: When the pain comes back: A post-appendectomy case
clinical_history: A 45-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with a 4-day history of right iliac fossa pain. He denied fever, nausea, or vomiting. Physical examination revealed rebound tenderness. Laboratory tests showed elevated C-reactive protein (19.6 mg/L) with a normal white-cell count. Two months earlier, he had undergone a laparoscopic appendectomy.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound (Figure 1) revealed a blind-ending, aperistaltic, non-compressible tubular structure (luminal diameter ≈ 10 mm) arising from the caecum at the appendectomy bed. The wall was thickened with surrounding echogenic fat. A minimal amount of free fluid was also observed. In contrast-enhanced computer tomography (CT), multiplanar reformats demonstrated an enhancing tubular remnant arising from the caecum, capped by two metallic clips at its distal end (Figures 2a, 2b, and 3). The stump showed concentric mural thickening, pericaecal fat stranding, and a trace of free fluid. No evidence of abscess or pneumoperitoneum was identified.
discussion: Background Stump appendicitis is a rare complication, occurring in approximately 1 in 50,000 appendectomies [1], reported from 9 weeks to 50 years after surgery [2]. Since prior appendectomy often lowers clinical suspicion, it is frequently overlooked in patients presenting with right-lower-quadrant pain [3]. Risk factors include a residual stump > 5 mm, distorted anatomy, and marked local inflammation during the index operation [4]. Clinical Perspective Symptoms mirror primary appendicitis. Delayed diagnosis increases perforation rates; therefore, imaging is crucial whenever right-iliac-fossa pain recurs after appendectomy. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound typically shows an incompressible, blind-ending stump (> 6 mm) with Doppler hyperaemia and adjacent fat echogenicity; surgical clips aid localisation. CT is the reference standard, depicting an enhancing stump, mural thickening, pericaecal stranding, and free fluid, while excluding mimics such as terminal ileitis, mesenteric adenitis or inflammatory bowel disease [5]. Outcome Definitive treatment is completion appendectomy, often with wedge resection of the caecal base to ensure complete removal. In our patient, laparoscopy confirmed stump inflammation, and an appendectomy with caecal flap was performed. Early imaging shortened the diagnostic interval, prevented perforation, and enabled rapid recovery. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged 3 days after admission. Thorough operative documentation at the primary surgery is essential, as it provides valuable clues should the patient re-present. In our case, no difficulties were encountered during the initial operation. Teaching Points Recurrent right-iliac-fossa pain after appendectomy should raise suspicion for stump appendicitis. CT reliably identifies the inflamed stump and surgical clips, expediting urgent surgery. Creating an appendiceal stump < 5 mm at the primary operation is the best prevention. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: A florid case of acromegaly
clinical_history: A 47-year-old male presented with complaints of headaches for 6 months. No history of loss of consciousness, projectile vomiting or seizures. No history of trauma. The patient is a known case of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension on treatment for 10 years. On examination, macrognathia and frontal bossing were noted.
imaging_findings: The skull radiograph (Figure 1a) shows an enlarged sella turcica, frontal sinus hyperpneumatisation, and calvarial hyperostosis. Prognathism and widened mandibular angle are seen (Figure 1b). Hand and feet radiographs (Figures 2a and 2b) show spade-like distal phalanges with prominent ungual tufts. The chest radiograph (Figure 3) reveals widened glenohumeral joints and thickened scapular borders. CT brain shows calvarial hyperostosis (Figure 4a) and a hyperdense sellar mass (Figure 4b). MRI reveals a lobulated sellar-suprasellar lesion—T1 isointense (Figure 7), T2 and FLAIR hyperintense with “snowman” appearance—causing sella widening and displacing adjacent vessels (Figures 5a, 5b, and 6), with heterogeneous enhancement (Figures 9b and 9c).
discussion: Background Acromegaly is a rare endocrine disorder characterised by persistent elevation of growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor 1 after fusion of the growth plates [1]. The vast majority of acromegaly cases are attributable to a pituitary adenoma secreting excess GH. Less frequently, the condition may result from a hypothalamic tumour producing GHRH (growth hormone–releasing hormone), ectopic GHRH secretion from non-endocrine neoplasms, or, in exceedingly rare situations, ectopic GH production [2]. Clinical Perspective Acromegaly typically presents insidiously in adults. Common symptoms include headache, excessive sweating, fatigue, arthralgia, and visual disturbances such as bitemporal hemianopia. Physical signs develop gradually and include coarse facial features, frontal bossing, prognathism, macroglossia, enlarged hands and feet and widened interdental spacing. Patients may also experience carpal tunnel syndrome, skin thickening, and organomegaly. Systemic complications include hypertension, diabetes mellitus, cardiomyopathy, sleep apnoea, and increased risk of colonic neoplasia [3]. Pseudoacromegaly, a rare mimic of acromegaly, presents with phenotypic features such as coarsened facial features, enlarged hands and feet, and soft tissue overgrowth—but with normal GH and IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1) levels and unremarkable pituitary imaging. It may arise from severe insulin resistance, congenital lipodystrophy, hypothyroidism, or medications like minoxidil, phenytoin, and antiretrovirals, and should be considered when biochemical and imaging findings do not support true acromegaly. Imaging Perspective Imaging is essential in the diagnosis and management of acromegaly, primarily to identify the presence of a pituitary adenoma and to evaluate related anatomical and systemic changes [4]. Key radiographic findings include thickening of the calvaria, enlarged frontal sinuses and an expanded sella turcica on skull radiographs. Hand and feet X-rays typically show spade-like distal phalanges, soft tissue thickening, increased heel pad thickness and phalangeal base enlargement. Recognising these patterns can prompt earlier diagnosis and improve clinical outcomes [5]. At diagnosis, GH-secreting pituitary adenomas typically present as macroadenomas, with a median size reported to range between 11 and 20 mm [6,7]. Pituitary macroadenomas typically appear as intra and suprasellar masses inseparable from the pituitary gland, effectively replacing it. On CT, they often cause remodelling and enlargement of the sella turcica with intact lamina dura, although large (“giant”) adenomas may erode the skull base. They are usually isodense to grey matter. Cystic changes (15–20%) and haemorrhage (10%) are common, with rare calcifications. On MRI, macroadenomas are generally isointense to cortex on T1 and T2-weighted images, with heterogeneous enhancement post-contrast. The posterior pituitary bright spot is displaced or absent. Compression of the optic chiasm may cause T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity along the optic pathways. Haemorrhagic foci may bloom on T2*, and fluid-fluid levels may appear in apoplexy [8]. T2-weighted MRI helps refine diagnosis and prognosis in GH-secreting pituitary adenomas. T2-hyperintense tumours are typically larger, more invasive, and associated with sparsely granulated histology and low somatostatin receptor subtype 2 (SSTR2) expression, both markers of poor response to somatostatin analogues. They also show higher somatostatin receptor subtype 3 (SSTR3) and dopamine receptor D5 (DRD5) expression, indicating aggressive behaviour. In contrast, T2 hypointense tumours tend to be smaller, densely granulated, with higher SSTR2 expression and better treatment outcomes [6,9]. Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated IGF-1 levels, failure of GH suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test, and MRI evidence of a pituitary mass [10]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Acromegaly, often due to pituitary adenomas, requires early recognition for optimal management. Radiological findings, including thickened calvaria, enlarged sella turcica, spade-like distal phalanges, and suprasellar mass on MRI, are crucial for diagnosis. Early identification via imaging can guide treatment and prevent complications like visual disturbances and systemic comorbidities.
