title: Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum and associated coronary artery fistula
clinical_history: A newborn male at 37 weeks of gestation with a prenatal diagnosis of congenital heart disease presented with increasing cyanosis shortly after birth.
imaging_findings: An electrocardiogram (ECG-gated) prospective coronary computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the chest was performed after the postnatal echocardiogram. On CTA chest, atretic pulmonary valve was noted and branch pulmonary arteries supplied by the tortuous patent ductus arteriosus (Figure 1). The interventricular septum was intact with a hypoplastic right ventricle. There was a small patent foramen ovale. The left coronary artery (LCA) and left anterior descending artery (LAD) were dilated with a distal fistulous communication with the right ventricle. There was no evidence of proximal coronary arterial stenosis or atresia (Figures 2, 3, and 4). Multiple fistulous connections from the right coronary artery (RCA) to the right ventricle were also seen, without proximal coronary artery stenosis (Figure 4). The correlated echocardiogram showed moderate tricuspid valve hypoplasia with no tricuspid regurgitation.
discussion: Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum (PA-IVS) is a rare congenital heart defect defined by the absence of communication between the right ventricular outflow tract and pulmonary arteries due to complete atresia of the pulmonary valve. It also features a hypoplastic right ventricle and no connection between the right and left ventricles. This condition accounts for less than 1–3% of all congenital heart defects [1]. Echocardiography is the primary imaging method, while CT offers superior spatial resolution for assessing right ventricular morphology, pulmonary artery anatomy, coronary circulation, ductus arteriosus, and major aorto-pulmonary collaterals [2]. In PA-IVS, outflow obstruction from the right heart requires an interatrial communication (patent foramen ovale/atrial septal defect), major aorto-pulmonary collateral arteries (MAPCAs), or patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) to ensure pulmonary blood flow. Cyanosis worsens as the foramen ovale and PDA close. Initial management includes maintaining PDA with prostaglandins and PDA stenting. Management depends on factors like pulmonary atresia (membranous or muscular), right ventricle (RV) morphology, tricuspid valve condition, and coronary artery anomalies [1,3]. In PA-IVS, although the RV is hypoplastic, it becomes hypertensive due to its inability to eject blood into the pulmonary circulation, particularly in patients without tricuspid regurgitation. In 50–70 % of patients, the elevated pressure may result in the formation of communications with the epicardial coronary arteries or coronary sinusoids, creating coronary fistulas. In one-quarter of these patients, the proximal coronary arteries can be atretic or stenotic, and CT or catheter coronary angiogram has a pivotal role in their detection. For these individuals, the coronary supply is dependent on the RV pressure, presenting a critical condition that complicates management. RV decompression by interventional or surgical opening of the RV outflow tract can lead to catastrophic myocardial ischaemia and haemodynamic collapse due to the sudden reduction in RV pressure in such cases [3,4]. The neonate in this case report was treated with prostaglandins immediately after birth. However, he developed apnea, requiring ventilation and higher ionotropic support and prostaglandin infusion, suggesting closure of the ductus arteriosus. Therefore, PDA stenting was done. Depending on the clinical course of the patient, single ventricular procedure with bidirectional Glenn procedure (surgery connecting the superior vena cava to the pulmonary arteries) followed by Fontan procedure (surgery connecting the inferior vena cava return to the pulmonary arteries) need to be planned for proper blood flow to the pulmonary circulation [5]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

final_diagnosis: Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum

title: Wallerian degeneration of pontocerebellar tracts secondary to unilateral pontine infarction
clinical_history: A 61-year-old male, with a history of a pontine stroke 10 weeks before, presented with new neurological symptoms of staccato speech and an uncoordinated gait. Neurological examination revealed nystagmus, mild dysarthria, truncal and limb ataxia, and an unsteady gait. An MRI was performed to rule out a new ischemic stroke.
imaging_findings: Brain MRI showed a cavitated lesion in the left paramedian pons, hypointense on T1-weighted images (WI) (Figure 1a), hyperintense on T2WI (Figure 1b), without diffusion restriction (Figure 1c), consistent with the previous pontine stroke. Additionally, symmetrical ovoid lesions in the middle cerebellar peduncles (MCPs), hypointense on T1WI (Figure 1d) and hyperintense on T2WI (Figure 1e), and mild T2WI hyperintensity in the left anterior pyramid (Figure 1g), without diffusion restriction (Figures 1f and 1h), were also noted.
discussion: Wallerian degeneration (WD) is a progressive anterograde disintegration and demyelination of axons, which occurs after injury to the proximal axon or cell body [1]. Infarction is the leading cause of WD [2,3]. Nonetheless, other conditions, such as tumours, haemorrhage, epilepsy, and degenerative diseases, can also contribute to WD [2,3]. Although WD usually involves the corticospinal tract, other neuronal circuits, such as corticopontocerebellar or dentate-rubro-olivary tracts, can be affected [4]. MCPs serve as the primary pathway for pontocerebellar tracts (PCT), linking the basal pons to the cerebellum [2]. PCT originate from the contralateral pontine nuclei, which receive cortico-pontine tracts, crossing the midline at a higher pontine level before travelling through the MCP to access the cerebellar cortex. Consequently, a lesion on one side of the pontine nuclei, such as ischemic stroke (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c), can result in WD of the PCT, leading to symmetrical hyperintense lesions in the MCPs (Figures 1d, 1e, and 1f) [2,3,5]. T2WI hyperintensity in the left medullary pyramid (Figures 1g and 1h) represents concomitant Wallerian degeneration of the corticospinal tract. The differential diagnoses of symmetrical lesions on the MCPs include bilateral anterior inferior cerebellar artery ischemic stroke, basilar artery thrombosis, demyelinating diseases, toxic or metabolic diseases, such as adrenoleukodystrophy, Wilson’s disease, and hypoglycaemic encephalopathy, and neurodegenerative diseases, such as multiply system atrophy, fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome, and spinocerebellar ataxia [6]. Rehabilitation is crucial for minimising sequelae after stroke [7]. However, the presence of WD may adversely impact the recovery [8]. Cross-sectional studies suggested that the decrease of fractional anisotropy in the pyramidal tract following a stroke was associated with worse motor outcome [8,9]. WD can be a marker for poor motor recovery and functional outcome, and its detection may help prognostication and guide rehabilitation programs [10].
differential_diagnosis: Bilateral middle cerebellar peduncles ischemic stroke Wallerian degeneration of pontocerebellar tracts secondary to unilateral pontine infarction Multiple system atrophy Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome Wilson’s disease
final_diagnosis: Wallerian degeneration of pontocerebellar tracts secondary to unilateral pontine infarction

title: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XPN) in a child
clinical_history: An 8-year-old male patient presented with chronic left lumbar discomfort, claudication, anaemia (Hb = 8 g/dL), and hyperleukocytosis (12000/mm3). He has been receiving therapy for anaemia for two years.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound (US) shows multiple thick-walled collections with echogenic fluid content occupying the left renal fossa and loss of renal parenchyma’s architecture with no corticomedullary differentiation. The thin remaining peripheric parenchymal bundle shows no limits with the thick-walled collections. There is a central pyelic stone measuring 20 mm with a posterior acoustic shadow and a hyperechoic aspect of the perirenal fat. CT (computed tomography) shows left renal enlargement with destruction of parenchymal architecture and dilated calyces consistent with the “bear paw sign” (Figure 1a), coexisting blurring of perirenal fat, psoas muscle enlargement and abscess formation (Figure 1b), as well as nephroureterolithiasis (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d). The left kidney was nonfunctional at the excretory phase scan (Figures 1e and 1f). On renal scintigraphy (Figure 2), DTPA injection demonstrates reduced relative renal function on the left (17.7% left and 82.3% right), with pyelocaliceal stasis at the excretory phase. Reduced cortical uptake, particularly in the left upper pole, was seen both at DMSA and DTPA scans.
discussion: Background Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XPN) is a rare form of renal and perirenal destructive infection that is generally considered an adult condition [1] and is uncommon in children. Several hypotheses have been put forward to understand the physiopathology of XPN, including urinary tract obstruction due to lithiasis or malformation, and a neglected or ineffectively treated urinary tract infection. Symptoms are mild, which explains the delay in diagnosis. Our case presents an 8-year-old male patient with a delayed diagnosis of XPN, whose only symptoms included chronic lumbar pain and anaemia. Clinical Perspective Clinical presentation varies depending on the form of the disease: lower back pain, recurrent fever, altered general condition with malaise, and sometimes urinary symptoms. Clinical examination reveals a lumbar mass in 50% of cases [2]. Exceptionally, it may present with fistulisation toward the subcutaneous tissue [2]. The biological disturbances observed during XPN include hyperleukocytosis, leukocyturia, pyuria, inflammatory anaemia or erythropoietin deficiency [3]. Imaging Perspective CT and MRI are more sensitive than US for the diagnosis of XPN. MRI is a great alternative to CT scan, especially in children, due to the lack of radiation exposure. The pathognomonic sign of “bear paw”, added to the identification of obstructive Staghorn calculus, on CT images, are very suggestive of the diagnosis [5]. CT images allow for evaluation of the stage of the disease based on local extension, accordingly [3]: Stage I – focal intrarenal involvement. Stage II – extension beyond the kidney, respecting Gerota’s fascia. Stage III – extra renal extension to neighbouring tissues. Outcome The treatment of XPN is both medical and surgical. In the diffuse form with total and irreversible renal destruction, nephrectomy is performed [4]. In the focal form, percutaneous drainage of the abscess and adjunctive antibiotic therapy prior to partial nephrectomy can be discussed [6]. In our case, broad-spectrum antibiotherapy was administered both before and following left nephrectomy. The patient received blood transfusion post-operatively. The nephrectomy specimen was macroscopically friable and fragmented, with multiple pockets of pus and staghorn lithiasis within the renal pelvis (Figure 3). The histopathology study revealed chronic inflammatory lesions and enlarged lipid-laden vacuolated macrophages, confirming the diagnosis of XPN. The prognosis after total nephrectomy is excellent. Two weeks after surgery, the child came back with marked improvement in his general state. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XPN) is rarely seen in children. Mild, non-specific symptoms may cause a delay in diagnosis. CT images are very suggestive of the diagnosis, which is confirmed only with histological studies. Treatment is surgical. Excellent prognosis if XPN is early diagnosed and adequately treated.

title: Twin circumflex coronary arteries with accessory circumflex from left coronary sinus
clinical_history: A 62-year-old male patient, without diabetes or hypertension, presented with chest pain for a computed tomography coronary angiography (CTCA).
imaging_findings: CTCA was retrospectively triggered by electrocardiography (ECG) using a Philips 128-slice CT scanner, 60 ml non-iodinated contrast, flow rate 5 ml/s, 120 keV and tracking method. The study showed a normal origin of both the right coronary artery (RCA) and left coronary artery (LCA). The LCA bifurcates into left anterior descending (LAD) and circumflex arteries (Cx) (Figure 1). An accessory Cx arises directly from the left coronary sinus by a separate ostium and then runs at the left atrioventricular groove, giving off a small posterior descending artery (PDA) and posterolateral artery (PLA) (Figures 1 and 2). The proximal segment of the native left circumflex artery (LCx) showed concentric plaques exerting mild stenosis (Figure 5).
discussion: The identification and assessment of coronary artery abnormalities are greatly aided by multi-detector computed tomography (MDCT). Rapid, high-resolution views of the coronary arteries are provided by MDCT, a noninvasive imaging method that makes it possible to examine the vascular structure of the heart in great detail. This feature is particularly useful for identifying anomalous patterns in the coronary artery branching off the heart that conventional imaging techniques can miss [1–3]. Coronary artery anomalies are innate vascular abnormalities that can remain undetected and symptom-free throughout a person’s life. These variants are uncommon and are found in approximately 1% of the population. Approximately 20% of coronary abnormalities (deep myocardial bridge with significant calibre attenuation and systolic milking, inter-arterial intra-mural course of coronary artery, transseptal LAD, coronary fistula, ALCAPA, ARCAPA) result in severe symptoms such as arrhythmia, syncope, myocardial infarction, or sudden death [4–6]. Cx is one of the two major coronary arteries that arise from the bifurcation of the LCA (the other branch is the LAD artery) [7]. The most reported anomaly concerning Cx is its origin from the right aortic sinus or right coronary artery with a retroaortic course. Moreover, twin or dual Cx arteries have also been reported to originate from both the RCA and LCA, where the accessory Cx was seen to originate from the RCA or right aortic sinus [8,9]. The most recent reported anomaly is the dual Cx arteries with a direct origin of the accessory Cx from the left aortic sinus [10]. Dual left Cx is a benign anomaly that specifically arises from the left coronary sinus by separate ostia. Symptoms related to accessory LCx as chest pain, heart failure and arrhythmia, occur if accessory LCx arises from the right coronary sinus with retroaortic course due to accelerated atherosclerosis and compression by the aortic root. Although a benign anomaly, it is important to be reported with a full description of its course to avoid accidental surgical injury, as clamping or transection [11]. We present a case of twin Cx (circumflex arteries) with a direct origin of the accessory Cx from the left coronary sinus.

title: Incidental discovery of a stage 2A primary adrenocortical adenocarcinoma
clinical_history: A 40-year-old male presented to the emergency department following the onset of acute right lower quadrant abdominal pain, later diagnosed as inflamed, nonperforated appendicitis. On CT abdomen and pelvis (CTAP), an incidental adrenal mass was found on the left kidney. Work-up for the adrenal mass was conducted.
imaging_findings: In 2018, a CTAP noted a 17 mm left adrenal nodule without normal washout characteristics (Figure 1). The work-up at the time revealed no functional secretion, and the patient was also asymptomatic. A new CTAP revealed that the previous nodule had grown to a size of 6.4 x 6 x 6.7 cm (Figure 2). A chest CT with contrast was unremarkable. An MRI was ordered for further characterisation of the mass. T1 MRI visualised a heterogeneous enhancing left adrenal mass that was suspicious of malignancy (Figure 3). The size of the lesion was consistent compared to the CTAP.
discussion: Background Primary adrenocortical adenocarcinoma (PACC) is an extremely rare and insidious cancer typically found incidentally on imaging for reasons unsuspecting of adrenal disease. It has an incidence of 0.07 per 100,000 in patients 15–49 years old that increases with age; 40–70% of incidentalomas are nonfunctional, and 0.4–4% are PACCs [1,2]. Incidentalomas are most commonly benign nonfunctioning adenomas, but primary malignancy may rarely exist. PACC is a rare but aggressively malignant form of adrenal incidentaloma that involves the adrenal cortex, causing Cushingoid sequelae due to excess steroid hormone production [2]. PACCs are divided into subtypes by cytomorphological features, including conventional, oncocytic, myxoid, and sarcomatoid [3]. Imaging Perspective Differentiation of benign from malignant adrenal tumours is primarily through radiological imaging using CT, MRI, or FDG-PET scanning. Standard non-contrast CT scanning is the most reliable imaging tool for the detection of PACCs [2]. In our case, the patient was asymptomatic with normal hormone levels, highlighting the insidious nature of early-stage disease. Given the low prevalence but high malignancy potential, adrenal incidentalomas require careful evaluation. Imaging plays a crucial role in characterising tumour behaviour and guiding management decisions. Non-contrast CT is the most reliable initial modality, showing mass density and morphology suggestive of malignancy [2]. In this case, a stage 2A PACC was incidentally discovered on CT during an evaluation for appendicitis. Key imaging findings that raise suspicion include size > 4 cm, irregular borders, and high unenhanced attenuation. FDG-PET and MRI may further characterise lesions, but histopathological confirmation using Lin–Weiss–Bisceglia criteria remains definitive [7]. Outcome Our patient underwent a successful adrenalectomy, and the specimen was obtained for cytologic analysis (Figure 4). The specimen was removed with clear margins. Sentinel lymph node biopsy was also obtained with no evidence of disease extension. No contiguous spread was observed in the final excision. Post-operative monitoring showed no recurrence, and adjuvant therapy was deemed unnecessary. Surgical resection is the primary treatment for early-stage PACC. Prognosis remains poor overall, with a 5-year survival rate below 60% and a high metastasis risk even in stage I–III disease [8,9]. Genetic analysis in our patient revealed TP53 , PTEN , and MSH6 variants—mutations associated with poor prognosis and cancer susceptibility [8]. Mitotane may be considered for unresectable or high-risk cases, but was not indicated here due to early-stage, complete resection [9]. Take Home Message In summary, PACC (primary adrenocortical adenocarcinoma) is a rare but highly malignant tumour that may be incidentally discovered in asymptomatic patients. Imaging is central to detection and staging; CT remains the cornerstone of diagnosis. Histologic evaluation and genetic profiling are essential for definitive diagnosis and prognostic assessment. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for incidental adrenal masses to avoid missing early-stage malignancies [10–12]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Chondroblastic osteosarcoma of the proximal humerus in a young man
clinical_history: An 18-year-old healthy male presents with three months of left shoulder pain during activities, followed by a gradual restriction in arm abduction. He denies any trauma, fever, or involvement of other joints. Physical examination reveals swelling in the deltoid region and an inability to raise the left arm to 90°.
imaging_findings: Left shoulder x-ray (Figure 1) revealed a mixed sclerotic-lytic lesion involving the proximal diaphysis and metaphysis of the humerus, characterised by poorly defined margins, a wide transition zone, permeative osteolysis, cortical thinning, and a spiculated periosteal reaction with Codman’s triangle, consistent with a Bone-RADS 4 lesion. MRI demonstrated a large lobulated mass centred in the proximal humerus, hypointense on T1-weighted images (Figure 2a), hyperintense on T2 (Figure 2b) and STIR (Figures 2c and 2d) sequences, with associated extraosseous soft tissue extension and glenohumeral joint effusion. Post-contrast fat-suppressed T1-weighted imaging (Figure 2e) showed heterogeneous enhancement with central non-enhancing areas. Diffusion-weighted imaging (Figure 2f) revealed restricted diffusion with corresponding low signal on the ADC map (Figure 2g) indicating high cellularity. PET/CT (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d) confirmed an intraosseous mass with osteoid matrix and aggressive periosteal reaction, demonstrating hypermetabolic activity in the proximal humerus, adjacent soft tissues, and secondary foci in the lungs and spinal canal.
discussion: Background Osteosarcomas are rare malignancies, accounting for less than 1% of all cancers [1]. Chondroblastic osteosarcoma is a rare and aggressive subtype of osteosarcoma, representing 25% of all cases. It is associated with higher rates of recurrence, metastasis, and a median overall survival estimated at 28 months [2]. It is characterised by a mineralised tumour matrix containing chondrocyte cell lines [1]. The incidence is higher in men, with a ratio of 1.5:1. This condition primarily occurs in the metaphysis of long bones [3]. Rapid bone growth predisposes individuals to developing osteosarcoma, which commonly manifests during the pubertal growth spurt and near the growing physis [4]. The most frequently affected bones are the tibia and femur [5]. Clinical Perspective The main symptoms include bone pain during activity and swelling at the end of a long bone [6]. Imaging modalities allow for assessing disease aggressiveness and extent, establishing prognosis, guiding treatment, and facilitating follow-up evaluations. Imaging Perspective Radiological X-ray findings detailed in Bone-RADS provide an estimate of malignancy risk for a given lesion. Bone-RADS scores range from 0 (incompletely characterised) to 4 (high risk) [7]. High-risk radiological findings predictive of malignancy include poorly defined margins with a mottled or permeative pattern of osteolysis. Malignant periosteal reactions consist of lamellated, parallel spiculated, and divergent spiculated types. Additionally, the degree of endosteal erosion, pathological fractures, and extraosseous soft tissue masses are significantly high suspicious predictors [7]. CT allows for the evaluation of bone matrix and architecture, identifies calcified bone matrix deposits, and detects pathological fractures. MRI provides superior soft tissue characterisation, enabling assessment of marrow infiltration, joint involvement, extraosseous extension, and neurovascular involvement. In this case, the lesion appears hypointense on T1-weighted sequences, hyperintense on T2 and STIR imaging, due to the soft tissue and matrix component, and shows heterogeneous enhancement with central non-enhancing areas after contrast administration. Restricted diffusion with low ADC values is consistent with high cellularity. PET/CT is utilised for staging and treatment follow-up [8]. Outcome A definitive diagnosis of chondroblastic osteosarcoma is established through a biopsy study that shows hyaline cartilage with a predominant component of cytological atypia [9]. This patient underwent an incisional bone biopsy that revealed areas of chondroid and osteoid matrix consistent with chondroblastic osteosarcoma. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy was indicated, followed by subsequent block resection of the proximal humerus and installation of a reverse humerus prosthesis (Figure 4). Palliative radiotherapy was indicated after follow-up images showed progression of secondary disease.

title: A case of primary prostatic urethral neoplasm
clinical_history: An 83-year-old gentleman presented to the Urosurgery department with a history of lower urinary tract symptoms in the form of increased frequency and incomplete evacuation of urine. No history of haematuria, burning micturition or fever. On digital rectal examination, the prostate gland was felt to be enlarged with nodularity within felt. On biochemical evaluation, prostate specific antigen (PSA) was marginally raised.
imaging_findings: On ultrasound examination, an enlarged prostate with a volume of 36 cc. There were features of chronic bladder outlet obstruction seen in the form of thickening of the bladder wall (maximum thickness of 8 mm) and a few trabeculations in the bladder wall. In view of the elevated PSA levels, an MRI prostate was done, which revealed a well-defined, solid, irregularly shaped lesion measuring 3.5 x 5.4 x 5.7 cm (AP x TR x CC) arising from the prostatic urethra and causing its widening and extending into the bladder. This lesion was homogeneously hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted and T2-weighted fat-saturated images (Figures 1 and 2). It was showing homogeneous restriction of diffusion on DWI (Figures 3a and 3b) and was heterogeneously enhancing on post-contrast images. Also, multiple well-defined T2 heterogeneous nodules were seen in the transitional zone (Figure 4). No T2 hypointense or diffusion-restricting lesion was seen in the prostate.
discussion: Diagnosis With those findings, an impression of a primary urethral neoplasm arising from the prostatic urethra with resultant chronic bladder outlet obstruction was given. HPE examination revealed the mass to be a primary urothelial carcinoma with origin from the prostatic urethra. Background Primary urethral neoplasms are very rare in occurrence, accounting for < 1% of all malignancies [1]. These neoplasms have a peak incidence in the elderly population over 75 years of age, with a predilection to males [2]. Most common carcinomas involving the urethra are urothelial carcinoma (54–60%), followed by squamous cell carcinoma (16–22%) and adenocarcinoma (10–15%) [3]. The most common site for urethral urothelial carcinoma is the prostatic urethra. The aetiology of urethral malignancies is unclear. However, many predisposing factors such as urethral strictures, external beam irradiation therapy, chronic urethral inflammation or urethritis, urethral diverticula, and recurrent urinary tract infections have been identified in various studies [4–6]. Clinical Perspective Due to the rare nature of urethral neoplasms, the clinical presentation is not very well studied. It can present with advanced symptoms in half of the patients. The most common presenting complaint is haematuria or bloody urethral discharge (62%). Other late symptoms can be an extra-urethral mass (52%), bladder outlet obstruction (48%) or pelvic pain (33%) [7]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Although a rare type of malignancy, it can be kept as a differential diagnosis in cases with a mass within the urethra causing its widening. The primary goal of radiological imaging is to assess local tumour extent and detect lymphatic and distant metastatic spread. Written informed consent from the patient was obtained for publication.

title: Hidden in the muscle: Incidental detection of a quadratus femoris haemangioma
clinical_history: A 68-year-old female presented to the emergency department with acute lower abdominal pain, accompanied by chronic burning sensations and stabbing pain in the right lower leg. Based on the initial clinical presentation, diverticulitis was suspected, and a routine abdominal CT scan was performed for further evaluation.
imaging_findings: CT imaging demonstrated a lipomatous, highly vascularised mass located posterior to the proximal femoral diaphysis of the right hip, with extension into the ischiofemoral space (Figures 1a and 1b). The lesion was predominantly composed of fatty tissue and exhibited intense arterial enhancement, consistent with a hypervascular process. Subsequent MRI offered further characterisation, identifying a complex intramuscular mass within the right quadratus femoris muscle, composed of both lipomatous (hyperintense on T1-weighted images) and nodular components (Figure 2). The nodular areas appeared hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2 fat-suppressed sequences (Figure 3). These regions demonstrated moderate, heterogeneous contrast enhancement, indicating variable internal vascularity (Figure 4). There were no significant signal voids on T2* sequences, effectively excluding haemorrhage or calcification. The lesion did not invade surrounding structures. However, the adjacent sciatic nerve exhibited focal thickening, which was suggestive of possible irritation due to mass effect or local inflammation (Figure 5).
discussion: Diagnosis An ultrasound-guided biopsy was performed. Histopathological analysis confirmed the diagnosis of an intramuscular haemangioma. Background Intramuscular haemangiomas are rare, benign vascular tumours accounting for about 0.8% of benign soft tissue tumours. They arise from abnormal blood vessel growth, mostly congenital, though up to 20% are linked to trauma. These tumours do not metastasise and typically follow a natural progression involving growth, fibrofatty replacement, thrombosis, atrophy, and eventual involution. They most commonly occur in subcutaneous fat but may also develop within muscles, especially in the thigh (36%) and calf (17%) [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Many intramuscular haemangiomas are small and asymptomatic, which likely leads to underreporting. However, they should be considered in patients with chronic musculoskeletal pain, especially without clear trauma or degenerative causes. Pain is present in around 60% of cases, often involving long, narrow muscles, and worsens with exercise due to vascular dilation and increased pressure. The average symptom duration before diagnosis is roughly 13 months, indicating delayed recognition [3]. Imaging Perspective MRI is the preferred diagnostic tool, reliably differentiating haemangiomas from malignant tumours. On T1-weighted MRI, lesions show high signal intensity reflecting fat, with low-signal areas corresponding to fibrous tissue or thrombi. T2-weighted images reveal high signal intensity with a characteristic multilobulated or “bag of worms” pattern and a central low-intensity “dot sign” specific to haemangiomas. Ultrasound may show hyperechoic masses and abnormal Doppler flow, but is less specific. CT scans help evaluate bone involvement or when MRI is contraindicated, revealing poorly defined soft tissue masses with fat attenuation and detecting phleboliths. The presence of phleboliths—calcified thrombi—is also considered pathognomonic for haemangiomas. Angiography is useful in complex or high-flow cases to guide embolisation or surgery [4]. Outcome Conservative management is the first line for minimally symptomatic patients and often results in gradual symptom resolution. Surgery is reserved for cases with functional impairment, fast growth, or malignancy concerns, but carries a risk of recurrence if excision is incomplete. Other treatments like sclerotherapy, embolisation, or radiation are options when surgery is not feasible. Regular follow-up is essential regardless of treatment to monitor progression or recurrence [5]. Take Home Message Intramuscular haemangiomas are an uncommon but important cause of chronic musculoskeletal pain. Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical, imaging, and histopathological findings. Most cases are managed conservatively, reserving surgery for specific indications. Early diagnosis and ongoing monitoring improve outcomes and avoid unnecessary interventions. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Intraneural ganglion cyst of the common fibular nerve
clinical_history: A 75-year-old woman with diabetes presents with lower back pain, neurogenic claudication, and left leg weakness after a fall. She reports paraesthesia and electric shock-like pain along the fibular nerve. Physical examination shows grade I muscle strength. Electromyography indicates polyneuropathy and fibular nerve injury. Magnetic resonance imaging was subsequently requested based on these findings.
imaging_findings: Axial T1-weighted and T2-weighted fat-suppressed images of the upper, middle (Figures 1a and 1b), and lower thirds of the leg reveal signal alterations and an oedema pattern in the anterior compartment muscles and part of the fibularis muscle fibres, indicating denervation. Complementary coronal T1-weighted (Figure 2a), coronal T2-weighted fat-saturated (Figure 2b), sagittal proton density-weighted (Figure 2c), sagittal T2-weighted fat-saturated (Figure 2d), and axial T2-weighted fat-saturated (Figure 2e) images demonstrate a cystic lesion within the topography of the common fibular nerve, along with fluid distension of the proximal tibiofibular joint—findings consistent with a ganglion cyst with intraneural extension.
discussion: Background Intraneural ganglion cysts are benign mucinous lesions that affect peripheral nerves, most commonly the common peroneal nerve near the superior tibiofibular joint [1,2]. Although relatively rare, their diagnosis is increasing due to advances in imaging techniques [3]. A meta-analysis by Desy et al. involving over 600 cases revealed that 60.6% of these cysts involve the common peroneal nerve [2,3], while only a small percentage—about 15 cases—affect the tibial nerve [4]. Figure 3 highlights the lower limb nerves, with the common fibular (peroneal) nerve (shown in pink) representing the typical site for intraneural ganglion cyst development. The unified articular theory, supported by clinical, MRI, and surgical evidence, is the most widely accepted explanation for their pathogenesis. It proposes that synovial fluid dissects through the articular branch of a joint, entering the nerve and forming a cyst [1,5,6]. These cysts typically originate from the superior tibiofibular joint and travel along the articular branch of the deep peroneal nerve, expanding within the epineurium and compressing nerve fascicles, which can result in swelling and neurological symptoms [1,3]. Clinical Perspective Clinically, intraneural cysts can cause pain, paraesthesia, muscle weakness, denervation, and atrophy. Patients may present with motor deficits, foot drop, a high-stepping gait, and sensory changes [2,7]. Imaging Perspective Magnetic resonance imaging is the gold standard for diagnosis, offering detailed visualisation of soft tissues and characteristic signs such as the “tail sign” (narrow pedicle connecting the cyst to the joint), “popliteus sign” (denervation atrophy of the popliteus muscle), and the “signet ring sign” (eccentric displacement of fascicles) [4]. Ultrasonography is a useful alternative for superficial structures and can help distinguish cystic from solid lesions, particularly when MRI is contraindicated [4,8,9]. Several differential diagnoses were considered but excluded based on MRI features and lesion location. Cystic nerve sheath tumours, such as schwannomas and neurofibromas, typically present as well-defined fusiform masses along the nerve path, showing isointensity on T1 and hyperintensity on T2-weighted images. Neurofibromas may display a “target sign”, and post-contrast enhancement is often heterogeneous, features not seen in this case. Atypical Baker’s cysts, which may extend in unusual directions or dissect into neurovascular structures, are fluid-filled on MRI, with possible internal debris, haemorrhage, or wall enhancement. However, their origin and morphology were inconsistent with the observed findings. Extraneural ganglion cysts often arise near the proximal tibiofibular joint but remain separate from nerve structures. On MRI, they appear lobulated and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, without intraneural tracking. In contrast, the cyst in this case clearly followed the course of the common fibular nerve, supporting the diagnosis of an intraneural ganglion cyst of the common fibular nerve. Outcome The primary treatment is surgical and involves decompression, cyst evacuation, and disconnection of the articular branch to the joint to prevent recurrence [2,5,10]. Addressing the articular connection is essential to reduce recurrence and avoid iatrogenic nerve injury [3]. However, recurrence still occurs in about 11% of cases and depends on the initial surgical technique [2,3]. Desy et al. describe three main recurrence patterns, emphasising the need for precise technique to prevent future cyst formation [2,3]. Ultrasound-guided aspiration is a less invasive alternative, though it carries a risk of injury to surrounding structures and lacks long-term data on recurrence rates [4]. In this particular case, however, ultrasound imaging was not utilised. Take Home Message / Teaching Points In conclusion, although intraneural ganglion cysts are uncommon, accurate imaging and appropriate surgical intervention are key to effective treatment and minimising recurrence. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Cystic nerve sheath tumour Intraneural ganglion cyst of the common fibular nerve Atypical Baker’s cyst Extraneural ganglion
final_diagnosis: Intraneural ganglion cyst of the common fibular nerve

title: Pott’s disease with multiloculated psoas abscess
clinical_history: A 20-year-old male presented with worsening lower back pain for 6 months. On physical examination there was no deformity or neurological deficits noted. There was no history of fever, night sweats or weight loss.
imaging_findings: An anteroposterior (AP) and lateral radiograph (Figures 1a and 1b) of the lumbar spine was done initially. It showed reduced intervertebral disc space at the L2–L3 level with adjacent end plate erosions and sclerosis, and soft tissue opacity in the paravertebral region at the L2–L3 lumbar vertebral level. Loss of the psoas muscle outline was also noted. On MRI, partial destruction of the posteroinferior aspect of L1 and posterosuperior aspect of L2 is seen with involvement of the intervening IV disc (Figures 2a and 2b). Altered signal intensity is seen in the vertebral bodies of L4 and L5, which appear hypointense on T1-weighted (T1WI) and hyperintense on T2-weighted (T2WI). There is an associated extensive, multiloculated prevertebral and bilateral paravertebral collection seen (Figures 3a, 3b, 4a, and 4b). The soft tissue components appear hypointense on T1WI and hyperintense on T2W images. These show peripheral restriction of diffusion (Figures 7a and 7b). On post-contrast imaging (Figures 5a, 5b, and 6), there is enhancement of the soft tissue components with central necrotic areas and the involved parts of L1 and L2 vertebral bodies.
discussion: Background Tuberculosis (TB) is one of the oldest documented infectious diseases in the world, which still has a significant disease burden in endemic countries [1]. Pott’s disease refers to the extrapulmonary form of TB, which has spread haematogenously to involve the spine, preferentially the thoracolumbar spine [2]. Pott’s spine is the most common form of skeletal TB approximately constituting 50% of the cases [3]. Clinical Perspective Pott’s disease presentation can be variable depending upon the duration, severity and presence of complications, such as deformity or neurological deficit [4]. Symptoms are usually insidious in onset and progression of the disease is slow. The most common and earliest symptom is back pain. Constitutional symptoms usually associated with pulmonary TB are less commonly associated with extrapulmonary TB [5]. Imaging Perspective The goal of imaging is not only to confirm the diagnosis but also to evaluate the extent of disease, detect complications, and aid in treatment planning. A chest X-ray is a valuable diagnostic tool, as up to one-third of these patients may also have coexisting pulmonary tuberculosis [6]. The disease commonly affects two adjacent vertebrae and the disc, but extension to three or more levels is frequent and characteristic [7]. Early signs on plane radiograph include radiolucency and unclear endplates. Common features are anterior vertebral destruction, disc height loss, endplate erosion, and paravertebral masses, often with calcification, suggesting TB. In advanced stages, the disease spreads, causing sclerosis, vertebral collapse, and kyphotic deformities. Typical MRI findings include low signal intensity on T1WI and high signal on T2WI in affected vertebrae. Paraspinal and epidural abscesses are commonly visualised, often with rim enhancement after gadolinium administration. MRI also effectively identifies subligamentous spread, spinal cord compression, and the presence of multilevel involvement, all of which are crucial for assessing disease severity and guiding management. Outcome Our patient was diagnosed with TB spine and was started on antitubercular drugs. No neurological complications developed during treatment. The patient continues to be monitored clinically and radiologically, with no signs of disease progression or complications. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Consider spinal TB in patients with chronic back pain, especially in endemic areas, even in the absence of constitutional symptoms. MRI is the most sensitive modality for detecting early vertebral involvement, abscesses, and complications. Early diagnosis and prompt initiation of anti-tubercular treatment are essential to prevent irreversible spinal deformity and neurological damage.

title: Congenital femoral deficiency and absence of the anterior cruciate ligament
clinical_history: A 15-year-old female patient with right lower limb shortening since childhood was evaluated in consultation for limb lengthening surgery. Her personal history was negative for trauma. On physical examination, she had a clinically measured leg-length discrepancy of 4 cm.
imaging_findings: Full-length standing anteroposterior view radiograph (Figure 1a) demonstrated right lower limb shortening secondary to femoral hypoplasia, with normal ossification and no proximal deformity, consistent with Paley type 1A congenital femoral deficiency (CFD). Mild proximal fibular shortening was also noted, compatible with fibular hemimelia (Achterman–Kalamchi type IA). On the magnified AP radiograph of the right knee (Figure 1b), the femoral intercondylar notch appeared shallow, and the tibial spines were markedly hypoplastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur (anterior drawer sign) and uncovering of the lateral meniscus posterior horn (Figure 2b), findings suggestive of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) insufficiency. On mid-sagittal fat-suppressed proton-density (PD) and oblique sagittal PD-weighted images (Figures 2c and 2d), the ACL was not visualised. The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) was present and vertically oriented (positive PCL line sign). No bone marrow oedema was seen, and the menisci were unremarkable.
discussion: Background CFD encompasses a spectrum of femoral anatomical disorders that ranges from congenital short femur to severe proximal focal femoral deficiency. Most CFD cases are unilateral, with the right femur more commonly affected [1]. Diagnosis may be made prenatally on obstetric ultrasound, postnatally, or even later in childhood due to leg–length discrepancy and impaired mobility [1,2]. Several classification systems have been described, including the Paley classification, which focuses on the degree of development and integrity of the femur [2]. Other congenital musculoskeletal abnormalities of the ipsilateral lower limb may be present, with fibular hemimelia being the most common [1,3,4]. Notably, Manner et al. reported that, in a study of 34 knees with CFD, the ACL was affected in all cases—15% were hypoplastic and 85% were absent—while the PCL was hypoplastic in 21% and absent in 24% [5]. Imaging Perspective Radiographs are used to assess the configuration of the proximal femur and measure the lengths of the femur and tibia. Femoral abnormalities range from mild shortening to subtrochanteric pseudoarthrosis, with severe deficiency of the hip joint and proximal femur [3]. The shape of the distal femur and proximal tibia can be classified using the Manner et al. classification, and the absence of cruciate ligaments may be inferred from the narrowing of the femoral intercondylar notch and the flattening of the tibial spines [2,5]. MRI is particularly useful for assessing the proximal femur and subtrochanteric pseudoarthrosis, but knee MRI may be indicated when clinical and radiographic evaluation suggests deformity or instability. In our case, given the radiographic suspicion of cruciate ligament hypoplasia or agenesis, a knee MRI was obtained. Sagittal images through the lateral femorotibial compartment demonstrated anterior tibial translation (anterior drawer sign) and the uncovering of the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus, findings suggestive of ACL insufficiency. Additionally, non-visualisation of ACL fibres in the intercondylar region and the absence of bone marrow oedema or associated injuries (e.g., meniscal ramp lesions) support the possibility of congenital ACL agenesis. The PCL was present and vertically oriented, indicating a positive PCL line sign, in which a line tangent to the upper border of the PCL does not intersect the medullary cavity of the distal femur and suggests ACL insufficiency. Outcome Treatment of congenital femoral deficiency (CFD) depends on the severity and associated anomalies, with goals including hip stability, limb length equalisation, and near-normal anatomical alignment. Regarding anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) agenesis, asymptomatic knee instability is not necessarily an indication for reconstructive surgery, although reconstruction may be considered if the patient is undergoing concurrent corrective procedures. Our patient is currently awaiting definitive surgical planning; however, in the absence of major associated abnormalities or symptoms, she is expected to undergo isolated limb lengthening surgery. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Small bowel intussusception after gastric bypass surgery
clinical_history: A 35-year-old female presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain, nausea, and intense restlessness. She had no fever, vomiting, or signs of systemic illness. Her surgical history included a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass in 2016 (9 years ago) and a separate laparoscopic small bowel revision procedure in 2019 (6 years ago) due to suspected adhesive obstruction.
imaging_findings: CT of the abdomen (Figures 1a and 1b) demonstrated a pronounced small bowel intussusception at the entero-enteric anastomosis. The involved bowel loop showed a sac-like configuration with central, tortuous, and congested mesenteric vessels. The intussuscepted segment measured approximately 12 cm, with mild pre-stenotic dilation. Minimal enhancement of the bowel wall was noted (Figure 2), indicating reduced enhancement compared to normal adjacent bowel loops, suggesting venous congestion and early ischemia. CT was performed in the portal-venous phase without oral contrast. Hyperattenuating suture material was visible at the lead point of the intussusception, consistent with the previous anastomosis.
discussion: Background Intussusception in adults is rare and even more uncommon after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB). The entero-enteric anastomosis is a known complication site, which can lead to bowel obstruction, ischemia, and frequently requires surgical intervention [1,2]. Clinical Perspective The patient presented with signs of acute abdomen and obstruction. Her history of previous intussusception after RYGB heightened clinical suspicion and expedited imaging. The previous intussusception was reduced without resection or revision of the anastomosis, although mesenteric defects were closed. Imaging Perspective CT is the diagnostic modality of choice and, in this case, demonstrated typical findings of telescoping bowel loops with central mesenteric vessel crowding and reduced wall enhancement. The absence of portal venous gas or pneumoperitoneum was reassuring, but signs of venous congestion warranted urgent surgical management. An intussusception length >100 mm on CT in RYGB patients is a sign indicating the patient requires emergent surgery [3]. Outcome Laparoscopic exploration confirmed a long-segment small bowel intussusception involving the common limb, causing entero-enteric obstruction. Despite evidence of strangulation, there was no ischemia. The bowel was reduced, mesenteric defects were closed, and serosal tears, attributed to traction during the intussusception, were repaired. The patient recovered uneventfully post-operatively, receiving prophylactic antibiotics for 48 hours. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Intussusception after gastric bypass should be considered in post-RYGB patients with acute abdominal pain. CT is the preferred imaging modality for diagnosis and management planning. Prompt surgical intervention is key to avoiding irreversible ischemia.

title: Anaplastic meningioma presenting with subdural haematoma: A diagnostic challenge
clinical_history: A 55-year-old male presented with headache, giddiness, disorientation, and right lower limb weakness. He had a recent history of a fall.
imaging_findings: Initial MRI revealed a crescent-shaped extra-axial lesion along the right frontoparietotemporal convexity, hyperintense on T1 and FLAIR-weighted sequences (Figures 1a and 1b), with mild mass effect and midline shift, suggesting a subacute subdural haematoma. A similar extra-axial collection was seen on the left side. No diffusion restriction was observed on DWI (Figure 1c). A well-defined enhancing lesion was also seen in the right lateral ventricle (persistent in serial imaging). The patient was initially managed conservatively and scheduled for follow-up. Two months later, a non-contrast CT was performed due to recurrence of symptoms, including disorientation and right lower limb weakness. CT revealed a well-defined subdural extraxial crescent-shaped collection along the cerebral convexity in the left frontoparietal region. It was causing a mass effect on the underlying cerebral parenchyma. Midline shift was noted towards the right, with left uncal herniation and dilatation of the contralateral lateral ventricle. A heterogeneous predominantly iso to hypodense lesion was seen along the left frontoparietal convexity, causing mass effect on the underlying brain parenchyma and left lateral ventricle (Figure 2a). Mild periosteal reaction along the inner table of the left parietal bone was observed (Figure 2b). No update MRI with gadolinium contrast was performed between this CT and surgery. This may have limited diagnostic clarity and contributed to incomplete preoperative planning. Intraoperatively, no haematoma was identified. Instead, thickened dura, granular periosteum and hyperostosis of underlying bone were noted, raising concern for an underlying neoplastic process (Figure 3). Postoperative contrast-enhanced MRI revealed a well-defined extra-axial lesion in the left frontoparietotemporal region. It was hyperintense on T2/FLAIR, isointense on T1, with mild diffusion restriction and heterogeneous peripheral enhancement (Figures 4a, 4b, 4c and 4d). There was also a significant mass effect on the adjacent brain parenchyma and ventricles. T1 hyperintense and T2 hypointense areas likely represented postoperative changes. A thin underlying T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense, and non-enhancing collection were also noted.
discussion: Background Anaplastic meningiomas (WHO Grade III) account for less than 2% of all meningiomas and are characterised by rapid growth, aggressive local invasion, necrosis, and a high risk of recurrence [1,2]. These tumours may arise de novo or through malignant progression of lower-grade meningiomas. Their imaging appearance can vary significantly, especially in the presence of haemorrhage, necrosis, or secondary inflammatory changes. Clinical Perspective Given the clinical context of our patient and the initial MRI findings of a crescentic extra-axial hyperintensity along the right frontoparietotemporal convexity, a diagnosis of subacute subdural haematoma was favoured. A second collection was noted contralaterally. The patient was managed conservatively. However, two months later, he presented again with worsening neurological symptoms. At this point, non-contrast CT revealed a hyperdense left extra-axial lesion with significant mass effect. While initially interpreted as a subacute subdural haemorrhage, no haematoma was found intraoperatively, and a thickened dura and abnormal periosteum were instead encountered. Imaging Perspective Initial MRI showed crescentic extra-axial lesions that were hyperintense on T1 and FLAIR-weighted sequences, with no diffusion restriction, suggesting subacute haematoma. However, the presence of bilateral collections, a stable, enhancing intraventricular lesion, and extracranial soft tissue thickening on CT raised subtle but important concerns. Critically, a follow-up contrast-enhanced MRI was not performed prior to surgery, despite progressive symptoms and changing CT findings. Postoperative MRI revealed a heterogeneously enhancing extra-axial mass with diffusion restriction, midline shift, and persistent mass effect. Histopathology confirmed the diagnosis of anaplastic meningioma. Although a traumatic subdural haematoma was initially a reasonable diagnosis given the history of trauma, the atypical features and evolving clinical course warranted re-evaluation. In retrospect, the lesion was not a case of anaplastic meningioma mimicking subdural haematoma, but rather a high-grade meningioma complicated by subdural haemorrhage, which constituted its initial and misleading imaging appearance. This dual pathology tumour with secondary haemorrhage in the context of trauma obscured the underlying neoplastic process. Outcome Surgery revealed no haematoma but thickened dura, thickened granular periosteum and hyperostosis of underlying bone. Histopathology confirmed a WHO Grade III anaplastic meningioma with bone involvement. Postoperative imaging clarified the extent of the lesion, including mass effect and heterogeneous enhancement. While the patient’s presenting symptoms were initially attributed to post-traumatic haemorrhage, the underlying aggressive tumour ultimately accounted for the clinical progression. Teaching Points Subdural haematomas secondary to trauma can coexist with or obscure underlying neoplastic lesions. Persistent or atypical imaging features, such as enhancement, extracranial soft tissue thickening, or bilateral involvement, should raise suspicion even in the presence of trauma history. Delayed contrast-enhanced imaging may miss the window for appropriate preoperative diagnosis. A multimodality approach, including contrast MRI and CT, is essential for surgical planning in complex extra-axial lesions. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Infection by Mycobacterium avium
clinical_history: A 74-year-old female undergoing immunosuppressive therapy was referred to the orthopaedic department for evaluation of a progressively enlarging mass on the medial side of the left knee, evolving over six months. Initially asymptomatic, the lesion became painful. Notably, she had undergone an articular puncture one year earlier.
imaging_findings: The patient presented with a large mass on the medial aspect of the left knee (Figures 1a and 1b), which was also evident on plain radiography (Figure 2). Ultrasonography demonstrated a sizable extra-articular heterogeneous lesion with no internal vascularisation, accompanied by a moderate joint effusion and synovial hypertrophy (Figures 3a and 3b). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed a large extra-articular collection, hyperintense on proton density-weighted fat-suppressed sequences (Figures 4a and 4b) and hypointense on T1-weighted sequences (Figure 4c), with extensive peripheral enhancement following gadolinium administration (Figures 5a and 5b) and no enhancement of solid components. Additionally, MRI revealed extensive synovitis and bone marrow oedema, along with juxta-articular and intra-articular erosions exhibiting peripheral contrast enhancement. No blooming artefacts were identified (Figure 5c).
discussion: Diagnosis A surgical debridement of the collection was performed in this case. Microbiological testing identified Mycobacterium avium . Background Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), including Mycobacterium avium , are ubiquitous in the environment, commonly found in soil and water. Musculoskeletal infections caused by NTM are rare but increasingly reported, likely due to improved detection methods and rising use of immunosuppressive therapies [1,2]. Although distinct from Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MT), clinical knowledge of NTM infections is often derived from tuberculosis literature due to limited case numbers [3]. NTM infections can spread haematogenously but more frequently occur via direct inoculation through trauma or invasive procedures, such as prosthetic joint implantation or surgical interventions, as seen in our patient [1,3]. Clinical Presentation The clinical presentation is typically chronic and nonspecific, with symptoms including localised pain and swelling, joint stiffness, low-grade fever, weight loss, and night sweats. The disease course is generally milder than tuberculous infections [3,4]. NTM can affect all parts of the musculoskeletal system, presenting as, for example, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, cellulitis, abscesses, and septic myositis [3]. Following percutaneous inoculation, NTM may induce subacute or chronic soft tissue infections that progress slowly over months, sometimes forming large fluid collections [2–6]. These can extend to adjacent joints and bones, resulting in osteomyelitis and destructive arthritis [2,3]. Imaging Perspective Although imaging cannot reliably distinguish NTM from tuberculous infections, certain features can raise suspicion [3]. Early radiographs may show soft-tissue swelling and localised bone resorption due to hyperaemia. In chronic stages, findings may include osteolysis, cortical destruction, abscesses and sinus tracts. Synovial invasion may manifest as marginal or subchondral erosions and regional osteopenia [3,7]. MRI is the most sensitive modality, offering early detection and evaluation of soft tissue involvement [3]. Key differential diagnoses include pyogenic and inflammatory arthritis. Therefore, synovial fluid aspiration should be performed as an initial diagnostic step. Although no specific imaging finding definitively separates these conditions, mycobacterial infections typically show a chronic pattern with peripheral erosions and gradual joint space narrowing, attributed to the lack of proteolytic enzymes in the exudate [2,3,7,8]. Outcome Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical, imaging, and laboratory findings, but definitive confirmation requires microbiological culture. Prompt recognition is critical, as delayed diagnosis can lead to severe outcomes. Management typically involves both antimicrobial therapy and surgical debridement. Due to limited drug susceptibility, radical interventions—including amputation or hemipelvectomy—may occasionally be necessary [1–3]. Large superficial fluid collections, particularly associated with osteomyelitis, should raise suspicion for NTM (non-tuberculous mycobacteria) infection, given the potential for significant morbidity. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
differential_diagnosis: Infection by Mycobacterium avium Infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis Pyogenic arthritis Inflammatory arthritis

title: Neuropathic arthropathy (Charcot joint) in a case of syringomyelia
clinical_history: A 57-year-old diabetic man, with 25 years of bilateral lower limb weakness, presented with a 1.5-month history of a mildly painful, firm, non-tender swelling over the left shoulder. Limited shoulder movement, reduced sensation, and a scar noted (Figures 1a and 1b). No trauma or aspiration records.
imaging_findings: X-ray of the left shoulder (Figure 2) showed joint destruction, including humeral head and glenoid resorption, widened joint space, periarticular calcifications, and soft tissue inflammation. MRI of the left shoulder (Figures 4, 5, 6, 7a, and 7b) revealed extensive bony damage, complete tears in the rotator cuff tendons and complete destruction of the glenoid labrum, glenohumeral ligaments, and biceps-labral anchor. A large, thick-walled fluid collection with peripheral enhancement extended into the intermuscular and intramuscular planes of the rotator cuff muscles. MRI of the spine (Figures 3a and 3b) showed a syrinx extending from the cervico-medullary junction to the thoracic vertebra at T11, consistent with syringomyelia, and a wedge collapse of the vertebral body of T12 thoracic vertebra, indicating chronic vertebral involvement.
discussion: Background Neuropathic arthropathy, or Charcot joint, is a degenerative joint condition caused by impaired sensory feedback, leading to joint destruction from repeated microtrauma. In syringomyelia, the shoulder and elbow are commonly affected due to cervical spinal cord involvement [1–3]. This rare condition has fewer than 70 reported cases, with 25% of syringomyelia patients developing neuropathic arthropathy, predominantly in males [5,7]. Syringomyelia involves a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) in the cervical spinal cord, disrupting spinothalamic pathways and anterior horn cells. This results in loss of pain and temperature sensation, making joints more susceptible to damage [1,3,4]. Clinical Perspective Patients often present with painless swelling, joint deformity, and restricted movement, usually in the shoulder, elbow, or wrist (Figures 1a and 1b). Sensory loss in the upper trunk and arms suggests central spinal cord involvement [1,3,5]. Shoulder joint destruction and subtle neurological signs can lead to misdiagnosis as septic or inflammatory arthritis, or neoplastic processes [1,4]. It should be differentiated from other disorders like: Gorham–Stout disease, also known as vanishing bone disease, involves progressive osteolysis due to vascular proliferation [9]. Septic arthritis, a rapidly progressive infection that can cause joint destruction usually accompanied by inflammatory signs [10]. Milwaukee shoulder syndrome, a rare destructive arthropathy associated with basic calcium phosphate crystal destruction [8]. Osteolytic tumour, a bone destruction secondary to malignancy or metastasis that may be associated with soft tissue component [11]. Imaging Perspective Imaging is essential to detect joint abnormalities and underlying causes like syringomyelia, especially in upper limb involvement [3,5]. X-ray and CT reveal joint fragmentation, dislocation, sclerosis, or bone loss in the shoulder or elbow (Figure 2) [2,3,6]. MRI shoulder identifies severe joint damage, including rotator cuff tears, ligament injuries, and fluid collections (Figures 4, 5, 6, 7a, and 7b) [1,3]. MRI spine is essential for detecting a syrinx (usually cervical) and associated abnormalities like Chiari type I malformation (Figures 3a and 3b) [1,3,6]. Outcome and Management Non-surgical treatment options include bracing and physiotherapy, while surgery may be needed for joint stabilisation or syrinx decompression, especially in cases of Chiari malformation [1,5]. Joint damage is often irreversible. Early recognition and intervention are crucial to limit progression and preserve function [2,4,6]. Take Home Message Consider syringomyelia in upper limb Charcot joints. Spinal MRI is key for diagnosis, and radiologists play a vital role in early detection and treatment [3,5].

title: Osteochondral lesion of the tibial plafond in a child
clinical_history: A 5-year-old male presented with persistent right ankle pain and mild swelling for two months following minor trauma. He was previously active and otherwise healthy, with no significant past medical history. Localised tenderness was noted over the lateral ankle during examination, although range of movements remained unrestricted. No signs of systemic illness or infection were present.
imaging_findings: Initial radiographs were inconclusive. Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the right ankle (Figures 1a and 1b) demonstrated a subtle radiolucent defect in the inferolateral aspect of the distal tibial epiphysis, surrounded by a thin sclerotic rim—an early clue often missed on plain films, especially on the lateral projection. MRI was performed for further evaluation. T1-weighted coronal image (Figure 2a) confirmed the presence of an osteochondral defect in the lateral tibial plafond. Coronal and sagittal PDFS (proton density fat-saturated) images (Figures 2b and 2c) showed fluid signal intensity within the donor defect, along with underlying subchondral marrow oedema and a subtle PD hyperintense unstable osteochondral fragment. T2-weighted sagittal and coronal sequences (Figure 3a and 3b) demonstrated the chondral-predominant fragment with a thin rim of intervening fluid, indicating instability. These findings are consistent with a Berndt and Harty grade III lesion. Mild joint effusion was also noted. No signs of physeal plate involvement or other soft tissue or osseous abnormalities were observed. The talar dome cartilage and subchondral bone were also carefully evaluated on MRI and appeared normal, with no evidence of marrow oedema, cartilage irregularity, or osteochondral defect.
discussion: Background Osteochondral lesions (OCLs) of the ankle are focal injuries affecting the articular cartilage and underlying subchondral bone. The talar dome is by far the most commonly involved site, with isolated involvement of the tibial plafond being considerably rare, especially in skeletally immature patients [1,2,5]. Aetiological factors include acute trauma, repetitive microtrauma, or vascular insufficiency. In children, the cartilaginous and vascular anatomy differs from that of adults, which may alter the pattern of injury and healing response. Importantly, these lesions may involve the secondary ossification centre and lie close to the physis, potentially affecting normal skeletal growth or epiphyseal development if left untreated. Clinical Perspective Children with OCLs may present with nonspecific symptoms such as prolonged joint pain, mild swelling, or altered gait. In this case, there was a clear history of minor trauma, but the radiographs were subtle and easily overlooked. The rarity of tibial plafond involvement in children can contribute to delays in diagnosis unless MRI is performed [1,3]. Clinical examination may not reveal gross deformity or instability, which further underscores the need for imaging in persistent cases. Imaging Perspective MRI remains the gold standard for the evaluation of osteochondral injuries in children, offering high sensitivity in identifying chondral and subchondral pathology, marrow changes, and fragment stability [3]. Key imaging features include fluid signal within the defect, a hyperintense rim around the displaced fragment on T2-weighted images, and associated marrow oedema. Recognition of a predominantly chondral fragment is essential, as it may be missed on radiographs or CT. While classification systems such as Berndt and Harty are primarily designed for talar dome lesions, the same principles of lesion stability and morphology can be cautiously applied to tibial plafond injuries. In this case, imaging features correspond to a Berndt and Harty grade III lesion, reflecting an unstable osteochondral fragment. Although MRI in this case did not reveal any abnormalities in the opposing talar dome, it is important to recognise that osteochondral lesions of the tibial plafond may occur concurrently with talar dome injuries, particularly in paediatric trauma. These are often described as “kissing lesions”. MRI allows comprehensive joint assessment, and careful evaluation of the talar dome should be part of routine imaging interpretation in such cases [3,6]. Outcome Given the patient’s age and imaging features indicating an unstable chondral-predominant fragment, conservative management involving immobilisation and reduction of weight-bearing would typically be the first line of treatment. Should symptoms persist or lesion progression be noted, surgical options such as fragment fixation or osteochondral grafting may be explored [4]. Recent literature also supports favourable outcomes with procedures like microfracture and bone marrow-derived cell transplantation (BMDCT), particularly in improving pain and joint function in tibial plafond lesions [7]. The prognosis in children is generally favourable with timely diagnosis and appropriate management. However, the patient was unfortunately lost to follow-up before treatment could be initiated. Take Home Message OCLs involving the tibial plafond are uncommon in children and can present subtly on initial imaging. MRI plays a crucial role in diagnosis and management planning. A high index of suspicion is necessary when evaluating persistent ankle pain following trauma in paediatric patients. Written informed consent for publication was obtained from the patient’s legal guardian.

title: Heterotopic ossification following prolonged Intensive Care Unit admission
clinical_history: A 35-year-old male with a background of asthma, migraine and chronic back pain, was admitted with shortness of breath and fever. Chest x-ray showed severe COVID pneumonitis, leading to ICU (intensive care unit) admission for invasive ventilation, complicated by recurrent pneumothoraxes and chest infections. Three months post-discharge, he describes pain in his shoulders.
imaging_findings: The initial CT examination of the chest, a coronal multiplanar reconstruction (MPR) image taken in October 2021, demonstrated bilateral mineralisation/immature ossification in the region of the inferior joint capsule of glenohumeral joints abutting the glenoid (Figure 1). Bilateral pulmonary fibrosis was present. A subsequent MRI (T1 and STIR coronal images), seven months later (May 2022), revealed further maturation of heterotopic ossification of the inferior recesses of shoulder joint capsules (red arrows in Figures 2a and 2b). One year and 4 months after the MRI (in September 2023), a CT of the left shoulder showed a mature osseous tissue with cancellous and cortical bones (Figure 3), which was more conspicuous on a follow-up radiograph of the left shoulder in 2024, i.e., three years after the initial presentation (Figure 4).
discussion: Background Heterotopic ossification (HO) is an abnormal process in which extra-skeletal bone develops within the soft tissue, muscles, and other connective tissue sites. HO is a typical complication post-surgery, trauma, and different systemic injuries, and can define an atypical tissue repair [1]. The link between COVID-19 and the HO pathogenesis is uncertain. A potential cause might be a systemic inflammatory response combined with extended immobilisation, especially in patients requiring lengthy intensive care stays [2]. There is some evidence that implies that SARS-CoV-2 could target cells within the musculoskeletal system; yet, it remains unclear whether this might be related to the development of HO and needs further research [3]. Clinical Perspective Prior to admission, the patient was fit and well, working as a taxi driver. He was a current smoker of 1–2 cigarettes/day. His regular medication was naproxen and dihydrocodeine for his back pain. His asthma was well controlled with no prior hospital admissions. Clinical examination revealed a severely restricted range of movement, with the inability to abduct both shoulders beyond 90 degrees, limited by pain. Initially, pain relief and physiotherapy were the treatment options chosen to manage his symptoms. After two months, his shoulders movements were recovering well, with internal rotation to the lower lumbar spine, external rotation of about 20 degrees, and active elevation of about 120 degrees. Imaging Perspective Plain film is often the first image modality used to diagnose HO, because it demonstrates a mineralised soft tissue mass, which later evolves into an ossified lesion with a mature cortical bone. Non-contrast CT is a great imaging method for investigating HO when suspected, as it allows for early detection of mineralisation of HO, defining the different stages of ossification. It also allows differentiation from other lesions and provides good anatomical information for surgical planning. MRI findings could often be misleading, particularly in the early stages, mimicking other pathologies, such as a neoplasm. However, once HO is matured, MRI could be confirmatory. Outcome The first therapeutic option is physiotherapy, consisting of passive movement exercises to avoid joint ankylosis in association with pain relief, NSAIDs, and bisphosphonates [4]. Definitive treatment is usually surgical resection once the HO has fully matured and has a good prognosis [5]. In our case, we ruled out other differentials based on clinical presentation and imaging as follows: Myositis ossificans is a type of heterotopic calcification occurring in muscles, not joint soft tissues. Dystrophic calcification involves calcium deposition in necrotic tissue. Tumoral calcinosis is typically associated with underlying metabolic disorder. Primary osteosarcoma is a malignant tumour usually seen in children and young adults. Take Home Message / Teaching Points A clinic presentation involving joint pain/stiffness after a prolonged critical care admission with immobilisation should raise suspicion for potentially heterotopic ossification (HO). Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
differential_diagnosis: Myositis ossificans Heterotopic ossification Tumoral calcinosis Primary osteosarcoma Dystrophic calcification

title: Pulmonary artery mucormycosis – A rare site of fungal vasculitis in early infancy
clinical_history: A 28-week gestational age very low birth weight (VLBW) preterm male child was referred at age one and a half months with an outside diagnosis of pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE) on 2D echocardiogram. He had a history of neonatal sepsis and prolonged neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) stay requiring central venous catheter insertion. A 2D echocardiogram was performed to evaluate for pulmonary hypertension or underlying structural cardiac anomaly, in light of persistent respiratory symptoms and recurrent lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI).
imaging_findings: CT angiogram (CTA) revealed a large, non-enhancing, hypodense, tubular filling defect suggestive of PTE in the main pulmonary artery (MPA), extending to the origin of the left pulmonary artery (LPA) and the lower lobar branch of the right pulmonary artery (RPA) (Figures 1a and 1b). Due to high clinical suspicion of fungal aetiology in view of the VLBW and prolonged NICU stay, complete surgical resection of the lesion was performed. Histology confirmed mucormycosis within the thrombus (Figure 2). Follow-up 2D echo at 3 months showed suspicious vascular dilatation and left lower lobe opacity on a chest radiograph (Figure 3). A repeated CTA revealed focal aneurysmal dilatation of the lower lobar branch of the LPA, likely representing a mycotic aneurysm. Additionally, mediastinal and perivascular necrotic soft tissue was seen along the lobar branches bilaterally, with 70–80% luminal narrowing of the lower lobar branch of the RPA (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c).
discussion: Neonates with predisposing factors such as prematurity and VLBW are at high risk for both bacterial and fungal infections [1] due to poor immunity, inadequate development of mucosal linings, injury due to catheters and hypertonic solutions, and the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics. The common fungal pathogens are Candida species, and rarely mucormycosis and Malassezia . The indwelling catheters are a source of injury and provide a surface for the formation of biofilm and proliferation of organisms, creating a focus for thrombosis and infection [2]. Mucormycosis is a rare, fulminant, aggressive disease commonly affecting the skin, paranasal sinuses, orbits, brain, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract [3], usually in an immunocompromised host, and requires prompt surgical and medical management to reduce mortality and organ loss [4]. Site-specific involvement can occur, as in our case, where an indwelling catheter led to vascular fungal disease followed by mediastinal spread. A mortality rate of 83% due to mediastinal mucormycosis is reported [5]. A multimodality approach to diagnosis and follow-up of these patients is important. The first line of investigation for cardiac fungal disease remains 2D echocardiogram, which commonly shows findings of endocarditis or a mass lesion. Cross-sectional imaging by CT and cardiac MRI provides better tissue characterisation and is superior in defining the extent of disease, including mediastinal spread. Cross–sectional findings of fungal vasculitis are rarely described. Talib et al. have described a case of intracardiac fungal mass showing peripheral enhancement and central hypointensity on perfusion cardiac MRI (CMRI) and LGE images with long inversion time (TI) main document of 600 ms [6]. Another case of adult fungal mediastinitis following stent–graft placement described an invasive disease, causing aortic rupture and mediastinal leak with demonstration of hyphae from purulent mediastinal tissue [5]. Our case showed a similar further extension of the disease with the formation of necrotic mediastinal tissue and a mycotic aneurysm of the lobar branch of LPA. The disease progressed even after surgical clearance and dual antifungal therapy, indicating a highly aggressive nature of the disease. The focal aneurysmal dilatation seen in our case is interpreted as a mycotic aneurysm—an important sequel of fungal vasculitis. It is important for radiologists to be aware of the risk of serious fungal disease in immunocompromised hosts, low birth-weight and preterm babies and those with long NICU stay and inserted catheters or devices. While the second case cited involved adult fungal mediastinitis post stent-graft placement, it is here referenced to illustrate the aggressive disease progression with mediastinal spread, and despite the demographic and imaging differences. Take Home Message Radiologists should consider mucormycosis in premature, VLBW neonates with immune compromise and catheter history who present with intravascular filling defects, particularly when associated with perivascular necrosis or aneurysmal changes. In such patients, what appears as PE may in fact be fungal vasculitis. Early suspicion and multimodal imaging are critical for diagnosis and prompt management.
differential_diagnosis: Pulmonary artery thrombosis Pulmonary artery vasculitis Pulmonary artery acute or chronic thromboembolism Pulmonary artery mucormycosis with fungal mediastinitis Pulmonary artery sarcoma
final_diagnosis: Pulmonary artery mucormycosis with fungal mediastinitis
