title: Traction apophysitis of the patella: Imaging hallmarks of Sinding–Larsen–Johansson disease
clinical_history: A 14-year-old male cricket player presented with anterior knee pain for 3 months, aggravated by jumping and stair climbing. No history of trauma or systemic symptoms. Localised tenderness was noted at the inferior patella without swelling or effusion.
imaging_findings: A skyline Merchant radiograph of the right knee (Figure 1) showed irregular ossification and subtle fragmentation at the inferior pole of the patella, with a normal tibial tuberosity. Sagittal and axial musculoskeletal ultrasound images (Figures 2a and 2b) revealed cortical irregularity and fragmentation of the inferior patellar pole. The patellar tendon was intact. A sagittal ultrasound image (Figure 3) also revealed a hyperechoic, mildly prominent Hoffa’s fat pad, suggestive of reactive inflammatory changes.
discussion: Background Sinding–Larsen–Johansson disease (SLJD) is a type of traction apophysitis affecting the secondary ossification centre at the inferior pole of the patella. It typically occurs during rapid skeletal growth in physically active adolescents [1]. SLJD represents a stress response due to repetitive traction from the patellar tendon, leading to changes in the immature osteocartilaginous junction. Clinical Perspective SLJD usually presents with localised anterior knee pain at the inferior pole of the patella, especially in adolescents involved in jumping sports. The pain is activity-related and focal in nature, helping distinguish it from other anterior knee pain aetiologies. Timely recognition is essential to avoid unnecessary investigations and to initiate effective conservative treatment [2,3]. Imaging Perspective Radiographs may reveal fragmentation, irregular ossification, or sclerosis at the inferior patellar pole [3]. Ultrasound serves as a valuable adjunct by demonstrating cortical irregularity, fragmentation, and associated soft tissue changes such as reactive Hoffa’s fat pad inflammation [4]. In this case, the classic imaging findings of inferior pole fragmentation with an intact tibial tuberosity and patellar tendon confirmed the diagnosis of SLJD. Although differential diagnoses exist, experienced radiologists can confidently identify SLJD based on imaging morphology and location. Outcome The patient was advised to temporarily cease high-impact sports, prescribed NSAIDs, and enrolled in a physiotherapy program focused on stretching and biomechanical unloading. At 6-week follow-up, the patient reported complete symptomatic relief. Repeated imaging was deemed unnecessary. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Sinding–Larsen–Johansson disease (SLJD) is a self-limiting overuse injury affecting the inferior patellar pole. Imaging confirms the diagnosis and helps exclude mimics such as patellar tendinopathy or sleeve fracture. Ultrasound and radiographs together enable confident, non-invasive diagnosis and reduce unnecessary workup.
differential_diagnosis: Jumper’s knee (patellar tendinopathy) Hoffa’s fat pad impingement Sinding–Larsen–Johansson disease (SLJD) Patellar sleeve fracture Osteochondrosis of the inferior patella Osgood–Schlatter disease

title: Pancreatitis beyond boundaries: Ectopic pancreas as a diagnostic challenge
clinical_history: A 43-year-old male patient visited the emergency room with two episodes of vomiting and epigastric pain over the past 2 days. On examination, vital signs were stable, and abdominal palpation revealed tenderness in the upper abdomen and left hypochondrium. Haematological examination revealed a rise in lipase level (470 U/L; normal 20–250 U/L) with normal complete blood count and liver panel.
imaging_findings: Abdominal CT demonstrated the presence of a homogeneously enhancing mass lesion closely related to the inferior aspect of the third part of the duodenum (Figure 1a). Notably, the lesion’s attenuation characteristics mirrored those of normal pancreatic parenchyma across all phases, suggesting a pancreatic origin (Figure 1b). The mass appeared mildly oedematous, with few identifiable clefts similar to the feathery pattern of normal pancreatic parenchyma. Adjacent to the mass, moderate fat stranding was observed in the mesentery, indicative of inflammatory changes. Interestingly, the mass appeared to be completely separate from the normal anatomical pancreas, which was visualised in the retroperitoneum and appeared normal in terms of size, shape, and attenuation (Figures 2a and 2b). Further evaluation with MRI confirmed the CT findings, demonstrating signal intensity characteristics similar to those of normal pancreatic tissue in all sequences. The MRI also highlighted fat stranding in the surrounding mesentery and minimal free fluid (Figure 3), consistent with acute pancreatitis arising within ectopic pancreatic tissue (Figures 4a and 4b). MR cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) further confirmed the presence of an ectopic duct within the ectopic pancreas draining into the proximal jejunum (Figures 5a and 5b).
discussion: Background Ectopic/heterotopic pancreas (HP) is pancreatic tissue without anatomical connection to the normal pancreas [1]. About 90% of cases occur in the upper gastrointestinal (GI) tract, mainly in the stomach, duodenum, or proximal jejunum [2,3]. Rarely, HP is found in the liver, gallbladder, spleen, lungs, or mediastinum [4]. In the GI tract, HP typically develops in the submucosal (73%), mucosal (17%), or subserosal (10%) layers. Most cases are asymptomatic, but HP can undergo pathological processes like acute pancreatitis, similar to the orthotopic pancreas. Clinical Perspective Ectopic pancreas often flies under the radar, typically remaining asymptomatic and being discovered incidentally. However, it can become inflamed, leading to complications like acute and chronic pancreatitis [5], pseudocysts, or malignancy [6]. Associated complications include GI bleeding [7], strictures, ulcers, and pseudocysts resulting from recurrent inflammation of the ectopic tissue. The diagnostic challenge lies in its ability to mimic pancreatitis clinically, even when the native pancreas appears radiologically normal. This is particularly significant in cases of gastrointestinal ectopic pancreas, where it can be mistaken for gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GISTs) [8], neuroendocrine tumours, or other lesions. Imaging Perspective Recently, endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) has been of great help in precisely localising the HP sites in the GI wall, characterised by indistinct borders, lobulated margins, duct-like anechoic structures, and involvement of multiple wall layers. HP typically appears as a hypoechoic submucosal mass, isoechoic to the muscularis propria, with possible anechoic tubular or cystic areas, aiding preoperative diagnosis [9], and with the additional benefit of guiding an FNAC or biopsy. On CT, HP shows attenuation and a degree of enhancement similar to that of normal pancreas in almost all phases. Sometimes the HP in submucosal regions can be mistaken for other mass lesions. In such cases, the presence of prominent overlying mucosal enhancement will be a useful sign for differentiating it from other lesions [10]. MR imaging is accurate to evaluate for HP, as it shows signal intensities similar to those of normal pancreas in all sequences. MRCP may reveal the “ectopic duct sign”, indicating a rudimentary ductal system [10]. In some cases, enhancement on MRI may exceed that of the native pancreas. However, histopathological examinations remain the gold standard to confirm the diagnosis. Outcome Most cases respond well to conservative treatment, including bowel rest, hydration, and analgesia. Surgical intervention is reserved for complications such as persistent obstruction, suspicion of malignancy, or failure of conservative management. Laparoscopic wedge resection or endoscopic removal is often curative when needed [11]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Heterotopic pancreas (HP) is a rare but important differential diagnosis in patients with unexplained gastrointestinal symptoms and submucosal lesions, particularly when the orthotopic pancreas is unremarkable on imaging. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Extensive skeletal involvement in multiple hereditary exostoses: Rare locations
clinical_history: A 19-year-old patient with no notable personal or family medical history. The patient has been complaining for the past 3 years of bilateral gonalgia, right shoulder pain, and rachialgia, with more significant functional discomfort in the lower limbs. Clinical examination reveals tenderness upon palpation of the knees and right shoulder.
imaging_findings: A radiological assessment was performed (x-rays and full-body scan) revealing multiple exostotic lesions of the dorsolumbar spine, sternoclavicular joints, costal arches, scapulas, as well as in bones of the upper limbs (bilaterally, more marked at the metaphyseal-epiphyseal region of the right proximal humerus), pelvic girdle, and bones of the lower limbs and feet (bilaterally, more marked at the knees).
discussion: Background Multiple exostoses disease (MED) is a rare genetic disorder characterised by the proliferation of multiple bony growths that can be sessile or pedunculated. They develop near the metaphysis of bones formed through endochondral ossification, sharing the common feature of full canal communication with the affected bone [1,2]. The disease is associated with mutations in exostosis genes [3]. A family history is present in two-thirds of cases, but sporadic cases due to de novo mutations are possible in about one-third of patients [4]. The number of exostoses found in patients with MED varies, potentially reaching thousands. The most common site for osteochondromas is the distal femur, proximal tibia or fibula. The proximal humerus is also a common site [1,2]. Other locations are rare but potentially serious, including the ribs, spine, or pelvis, with a risk of complications (pulmonary consolidation, spinal cord compression, malignant transformation) [1,5]. Our patient presents with lesions at the frequent locations described above (Figures 1 and 2) along with other rare locations, notably the sternoclavicular joints, costal arches, scapulas, and the dorsolumbar spine (Figure 3). Clinical Perspective The cardinal symptom is chronic pain and discomfort. Imaging Perspective X-ray is the initial radiological examination often performed and allows a definitive diagnosis, especially in pedunculated forms [6]. The typical appearance of a pedunculated lesion is seen as a metaphyseal addition image on long bones, or at the level of the girdles or axial skeleton, with a narrow implantation base, in contrast to sessile lesions, which have a broad base of attachment (cauliflower appearance) [6]. Other imaging methods are used, including CT scans, which allow the assessment of various locations of exostotic lesions and highlight the continuity between the trabecular bone of the metaphyseal spongy bone and the centre of the exostosis [6]. This full canal communication is also visible on MRI, which remains the best imaging method to measure the thickness of the cartilage cap. A thickness ≥ 2 cm on CT or MRI helps differentiate between a benign exostosis and chondrosarcoma [1]. Enhancement after gadolinium injection is also a sign of sarcomatous degeneration [6]. Ultrasound can also be used to measure the thickness of the cartilage cap. Some studies suggest that ultrasonography is more accurate than CT, with results similar to MRI [6]. Bone scintigraphy may also have its place, by showing fixation of enchondral bone [1,7]. Outcome Surgical intervention should be pursued without delay whenever there is a clinically or radiologically suspicious exostotic lesion. Take Home Message Multiple hereditary exostoses is a rare genetic disorder. Conventional radiography is the first line imaging modality, followed by whole body CT to identify the various locations. Ultrasound—and even more so MRI—allows for monitoring of suspicious lesions through measurement of the thickness of the cartilaginous cap.

title: L1 syndrome disorder: MASA syndrome
clinical_history: A 3-year-old male presented with severe triventricular ventriculomegaly and cortical thinning at 35 weeks on prenatal ultrasound. At birth, he had an unusual phenotype, adducted thumbs and poor spontaneous mobility. Progressive ventriculomegaly required ventriculoperitoneal derivation (VPD). Currently, the patient has severe neurological involvement, flaccid paresis with paroxysms of rigidity and epilepsy.
imaging_findings: Transfontanelar US and postnatal MRI at 1 day and 1 week, respectively, show severe triventricular hydrocephaly and large massa intermedia (Figures 1a and 1b), aqueductal stenosis, enlarged quadrigeminal plate, corpus callosum agenesis, vermian hypoplasia, severe cortical thinning and diencephalic–mesencephalic junction dysplasia (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d). The latest MRI, at the age of 3 years, before VPD treatment and mild improvement of ventriculomegaly, demonstrates better visualisation of the previous findings (Figure 3a), in addition to diffuse hypoplasia of cerebral white matter, polymicrogyria (Figures 3b and 3c), diencephalosynapsis (Figure 3d) with diencephalic–mesencephalic junction dysplasia in a so-called “butterfly-like pattern” (Figures 3e and 3f), and hypoplastic and poorly differentiated hippocampi.
discussion: Background L1 syndrome is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the neuronal L1CAM, a membrane glycoprotein primarily expressed in the developing nervous system that mediates cell-to-cell adhesion at the cell surface. These mutations disrupt normal neural connectivity and axonal guidance. The clinical spectrum of the syndrome comprises several major X-linked disorders, including X-linked congenital hydrocephalus with or without congenital aqueductal stenosis (CAS), MASA syndrome (mental retardation, adducted thumbs, shuffling gait, aphasia), spastic paraplegia type I and corpus callosum agenesis (CCA) or hypoplasia [1]. Clinical Perspective It is a disease to be considered in all patients with congenital hydrocephalus, especially if syndromic and male, as it is the most frequent genetic cause of hydrocephalus associated with spastic paraplegia, accounting for 10% to 30.1% in some series [2,3]. In utero US allow prenatal detection of foetal hydrocephalus in most cases, allowing early initiation of a battery of diagnostic tests for differential diagnosis between genetic or acquired causes (Chiari type 2 malformation, aqueductal gliosis or CAS due to infection, intraventricular haemorrhage or extrinsic compression) [4,5]. Foetal MRI and, especially, postnatal MRI, better characterise associated central nervous system malformations. L1CAM genetic analysis will set the final diagnosis. Imaging Perspective Postnatal MRI main imaging features include obstructive hydrocephalus with CAS, CCA, enlarged quadrigeminal plate, large massa intermedia due to hypertrophy and interthalamic adhesion (diencephalosynapsis) with diencephalic–mesencephalic junction dysplasia type A (midbrain–hypothalamus fusion with “butterfly-like pattern”) and type B (fusion between midbrain and thalamus), brainstem kinking, vermian and pontine hypoplasia, absence of corticospinal tracts and diffuse hypoplasia of cerebral white matter [3,6]. DWI of the brainstem can be used to demonstrate a lack of anisotropy in the corticospinal tracts of the basis pontis, as bilateral hypoplasia of the corticospinal tracts is almost pathognomonic. According to the two main patterns of L1 syndrome described by Accogli et al., our case corresponded to the L1 phenotype type 1 [6]. Our patient presented with diffuse polymicrogyria, a malformation of cortical development, a feature described but rare [5]. Brainstem kinking was not present. Outcome Therapeutic options include VPD and secondary prevention due to its poor prognosis, as many die in infancy or early childhood, with severe motor and cognitive neurologic deficits invariably present. Take Home Message / Teaching Points The recognition of the structural alterations and the most characteristic and frequent imaging findings of the entity will allow to suspect genopathy, and guide the radiologist to perform a structured and systematic reading to search for alterations included in the spectrum of the disease that could go unnoticed in a first diagnosis.

title: Seizures and scars: Decoding lipoid proteinosis through neuroimaging
clinical_history: A 28-year-old pregnant female presented to the neurology department with new-onset generalised tonic-clonic seizures. Neurological examination was normal. A dermatological consultation revealed multiple acneiform scars over the flexor surface and pearly papules along the eyelid margins and on the forehead (Figures 1 and 2), for which she had been under evaluation. No family history of similar illness was noted. MRI brain was performed to investigate the aetiology of seizures.
imaging_findings: Clinical photographs taken show acneiform scars over the flexor aspect of the left elbow (Figure 1) and pearly papules along both eyelid margins, and also seen on the forehead (Figure 2). An MRI brain was done. Axial T2 image (Figure 3) shows bilateral symmetrical hypointensities in the amygdala. There is no mass effect, oedema, or acute infarct. There is no space-occupying lesion. Axial SWI (susceptibility-weighted imaging) of the MRI brain (Figure 4) sequences shows blooming in the amygdala, likely due to calcification.
discussion: Lipoid proteinosis, also known as Urbach–Wiethe disease, is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ECM1 gene on chromosome 1q21 [1]. It is characterised by the deposition of periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive hyaline-like material in the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs [2]. Common clinical features include early-onset hoarseness, acneiform scarring, and beaded papules along the eyelid margins [2]. Although central nervous system (CNS) involvement is uncommon, it may present with characteristic neuroimaging features showing calcifications of the amygdala and medial temporal lobes, which are bilateral and symmetrical [3]. In our patient, the identification of bilateral symmetrical amygdala calcifications was considered pathognomonic for lipoid proteinosis [3,4]. While this condition usually manifests early in life with vocal and dermatological signs, it may remain undiagnosed until neurological symptoms such as seizures, memory impairment, or behavioural changes prompt imaging [3,4]. These amygdala calcifications, a hallmark imaging finding, are best detected on CT, although they may also be visualised on susceptibility-weighted MRI sequences [3]. While the differential diagnosis includes epilepsy, prior infections, trauma, or metabolic disorders, the presence of cutaneous manifestations helps significantly narrow the diagnosis [4]. Early diagnosis is crucial for guiding genetic counselling, symptom management, and screening of family members [1,2]. Despite its rarity, lipoid proteinosis has a distinctive radiologic signature that radiologists should recognise, particularly in patients with neuropsychiatric symptoms and associated dermatologic features. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: An unusual case of hepatitis
clinical_history: A 55-year-old male with epigastric pain primarily localised to the right upper quadrant, a positive Murphy’s sign, associated with vomiting and hypotension. The patient presented with a fever spike of 38.1ºC as the only infectious clinical sign observed. Among the analytical parameters, there is a marked elevation of C-reactive protein (CRP; 12.8 mg/dL), procalcitonin (29.8 ng/mL), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; 2488 U/L), and leukocytosis (24×10^9/L) with neutrophilia (18.9×10^9/L). The family reports diarrhoea in the preceding days.
imaging_findings: In a portable chest x-ray, a small left pleural effusion and the presence of gas in the right upper quadrant are seen (Figure 1). An abdominopelvic CT scan was performed with intravenous contrast in the arterial and portal venous phases. The main findings include numerous subcentimeter gas bubbles arranged in two clusters, primarily affecting the right liver lobe, with maximum axial diameters of 80 mm and 69 mm. Free gas bubbles within the parenchyma and perfusion abnormalities in the affected segments are also observed, along with predominantly central periportal oedema (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 3).
discussion: Background Emphysematous hepatitis is a rare condition characterised by severe inflammation of the liver and the presence of gas within the hepatic parenchyma [1]. In such settings, necrotic hepatic tissue or bacterial fermentation leads to the production of a gas mixture, which accounts for the radiological findings [1]. The pathophysiology remains unclear; however, it is believed to involve glucose fermentation by the causative bacteria, resulting in a gas mixture composed of approximately 60% nitrogen, 15% hydrogen, 5% carbon dioxide, and 5% oxygen [1–4]. Clinical Perspective This case involves a 55-year-old male patient with a history of diarrhoea in the preceding days, along with epigastric abdominal pain localised to the right upper quadrant and vomiting. Subsequently, the patient developed signs of shock, including altered consciousness, hypotension (blood pressure of 70/35 mmHg), tachypnoea, hypothermia (31ºC), and acute renal failure, evidenced by a serum creatinine level of 2.56 mg/dL. Blood cultures were positive for Clostridium perfringens and Enterococcus faecium in both the first and second samples. The symptomatology in these patients is nonspecific (such as abdominal pain and fever) and overlaps with that of most acute pathologies affecting the right upper quadrant, as well as elevated acute-phase reactants (such as CRP and leukocytosis) [1,2,4]. Although clinical suspicion is challenging, a distinguishing feature of this entity is its tendency to rapidly progress to sepsis, a frequent complication and the principal factor contributing to the poor outcome associated with this condition. In fact, in most reported cases, death has occurred within three days of hospital admission, underscoring the condition’s extremely poor prognosis [1,4]. Imaging Perspective Given the nonspecific nature of the clinical and laboratory findings, radiology plays a pivotal role in the diagnosis. The gold standard imaging modality is computed tomography (CT) with contrast [2]. CT enables precise identification of the hallmark finding: multiple foci of gas within the hepatic parenchyma [1,2], without associated mass effect or significant free fluid. This radiologic appearance is highly specific and facilitates the differentiation of emphysematous hepatitis from other hepatobiliary conditions, such as abscesses, where gas is typically localised within collections often surrounded by a defined wall, and infarctions, which manifest as ill-defined wedge-shaped areas of hypoattenuation without the presence of intraparenchymal gas [1,3,5]. Outcome Management of this condition typically includes the administration of intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and, when indicated, percutaneous drainage of hepatic collections [1]. Despite the implementation of both interventional and pharmacological therapies, the condition remains associated with a high mortality rate [1,4]. In the present case, the patient experienced rapid clinical deterioration, progressing to shock and death within a few hours of presentation. Emphysematous hepatitis was attributed to infection with Clostridium perfringens and Enterococcus faecium . Take Home Message Emphysematous hepatitis is a rare disease caused by gas-producing microorganisms, characterised by a rapidly progressive and often fatal course, for which contrast-enhanced computed tomography is essential for diagnosis. All patient data have been fully anonymised throughout the manuscript and in related files.

title: Progressive fibrodysplasia ossificans: A radiologically diagnosed disease
clinical_history: A 22-year-old female presented with hallux valgus deformity of both first toes since birth (Figure 1). At the age of 12, she began experiencing difficulty walking and progressive joint stiffness. On physical examination, there was an inability to fully open the temporomandibular joints bilaterally and restricted flexion and abduction of the extremities.
imaging_findings: On plain radiographs of the feet, there was absence of the distal phalanges of the first toes and hallux valgus with metatarsophalangeal angles >15°, supporting early skeletal deformities (Figure 2). CT imaging of the cervicothoracic spine demonstrated heterotopic ossification of the supraspinous and posterior nuchal ligaments (Figure 3). Three-dimensional reconstructions showed multiple bridging ossifications forming tubular bone between the iliac bones and the twelfth ribs, as well as ossified extensions from the right iliac bone to the right humerus (Figures 4a and 4b).
discussion: Background The radiographic and CT imaging on our patient revealed key diagnostic features of fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva. Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (also known as Münchmeyer disease) is an ultrarare autosomal dominant disorder with a prevalence below 1 per 2 million individuals [1]. It is caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the ACVR1 gene on chromosome 2q24.1, which activates bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4), leading to abnormal bone formation [1,2]. Clinical Perspective One of the initial clinical features is usually the presentation of deformities in the big toes with a shortened first metatarsal with hallux valgus deformity [3]. Other imaging findings may be shortened thumbs, shortened femoral necks and spinal anomalies such as narrow vertebral bodies and the presence of cervical and paraspinal soft tissue masses. These findings are present from birth and progress over time, causing fusion of the vertebral bodies, as well as the costovertebral and costotransverse joints, accompanied by stages of early inflammation characterised by episodic swelling of soft tissues (sprouts) that can progressively transform into heterotopic bone with a limitation in normal mobility [4]. Imaging Perspective Those musculoskeletal alterations can be initially demonstrated with radiographs of the foot and hands; however, their usefulness is limited in demonstrating lesions in the early inflammatory stage, so ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging are preferred as a complement [5]. Computed tomography with a bone window and volumetric reconstructions becomes essential for demonstrating the volumes of calcified heterotopic tissues, as well as the fusions that condition and restrict movement [6]. Typically, we will observe heterotopic calcifications connecting structures of the axial and appendicular skeleton. Sites of ossification include the sternocleidomastoid, paraspinal, mandibular, scapular, pelvic girdle muscles, and the scalp [3,6]. They also allow the evaluation of ligamentous calcifications, with the spinal longitudinal ligaments and some tendons being more affected [4,6]. Outcome These ectopic ossifications result in progressive joint ankylosis. Trismus and restricted rib cage expansion due to ossification of respiratory muscles occur in later stages [7]. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by imaging features, and genetic confirmation should not delay diagnosis or management [7,8]. Many cases are diagnosed late, leading to erroneous diagnoses and delayed care with consequences that worsen heterotopic ossifications, which leads to a deterioration in the quality of life [1,8]. Teaching Points Consider the diagnosis of fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva in paediatric patients with hallux valgus deformities that are accompanied by episodic swelling of soft tissues. Computed tomography is crucial to demonstrate the anatomical locations of heterotopic ossifications and bone fusions of the axial and appendicular skeleton. Early diagnosis prevents unnecessary procedures (e.g., biopsies or surgeries), which may worsen heterotopic ossifications. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease: Probable diagnosis in a middle-aged man
clinical_history: A previously healthy 45-year-old gentleman presented in the neurology department with a 6-month history of neurocognitive decline with behavioural and personality changes associated with myoclonus and gait imbalance.
imaging_findings: MRI brain demonstrated asymmetrical areas of high signal in DWI and T2/FLAIR with corresponding normal to low signal in ADC along the cortical convexities of the right frontoparieto-temporal lobes and the right parasagittal region (Figures 1a, 1b, 2a, and 2b). Bilateral symmetric high signal in DWI and T2/FLAIR with corresponding low signal in ADC are seen in the bilateral caudate nucleus, globus pallidus and bilateral posteromedial thalamus (Figures 3a, 3b, and 4).
discussion: Background Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) is a rare, fatal and transmissible neurodegenerative disease caused by prions. It results from the transformation of the normal form of prion protein, PrPC (prion-related protein, where C represents the cellular form of the protein), with a primarily alpha-helical structure into an abnormal form of the protein, PrPSc (proteinaceous infectious particle, where Sc represents scrapie, the prion disease of sheep and goats), which has a primarily beta-pleated sheet structure. This abnormal form of prion protein then spreads and accumulates throughout the brain, resulting in spongiform neurodegeneration [1]. Clinical Perspective CJD is characterised by a rapidly progressive dementia (RPD), myoclonus, cerebellar, pyramidal, extrapyramidal, and psychiatric manifestations, and visual symptoms [1]. In the early stages of the disease, CJD is frequently confused with psychiatric disorders because of the substantial behavioural and personality changes that might mask the cognitive symptoms. However, neurologic symptoms become more noticeable as the disease progresses, and a dementia syndrome evaluation is typically conducted. Other dementias that are linked to myoclonus and progress more quickly, like Alzheimer’s disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and corticobasal degeneration, must be distinguished from it. Paraneoplastic syndrome and autoimmune encephalitis, being possible treatable differentials, make neuroimaging and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis essential [2]. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in 2018, a definite diagnosis of CJD can only be made through the presence of positive brain tissue pathology. A probable diagnosis may be considered if the patient shows rapidly progressing dementia along with at least two of the following symptoms: myoclonus, visual and/or cerebellar abnormalities, pyramidal and/or extrapyramidal symptoms, or akinetic mutism. Additionally, a probable diagnosis requires positive results from one of the following tests: brain MRI, electroencephalogram (EEG), or CSF analysis [3] Imaging Perspective Based on the diagnostic criteria from the CDC in 2018, this patient was diagnosed as a probable case of CJD, meeting the necessary clinical and MRI criteria, in addition to elevated levels of CSF 14-3-3 proteins, and EEG results showing periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWCs). Outcome Currently, there is no existing cure for CJD. Treatment emphasises managing symptoms and providing palliative care. Take Home Message / Teaching Point Familiarising with characteristic MRI findings can help in early diagnosis.
differential_diagnosis: Autoimmune encephalitis Metabolic encephalopathy (hepatic, uremic, or hypoglycaemic) Hypoxic/anoxic brain injury Osmotic demyelination Mitochondrial disease Probable Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease

title: Cerebellar paediatric-type diffuse low-grade glioma, MAP kinase pathway altered
clinical_history: An 11-year-old male presented to the emergency department at our institution with the chief complaints of insidious, throbbing frontal headache, dizziness, photo-phonophobia and emesis for one week. Neurological examination revealed a positive Kernig sign, ataxia and impaired finger-to-nose testing.
imaging_findings: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head demonstrated a diffuse, heterogeneous solid-cystic lesion in the right inferomedial cerebellar hemisphere involving the adjacent vermis. The solid component was fairly defined with irregular margins, manifesting as mild expansion of the cerebellar folia with abnormal low T1 (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d) and high T2 FLAIR signal interspersed with thick T2 dark striations (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). The lobulated cystic component showed high signal on T2WI, intermediate on T1WI and incomplete FLAIR suppression without diffusion restriction. Post-contrast images demonstrated nodular and linear enhancement within the folia and peripheral enhancement of the cyst (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d). Mass effect in the posterior fossa included mild perilesional oedema and partial effacement of the fourth ventricle. There was no evident enlargement of supratentorial ventricles or periventricular oedema. We observed an inferior cerebellar tonsillar descent of 7 mm. CT showed thick, linear striated calcifications mimicking a “tiger-striped” appearance. Bony remodelling with scalloping of the overlying occipital bone suggested an indolent long-standing lesion (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c).
discussion: Background Paediatric-type diffuse low-grade gliomas (pDLGG), MAP (mitogen-activated protein) kinase pathway altered (MAPK-altered), are a subclassification within the pDLGG category according to the 2021 WHO CNS (central nervous system) tumour classification. They occur in children and contain genetic alterations causing deregulation of the MAP kinase signalling pathway [1], encompassing a spectrum of imaging, morphologic, and molecular features [2,3]. Clinical Perspective The clinical presentation includes symptoms related to increased intracranial pressure, such as headache, nausea, and vomiting. Although not encountered in our patient, seizures with or without longstanding epilepsy are also a feature [4]. Imaging Perspective The imaging findings in our case of pDLGG, MAPK-altered, overlap with a few posterior fossa lesions, creating a diagnostic dilemma. Initially, we favoured dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma (DCG). Characteristic imaging findings of DCG include ill-defined margins, thickening and expansion of the folia, and “tiger-striped” folial pattern appearance on T2W images from alternating low and high signal areas. Enhancement is distinctly rare. However, when present, it is faint or densely striated, appearing punctate when viewed in an orthogonal plane, as observed in our case. Cysts are rarely described and are thought to be reflective of extensive vacuolation [5]. Calcifications, both scanty as well as coarse and striated, have been described [5–7]. The presence of a large cerebellar cyst with peripheral rim enhancement and mass effect on adjacent parenchyma was also reminiscent of pilocytic astrocytoma (PA) [8]. However, the cystic component in PA typically shows a brightly enhancing mural nodule, absent in our case. Also, PAs can have a bigger solid component bordering the cyst, but these are usually well-marginated and less diffusely spread in the brain parenchyma [9]. Lastly, a more diffuse high-grade glioma was less likely due to the limited mass effect, perilesional oedema, and calcification pattern [3]. Histological examination with molecular sequencing was required to make the precise, integrated diagnosis (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, and 3d) [5]. In our patient, by immunohistochemistry, tumour cells were positive for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), synaptophysin and Olig2, and negative for BRAFV600E mutant protein (not shown). RNA sequencing of tumour tissue identified a FGFR1::TACC1 fusion, which in combination with the histology, led to the final diagnosis of paediatric-type diffuse low-grade glioma, MAP kinase pathway altered (pDLGG, MAPK-altered). While few cases of pDLGG, MAPK-altered in the posterior fossa have been documented [10,11], they may appear as a heterogeneously enhancing mass with cystic components on imaging [10]. Outcome Surgery is the mainstay for management of resectable pDLGG and our patient underwent midline suboccipital craniotomy with gross total tumour resection. Prognosis depends on location, age, histology, and molecular alterations. These tumours rarely undergo malignant change. Molecular alterations provide important prognostic information regarding specific MAPK pathway targeted chemotherapies [1]. Imaging was key in defining the anatomic extent and for preoperative planning. Although some findings were nonspecific, the presence of a complex cyst with a solid component suggested neoplasia and informed the differential diagnosis. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Imaging features of pDLGGs, MAPK-altered, can be nonspecific. They help narrow differential diagnoses and are valuable for preoperative planning. Most pDLGGs may demonstrate solid and cystic components with some degree of enhancement within solid components. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Haberland syndrome: Radiological clues in a rare neurocutaneous disorder
clinical_history: A 5-year-old girl presented with a progressively enlarging occipital swelling and mild pain. She had prior right-eye surgeries for eyelid coloboma, with corneal opacification of uncertain cause. She had no light perception in the right eye and reduced vision in the left. No systemic issues. Siblings were healthy.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a 2.8 cm bony defect at the posterior fontanelle, through which a partially calcified lipomatous lesion was herniating into the subcutaneous scalp (Figure 1a). This lesion extended intracranially along the posterior falx, causing indentation of the superior sagittal sinus (Figure 1b). A second linear lipoma (10 × 2 mm) was seen at the splenium of the corpus callosum (Figure 1c). A 3D volume-rendered reconstruction of the cranial defect shows the 2.8 cm bony defect at the posterior fontanelle (Figure 1d). MRI confirmed T1-hyperintense lipomas at the posterior fontanelle and splenium, with an extracranial component (Figure 2a). T2-weighted MRI revealed an arachnoid cyst at the left cerebellopontine angle (Figure 2b), and confirmed bilateral colobomas and absence of the right lens (Figure 2c).
discussion: Background Encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis (ECCL), or Haberland syndrome, is a rare neurocutaneous disorder characterised by unilateral involvement of the skin, eyes, and central nervous system [1]. It is a sporadic condition caused by postzygotic somatic activating mutations in the FGFR1 gene (#613001 OMIM) leading to mosaicism, affecting ectomesodermal development and neural crest derivatives [1,2]. Approximately 60 cases have been reported to date, underscoring its rarity. Common features include lipomatous hamartomas, intracranial anomalies, and ocular malformations [2]. Clinical Perspective ECCL typically presents in infancy or early childhood with cutaneous findings such as nevus psiloliparus (a soft, hairless fatty scalp lesion), ocular anomalies (including colobomas, epibulbar dermoids, or microphthalmia), and variable neurologic features [2]. In this case, the child presented with a congenital occipital mass, bilateral vitreous colobomas, and an absent right lens. She also had a history of right eyelid coloboma. Given this constellation of features, ECCL was high on the differential. Imaging is essential for diagnosis, delineation of lesion extent, and evaluation of associated intracranial abnormalities [2,3]. Imaging Perspective CT and MRI are crucial in the diagnostic workup of ECCL. In this case, CT revealed a bony defect at the posterior fontanelle with herniation of a partially calcified lipomatous lesion, corpus callosal lipoma, and bilateral colobomas. MRI confirmed the lipomatous nature of the lesion and revealed an additional arachnoid cyst at the left cerebellopontine angle. Intracranial lipomas, especially in the interhemispheric fissure or corpus callosum, and arachnoid cysts are common in ECCL [4]. These imaging findings not only support the diagnosis but also help differentiate ECCL from syndromes with overlapping features, such as oculocerebrocutaneous syndrome or Goldenhar syndrome [5]. Outcome There is no curative treatment for ECCL. Management is symptomatic and often requires a multidisciplinary approach. Neurosurgical intervention may be warranted in cases of mass effect or hydrocephalus. Visual rehabilitation and developmental support are critical [6]. Prognosis varies with the extent of neurologic involvement but may be stable in the absence of progressive lesions [5–7]. Our patient had prior ophthalmologic surgeries for eyelid coloboma and corneal opacification but has received no intervention for the scalp or intracranial findings. The patient is currently being managed conservatively under observation. Take Home Message Encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis (ECCL) should be considered in patients with congenital scalp masses and ocular anomalies. Neuroimaging is pivotal in diagnosis, characterisation, and guiding long-term care.

title: Giant tuberculoma: An uncommon cause of intracranial space-occupying lesion
clinical_history: A 35-year-old gentleman presented with a gradually progressive headache since 6 months, which was eventually accompanied by visual disturbance, giddiness and difficulty in walking. There was no history of trauma or any other systemic complaints. Fundoscopic examination was unremarkable.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced MRI brain revealed a 3.1 x 3.4 x 3.5 cm-sized T2 hypointense (Figure 1), and thick-walled, ring-enhancing (Figure 2) lesion in the left hemicerebellum. The lesion showed T1 isointense signal (Figure 3) without any diffusion restriction (Figures 4a and 4b). Associated, there was significant perilesional oedema and mass effect causing compression of the fourth ventricle (Figure 1) with resultant moderate upstream hydrocephalus and periventricular cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) seepage. On MR spectroscopy, the lesion showed a prominent lipid lactate peak with reduced choline and N-acetylaspartate levels (Figures 5a and 5b).
discussion: Background Tuberculosis is a major cause of healthcare burden in developing countries and usually involves the pulmonary and lymphoid systems, although other organ systems, including the central nervous system (CNS) may also be involved. Clinical Perspective CNS involvement occurs due to haematogeneous spread and patients may present with signs of raised intracranial pressure (headache, vomiting), focal neurological deficits, or systemic symptoms such as fever, weakness and weight loss. The diagnostic workup of suspected patients of CNS tuberculosis relies on CSF analysis. Contrast-enhanced imaging may not only aid in diagnosis, but also help in defining disease extent, rule out complications and monitor treatment response. In CNS, tuberculosis may involve neuroparenchyma as well as meninges, manifesting as meningitis, tuberculomas, abscesses or focal cerebritis. Rarely, it may present as a giant tuberculoma, mimicking space-occupying lesions such as glioma. In advanced cases, complications such as hydrocephalus and infarcts may occur. Imaging Perspective Contrast-enhanced MRI allows better delineation of anatomy and imaging characteristics of the lesion as compared to CT, and combined with MR spectroscopy, is the modality of choice. Tuberculomas may be caseating or noncaseating, depending on the composition of granulation tissue, with MRI playing a vital role in distinguishing between the two [1]. Tuberculomas with caseating centre appear hypointense on T2WI, with a T2 hyperintense rim, and demonstrate peripheral rim enhancement. Noncaseating tuberculomas are hypointense on T1WI, hyperintense on T2WI, and show nodular solid enhancement. Tuberculomas with central liquefaction are hyperintense on T2WI with peripheral T2 hypointensity and show peripheral rim enhancement [2]. MR spectroscopy shows a lipid lactate peak and is useful in differentiating tuberculomas from other lesions [3]. It is also important to differentiate tuberculomas from tuberculous abscesses, which also show peripheral enhancement. Here, MRI plays an important role: abscesses show intense diffusion restriction on DWI in contrast to granulomas. Nevertheless, abscesses are rare and are usually seen in immunocompromised patients, but can be treated immediately using surgical drainage [1]. Take Home Message Tuberculomas should be considered as a differential diagnosis in case of solitary intracranial mass lesions. Nevertheless, a definite diagnosis is difficult because the imaging presentation is inconsistent and nonspecific, and a definitive diagnosis can sometimes only be established with a biopsy. A long course (9–18 months) of antitubercular drugs is usually effective in treatment. Surgical intervention may be reserved for complications such as hydrocephalus, large lesions with significant mass effect, or for tissue sampling when clinical-imaging diagnosis is not certain [3]. title: Haemorrhagic cholecystitis with pseudoaneurysm of replaced right hepatic artery
clinical_history: A 60-year-old male initially presented with acute right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea and dyspepsia. Ultrasonography revealed acute calculous cholecystitis. The patient was managed conservatively. Two weeks later, he presented to the emergency department with severe right abdominal pain, abdominal distention and melena.
imaging_findings: Non-contrast CT (NCCT) reveals a grossly distended gallbladder with heterogeneous hyperdense intraluminal contents, likely representing haemorrhage, biliary sludge, or gallstones (Figure 1). Triple phase contrast enhanced CT (CECT) reveals a defect in the wall of the distal body (Figure 2) of the gallbladder with a heterogeneous collection within the lumen, extending into the left subphrenic space (measuring approximately 7 x 21 x 7 cm). The collection compresses the adjacent stomach, bowel loops and the mid portion of the common bile duct (Figure 3), resulting in upstream mild prominence of bilateral intrahepatic biliary radicles. There is also the presence of pericholecystic fat stranding, omentomesenteric fat stranding and minimal ascites (Figure 2). Late arterial phase CT (Figure 4) shows a focal hyperdensity adjacent to the gallbladder wall, which is showing intense enhancement and continuity with a vessel, consistent with a pseudoaneurysm. No evidence of significant pooling is noted. However, minimal contrast extravasation cannot be definitively ruled out. Maximum intensity projection (MIP) (Figure 5) and volume rendered (VR) reconstructions (Figure 6) depict a pseudoaneurysm involving the replaced right hepatic artery, which is arising from the superior mesenteric artery.
discussion: Background Acute calculous cholecystitis (ACC) complicated by gallbladder perforation accounts for only 4.5% of the cases operated for ACC [1]. Increased intraluminal pressure from cystic duct obstruction typically leads to ischemia, wall necrosis and perforation. According to Niemeier’s classification, type 1 gallbladder perforation involves free perforation into the peritoneal cavity, resulting in generalised peritonitis [2]. The presence of vascular complications such as pseudoaneurysms or arterial ruptures within the gallbladder lumen are extremely rare. A replaced right hepatic artery arising from the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) accounts for only 12% of the hepatic artery variations [3]. Arterial wall compromise, as in this case, can lead to life-threatening haemorrhagic cholecystitis. Clinical Perspective Patients with complicated cholecystitis may present with signs of sepsis, abdominal tenderness and peritoneal irritation. The clinical challenge lies in distinguishing uncomplicated cholecystitis from life-threatening complications such as gangrene, perforation or haemorrhagic cholecystitis. Imaging plays a pivotal role in detecting early complications and guiding early surgical or interventional management [4]. Imaging Perspective A non-contrast CT scan demonstrates haemorrhage, calculi and sludge within the gallbladder as hyperdense contents. Triple phase CECT imaging is the modality of choice for detecting cholecystitis complications such as emphysematous cholecystitis, gallbladder perforation, abscess and haemorrhagic collections [5]. CECT offers superior detection of gallbladder wall defects compared to ultrasound [6]. The presence of pseudoaneurysm formation suggests arterial involvement. Multiplanar reconstructions (MPRs) in coronal and sagittal planes aid in evaluating subphrenic extension and involvement of adjacent organs. MIP images help in the assessment of the vascular anatomy and identification of anomalous hepatic artery variants [7]. Outcome Our patient developed neurological symptoms, including deviation of the mouth and inability to walk, a day after undergoing CECT of the abdomen. The patient was managed conservatively with intravenous fluids, multiple blood transfusions, antibiotics and aspiration of peritoneal fluid. The neurological symptoms were attributed to metabolic derangements secondary to anaemia and volume loss. Due to the patient’s unstable condition and refusal to undergo further interventions, no endovascular or surgical treatment was pursued. CECT findings were pivotal in explaining the falling haematocrit, melena, abdominal distention and pain. CECT is essential in accurate detection of complicated cholecystitis and vascular injury, which aids in guiding the clinician to offer surgical or endovascular interventions. Teaching points Gallbladder perforation associated with arterial rupture and pseudoaneurysm formation is a rare but life-threatening complication of acute calculous cholecystitis. Performing triple phase CECT is essential in identifying both the biliary and vascular complications. Early imaging and accurate interpretation significantly impact surgical decision making, reduce diagnostic delay and improve patient outcomes.

title: Sturge–Weber syndrome unveiled: A radiologic perspective
clinical_history: Case 1 An 8-year-old boy presented with recurrent focal seizures since infancy and progressive developmental delay, along with a port-wine stain on the right side of his face, present since birth. Case 2 A 54-year-old male with a right hemifacial port-wine stain presented with long-standing epilepsy, progressive left-hemiplegia, cognitive decline and migraine-like headaches. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed visual field defects and glaucoma.
imaging_findings: Case 1 Non-contrast CT images of the brain revealed gyriform, curvilinear cortical and subcortical calcifications along the right parieto-occipital region, with a “tram-track” appearance and associated mild cortical atrophy (Figure 1a). Post-contrast CT images demonstrated pial enhancement over the right parieto-occipital cortex, consistent with pial angiomas. There was also enlargement and enhancement of the ipsilateral choroid plexus (Figure 1b). Additionally, homogeneous crescentic enhancement of the choroid was found along the posterior segment of the right globe, consistent with a choroidal angioma (Figure 1c). Case 2 T2-weighted and FLAIR axial MR images show right cerebral volume loss with diffusely thinned cortex, ex vacuo dilatation of ipsilateral lateral ventricle, and extensive curvilinear cortical hypointensity (Figures 2a and 2b). Axial susceptibility-weighted image (SWI) shows “blooming” of the extensive cortical/subcortical calcifications on the right cerebral hemisphere (Figure 2c). Post-contrast T1-weighted image shows serpentine gyriform enhancement, and enlargement and enhancement of choroid plexus (Figure 2d).
discussion: Background Sturge–Weber Syndrome (SWS), also referred to as encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis, is one of the very few syndromes that is sporadic [1]. Most affected individuals exhibit a prominent port-wine stain, making it one of the most disfiguring neurocutaneous syndromes. Neurological complications such as epilepsy, mental retardation and focal deficits are frequently observed. Imaging continues to play a crucial role in the diagnosis, evaluation, and management [2]. Clinical Perspective The classical characteristics of SWS encompass a spectrum of (1) a dermal capillary-venular malformation along the sensory branches of the trigeminal nerve, (2) retinal choroidal angioma (with or without glaucoma), and (3) a cerebral capillary-venous leptomeningeal (pial) angioma [2]. Seizures developing in infancy (75–90%) are often medically refractory and progress with time. Other common manifestations include glaucoma (70%), hemiparesis (30–65%), and migraine-like headaches [2,3]. These two cases underscore the pivotal role of radiological evaluation in the diagnosis and management of SWS. Imaging Perspective Neuroimaging plays a central role in SWS, as it is used to detect the intracranial pial angiomas. It not only confirms the diagnosis but also delineates the extent and severity of intracranial involvement, including the sequelae of prolonged venous ischaemia. SWS is unilateral in 80% and bilateral in 20% of cases; infratentorial lesions are seen in 11% of cases. When unilateral, it typically occurs ipsilateral to the facial angioma. The parietooccipital region is the most commonly affected location, followed by the frontal and temporal lobes. The degree of involvement can vary from localised lesions to the involvement of an entire cerebral hemisphere [2,4]. On CT, there is cortical atrophy of the affected hemisphere, with associated ipsilateral calvarial thickening and enlargement of the paranasal sinuses. Cortical calcifications, located in the underlying brain parenchyma (not within the angioma itself), typically exhibit a tram-track or gyriform pattern and tend to progress with age. On MRI, the affected cortex and subcortical white matter demonstrate T2 hypointensity, with susceptibility blooming of calcifications on gradient/SWI sequences. Post-contrast T1-weighted images best demonstrate the leptomeningeal angioma, and typically show serpentine enhancement. Additional findings include ipsilateral choroid plexus enlargement and enlarged medullary veins, sources of compensatory collateral venous drainage. Sequential examinations reveal progressive cerebral cortical and subcortical atrophy, particularly during the first years of life. In newborns, initial findings may be subtle or absent, highlighting the importance of follow-up imaging in suspected cases [2,5,6]. Outcome Outcomes in SWS depend on the extent of brain involvement and seizure control. Early-onset, refractory seizures are associated with poorer cognitive and motor outcomes. Periinsular hemispherotomy is the last resort to manage catastrophic epilepsy associated with hemispheric lesions [7].

title: Mycobacterium kansasii tenosynovitis in a patient receiving etanercept
clinical_history: A 42-year-old woman taking etanercept for psoriatic arthritis presented to the emergency department with pain in her right wrist for three weeks, predominantly in the fourth and fifth fingers. She reported no history of trauma or prior procedures. Clinical examination revealed swelling on the palmar surface and pain with movement. An ultrasound was performed, which showed synovial fluid (images not available).
imaging_findings: MRI of the right hand showed fluid in the synovial sheath of the flexor tendons (Figure 1a), extending from the distal radioulnar joint to the metacarpals, with multiple small nodules within the tendon sheath, ranging from hypointense to isointense, consistent with “rice bodies” (Figures 1b, 1c, and 1d). Soft tissue enlargement and thickening of the flexor sheath tendons were also observed (Figures 1e and 1f). Two months after starting treatment, a follow-up MRI was performed, which showed the disappearance of the “rice bodies” with a slight persistence of synovial fluid in the flexor tendon sheath (Figures 2a and 2b). A decrease in soft tissue enlargement and flexor sheath thickening was also observed (Figure 2c).
discussion: Background Nontuberculous mycobacterial tenosynovitis is a rare condition that mainly affects the hand and wrist [1,2]. M. kansasii ( Mycobacterium kansasii ) is an atypical Mycobacterium . It is photochromogenic, acid-fast, and slow-growing [1]. M. kansasii infection mainly impacts immunosuppressed patients or those on immunosuppressive therapy. The infection is typically pulmonary; when it involves the musculoskeletal system, it presents as arthritis, osteomyelitis, and septic tenosynovitis. About 5% to 10% of patients with atypical mycobacterial infections show musculoskeletal involvement; the most common associated species are M. kansasii and Mycobacterium marinum [1,2]. Diagnosis is microbiological [1]. In our case, culture samples were obtained by aspiration during ultrasound, which revealed growth of M. kansasii . Etanercept is an antitumour necrosis factor agent used to treat psoriatic arthritis and other immune-mediated or inflammatory diseases [3,4]. It may be related to atypical infections by the Mycobacterium complex [5]. Clinical Perspective Septic tenosynovitis caused by nontuberculous mycobacteria has an insidious clinical presentation and chronic course, manifesting symptoms such as pain, mass effect, hyperaemia, oedema, and stiffness [2,6]. Complications (stiffness, persistent infection) and sequelae (functional limitation, chronic pain) may occur [7]. Imaging Perspective Radiological findings in tenosynovitis caused by M. kansasii or atypical mycobacteria are nonspecific. Conventional radiographs show soft tissue enlargement and, in advanced cases, even bone erosions. Ultrasonography may reveal joint effusion, soft tissue swelling, tendon thickening, and even rupture [6]. MRI may reveal increased soft tissue volume, diffuse thickening and enhancement of the synovial membrane, joint or tendon involvement, and the presence of joint collections or effusions, along with “rice bodies” [8–10]. The appearance of “rice bodies” on MRI is an uncommon finding, linked to chronic inflammation of the synovial membrane. These are believed to form from microinfarcts or fibrin deposits [9]. Outcome Treatment involves traditional antituberculosis drugs. In resistant cases, azithromycin and a fluoroquinolone can be used with excellent responses. When dealing with immunosuppressed patients, it is crucial to improve the immune status [11,12]. Approximately 82% of patients may need surgery, while 18% respond to medical treatment alone. Half of the cases will recover without sequelae [13]. In our case, we administered isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, followed by 12 months of isoniazid with rifampin and discontinuation of etanercept, and the patient is recovering without sequelae. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Atypical mycobacterial tenosynovitis ( M. kansasii ) is a rare infection that should be considered in immunosuppressed patients or those receiving immunosuppressive therapy. “Rice bodies” on MRI are not specific but should raise suspicion of the condition based on clinical signs. Diagnosis relies on microbiology, and treatment is pharmacological. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Orbitofacial arteriovenous malformation. The utility of MR angiography fused with CT
clinical_history: A 51-year-old female presented with a reddish colouration of the left periorbital tissue since birth, with enlargement of the soft tissues of the nose and left orbital region, resulting in multiple ulcers requiring surgical treatment. She currently presents with left ocular pain and ipsilateral proptosis.
imaging_findings: Magnetic resonance imaging shows multiple flow voids in T2-weighted sequences located in the periorbital and nasal region on the left side. In MR angiography sequences fused whit computed tomography, multiple efferent vessels are identified coming from the branches of the left external carotid artery, a diffuse nidus located in the periorbital and left nasal region with an enlarged afferent vessel crossing the frontal bone joining the superior sagittal sinus, with an increased calibre and flow of the sagittal sinus and cortical veins of the frontal lobe and insular region of the left cerebral hemisphere.
discussion: Background Vascular anomalies of the orbital region account for 10% of all orbital masses. Arteriovenous malformations are characterised by rapid arterial flow, the presence of a nidus and draining venous channels [1]. Pathophysiologically, these are developmental errors that take place during embryogenesis, just after the primitive capillary plexus has formed, leading to genetic errors damaging the endothelial cells during this period [2]. Clinical Perspective Clinically, they present as pulsating proptosis and with the presence of orbital masses. They can be classified by the Schobinger clinical classification of arteriovenous malformations, ranging from skin discolouration and redness (stage 1) to destruction and ulceration (stage 3) and subsequently cardiac decompensation (stage 4) [3]. Other clinical features that can be present are oedema, congestion of the episclera, pain, reduced vision and diplopia [4]. Imaging Perspective In orbital masses, computed tomography and resonance imaging tend to be the first imaging modality of choice, with the presence of intense contrast enhancement with prominent vessels suggesting a vascular origin of the lesion [5]. The advantages of using MRI include improved delineation of adjacent structures and the use of gadolinium, which is better tolerated and provides excellent spatial relationships. CT offers improved visualisation of bony structures, which may be important when observing penetrating vessels. In magnetic resonance imaging, the presence of flow voids and serpiginous enhancing structures suggests an arteriovenous malformation [6]. 4D time-resolved MR angiography (4D-TRAK) is a technique of CE–MRA that can obtain dynamic filling of the arteries and veins similar to digital subtraction angiography (DSA) [7]. The presence of a nidus is crucial for diagnosis. This is the site where the arterial blood is shunted to veins, appearing in angiography MRI as enlarged vascular channels associated with dilated feeding and draining vessels; the mass-like feature is an atypical finding and are attributed to oedema and a fibrofatty matrix within the surrounding tissue, and the use of this imaging technique help to the marginal demarcation of the lesion and delimitate extension to the adjacent structures [8]. Angiography is the gold standard method for diagnosis. Angiography sequences contribute to differentiating arteriovenous malformations from venous malformations, in which a spongy mass is typically observed that is composed of abnormal veins with lobulated margins and multiple, rounded, signal voids that represent phleboliths, with ventral enhancement and patchy [9]. Outcome Treatment varies depending on the extent of the injury and ranges from sclerotherapy to surgery, and is rarely cured, only controlled [10].

title: Congenital cochlear nerve deficiency – A case series
clinical_history: Case 1 : A 9-year-old girl presented to the otorhinolaryngology (ENT) department with profound hearing loss. On evaluation, she was detected to have right-sided sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). Case 2 : A 6-year-old boy was referred from the ENT department with a clinical diagnosis of severe right-sided SNHL. Case 3 : A 2-year-old child was referred with a clinical diagnosis of right-sided SNHL for MRI.
imaging_findings: MRI brain were performed, and the most relevant findings for each case are noted below: Case 1 : Thinned-out cochlear division of the right vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) (Figure 1b). Stenosed right internal auditory meatus (IAM) (Figure 1a). The facial nerve CN VII appeared normal. Case 2 : Non-visualised cochlear division of the right CN VIII (Figure 2a). CN VII appeared normal. Case 3 : The cochlear nerve is not visualised in the anteroinferior aspect of the right IAM (Figure 3a).
discussion: Background Cochlear nerve deficiency (CND) is among the few aetiologies of congenital sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). They may be either defined as a small which may be hypoplastic or absent (aplastic) cochlear nerves (VIII cranial nerve) due to agenesis or degeneration [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Patients with CND present to the hospital with complaints of poor response to verbal commands in early childhood. In such cases, imaging is crucial to rule out anatomical causes of hearing loss, either in the form of nerve deficiency or dysplastic development of middle/inner ear structures. Epidemiologically, the prevalence of cochlear nerve aplasia in the Indian population is scarce. However, the prevalence of SNHL averages 2–3 per 1,000 live births among the Indian population. Inner ear malformations (IEMs) amount to 20% of congenital SNHL, making it a relatively rare developmental abnormality [3–6]. Imaging Perspective MRI plays a crucial role in differentiating between developmental and birth trauma-related CN VIII hypoplasia/aplasia [1–3]. This is done by analysing the course of the nerve segments and their brainstem nuclei. The most important sequences to characterise CN VIII are the three-dimensional (3D) high-resolution T2-weighted sequences (also known as T2W 3D DRIVE), providing an excellent contrast between the cerebrospinal fluid and cranial nerves. Aplasia of the cochlear nerve is diagnosed when the nerve is not visible on imaging, whereas hypoplasia is detected when the cochlear nerve is thinner in relation to other nerves in the ipsilateral internal auditory canal (IAC) [3]. Outcome Patients with CND can further be managed with either cochlear implants or auditory brainstem implants. Take Home Message / Teaching Points In clinically suspected cases of cochlear nerve deficiency (CND), it is always recommended to examine the study in sagittal or oblique sagittal sections in T2W 3D DRIVE sequence for better characterisation of the nerve complex. Since all the patients were under the age of 18, informed consents were obtained from the patients’ guardians to participate in this study.
differential_diagnosis: Cochlear nerve deficiency Auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder Mondini dysplasia Acoustic neuroma

title: Colonic lipoma causing large bowel intussusception
clinical_history: A 50-year-old female patient, with no important pathological or family history, presented with lower right quadrant intermittent abdominal pain for one month along with chronic constipation, bloating and lower abdominal fullness. She denied weight loss, vomiting, nausea, fever or change in her bowel habits.
imaging_findings: An abdominal and pelvic computed tomography (CT) was performed and showed a well-circumscribed, homogeneous tumour with fat density in the ascending colon, measuring 6 x 3 x 3 cm, in the longitudinal, anteroposterior and transverse axes, respectively (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d). The use of positive oral contrast, in accordance with the institution’s standard protocol for suspected bowel obstruction at the time, may have limited the evaluation of intraluminal and mucosal details. Intravenous iodinated contrast administration was contraindicated due to the patient’s documented hypersensitivity. The tumour caused ascending colocolic intussusception (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, and 1d). Although some classical radiological features of intussusception, such as concentric “target” sign, were not clearly seen, some reformatted sequences (Figures 1b and 1c) suggested a bowel-within-bowel configuration. There was no evidence of abnormal proximal bowel loop distension, ascites, or pneumoperitoneum. The preoperative diagnosis was colocolic intussusception due to an ascending colonic lipoma.
discussion: Background Intussusception occurs when a segment of the intestine, along with its mesentery (intussusceptum), telescopes into the lumen of a contiguous portion of bowel (intussuscipiens) by peristaltic movements. Intussusception is uncommon in adults, accounting for around 5% of cases, and is usually caused by a pathological lead point. Malignant tumours are the most common cause of colocolic intussusception [1]. Lipomas are non-epithelial benign adipose tumours and they are the most common benign cause of colocolic intussusception in adults. In about 90% of cases, these tumours are found in the submucosal layer of the colon [1]. Colonic lipomas leading to colocolic intussusception usually occur when the tumour is over 4 cm in diameter and are commonly found in the transverse colon (28%), followed by the sigmoid colon (20%), cecum (19%), ascending colon (15%), descending colon (14%), and rectum (4%) [2,3]. Clinical Perspective In most cases, colonic lipomas are asymptomatic and are detected incidentally. Lipomas over 2 cm in diameter can be symptomatic, presenting with clinical features such as abdominal pain, changes in bowel habits and, in rare instances, intussusception [3,4]. The patient’s clinical presentation and physical examination findings are nonspecific, making the diagnosis challenging. Therefore, colonoscopy and abdominal and pelvic CT are commonly requested in clinical practice [5]. Imaging Perspective In large bowel intussusception, a lead mass can often be seen on CT imaging. However, it is usually hard to determine the underlying cause, except in the case of a lipoma, which shows a well-marginated mass with fat attenuation. Intussusception with a pathological lead point typically presents as an abnormal target-like lesion and may be associated with proximal bowel obstruction [1]. In this case report, considering the patient’s age and her subacute symptoms, a malignant lesion was initially suspected. Imaging was crucial for establishing the diagnosis, despite the limitations of the CT protocol used. Nevertheless, this case represents a valuable example of the rare occurrence of benign lipoma-induced intussusception mimicking malignancy, consistent with the few similar cases reported in the literature. Outcome The approach of colonic lipomas depends on their size and symptoms. The treatment of intussusception in adults usually requires surgical intervention [5]. In our patient, a right hemicolectomy was performed, and histopathological examination showed mature adipose tissue with no signs of atypia, compatible with submucosal lipoma (Figure 2). The patient recovered well and was discharged after a few days. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Lipomas are the most common benign cause of colocolic intussusception in adults. CT plays a crucial role in diagnosing intussusception and evaluating its underlying aetiology. Colonic lipomas, in particular, can be easily identified on CT due to their characteristic fat attenuation. Surgery is the treatment of choice for colonic lipoma-induced intussusception. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Calcified cerebral emboli (“Salted pretzel” sign)
clinical_history: An 85-year-old patient presented at the emergency department after experiencing nausea for the past two hours. During the clinical examination, the patient exhibited motor deficits, hemianopia, and facial asymmetry.
imaging_findings: Brain CT showed multiple calcified foci in the distal pial branches of the left middle cerebral and posterior cerebral artery resembling the salt on a pretzel (arrows in Figure 1). Compared with the previous brain CT, obtained 4 years before, new calcified foci were visible (arrow in Figure 2). Diffusion-weighted brain MR imaging revealed several areas of recent ischaemia in regions supplied by the left middle cerebral artery and the left posterior cerebral artery (Figure 3). The CT angiogram (CTA) showed extensive calcified plaques at the left carotid bifurcation with a floating thrombus. A foetal posterior communicating artery explained the presence of calcified emboli in both vascular territories.
discussion: Background Calcified cerebral emboli are a rare cause of stroke. These emboli typically originate from extensive atherosclerotic disease at the cardiac valves, the aorta or the blood vessels of the neck. Calcified emboli can occur spontaneously or be triggered by cardiovascular interventions [1]. Clinical Perspective There is an increased risk of recurrent strokes. As a result, further cardiovascular investigations are crucial. If large vessel occlusion can be demonstrated, thrombolysis can be considered. However the efficacy of thrombolysis in calcified cerebral emboli has not been studied yet. Imaging Perspective CT is key in detecting calcified emboli, often visible as hyperdense, punctate foci within cerebral arteries. Diffusion-weighted MRI can confirm the ischaemic areas. CTA can reveal the embolic source and guide further management. Outcome Calcified emboli indicate an elevated risk for recurrent strokes. Cardiovascular evaluation is essential to identify and treat the underlying cause. Endovascular thrombectomy can be considered in cases of large vessel occlusion; however, there is a worse outcome and a higher mortality compared to non-calcified thrombi. Thrombolysis may also be considered, though efficacy remains uncertain. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Calcified cerebral emboli are a rare but distinct stroke aetiology. Recognition of this pattern can guide immediate and long-term management and should prompt a thorough vascular assessment. title: Right bronchial artery aneurysm in a patient with post-infectious bronchiectasis
clinical_history: A 89-year-old woman was being treated with anticoagulation for her aortic valve prosthesis. She had a history of recurrent respiratory infections, postinfectious bronchiectasis, and episodes of mild haemoptysis. She presented to the emergency department with symptoms of respiratory infection and severe haemoptysis and underwent chest computed tomography angiography (CTA chest).
imaging_findings: CTA chest in coronal and axial projections (Figures 1 and 2) using a soft tissue window with maximum intensity projection (MIP) showed a right bronchial artery of orthotopic origin, originating from the lower medial border of the aortic arch. It is tortuous and has a sac-like aneurysmal dilation. Bronchiectasis and consolidation in the right lower lobe (RLL) were observed. Two 3D vascular reconstructions of the orthotopic bronchial artery are shown (Figure 3). CT (computed tomography) of the chest with a pulmonary window at the level of the main bronchi showed an aneurysm and dilation of the right bronchial artery, along with condensation in the RLL (Figure 4). A previous chest CT in pulmonary window revealed multiple sacular and cystic bronchial dilations in the right upper lobe and middle lobe (Figure 5).
discussion: Background The bronchial arteries typically arise from the thoracic aorta, with their most common origin (orthotopic) being from the descending aorta between the 5th and 6th thoracic vertebrae. Bronchial arteries that originate outside this location are referred to as ectopic [1]. Most patients have two left bronchial arteries and one right bronchial artery [1]. The right bronchial artery usually arises as the intercostobronchial trunk, sharing its proximal course with an intercostal artery [1,2]. On imaging, they appear as thin vessels with a diameter of less than 2 mm [1]. Bronchial artery aneurysms (BAA) are uncommon. Their aetiology is linked to chronic inflammatory changes in the lungs that increase blood flow. Additionally, patients with pulmonary hypertension, chronic infections, bronchiectasis, and neoplasia are more likely to present with BAA [1,3,4]. Clinical Perspective Bronchial artery dilations and BAA are usually asymptomatic, with most of them being incidentally found. When symptomatic, patients present with haemoptysis, cough, dyspnoea and chest pain [3,4]. When a BAA ruptures, the clinical presentation resembles that of an acute aortic syndrome [5]. Imaging Perspective CTA chest with reconstructed slices at 1.00–1.25 mm is the preferred modality for imaging bronchial arteries. MIP reconstructions can help with vascular anatomy. It allows radiologists to define the number, origin, and trajectory of the bronchial arteries, as well as other blood vessels. Additionally, the size, dilation, or hypertrophy of bronchial arteries can be reliably assessed [1,5]. In most cases, it creates an accurate vascular map to guide interventional procedures [1]. Selective bronchial angiography is an invasive test; it was considered the gold standard for diagnosing BAA, but currently, CT angiography is an alternative imaging modality that acquires thin sections that can be used to create multiplanar and three-dimensional reconstructions, producing images comparable to or even better than conventional angiography in representing bronchial or non-bronchial systemic arteries [1,6]. Outcome BAA embolisation is the preferred treatment. Ideally, all aneurysms should be treated promptly after diagnosis, regardless of symptoms, due to the high risk of bleeding and death [1,5,7]. Although our patient did not show a ruptured aneurysm, conservative management was decided upon due to haemodynamic instability, age, and comorbidities, and the patient ultimately passed away. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Bronchial artery aneurysms (BAA) are a rare but potentially life-threatening condition. They should be included in the differential diagnosis of patients presenting with haemoptysis, especially if they have a history of recurrent lung infection, pulmonary hypertension or bronchiectasis. The most accessible, fast and non-invasive imaging modality is CTA chest, which should not be postponed if clinically suspected. All BAA require prompt treatment. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
