title: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome
clinical_history: A 55-year-old woman with hypertension, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and biliopancreatic bypass, who has visited the emergency department multiple times due to thunderclap headaches with normal cranial CT scans. She returns for consultation one week later, presenting with hemianopsia, without any other associated symptoms.
imaging_findings: In the initial studies performed for the thunderclap headache, cranial CT scans with and without contrast were completely normal. In a non-contrast cranial CT scan one week later, when she presented with hemianopsia, there was an infarct area in the superficial territory of the left posterior cerebral artery (Figures 1a and 1b). The main arterial structures of the supraaortic trunks and intracranial arteries were patent, although irregularities and focal stenoses were noted (as seen in Figures 2a, 2b and 2c).
discussion: Background Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) is a neurological disorder characterised by a temporary vasoconstriction of the blood vessels in the brain, leading to various neurological symptoms [1]. Clinical Perspective The initial hallmark symptom is a thunderclap headache, described as sudden and severe, reaching peak intensity within seconds, prompting urgent medical evaluation. Patients may experience nausea, vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia, which can mimic other acute headache syndromes such as subarachnoid haemorrhage or migraine. Neurological deficits occur (8%–43% of cases) and may include encephalopathy, visual disturbances, dysarthria, aphasia, and ataxia. Despite its potentially alarming presentation, RCVS is typically reversible, with resolution within a few weeks. However, in some cases, more serious neurological symptoms can develop, including seizures, motor weakness, and disturbances in speech or vision. These complications occur in 25–33% of patients and include posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), seizures, ischemic stroke, subarachnoid haemorrhage, or intraparenchymal haemorrhage. Haemorrhagic events typically occur in the first week, while ischemic complications are more common in the second week, underscoring the importance of early recognition and management [1]. Triggering factors include intense physical exertion, sexual activity, emotional stress, vasoactive substances, postpartum state, or recreational drug use (cannabis, cocaine) [2]. Imaging Perspective Diagnosis must be made through imaging, with segmental vasoconstriction of intracranial arteries as the key finding. Angiography is the gold standard for this purpose, as seen in Figures 2a, 2b and 2c. Studies show that smaller-calibre arteries are the first to be affected and may appear normal initially. Therefore, if clinical suspicion is high, repeating the study after 2–3 weeks is recommended, and an MRI can be performed at a later stage to evaluate for complications such as infarctions or haemorrhages and rule out other causes such as vasculitis, aneurysms, or subarachnoid haemorrhage [3]. Outcome Prognosis is generally favourable. Early diagnosis and close monitoring remain essential to prevent severe complications such as stroke, haemorrhage, or seizures. Delayed diagnosis or severe presentation can lead to stroke or irreversible brain injury. Prognostic factors include initial symptom severity, associated conditions (e.g., autoimmune disease or postpartum state), and timeliness of treatment. Postpartum cases carry worse outcomes, with residual deficits in 30% and mortality up to 20% [3]. Treatment remains supportive, as no definitive therapy has proven effective. Management includes removing triggers and symptomatic care. NSAIDs, antiemetics, antiepileptics, and occasionally corticosteroids may be used, though corticosteroids may worsen outcomes. Nimodipine may relieve headache but does not affect long-term prognosis [1]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Early recognition is crucial. Initial imaging may appear normal, increasing the risk of missed diagnosis and delayed treatment, which can lead to preventable complications. title: Septal placental implantation in a gravid septate uterus
clinical_history: A 27-year-old nulliparous female came for her first antenatal scan at 32 weeks of gestation with no prior early antenatal scans. She presented with a bilobed abdominal contour seen externally as two distinct bulges with a central vertical depression. No earlier imaging had been done.
imaging_findings: An ultrasound examination revealed a thin central septum partially dividing the uterus into two hemicavities. The amniotic sac was seen occupying both the uterine hemicavities. The foetus was viable, with the foetal abdomen and lower extremities seen in the right hemicavity, and the foetal head and upper extremities extending into the left hemicavity across the central septum (Figures 1 and 2). Nearly two-thirds of the placenta was implanted on the left side of the central septum, with the rest of it implanted on the anterior wall of the left hemicavity (Figure 3). No vascularity was detected in the uterine septum on Doppler ultrasound.
discussion: Background A uterine septum is a congenital Müllerian anomaly where a fibrous or fibromuscular band divides the endometrial cavity partially or completely. It results from incomplete resorption of the medial walls of the fused Müllerian ducts. The septum is typically avascular and poorly distensible, which can impair implantation and placental development in pregnancy [3,4]. Clinical Perspective In a septate uterus, pregnancy typically occurs in one hemicavity, as the septum restricts expansion into both sides, with implantation usually occurring on the well-vascularised lateral wall [2,3]. In rare cases, pregnancy can continue despite placental implantation on the septum, representing an unusual presentation as mentioned in some case reports, and cited in Calis et al. (2018) and in Martinez‑Peñuela et al. (2019) [1,6]. Such cases may lead to complications like foetal growth restriction or preterm birth, yet may occasionally result in successful outcomes with close monitoring [1,3,4]. Hence, in such cases, ultrasound monitoring of placental location and foetal growth is needed [5,6]. Imaging Perspective Diagnostic pearls include a narrowed uterine contour with persistent midline echo and extension of the gestational sac across the septum. Key findings include abnormal uterine shape on 2D ultrasound, placental tissue implanted on the midline septum and foetal parts extending across the septum to occupy both uterine cavities. Final diagnosis is best confirmed with 3D ultrasound, MRI or hysteroscopy, which clearly delineate the septum, uterine morphology, and placental location [1,6]. Outcome Therapeutic options in pregnancies with a septate uterus and placental implantation on the septum are limited to close monitoring, as surgical correction (metroplasty) is contraindicated during pregnancy [1,4]. Prognosis depends on septum vascularity and placental function; risks include miscarriage, growth restriction, and preterm labour [1,4,5]. Imaging plays a crucial role in therapy planning—3D ultrasound and MRI help assess septal extent, placental location, and foetal growth, guiding surveillance strategies and delivery planning to optimise maternal and foetal outcomes in these rare presentations [1]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Placental implantation on the uterine septum is a rare condition that clinicians should be aware of during antenatal care. Accurate diagnosis requires the use of advanced imaging techniques, which can help differentiate it from more common placental positions. Once diagnosed, these cases need close monitoring for potential foetal growth restriction and placental insufficiency. A carefully planned delivery strategy is essential to minimise maternal and foetal risks.

title: Mesenteric lymphangioma causing small bowel obstruction
clinical_history: A 38-year-old male presented to the emergency room with a three-day history of gradually progressive, intermittent abdominal pain, abdominal distention, vomiting, and reduced bowel movements. His medical history included schizophrenia, well-controlled with antipsychotic medication. He had no prior abdominal surgeries. An abdominal CT with intravenous contrast (portal venous phase) was obtained.
imaging_findings: A large fluid-attenuating mass, composed of multiple confluent cystic lesions, was noted in the right lower quadrant and pelvis, extending into the right inguinal canal (Figure 1). The confluent cystic spaces showed internal densities of fluid, imperceptible walls, lobulated margins, and thin, smooth, enhancing septae (Figure 2). The lesion exerted mass effect on the bladder and adjacent small bowel loops (Figures 3a and 3b). Small bowel obstruction was evident, with prominent dilation of the jejunum and multiple ileal loops. A transition point in the pelvis adjacent to the cystic lesion was evident. Twisting of the mesentery with a prominent whirlpool sign was observed (Figure 4).
discussion: Background Lymphangiomas are rare benign tumours of lymphatic origin. They are considered congenital macrocystic lymphatic malformations, due to embryonic sequestration of lymphatic tissue [1]. Although seen most often in the paediatric population in the head, neck, and axilla, they have been reported in adults and can occur throughout the body [2]. Peritoneal involvement is exceedingly rare. Clinical Perspective Mesenteric lymphangiomas (MLs) are uncommon intra-abdominal tumours, with a reported incidence of 1 in 20,000–250,000 hospital admissions. Most are diagnosed in early childhood, with adult cases being rare [1,2]. Clinical presentation varies widely, ranging from asymptomatic incidental findings to acute abdominal emergencies. Complications such as haemorrhage, infection, torsion, and rupture, as well as small bowel obstruction, either from extrinsic compression or volvulus, have been reported [1,3]. Due to the nonspecific and variable presentation, especially in emergency settings, urgent surgical exploration is often necessary. Imaging plays a crucial role in the diagnostic process, identifying the cystic nature of the lesion, its effect on surrounding structures, and potential complications, thereby guiding appropriate surgical planning and management. Imaging Perspective MLs are thin-walled multiloculated cystic masses with thin internal septa, containing chylous, serous or haemorrhagic fluid. On ultrasound, they often present as anechoic or hypoechoic lesions with internal septa. Computed tomography reveals fluid-attenuating, multiloculated, lobulated cystic structures. Magnetic resonance imaging is particularly useful. MLs usually exhibit high signal intensity on T2-weighted images and low signal on T1-weighted images. Less commonly, T1 hyperintensity and intermediate T2 signal may be observed when the content is rich in chyle or proteinaceous material. Fat density on CT or signal consistent with fat on MRI from chylous fluid can be a very helpful imaging finding, narrowing the differential diagnosis. Enhancement of wall and septa is seen, while mass effect on adjacent organs is present [4]. Whereas imaging strongly suggests the diagnosis, definitive confirmation requires histopathological examination [5]. Accurate imaging interpretation is essential to guide diagnosis, assess the extent, and support surgical planning. Outcome Complete surgical excision is the treatment of choice for cystic lymphangiomas, even in asymptomatic cases. Prognosis is generally favourable, with low rates of postoperative complications and recurrence. Increased tumour size may preclude complete resection and increase the risk of local recurrence. Segmental bowel resection may be necessary in cases of intestinal wall and mesenteric vessel involvement [5,6]. In our case, small bowel volvulus due to a large cystic mesenteric mass was confirmed intraoperatively. Complete excision of the lesion with small bowel resection, due to bowel wall ischemic changes and encasement of mesenteric arterial branches was performed. Histology confirmed the presumed radiological diagnosis. Complete resolution of symptomatology and no recurrence were noted 6 months post-resection, but the patient was subsequently lost to follow-up. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Mesenteric lymphangiomas (MLs) are rare, especially in adults. They may be present with an acute abdomen due to complications such as bowel obstruction or volvulus. Imaging, particularly contrast-enhanced CT and MRI, plays a crucial role in suggesting the diagnosis and guiding surgical planning. Prompt surgical intervention is essential for both diagnosis and treatment. MLs should be considered in the differential diagnosis of cystic intra-abdominal masses, even in adult patients. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Crossed pulmonary arteries: A rare congenital vascular variant
clinical_history: A 67-year-old female patient undergoing routine staging CT for oncologic follow-up. No known history of congenital heart disease. No cardiopulmonary symptoms reported.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax demonstrated an anomalous origin of the pulmonary arteries: the right pulmonary artery arose from the left side of the pulmonary trunk and crossed behind it to reach the right lung, while the left pulmonary artery originated in normal fashion.
discussion: Background Crossed pulmonary arteries (CPA) are a rare congenital anomaly characterised by the transposition and crossing of the right and left pulmonary arteries. In this condition, the left pulmonary artery originates superior and to the right of the right pulmonary artery, and both arteries cross each other as they proceed to their respective lungs. Crossed pulmonary arteries are often isolated findings, but they may also be associated with other congenital cardiovascular anomalies. Reported associations include ventricular septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, atrioventricular septal defects, and complex anomalies such as tetralogy of Fallot or double outlet right ventricle. Additionally, a right-sided aortic arch has been noted in some cases. Recognition of these potential coexisting anomalies is important, particularly in paediatric patients, to guide further cardiac evaluation. However, in this case, no evidence of associated anomalies was found on imaging or clinical examination [1]. Clinical Perspective CPA is typically asymptomatic and discovered incidentally during imaging for unrelated conditions. Recognition is crucial for surgical planning or interventional procedures [3]. Imaging Perspective CT angiography or enhanced CT chest reliably demonstrates the anomalous crossing pattern of the pulmonary arteries. The key diagnostic feature is the origin of the right pulmonary artery from the left side of the pulmonary trunk [1]. Outcome In this case, no intervention was required. The finding was incidental and clinically insignificant but recorded for future procedural awareness. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Crossed pulmonary arteries (CPA) are a rare and benign congenital variant. Important to recognise on thoracic imaging, especially for pre-operative planning. CT is the modality of choice for diagnosis.

title: Genes to scans: Bardet–Biedl syndrome with post-renal transplant encephalopathy
clinical_history: A 15-year-old female presented with loss of appetite and anorexia since 2 months, oliguria for 6 months, primary amenorrhea, polydactyly and a short neck (Figure 5). She was overweight, showed pedal oedema and retinal pigment epithelium atrophy changes leading to diminished vision. Blood investigations indicated elevated serum urea and creatinine levels, with low eGFR, LH, FSH, and oestradiol. Patient was normotensive (117/79 mmHg) when she developed seizures post-renal transplant on day 3.
imaging_findings: In the MRI abdomen, bilateral kidneys appear small with relatively thin parenchyma and multiple cortical cysts with corticomedullary differentiation. No dilatation of both the pelvicalyceal system or the ureters—chronic kidney disease or sequelae of renal dysplasia (Figure 1). There is an anteflexed hypoplastic uterus, relatively small for age, measuring about 14 x 27 x 49 mm (AP x TD x CC) with hyperintense myometrium and thin endometrium measuring about 1mm (Figure 2a). Bilateral ovaries show multiple small peripherally arranged follicles (Figures 2b and 2c). The vagina is also relatively hypoplastic (Figure 2d). MRI brain post renal transplant (day 3) shows bilateral symmetrical cortical and subcortical T2W/FLAIR hyperintensities, seen involving bilateral parieto-occipital lobes, the right basal ganglia (Figure 3a), and bilateral high frontal lobes (Figures 3b and 3c). There is no diffusion restriction with high ADC values (Figures 3d and 3e)—posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). Sagittal and coronal T2-weighted images show predominantly posterior distribution of hyperintensities (Figures 4a and 4b).
discussion: Background Bardet–Biedl syndrome (BBS), also known as Laurence–Moon–Bardet–Biedl syndrome, is a rare, autosomal recessive hereditary multisystem illness resulting from primary cilia malfunction. The malfunction of the primary cilia, both motile and non-motile, results in ciliopathies [2]. The molecular basis was demonstrated to involve pathogenic mutations in 26 genes, BBS12 being the most common [3]. Genetic testing can validate the diagnosis, which is based on clinical signs and symptoms [4]. In this instance, BBS was detected by genetic testing, which was positive for the BBS7 gene. Clinical Perspective BBS is characterised by cone-rod dystrophy, skeletal abnormalities (polydactyly, rib cage), central obesity, learning disabilities, hypogonadism in males, renal anomalies, nystagmus, speech disorders, developmental delay, polyuria/polydipsia, ataxia, poor coordination/clumsiness, and intellectual disability [1,5]. In this case, the patient had positive genetic testing with more than one major criterion (Figure 6). Among the differential diagnoses are: Joubert syndrome, which excludes hypogonadism and genitourinary abnormalities; Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome, which excludes polydactyly and retinal changes; Alström syndrome, which excludes polydactyly; and McKusick–Kaufman syndrome, which excludes obesity and retinal disease [8]. Imaging Perspective Foetal MRI and ultrasound are the first-line for prenatal diagnosis of BBS. The presence of echogenic kidneys during a level II ultrasound should raise suspicion for BBS. Additionally, ultrasound findings of polycystic kidneys, with or without polydactyly, suggest a high likelihood of the condition [6]. The antenatal scans for this patient were inconclusive. She later presented with echogenic kidneys and a loss of corticomedullary differentiation on an ultrasound performed at 14 years of age. Further evaluation using MRI of the abdomen and pelvis revealed chronic kidney disease, a hypoplastic uterus with vagina, and multicystic ovaries. Outcome BBS is a chronic disease that currently has no specific cure. The treatment for BBS primarily focuses on symptomatic relief [7]. In our case, the patient underwent renal transplantation due to chronic kidney disease and was prescribed the immunosuppressant tacrolimus. On postoperative day 3, she developed posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) due to tacrolimus toxicity (levels 9.76 ng/mL), which was resolved after switching the immunosuppressant to cyclosporine. PRES is not a neurological aspect of BBS but rather a consequence of immunosuppression (tacrolimus) or transplantation. Tacrolimus damages the endothelium, which results in cerebral dysregulation and vasogenic oedema. Even at subtherapeutic concentrations, tacrolimus can cause PRES in the early post-renal transplant interval [1]. According to reports, the incidence varies between 0.34% and 5% [9]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Bardet–Biedl syndrome (BBS) is a rare syndrome that necessitates early diagnosis and expert multidisciplinary management. Prenatal diagnosis of BBS can be achieved through ultrasound, foetal MRI, and genetic testing. Parents should receive comprehensive counselling and appropriate guidance regarding the potentially life-threatening systemic complications associated with the syndrome. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: When white matter and atrophy whisper: Adult-onset Alexander disease
clinical_history: A 38-year-old woman presents with a nearly one-year history of progressively worsening dysphagia, dysarthria, and palatal myoclonus. She reports a previous diagnosis of multiple sclerosis; however, no medical documentation is available to confirm this, and there is no record of a prior neurological evaluation. Current clinical findings raise suspicion of involvement of Mollaret’s triangle.
imaging_findings: An axial 3D FLAIR image (Figure 1) reveals confluent, bilateral and symmetrical hyperintensities in the periventricular white matter. A midline sagittal T1-weighted MPRAGE image (Figure 2) shows atrophy of the corpus callosum, frontal lobe, medulla oblongata, cerebellum, and cervical spinal cord. The striking preservation of the midbrain and pons, in contrast to the atrophy of adjacent structures, results in a configuration suggestive of the “tadpole sign” described in Alexander disease. An axial post-contrast T1-weighted MPRAGE image (Figure 3) shows a small, punctate enhancing focus in the white matter adjacent to the left dentate nucleus. An axial T2-weighted TSE image (Figure 4) shows bilateral and symmetrical hyperintense signal in the paramedian medulla oblongata, suggestive of the “chipmunk sign” described in Alexander disease. Bilateral atrophy of the dentate nuclei was noted on axial T1-weighted images (Figure 5), with corresponding perinuclear hyperintensities on 3D FLAIR (Figure 6), consistent with gliotic changes secondary to chronic demyelination.
discussion: Background Alexander disease is a very rare neurodegenerative disorder that typically presents during infancy, although adult-onset forms have also been described. It belongs to the group of leukodystrophies—a set of progressive, genetic metabolic disorders that primarily affect the white matter of the central nervous system (CNS). In Alexander disease, the underlying cause is a mutation in the GFAP gene, which encodes the glial fibrillary acidic protein. This leads to the accumulation of Rosenthal fibres within astrocytes [1]. According to age, symptoms, and imaging, two main forms are recognised: Type I (infantile) : usually presents with macrocephaly, seizures, developmental delay, encephalopathy, and typical MRI features. Type II (later-onset) : associated with bulbar dysfunction, autonomic disturbances, abnormal eye movements, and variable MRI findings. The prevalence is unknown, although a Japanese study estimated it at 1 per 2.7 million individuals [2]. Clinical Perspective From a clinical perspective, adult-onset Alexander disease can mimic other neurologic conditions such as multiple sclerosis or other leukodystrophies, especially in patients with nonspecific brainstem or bulbar symptoms. In this case, the initial clinical suspicion was low, influenced by an inaccurate prior diagnosis of multiple sclerosis without neurologic evaluation or previous confirmatory imaging. The diagnosis was reconsidered only after imaging findings raised the possibility of a leukodystrophic process. This shows the key role of MRI in raising suspicion of this rare entity and prompting genetic testing. Imaging Perspective In our case, only three of the five van der Knaap criteria were met: predominant frontal white matter changes, brainstem abnormalities, and contrast enhancement of the dentate nuclei. Periventricular rim and deep grey matter involvement were absent [3]. This supports previous observations that adult-onset forms may not fulfil the classical MRI criteria, and that infratentorial findings are often more diagnostically relevant in these patients [4,5]. Additional findings include signal changes in the upper cervical cord and medulla, cerebellar peduncles, and the “ventricular garland” sign. The “chipmunk sign” (T2 hyperintensity in the dorsal medulla, pyramids, and central portion of the inferior olivary nuclei, with peripheral hypointensity) and the “tadpole sign” (atrophy of the medulla and cervical cord with pontine sparing) are hallmark features of adult-onset Alexander disease [6,7]. Outcome There is no curative treatment. Management is supportive and multidisciplinary. Prognosis depends on age of onset: the infantile form has a median survival of 14 years; adult-onset forms may progress more slowly, with a median survival of around 25 years [8]. Take Home Message When brainstem atrophy and white matter changes create diagnostic uncertainty, let the “tadpole” and “chipmunk” signs speak—they might whisper Alexander disease. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Atherosclerosis causing giant arc of Riolan and visceral artery aneurysm
clinical_history: A 79-year-old female with no known comorbidities and previous surgical history came with complaints of low back ache and lower abdominal pain, which was on and off for 6 months, with no other significant complaints. Per-abdomen examination revealed a small, minimally mobile, palpable mass in the umbilical region, and the baseline blood investigations were within normal limits.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound of the abdomen showed a peripherally calcified intraperitoneal anechoic structure of size ~ 2.6 x 2.2cm in the right paraumbilical region, which showed pulsating colour flow and arterial waveforms within on colour Doppler (Figures 1a and 1b). A few other dilated intraperitoneal vessels were noted (Figure 1c). CT aortogram revealed an extensive circumferential atherosclerotic wall calcification of the abdominal aorta (Figure 2a) with significant multilevel stenoses and abrupt contrast cut-off in the infrarenal part of the abdominal aorta (Figure 2b). A peripherally calcified, fully opacifying aneurysm is seen arising from the middle colic artery (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c) corresponding to the intraperitoneal pulsatile structure seen in ultrasound. The post-stenotic part of the aorta is reformed by the collateral pathway between the superior mesenteric (SMA) and inferior mesenteric (IMA) arteries called the arc of Riolan (Figures 4a, 4b, 4c, 5a, and 5b), which is dilated and tortuous in course and is seen supplying the bilateral iliac arteries. The post-stenotic part of the aorta and iliac arteries showed reduced contrast opacification in the arterial phase and normal opacification in the venous phase owing to the altered flow dynamics (Figures 6a and 6b).
discussion: Background The arc of Riolan (AoR) is a collateral vessel connecting the branches of SMA and IMA and runs as a loop close to the root of the mesentery [1]. This is a very minute artery, which is difficult to visualise in CECT images under normal circumstances, and thus it is predominantly seen only in 20–30% of the population, with a reported occurrence of 5.5–11.4% [2] in angiography and clinical surgery while in others it can be rudimentary or absent. Dilatation of the AoR primarily occurs as a compensatory mechanism in cases with severe stenosis of major aortic branches like the celiac trunk, SMA and IMA. The most common cause of occlusion is chronic ischemia by atherosclerosis, aortitis, vasculopathies [2], and acute embolism due to atrial fibrillation. Other causes of AoR expansion include colonic tumours to compensate for its increasing vascular demand and ulcerative colitis [3,4]. Clinical Perspective Dilated AoR is usually an incidental finding with no specific symptoms. Patients may present with abdominal pain pertaining to mesenteric ischemia and symptoms specific to other causes, like ulcerative colitis and colonic tumours. Imaging Perspective Although ultrasound can be used as a screening investigation, CT angiography with 3D reconstruction is the investigation of choice [1] for diagnosis and presurgical planning. MR angiography can be done but has limitations due to increased scanning time and motion artifacts due to respiration and bowel peristalsis. DSA is very useful in the endovascular management of the visceral artery aneurysm. The collateral pathway of AoR must be differentiated from the artery of Drummond, which is also a collateral pathway and runs close to the mesentery connecting the branches of SMA and IMA near the splenic flexure. In our case, there was a complete atherosclerotic occlusion of the infrarenal part of the abdominal aorta, and the post-stenotic part was reformed by the dilated AoR and IMA, which supplied blood to the iliac arteries. The probable explanation for the formation of the middle colic artery aneurysm is due to the hyperdynamic flow within. Outcome Endovascular procedures like coil embolisation and stent graft placements is the treatment of visceral artery aneurysms, but due to the difficult approach in these long, tortuous vessels and wider neck aneurysms, open surgical approach is considered [5]. In our case, the patient denied treatment and was discharged against medical advice. Teaching Points The arc of Riolan (AoR) is an important collateral pathway between the superior mesenteric (SMA) and the inferior mesenteric (IMA) arteries. It is a minute and inconspicuous artery, which dilates in cases of stenoses of major aortic branches and mesenteric ischemia. Formation of visceral artery aneurysms occurs due to compensatory high flow dynamics. Identifying the enlarged AoR and knowledge of other collateral pathways is useful for prognostic evaluation of acute and chronic ischemia and in planning for colonic surgeries. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: A pain in the butt
clinical_history: An 82-year-old woman presented with gait impairment, cramping back pain, and numbness. After a negative head CT, unenhanced CT and MR of the column showed vertebral metastases causing medullary stenosis in the D3–D5 segment (Figures 1a and 1b). A whole-body contrast-enhanced CT was requested to search for the primitive lesion.
imaging_findings: CT showed a 7.5 cm oval lesion between liver segments VII and VIII (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d), with inhomogeneous hyperenhancement on the arterial phase, wash-out within the lesion on the portal-venous phase—consistent with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)—, and different components progressively enhancing on the delayed phase. Apart from a slight enlargement of the left lobe and an inhomogeneous enhancement pattern, no signs of chronic liver disease were evident. The diagnosis of probable HCC was made (Figures 1a, 1b, 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d). Concomitantly, a lesion of the left gluteus maximus and gluteus medius muscles was observed (maximum axial diameter of 9.2 cm), though without concomitant areas of altered enhancement, with a non-specific aspect (Figures 3a, 3b, 3c, 3d, and 3e). On these bases, a biopsy was requested to determine whether it was a metachronous lesion of musculoskeletal origin or an undetermined secondary lesion. The final diagnosis was in line with metastasis from HCC.
discussion: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide [1] and is usually diagnosed via contrast-enhanced CT or MR [1]. Biopsy is reserved for dubious cases only. As for our patient, biopsy was unavoidable because of the rarity of musculoskeletal HCC metastases, no history of hepatopathy, and the paucity of clinical history (opening to the possibility of a synchronous tumour). HCC is usually confined to the liver [2]. Extensive disease is more commonly due to peritoneal and nodal invasion, while vascular invasion is generally responsible for extra-abdominal extension. Metastases to the skeleton and muscles are rarely found, and the pathogenesis is still unknown. Muscle metastatic disease is rare, probably due to lactic acid and pulsatile blood flow, which obstruct the rooting of malignant cells [3–6]. The most common tumours metastasising to the skeletal system are from the thyroid, breast, gastrointestinal and urogenital system [7]. Bony lesions from HCC are usually due to vascular spread [8] and cause lysis of the osseous cortex, with secondary involvement of the surrounding skeletal muscles. Our case is challenging due to the absence of osseous involvement adjacent to the gluteal muscle and no arterial hyperenhancement. Our patient did not report any recent trauma, nor did she take anticoagulants, which could suggest a gluteal haematoma. Besides, the lesion lacked basal hyperdensity and was too inhomogeneous to support the hypothesis. A muscle abscess is also unlikely, as no laboratory findings of inflammation were found, and there were no well-marginated lesions with rim-enhancement, central necrosis and inflammatory changes in the surrounding tissues. A soft-tissue tumour was the most probable differential diagnosis: both sarcoma and schwannoma would have required an MR for further characterisation; however, schwannomas tend to be homogeneous single lesions, while sarcomas are aggressive lesions, usually demarcated and heterogeneous, disrupting the surrounding tissues [9]. Neither diagnosis was entirely satisfactory, as in our case, no marginated mass was visible, and the entire muscle was enlarged and inhomogeneous, thus suggesting the presence of more than one lesion. Only pathological examination showed the architectural and immunohistochemical characteristics typical of HCC cells. Due to the high disease burden and unsatisfactory clinical conditions, the patient was deemed unfit for both radiotherapy and systemic treatment and was referred to palliative care. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: A rare case of benign sacral myoepithelioma mimicking a chordoma
clinical_history: A 64-year-old woman, a housewife, presented with chronic dull low back pain persisting for the past year. She had no significant medical or surgical history, nor any history of trauma or malignancy. She reported normal bladder and bowel function and denied any history of night sweats, weight loss, or loss of appetite. Clinical examination revealed no neurological deficits.
imaging_findings: An initial CT scan of the lumbosacral spine revealed a destructive midline lesion of the sacrum with a sclerotic rim, involving the S2–S4 segments, along with an extraosseous soft tissue component extending into the sacral canal (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, 1d, 1e, and 1f). No other significant findings were noted. Subsequent MRI with T1, T2-weighted, and STIR sequences was performed for further characterisation. The lesion appeared slightly hyperintense relative to skeletal muscle on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on fluid-sensitive sequences (T2) (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, 2d, and 2e).
discussion: Background Myoepitheliomas are rare tumours, most commonly arising in the salivary glands. They may be benign or malignant, with the majority being benign [1]. The average age of onset is in the fifth decade, with no apparent gender predilection [1]. While they can occur in a variety of soft tissue sites, intraosseous myoepitheliomas are exceedingly rare. The exact pathophysiology remains unclear but is presumed to originate from myoepithelial cells, which are typically found in the salivary glands. Notably, in this case, there was no prior pathology involving the sacral bone. Clinical Perspective On examination, no swelling or tenderness was noted over the lower back. The history was inconclusive regarding prior trauma. Wide local excision with tumour-free margins remains the treatment of choice [2]. The role of radiotherapy remains controversial [3]. In this case, the patient’s age, sex, clinical history, and imaging findings were nonspecific for myoepithelioma. Differential diagnoses for lytic sacral lesions include primary tumours such as chordoma and chondrosarcoma, benign entities like giant cell tumour (GCT), and metastatic disease. While intraosseous myoepitheliomas are rare, previous literature has reported such lesions in bones outside the head and neck, such as the femur, tibia, phalanges, and iliac bone [1–5,8,9]. These lesions often mimic other entities on imaging, typically presenting as well-defined, expansile lytic lesions. On MRI, they generally appear slightly hyperintense or isointense on T1, and hyperintense on T2 sequences [8,9]. Imaging Perspective Radiologically, intraosseous myoepitheliomas appear as aggressive, expansile lytic lesions. They tend to be slightly hyperintense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on fluid-sensitive sequences [1]. These imaging features overlap significantly with other destructive sacral lesions such as chordoma, GCT, or metastasis [1,4]. Reported cases involving the femur, tibia, radius, phalanges, and ilium consistently demonstrate lytic lesions. However, other imaging characteristics are typically nonspecific, necessitating histopathological examination (HPE) for definitive diagnosis. Immunohistochemically, these tumours commonly express epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), S100 protein, and frequently harbour the EWSR1::PBX3 fusion gene. Sacral chordoma remains the most common primary lesion in the sacrum [5], closely mimicking myoepithelioma on imaging. Hence, histopathological confirmation is crucial. Histologically, myoepitheliomas can resemble their salivary gland counterparts. Microscopy often reveals epithelioid cells, as seen in this case (Figure 3), but may also include spindle cells, clear cells, squamous cells, or plasmacytoid cells [1]. These are embedded in a fibrous, hyaline, myxoid, or myxohyaline stroma. Nuclear atypia is more common in malignant variants [1]. Immunohistochemically, these tumours express cytokeratin (AE1/AE3, CAM5.2, 34βE12, CK5/6, CK7, CK14), smooth muscle actin (SMA), calponin, S100, vimentin, GFAP, and p63 [7]. In this case, the tumour showed diffuse positivity for AE1/AE3 and focal positivity for S100, along with the EWSR1::PBX3 gene fusion. Notably, epithelioid areas in myoepitheliomas can resemble chordomas, adding to the diagnostic challenge [1,4,6,7]. Outcome Given the diagnostic uncertainty on imaging and the possibility of malignancy, wide local excision with tumour-free margins was performed. The top radiological differential was sacral chordoma, but biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of sacral myoepithelioma. This case highlights the challenges in differentiating these entities radiologically due to their similar appearances. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Intraosseous myoepitheliomas are rare, especially in the sacrum. Imaging features often mimic more common lesions like chordoma, GCT, or metastases. Histopathological examination and immunohistochemistry, including molecular testing for EWSR1 fusion genes, are crucial for diagnosis. Clinicians and radiologists should consider myoepithelioma in the differential diagnosis of lytic sacral lesions and pursue biopsy before initiating management.

title: Intrathoracic accessory rib and associated findings
clinical_history: A 51-year-old woman with no past medical or surgical history consulted with 8 months of pain in the dorsal column and left hemithorax, which was exacerbated with mobilisation and improved with rest and analgesics. Physical examination was unremarkable.
imaging_findings: Due to the localisation of the pain, a chest radiograph was performed. It showed a linear, curved and vertical dense opacity, similar to vertebrae opacity, in the left hemithorax superimposed on the hilum and cardiac silhouette (Figures 1a and 1b). An intrathoracic rib was suspected due to its shape and density, so a non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest was performed, which confirmed the presence of a left dorsal accessory rib. This accessory rib originated from the T3 and T4 vertebral bodies, which were fused with an associated fibrous tract at its distal portion. The fibrous tract was contacting the posterior region of the homolateral hemidiaphragm (Figures 2a and 2b), which could explain the symptoms.
discussion: Background Intrathoracic ribs are a very rare congenital anomaly resulting from abnormal rib development and consisting of a normonumerary or supernumerary rib that has an abnormal origin and path within the thoracic cavity. It was first described in 1947 and since then approximately 50 cases have been reported in the literature [1,2]. The aetiology is not clear. Some embryological hypotheses have been formulated to explain the development of an intrathoracic rib, among them it has been postulated that it is due to an incomplete fusion between the caudal and rostral half of the sclerotome, in addition to changes in the intrathoracic pressure in the embryo [3,4]. Clinical Perspective It is usually asymptomatic and is found as an incidental finding in both paediatric and adult populations. Some reported symptoms and signs consist of chest pain, dyspnoea, mass sensation, haemoptysis, pneumothorax and liver injury [4]. In our case, the patient was symptomatic, which led to the performed studies. The finding, such as the proximity to the left diaphragm, could explain the patient’s symptoms. Imaging Perspective Radiography and CT are the imaging modalities of choice in these anomalies. When they present with a typical location and appearance, the diagnosis can be made with a chest radiograph. However, when the location or appearance is atypical or there are doubts, CT is the modality of choice, allowing the determination of the cortical and medullary components, origin and path, as well as to characterise possible associated findings, such as intrathoracic fat or the presence of a fibrous insertion in the diaphragm, which could cause a restrictive ventilatory defect and even pain. In addition, 2D and 3D multiplanar reconstructions allow a better characterisation of an intrathoracic rib [5,6]. Our patient underwent a CT scan that confirmed the diagnosis and showed fusion of vertebral bodies and fibrous tract at the distal end of the rib contacting the posterior region of the homolateral hemidiaphragm (Figures 2a and 2b). Outcome Treatment of intrathoracic rib is generally not necessary due to its natural asymptomatic nature. Patients with symptoms may require management, but the appropriate technique and the success of the procedures performed are unknown. It has even been documented that surgery does not improve respiratory function if it was compromised; however, thoracoscopic interventions have been documented in some cases [4–10]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points It is essential to be aware of this uncommon and innocuous anomaly to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary additional interventions. It should be considered among the differential diagnoses of mediastinal, pulmonary, pleural and chest wall pathology. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
differential_diagnosis: Scimitar syndrome Hilar or mediastinal mass Intrathoracic accessory rib Heterotopic calcification Atelectasis Pleural calcifications

title: The elusive mucocele: A rare presentation
clinical_history: A 48-year-old female presented to the neurosurgery department with a history of headache and diplopia for 6 months. On clinical examination, left VI cranial nerve palsy was noted. The systemic examination and the laboratory findings were within normal limits.
imaging_findings: MRI brain showed a well-defined, expansile lesion in the left sphenoid sinus, which was isointense on T1WI and hyperintense on T2WI (Figures 1a and 1b). The lesion showed no restricted diffusion on DWI or any post-contrast enhancement. The lesion was causing expansion of the sphenoid sinus with remodelling of the sinus wall. It was causing lateral displacement of the left ICA (internal carotid artery) and the left temporal lobe. This lesion was closely abutting the cisternal segment of the left VI cranial nerve and the Dorello’s canal (Figures 2a and 2b). On non-contrast CT, no hyperdensity was seen within the lesion (Figure 3a). On CT angiography, the left ICA canal was dehiscent, and the left ICA was seen coursing through the lesion (Figures 3b and 3c).
discussion: The patient underwent endoscopic transnasal resection of the lesion and was confirmed to be a sphenoid mucocele on histopathological examination (Figures 4a and 4b). Background Mucocele is the accumulation of mucus within the paranasal sinuses, which can lead to erosion of the sinus wall and adjacent structures. It commonly involves the frontal sinus with mucocele of the sphenoid sinus, a rare entity comprising just 1–2% of all cases [1]. Clinical Perspective Headache is the most common symptom, localised to the retroorbital region, with visual symptoms being the second most common presenting complaint, most commonly due to involvement of the optic nerve. Involvement of the III, IV, and VI nerves can cause diplopia due to restriction of ocular movements [2]. Complications include superadded fungal infection, compression of the adjacent structures such as the optic nerve, the cavernous sinus and the II, IV and VI cranial nerves. Imaging Perspective CT shows that mucoceles tend to cause expansion of the affected sphenoid sinus with bony remodelling and displacement of the adjacent structures. CT angiography is useful to look for vascular displacement, particularly to assess the relationship with the ICA, crucial information for endoscopic surgery planning. On MRI, mucoceles appear isointense to hyperintense on T1WI, depending on their protein content, and hyperintense on T2WI. Mucoceles normally do not show restriction of diffusion or post-contrast enhancement. Heavily T2-weighted images are used to demonstrate a relationship with adjacent cranial nerves such as II, III, IV, and VI cranial nerves [3]. Outcome This case emphasises the role of radiological investigations, like MRI, which remains the investigation of choice to diagnose this condition, and CT scan and CT angiography to look for the bony remodelling, vascular involvement and pre-op planning. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Sphenoid sinus mucocele makes up 1–2% of all paranasal sinus mucoceles and has varied presentations. Among symptoms, headache is the most common one, followed by visual complaints. MRI and CT are the imaging modalities of choice for early diagnosis and pre-op planning. Endoscopic transnasal sphenoidotomy is the surgery of choice. Written informed consent from the patient was obtained for publication.

title: Reading between the rings and blooming: Coats plus syndrome
clinical_history: A 31-year-old male with persistent purulent discharge from the site of a right proximal femoral nail implant, placed two years ago following trauma. The patient has a history of developmental delay, including absence of speech since early childhood, and was considered a neglected child with no formal developmental assessments. No recent systemic symptoms. Currently scheduled for orthopaedic implant removal.
imaging_findings: Non-contrast CT revealed symmetrical calcifications in the basal ganglia, thalami, deep cerebellar nuclei, and cortical/subcortical regions of both frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes (Figures 1a and 1b). Multiple cerebral and cerebellar cysts, including porencephalic cysts communicating with lateral ventricles, were present, with the largest cyst (37 × 48 × 26 mm) in the right cerebellum causing mass effect. There was loss of grey-white differentiation and mild ex-vacuo ventricular dilatation. The right globe showed vitreous haemorrhage, retinal calcification, and aphakia/microphakia. MRI showed multiple altered signal cysts in cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres (Figures 2a and 2b), severe thinning of the corpus callosum, periventricular T2/FLAIR hyperintensities (Figures 3a and 3b), and blooming artefacts (suggesting calcifications) on SWI. Ocular findings included posterior vitreous haemorrhage, optic nerve atrophy, and absent right lens (Figure 4). Fundus examination (Figure 5) revealed telangiectatic retinal vessels and extrafoveal exudates, consistent with Coats disease-like changes. These findings, combined with intracranial calcifications and cysts, established the diagnosis of Coats plus syndrome.
discussion: Background Coats plus syndrome (cerebroretinal microangiopathy with calcifications and cysts; CRMCC) is an autosomal recessive disorder marked by retinal telangiectasia, intracranial calcifications, white matter changes, and cystic parenchymal lesions. Mutations in the CTC1 gene and telomere maintenance pathway underlie the pathophysiology [1]. Clinical Perspective Clinically, patients present with neurodevelopmental delay, seizures, visual impairment, and systemic complications (osteopenia, gastrointestinal bleeding) [2]. In this case, persistent orthopaedic infection prompted imaging, revealing features inconsistent with metastatic disease and suggestive of a cerebroretinal microangiopathy. Imaging Perspective Imaging is decisive for diagnosis, especially when genetic confirmation is unavailable. Diagnostic pearls include the triad of symmetrical intracranial calcifications, cysts (including porencephalic), and leukoencephalopathy on CT and MRI [1,3]. Ocular findings such as vitreous haemorrhage and retinal telangiectasia, confirmed on fundus, strongly support Coats plus [2]. MRI with SWI is particularly useful for detecting calcification and cyst walls [3]. Recognition of these features prevents misdiagnosis as metastasis or infectious pathology. Outcome Diagnosis via imaging enables targeted multidisciplinary management, prevents unnecessary oncological/infectious workup, and guides appropriate surgical planning. Prognosis is guarded due to progressive neurological and systemic deterioration [1]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Coats plus syndrome should be considered in young adults with a neuroimaging triad (calcifications, cysts, leukoencephalopathy) and retinal telangiectasia. Advanced MRI techniques aid in differentiating rare microangiopathies from common mimics. Early recognition impacts therapeutic decisions and prevents diagnostic delay [2,3].

title: Retroperitoneal mass as a presentation of a burned-out testicular tumour
clinical_history: A 42-year-old man with a prior appendectomy presented with progressive abdominal pain for 4 weeks, which worsened at night. Initially developed low-grade fever after suspected foodborne illness. No vomiting or diarrhoea. Reported 3–4 kg weight loss. External CT revealed a retroperitoneal mass, prompting referral to our hospital for further evaluation.
imaging_findings: Abdominal CT (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c) revealed a solid-cystic lesion with thickened walls in the left anterior pararenal space, containing internal septa. Fine needle aspiration and drainage catheter placement were performed on the cystic component (Figures 2a and 2b) to rule out infection, alongside core needle biopsy of the solid portion (Figure 2c). The histopathology (not shown) suggested fibrotic mesenchymal proliferation with an inflammatory component (positive IgG4 immunostaining). Due to discordance between imaging findings and pathology, an 18F-FDG PET/CT was obtained (Figures 3a and 3b), showing hypermetabolism in the solid component, with ametabolic, likely necrotic-cystic, changes. A repeated biopsy of the hypermetabolic area (Figure 4) confirmed malignant neoplastic infiltration compatible with germ cell tumour (Figures 5a and 5b). Scrotal ultrasound (Figure 6) identified a poorly defined hypoechoic area, and perineal MRI (Figures 7a, 7b, 7c, and 7d) demonstrated signal alteration with mild diffusion restriction. Left orchiectomy confirmed a burned-out testicular tumour (Figures 8a, 8b, and 8c), and the retroperitoneal lesion was subsequently resected (Figures 9a and 9b).
discussion: Background Testicular cancer is the most common nonhaematologic malignancy in men between 15 and 49 years old [1]. Although this disease is relatively rare, its incidence has more than doubled in the last forty years [2]. The most common route of dissemination is lymphatic, and therefore, the initial presentation may occasionally be a retroperitoneal mass, with testicular imaging not revealing an evident lesion. In such cases, a testicular malignancy should be considered, as the primary tumour may have undergone spontaneous regression (“burned out”), rendering it radiologically inconspicuous or subtle on imaging studies [3]. Clinical Perspective Typical presentations of testicular cancer include a painless mass in the testicle or groin [4]. At initial diagnosis, approximately 20% of patients will have metastatic disease and may present with abdominal or back pain, malaise, or lethargy, which may be an indication of bulky lymphadenopathy in the abdomen or retroperitoneum. Patients with a retroperitoneal mass often present with progressive abdominal pain, weight loss, and systemic symptoms. In these cases, imaging plays a crucial role in differentiating benign, infectious, and malignant causes, guiding biopsy procedures, and assisting in treatment planning. Imaging Perspective In cases of suspected retroperitoneal masses, contrast-enhanced CT is highly valuable for evaluating the lesion characteristics and extent, and for guiding biopsy procedures. Given the frequent lymphatic spread of testicular tumours, it is crucial to perform a scrotal ultrasound in young male patients presenting with retroperitoneal lesions, as these may represent metastases from a primary testicular tumour. Ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality to distinguish intra from extratesticular lesions and is routinely performed prior to orchiectomy. Testicular tumours typically appear as well-defined, hypoechoic masses relative to normal testicular tissue, but can show heterogeneity due to calcifications or cystic changes. Increased vascularity, however, is not specific for malignancy [5]. In cases of burned-out tumours, ultrasound findings can be very subtle or even absent, complicating diagnosis. When ultrasound is inconclusive, MRI can provide additional information. Solid testicular tumours usually demonstrate lower signal intensity on T2-weighted MRI sequences compared to the high signal intensity of normal testicular parenchyma. Nonetheless, the definitive role of MRI as a replacement or complement to ultrasound in testicular tumour evaluation remains to be fully established [6]. Outcome The standard treatment involves radical orchiectomy followed by surgical resection of metastatic retroperitoneal masses when feasible. Depending on the stage and histology, adjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy may be indicated. Imaging is crucial for surgical planning and treatment response monitoring [7]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Retroperitoneal masses in young male patients can be the initial manifestation of metastatic testicular cancer, even when testicular imaging appears normal. Contrast-enhanced CT and scrotal ultrasound are key imaging tools for diagnosis, biopsy guidance, and treatment planning in suspected testicular cancer. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

final_diagnosis: Retroperitoneal seminoma metastatic from a burned-out testicular tumour

title: Combined renal artery and vein recanalisation restores kidney function post-surgery
clinical_history: A 25-year-old woman with metastatic endometrial carcinoma involving the lymph nodes and ovaries underwent hysterectomy and retroperitoneal lymphadenectomy. Postoperatively, she developed deteriorating renal function due to a right ureteral injury, which was initially managed with a double-J catheter. Although her renal function improved, her glomerular filtration rate (GFR) subsequently declined from 86 to 43 ml/min.
imaging_findings: Abdominal computed tomography (CT) imaging revealed proximal occlusion of the left renal artery and thrombosis of the left renal vein (Figures 1a and 1b). Given the necessity for optimal renal function before initiating platinum-based chemotherapy, she was referred for interventional radiology assessment. Digital subtraction angiography confirmed a proximal occlusion of the left renal artery, resulting in significantly reduced renal parenchymal perfusion. Additionally, venous-phase imaging demonstrated extensive thrombosis of the left renal vein with evidence of collateral circulation.
discussion: Revascularisation was performed via a multi-modal approach (Figure 2): A guidewire was advanced across the arterial occlusion, restoring partial arterial perfusion. Intra-arterial alteplase (10 mg) was administered for thrombolysis. Mechanical venous thrombectomy was performed using the AngioJet system, significantly improving venous outflow. A 6 x 17 mm bare-metal stent was deployed in the proximal left renal artery, achieving full arterial perfusion. The patient was placed on anticoagulation therapy and dual antiplatelet therapy for four weeks, followed by lifelong aspirin. This case illustrates a successful endovascular approach for managing postsurgical renal artery and vein occlusions in a cancer patient. Early intervention with combined thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy, and stenting facilitated the restoration of renal function. While previous case reports and small studies have discussed venous thrombectomy or lysis [1], and arterial stenting [2,3] individually, the combined treatment approach, particularly applying lysis through the artery to revascularise the vein, has not been reported before in acute kidney failure. However, the integration of these techniques is crucial in preventing ischemic nephropathy and maintaining renal function in patients requiring nephrotoxic chemotherapeutic agents [4]. Additionally, consideration of arterial inflow is crucial, as patients with thrombosis and compromised inflow (e.g., arterial dissection, stenosis, or occlusion) are at higher risk of early re-thrombosis in the venous drainage. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Endovascular intervention offers a minimally invasive solution for complex renal vascular obstructions. A combination of thrombolysis and thrombectomy can significantly enhance venous drainage in thrombosed renal veins. Early revascularisation is critical in preserving renal function, particularly in oncology patients requiring nephrotoxic therapy. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Left adrenal infarction post Hartmann’s procedure
clinical_history: A 66-year-old female presented with left iliac fossa pain. A CT abdomen/pelvis (portal venous phase contrast) was performed, which diagnosed sigmoid diverticulitis with localised perforation and involvement of the left fallopian tube. A Hartmann’s procedure and left salpingectomy were performed. Seven days later, a follow-up CT abdomen/pelvis (portal venous phase contrast) was performed.
imaging_findings: The initial contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed sigmoid diverticulitis with localised perforation and involvement of the left fallopian tube. Adrenal glands were of normal size and morphology (Figure 1). The patient subsequently underwent Hartmann’s procedure and left salpingectomy. A second enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis performed seven days postoperatively showed a collection in the pelvis at the site of previous surgery. The adrenal glands were bilaterally enlarged with peri-adrenal fat stranding and subtle hypoattenuation, left more so than the right (Figures 2a and 2b). A follow-up contrast-enhanced MRI of the adrenals was performed two days after the latest CT scan (i.e., nine days postoperatively), which showed only peripheral enhancement of the enlarged left adrenal gland and no enhancement of the bulk of the gland. The right adrenal gland was enlarged but enhancing normally (Figures 3a and 3b).
discussion: Adrenal infarction is a rare but serious complication that can occur in the context of severe systemic illness, including septic states and major abdominal surgery. Increased arterial inflow—typically due to stress, surgery, or systemic illness—overwhelms the adrenal gland’s limited venous drainage. Each adrenal gland is supplied by three arteries (the superior, middle, and inferior adrenal arteries), but drained by a single central vein, creating a predisposition to venous stasis. This imbalance leads to glandular enlargement, interstitial oedema, and rising intraglandular pressure. This state can be termed “adrenal congestion”. If sustained, it can compromise perfusion and result in adrenal infarction, or if vascular rupture occurs, it leads to adrenal haemorrhage. There are few case reports of adrenal haemorrhage or infarction with imaging findings in the literature. Cases of bilateral adrenal infarction and haemorrhage have been reported in patients with hypercoagulable states such as antiphospholipid syndrome, with imaging findings including asymmetric gland enlargement, hypoattenuation, and periadrenal fat stranding on CT [1]. Dual-energy CT studies have further demonstrated perfusion deficits in bilateral adrenal infarction, highlighting its utility in evaluating adrenal vascular compromise [2]. Adrenal congestion—manifested as gland enlargement and peri-adrenal fat stranding on CT—can precede infarction or haemorrhage, indicating a pathophysiological progression from venous stasis to ischemia and vascular rupture [3]. Recognition of these imaging patterns is critical in at-risk populations, as bilateral involvement may precipitate life-threatening adrenal insufficiency requiring urgent corticosteroid therapy. Not all cases of adrenal infarction lead to adrenal insufficiency as in the case of our patient, who was discharged home, as they have no clinical signs or biochemical parameters to suggest adrenal insufficiency. The changes in our patient’s right adrenal could possibly be attributed to adrenal congestion with no subsequent infarction or haemorrhage. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: A rare cause of hypoglossal palsy
clinical_history: A 64-year-old man diagnosed with metastatic colorectal cancer, treated with chemotherapy (FOLFIRINOX and bevacizumab), presented with dysarthria and dysphagia 72 hours following the placement of a central venous catheter (CVC) through the right subclavian vein under ultrasound guidance at another hospital. On physical examination, right tongue weakness and right-side tongue deviation on protrusion were noticed.
imaging_findings: A plain CT of the neck (Figures 1a and 1b) revealed the misplacement of a CVC, whose tip was in the proximal cervical segment of the right internal jugular vein (IJV). The patient underwent removal of the previous CVC on the right side (Figure 2a) and positioning of a new CVC on the left side (Figure 2b). The MRI performed after the removal of the CVC demonstrated extensive thrombosis of the right IJV up to the jugular foramen, while the right sigmoid and the transverse dural venous sinuses remain patent (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c); no thickening or pathological enhancement along the cisternal or intracanal path of the XIIth right cranial nerve was observed (Figures 3b and 3c). Intense enhancement is observed along the wall of the IJV, reflecting thrombophlebitis (Figure 4). Indirect signs of right hemitongue paresis were observed: high signal intensity on T2-weighted images (Figure 5a and 5b), enhancement following the administration of gadolinium (Figure 5c), and the posterior protrusion of the tongue base in the supine position (Figures 5b and 5c).
discussion: Central venous catheters (CVCs) are commonly used in oncologic patients to provide safe and efficient administration of long-term chemotherapy. Real-time ultrasound guidance is often the standard procedure for central venous access [1]. Ultrasound facilitates the CVC insertion into the appropriate vessel, having, however, limited value in confirming the optimal CVC tip position into the superior vena cava [2,3]. Therefore, CVC malposition may still occur, which increases the risks of catheter dysfunction, local venous thrombosis, vessel wall perforation, and cranial retrograde injection [4]. The subclavian or left-sided venous approach proved to be more prone to CVC misplacement, as it requires navigating around corners [5]. Cranial nerve injury following CVC insertion is an extremely rare complication reported in the literature [6]. In our case, the patient presented hypoglossal nerve palsy, which was assumed to be iatrogenic, caused as a consequence of the CVC mispositioning in the proximal part of IJV or secondary to the inflammatory process of thrombophlebitis at the level of the post-styloid compartment. After catheter removal, the patient underwent treatment with antibiotics and heparin, with only partial recovery of the cranial nerve deficit. The hypoglossal nerve provides motor innervation to both the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue (except for the palatoglossus). Clinical manifestations of hypoglossal palsy include ipsilateral tongue deviation, dysarthria, and dysphagia [7]. MRI is particularly useful in assessing tongue denervation changes, which are time-dependent to the initial insult. In the acute/subacute phase, due to the increased interstitial water content, the affected tongue side appears hypointense on T1-weighted and hyperintense on T2-weighted, presenting an increased contrast uptake. In the chronic phase, there is volume loss of the affected tongue side, with progressive fatty infiltration resulting in high signal intensity on both T1 and T2 and mild to no enhancement [8]. Another important differential diagnosis for unilateral hypoglossal nerve palsy, which should be taken into consideration in our patient given his oncologic context, is bone metastasis in the skull base that would encompass the hypoglossal canal or second primary tumour with perineural spread, both excluded in our case [7]. Teaching Points International guidelines recommend that CVC placement should be confirmed with a chest X-ray after each catheterisation before treatment administration, even if ultrasound guidance is used [9]. If new neurological symptoms ensue after a CVC placement, imaging with CT or MRI is advised to assess its location and identify potential complications [5]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Intravascular leiomyomatosis causing right heart dysfunction
clinical_history: A previously healthy 52-year-old female with a two-day history of severe, persistent dyspnoea on exertion and chest pain. She denied any infectious symptoms. A pulmonary embolism was suspected.
imaging_findings: Initial work-up with a CT pulmonary angiogram (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c) revealed what was initially thought to be a large saddle embolus with extension through the right heart and into the inferior vena cava (IVC). Marked enlargement of the pulmonary trunk, flattening of the intraventricular septum, and an elevated RV:LV ratio of 1.5 (Figure 1b) indicated right heart dysfunction. Bilateral lower extremity ultrasounds for deep venous thrombosis (DVT) were negative. To further characterise the extent of filling defect, a CT abdomen/pelvis was performed, which demonstrated thrombus enhancement in the IVC (Figures 2a and 2c), indicating the filling defect was composed of soft tissue, rather than clot. The confluent linear filling defect extended through to the distal right gonadal vein (Figure 2d), raising suspicion for a pelvic source. Multiple large uterine fibroids were noted and further assessed with a pelvic MRI (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c). No other intra-abdominal malignancy was present, giving us the presumptive diagnosis of intravenous fibroid. A transoesophageal echocardiogram was used to further understand the extent of the intracardiac mass for presurgical planning (Figures 4a and 4b). A repeat CT pulmonary angiogram (Figure 5) demonstrated no interval change in the filling defect despite anticoagulation. The diagnosis of intravenous leiomyomatosis extending into the right heart and pulmonary trunk was confirmed by pathology following surgical excision.
discussion: Background Intravascular leiomyomatosis (IVL) is a rare, benign variant of uterine leiomyoma characterised by the proliferation of smooth muscle cells within venous walls. Although this tumour is benign, it can show aggressive behaviour by extending intraluminally from the pelvic veins through the inferior vena cava and potentially into the right heart [1]. Although the mass usually does not invade the walls of the vessels, these intravascular fibroids can be firmly fixed to the wall [2]. The presentation of IVL varies with the extent and size of the tumour thrombus; a particularly life-threatening form is intracardiac leiomyomatosis. Occurring in 10% to 30% of IVL cases, this tumour within the heart carries a high risk of mortality, particularly once the tumour crosses the tricuspid valve, causing outflow tract obstruction, cor pulmonale, and pulmonary oedema. Further progression into the pulmonary arteries results in the same symptoms of standard pulmonary embolism, as seen in this case [3,4]. Clinical Perspective Intravenous leiomyomatosis presents with a wide range of symptoms depending on the site of involvement, from asymptomatic cases to abdominal pain, irregular bleeding, pelvic mass, lower extremity swelling, ascites, and hepatosplenomegaly. The most common symptoms associated with intracardiac leiomyomatosis are dyspnoea on exertion, shortness of breath, orthopnoea or syncope [3]. Imaging Perspective CT pulmonary angiogram is the most common test used to diagnose intrathoracic vascular filling defects within the pulmonary trunk and cardiac chambers. Contrast-enhanced gated cardiac CT and echocardiogram are helpful adjunctive modalities. Differentiation between tumour thrombus and standard blood clot is confirmed by visualising enhancement within the thrombus on contrast images and unchanged thrombus morphology (size and shape) after long-term anticoagulation [5]. The most common tumours to form tumour thrombus are renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and adrenal cortical carcinomas. Outcome Complete surgical resection remains the most effective treatment, offering the highest chance of cure. When resection is incomplete, the risk of recurrence can be as high as 33% [3]. Long-term imaging follow-up is essential due to the high risk of recurrence. Furthermore, given that IVL is a hormone-dependent tumour, antioestrogen therapy can be additionally helpful against recurrence [6,7]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Intravenous leiomyomatosis (IVL) is a rare yet potentially life-threatening condition that can lead to right heart dysfunction, pulmonary artery obstruction, and significant morbidity if left untreated. Early recognition via advanced imaging techniques is critical for diagnosis, and immediate surgical resection remains the most effective treatment.

title: CT imaging diagnosis of partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage
clinical_history: A 43-year-old woman with a clinical history of symptomatic sick sinus syndrome and recurrent syncope underwent dual-chamber pacemaker implantation. Subsequently, she began experiencing exertional chest pain and dizziness. An echocardiogram (ECG) was therefore performed, which revealed right ventricular enlargement and raised suspicion for multiple anomalous pulmonary venous connections. Given these findings and her symptoms, further assessment was indicated to evaluate for possible coronary involvement and the presence of a significant left-to-right shunt, leading to the decision to proceed with a CT scan.
imaging_findings: The imaging protocol consisted of a dedicated cardiac computed tomography angiography (CTA) tailored for mapping the pulmonary venous system. Following a whole-chest topogram, a biphasic contrast protocol was administered, with timing optimised via a test bolus in the left atrium. A single, high-pitch ECG-gated acquisition was performed to cover the entire thorax, ensuring visualisation of any potential anomalous drainage pathways. From the acquired data, multiplanar and 3D volume-rendered reconstructions were created to precisely delineate the venous anatomy and its connection to the cardiac chambers. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrates convergence of the left superior pulmonary veins, forming a vertical vein that ascends adjacent to the aortic arch and drains into the left brachiocephalic (innominate) vein, consistent with partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (PAPVD) (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, 2, and 3). The remaining pulmonary veins show normal drainage into the left atrium (Figure 4). The right atrium is enlarged, and the atrial septum appears thin, likely membranous, and bulging (Figure 5). Right atrial enlargement is consistent with a volume overload state secondary to the left-to-right shunt. The atrioventricular connections are normal, and there is no evidence of pulmonary embolism, pericardial effusion, or pleural effusion. Coronary arteries are unremarkable. No features of scimitar syndrome are present, and lung parenchyma and perfusion are preserved.
discussion: Background Partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (PAPVD) is a rare congenital cardiovascular anomaly where one or more (but not all) pulmonary veins drain into the right atrium or systemic venous system instead of the left atrium. This creates a left-to-right shunt, potentially leading to right heart enlargement and pulmonary hypertension over time. The pathophysiology involves abnormal embryologic development of pulmonary venous connections, resulting in partial mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood [1]. The incidence is 0.4%–0.7% and is associated with sinus venosus atrial septal defect (ASD)[2]. Clinical Perspective PAPVD often presents with non-specific symptoms or may be asymptomatic, especially in isolated cases. When symptomatic, patients may report exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, or palpitations. Clinical suspicion often arises in the context of unexplained right heart enlargement or pulmonary hypertension [3]. Imaging is essential because physical findings and basic tests (like ECG or chest X-ray) are often non-specific. The key clinical problem is to identify the anomalous venous drainage and quantify the shunt, as this has implications for management and prognosis. Imaging Perspective The definitive diagnosis of PAPVD often relies on a multimodal imaging approach, particularly when echocardiographic findings are ambiguous. Cardiac CT is highly effective for anatomical characterisation, providing unparalleled spatial resolution to map the number and course of pulmonary veins and identify their anomalous drainage sites [4]. However, to fully evaluate the condition’s haemodynamic impact, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (cardiac MRI) is indispensable. By utilising phase-contrast sequences, cardiac MRI allows for precise, non-invasive quantification of the left-to-right shunt volume. This measurement is crucial for clinical decision-making, as the magnitude of the shunt is a primary determinant for surgical intervention [5]. Therefore, the diagnostic strength lies in using CT for its anatomical clarity and cardiac MRI for the essential functional data required for patient management. Outcome Therapeutic options depend on the degree of shunt and symptoms. Asymptomatic patients with small shunts may only require monitoring. Symptomatic patients, or those with significant left-to-right shunt or pulmonary hypertension, may need surgical correction. Imaging findings directly impact therapy planning by identifying candidates for surgery and guiding the surgical approach. Prognosis is generally good if PAPVD is recognised and treated before irreversible pulmonary vascular damage ensues. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (PAPVD) should be considered in cases of unexplained right heart enlargement or pulmonary hypertension. Cardiac CT is a key diagnostic tool, allowing precise mapping of anomalous pulmonary veins and guiding management. Early recognition and accurate imaging are crucial for optimal outcomes, as timely intervention can prevent long-term complications. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
