title: Cement leakage into pulmonary and intracardiac circulation after percutaneous vertebroplasty
clinical_history: A 51-year-old female patient underwent elective computed tomography (CT) enterography for persistent abdominal pain and suspected segmental mural thickening of the small bowel. Her medical history included L4–L5 percutaneous vertebroplasty ten years before, in 2015, performed for a compressive disc herniation with associated radiculopathy. She was asymptomatic and had no known cardiopulmonary disease.
imaging_findings: CT enterography was performed utilising volumetric acquisition before and after intravenous contrast administration, encompassing enteric and portal venous phases, with multiplanar reconstructions. Imaging revealed the presence of orthopaedic hardware at the L4 and L5 vertebral bodies, comprising bilateral transpedicular fixation screws and hyperdense material consistent with polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) cement, in accordance with the patient’s prior percutaneous vertebroplasty. Notably, there was clear evidence of cement extravasation extending into the adjacent lumbar venous plexuses (Figures 1a and 1b). Further detailed evaluation of the lower pulmonary fields revealed multiple discrete hyperdense foci bilaterally within the subsegmental pulmonary arterial branches, compatible with pulmonary cement embolism (PCE) (Figures 2a and 2b). Additionally, a similar small hyperattenuating residue was detected within the right ventricle, strongly indicative of an iatrogenic intracardiac cement embolus (ICE) (Figures 3a and 3b). Retrospective evaluation of available prior imaging studies from 2012 and 2008 (pre-vertebroplasty) showed no hyperdense material, lending further support to the diagnosis.
discussion: Background Percutaneous vertebroplasty (PV) is a minimally invasive procedure widely used for the treatment of painful vertebral compression fractures, most frequently secondary to osteoporosis or metastatic disease. The technique involves the injection of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) cement into the vertebral body under fluoroscopic or CT guidance. Cement leakage is a well-recognised complication of PV. In rare cases, PMMA may migrate into the venous system, potentially leading to pulmonary cement embolism (PCE) or, more rarely and severely, intracardiac cement embolism (ICE) [1–3]. The underlying mechanism involves extravasation of cement into the paravertebral venous system during injection, which may allow access to the azygos system, inferior vena cava and ultimately the right heart and pulmonary vasculature. Recognised risk factors include low cement viscosity, high injection pressure, and disruption of the vertebral cortical wall [1,2,4]. Clinical Perspective Fortunately, most cases of PCEs and even ICEs are asymptomatic, often being discovered incidentally on imaging, as in this case. However, symptomatic presentations may occur and include dyspnoea, chest pain, arrhythmias, haemodynamic instability, or even cardiac arrest. The diagnosis should be considered, particularly when such symptoms emerge immediately after the vertebroplasty procedure [1–3]. Imaging Perspective CT remains the modality of choice for definitive diagnosis, typically revealing high-density linear or tubular opacities (>1000 HU) within the pulmonary arteries or right heart chambers [1,3]. Echocardiography may provide complementary information, particularly regarding the precise localisation of the embolus and its potential impact on cardiac function. This is especially relevant in cases involving cement fragments larger than 10 mm, which have been associated with an increased risk of cardiac perforation and tamponade [2–4]. Outcome Currently, there are no standardised treatment guidelines. Most studies recommend a conservative approach for asymptomatic patients or those with mild symptoms. Conversely, in patients presenting with severe symptoms, haemodynamically unstable conditions, or a high risk of complications, interventional or surgical removal may be the treatment of choice. The role of anticoagulation remains controversial but may be considered to prevent thrombus formation on the cement fragment by facilitating encapsulation [1–3]. Teaching Points This case illustrates a rare presentation of concurrent asymptomatic pulmonary and intracardiac cement embolism, incidentally diagnosed years after vertebroplasty. It underscores the importance of a systematic evaluation of all included anatomical structures in cross-sectional imaging, even when not directly related to the clinical suspicion, and reaffirms the need for long-term vigilance in patients with a history of cement augmentation procedures, as it consolidates the recognition of potentially delayed complications. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Atretic parietal cephalocele in a one-year-old child
clinical_history: A 12-month-old male presented with a 1 cm alopecic, soft, mid-parietal scalp swelling present at birth. The lesion was not associated with seizures, developmental delay, or neurological deficits. Apart from this lesion, the antenatal and perinatal courses were unremarkable.
imaging_findings: Soft tissue ultrasound demonstrated a well‑circumscribed, ovoid, predominantly hypoechoic subcutaneous nodule measuring 11 × 5 mm over the mid-parietal region (Figure 1a). Colour Doppler showed no internal vascularity (Figure 1b). A narrow hypoechoic fibrous tract was visualised traversing a focal cortical discontinuity, compatible with a small calvarial defect and intracranial dural attachment. MRI revealed a T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense lesion, connected to the dura by a fibrous stalk (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d). Contrast-enhanced study depicted a persistent falcine sinus contiguous with the lesion (Figures 3a and 3b). No hydrocephalus or cortical malformations were identified.
discussion: Background Atretic cephaloceles (ACs) are rudimentary, skin-covered lesions composed of fibrous tissue, meninges, and sometimes glial rests [1]. Cephaloceles occur in approximately 1 per 10,000 live births [2]. Atretic cephaloceles comprise 4–17% of all cephaloceles, and parietal ACs account for 40–50% of ACs [3]. These lesions often overlie a fenestrated superior sagittal sinus [4]. Clinical Perspective Lesions usually present as small, alopecic scalp masses detected in infancy. Their size can transiently increase with Valsalva or crying. Neurological examination is typically normal, but ACs are frequently associated with intracranial venous anomalies such as persistent falcine or fenestrated superior sagittal sinus, which may influence surgical planning [1]. Imaging Perspective Soft-tissue ultrasound depicts a small, alopecic, ovoid, predominantly hypoechoic subcutaneous mass in the parietal midline with sharply defined margins. In our case, no flow was seen on Doppler, likely due to compression of the lesion. Generous use of gel with minimal transducer pressure may enable visualisation of flow within the stalk. Complementary MRI characterises the nodule as iso to hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, confirms that no functional cortical tissue is herniated, and clearly delineates the fibrous stalk as it inserts into the dura. After gadolinium administration, high‑resolution 3D T1-weighted sequences highlight venous variants—such as fenestration of the superior sagittal sinus or a persistent falcine sinus [5]. Outcome The child is currently being observed with periodic clinical and imaging follow-up. He remains neurologically intact, and the scalp nodule has shown no interval growth. Surgical excision—including removal of the fibrous stalk and closure of the dural attachment—may be indicated in the future for cosmetic reasons or if clinical symptoms arise, such as pain resulting from stretching of the underlying dura or progressive skin changes [6]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Small alopecic parietal scalp nodules in infants should raise suspicion for atretic cephalocele (AC). MRI is essential to characterise the lesion and delineate venous anatomy. Surgical excision is curative, but awareness of associated venous variants avoids intraoperative haemorrhage. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Unilateral tensor fascia lata hypertrophy mimicking a soft tissue tumour
clinical_history: A lady in her 60s who had a left anterolateral proximal thigh painless swelling over the past 2 years, presented to our service complaining of left hip pain over the past few weeks. No history of trauma or previous orthopaedic surgery was mentioned. History of bilateral hip osteoarthritis with chronic hip pain for the last 4 years. Upon physical examination, the referring physician found a left anterolateral proximal thigh non-tender mass lesion with normal overlying skin. No neurological complaint, i.e., lumbar pain or limb paraesthesia. A tumoural lesion was suspected, and imaging investigations were requested.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound shows a diffusely enlarged left tensor fascia lata (TFL) muscle manifested by an increase in its anteroposterior (AP) diameter, measuring about 30 mm at the left, compared to 13 mm at the right, with preserved muscle and fascial echopattern (Figures 1a and 1b). No mass lesions were identified. Doppler imaging showed no specific vascular pattern (images not included). Unenhanced pelvic MR scan revealed asymmetrical tensor fascia latae muscles with hypertrophied left side showing preserved fascial planes and no focal muscle lesions or localised fluid collections (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, 2d, and 2e). No local mass effects are exerted on the surrounding soft tissue. A note is made of an atrophied left gluteus minimus as well, with decreased muscle bulk and intramuscular high T1 signal, in keeping with fatty degeneration of the muscle. As an asymmetrical enlarged muscle with intact muscle configuration and fascial planes with no definite focal cystic or solid mass lesion, distorting its fibres, a radiological diagnosis of isolated pseudotumour (hypertrophy) of the left tensor fascia lata muscle was made.
discussion: Background Muscle hypertrophy is recognised as an increase in muscle volume with an increased number and size of its fibres. However, in pseudohypertrophy, an increase in volume happens due to the infiltration of the muscle by fat and connective tissue in between muscle fibres rather than affecting muscle fibres per se [1]. Unilateral compensatory hypertrophy of the TFL muscle is an uncommon clinical entity that has been sporadically reported in the literature [2]. It is defined as an enlargement of the tensor fascia lata with pathological changes in the gluteus muscles (minimus and/or medius), like muscle tears or atrophy [3]. Pseudotumour of the tensor fascia lata is explained by either denervational or mechanical aetiologies. TFL hypertrophy can be seen in patients following hip surgery or advanced hip degenerative disease with altered hip biomechanics [4]. In our case, left gluteus minimus atrophy secondary to hip osteoarthritis is considered the cause of left side THL compensatory hypertrophy of the same side. Clinical Perspective The pain is not a common presenting symptom of THL hypertrophy, unless it is secondary to a previous total hip replacement. A painless anterolateral thigh mass is the most common presentation, in keeping with our case [5]. The general differential diagnosis of thigh mass includes malignancy (such as sarcoma) versus other benign lesions (like lipoma, focal lipomatosis or abscess). TFL hypertrophy presentation, as progressively increasing mass, is considered a soft tissue sarcoma mimicker, which necessitates invasive tissue biopsy to differentiate. Imaging Perspective MRI is the imaging modality of choice as it helps in confirming the muscle hypertrophy with preserved muscle configuration, depicting intramuscular fat and connective tissue infiltration, thus differentiating muscle hypertrophy from pseudohypertrophy, as well as excluding other causes [5] with an absence of any focal mass lesion or loculated collection. Ultrasound (US) also plays a valuable role in corroborating the diagnosis, as a noninvasive real-time diagnostic tool, along with electromyography [4]. Using US and MRI imaging modalities to diagnose THL hypertrophy almost eliminates the need for invasive procedures such as tissue biopsy to exclude soft tissue sarcoma. Outcome The treatment of TFL usually involves hip physiotherapy to strengthen the hip abductors, and local botulinum toxin injections may also be beneficial, by eliminating symptoms and decreasing the size of the TFL [6]. We are reporting this rare case of compensatory hypertrophy following gluteus minimus atrophy and chronic tear of the gluteus muscles. After MRI and US diagnosis neither biopsy nor surgical intervention were required. The patient was reassured by the treating physician and is currently undergoing physiotherapy. Teaching Points Unilateral tensor fascia lata hypertrophy is a rare entity that clinically mimics soft tissue tumours. Patients may present with a painless swelling in the anterolateral proximal thigh area, which may clinically raise the suspicion of soft tissue malignant lesions (sarcoma) among other differential diagnoses. Non-invasive US and MRI imaging features help reach the correct diagnosis and avoid the need for invasive tissue biopsy. Although TFL hypertrophy is a rare entity, clinicians should consider it at the differential diagnosis of anterolateral upper thigh painless masses. With the use of US and MRI as non-invasive tools, they can reach the correct diagnosis. Take Home Message Isolated hypertrophy or pseudohypertrophy of the tensor fascia lata is a rare benign condition that may mimic a soft tissue tumour. Awareness of this entity and appropriate imaging can prevent misdiagnosis and avoid unnecessary biopsy or surgery.

title: Primary nasopharyngeal Burkitt’s lymphoma in a child
clinical_history: A 9-year-old boy with a 6-month history of nasal obstruction, epistaxis, right facial swelling, nocturnal snoring, and mild right ocular proptosis. Physical examination revealed cervical lymphadenopathy, bilateral seromucous otitis and unexplained weight loss. HIV serology was negative. The lumbar puncture and bone marrow biopsy showed no evidence of tumour invasion. The complete blood count and standard biochemistry panel did not reveal any significant abnormalities.
imaging_findings: MRI revealed a 77 × 54 × 67 mm homogeneous nasopharyngeal mass with intermediate T2 signal and marked diffusion restriction (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c). The lesion extended into the right nasal cavity, maxillary sinus (with posterior wall lysis), pterygopalatine fossa, pterygoid muscles, parapharyngeal fat, sphenoid sinus, ethmoid cells, extraconical intraorbital fat, orbital apex, and right foramen ovale. Homogeneous gadolinium enhancement was observed (Figure 2). Cervical lymphadenopathy was present. The extension work-up with cervical/thoracic/abdominopelvic CT confirmed bone involvement adjacent to the cervical mass without distant metastases (Figures 4a, 4b, 4c, and 4d). A CT-guided biopsy of the cervical mass confirmed Burkitt’s lymphoma. The disease was therefore staged as Ann Arbor stage IB.
discussion: Background Burkitt’s lymphoma (BL) is a high-grade B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with rapid growth and high proliferation index [1,2]. It is the most common malignant lymphoma in children (35–45% of paediatric lymphomas) but is rare in the nasopharynx [3,4]. Three clinical forms exist: endemic (Epstein–Barr virus-related, Africa), sporadic (Western countries), and HIV-associated [5]. Clinical Perspective Nasopharyngeal BL presents with non-specific symptoms—nasal obstruction, epistaxis, facial swelling—often mimicking nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). Early imaging is crucial due to its rapid progression and therapeutic urgency [6,7]. The prognosis for patients with BL is generally favourable, with a reported 5-year overall survival rate of 80–90% [7]. Imaging Perspective On MRI, BL typically appears as a symmetrical, homogeneous mass with intermediate T1/T2 signal, strong gadolinium enhancement, and low ADC values due to hypercellularity. These features help distinguish it from NPC, which is often asymmetric, less homogeneous, and has higher ADC values, or from parameningeal rhabdomyosarcoma, which shows more necrosis, heterogeneous enhancement, and minimal lymphadenopathy [7–9]. Outcome The patient received multi-agent chemotherapy (COP, COPADM, CYM). Follow-up MRI showed residual fibroinflammatory tissue. Clinical improvement and lymph node regression were noted, despite treatment complications (medullary aplasia, febrile neutropenia). Take Home Message / Teaching Points Consider Burkitt’s lymphoma (BL) in paediatric nasopharyngeal masses with homogeneous enhancement, low ADC, and Waldeyer’s ring involvement. MRI is essential for assessing tumour extent and differentiating from nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) and rhabdomyosarcoma. Prompt histopathological confirmation is critical to initiate urgent chemotherapy.

title: Intraureteral toothpick foreign body: A rare migration case
clinical_history: A 34-year-old male presented with 3 months of right flank pain. No haematuria or urinary symptoms. Physical examination revealed right costovertebral angle tenderness.
imaging_findings: Non-contrast abdominal CT showed a linear hyperdensity (13 × 17 mm, ~40 HU) in the distal right ureter (Figure 1). The object exhibited smooth margins without calcification. Ureteroscopy confirmed an elongated foreign body, later extracted intact via forceps.
discussion: Background Ureteral foreign bodies are exceptionally rare, typically resulting from iatrogenic causes or migration from adjacent organs [1]. Retrograde migration from the bladder through the ureteral orifice is a recognised but uncommon mechanism, facilitated by object morphology. Clinical Perspective Flank pain mimicking ureteric colic is the primary symptom. Imaging is critical to differentiate from ureteral stones or tumours, especially when the history is unclear. Prompt identification prevents complications like obstruction or perforation. Imaging Perspective Absence of calcification in elongated objects should raise suspicion for organic foreign bodies. Key diagnostic clues on CT are linear hyperdensities (HU < 100), that distinguishes it from calculi. Endoscopy is the gold standard for confirmation and retrieval. Outcome Endoscopic removal is the first-line treatment, with a success rate > 90% [2]. Open surgery is reserved for embedded objects. Prognosis is excellent post-removal, with symptom resolution as in this case (removal of an intraureteral bamboo toothpick foreign body). Take Home Message Consider a foreign body in atypical “stone” cases with low HU density. Object shape enables retrograde ureteral migration. Endoscopy achieves definitive diagnosis/therapy.
differential_diagnosis: Intraureteral foreign body Ureteral calculus Urothelial carcinoma Blood clot

title: Atlanto-occipital assimilation with isolated abducens palsy: A rare stroke pathway
clinical_history: A 22-year-old woman began her illness after a nap with complete paralysis of the right abducens nerve. No other signs or symptoms were present.
imaging_findings: Magnetic diffusion-weighted imaging in B=1000 demonstrated an acute ischemic stroke in the right pons at the level of the right sixth cranial nerve nucleus. Angiographic sequences revealed an aberrant bone channel of the right vertebral artery in its V3 segment. Complementary CT angiography of the atlanto-occipital assimilation, which formed an irregular osseous canal through which the right vertebral artery passed, compressing it. This led to an embolic event that resulted in pontine ischemia. Other causes were excluded.
discussion: Background Atlanto-occipital assimilation is the most common developmental anomaly of the craniocervical junction [1], affecting (0.08–2.8%) of the population [2]. It is characterised by partial or complete fusion of the atlas with the occipital condyles due to segmentation failure between the caudal occipital and cranial cervical sclerotomes [3]. Clinical Perspective Clinical manifestations usually begin in early adulthood and are often associated with atlantoaxial instability, presenting with headache, neck pain, weakness, or ataxia. In some cases, symptoms result from stenosis or haemodynamic alterations in the vertebrobasilar system [4,8]. Imaging Perspective CT angiography enables accurate vascular characterisation through multiplanar and 3D reconstructions, allowing visualisation of complete or incomplete fusion between the atlas and occipital condyles. Aberrant osseous canals may form, through which the vertebral arteries pass [3]. Four vertebral artery courses have been described [5]: Type 1: The vertebral artery enters the spinal canal below the posterior arch of C1 and courses beneath the occipitalised lateral mass of C1. Type 2: The vertebral artery enters below the posterior arch of C1 and courses along or curves over the posterior surface of the occipitalised lateral mass of C1. Type 3: The vertebral artery ascends externally and laterally after leaving the transverse foramen of the axis, enters a bony foramen formed between the atlas and the occipital bone, and then proceeds into the cranial cavity. This is the most frequent type and is strongly associated with vascular complications or dissection. Type 4: Absence of the vertebral artery. Outcome In type 3 anomalies, the osseous canal often appears narrowed and irregular, particularly at the entry to the cranial cavity [6]. This may precipitate sudden ischemic events triggered by head movements, affecting territories supplied by the vertebral, basilar, or posterior cerebral arteries [7]. MRI is preferable for detecting posterior fossa infarcts, as CT may be limited by beam-hardening artefacts [8]. Treatment is often surgical to prevent further compressive or thromboembolic events [7,9]. Teaching Points In young adults presenting with ischemic stroke, secondary vascular causes should always be considered, including anomalies in the arterial course.

title: CAlcifying PseudoNeoplasm Of the Neuraxis (CAPNON): A rare CNS lesion
clinical_history: A 52-year-old female with a history of epilepsy since the age of 8, with no seizure recurrence until adulthood, was referred to our centre following the reappearance of seizures, for reassessment and adjustment of antiepileptic therapy. She had never undergone a brain MRI before.
imaging_findings: MRI revealed a well-defined, intra-axial, macronodular lesion (maximum axial diameter: 35 mm), located in the left insular and temporal lobes. The lesion appeared lobulated and hypointense on all sequences (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, 1d, and 1e), with no enhancement after contrast administration (Figure 1f), consistent with extensive calcification. No parenchymal components, vasogenic oedema, or mass effect were observed. CT confirmed the diagnosis consistent with a completely calcified lesion, without adjacent oedema (Figure 2).
discussion: Background Calcifying pseudoneoplasm of the neuraxis (CAPNON) represents infrequent, benign, calcified lesions that can develop along the neuraxis, intra and extra-axial, with a peak incidence between 40 and 60 years. The precise aetiology is not perfectly known, and it seems to be secondary to different factors [1,2]. Clinical Perspective The clinical symptoms appear accordingly to their location, dimensions or mass effect. Most frequently, patients with brain lesions present with seizures, headache, hemiparesis, cranial nerve symptoms, tinnitus, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting [2–4]. Imaging Perspective CT represents the most sensitive imaging modality for detecting these calcifications, and its findings consist of a heavily calcified lesion (usually a complete calcified lesion) [1,3,5]. MRI is indicated for a better characterisation of the lesion, which appears hypointense on T1 and T2-weighted, without or with mild “blooming” on SWI, no restricted diffusion, usually no enhancement (when present it is mild), without parenchymal components, and usually without vasogenic oedema. Sometimes vasogenic oedema can be present and differential diagnosis is required [3]. The differential diagnoses include complete calcified meningiomas (sometimes with vasogenic oedema, and usually with at least a small parenchymal area), cavernomas (“popcorn” appearance, different enhancement compared to CAPNON, sometimes with oedema), glial lesion such as oligodendrogliomas (usually hyperintense on T2-weighted, with contrast enhancement and vasogenic oedema) or calcified brain metastasis (primary malignancy known, can have contrast enhancement, vasogenic oedema) [1,3,5]. Outcome Imaging techniques such as CT and MRI play a pivotal role in making the correct imaging diagnosis. The definitive diagnosis is based on histopathology, but not all cases have the indication for surgery. The management is built on clinical presentation, location and size. An asymptomatic lesion can be followed up, while lesions with important clinical symptoms can be resected. Being a benign entity, the prognosis is favourable and it does not require further treatment modalities such as radio or chemotherapy [1,6,7]. In our case, antiepileptic drug therapy was adjusted, resulting in complete seizure control, and the patient was dismissed without surgery needed at the moment of examination. Given the location of the lesion, a conservative approach with radiological surveillance was chosen to monitor for potential growth. A follow-up MRI performed 5 years later showed no changes in size or signal characteristics. Take Home Message / Teaching Points CAPNON represents a rare, but benign lesion of which radiologists should be aware of, to not misinterpret it as an aggressive entity. If asymptomatic, long-term follow-up confirms the radiological suspicion of CAPNON. It should be taken into consideration when we face heavily calcified brain lesions. Vasogenic oedema is usually not detected, but when present, differential diagnosis should be taken into account. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Osteolytic temporal bone mass in a young male
clinical_history: Young male with a history of a slowly growing, painless swelling in the right temporal region, with associated mild hearing loss and occasional headaches. No history of trauma, fever, or systemic symptoms. Physical examination revealed a firm, non-tender mass in the temporal region, which elicited further imaging characterisation.
imaging_findings: Serial CT and MRI demonstrated a large, expansile lytic lesion centred on the right temporal bone, with the largest axis of 61 mm, with stable dimensions over multiple follow-up studies (Figures 1a, 1b, 3a, and 3b). The lesion involved both squamous and petrous portions, eroding the outer and inner cortices, and extensively invading the mastoid air cells, with marked narrowing and focal erosion of the external auditory canal (Figures 1a and 1b). Anteriorly, mild epicranial soft tissue extension was noted (Figures 1b and 1c). The mass abutted the articular surface of the right temporomandibular joint over a 12 mm segment, without invasion of the condyle or joint space (Figure 1b). It also contacted but did not invade the foramen ovale or spinosum. MRI revealed a predominantly T2-hyperintense central component, surrounded by a hypointense peripheral fibrous rim (Figure 2a), with vivid peripheral and septal enhancement (Figure 2b). The central component remained non-enhancing. The lesion moulded the temporal lobe without parenchymal invasion or oedema (Figure 2a). No periosteal reaction, muscle atrophy, cranial nerve involvement or regional lymphadenopathy was present.
discussion: Background Giant cell tumour (GCT) is typically a benign locally aggressive neoplasm, most often seen in the epiphysis of long bones in young adults. Cranial involvement, especially in the temporal bone, is reported to be extremely rare, occurring in about 1% of all GCTs [1]. Imaging Perspective In long bones, GCTs typically present as an expansile, lytic lesion with well-defined, non-sclerotic margins, located in the meta-epiphyseal region of bones. Cortical thinning is a classical feature in this lesion. It lacks matrix mineralisation and periosteal reaction. On MRI, they present on T1 with a hypointense signal and on T2 with a heterogeneous iso to hyperintense signal, due to areas of haemorrhage or cystic degeneration. Sometimes there are fluid–fluid levels. Solid components enhance avidly. In the skull, their appearance can be different. On CT they may present as an expansile, osteolytic lesion with associated patchy cortical irregularity due to the thinness of cranial bones [2]. Due to proximity to other structures, they may extend to the middle cranial fossa, external auditory canal, or middle ear [3]. On MRI, their appearance is variable, usually presenting as a hypo or isointense lesion on both T1 and T2 sequences, with the solid components enhancing moderately to irregularly [2]. Rim or septal enhancement can be present, particularly if the lesion is partially cystic or lobulated [4]. Musculoskeletal (MSK) radiologists are trained to recognise an expansile, lytic bone lesion with associated cortical thinning and absent periosteal reaction (especially in young adults) as suspicious for GCT. This case demonstrates why the same logic applies to the skull. The key to recognising GCT in the skull is to apply MSK reasoning even outside the appendicular skeleton: identify aggressive, expansile, lytic lesions—even if cortical thinning is less conspicuous. Always assess for the presence of a soft tissue component, signal variability, and extension into adjacent anatomical compartments. Outcome This patient’s diagnosis was confirmed histologically after neuronavigation-guided excision. The lesion remains stable on follow-up, but, as in any location, recurrence is possible and mandates long-term surveillance. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Always apply MSK reasoning to lytic cranial bone lesions: Endosteal scalloping and lack of periosteal reaction in a lytic, expansile lesion should always prompt consideration of GCT, even in the temporal bone. In the temporal bone, GCTs are also expansile and lytic, but may show more subtle cortical irregularity, variable T2 signal (sometimes central hyperintensity with a hypointense rim), and moderate, irregular enhancement. Biopsy is essential for confirmation, and recurrence is possible even after complete excision—follow-up is mandatory. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Sella spur mimicking a pituitary adenoma in a 13-year-old female
clinical_history: A 13-year-old female presented with persistent headaches and decreased peripheral vision. Visual acuity was 6/6 in the right eye and 6/36 in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated temporal nerve fibre layer thinning corresponding to nasal field defects, without evidence of bitemporal hemianopia. Endocrine evaluation revealed normal results, which can occasionally be observed in non-functioning pituitary adenomas.
imaging_findings: MRI of the head revealed a bulky pituitary gland with a T1-hypointense area, initially raising suspicion for a microadenoma. On dynamic post-contrast sequences, however, the gland demonstrated homogeneous enhancement without delayed filling. A focal midline indentation arising from the dorsum sellae was observed, resulting in gland asymmetry and a small central T1-hypointense focus. Importantly, there was no sellar expansion or suprasellar extension. A thin-section CT, performed several months later during trauma evaluation, redemonstrated the presence of a well-defined midline bony spur arising from the dorsum sellae and projecting into the pituitary fossa.
discussion: Background Sellar spine is a rare congenital anatomical variant, with an estimated incidence of 1 in 5,000–8,000 [1]. It results from ossification of a persistent segment of the cephalic notochord, where failure of regression during embryogenesis gives rise to a midline bony spur projecting into the pituitary fossa. An alternative proposed mechanism suggests ossification of a dural fold containing a vascular channel [2]. Clinical Perspective Most patients are asymptomatic, with the sellar spine detected incidentally on imaging. When symptomatic, presentations may include headaches, visual disturbances such as bitemporal hemianopia from optic chiasm compression, and endocrine dysfunction including hypopituitarism, galactorrhoea, and oligomenorrhoea [3,4]. Symptoms typically arise after puberty, when physiological pituitary enlargement increases the likelihood of gland or stalk deformation by the bony spur. Imaging Perspective On MRI, the sellar spine appears as a sharply marginated linear projection arising from the dorsum sellae and extending into the pituitary fossa. Signal intensity depends on marrow content: cortical bone demonstrates uniformly low signal on both T1 and T2-weighted sequences, whereas marrow-containing bone exhibits high T1 signal and variable T2 signal [5]. CT remains the gold standard for diagnosis, clearly depicting a well-ossified spur continuous with the dorsum sellae and sellar floor. It allows confident differentiation from pituitary microadenomas and other calcified sellar or parasellar lesions [6]. Outcome Asymptomatic cases require no intervention; correct identification prevents unnecessary investigations or surgery. Symptomatic patients—particularly those with optic chiasm compression or pituitary dysfunction—may benefit from endoscopic resection and decompression. Most lesions remain stable over time, and no cases of malignant transformation have been reported [4]. Given that our patient had mild and stable clinical symptoms, a wait-and-watch strategy was adopted. She remains under regular clinical and radiological follow-up. Take Home Message Awareness of sellar spine as a standard anatomical variant is essential to avoid misdiagnosis as a pituitary adenoma and to prevent unwarranted interventions. Correlation between MRI and CT findings is key to establishing the diagnosis with confidence. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Multimodal imaging in Erdheim–Chester disease
clinical_history: A 45-year-old man presented with two months of progressive left knee pain and reduced exercise tolerance. Physical examination revealed bilateral xanthelasmata on the eyelids. He had no relevant past medical history, toxic habits, or systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats.
imaging_findings: Initial radiographs of the left knee demonstrated diffuse osteosclerosis and mild cortical thickening involving the distal metaphysis and diaphysis of the femur (Figures 1a and 1b). Computed tomography (CT) revealed soft tissue masses adjacent to the distal femoral metaphyses of both lower extremities, more evident on the medial aspect of the left thigh. A CT-guided Tru-Cut biopsy was performed targeting these peri-osseous soft tissue lesions, as they were more accessible, using a 14G needle to obtain multiple core samples. CT also confirmed bilateral metaphyseal and diaphyseal osteosclerosis with epiphyseal sparing (Figure 2). Bone scintigraphy (Tc-99m MDP) showed intense, symmetric radiotracer uptake in the distal femurs and tibias, sparing the epiphyses (Figure 3). Abdominal ultrasound revealed bilateral perirenal soft tissue thickening (Figure 4), which was corroborated on contrast-enhanced CT, showing the typical “hairy kidney” appearance and retroperitoneal soft tissue infiltration (Figure 5). Histopathology confirmed foamy and multinucleated histiocytes with BRAF V600E mutation (Figures 6a and 6b).
discussion: Background Erdheim–Chester disease (ECD) is a rare, multisystemic, non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis characterised by xanthogranulomatous infiltration of foamy histiocytes within a fibrotic stroma. It predominantly affects middle-aged adults, typically between the fifth and seventh decades of life. The disease is strongly associated with somatic mutations in the MAPK pathway, most commonly the BRAF V600E mutation, present in over half of all cases [1,2]. Clinical Perspective ECD presents with a broad clinical spectrum depending on the organs involved. Bone pain, especially in the long bones of the lower extremities, is the most frequent initial symptom, reported in approximately 50% of patients [2]. Other manifestations include exophthalmos, central diabetes insipidus, and xanthelasma-like cutaneous lesions. Due to its protean nature and often indolent course, early diagnosis requires high clinical suspicion. Imaging is critical not only for detecting organ involvement but also for guiding biopsy and assessing disease extent. Imaging Perspective Typical imaging findings in ECD include bilateral, symmetric osteosclerosis of the diaphysis and metaphysis of long bones, with sparing of the epiphyses—a hallmark feature that helps distinguish ECD from other sclerotic bone diseases [3]. Radiographs and CT commonly confirm the symmetric pattern of long bone involvement, while MRI typically shows hypointense marrow signal on both T1 and T2-weighted images, often associated with enhancing periosteal or soft tissue components. Bone scintigraphy characteristically reveals intense, symmetric uptake in the distal femurs and tibias, frequently extending to the tarsal bones, distal radii, femoral necks, and tibial shafts—findings consistent with the classic skeletal distribution seen in ECD [1,3]. Abdominal imaging, particularly ultrasound and CT, may reveal bilateral perirenal soft tissue infiltration, producing the characteristic “hairy kidney” sign. These retroperitoneal changes are present in over 50% of patients and can lead to obstructive uropathy [1,2]. Histological confirmation remains essential. Biopsies typically demonstrate foamy and multinucleated histiocytes within a fibrotic background, and immunohistochemical analysis frequently reveals the presence of BRAF V600E mutations, supporting the diagnosis and guiding targeted therapy. Outcome Targeted therapy with BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib has shown excellent efficacy in BRAF-mutant cases. Treatment led to symptom resolution and regression of imaging findings. MEK inhibitors may be considered in BRAF-negative disease [1]. Take Home Message Multimodality imaging is key for early identification, diagnosis, and monitoring of Erdheim–Chester disease (ECD). Integration of clinical, imaging, and pathological findings is essential for appropriate management.

title: Typical bronchial carcinoid of the bronchus intermedius: A radiologic classic
clinical_history: A 29-year-old male nonsmoker presented with a persistent dry cough for two months with intermittent scanty haemoptysis. There was no history of fever, weight loss, other constitutional symptoms or comorbidities. The chest radiograph was unremarkable, except for subtle increased lucency in the right lung. The patient was referred for further evaluation with a contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) thorax.
imaging_findings: Computed tomography (CT) of the thorax in the lung window demonstrated a well-defined, soft tissue attenuating, partially obstructing endobronchial mass located within the bronchus intermedius (BI), in close proximity to the origin of the right middle lobe (RML) bronchus (Figures 1a and 1c). The lesion caused partial luminal obstruction, particularly at the RML bronchial origin, resulting in hyperinflation of the RML, indicative of a ball-valve mechanism (Figures 1b and 1c). Additional findings included a few centrilobular nodules and tree-in-bud opacities in the right upper lobe, suggestive of a superadded infection. Following intravenous contrast administration, the lesion exhibited intense, homogeneous enhancement (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). No evidence of intralesional calcification, mediastinal invasion, or regional lymphadenopathy was observed. A virtual bronchoscopy, reconstructed from thin-section CT images, revealed a smooth-surfaced, endobronchial lesion partially occluding the bronchial lumen at the same anatomical level (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Bronchial carcinoid tumours are rare, accounting for less than 2% of all lung malignancies [1]. These neuroendocrine tumours arise from Kulchitsky cells and are classified by the WHO into typical and atypical subtypes. Typical carcinoids are low-grade, slow-growing tumours affecting tracheobronchial tree with an excellent prognosis and a strong predilection for central airways [2]. Clinical Perspective Typical bronchial carcinoids commonly affect younger adults and present with nonspecific respiratory symptoms such as cough, wheezing, or recurrent infections. Haemoptysis is common due to the tumour’s vascular nature. In some cases, the tumour is detected incidentally on imaging performed for other reasons. Carcinoid syndrome is rare unless hepatic metastases are present, which is uncommon in typical carcinoid tumours [3]. Imaging Perspective Chest radiographs are often normal or may show indirect signs such as lobar overinflation or atelectasis. CT is the preferred modality, typically demonstrating a well-circumscribed, avid enhancing endobronchial mass. Hypervascularity manifests as intense homogeneous enhancement in arterial phase. Calcification may be present in one-third of cases. Obstructive changes such as air trapping or post-obstructive pneumonia may be seen [3,4]. Virtual bronchoscopy can non-invasively depict the intraluminal mass and its location. In this case, the lesion caused partial obstruction and lobar hyperinflation of RML with superadded infection in the right upper lobe. MRI has a limited role but may assist in assessing mediastinal invasion or nodal involvement. Among functional imaging modalities, FDG PET/CT has limited sensitivity for typical carcinoids due to low FDG avidity; however, it is helpful in detecting aggressive or atypical variants. In contrast, 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT offers superior sensitivity (up to 95%) and specificity by targeting the somatostatin receptor subtype 2 expression on neuroendocrine cells, making it highly valuable for staging, detecting multifocal disease, and surveillance [5]. Outcome The patient underwent rigid bronchoscopy, which revealed a fleshy vascular mass obstructing the BI, and the tumour was ablated using laser and cryotherapy in the same setting (Figures 4a, 4b, 4c, and 4d). Histopathological examination confirmed a typical carcinoid tumour (Figures 5a and 5b). The patient remains asymptomatic on follow-up with no evidence of recurrence. Bronchoscopic intervention is suitable for centrally located, non-invasive carcinoids. Surgical resection is reserved for larger or peripherally situated tumours or those with nodal involvement [6]. Take Home Message This case underscores the need for vigilance when evaluating persistent cough and subtle radiographic abnormalities. Central endobronchial lesions such as typical carcinoids may appear deceptively inconspicuous on plain radiographs, yet demonstrate characteristic features on contrast-enhanced CT and virtual bronchoscopy. Their intense vascular enhancement, well-circumscribed margins, and tendency to cause obstructive changes should prompt radiologists to include carcinoid in the differential. Early diagnosis and minimally invasive management can yield excellent outcomes in appropriately selected cases. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding secondary to giant splenic artery aneurysm
clinical_history: A 52-year-old male presented with epigastric pain, melena, and syncope post-defecation. Physical examination was unremarkable. An upper endoscopy was performed, revealing an ulcerated subepithelial lesion in the gastric fundus (Figure 1), suspected to be a gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST). A full-body CT scan was conducted to complete the staging evaluation.
imaging_findings: A CT body scan with intravenous contrast in arterial and portal venous phases was performed. A lesion originating from the distal segment of the splenic artery was observed, partially thrombosed (Figures 2a and 2b), measuring 12 x 7.5 x 7 cm (L x AP x T), with no signs of rupture, but eroding the wall of the gastric fundus (Figures 2c and 2d). Subsequently, a diagnostic-therapeutic and selective arteriography of the splenic artery was performed, confirming the presence of an aneurysm of 12 cm (Figure 3a), over which coils and controlled-release microcoils were placed (Figure 3b). The control CT demonstrated a reduction in blood flow within the aneurysm (Figure 4a), which allowed for a safer execution of the definitive surgical treatment: distal pancreatectomy, aneurysmectomy, and splenectomy (Figures 4b and 4c).
discussion: A blood vessel is considered aneurysmal when its diameter exceeds its usual size by 50%, and this dilatation may be saccular or fusiform. Based on histological criteria, it can be classified as a true aneurysm (when the vessel walls remain intact) or a pseudoaneurysm [1,2]. The most common aneurysms originate in the infrarenal abdominal aorta, followed by those in the iliac arteries. About 5% of intra-abdominal aneurysms are visceral, and splenic artery aneurysms (SAA) account for 60% of those in the splanchnic territory, making them the most frequent visceral aneurysms. However, giant splenic aneurysms are considered rare [1,3,4]. The splenic artery typically measures 0.5 cm, increasing to 1 cm with an aneurysm [5]. A giant SAA is commonly defined as ≥ 5 cm, with an increasing rupture risk as size augments: aneurysms < 2 cm pose a 2–10% rupture risk, while giant aneurysms may have up to 30% risk. Small aneurysms (< 2 cm) are often asymptomatic and found incidentally, whereas giant aneurysms may present with left upper quadrant pain radiating to the epigastrium, back, or left flank, and 30% may have a palpable mass. Rupture can lead to intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal bleeding, causing compression damage, fistulas, or haemodynamic instability with symptoms of upper gastrointestinal bleeding, nausea, vomiting, or jaundice [1)]. For suspected SAA, CT angiography is the preferred non-invasive imaging modality. SAA are identified on CT as nodular lesions, typically small, with a density similar to the originating vessel. Many of these aneurysms may be partially or completely thrombosed and exhibit mural calcifications. In the presence of an aneurysm, it is crucial to assess potential complications, including signs of rupture or fistulisation [6]. However, arteriography remains the gold standard due to its diagnostic and therapeutic capabilities. Treatment depends on rupture risk—aneurysms < 2 cm may be monitored if asymptomatic. The approach may be endovascular, surgical, or sequential to minimise intraoperative bleeding. Endovascular techniques are preferred. Surgical intervention is reserved for cases with local complications or haemodynamic instability [1,3,4]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Splenic artery aneurysms (SAA) are the most frequent visceral aneurysms. SAA < 2 cm are usually asymptomatic, whereas giant aneurysms may present with abdominal pain, a palpable mass, and signs of gastrointestinal bleeding. The risk of rupture is directly related to size, reaching up to 30% in giant aneurysms. Angiography is the gold standard due to its diagnostic and therapeutic capabilities, while CT imaging provides better anatomical characterisation in the perioperative setting. title: Ultrasonographic diagnosis: Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery aneurysm and coeliac trunk stenosis
clinical_history: A 55-year-old patient presented to the outpatient ultrasound department, having been referred by her general practitioner for chronic vague abdominal pain and weight loss. Clinically, abdominal examination, blood workup and gastroscopy were normal. An ultrasound was requested to assess for intra-abdominal pathology, particularly for evidence of malignancy.
imaging_findings: B-mode and Doppler ultrasound showed a focal anechoic fusiform dilatation (14 mm x 11 mm; Figures 1a and 1b) of the proximal first branch of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), at the level of the pancreatic head, in keeping with an inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery aneurysm (IPDAA). There was turbulent blood flow within the aneurysm, but no evidence of thrombosis. The proximal coeliac trunk was kinked and severely stenotic, measuring 2 mm in diameter (Figure 2). The remainder of the sonographic examination of the abdomen was normal. Subsequent computed tomography (CT) imaging was performed, acquired in both arterial and portal venous phases. This confirmed IPDAA with severe coeliac trunk stenosis and collateralisation of the pancreaticoduodenal arcades (Figures 3a and 3b), secondary to compression by the median arcuate ligament. There were no further abnormalities.
discussion: Background True IPDAA is defined as dilatation involving all three layers of the arterial wall without a radiologically demonstrable traumatic, infective or inflammatory cause [1]. This may occur secondary to coeliac artery (CA) stenosis or occlusion, usually resulting from entrapment by the median arcuate ligament (MAL) or arteriosclerosis. Rarer causes include systemic vasculitis and fibromuscular dysplasia [3]. Although the pathophysiology is incompletely understood, collateralisation of pancreaticoduodenal arcades via the SMA is thought to result in increased retrograde blood flow, focal hypertension, vessel wall remodelling, and aneurysmal dilatation [1–3]. Clinical Perspective IPDAAs account for 2% of all visceral artery aneurysms with an overall prevalence of 0.01–0.2% [4,5]. A quarter of patients with IPDAA are asymptomatic. Presentation of unruptured IPDAA includes abdominal pain, weight loss, pancreatitis, duodenal obstruction and painless jaundice, due to mass effect. The median age of diagnosis for ruptured IPDAA is 52 years, and 57 years for unruptured, with no gender predilection [2,3]. IPDAA diameter ranges from 4 mm to 70 mm (mean 22 mm), with no reported relationship between aneurysm sac size and rupture risk [6]. Most IPDAAs are diagnosed following rupture, typically presenting with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and hypovolaemic shock secondary to retroperitoneal or gastrointestinal haemorrhage [2,3]. Imaging Perspective Larger IPDAAs may be diagnosed on ultrasound with colour Doppler imaging (CDI) [2]. Features include a hypoechoic, well-defined retroperitoneal peripancreatic mass occasionally containing echogenic thrombus. CDI may demonstrate turbulent arterial flow and communication with a SMA branch [8]. Biliary dilatation might also be seen [9]. Arterial phase thin-slice contrast-enhanced multi-detector CT is the most common diagnostic modality; however, selective catheter angiography is the gold standard [2,7]. Outcome Management of IPDAA is based on case reports and literature reviews [10]. Clinically stable patients may undergo serial imaging to monitor aneurysm dimensions, evaluate for sac thrombosis and secondary complications [9]. Interventional procedures include embolisation of the aneurysm sac [2], with coiling being the treatment of choice, although particle or glue embolisation and covered stenting are alternative options [11]. Surgical or endovascular management of concomitant CA stenosis remains controversial, given the favourable outcomes of IPDAA treatment without recurrence [12,13]. In our case, based on numerous factors, including aneurysm morphology, the vascular surgical decision was for surveillance and ongoing consideration of bypass surgery, rather than endovascular intervention. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Sonographic diagnosis of inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery aneurysm (IPDAA) is rare. An understanding of normal vascular anatomy and sonographic features of IPDAA is key in identification, determining the likely cause, and evaluating for complications. In this case, early diagnosis optimised clinical management under the care of vascular surgery. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Multisystem involvement in cystic echinococcosis: Focus on the cardiopulmonary system
clinical_history: A 76-year-old female patient presented with several weeks of dyspnoea and generalised weakness. She also reported occasional night sweats, although her body temperature had not been recorded. Electrocardiography revealed signs of incomplete left bundle branch block and left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH). Echocardiography revealed biatrial and right ventricular dilation, LVH with global hypokinesia, mitral and aortic valve stenosis and regurgitation, tricuspid insufficiency, and evidence of pulmonary hypertension.
imaging_findings: A contrast-enhanced chest CT was initially performed, revealing a well-defined, non-enhancing, low-attenuation mass within the interventricular septum (Figures 1a and 1b). Multiple solid and cavitary nodules were noted in both lungs, along with left-sided pulmonary infiltrates and pleural effusion (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). Subsequent abdominal CT imaging demonstrated several non-enhancing cystic lesions in both the liver and spleen (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Cystic echinococcosis is a widespread parasitic infection primarily affecting the liver, followed by the lungs. Although cardiac involvement is rare, it often results in severe outcomes when it occurs [1]. Clinical Perspective In the early stages, hydatid cysts are typically asymptomatic. A definitive diagnosis requires a combination of clinical presentation, imaging features, and laboratory tests [1–3]. Imaging Perspective Imaging plays a crucial role in identifying parasitic cysts, with ultrasound and chest X-ray being the initial modalities. For a more detailed assessment and to characterise the extent of the disease, CT and/or MRI are preferred [1,2]. The imaging appearance of echinococcal cysts varies depending on the disease stage [1]. In stage I, the cysts typically appear as well-defined, non-enhancing fluid-filled masses. In more advanced stages, features such as daughter cysts, detached floating membranes, hydatid sand, and calcifications may be observed. On chest CT, parasitic pulmonary cysts usually present as well-defined, round masses with homogeneous soft-tissue opacity. When cysts rupture into the bronchial system, an “air-crescent” sign may appear. Pulmonary echinococcosis is often associated with adjacent pneumonitis, atelectasis, or pleural effusion, which may obscure cyst margins. Our case was noteworthy for the multifocal presentation of the disease. Unfortunately, echocardiography failed to detect the parasitic cyst, which was only identified on the chest CT. Due to the patient’s dyspnoea, more advanced imaging techniques, such as cardiac CT or MRI, could not be performed. However, the multiorgan involvement coupled with the positive anti- Echinococcus antibody test led to the final diagnosis. Outcome In our case, a serum anti- Echinococcus antibody (IgG) level of 1.998 U/L was detected. The patient resided in a rural area and had frequent contact with various domestic animals. Treatment options for cystic echinococcosis vary based on the location of the cysts and the course of the disease. Approaches can include surgery, conservative management, or a combined strategy of treatment along with surgical cyst removal [2]. In our case, given the multiorgan involvement and cardiopulmonary insufficiency, medication-based antiparasitic therapy was preferred. Subsequently, the patient recovered well and is free of symptoms. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Segmental testicular infarction as a rare complication of severe epididymo-orchitis
clinical_history: An 80-year-old male patient with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and no prior scrotal pathology presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of progressive left testicular pain, erythema, and swelling. Laboratory investigations revealed an elevated C-reactive protein level (23 mg/dL) without leukocytosis. A testicular ultrasound was requested.
imaging_findings: B-mode ultrasound revealed marked asymmetry in testicular volume, with significant enlargement of the left testis, which exhibited a heterogeneous, patchy echotexture with a well-demarcated geographic area of decreased echogenicity in the upper pole, showing absent vascularity on colour Doppler ultrasound. The epididymis was diffusely enlarged and globular, with intense hypervascularity on colour Doppler ultrasound, harbouring an internally non-vascularised complex fluid collection in its head, measuring approximately 18 mm, with internal mobile echoes suggestive of a localised abscess. Additional findings consistent with complicated epididymo-orchitis included an ipsilateral loculated pyocele and funiculitis extending along the spermatic cord. The abscess was surgically drained, and the purulent material was submitted for microbiological culture. The patient was discharged on oral cefuroxime but returned to the emergency department due to a lack of clinical improvement. Despite isolation of Escherichia coli sensitive to the prescribed antibiotic, follow-up ultrasound revealed progressive pathological changes, prompting a left orchiectomy.
discussion: Background Testicular infarction is a rare and often idiopathic complication of epididymo-orchitis, occurring in approximately 1–2% of cases and predominantly affecting men between 20–40 years [1,2]. The pathophysiology behind this para-infectious thrombosis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include venous outflow obstruction or arterial compromise secondary to inflammation and oedema of the spermatic cord [3]. The microbiological profile varies with age. In younger patients, Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are the most frequent pathogens, although they are rarely associated with testicular infarction. Conversely, in older individuals, Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa are more commonly isolated and have been implicated in vascular complications [4]. Depending on the extent of vascular occlusion, testicular infarction may be segmental or diffuse. The segmental form typically involves the upper pole of the testis, which relies solely on the testicular artery [2,3]. Clinical Perspective Clinical presentation is variable and often nonspecific, particularly in patients with comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus, who are predisposed to genitourinary infections and impaired tissue repair. Acute scrotal pain is the most common symptom, requiring differentiation from testicular torsion or testicular tumours. A comprehensive approach combining clinical evaluation, laboratory work-up, and imaging studies is essential to establish an accurate diagnosis [5]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound, particularly colour Doppler, is the first-line imaging modality for acute scrotal pain assessment. Key sonographic findings include well-demarcated, avascular, hypoechoic areas within the testicular parenchyma in a background of inflammatory changes. Differentiation from small intratesticular tumours may be challenging when relying solely on the absence of vascularity [4,5]. Nonetheless, a geographic pattern of infarction, associated with infectious complications findings such as epididymal abscess, pyocele and funiculitis, favours an infectious aetiology. In uncertain cases, scrotal MRI may be decisive in establishing a definitive diagnosis [4]. Outcome Although conservative management with careful follow-up represents a reasonable option, the risk of progression from reversible ischemia to irreversible infarction, as well as complications such as testicular atrophy, endocrine dysfunction, or contralateral torsion, must be considered [4,5]. In this case, due to clinical nonresponse to antimicrobial therapy and worsening imaging findings, the patient underwent left-sided orchiectomy. The patient’s age and absence of clinical improvement supported the decision to proceed with orchiectomy, with no postoperative complications. Teaching Points Testicular infarction, though rare, should be considered in patients presenting with severe or refractory epididymo-orchitis. Ultrasonography plays an indispensable role in diagnosing and managing post-infectious testicular necrosis, avoiding misdiagnosis and preventing delays in surgical intervention. In cases managed conservatively, serial Doppler ultrasound assessments are essential for monitoring progression or complications. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Spontaneous brain and spinal subdural haematomas
clinical_history: A patient diagnosed with acute myeloid leukaemia was admitted for an inaugural generalised seizure. His medical history was relevant for hypertension, hyperuricaemia and chronic renal insufficiency. Laboratory findings disclosed pancytopaenia and thrombocytopaenia (28,000), and normal PCR (0.29). He was waiting to initiate treatment with azacitidine and venetoclax. The seizure was witnessed by a family member who denied any head trauma before or during the episode.
imaging_findings: The head CT shows mild supratentorial hydrocephalus with dilatation of the frontal and temporal horns, transependymal effusion and sulcal effacement at the frontoparietal convexity (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c). Sagittal reconstructions demonstrate a small posterior fossa, inferior displacement of the tentorium and abnormal soft tissue density in the retroclival and retrocerebellar regions extending into the upper cervical spinal canal (Figure 1d). These findings were considered suspicious for pachy and/or leptomeningeal infiltration, and a brain MRI was recommended. Brain and spine MRI shows several spontaneously T1 hyperintense extra-axial collections with no enhancement after gadolinium and no signal suppression on the fat-suppressed T1-weighted images, extending from the dorsum sella to the C3–C4 level (Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, 2d, and 2e). The distribution and morphology of these fluid collections suggested a subdural location with mass effect upon the brainstem and spinal cord. All collections had similar signal intensities, suggesting a simultaneous occurrence. T2-weighted and FLAIR images confirmed the supratentorial hydrocephalus. There was no abnormal leptomeningeal or ependymal enhancement. Although an MR angiography was not performed, there was no evidence of vascular malformations on other sequences.
discussion: Background Subdural haematomas are spontaneous in the absence of a history of accidental or iatrogenic trauma. They are rare and often result from blood dyscrasias or vascular malformations, but in 5% of cases, no potential cause is found [1]. Simultaneous occurrence of both intracranial and spinal subdurals is even rarer. Spinal subdural haematoma (SSDH) is a rare disease due to the absence of bridging veins in the spinal subdural space. In the case of concomitant intracranial and SSDH, the involvement of the spinal canal results from the contiguity of the subdural spaces and the effect of gravity. SSDH should be promptly recognised and managed as it can lead to devastating neurological dysfunction with significant morbimortality [2,3]. Clinical Perspective Presenting symptoms depend on the size, location and onset of the SSDH. The most common include headache, dizziness and behavioural changes. Seizures are a less common presenting symptom. When affecting the spinal canal, back pain, altered sensitivity, sphincter dysfunction, and motor weakness are the most common presentations [4]. As symptoms can be varied, clinical diagnosis is difficult and imaging, preferably with MRI, is mandatory. In patients with underlying conditions in which meningeal involvement needs to be excluded, imaging should always be performed before lumbar puncture. Imaging Perspective The findings in the head CT and the patient’s history prompted us to favour leptomeningeal dissemination. However, brain MRI revealed several crescent-shaped T1 hyperintense lesions in the posterior fossa and along the cervical spinal canal, with no enhancement, which, together with thrombocytopaenia, was very suggestive of spontaneous subdural haematomas. In the spine, the distinction between subdural (SH) and epidural haematoma (EH) is not easy. SH are most often ventral to the spinal cord or have a semicircular/circumferential distribution and tend to compress the cord, whereas EH are usually dorsal to the cord, their spread limited by the fixation of the dura to the posterior longitudinal ligament, and tend to displace the L cord. In our case, the crescent shape of the haematoma along with the diffuse spread in the posterior fossa and the involvement of cervical spine levels below the C2 level (level of the inferior attachment of the tectorial membrane to the spinal dura) favoured the hypothesis of SSDH. Outcome Three treatment options exist in the management of SSDH: surgical evacuation, percutaneous drainage, or conservative medical management, depending on the neurological deficits, performance status, and underlying conditions [5]. In our case, due to the patient’s underlying condition and poor performance status, the patient was treated conservatively. Unfortunately, the patient developed signs of infection and was started on antibiotics, but ultimately expired. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Spinal subdural haematomas (SSDHs) are an emergency requiring urgent recognition and management. The morphology and mass effect upon the spinal cord can help differentiate subdural from epidural haematomas. title: Hemimyelomeningocele with diastematomyelia: A rare spinal trio
clinical_history: A 1.5-month-old female infant presented with a congenital midline back swelling with a skin defect. She was born full-term via normal vaginal delivery, with no relevant family history. Developmental milestones were age-appropriate. Neurologically, the left lower limb function was normal, while the right lower limb showed minimal movement.
imaging_findings: MR imaging of the lumbosacral spine revealed a low-lying cord terminating at the S1 level, associated with spina bifida from the L2 to S5 levels and tethering of the cord. Splitting of the spinal cord (Figure 1a) is seen at the L2–L3 level with a bony bar at the L3–L4 level (Figures 1b and 1c): type I diastematomyelia. The right hemicord, along with meninges and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), is herniating through posterior elemental defects of the spina bifida, forming a large subcutaneous mass containing dysplastic soft tissue appearing T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense, not showing suppression on STIR (Figure 6), with an intervening T1 and T2 low-signal-intensity spiculated structure in the centre (Figures 7a and 7b) and a well-defined CSF fluid-intensity cyst within (Figures 2 and 4). Both hemicords reunite below the level of herniation. A slightly prominent central canal is seen from the T10 to S1 vertebral levels (Figure 3). The rest of the vertebral bodies appear unremarkable.
discussion: Background Split cord malformations (SCMs) are rare spinal dysraphisms that involve a longitudinal splitting of the spinal cord into two hemicords. Type I SCM is defined by two hemicords, each within its own dural sac, separated by a rigid osseous or fibrous septum. Type II SCM is characterised by two hemicords located within a single dural sac, separated by a flexible, fibrous median septum [1]. Hemimyelomeningocele is an exceptionally rare variant in which one hemicord, along with meninges and CSF, herniates through a posterior vertebral defect, forming a localised neural tube defect [2–4]. These anomalies result from faulty gastrulation and notochordal duplication, occurring during early embryogenesis. In our case, the presence of a dysplastic subcutaneous soft tissue mass suggests that, in addition to errors in primary neurulation, there may have been an associated defect in mesenchymal differentiation, as indicated by the presence of dysplastic tissue components within the lesion [1,3,4]. Clinical Perspective Clinically, SCMs often present during infancy with midline back swelling, cutaneous stigmata, or neurological asymmetry such as unilateral limb weakness or deformities. In our case, the infant had a congenital back swelling and reduced movement in the right lower limb. The combination of hemimyelomeningocele and diastematomyelia may present with variable neurological outcomes depending on the degree of cord tethering and associated anomalies. Imaging is essential not only for diagnosis but also for presurgical anatomical mapping [2,5]. Identifying the full extent of the lesion helps surgeons to prevent incomplete repair or recurrence of tethering. Imaging Perspective MRI is the modality of choice for diagnosing complex spinal dysraphisms, offering high-resolution multiplanar assessment of anomalies such as cord duplication (diastematomyelia), tethered cord, syringomyelia, dysplastic or lipomatous tissue, and, in hemimyelomeningocele, a CSF-filled sac containing a herniated hemicord [1,2]. Key sequences include sagittal and axial, T1 and T2-weighted images, with 3D T2-weighted (e.g., SPACE or CISS) and STIR or fat-suppressed T2 aiding in the evaluation of soft tissue and tethering elements [6]. Accurate imaging is essential for defining anatomy, guiding surgical planning, and correlating with embryological theories [1,5]. Identifying the type of split cord and any tethering elements is crucial for optimal preoperative assessment [3,5]. Advanced bone MRI techniques like zero echo time (ZTE) imaging offer promising bone visualisation, but currently they complement rather than replace CT, which remains essential for detailed assessment of complex osseous abnormalities [7]. Outcome Surgical management includes resection of the osseous spur, detethering of the spinal cord, and repair of the neural herniation. While early correction can prevent further deterioration, existing neurological deficits are often permanent. Prognosis is generally better with timely intervention, but delayed diagnosis increases the risk of irreversible damage [5]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Hemimyelomeningocele with type I split cord malformation (SCM) is a rare but surgically manageable spinal dysraphism. MRI with CT correlation is essential for accurate diagnosis and surgical planning. Early intervention helps prevent neurological deterioration further, though existing deficits are usually irreversible. Always assess for associated bony anomalies, tethered cord, and syringohydromyelia. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Pulmonary histoplasmosis in a returning immunocompromised traveller
clinical_history: A 30-year-old male with a medical history of liver transplant for primary sclerosing cholangitis and severe Crohn’s disease returned from a trip to Mexico with the development of a fever over the prior week. His medications included infliximab, tacrolimus, and azathioprine. An infectious workup was conducted.
imaging_findings: The initial chest radiographs (Figures 1a and 1b) revealed a dense focal consolidation in the left lower lobe retrocardiac region, annotated with red circles. Further characterisation with CT (Figure 2a) confirmed this area of consolidation with air bronchograms. Perihilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy was also noted on this study (Figure 2b, yellow arrow), prompting bronchoscopy. Cultures returned positive from bronchoalveolar lavage for Histoplasma capsulatum three weeks after the initial presentation; this diagnosis was further confirmed by additional serology testing, and antifungal medications were started. A subsequent CT six weeks after the initial presentation showed that the area of consolidation had increased in size and there was interval development of diffuse miliary nodules (Figures 3a and 3b), suggesting that a prolonged course of antifungal treatment would be required. The micronodules were randomly distributed with no particular apicobasal predominance and the degree of lymphadenopathy was unchanged. After completing a six-month course of antifungal treatment, the surveillance CT scan demonstrated complete resolution of both the miliary nodules and left lower lobe consolidation (Figure 4a). The thoracic lymphadenopathy had improved but not completely resolved (Figure 4b, purple arrow).
discussion: Background Pulmonary histoplasmosis is an infectious disease caused by the dimorphic fungus Histoplasma capsulatum . Belonging to the Ascomycota phylum, this fungus thrives in moderate to warm temperatures, rich soil, and moist environments contaminated with bird or bat excrement. This has led to a preponderance for river valleys, with high prevalence regions including the Southeastern United States, Mexico, and Latin America. Although the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys in North America maintain the highest number of endemic infections, changing climate, travel, and immigration patterns have highlighted that histoplasmosis is global in nature [1]. Clinical Perspective The majority of histoplasmosis infections in immunocompetent individuals (> 90%) are asymptomatic or mild in nature, often making a confirmed diagnosis elusive. Patients usually present with nonspecific symptoms, including fever, malaise, cough, and chest pain. As a result, histoplasmosis is often misdiagnosed as a viral or bacterial infection. However, clinical presentation in immunocompromised individuals can also be severe, including respiratory failure and septic shock. Failure to establish the correct diagnosis in these patients can be fatal [2]. Imaging Perspective There is a wide variety of thoracic imaging presentations of histoplasmosis based on the infection timeline. Acute pulmonary histoplasmosis commonly results in pulmonary nodules, segmental or lobar consolidation (mimicking bacterial pneumonia), and mediastinal/perihilar lymphadenopathy [3]. Pleural or pericardial effusions are rare, but can occur in the setting of immune reconstitution syndrome [4]. Acute infections in the immunocompromised patient can progress to disseminated histoplasmosis. The intrathoracic CT findings are diverse and can include patchy multifocal consolidation, ground glass opacities, cavitary lesions, and miliary micronodules (as in our case) [5,6]. Chronic histoplasmosis infection can result in calcified thoracic lymph nodes, calcified pulmonary granulomas, and upper lobe cavitations. Granulomas that continue to enlarge, termed histoplasmomas, are of particular importance because they mimic progressing malignancy [6]. The slow outward growth of granulation tissue often results in lamellated calcification, although they can also exhibit a diffuse or central calcification pattern. Take Home Message The diagnosis of histoplasmosis in atypical geographic locations is challenging, exacerbated by the lack of disease awareness, nonspecific clinical and radiologic presentation, and imperfect laboratory tests [7]. Therefore, it is essential to consider the immune status and travel history of the patient when investigating thoracic imaging with atypical findings.
