title: Neuroimaging clues to an organic aciduria: L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria
clinical_history: A seven-year-old boy came with chief complaints of large head size, developmental delay, seizures and clumsiness from two years of age. No other relevant history. Antenatal history was uneventful.
imaging_findings: A plain MRI brain was done. Diffuse and symmetrical T2 hyperintensities (Figures 1a and 1c) were noted involving bilateral frontal-temporal-parietal-occipital subcortical white matter, which shows T2 shine-through effect on ADC map (Figures 5a and 5b), with periventricular white matter showing normal signal intensities (Figure 1c). No white matter cystic areas noted. Symmetrical T2 hyperintensities were noted in the bilateral globus pallidus (Figure 1a) and dentate nucleus (Figure 1b), showing diffusion restriction on DWI sequences (Figures 3a and 3b). Prominent ventricular system and mildly prominent extra-axial cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) spaces and cerebellar folia suggest mild atrophy. A prominent retrocerebellar space was noted—mega cisterna magna (Figure 7). The corpus callosum appears thinned along its entire length but shows normal signal intensities (Figure 7). Bilateral thalami, brainstem and cerebellar white matter appear normal.
discussion: Background L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (L2HGA) is a rare autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder caused by abnormal variants of the L2HGDH gene, located on chromosome 14q22.1, which encodes L-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase (encoded by mitochondria). This disease was initially reported in 1980, and many cases have been documented worldwide subsequently, with a prevalence rate of <1 per 1,000,000 live births [1]. Clinical Perspective Cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, and cognitive decline are among the progressively increasing neurological symptoms of L2HGA that usually appear during the first year of life. Seizures, macrocephaly, pyramidal and extrapyramidal symptoms, and growth retardation are some of the additional hallmarks [1]. Imaging Perspective On MRI, bilateral symmetrical subcortical white matter typical abnormalities are a preferential involvement of the frontal white matter (more than the occipital one), of the subcortical white matter (more than the deep and periventricular one), while the internal capsule, corpus callosum, cerebellar white matter, and brainstem are spared [2]. The grey matter in the dentate nucleus and putamen is almost always affected, but in the globus pallidus and caudate nucleus, it has been inconsistently reported, despite seen in most patients [2]. Cerebellar vermis and hemispheric atrophy are present only in some patients [2]. Occasional MRI findings in subsets include oedema of cerebral white matter with broadening of gyri, thinning of subcortical white matter, rarely with cyst formation, and cerebral white matter atrophy [2]. Relatively spared periventricular white matter is a key differentiator from Canavan disease and some mitochondrial disorders. A normal appearance of the thalami, brainstem, and cerebellar white matter helps to rule out Kearns–Sayre and advanced mitochondrial diseases. The absence of subcortical cysts helps to differentiate it from megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts. The molecular hallmark of L2HGA is a markedly increased level of L-2-hydroxyglutaric acid, most prominently in urine, followed by cerebrospinal fluid and plasma. Urinary organic acid screening using gas chromatography–mass spectrometry and liquid chromatography yields an accurate diagnosis [1]. Outcome Currently, there is no definitive therapy for L2HGA. Supportive management is indicated, with some reports suggesting potential symptomatic benefits from flavin adenine dinucleotide sodium (FAD) and levocarnitine chloride supplementation [1]. Treatment response in L2HGA may relate to residual enzyme activity, though no consistent correlation is known. One child with a homozygous exon 10 L2HGDH mutation remained seizure-free and demonstrated developmental gains at 6-month follow-up [3]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria (L2HGA) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by L2HGDH gene mutations on chromosome 14q22.1. It presents in childhood with ataxia, dysarthria, seizures, macrocephaly, and cognitive decline. MRI shows bilateral subcortical white matter changes, as well as dentate nucleus and putamen involvement. Urinary L-2-hydroxyglutaric acid elevation confirms the diagnosis. There is no cure. Supportive care is indicated. Riboflavin/carnitine may help.

title: Penetrating thoracic injury from a fall onto a pencil
clinical_history: An 8-year-old presented as a level 1 trauma at a tertiary paediatric care hospital after tripping and falling directly onto a pencil at school. On examination, a portion of the pencil was protruding from the left chest wall at the mid-thoracic level (Figure 1).
imaging_findings: Initial chest radiograph identified the tubular foreign body (pencil) penetrating the left paramediastinal chest with no pneumothorax (Figure 2). Contrast-enhanced axial computed tomography (CT) showed the tip of the foreign body adjacent to the left superior pulmonary vein and left upper lobe bronchus (Figure 3a), and demonstrated a small parenchymal haemorrhage and pneumatocele at the site of the penetrating injury, consistent with an American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) grade 2 injury [1] (Figure 3b). The image taken during the surgery shows that the pencil was penetrating the left lung (Figure 4).
discussion: Background Penetrating trauma accounts for up to 20% of paediatric trauma admissions in the United States of America, with management of these injuries guided by specific anatomic location [2]. Writing instruments in the school setting are of particular risk for penetrating injury in children [2,3]. Large prospective studies assessing the incidence of injury from writing utensils are not currently available. Clinical Perspective One of the largest case series assessing injury from writing instruments at a large urban paediatric hospital identified 14 such injuries over a 5-year period: 9 involved the head and neck (one resulting in death from transhemispheric brain injury after orbital penetration), 1 the chest, 2 the bladder/perineum, and 2 the extremities [4]. Of the 14 cases, 8 required surgical intervention to remove the foreign body and/or treat penetrating injury. In another series, 1 case of penetrating brain injury due to accidental trauma from a pencil was reported with resultant intact neurological function [5]. One case report illustrates trauma to the chest from a pencil in a 2-year-old [6]. In these instances, operative intervention is recommended even if the patient is haemodynamically stable, due to the possibility of proximity of the foreign object to critical vascular structures that the object may be occluding. Imaging Perspective Pre-operative contrast-enhanced CT is used to identify the proximity of the foreign body to critical neurovascular structures and to determine the optimal operative approach in the event of rapid bleeding upon removal. Attention should be made to small fragments, which may result in subsequent infection. Echocardiography may exclude the possibility of cardiac rhythm alteration or tamponade [6]. There should be a low threshold for imaging, given that children may bleed up to 50% of their blood volume into their chest and may not show haemodynamic alteration prior to losing up to 30% of their blood volume [7]. Outcome This case details trauma to the chest in a school-aged child related to falling onto a pencil. Although haemodynamically stable on presentation, prompt CT demonstrated proximity of the injury to the left superior pulmonary vein and left upper lobe bronchus, placing the patient at risk for pulmonary haemorrhage or pneumothorax. Parenchymal injury to the lung was graded as AAST 2. The patient was discharged home in stable condition 48 hours after the operative removal. Take Home Message / Teaching Points This case illustrates the utility of contrast-enhanced CT and of a multidisciplinary approach for risk analysis in determining the best approach to treating penetrating trauma to the chest from a writing utensil in a school-aged child. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Organophosphate-linked amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: An uncommon case in agricultural work
clinical_history: We report the case of a 29-year-old male farmer with a history of prolonged exposure to organophosphates. He presented with progressive lower limb motor weakness over two years, with preserved cognitive and intellectual functions.
imaging_findings: A cerebromedullary MRI revealed bilateral and symmetric T2 hyperintensity in the centrum semiovale, the posterior limb of the internal capsule, and along the corticospinal tracts, accompanied by a slight hyperintensity on DWI sequences and no enhancement following gadolinium administration (Figures 1a, 1b, 1c, 2, 3a, and 3b). The spinal cord sequences showed no abnormalities (Figures 4a and 4b). An electroneuromyography (ENMG) demonstrated findings consistent with both active and chronic denervation, including fibrillation potentials, positive sharp waves, large polyphasic motor unit potentials, reduced motor unit recruitment, and preserved sensory nerve conduction.
discussion: Background Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), or Charcot disease, is a rapidly progressive and fatal neurodegenerative disorder marked by degeneration of upper motor neurons in the motor cortex and lower motor neurons in the spinal cord and brainstem. This results in progressive paralysis and eventual death, usually from respiratory failure. It is the most common adult-onset paralytic disease, with 90–95% of cases occurring sporadically, suggesting strong environmental contributions. Among the implicated factors, chronic exposure to organophosphates (OPs)—used in agriculture, industry, and as nerve agents—has been associated with increased ALS risk in farmers, soccer players, and Gulf War veterans. Despite extensive study, mechanisms remain unclear, limiting therapeutic advances [1,2]. Clinical Perspective ALS typically presents with progressive motor weakness, muscle atrophy, and bulbar or diaphragmatic involvement, while cognition and sensation are preserved. A distinctive finding is the “split hand sign”. Diagnosis is based on El Escorial criteria, requiring evidence of both lower and upper motor neuron degeneration, progressive spread of symptoms, and exclusion of alternative causes [1,2]. OPs exposure is of particular interest: unlike OP-induced delayed neuropathy caused by acute high doses, ALS is thought to arise from chronic, low-level exposure. Veterans exposed to OP-related prophylaxis showed doubled ALS incidence, reinforcing this link [2,3]. Imaging Perspective MRI is central to ALS evaluation, mainly to exclude mimics. Subtle supportive findings may include [3,4]: Corticospinal tract hyperintensity on T2/FLAIR in the internal capsule, centrum semiovale, or ventral brainstem, though nonspecific. Motor cortex hypointensity on T2, though rarely seen, possibly reflecting iron deposition or gliosis. Brain atrophy, typically mild, but extending beyond the motor cortex to frontal, temporal, and parietal regions; more severe in ALS with frontotemporal dementia. White matter loss, particularly in the corpus callosum and cerebellum, has also been reported. Outcome Treatment focuses on symptom control, slowing progression, and mitigating toxic effects. Acute OP poisoning is treated with atropine and pralidoxime, whereas chronic exposure is managed with antioxidants and neuroprotective agents. Standard ALS therapies—riluzole, edaravone, respiratory and nutritional support—are complemented by physical therapy and lifestyle measures to reduce ongoing OP exposure. Experimental approaches and palliative care remain essential for maintaining quality of life [4,5]. The treatment plan for our patient focused on symptomatic management with riluzole, physical therapy, and antioxidants, while addressing any potential acute or chronic effects of OP toxicity and providing psychological and palliative care. Take Home Message MRI and neuroimaging are key to excluding amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) mimics in farmers with progressive weakness. While MRI may be normal, corticospinal tract hyperintensity can support diagnosis in appropriate clinical settings. Chronic organophosphate (OP) exposure in agricultural workers represents a potential ALS risk and should be systematically assessed. Combining imaging with detailed occupational history improves diagnostic accuracy and highlights the role of environmental contributors in neurodegeneration. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Ketamine-induced uropathy
clinical_history: Case 1, a male in his 20s, and Case 2, a male in his 40s, both presented with progressively worsening flank pain and macroscopic haematuria accompanied by variable lower urinary tract symptoms, including urinary dribbling, frequency, urgency, and dysuria. Neither patient had a history of renal calculi or prior urological interventions. Systemic features such as fever, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms were absent. In both cases, there was a longstanding history of recreational ketamine use.
imaging_findings: Case 1 underwent an unenhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c) due to impaired renal function, while Case 2 had a single portal venous phase contrast-enhanced CT (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). Imaging in both patients demonstrated moderate hydroureteronephrosis (Figures 1a and 2a), without evidence of calculi. The ureters showed diffuse urothelial thickening (Figures 1b and 2b), extending distally into the urinary bladder. The bladder appeared tense with small volume capacity, and with diffuse circumferential wall thickening (Figures 1c and 2c).
discussion: Background Ketamine uropathy is a chronic condition associated with prolonged recreational ketamine use. The urinary bladder and ureters are the primary sites affected, owing to the direct toxic effects of ketamine and its metabolites on the urothelium. This urothelial injury initiates an inflammatory cascade, resulting in tissue fibrosis, ischemia, and progressive loss of bladder compliance and capacity [1]. Clinical Perspective Ketamine uropathy most commonly presents with lower urinary tract symptoms, including urgency, frequency, dysuria, haematuria, and pelvic or suprapubic pain. In advanced or untreated cases, the upper urinary tract becomes involved, leading to obstructive uropathy and progressive renal impairment. Imaging, particularly ultrasound and CT, have a crucial role in the diagnosis and provides a baseline for guiding further management [2]. Imaging Perspective Imaging enables a detailed assessment of the extent of urinary tract involvement in ketamine uropathy. Ultrasound may demonstrate focal or diffuse bladder wall thickening, intramural calcifications, and variable degrees of hydronephrosis [3]. CT largely contributes to the evaluation of disease extent and severity, and exclusion of malignancy in patients presenting with haematuria. Typical CT features include mucosal enhancement, diffuse or localised bladder wall thickening, and a reduced bladder capacity. As the clinical presentation often overlaps with urinary tract infections and interstitial cystitis, integration of imaging findings with the clinical context is essential for accurate diagnosis [3]. Outcome Early recognition and timely management of ketamine-induced uropathy are crucial to alleviate symptoms and prevent potential irreversible upper urinary tract damage. Complete cessation of ketamine use is mandatory, which may permit partial recovery if initiated promptly. Adjunctive measures include anti-inflammatory agents, anticholinergics, and intravesical botulinum toxin injections. In severe or refractory cases, surgical options such as bladder augmentation or ureteral reimplantation may be necessary [4]. Take Home Message In patients presenting with reduced bladder capacity and diffuse urothelial thickening, ketamine-induced uropathy should be considered, particularly in the appropriate clinical context. As individuals may be reluctant to disclose ketamine use, and presenting symptoms are often nonspecific, the attention of radiologists must be drawn to this condition with these imaging features. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Life-threatening lower gastrointestinal bleeding in Crohn’s disease with cytomegalovirus coinfection
clinical_history: A 26-year-old woman with Crohn’s disease presented with rectal bleeding, loose stools, and fever. Colonoscopy showed colonic ulcers with adherent clots, treated with adrenaline and haemoclips. She later developed massive rectal bleeding with haemodynamic instability and rapid haemoglobin drop (9 to 6.2 g/dL), necessitating urgent computed tomographic angiography during hospitalisation.
imaging_findings: CT angiogram demonstrated stratified mural thickening with skip lesions extending from the ascending to the sigmoid colon, along with increased mesocolic vascularity and small locoregional lymph nodes, but no evidence of active contrast extravasation (Figure 1). Histopathological analysis of colonoscopic biopsy specimens and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests confirmed active Crohn’s disease with concomitant cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. Following clinical deterioration, a repeated CT angiogram was performed, which revealed active arterial-phase contrast extravasation into the ascending colonic lumen, originating from a branch of the ileocolic artery (Figure 2). Progressive accumulation of contrast on delayed phases confirmed ongoing haemorrhage. Given critical instability and clear active bleeding on CT, immediate angioembolisation was preferred. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) validated the findings, identifying a single actively bleeding ileocolic branch of superior mesenteric artery (SMA) (Figure 3). Superselective catheterisation (Figure 4) and embolisation were performed using two 2 × 20 mm microcoils. The post-embolisation angiogram demonstrated complete haemostasis with preserved perfusion of the surrounding bowel segments (Figure 5). Celiac, SMA, and inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) angiogram showed no other active bleeders. No procedure-related complications were encountered.
discussion: Background Crohn’s disease is a chronic inflammatory disorder with transmural bowel involvement, typically presenting with abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss, melena, and anaemia. Although gastrointestinal bleeding is common, severe life-threatening haemorrhage requiring emergent endovascular or surgical intervention is rare, occurring in only 0.6–5.5% of cases [1]. The mean age at presentation is approximately 30 years, with reported cases typically ranging between 27 and 45 years [1]. Recent studies suggest CMV coinfection is associated with intensified mucosal inflammation, deep ulcerations, and erosions, leading to vascular disruption and bleeding complications [2]. Risk factors for CMV coinfection include long disease duration, severe or steroid-refractory colitis, immunosuppressive or biologic therapy, and older age [3]. Clinical Perspective Massive gastrointestinal bleeding in Crohn’s disease is an uncommon but clinically complex scenario, marked by sudden onset, risk of haemodynamic compromise, and the lack of standardised treatment protocols. Initial management involves haemodynamic stabilisation and resuscitation. Although endoscopy is typically the first-line diagnostic and therapeutic tool, its utility may be limited in the setting of diffuse inflammation obscuring the bleeding source, coexisting strictures limiting endoscopic access, and active haemorrhage, impairing visibility [1]. Additionally, the presence of CMV coinfection in our case necessitated the initiation of antiviral therapy and delayed the use of immunosuppressive biologics, which are otherwise effective in controlling both inflammation and bleeding [2–5]. Imaging Perspective When endoscopic evaluation is limited, such as in cases involving the small bowel, non-negotiable strictures or active massive haemorrhage, CT angiography serves as a valuable tool for identifying the source of bleeding and guiding further management. However, for CMV colitis, colonoscopic and CT findings are nonspecific, with histology required to establish the definitive diagnosis. DSA provides both diagnostic accuracy and therapeutic options, allowing precise embolisation while reducing the need for surgery and helping to preserve bowel length. Superselective embolisation with microcoils has demonstrated high technical success rates (up to 100%) and a low rate of complications, offering a prompt and effective approach to controlling bleeding [1,6]. In our case, coils were selected to minimise bowel ischemia, which is more commonly associated with liquid agents. Distal superselective embolisation in the vasa recta was performed, an approach ideal for reducing bowel ischemia and rebleeding. Intra-arterial vasopressin infusion is an alternative when embolisation is limited by diffuse disease or inability to achieve superselective catheterisation [7]. Outcome The patient remained stable following the procedure, with no further episodes of bleeding, and surgical intervention was avoided. CMV colitis was managed with antiviral therapy, while corticosteroids were continued. The patient was discharged in a stable condition, with plans to commence biologic therapy upon completion of antiviral treatment. This case highlights the importance of close clinical monitoring, timely imaging, and appropriate therapeutic intervention. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Severe, life-threatening lower gastrointestinal bleeding is an uncommon but critical complication of Crohn’s disease. Prompt utilisation of CT angiography and digital subtraction angiography (DSA) can be lifesaving in acute settings. Superselective embolisation offers a safe and effective minimally invasive alternative, potentially eliminating the need for bowel resection. Co-existing cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection increases mucosal fragility and bleeding risk, while also necessitating a temporary pause in immunosuppressive biologic therapy. Coordinated multidisciplinary management is crucial to achieving favourable clinical outcomes.

title: Extrapulmonary enigma: Tubercular wrist arthritis with ankylosis
clinical_history: A woman in her 30s presented with a 4–5 year history of right wrist pain, initially diagnosed as seronegative inflammatory arthritis based on weakly positive ANA-IF tests and negative rheumatoid arthritis (RA) factor. She was started on immunosuppressants, but was inconsistent with follow-up. Her symptoms worsened over time, leading to restriction of movements.
imaging_findings: The initial X-ray of the right wrist, taken 4 years ago, revealed features of the Phemister triad: marginal erosions of the scaphoid, subtle juxta-articular osteopenia, reduced radiocarpal joint space, and mild soft tissue swelling (Figure 1). The current MRI showed bone marrow oedema involving the distal radius, ulna, all carpal bones, and metacarpal bases (Figure 2a), as well as extensive erosions and deformity of the carpal bones with synovial thickening displaying T1 hypointensity (Figure 2b) and T2 intermediate signal intensity (Figure 2c), leading to near-complete loss of joint space. Ankylosis between the radius and lunate was suspected. A CT scan confirmed severe joint space narrowing, juxta-articular osteopenia, deformity, erosions of the carpal bones, and bony fusion of the radius and lunate (Figure 3). The left wrist was normal. These findings were consistent with advanced tubercular arthritis.
discussion: Background Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major public health issue in developing countries, especially among immunocompromised individuals, and due to emerging drug resistance. Pulmonary TB accounts for 70–80% of cases, while extrapulmonary TB makes up 15–20%. Of these, only about a third involve the osteoarticular system, most commonly the spine, hip, and knee. TB of the wrist is rare, comprising less than 1% of extrapulmonary cases, and often requires a high index of suspicion for diagnosis [1,2]. TB wrist may occur primarily or follow pulmonary TB or trauma. In a study by Yushan et al., only 9 of 84 patients had prior pulmonary TB, 24 had a history of trauma, and 51 had no TB history [3]. Clinical Perspective Clinically, TB osteoarthritis presents as a monoarticular disease with vague symptoms like swelling and pain, often without the classic signs of inflammation. Its slow course can lead to delayed diagnosis and complications. Pyogenic arthritis, in contrast, usually progresses rapidly. TB may rarely present acutely in immunocompromised individuals [4]. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a key differential, typically shows bilateral involvement and seropositivity for RA factor [5]. Imaging Perspective In early stages of TB arthritis, X-ray and CT may reveal the “Phemister triad”: juxta-articular osteopenia, bone erosions, and gradual joint space narrowing [2]. In advanced cases, carpal erosions and subchondral cysts may produce a moth-eaten appearance. Delayed treatment can lead to ankylosis. MRI is the preferred investigation modality, showing early marrow oedema (T2/PDFS hyperintensity), joint effusion, and synovitis. TB synovium characteristically exhibits low to intermediate T2 signal intensity. Erosions are observed in about 70% of cases. Diagnosis Misdiagnosis is common in cases of TB arthritis. Our case was initially mistaken for inflammatory arthritis due to a weakly positive ANA (antinuclear antibody) report and treated with immunosuppressants, which worsened the TB due to immune suppression. Immunosuppressants are known to cause reactivation of pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB [6]. ANA is a known confounding factor as it can occur transiently in infections like TB, potentially misleading clinicians. It is important to use caution while interpreting these reports, especially in countries endemic for TB, and they should be interpreted alongside clinical and imaging findings [7]. Definitive diagnosis requires synovial fluid aspiration, though it may be challenging in severely deformed or ankylosed joints. Ultrasound-guided aspiration can be helpful. Due to high suspicion of a tubercular aetiology in our case, an interferon-gamma release assay ( IGRA) test, QuantiFERON, was performed and returned positive. IGRAs are useful adjuncts in diagnosing extrapulmonary TB, including osteoarticular disease, though they cannot replace microbiological or histopathological confirmation. Meta-analyses report a pooled sensitivity of 84% and specificity of 82% [8]. Compared with the tuberculin skin test (TST), they offer greater specificity in BCG-vaccinated populations, require only a single visit, and avoid false positives. In our case, IGRA was used to support the presumptive diagnosis when aspiration was unsuccessful [9]. Outcome Joint aspiration was attempted but resulted in a dry tap due to severe joint space reduction, ankylosis, and minimal effusion. The patient declined an invasive synovial biopsy. Anti-tubercular therapy (ATT) is a standard treatment. Surgery, including debridement, synovectomy, arthrodesis, or arthroplasty, may be considered in advanced cases with severe joint destruction [3]. Imaging plays a crucial role, and early diagnosis is important to help preserve and restore the range of motion and improve quality of life.

title: Iatrogenic arteriovenous fistula
clinical_history: An 84-year-old renal transplant recipient, three months post-transplant, developed obstructive hydronephrosis from a perigraft lymphocele. He was on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, steroids, and basiliximab, plus apixaban for atrial fibrillation. He presented with acute dysfunction, anaemia, and haematuria. Initial ureteral stenting failed; nephrostomy was chosen for persistent obstruction.
imaging_findings: A renal Doppler ultrasound performed one week after nephrostomy placement showed echogenic content within the renal collecting system, compatible with haematuria (Figure 1). Suspicion of a vascular lesion prompted a triple-phase angio CT. The non-contrast, arterial, and portal venous phases demonstrated early opacification of the renal vein and right common iliac vein, indicating an arteriovenous fistula (AVF) (Figures 2a and 2b). No aneurysms were detected. Catheter angiography confirmed these findings, revealing early venous filling from the renal artery. Endovascular coil embolisation was performed with successful occlusion of the fistula (Figures 3a and 3b).
discussion: Background Renal arteriovenous fistulas (RAVFs) are rare vascular anomalies that represent a direct communication between the renal artery and vein, bypassing the capillary bed. These lesions are classified into traumatic (mostly iatrogenic, such as after renal biopsy, surgery or nephrostomy) and non-traumatic (congenital or acquired) [1]. Iatrogenic RAVFs are the most frequent and typically involve a single communication that may also be associated with pseudoaneurysms resulting from vascular injury [1]. Clinical Perspective While many RAVFs are clinically silent and may be incidentally discovered during imaging for unrelated conditions, others can produce significant symptoms such as gross haematuria, flank pain, or acute urinary retention due to clot formation. Iatrogenic AVFs often present within days to weeks after the causative intervention [1,2]. In rare cases, large, high-flow fistulas may lead to high-output cardiac failure. The likelihood of a RAVF should be considered in patients with a recent history of renal interventions presenting with unexplained haematuria or haemodynamic changes. Imaging plays a pivotal role, not only in confirming the diagnosis but also in assessing the haemodynamic significance and guiding clinical decisions. The radiologist should clearly describe the location, size, flow characteristics of the fistula, and associated findings such as pseudoaneurysms or venous thrombosis [2,3]. Imaging Perspective Doppler ultrasound is often the initial diagnostic modality, showing turbulent high-velocity flow and arterialised venous waveforms. Contrast-enhanced CT angiography provides high-resolution images of renal vascular anatomy and is particularly useful for detecting early venous opacification, intraparenchymal pseudoaneurysms, and guiding interventional planning. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA), while invasive, remains the gold standard due to its detailed vascular mapping and the possibility of performing therapeutic embolisation in the same session [2,4]. In this case, CT/CTA was preferred over non-contrast MRA/TOF because of its rapid availability and superior sensitivity for detecting active bleeding and pseudoaneurysms in potentially unstable patients. MR angiography may be appropriate in stable individuals with contraindications to iodinated contrast. Outcome Small and asymptomatic RAVFs may be managed conservatively with imaging follow-up. However, symptomatic lesions or those with high flow generally require treatment. Endovascular transarterial embolisation (TAE) is the preferred method, offering high technical (100%) and clinical (96%) success rates with minimal impact on renal function [1,4]. The choice of embolic material and technique depends on the fistula’s size, flow rate, and vascular anatomy. Surgical treatment is reserved for failures or cases unsuitable for embolisation 4]. As a treatment algorithm, we propose conservative management in stable patients without imaging evidence of active bleeding or obstruction, endovascular therapy in patients with transfusion-dependent haematuria or demonstrable pseudoaneurysm/AVF, and, finally, surgery in cases of endovascular failure, unsuitable vascular anatomy, or refractory/infected lymphocele. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Renal arteriovenous fistulas (RAVFs) are uncommon but important vascular complications, often following renal procedures. Timely imaging diagnosis is essential, with Doppler US and CT as first-line modalities, and DSA for definitive evaluation and treatment. TAE is safe, effective, and organ-preserving. Radiologists play a central role in detection, characterisation and therapeutic planning. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: MRI markers and morphometric indices in progressive supranuclear palsy
clinical_history: A 69-year-old man presented with recurrent falls over 1 year, progressive difficulty in swallowing, and impaired vertical gaze. Neurological examination revealed supranuclear limitation of vertical eye movements, axial rigidity, bradykinesia, and dysarthria. There was no significant response to levodopa therapy.
imaging_findings: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated hallmark features of progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP). Mid-sagittal T2-weighted imaging showed selective midbrain atrophy with preserved pontine volume, producing the "hummingbird" sign (Figure 1a) [1]. Axial T2-weighted and T1-weighted imaging, respectively, revealed lateral concavity of the tegmentum (“morning glory” sign, Figure 1b) [2] and thinning of the tegmentum with preserved peduncles (“Mickey Mouse” sign, Figure 1c) [3]. Quantitative measurement demonstrated a reduced midbrain-to-pons width ratio (Figure 1d) [4]. Additional morphometric indices included decreased midbrain-to-pons area ratio (Figure 2a), thinning of the superior cerebellar peduncles (Figure 2c), with preserved middle cerebellar peduncles (Figure 2b). The magnetic resonance parkinsonism index (MRPI) was elevated (~62.38), supporting the diagnosis of PSP [4].
discussion: Background Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is an atypical parkinsonian tauopathy characterised by early postural instability, supranuclear gaze palsy, and axial rigidity. Neurodegeneration primarily involves the midbrain, superior cerebellar peduncles, and basal ganglia structures, producing characteristic MRI features [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Clinically, PSP often overlaps with idiopathic Parkinson’s disease, especially in early stages. However, poor response to dopaminergic therapy, vertical gaze palsy, and recurrent falls are diagnostic clues. Distinguishing PSP from Parkinson’s disease and multiple system atrophy is vital, as prognosis and therapeutic strategies differ substantially. Imaging is requested to support diagnosis, rule out mimics, and guide counselling of patients and families [3]. Imaging Perspective MRI plays a central role in establishing a diagnosis. Qualitative signs include the “hummingbird” sign (selective midbrain atrophy with preserved pons), the “morning glory” sign (lateral concavity of the tegmentum), and the “Mickey Mouse” sign (thinning of the tegmentum with preserved peduncles) [1–3]. Quantitative metrics further improve diagnostic confidence. A reduced midbrain-to-pons ratio and elevated MRPI provide reproducible markers with high sensitivity and specificity for PSP [4]. In this case, both qualitative and morphometric findings corroborated the clinical suspicion. Pathological confirmation, though not performed in this patient, has consistently validated these imaging markers in prior studies. Outcome PSP is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with limited therapeutic options. Symptomatic treatment with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and speech therapy is beneficial. Levodopa provides minimal and transient benefit. Accurate radiological diagnosis allows realistic prognostication, avoids unnecessary trials of dopaminergic therapy, and helps in planning supportive care and fall-prevention strategies. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Qualitative MRI signs (hummingbird, morning glory, Mickey Mouse) combined with quantitative measures (midbrain-to-pons ratio, MRPI) provide reliable and specific imaging markers for progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP). Radiologists should recognise these features to distinguish PSP from other parkinsonian syndromes. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Cellular angiofibroma of the prostate: A rare location
clinical_history: A 72-year-old male presented with progressive lower urinary tract symptoms and acute urinary retention. Cross-sectional imaging identified a large pelvic mass with additional satellite lesions, compressing adjacent structures. He was referred to an oncological specialised hospital.
imaging_findings: MRI demonstrates a large lesion arising from the prostate, with heterogeneous signal intensity on sagittal and axial T2-weighted images (Figures 1a and 1b). Hyperintense areas suggest myxoid components, while hypointense regions exhibit avid enhancement after gadolinium-based contrast administration (Figure 1d), consistent with fibrotic tissue. The lesion has well-defined margins, appears homogeneously hypointense on T1-weighted imaging (Figure 1c), and shows no diffusion restriction (Figures 1e and 1f). It displaces the bladder (asterisk) and small bowel loops medially, and the rectum posteriorly. Two additional tumour foci are identified: one within the mesorectal fat (orange arrows, Figures 2a, 2b, 2c, and 2d) and another involving the right puborectalis muscle (blue arrows, Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c). The imaging findings suggest a locally aggressive yet well-circumscribed neoplasm with potential for multifocal involvement, highlighting the importance of assessing both the primary tumour extent and secondary foci in adjacent pelvic compartments for optimal treatment planning.
discussion: Background Cellular angiofibroma (CAF) is an uncommon benign mesenchymal tumour, equally frequent in both sexes. In men, it is usually seen in the inguinoscrotal region during the seventh decade of life. Originally characterised by Nucci et al. in 1997 [1], this neoplasm is defined histologically by two predominant components: bland spindle-shaped cells and a prominent vascular network [1–3]. Although predominantly found in the genital region, CAF has also been documented in both pelvic and extrapelvic locations [4]. Clinical Perspective When a cellular angiofibroma arises in the prostate, lower urinary tract symptoms are the most commonly reported clinical manifestation. Although the imaging characteristics of cellular angiofibroma are non-specific, radiological assessment plays a crucial role in excluding more aggressive neoplasms. Certain imaging findings may be suggestive of a mesenchymal origin. Imaging Perspective On ultrasound, an enlarged prostate may be seen. On MRI, prostatic cellular angiofibroma typically appears as a well-circumscribed, encapsulated mass with a heterogeneous internal architecture and heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted images, reflecting the fibrous and myxoid areas. It is usually hypointense on T1-weighted MRI sequences. Post-contrast sequences reveal marked and homogeneous enhancement of the solid soft-tissue component. Up to half of cellular angiofibromas may show fat. It usually does not show areas of restricted diffusion [5,6]. While not specific, these imaging features may suggest a mesenchymal tumour and help distinguish it from more aggressive prostate cancers [5]. Outcome Local excision with negative margins is usually curative due to the low risk of recurrence and metastatic potential. Rare cases of local recurrence without distant dissemination have been described [6,7]. Accordingly, surgical removal followed by clinical surveillance is considered an appropriate long-term approach. Take Home Message Prostatic cellular angiofibromas are rare benign mesenchymal tumours that can resemble malignancy, and are usually large at diagnosis. MRI can suggest a mesenchymal origin, but diagnosis depends on histology. Surgical excision is typically curative, with follow-up being the recommended management to avoid unnecessary treatment.

title: Exploding fat: Ruptured intracranial dermoid cyst
clinical_history: A 19-year-old male with a history of moderate traumatic brain injury presented with new-onset neurological symptoms. While at work, the patient developed dizziness, collapsed, had one episode of vomiting and retrograde amnesia for the event and for the preceding three days. Witnesses reported no abnormal movements or loss of consciousness.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced CT of the brain showed a bilobulated fat-density lesion in the right temporal lobe measuring 17 × 23 × 44 mm, with peripheral and septal calcifications. Fat attenuation material was seen disseminated within the subarachnoid space of both hemispheres, consistent with rupture dermoid cyst. Midline structures were preserved, and there was no hydrocephalus or evidence of ischemia.
discussion: Background Intracranial dermoid cysts are exceedingly rare lesions with distinctive embryologic and imaging features. While typically benign and slow-growing, rupture—either spontaneous or secondary to trauma—can significantly alter the clinical course [1–3]. Clinical Perspective The release of lipid material into cerebrospinal fluid spaces can trigger an inflammatory response, resulting in symptoms such as headache, seizures, focal neurological deficits, or chemical meningitis [1–3,6]. Symptom severity correlates with the extent of dissemination and the rupture site. Imaging Perspective Radiologic diagnosis is straightforward when fat droplets are seen within the subarachnoid space or ventricles. MRI (T1-weighted and fat-suppressed sequences) is particularly sensitive for detecting fat, while CT effectively depicts fat attenuation and calcifications (see the Imaging Findings section above). Preoperative imaging should evaluate the cyst’s relationship with neurovascular structures to guide surgical planning [7–9]. Outcome Total surgical excision is curative and prevents recurrence. However, adherence to critical structures may require subtotal resection. Intraoperative rupture should be avoided to minimise dissemination and the risk of postoperative chemical meningitis. Corticosteroids can be used perioperatively to control inflammatory symptoms. Take Home Message This case underscores the importance of early recognition of radiologic hallmarks, particularly in trauma-related settings, and highlights the need for individualised surgical strategies based on lesion location and patient presentation. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Thymic hyperplasia due to Graves’ disease
clinical_history: A 55-year-old woman with a recent diagnosis of Graves–Basedow disease and a history of non-invasive urothelial bladder carcinoma, treated by tumour resection. She has remained stable for two years under urological follow-up, during which no mediastinal lymphadenopathy or evidence of distant urothelial disease has been observed. The patient tested negative for autoimmune markers related to myasthenia gravis.
imaging_findings: As part of the urological follow-up, a thoracoabdominal computed tomography (CT) scan, performed without contrast due to the recent diagnosis of hyperthyroidism, revealed no mediastinal lymphadenopathy or signs of distant urothelial disease (Figures 1a and 1b). However, it demonstrated an increased density in the anterior mediastinal fat without signs of mass effect (Figures 1a and 1b), suggestive of a newly developed suspicious thymic enlargement. A thymic gland with pyramidal morphology and homogeneous appearance with intraglandular fatty streaks was visualised (Figures 1c and 1d), compatible with thymic hyperplasia, likely secondary to Graves–Basedow disease. This finding was not present in previous studies (Figures 2a and 2b), where no mediastinal lymphadenopathy or evidence of distant urothelial disease was observed.
discussion: Background Thymic hyperplasia (TH) in the context of Graves’ disease (GD) is a rare finding, with very few cases documented in the literature [1]. TH is generally benign and of uncertain pathogenesis. It is proposed that TH may result from a combination of autoimmune and hormonal factors that stimulate thymic growth [1,2]: Autoimmune stimulation: In Graves’ disease, the immune system produces high levels of antibodies that stimulate the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which is also found in extrathyroidal tissues such as the thymus, resulting in glandular enlargement. Excess thyroid hormones: The hyperthyroid state (elevated T3 and T4 levels) has a trophic and proliferative effect on thymic tissue. TH is usually reversible once the hyperthyroidism is treated. There are two forms of TH: the follicular form and true hyperplasia. For diagnosis, radiological features on CT or MRI, and reduction in size after antithyroid treatment are key. Imaging Perspective On CT scan, imaging characteristics include a homogeneous mediastinal mass with pyramidal shape, lacking calcifications, septa, or cystic components, and with no invasion into adjacent structures (Figure 1) [3,4]. In case of doubt, MRI provides additional information (chemical shift for fat, which is absent in thymic tumours; T2 hyperintensity to differentiate it from cysts [3,4]; MRI with contrast to highlight septa present within a cystic thymoma, etc.). Alternatively, a follow-up CT scan at three months can be performed. On octreoscan, TH does not demonstrate octreotide uptake, whereas thymic tumours typically do [3,4]. FDG-PET is useful for evaluating potential thymic malignancy but is limited by physiological FDG uptake in the thymus, particularly before puberty and occasionally in young adults [1,3,4]. Diagnosis In this case, the patient had Graves’ disease, tested negative for myasthenia gravis antibodies, and showed no evidence of mediastinal lymphadenopathy or distant urothelial disease. Therefore, her thymic hyperplasia was attributed to Graves’ disease. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Intrascrotal and extratesticular epidermoid cyst – An extremely rare case
clinical_history: A 58-year-old man with no relevant medical history presented with a long-standing, painless right-sided scrotal nodule, confirmed on physical examination with the absence of erythema or inflammatory signs. Laboratory tests for chorionic gonadotropin hormone and alpha-fetoprotein were negative.
imaging_findings: Ultrasonography identified a well-circumscribed, oval right intrascrotal extratesticular mass measuring 16 × 10 mm, associated with a moderate ipsilateral hydrocele. The lesion exhibited the characteristic “onion ring” pattern together with a central echogenic target-like feature (Figure 1) and showed no vascular flow on colour Doppler imaging (Figure 2). Both testes appeared normal (Figures 3a and 3b).
discussion: Background Epidermoid cysts (ECs) are rare benign lesions filled with keratin, accounting for approximately 1–2% of all testicular tumours. Despite their rarity, they represent the most common benign neoplasm arising within the testis [1,3], while extratesticular presentation is exceedingly uncommon [5]. Clinical Perspective ECs usually present in young adulthood, with a median age of 26 years, although cases have also been reported in prepubertal patients (age range 11–34 years) [2,7]. Most ECs are asymptomatic and are often detected incidentally during routine physical examination. In some cases, however, patients may report mild pain or discomfort [1]. They may occur as multiple and/or bilateral lesions [5]. Imaging Perspective The most frequently described ultrasonographic features include: Mural calcifications, with scattered or dense foci deposits, are the most common pattern [1–6]. Well-circumscribed, round to oval-shaped lesions with the classic “onion ring” appearance, characterised by alternating hyperechoic and hypoechoic concentric layers, corresponding to keratin debris surrounded by keratinising squamous epithelium [1–6]. Target-like pattern, with a hypoechoic rim and a central echogenic core [1–6]. Although they may appear solid, ECs are cystic lesions, typically showing no internal vascular flow on colour Doppler. Characteristics as ill-defined margins or internal heterogeneity may be suggestive of malignancy [6]. ECs are benign lesions, although they can be associated with invasive germ cell tumours, particularly teratomas [3]. Rare reports describe cases initially interpreted as “simple” ECs on preoperative imaging, which were later found to be associated with embryonal carcinoma or germ cell neoplasia in situ [3]. Outcome When EC is suspected radiologically, the urologist may consider intraoperative frozen section analysis, biopsies of adjacent testicular tissue, and possibly testis-sparing surgery. Nevertheless, many surgeons still prefer orchiectomy rather than enucleation, since sonographic findings are nonspecific and cannot reliably distinguish ECs from malignant testicular tumours [7]. Take Home Message Therefore, the diagnosis of epidermoid cyst (EC) should be considered whenever a scrotal mass demonstrates the “onion ring” pattern on ultrasound in the absence of Doppler vascularity. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Sacral insufficiency fractures: An axial spondyloarthropathy impersonator
clinical_history: A 74-year-old female presented to her GP with an acute onset of pain in her lower back, buttocks, thighs and pubic region, of 6 months duration after gardening. She was previously very active, but she now requires a stick for outdoor activities due to the worsening pain.
imaging_findings: The initial pelvic radiograph revealed oval lucencies in the left hip and recommended MRI to rule out malignancy. The MRI pelvis confirmed that the hip appearances were related to osteoarthritis. However, there was diffuse bone marrow oedema in both sacral alae adjacent to the sacroiliac joints (SIJs) (Figure 1), along with erosions and oedema around the pubic symphysis. The initial report suggested that these findings together could represent an axial spondyloarthropathy (AxSpA) and recommended rheumatology referral. Dual-energy CT (DE-CT) performed after multi-disciplinary team (MDT) discussion showed no erosions in the SIJs, but noted a lucent line with a sclerotic margin in the right sacral ala (Figure 2). Follow-up MRI displayed interval reduction in marrow oedema in the sacral alae and pubic symphysis, and new T1 hypointense lines parallel to both sacral alae. (Figures 3a and 3b). Overall appearances were of resolving sacral insufficiency fractures and separate osteitis pubis, not AxSpA.
discussion: Background Sacral insufficiency fractures (SIFs) are a subtype of stress fractures, whereby there is normal stress on abnormal bone, occurring in the sacral alae parallel to the sacroiliac joints [1]. The most common cause is osteoporosis, and, therefore, the majority of cases occur in postmenopausal women. Sacroiliitis and osteitis pubis are both manifestations of AxSpAs, but would typically present before the age of 45 in 92% of cases [2]. Clinical Perspective SIFs typically present with lower back pain causing reduced mobility, without a history of significant trauma. It can pose a diagnostic challenge due to nonspecific symptoms, lack of positive laboratory tests and misinterpretation of imaging findings [3]. Our patient presented with typical symptoms of SIFs and had normal blood results, including inflammatory markers. In addition, her gender, age at presentation, short history and onset of symptoms after a day of gardening pointed away from a diagnosis of AxSpA. This led to a radiology review of her imaging in MDT to revise the original MRI diagnosis. Imaging Perspective The gold standard imaging test for SIFs is MRI, which has a 99% sensitivity [1]. The presence of both oedema on STIR and T1 hypointense fracture lines in the sacral alae with a non-traumatic history is diagnostic [1]. However, uncertainty has been noted in cases without a clear fracture line, such as our case [4]. Originally, AxSpA was considered as the oedema on MRI extended from the sacral alae to the SIJs. On review, the oedema was centred on the sacral alae rather than the SIJs, which was more in favour of SIFs. There were also no other features to suggest an AxSpA, such as joint erosions or fat metaplasia. Furthermore, the pubic symphysis appearances added to the diagnostic uncertainty. It was eventually diagnosed as idiopathic osteitis pubis, as there were classic findings (erosions and bone marrow oedema) and no clinical evidence of infection. Follow-up imaging played a key role in confirming the diagnoses, as it showed characteristic hypointense T1 lines indicating healing fractures in the sacral alae bilaterally. Outcome SIFs are managed conservatively with pain management and treatment of the underlying cause, in this case osteoporosis [3]. If the patient had been misdiagnosed, not only would her osteoporosis be left untreated, but she would have been commenced on biologic treatment for the rest of her life with its associated risks. Take Home Message Radiology reports should be interpreted in the context of the patient’s clinical presentation to avoid misdiagnosis. Evolution of MRI appearances from STIR hyperintensity (oedema) to T1 hypointense fracture lines represents a classic appearance of stress fractures. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Giant intradiploic epidermoid cyst of the occipital bone
clinical_history: A man in his late sixties presented with neck pain and restricted neck movement, preceded by episodes of intermittent dizziness, blackouts, difficulty walking and balance disturbance. His medical history included cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, hyperlipidaemia, non-alcoholic hepatic steatosis and type 2 diabetes mellitus complicated by nephropathy, neuropathy and peripheral vascular disease.
imaging_findings: Initial MRI spine showed a posterior cranial fossa extradural lesion extending from the occipital bone through the foramen magnum to the C1 vertebral body level (Figure 1). CT head showed the cystic lesion with calcified zones from the left occipital bone eroding the outer cortical table, with midline extension and early right occipital bone involvement (Figure 2). MRI brain non-contrast (due to nephropathy) visualised the 6 x 9 cm mass impinging on the left cerebellar hemisphere, compressing the left posterior brainstem, with left petrous temporal outer table erosion and early occipital outer table destruction near the occipital suture (Figure 3). It showed hyperintensity with low intra-tumoural signal on T2, hypointensity with high intra-tumoural signal on T1 and FLAIR and restricted diffusion with classic hyperintensity on DWI with corresponding low ADC signal. The patient was diagnosed with a giant intradiploic epidermoid cyst and underwent posterior fossa craniectomy with tumour decompression and mesh cranioplasty.
discussion: Background Epidermoid cysts are rare, benign tumours accounting for less than 2% of all intracranial tumours, occurring within the first seven decades of life [1]. Epidermoid cysts may be congenital, arising from vestigial ectodermal tissues during neural tube closure, subsequently remaining in the cranial bones, or acquired from post-traumatic or post-surgical implantation [2,3]. Intradiploic epidermoid cysts are an extradural subtype accounting for only ~10–25% of all epidermoid cysts and may occur in any skull diploë [4–6]. Giant intradiploic epidermoid cysts can reach impressive sizes, extending through the dura and causing mass effect on the underlying parenchyma. Once over 5 cm, these are classified as giant Intradiploic epidermoid cysts, which are extremely rare with limited reported cases [5,7]. Clinical Perspective Intradiploic epidermoid cysts classically present as a painless, indolent, well-defined scalp swelling. However, they can grow quite large without neurological symptoms, often presenting later on in life. Occasionally, they invade the underlying dura, extending into the brain parenchyma, causing progressive non-specific or neurological symptoms, such as in this case. Imaging Perspective On plain radiograph, these lesions are characteristically well-delineated, rounded or lobulated with sclerotic or scalloped margins. CT scan classically demonstrates a hypodense, non-enhancing extradural lesion with well-defined bony defects and calcified regions, more often affecting the inner than the outer skull table. MRI scan displays an extradural lesion, iso/hyperintense to cerebrospinal fluid on T2-weighted sequence and slightly hyperintense on T1-weighted sequence with restricted diffusion areas. They do not demonstrate contrast enhancement. Outcome An indication for neurosurgery is raised intracranial pressure and neurological fallout caused by intradural extension and parenchymal extension. When giant intradiploic epidermoid cysts extend into the posterior cranial fossa, they can invade vital structures such as the brainstem and fourth ventricle and result in obstructive hydrocephalus. In these instances, neurosurgical intervention is required. Conclusions The purpose of this case report is to enhance the database of cases available for review and contribute to the growing body of knowledge surrounding these rare tumours. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Central pontine myelinolysis
clinical_history: A 38-year-old woman presented with chronic vomiting, bowel changes, weight loss and delirium with seizures. Labs revealed hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia. Rapid sodium correction led to subsequent quadriparesis with bulbar symptoms, consistent with osmotic demyelination syndrome. There was some improvement in her speech; however, the quadriparesis persisted despite the intervention.
imaging_findings: A non-contrast brain computed tomography (CTB) was done on admission and was noted to be normal. A repeat CTB was done 14 days after admission and showed an area of hypoattenuation (25 x 15 x 16 mm) that was well-defined and crossed the midline within the pons (Figures 1a and 1b). There was no associated mass effect, hydrocephalus or haemorrhage. A non-contrast MRI was done 3 days later and noted increased T2 signals (Figure 2) and decreased T1 signals (Figure 3) within the central pons. DWI shows a hypointense signal (Figure 4a) and ADC shows a hyperintense lesion (Figure 4b), indicating a T2 shine-through effect and not a true restricted diffusion. This also suggests resolution of the cytotoxic oedema and persistence of myelin damage.
discussion: Background Central pontine myelinolysis (CPM) is a neurological condition most often caused by rapid correction of hyponatraemia, leading to symmetrical demyelination in pontine white matter tracts. Extrapontine involvement occurs in at least 10% of patients, affecting regions such as the midbrain, thalamus, basal nuclei, and cerebellum [1]. CPM is part of osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), with an estimated incidence of 2.5% in intensive care admissions [2]. Histologically, lesions show myelin and oligodendroglia loss with relative axonal and neuronal sparing, along with astrocytosis and infiltration by leukocytes and macrophages [3]. ODS typically arises in patients who have chronic hyponatraemia (> 48 hours) as the brain adapts to hyponatraemia by losing osmotically active organic solutes out of the cell, allowing equal osmolarity with the extracellular compartment, and consequently, this provides protection against brain swelling. However, such solutes cannot be rapidly replaced during sodium correction, resulting in astrocyte apoptosis and release of inflammatory cytokines with eventual loss of myelin from oligodendrocytes [4]. Clinical Perspective Symptoms appear 2–6 days after correction and may include dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis, seizures, confusion, and coma [5–8]. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, with emphasis on sodium correction rate. MRI is preferred but may not show changes until up to four weeks after onset, sometimes requiring repeat scans [7]. Imaging Perspective Early findings are usually on MRI with DWI hyperintensity and ADC signal loss crossing the midline [9], followed by T2/FLAIR hyperintensity sparing the periphery and corticospinal tracts. T1 images may show low signal intensity with possible gadolinium enhancement [9–11]. CT may demonstrate midline-crossing low attenuation, but it is less reliable due to the beam hardening artefact when examining the base of the skull. Outcome If ODS is suspected, intensive care management should begin without waiting for imaging. Supportive measures include ventilation, seizure prevention, and physiotherapy. Therapeutic options are limited: reinduction of hyponatraemia and immune-modulating therapies have been tried. Lowering sodium by < 16 mEq/L of initial levels using D5W and desmopressin has shown benefit in case studies [13,14]. Immune therapies, including steroids, plasmapheresis, and immunoglobulins, have also been reported [15,16]. Radiological follow-up shows lesions usually shrink at six months, with persistence possible at one year. Importantly, lesion size or persistence does not necessarily correlate with clinical outcome [12]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Preventing overcorrection of sodium remains the most effective strategy. Since osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS) symptoms typically arise after two days, and MRI changes may lag further, normal imaging does not exclude the diagnosis, and early treatment should not be delayed. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Dual rim sign in a pyogenic brain abscess
clinical_history: A 29-year-old immunocompetent woman presented with a one-week history of progressively worsening nocturnal headache, initially mild but becoming more intense and resistant to analgesics. The headache was accompanied by episodes of nausea and recurrent vomiting. Shortly before hospital admission, she experienced a syncopal event, which prompted urgent neurological evaluation.
imaging_findings: Non-contrast CT showed a right frontal intra-axial mass with surrounding oedema, significant mass effect, and midline shift (Figure 1). On MRI, the lesion was multilobulated with central T1 hypointensity (Figure 2) and marked T2/FLAIR hyperintensity (Figure 3). Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated restricted diffusion of the central cavity with corresponding low ADC values (Figures 4a and 4b), consistent with purulent material. A characteristic “dual rim sign” was identified on T2-weighted images, defined by an inner hyperintense rim (white arrow) and an outer hypointense rim (blue arrow) at the capsule–parenchyma interface (Figure 5). Post-contrast T1-weighted sequences revealed a thin, smooth peripheral ring enhancement (Figure 6), confirming capsule formation. The combination of multilobulated morphology, restricted diffusion, peripheral enhancement, and the dual rim sign strongly supported the diagnosis of a pyogenic brain abscess, helping to differentiate it from necrotic tumours or metastases.
discussion: Background Pyogenic brain abscess is a severe intracranial infection characterised by a suppurative collection within the brain parenchyma. It evolves from early cerebritis to capsule formation. The most common aetiologies are contiguous spread from sinusitis or otitis, haematogenous dissemination, and iatrogenic causes. Despite modern antibiotics and neurosurgery, morbidity and mortality remain significant [1,2]. Early neuroimaging is crucial for timely management [5]. Clinical Perspective Clinical presentation is often nonspecific. The classic triad of headache, fever, and focal neurological deficit occurs in less than half of cases [2]. Seizures, nausea, vomiting, or raised intracranial pressure may also be seen. In this patient, progressive nocturnal headache and vomiting suggested intracranial pathology. Immunocompetent status and lack of systemic signs initially reduced suspicion for abscess, highlighting the limited reliability of clinical findings alone. Imaging Perspective When evaluating ring-enhancing intracranial lesions, the most important diagnostic challenge is differentiation from necrotic tumours. Both may appear as ring-enhancing lesions with oedema. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is the most reliable discriminator: pyogenic abscesses show marked central diffusion restriction due to purulent content, while necrotic tumours usually display facilitated diffusion [2,3]. Another characteristic clue is the “dual rim sign” on T2-weighted imaging, defined by an inner hyperintense and an outer hypointense rim at the capsule–parenchyma interface, strongly favouring an abscess [4]. Thin, smooth peripheral ring enhancement and extensive vasogenic oedema also favour an abscess. Other mimics include subacute haematoma, which changes over time, tumefactive demyelination, often with open-ring enhancement, and atypical infections such as tuberculous, fungal, or parasitic abscesses [2,5]. Outcome The patient underwent urgent craniotomy and surgical drainage. Cultures grew Fusobacterium spp., confirming the infectious origin. She received prolonged targeted intravenous antibiotics, followed by oral therapy. Clinical symptoms improved rapidly, and follow-up MRI showed gradual resolution of the cavity and oedema. Take Home Message In ring-enhancing intracranial lesions, the combination of central diffusion restriction and the T2 dual rim sign strongly supports the diagnosis of pyogenic brain abscess. Early recognition is essential to distinguish abscess from necrotic tumour and to guide appropriate surgical and antimicrobial treatment [2,5].

title: Dural arteriovenous fistula mimicking diffuse hemispheric pathology
clinical_history: A 47-year-old male presented with a history of generalised tonic-clonic seizures three months ago, followed by progressive forgetfulness, imbalance, and left-sided weakness. There was no history of trauma, fever, or prior neurosurgical intervention.
imaging_findings: MRI, T2 axial, of the brain showed hyperintensity in the right frontal, parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes, as well as the gangliocapsular region, with mass effect, suggestive of vasogenic oedema. Multiple serpiginous flow voids noted in bilateral cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres, especially around the tentorium, with transosseous vessels (Figures 1a and 1b). MRI TOF (time-of-flight) demonstrated flow-related enhancement in the superior sagittal and right transverse sinuses (Figures 2a and 2b), with prominent occipital artery branches from both external carotid arteries (ECAs) and the right vertebral artery (Figure 2c). Contrast-enhanced CT showed diffuse white matter hypodensity in the right hemisphere with preserved grey–white differentiation and no acute haemorrhage (Figure 3). CT angiography revealed multiple tortuous vascular channels in bilateral cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres, prominent occipital branches, and early filling of dural sinuses (Figures 4a, 4b, 4c, and 4d), with non-opacification of the right sigmoid sinus, suggestive of chronic thrombosis (Figure 5). Digital subtraction angiography demonstrated multiple collaterals from the right occipital, left ECA, and right vertebral arteries draining into the posterior superior sagittal sinus, with retrograde cortical venous filling (Figures 6, 7, and 8), consistent with Cognard IIa+b (Figure 9).
discussion: Background Dural arteriovenous fistulas (dAVFs) are acquired intracranial vascular malformations defined by abnormal shunts between dural arteries and dural venous sinuses, meningeal veins, or cortical veins. They account for 10–15% of intracranial vascular malformations [1]. Many are clinically silent or involuted spontaneously, so the true incidence is higher. The first description of dAVFs dates to the early 20th century, when angiography revealed abnormal arterial–venous sinus connections. In 1972, Houser et al. highlighted venous hypertension in symptom development, before which they were thought to be congenital [2]. Advances in angiography have since refined classification and treatment. dAVFs are considered acquired, unlike parenchymal arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) [1]. The prevailing hypothesis is that dural sinus thrombosis or venous outflow obstruction increases venous pressure, stimulating angiogenesis in the dura. Persistent venous hypertension recruits dural arteries, usually external carotid branches, which form pathological shunts. These may drain retrogradely into cortical veins, causing venous hypertension, vasogenic oedema, seizures, cognitive decline, or haemorrhage [4]. The transverse and cavernous sinuses are the most frequent sites, but any dural location can be involved. Clinical Perspective Clinical manifestations depend on venous drainage rather than fistula size [5]. Symptoms include tinnitus, papilledema, altered sensorium, headache, seizures, or cranial nerve palsies. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) remains the gold standard for diagnosis. In the presented case, chronic thrombosis of the right sigmoid sinus and internal jugular vein likely triggered arterial recruitment and cortical venous reflux, explaining seizures and hemiparesis due to venous congestion and oedema. Imaging Perspective On CT, dAVFs may appear subtle, with findings such as parenchymal oedema, haemorrhage, or engorged cortical veins. CT angiography can show early venous opacification, irregular dural sinuses, and dilated feeders. MRI is superior, demonstrating serpiginous flow voids, venous congestion (T2/FLAIR hyperintensity), and haemorrhage. MRA identifies feeders and drainage, while SWI highlights venous hypertension. Arterial spin labelling (ASL) has emerged as a useful non-contrast technique, showing arterialised venous signal as abnormal hyperintensity in venous sinuses and cortical veins, suggestive of shunting. ASL is particularly valuable in patients where contrast is contraindicated and in follow-up. Imaging plays a pivotal role in differentiating dural arteriovenous fistula (dAVF) from its mimics. Unlike proliferative cerebral angiopathy, which shows a diffuse vascular network interspersed with normal parenchyma, dAVF demonstrates direct arteriovenous shunting without intervening brain tissue. In contrast to AVMs, which have a compact nidus within brain parenchyma, dAVFs lack a nidus and drain into dural venous sinuses or cortical veins. Moyamoya disease is characterised by progressive internal carotid artery stenosis with basal collateral networks, whereas dAVF shows venous sinus arterialisation without arterial occlusion. Similarly, chronic venous sinus thrombosis manifests as sinus non-opacification or filling defects without early venous filling, unlike the early arterialised venous drainage seen in dAVF. Classification and Management Venous drainage is described by the Borden and Cognard classifications, stratifying lesions by haemodynamics and clinical risk. Low-grade lesions (Borden I; Cognard I–IIa) are usually benign, whereas high-grade lesions (Borden II–III; Cognard IIb–V) carry a higher risk of seizures, haemorrhage, and morbidity [1,3]. DSA is essential for classification and management. Endovascular embolisation is first-line treatment, with surgery or radiosurgery reserved for refractory cases [4]. Take Home Message In summary, dural arteriovenous fistulas (dAVFs) are acquired vascular malformations related to venous hypertension after sinus thrombosis or obstruction. Prognosis depends on venous drainage. CT and MRI can suggest the diagnosis, but DSA remains indispensable for classification and treatment planning, especially for high-grade lesions with cortical venous reflux.
differential_diagnosis: Proliferative cerebral angiopathy Arteriovenous malformations Moyamoya disease Dural arteriovenous fistula Chronic venous sinus thrombosis

title: Glomangiopericytoma – An unusual sinonasal tumour
clinical_history: A 44-year-old female patient presented with worsening unilateral right nasal obstruction that began two years prior. She also reported occasional epistaxis. Physical examination revealed a polypoid, friable lesion occupying the entire right nasal fossa extending to the choanal orifice. Prior medical history was unremarkable. A computed tomography (CT) scan was ordered.
imaging_findings: CT scan (Figure 1) showed an expansile soft-tissue polypoid mass filling the right nasal fossa and the osteomeatal unit, which obstructed the right choanal orifice and protruded into the nasopharynx lumen. There was smooth bone expansion and remodelling without destruction (arrows) and complete filling of the right paranasal sinuses (PNS) that could represent post-obstructive changes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure 2) showed a nasochoanal expansile lesion, isointense to muscle on T1 (with a few spontaneously hyperintense foci) and hyperintense on T2 images with avid and homogeneous contrast enhancement and no restricted diffusion. There were no signal changes in the surrounding bone and no signs of intracranial extension. Post-obstructive changes were present in the right PNS, displaying a distinctive signal on both T2 and T1 and no enhancement. Biopsy disclosed a submucosal hypercellular tumour with a diffuse/solid, fascicular pattern composed of monomorphic spindle cells with clear/eosinophilic cytoplasm (Figure 3). Immunohistochemistry (IHC) was positive for beta-catenin. Molecular studies demonstrated a pathogenic variant of the CTNNB1 gene, leading to the final diagnosis of glomangiopericytoma.
discussion: Background Glomangiopericytomas are rare tumours of mesenchymal origin [1], thought to originate from perivascular pericytes, formerly known as sinonasal-type haemangiopericytoma, accounting for < 0.5% of all sinonasal tumours (SNT) [2–6]. They occur primarily in the nasal cavity and less frequently in the PNS [4,5]. They are classified as borderline tumours of uncertain malignant potential and, on histopathology, demonstrate a perivascular myoid differentiation pattern consisting of spindle cells packed around thin-walled branching vessels with a staghorn appearance [7]. Immunohistochemistry is positive for SMA, vimentin, cyclin D1 and beta-catenin nuclear staining and negative for vascular markers. Molecular analysis demonstrates CTNNB1 mutation. Their aetiology remains unknown [3]. Clinical Perspective Symptoms include unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis and facial pain [3–6]. These lesions are readily accessible to endoscopic examination and biopsy, and present as submucosal polypoid reddish masses in the nasal cavity. Imaging Perspective The role of imaging is to depict tumour extension prior to surgical planning, paying attention to signs of tumour aggressiveness (bone erosion, orbital, dural, or intracranial invasion). Lymph node metastasis must be sought [5]. MR is the preferred modality owing to its superior soft-tissue contrast. Key imaging features include intermediate-to-high signal intensity on T2, avid and homogeneous enhancement, the presence of blood degradation products and high ADC values. Flow voids on both T1 and T2 can also be present. On dynamic contrast-enhanced perfusion (DCE PWI), these tumours display a rapid wash-in and wash-out pattern [2]. CT is helpful to delineate bone involvement, showing an expansile and slow-growing tumour causing bone remodelling [2]. Although the combination of imaging features can suggest this entity, a tissue biopsy is necessary to reach the diagnosis [2–6]. Outcome Complete surgical resection is the preferred treatment, either through an endoscopic or an open approach, and offers the best prognosis. Pre-operative embolisation may be performed to minimise bleeding. Recurrence rates are not negligible, particularly in cases of incomplete resections, varying between 17% and 30%, and requiring long-term follow-up. Metastases are rare, with a reported rate of 5–10%, usually preceded by multiple recurrences [3–6]. Our patient underwent open surgery with complete tumour resection and is currently under clinical and imaging follow-up with no evidence of recurrence after seven months (Figure 4). Take Home Message Glomangiopericytomas are rare mesenchymal tumours arising predominantly in the nasal cavity with an indolent course. It is important to include them in the differential diagnosis of hypervascular sinonasal lesions, and both CT and MRI play a complementary role in their work-up. Ultimately, its radiologic features are non-specific, and tissue biopsy is required. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
