title: Crossed cerebellar diaschisis secondary to extensive stroke
clinical_history: A 90-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital for left hemiparesis. No personal history of interest or significant analytical alterations were present.
imaging_findings: Baseline CT showed right extensive hypodensity on the middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory related to an established ischemic lesion (Figure 1). CT angiography revealed an occlusion in the right M1 segment (Figure 2). Functional maps showed alterations in the right MCA territory with an increased mean transit time (MTT), decreased cerebral blood flow (CBF) and a globally preserved cerebral blood volume (CBV), associated with a large area of penumbra (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c). Same alterations were also observed in the left cerebellar hemisphere (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c).
discussion: Background Crossed cerebellar diaschisis (CCD) is a recognised phenomenon following cerebral infarction or other significant supratentorial lesions (haemorrhage, tumours, encephalitis, etc), consisting of an acute depression in function, metabolism and perfusion of the contralateral cerebellar parenchyma due to an interruption of the cortico-ponto-cerebellar pathway [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Although this condition is generally asymptomatic with no other clinical features or neurological deficits associated with the contralateral supratentorial lesion, the relationship between infarct volume and the severity of CCD is still up for dispute in the research. According to some reports, one of the most important elements influencing the development of CCD is the quantity of low perfusion volume in the supratentorial brain [2]. Imaging Perspective CT perfusion obtained during an acute stroke may show abnormal perfusion dates, especially affecting CBF and CBV maps [1,2] of the contralateral cerebellar hemisphere, with a mild to moderate reduction of these parameters that are not low enough to be classified as infarction. Despite the fact that brain perfusion in acute stroke cases is typically studied using CT perfusion (CTP) imaging, imaging studies of this entity based on CT perfusion have not yet been published [2]. For that reason, nuclear medicine studies should be performed to formally detect hypometabolism. Outcome No treatment other than management of the supratentorial insult is available or necessary. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Abnormal findings on CT perfusion, such as crossed cerebellar diaschisis due to a contralateral acute cerebral infarct, can be found on all types of perfusion maps (MTT, CBF, and CBV). These findings can be challenging and constitute a pitfall. Thus, the radiologist’s knowledge of this entity can be the key to interpreting the study correctly.
differential_diagnosis: Wallerian degeneration Contralateral cerebellar infarction Crossed cerebellar diaschisis Asymmetric cerebellar atrophy

title: Tubular adenoma of the breast: An uncommon benign tumour
clinical_history: A 40-year-old woman was referred to our institution for a self-detected, painless lump in her left breast. Examination revealed a soft, slightly mobile nodule with a diameter of 1 cm in the lower inner quadrant. No nipple discharge, skin changes, or palpable lymph nodes were present, and there was no relevant personal or family history.
imaging_findings: A mammogram was acquired (craniocaudal and mediolateral oblique views) showing a mass with indistinct margins, without associated calcifications, in the lower inner quadrant of the left breast (Figures 1a and 1b). Ultrasound revealed a solid mass with irregular shape and irregular margins, measuring 43 mm, with its longest axis parallel to the skin (Figures 2a and 2b). No posterior shadowing, calcifications or associated features, and skin thickening were present. The lesion was classified as BI-RADS 4b, and a core biopsy was subsequently performed, revealing a ductal adenoma. Following the initial core biopsy, a breast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was acquired for further characterisation, demonstrating an irregular, T2-hypointense mass with spiculated margins and early homogeneous enhancement (Figures 3a and 3b), followed by a plateau-type II kinetic curve (Figure 3c), features that justified an upgrade to BI-RADS 4c. Due to radiopathological discordance, a vacuum-assisted biopsy (VAB) was performed to acquire larger samples, which confirmed the initial histological diagnosis. However, after multidisciplinary discussion and in accordance with the patient’s preference, a decision was reached to surgically excise the lesion. Final histopathology revealed a tubular adenoma (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c).
discussion: Background Tubular adenoma (TA) of the breast is a rare benign epithelial neoplasm representing 0.13% to 1.7% of all benign breast tumours [1]. According to the 2019 World Health Organisation classification, TA is grouped under adenomas, alongside lactating and ductal adenomas [2]. Histologically, it comprises tightly packed uniform tubular structures, lined by epithelial and myoepithelial cells, with minimal fibrous stroma and no true capsule [1,3,4]. Clinical Perspective TA typically presents in premenopausal women, with over 90% of cases diagnosed before age 40 [5,6]. Clinically, it is indistinguishable from other benign tumours, presenting as a palpable, smooth, mobile lump, without skin or nipple involvement, usually incidentally discovered on breast examination [7]. Imaging Perspective Like the clinical presentation, the radiological features are also nonspecific. On mammography, it often appears as a well-circumscribed lesion without calcifications; though, in older women, grouped microcalcifications may be seen, prompting the need for biopsy [7,8]. Ultrasound typically shows an oval or lobulated, circumscribed, hypoechogenic and parallel-oriented mass. Nevertheless, irregular margins can occur, as in our case, raising suspicion for malignancy and reinforcing the need for biopsy [8,9]. On MRI, TAs usually show rapid and homogeneous enhancement, mirroring their uniform epithelial composition [10]. Based on the overall imaging findings, differential diagnoses include other benign tumours such as fibroadenomas, also typically circumscribed, oval and parallel-oriented lesions. However, on MRI, they may exhibit low signal non-enhancing internal septations, which show high specificity [11]. The final distinction is histopathological, and, unlike TAs, fibroadenomas have a prominent stromal component [6]. Also to be considered are lactating adenoma (in pregnant women or during the postpartum), phyllodes tumour (typically large and rapidly growing), sclerosing adenosis, and ductal adenoma [6,12]. In our case, ductal adenoma was indeed the histopathologic result obtained in the two pre-surgical biopsies. Both tumours can show epithelial proliferation and tubular structures, but ductal adenomas are confined to a single duct surrounded by a fibroelastic wall, while TAs arise from the terminal duct-lobular unit and lack encapsulation [13]. The lesion’s large size may have limited the representativeness of the VAB, precluding an accurate preoperative diagnosis. The constellation of imaging findings—large size, irregular morphology, spiculated margins and avid contrast uptake on MRI—was not fully concordant with the benign histological result. This radiology–pathology discordance raised concern for underestimation on biopsy and justified stepwise escalation from core biopsy to VAB and, ultimately, surgical excision, as decided in a multidisciplinary setting. Outcome Although benign and not associated with increased malignancy risk, excision is often required for definitive diagnosis, especially in large lesions, and in those presenting with worrying imaging features [6]. Rare reports of coexistent carcinoma within TAs exist, but these are exceptional and likely reflect incidental coexistence, rather than true malignant transformation [14]. In the present case, the patient was discharged from our breast clinic 1 month after surgery and remains under the care of her family physician. At 12-month follow-up, her breast examination was normal, with no evidence of recurrence. Teaching Points Tubular adenoma (TA) is a rare benign breast tumour typically presenting in premenopausal women. Imaging features are nonspecific and may mimic fibroadenoma or, occasionally, malignancy. While histopathology is essential for definitive diagnosis, in large lesions, biopsy may fail to capture the lesion’s full architecture. When imaging features are not fully explained by core biopsy, radiology–pathology discordance should be acknowledged; consider repeat sampling (e.g., VAB) or surgical excision following multidisciplinary discussion. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Bowel-within-bowel sign in an adult: Intestinal lipoma
clinical_history: A 53-year-old male referred to our Emergency Department with haematochezia, weight loss, and progressive clinical deterioration. Colonoscopy revealed an obstructive mass in the right colon. A right hemicolectomy was scheduled, and the diagnostic workup was completed with contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT).
imaging_findings: An abdominopelvic CT scan with intravenous contrast in the portal venous phase and oral water was performed. The classic “bowel-within-bowel” sign was visualised, with the cecal appendix contained within the intussuscepted segment (Figures 1a and 1b). Imaging also showed a 4 cm endoluminal mass in the ascending colon with fat attenuation values, serving as the lead point of an ileocolic intussusception with an invaginated segment approximately 7 cm in length (Figures 2a and 2b). No proximal bowel loop dilatation was observed. Subsequent histopathological examination identified the lesion as a submucosal lipoma in the right colon, near the cecum, confirming the absence of malignancy (Figure 4).
discussion: Background Intestinal intussusception is a rare entity in adults and is often associated with an underlying pathological lesion, with a high likelihood of malignancy, thus posing a significant diagnostic challenge. Unlike in pediatric patients, where intussusceptions are far more common, in adults they represent only about 5% of all cases and 1% of intestinal obstructions, most commonly involving the small bowel. Colonic intussusceptions, however, are more frequently linked to malignant lesions given the higher prevalence of colonic neoplasms. Nonetheless, studies of colonic intussusception indicate that roughly 30% of cases have a benign aetiology, including lipomas, polyps, other non-malignant lesions (stromal tumours, endometriosis) or prior anastomoses. Gastrointestinal (GI) tract lipomas are uncommon benign tumours that may occur anywhere along the GI tract, with a predilection for the submucosa of the colon, particularly the right colon. These lesions typically arise in middle-aged adults and show a higher incidence in females, while adenomatous polyps and carcinomas remain important differential diagnoses [1–3,6]. Clinical Perspective Colonic lipomas are generally asymptomatic but may present with rectal bleeding or obstructive symptoms, often mimicking malignancy. The risk of intussusception and symptomatic presentation is directly proportional to the size of the lesion [1,3,4]. Imaging Perspective CT is the imaging modality of choice for diagnosis, due to its ability to characterise lesions (e.g., attenuation values and typical radiologic signs), detect associated findings, and assist in preoperative planning. Additional modalities such as endoscopy and magnetic resonance (MRI) serve as complementary tools. Definitive diagnosis is confirmed via histopathological examination of the resected surgical specimen [1,5]. Outcome Most colonic lipomas are asymptomatic, and optimal management remains a subject of debate, ranging from conservative clinical observation to segmental colectomy. Treatment is generally reserved for symptomatic cases or those mimicking malignancy. In adults, intussusception is commonly an indication for urgent surgical intervention, with resective surgery being the classic therapeutic approach. Recently, endoscopic management has emerged as an effective and less invasive alternative [3,4]. Take Home Message Colonic lipomas as the underlying cause of adult intussusception are rare and diagnostically challenging. A comprehensive evaluation using clinical assessment, colonoscopy, and CT imaging constitutes the cornerstone for accurate diagnosis and appropriate therapeutic planning [3]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Cholecystocolonic fistula complicated by ischaemic and perforated colon
clinical_history: An 85-year-old female, a nursing home resident with multiple comorbidities, presented with lower abdominal pain and shock (hypotension, tachypnoea, severe lactic acidosis). Due to dementia, she was unable to provide her history.
imaging_findings: CT examination was performed including native, arterial, and venous phases. The venous phase appeared somewhat earlier than usual, likely due to the patient’s hypotensive state affecting contrast circulation dynamics. Abdominal CT revealed extensive pneumoperitoneum beneath the anterior abdominal wall, most likely due to ischaemic colonic perforation (Figure 1). A 12 mm cholecystocolonic fistula was seen at the hepatic flexure (Figures 2, 3a, 3b, and 3c). A 3 cm gallstone was impacted in the sigmoid colon, with wall thinning, hypoenhancement, pericolonic fat stranding, free fluid, and small foci of extraluminal air—features consistent with ischaemia and perforation (Figures 2, 4, 5a, 5b, and 5c). Similar hypoenhancement and mural thinning suggested ischaemia in the cecum and ascending colon (Figures 6a, 6b, and 6c). Additional findings indicated hypoperfusion syndrome: a narrow inferior vena cava, hypoenhancement of the liver and spleen, and bilateral adrenal hyperdensity (Figure 7). Subtotal stenosis of the superior mesenteric artery further compromised bowel perfusion (Figure 8).
discussion: Background Cholecystocolonic fistula is a rare complication of chronic gallbladder disease, accounting for 8–26% of biliary-enteric fistulas. It typically arises at the hepatic flexure due to the close anatomical relationship with the gallbladder. Persistent inflammation from gallstones leads to adhesions, erosion of the adjacent bowel wall, and eventual fistula formation. Less common causes include peptic ulcer disease, Crohn’s disease, diverticulitis, infection, malignancy, and trauma. The fistula allows gallstones to pass directly into the colon, which may result in obstruction, ischaemia, or perforation [1–5]. Clinical Presentation Clinically, presentations are often nonspecific, including abdominal pain, diarrhoea, or features of bowel obstruction. In elderly multimorbid patients, especially those with cognitive impairment, recognition of symptoms may be delayed, making imaging crucial for diagnosis [1,4,5]. Imaging Perspective CT is the modality of choice, as it enables direct visualisation of the fistula, impacted gallstones, and complications such as pneumoperitoneum and ischaemic bowel. Signs of ischaemia include mural thinning, hypoenhancement, pericolonic fat stranding, free fluid, and extraluminal air. In our case, the cholecystocolonic fistula most likely represented a chronic process, and the gallstone was not causing complete obstruction. The widespread hypoenhancement of the cecum and ascending colon is better explained by systemic hypoperfusion in the context of profound shock, with subtotal stenosis of the superior mesenteric artery further reducing mesenteric perfusion reserve. Locally, however, the impacted sigmoid gallstone likely resulted in pressure necrosis, mural thinning, and focal perforation. This mechanism has been described in the literature even in the absence of frank obstruction, highlighting that gallstones may act as a precipitating factor for localised wall injury and perforation in ischaemic settings [1,4,6]. Outcome Unfortunately, despite supportive care, the patient’s condition deteriorated, and she ultimately died. While surgical correction remains the definitive treatment for biliary-enteric fistulas and ischaemic bowel, it may not be feasible in elderly or frail patients with multiple comorbidities. In such cases, only conservative and supportive care is possible [2,3]. Take Home Message This case highlights the vital role of CT in detecting biliary-enteric fistulas and ischaemic complications, and in recognising hypoperfusion signs that directly impact prognosis and management in vulnerable patients [1,2]. Teaching Points Cholecystocolonic fistula is a rare but important complication of chronic gallbladder disease. CT allows detection of fistulas, gallstone impaction, and associated ischaemic or perforation changes. Recognition of the CT hypoperfusion complex is essential, as it signals severe circulatory compromise and guides management. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma: An unknown neoplasm
clinical_history: A 70-year-old patient with chronic pain and a limited range of motion in the elbow. On physical examination, limitation of extension and pronation–supination. No history of previous trauma and no relevant medical background.
imaging_findings: The plain radiograph shows advanced osteoarthritis with joint space narrowing and periarticular calcifications (Figures 1a and 1b). In CT without contrast (Figures 2a and 2b), in addition to the findings described on the x-ray, an intra-articular soft tissue lesion with adjacent bone erosion is observed (arrows). Based on the findings, it was decided to proceed with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). MRI T1-weighted image (Figure 3a), STIR sequence (Figure 3b), and T1 post-contrast image (Figure 3c) show an intra-articular, multilobulated lesion that is hyperintense on fluid-sensitive sequences, with heterogeneous and septal enhancement. No significant bone involvement is observed. A decision was made to perform an ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy (Figures 4a and 4b). A staging study was performed (not shown), revealing no evidence of distant disease.
discussion: Background Extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma is an extremely rare subtype of sarcoma (< 1/1,000,000 inhabitants/year). It usually occurs in adults with a mean age of 50 years, predominantly in males [1,2]. Most arise from the deep soft tissues of the proximal extremities and shoulder girdle, with the thigh being the most frequent site [2]. Despite its name, recent studies have shown that it is a mesenchymal tumour rather than of chondroid origin, and in the latest WHO classification, it is categorised as a “tumour of uncertain differentiation” [3]. From a histopathological standpoint, it is a neoplasm with tumour cells connected by cords or in small clusters, surrounded by fibrous strands within a myxoid matrix, without chondroid differentiation. It harbours the specific mutation of the NR4A3 gene translocation on chromosome 9 [4]. Clinical Perspective Patients are generally asymptomatic, as it is a slow-growing tumour, although approximately 13% have metastases at diagnosis, usually in the lungs. Symptoms are usually caused by significant intra-articular involvement, which can lead to impaired mobility [2]. Imaging Perspective The main finding consists of a lobulated extraskeletal soft tissue mass that is hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences and variable on T1-weighted sequences, depending on the presence of haemorrhage, necrosis, or cystic degeneration. In studies performed after intravenous contrast administration, heterogeneous enhancement is observed, predominantly septal and peripheral [1]. It generally does not significantly affect the bone, although it can cause bone erosions by contiguity. Due to these erosions and other factors, peripheral calcifications are commonly observed. The described findings are nonspecific and may be present in other pathologies, both tumoural and non-tumoural, so a definitive diagnosis must be made through histopathological and genetic studies [4]. Outcome The prognosis is generally better compared to other soft tissue sarcomas, although it depends on whether the disease is localised or disseminated [1,5]. Treatment is variable, especially in the presence of distant metastases. In localised disease, wide local resection is usually chosen, with the option of adjuvant radiotherapy. In cases of disseminated disease, numerous therapeutic regimens have been tried, some still in clinical trial phases; however, no clear survival benefit has been observed given the limited number of cases reported in the literature [5]. In our case, following the absence of distant disease, a transhumeral amputation was chosen (Figure 5). No residual disease was found at the surgical margins. title: Diastematomyelia and tethered cord in a paediatric patient
clinical_history: A 13-year-old female with congenital scoliosis (Figure 1) was evaluated for surgical treatment.
imaging_findings: An initial non-contrast CT scan of the thoracic spine (Figures 2a and 2b) showed upper thoracic rotoscoliosis with a rightward curve and thoracolumbar scoliosis with a leftward curve. The vertebral bodies from T1 to T6 showed decreased size and wedging on their left lateral wall, associated with narrowing of the intercostal spaces and partial fusion of the intervertebral disks. Irregularity and sclerosis were observed in their superior and inferior endplates, as well as marginal osteophytes, resulting in narrowing of the bilateral neuroforamina. A vertebral segmentation defect characterised by a longitudinal bony septum dividing the spinal cord into two segments, consistent with a butterfly vertebra at the level of T10, was observed (Figures 2c and 2d). A month later, a thoracic column MRI revealed division of the spinal canal by a bony septum at the level of L1, in relation to diastematomyelia (Figure 3a). The spinal cord presents dilation of its central canal at the level of C4 to be considered hydromyelia (syrinx) (Figure 3b), and medullary conus at the level of L3 is compatible with a tethered cord.
discussion: Background Diastematomyelia is an uncommon congenital malformation of the spine characterised by the splitting of the spinal cord or cauda equina at the extent of one or a few vertebrae. Although spinal dysraphism has an estimated incidence of 1 to 3 cases per 1,000 live births, the exact prevalence of diastematomyelia remains unclear. However, it is thought to represent approximately 5% of all congenital spinal anomalies [1]. The aetiology is unknown, but it has been suggested that the cause of this anomaly is the presence of a connection between the neural tube and the amniotic cavity or primitive bowel [2]. Clinical Perspective The clinical presentation includes cutaneous abnormalities overlying the spine, neurologic deficits such as back pain, asymmetric reflexes, progressive weakness, muscle atrophy, loss of sensation, paraesthesias, bowel and bladder dysfunction, spasticity, or paresis, and orthopaedic abnormalities including congenital scoliosis, clubfoot, lower limb discrepancy [3,4]. Imaging Perspective The diagnosis of diastematomyelia is conventionally based on its clinical manifestations and radiological examination. Plain radiography has been traditionally used to identify the interpedicular space or bony spur. However, with the improvements in imaging technology, computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are now established as the primary diagnostic strategies for evaluating cases of diastematomyelia [5]. During the patient’s initial examination, the neurosurgery service requested a non-contrast thoracic column CT to correct the scoliosis. The decision to perform the subsequent non-contrast thoracic column MRI was based on the need to identify the presence of two hemichords, syringohydromyelia and tethered cord. Teaching Points We discussed the typical findings of diastematomyelia in paediatric patients using different imaging modalities before surgical treatment. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Pivot-shift injury with multi-ligamentous knee involvement
clinical_history: A 30-year-old female presented with left knee instability after a pivoting injury while planting and twisting the knee. She subsequently experienced mechanical locking, which required manual manipulation to achieve full extension.
imaging_findings: Plain radiographs demonstrated a large suprapatellar effusion without fracture (Figure 1). MRI showed a complete grade III anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear with a large joint effusion (Figure 2c). There was a grade II medial collateral ligament (MCL) tear, primarily involving the deep fibres (Figure 3a). A grade I–II lateral collateral ligament LCL sprain was noted near the femoral origin (Figure 3c). A horizontal, non-displaced tear of the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus was present (Figure 2a). Bone marrow oedema in the posterior tibial plateau and lateral femoral condyle formed a classic kissing contusion pattern (Figures 4a and 4b). The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL), extensor mechanism, and articular cartilage appeared intact (Figure 2b).
discussion: Background ACL tears are common in pivoting sports and activities. The ACL prevents anterior tibial translation and controls rotational stability. Injuries often co-occur with meniscal and collateral ligament damage. The MCL and LCL provide stability to valgus and varus forces, respectively. Clinical Perspective ACL injuries typically occur during pivoting or twisting movements, especially when the foot is planted. Patients often report a popping sensation, followed by swelling and instability. A positive Lachman test or pivot-shift test is highly suggestive of ACL rupture. Clinical examination may be limited by pain or swelling in the acute setting, making imaging essential. In this case, the patient experienced mechanical locking, which raised concern for meniscal pathology, especially involving the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus. Imaging Perspective MRI is the gold standard for assessing soft tissue knee injuries [1,2]. MRI is required to assess the full extent of soft tissue injury and bone contusions. Identifying which structures are involved and the degree of tears has direct implications for rehabilitation, surgical planning and graft selection. Radiologists must clearly report the location, grade and chronicity of ligament injuries and describe meniscal tears in terms of type, location, displacement and reparability. These details help the physiotherapist and surgeon determine rehabilitation goals, operative timing, technique and the need for concomitant procedures. In this case, the rupture of the ACL with surrounding oedema and fluid cleft confirmed a functionally complete tear. High-grade MCL and low-grade LCL tears are well visualised on coronal proton density imaging. While the horizontal posterior horn tear of the lateral meniscus was non-displaced, its configuration raised concern for a potential bucket-handle component, which may explain the mechanical locking. The kissing bone contusions of the lateral femoral condyle and posterior tibial plateau are characteristic of a pivot-shift mechanism. The intact PCL and cartilage helped exclude a more extensive injury. Outcome Physiotherapy is used to regain range of motion and build muscle pre-operatively. The MCL, with a relatively robust blood supply, is expected to heal over a period of 6–8 weeks, with conservative management of bracing, particularly when the superficial fibres remain intact. Surgical intervention included ACL reconstruction with ipsilateral hamstring graft and ultimately posterolateral meniscectomy, as on inspection arthroscopically, the horizontal tear involved the white zone. Graft choice depends on multiple factors, including patient activity level, anatomy, and surgeon preference. Common graft options include hamstring (semitendinosus/gracilis), patellar tendon, quadriceps tendon autografts or an allograft. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Pivot-shift injuries often involve multiple ligamentous structures and menisci. MRI is essential for diagnosis and pre-surgical planning. Bone contusions provide insight into the injury mechanism to classify the injury. Meniscal tears may cause locking even without fragment displacement.

title: Spontaneous rupture of a suprasellar dermoid cyst with subarachnoid fat dissemination
clinical_history: A 20-year-old woman with prior neurosurgery attended a routine follow-up. She denied headache, fever, seizures, or visual symptoms. Neurological examination was normal, except for persistent partial anosmia since the operation. No recent trauma or infection. A follow-up review was requested by her neurosurgical team.
imaging_findings: Axial post-contrast T1-weighted MRI demonstrated a well-defined hyperintense nodular lesion in the frontobasal region, consistent with residual dermoid cyst content. Multiple small, punctate T1-hyperintense foci were scattered within the subarachnoid spaces, predominantly in the left Sylvian fissure, suggestive of disseminated fat droplets secondary to spontaneous cyst rupture (Figure 1). An upper axial slice revealed additional fat droplets within cortical sulci bilaterally, with a left-sided predominance (Figure 2). Midline sagittal T1-weighted MRI confirmed suprasellar and frontobasal fat-containing lesions, accompanied by scattered hyperintense foci along the basal cisterns (Figure 3). Coronal T1-weighted MRI further delineated the distribution of fat droplets in suprasellar and frontobasal subarachnoid spaces, without pathological enhancement or ventricular dilatation (Figure 4). The absence of diffusion restriction, surrounding oedema, or mass effect favoured a chronic or subacute process rather than acute rupture.
discussion: Background Intracranial dermoid cysts are rare, benign, congenital lesions arising from ectodermal inclusions during neural tube closure, representing <0.5% of intracranial tumours [1]. They consist of a cystic cavity lined by stratified squamous epithelium and filled with lipid-rich material such as sebum, cholesterol crystals, and occasionally hair. Most occur in midline locations—suprasellar or parasellar cisterns, posterior fossa, or fourth ventricle. Although slow-growing, they may cause symptoms by mass effect or, rarely, rupture. Spontaneous rupture is uncommon, more often following trauma or surgery, and poses a unique diagnostic challenge [2,3]. Clinical Perspective Rupture releases fatty contents into the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), potentially causing chemical meningitis, seizures, vasospasm, or obstructive hydrocephalus [2]. The inflammatory reaction results from lipid irritation of the meninges. Presentation ranges from acute neurologic deterioration with meningeal signs to incidental radiological findings. The present case was clinically silent: the patient remained asymptomatic after rupture except for partial anosmia from the initial surgery, illustrating that rupture may go unnoticed for years. Imaging Perspective MRI remains the gold standard for diagnosis and follow-up of intracranial dermoid cysts [1,3]. Fatty droplets disseminated into the subarachnoid or ventricular spaces appear hyperintense on non-fat-suppressed T1-weighted images and lose signal on fat-suppressed sequences, a finding that allows confident differentiation from subacute haemorrhage. On CT, fat is recognised as hypodense material with attenuation values between -50 and -100 HU [1]. The classic hallmark of rupture is the presence of multiple, scattered T1-hyperintense foci in the basal cisterns or cortical sulci [3]. In the present case, the absence of meningeal enhancement, oedema, or ventricular enlargement favoured a subacute or chronic rupture without active inflammation, in keeping with the benign clinical course. Outcome In asymptomatic patients without complications, conservative management with regular clinical assessment and serial MRI is preferred [4]. Surgical intervention is generally reserved for residual lesions producing significant mass effect, progressive neurological symptoms, or secondary complications [4]. Over one year of follow-up, our patient remained neurologically stable, and imaging revealed no progression. Take Home Message Dermoid cyst remnants may persist and rupture years after resection. Recognising their imaging pattern and natural history prevents misdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment in stable patients. Long-term imaging surveillance is recommended.

title: Obturator neuropathy secondary to entrapment by iliac adenopathies
clinical_history: A 61-year-old male patient, with known metastasised rectal cancer, presented with severe pain in the left hip since a few months. The pain was situated in the dorsal gluteal region, radiating to the perineum and the left groin and knee, and was worse in the evening and at night.
imaging_findings: An x-ray and ultrasound of the left hip did not reveal any significant abnormalities or degeneration. The most recent CT in the context of his oncologic follow-up, a few weeks earlier, showed increased enlargement and partial confluence of the known iliac adenopathies on the left (Figure 1). Subsequently, a contrast-enhanced MRI of the pelvis was performed for further evaluation. This showed a thickened and oedematous obturator nerve on the left side, completely encased by the iliac adenopathies on its proximal course (Figures 2, 3a, 3b, and 3c). Muscle oedema was present in the left obturator externus muscle and, to a lesser extent, in the left adductor magnus, brevis and longus muscles, all innervated by the obturator nerve, as a sign of denervation (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c). Secondary asymmetrical, mild fatty atrophy was already present in the previously described muscles (Figures 5a and 5b). There was no evidence of additional metastatic lesions, aside from the known adenopathies.
discussion: Background The obturator nerve originates from the L2–L4 spinal nerve roots, travels along the iliopectineal line into the obturator canal and then descends along the inner thigh. The anterior branch innervates the adductor brevis, adductor longus, and gracilis muscles, as well as providing sensory input to the inner thigh. The posterior branch supplies the obturator externus and part of the adductor magnus and provides sensory branches to the knee joint [1–3]. Obturator neuropathy is relatively uncommon in comparison to other lower extremity neuropathies [4]. Multiple different causes have been described, for example, trauma, surgery, chronic adductor tendinopathy or osteitis pubis, obturator hernia, compression by mass lesions, childbirth, et cetera [1,2,4]. Clinical Perspective Patients usually present with paraesthesia, sensory deficits, or pain in the medial thigh or groin, and extension or abduction of the thigh can worsen the pain. Other symptoms can include weakness in thigh adduction, an abnormal gait pattern, and muscle atrophy [5]. Obturator neuropathy can occasionally present in atypical forms, with symptoms confined to the groin or pelvic region, potentially leading to a delay in diagnosis [4]. Needle electromyography can be useful in confirming suspected obturator neuropathy, but imaging is needed to identify the exact cause of the neuropathy. Imaging Perspective Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the preferred imaging modality for the diagnosis of obturator neuropathy. The nerve itself usually shows abnormal signal intensities and can be increased in size. Muscle changes secondary to the denervation can be seen, like muscle oedema and fatty atrophy. MRI is also useful to examine the cause of the neuropathy, for example, a mass lesion that causes compression. Outcome The treatment is usually conservative, including pain management and physical therapy. When the symptoms are refractory to treatment or when there is a mass lesion present, other therapy options, like a surgical intervention, need to be considered. Patients with an acute onset of the neuropathy tend to have a better outcome and prognosis, as opposed to patients with chronic neuropathy, whose prognosis is usually poorer [6]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Obturator neuropathy is a relatively uncommon entity compared to other lower limb neuropathies and can have multiple different causes. Nonetheless, it is important to recognise it as a clinician and as a radiologist, given that, if treated early in the disease course, the prognosis is much better. It is also important to remember that this neuropathy can be caused by compression/entrapment by mass lesions, possibly malignant, like in our case.

title: Juvenile xanthogranuloma
clinical_history: A 2-month-old infant with skin nodules of 2 months of evolution (Figure 1), with no known history. On physical examination of the patient, a well-defined subcutaneous nodule was observed in the region of the hand, with a rounded appearance and colouration that varied between yellowish and orange, as well as hepatomegaly associated with ascites.
imaging_findings: From the moment the patient entered the hospital, images were taken in the following sequence. An anteroposterior abdominal x-ray revealed ascites (Figure 2), possibly linked to hepatomegaly due to hepatic infiltration in systemic juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG). Ultrasound showed hepatomegaly with multiple hypoechoic nodules, lacking Doppler flow, consistent with histiocytic infiltration (Figures 3a and 3b). MRI with contrast confirmed liver involvement, displaying hyperintense T2 nodules with peripheral enhancement, characteristic of JXG (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c). Chest x-ray and MRI revealed multiple solid lung nodules, suggesting pulmonary spread in a systemic presentation (Figures 5a and 5b). MRI also identified a right occipital nodule, hyperintense on T1 and hypointense on T2, with peripheral contrast enhancement, indicating a rare central nervous system involvement (Figures 6a, 6b, and 6c). Neck MRI showed a right mandibular nodule, hypointense on T2, with no diffusion restriction, consistent with soft tissue JXG (Figures 7a and 7b). A full-body x-ray showed no skeletal lesions (Figures 8a, 8, 8c, 8d, and 8e), a favourable prognosis indicator. Ultrasound of a dorsal cutaneous nodule revealed a well-defined hypoechoic lesion without vascularisation (Figure 9), from which the biopsy sample was obtained to identify the patient’s final diagnosis.
discussion: Juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG) is a rare histiocytic disorder in paediatrics, typically presenting as isolated skin lesions. However, multisystem involvement, as seen in this case of a 2-month-old female, is highly uncommon. The patient exhibited cutaneous nodules on the hand and back, along with abdominal distension due to ascites. Given these findings, a broad differential diagnosis was considered, including benign haemangioendotheliomas and malignant metastatic neuroblastoma. The presence of hepatomegaly and ascites is rare in JXG, necessitating extensive diagnostic studies [1]. Laboratory tests revealed thrombocytopenia, anaemia, cholestasis, elevated D-dimer levels, and prolonged coagulation times, indicative of a systemic inflammatory response. While Kasabach–Merritt syndrome was considered, it was ruled out due to the absence of sepsis or disseminated intravascular coagulation [2]. Imaging played a crucial role in characterising the lesions and narrowing the diagnosis. Ultrasound revealed hepatomegaly with hypoechoic nodules lacking Doppler flow, suggesting a benign infiltrative or neoplastic process. MRI demonstrated multiple hyperintense T2 liver nodules with contrast enhancement, supporting a nonvascular inflammatory aetiology [6]. Additional findings included pulmonary nodules, a right occipital nodule, and a mandibular nodule. Skeletal imaging ruled out lytic lesions, excluding malignant bone pathology. The imaging findings helped differentiate between systemic infections (e.g., liver abscesses) and histiocytic (JXG) or neoplastic (neuroblastoma) disorders [4]. Histopathological analysis ultimately confirmed the diagnosis. A key differential diagnosis was metastatic neuroblastoma, as 10–20% of neuroblastomas without primary adrenal lesions can present with multisystem involvement. However, the absence of a primary lesion and characteristic histopathological findings ruled out this possibility. Additionally, the lack of Doppler flow and final histological features excluded haemangioendotheliomas [7]. Histopathological analysis was definitive in confirming JXG. The biopsy revealed epithelioid cells with foamy cytoplasm, indicative of lipid accumulation, along with characteristic Touton giant cells. Immunohistochemistry showed BRAF V600 positivity, confirming the histiocytic nature of the proliferation and supporting the JXG diagnosis [8]. This case underscores the potential for JXG to extend beyond the skin, affecting the liver (hepatomegaly with nodules), lungs (solid nodules), central nervous system (occipital nodule), and soft tissues (mandibular lesion). While these manifestations are rare, their recognition was crucial in ruling out aggressive malignancies and guiding conservative management [3]. Multisystem JXG is rarely fatal and typically has a favourable prognosis with conservative follow-up. Notably, this patient did not exhibit ocular involvement, which can sometimes lead to complications such as hyphaema or glaucoma. A structured follow-up plan, including ophthalmologic evaluations, ultrasound, and MRI, is recommended to monitor for progression or recurrence [5]. Take Home Message This case highlights the importance of a comprehensive, multidisciplinary diagnostic approach. Imaging techniques, including ultrasound, MRI, and x-rays, provide critical insights into disease extent, facilitating diagnosis, management, and differentiation from malignant conditions in multisystem JXG cases. The integration of clinical, imaging, and pathological findings facilitated the confirmation of a rare yet benign condition, preventing unnecessary interventions and expanding the understanding of multisystem JXG.

title: An unexpected recurrence: A mandibular clue to abdominal disease
clinical_history: A 59-year-old HIV-positive patient on antiretroviral therapy with undetectable viral load and prior remission of mandibular plasmablastic lymphoma (2020) underwent routine follow-up. Thoracic CT incidentally revealed right-sided hydronephrosis. A subsequent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT was performed to assess the underlying cause of the urinary tract obstruction.
imaging_findings: Abdominal CT (Figure 1) showed isolated retroperitoneal lymphadenopathies and right-sided hydronephrosis. A focal calibre change in the proximal ureter was noted, adjacent to an oval-shaped heterogeneous structure, distal to which the ureter appeared collapsed. Abnormally dense filling of the inferior vena cava and a branch of the superior mesenteric vein, likely the ileocolic vein, suggested extensive tumoural venous thrombosis. These findings also pointed to hydronephrosis due to either a primary urinary tract neoplasm or extrinsic compression from a necrotic adenopathy secondary to lymphoproliferative disease. FDG-PET-CT (Figure 2) demonstrated hypermetabolic activity in retroperitoneal lymph nodes (SUV max: 2.7) and within the inferior vena cava and superior mesenteric vein branch thrombus (SUV max: 4.3), consistent with malignancy. The ureteral narrowing was metabolically inactive. Phlebography (Figure 3) confirmed complete inferior vena cava occlusion, and thrombus biopsies were obtained. Percutaneous pyelography (Figure 4) showed extrinsic ureteral compression, likely from a lymph node. Histopathology (Figure 5) revealed plasmablastic lymphoma recurrence, matching the original mandibular lesion.
discussion: Plasmablastic lymphoma (PBL) is a rare and aggressive subtype of B-cell lymphoma, originally described in the oral cavity of HIV-positive patients. It typically presents as a rapidly enlarging mass, most often affecting the oral mucosa in HIV-associated cases [1–3]. However, plasmablastic lymphoma may also occur in immunocompetent individuals and transplant recipients, in whom it shows a more heterogeneous anatomical distribution. In these patients, up to 50% of cases arise outside the oral cavity, commonly involving the gastrointestinal tract, skin, and soft tissues. Primary nodal disease is rare, except in transplant recipients, who may also show cutaneous involvement [1]. Epstein–Barr virus infection and MYC gene rearrangements are frequently implicated in the pathogenesis of PBL [1–3]. Imaging findings are variable and often non-specific, depending on the site of disease. CT and FDG-PET-CT may reveal large, necrotic, or hypermetabolic masses, frequently without associated nodal clustering. The standard treatment consists of intensive chemotherapy regimens, often followed by autologous stem cell transplantation [3]. Nonetheless, prognosis remains poor, with reported 5-year overall survival rates ranging from 22% to 60% and median survival between 4 and 32 months [4]. Complete responses are rare and have been described only in small case series [5]. Given its low incidence and aggressive behaviour, data on recurrence patterns in PBL are limited. To our knowledge, recurrence with tumour thrombus in the inferior vena cava and superior mesenteric vein has not been previously reported. Tumour thrombosis is typically associated with solid tumours such as hepatocellular or renal cell carcinoma and is rarely seen in haematologic malignancies [6]. In this case, histopathologic confirmation of malignant cells within the thrombus established the diagnosis of tumour thrombus secondary to PBL recurrence. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Plasmablastic lymphoma (PBL) is a rare and aggressive lymphoma, typically involving the oral cavity in HIV-positive patients, but it may also affect other anatomical sites in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised individuals. This case illustrates a unique abdominal recurrence of mandibular plasmablastic lymphoma, manifesting as tumoural thrombosis of the inferior vena cava and superior mesenteric vein branch, mimicking vascular involvement by solid tumours, associated with retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis was established through FDG-PET-CT imaging and biopsy, confirming Epstein–Barr virus-positive PBL with identical morphology to the original mandibular lesion. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Azygos vein aneurysm: A rare posterior mediastinal mass
clinical_history: A 79-year-old patient presented to the emergency department of another institution with complaints of dizziness and a near-syncope episode. Medical history and physical examination were unremarkable. A chest radiograph was performed as part of the initial workup and revealed an incidental right paratracheal opacity unrelated to the presenting symptoms.
imaging_findings: The chest radiograph revealed an opacity along the right paratracheal contour. As it was obtained in another institution, the computed tomography (CT) localiser radiograph is shown here (Figure 1), where widening of the right mediastinal contour can be seen. A CT was performed, including pre-contrast and post-contrast venous phases, revealing a well-defined mass in the posterior mediastinum, with similar density to nearby vascular structures on pre-contrast images (Figures 2a and 2b) and identical enhancement pattern to surrounding veins (Figures 3a and 3b). The lesion was in continuity with the azygos vein. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), including T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and post-contrast T1-weighted images, confirmed these findings, showing a posterior mediastinal mass in continuity with the azygos vein, demonstrating similar characteristics and enhancement to this vessel (Figures 4a, 4b, 5a, and 5b). Maximum intensity projection and multiplanar reconstructions were generated from post-contrast CT and MRI images (Figures 6a and 6b), providing enhanced visualisation of the azygos vein trajectory and dilation.
discussion: Background An azygos vein aneurysm (AVA) is a rare cause of a posterior mediastinal mass. It may develop due to trauma or conditions that increase the flow or pressure in the azygos venous system, such as heart failure. AVAs can also be idiopathic [1–7]. The normal azygos vein can have a diameter up to 1 cm, with the arch reaching 1.5 cm [2]. Definitions of what constitutes an AVA vary. Some authors define it as a focal dilation of the azygos vein exceeding 2.5 times the normal diameter of the azygos vein in adults [2,5,6]. Clinical Perspective AVAs are often incidental findings. When symptoms occur, they usually result from compression of nearby structures like the oesophagus or the trachea, causing cough, dyspnoea, or dysphagia [2–7]. Complications are rare but may arise. They include thrombus formation within the aneurysm, which may lead to pulmonary embolism [2–7]. Imaging Perspective Chest radiographs often provide the initial clue to the presence of AVAs, showing a mass or an enlargement of the right mediastinum. This mass changes in size with respiratory movements and with the Valsalva manoeuvre [2–4]. CT and MRI show a well-defined posterior mediastinal mass with homogeneous enhancement in the venous phase, with imaging characteristics and enhancement similar to the azygos vein. These imaging modalities also allow for an evaluation of the surrounding structures and detection of complications such as thrombosis [2–6]. Outcome There are no universally accepted guidelines for AVA management [2–6]. Asymptomatic patients may be managed conservatively, although some authors advocate for surgical resection due to the risk of complications [2,5]. Despite there being no defined criteria for surgical resection, it may be the best option when complications arise or to reduce symptoms caused by compression of adjacent structures [2–4]. Endovascular treatment may be considered as an alternative to surgical excision [2,3]. In our patient’s case, a conservative approach was chosen. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Although rare, azygos vein aneurysms (AVAs) should be considered in the differential diagnosis of posterior mediastinal masses. Awareness of this entity is essential in order to avoid invasive procedures such as biopsies, which carry a risk of life-threatening bleeding. CT is essential for diagnosing this condition and detecting complications such as thrombosis, with MRI serving as an adjunct imaging modality when further characterisation is needed [1–7]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Rectal vascular malformation (haemangioma): A rare cause of rectal bleeding
clinical_history: A 13-year-old male was sent to our clinic from another institution with a lifelong history of intermittent, unexpected, painless rectal bleeding. The episodes were unpredictable, caused discomfort, and progressively affected his quality of life. Initially, they occurred once per month; however, the frequency gradually increased to once every week, accompanied by a larger volume of blood loss.
imaging_findings: Colonoscopy revealed diffuse, confluent bluish areas in the rectum, suggestive of vascular structures (Figure 1). Axial, coronal, and sagittal T2-weighted MR images demonstrate a long segment of high signal, regular, and circumferential thickening of the rectal wall, extending from the anorectal junction to the rectosigmoid junction (Figure 2). High signal intensity is also seen on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with a high b-value, as well as on the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map (Figure 3). Numerous serpiginous flow voids are noted in the surrounding mesorectal fat, which enhance on post-contrast fat-saturated T1-weighted MR images, indicating their vascular nature. Additionally, progressive enhancement of the rectal wall is observed, supporting the diagnosis of a vascular malformation (haemangioma) (Figures 2 and 4).
discussion: Background As the name suggests, vascular malformations (VMs), also known as haemangiomas, are benign congenital proliferations of blood vessels and mesenchymal tissue [1]. Although first described in 1839, their pathogenesis remains incompletely understood, but is thought to be related to abnormalities in the angiogenesis process [2,3]. Localisation in the gastrointestinal tract is exceedingly rare, accounting for only about 0.05% of all intestinal tumours [1]. Clinical Perspective Although patients can present at any age, the condition most commonly affects children and young adults [1,4]. Symptoms can range from long-standing, recurrent painless bleeding to anaemia and even massive, life-threatening haemorrhage [2,4–7]. One of the major challenges is that, due to the rarity of the condition, misdiagnosis is common, occurring in up to 80% of cases. More prevalent conditions, such as inflammatory bowel disease or internal haemorrhoids, are often suspected instead, which ultimately delays diagnosis and contributes to poorer outcomes [2,6]. Colonoscopy is considered the gold standard for diagnosis, as it enables assessment of the lesion’s morphology, location, and extent of infiltration. CT and MRI offer precise evaluation of vascularisation, size, and potential involvement of adjacent structures [1,6–8]. MRI also plays a crucial role in surgical planning by helping to assess anal canal and sphincter involvement [8]. Biopsy should be avoided due to the high risk of bleeding [1,2,8]. Imaging Perspective On MRI, VMs typically appear hyperintense on T2-weighted images and hypointense on T1-weighted images, with a characteristic discontinuous, progressive, nodular post-contrast enhancement pattern. However, minimal or heterogeneous enhancement may occasionally be seen, likely due to internal fibrosis. CT, while less sensitive for diagnosing the condition, allows for direct visualisation of calcifications (phleboliths), which are considered characteristic findings [1,6–8]. Outcome Surgical resection remains the definitive treatment of choice, with preservation of the anal sphincter whenever technically feasible [2,8]. Several less invasive procedures have been introduced in recent years, including cryotherapy, low-dose radiation, and sclerotherapy; however, these are associated with high recurrence rates [1]. Endovascular embolisation technique has been introduced, and according to Pospisilova et al., it should be considered in symptomatic patients in whom the risk of surgery and disadvantages, such as having a stoma, outweigh the potential benefits [8]. Conservative treatment approaches have also been described, primarily aimed at symptom control [4,9,10]. In our case, the patient was managed with iron supplementation, propranolol, and sirolimus to control the episodes. Due to the extent of the disease and the patient’s preferences, surgical intervention has not yet been pursued. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Patients may present at any age, but children and young adults are most commonly affected. Symptoms may range from painless rectal bleeding to life-threatening haemorrhage. A high suspicion index is important due to the rarity of the pathology. Typical MR features include a T2 hyperintense and a T1 hypointense structure with a discontinuous, progressive, nodular post-contrast enhancement pattern. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Lemierre’s syndrome complicated by a mycotic aneurysm
clinical_history: A 22-year-old previously healthy patient presented with headache, weakness, and sore throat. At the emergency department, he was febrile, cognitively impaired (Glasgow Coma Scale 12), and had positive meningeal symptoms. Laboratory tests showed markedly elevated inflammatory markers: C-reactive protein 203 mg/L and procalcitonin 7.8 ng/mL.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced CT showed a large left palatine tonsil abscess with inflammatory extension into the temporalis and masseter muscles (Figure 1). Chest and abdominal CT showed bilateral pulmonary densities consistent with septic emboli and hepatomegaly. Central nervous system (CNS) and craniofacial MRI confirmed previously suspected left superior ophthalmic vein thrombosis (Figure 2a) and additionally demonstrated thrombi in both cavernous sinuses (Figure 2b) as well as five cerebral focal lesions compatible with septic emboli (Figure 3). Later CT angiography, performed due to severe headaches, revealed an 11 × 8 mm mycotic aneurysm in the cavernous segment of the left internal carotid artery, absent on a scan 14 days earlier. Urgent coil embolisation was performed (Figure 4). Follow-up contrast-enhanced MRI with MR angiography confirmed successful aneurysm occlusion.
discussion: Background Lemierre’s syndrome typically affects healthy young adults at the median age of 21 and is caused by an anaerobic Gram-negative species Fusobacterium necrophorum originating from the oropharynx [1]. Clinical Perspective Lemierre’s syndrome typical clinical presentation includes thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein, sepsis, and formation of septic emboli [1]. Rarely, septic emboli can spread to the CNS, which is associated with mortality of up to 30% [2]. CNS involvement can result in severe complications that may include meningitis, sinus thrombosis, and septic-embolic encephalitis [3]. Imaging Perspective Patients may present with non-specific neurological symptoms. Previous studies indicated the special role of diagnostic imaging, especially of the neck region [4]. However, if symptoms such as headache, cognitive impairment or positive “meningeal” signs are observed, it is necessary to perform an urgent CNS CT scan or, if possible, an MR scan. Outcome Mycotic aneurysms are prone to rupture and have a mortality rate of 60–90% [5]. Management strategies include conservative treatment, internal carotid artery ligation, balloon or coil occlusion, and stenting, with variable outcomes [6]. Take Home Message Mycotic aneurysm is a severe, rare complication of Lemierre’s syndrome [7], but being diagnosed early enough is a potentially manageable condition. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Medullary cap dysplasia with spinal dysraphism: A rare association
clinical_history: A 2-year-old female child was referred for evaluation of developmental delay and a sacral midline cutaneous lesion. Birth history was unremarkable, and prenatal ultrasonography had shown no anomalies. Postnatal examination revealed axial hypotonia, poor head control, and a midline lumbosacral dimple with overlying hair tuft. An MRI of the brain and spine was performed to assess for neurodevelopmental and spinal anomalies.
imaging_findings: Brain MRI, axial and mid-sagittal T1 and T2-weighted imaging, demonstrated a smooth, well-defined dorsal protrusion from the medulla, isointense to adjacent grey matter, consistent with a medullary cap (Figures 1a, 1b, 2a, and 2b). There was no hydrocephalus or supratentorial anomaly. Spinal MRI, sagittal and axial T1 and T2-weighted sequences, revealed a lipomeningomyelocele at the L4–S1 level, with dorsal herniation of neural elements through a spina bifida defect into a subcutaneous lipomatous mass (Figures 3a, 3b, 4a, and 4b). A filar lipoma extended from the low-lying conus medullaris, which terminated at the L3 level (Figures 5a and 5b). A dermal sinus tract communicated from the skin surface to the dorsal aspect of the thecal sac (Figures 3a, 3b, 4a, and 4b). An inclusion cyst consisted of an anteriorly located multiloculated cerebrospinal fluid signal intensity lesion seen in the spinal canal at the axial level of the LV3 vertebral body. No syrinx or vertebral segmentation anomalies were seen. The findings confirmed complex occult spinal dysraphism coexisting with a hindbrain malformation.
discussion: Medullary cap dysplasia (MCD) is a rare congenital brainstem malformation characterised by a non-enhancing dorsal protrusion of the medulla, often appearing as a symmetric, cap-like structure without mass effect. It is frequently accompanied by hypoplasia of the ventral pons and associated cerebellar anomalies, such as vermian hypoplasia and thickened cerebellar peduncles—components of the molar tooth sign classically seen in Joubert syndrome and related disorders (JSRD) [1–3]. The pathogenesis of MCD likely involves aberrant axonal pathfinding or defective midline decussation, leading to ectopic or disorganised white matter tracts in the dorsal medulla [4,5]. Histopathological studies have demonstrated heterotopic neurons and axonal spheroids in the cap region, supporting its developmental rather than neoplastic origin [1]. Spinal dysraphism encompasses a wide range of spinal anomalies resulting from incomplete neural tube closure or abnormal secondary neurulation. The most common forms of occult dysraphism include [6–8]: Lipomeningomyelocele , where neural elements protrude dorsally into a lipomatous subcutaneous mass. Filar lipoma , an intradural fat-containing lesion that may tether the spinal cord. Dermal sinus tract , an epithelium-lined tract extending from the skin to neural structures, carrying a risk for infection or tethering. The co-occurrence of MCD and complex spinal dysraphism, as illustrated in this case, is extremely rare and may indicate a shared embryologic disruption during axial development. Both hindbrain malformations and spinal dysraphism have been linked to defective dorsal midline signalling and cilia-related gene mutations, emphasising their syndromic overlap [9–11]. Medullary tegmental cap dysplasia has been further characterised by many authors based on shape, size in relation to the medulla (anterior–posterior diameter in the midsagittal plane), craniocaudal extension (pontomedullary, low medullary), axial projection (unilateral, bilateral), relation to the cerebellar peduncles (connected, separated, or unknown), and signal intensity [1]. Five types were identified [1]: Smooth – the cap borders blend into the medulla, and the contour is smooth. Stick sign – the cap is thin and elongated. Globular – the cap is round. Straight-angled, “step sign” – there is a straight angle between the cap and the medulla. Tuberal, “caterpillar sign” – the cap consists of multiple tuberlike protuberances. Teaching Points Medullary cap dysplasia (MCD) is a rare dorsal brainstem malformation best recognised on MRI by a non-enhancing dorsal medullary protrusion. It often coexists with cerebellar vermian hypoplasia and thickened superior cerebellar peduncles, forming a molar tooth configuration. Spinal dysraphism—including lipomeningomyelocele, filar lipoma, and dermal sinus tract—can present concurrently and must be investigated when cutaneous or neurologic signs are present. Full neuroaxis imaging is essential in suspected congenital brainstem malformations, especially when physical stigmata or motor deficits are observed. The combination may point to an underlying genetic syndrome or midline developmental disorder, guiding genetic counselling and surgical management.

final_diagnosis: Medullary tegmental cap dysplasia with spinal dysraphism

title: Primary spinal cord glioblastoma of the conus medullaris
clinical_history: A 43-year-old male patient presented to the neurology department with a six-week history of progressive spastic paraparesis, more pronounced on the right, with tetraparetic features. He mentioned an upper respiratory tract infection ten weeks prior. Past medical history was otherwise unremarkable.
imaging_findings: Brain MRI was normal. Whole-spine MRI showed a large intramedullary ovoid mass at the T12 level, involving the conus medullaris, measuring ~ 29 × 16.5 × 18.5 mm (craniocaudal × anteroposterior × transverse). The lesion expanded the cord with near-complete effacement of the perimedullary cerebrospinal fluid, and showed a hyperintense signal in T2-weighted and STIR sequences and an intermediate signal in T1-weighted sequences. No intralesional blood products were identified (Figures 1 and 2). After intravenous gadolinium administration, enhancement was heterogeneous with peripheral predominance. Cranial to the lesion, cord T2 hyperintensity extended to the lower T10 level without cavitation or post-contrast enhancement, indicating peritumoral oedema (Figures 2 and 3). Surgical biopsy and histopathology of the intramedullary lesion revealed spinal cord glioblastoma. The patient underwent radiotherapy and chemotherapy. At 6-month follow-up, MRI showed no significant reduction in size but a marked decrease in the extent and intensity of contrast enhancement, with a large central non-enhancing necrotic component (Figures 4 and 5).
discussion: Background Primary spinal cord glioblastoma (scGB) is a WHO grade-4 intramedullary astrocytoma [1,2]. It is exceedingly rare—representing ~1.5% of all primary spinal neoplasms and ~7.5% of intramedullary gliomas—and biologically aggressive [3,4]. scGB affects younger patients—median age 32 years at diagnosis—compared to cranial GB, and shows a male predominance [3]. Clinical Perspective scGB is predominantly localised in the thoracic, followed by the cervical cord, with rarer involvement of the conus medullaris [3,5], as in this case. Patients typically develop subacute progressive motor and sensory deficits, axial and radicular pain, and bowel/bladder dysfunction [2,3]. Imaging is essential to localise the disease, assess craniocaudal extent, and screen the neuraxis for skip lesions or dissemination, which influence therapeutic decisions [1]. Imaging Perspective MRI is the modality of choice for diagnosis and preoperative assessment. Typical scGB appears as an expansile, infiltrative intramedullary lesion with high signal on T2-weighted images, iso or low signal on T1-weighted images, and heterogeneous or ring-like enhancement; necrosis, haemorrhage, and long-segment involvement are common [1,5]. However, imaging features are not specific, and the differentiation from less aggressive neurogenic tumours and from inflammatory and infectious disorders is often difficult [5,6]. scGB should be distinguished from ependymomas, which are usually centrally located, well-marginated, more homogeneously enhancing, and commonly associated with syringohydromyelia [1,7]. In contrast, high-grade astrocytomas/GBs tend to be ill-defined and heterogeneously enhancing with infiltrative margins, limiting gross-total resection [7]. Whole-spine and brain MRI is vital to evaluate dissemination; DWI, DTI and perfusion may assist grading in select cases, but are technically challenging in the cord [1,5,6]. When MRI is contraindicated, CT is an acceptable second-line study despite its inferior soft-tissue contrast; CT myelography can delineate the full tumour extent for preoperative planning [1]. Histology remains definitive for diagnosis, and biopsy should be performed once infection/inflammation are excluded [5,6]. Outcome Maximal safe resection followed by chemoradiation is standard by extrapolation from cranial GB [3]. Resection is often constrained by infiltrative margins, and its survival impact appears less consistent than in other intramedullary gliomas [8]. Median overall survival is ~10–14 months despite multimodality therapy [4]. Although rare, secondary cerebral dissemination via craniospinal spread has been reported, sometimes months after initial treatment [9]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points In adults, a long-segment, poorly marginated, heterogeneously enhancing intramedullary mass should raise suspicion for glioblastoma [7]. Imaging should include the whole neuraxis and convey tumour length, margins, syrinx, exophytic components, and anticipated resectability to guide neurosurgical strategy and radiotherapy [1,7]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: An unusual presentation of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in breast
clinical_history: A 74-year-old female with no family history of breast cancer presented with multiple palpable masses in bilateral breasts and abdomen since 4 months with no history of trauma/malignancy. On clinical examination, all of these lumps were mobile and were inferred to be present in the subcutaneous plane.
imaging_findings: Bilateral mammogram, USG breast and contrast-enhanced CT thorax, abdomen and pelvis were performed. On digital mammogram, multiple variable-sized oval isodense and high-density lesions with circumscribed, lobulated, and some irregular margins were seen scattered in bilateral breast parenchyma (Figures 1a and 1b). Enlarged left axillary lymph nodes were also seen. No associated microcalcifications, skin changes or nipple retraction were noted. Ultrasound showed multiple variable-sized, well-defined, heterogeneous lesions with hyperechoic and hypoechoic parts. Some of them have a target appearance, hypoechoic in the central and hyperechoic in the peripheral part (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c), and increased vascularity (Figure 2d), seen mostly arising from the subcutaneous plane and the remaining from the skin. These lesions appeared soft on shear wave elastography (Figure 2e) and show mild posterior acoustic enhancement. Enlarged left axillary nodes with increased cortical thickness were also seen (Figure 3). A combined BIRADS 4C (high suspicion of malignancy) category was assigned. Contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) thorax, abdomen and pelvis showed multiple heterogeneously enhancing bilateral breast lesions (Figure 4a), with other multiple diffuse innumerable well-defined enhancing soft tissue lesions in the subcutaneous plane of the entire body (Figure 4b and 4c). A few enlarged left axillary nodes were also seen. No other organ was seen involved beyond the breast and subcutaneous lesions. PETCT was not performed for this case. Core biopsy was performed from the largest lesion in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, which, on histological diagnosis, was suggestive of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, large cell type, favouring diffuse large B-cell lymphoma that was CD20, BCL2-positive.
discussion: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) is a diverse group of haematologic malignancies that originate in the lymphatic system. Unlike Hodgkin lymphoma (HL), which is characterised by the presence of Reed–Sternberg cells, NHL encompasses a broad range of lymphoid cancers, typically originating from B-cells, T-cells, or NK-cells [1,2]. NHL has a higher tendency for extra-nodal involvement than Hodgkin lymphoma. It commonly presents as painless lymphadenopathy, with B-symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats, and fatigue). Although isolated breast lymphoma most often appears in the literature as a solitary, unilateral, non-calcified mass, several published teaching cases (including multiple Eurorad reports) characterise breast lymphoma as a single lesion or a limited unilateral process rather than diffuse cutaneous/subcutaneous disease. For example, Eurorad case reports [3,4] commonly illustrate solitary or localised breast masses. Our patient’s presentation—multiple bilateral breast lesions with innumerable enhancing subcutaneous nodules throughout the body—is therefore atypical and more consistent with disseminated extranodal disease rather than the focal presentations usually illustrated in teaching cases. This pattern of widespread subcutaneous involvement is rarely described for breast lymphoma and better aligns with reports of primary cutaneous or subcutaneous B-cell lymphomas in the dermatologic literature, underscoring the diagnostic challenge and the need for histologic confirmation. When considering the imaging findings, the differential diagnosis included lymphoma, neurofibromatosis, metastasis, and multiple fibroadenomas/phyllodes. Neurofibromatosis was unlikely given the advanced age of presentation and absence of typical cutaneous manifestations. Metastatic disease was also less probable, as no known primary malignancy was identified, and the morphology of the lesions was less aggressive (soft on elastography) than usually expected for breast metastases. Multiple fibroadenomas or phyllodes tumours, while potentially mimicking multifocal breast masses, are unusual in this age group and would not explain the diffuse systemic subcutaneous lesions seen on CT. In contrast, the histopathologic confirmation of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma correlated best with the atypical radiologic presentation in this patient. Key imaging modalities and diagnostic pearls include: CT and PET/CT imaging evaluate lymphadenopathy and extra-nodal disease. MRI is useful for evaluating central nervous system involvement. Ultrasound is helpful in identifying superficial lymphadenopathy or evaluating abdominal organs. It is also used for biopsy guidance. Biopsy is the gold standard diagnostic procedure for confirming NHL. Final diagnosis is made by combining imaging findings with histopathologic and molecular studies. Our case presented with multiple, discrete, variable-sized lesions scattered all over the body in the subcutaneous plane, which is an atypical presentation for diffuse extralymphatic disease. Hence, stage IV was assigned. Multiple therapeutic options, including chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunotherapy, stem cell transplantation and targeted therapy, are available [5,6]. However, prognosis of NHL depends on several factors, including the histologic subtype, staging, age and comorbidities. In conclusion, this case provided an insight into a rare clinical and radiological presentation of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, which should be borne in mind as one of the differentials of bilateral multiple breast lesions. Teaching Points Breast lymphoma can mimic benign lesions such as fibroadenomas, particularly when margins appear circumscribed or lobulated. Shear wave elastography may be misleading, as lymphomatous lesions can appear soft despite being malignant. Disseminated subcutaneous involvement in lymphoma is rare, and its recognition is essential to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary surgery. Informed consent has been obtained from the patient.

title: Orbital brown tumour in a chronic kidney disease patient
clinical_history: A 25-year-old female with a history of end-stage chronic kidney disease (CKD) since 8 years and tertiary hyperparathyroidism presented with proptosis and restriction of left eye movement.
imaging_findings: Contrast material was not administered for either CT or MRI studies due to the patient’s underlying medical condition. Non-contrast-enhanced CT revealed the skull exhibiting a diffuse salt-and-pepper appearance with areas of bone resorption (Figure 1). A well-defined, expansile, predominantly lytic lesion involving the left orbital roof is seen. The lesion causes cortical thinning with evidence of cortical breach predominantly at its superior aspect. The lesion shows a narrow transition zone. No separate soft tissue component or periosteal reaction is seen. An MRI was performed, revealing a well-defined, expansile lesion involving the posterolateral aspect of the left orbital roof. Proptosis of the left eye is seen (Figure 2a), but no ptosis is clinically seen. The lesion is of intermediate signal intensity on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted (Figures 2b and 4a), and does not show restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging (Figures 3a and 3b). There is no evidence of cystic change or necrosis within this lesion. The lesion exhibits significant mass effect on the superior rectus and levator muscles (Figure 4b).
discussion: Background Brown tumours are giant cell lesions that develop due to abnormal bone metabolism associated with hyperparathyroidism [1]. The term “brown tumour” comes from its characteristic colour, which results from increased vascularity, haemorrhage, and the accumulation of haemosiderin [2]. In secondary hyperparathyroidism, increased bone turnover occurs due to chronic stimulation of the parathyroid glands, leading to heightened osteoblastic and osteoclastic activity; this explains the thickened appearance of other bones on imaging. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism develops when the parathyroid glands continue to secrete excessive amounts of parathyroid hormone, typically following prolonged secondary hyperparathyroidism, most commonly seen in patients with CKD [3]. Clinical Perspective Brown tumours usually manifest as gradually enlarging, noticeable bone swellings and can lead to bone pain or fractures resulting from weakened bone structure [4]. Brown tumours can develop throughout the skeleton, but they most commonly affect the pelvis, ribs, clavicle, and skull bones—particularly the mandible [4]. Orbital involvement is rare and may present with symptoms such as proptosis and restricted eye movement, as seen in this patient. To evaluate the complete extent of musculoskeletal involvement, dedicated CT or MRI imaging is often utilised. Imaging Perspective Brown tumours typically appear as well-defined lytic lesions with thinning of the cortex, though they seldom lead to outright bone destruction [5]. A small transition zone is generally expected, consistent with the slow-growing nature of these lesions, as also noted in this case. Less frequently, they may present as poorly defined lesions, show a combination of lytic and sclerotic changes, or involve adjacent soft tissues [6]. These lesions often comprise a mix of solid, cystic, and haemorrhagic areas, resulting in heterogeneous MRI signals [7]. CT, using high resolution bone algorithm, is particularly valuable for assessing bone detail. MRI offers superior soft tissue characterisation, helps assess lesion composition, and rules out alternative diagnoses by evaluating diffusion and perfusion parameters. The diagnosis of a brown tumour is made by integrating imaging features with clinical history and biochemical evidence of elevated PTH levels. In ambiguous cases, a biopsy may be required to exclude other giant cell lesions or malignancies. Outcome Treatment focuses on correcting the underlying hyperparathyroidism, often by parathyroidectomy, which typically results in lesion regression. Medical management includes phosphate binders and vitamin D analogues to control secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD patients. Early diagnosis via imaging is crucial to avoid unnecessary aggressive surgical interventions. Take Home Message / Teaching Points In patients with chronic kidney disease and tertiary hyperparathyroidism, brown tumours should be included in the differential diagnosis of lytic bone lesions, particularly when presenting in atypical locations such as the orbit. Though rare, orbital brown tumours can mimic malignancy and may present with proptosis and restricted ocular movement. Recognising this entity is crucial for avoiding misdiagnosis and guiding appropriate management.
