title: Bilateral breast syringomatous tumour with non-areolar involvement
clinical_history: A 47-year-old woman was referred to our Breast Unit for evaluation of bilateral breast lesions incidentally detected on screening imaging. Her medical history included a laparoscopic hysterectomy for endometriosis. Family history was significant for uterine and breast carcinoma in two maternal aunts and leukaemia in her father. Physical examination was unremarkable.
imaging_findings: Mammography with tomosynthesis revealed extremely dense breast tissue and two areas of architectural distortion: one in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast (periareolar), and the other in the retroareolar region of the left breast (Figure 1). Ultrasound (US) demonstrated two irregular, hypoechoic lesions with spiculated margins and increased stiffness on elastography (Figure 2). Given the suspicion of a bilateral malignant process, the patient underwent dynamic contrast-enhanced breast Magnetic Resonance (MR). This revealed a 10 mm spiculated mass in the right periareolar region, demonstrating rapid initial and persistent delayed enhancement (type I kinetic curve), with associated non-mass enhancement extending toward the retroareolar region (Figure 3). A second 12 mm spiculated lesion was detected in the left breast, more than 3 cm from the nipple–areolar complex (NAC), with similar kinetic features (Figure 4). Both lesions were classified as BI-RADS 4C, Kaiser score 6 and underwent US-guided core needle biopsy.
discussion: Syringomatous tumour of the breast, also called syringomatous adenoma of the nipple, is a rare benign neoplasm that typically originates from eccrine sweat ducts within the NAC [1,2]. First described by Rosen in 1983 [3], syringomatous tumour most commonly presents as a solitary, unilateral lesion located in the subareolar region, with clinical manifestations such as nipple tenderness and pruritus. Ulceration, nipple inversion, or discharge are less frequent [1]. In our case, no evidence of nipple changes or palpable abnormalities was found during physical examination. The patient underwent bilateral periareolar surgical excision followed by retroareolar coring, as recommended by the multidisciplinary tumour board. Histopathological analysis confirmed the diagnosis of syringomatous tumour, showing an infiltrative proliferation of irregular ductal and tubular structures within a fibrous stroma. These were composed of a bilayered epithelium—an inner epithelial and an outer myoepithelial layer—forming the characteristic “tadpole” or “comma” shapes. No lymphovascular or perineural invasion was present. Immunohistochemistry showed strong expression of p63, CK5/6, CK14, and smooth muscle actin (SMA) in the myoepithelial cells, with CK8/18 positivity in the luminal cells. These features help distinguish syringomatous tumour from malignant mimickers such as low-grade adenosquamous or tubular carcinoma [2,4]. Although syringomatous tumours may clinically and histologically mimic malignancy, they are benign and locally infiltrative. Complete excision with negative margins is the standard treatment, as residual disease is associated with recurrence rates up to 45% [1]. In our patient, both lesions were completely excised with clear margins. A follow-up strategy was adopted. Neither breast lesion showed radiological or histological involvement of the NAC, and no retroareolar involvement was detected on the left side, typically defined as within 2 cm of the NAC [5]. To the best of our knowledge, only two cases of bilateral syringomatous tumours have been reported in the international literature [6,7], and in both instances the lesions were confined to the nipple or subareolar region. No well-documented cases have described a syringomatous tumour arising within the breast parenchyma independently of the NAC. This makes our case a rare example of bilateral syringomatous tumour with no clinical, radiological, or histological involvement of the NAC on the left side. Take Home Message Although benign, syringomatous tumours can mimic malignancy. Complete excision with negative margins is mandatory to prevent recurrence. Bilateral presentation is extremely rare, and this case highlights the possible occurrence outside the NAC. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: An incidental finding of pneumoparotid on “puffed cheeks” CT
clinical_history: An 87-year-old male patient underwent a maxillofacial CT scan for the clinical finding of swelling in the left buccal mucosa, awaiting surgery.
imaging_findings: The “puffed-cheeks” CT scan, performed before and after the administration of contrast medium, confirms a roundish swelling of about 1 cm in the left buccal mucosa, with contrast-enhancing thickening of the adjoining mucosa. The left parotid gland shows fatty replacement and reduction in volume, indicating chronic obstruction. A biopsy was subsequently performed on the lesion, which confirmed the diagnostic suspicion of adenoid cystic carcinoma. The examination also showed the right parotid gland to be modestly increased in size compared to the contralateral one. Within it, there is evidence of diffuse gas occupying almost the entire course of Stensen’s duct and secondary ducts, with an arborescent appearance (visible on all scans). No images of calculi within the ducts are documented. These signs, combined with the absence of clinical symptoms and signs, are indicative of an incidental finding of pneumoparotid.
discussion: Background Pneumoparotid is a rare condition characterised by the presence of air within the Stensen’s duct or the parotid gland. It represents one of the less frequent causes of parotid swelling and can be either unilateral or bilateral. It is generally caused by increased endoral positive air pressure, which can lead to air reflux within the main duct and/or into the gland. There are various causes, including occupational (scuba divers, glassblowers, wind instrument players), lung diseases associated with recurrent coughing, iatrogenic causes (spirometry, positive pressure ventilation, dental procedures with compressed air, fine needle aspiration), self-induced insufflation (Valsalva manoeuvre, puffing, cough suppression, altered airway pressure) or trauma [1]. The opening of the Stensen’s duct is located near the second upper molar tooth bilaterally. The duct has three anatomical features that prevent the reflux of air and saliva into the parotid gland: the diameter of the duct orifice is smaller than the duct itself; the opening of the duct is lined with a thick layer of mucosa, which covers the orifice when there is an increase in intraoral pressure; in its lateral course, the Stensen’s duct is compressed along the masseter muscle and during its passage through the buccinator muscle with increased oral pressure. If the intraoral pressure exceeds the protective mechanism, air can reflux through the duct into the parotid gland, leading to pneumoparotiditis. Clinical Perspective Pneumoparotid usually does not present significant clinical manifestations, except for modest parotid swelling. Rarely, crepitus may be noted upon palpation [1]. However, complications include subcutaneous emphysema, infectious parotitis (in the case of recurrent pneumoparotid), and, more rarely, pneumomediastinum and pneumothorax [2]. Recurrent pneumoparotid can predispose to infectious parotitis by retrograde blowing oral bacteria into the parotid gland. Pressure changes in the parotid parenchyma further favour bacterial growth [3]. Imaging is essential to differentiate pneumoparotid from other causes of parotid swelling. In particular, CT, which has very high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosis [4], is adequate for differential diagnosis. Imaging Perspective In the diagnosis of pneumoparotid, the hallmark is the finding of gas within the parotid gland or parotid ducts. Therefore, CT, due to its sensitivity and spatial resolution, is the most accurate method for detecting this finding [5]. Ultrasound [4] is less specific because gas can be confused with ductal calculi (which are more frequently encountered); however, while gas produces reverberation or ring-down artefacts, calculi generate posterior shadow cone artefacts [6]. Some experience on the part of the operator is required for the diagnosis. However, compared to CT, ultrasound examination is a more widely available, low-cost and radiation-free method. Outcome Prognostically, pneumoparotitis is self-limiting. Most patients respond to conservative treatment. Antibiotics may be administered to prevent overinfection, analgesics in cases of pain, sialogogues to facilitate gas expulsion, glandular massage, or warm compresses. Surgery is reserved for more severe or recurrent pneumoparotid cases complicated by sialectasias and recurrent infections [1]. Take Home Message Imaging plays a key role in diagnosing pneumoparotid, as the clinical picture is often blurred and symptoms may even be absent, but this condition is not without its complications, albeit infrequent. In particular, the high sensitivity and specificity of CT scans make it possible to rule out potential diagnostic mimics and thus establish a correct therapeutic framework. Retrograde air insufflation during CT scans with puffed cheeks performed to evaluate oral cavity lesions can be observed in approximately 15% of patients [7]. In otherwise asymptomatic patients, it does not require further investigation or treatment beyond conservative measures. Therefore, awareness of this finding is important to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary concern. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Corynebacterium kroppenstedtii-associated granulomatous mastitis: A diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
clinical_history: A 64-year-old woman was referred to our hospital for second-opinion breast imaging due to left-sided bloody nipple discharge and nipple inversion, as the nature of the lesion could not be determined with certainty at the referring centre. Clinical examination revealed a firm, palpable area in the left breast with associated pain. The patient had no history of chronic illness and was not on any long-term or specific medication.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound at our centre revealed a left-sided peri-areolar heterogeneous well-circumscribed mass, in keeping with a dilated duct full of hypoechoic material, suggesting haemorrhagic ducts or intraductal debris (Figure 1). No significant intralesional vascularisation was observed, and no axillary adenopathy or other signs of malignancy were noted. In addition, bilateral mammography in standard craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO) views demonstrated benign appearing calcifications bilaterally, as well as several well-circumscribed opacities corresponding to filled dilated ducts (Figure 2). MRI, performed to assess the extent of the lesions and to further rule out malignancy, demonstrated multiple dilated ducts containing T1 hyperintense material, which appeared hypointense on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, suggestive of proteinaceous or mucinous content with fatty components. This imaging pattern has been previously reported in granulomatous mastitis cases [1]. In the inferolateral quadrant of the left breast, a subtle periductal T2 hyperintense signal with associated contrast enhancement was noted. These features are indicative of a focal inflammatory process, most likely periductal mastitis (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Granulomatous mastitis (GM) is a rare chronic breast inflammatory disease that mimics breast cancer and is considered a diagnosis of exclusion. The disease typically affects women of childbearing age, especially with a recent history of pregnancy and lactation. The pathogenesis is multifactorial with contributors including immune dysregulation, hormonal components and bacterial infection [2]. Corynebacterium kroppenstedtii was first isolated from the sputum of a patient with pulmonary disease. At present, the bacterium is almost exclusively obtained from female patients with breast abscesses and GM. Nevertheless, its exact role in breast diseases remains unclear [3]. Psychiatric illness and use of antipsychotic medication have been associated with a higher incidence of C. kroppenstedtii -related mastitis. Hyperprolactinemia, through antipsychotic medication or pituitary tumours (micro/macroadenoma), was suggested as a probable aetiological agent. It induces ductal ectasia and milk stagnation, predisposing factors for GM. Additionally, prolactin has proinflammatory effects in animal mammary epithelial cells, leading to the formation of granulomas [4]. Clinical Perspective Patients typically present with breast pain, palpable mass, and nipple discharge, features also associated with malignancy. Imaging is essential to characterise the lesion and guide biopsy. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound shows a mass-like tubular or nodular hypoechoic structure, often requiring histology for differentiation. MRI demonstrates asymmetrical T1 low and T2 high signal changes without significant mass effect, with contrast enhancement (mass, nodular, or ring-like) [6]. Outcome Treatment depends on the underlying aetiology. Antibiotics, steroids and surgical procedures are included as options. Recurrence occurs in approximately 25% of cases [5]. In our case, FNAC (fine needle aspiration cytology) followed by core biopsy confirmed chronic inflammatory duct ectasia with dense macrophage infiltration. Corynebacterium kroppenstedtii was isolated on two separate samples from culture. Initial antibiotic treatment with clindamycin (switched to doxycycline due to hypersensitivity) led to partial improvement. Following it, PET/CT and MRI revealed persistent bilateral duct ectasia, with mild residual periductal inflammation in the left infero-external quadrant (Figure 4). In consultation with an external academic centre, doxycycline was maintained, with a one-week course of ciprofloxacin and monthly intramuscular penicillin for one year. Nevertheless, subsequent ultrasound showed recurrent filled duct ectasia with abscess formation. The patient was hospitalised and treated with intravenous vancomycin and high-dose penicillin, resulting in significant but incomplete clinical improvement. Follow-up MRI demonstrated a reduction of the retroareolar dilated duct in the left breast, with persistent periductal enhancement and inflammation. The latest follow-up MRI revealed a similar appearance, with no significant interval change (Figure 5). Current treatment includes continued vancomycin administration and monthly intramuscular penicillin for a minimum of six months. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Granulomatous mastitis (GM) may mimic malignancy; biopsy and microbiological evaluation are essential. Corynebacterium kroppenstedtii is increasingly implicated in chronic or recurrent GM, though its role in breast diseases remains unclear. Treatment is often prolonged and may require antibiotics, steroids, or surgery. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Bilateral pelvic kidneys and pancake adrenal glands
clinical_history: A 50-year-old female with a past medical history of sphincter of Oddi dysfunction status post sphincterotomy, and stage 4 chronic kidney disease, presented to the hospital with left upper quadrant abdominal pain and vomiting, which started the night prior. In the emergency department, the patient was noted to have leukocytosis, and a computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis was ordered.
imaging_findings: CT of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast demonstrated no acute abnormality. However, the kidneys were not visualised in the renal fossae. Bilateral pancake morphology of the adrenal glands (Figure 1) and bilateral pelvic kidneys (Figure 2) was visualised. Subsequently, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) was performed and demonstrated no acute abnormality. The pelvic location of the bilateral kidneys and bilateral pancake adrenal glands was again noted (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Pelvic renal ectopia is considered the most common renal ectopia, with a prevalence of unilateral ectopia representing 1 in 2,100–3,000 in autopsies [1,2]. Bilateral pelvic kidneys represent approximately 10% of all renal ectopia cases. The true incidence of bilateral pelvic kidneys is unknown, with only a few cases reported in the literature. During normal embryological development, cephalic migration of the kidneys results in their normal retroperitoneal location, with an ectopic location the result of migration arrest. Ectopic kidneys are often associated with other abnormalities such as renal agenesis of the contralateral kidney, vascular malformations, and genital anomalies. Clinical Perspective Patients with pelvic kidneys can be asymptomatic, and the diagnosis is often incidental. However, patients may experience signs and symptoms including palpable pelvic masses, incontinence, urinary tract infections, nephrolithiasis, hydronephrosis, and renovascular hypertension secondary to anomalous vascular supply [3,4]. Special attention is required with concomitant presence of aortic and iliac aneurysms, given potential complications that can arise during surgical intervention [5]. In females, dystocia from a pelvic kidney can occur during pregnancy due to obstruction of the birthing canal. In our case, the patient was unaware of her condition and did not report previously experiencing any of the above-mentioned complications or other congenital anomalies. The patient’s glomerular filtration rate (GFR) at the time of her scan was 17, compatible with her known chronic kidney disease; this was unchanged compared to prior GFR measurements. Imaging Perspective Pelvic ectopic kidneys can be detected on ultrasound, intravenous pyelogram, CT, and MRI. Imaging can be helpful in assessing vascular and non-vascular anatomy as well as functional and structural assessment. These imaging modalities can additionally be useful in detecting potential associated urogenital abnormalities. In our case, given the lack of normal renal development within the renal fossae, the typical V-shaped adrenal gland development did not occur, resulting in the pancake configuration of the adrenal glands. Outcome Patients are often asymptomatic, and the diagnosis can be incidental, such as in our case. Treatment depends on the patient’s symptoms and the aetiology of the complications that may arise. Take Home Message Identifying ectopic kidneys and understanding the potential complications that can arise, as well as understanding the strengths and weaknesses of the different available modalities, can help in narrowing down the differential diagnoses when complications arise. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Papillary carcinoma in a thyroglossal duct cyst
clinical_history: A woman in her mid-20s presented with a painless, progressively enlarging midline neck mass over a period of 8 months. She had no history of dysphagia, dysphonia, or systemic symptoms. Physical examination revealed a firm, mobile mass in the anterior neck with mild movement on tongue protrusion and deglutition. Laboratory investigations revealed elevated serum thyroid-stimulating hormone and low free T4 levels.
imaging_findings: Plain CT images revealed a well-defined multilocular heterogeneous solid cystic lesion with clusters of calcifications in the anterior midline neck measuring 7.5 x 7 x 5 cm (Figure 1a). The thyroid gland appeared normal, and there were no suspicious cervical lymph nodes (Figure 1b). Contrast-enhanced CT images demonstrated enhancing papillary excrescences and internal septations (Figures 1c, 2a, and 2b). There was mild perilesional fat stranding with a mildly thickened investing layer of deep cervical fascia and left platysma. The lesion was infiltrating the strap muscles, also abutting the thyroid gland and left sternocleidomastoid with indistinct fat planes. The lesion also abuts the anterior wall of the trachea without luminal narrowing (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c). There was infiltration of the mylohyoid, geniohyoid and anterior belly of digastric muscles bilaterally, more so on the right (Figures 2a and 2b). However, the intrinsic muscles and the base of the tongue were preserved. The lesion is also abutting the hyoid bone, but no features of bone invasion or remodelling were identified (Figure 2b). CT findings raised the suspicion of papillary carcinoma within a thyroglossal duct cyst. The patient underwent ultrasound-guided needle aspiration, which revealed clusters of single scattered and focal papillaroid clusters of follicular cells. Histopathological examination (HPE) following Sistrunk procedure with total thyroidectomy confirmed classic-type papillary carcinoma arising in the thyroglossal duct cyst (Figures 3a and 3b). The excised thyroid also revealed features of nodular Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, and the hyoid bone was free of tumour.
discussion: Background Thyroglossal duct cysts (TGDC) are the most common congenital cervical cystic lesions resulting from incomplete obliteration of the thyroglossal duct during embryogenesis. TGDC can develop anywhere along the embryological tract from the foramen cecum to the suprasternal region, with the most common location being near the hyoid bone [1]. Papillary carcinoma arising within a TGDC is an uncommon entity, accounting for approximately 1% of all TGDC cases [1]. Given its rarity, the diagnosis and management pose significant challenges. This case highlights the importance of preoperative imaging in TGDC in differentiating benign and malignant lesions and also in planning surgical management. Clinical Perspective The clinical presentation of thyroglossal duct carcinoma is often indistinguishable from benign TGDC, as patients typically exhibit a painless, slow-growing midline neck mass [2]. The presence of malignancy is usually confirmed by HPE, emphasising the need for a high index of suspicion in select cases [3]. Imaging Perspective Imaging plays a crucial role in the evaluation of TGDC malignancy. Ultrasonography is often the initial modality, revealing a cystic mass with solid components or calcifications, which may raise suspicion for malignancy [4]. CT imaging typically reveals a solid-cystic mass, and the presence of soft tissue within a TGDC raises concern for the possibility of carcinoma; additionally, calcification may serve as a specific marker for papillary carcinoma [5,6]. Extra cystic extension into surrounding tissues and cervical lymphadenopathy may indicate aggressive disease [7]. These findings aid in distinguishing malignant from benign TGDCs and guide surgical planning. Fine-needle aspiration cytology has limited sensitivity in detecting carcinoma within TGDC due to the cystic nature of the lesion and low cellular yield [8]. HPE remains the gold standard for diagnosis. Papillary carcinoma is the most frequently reported histological variant, accounting for over 80% of cases [9]. The presence of papillary structures, nuclear grooves, intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions, and a large optically clear nucleus are hallmark microscopic features of papillary thyroid carcinoma. Outcome Sistrunk procedure, which involves excision of the cyst, along with the central portion of the hyoid bone and a core of the surrounding tissue, is considered the standard treatment, especially for those who are categorised as low-risk patients [10]. TGDC warrants thorough evaluation of the thyroid for synchronous malignancy, and of central and lateral compartment lymph nodes for nodal metastasis, as total thyroidectomy with nodal dissection is warranted in high-risk patients and to facilitate radioactive iodine therapy when indicated [11,12]. Our patient underwent a Sistrunk procedure with total thyroidectomy followed by close postoperative surveillance. Radioactive iodine ablation was not pursued in our case, given the clear surgical margins on pathology and the absence of malignancy in the thyroid. Prognosis for patients with papillary carcinoma in TGDC is generally favourable, with low recurrence rates and a five-year survival rate of about 95% following complete surgical excision[13]. However, long-term follow-up is recommended due to its potential for recurrence or metastasis, especially in cases with positive lymph nodes or aggressive histological features. The authors would like to thank the patient for allowing this rare case to be presented in this report.

title: Preoperative computer tomography-guided dye marking before minimally-invasive retroperitoneal lymph node resection
clinical_history: A 60-year-old man diagnosed with a G2 neuroendocrine tumour (NET) in the pancreas tail underwent left-sided pancreatectomy and splenectomy two years ago. During oncological follow-up, a new retroperitoneal hypervascularised nodule was detected, recommended for resection by the multidisciplinary tumour board.
imaging_findings: Abdominal positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) imaging revealed a metabolically active 9 mm nodule adjacent to the left renal vein (Figure 1). Additionally, at multi-phase magnetic resonance imaging (MRI; using a T3 scanner and Gadovist), the lesion showed diffusion restriction and arterial hyper-enhancement (Figure 1). Given the small size of the target lesion, the patient was sent for preoperative CT-guided dye marking.
discussion: CT-guided percutaneous marking was performed using patent blue V (PBV) and indocyanine green (ICG) injection (Figure 2): A contrast-enhanced arterial-phase CT was acquired to differentiate the target lesion from surrounding lymph nodes and ganglia. Following superficial and deep local anaesthesia, a 22-gauge Chiba needle was advanced under CT-fluoroscopic guidance until its tip lay immediately adjacent to, but not through, the target lesion. Care should be taken to avoid injecting dye directly into the target nodule, as this may increase the potential for malignant cell spread and interfere with subsequent pathological assessment. A total of 0.3 mL each of PBV and ICG were injected using a 1 mL Luer-lock syringe, followed by prompt needle withdrawal without saline flushing to avoid dye dilution. After applying a bandage, the patient was sent for surgical preparation, with surgery performed 3 hours after marking. daVinci-assisted resection of the target lesion using the Firefly camera system was completed in 47 minutes from incision to closure, despite prominent intra-abdominal adhesions following previous left-sided pancreatectomy and splenectomy (Figure 3). This case illustrates how interventional radiology-guided preoperative dye marking enhances surgical precision in minimally invasive resections of intra-abdominal targets. While intravenous and intracholangiographic use of ICG in abdominal procedures [1,2] and percutaneous ICG lung markings in thoracic surgery [3,4] are emerging technologies for surgical decision-making over the past decade, to our knowledge, this is the first case demonstrating CT-guided percutaneous marking as feasible for efficient resection of retroperitoneal lesions. In our experience, CT-guided marking is a brief and almost painless intervention performed under local anaesthesia that enhances target identification during surgery, reduces operative duration, and improves oncological safety [5]. Teaching Points CT-guided percutaneous dye marking using patent blue V and/or indocyanine green for retroperitoneal lesions is a straightforward and safe radiological intervention. Preoperative marking enabled quick intraoperative identification and complete resection of a small retroperitoneal lesion. An interdisciplinary approach to surgery planning, including interventional radiology-guided lesion marking, is likely to enhance surgical precision. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Otogenic brain abscess
clinical_history: A 38-year-old man with no past medical history presents with a 4-day history of headache, right-sided otalgia and otorrhoea. He has had intermittent right-sided hearing loss and ear “fullness” for 2 years. He then becomes pyrexial and begins to behave erratically. Clinical examination is unremarkable.
imaging_findings: Initial non-contrast CT showed pneumocephalus and a hypodensity in the temporal lobe (Figures 1a and 1b). Bone windows revealed widespread opacification of the right petromastoid air cells (Figure 1c). CT mastoid confirmed air cell pneumatisation and defects in the tegmen mastoideum (Figures 2a and 2b). MRI T2/FLAIR images showed a hyperintense lesion, a hypointense rim and an internal air locule in the right inferior temporal gyrus, with adjacent hyperintense cerebritis and vasogenic oedema (Figures 3a and 3b). There was T2 hyperintense fluid in the petromastoid air cells and a tegmen (Figures 3c). T2 GRE images displayed a hyperintense centre with a hypointense rim and blooming artifact, the “dual rim” sign (Figure 3d) [1]. The temporal lobe lesion was T1 hypointense with classic T1 post-contrast ring-enhancement (Figures 4a and 4b). Post-contrast cochlear enhancement suggested secondary suppurative otogenic labyrinthitis. The lesion and mastoid air cells showed diffusion restriction, high DWI and low ADC signal (Figures 5a and 5b).
discussion: Background Brain abscesses often stem from a nearby infected source [2]. Temporal lobe abscesses primarily originate from otogenic sources, i.e., otitis media or mastoiditis [3]. Intracerebral invasion usually occurs through a bone defect, caused by mucopurulent secretions in the mastoid air cell space that gradually break down bony trabeculae through mechanical compression, inflammatory hyperaemia and local acidosis, in a disease process known as coalescent mastoiditis [4]. Clinical Perspective A 2014 systematic review found patients with brain abscesses presented with headache, fever, altered mental status, focal neurologic symptoms, and nausea and vomiting. The incidence of symptoms varied considerably from 14% to 93% [5]. As brain abscesses cannot be easily differentiated on presentation from other space-occupying lesions, meningitis, encephalitis, or even psychiatric disorders, neuroimaging is a critical tool for definitive diagnosis. Imaging Perspective While brain abscesses have a characteristic appearance on CT and MRI, several important differentials must be considered. Cerebritis, an early precursor, appears as an ill-defined area of inflammation with T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and restricted diffusion. Incomplete capsule development results in little to no ring enhancement on contrast scans [6]. Similarly, partially treated abscesses may display less intense/irregular ring enhancement. Some intracranial malignancies can be difficult to differentiate from abscesses. The fluid-filled necrotic cores of most tumours show facilitated diffusion (low DWI, high ADC). Abscesses contain viscous pus and show restricted diffusion. However, highly cellular tumours (e.g., lymphomas) can mimic this finding [7]. By measuring relative cerebral blood volume, perfusion imaging can show that abscess capsules are avascular, whereas high-grade tumours show hypervascularity secondary to neovascularisation [8]. Subacute haematomas can also mimic brain abscesses by demonstrating ring enhancement. However they are differentiated by T1 hyperintensity and T2* hypointensity due to the presence of blood products [9]. Finally, not all brain abscesses have a typical appearance. Fungal abscesses demonstrate a heterogeneous/patchy diffusion on DWI/ADC maps, unlike the uniform restricted diffusion in pyogenic abscesses (Figures 5a and 5b). Fungal abscess capsules are often irregular and thicker with internal spicules and the T2* “dual-rim sign” is usually absent [10]. Outcome Brain abscesses usually require prolonged antibiotic courses and surgery for definitive management [11]. CT and MRI imaging is crucial for timely diagnosis and is the cornerstone of planning emergent surgical procedures. This patient required a joint ENT and neurosurgical procedure involving mastoidectomy, aspiration and resection of the temporal lobe abscess and repair of middle fossa defects (Figures 6a and 6b). He has since returned to work and is largely asymptomatic.
differential_diagnosis: Right temporal lobe abscess secondary to chronic coalescent otomastoiditis Primary cerebral tumours/metastases Subacute haemorrhage/infarcts Fungal brain abscess
final_diagnosis: Right temporal lobe abscess secondary to chronic coalescent otomastoiditis

title: Rare pelvic presentation of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour
clinical_history: A 59-year-old male presented with a two-month history of tenesmus and urinary urgency. He had obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus, without features of hereditary tumour syndrome. Digital rectal examination revealed a firm mass 3 cm from the anal verge, and rigid rectosigmoidoscopy showed rectal stenosis from extrinsic compression.
imaging_findings: Computed tomography (CT) of the pelvic region revealed a large, well-defined lesion measuring 10 × 9 cm, with heterogeneous enhancement (Figure 1). No clear cleavage plane was observed between the lesion and adjacent structures, including the rectum and prostate (Figure 2). On magnetic resonance (MR), the lesion abuts the left rectosigmoid wall, prostate, and seminal vesicles, without imaging signs of invasion. Additionally, the mass compressed and displaced the upper rectum to the right and displaced the prostate and seminal vesicles anterosuperiorly (Figure 3). There is also a fat plane separating the mass from the sacral plexus, as well as from the obturator and sciatic nerves. There are no indirect signs of invasion, such as oedema or abnormal enhancement of the major nerve structures. The lesion exhibited marked heterogeneity, with extensive necrotic areas, significant diffusion restriction, and intense enhancement of the solid peripheral components following contrast administration (Figures 3, 4, 5, and 6).
discussion: Background Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST) is a rare, aggressive neoplasm that arises from the peripheral nerve sheaths, accounting for 5% of soft-tissue sarcomas and occurring in 0.001% of the population [1,2]. Clinical Perspective MPNST typically affects young to middle-aged adults, with no sex predilection [1]. About half of the cases are associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), and the remainder are sporadic [1]. Common sites include the extremities, head, neck, and trunk, while pelvic involvement is rare [1,3]. The symptoms are related to the location and size of the lesion [4]. Pain and weakness are the most commonly reported [4]. The prognosis is poor, and the association with NF1 further worsens survival [4]. Imaging Perspective MRI is the modality of choice for soft tissue tumours [5]. On T1-weighted sequences, MPNST shows signal intensity similar to muscle with peripheral gadolinium enhancement [5]. T2-weighted sequences reveal heterogeneous signal with hyperintense areas reflecting necrosis or cystic degeneration [5]. Although imaging cannot definitively distinguish benign from malignant nerve sheath tumours, features such as large size, necrotic or cystic areas, peripheral enhancement, perilesional oedema, absence of the “target sign”, and low ADC on diffusion-weighted imaging may suggest MPNST [6,7]. Several entities can present as presacral or pelvic masses [8]: Colorectal cancer arises from the bowel wall and may cause obstruction or infiltration; Rectal GIST originates in the rectal wall and may show intraluminal involvement; Acrococcygeal chordoma shows midline sacral destruction and canal extension; Teratomas occur in younger patients and contain fat or calcifications; Tailgut cysts are congenital multiloculated cystic lesions that can rarely undergo malignant transformation [8]. Outcome CT-guided biopsy revealed a spindle cell sarcoma with myogenic differentiation. The patient received neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by extended pelvic excision, including abdominoperineal resection and perineal reconstruction. Histopathology showed a high-grade spindle cell neoplasm with nuclear pleomorphism, desmin and CD34 positivity, less than 50% necrosis, and CDKN2A inactivation, consistent with MPNST. Although S100 expression is relatively specific for tumours of nerve sheath origin, it was negative in this case. Nonetheless, up to 50% of MPNSTs may demonstrate patchy or focal S100 positivity [1]. Eight months later, recurrence was detected in the presacral region, confirmed by biopsy. The patient underwent extended excision with partial sacrectomy and adjuvant brachytherapy. Take Home Message Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST) is a rare, aggressive soft-tissue sarcoma that may occur sporadically, without neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). Imaging features, such as large size, heterogeneous signal, and peripheral enhancement, aid in diagnosing MPNST. The pelvic region is a rare location for MPNST, with few cases reported in the literature. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour Rectal gastrointestinal stromal tumour Sacrococcygeal chordoma Teratoma Tailgut cyst

title: Radiological perspectives on immunotherapy-related effects – A diagnostic challenge
clinical_history: A 59-year-old man, smoker (42 pack-years), with a history of penile cancer at age 54 and rhinosinusitis with lung adenocarcinoma (PD-L1 60–70%), without targetable mutations and initially staged as IIIB, underwent chemotherapy with concurrent radiotherapy. However, due to progression to metastatic disease, he started treatment with pembrolizumab.
imaging_findings: The re-evaluation computed tomography (CT) scan after five cycles of immunotherapy (Figures 1b, 2b, 3b, and 4b) showed a partial response. However, new retractile perihilar peribronchovascular consolidations appeared, diffusely distributed across all lung lobes, with irregular contours and internal traction bronchiectasis. These findings were associated with fissural and pleural retraction, as well as reduced lung volume in the affected areas. Moderate bilateral centrilobular emphysema was also observed. These newly emerged changes were interpreted as pembrolizumab-related organising pneumonia.
discussion: Pembrolizumab is a drug within the category of immunotherapy that functions as an immune checkpoint inhibitor and has revolutionised oncology [1]. However, it has documented immune-related adverse effects that can be potentially life-threatening. The most common side effects occur at the dermatological, endocrinological, gastrointestinal, pulmonary, and hepatic systems [2]. Pneumonitis related to pembrolizumab is reported in studies with an incidence of 3–5% and is more common in smokers or former smokers [1,3]. The changes typically appear, on average, 2.8 months after the initiation of therapy [1]. The radiological pattern is classified as interstitial lung disease (ILD) and may present with ground-glass opacities or consolidations, typically with a peribronchovascular distribution, most commonly involving the lower lobes. Interlobular septal thickening and a “crazy paving” pattern may also be present [4]. Clinically, patients may be asymptomatic or present with mild cough, chest pain, and progressively worsening dyspnoea [1]. In terms of severity, pneumonitis can be classified into four grades: the lowest, grade one, is the mildest form, in which the patient is asymptomatic or presents with mild symptoms; grade two, where the patient experiences symptoms that affect daily activities; grade three, characterised by severe clinical manifestations; and, grade four, the most severe, which is life-threatening and often requires admission to intensive care [4,5]. Our patient, despite the extensive radiological findings, was asymptomatic from a respiratory standpoint, experiencing only generalised itching that resolved with antihistamines. The patient continued the treatment under close monitoring, without any further complaints to date. The treatment of pembrolizumab-related pneumonitis primarily involves discontinuing the drug. In some cases, corticosteroid therapy is necessary, with a typical treatment duration of around six weeks, depending on the individual situation [3]. In certain cases, it is possible to resume treatment; however, in others, permanent discontinuation is required [1]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points This case reports an adverse effect of immunotherapy, which, although recognised, is relatively uncommon and presents a diagnostic challenge. Other potential causes—particularly infections and even disease progression—must always be carefully excluded. Radiologically, it can present with multiple patterns, most notably peribronchovascular involvement. Pembrolizumab-related pneumonitis is a potentially fatal condition that requires a high index of suspicion.
differential_diagnosis: Radiation pneumonitis Pneumonitis secondary to pembrolizumab Early pulmonary oedema Tumour progression

title: Appendiceal intussusception: An ileocecal intussusception mimic
clinical_history: A teenage patient presented to the emergency department with acute abdominal pain in the lower quadrants, more intense in the right iliac fossa. Medical history was unremarkable. The patient was afebrile. Blood tests showed leukocytosis (43.65 x 10^9/L) and elevated C-reactive protein levels (38.8 mg/L).
imaging_findings: Ultrasound revealed concentric alternating echogenic and hypoechoic bands of bowel wall in the right iliac fossa (target sign) (Figure 1). The appendix and the last ileal loop could not be definitively identified. An abdominopelvic computed tomography (CT) scan performed in the portal venous phase showed the appendix invaginating into the caecum and ascending colon, enlarged and with hyperenhancing walls (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). The caecum showed thickened and hyperenhancing walls. Fat stranding surrounding the caecum and free intra-abdominal fluid were also seen. The last ileal loop showed no significant alterations (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Appendiceal intussusception is a rare condition characterised by invagination of the appendix into itself or into the caecum, with an estimated incidence of 0.01% among patients who underwent appendectomy [1–6]. It is thought to result from abnormal appendiceal peristalsis triggered by factors such as fecaliths, foreign bodies, lymphoid hyperplasia or neoplasms such as adenocarcinomas. It may also be idiopathic [1–6]. Clinical Perspective Clinical presentation is often nonspecific. Patients may show symptoms similar to acute appendicitis or ileocecal intussusception, such as right lower quadrant abdominal pain and vomiting. Others may present with symptoms of bowel obstruction or recurrent abdominal pain. It can also be found incidentally in asymptomatic patients [1–4,6]. Imaging Perspective Plain abdominal radiographs are typically normal unless obstruction is present, in which case dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels will be seen [1,5]. Barium enema, primarily performed in paediatric patients, may demonstrate a finger-like filling defect in the caecum or a coiled-spring appearance. However, it is rarely used in acute cases, especially in older patients, due to the risks such as perforation [1,5]. Ultrasound may show similar findings to ileocecal intussusception, such as the target sign (alternating echogenic and hypoechoic layers of bowel wall). Identifying the insertion of the appendix and the terminal ileum helps differentiate these conditions [1,5,6]. CT imaging will show a layered, target-like appearance of the caecum, with a well-encapsulated structure protruding into the lumen. It will effectively distinguish appendiceal from ileocecal intussusception and detect complications [1–3]. Outcome When managing an appendiceal intussusception, children may respond to reduction with barium or air enemas. Reduction should be avoided when malignant lesions are suspected, to avoid dissemination. Adults generally require surgery, with some authors advocating for a reduction attempt with gentle traction to be made initially, followed by a simple appendectomy. Colonoscopy reduction has also been described. If reduction is not achieved, a more complex surgery is performed, usually involving opening the caecum. Right hemicolectomy should be considered when malignant lesions are detected [2,3,7]. In our case, an appendectomy was performed, and histologic analysis revealed a mucinous adenocarcinoma of the appendix with inflammatory infiltrate in the subserosa and surrounding tissue. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Appendiceal intussusception is an uncommon cause of abdominal pain. Causes vary from benign (such as fecaliths) to malignant (such as adenocarcinomas). Clinical presentation is nonspecific, and ultrasound and CT play an essential role in this diagnosis [1–6]. title: Bilateral nontraumatic spontaneous femoral neck fractures in chronic kidney disease
clinical_history: A 65-year-old female with end-stage renal disease on long-term peritoneal dialysis presented with progressive weakness, poor appetite, and inability to ambulate. Two weeks prior, she developed bilateral hip and leg pain after a cracking sound while seated, without any history of trauma. Labs showed severe hyperparathyroidism and low vitamin D.
imaging_findings: Pelvic radiographs (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c) demonstrate bilateral basicervical femoral neck fractures (Garden type III) with superior displacement of both femoral shafts and diastasis of the pubic symphysis. Irregular periosteal thickening is noted along the proximal femurs, with diffuse demineralisation of the femoral heads and pelvic bones. Both acetabular rims remain intact but show mild right-sided bulging into the pelvic rim. Findings suggest markedly weakened bone structure and chronic metabolic changes predisposing to insufficiency fractures.
discussion: Background Femoral neck fractures commonly occur in older women, often due to osteoporosis or metabolic bone disease. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) results in renal osteodystrophy, marked by altered bone remodelling and impaired mineralisation. Declining kidney function leads to phosphate retention and lower 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, which triggers hyperparathyroidism, driving cortical thinning and fragility [1–3]. Dialysis patients face an approximately 4.4-fold higher risk of hip fractures compared to the general population [4]. This case is unusual: spontaneous, bilateral femoral neck fractures without a history of trauma. While most femoral neck fractures follow falls, external rotation may also cause fractures in weakened bone [5]. In this patient, minimal rotational force while seated likely caused symmetric fractures in osteopenic bone. Clinical Perspective This dialysis patient presented with sudden bilateral hip pain and inability to walk, without any trauma. Laboratory data revealed markedly elevated parathyroid hormone and low vitamin D, consistent with hyperparathyroidism. Imaging was indispensable to uncover the structural aetiology of the immobility, to delineate fracture patterns, and to coordinate orthopaedic and endocrine care in a metabolically fragile patient. Imaging Perspective Pelvic radiographs showed bilateral displaced femoral neck fractures (Garden type III). These findings, without trauma, point toward insufficiency fractures secondary to metabolic bone disease. Plain radiographs are sufficient for diagnosis in most femoral neck fractures, while MRI or CT are reserved for equivocal or occult cases [5]. The radiographic appearance, along with her metabolic derangements, supports renal osteodystrophy as the aetiology. Outcome After diagnosis, the patient was co-managed by the orthopaedics and endocrinology departments. Work-up revealed low bone stock, making surgical fixation inadvisable. Thus, conservative management was chosen. She received analgesia and rehabilitation, while endocrine therapy targeted tertiary hyperparathyroidism and subclinical hyperthyroidism. Therapeutic options for similar cases include parathyroidectomy, phosphate binders, vitamin D analogues, and antiresorptive or anabolic agents tailored to bone turnover status [6]. Prognosis is guarded: CKD patients sustaining hip fractures exhibit high mortality (up to 70% at one year in some series) [7]. Early imaging is critical, enabling timely intervention and may reduce further morbidity. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Renal osteodystrophy predisposes to spontaneous insufficiency fractures. Bilateral femoral neck fractures in this setting should prompt evaluation for metabolic bone disease. Imaging is essential for diagnosis, characterisation, and guiding operative vs. conservative decisions. Rapid metabolic correction and multidisciplinary management are vital for improving outcomes. title: Masson’s tumour of the elbow: Rare presentation in paediatric patient
clinical_history: A 10-year-old girl presented with a 6-month swelling at the posteromedial aspect of the right elbow with fixed flexion deformity of the elbow (Figure 1). The swelling was painless, progressive in nature, and firm in consistency.
imaging_findings: A plain radiograph initially performed (Figure 2) showed soft tissue opacity at the posteromedial aspect of the right elbow, along with a few calcific foci associated with it. Expansion of the distal humerus was also noted. CT angiography of the right upper limb showed a heterogeneous lesion (Figure 3) with multiple calcific foci within the posteromedial aspect of the right elbow. No definite arterial feeders were seen supplying the lesion. The lesion was being drained by tributaries from branches of the right basilic vein (Figure 4). MRI was performed using PD/TSE (proton density/turbo spin echo) T2-weighted and SE T1-weighted sequences in the sagittal and coronal planes, along with fat-saturated PD/TSE T2-weighted and SE T1-weighted sequences in the transverse plane. On MRI, a well-defined lobulated lesion (Figure 5) was noted arising from the right elbow joint, located on the posterior aspect of the distal right arm in the intermuscular plane and seen displacing the triceps posteriorly. The lesion was heterogeneously isointense to the muscle on T1-weighted and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted and PDFS (proton density fat-saturated) sequences (Figure 6). On post-contrast images, it showed heterogeneous and patchy contrast enhancement (Figure 8). The lesion was causing cortical breach and infiltrating the medullary compartment of the underlying distal humerus. Intra-articular extension into the right elbow joint is seen with associated narrowing of the joint space. The olecranon process and proximal 1/3 of the ulna are also involved, with associated erosion of the proximal ulna. No obvious involvement of the neurovascular bundle was seen.
discussion: Background Masson’s tumour, another name for intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia (IPEH), is a rare vascular tumour thought to originate from the proliferation of injured endothelial cells within a vessel, often thought to be a form of special thrombus organisation. It typically manifests in various parts of the body, including the limbs and upper regions, but is especially prevalent in the fingers and vascular structures [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Due to its rarity and clinical similarity to other vascular tumours like pyogenic granuloma, haemangioma, and angiosarcoma, diagnosing it can be difficult [1,3]. It typically presents as a slow-growing mass or swelling, appearing as a firm, subcutaneous nodule or papule with an ovoid, rounded, or lobulated shape, located superficially and often accompanied by bluish or reddish discolouration of the overlying skin. From a clinical standpoint, the overlapping features with both benign and malignant vascular lesions make accurate differentiation crucial. Imaging is essential not only for localisation and assessment of lesion extent but also to help distinguish IPEH from more aggressive pathologies. Imaging Perspective Imaging findings offer crucial diagnostic clues and help differentiate IPEH from aggressive vascular neoplasms. Lesions often appear isointense or slightly hyperintense on T1-weighted images, and they demonstrate heterogeneous signals on T2-weighted images, including peripheral hyperintensity, hypointense nodules, or hyperintensity with hypointense rims, reflecting a mix of thrombi and endothelial proliferation [4,5]. Post-contrast MRI typically shows rim, septal, or heterogeneous enhancement, corresponding to fibrovascular tissue and thrombotic regions [4,6]. Mixed-type IPEHs may exhibit central or septal enhancement and variable internal signals [6]. Ultrasound is useful for superficial lesions, revealing hypoechoic masses with peripheral or septal vascularity on Doppler, correlating with papillary architecture and fibrous septa [6,7]. Although histopathology confirms the diagnosis, recognising these imaging features helps narrow the differential and guides biopsy or excision, reducing the risk of misdiagnosis as an aggressive vascular tumour. Differential diagnosis: Pyogenic granuloma – Superficial, rapidly growing soft tissue lesion with intense homogeneous contrast enhancement, usually lacking internal thrombi, calcifications, or flow voids. Haemangioma – Common in childhood/young adulthood, shows T2 hyperintensity with flow voids on MRI, phleboliths as calcifications on CT, and a characteristic progressive nodular centripetal enhancement pattern. Angiosarcoma – Ill-defined infiltrative soft tissue mass demonstrating heterogeneous enhancement, areas of haemorrhage and necrosis, restricted diffusion on MRI, and possible local invasion or distant metastases. Organised thrombus – Non-enhancing or showing only thin peripheral rim enhancement, without internal flow voids or nodular vascularity, often associated with adjacent venous structures. Haemophilic pseudotumor – Expansile lytic bone lesion with fluid–fluid levels and haemosiderin deposition causing blooming on GRE/SWI MRI, non-vascular in nature with only peripheral capsule enhancement, and seen in patients with haemophilia. Kaposi sarcoma – Presents as multiple enhancing cutaneous or subcutaneous nodules with intermediate T1 and hyperintense T2 signals on MRI, showing strong enhancement, typically involving skin, mucosa, and visceral organs in the setting of HIV/AIDS or immunosuppression. Outcome In our case, initial cytological evaluation showed no evidence of malignancy, helping to exclude more aggressive vascular tumours. Subsequent histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen confirmed the diagnosis of Masson’s tumour. Given the benign nature but potential for local recurrence, surgical excision is being planned as definitive treatment. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Masson’s tumour is a rare, benign vascular lesion that can closely mimic both benign and malignant vascular neoplasms, particularly angiosarcoma. Its variable presentation and overlapping features often pose diagnostic challenges. MRI plays a critical role in evaluation, with characteristic findings such as heterogeneous T2 signal intensity and rim or septal enhancement, reflecting internal thrombi and proliferative endothelial components. Although imaging can suggest the diagnosis, histopathology remains essential for confirmation. Recognising the typical imaging features of IPEH (intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia) is crucial to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary aggressive treatment, allowing for appropriate surgical management and favourable outcomes.

title: Anti-synthetase syndrome
clinical_history: A 39-year-old aluminium worker presented with a year-long history of diffuse hand pain, swelling, and bilateral finger desquamation, partially responsive to prednisolone. The exam revealed mechanic’s hands, Gottron’s papules, elbow and knee desquamation, high creatine kinase/myoglobin, but preserved muscle strength and no joint inflammation.
imaging_findings: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis and thighs demonstrated diffuse interstitial oedema within the pelvic and thigh muscle groups (Figures 1 and 2), without significant associated atrophy or fatty infiltration, findings suggestive of non-specific myositis. There was also associated intermuscular fascial oedema (Figure 3). Computed tomography of the chest revealed areas of ground-glass opacification (Figure 4) in both lower lobes, the middle lobe, and the lingula, suggestive of involvement by interstitial lung disease.
discussion: Background Anti-synthetase syndrome (ASS) is a rare autoimmune disorder characterised by autoantibodies against aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, often anti-Jo-1. It is part of idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, defined by the triad of myositis, interstitial lung disease (ILD), and dermatologic features like “mechanic’s hands” and Gottron’s papules. Other symptoms include arthritis, Raynaud’s phenomenon, and fever. The presentation is variable, with not all patients showing the full triad at onset [1]. Clinical Perspective ASS typically affects adults in their 40s–60s, with a higher prevalence in women [5]. Patients may present with myositis, pulmonary, or cutaneous involvement. “Mechanic’s hands” are a common but non-specific sign [1]. Muscle involvement ranges from mild to severe, and some may only show elevated muscle enzymes without clinical weakness [4]. ILD is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, with varying progression [3]. Imaging Perspective In musculoskeletal imaging, MRI is sensitive in detecting muscle inflammation, showing diffuse muscle oedema without significant atrophy (Figure 1) in early stages. Intermuscular fascial oedema (Figure 3) is also common [4]. In pulmonary imaging, high-resolution CT is essential for evaluating ILD, commonly showing patterns like nonspecific interstitial pneumonia and organising pneumonia, with ground-glass opacities (Figure 4) and traction bronchiectasis, primarily in the lower lobes [2]. Early ILD detection is crucial for prognosis [2]. Ultrasound and chest radiography have lower sensitivity but may be useful in initial assessment [2]. Imaging findings in ASS overlap with other inflammatory myopathies and ILD causes. Diagnosis relies on combining imaging, clinical, and serologic data [1]. Outcome Early treatment with corticosteroids and immunosuppressive agents is key to preventing irreversible damage. MRI and high-resolution CT are important for monitoring treatment response [3]. Take Home Message Anti-synthetase syndrome (ASS) is a rare cause of myositis and interstitial lung disease (ILD). MRI is sensitive for detecting muscle inflammation, and high-resolution CT is essential for ILD assessment. Radiologists should be familiar with these imaging features for early diagnosis and management [1].

title: Neurobrucellosis – Diffuse white matter inflammation pattern mimicking leukodystrophy
clinical_history: A 50-year-old male farmer presented with a 1-year history of progressive ataxia, seizures, and speech difficulties. On examination, he exhibited bilateral lower limb spasticity, prominent cerebellar signs, and a broad-based spastic-ataxic gait.
imaging_findings: MRI of the brain revealed diffuse subcortical white matter hyperintensity on T2-weighted (Figure 1) and FLAIR (Figure 2) sequences, predominantly affecting the frontal, parietal, and anterior temporal lobes. Similar signal changes were observed in the bilateral subcortical cerebellar white matter (red arrow in Figure 2d). No abnormalities were detected on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) or susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI). Additionally, no leptomeningeal or neuroparenchymal contrast enhancement was noted (Figure 3). Enhancement of the cranial nerves was not evident.
discussion: Background Brucellosis is a common zoonotic disease worldwide. Farmers involved in animal husbandry are frequently exposed to infections by consuming uncooked meat or unpasteurised dairy products. Neurobrucellosis is a rare but serious complication and occurs in up to 25% cases of brucellosis [1]. Clinical Perspective Neurological manifestations are diverse and often non-specific. Usually, patients present with headache, low-grade fever, hearing loss, and neuropsychiatric disturbances. The frequent occurrence of sensorineural hearing loss indicates that brucellosis preferentially affects the auditory system. Other manifestations are chronic meningitis, encephalitis, meningoencephalitis, myelitis, myelopathy, stroke, paraplegia, radiculoneuritis, demyelination, intracranial hypertension, Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), cerebral abscess, cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT), subdural haemorrhage, cranial nerve involvement, or a combination of these manifestations [2]. Imaging Perspective The imaging abnormalities in neurobrucellosis vary widely, from a normal appearance to features of meningitis, meningoencephalitis, diffuse inflammatory white matter changes, cerebral abscess formation and vascular insult. Inflammation may cause granuloma formation and enhancement of perivascular spaces, meninges, or lumbar nerve roots. A diffuse inflammatory white matter pattern is described in approximately 25% of cases, predominantly affecting the subcortical arcuate fibres, periventricular white matter and focal demyelinating plaques. Microhaemorrhages and enhancement are uncommon. White matter changes may mimic those seen in multiple sclerosis, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, or Lyme disease; however, corpus callosal involvement and subcortical enhancing lesions, typical of these conditions, have not been described in neurobrucellosis [3,4]. Outcome In our case, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (70 cells/µL), elevated protein (80 mg/dL), and low glucose (13 mg/dL). Oligoclonal bands were also present in the CSF. Additionally, both CSF and serum tested positive for anti- Brucella IgG antibodies via ELISA, confirming the diagnosis. Take Home Message Neurobrucellosis is a serious complication of brucellosis with highly variable clinical and imaging presentations. On imaging, at least five imaging patterns have been described. Detection of IgG and IgM anti- Brucella antibodies by ELISA is the most commonly used diagnostic method. With early diagnosis and standard treatment, recovery is generally good.

title: Pelvic MRI as a diagnostic tool in atypical male sexual dysfunction
clinical_history: A 43-year-old fit male, who sought medical attention for dysuria and perianal pain. On examination, he had a tender prostate and mildly raised PSA, and therefore was treated for prostatitis. However, his symptoms worsened, and he developed painful ejaculation. His physician ordered a pelvic MRI and CT urogram.
imaging_findings: A pelvic MRI revealed a large cystic lesion arising in the region of the right ureteric orifice, which appeared extravesical. This extended superiorly and communicated with an abnormally distended and dilated right distal ureter (Figure 1). On the coronal T1-weighted images, the right seminal vesicles and large cystic tubular structure showed increased signalling, in keeping with haemorrhagic/proteinaceous contents (Figure 2). No suspicious pelvic lymphadenopathy or destructive osseous lesions were shown. Based on these findings, a working diagnosis of Zinner syndrome was raised, which is extremely rare. The diagnostic workup was completed with a CT urogram, confirming an absent right kidney. There was dilatation of the distal right ureter, which was seen to extend to a 5.0 x 4.4 cm cystic stricture, in keeping with a large right seminal vesicle cyst (Figure 3). The urinary bladder appeared unremarkable, along with the left kidney and ureter. Based on these findings, there was a multidisciplinary team discussion regarding a transperineal aspiration of the seminal vesicle cyst. However, ultimately, a conservative approach was adopted.
discussion: Background Zinner syndrome is a rare congenital disorder of the male urogenital tract, first coined by A. Zinner in 1914 [1]. Fewer than 300 cases have been reported in the literature, and it is often asymptomatic till found incidentally in the third or fourth decade of life through diagnostic imaging. It comprises a triad of mesonephric (Wolffian) duct anomalies involving unilateral renal agenesis, ipsilateral seminal vesicle cyst and ejaculatory duct obstruction [2]. Clinical Perspective Zinner syndrome remains an underdiagnosed entity by clinicians due to its non-specific presentation and the reliance on advanced diagnostic tools such as MRI for definitive diagnosis. Symptoms can be vague, such as those illustrated in this case, along with infertility, urinary frequency/urgency and some experiencing epididymitis or haematospermia [3]. Occasionally, complications such as recurrent epididymitis, urinary tract infections, or pelvic pain may occur due to secondary infection of the seminal vesicle cyst. Early radiology identification is essential to know the disease burden and any secondary effects, such as compression of the bladder or prostate, that influence management planning. Outcome Management depends on symptom burden and cyst size. A conservative approach is more appropriate for asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic patients, involving clinical observation and periodic imaging to monitor cyst progression. Minimally invasive interventions, including transrectal aspiration or transurethral deroofing, may offer temporary symptom relief but can be associated with recurrence. Definitive management involves surgical excision of the seminal vesicle cyst, which may provide long-term symptom relief. However, the long-term prognosis remains uncertain and can be variable depending on the function of the contralateral seminal vesicle and contralateral solitary renal unit. Fertility outcomes largely depend on the functionality of the contralateral seminal vesicle and vas deferens. From a renal perspective, patients should be advised on solitary kidney precautions, including avoidance of nephrotoxic agents, contact sports and other high-impact activities. MRI findings directly inform therapeutic planning, helping to distinguish patients for conservative monitoring from those requiring surgical referral. In this particular case, the patient experienced near-complete resolution of his symptoms following multidisciplinary discussion, and a decision was made to pursue a conservative management approach with ongoing surveillance rather than immediate surgical intervention. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Zinner syndrome, while rare, should be considered in men presenting with persistent genitourinary symptoms that do not respond to conventional treatment. This case underscores the importance of advanced imaging in identifying congenital anomalies when initial clinical and laboratory evaluations are inconclusive. Conservative management may be sufficient in symptomatic cases if the patient’s condition improves, with surgical options reserved for those with ongoing symptoms or complications. title: Frontal mass: A diagnostic challenge
clinical_history: A 69-year-old man was admitted to the Emergency Department because he had developed a painless, fluctuant frontal mass of two weeks’ duration, with no fever. He gave a history of previous sinusitis episodes for which he sought evaluation by a naturopathic practitioner.
imaging_findings: An initial CT scan with and without contrast was performed. It showed an extensive sinus disease involving all paranasal sinuses, associated with signs of osteitis of their walls. The right frontal sinus was completely opacified, and it demonstrated a large anterior paramedial bone dehiscence (Figures 1 and 2), which communicated with a large subperiosteal collection with peripheral enhancement and internal septation (Figure 3). The study was completed with an MR, which confirmed an abscessed collection, hypointense on T1-weighted and hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences, and with intense diffusion restriction content (Figures 4a and 4b). There was also a smaller posterosuperior bone dehiscence of the frontal right sinus, associated with a small adjacent epidural collection, dural thickening and enhancement (Figures 5a, 5b and 5c).
discussion: Background Pott’s puffy tumour, described by Sir Percival Pott in 1760, is defined as an osteomyelitis of the frontal bone with associated subperiosteal abscess and dural involvement [1]. It classically follows acute or inadequately treated bacterial sinusitis, but may also result from trauma. Its pathophysiology is explained by the existing anastomosis between the dural venous sinus and the veins of the scalp, diploic and emissary veins. Though rare in the antibiotic era, it remains a serious entity due to its potential intracranial and orbital complications [2]. Imaging Perspective CT is the imaging modality of choice, showing sinus opacification, bony erosion, and subperiosteal abscess. The main differential diagnoses include: Destructive metastasis to frontal sinus: no diffusion restriction. Infected mucocele: typically expansile and well-circumscribed, with smooth bone remodelling rather than irregular destruction. Primary osteomyelitis: shows more diffuse bony sclerosis/destruction without a characteristic sinus origin; often accompanied by periosteal reaction. Outcome Our patient underwent surgical drainage of the abscess and received broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics targeting both anaerobic and aerobic organisms. The prompt intervention avoided further complications. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Frontal swelling with subperiosteal abscess and frontal bone destruction is a hallmark of Pott’s puffy tumour [3]. CT detection is crucial as systemic symptoms may be absent, but intracranial complications are common. Pott’s puffy tumour remains a rare but life-threatening complication of frontal sinusitis. CT findings should trigger immediate diagnosis and intervention. Early recognition is essential to prevent devastating intracranial sequelae. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Secondary synovial chondromatosis of the elbow
clinical_history: A 62-year-old man with no other significant clinical history besides dyslipidaemia, with right elbow stiffness for 1.5 years, with no history of trauma.
imaging_findings: Lateral radiographs of the elbow (Figure 1) show multiple well-defined radio-opacities in the anterior aspect of the cubital fossa (loose bodies), with reduced joint space, subchondral sclerosis and marginal osteophytes. Axial T2-weighted gradient echo (GRE) sequences (Figure 2) and sagittal T1-weighted (Figures 3, 4a, and 4b) images confirm the radiographic findings and show multiple, corticated T1 and T2 hypointense round to ovoid foci within the elbow joint, showing blooming on the GRE sequences (Figure 2). These findings are consistent with intra-articular loose bodies.
discussion: Background Synovial chondromatosis is an uncommon, benign condition characterised by the formation of cartilaginous nodules within the synovium, which subsequently calcify and ossify, producing intra-articular loose bodies. It is further divided into primary and secondary types. Primary forms occur more in younger age groups (4th to 5th decades of age) and are aggressive, attributed to underlying cartilaginous metaplasia, with higher recurrence and occasional malignant potential [1,3]. Secondary synovial chondromatosis (5th or 6th decades of age) is more common, associated with osteoarthritis (therefore occurring in older patients), post-traumatic changes, or inflammatory causes, and attributed to detached cartilaginous fragments ossifying within the joint [1,2,4]. Clinical Perspective Patients usually present with chronic pain and restriction of movement. A male predominance is reported [2]. The critical distinction between primary and secondary synovial chondromatosis needs to be made—primary synovial chondromatosis is more aggressive and needs more intensive management due to underlying cartilaginous metaplasia of the synovium [3,4]. Imaging Perspective Radiographs are the first-line investigation to identify bony abnormalities, osteoarthritic changes and exclude trauma. Findings include subchondral sclerosis, reduction in joint space, and marginal osteophytes that indicate osteoarthritis. Loose bodies are visualised as multiple round to oval, intra-articular radio-opacities showing ring and arc calcifications that indicate a chondroid origin. Sometimes, a “sac of pebbles” appearance is described [2,5]. Associated joint effusions may obliterate fat pads. MRI is superior for soft tissue assessment, detecting both calcified and non-calcified nodules, synovial thickening and the presence of neurovascular impingement (commonly the ulnar nerve). Synovial thickening on MRI with intra-articular T1 isointense and T2 hypointense foci showing blooming on GRE sequences (suggesting calcification) is typical, along with osteoarthritic changes [3]. Differentiation from primary forms is made on imaging by fewer, larger, loose bodies in secondary chondromatosis, with co-existing osteoarthritis. Other modalities include ultrasound for synovitis and effusions [4]. Differentials include tumoral calcinosis, which has amorphous, poorly defined, peri-articular calcific masses [3]. Linear/cartilaginous calcifications in cartilage without discrete intra-articular bodies favour crystal deposition disease. Outcome Initial management is done with NSAIDs and physical therapy in the absence of significant mechanical obstruction to movement. Arthroscopic removal of foreign bodies is sufficient in more severe cases. Some approaches prefer limited synovectomy [5]. In primary forms, where synovectomy is more commonly performed due to a more aggressive course and risk of recurrence [3]. Take Home Message Secondary synovial chondromatosis is distinct from primary forms by age, clinical setting, osteoarthritic changes and imaging features. It is often responsive to the removal of loose bodies. Imaging evaluation is imperative to diagnosis and planning of therapy. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Bilateral Hutch diverticulum diagnosed in adulthood
clinical_history: A 52-year-old man presented to the emergency department with one week of abdominal pain, diarrhoea and an initial febrile episode. Physical examination revealed tenderness with guarding in the right iliac fossa, raising clinical suspicion of appendicitis. An ultrasound was requested for further evaluation.
imaging_findings: Abdominal ultrasound confirmed acute appendicitis with an inflammatory phlegmon. Incidentally, two rounded, symmetrical, anechoic structures were identified between the seminal vesicles and the bladder (Figure 1). A subsequent contrast-enhanced CT urogram with 3D reconstruction demonstrated rounded structures adjacent to the bladder, showing contrast opacification and originating at the level of the ureteral orifices (Figure 2). Pelvic MRI with T2-weighted spin-echo and diffusion sequences was then performed to further characterise the incidental bladder finding. Axial images revealed dilatation of both ureterovesical junctions, each surrounded by a thin muscular layer and directly communicating with the bladder. The ureters were orthotopically positioned with preserved urinary drainage, consistent with bilateral Hutch diverticula (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Hutch diverticulum is a congenital paraureteral bladder diverticulum located at the ureterovesical junction, more often unilateral but occasionally bilateral [1]. For a diverticulum to be considered a true Hutch diverticulum, histological examination must demonstrate smooth muscle fibres within its wall [2]. In contrast, acquired bladder diverticula result from mucosal herniation through a defect in the detrusor wall, secondary to increased intravesical pressure. The majority of cases have been reported in males, with an incidence of approximately 3:1, and they are usually diagnosed during childhood. Hutch diverticula have also been described in association with congenital conditions, including Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, posterior urethral valves, neurogenic bladder dysfunction, and prune belly syndrome [3]. Clinical Perspective Clinically, Hutch diverticula may remain asymptomatic or present with recurrent urinary tract infections, usually secondary to urinary stasis or vesicoureteral reflux. In larger diverticula, obstructive urinary symptoms or compression of adjacent vascular or pelvic structures may occur. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound is a useful first-line modality for assessing diverticular morphology, bladder wall characteristics and potential complications, as well as for detecting vesicoureteral reflux through contrast-enhanced voiding urosonography [3]. In this case, a subsequent contrast-enhanced CT urogram with three-dimensional reconstruction demonstrated rounded structures adjacent to the bladder, containing contrast and originating at the level of the ureteral orifices. Pelvic MRI further characterised the findings, revealing dilatation of both ureterovesical junctions with direct communication to the bladder, orthotopic ureteral insertion, and preserved urinary drainage, confirming the diagnosis of bilateral Hutch diverticula. In congenital Hutch diverticula, the bladder wall appears smooth, unlike acquired diverticula, where it is typically thickened and trabeculated (“fighting bladder”). Congenital diverticula generally have a short and wide neck, are solitary, and are located paraureterally, whereas acquired diverticula tend to have a long and narrow neck, are often multiple, and may occur in any part of the bladder wall [4]. Outcome Management depends on symptomatology. Asymptomatic patients are generally managed conservatively with observation and periodic imaging follow-up. Surgical diverticulectomy remains the treatment of choice in symptomatic cases, especially when recurrent infections, reflux or obstructive symptoms are present [5]. In this patient, the diverticula were incidental findings without functional compromise, favouring a conservative approach. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Bilateral Hutch diverticulum in adulthood is an uncommon finding, usually diagnosed incidentally. Awareness of this entity is important to avoid misinterpretation and to guide appropriate management. Imaging plays a key role in establishing the diagnosis and assessing complications, while treatment decisions should be based on the presence or absence of symptoms. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
