title: Mixed epithelial and stromal tumour in a young woman
clinical_history: A 29-year-old woman with a history of reflux esophagitis presented to her general practitioner with upper abdominal pain. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a right renal mass (Figure 1), and she was referred to the urology clinic for further evaluation.
imaging_findings: Abdominal CT confirmed a multilocular cystic mass of approximately 10 cm arising from the interpolar and lower pole region of the right kidney, with fine septations and without solid enhancing nodules or coarse calcifications (Figures 2a and 2b). MRI showed a well-defined, encapsulated, multilocular cystic mass with some cysts with an atypical content, but without solid contrast-enhancing components (Figures 3a, 3b, and 3c). No lymphadenopathy was detected. Interval imaging revealed slow growth without additional malignant features. After pregnancy and a prolonged follow-up period, the patient underwent a partial nephrectomy. Macroscopic examination revealed a cystic lesion (Figure 4), with a white to pink coloration. No distinct papillary structures or solid masses were identified within the cyst lumina, which were smoothly lined. Microscopically, no necrosis, atypia, or increased mitotic activity was present. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated PAX8 positivity in the epithelial component and oestrogen/progesterone receptors in the stroma, confirming the diagnosis of mixed epithelial and stromal tumour (MEST) of the kidney.
discussion: Background Mixed epithelial and stromal tumour (MEST) is a rare benign renal neoplasm, although some cases of malignant transformation have been reported [1]. It is classified in the 2022 WHO classification of renal tumours as a mixed epithelial and stromal tumour family together with adult cystic nephroma [2,3]. Histologically, it is characterised by cystic spaces lined by epithelium within a spindle-shaped cell stroma [3]. It typically occurs in middle-aged and older women, often linked to hormonal influences due to expression of oestrogen and progesterone receptors in the stromal component [3–5]. Clinical Perspective Patients with MEST are often asymptomatic, and lesions are frequently detected incidentally during imaging. When symptoms occur, patients may present with abdominal or flank pain, haematuria, palpable mass, or urinary tract infections [3,4,6]. Clinical evaluation alone is insufficient to establish the diagnosis of MEST, as symptoms are nonspecific [1]. Imaging has a central role in guiding management and informing the referring physician about the potential malignancy risk. Imaging Perspective On cross-sectional imaging, MEST appears as a well-circumscribed heterogeneous renal lesion with variable cystic and solid components [1,7]. Septal enhancement and delayed contrast uptake are commonly observed. Lack of nodular enhancement is an imaging feature suggestive of benignity. MRI is valuable for evaluating cystic contents and assessing involvement of the collecting system. In some cases, MEST may protrude into the renal pelvis, causing proximal collecting system dilatation, although this is less frequent than in adult cystic nephroma [4]. Cystic renal cell carcinoma often exhibits thicker, irregular septa and enhancing solid nodules, features uncommon in MEST [6]. However, definitive diagnosis requires histopathology. Outcome Therapeutic options include partial nephrectomy, especially for larger lesions or when malignancy cannot be excluded. Prognosis is favourable, as MESTs are benign and surgical excision is curative. In this case, partial nephrectomy confirmed the diagnosis and achieved complete removal without local recurrence. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Mixed epithelial and stromal tumour (MEST) is a rare benign renal tumour, predominantly affecting middle-aged and older women. Imaging shows a multilocular cystic lesion without enhancing solid components. Differentiation from other cystic lesions can be challenging and requires histopathological confirmation. Surgical excision offers favourable outcomes. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Polysubstance-induced leukoencephalopathy and haemorrhagic globus pallidus necrosis
clinical_history: A 25-year-old male was admitted in a comatose state after suspected polysubstance intoxication. Toxicology screening detected cocaine, MDMA, cannabis, and benzodiazepines. Secondary aspiration pneumonia led to severe respiratory failure, hypoxia, pre-renal acute kidney injury, and rhabdomyolysis.
imaging_findings: Initial non-contrast head CT revealed bilateral, symmetric hypoattenuation of the globus pallidus (Figure 1). Follow-up MRI showed extensive patchy hyperintensities on T2/FLAIR with a centripetal distribution, predominantly affecting the lentiform nuclei, periventricular white matter, and deep limbic structures (Figure 2). T1-weighted images displayed symmetric hyperintensities in the globus pallidus. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) demonstrated central hyperintensity with a hypointense halo (Figure 4a), and ADC maps revealed corresponding central hypointensity with a hyperintense halo (Figure 4b), consistent with restricted diffusion and subacute haemorrhage—likely due to hydrophobic macromolecule accumulation from haemoglobin breakdown. SWI confirmed petechial central haemorrhage (Figure 3). Post-contrast T1 imaging showed peripheral halo enhancement in the globus pallidus only. Findings were suggestive of haemorrhagic necrosis. The affected white matter exhibited diffusion hyperintensity with matched ADC hyperintensity (Figure 4b), consistent with T2 shine-through effect and parenchymal oedema.
discussion: Background Toxic leukoencephalopathy (TL) refers to white matter injury caused by exposure to neurotoxic substances such as recreational drugs, chemotherapy agents, or environmental toxins. The basal ganglia, particularly the globus pallidus, are especially vulnerable due to their high metabolic demands and vascular anatomy. Haemorrhagic necrosis of the globus pallidus is rare and severe [1,4,6]. Clinical Perspective Our patient was found unresponsive at home and presented to the emergency department with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 3, requiring intubation and ICU admission. Toxicology revealed methadone, benzodiazepines, MDMA, THC, and cocaine [1–3]. The patient developed severe respiratory failure secondary to aspiration pneumonia, requiring prone positioning cycles, neuromuscular blockade, and deep sedation. Persistent low consciousness following sedation withdrawal prompted an additional brain MRI. Imaging Perspective Initial non-contrast CT demonstrated bilateral symmetric hypodensities in the globus pallidus (Figure 1), suggestive of toxic or metabolic aetiology. MRI revealed symmetric involvement of the lentiform nuclei, periventricular white matter, and limbic structures, sparing the cortex, peripheral white matter, thalami, and cerebellum (Figures 2, 4a, and 4b). SWI showed petechial haemorrhages in the globus pallidus (Figure 3). DWI findings (Figure 4a) supported the coexistence of necrotic and haemorrhagic damage. Imaging findings were consistent with toxic leukoencephalopathy with bilateral haemorrhagic necrosis of the globus pallidus [4–6]. Outcome After a prolonged ICU stay, with improvement in respiratory function and resolution of renal failure and rhabdomyolysis, the patient underwent tracheostomy. Neurologically, he remained in a minimally conscious state with myoclonus and limited response to stimuli. EEG showed encephalopathy without epileptiform activity. Clinical and imaging findings indicated a poor neurological prognosis. Teaching Points Consider toxic leukoencephalopathy in comatose patients with a history or suspicion of substance abuse. Bilateral, symmetric involvement of the globus pallidus and periventricular white matter is characteristic. Haemorrhagic necrosis of the globus pallidus is rare and associated with severe, irreversible injury. MRI, including diffusion and susceptibility sequences, is essential for diagnosis and assessment of lesion distribution and extent. Prognosis depends on the degree of neurological involvement and associated systemic complications. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Toxic haemorrhagic necrosis of globus pallidus and leukoencephalopathy Delayed post-hypoxic leukoencephalopathy Carbon monoxide poisoning Hypoglycaemic encephalopathy Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) Mitochondrial encephalopathy
final_diagnosis: Toxic haemorrhagic necrosis of globus pallidus and leukoencephalopathy

title: Dialysis derailed: Reversible leukoencephalopathy
clinical_history: A 36-year-old male with chronic kidney disease and hypertension presented with seizures. Blood urea was 325 mg/dL, and haemodialysis was initiated. Within 48 hours, his condition worsened, requiring intubation. Despite falling urea levels, the neurological status did not improve, prompting a brain MRI for evaluation.
imaging_findings: The brain MRI reveals symmetric T2-weighted (Figure 1a) and symmetric FLAIR (Figure 1b) hyperintensities involving the bilateral periventricular and subcortical white matter with a chronic lacunar infarct in the left corona radiata. The involved areas show no associated diffusion restriction on DWI and ADC sequences (Figures 2a and 2b), and multiple chronic microbleeds in SWI (Figure 3). There is no abnormal enhancement in post-contrast T1FS images (Figure 4).
discussion: Background Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome (DDS) occurs in patients with severe uraemia who undergo rapid or aggressive haemodialysis. Manifestations usually begin within 24 hours of dialysis and resolve within hours. Diagnosis is clinical, made after excluding metabolic or intracranial causes [1]. Clinical Perspective DDS represents a spectrum of neurological symptoms ranging from mild headache, nausea, and tremors to seizures, coma, or death from cerebral oedema [2]. Symptoms often emerge toward the end of dialysis, particularly with rapid urea clearance. This creates an osmotic gradient between plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), driving water into the brain parenchyma and producing cerebral oedema. Clinical worsening may paradoxically occur despite biochemical improvement, especially in patients with high pre-dialysis urea [2]. Brain oedema-related leukoencephalopathy typically involves white matter, where extracellular spaces between glial cells and capillaries allow fluid accumulation [3]. Proposed mechanisms include the reverse urea effect, generation of idiogenic osmoles, and paradoxical intracellular acidosis [4]. Imaging Perspective On CT, affected white matter appears hypodense, sometimes with oedematous basal ganglia or mimics such as haemorrhage or infarct. MRI is the investigation of choice, showing diffuse T2/FLAIR hyperintensity of white matter, often with facilitated diffusion. A posterior reversible encephalopathy pattern may be seen [3]. Contrast enhancement is usually absent. MR spectroscopy demonstrates reduced NAA and elevated choline. Outcome DDS can be fatal, particularly in high-risk patients. Risk factors include pre-existing central nervous system pathology, severe cerebral acidosis, rapid correction of hyperosmolality, relative hypercapnia, and post-dialysis haemodynamic instability [5]. The patient showed clinical improvement in the subsequent weeks but declined further imaging. Given the transient nature of the pathology, the findings are consistent with a diagnosis of DDS. Take-Home Message / Teaching Points Rapid correction of severe uraemia can precipitate dialysis disequilibrium syndrome (DDS), especially with high pre-dialysis urea or central nervous system vulnerability. DDS-related leukoencephalopathy is underrecognised, often presenting with seizures, coma, or altered sensorium, and mimicking other metabolic or vascular causes. MRI best detects early white matter changes and distinguishes DDS from uremic encephalopathy or osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS). Uremic encephalopathy, DDS, and ODS lie on a spectrum of metabolic brain injury; differentiating them carries prognostic and therapeutic value. Slow, controlled dialysis initiation in high-risk patients is essential to reduce risk. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Low-grade chondrosarcoma arising from osteochondroma
clinical_history: A 22-year-old male football player presented after sustaining a posterior thigh muscle injury during soccer practice. Because of the traumatic mechanism, a hip and thigh radiograph was obtained to exclude associated bone injury. The radiograph incidentally revealed a lesion in the hip region. The patient had no hip-related symptoms, was otherwise healthy, and had no relevant family history.
imaging_findings: Radiograph showed a large lobulated, extra-osseous mass adjacent to the right iliac wing, containing prominent internal calcifications (Figure 1). MRI revealed a large, lobulated nodular lesion in the right gluteal region, measuring 14.4 × 9.2 × 9 cm (craniocaudal × transverse × anteroposterior). The lesion contains a central calcified/ossified component (5 cm) that appears to communicate with the external surface of the iliac wing (Figure 2a). The peripheral component is voluminous, hyperintense on fluid-sensitive sequences, and demonstrates septations, calcifications, as well as peripheral and septal enhancement, likely indicating a chondroid matrix (Figures 2a and 2b). Imaging features are suggestive of an aggressive lesion, most likely osteochondroma with secondary chondrosarcomatous transformation. The mass extensively involves the gluteus minimus muscle and appears to invade the anterior portion of the gluteus medius, with no clear separation from the origin of the iliotibial band at the iliac crest tubercle (Figure 2c).
discussion: Background Low-grade chondrosarcoma is a malignant cartilage tumour that produces a hyaline cartilage matrix. It typically occurs in adults between the fourth and sixth decades but can appear in younger individuals, as seen in this case. The pelvis, femur, and proximal humerus are the most common sites, though it can arise in any bone. Low-grade lesions are slow-growing and may develop de novo or from pre-existing benign cartilage tumours like osteochondromas or enchondromas [1]. Clinical Perspective Patients with low-grade chondrosarcoma often present with non-specific symptoms, such as pain or swelling, or the tumour may be discovered incidentally, especially in slow-growing or deep-seated lesions [1]. In this case, the lesion was detected following trauma, with no symptoms related to the hip. Malignant transformation of osteochondroma should be suspected if there is new pain, rapid growth, or imaging features suggestive of aggressive behaviour [1]. Imaging Perspective MRI is the preferred imaging modality for characterising cartilaginous tumours and assessing their local extent [2]. Low-grade chondrosarcomas typically appear as lobulated masses with a chondroid matrix, hyperintense on fluid-sensitive sequences (T2/STIR), and may show internal septations and calcifications. After contrast, peripheral and septal enhancement is common [2]. Features suggestive of malignant transformation in osteochondroma include a cartilage cap thickness greater than 1.5–2 cm in adults, an irregular or nodular cap, and soft tissue invasion [3]. In this case, the lesion had a large peripheral soft tissue mass with a central calcified component communicating with the iliac wing, consistent with secondary chondrosarcoma from an osteochondroma [2]. Although MRI is essential for surgical planning and local staging, radiography plays a key role in the initial detection and characterisation of bone tumours [4]. In this case, radiographic imaging revealed a centrally located calcified component with dense, osteoid-like matrix, surrounded by a more lucent, chondroid-like matrix at the periphery. This combination of central osteoid-like and peripheral chondroid-like appearance is a classic radiographic feature suggestive of cartilaginous malignancy, highlighting the importance of plain radiographs in initial tumour assessment [5]. Differential Diagnosis The differential diagnosis includes benign cartilaginous tumours like osteochondroma or enchondroma, chondroblastic osteosarcoma, and other soft tissue sarcomas [2]. Imaging features, clinical history, and lesion location help narrow the differential. A definitive diagnosis requires histopathological confirmation. Outcome and Management Surgical resection with wide margins is the primary treatment for low-grade chondrosarcoma, as these tumours are resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy [1]. Prognosis is favourable for low-grade lesions, with a low metastasis risk but with a potential for local recurrence if excision is incomplete. Long-term follow-up is recommended [1]. Take Home Message Low-grade chondrosarcoma should be considered in the differential diagnosis of large, lobulated, calcified masses in the pelvis, especially in young adults and in the setting of pre-existing osteochondroma. While MRI is crucial for local staging and surgical planning, conventional radiography remains a vital tool in the initial assessment, especially for evaluating the matrix characteristics of bone/cartilage tumours [5]. Early recognition and appropriate management are essential to ensure optimal outcomes.

title: Lesion of the Kaplan fibres of the iliotibial band
clinical_history: A 23-year-old female with two weeks of insidious anterolateral right knee pain, which worsened with load and knee flexion. No history of trauma or recent sports activities. Physical examination revealed only tenderness over the antero-lateral supra-patellar region. She later had a cycle of NSAIDs for one week, becoming symptom-free afterwards.
imaging_findings: MRI of the left knee demonstrated thickening, heterogeneity and interstitial T2 signal hyperintensity in the femoral insertion of the inferior Kaplan fibres (KF) of the iliotibial band (ITB), associated with and surrounding a soft tissue oedema (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c). No signs of rupture were seen. The main iliotibial band was intact, without significant friction-related signal abnormalities. No joint effusion or evidence of other significant lesions in the meniscus, cartilage, ligaments or remaining musculotendinous structures.
discussion: Background The KF are connections of the ITB, inserting onto the lateral distal femoral metaphysis, with two bundles (proximal and distal) [1] (Figure 2). The proximal bundle attaches to a ridge on the upper distal femoral shaft, about 50 mm above the lateral epicondyle. The distal bundle anchors to a supracondylar ridge roughly 30 mm above the lateral epicondyle [2]. They play an important role in maintaining knee rotational stability, particularly with anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture [3,4]. Clinical Perspective Isolated KF lesions can be symptomatic. MRI can identify these lesions and exclude other causes of anterolateral knee pain. This is crucial given clinical overlap with iliotibial band friction syndrome, patellar tendon–lateral femoral condyle friction syndrome, excessive lateral pressure syndrome, popliteus tendinopathy, stress fracture, and meniscus tears. Imaging Perspective MRI frequently identifies KF on routine knee sequences (96% on sagittal images), anterior and laterally to the superior lateral geniculate artery (Figure 2) [3]. KF injuries may occur in isolation or with lateral meniscus, lateral collateral ligament, anterolateral and anterior cruciate ligament lesions [4]. Batty et al. suggested MRI diagnostic criteria for KF injury of at least one direct sign or two indirect signs in any plane. Direct signs are partial/complete discontinuity or femoral avulsion; indirect signs are thickening and/or intra-substance signal change, focal bone marrow oedema at femoral insertion, surrounding soft tissue oedema, and wavy appearance [5]. In this case, inferior KF thickening, intra-substance signal change and soft tissue oedema confirmed the diagnosis per Batty et al., with two indirect signs and intact structural integrity. Outcome In the context of ACL rupture, KF lesions are particularly important as they contribute to clinically relevant anterolateral knee rotational instability, potentially altering treatment approach [1,4]. KF surgical repair is mainly required when associated with ACL rupture and instability. Symptomatic isolated KF injuries rarely need surgery unless instability persists [4,6]. Take Home Message This case highlights the need for radiologists and clinicians to consider Kaplan fibre (KF) lesions in anterior and lateral knee pain and the use of MRI to differentiate them from overlapping pathologies, ensuring proper management and timely recovery.

title: Systemic hydatid disease: Central nervous system, pulmonary, hepatic and musculoskeletal involvement
clinical_history: A 14-year-old boy presented with left-sided headache, right-sided visual loss, nausea, and vomiting. Neurological exam showed right homonymous hemianopsia. Blood tests revealed eosinophilia and elevated ALT and γ-GT. No relevant medical history.
imaging_findings: Brain MRI revealed a thin-walled cyst in the left temporal and parietal lobes, located along the course of the optic radiation (Figure 1a). The cyst was iso-intense to cerebrospinal fluid on T2-weighted imaging, and there was associated hydrocephalus, including bilateral dilatation of the temporal horns due to compression of the third ventricle and aqueduct of Sylvius (Figure 1b). The posterocranial wall of the cyst showed contrast enhancement (Figure 1a). A tumoral cyst could not be excluded. Chest CT demonstrated mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with multiple bilateral pulmonary cysts (Figure 2a). One of the cysts showed a crescent sign, suggesting rupture (Figure 2b). Additionally, a cystic lesion was identified in the right subscapularis muscle (Figure 2c). Abdominal CT revealed multiple cysts in the liver (Figure 3a), in the anterior upper pole of the left kidney (Figure 3a), and in the right iliac fossa with a thickened wall and increased density, raising suspicion for superinfection (Figure 3b). Further cystic lesions were seen in the left paraspinal muscles at the L1–L2 level and in the right gluteus maximus muscle (Figure 3c).
discussion: Background Hydatid disease is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of Echinococcus tapeworms. The two primary forms in humans are cystic echinococcosis (CE), caused by Echinococcus granulosus , and alveolar echinococcosis (AE), caused by E. multilocularis . Carnivores, such as dogs, serve as definitive hosts, while herbivores like sheep act as intermediate hosts. Humans become infected through ingestion of food or water contaminated with the eggs of infected animals [2,5]. According to the World Health Organisation Informal Working Group on Echinococcosis (WHO–IWGE) classification, hydatid cysts can be staged as follows: Type I: simple cyst with no internal architecture. Type IIa: cyst with daughter cyst(s) and matrix – round daughter cysts at the periphery. Type IIb: cyst with daughter cyst(s) and matrix – larger, irregularly shaped daughter cysts occupying almost the entire volume of the mother cyst. Type IIc: cyst with daughter cyst(s) and matrix – oval masses with scattered calcifications and occasional daughter cysts. Type III: calcified (dead) cyst. Type IV: complicated cyst (e.g., ruptured cyst). In our case, most hepatic and pulmonary cysts correspond to type I and type IIa cysts, while the cyst in the right iliac fossa with a thickened wall represents a type IV complicated cyst [1]. Clinical Perspective The liver (∼75%) and lungs (∼15%) are the most involved organs. Involvement of the brain, kidneys, and muscles is rare. Clinical symptoms are often non-specific and may only appear once cysts enlarge or rupture. Involvement of the central nervous system can present as space-occupying lesions, complicating diagnosis [3,4,6]. Imaging Perspective CT and MRI are key imaging modalities for diagnosing and staging hydatid disease. MRI is particularly useful for evaluating intracranial or soft tissue involvement, offering superior soft tissue contrast and the ability to assess cyst wall morphology. Hydatid cysts appear as well-defined, thin-walled, cerebrospinal fluid-isointense lesions. Contrast enhancement and irregular walls suggest rupture or infection. CT is superior for detecting calcifications, identifying daughter cysts, and staging systemic disease, especially in the thorax and abdomen. In cases of rupture, signs like the crescent sign or air-fluid levels may be observed [3,5,7]. On ultrasound, the pathognomonic “water lily sign”—representing detached endocyst membranes floating in cystic fluid—is characteristic of ruptured hydatid cysts [8]. Unfortunately, in this patient, an abdominal ultrasound has not been performed yet. Outcome Surgical excision is the primary treatment for intracranial hydatid cysts, though complications such as cyst rupture during surgery can lead to subarachnoid dissemination and increased risk of recurrence. For hepatic and extrahepatic cysts, minimally invasive procedures such as PAIR (puncture, aspiration, injection of a protoscolicidal agent, and reaspiration) are also increasingly used, depending on cyst stage and location [9]. In our case, albendazole was administered postoperatively to prevent parasitic reinfection. Praziquantel was also prescribed, with both drugs effective in treating hydatid disease. After surgery, the patient’s visual symptoms improved, indicating successful cyst removal. Hepatic cysts remained stable at follow-up imaging and will be monitored via ultrasound every 3 months. Conservative management is in place for pulmonary and renal cysts, with periodic imaging for monitoring [3,6]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Consider hydatid disease in cystic lesions with systemic involvement, especially in endemic regions. Multimodal imaging is essential for diagnosis and staging. MRI is preferred for central nervous system involvement; CT for systemic disease. Early diagnosis is crucial to avoid complications such as rupture or dissemination. Management of extensive hydatid disease often requires coordination between neurosurgeons, infectious disease specialists, and radiologists to ensure comprehensive care and optimal outcome Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Monostotic Paget’s disease of the mandible
clinical_history: A 54-year-old woman was referred for a second opinion because of an increasing alkaline phosphatase level since 2017. The patient has complaints of a long-standing loss of taste and a gradual prominence of her jaw. She did not have any pain or other neurological symptoms.
imaging_findings: Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) revealed diffuse expansion and sclerosis of the mandibular bone with coarsened trabecular architecture; also, there was an increased uptake of the tracer (technetium) in the mandible (Figure 1). CT confirmed symmetrical widening of the mandibular corpus and ramus bilaterally, with a preserved cortical outline. The bone appeared globally hypodense, with coarse internal trabeculae, slightly denser in the right ramus and condyles. The mandibular canals appeared intact bilaterally (Figures 2 and 3). These findings are compatible with mandibular Paget’s disease and make fibrous dysplasia unlikely.
discussion: Background Paget’s disease of bone is a chronic condition characterised by abnormal bone remodelling with phases of osteoclastic resorption and disorganised osteoblastic repair. This leads to structurally weakened and deformed bones with altered architecture. Common sites include the pelvis, femur, lumbar spine, and skull [1]. Clinical Perspective Many cases of Paget’s disease are asymptomatic and are first detected via elevated alkaline phosphatase levels. When symptomatic, patients may experience bone pain, deformity, or complications related to cranial nerve compression. In this case, the patient did not experience pain but reported taste loss and a change in facial shape, likely due to chronic mandibular expansion. However, no direct anatomic nerve compression was apparent on CT. Imaging was essential to confirm the diagnosis, rule out malignancy, and assess treatment need. Imaging Perspective SPECT allowed precise localisation and showed extensive involvement of the mandible with hypermetabolism, sclerotic changes, and trabecular disorganisation. CT confirmed a preserved cortex, absence of a soft tissue mass, symmetrical involvement and the mosaic pattern of bone involvement, which are key to differentiating Paget’s disease from other entities such as fibrous dysplasia, which often shows a ground-glass matrix and typically affects younger individuals. Malignant transformation (osteosarcoma) is rare but important to exclude. No imaging signs of malignancy were present in our case. Outcome Despite the absence of pain or fracture risk, treatment is indicated due to progressive disease activity and aesthetic and functional impact. The patient will receive intravenous zoledronate (Aclasta ® ). Follow-up will include monitoring biochemical markers (alkaline phosphatase, bone turnover markers) at 3 and 6 months post-treatment. A recent dental evaluation was unremarkable, reducing concern for medication-induced osteonecrosis of the jaw as a possible complication of zoledronate therapy. Take Home Message / Teaching Points The differentiation between Paget’s disease and fibrous dysplasia can be suggested based on the patient’s age, the pattern of bone involvement, and biochemical markers. Paget’s disease typically occurs in older adults and is characterised by symmetrical bone involvement along with elevated alkaline phosphatase levels. Another feature to distinguish the two is the mosaic pattern of bone involvement in Paget’s, where there will be lytic parts and blastic parts. In fibrous dysplasia, this involvement is more uniform. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Retroperitoneal liposarcoma: CT and PET/CT correlation
clinical_history: A 44-year-old male presented with progressive abdominal discomfort, otherwise healthy. Physical examination revealed abdominal pain in the upper region of the abdomen. Laboratory findings were unremarkable. The patient was referred for imaging evaluation to assess lesion burden and extent.
imaging_findings: Cross-sectional imaging of the abdomen demonstrates two large, well-defined but heterogeneous retroperitoneal masses, one located in the upper abdominal quadrant on the right side (Figure 2) and the other in the contralateral upper quadrant on the left (Figure 1). Within each mass, there are extensive regions of fat attenuation intermixed with irregular soft-tissue components of higher density, producing a variegated internal architecture. This mixture of fatty and non-fatty elements is highly suggestive of a lipomatous neoplasm, and the irregular solid portions raise concern for a more aggressive or dedifferentiated component. On metabolic imaging, both retroperitoneal tumours demonstrate markedly heterogeneous uptake of fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG). Large fatty regions show little to no metabolic activity, consistent with their low-grade lipomatous nature, whereas the non-lipomatous solid areas reveal intense hypermetabolism, strongly correlating with dedifferentiated or higher-grade tumour components (Figure 3). The distribution of FDG activity is patchy but concordant with the solid nodular areas seen on CT, reinforcing the suspicion of dedifferentiated liposarcoma within an otherwise well-differentiated lipomatous tumour.
discussion: Background Retroperitoneal liposarcomas are rare malignant mesenchymal tumours, yet they represent the most frequent primary retroperitoneal sarcoma in adults. They usually present between the fourth and sixth decades of life and are characterised by insidious growth, often reaching large dimensions before detection. The World Health Organisation (WHO) classifies liposarcomas into well-differentiated, dedifferentiated, myxoid, and pleomorphic subtypes, with prognosis strongly dependent on histology. Dedifferentiated liposarcomas are more aggressive, with a higher recurrence and metastatic potential [1]. Clinical Perspective Patients frequently present with vague abdominal discomfort, distension, or symptoms related to mass effect, such as bowel obstruction or urinary complaints. Systemic symptoms are uncommon. Laboratory results are usually nonspecific, and tumour markers have no diagnostic role. In our patient, progressive abdominal discomfort prompted imaging, which revealed a large retroperitoneal mass [2]. Imaging Perspective CT is the first-line imaging modality. Well-differentiated tumours typically contain macroscopic fat with thick septa or nodular non-adipose components. Dedifferentiated subtypes demonstrate more prominent solid enhancing areas within the fatty mass [1]. MRI provides superior soft-tissue contrast, confirming fat and delineating tumour margins and relation to adjacent organs and vessels, which is crucial for surgical planning. PET/CT plays an important role in functional characterisation, detecting hypermetabolic dedifferentiated components and excluding distant metastases [2]. Outcome Complete surgical resection with negative margins remains the cornerstone of treatment, as chemo and radiotherapy offer limited benefit. Even with optimal resection, recurrence is common, especially in dedifferentiated forms, justifying close surveillance with CT or MRI. Our patient underwent surgical resection with histopathological confirmation of dedifferentiated retroperitoneal liposarcoma. Regular imaging follow-up is ongoing to monitor for recurrence [3]. Take Home Messages / Teaching Points Large retroperitoneal fat-containing masses should raise suspicion of liposarcoma. PET/CT helps identify dedifferentiated components. Differential diagnoses include lipoma, teratoma, and other retroperitoneal sarcomas.

title: Nutcracker syndrome with varicocele and spontaneous scrotal haematoma
clinical_history: A 32-year-old patient presented to the emergency department with atraumatic pain and swelling of the left testis. The patient was afebrile and reported no history of unprotected sexual encounters. Clinical examination revealed a hard, enlarged left testis with bluish discolouration. Biochemical values were normal.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound of the scrotum (Figures 1a and 1b) visualised a large, heterogeneous hyperechogenic mass adjacent to the left testis at the site of the swelling, compatible with a parascrotal haematoma. Furthermore, there were clear signs of varicocele on the left side, such as a dilated, serpiginous appearance of the pampiniform plexus and flow reversal in the veins when the patient performed a Valsalva manoeuvre. There were no signs of testicular torsion, orchitis or epididymitis based on normal Doppler signal and greyscale appearance of both testes and epididymides. Finally, a small reactive hydrocele was noted on the left side. Subsequently, a CT scan (Figures 2a and 2b) was performed to exclude an intra-abdominal mass causing the varicocele. The scan demonstrated compression of the left renal vein between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta, which caused engorgement of the testicular vein, explaining the dilated pampiniform plexus.
discussion: Background Nutcracker syndrome is a rare disease caused by extrinsic compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery [1]. Varicocele is defined as the dilation and increased tortuosity of the pampiniform plexus [2]. Since the veins of the spermatic cord drain into the renal vein, compression and dilation in the left renal vein can cause varicocele. Clinical Perspective Common symptoms of nutcracker syndrome are abdominal or flank pain, orthostatic proteinuria, and haematuria. In selected cases, varicocele is one of the presenting symptoms. Varicocele is frequently associated with infertility in adolescents, but the exact pathophysiology of this relation is still poorly understood. Chronic venous compression can provoke the formation of collateral pelvic veins, potentially overlapping with pelvic congestion syndrome [3]. Imaging is essential in excluding or diagnosing a possible underlying cause of the varicocele. It is important to communicate the causal relationship of nutcracker syndrome and varicocele to the requesting physician because, without surgical intervention, symptoms will not resolve. Imaging Perspective Duplex ultrasound, CT and, occasionally, MR venography are utilised in the diagnosis of nutcracker syndrome and varicocele. These modalities can measure the diameter of the left renal vein, but only duplex ultrasound can assess flow velocities, providing additional information and value to the treating physician. Key imaging findings in varicocele are dilation of the pampiniform plexus (> 3 mm), serpiginous appearance, flow reversal with Valsalva manoeuvre and vascular reflux [4]. Imaging findings in nutcracker syndrome are compression of the left renal vein with pre and poststenotic dilatation and dilatation of the downstream gonadal vein. A parascrotal hematoma can be differentiated from other scrotal masses by its lack of enhancement, spontaneous T1-hyperintensity, and often restricted diffusion. Furthermore, the spontaneous regression also suggests a benign process. Outcome Nutcracker syndrome can be treated with either open or endovascular surgery. Open surgery involves reimplantation of the left renal vein in the inferior vena cava. Endovascular surgery consists of percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) with stenting of the compressed left renal vein [5]. A full recovery with spontaneous resolution of the scrotal haematoma and regression of the varicocele is expected. However, one in three patients eventually needs surgical reintervention. In this case, imaging dictates the treatment of the clinical problem and acts as a roadmap for the vascular surgeon. Take Home Message Nutcracker syndrome is an underdiagnosed cause of therapy-resistant varicocele and should be routinely excluded as a possible underlying cause. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Chondrosarcoma of the distal femur: CT and MRI findings
clinical_history: The patient presented with progressive pain and swelling around the right knee for 4 months. There was no history of trauma, fever, or weight loss. Local examination revealed swelling and tenderness over the distal thigh. Laboratory values were within normal limits.
imaging_findings: Axial non-contrast CT (Figure 1) demonstrates a lobulated lytic lesion in the distal femur with endosteal scalloping, cortical breach, and multiple foci of chondroid matrix calcifications showing a “rings and arcs” pattern. Sagittal reformatted CT (Figure 2) shows the lesion extending from the distal metaphysis to the epiphysis, with cortical thinning and focal cortical breach. MRI was performed on a 1.5-Tesla scanner using a dedicated knee coil, with T1 and T2-weighted sequences in sagittal and axial planes, slice thickness of 4 mm. Sagittal T1-weighted MRI (Figure 3) shows a predominantly hypointense lesion relative to muscle, with cortical breach and adjacent extraosseous soft-tissue component. Sagittal T2-weighted MRI (Figure 4) demonstrates a lobulated, predominantly hyperintense lesion with multiple internal hypointense septations. Two oval fluid–fluid levels are also noted within the lesion, suggesting secondary aneurysmal bone cyst-like changes. Axial T2-weighted MRI (Figure 5) shows the lobulated hyperintense lesion with cortical destruction and anterolateral soft-tissue extension. No periosteal reaction is evident. Histopathology (Figure 6) shows lobules of malignant cartilage with enlarged, binucleated chondrocytes in a myxoid matrix, consistent with grade II conventional chondrosarcoma. No secondary aneurysmal bone cyst component was identified histologically.
discussion: Chondrosarcomas are malignant cartilage-producing tumours representing around 20% of primary bone sarcomas. They typically affect adults between the fourth and seventh decades. The pelvis, proximal femur, and proximal humerus are the most common sites, while distal femoral involvement is less frequent [1]. Radiographically, they appear as lytic lesions with endosteal scalloping and chondroid matrix mineralisation. CT is ideal for evaluating calcification patterns and cortical disruption [2]. MRI provides superior assessment of intramedullary involvement and soft-tissue extension, with characteristic low-to-intermediate T1 signal, high T2 signal, and hypointense septations [3]. Secondary aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC)-like changes can occasionally occur in chondrosarcomas and may manifest as fluid–fluid levels on MRI. This was observed in our case, but these changes were not confirmed histologically. Such secondary ABC formation may represent intralesional haemorrhage or cystic degeneration within the tumour [4]. Histological grading is critical for prognosis. Grade II lesions show increased cellularity, nuclear atypia, and a myxoid background. Wide surgical excision is the treatment of choice, as chondrosarcomas are relatively resistant to chemotherapy and radiotherapy [5].

title: Double trouble – Incarcerated hernia causing obstructive jaundice
clinical_history: A 42-year-old woman presented with abdominal pain and an irreducible right lumbar swelling at the previous surgical scar. She had a history of common bile duct (CBD) injury during laparoscopic cholecystectomy, leading to CBD stricture. The stricture was managed by Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy. Laboratory evaluation revealed hyperbilirubinemia with elevated direct bilirubin.
imaging_findings: The ultrasound of the abdomen shows herniated bowel loops with a dilated proximal loop measuring ~3.6 cm in diameter (Figure 1). The dilated bowel loop is traced to the porta, showing that the CBD is dilated and opening into the bowel loop (Figure 2). The contrast-enhanced CT reveal a right abdominal wall hernia at the prior surgical scar (Figures 3a and 3b). The afferent limb of a Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy is herniated, causing a small bowel obstruction, upstream biliary dilatation, and obstructive jaundice. The herniated bowel shows maintained mural enhancement (Figures 3c and 3d). Axial T2 HASTE MR cholangiography shows dilated intrahepatic biliary radicles (Figure 4). The MIP (maximum intensity projection) image of the MR cholangiogram shows a markedly dilated proximal jejunal loop arising from the Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy site, with associated upstream dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts (Figure 5).
discussion: Background Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the standard management for cholelithiasis; however, sometimes it is associated with major biliary complications due to injury to the CBD [4]. The preferred surgical management of iatrogenic CBD injury/strictures is Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy [5]. This procedure creates a jejunal loop as a biliary limb that drains bile. An external hernia can occur due to a defect in the abdominal or pelvic wall, typically at sites of previous surgical intervention. Hernias are a common cause of small bowel obstruction [1]. The presence of irreducible swelling at the surgical site raises suspicion of an incarcerated incisional hernia, which is a surgical emergency. A mechanical obstruction in the biliary drainage leads to obstructive jaundice. If there is an obstruction in the biliary limb of Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy, it leads to obstructive jaundice. Imaging Perspective The initial modality for evaluation of abdominal pain is an ultrasound. The ultrasound shows a defect in the abdominal wall, with herniation of bowel loops, a dilated proximal loop, which suggests obstruction. In our case, the dilated proximal bowel loop was traced to the porta with dilated CBD and intrahepatic biliary radicles [6]. The contrast-enhanced CT scan is the investigation of choice in cases of hernia and small bowel obstruction [1]. In mechanical small bowel obstruction, CT shows a transition point that could be a hernia, mass, stricture, or intussusception. A clinically irreducible hernia with a narrow neck on imaging is consistent with an incarcerated hernia [7]. The presence of mural enhancement in herniated loops differentiates an incarcerated hernia from a strangulated hernia. In our case, the biliary limb of hepaticojejunostomy herniated through the surgical site and progressed to incarceration, leading to biliary obstruction, which caused obstructive jaundice and hyperbilirubinemia. MR cholangiography is very useful in the evaluation of biliary anatomy. It uses heavily T2-weighted sequences that accentuate the high signal from relatively static fluid in the biliary tract [3]. Normally, the fluid signals in the bowel loops are suppressed due to heavy T2-weighted imaging, but due to obstruction of the jejunal loop of the biliary limb, high signal intensity is seen on MRCP [3,6]. Outcome The patient underwent open hernioplasty in view of incarceration. A herniated jejunal loop through a narrow defect and congestion [7] were observed during the surgery (Figure 6). After it, bilirubin levels normalised. The herniated bowel segment was preserved, as it showed normal perfusion after repositioning. Teaching points Incarceration of the biliary limb after Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy is an uncommon cause of obstructive jaundice. Fluid-filled, obstructed jejunal biliary limb appears hyperintense on heavily T2-weighted sequences due to stasis. A CT scan is crucial for identifying the transition point, confirming the hernia as the cause, and assessing bowel viability to distinguish incarceration from strangulation.

title: Extra-abdominal desmoid fibromatosis of the posterior mediastinum
clinical_history: A 31-year-old female presented with complaints of fever and cough for 2 weeks. She had no significant past medical history.
imaging_findings: CT thorax revealed a large, well-defined, lobulated paraspinal mass extending from D1 to D5, causing widening of the posterior superior mediastinum (Figure 1). MRI further characterised the 8.6 × 8.4 × 5.5 cm mass, which was “horseshoe-shaped” in the paravertebral regions. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with characteristic T2 hypointense bands representing fibrous collagen content (Figure 2). The mass conforms to the anterior aspect of the vertebral body without bony erosion or calcification and showed heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Desmoid fibromatosis (DF), also known as aggressive fibromatosis, is a rare, locally aggressive, benign soft-tissue tumour characterised by the monoclonal proliferation of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts [1]. It only accounts for approximately 0.03% of all neoplasms. While extra-abdominal DF most commonly affects the trunk and extremities, its localisation in the mediastinum is exceedingly rare. DF presenting as a posterior mediastinal mass, particularly in a young female, is highly unusual. Its rarity, coupled with the patient’s non-specific symptoms (fever and cough), led to the incidental discovery during initial workup. Clinical Perspective The clinical presentation of mediastinal DF is often non-specific, with symptoms related to compression of adjacent structures (chest pain, back pain, cough) or, as in this case, general constitutional symptoms [2]. Due to the rarity of this condition, it is often misdiagnosed as other, more common mediastinal tumours, such as lymphomas or neurogenic tumours. Imaging plays a crucial role in characterisation and pre-biopsy planning. Imaging Perspective On imaging, DF typically appears as a well-defined or lobulated soft-tissue mass. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is considered the gold standard for assessing DF [3]. On MRI, the lesion is characteristically isointense or hypointense on T1-weighted images and shows a heterogeneous signal on T2-weighted images. This heterogeneity on T2-weighted images is a key diagnostic feature, resulting from the variable content of myxoid stroma (high signal) and dense collagen/fibrous tissue (low signal) [4]. The T2 hypointense bands seen in this case are highly suggestive of the dense fibrous collagen within the tumour [5]. Post-contrast enhancement is typically heterogeneous due to the varying amounts of cellularity and stroma. CT-guided core-needle biopsy is required for a definitive diagnosis, as was done in this case, confirming the presence of desmoid fibromatosis. Outcome Management of desmoid fibromatosis varies based on location and symptomology. Given the benign but locally aggressive nature and the critical location in the mediastinum, a conservative approach of watchful waiting may be an option for asymptomatic or slowly growing tumours, with surgical resection reserved for symptomatic cases. The patient in this case was put on conservative management with close follow-up due to the lesion’s complex location and size, which posed a high risk for surgical morbidity. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Posterior mediastinal desmoid fibromatosis (DF) is an extremely rare finding, especially in young females presenting with non-specific symptoms. MRI is the key imaging modality, revealing a characteristically T1 hypointense and T2 heterogeneous mass with fibrous bands. Biopsy is essential for a definitive diagnosis. Treatment is often conservative due to the high risk of recurrence and surgical morbidity.

title: Pancreatic graft thrombosis and pancreatitis following simultaneous kidney transplant
clinical_history: A 45-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes and end-stage renal disease underwent simultaneous pancreas-kidney transplantation. Six weeks post-transplant, while on heparin, she presented with abdominal discomfort and persistent vomiting unresponsive to antiemetics. Laboratory tests showed normal renal and pancreatic graft function, without biochemical abnormalities.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis was performed in portal venous and delayed excretory phases. The pancreatic graft in the right iliac fossa showed diffuse enlargement with mildly decreased parenchymal enhancement and surrounding fat stranding, consistent with interstitial oedematous pancreatitis (Figures 1a and 1b). The native pancreas was unremarkable. In the venous drainage, a stenotic luminal filling defect extended from the graft venous outflow into the inferior vena cava, involving the native left renal vein (Figures 1c and 1d). The renal graft, located in the left iliac fossa, demonstrated a small cortical cyst in the upper pole, mild pyelocaliceal and ureteral wall thickening, and slight ectasia. Two ureteral calculi (9 mm mid-ureter, 4 mm distal ureter) were noted, with preserved distal excretion to the bladder (Figures 2a and 2b). Additionally, the native kidneys were atrophic. The portal vein, hepatic veins, and suprahepatic veins remained patent.
discussion: Background Simultaneous pancreas-kidney transplantation (SPKT) is the treatment of choice for type 1 diabetes with end-stage renal disease [1]. Early vascular complications remain the leading cause of graft loss, with venous thrombosis reported in 3–10% of cases [2]. Pancreatitis of the graft, whether acute oedematous or necrotising, occurs in up to 35% of recipients within the first month post-transplant. Both complications may coexist, complicating diagnosis. Acute rejection and the presence of pancreatitis on imaging are recognised risk factors for graft thrombosis [3]. Clinical Perspective Venous thrombosis of the pancreatic graft presents with nonspecific features, including abdominal pain, graft tenderness, or elevated pancreatic enzymes, which overlap with rejection or pancreatitis. Interstitial oedematous pancreatitis similarly manifests with abdominal discomfort and enzyme elevation, making imaging essential for accurate diagnosis [3]. On the other hand, early post-transplant ureteral stones are uncommon, usually detected around one year after surgery, and often composed of calcium oxalate. In this case, the finding was incidental, as the patient was asymptomatic due to partial graft denervation, which can delay recognition of hydronephrosis and graft dysfunction. Despite subtle presentation, lithiasis remains a potentially serious threat to graft function, highlighting the importance of early imaging. [4]. Imaging Perspective In venous thrombosis, Doppler ultrasound may show absent or reversed flow, but it is operator-dependent and limited by bowel gas. Multidetector CT angiography is the reference standard, demonstrating intraluminal filling defects, absent venous enhancement, vessel stenosis or dilation, and occasionally collateral circulation. Secondary signs include graft swelling and impaired perfusion [2,3]. In pancreatitis, CT findings include graft enlargement, peripancreatic fat stranding, homogeneous enhancement, and absence of necrosis, similar to the native pancreas. In transplanted grafts, pancreatitis may result from venous outflow obstruction, as thrombosis impairs drainage and leads to interstitial oedema [2,3]. Outcome Venous thrombosis requires prompt intervention, ranging from anticoagulation to surgical thrombectomy or graft pancreatectomy, depending on severity. Interstitial pancreatitis is usually managed conservatively but may mimic or mask rejection, necessitating close imaging follow-up [3]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Venous thrombosis and acute graft pancreatitis are key early complications following simultaneous pancreas-kidney transplantation (SPKT). Clinical and biochemical findings are nonspecific; imaging is crucial for diagnosis. CT angiography provides a comprehensive evaluation of vascular patency and parenchymal changes. Pancreatitis may be secondary to venous obstruction, emphasising the importance of systematic vascular assessment. Early post-transplant urolithiasis is rare but should be considered, especially if pre-existing stones were present.

title: Symptomatic unilateral absence of pulmonary artery with right-sided aortic arch
clinical_history: A 21-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of cough and haemoptysis. He had no known past medical history.
imaging_findings: Chest radiography revealed a leftward mediastinal shift with reduced left lung volume (Figure 1). Given the haemoptysis and notable radiographic findings, a chest CT angiography scan was requested. Chest CT angiography confirmed a leftward mediastinal shift and reduced left lung volume, along with multiple areas of ground-glass opacity, which in this clinical context was consistent with alveolar haemorrhage (Figure 2a). The left main pulmonary artery was absent (Figure 2b), with several hypertrophic bronchial arteries visible at the left hilum (Figure 2c), as well as hypertrophic and tortuous left intercostal arteries (Figure 2d). A right-sided aortic arch with mirror-image branching (first branch: left brachiocephalic artery; second branch: right common carotid artery; third branch: right subclavian artery) and a retro-aortic left brachiocephalic venous trunk were also identified (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Isolated unilateral absence of pulmonary artery (UAPA) is a rare congenital disease (with a prevalence of 1/200,000), resulting from an altered development of the sixth aortic arch segment [1]. Due to its usual association with other cardiovascular anomalies, it is usually diagnosed during the first year of life; rarely, it may present in the adult age, in the context of haemoptysis (as in this case), pulmonary hypertension or exercise intolerance [2–4]. They can also be incidentally discovered in chest radiographs [4]. Clinical Perspective This anomaly can occur isolated or in association with other congenital abnormalities (such as tetralogy of Fallot, septal defects, etc.) [2]. Due to embryologic relationships, UAPA commonly occurs on the side of the chest opposite the aortic arch: half of the patients with left pulmonary artery absence have a right-sided aortic arch, whereas patients with right pulmonary absence have mainly a left aortic arch [1,2]. Distal intrapulmonary branches of the affected artery can be supplied by collateral vessels from bronchial (usually), intercostal, internal mammary, subdiaphragmatic or subclavian arteries, which may undergo hypertrophy and dilation, with a propensity to bleed, resulting in haemoptysis [2]. Outcome There is no consensus regarding the treatment of UAPA. Early detection of UAPA might offer the opportunity of surgical repair, either with creation of an aortopulmonary shunt or by connection of the affected pulmonary artery to the main pulmonary artery [3]. It is known that ensuring adequate antegrade blood flow to the unilaterally absent pulmonary artery before hypoplasia develops may improve the likelihood of long-term patency [4]. Regarding adult patients, most agree that the treatment should be reserved for patients with haemoptysis, pulmonary hypertension, or recurrent infections [4]. A detailed discussion of therapeutic options is beyond the scope of this article; however, haemoptysis can be managed with embolisation of systemic collaterals, lobectomy, or pneumonectomy [2]. Embolisation may also be used as an adjunct to surgery to reduce subsequent surgical blood loss [4]. This patient was admitted to the pulmonology ward, where he experienced several further severe episodes of haemoptysis. He was initially treated by undergoing an angiography with bronchial artery embolisation and embolisation of several tortuous hypertrophic intercostal arteries in order to control the haemorrhage (Figures 4a and b). However, he continued to develop recurrent haemoptysis afterwards and, hence, subsequently underwent left pneumonectomy on the next day, with resolution of the haemoptysis. Take Home Message Although usually diagnosed in early childhood, unilateral absence of pulmonary artery (UAPA) may, rarely, present in adults, either incidentally on imaging studies or with pulmonary hypertension or haemoptysis, resulting from systemic collaterals that are prone to rupture/bleeding.

title: Elderly diabetic with acute fever and lower limb swelling
clinical_history: A 69-year-old man with uncontrolled type II diabetes mellitus and diabetic foot presented to the emergency department with a three-day progressive worsening skin pallor and oedema of the right lower limb without trauma, culminating on the last day in acute fever (38.6ºC), anorexia and asthenia without improvement. The family explained that he was not taking his medication and did not have his risk factors under control (he smokes 15 cigarettes/day and consumes alcohol recreationally). Clinical examination revealed pallor of the skin and oedema in the right lower limb. Laboratory results showed hyperglycaemia (374 mg/dL), ketonaemia (1.7 mmol/L), leucocytosis (10,000/µL) with a predominance of neutrophils (90.49%), C-reactive protein of 484 mg/L. As an MRI was not possible for technical reasons and the patient reported a previous reaction to iodinated contrast media, a CT scan was performed without contrast media.
imaging_findings: The unenhanced CT provided detailed anatomical information on bone and soft tissue in a short time and with high sensitivity. Extensive gas bubbles were found in the plantar region of the forefoot and around the ankle, which were more pronounced on the lateral side of the ankle. Fat stranding was also seen around the ankle and on the dorsum of the foot (Figure 1). Marginal erosions on the proximal phalanx of the 3rd finger, with small foci of intraosseous gas, were present. There was also intraosseous gas and marginal erosions in the head of the third metatarsal (Figure 2). No obvious collections were noted. Absence of the distal and middle phalanges of the 5th ray was observed (previous amputation).
discussion: Background Necrotising soft tissue infections (NSTI) are rare but highly fatal [1]. The incidence of NSTI has increased, but the exact reason for this remains speculative. Possible explanations include increased microbial virulence and resistance due to overuse of antibiotics, better reporting of the disease, or both [2,3]. The spectrum of the disease includes necrotising forms of cellulitis, fasciitis, myositis [4] and emphysematous osteomyelitis, which represent the extreme end of the spectrum [5]. Risk factors include injury to the skin or mucous membranes, traumatic wounds, diabetes, or other immunosuppressive conditions [6]. There are two subtypes of NSTI, based on the involved microorganisms. Type I (polymicrobial) is the most common form and includes anaerobic (gas-forming bacteria) and aerobic organisms. Type II (monomicrobial) is less common and includes group A streptococci, which can lead to toxic shock syndrome [3,7]. Pathophysiology is due to tissue ischaemia caused by widespread occlusion of small subcutaneous vessels, leading to skin infarction and necrosis, which favours bacterial growth. The superficial nerves are often damaged, leading to local anaesthesia. Oedema is caused by the infection-induced release of cytokines at the local level, which spread to the veins and lymphatic vessels [4]. Clinical Perspective NSTIs can manifest in subtle ways, but pose a significant life risk. They are characterised by their heterogeneity in terms of microbiology, risk factors and anatomical involvement, and often present with non-specific symptoms, leading to a high rate of delayed diagnosis [8,9]. Imaging techniques are crucial for early diagnosis, especially when the results of the physical examination are inconclusive and venous thrombosis and septic thrombophlebitis have been ruled out based on the clinical findings (pallor and disproportionate pain). In our case, the CT scan showed the extent of the NSTI and confirmed the presence of emphysematous osteomyelitis, indicating a severe type I NSTI. Imaging Perspective Although MRI and CT with contrast enhancement best describe soft tissue and collections, and MRI is better at detecting early bone involvement, CT without contrast is, however, better than ultrasound and X-ray in assessing bone and the presence of tissue gas. Imaging procedures are often performed to confirm the diagnosis, assess the extent of disease and assist in treatment planning [10,11]. In this case, non-enhanced CT showed features of NSTI, soft tissue and bone emphysema without collections, ruling out the diagnosis of erysipelas or subcutaneous abscess. Cross-sectional imaging provides higher sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis of NSTI compared to radiographs and ultrasound. CT was chosen because it quickly and sensitively provides detailed anatomical information, examines bone and soft tissue, and detects gas and fluid collections along the fascia [5,12]. CT, therefore, plays an important role in the assessment of a possible NSTI in the emergency department. Outcome In our case, treatment outcomes were poor due to the advanced stage of NSTI and the patient’s comorbidities. Early surgical debridement was performed as this is the most important therapy and is crucial in improving survival. Due to extensive soft tissue and bone involvement, the patient underwent two surgical debridements without clinical improvement, resulting in a poor outcome and amputation of the limb. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics were also initially administered and adjusted once microbiological results were available. Take Home Message This case emphasises the aggressive nature of necrotising soft tissue infections (NSTI) associated with diabetes mellitus, and highlights the critical importance of early recognition and intervention. The unusual course of symptoms, including disproportionate pain due to neuronal damage, paraesthesia and rapid systemic involvement, presents a clinical challenge that is often underestimated in NSTI in diabetic patients. This case adds to the existing literature emphasising the need for vigilance and early recognition of NSTI in this high-risk group. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Osteochondroma of the acromion: An uncommon site of origin
clinical_history: A 27-year-old female with a 7-year history of swelling over the right shoulder noticed an accelerated increase in the size of the lump over the past 5 months. The range of motion of the shoulder was reduced, along with intermittent tingling radiating down the entire right arm in a non-dermatomal pattern. No significant past medical or family history.
imaging_findings: Plain radiograph of the shoulder (Figure 1) shows a well-defined calcified opacity overlying the humeral head, initially raising suspicion for a loose body, and possibly related to synovial osteochondromatosis. MRI shoulder (Figure 2) reveals a pedunculated osseous lesion arising from the undersurface of the distal acromion, extending posteriorly into the glenohumeral joint. The lesion measures approximately 3.5 × 3.2 × 2.9 cm and exhibits a thin cartilaginous cap, consistent with osteochondroma. Mild remodelling of the adjacent posterior humeral head and glenoid is seen. The lesion displaces the infraspinatus tendon, which shows signal changes suggestive of tendinopathy. CT shoulder (Figure 3) confirms a large osteochondroma originating from the undersurface of the acromion, projecting into the posterior glenohumeral joint. An apparent pseudoarthrosis is noted between the lesion and the posterior humeral head, which likely accounts for the surrounding bone marrow oedema observed on MRI.
discussion: Background Osteochondroma is the most common primary benign tumour and constitutes 36% to 41% of all tumours [1]. It can present as a solitary lesion or as part of a generalised skeletal disorder (multiple hereditary exostoses). Histologically, it is characterised by a cartilage-capped bony outgrowth that develops through endochondral ossification. While osteochondromas most commonly arise in the metaphyseal regions of long bones (e.g., femur, tibia, humerus), occurrence in flat bones or unusual sites, such as the acromion, is rare. In such locations, they may cause mechanical symptoms due to impingement or proximity to neurovascular structures, as in this case. Imaging Perspective In our case, imaging played a crucial role in diagnosis. The acromial osteochondroma caused posterior glenohumeral joint impingement and secondary infraspinatus tendinopathy—an unusual yet clinically significant presentation. According to the World Health Organisation (WHO) Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours (5th edition), essential diagnostic features of osteochondroma include: A cartilaginous cap < 2 cm in adults. Growth-plate-like architecture in children or extensive calcification in older patients. Cortical and medullary continuity with the underlying bone [2]. On plain radiography, osteochondromas appear as sessile or pedunculated osseous projections from the metaphyseal region, typically pointing away from the epiphysis. The lesion often causes metaphyseal widening. The cartilage cap may show rings and arcs calcification or may be indistinct. In flat bones, the pathognomonic is the feature of corticomedullary continuity with the parent bone on plain radiographs. CT provides superior visualisation of cortical and medullary continuity. It is particularly helpful in delineating the lesion’s relationship with adjacent bony structures and for preoperative planning. Septal enhancement within the cartilaginous cap may also be noted [3]. MRI is the modality of choice for evaluating the cartilage cap and assessing for malignant transformation. The cap typically demonstrates low-to-intermediate signal on T1-weighted images and high signal on T2-weighted images. A cartilage cap > 1.5 cm in thickness in skeletally mature individuals raises suspicion for malignant transformation. Post-contrast imaging typically shows peripheral enhancement of the fibrovascular tissue surrounding the cap, whereas the cartilaginous portion itself should not enhance [3]. Outcome Following the radiological findings of osteochondroma, this patient was informed about surgery as the treatment option. Finally, the patient agreed, and the excision was performed successfully. Meanwhile, the case was also discussed in a multidisciplinary team. The conclusion from histology was debulking of bone on the right acromion, as remodelled bone in areas may represent part of an exostosis, but this must be correlated with radiological findings. There was no evidence of inflammation or malignancy in the sample. The patient was asked to be reviewed in the orthopaedic clinic. The diagnosis was right subacromial exostosis; excision was done. Histology of the osteochondroma showed no sinister features. The treatment included physiotherapy of the right shoulder and a review after 3 months. The surgeon also stated that neurovascular examination of the right upper arm remains normal, axillary nerve sensation intact, that she has a slight decreased range of motion on the right in comparison to the left side, which was expected at this time after surgery but she will need to have physiotherapy and exercises and encourage movement. Teaching Points Osteochondromas can arise in atypical locations, including flat bones such as the acromion. Imaging plays a pivotal role in diagnosis, characterisation, and surgical planning. A thorough radiological evaluation, including assessment of the cartilage cap and surrounding structures, is essential, especially in adults with new or progressive symptoms. Osteochondroma should remain a differential diagnosis in patients presenting with chronic shoulder swelling, particularly when imaging reveals a well-demarcated, exophytic lesion with medullary continuity. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: MELAS presenting as a stroke-like episode in Down syndrome
clinical_history: A 4-year-old boy with Down syndrome presented with left-sided weakness for 5 days. He had a developmental delay and recurrent headaches with vomiting. No trauma, fever, or infection was reported. Laboratory and cerebrospinal fluid studies were unremarkable, excluding infectious or inflammatory encephalopathy. Genetic or muscle biopsy confirmation could not be obtained. External report suggested a possible lactate peak, though independent verification was not possible.
imaging_findings: On MRI brain, performed on a 1.5T system, areas showing restricted diffusion with low ADC values, appearing hyperintense on T2/FLAIR, and predominantly hypointense on T1-weighted are noted in the right high frontoparietal parenchyma, right perirolandic region, right frontoparietal parenchyma, right centrum semiovale, right corona radiata, and right temporal lobe, associated with gyral thickening and effacement of overlying sulci in the right high frontoparietal parenchyma. A T1/FLAIR hypointense area appearing hyperintense on T2-weighted, with surrounding FLAIR hyperintensity, is noted involving the genu of the corpus callosum with mild dilatation of the anterior horn of the left lateral ventricle, suggestive of gliosis (Figures 1c and 4c). These are seen involving cortical and subcortical regions of bilateral parietal and occipital lobes, with asymmetrical distribution. Areas of restricted diffusion were not typical of arterial infarction (Figures 2 and 3). On MR angiography, also performed on a 1.5T system, intracranial arteries were patent with no evidence of stenosis, occlusion, or moyamoya pattern (Figure 5).On SWI, no haemorrhage was observed (Figure 6). MR spectroscopy was not available within our institute, and thus, a possible lactate peak could not be confirmed. Imaging findings suggested a stroke-like episode. The non-territorial distribution, cortical involvement, and absence of vascular occlusion were strongly suggestive, particularly of MELAS syndrome.
discussion: Background MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes) is a mitochondrial disorder, most often linked to mutations in the mitochondrial tRNALeu gene [1,2]. Clinically, it manifests with repeated stroke-like episodes, epilepsy, and progressive neurological impairment [3,4]. Clinical Perspective Children with Down syndrome are predisposed to vascular strokes, most often related to congenital cardiac disease or moyamoya vasculopathy [5]. If vascular studies are unremarkable, alternative diagnoses such as MELAS should be entertained. Imaging Perspective On MRI, MELAS typically affects cortical and subcortical areas without respect to vascular territories, with a predilection for the parieto-occipital lobes [6,7]. Diffusion restriction is variable, reflecting both vasogenic and cytotoxic oedema, and MR spectroscopy often reveals a lactate peak [8]. In our case, although MR spectroscopy and genetic confirmation were not available, the imaging distribution and clinical presentation strongly supported a diagnosis of MELAS. The lack of molecular confirmation is acknowledged as a limitation. Nevertheless, this case highlights the radiological hallmarks that should raise suspicion for MELAS, prompting further testing. Definitive diagnosis of MELAS requires demonstration of mitochondrial mutation or characteristic muscle biopsy findings. In this case, such confirmation was not feasible; therefore, the diagnosis remains presumptive based on clinical and radiologic correlation. Outcome No curative therapy exists. Supportive treatments include L-arginine, antioxidants, and coenzyme Q10, which may reduce the severity of episodes [9,10]. Recognition of imaging features prevents misdiagnosis as ischemic stroke, avoiding inappropriate anticoagulation or surgical interventions. Teaching Points In Down syndrome, vascular stroke is common, but MELAS should be suspected when lesions are non-territorial with normal angiography. Radiologists must recognise these imaging features to guide appropriate diagnosis and management. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Ischemic stroke MELAS syndrome Moyamoya syndrome Encephalitis Leigh syndrome

title: Bronchogenic cyst: Exploring CT capabilities for the definitive diagnosis
clinical_history: A 37-year-old male was referred to our institution following the incidental detection of a mediastinal mass on a routine chest radiograph. The patient was asymptomatic, with no abnormalities found on physical examination. Routine laboratory tests were normal.
imaging_findings: Posteroanterior chest radiography (Figure 1a) showed a well-circumscribed, rounded opacity projecting over the cardiac silhouette, suggestive of a middle mediastinal mass. On the lateral view (Figure 1b), the lesion margin was poorly defined in relation to the adjacent mediastinal structures. Subtle layering calcifications with a horizontal upper margin were noted within the lesion. The findings prompted further cross-sectional imaging. Chest CT (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c) revealed a well-defined, homogeneous, low-attenuation mass (8 HU) located in the middle mediastinum, inferior to the carina. The lesion measured 9.0 × 7.0 cm, had a thin wall and showed no evidence of enhancement following intravenous contrast administration (Figure 3). Fine, dependent calcifications with a horizontal fluid–calcium level were identified within the lesion, consistent with milk of calcium. Repeat imaging in different patient positions demonstrated a shift in the calcium layering from dorsal to ventral decubitus, confirming its mobility. No signs of invasion into adjacent structures, lymphadenopathy, or pleural effusion were observed.
discussion: Background Bronchogenic cysts are congenital anomalies arising from abnormal budding of the bronchial tree during early embryonic development and represent a subtype of bronchopulmonary foregut malformations. Histologically, they are lined by secretory respiratory epithelium, typically composed of ciliated cuboidal or columnar cells [1,2]. Bronchogenic cysts typically do not communicate with the bronchial tree, and as a result, they are generally not air-filled. Instead, they contain fluid, along with varying amounts of proteinaceous material, blood products, and, occasionally, calcium oxalate [3]. These cysts may occur within the mediastinum or the lung parenchyma, with the middle mediastinum being the most common location [4]. Clinical Perspective Although frequently identified incidentally during the neonatal period, they can also present in adulthood. In adults, clinical presentation varies widely, ranging from asymptomatic lesions detected on routine chest radiography to symptomatic cases presenting with haemoptysis, pneumothorax, or pneumonia when located within the lung parenchyma, or with chest pain, dysphagia, or central venous compression due to mediastinal mass effect [4]. Imaging Perspective On CT, bronchogenic cysts typically appear as well-circumscribed lesions with smooth margins and no post-contrast enhancement. They usually demonstrate water attenuation values (< 20 Hounsfield Units), as observed in our case, although soft tissue attenuation may also be present, depending on the cyst contents. In rare cases, dependent high-attenuation material consistent with milk of calcium may be seen. This finding can be distinguished from peripheral wall calcifications by demonstrating a shift in calcium layering with changes in patient positioning from dorsal to ventral decubitus. Although uncommon, this feature is considered characteristic and can be suggestive of the diagnosis [1]. MRI can be useful in atypical cases where the characteristic horizontal fluid–calcium level is absent, typically showing variable T1 signal intensity and high T2 signal intensity [3]. Differential Diagnoses Other congenital cystic lesions to consider in the differential diagnoses include oesophageal duplication cysts, neurenteric cysts, and pericardial cysts. Oesophageal duplication cysts are typically located adjacent to the oesophagus and may demonstrate communication with the oesophageal lumen. Bronchogenic cysts are sometimes associated with other congenital pulmonary malformations such as sequestration and lobar emphysema. Oesophageal duplication cysts and neurenteric cysts are both typically located in the posterior mediastinum. Pericardial cysts, on the other hand, are most commonly found in the right cardiophrenic angle [1,5]. Outcome In this case, endobronchial ultrasound was employed both for diagnostic confirmation and therapeutic drainage. Other management options include surgical excision or percutaneous aspiration under CT guidance. Small asymptomatic lesions may be managed conservatively with radiological follow-up [1,6].
