title: Misdiagnosed bipartite talus as a traumatic fracture of the talus
clinical_history: A 38-year-old female dog groomer and horseback rider sustained a right ankle inversion injury. Persistent hindfoot pain and stiffness despite conservative management. Difficulty on uneven terrain and restricted plantar flexion. The exam revealed full ankle range, pain, limited subtalar inversion/eversion, and no malalignment or gait abnormality.
imaging_findings: Initial ankle radiograph suggested a lateral malleolus fracture (Figure 1). CT revealed a posterior sagittal split in the talar body with chronic osteochondral defect of the medial talar dome, incomplete fibrocartilage talocalcaneal coalition with smooth ossicles, and a prior fibular tip trauma with ossicle (Figure 2). A large accessory navicular and minimal degenerative changes in the talonavicular and great toe metatarsophalangeal joints were also present. MRI confirmed the split and coalition, initially interpreted as post-traumatic but later recognised as congenital bipartite talus, based on smooth, corticated fragment margins (Figure 3).
discussion: The talus is central to hindfoot biomechanics, articulating with the tibia, fibula, and calcaneus. Talar fractures are rare, usually linked to high-energy injuries, and can be challenging to diagnose [1,2]. Congenital anomalies such as bipartite talus, where the talar body is divided into two ossified segments, may mimic fractures on plain radiographs, especially when seen in the context of trauma [3]. In this patient, the posterior sagittal split in the talar body, coupled with an osteochondral defect, initially raised concern for a fracture, an unusual finding following a low-energy inversion injury. The incomplete talocalcaneal coalition added complexity; coalitions can be asymptomatic but may cause altered biomechanics and ankle sprains [4]. A key diagnostic clue emerged during the multidisciplinary review. The talar fragment margins were smooth and corticated, suggesting a chronic congenital variant rather than an acute injury. The absence of displacement, soft tissue swelling, or bone marrow oedema further supported this. The coalition likely became symptomatic due to altered load and motion after the injury. This case highlights the risk of over-reliance on initial trauma imaging, especially in the presence of anatomical variants. Congenital anomalies should remain in the differentials when imaging appearances and clinical findings are discordant. Advanced modalities, particularly CT for cortical detail and MRI for soft tissue and marrow assessment, can differentiate between chronic variants and acute pathology. Definitive management depended on symptom persistence. Given the patient’s ongoing pain and functional limitation, talocalcaneal coalition excision was performed. This case underscores the value of correlating mechanism, clinical signs, and advanced imaging, as well as the importance of multidisciplinary collaboration in achieving diagnostic accuracy and avoiding unnecessary interventions. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Splenic haemangioma mimicking metastasis
clinical_history: A 65-year-old male, a chronic smoker, presented with a chronic cough, for which a non-contrast chest CT was performed.
imaging_findings: The non-contrast CT revealed a locally advanced pulmonary process, with an incidental finding of a large splenic mass at the edge of the abdominal CT slices. The mass was well-defined, hypodense, and heterogeneous (Figure 1). Given the heterogeneous appearance of this splenic mass in the neoplastic context of the patient, the diagnosis of splenic metastasis was considered. Abdominal sonography and an MRI were requested to analyse the mass further. The mass was hyperechoic and heterogeneous on ultrasound without a colour Doppler signal (Figure 2). The MRI revealed a large splenic mass with a low-intensity signal on T1-weighted, heterogeneous high signal intensity on T2-weighted, and high signal intensity in DWI (Figure 3). This mass demonstrates peripheral contrast uptake in the arterial phase, then exhibits gradual centripetal enhancement during the portal venous phase, resulting in iso-enhancement compared to adjacent vessels in the late phase (Figure 4). Given these radiological characteristics, the diagnosis of a splenic haemangioma was confirmed.
discussion: Haemangiomas are benign tumours originating from the sinusoidal epithelium and comprise non-encapsulated, non-neoplastic vascular channels that vary in size from capillary to cavernous types, each lined by a single layer of epithelium [1]. Although they are rare, haemangiomas remain the second most common focal lesion of the spleen after simple splenic cysts [1]. Their clinical presentation is typically subtle, and they are often identified incidentally during investigations for other health issues, as in our case [1]. Ultrasound often demonstrates round, echogenic masses, with or without cystic areas. Cavernous haemangiomas generally appear as solid masses with a homogeneous hyperechoic pattern, while sclerosed and capillary haemangiomas may present as hypo or isoechoic. As observed in our patient, voluminous lesions often exhibit lobulated contours and tend to become inhomogeneous [2]. CT scans typically reveal a homogeneous, hypodense, or multicystic mass, which may contain calcifications. Regarding enhancement, most haemangiomas show discontinuous peripheral globular uptake in the arterial phase. In the portal venous phase, they demonstrate gradual centripetal filling, with uniform enhancement in the late phase [3]. Unusual enhancement patterns can occur, particularly in lesions with atypical ultrasound characteristics or in small haemangiomas; these may include rapid homogeneous (flash-filling) enhancement or persistent peripheral and delayed enhancement only. The MRI features are comparable to those of hepatic haemangiomas [2]. These lesions appear iso or hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images compared to the spleen. Due to their low cellularity, haemangiomas do not exhibit restricted diffusion on DWI. The pattern of dynamic enhancement is identical to that described for CT. Given their low cellularity and benign nature, most splenic haemangiomas require no treatment. However, surgical resection or selective splenic artery embolisation may be warranted in patients with large lesions, as large haemangiomas carry a higher risk of spontaneous rupture [4,5].

title: Penile Mondor’s disease: An exceedingly rare diagnosis
clinical_history: A 66-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 15-day history of penile swelling at the base, accompanied by tenderness. He had no relevant past medical history. On examination, swelling at the base of the penis was confirmed. An ultrasound was requested to exclude the presence of abscesses.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound revealed a heterogeneous collection measuring 38 × 15 mm at the base of the penis, which, in the current clinical context, was compatible with an abscess (Figure 1a). Additionally, the superficial dorsal vein of the penis was non-compressible, contained heterogeneous endoluminal material, and demonstrated absence of flow on colour Doppler ultrasound, findings consistent with thrombosis (Figures 1b and 1c).
discussion: Background Penile Mondor’s disease refers to the thrombosis of the superficial dorsal vein of the penis [1]. It is an exceedingly rare diagnosis, with only 53 cases reported in the literature, although it is likely significantly underdiagnosed [2,3]. Its aetiology remains largely unknown, but it has been linked to various factors, which fit the Virchow’s triad: vessel wall damage (e.g., due to vigorous sexual activity, penile trauma, pelvic/genital surgery), blood stasis (e.g., prolonged erection, prolonged sitting position, pelvic tumours, etc.), and hypercoagulation (e.g., urogenital infection, paraneoplastic thrombosis, thrombophilia) [3]. It typically affects men between 21 and 70 years old, presenting with complaints of a painful cord or fibrotic area along the dorsal surface of the penis, often accompanied by intense pain [1]. It may be asymptomatic [3]. Clinical and Imaging Perspectives Diagnosis is generally clinical, established through patient history and physical examination. Imaging plays a role in confirming the presence of intravascular thrombus; grey-scale and Doppler ultrasound are valuable in cases of diagnostic uncertainty, as they can assess the extent of thrombosis by demonstrating echogenic heterogeneous material within the venous lumen, vessel incompressibility, absence of flow on Doppler interrogation, and pain upon selective pressure; the affected vein may also appear dilated with inflammatory wall changes [3]. Sclerosing lymphangitis and Peyronie’s disease should both be considered in the differential diagnosis when evaluating a painful, fibrotic lesion of the penis [1]. Outcome Regarding the treatment, penile Mondor’s disease is typically self-limiting within 4–6 weeks. Treatment is essentially supportive, with measures such as sexual abstinence and warm compresses, as well as oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and topical anticoagulants [4], and oral antibiotics in case of infection [3]. Regarding thrombosis of the deep dorsal vein, a rarer entity beyond the scope of this case report, some authors advocate the use of oral anticoagulation due to its potential association with pulmonary embolisation [5]. The prognosis is excellent, and no long-term irreversible sequelae have been described [4]. Take Home Message Radiologists’ encounter with this pathology is exceedingly rare, due to the fact that penile Mondor’s disease itself is uncommon and is generally diagnosed clinically. Nevertheless, radiologists should be aware of this entity in cases presenting with penile tenderness and swelling.
differential_diagnosis: Penile Mondor’s disease Sclerosing lymphangitis Peyronie’s disease

title: Man with acute brainstem–cerebellar syndrome
clinical_history: A 45-year-old man with no prior history presented with dizziness and neck pain. Two weeks earlier, he had febrile pharyngotonsillitis with diarrhoea. On examination, he was alert but showed dysarthria, nystagmus, gait instability, and dysmetria (brainstem–cerebellar syndrome). The stroke code was activated, and he was admitted for evaluation.
imaging_findings: The initial stroke protocol (non-contrast CT and CT angiography) showed no abnormalities. The following day, a brain MRI was performed before and after intravenous contrast, including T2 perfusion. It revealed extensive T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the pons with mild expansion, more prominent on the left side (Figures 1 and 2). Perfusion showed a slight increase in cerebral blood flow and relative cerebral blood volume, below 1.8 (Figure 3). No contrast enhancement or diffusion restriction was observed. These findings are compatible with rhombencephalitis of inflammatory, infectious, or post-infectious autoimmune aetiology, such as Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis. Demyelinating disease, such as acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM), is considered less likely, and neoplastic aetiology is much less probable.
discussion: Background Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis (BBE) is an acute, immune-mediated inflammatory disorder of the brainstem belonging to the anti-GQ1b antibody spectrum, which also includes Miller Fisher syndrome (MFS) and overlaps with Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) [1,2]. It typically follows a recent infection, often C. jejuni , or viral upper respiratory illness, through molecular mimicry between microbial antigens and neuronal gangliosides, particularly GQ1b, abundant in ocular motor nerves and brainstem structures [1,3]. Pathophysiologically, both central nervous system structures (brainstem, thalami, cerebellum) and peripheral nerves may be involved, explaining the overlap of encephalopathy, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia with or without peripheral weakness [2]. Clinical Perspective Our patient presented with a brainstem–cerebellar syndrome, following a febrile pharyngotonsillitis with diarrhoea two weeks earlier. The triad of ophthalmoplegia/ataxia (here manifest as cerebellar signs) and brainstem involvement is characteristic of BBE [1,4]. Although consciousness was preserved, brainstem signs prompted urgent stroke evaluation. Imaging is essential to exclude vascular, infectious, or demyelinating mimics, and to identify subtle inflammatory changes that may guide early immunotherapy. Communication with the referring physician should highlight that early MRI can be normal in BBE and that diagnosis remains primarily clinical, supported by serology (anti-GQ1b IgG) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis (albuminocytologic dissociation), although seronegativity does not exclude BBE [2–5]. In our case, serological testing for antiganglioside antibodies (anti-GQ1b IgG) was negative, and CSF analysis showed mild protein elevation without pleocytosis consistent with albuminocytologic dissociation. No infectious agents were detected. Imaging Perspective MRI abnormalities are present in a minority of cases (≈10–30%), often as T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the brainstem, periaqueductal grey, thalami, or cerebellum, without significant enhancement [1,5]. In our patient, the MRI performed on day two showed an isolated FLAIR hyperintensity in the pons, consistent with inflammatory brainstem involvement. Diffusion restriction is uncommon, and lesions typically resolve within weeks [5]. Outcome First-line treatment includes intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or plasma exchange [4,6]. Our patient received IVIG, corticosteroids, and empirical antibiotics for possible Listeria brainstem infection. Prognosis is generally favourable, with most patients achieving substantial recovery within weeks to months; early treatment may accelerate improvement [1,6]. After several months following treatment and the acute episode, our patient has improved neurologically, although horizontal nystagmus and mild ataxia persist. Take Home Message Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis (BBE) should be suspected in patients with acute brainstem/cerebellar signs following infection, even with a normal early MRI. Subtle pontine FLAIR lesions, as in our case, support the diagnosis when correlated clinically. Prompt exclusion of vascular and infectious causes, and early initiation of immunotherapy, are critical for good outcomes. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Cystic ductal adenocarcinoma of the prostate: A rare presentation
clinical_history: A 78-year-old male was referred to an oncologic hospital for urinary retention and a palpable lower abdominal mass. A pelvic lesion had been incidentally detected on CT for suspected diverticulitis three years earlier, but was not investigated. A prostatic origin was suspected, and PSA was 7 ng/ml.
imaging_findings: A pelvic MRI demonstrated a large multilocular, multiseptated tumour (Figure 1a) with several loculi predominantly hyperintense on T2-weighted images (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c), while others showed variable signal on T1 and T2-weighted images (Figures 1c, 1e, and 1f), corresponding to haemorrhagic content, confirmed on pathology. The lesion originates from the right peripheral zone of the mid-third of the prostate (Figure 1d), contacting and displacing the seminal vesicles, causing medial displacement of the bladder and posterior displacement of the rectum (Figure 1b). The mass is predominantly well circumscribed, causing slight bulging of the anterior and lateral pelvic wall. Some multilocular cysts project posteriorly from the main lesion into the mesorectal fat (Figure 1e). The lesion contains internal septa, hypointense on T2-weighted images (Figure 1c), and a few eccentric papillary solid components with intermediate T2 signal (Figure 1a). These solid areas show no restricted diffusion (Figures 2a and 2b) and mild enhancement following intravenous gadolinium-based contrast (Figures 2c and 2d). No direct invasion of adjacent organs is observed. Staging thoracic and abdominal CT was also performed and showed no suspicious lesions for metastatic disease.
discussion: Background Prostate tumours can arise from epithelial, stromal, or ectopic glandular cells. Adenocarcinoma is the most frequent type, with ductal adenocarcinoma representing only 0.1–2.0% of prostate cancers [1]. It often coexists with acinar adenocarcinoma and typically involves the peripheral zone and prostatic urethra, less frequently the transition zone [2]. Clinical Perspective Ductal adenocarcinoma usually affects men in their sixth to eighth decades. Symptoms include urinary retention from bladder outlet obstruction, haematuria, constipation, and pelvic pain [1,3]. Haematuria is the most frequent presentation, often linked to an exophytic endourethral lesion. Prostate biopsies may be negative, and diagnosis is frequently made at transurethral resection (TURP) [4]. When a large cystic pelvic lesion is identified, particularly involving the prostate, bladder, or rectum, determining the organ of origin may be difficult. In such cases, imaging is essential for diagnosis, staging, and treatment planning [3,5]. Imaging Perspective Cystic variants of prostatic carcinoma are extremely rare, with only nine macrocystic ductal cases reported between 1991 and 2016 [6]. Conventional ductal adenocarcinomas typically show solid, papillary, and cribriform architecture, with other reported variants including mucinous, foamy gland, and cystic papillary patterns [3,6–9]. Typically, they appear as large, exophytic, multiloculated lesions with papillary or polypoid solid components [6]. Solid areas may show papillary fronds or cribriform patterns, often with haemorrhage and restricted diffusion on MRI [7]. Outcome Ductal adenocarcinoma, either pure or mixed with acinar elements, is an aggressive, distinct subtype [3,5,8,10]. Most cases present at advanced stages (T3–T4 in 75%) and tend to metastasise to bone, lymph nodes, and visceral organs such as the lung and liver [3,5,11]. Prognosis is poorer, with reported five-year metastasis-free survival of 75% versus 95% after radical prostatectomy, and 62% versus 93% after radiotherapy [11,12]. Standard management includes radical surgery, often combined with hormonal or systemic therapy [3,5,7]. Our patient underwent a radical prostatectomy. At 23-month follow-up, he remains alive and without radiological recurrence. Pathology confirmed ductal cystadenocarcinoma (Gleason 8, grade group 4), completely excised, with focal adipose tissue involvement and no lymphovascular or perineural invasion. Take Home Message Cystic ductal adenocarcinoma is a rare, aggressive prostate cancer subtype. Accurate diagnosis requires histopathological and imaging correlation, with imaging being essential to assess the extent and guide therapy. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Enchondroma protuberans: Multimodal imaging features of a rare tumour
clinical_history: A 10-year-old boy presented because of painless swelling in the 1st finger of the left hand for several years. The patient did not recall any previous history of trauma or infection. A hard fixed subcutaneous mass was found, without signs of inflammation. Range of motion was preserved.
imaging_findings: Plain radiographs of the thumb (Figure 1) revealed a solitary well-defined, predominantly lytic lesion in the proximal diaphysis of the thumb’s proximal phalanx, with both medullary and exophytic components. Marked endosteal scalloping and thinning of the expanded cortex were present, without signs of aggressive periosteal reaction. CT imaging (Figure 2) confirmed these findings, revealing a sclerotic border, contiguous exophytic extension and foci of chondroid calcification. On MRI (Figure 3), the lesion appeared moderately hypointense on T1-weighted sequences and hyperintense with a lobulated contour on T2-weighted fat-saturated images, similar to hyaline cartilage. Small foci of curvilinear calcification were evident, supporting the presence of a chondroid matrix. MRI also showed a continuous rim of calcified periosteum. No evidence of soft tissue extension or periosteal reaction was present on any modality throughout the evaluation.
discussion: Background Enchondroma is a benign cartilaginous bone tumour, the most common in the hand (90%). Enchondroma protuberans (EP) is a very rare subtype of enchondroma. Phalanges and metacarpals are the most frequent locations. EP is characterised by an intramedullary enchondroma that grows exophytically, breaching the cortex. The pathophysiology involves cartilaginous proliferation from chondrocytes near the growth plate [1–3]. Clinical Perspective EP typically presents as a slow-growing, painless and firm mass in the small bones of the hand. Some patients may experience discomfort and pain, mainly if a pathological fracture is present. Clinically, EP’s appearance is nonspecific, but careful search for soft tissue haemangiomas must be included in the examination. Imaging is critical in the diagnosis and risk assessment, guiding appropriate patient management. Similar lesions, like periosteal chondroma and chondrosarcoma, have differing management and prognostic implications. If imaging is not clearly diagnostic, a biopsy should take place [2–5]. Imaging Perspective Radiographs and CT commonly show a well-defined lytic medullary cavity in the diaphysis, with endosteal scalloping, cortical thinning, and a contiguous exophytic component extending through the cortex. Chondroid matrix calcifications may be present [1,4]. MRI is useful for diagnostic clarity, demonstrating clear continuity between the medullary and exophytic components, with mostly chondroid signal characteristics, hypointense on T1 (Figures 3a and 3b) and hyperintense on T2 (Figures 3c and 3d), with regular sclerotic margins and septations or nodular low-signal areas of calcification. MRI better depicts lesion morphology and location to distinguish it from periosteal chondroma, which has a subperiosteal origin, causing cortical interruption from the outer surface. The presence of aggressive soft tissue infiltration, aggressive periosteal reaction and growth would raise the suspicion for chondrosarcoma [1,4]. In most cases, diagnosis can be made on radiographs. CT or, ideally, MRI should be used when doubt persists. If multiple lesions were present, the suspicion for Ollier disease should be stated. If the patient also had soft tissue haemangiomas, then Maffucci syndrome would be the diagnosis [5]. Outcome The therapeutic approach is usually surgical with marginal excision of the exophytic portion and intralesional curettage of the medullary component. Prognosis is excellent, with low rates of recurrence. Imaging is essential in preoperative planning to delineate lesion extent, confirm the diagnosis, and guide appropriate surgery. It also minimises the risk of misdiagnosis and thus unnecessary radical procedures or undertreatment [1,2]. Teaching Points Enchondroma protuberans (EP) should be considered in exophytic lytic lesions of the hand. Multimodality imaging helps distinguish EP from periosteal chondroma and chondrosarcoma. Curettage ensures an excellent prognosis.

title: Acute quadriceps denervation oedema following inguinal hernia repair
clinical_history: A 65-year-old male, with a history of open right-sided inguinal hernia repair, underwent laparoscopic treatment for a recurrent bilateral inguinal hernia. Postoperatively, he experienced right-sided weakness with limping, hypoesthesia, and progressive pain in the thigh. There were no local anaesthetics used during the procedure.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound of the right groin (Figure 1) revealed a large collection of fluid around the inserted mesh, suggestive of a postoperative seroma. This was located superficial to the iliopsoas muscle, possibly compressing the femoral nerve. Distally to this collection, ultrasound showed non-specific infiltrative features around the femoral nerve at the inguinal region, lateral to the femoral vessels. Furthermore, an additional lipomatous mass was identified near the mesh, suspicious for a recurrent hernia (Figure 2). MRI with T2-TIRM (turbo inversion recovery magnitude) images (Figure 3) confirmed a recurrent indirect inguinal hernia and large postoperative seroma with probable compression of the femoral nerve. The right femoral nerve and quadriceps muscle both presented hyperintensity on T2-weighted images, which is consistent with femoral neuropathy and subsequent acute denervation muscular oedema.
discussion: Acute femoral neuropathy after hernia repair is a rare complication, with a higher chance after redo surgery (recurrent hernia, evacuation of haematoma, or debridement of infection) [1]. It poses a typical clinical presentation with sensory and motor deficit (cf. infra), best objectified using the MRC (Medical Research Council) muscle grading system. Nerve conduction studies, electromyography, and imaging investigations can be used in diagnosis to define the aetiology and locate possible compression. Most cases are resolved within a few weeks to one year using physical therapy and rehabilitation. When a compressive cause is identified, initial surgery can be indicated. Only in a small percentage of cases, more radical surgery such as neurolysis and nerve grafting is needed. Although the long-term prognosis is good, some cases can cause significant medicolegal implications. This has to do with the fact that there are several preventive measures that can be taken, such as adjusting the retractor during the operation so that traction of the femoral nerve can be averted. Peripheral neuropathies are generally classified as compressive or non-compressive [2]. Both types influence this case: the femoral canal as a compressive site and the postoperative state (with possible trauma, infection, and/or inflammation) as a non-compressive factor. The typical clinical presentation of peripheral femoral neuropathy is well-illustrated in this case. The femoral nerve originates from the lumbar plexus, passing between and innervating the psoas and iliacus muscles [1–3]. After crossing the inguinal ligament, it divides into an anterior branch to the pectineus and sartorius muscles and a posterior branch to the thigh’s anterior compartment, also innervating anteromedial leg skin (saphenous nerve). Here, the compressive seroma was distal to the iliopsoas branches, sparing the force of the iliopsoas muscle. In contrast, the quadriceps muscle, located more inferiorly, showed reduced strength (MRC 3/5) and loss of patellar reflex. The patient also experienced hypoesthesia and pain in the anteromedial thigh (saphenous nerve). Electromyography showed acute-on-chronic L5-neuropathy. Together with ultrasound and MRI, the diagnosis of a large seroma leading to compressive femoral neuropathy and subsequent acute quadriceps denervation oedema could be made. No lipomatous muscle atrophy was present, with leg circumference preserved. The differential diagnosis should include intra-operative nerve damage, both mechanical (lesion to the nerve) and pharmaceutical (e.g., due to misuse of local anaesthetics), as well as stretching and compression of the nerve by scar tissue, central neuropathy (such as radiculopathy), and other inflammatory neuropathies. Ultrasound effectively evaluates peripheral nerves on their superficial course [1,2]. Neuropathy appears as nerve enlargement with hyporeflectivity. MRI is preferred for assessing deeper nerve segments and identifying compression causes, making it easier to evaluate associated muscle groups [1–3]. A compressed nerve is T2-hyperintense and enlarged. Denervated muscles show T2-hyperintense oedema in the acute phase, and progress to T1-hyperintense lipomatous atrophy when chronic. STIR-imaging is indispensable in MR neurography for its robust, homogeneous fat suppression and high nerve-to-fat contrast, making it ideal for detecting nerve oedema and inflammation. 3D isotropic T2-FatSat imaging is the current state-of-the-art, providing higher resolution and multiplanar reconstructions with excellent nerve-soft tissue contrast and continuous nerve tracking [4]. Persistent denervation may cause muscular atrophy, which was not yet present in this case. Timely pressure relief can partially reverse symptoms [2]. Surgical decompression poses risks, favouring initial conservative treatment [1,3]. In our case, seroma aspiration provided little improvement. Physiotherapy and electrotherapy initially showed minimal effect, but reduced symptoms later on, with strength returning gradually. Physiotherapy was continued alongside neuropathic pain management with duloxetine, a serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI). Another type of iatrogenic femoral neuropathy is after an ilioinguinal nerve block, through trauma with puncture of the nerve or toxic damage related to high doses [1]. This can be prevented by using ultrasound-guided injection. Take Home Message This case demonstrates the usefulness of MRI in diagnosing (acute and/or chronic) muscular denervation, especially in cases of unusual compressive causes. Acute denervation shows neurogenic muscular oedema (T2-hyperintense), progressing to lipomatous atrophy (T1-hyperintense) when chronic. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Brown tumour mimicking giant cell tumour of bone
clinical_history: A 45-year-old man with right knee pain and swelling. Imaging revealed an expansile lytic lesion in the distal femur. The lesion underwent biopsy in June 2024, which reported a giant cell-rich bone lesion. The patient subsequently underwent surgical curettage with adjuvant phenol application and bone grafting in July 2024. Two weeks later, he sustained a subtrochanteric femoral fracture. Staging imaging demonstrated multiple additional lytic bone lesions and abnormal uptake in the neck region. Serum calcium was 3.15 mmol/L, phosphate 0.7 mmol/L, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) 1450 pg/mL.
imaging_findings: Radiographs (Figure 1), CT (Figure 2) and MRI (Figure 3) of the right knee showed an expansile, lobulated lytic lesion in the distal femur with cortical thinning and heterogeneous enhancement. Later radiographs (Figure 4) demonstrated a subtrochanteric fracture through a lytic lesion and multiple additional lytic lesions in the pelvis and spine. CT confirmed multifocality (Figure 5). PET/CT revealed hypermetabolic bone lesions (Figure 6). Parathyroid scintigraphy demonstrated a hyperfunctioning right superior parathyroid gland (Figure 7). Follow-up radiographs showed consolidation of the fracture and progressive calcification of the lesions after surgical treatment of the neck lesion (Figures 8 and 9).
discussion: Background Brown tumours are rare, non-neoplastic giant cell-rich bone lesions secondary to hyperparathyroidism. Excess parathyroid hormone (PTH) stimulates osteoclastic bone resorption, replaced by fibroblastic tissue and multinucleated giant cells [1]. Haemosiderin from repeated haemorrhage gives their brown gross appearance. They may be solitary or multifocal, most commonly affecting ribs, pelvis, mandible, long bones and spine. Incidence is ~3% in primary hyperparathyroidism and 1.5–2% in secondary disease [2,3]. Clinical Perspective Patients can present with pain, swelling, or pathological fractures. Solitary lesions may mimic giant cell tumour (GCT) radiologically and histologically, delaying recognition of the underlying endocrine disorder. Multifocal lesions or systemic signs such as bone pain, renal calculi or neuropsychiatric symptoms should prompt investigation for hyperparathyroidism [2,3]. In our case, the initial biopsy performed demonstrated a giant cell-rich lesion interpreted as compatible with a GCT. Surgical curettage with adjuvant treatment was subsequently performed. However, following a pathological subtrochanteric fracture and identification of multifocal lytic lesions, a histological review raised the differential diagnosis of a brown tumour associated with primary hyperparathyroidism, prompting biochemical evaluation and definitive diagnosis. Imaging Perspective On radiographs, brown tumours appear as expansile lytic lesions without periosteal reaction or sclerotic margins. CT delineates cortical thinning and trabecular destruction. MRI is typically hypointense on T1, heterogeneous on T2/STIR, and enhances after contrast [1,2]. Multifocality should raise suspicion for metabolic bone disease. PET/CT may show hypermetabolism in bone and parathyroid glands, as in this case. Sestamibi scintigraphy and cervical ultrasound are standard for localising parathyroid adenomas before surgery [3,4]. Outcome Treatment is parathyroidectomy. Lesions usually regress or calcify within months. Our patient’s subtrochanteric fracture required intramedullary nailing prior to diagnosis. Immediate postoperative laboratory tests showed hypocalcaemia (calcium 2.05 mmol/L), hyperphosphataemia (1.9 mmol/L) and suppressed PTH (18 pg/mL), consistent with hungry bone syndrome. Intensive calcium and vitamin D supplementation was initiated. Follow-up laboratory tests at six months demonstrated normalisation of serum calcium (2.30 mmol/L), phosphate (1.2 mmol/L) and PTH (45 pg/mL), indicating metabolic recovery. A ten-month follow-up imaging (Figure 9) confirmed fracture consolidation and lesion calcification, consistent with metabolic recovery [4]. Teaching Point Brown tumours can closely mimic giant cell tumour (GCT) radiologically and histologically. Multifocal lytic lesions should prompt measurement of serum calcium and parathyroid hormone (PTH) to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary aggressive orthopaedic procedures. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Benign enhancing foramen magnum lesions: A bright-side imaging perspective
clinical_history: A 52-year-old woman with a history of partially resected dorsal spinal meningeal melanoma treated with adjuvant radiotherapy in 2011 was under regular neuroaxis MRI surveillance for post-treatment follow-up. She had remained clinically and radiologically stable on long-term follow-up.
imaging_findings: The latest follow-up MRI of the brain and spine demonstrated bilateral, well-defined, small enhancing nodules located posterior to the intradural vertebral arteries at the level of the foramen magnum. These lesions showed marked hyperintensity on 3D T2-FLAIR images (Figure 1), signal intensity similar to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) on T2-weighted sequences, no restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging or blooming effect on susceptibility-weighted imaging, and avid, homogeneous enhancement on post-contrast T1-weighted imaging (Figure 2). A retrospective review confirmed their presence on prior examinations, with a slight increase in size over the years compared with the baseline study from 2011 (Figure 3), without associated mass effect or additional parenchymal or meningeal lesions. The dorsal spinal MRI demonstrated local disease control, with stable post-surgical changes and no evidence of tumour recurrence.
discussion: Background Benign enhancing foramen magnum lesions (BEFMLs) is a recently described imaging entity characterised by small, enhancing T2-hyperintense nodules located posterior to the intradural vertebral artery, typically in contact with the dorsal root of the spinal accessory nerve (SAN) [1,2]. Histologically, BEFMLs are believed to represent fibrotic arachnoid nodules adherent to the pia mater of the SAN [2]. Clinical Perspective Although often detected incidentally on imaging [4], BEFMLs carry a clinical risk of overdiagnosis and overtreatment, as they may be mistaken for malignant or vascular pathology [2,3]. It is essential to clearly communicate their benign nature to the referring physician, since they may slightly enlarge over time without malignant potential or need for intervention [1,2]. Imaging Perspective Radiologically, BEFMLs are best appreciated on high-resolution 3D FLAIR and post-contrast 3D T1-weighted sequences, whereas they often remain occult on conventional T2 and T1-weighted spin-echo sequences, as well as on routine 2D FLAIR imaging due to CSF flow artefacts [3]. Their typical imaging appearance includes small, round or ovoid, well-defined foci located posterior to the intradural vertebral arteries and in contact with the SAN [2–4]. High-resolution balanced steady-state sequences, such as 3D-CISS, may further demonstrate their attachment to the SAN [1,2,5]. BEFMLs typically show marked T2-FLAIR hyperintensity, are inapparent on conventional T2 spin-echo sequences, and demonstrate intense, homogeneous post-contrast enhancement without diffusion restriction or blooming effect on susceptibility-sensitive images[1–3]. Their invisible T2 signal helps distinguish them from other avidly enhancing lesions in this region, including meningiomas, nerve sheath tumours, metastatic or inflammatory deposits (e.g., sarcoidosis), as well as vascular lesions such as dissecting posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) aneurysms, which usually exhibit T2 flow voids and/or vascular signal on angiography unless thrombosed [2,3]. When uncertain, angiographic evaluation with 3D time-of-flight MR angiography or CT angiography may be performed to exclude vascular pathology. Conversely, other T2-occult cystic lesions, such as arachnoid, neuroenteric, epidermoid or synovial cysts, do not demonstrate post-contrast enhancement, allowing confident differentiation [3]. Finally, the characteristic location, symmetry, absence of mass effect, long-term stability or minimal growth on follow-up imaging are key diagnostic features supporting their benign nature and preventing unnecessary intervention [2–4]. Outcome BEFMLs are considered “do-not-touch” entities, with a benign prognosis and no indication for surgical resection or long-term follow-up [1,2]. The implications of accurate imaging interpretation are particularly important in oncologic patients, as in our case, where misclassification as recurrent or metastatic disease could result in unwarranted therapeutic interventions or changes in treatment planning. Take Home Message / Teaching Point Awareness of this benign entity by radiologists prevents misdiagnosis and unnecessary interventions [2]. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Unilateral upper limb elephantiasis neuromatosa: Imaging findings
clinical_history: A 15-year-old boy presented with congenital, painless swelling of the left upper limb, progressively enlarging since birth, causing limb deformity and restricted elbow and wrist movement (Figure 1a). The swelling increased gradually in childhood and more rapidly in recent years. The patient came from a rural background with limited healthcare access and had not sought treatment earlier. There was no prior medical or surgical intervention. Examination showed diffuse soft swelling, nodular skin thickening, multiple café-au-lait macules, and cutaneous neurofibromas (Figures 1a and 1b), suggestive of neurofibromatosis type 1.
imaging_findings: Ultrasonography revealed multiple elongated soft-tissue masses infiltrating along major neurovascular bundles, forming a characteristic worm-like configuration with mixed echotexture and concentric appearance suggestive of neural origin (Figure 2a). Colour Doppler demonstrated dilated, tortuous vascular channels within and around the lesions (Figure 2b). Plain radiographs showed diffuse soft-tissue overgrowth, cortical thinning, and bony remodelling of the humerus, radius, ulna, and hand bones, with overall limb lengthening and digital asymmetry due to disproportionate ring finger phalangeal growth (Figures 3a and 3b). Multiple healed fracture lines with callus formation indicated recurrent pathological fractures. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed diffuse skin and subcutaneous thickening with infiltrative, low-attenuation masses involving subcutaneous and muscular compartments, associated muscle atrophy, and mild patchy enhancement (Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c). Additional findings included humeral bowing with pseudoarthrosis, fusiform masses along the ulnar nerve consistent with plexiform neurofibromas, and numerous dilated tortuous vascular channels, confirming neurofibromatosis-related elephantiasis neuromatosa. MRI was not performed due to financial constraints; however, CT and USG findings were diagnostic of neurofibromatosis-related elephantiasis neuromatosa.
discussion: Background Elephantiasis neuromatosa (EN) is an uncommon but dramatic manifestation of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), characterised by diffuse hypertrophy of skin, subcutaneous tissues, and underlying bones, resulting in progressive limb enlargement and deformity [1,4]. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) results from mutations in the NF1 gene located on chromosome 17q11.2, which encodes neurofibromin, a tumour-suppressor protein regulating RAS pathway activity. The pathogenesis is thought to involve proliferation of plexiform neurofibromas with lymphatic obstruction, chronic venous congestion, and adipose tissue proliferation, leading to overgrowth [3,4]. Skeletal changes include cortical thinning, bone lengthening, bowing deformities, and pseudoarthrosis [1–3]. Clinical Perspective Clinically, EN presents as painless, gradually progressive limb swelling causing deformity, restricted mobility, and functional impairment. The presence of café-au-lait macules and cutaneous neurofibromas usually raises suspicion of NF1 [1,2]. Imaging is requested to differentiate EN from other causes of massive limb enlargement and to evaluate the extent of disease for management planning. Imaging Perspective Imaging plays a crucial role in diagnosis and surgical planning. Ultrasound typically shows elongated, infiltrative masses following neurovascular bundles with a worm-like configuration and concentric appearance suggestive of neural origin [4]. Doppler demonstrates associated vascular channels. Radiographs show soft-tissue overgrowth, cortical thinning, bony remodelling, limb lengthening, and sometimes pathological fractures [1,3]. CT or MRI confirm diffuse soft-tissue thickening, muscle atrophy, plexiform neurofibromas, and vascular involvement, and helps exclude malignant transformation [3,4]. Together with clinical stigmata, these findings are diagnostic of EN. Outcome Management is challenging and often multidisciplinary. Surgical debulking, orthopaedic correction, and physiotherapy may improve function and cosmesis, but recurrence is common due to the infiltrative nature of plexiform neurofibromas. Imaging significantly influences therapeutic planning by mapping lesion extent and identifying complications such as pseudoarthrosis or malignant change [3,4]. Prognosis depends on the severity of deformity, surgical feasibility, and the absence of malignant transformation. In this case, the patient declined surgical intervention and is being managed conservatively with limb support and physiotherapy, showing a stable condition without ulceration or malignant change on follow-up. Take Home Message Elephantiasis neuromatosa (EN) is a rare and severe phenotype of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) with striking limb overgrowth and functional limitation. Multimodality imaging is indispensable for diagnosis, differentiation from other causes of limb enlargement, and treatment planning. Early recognition and a coordinated, multidisciplinary approach are essential for optimal functional and psychosocial outcomes.

title: An uncommon diagnosis: Diabetic mastopathy in a male patient
clinical_history: A 37-year-old male presented with a one-week history of a painless firm left breast lump, retroareolar on palpation, extending toward the upper-outer quadrant (12–3 o’clock). Skin and nipple were normal. No systemic symptoms. Medical history notable for poorly controlled insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus.
imaging_findings: Mammography revealed bilateral gynecomastia, more prominent and dense on the left, with a focal asymmetry and obscured margins in the retroareolar/upper-outer quadrant (Figure 1). Ultrasonographically, the area described on mammography corresponded to a mass located between the 12 and 3 o’clock positions, with posterior shadowing, horizontal orientation, oval shape, indistinct margins and minimal Doppler flow (Figure 2). No suspicious lymph nodes were observed in either axilla. The lesion initially corresponded to BI-RADS category 4B, but in a male patient, the category was upgraded to 4C. Given these findings, a core needle biopsy was performed due to the high suspicion of malignancy. Histological analysis revealed dense stroma with a marked lymphocytic infiltrate in perilobular and pericanalicular areas, along with a mild perivascular infiltrate. No histological signs of malignancy were observed, confirming the diagnosis of diabetic mastopathy.
discussion: Background Diabetic mastopathy is an uncommon benign breast condition that mimics malignancy and is primarily associated with long-standing insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. Its pathogenesis remains unclear, but an autoimmune mechanism has been proposed, involving fibroinflammatory changes driven by chronic hyperglycemia and immune dysregulation. Histologically, it shows dense keloid-like stromal fibrosis and a marked lymphocytic infiltrate, predominantly B-cells, distributed in periductal, perilobular, and perivascular areas. These features resemble those of other autoimmune-related breast disorders, supporting the hypothesis of an immunologically mediated process. Although most frequently reported in premenopausal women with poorly controlled diabetes, it may also occur in males and is rarely seen in type 2 diabetes or other autoimmune conditions [1–6]. Cases have also highlighted diagnostic challenges in the emergency setting, where diabetic mastopathy can be easily misinterpreted [9]. Clinical Perspective The clinical presentation typically consists of a large, firm, painless breast mass, usually located in the retroareolar region, clinically indistinguishable from cancer. Although often unilateral, diabetic mastopathy may also present as bilateral, multifocal, or multicentric disease, and recurrences after excision are not uncommon [2–6]. Awareness of these patterns is crucial to avoid unnecessary surgical interventions [7]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice in the initial work-up, as it typically demonstrates irregular hypoechoic lesions with posterior acoustic shadowing, classic features of this entity [4–6,9]. Mammography, although often nonspecific, may show ill-defined masses or focal asymmetries in dense breasts [8]. Magnetic resonance imaging serves as a complementary tool in complex or equivocal cases. Reported MRI patterns are variable and nonspecific, frequently showing delayed or minimal enhancement, which hampers reliable differentiation from malignancy [4–6]. For this reason, definitive diagnosis relies on core needle biopsy, since the marked stromal fibrosis reduces the diagnostic yield of cytology [1–6]. Outcome This is a benign, self-limited condition, and, therefore, management is usually conservative and based on clinical and radiological follow-up. Surgical intervention is not routinely indicated, as recurrences are frequent even after resection [2–6]. Take Home Message Diabetic mastopathy is a benign entity that can clinically and radiologically mimic breast cancer, especially in young patients with long-standing type 1 diabetes. Proper recognition of clinical and radiological features, and performing a core needle biopsy to confirm the diagnosis, are essential to avoid unnecessary aggressive treatments [1,5,6]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Bilateral tympanic membrane pneumatoceles: A rare radiologic and clinical entity
clinical_history: A 40-year-old man presented with bilateral ear irritation and itching for 3–4 years, recently accompanied by ear fullness and pressure. He denied ear discharge, hearing loss, tinnitus, recent infection or barotrauma. On otoscopy, bilateral attic-level tympanic membrane outpouchings, more prominent on the right side, were noted (Figure 1), with intact, non-inflamed membranes and no middle-ear effusion. Pure-tone audiometry and tympanometry were not performed, as there was no subjective hearing loss. Prior medical history was relevant for asthma, diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, and smoking.
imaging_findings: High-resolution CT coronal reconstructions of the petrous temporal bones (Figure 2a) reveal bilateral tympanic membrane pneumatoceles arising from the pars flaccida and protruding into the external auditory canals. Axial CT images (Figure 2b) further delineate these air-filled outpouchings. The middle ear cavities and mastoid air cells are well-aerated, showing no evidence of opacification. No ossicular chain or scutum erosion is observed. Additional MRI demonstrated air-filled sacs arising from the tympanic membranes with normal middle-ear cavities and an unremarkable nasopharynx (Figure 3). Following multidisciplinary review by ENT (ear, nose, and throat) and radiology, these findings were considered consistent with bilateral tympanic membrane pneumatoceles.
discussion: Background Tympanic membrane (TM) pneumatoceles are exceptionally rare air-filled lesions arising from the TM, typically involving the pars flaccida [1,5]. They are more commonly reported unilaterally and often in association with identifiable triggers such as trauma, barotrauma, positive pressure ventilation, infection or inflammation [2–4]. Although their exact pathogenesis remains unclear, several mechanisms have been proposed. Positive pressure, as seen with CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) therapy, may distend structurally vulnerable areas of the TM, promoting cystic air entrapment [1,4]. Repetitive Valsalva manoeuvres or auto-insufflation in the context of eustachian tube dysfunction may cause similar ballooning via a ball-valve mechanism [3,5]. In cases of infection or inflammation, pneumatoceles may develop after fluid resorption and subsequent filling of a transient potential space by air. Congenital or acquired weaknesses of the tympanic membrane, particularly at the pars flaccida, may predispose individuals to pneumatocele formation even without obvious triggers and may account for idiopathic cases [1,3,5]. Clinical Perspective Patients may be asymptomatic or present with vague aural symptoms such as fullness, pressure, or irritation [1,3]. In our case, the patient reported a long-standing history of bilateral irritation and pressure, without otorrhoea, hearing loss, or prior barotrauma (diving, CPAP use, etc). The bilateral nature of the findings, in the absence of precipitating events, makes this case particularly unusual. Imaging Perspective High-resolution CT is critical in visualising the pneumatoceles as air-filled outpouchings of the pars flaccida protruding into the external auditory canal, and should remain the first-line imaging method. MRI can be a helpful additional tool when CT findings are unclear, particularly to rule out infection or cholesteatoma. However, tympanic pneumatoceles may be difficult to depict on MRI when the tympanic membrane is surrounded by air in the external auditory canal (EAC) and middle-ear cavity (MEC). Outcome Our patient was managed conservatively for symptomatic itching with topical therapy, resulting in partial symptom relief. He is under regular follow-up in the microsuction clinic, with no progression or new symptoms. Management depends on symptom severity and risk of progression. Conservative observation is appropriate for stable, asymptomatic cases without evidence of cholesteatoma or bone erosion. Surgical intervention (e.g., tympanoplasty) may be warranted if symptoms persist or imaging suggests progressive pathology or secondary complications. Long-term outcomes are generally favourable when appropriately managed [1]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Tympanic membrane (TM) pneumatoceles, while rare, can present bilaterally and without classical risk factors such as trauma or CPAP use. High-resolution CT remains the first-line investigation for tympanic-membrane and middle-ear pathologies. MRI serves as a useful adjunct when CT findings are ambiguous, helping to distinguish benign air-filled lesions from soft-tissue disease. On MRI, the very thin tympanic membrane can be difficult to differentiate from adjacent aerated spaces, a potential interpretative pitfall that may obscure small air collections. Awareness of this rare entity can prevent unnecessary surgical intervention and enhance diagnostic precision in otologic imaging.

title: Paradidymis on the loose: A painless paratesticular mass after testicular cancer
clinical_history: A 46-year-old man with a history of right testicular seminoma (pT1N0M0) treated with orchidectomy presented with an incidentally detected, painless left scrotal mass. Clinical examination revealed a firm, well-circumscribed paratesticular lesion, distinct from the testis. The left testicle was normal in size and position, with preserved cremasteric reflex.
imaging_findings: Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated a right testicular prosthesis (Figure 1). The left testis was normal in size and echotexture, with no focal lesions (Figure 2). Adjacent to the head of the left epididymis, a small, well-circumscribed, isoechoic nodular structure was identified at the inferior portion of the spermatic cord (Figure 3). The lesion was avascular on colour Doppler and contained a tiny anechoic component consistent with a cyst in the paradidymis (organ of Giraldes) (Figure 4).
discussion: Background The paratesticular space includes intrascrotal structures adjacent to the testis, such as the epididymis, spermatic cord, and fascial elements derived from testicular descent. Unlike intratesticular lesions, which are often malignant, most paratesticular nodules in adults are benign [1,2]. Five main testicular appendages exist: the appendix testis, appendix epididymis, superior and inferior aberrant ducts (organs of Haller), and the paradidymis. The paradidymis is a mesonephric (Wolffian) remnant, homologous to the paroophoron in females, consisting of vestigial convoluted tubules located anteroinferiorly in the spermatic cord near the epididymal head. It is the rarest appendage, found in only 1–3% of males [3]. Clinical Perspective Without torsion, the paradidymis usually presents as a painless, well-circumscribed paratesticular nodule. When torsion occurs, it can mimic testicular torsion, presenting with acute pain and sometimes nausea or vomiting [4]. It is a rare cause of a scrotal mass, typically due to cystic change or torsion, with only isolated reports. Standard evaluation like physical examination, ultrasound, and tumour markers often cannot provide a definitive diagnosis, and surgical exploration may be required [4,5]. In our case, the palpable solid nodule with a tiny internal cystic focus represented the paradidymis with cystic change, explaining both the nodular and anechoic components seen on ultrasound. Given the patient’s prior right seminoma, recognising the contralateral benign extratesticular lesion was crucial to avoid misinterpreting it as tumour recurrence or a new malignancy. Imaging Perspective High-resolution ultrasound with colour Doppler is the modality of choice for paratesticular lesions. The paradidymis appears as a small, avascular, well-defined structure near the epididymal head or body, usually isoechoic or slightly hypoechoic. With cystic change, it appears anechoic and avascular. In torsion, ultrasound may show a heterogeneous, enlarged appendage with surrounding hypervascularity. MRI, though rarely needed, may depict a small soft-tissue or cystic lesion without enhancement. Recognising these features helps avoid misdiagnosis and guides management [2,4–6]. A spermatic cord lipoma appears echogenic and compressible, whereas an adenomatoid tumour, the most common benign paratesticular neoplasm, shows internal vascularity [6]. Outcome Incidental findings need no treatment and can be monitored. Acute torsion may require surgical exploration [5,6]. Prognosis is excellent, as the paradidymis has no malignant potential. When excised, histology confirms the diagnosis and no further therapy is required [4,5]. Take Home Message The paradidymis is a rare paratesticular remnant that may mimic pathology. Recognising its imaging features prevents misdiagnosis and unnecessary intervention. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: The use of ultrasound in anterior interosseous nerve neuralgic amyotrophy
clinical_history: A 62-year-old woman presented to the neurosurgery department with a 10-day history of muscle weakness, preventing active flexion of the interphalangeal joint of her right thumb and the distal interphalangeal joint of her index finger. Electromyography (EMG) showed abnormal motor unit activity in the flexor pollicis longus and pronator quadratus. One month earlier, the patient experienced severe neck and shoulder pain on both sides. The symptoms have since improved spontaneously and showed marked relief following a cervical epidural steroid injection.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound demonstrated a clear atrophy of the pronator quadratus and flexor pollicis longus muscle bellies in the forearm (Figure 1). Detailed evaluation of the median nerve using a 22 MHz high-resolution probe identified two isolated thickened fascicles on the posterior side of the nerve (Figure 2a), approximately 3 cm proximal to the elbow crease, one exhibiting a distinct hourglass-shaped constriction (Figure 2b). These findings confirm the diagnosis of neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage–Turner syndrome) affecting the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) fascicles within the median nerve.
discussion: Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome (AINS) is a form of neuralgic amyotrophy (NA), a neuromuscular disorder, believed to result from an interaction between genetic susceptibility and/or an autoimmune trigger. AINS typically presents with prodromal arm or forearm pain lasting for hours to days, followed by an isolated palsy of the flexor pollicis longus, the flexor digitorum profundus (index) and the pronator quadratus muscles. This leads to weakness in the thumb-index finger pincer movement. It predominantly affects individuals in their 40s, with a slight female predilection, though it can occur at any age. Diagnosis of AINS involves clinical history, EMG, and imaging findings. The AIN is a purely motor branch of the median nerve, with its fascicles located in the posterior of the median nerve trunk in the distal upper arm. The AIN emerges from the epineurium 3–5 cm distal to the humeral intercondylar axis. Targeted high-resolution ultrasound can identify enlarged fascicles within the median nerve trunk proximal to the AIN branch point, eventually accompanied by nearly pathognomonic hourglass-shaped constrictions and muscle atrophy. These imaging findings help confirm the diagnosis and assess the need for surgery during follow-up. MRI may also show muscle atrophy, next to T2 signal hyperintensity in the AIN distribution, but it is more expensive and offers lower resolution [1]. Initial treatment includes analgesics, corticosteroids and physiotherapy. If the patient shows no signs of recovery after 6–12 months of conservative therapy, exploratory surgery with interfascicular neurolysis may be considered, particularly when hourglass constriction is demonstrated on ultrasound, as in our case. Neurolysis with release of perineural fibrous strands was therefore performed. At 3-month follow-up, the patient showed clinical improvement, with partial recovery of strength and EMG evidence of reactivation of the flexor pollicis longus muscle. Overall, surgical treatment for hourglass-like nerve constrictions in patients who fail to recover with conservative management may offer an effective therapeutic option [2,3]. Take Home Message Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome (AINS) is a rare manifestation of neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage–Turner syndrome), where targeted high-resolution ultrasound can reveal characteristic hourglass-shaped constrictions and fascicular thickening of the anterior interosseous nerve fascicles within the median nerve proximal to the elbow crease. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Patellar sleeve fracture in a 12-year-old boy
clinical_history: A 12-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with direct trauma to the knee sustained the previous day. He reported pain and functional limitation. Physical examination revealed mild knee oedema, tenderness over the inferior pole of the patella, and signs of extensor mechanism insufficiency. No haematoma was observed.
imaging_findings: Initial knee radiographs showed subtle irregularities at the inferior pole of the patella, raising suspicion of cartilage avulsion (Figure 1). Ultrasound revealed hypoechoic discontinuity of the distal patellar cartilage with adjacent soft tissue swelling, further supporting the diagnosis of a sleeve fracture (Figure 2). MRI confirmed the lesion, showing disruption of the patellar cartilage and partial detachment (2 mm) of surrounding soft tissues, compromising the extensor mechanism (Figure 3). Adjacent soft tissue oedema was also noted. No significant joint effusion or bone marrow oedema was present. MRI excluded diagnoses such as patellar dislocation or ligamentous injury.
discussion: Background Patellar sleeve fractures are rare injuries, almost exclusively observed in skeletally immature patients, particularly those engaged in high-impact sports. They involve avulsion of the cartilage and periosteum at the inferior pole of the patella, often accompanied by detachment of adjacent soft tissues such as tendons or ligaments. These fractures are classified as type I, when only soft tissue is avulsed, or type II, when both bone and soft tissue are involved. The injury typically results from indirect tractional forces acting on the immature osteochondral junction, leading to disruption of the extensor mechanism [1]. Clinical Perspective Patients typically present with localised pain at the inferior aspect of the patella and loss of active knee extension [2]. Swelling is often mild, and haematoma may be absent. The clinical presentation can overlap with other conditions, such as patellar dislocation or tendinopathy, which may lead to delayed diagnosis. Imaging is essential to confirm the lesion, exclude differential diagnoses, and determine the need for surgical intervention [3]. Imaging Perspective MRI is the imaging modality of choice for diagnosing patellar sleeve fractures, as it provides optimal visualisation of cartilage, periosteum, and soft tissue structures. While radiographs may show subtle irregularities or even appear normal, MRI can clearly demonstrate cartilage disruption and associated soft tissue detachment [2]. Ultrasound may aid in the early assessment by identifying hypoechoic discontinuity and soft tissue swelling, but it is operator-dependent and less specific. A key diagnostic feature on MRI is the involvement of the extensor mechanism, which helps confirm the diagnosis and guide therapeutic planning. MRI is also essential in excluding other pathologies such as ligamentous injury or osteochondral lesions [3]. Outcome Management of patellar sleeve fractures depends on the degree of displacement and integrity of the extensor mechanism. Conservative treatment may suffice in cases with minimal displacement and preserved function [2,3]. Surgical repair is usually required when there is significant soft tissue avulsion or disruption of the extensor mechanism. Prognosis is favourable with early diagnosis and appropriate management. Delayed treatment may lead to complications such as extensor lag, anterior knee pain, or patellofemoral instability. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Patellar sleeve fractures are rare but important causes of knee pain and extensor mechanism failure in children. MRI is the modality of choice for identifying cartilage disruption and soft tissue avulsion. Early diagnosis and proper treatment are key to avoiding long-term functional impairment. Always consider this diagnosis in children with knee trauma and extension deficit, even without significant swelling.

title: Disseminated melioidosis on FDG PET/CT: A potential mimicker of metastatic malignancy
clinical_history: A 94-year-old woman with multiple comorbidities presented to the accident and emergency department of our hospital with reduced verbal responsiveness and desaturation. She appeared tired-looking and afebrile upon initial presentation. Investigations found elevated white blood cell count and C-reactive protein. Blood culture, sputum culture, and tuberculosis workup were negative. She denied recent travel history. Her urine culture yielded B. pseudomallei . Her serum B. pseudomallei IgG and IgM were also positive.
imaging_findings: Chest radiograph showed opacity in the left lung field (Figure 1). Ultrasound of the abdomen was mostly unremarkable, showing only gallstones and sludge (images not included). 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/CT was performed in search of metastatic infection for suspected melioidosis. Multiple FDG-hyperactive lesions were identified, including a left lung upper lobe mass (Figures 2 and 3), multiple enlarged lymph nodes at bilateral hilar-interlobar and mediastinal stations (Figure 4), several hyperactive lesions at the right kidney (Figure 5a), and another focal hyperactivity at the spleen (Figure 5b). Reduced FDG activity is observed at the centre of the left lung mass and in some enlarged intrathoracic nodes. Diffuse increased bone marrow activity is seen on the MIP image (Figure 6), likely of reactive nature.
discussion: Background Melioidosis is a disease caused by the bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei . It is endemic in southeastern Asia, northern Australia, southern Asia, and China [1]. Occupational or recreational exposure to soil and surface water is the main risk factor [2]. Severe or fatal melioidosis occurs more often in individuals with comorbidities, including diabetes, hazardous alcohol use, and chronic kidney or lung diseases [3]. Clinical Perspective Most infections with B. pseudomallei are asymptomatic, with severe clinical disease usually seen in those with multiple comorbidities [4]. Manifestations of acute infection include pneumonia, bacteraemia, skin and genitourinary tract infections (e.g., urinary tract infection, abscesses at the prostate and kidneys) [5], septic arthritis, parotitis, or abscesses at other organs. Imaging Perspective Cross-sectional imaging with CT is routinely performed to look for sites of metastatic infection in the setting of melioidosis [6]. Findings of non-pulmonary focal sites of infection can prompt antibiotic therapy optimisation (antibiotic choice and duration [7]). Drainage can be considered if abscesses are identified [8]. FDG PET/CT is well-validated for evaluating fevers of unknown origin (FUO) or metastatic infection/septic emboli in the setting of bacteraemia/septicaemia [9]. It has been shown to be superior to CT alone in the setting of FUO [10]. However, literature evaluating its applications in the setting of melioidosis is sparse. Outcome Patient’s clinical condition improved after optimised antibiotic therapy with meropenem. The lung mass shows resolution following antibiotic therapy on subsequent serial chest x-rays, suggesting its infective nature. The infectious disease team established the diagnosis of disseminated melioidosis following the combination of clinical and serial imaging findings as described above. Unfortunately, she suffered from recurrent pneumonia three months after discharge and sadly succumbed. Teaching Points Disseminated melioidosis can give an appearance that mimics metastatic malignancy in FDG-PET [11]. In our case, the left lung mass and mediastinal lymphadenopathies can be misdiagnosed as primary lung malignancy with regional nodal metastases. The renal and splenic lesions also mimic the appearance of metastases or other malignancies. Lung lesions with reduced central FDG activity are indicative of abscesses or cavitatory neoplasms [12]. Visualisation of this sign should prompt consideration of potential infective aetiology during image interpretation. Familiarity with the distributions of FDG-hyperactive lesions may also help distinguish between melioidosis and malignancy. In our case, FDG-hyperactive lesions were seen affecting the spleen and kidneys. This pattern is more typical of disseminated melioidosis than lung cancer with metastases [13,14]. Careful correlation with clinical profile and microbiological/histopathological investigations may help elucidate the aetiology. Written informed consent for publication has been obtained from the patient’s next of kin.
differential_diagnosis: Primary lung cancer with metastases Tuberculosis Disseminated melioidosis Fungal infection Other bacterial abscesses (e.g., typhoid fever)

title: From lymphoid interstitial pneumonia to secondary amyloidosis in Sjögren’s
clinical_history: A 67-year-old woman with a known history of Sjögren’s syndrome was diagnosed with lymphoid interstitial pneumonia (LIP) two years earlier (Figure 1), confirmed by transbronchial biopsy. She presented with worsening respiratory symptoms, and antibiotic therapy was ineffective.
imaging_findings: A chest CT performed two years earlier (Figure 1), at the time of lymphoid interstitial pneumonia (LIP) diagnosis, showed diffuse bilateral interstitial involvement with interlobular septal thickening, patchy consolidations with focal calcifications, and air trapping on expiratory images. A recent CT demonstrated marked progression, with increased peribronchovascular and interlobular septal thickening, numerous septal calcifications, and new subsegmental peribronchovascular consolidations, predominantly in the lower lobes (Figures 2a and 2b). Small bilateral pleural and pericardial effusions with associated pleuropericardial thickening were also evident. These findings indicated progressive interstitial lung disease with imaging features highly suggestive of pulmonary amyloidosis involving both lung parenchyma and serosal surfaces. 18 F-FDG PET/CT showed no abnormal metabolic activity, excluding infection or malignancy (Figure 3). A repeated transthoracic biopsy confirmed AA (secondary) amyloidosis. Histopathology revealed amorphous eosinophilic deposits thickening alveolar septae and vessel walls (Figure 4a) with apple-green birefringence on Congo red staining, confirming amyloid deposition (Figure 4b).
discussion: Background Amyloidosis is a disorder characterised by the extracellular deposition of insoluble fibrillar proteins that disrupt normal tissue architecture and function. It is classified as primary (AL) or secondary (AA) according to the precursor protein involved. AA amyloidosis arises as a complication of chronic inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and—less commonly—Sjögren’s syndrome. Pulmonary involvement in AA amyloidosis is extremely rare, particularly as a dominant clinical feature [1]. Clinical Perspective Sjögren’s syndrome is a chronic autoimmune disease characterised by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands, which may also affect the lungs, kidneys, skin, and nervous system. The most frequent pulmonary manifestations are nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) and lymphoid interstitial pneumonia (LIP). When imaging findings deviate from the usual pattern, rare complications such as amyloidosis, lymphoma, or pulmonary hypertension should be considered [3]. Imaging Perspective Pulmonary amyloidosis presents in three main forms: Tracheobronchial amyloidosis shows nodular or circumferential thickening of the tracheobronchial walls, sometimes calcified, and may cause airway obstruction. Nodular pulmonary amyloidosis manifests as well-defined, often calcified, subpleural nodules that are metabolically inactive on PET/CT and usually localised. Diffuse alveolar septal amyloidosis, as in the present case, is the rarest form and is typically systemic. Characteristic CT findings include reticular or septal thickening, ground-glass opacities, small nodules, and punctate septal calcifications, with possible pleural or pericardial thickening or effusion in advanced disease [2]. In our patient, diffuse peribronchovascular and interlobular septal thickening, calcifications, and serosal involvement were highly suggestive of diffuse alveolar septal amyloidosis. The absence of FDG uptake on PET/CT excluded infection or malignancy. Histopathological examination confirmed AA-type amyloid deposition, likely secondary to chronic autoimmune inflammation from Sjögren’s syndrome. Outcome and Clinical Relevance This rare association of Sjögren’s syndrome with diffuse alveolar septal amyloidosis emphasises the importance of recognising atypical imaging patterns. Although there is no curative treatment, controlling the underlying inflammatory process may slow progression. Corticosteroids or immunosuppressive therapy can stabilise pulmonary involvement and improve symptoms [1,2]. Teaching Points Diffuse pulmonary amyloidosis should be suspected when calcifications coexist with interstitial thickening in autoimmune disease. PET/CT can help exclude infection or malignancy, but cannot replace biopsy confirmation. Histopathology with Congo red birefringence remains the diagnostic gold standard. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Contained perforation of a small intestine loop by a fishbone
clinical_history: A 79-year-old male presented to the emergency department with mesogastric and lower abdominal pain, nausea and diarrhoea. On physical examination, he complained of pain in the lower quadrants of the abdomen on palpation. Blood work analysis showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, with an insignificant C-reactive protein. An abdominal ultrasound was requested.
imaging_findings: On ultrasound at the location of pain (Figure 1), in the hypogastric region, there was increased echogenicity of intra-abdominal fat, surrounding a bowel loop that showed a hyperechoic linear structure transversing it. No changes were observed in the remaining abdominal organs. Upon questioning the patient, he acknowledged having had an episode of choking when eating a fish meal recently. Subsequently, a computed tomography (CT) scan was performed (Figure 2), revealing a hyperdense linear structure corresponding to the impacted fishbone, with extraluminal extension of its upper edge, suggesting focal perforation. In addition, extensive stranding of the adjacent mesenteric fat and stratification of the intestinal wall were observed. No fluid collections, free fluid or pneumoperitoneum were identified.
discussion: Background Fishbones are the most frequently ingested foreign objects. Although most fishbones pass through the gastrointestinal tract uneventfully, various complications may occur, including perforation, fistulisation, bleeding and sepsis. Gastrointestinal perforation occurs in less than 1% of cases of fishbone ingestion [1,2]. Numerous risk factors for fishbone ingestion have been identified, including the use of dentures, people in the extremes of life, imprisoned and psychiatric patients, and alcohol or drug abusers [3]. CT is the imaging of choice to diagnose fishbone impactions [4]. Clinical Perspective The diagnosis of visceral perforation caused by a fishbone can be challenging, as patients usually do not remember ingesting a fishbone and typically present with nonspecific symptoms. Patients usually complain of abdominal pain and fever, with bowel obstruction and peritoneal irritation being less frequent [3]. Since the degree of clinical suspicion is generally low, in patients presenting with non-specific abdominal pain, the gastrointestinal tract should be meticulously evaluated on imaging in order to determine whether a foreign body is present [2]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound is a dynamic technique that combines real-time imaging with physical examination, allowing the clinician to direct the sonographic study to the most symptomatic abdominal areas. It makes it possible to identify foreign bodies based on their high reflectivity [3]. However, CT with intravenous contrast administration is the gold standard to detect fishbone impactions and their complications. The common findings of visceral perforation include bowel wall thickening, mesenteric fat stranding, abscess formation and localised pneumoperitoneum. Free pneumoperitoneum is rare, as bowel perforation is a slow and gradual process, allowing inflammatory components to seal the perforated area [5]. A linear hyperdense structure, corresponding to a fishbone, surrounded by inflammatory changes, may be encountered [3]. Outcome If the patient presents with peritoneal signs secondary to perforation, surgical management is indicated. This usually involves resection of the affected bowel or suturing of the perforated area [3,6]. Our patient underwent laparotomy with foreign body removal and enterorrhaphy. He also completed five days of intravenous antibiotics (ceftriaxone and metronidazole). Nonsurgical management depends on a variety of factors, with the patient’s condition, location of perforation in the gastrointestinal tract, and degree of contamination being the most significant [6]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Fishbone ingestion is a known cause of visceral perforation. Clinical suspicion is usually low, and thus, analysing CT findings with special caution is key for establishing the diagnosis. The common CT features of contained visceral perforation include bowel wall thickening, mesenteric fat stranding, abscess formation and localised pneumoperitoneum.
