title: Acute gastric diverticulitis identified on chest CT in immunocompromised patient
clinical_history: A patient in his 50s with rheumatoid arthritis, on methotrexate and adalimumab, presented with several days of fever, rigours, diffuse myalgia, and acute epigastric pain radiating to the back. Chest radiography demonstrated right lower lobe consolidation, and CT was performed to further evaluate.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced CT chest demonstrated a cavitary right lower lobe consolidation typical of Legionella pneumonia (Figure 1). Incidentally, a 2.5 × 1.9 cm posterior fundal gastric diverticulum was noted with an intradiverticular air–fluid level and perifocal fat stranding, consistent with acute gastric diverticulitis (Figure 2). At a 6-week follow-up, the repeat CT assessing for resolution of pneumonia showed interval resolution of fat stranding surrounding the diverticulum, while the diverticulum itself persisted (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Gastric diverticula are the rarest diverticula of the gastrointestinal tract, with an estimated prevalence of only 0.01% on upper endoscopy [1]. While most remain clinically silent, complications such as bleeding, perforation, and acute inflammation (gastric diverticulitis) may occur [2]. Since the first description in 1906, fewer than 25 CT-confirmed cases of gastric diverticulitis have been reported in the literature, leaving its natural history and optimal management largely undefined [3]. Clinical Perspective In this case, the patient presented with fever, rigours, myalgia, and acute epigastric pain, prompting imaging for suspected pulmonary infection. Given his background of rheumatoid arthritis managed with methotrexate and adalimumab, he was immunocompromised and at increased risk for atypical pathogens such as Legionella pneumophila [4]. Chest CT confirmed cavitary Legionella pneumonia, but careful review of the upper abdomen revealed the additional finding of an inflamed gastric diverticulum. Recognition of this incidental but clinically significant lesion helped explain the acute epigastric pain, preventing misattribution of symptoms solely to pneumonia. Imaging Perspective CT is a useful imaging modality for identifying gastric diverticular disease, although endoscopy remains the preferred method for direct visualisation of the gastric mucosa. However, CT can be valuable in demonstrating associated complications—such as inflammation, perforation, or bleeding—and in incidental detection, as in this case. The characteristic features of gastric diverticulitis include a posterior-fundal outpouching contiguous with the gastric lumen, the presence of an intradiverticular air–fluid level, and surrounding fat stranding [5]. Misinterpretation is possible if the luminal communication is not identified, leading to confusion with left adrenal, renal, or pancreatic pathology. In this case, the triad of findings was evident on initial imaging, and follow-up CT demonstrated complete resolution of fat stranding, confirming inflammatory resolution, while the structural diverticulum persisted—consistent with its congenital origin. Outcome Management of gastric diverticulitis is typically conservative. Proton-pump inhibition and systemic antibiotics are usually sufficient, with surgery reserved for severe complications such as bleeding, perforation, or refractory infection [2,3]. Our patient improved with azithromycin prescribed for Legionella , which also provided incidental coverage for gastric flora. His clinical course was favourable, and follow-up CT further supported resolution of inflammation without recurrence. Take Home Message / Teaching Points This case underscores the importance of carefully scrutinising extra-thoracic structures when interpreting thoracic imaging. In immunocompromised patients, dual pathology is possible, and clinicians must remain vigilant to avoid diagnostic overshadowing. While gastric diverticulitis is exceptionally rare, awareness of its imaging features ensures accurate diagnosis, guides conservative management, and prevents unnecessary interventions. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Fabry cardiomyopathy
clinical_history: A 36-year-old male with heterozygosity for the known pathogenic mutation in the galactosidase alpha ( GLA ) gene, consistent with Fabry disease, presents with shortness of breath on exertion, heart palpitations and fainting.
imaging_findings: Cardiac MRI (CMR), carried out at 1,5T, demonstrated markedly reduced native T1 values (Figures 1a and 1b) consistent with intracellular sphingolipid accumulation. Normal values on the T2* mapping (Figure 2) excluded myocardial iron deposition. There was no evidence of focal myocardial oedema or inflammation based on the T2 maps (Figure 3). There was focal, non-ischemic mid-wall fibrosis in the basal inferolateral left ventricular wall, as evidenced by late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) (Figure 4). In addition, mild concentric left ventricular hypertrophy was present with a maximal wall thickness of 14 mm (Figures 5a and 5b).
discussion: Background Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in the GLA gene, resulting in deficient α-galactosidase A [1]. This results in glycosphingolipid buildup within lysosomes, which disrupts cellular function, especially in endothelial cells, causing hypoperfusion, inflammation, oxidative stress and cell death, eventually leading to fibrosis [2]. The biological diagnosis typically involves two steps: screening for deficient α-galactosidase A (α-gal A) enzyme activity (reliable in males) and measuring the accumulating substrate, globotriaosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb3), in plasma or urine [3]. Due to random X-chromosome inactivation, α-gal A enzyme activity can be normal in female carriers, and lyso-Gb3 levels may also overlap with the normal range in up to two-thirds of affected women [4]. Therefore, molecular genetic testing for GLA gene mutations is essential for a definitive diagnosis in all individuals, but particularly in women, where enzymatic and biomarker assays can be inconclusive [5]. Cardiac involvement is a major determinant of morbidity and mortality. Fabry cardiomyopathy is typically characterised by concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), fibrosis, arrhythmias, and eventual heart failure [1]. Clinical Perspective Patients may present with non-specific symptoms such as exertional dyspnoea, palpitations, syncope or chest pain [1]. Because Fabry cardiomyopathy can mimic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and hypertensive heart disease, early recognition is challenging [1]. CMR with native T1 mapping is crucial in the detection of Fabry disease, prompting genetic testing and enabling timely therapy initiation [1]. Imaging Perspective CMR is the gold standard of imaging. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) typically can show mid-wall fibrosis of the basal inferolateral wall, indicating myocardial inflammation and/or fibrosis [1]. T1 mapping reveals reduced T1 values due to intracellular sphingolipid accumulation [1]. This unique characteristic makes T1 mapping essential in differentiating Fabry disease from other phenocopies of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, as the reduced T1 is highly specific to the storage of sphingolipids. Moreover, there is an evolving clinical perspective that the presence of reduced native T1 time, even in the absence of LVH or LGE, should prompt consideration for timely therapy initiation to prevent progression to irreversible myocardial fibrosis [6,7]. Beyond lipid storage, CMR can detect myocardial inflammation indicated by increased native T2 values, a finding often linked to chronic troponin elevation and suggesting chronic myocardial oedema; specific Fabry disease treatments appear to be effective on this inflammation, as shown by the comparative evolution of T2 values over time [8,9]. Outcome Disease-modifying therapies include enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) [1]. These interventions may prevent progression if started before irreversible fibrosis occurs [1]. Gene therapy and substrate reduction therapy are under investigation [1]. Imaging plays a central role in identifying early myocardial involvement, monitoring treatment response and determining prognosis, as the presence of extensive fibrosis on CMR is associated with worse outcomes and reduced treatment response [1]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Fabry cardiomyopathy should be suspected in patients with unexplained concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, especially when accompanied by systemic features or family history [1]. Cardiac MRI (CMR) with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and T1 mapping provide key imaging and diagnostic clues. Early imaging and recognition enable a timely initiation of disease-specific therapy, which may alter prognosis [2]. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Mature ovarian teratoma with torsion and rupture
clinical_history: A 32-year-old female presented with progressively worsening lower abdominal pain, initially managed as constipation. Her symptoms intensified, with the development of severe pain localised to the left iliac fossa and hypogastric region, accompanied by anorexia, vomiting, chills, and watery stools. On examination, the abdomen was distended and tender, though no fever was documented.
imaging_findings: The supine abdominal radiograph (Figure 1) shows multiple dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels in the central and upper abdomen, displaying a stepladder pattern. No free intraperitoneal air is seen, excluding perforation. Abnormal pelvic calcifications are also noted. CT imaging demonstrates a heterogeneous, predominantly cystic pelvic mass measuring approximately 13 cm, located in the midline pelvis, anterior to the uterus, and displacing it posteriorly and to the right. The mass contains macroscopic fat, fluid-attenuation areas, and coarse calcifications, including a well-defined Rokitansky nodule (Figures 2 and 3). The right ovary is not separately visualised, likely replaced by the mass, while the left ovary appears normal (Figure 4). A twisted tubular structure in the right adnexal region shows the characteristic whirlpool (swirl) sign of a twisted vascular pedicle, consistent with adnexal torsion (Figure 5). Free intraperitoneal fat, fat-fluid levels ascites suggest rupture (Figures 2 and 6). Mild small-bowel dilatation without a transition point indicates reactive localised functional small bowel ileus secondary to an adjacent inflammatory process (Figure 7).
discussion: Background Mature cystic teratomas (dermoid cysts) are the most common benign ovarian neoplasms in reproductive-aged women, arising from germ cells and containing elements from all three germ layers [1,2]. Although usually asymptomatic, they may cause complications such as torsion, rupture, infection, or, rarely, malignant transformation [1,3]. Torsion occurs in about 15% of cases, particularly in lesions > 5 cm, while rupture is rare (< 2%) and may lead to chemical peritonitis from spillage of sebaceous material [3,4]. Clinical Perspective Symptoms are often nonspecific and may mimic gastrointestinal disorders. In this case, initial constipation-like symptoms delayed diagnosis until severe pain, vomiting, and systemic inflammatory signs developed. Ovarian torsion and rupture are gynaecological emergencies requiring prompt imaging to prevent infarction or generalised peritonitis. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for adnexal pathology in women of reproductive age presenting with acute lower abdominal pain [3]. Imaging Perspective The abdominal X-ray revealed mild small bowel dilatation with a stepladder pattern, indicating localised ileus secondary to peritoneal irritation rather than mechanical obstruction. Absence of free air excluded perforation, while pelvic calcifications suggested the presence of a calcified pelvic lesion. Ultrasound, the first-line modality, typically demonstrates a heterogeneous adnexal mass with echogenic components and posterior acoustic shadowing, raising suspicion for a dermoid cyst. CT plays a key role in identifying the cause and complications of adnexal pathology, especially when torsion and/or rupture are suspected. In this case, CT confirmed a mature cystic teratoma and demonstrated dual complications—torsion and rupture—through findings such as the whirlpool sign, free intraperitoneal fat, fat–fluid levels, and peritoneal inflammatory reaction. Its ability to define the lesion’s origin, identify fat components, and assess secondary effects underscores its diagnostic superiority [1,3]. The teratoma’s size and mobility predisposed it to torsion, leading to ischaemia, necrosis, and rupture with sebaceous spillage causing chemical peritonitis. Imaging findings were confirmed intraoperatively. Localised small-bowel dilatation represented a reactive functional ileus, a transient response to inflammation rather than true obstruction—a key distinction to avoid unnecessary surgery [4]. Outcome Urgent laparotomy revealed a large ruptured teratoma with adnexal torsion and sebaceous spillage. Right adnexectomy was performed. Histology confirmed a mature cystic teratoma without malignant features. The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day 4. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Mature cystic teratomas may undergo torsion or rarely rupture—both require emergency surgery. Presentation is often nonspecific; prompt imaging is essential. Ultrasound suggests the diagnosis; CT confirms and defines complications. Torsion appears as a twisted pedicle with abnormal ovarian position or displacement. Localised ileus reflects reactive bowel dilatation near inflammation, rather than a true mechanical obstruction, helping to avoid unnecessary surgery. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Critical illness-associated cerebral microbleeds mimicking emboli in sepsis
clinical_history: A 79‑year‑old male with right lower limb necrotising fasciitis, post-debridement and fasciotomy, was admitted with confusion, disorientation, and respiratory distress. He developed septic shock, encephalopathy, and acute kidney injury. No meningism was noted, but severe quadriparesis was present.
imaging_findings: MRI brain revealed multiple punctate foci of susceptibility weighted imaging (SWI) blooming in bilateral cerebral (predominant subcortical white matter) and cerebellar hemispheres, corpus callosum, bilateral internal and external capsules, and pons. No diffusion restriction was seen. The classical pattern of SWI blooming and clinical setting favoured critical illness–associated cerebral microbleeds (CIACM) over embolic lesions.
discussion: Background Critical illness–associated cerebral microbleeds (CIACM) represent a distinctive neuroimaging entity increasingly recognised in severely ill patients. These microbleeds diffusely involve the juxtacortical white matter, corpus callosum, and cerebellum, sparing the deep and periventricular white matter, as well as the cerebral cortex. The proposed mechanism centres on hypoxaemia-induced endothelial injury and blood–brain barrier disruption, which cause leakage of erythrocytes into the parenchyma. Oxidative stress and inflammatory mediators during sepsis or respiratory failure further aggravate vascular permeability. This pattern closely resembles microbleeds seen in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) therapy, and high-altitude cerebral oedema, supporting a unifying hypoxic–vascular pathogenesis [1,4,5]. Clinical Perspective Patients with CIACM are typically critically ill, with conditions such as sepsis, respiratory failure, or shock, and often require intensive care or ventilatory support. Neurological manifestations are non-specific, including altered sensorium, encephalopathy, or generalised weakness. In this case, the patient presented with septic shock and quadriparesis in the absence of focal deficits or meningism. Recognition of CIACM is important to avoid overdiagnosis of embolic or haemorrhagic pathology and to guide appropriate clinical management. Imaging Perspective MRI using susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) or T2*-gradient echo sequences is diagnostic, showing numerous punctate hypointense foci with a characteristic distribution. In contrast to hypertensive or amyloid angiopathy microbleeds, CIACM lesions cluster at the grey–white junction and the corpus callosum, while sparing the basal ganglia and thalami. The absence of diffusion restriction or infarction supports a non-embolic origin [1–3]. Outcome Most patients exhibit neurological recovery as systemic illness resolves, although cognitive sequelae may persist. Follow-up MRI often demonstrates partial resolution or stabilisation of lesions without new haemorrhages. Teaching Points Critical illness–associated cerebral microbleeds (CIACM) is a distinct, hypoxaemia-related microvascular phenomenon. Juxtacortical and callosal microbleeds with deep grey sparing are diagnostic clues. Recognition prevents misinterpretation as embolic lesions and avoids unnecessary therapy escalation.

title: Renal aspergilloma imitating a renal cell carcinoma
clinical_history: A 42-year-old man presented to the surgical outpatient department with vague abdominal pain. No history of fever, burning micturition, and haematuria.
imaging_findings: Ultrasonography revealed an incidental heterogeneously hypoechoic mass in the mid-pole of the left kidney. A contrast-enhanced CT with corticomedullary, nephrographic, and delayed phases was performed for further evaluation. CT showed a 2.5 cm high-density lesion in the posterior midpole, correlating with the ultrasound finding. The lesion had a mean attenuation of 70 HU on non-contrast, suggesting haemorrhagic or proteinaceous content, possibly with calcification. No definite calcification or fat was identified. Post-contrast images showed a mean attenuation of 92 HU, which remained indeterminate for enhancement (Figure 1). A primary renal neoplasm was considered, and further evaluation with contrast-enhanced MRI (CEMRI) was recommended. On MRI, the lesion was markedly T2 hypointense with susceptibility artefacts on GRE images, consistent with haemorrhage and/or calcification (Figure 2). There was focal enhancement involving approximately 5–10% of the mass. No diffusion restriction was observed.
discussion: Background Aspergillus is a sporophytic fungus found throughout the globe, and Aspergillus fumigatus has been identified as a cause of urinary infections [1]. It mainly affects patients who are immunosuppressed by any condition, such as bone marrow transplantation, organ transplantation, diabetes, steroid therapy, any malignancy, or chemotherapy [2]. Some cases have been reported post-instrumentation as well [3]. Renal aspergillosis can occur in three different modes: the first one is the haematogenous mode of spread, the second one is the isolated fungal cast, and the third one is ascending infection from the lower urinary tract [4]. Clinical Perspective Patients usually present with fever and vague abdominal pain. Primary renal aspergillosis is very uncommon in immunocompetent individuals, and no specific clinical features have been well-characterised so far [5]. Imaging Perspective Marked T2 hypointensity, the presence of calcifications, and haemorrhage within a renal mass disproportionate to the degree of enhancement and diffusion restriction are radiological clues. In our case, the final diagnosis was made after histopathological examination of the surgically resected specimen, which showed fruiting bodies of Aspergillus fumigatus along with foci of necrosis and cellular debris (Figure 3). Outcome In general, the management of renal aspergillosis involves a combination of medical and surgical intervention [6]. However, the mainstay of management is evacuation of the aspergilloma. This can occur naturally if the aspergilloma is in the renal pelvis or by nephrectomy [2]. In an immunocompetent patient, evacuation alone is sufficient [2]. The prognosis for the disease itself is excellent. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Renal aspergilloma is a rare but possible differential for renal incidentaloma even in immunocompetent patients. Marked T2 hypointensity, the presence of calcifications, and haemorrhage within a renal mass disproportionate to the degree of enhancement and diffusion restriction are radiological clues. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Ovarian torsion on MRI in polycystic ovarian syndrome
clinical_history: A 31-year-old female with known polycystic ovarian syndrome presents with sudden-onset right abdominal pain. A preliminary ultrasound showed an enlarged right ovary with multiple follicles and minimal free fluid.
imaging_findings: Non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters, and urinary bladder reveals a midline right ovary with peripherally arranged follicles, displacing the urinary bladder, and ascites (Figure 1). Contrast-enhanced MRI shows an enlarged right ovary situated in the midline, with multiple peripherally arranged follicles and T2 hyperintense central stroma, reflecting preserved architecture (Figures 2a and 2b). The ovarian cortex is significantly T2 hypointense and shows reduced contrast enhancement. The supplying vascular pedicle is twisted around its own axis, with a dilated fallopian tube showing fluid–fluid levels within, reflecting areas of haemorrhage (Figures 3a and 3b). Features indicate right ovarian torsion. The left ovary shows normal vascularity with multiple peripherally arranged follicles, consistent with polycystic ovarian syndrome. Intra-operatively, the radiological findings were confirmed, and detorsion of the right ovary and tube was done.
discussion: Background Ovarian torsion is a gynaecologic emergency that presents in young females as acute pelvic pain, with nausea, vomiting, and fever being the other symptoms. Twisting of the vascular and supporting ligamentous structures (suspensory or ovarian ligaments) causes lymphatic, venous and, eventually, arterial compromise, leading to haemorrhage and infarction. Ovarian cysts > 5 cm, dermoid cysts, and pregnancy are some of the predisposing risk factors [1]. The most common endocrine disorder in women of reproductive age is polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), characterised by hyperandrogenism, menstrual abnormalities, and an enlarged ovary (> 10 mL) or multiple peripherally arranged subcentimetric follicles with a centrally displaced cortex on imaging. These enlarged ovaries with multiple cysts are heavier in weight, likely predisposing them to twisting around the vascular pedicle or the infundibulopelvic ligament. Ovarian torsion in PCOS is a diagnostic and management challenge, since it can be recurrent, and the underlying risk factor is surgically non-modifiable [2]. Imaging Perspective Since the symptoms are commonly non-specific, an initial pelvic ultrasound allows vascular assessment without contrast or radiation. Findings include a hypoechoic, asymmetrically enlarged ovary (> 4.0 cm max. dimension) in the midline, with altered stromal echotexture (hypoechoic due to oedema or hyperechoic due to haemorrhage) and peripherally arranged follicles (a “string of pearls” sign) [3]. The typical “whirlpool sign” depicts a twisted vascular pedicle. Additional findings include a dilated fallopian tube and ascites [4]. However, Doppler assessment may be normal due to preserved perfusion from dual arterial supply. Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI, if ultrasound is indeterminate or suggests underlying masses, allow vascular assessment with concomitant characterisation/exclusion of underlying ovarian masses. A T1 hypointense rim surrounding the ovary correlates to perifollicular haemorrhage and intra-operative viability. Haemorrhage may result in haematosalpinx with tubal dilatation or haemoperitoneum. MRI signs indicating ovarian infarction include haemorrhage and absence of internal enhancement [5,6]. Outcome Differentiation from ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome can be made by the absence of the “whirlpool sign”, with no adnexal masses, bilaterally enlarged ovaries and a history of in-vitro fertilisation. Additionally, bowel causes of pain, such as diverticulitis or appendicitis, must be excluded. Reports must include ovarian size, laterality, twisting of vascular pedicle, haemoperitoneum, associated ovarian lesions or lead points, if any. Emergency laparoscopy with ovarian or adnexal detorsion constitutes management. Teaching Points In a patient with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) presenting with acute pelvic pain, ovarian torsion must be high on the list of differentials, even in the absence of an adnexal mass. Ultrasound shows an enlarged ovary, peripheral follicles and whirlpool sign. Doppler may be normal. MRI and CT show twisting of the pedicle and haemorrhage. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome Right ovarian torsion Ruptured haemorrhagic cyst Ectopic pregnancy

title: Intramuscular myxoma with radiological-pathological correlation
clinical_history: A 46-year-old patient presented with a gradually enlarging, painless swelling in the posterior right thigh, first noticed two years earlier. There was no history of trauma. Discomfort was mainly triggered by sitting or exertion. Examination revealed a soft, mobile, non-adherent mass without neurological deficits.
imaging_findings: MRI of the right thigh (Figure 1) demonstrated a well-circumscribed, ovoid lesion within the proximal semitendinosus muscle, measuring 5.6 cm craniocaudally. The lesion exhibited marked hyperintensity on T2-weighted and fluid-sensitive sequences, with fine internal hypointense septa, and low signal on T1-weighted images. Subtle adjacent muscle oedema and limited fatty infiltration indicated slow growth. No evidence of tendon or neurovascular involvement, haematoma, or bone marrow abnormality was observed. Follow-up MRI at 15 months post-excision (Figure 2) confirmed complete resection, with no residual mass or recurrence and preserved surrounding muscle architecture.
discussion: Background Intramuscular myxoma is a rare mesenchymal tumour and most frequently arises in the deep muscles of the lower extremities, particularly the thigh. Patients are typically middle-aged adults with a slight female predominance [1,2]. Histologically, it is characterised by an abundant extracellular myxoid matrix with absent mitotic activity and necrosis [1]. Multiple myxomas with associated polyostotic fibrous dysplasia represent the rare Mazabraud syndrome, but no imaging or clinical features suggestive of this syndrome were present in our patient. Clinical Perspective Patients often report a slow-growing, deep, painless mass, although mild local discomfort or pressure can be present, especially during physical activity or when sitting. Typically, there is no history of trauma or systemic symptoms. Clinical suspicion is often low, and imaging is essential for lesion characterisation, evaluation of its relationship with adjacent structures, and exclusion of aggressive features. Imaging Perspective The classic MRI features of intramuscular myxoma are a well-defined, ovoid intramuscular lesion with low T1 and marked T2 hyperintensity (reflecting the myxoid matrix’s high-water content). Fine internal hypointense septa are highly characteristic and, when present, strongly support the diagnosis. Mild adjacent muscle oedema and limited fatty infiltration are commonly present, supporting the diagnosis of a slow-growing, expansile benign tumour. Occasionally, a “bright cap” or “bright rim” may be visible on T2-weighted images at the lesion’s poles or periphery. Differentials include myxoid liposarcoma, which presents as a heterogeneous, infiltrative mass with ill-defined margins, areas of haemorrhage and necrosis, as well as prominent enhancement after contrast administration [3,4]. Myxofibrosarcoma, another differential, frequently displays a “tail sign” that represents curvilinear extensions of the tumour along the fascial planes, as well as a more infiltrative growth. Chronic organised haematoma may be considered if there is a history of trauma, especially if the lesion has changed in size or signal over time, or if blood products are seen. Although less common, intramuscular haemangiomas are also a differential, often containing vascular channels, phleboliths, or flow voids [5]. Outcome In this case, histology demonstrated a hypocellular myxoid stroma with scattered bland spindle cells, focal permeation of muscle fibres (“checkerboard” pattern), and no evidence of atypia, mitosis, or necrosis (Figure 3). Surgical margins were free of tumour, confirming complete excision, which is almost always curative [1,5]. Recurrence is exceedingly rare. Imaging follow-up at 15 months post-resection showed no signs of recurrence or complications (Figure 2). Take Home Message / Teaching Points Intramuscular myxoma presents on MRI as a well-circumscribed T1-hypointense and T2-hyperintense lesion with fine septa and mild perilesional oedema. Stable slow growth and an absent history of trauma help differentiate it from a haematoma. Malignant myxoid tumours, such as myxoid liposarcoma, often show heterogeneous signal, infiltrative margins, or aggressive features. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Myxoid liposarcoma Myxofibrosarcoma Intramuscular myxoma Chronic organised haematoma Intramuscular haemangioma

title: An atypical presentation of a primary central nervous system lymphoma
clinical_history: A 59-year-old woman with no known significant medical history presented with vertigo, nausea, vomiting, urinary retention, and vertical nystagmus. Laboratory findings were unremarkable. Treatment with high-dose intravenous steroids resulted in an initial favourable clinical response. At one-month follow-up, she developed ataxia, bradykinesia, altered speech and behavioural disturbances.
imaging_findings: On initial MR imaging, FLAIR and T2-weighted sequences revealed diffuse, confluent, periventricular hyperintensities in both supratentorial and infratentorial regions (Figures 1a and 1b). The lesions showed no diffusion restriction and no contrast enhancement on the T1-weighted MP-RAGE sequence (Figures 1c and 1d). No evidence of haemorrhage was seen. At two-month follow-up, repeat MRI demonstrated a clear enlargement of these signal abnormalities without contrast enhancement (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). A third MRI, performed 2 months and 3 weeks after initial presentation, showed new contrast enhancement within the previously described parenchymal lesions (Figures 3a and 3b).
discussion: Background Primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) is an uncommon subtype of primary central nervous system (CNS) tumours, representing only 3–4% of cases [1,2]. It arises exclusively in the brain, spinal cord, cranial nerves, leptomeninges, and/or eyes, with the brain parenchyma being the most frequent site. The pathophysiology of PCNSL is incompletely understood. It likely involves immunoglobulins binding CNS self-antigens, along with genetic alterations driving dysregulation of B-cell receptor, toll-like receptor, and NF-κB signalling pathways [1]. Congenital or acquired immunodeficiency is the only well-established risk factor for PCNSL, with HIV-infected individuals being particularly susceptible to developing this tumour [1,3]. Clinical Perspective PCNSL presents variably depending on CNS location, most commonly in the brain parenchyma (92%). Focal neurological deficits and altered mental status are the typical clinical presentations, usually prompting brain imaging and facilitating rapid diagnosis. Systemic “B symptoms” such as fever, night sweats, or weight loss are rare in PCNSL [1]. Imaging Perspective MRI is the imaging modality of choice for PCNSL. Lesions typically appear iso to hypointense on T1 and T2-weighted images and are frequently associated with mild to moderate perilesional oedema. In a minority of cases, atypical signal characteristics may be observed, such as hyperintensity on T1 (5.5%) or T2 (19.5%). Contrast enhancement is usually homogeneous, but some lesions may lack enhancement or display features such as haemorrhage, calcification, cysts, or necrosis, potentially mimicking non-malignant CNS disease. Approximately 25% of cases present with such atypical features, which can contribute to diagnostic delay. Lesions most commonly involve the supratentorial compartment, particularly the periventricular region, but can also affect the basal ganglia, thalami, corpus callosum, ventricles, and cerebellum [4,5]. Outcome A brain biopsy was performed following the third MRI, and histopathological analysis confirmed the diagnosis of primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the central nervous system. The patient subsequently commenced chemoimmunotherapy with the MATRix regimen. Follow-up data regarding treatment response were unavailable, as the patient was referred to another institution for further management. Teaching Points Primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) can present as diffuse non-enhancing confluent lesions on MRI and should therefore be considered in the differential diagnosis in immunocompetent patients with this imaging pattern. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Diagnostic capabilities of CEUS in the steatotic liver: Atypical becomes typical
clinical_history: A 72-year-old female with a known history of mild to moderate hepatic steatosis and no other signs of hepatic dysfunction was referred for evaluation of a liver lesion in segment 3. A previous ultrasound examination of the liver in 2012 showed no focal abnormalities. A magnetic resonance (MR) imaging was contraindicated due to an incompatible cardiac pacemaker in situ.
imaging_findings: Baseline ultrasound showed moderate hepatic steatosis, with some minor parenchymal heterogeneity. A 4.5 × 4.0 cm solid lesion, isoechoic to the increased echogenicity of the underlying steatotic liver parenchyma, with cystic components, was identified in segment 3 of the liver (Figure 1). The triphasic CT demonstrated a 4 × 3 × 3 cm part-solid, part-cystic capsular lesion with arterialised components and no convincing washout in the portal venous phase (Figure 2). The hepatic vasculature was patent, and the liver showed no convincing chronic liver disease, with multiple small hepatic cysts also present. On the CEUS examination with 2.4 mL of SonoVue ® (Bracco S.p.A.) as the intravenous contrast agent, the lesion clearly demonstrated peripheral globular enhancement with centripetal progression, evident at the very early arterial phase (Figures 3a and 3b), with temporal observed in-filling during the portal-venous phase (Figure 3c), with complete in-filling observed, sparing two small cystic areas. On the delayed phase imaging at 4.5 minutes, there was no washout (Figure 4). These features were consistent with an atypical haemangioma, with a cystic component.
discussion: Background Hepatic haemangiomas are the most common benign liver tumours, composed of vascular channels lined by endothelium. B-mode ultrasound appearances of classic haemangiomas are described as echogenic compared to the background non-steatotic liver, and occur in characteristic positions, rarely with cystic components. On the CEUS examination, the pathognomonic feature of any haemangioma is a typical homogeneous peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in. The atypical haemangiomas may present with heterogeneous internal architecture, cystic degeneration, or altered perfusion patterns [1–3]. Clinical Perspective Steatosis is known to modify parenchymal echotexture and vascular dynamics, which may in turn alter the well-recognised enhancement patterns of focal lesions, complicating diagnosis [2,4]. In addition, cystic degeneration within haemangiomas, as in this case, further challenges differentiation from malignant necrotic tumours [3]. Careful imaging characterisation is therefore essential to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary invasive procedures. Imaging Perspective Triphasic CT demonstrated arterialisation of the lesion but no convincing washout in the portal venous phase, which raised concern for hepatocellular carcinoma but was inconclusive. CEUS offered a clear diagnostic advantage. By providing continuous, real-time observation throughout all vascular phases, from injection through arterial, portal venous, and very delayed phases, CEUS enables detection of transient or atypical patterns [5]. In this case, early peripheral globular enhancement was already visible in the pre-arterial phase, with progressive centripetal fill-in, and importantly, no washout was demonstrated even at the very delayed phase (4.5 minutes). Such subtle dynamic changes may be missed with the fixed time-point acquisitions of CT or MR imaging. Outcome CEUS confirmed the benign nature of the lesion, sparing the patient from biopsy or surgery. Conservative follow-up was pursued. Teaching Points In patients with hepatic steatosis or atypical haemangiomas undergoing cystic degeneration, CEUS remains a powerful modality for reliable characterisation. Its real-time capability allows detection of enhancement behaviour that distinguishes benign from malignant lesions, even when CT or MRI are inconclusive or contraindicated.

title: Starfield in the storm – Cerebral fat embolism following long bone fracture
clinical_history: A 32-year-old male was referred to the emergency department 36 hours after a road traffic accident, sustaining injuries to the head and lower limbs. He presented with confusion and altered sensorium. However, there were no obvious focal or lateralising neurological findings. His neurological status deteriorated, requiring sedation, intubation and mechanical ventilation with subsequent intensive care admission.
imaging_findings: Bilateral leg radiographs demonstrated a comminuted fracture of the proximal third of the right tibia (Figure 1). Non-contrast MRI of the brain demonstrated multiple, bilateral, near-symmetrical, non-confluent hyperintense foci on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences (Figure 2), exhibiting diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and forming the characteristic “starfield pattern” (Figure 3). The lesions involved the bilateral centrum semiovale, corona radiata, basal ganglia, splenium of the corpus callosum, and white matter of both cerebral hemispheres. In addition, numerous punctate hypointense foci were observed on susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) within the same regions, consistent with microhaemorrhages (Figure 4).
discussion: Background Fat embolism syndrome (FES) is a multisystem disorder usually following long bone fractures or orthopaedic trauma, with a neurological involvement termed cerebral fat embolism syndrome (CFE) [2]. CFE is a rare but potentially lethal complication of long bone fractures [1], and isolated cerebral fat embolism without pulmonary symptoms is even rarer [2,7]. Neurological manifestations generally appear 12–72 hours after the initial insult [7]. Clinical Perspective Neurological manifestations of CFE range from confusion to coma. Poor Glasgow Coma Score at admission and early neurological deterioration are recognised markers of severity [2]. In many trauma patients, initial neurological deficits may mimic diffuse axonal injury (DAI) or hypoxic-ischaemic injury, especially if MRI is delayed. Prompt imaging is therefore essential to avoid misdiagnosis. Case-specific Diagnostic Reasoning In the present case, the patient had sustained a head injury with a comminuted fracture of the proximal third of the right tibia. Neurological symptoms prompted brain imaging. The differential diagnosis included: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI): Considered due to trauma. Typically presents with punctate haemorrhages at the grey-white matter junction, corpus callosum, and brainstem. In this case, lesions were bilateral, near-symmetrical and non-confluent, forming the classic “starfield pattern” on DWI, and presenting together with a long bone fracture, are more likely in favour of cerebral fat embolism. Hypoxic-ischaemic injury : Usually involves watershed and cortical/subcortical regions with diffusion restriction. The presence of multiple punctate microhaemorrhages on SWI and the distribution of lesions argue against hypoxic-ischaemic injury. Septic or thromboembolic emboli : Typically present as larger territorial infarcts or abscess-like lesions, and are usually considered in patients with a septic focus in systemic circulation and with a clinical history of fever and neurological symptoms. The tiny, scattered nature of lesions, combined with the temporal association with a long bone fracture, made embolic infection unlikely. Imaging Perspective CT is frequently normal in the acute stage [2], which may contribute to delayed diagnosis. MRI, however, is the preferred imaging modality for cerebral fat embolism. Incomplete forms of fat embolism, such as isolated cerebral involvement, pose diagnostic challenges, and MRI provides valuable information in these cases [8]. DWI is the most sensitive sequence for detecting cerebral fat embolism, often revealing lesions that may be missed on other modalities [4,5]. The hallmark “starfield pattern” on DWI appears as numerous tiny hyperintense foci representing cytotoxic oedemas [1,5,6]. GRE or SWI sequences can demonstrate associated petechial haemorrhages [2,5]. MRI lesion patterns are dynamic, and initially scattered embolic lesions may progress to confluent cytotoxic oedema or partially resolve on follow-up imaging [3]. Outcome Prognosis in cerebral fat embolism is highly variable. Neuroimaging is useful not only for diagnostic management but also for prognostic purposes. While many patients achieve complete neurological recovery, severe cases may result in long-term neurological deficits or even mortality [6]. Serial MRI findings—whether lesions resolve or progress—can help predict clinical outcome [3]. Supportive management with mechanical ventilation, haemodynamic stabilisation, and early fracture fixation remains the cornerstone of therapy. Teaching Points Cerebral fat embolism is a serious but under-recognised complication of long bone fractures. DWI showing the “starfield pattern” is virtually diagnostic. Cerebral fat embolism must be differentiated from diffuse axonal injury and hypoxic brain injury, as management and prognosis differ. Conclusion This case illustrates the classic MRI features of cerebral fat embolism, underscoring the importance of early diagnosis with diffusion-weighted imaging in polytrauma patients with unexplained neurological decline. We have obtained written informed consent from the patient.

final_diagnosis: Cerebral fat embolism (in the context of long bone fracture)

title: A rare case of ileal herniation in a right paraduodenal location
clinical_history: A 49-year-old male presented with acute onset, colicky, predominantly central abdominal pain and vomiting. On examination, the abdomen was distended but without guarding or rebound tenderness. He had no prior history of abdominal surgeries. Lab findings were unremarkable. Intestinal obstruction was suspected, and an x-ray of the abdomen was performed, followed by an abdominal CT. A nasogastric tube and urinary catheter were inserted in the meantime. The nasogastric tube relieved the vomiting and distension significantly. However, the patient still had absolute constipation, and the nasogastric tube aspirate was about 1500 ml per day.
imaging_findings: Initial x-ray of the abdomen showed some dilated bowel loops in the right upper abdomen (Figure 1). This x-ray hinted at the diagnosis of right paraduodenal hernia, as a dilated bowel loop in the right upper abdomen was noted, which was likely the initial site of bowel obstruction. The CT done later gave a more complex picture of almost the entire small intestine being dilated. CT of the abdomen was performed because of the persistently high nasogastric tube aspirate and constipation, which indicated ongoing intestinal obstruction. The contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis showed dilated bowel loops from the mid-duodenum to the distal ileum with a transition point in the distal ileum (the stomach and proximal duodenum were decompressed by a nasogastric tube). In addition, there was a cluster of dilated bowel loops to the right of the 2nd and 3rd parts of the duodenum, posterolateral to the superior mesenteric vessels (Figures 2 and 3). This cluster of bowel loops hinted at a paraduodenal hernia. Whirling of the small bowel mesentery was noted in the mid-abdomen (Figure 4), which further solidified the differential of internal hernia. Furthermore, the third part of the duodenum was pulled to the centre of the abdomen, instead of crossing to the left side of the abdomen as expected (Figure 5). Therefore, jejunal loops were noted lying to the right side of the abdomen. However, the normal relationship between the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and superior mesenteric vein (SMV) was maintained, and the caecum was located in the right iliac fossa (normal position). The altered position of the duodenum suggested an element of non-rotation, but the normal relationship between SMA and SMV, as well as a normal position of the caecum, excluded malrotation. Most of the distal part of the ileum was collapsed.
discussion: Background A right paraduodenal hernia is an internal hernia in which a loop of small bowel, usually jejunum, herniates through a defect in the small bowel mesentery (fossa of Waldeyer) at a right paraduodenal location. Typically, a cluster of dilated bowel loops is seen inferior and to the right of the third part of the duodenum, posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels. The superior mesenteric artery and vein are displaced anteriorly [1], forming the left anterolateral border of the herniated sac. Right paraduodenal hernia is rarer than left paraduodenal hernia [2], and it is even more uncommon for the ileum, rather than the jejunum, to herniate through the fossa of Waldeyer. Kim et al. reported a similar case in which both ileal and jejunal loops were present within the hernia intraoperatively [3]. Clinical and Imaging Perspectives In our patient, instead of a jejunal loop herniating through the fossa of Waldeyer (more common occurrence), it was an ileal loop that herniated through the latter. It is quite uncommon for the ileum to herniate in this location. The classical pattern of a clustered dilated bowel in the right paraduodenal region is typically seen when a jejunal loop herniates through. However, when an ileal loop herniates through, all bowel proximal to the herniated ileal loop will dilate as all of this proximal bowel is now obstructed. Thus, the typical finding of a cluster of dilated bowel loops in a right paraduodenal location was obscured in our patient by diffuse small bowel dilatation throughout the abdomen. This complicated the identification of the hernia. Additionally, the abnormal position of the third part of the duodenum suggests an element of non-rotation, which can occur in this type of hernia [2]. Active exclusion of malrotation is essential in cases of internal hernia. In our patient, however, the SMV was on the right of the SMA, the cecum was normally located in the right iliac fossa, and no malrotation was found intraoperatively. Outcome Surgical exploration revealed an internal hernia with a segment of distal ileum herniating in a right paraduodenal location. There was a volvulus of the herniated bowel segment, but it remained viable. The hernia was reduced, and the patient had an uneventful recovery. Take Home Message In cases of bowel obstruction without an obvious cause or prior surgery, an internal hernia should be considered. Whirling of mesenteric vessels, abnormal small bowel positioning and abnormal duodenal course are clues to look for when suspecting an internal hernia. Malrotation must be excluded in all patients with intestinal obstruction and internal hernia. Another possible cause for intestinal obstruction is adhesions. But this would be unlikely given the absence of previous bowel surgery or history of intra-abdominal inflammation. Adhesions are generally too thin to be seen on CT, but they can be suspected if there is abnormal angulation/stricture of bowel in a patient with risk factors for adhesion formation. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

final_diagnosis: Ileal herniation in a right paraduodenal location

title: Breast tubular adenoma: A rare benign lesion mimicking malignancy
clinical_history: A 54-year-old female patient with a history of squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix presented with a hypermetabolic focus in the left breast on PET-CT, corresponding to a 12 mm nodular lesion (Figure 1).
imaging_findings: Digital breast tomosynthesis revealed an 11 mm well-defined nodular lesion in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, visualised in both projections of mammography, partially included on the field of view on cranio-caudal (Figure 2) and more easily appreciated after contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM), showing a very mild enhancement (Figure 3). Ultrasound examination demonstrated a well-defined, hypoechoic solid lesion, without posterior acoustic attenuation (Figure 4). Although this lesion did not present unequivocally suspicious criteria, given the patient’s oncological context, the mild enhancement on contrast-enhanced mammography, and the metabolic behaviour observed on PET-CT, a histological verification was pursued via ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy. Histopathological examination confirmed a tubular adenoma of the breast. Histological analysis revealed a well-circumscribed lesion with benign ductal proliferation, composed of tubular structures of varying sizes and scant fibroelastic stroma. No cellular atypia or infiltration was identified (confirmed by p63 and CK5 immunohistochemistry), supporting the benign nature of the lesion (Figure 5).
discussion: Background Fibroepithelial breast lesions include a spectrum of entities such as tubular adenomas, fibroadenomas, and phyllodes tumours, with variable biological behaviour, some of which are malignant [1]. Tubular adenomas are rare benign epithelial tumours, typically found in young women, comprising 0.13% to 1.7% of all benign breast lesions [2]. Given the extreme rarity of tubular adenomas, malignant transformation and concurrent occurrence with carcinoma remain exceptionally uncommon [3]. While imaging plays a crucial role in initial characterisation, histological evaluation via core needle biopsy or surgical excision remains the gold standard for definitive diagnosis. Clinical Perspective Although usually found in young women, tubular adenomas may occasionally be identified in older patients, as in the present case. In oncologic patients, FDG-avid breast lesions may raise suspicion for secondary malignancy, warranting further investigation through targeted imaging and biopsy. Imaging Perspective On imaging, tubular adenomas are almost indistinguishable from fibroadenomas. Because these lesions typically occur in young women and share similar ultrasound features with fibroadenomas, they are often classified as benign fibroadenomas based on imaging alone [4]. On mammography, they typically appear as well-circumscribed, oval-shaped masses with a parallel orientation to the skin surface. On CEM, they usually show absent or minimal enhancement, a pattern common among many benign lesions. However, this low enhancement is not specific, as some fibroadenomas, certain phyllodes tumours, and occasionally malignant lesions can also demonstrate minimal enhancement. In older patients, calcifications may be present, which can mimic features of malignancy [1,2]. On ultrasound, these lesions are usually hypoechoic, well-defined, and solid, often leading to classification as BI-RADS 3 or 4, especially in the context of oncologic patients. Nevertheless, it is important to note that tubular adenomas can occasionally present with suspicious imaging features, including irregular or lobulated margins and an irregular shape, which may raise concern for malignancy and warrant biopsy. Given the considerable imaging overlap with other breast lesions, histological confirmation is often required to exclude malignancy. Histologically, tubular adenomas can be differentiated from fibroadenomas by the predominance of homogeneously packed tubular and acinar epithelial components and a paucity of stromal components [2,5] (Figure 5). Although FDG-PET is frequently used in oncologic settings, its sensitivity and specificity in breast lesions are limited, as benign lesions may appear FDG-avid, leading to diagnostic dilemmas [6]. Outcome In our case, histological confirmation through ultrasound-guided core biopsy was essential in establishing the benign nature of this lesion, a tubular adenoma. No further treatment was needed, and the lesion has remained stable under follow-up. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Tubular adenomas are rare benign breast tumours that can mimic fibroadenomas both clinically and radiologically. They may appear FDG-avid on PET-CT, leading to diagnostic challenges, especially in oncologic patients. Histopathological confirmation is essential to differentiate these lesions from malignant tumours due to imaging overlap with malignant lesions. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: An atypical haemorrhage location: Duret haemorrhage
clinical_history: An 85-year-old male arrived at the emergency department at 20:50 with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 5 and right hemiparesis. He was last seen asymptomatic at 17:00.
imaging_findings: Initial non-contrast CT on admission (Figure 1) revealed an extensive left middle cerebral artery (MCA) infarction, with diffuse loss of cortico–subcortical differentiation throughout the left MCA territory, including the insula, consistent with an ASPECTS score of 3. A hyperdense left M1 segment indicated acute thrombus. Primary thrombectomy was performed. Digital subtraction angiography (Figure 2) confirmed M1 occlusion and demonstrated complete recanalisation (TICI 3) after a single thrombectomy pass. Follow-up non-contrast CT performed 24 hours later (Figures 3 and 4) revealed a malignant left MCA infarction with extensive oedema causing sulcal effacement, collapse of the left lateral ventricle, and a 12 mm contralateral midline shift. Signs of subfalcine and descending transtentorial herniation were evident, with obliteration of the basal cisterns. The infarct showed haemorrhagic transformation (PH1 type) and multiple small haemorrhagic foci within the pons and midbrain, consistent with Duret haemorrhages.
discussion: Background Duret haemorrhage refers to linear or flame-shaped brainstem haemorrhages, typically involving the pons and midbrain, resulting from rupture of perforating vessels after the vasculature is severed from a downward displacement, most often the paramedian branches of the basilar artery [1]. It occurs secondary to descending transtentorial herniation, a consequence of increased intracranial pressure from various causes, such as traumatic brain injury, space-occupying lesions, or diffuse cerebral oedema after large ischemic strokes [1,2]. Historically, it was regarded as a postmortem finding until the advent of CT and MRI allowed in vivo recognition. Clinical Perspective Clinically, Duret haemorrhage is associated with sudden neurological deterioration, including coma, abnormal pupillary reflexes, and loss of brainstem function. Although frequently fatal, early diagnosis is critical, as prompt recognition of brain herniation can guide urgent therapeutic decisions to reduce intracranial pressure. Imaging plays a central role, as the clinical picture alone cannot reliably distinguish between herniation-related brainstem injury and other causes of rapid deterioration. Radiologists must immediately alert the treating team to the presence of mass effect, midline shift, and brainstem haemorrhage, as these findings have major prognostic and therapeutic implications [3]. Imaging Perspective Non-contrast CT is the first-line diagnostic tool, demonstrating small hyperdense foci within the pons or midbrain, typically in a midline distribution. Associated findings include massive hemispheric oedema, sulcal effacement, ventricular collapse, midline shift, and obliteration of basal cisterns, all indicating transtentorial herniation [4,5]. MRI, particularly susceptibility-weighted imaging or T2*-GRE sequences, can increase sensitivity for detecting microhaemorrhages and assessing the extent of brainstem involvement [6]. The final diagnosis relies on correlating these imaging features with the clinical context of increased intracranial pressure and herniation. Outcome The prognosis is generally poor, reflecting severe brain injury and brainstem compression. Nevertheless, Duret haemorrhage should not be considered an absolute indicator of brain death, as occasional reports describe partial neurological recovery following rapid decompression and effective intracranial pressure management. Imaging findings thus play a pivotal role in guiding prognosis, therapeutic planning, and family counselling [7]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Duret haemorrhage is a secondary brainstem haemorrhage caused by downward transtentorial herniation. CT remains the gold-standard technique for its rapid detection. It is a marker of severe intracranial hypertension but not synonymous with brain death. Early recognition allows immediate therapeutic action aimed at reducing intracranial pressure and may improve outcomes in selected cases. title: Multifocal IDH1-positive astrocytoma in Ollier disease
clinical_history: A 26-year-old female with a known history of Ollier disease (OD) presented with complaints of migraines. She had a history of cartilaginous and joint enchondromas involving the left proximal femur and left hand.
imaging_findings: Multiple appendicular skeletal enchondromas were previously identified on CT and radiographs (Figures 1a, 1b, and 2). During neurologic evaluation for migraine, brain MRI revealed six intracranial lesions. A FLAIR image showed lower signal intensity in the right insular mass (Figure 3a) compared with the corresponding T2 image (Figure 3b), demonstrating a T2/FLAIR mismatch. The lesion showed no significant enhancement on post-contrast images (Figure 3c). Additional tumours were identified in the lateral left parietal lobe and more superiorly at the midline within the left parietal lobe (Figures 4a and 4b). These lesions also demonstrated a T2/FLAIR mismatch, suggestive of IDH-mutant astrocytomas. The SWI sequence showed no low-signal foci to suggest haemorrhage (Figure 5a). The ADC map showed no evidence of restricted diffusion (Figure 5b), and the B1000 (trace) image demonstrated bright signal intensity as expected (Figure 5c).
discussion: Ollier disease (OD) is a disorder characterised by multiple enchondromas caused by mutations in the IDH1 or IDH2 genes [1]. Although OD is considered to be sporadic, meaning that the molecular changes are somatic and only occur in the affected tissues, there have been several reports of familial recurrence, albeit rare, suggesting that a dominant inheritance pattern with reduced penetrance is possible [2]. The enchondromas in OD may be distributed unilaterally or bilaterally, and malignant transformation of enchondromas to chondrosarcoma has been estimated to be as high as 40% [3]. Individuals with OD are at an increased risk for intracranial malignancies of glial origin, with 2.4% of OD patients diagnosed with a brain malignancy [4,5]. Within the differential would be Maffucci’s syndrome with similar occurrence rates, but Maffucci’s also demonstrates soft tissue haemangiomas and less commonly lymphangiomas in addition to enchondromas [3]. Although rare, brain malignancy must be considered in a patient presenting with neurological symptoms, such as migraine, in the setting of OD. The imaging study of choice for neurological evaluation in this case is brain MRI due to its ability to evaluate for intracranial lesions or structural variations that may be causing the patient’s presenting symptoms [6]. On MRI, astrocytomas appear confined to the white matter and cause expansion of the neighbouring cortex. The lesions are isointense or hypointense compared to white matter on T1 and are hyperintense on T2. Astrocytomas may involve the cortex in late stages. Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic and genetic examination of the lesions [6]. Maximal safe surgical resection is the cornerstone of the management of astrocytomas. MRI is essential for surgical planning, especially in this case of multifocal astrocytomas. MRI is also necessary for postoperative monitoring of astrocytomas, as well as serial monitoring for progression. Adjuvant therapy includes chemotherapy and radiation [7]. In this case, immunohistochemistry was positive for the IDH1 R132H (F1) genotype, and pathology was described as an IDH -mutant astrocytoma with hypercellularity and atypia. Because this patient had both OD, of which as many as 87% of enchondromas are known to harbour an IDH1 variant, and an IDH1 -positive astrocytoma, the possibility of a germline IDH1 variant was considered in this patient [8]. The prevalence of tumours in OD raises the question about whether screening for the IDH mutations and brain MRI should be a standard of care. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.
differential_diagnosis: Glioblastoma Astrocytoma Subacute infarction Encephalitis Oligodendroglioma

title: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: Ultrasound signs and their diagnostic value
clinical_history: A one-month-old infant, previously healthy and without family history of pyloric hypertrophy, was presented to the emergency department with projectile vomiting after each feeding and increased gastroesophageal reflux over the past 48–72 hours. The infant exhibits increased hunger post-vomiting, along with irritability. Stools and urinary output remain within normal limits. Laboratory tests revealed metabolic alkalosis and elevated liver enzymes.
imaging_findings: An abdominal ultrasound was performed, revealing the pyloric channel located parallel to the gallbladder in the upper right abdomen. It measured 24 mm in length and had a muscular layer 5 mm in thickness (Figure 1a). The muscular layer exhibited hypoechogenicity and enlargement, while the mucosa/submucosa appeared hyperechogenic (Figures 1a and 1b). The pyloric channel was elongated. A redundant pyloric mucosa protruding into the gastric antrum was also noted (Figure 1c). During the examination, the pyloric channel remained closed throughout, and no passage of gastric contents was observed. Additionally, gastric content retention was detected.
discussion: Background Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (HPS) is an acquired narrowing of the pylorus that results in obstruction of gastric emptying. It typically occurs in infants aged between 2 weeks and 3 months [1–3]. The condition shows a familial distribution, suggesting a possible genetic predisposition. The exact pathophysiology of the disease remains unclear, though the nitric oxide pathway has recently been implicated. It has been postulated that a nitric oxide synthase deficiency within the pyloric muscle may contribute to pylorospasm and, consequently, hypertrophy [2,3]. Additionally, the potential role of an infectious aetiology has been suggested [2], among other possible causes, although no specific aetiology has been definitively identified. Clinical Perspective Progressive pyloric hypertrophy leads to obstruction, which may progress to complete obstruction, resulting in postprandial projectile vomiting. This can subsequently cause dehydration, accompanied by hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis [1–3]. On physical examination, palpation of the “olive” and the presence of a “caterpillar sign” (contraction waves of the stomach visible in an emaciated child) may be observed [4]. Imaging Perspective Laboratory tests and ultrasonography are essential for establishing the diagnosis. Ultrasonographically, a pyloric muscle thickness greater than 3 mm and a pyloric canal length of 15 mm or more are typically considered diagnostic for HPS [1,2]. Several signs can be identified in HPS: The “cervix” sign refers to the sonographic appearance of the thickened and elongated pylorus, which resembles the typical longitudinal sonographic appearance of the cervix in the context of HPS. The “bull’s eye” sign, also known as the “donut” sign, is formed by the orthogonal view of the hypoechoic muscle surrounding the echogenic mucosa. The “antral nipple” sign specifically denotes redundant pyloric mucosa protruding into the gastric antrum, which is commonly observed in HPS on ultrasound. Outcome Initial treatment involves rehydration and correction of electrolyte imbalances to within normal ranges, preparing the patient for subsequent surgical intervention. Prior to surgery, the placement of a nasogastric tube is recommended to empty the stomach and minimise the risk of aspiration [1–3]. Definitive treatment consists of an extramucosal longitudinal pyloromyotomy, which involves splitting the pyloric muscle without suturing [1–3]. This procedure, known as Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy, can be performed via an open approach or laparoscopically. Laparoscopic surgery offers advantages such as shorter recovery time, reduced scarring, and lower cost, although it carries a small risk of incomplete pyloromyotomy. The only non-surgical treatment involves the administration of atropine sulfate, which inhibits muscle contraction and gastrointestinal peristalsis. It may only be a possible alternative in children who cannot undergo surgery. In any case, if not treated, it is a lethal disorder [5]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points The increased use of ultrasound has led to earlier diagnosis of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (HPS) in infants. Therefore, familiarity with the various ultrasound signs of HPS is crucial for accurate and timely diagnosis. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: The floating fat sign: Radiographic diagnosis of knee lipohemarthrosis
clinical_history: A 63-year-old female presented with complaints of pain in the right knee following an alleged slip and fall at home. She reported difficulty in walking and localised tenderness over the affected area. On clinical examination, the right knee exhibited swelling, redness, and tenderness.
imaging_findings: Horizontal beam lateral radiograph of the right knee (Figure 1) shows a comminuted intra-articular tibial plateau fracture. The suprapatellar region shows a fat-fluid level. The rest of the bones are normal. Sagittal and axial views of the proton density fat-saturated (PD-FS) right knee (Figures 2 and 3) show a fat-fluid level in the suprapatellar region. Fat, being the lightest component, settles at the top. The middle layer consists of serous joint effusion. The inferior layer consists of blood. There is subcutaneous oedema around the knee joint. There is also evidence of intramuscular oedema.
discussion: Background Lipohemarthrosis most commonly occurs as a result of intra-articular fractures of the knee joint. It results from a fracture of a marrow-containing bone, causing the release of fat into the joint space. Since fat has less density than blood, it floats on top of the blood, resulting in a visible fat-fluid level on imaging. Clinical Perspective Clinically, it usually presents with painful joint swelling after trauma. It also shows a restricted range of motion. It is most frequently associated with knee fractures, especially tibial plateau fractures, but has also been reported in fractures of the shoulder, elbow, and hip [2,3]. Imaging Perspective This phenomenon is best demonstrated with a horizontal beam lateral radiograph, particularly using a cross-table lateral view. However, one limitation of this technique is that small joint effusions may go undetected [1,2]. For optimal visualisation of the fat-fluid level, the patient should remain still for about five minutes before the radiograph is taken. This allows enough time for the fat and blood to separate and settle into visible layers. In cases of penetrating trauma to the knee, air-fluid levels may also be observed. The greater radiolucency of air compared to fat typically allows for easy differentiation between fat-fluid and air-fluid levels [1]. In some cases of traumatic lipohemarthrosis, a double fat-fluid level may be seen on horizontal beam radiographs, which can be attributed to the presence of a suprapatellar plica synovialis [3]. Diagnoses It is important to note that not all tibial plateau fractures are accompanied by lipohemarthrosis, although hemarthrosis itself is relatively common in such injuries. Therefore, the absence of lipohemarthrosis does not rule out the presence of an intra-articular fracture. However, when lipohemarthrosis is observed, it is almost always indicative of an underlying intra-articular fracture, with the tibial plateau being the most frequently involved site [2,3]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points We learned from this case that, on the basis of radiological signs, we can detect an intra-articular fracture, and it will be helpful to diagnose it as early as possible for further treatment. This reduces the chance of missing the fractures on imaging. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Ectopic thyroid in the hepatoduodenal ligament presenting as a liver incidentaloma
clinical_history: A 55-year-old woman consulted a gastroenterologist due to pain in the right hypochondrium for several months. The patient was afebrile and had mild hypertension. Other clinical parameters were normal. Clinical examination revealed abdominal obesity and local tenderness. Biochemical values were normal.
imaging_findings: A CT scan of the abdomen (Figure 1) showed a sharply defined mass of approximately 4 cm located in the hepatoduodenal ligament, adjacent to and focally indiscernible from segment 4b of the liver. The mass enhanced homogeneously following administration of IV contrast and contained a central calcification. Further evaluation was performed with an MRI scan of the liver (Figure 2). The lesion appeared isointense on both T2 and T1 fat-suppressed sequences (compared to the liver parenchyma) and enhanced homogeneously after administration of IV contrast. There was no restricted diffusion. Incidentally, a renal cell carcinoma was discovered simultaneously in the right kidney. Ultrasound was not performed in this case. A liver adenoma was initially suspected, resulting in a laparoscopic excision of the lesion. During surgery, the lesion was located in the hepatoduodenal ligament with no invasion in the liver. Macroscopical appearance resembled a gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST). Surprisingly, anatomopathological examination revealed the lesion to be ectopic thyroid tissue.
discussion: Background Ectopic thyroid is defined as a form of thyroid dysgenesis, with tissue presenting at abnormal sites in the body. The condition results from an error during embryologic migration of the thyroid. The thyroid originates at the base of the tongue near the first and second pharyngeal pouches. During the fifth week of gestation, it migrates caudally along the midline, anteriorly to the laryngeal cartilage [1]. The most common position for ectopic thyroid is the cervical region along the obliterated thyroglossal duct [2], but in rare cases it may be found along the hepatoduodenal ligament and misidentified as a liver incidentaloma. Clinical Perspective Ectopic thyroid at the hepatoduodenal ligament is usually asymptomatic. However, symptoms can arise due to mass effect, such as abdominal pain or jaundice, because of biliary obstruction. The condition is usually discovered incidentally during imaging for unrelated reasons [3]. Imaging is essential to correctly diagnose the ectopic thyroid and exclude other mimickers such as malignancies. The requesting physician must be assured that this is a benign lesion that does not require further follow-up or treatment in most cases. Imaging Perspective The key imaging characteristic of ectopic thyroid tissue is its identical appearance to normal thyroid tissue. However, variations in imaging protocols or isolated abdominal imaging can cause diagnostic issues. On MRI, the lesion is typically isointense on T1 and T2-weighted sequences compared to liver parenchyma, with homogeneous enhancement after contrast administration. There is no restricted diffusion. Occasionally, a central calcification can be present. Unfortunately, CT and MRI findings are not pathognomonic for an ectopic thyroid. Most notably, a GIST can present analogue signal characteristics. MRI of a GIST usually demonstrates T1 hypointensity, T2 hyperintensity, homogeneous to heterogeneous contrast enhancement depending on the size of the lesion, and restricted diffusion [4]. To confirm the diagnosis, a 131 I scintigraphy can be performed, demonstrating high uptake at the site of the lesion. Alternatively, a biopsy may be considered. Biochemically, elevated thyroglobulin levels can solidify the diagnosis but are not always present [5]. Malignant transformation of the ectopic thyroid presents with heterogeneous enhancement, restricted diffusion, infiltration in the adjacent structures and sometimes lymphadenopathy [6]. In our case, surgery was performed, and the final diagnosis was made by histological examination of the resected specimen. Outcome Typically, ectopic thyroid tissue does not demand surgery or follow-up because of its benign nature. If diagnosed correctly, the patient can be reassured that no malignant lesion is present and no further treatment is needed. In very rare instances, malignant transformation can occur, warranting surgery and/or radiometabolic 131 I therapy [7]. Take Home Message Ectopic thyroid tissue can rarely present as a liver incidentaloma. It is important to differentiate it from malignant liver lesions to ensure appropriate treatment and follow-up. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
