title: Relapsing polychondritis with tracheobronchial involvement
clinical_history: A 52-year-old man with a history of chronic sinusitis presented with low-grade fever and persistent cough. Blood tests showed elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and leukocytosis. Despite five courses of antibiotics over six weeks, symptoms persisted, and he was referred for a CT thorax/abdomen and whole-body FDG PET/CT for further evaluation.
imaging_findings: Initial thoracic and abdominal CT with contrast showed diffuse circumferential wall thickening of the trachea and main bronchi, with subtle peritracheal reaction and a few enlarged lymph nodes (Figure 1). A whole-body FDG PET/CT scan was subsequently performed. It showed intense symmetrical FDG uptake in the laryngeal cartilage, thickened tracheal wall, main bronchi, and bilateral segmental bronchi (Figure 2). Additional mild uptake was seen in the nasal septum and in a few mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes. The pattern of symmetric FDG uptake in cartilaginous structures of the upper airways in combination with wall thickening was interpreted as inflammatory and considered consistent with relapsing polychondritis.
discussion: Background Relapsing polychondritis (RP) is a rare, chronic, autoimmune disease characterised by repeated inflammation of cartilaginous tissues, including those of the auricles, nasal septum, respiratory tract, and joints [1]. The pathophysiology remains unclear but is believed to involve both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses against cartilage-specific proteins, such as type II collagen and matrilin-1 [2]. This results in inflammation, oedema, and progressive cartilage degeneration, which in the respiratory tract can become life-threatening. Typical onset is in mid-adulthood, often presenting with subtle or fluctuating symptoms, causing diagnostic delay [3]. Clinical Perspective RP often presents with non-specific, fluctuating symptoms such as low-grade fever, fatigue, cough, or localised pain, depending on the affected cartilage [1]. Respiratory involvement occurs in up to 50% of patients and can manifest as dyspnoea, stridor, or recurrent respiratory infections [4]. However, in early stages, symptoms may be subtle and transient, leading to significant diagnostic delay [5]. Imaging is essential to evaluate the extent and distribution of cartilaginous inflammation, particularly in the airways, where early detection of wall thickening or collapse is important [6]. Imaging Perspective In RP, contrast-enhanced CT is an essential first-line imaging modality for assessing airway involvement. A hallmark finding is smooth, circumferential thickening of the tracheobronchial wall with sparing of the posterior membranous portion [3], which helps distinguish RP from other causes of airway disease, such as malignancy or granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) [1]. Calcifications in affected cartilage may also be seen in chronic cases [3]. FDG PET/CT provides complementary information by highlighting metabolically active inflammation in cartilage structures, even before morphological changes become apparent on CT. This can be particularly useful in early cases [7]. Increased symmetrical FDG uptake in laryngeal, tracheal, or bronchial cartilage is highly suggestive of RP, and PET/CT can help assess disease extent and monitor treatment response [1]. While there is no single pathognomonic imaging feature, the combination of CT findings (cartilaginous airway thickening with posterior sparing) and PET/CT evidence of inflammatory activity strongly supports the diagnosis in the appropriate clinical context [8]. Biopsy is not always required, but may be considered when imaging and clinical features are inconclusive or to exclude mimics such as neoplasia [3]. Outcome The patient was referred to a rheumatology department for suspected relapsing polychondritis. Biopsy was considered but ultimately deferred due to airway risks. Medical treatment was initiated with high-dose prednisolone, followed by biologic therapy. Treatment response was assessed with follow-up MRI, demonstrating partial regression of the tracheobronchial wall thickening (Figures 3 and 4). Despite treatment, the patient continued to experience recurrent respiratory exacerbations.
differential_diagnosis: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) Tracheobronchial amyloidosis Relapsing polychondritis Sarcoidosis

title: Incidental finding during active surveillance of Gleason 3+3 prostate cancer
clinical_history: A 70-year-old male with a history of bladder cancer (Ta), treated with transurethral resection and periodic instillations of Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG), and a Gleason 3+3 prostate cancer in the right prostatic lobe under active surveillance, underwent a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for prostatic evaluation.
imaging_findings: Follow-up 3 Tesla (T) multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) showed a new 18 mm nodule located in the left posterolateral peripheral zone (PZ) at the prostatic apex. The nodule was homogeneously hypointense on T2-weighted images with a broad contact and bulging of the prostatic capsule (Figure 1). Moreover, it showed marked high signal intensity on diffusion-weighted images (DWI), prominent low signal intensity on apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) (Figure 2), and a peripheral rim enhancement on dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) T1-weighted images (Figure 3). Since the patient was under active surveillance for his Gleason 3+3 prostate carcinoma, a biopsy was scheduled 15 days after the MRI. Finally, the histological analysis confirmed the diagnosis suspected on the MRI.
discussion: Background Granulomatous prostatitis (GP) is a rare inflammatory condition of the prostate, found in 0.6–1.5% of prostate biopsies, histologically characterised by the presence of granulomas. GP has a broad aetiology, and can be idiopathic, infectious (tuberculosis, fungal), iatrogenic (post-biopsy or post-surgery), or related to systemic granulomatous diseases (sarcoidosis, vasculitis). BCG instillation for the treatment of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer is one of the most frequent causes of GP [1–6]. It has been proposed that idiopathic cases result from an autoimmune reaction caused by stasis of prostatic secretions and urinary reflux [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Patients may be asymptomatic or present with lower urinary tract symptoms, such as urinary frequency or dysuria. The PSA (prostate-specific antigen) value is usually raised, and a hardened nodule is often observed on digital rectal examination, which may raise suspicion of prostate cancer. For this reason, mpMRI is necessary to make an accurate differential diagnosis. However, in many cases, there may be an overlap between the imaging findings of both entities, making biopsy necessary [1–6]. Imaging Perspective On mpMRI, GP can be diffuse or nodular and affect the PZ, potentially extending to the transition zone. It is usually hypointense on T2-weighted images, hyperintense on DWI, and markedly hypointense on ADC [2–6]. It can also produce periprostatic fat stranding and bulging of the prostatic capsule, suggesting extraprostatic extension [2,5]. All these findings overlap with prostate cancer, resulting in PI-RADS 4 or PI-RADS 5 lesions [7]. On DCE, although it can show diffuse enhancement, GP usually shows peripheral rim enhancement in cases of caseous necrosis formation [2–6]. This enhancement pattern is rare in prostate cancer, as it usually demonstrates early diffuse enhancement with late washout on DCE [3,4]. Therefore, in a patient in an appropriate clinical setting (such as BCG instillation), the presence of peripheral rim enhancement with a central non-enhancing necrotic area may suggest GP diagnosis, thus avoiding biopsy [3–6]. Outcome Treatment is only necessary in symptomatic GP cases and will vary depending on the aetiology. Most idiopathic cases are self-limiting. Contrarily, symptomatic cases caused by BCG instillations are treated with anti-tuberculous medications and discontinuation of the instillations [1,2]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Granulomatous prostatitis (GP) may be indistinguishable from prostate cancer on imaging, resulting in PI-RADS 4 or PI-RADS 5 lesions. However, in an appropriate clinical setting, the presence of ring enhancement on DCE may suggest the diagnosis. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Granulomatous prostatitis Acute prostatitis with abscess formation Prostate cancer Post-biopsy haemorrhage

title: Multiple intracranial masses and progressive bilateral hearing loss
clinical_history: A 43-year-old woman with a 20-year history of progressive headaches and prior resections of intracranial masses (2014 and 2015) presented for follow-up evaluation. During the preceding year, she had developed severe bilateral hearing loss, seizures, and symptoms of intracranial hypertension, including new, intense headaches.
imaging_findings: The current contrast-enhanced cranial MRI demonstrates multiple bilateral intracranial lesions. Several extra-axial, contrast-enhancing masses were identified along the falx cerebri, consistent with meningiomas (Figures 1a and 1b). Bilateral vestibular schwannomas were also evident, characterised by heterogeneously enhancing lesions arising from both internal auditory canals (Figure 1c). Additionally, a distinct enhancing lesion was noted in the left eyelid. A non-contrast head CT obtained on an emergency basis revealed progressive ventriculomegaly with rounding of the lateral ventricles, consistent with developing hydrocephalus and correlating with the patient’s acute symptoms (Figure 2).
discussion: Background Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) is a rare autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NF2 tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 22 [1]. This gene encodes the merlin protein (also called schwannomin), a protein which regulates Schwann cell growth [2]. The absence of functional merlin leads to the classic triad of tumours: schwannomas, meningiomas, and ependymomas. The presence of bilateral vestibular schwannomas is the diagnostic hallmark of the disease [1]. Clinical Perspective NF2 typically presents in young adulthood, with an average age of diagnosis around 25 [2]. The most common presenting complaint is progressive sensorineural hearing loss, followed by tinnitus and balance issues, related to bilateral vestibular schwannomas (BVS). Our patient’s presentation with severe bilateral hearing loss, seizures, and intracranial hypertension is a classic, though advanced, manifestation. Case severity can be stratified into the mild “Gardner” phenotype or the severe “Wishart” phenotype; this patient’s early onset and multiple tumour burden align with the more severe form [2]. Imaging Perspective Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the imaging modality of choice for both diagnosis and lifelong surveillance [1]. In this case, the current (2025) contrast-enhanced cranial MRI was crucial for demonstrating the constellation of tumours, such as multiple inherited schwannomas and meningiomas. The pathognomonic BVS are seen emerging from the internal auditory canals (IACs), showing typical T2 hyperintensity and heterogeneous enhancement [1]. The multiple meningiomas, the second most common tumour in NF2, are also classic. They appear as dural-based, extra-axial masses that are T1 isointense to grey matter and demonstrate avid, homogeneous enhancement, often with a “dural tail” sign [3]. Longitudinal imaging is critical, not only to monitor tumour growth but to detect life-threatening complications, such as obstructive hydrocephalus. Outcome The management goal in NF2 is often palliative, not curative. Given the patient’s acute presentation with intracranial hypertension, the immediate life-saving intervention was a ventricular shunt followed by a staged surgical plan to resect the most symptomatic tumours. Radiotherapy was specifically contraindicated. Radiation use in NF2 patients must be carefully considered, as it can induce or accelerate new tumours in these patients. It has been reported that nearly 50% of all malignant post-radiation degenerations occur in the context of NF2, which fully justifies the decision to avoid it [2]. Teaching Points Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are pathognomonic for Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2). The presence of multiple intracranial tumour types (schwannomas and meningiomas) should immediately suggest NF2. Lifelong surveillance with high-resolution, thin-cut MRI of the brain and spine is essential for monitoring tumour growth and complications. Radiotherapy should be avoided in NF2 patients due to the high risk of radiation-induced secondary neoplasms. NF2 management is complex and must be handled by an experienced, multidisciplinary team. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Focal splenic lesions: A challenge for the radiologist
clinical_history: A 45-year-old asymptomatic woman, with a history of right nephrectomy 8 years ago for clear cell carcinoma (T2aN0M0, G2), and normal blood tests (biochemistry, haematocrit, and PCR), underwent a follow-up computed tomography (CT).
imaging_findings: The initial contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) showed multiple focal splenic lesions of approximately 1–1.5 cm, diffusely scattered throughout the parenchyma, which were solid, well-defined, hypovascular in the arterial phase, with mild progressive enhancement during the dynamic study, and without associated splenomegaly. Post-surgical changes from right nephrectomy were also observed, with no signs of local recurrence. No other relevant findings were observed in the thorax or the abdomen. Three months later, a close follow-up CT scan was performed, which demonstrated growth of the lesions (Figure 6). For this reason, a splenectomy was finally performed (Figure 7).
discussion: Background Sarcoidosis is a multisystemic disease of unknown origin, which is histologically characterised by the formation of non-caseating granulomas. It is more frequent in the USA, particularly in African American women in the 3rd–5th decades of life [1,2]. It predominantly affects the lungs and the mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes (90%), with possible involvement of extrathoracic locations (skin, lymph nodes, eyes, liver, spleen, etc.), usually in combination with the aforementioned. Infrequently, it may manifest with exclusively extrathoracic symptoms (10%), with isolated splenic involvement being a rare manifestation [1–4]. Clinical Perspective Although it can sometimes be asymptomatic, patients often present systemic symptoms (fever, malaise, weight loss) or symptoms related to the affected target organs. Splenic involvement can produce splenomegaly and/or hypersplenism [1–4]. Since the symptoms are nonspecific, the diagnosis is usually reached by a combination of clinical, radiological, and pathological findings after the exclusion of other entities that potentially cause non-caseating granulomas [1,2,4,5]. Imaging Perspective On imaging, splenic sarcoidosis typically presents as homogeneous splenomegaly or, less frequently, as multiple focal splenic lesions [1,2,4–6]. They are usually small nodules scattered in the splenic parenchyma. On ultrasound, well-defined nodules are usually hypoechoic, whereas smaller, discrete nodules can be difficult to identify, giving a heterogeneous appearance to the splenic parenchyma [1,2,5]. On dynamic CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), they are usually hypoenhancing on the arterial phase, with fading on the equilibrium phase. They are usually hypointense on T1 and T2-weighted images (WI), being more evident on T2-WI with fat suppression [1,2,5,6]. On PET/CT, nodules are usually hypermetabolic [4,6]. When these signs occur in combination with perilymphatic-distributed pulmonary nodules and/or symmetric hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, they are highly suggestive of sarcoidosis [2]. However, when these lesions occur in isolation, imaging findings are nonspecific due to overlap with other granulomatous diseases, splenic lymphoma, or metastases. Therefore, splenic biopsy or even, in some cases, splenectomy, are necessary to reach a diagnosis [1,2,5,6]. Outcome Sometimes, spontaneous regressions can occur in asymptomatic patients, whereas symptomatic patients are usually treated with corticosteroids. In cases of splenic sarcoidosis refractory to medical therapy, a splenectomy may be necessary. Approximately a third of patients may develop chronic sarcoidosis, with mortality related to pulmonary or cardiac involvement [1,2,6]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points The spleen is a potential site of involvement of sarcoidosis, manifesting as homogeneous splenomegaly or multiple focal splenic lesions on imaging. Although typically associated with thoracic manifestations, isolated splenic involvement can occur in rare cases. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: A rare and unique entity: High-grade astrocytoma with piloid features
clinical_history: A 56-year-old male presented with a two-month history of static and kinetic cerebellar syndrome, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. The patient underwent a CT and an MRI workup.
imaging_findings: Initial CT revealed a partially calcified left posterior fossa mass with apparent tentorial insertion (figures 1a and 1b). MRI confirmed a unique, circumscribed, left cerebellar lesion (32 mm), subtly hyperintense on T2-weighted and iso/hypointense on T1-weighted sequences, without diffusion restriction, with some peripheral calcifications and avid contrast enhancement (Figures 2a, 2b, and 2c). The lesion, surrounded by moderate perilesional vasogenic oedema, was causing mass effect on the adjacent cerebellar parenchyma as well as on the fourth ventricle, without obstructive hydrocephalus or signs of herniation. The suspected extra-axial origin and dural contact were suggestive of a meningioma. However, after surgery, the subsequent molecular analysis identified CDKN2A homozygous deletion, activating FGFR1 and NF1 mutations, and methylated MGMT promoter status, allowing the classification of the mass as a high-grade astrocytoma with piloid features (HGAP).
discussion: Background HGAP is a rare, neoplastic entity, recently included in the 2021 WHO classification (5th Edition) as a circumscribed glioma (IDH wildtype) defined by a specific methylation profile, which primarily affects adults (4th decade) [1,2]. It lacks a distinct histological profile, sharing features both with glioblastoma (GBM), i.e., high mitotic activity, microvascular proliferation, and necrosis, and with pilocytic astrocytoma (PA), i.e., elongated glial tumour cell processes (aka “piloid” features), Rosenthal fibres, and eosinophilic granular bodies [3,4]. Given their imaging and histologic variability, DNA methylation profiling represents the sole diagnostic method. Beyond the epigenetic fingerprint, HGAP also presents with characteristic molecular alterations (CDKN2A/B, NF1, BRAF, FGFR1, ATRX) that could also aid characterisation [5]. It can emerge de novo, usually with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) or as a progression of a lower-grade glioma, often PA [5,6]. As of now, HGAP are often diagnosed as a reclassification of previously diagnosed anaplastic astrocytoma or GBM [7]. Clinical Perspective Clinical presentation depends on tumour location. Even though it has a predilection for the posterior fossa (62–74%), it may be located anywhere in the central nervous system and even have intraventricular and leptomeningeal dissemination [4,5]. As in our case, posterior fossa lesions could determine mass effect leading to cerebellar symptoms, signs of intracranial hypertension, and headache. A comprehensive workup is essential to investigate NF1-related stigmata [5,6]. Imaging Perspective HGAP poses a significant challenge due to the limited availability of data and the lack of a consistent radiographic appearance [3,7,8]. It is mostly located in the cerebellum (midline or paramedian) [4,5]. It usually presents as a mass with low T1 and high T2/FLAIR signal (Figures 2b and 2c), without significant diffusion restriction and variable enhancement (homogeneous as seen in Figures 1a, 1b, and 2a, rim, heterogeneous), sometimes with necrotic areas [4,5]. Multiple imaging patterns often mirror diverse microscopic characteristics (cellularity, microvascular proliferation, necrosis), again occupying a spectrum between low and high-grade tumours [5]. Imaging is also necessary to investigate possible complications and guide surgical planning [3]. Outcome Considering its rarity and uniqueness, HGAP does not have an established standard of care [3,9]. Treatment typically involves maximal safe surgical resection associated with chemoradiotherapy (temozolomide), and following imaging surveillance [4]. Prognosis is between that of IDH wildtype GBM and IDH-mutant gliomas, i.e., a 5-year survival rate of 50% [3,5]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points High-grade astrocytoma with piloid features (HGAP) is a new neoplastic entity, still not well-defined, that should be considered as a differential diagnosis in posterior fossa tumours, with specific molecular alterations (ATRX, CDKN2A/B, and MAPK), in NF1 patients [3,4]. DNA methylation profiling is required for diagnosis [6,9]. Treatment consists of surgery with radiochemotherapy (temozolomide), with a prognosis of 50% at 5 years [3].

title: Visualisation of ischaemic priapism with sickle cell disease on CEUS
clinical_history: A 19-year-old boy diagnosed with homozygous SS sickle cell disease (SCD) 10 years previously, presented with persistent penile erection, without sexual stimulation and lasting more than 4 hours.
imaging_findings: The initial procedure was a non-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure 1). The T2-weighted sagittal plane showed lower signal intensity than expected in the normal erectile state. The scattered and unevenly distributed focal low signal intensity in the central corpus cavernosa indicated areas of small infarction or segmental thrombosis (Figure 1). Later the same day, colour Doppler ultrasound (Figure 2a) and micro-vascular imaging (Figure 2b) only demonstrated the vascular supply outside the corpora cavernosa surrounding the tunica albuginea. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS), 4.8 mLs of SonoVue™, demonstrated the patency of the cavernosal arteries in the late arterial phase, with limited filling of the arterial branches, and a truncated cavernosal artery (Figures 2c and 2d). There was no enhancement in the parenchyma of the penis. Enhanced MRI of the penis at 18 days (Figure 3) showed no enhancement on post-contrast imaging in the corpora cavernosa. A thin rim of peripheral enhancement was present bilaterally, without definite internal septal or trabecular enhancement. Patchy enhancement was seen towards the crura. The MRI features are consistent with the chronic sequelae of ischaemic priapism.
discussion: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is caused by a genetic mutation that results in an abnormal structure of haemoglobin. Homozygous patients with SCD may suffer from intermittent micro-vascular occlusive events that affect the entire body. Priapism is one of the common manifestations of SCD and may affect up to 42% of the male SCD population [1,2]. Priapism caused by SCD is an ischaemic, low-flow type of priapism, secondary to erythrocyte sickling, leading to stasis of the venous and sinusoidal penile vein drainage. On physical examination, a painful and rigid penis is usually seen. This patient underwent insertion of a malleable penile prosthesis (Coloplast Genesis ® ) bilaterally. Intraoperatively, the penis was rigid and fibrotic, with a “woody” consistency. At 10 days post-operation, the dressing was removed without complication. There were no signs of infection, and the patient reported adherence to oral antibiotics. Classical colour Doppler ultrasound findings are little or no cavernosal arterial inflow. Decreased colour Doppler flow also indicates possible thrombosis of the corpus cavernosa [3]. MRI could assess erectile tissue in ischaemic priapism and the extent of necrosis, with necrotic/infarcted tissue manifested as a low T2 signal in the central corpus cavernosa. MRI also plays an important role in differentiating ischaemic priapism from some mimicking penile metastasis, with post-contrast MRI adding further information, determining the degree of infarction for surgical planning [4–6]. Because a significant number of SCD patients have kidney dysfunction, the contrast agents of computed tomography (iodinated contrast) or magnetic resonance (gadolinium) arteriographies are not suitable. The ultrasound contrast agent used in our case is safe in the presence of renal impairment and provides better temporal and spatial resolution compared to MR or CT imaging. Ultrasound contrast agents are purely blood-pool agents that can clearly show very small blood vessels, allowing haemodynamic assessment of the cavernosal arteries. Importantly, ultrasound is radiation-free, portable, and inexpensive, and is particularly suitable for superficial male genital examinations [7]. Take Home Message This case illustrates the usefulness of CEUS to rapidly and accurately, without patient compromise and with patient comfort, establish patent cavernosal arteries, thrombosis of the corpora cavernosa in a SCC patient with low-flow priapism. This enabled early and definitive surgical intervention. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: A hit in the target: Baló’s concentric sclerosis
clinical_history: A 54-year-old male with a history of bronchial asthma and ankylosing spondylitis presented to the emergency department with progressive left-sided hemiparesis, primarily of the arm (strength of 4/5) and central left facial pain on examination.
imaging_findings: Magnetic resonance imaging showed pseudotumoural-like lesions affecting the corpus callosum, periventricular and juxtacortical white matter with apparent alternating T2 signal in concentric rings (Figures 1a, 1b and 1c), a peripheral ring of restriction (Figures 2a and 2b), and heterogeneous enhancement with different uptake patterns after intravenous contrast administration (Figures 3a and 3b). No significant mass effect or perilesional oedema were present. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination ruled out the presence of IgG oligoclonal bands and malignant cells.
discussion: Background Baló’s concentric sclerosis (BCS) is a rare demyelinating disease to be considered a subtype within the spectrum of multiple sclerosis [1–4]. This entity usually presents as a single or multiple concentric tumefactive-like lesions, which cause widespread neurologic dysfunction. Clinical Perspective Clinical course of this disease is considered similar to Marburg’s variant of multiple sclerosis, which shows a severe, monophasic course, with rapid and sometimes fulminant progression [1]. Most common symptoms include headache, aphasia, focal seizures or cognitive/behavioural dysfunction [1]. Cerebrospinal fluid analyses also often reveal a mononuclear inflammatory reaction and occasionally oligoclonal bands. Imaging Perspective The most characteristic feature of this condition is the alternating concentric layers of demyelination and preserved myelin, giving rise to the characteristic image seen on MRI of alternating bands or concentric rings appearance on T2-weighted and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images (bull’s-eye sign/onion bulb appearance) [3,4]. Lesions may be solitary or multiple and often mimic intracranial space-occupying lesions [4]. Although diagnosis has historically been made postmortem based on pathological findings, the most recent studies support the fundamental role of brain MRI for early and definitive diagnosis of BCS [3]. It is important to remark that this role may have a significant influence on morbidity and mortality associated with the disease [2]. In our case, diagnosis was based on clinical signs and symptoms consistent with Baló’s concentric sclerosis, the characteristic concentric rings on MR images, and exclusion of other neurologic diseases. Outcome As with other forms of multiple sclerosis, the use of corticosteroids in the acute phase is essential, although this subtype is usually rapidly progressive and responds poorly to treatment. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Although this subtype of multiple sclerosis is infrequent, the role of MRI is fundamental in early diagnosis. Radiological findings can be challenging and may be mistaken for intracranial occupying lesions, and thus, the radiologist’s knowledge of this entity can be the key to interpreting the imaging study correctly.

title: Persistent dorsal forefoot pain in an active adult
clinical_history: A female adult with weeks of progressive forefoot pain was referred by the occupational health department to radiology for a suspected Morton’s neuroma. She had recently increased physical activity. During scanning, the patient localised the maximal tenderness over the dorsal distal second metatarsal. There were no initial radiographs, as the request targeted soft tissue.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound of the left forefoot was initially focused on the third intermetatarsal space, given the patient’s complaints, but it was later extended to the symptomatic dorsal distal second metatarsal. Greyscale ultrasound showed mild periosteal reaction at the metatarsal neck with hyperechogenicity of adjacent fat and soft tissues, compatible with reactive oedema (Figure 1a). Conventional colour Doppler acquisitions were attempted but did not demonstrate visible periosteal hyperaemia, likely due to extremely low velocity flow, and therefore, no image was recorded. A microvascular Doppler mode was subsequently used, which successfully depicted subtle periosteal hypervascularity (Figure 1b). A small third-space Morton’s neuroma (≈ 6 x 5 mm) was also identified (Figure 2). No metatarsophalangeal joint effusion/synovitis or tendon abnormality was seen. MRI performed one month later revealed a stress fracture traversing the neck of the second metatarsal with marked marrow and soft-tissue oedema (Figure 3). No other osseous or articular abnormalities were seen.
discussion: Background Metatarsal stress fractures lie within the bone-stress spectrum from stress reaction to cortical break. The second metatarsal is most frequently involved due to repetitive forefoot loading and relative rigidity within the forefoot lever arm [1]. Early radiographs have low sensitivity and may remain normal for 2–3 weeks [2]. Clinical Perspective This case illustrates a common clinic-imaging discrepancy: the referral asked for a neuroma, yet the patient’s point of maximal tenderness was located over the dorsal distal second metatarsal. The referral from occupational health focused on a suspected Morton’s neuroma, and therefore, no initial radiography was obtained. Directed questioning revealed a recent increase in physical activity, a classical precipitating factor [1]. Proactively scanning where it hurts transformed a soft-tissue work-up into a bone-stress pathway, avoiding diagnostic delay that a normal early radiograph could have introduced. Imaging Perspective In our case, ultrasound raised suspicion and MRI confirmed/staged the lesion. Early radiographs have low sensitivity and may remain normal for 2–3 weeks [2]. Ultrasound findings of periosteal thickening or subtle reaction with adjacent soft-tissue oedema should raise suspicion for stress injury [3]. In our case, conventional Doppler was negative, a recognised limitation when periosteal flow is below the velocity detection threshold of standard Doppler modes. This justified the use of microvascular Doppler, which revealed subtle hyperaemia supporting an early stress response. Ultrasound is therefore considered a triage tool because it cannot evaluate medullary oedema or grade the injury. MRI is the reference standard: fluid-sensitive sequences depict marrow oedema and, when present, a low-signal fracture line at the metatarsal neck. MRI grading correlates with the time to return to activity, guiding prognosis and follow-up [2,4,5]. A small third-space Morton’s neuroma is common and may be incidental; insist on symptom–lesion concordance. Other differentials include extensor tendinopathy, plantar plate tear, Freiberg infraction at the metatarsal head, and osteomyelitis when clinically suspected [6]. Remember that bone marrow oedemas are non-specific; location/morphology (linear peri-cortical pattern, fracture line) separates stress fracture from bone contusion or infection. Outcome Second-metatarsal neck injuries are low-risk and usually respond to conservative treatment: activity modification, protected weight-bearing (stiff-soled shoe/boot), analgesia and optimisation of risk factors (training load, footwear, vitamin D). Routine imaging follow-up is unnecessary if symptoms improve, but persistent pain warrants reassessment [2,4]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points In forefoot pain, scan where it hurts: periosteal hyperaemia and focal peri-metatarsal oedema on US should be better characterised by MRI. Periosteal hyperaemia and soft-tissue oedema on ultrasound should prompt MRI for confirmation and grading. Microvascular Doppler may help detect low-flow periosteal hypervascularity when conventional Doppler is equivocal. MRI confirms and grades bone-stress injuries, which then affect expected recovery. In second-metatarsal neck stress fractures, conservative management is usually enough. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Partial caecal necrosis mimicking acute appendicitis
clinical_history: A 91-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with acute abdominal pain and fever. Physical examination demonstrated localised tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Laboratory tests showed a C-reactive protein level of 30 mg/dL. Acute appendicitis was suspected, and an abdominal and pelvic computed tomography (CT) was requested.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced CT in the portal venous phase (Figures 1a, 1b, and 1c) demonstrated a blind-ending saccular structure arising from the caecum, containing an air–fluid level with gas bubbles within the dependent fluid, along with a few small gas bubbles that appeared to lie within the wall of the structure. The lesion had a markedly thin, non-enhancing wall, although assessment was partially limited by motion artefact. The ileocaecal appendix was not visualised, and there was no adjacent fat stranding or diverticular disease elsewhere in the colon. Mesenteric vessels were normally enhanced, and no ascites was present.
discussion: Background Partial caecal necrosis (PCN) is a rare form of ischaemic colitis of unclear origin, predominantly affecting elderly patients. It typically occurs spontaneously and presents with acute right lower‑quadrant pain. PCN has been reported in association with trauma, hypotension, chronic heart disease, haemodialysis, open-heart surgery and systemic chemotherapy [1]. In our patient, advanced age and established cardiovascular disease were notable contributing factors. Clinical Perspective Patients with PCN commonly present with acute right lower-quadrant pain, often mimicking appendicitis or other caecal pathology such as diverticulitis or perforated malignancy [2,3]. Laboratory results are non-specific, and no serum biomarker reliably detects early colonic ischaemia [3]. Elevated lactate may support the diagnosis, but normal levels do not exclude ischaemia [4], as in this case (1.8 mmol/L). High clinical suspicion remains essential to ensure prompt recognition and prevent perforation, sepsis, and increased mortality. Imaging Perspective Findings of PCN are non-specific [1]. Intramural gas alone is a recognised imaging feature of bowel necrosis, with other cases of PCN also reporting localised pericaecal fluid collections [5] or mass-like lesions [6] indicative of a focal necrotic segment. Transmural necrosis thins the wall, allowing fluid or intramural gas to accumulate, producing a localised, sac-like protrusion that bulges from the surrounding viable bowel. In our case, CT showed a thin-walled, non-enhancing, blind-ending saccular structure arising from the caecum, containing intermixed fluid and gas, with additional gas suggestive of being intramural, raising concern for pneumatosis. Absence of wall thickening and surrounding fat stranding argued against an infectious-inflammatory process; however, due to the rarity of PCN, perforated appendicitis, diverticulitis and contained caecal perforation remained in the differential. Outcome The patient underwent laparoscopic surgery, which revealed a solitary necrotic caecal segment, with the remainder of the bowel appearing normal (Figures 2a and 2b). An uneventful ileocaecal resection was performed. Postoperatively, the patient reported a childhood appendectomy, which had not been known beforehand. Histopathology confirmed multifocal mucosal ischaemic necrosis with dense acute neutrophilic inflammation extending transmurally, establishing the diagnosis of severe ischaemic colitis. Take Home Message Partial caecal necrosis is a rare mimic of appendicitis. Early recognition is crucial to prevent complications such as perforation and sepsis, with diagnosis confirmed by surgery and histopathology. Advanced age and cardiovascular disease are key risk factors. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Bezold’s abscess as a complication of otomastoiditis
clinical_history: A 71-year-old man presented with a one-month history of right ear drainage. He underwent two courses of antibiotics, but there was no significant improvement. Additionally, he reported neck pain for the past week. A thorough examination revealed pronounced soft tissue swelling in the neck and the right subscapular region.
imaging_findings: Computed tomography (CT) of the neck in axial and coronal slices with bone window imaging shows slight soft tissue enlargement and partial erosion of the right mastoid air cells (Figures 1 and 2). Images acquired with soft tissue windowing show a hypodense area with peripheral enhancement corresponding to a large collection located in the right posterior prevertebral, paraspinal, and cervical spaces, measuring approximately 7 x 9 x 18 cm (Figures 3 and 4). Its extension reaches the suprascapular region and contacts the superior and anterior surface of the scapula (Figure 5). It also presents an intracranial component that causes partial obstruction of the right sigmoid venous sinus without completely impairing its patency (Figure 6).
discussion: Background Bezold’s abscess is a rare but serious complication of otomastoiditis, located deep in the lateral cervical region. It was described in 1885 by Friedrich von Bezold [1]. It can occur at any age but is more common in adult males. The percentage of patients with otitis or mastoiditis who develop this complication is unknown, but with the current use of and access to antibiotics, its incidence is very low [1–3]. Its pathogenesis involves the spread of an infectious process from the middle ear to the mastoid through an erosion in the digastric ridge, between the digastric and sternocleidomastoid muscles [1]. Clinical Perspective Bezold’s abscess can be difficult to recognise, as its clinical presentation is heterogeneous, ranging from signs of cervical inflammation or fever to otorrhea, hearing loss, or facial paralysis [1,4]. Evaluation by palpation is limited, since the collection is located deep in the neck [1]. Laboratory tests show leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers. Most frequent causative organisms are Streptococcus pneumoniae , group A streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus , and Haemophilus influenzae . It can occur alongside other complications such as subdural and epidural empyema, jugular venous thrombosis, and fistulas [2,4]. Imaging Perspective Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the temporal bone and neck is the ideal test for assessing the extent of otomastoiditis. It allows the detection of bone erosions, precise delineation of the anatomical boundaries of the cervical abscess, and surgical planning. It presents as a hypodense collection with rim enhancement and surrounding soft tissue oedema. In some patients, the abscess may extend through the deep cervical fascia and reach the surface, altering the cervical anatomy. Bone destruction of the mastoid air cells may also be observed. The CT scan may include intracranial structures if complications are suspected [1–3,5]. The role of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in the diagnosis of Bezold’s abscess is generally limited; it is primarily indicated when intracranial complications, cholesteatoma, and intravascular thrombi are suspected [1,2]. Outcome Treatment of Bezold abscess includes broad-spectrum antibiotics with good penetration into the cerebrospinal fluid and early surgery with drainage of the collection, as well as treatment of its complications [1,2,4,6]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Bezold’s abscess is a rare but very serious complication of otomastoiditis, and it is important to be aware of it. Clinical diagnosis is not easy and requires imaging tests for confirmation. Treatment involves antibiotic therapy and surgery. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Diffuse splenic lymphangiomatosis in an adult
clinical_history: A 35-year-old female presented with intermittent, vague pain in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen for approximately six months. She denied any history of fever, abdominal trauma, weight loss, or constitutional symptoms. There was no history of significant comorbidities and no relevant past medical or surgical history. Clinical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory investigations, including complete blood count and basic metabolic profile, were within normal limits. The patient had not undergone any prior abdominal imaging.
imaging_findings: To evaluate for possible splenic or left renal pathology, a whole-abdomen ultrasonography (USG) was performed, followed by contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the upper abdomen. USG (Figure 1) revealed a normally sized spleen with multiple hypoechoic and anechoic cystic lesions in the splenic parenchyma with no Doppler detectable flow within. There was a heterogeneous appearance of the splenic parenchyma. There were a few occasional internal septations. On contrast-enhanced MRI, the spleen was normal in size. On T2-weighted and STIR sequences (Figure 2), there were multiple thin-walled hyperintense cystic lesions of varying sizes with hypointense septa involving the entire splenic parenchyma. On the T1-weighted sequence (Figure 3), the spleen appeared mostly isointense with mildly heterogeneous parenchymal signal. On DWI (diffusion-weighted imaging), no obvious significant diffusion restriction is shown by the cystic lesions or the heterogeneous splenic parenchyma (Figure 4). On T1-weighted post-contrast study (Figure 5), no enhancement is seen on both arterial and delayed phases, with the angiography revealing multiple well-defined avascular lesions of various sizes that give the spleen a “Swiss cheese” appearance. For a definitive diagnosis, a USG-guided TruCut biopsy was done and sent for histopathological analysis. It confirmed the provisional diagnosis of diffuse splenic lymphangioma.
discussion: Background Splenic lymphangiomas or lymphangiomatosis represent a spectrum of benign lymphatic malformations affecting the spleen, ranging from solitary cystic lymphangiomas to multifocal diffuse lymphatic infiltration (lymphangiomatosis) [1]. Although classically paediatric, adult presentations are increasingly reported—often incidentally—because of a wider use of cross-sectional imaging [2]. The pathogenesis is thought to be a congenital maldevelopment of lymphatic channels, with occasional acquired/traumatic associations. Clinical Perspective Patients are often asymptomatic, with the lesion incidentally detected on imaging. Symptomatic cases may present with vague left upper quadrant pain, splenomegaly, or complications like rupture, infection, or hypersplenism [3]. Imaging is crucial for differentiation from other cystic splenic lesions such as hydatid cysts, haemangiomas, or metastases. Radiologists play a key role in identifying imaging features suggestive of lymphangioma and guiding further management [4]. Radiologic-pathologic correlation and awareness of this entity in adults are essential to avoid misdiagnosis and guide appropriate therapy [9,10]. Imaging Perspective On USG, splenic lymphangiomas appear as well-defined, anechoic or hypoechoic cystic lesions with thin septations and occasional calcifications. Internal debris may be present in case of haemorrhage [5]. On CT scans, they appear as multiloculated, non-enhancing cystic lesions with thin walls and possible peripheral or septal calcifications. No solid enhancing components are seen, which helps differentiate it from malignant lesions [6]. On MRI, T2-weighted images demonstrate a hyperintense multilocular lesion with fluid-fluid levels, while T1-weighted images show low signal intensity. Post-contrast imaging typically reveals minimal to no enhancement [7]. The final diagnosis is confirmed based on imaging features, clinical correlation, and histopathology in cases where the diagnosis is uncertain [9,10]. Outcome Management depends on symptoms and extent. Isolated lesions are often treated surgically (partial or total splenectomy) while multifocal disease may require conservative or multidisciplinary approaches. Because related symptoms were only mild discomfort, our patient was advised to undergo regular 6-monthly follow-ups with conservative management. She was informed that surgical splenectomy can be planned if complications or severe symptoms become present and that the prognosis is excellent with a minimal risk of malignant transformation [8,11]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Splenic lymphangiomas are rare congenital malformations of the lymphatic system that are often incidental findings. Imaging modalities like USG and MRI play a crucial role in diagnosis, distinguishing it from other splenic cystic lesions. Characteristic imaging features include multiloculated cystic morphology, absence of solid enhancement, and occasional calcifications. Asymptomatic cases require monitoring, while symptomatic cases may necessitate surgical intervention.

title: Tuberculous meningitis with cranial meningo-neuritis and incidental NF2
clinical_history: 37-year-old male with thunderclap headache, vomiting, and progressive bilateral visual and hearing loss. No fever, seizures, loss of consciousness, or focal limb weakness. Symptoms worsened over 10 days.
imaging_findings: MRI brain showed diffuse basal and perimesencephalic leptomeningeal enhancement (Figures 1a and 1b). Bilateral trigeminal nerves appeared thickened and intensely enhancing (Figures 2a and 2b). The optic chiasm was swollen with post-contrast enhancement, consistent with chiasmatic neuritis (Figure 3). Multiple venous haemorrhagic infarcts were seen in the bilateral temporal lobes (Figures 4a and 4b). Bilateral cerebellopontine angle masses with internal cystic areas and heterogeneous enhancement were present, compatible with vestibular schwannomas (Figure 5).
discussion: Background Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) results from haematogeneous dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis , producing dense exudates in the basal cisterns [1]. These exudates may encase cranial nerves and perforating vessels, leading to neuropathies and vasculitic or venous infarcts [2]. Clinical Perspective TBM often presents subacutely with headache, vomiting, visual impairment, or cranial neuropathies [1,3]. Early imaging is essential, as neurological deterioration may occur before laboratory confirmation. Identifying basal meningitis with cranial nerve involvement prompts urgent therapy. Imaging Perspective MRI features characteristic of TBM include thick basal leptomeningeal enhancement, cranial nerve involvement—especially II, III, V, and VI—and infarcts secondary to vasculitis or venous congestion [2]. Chiasmatic neuritis and bilateral trigeminal nerve enhancement are well-described manifestations of TBM-related neuritis [4]. Haemorrhagic infarcts, particularly in the temporal lobes or basal ganglia, result from the involvement of perforators and deep venous structures. Neurosarcoidosis may mimic TBM but tends to demonstrate nodular or dural enhancement and pituitary stalk thickening, which were absent here [6]. Autoimmune meningo-neuritis (IgG4-related or idiopathic) typically shows pachymeningeal involvement and lacks infarcts [5]. Incidental bilateral vestibular schwannomas fulfil diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) but are unrelated to the acute pathology [7]. Outcome Early antitubercular therapy plus corticosteroids improves outcomes and reduces infarct-related morbidity [1,3]. Visual and auditory deficits may persist if treatment is delayed. Recognition of incidental NF2 guides genetic evaluation and long-term surveillance. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Basal leptomeningitis with multiple cranial neuropathies strongly suggests tuberculous meningitis (TBM). Venous/vasculitic infarcts help differentiate TBM from neurosarcoidosis or autoimmune aetiologies. Coexisting pathology (e.g., NF2) may obscure the primary diagnosis; imaging pattern remains critical. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Incidental mediastinal mass in a young male with gynecomastia
clinical_history: A 20-year-old male, a smoker with a history of asthma and atopy, presented with left chest pain that increases with inspiration, lasting for 3 days. He also referred fatigue and chest tightness at night that required the use of a combined inhaler (budesonide + formoterol). No other symptoms or active prescriptions were documented. Blood test showed non-significant alterations.
imaging_findings: Initially, a plain chest x-ray revealing a mass in the left side of the anterior mediastinum was performed. Based on these findings, the mass was further evaluated with a contrast-enhanced body conventional CT-scan. The study showed a large, well-defined heterogeneous non-enhancing mass with small hypodense fatty areas (mean density: -83 Hounsfield units) located in the anterior mediastinum. It was in contact with the aortic arch and pericardium, compressed the brachiocephalic venous trunk, narrowed the left pulmonary artery and caused displacement of the arterial branches supplying the left upper lobe. Incidental gynecomastia was detected, which along with elevated hormone levels (β-HCG 575.3 mU/mL, AFP 6018 ng/mL, LDH 288 U/L) were clue in the radiological diagnosis. Non-specific bilateral hilar lymphatic cuffing were present. Finally, a PET scan was performed as a staging study, which allowed the evaluation of the mass behaviour and the identification of the area with the highest uptake, determining the most suitable region for CT-guided biopsy. Hilar nodes were FDG negative.
discussion: Background Extragonadal germ-cell tumours (GCTs) are rare neoplasms, most commonly affecting the anterior mediastinum, with a predilection for young males. Their estimated incident rate is 1.27 per 1,000,000 person-years [1]. Different origins are historically considered: metastases from gonadal GTCs and primary stem cells abnormally retained along the midline during embryonic migration. Non-seminomatous mediastinal GCTs (e.g., yolk sac tumours, embryonal carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, teratomas and mixed GCT) are more frequent than seminomas and have a worse prognosis [1–3]. Although not in our case, primary GTCs are associated with Klinefelter syndrome and haematologic malignancies. Abnormalities of the 12p chromosome are related, often gains and the presence of isochromosome i(12p) [1,2,4]. Like testicular GCTs, they typically secrete tumour markers alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-HCG) [4]. Clinical Perspective They can be found incidentally. Initial presentations comprise mainly dyspnoea, chest pain and cough, followed by fever and weight loss, vena cava syndrome when compression in advanced stages, and fatigue [3]. In some cases, haemoptysis, pericarditis or endocrine dysfunction have been described [5,6]. Imaging Perspective CT scan is the primary imaging tool. Seminomas appear as large, sharply marginated, homogeneous masses, some with ring-like and stippled calcifications, which tend to extend bilaterally within the mediastinum. Non-seminomatous GCTs might appear as large, heterogeneous masses with poor margins, some containing necrosis or haemorrhage, seen as low attenuation areas. The tumour occasionally invades the lung. Mature teratomas are usually well-defined, heterogeneous lesions containing fat, calcifications, teeth and/or fluid, usually extending unilaterally [5,7]. MRI helps in distinguishing tissue intensities and assessing tumour infiltration into the pericardium and great vessels [8]. Three stages are described, considering infiltration of adjacent structures (stage II) or metastatic disease (stage III) [1]. Imaging techniques, combined with elevated serum tumour markers (AFP and β-HCG, with normal values of < 10 ng/mL and 5 mU/mL, respectively), contribute to an accurate presumptive diagnosis by characterising masses and guiding targeted biopsy. Final diagnosis of GCTs is anatomopathological and immunohistochemical [3,5]. Outcome Management of non-seminomatous mediastinal GCTs generally involves neoadjuvant high-dose chemotherapy followed by surgical resection of residual tumour, with a poor prognosis, except for benign teratomas, which are treated with surgical excision alone. Despite seminomas being radiosensitive tumours, primary chemotherapy is nowadays the initial treatment. PET-CT is crucial for prognosis after treatment and follow-up [3]. In our patient, the association of a mediastinal mass, gynecomastia and elevated hormone levels strongly suggested a GCT. Primary biopsy reported a mixed mediastinal subtype with poor prognosis according to the IGCCCG (International Germ Cell Cancer Collaborative Group) criteria. Treatment consisted of chemotherapy and subsequent surgery. Surgical specimen revealed a mature teratoma with modifications attributable to neoadjuvancy.

title: Chasing the diagnosis of heroin induced toxic leukoencephalopathy
clinical_history: A 24-year-old male patient, a known heroin addict with a history of regular inhalation of heroin vapours, was brought to the emergency department by his family after an acute episode of generalised weakness followed by altered sensorium. MRI brain was done to rule out haemorrhage, infection, etc, and look for features of toxic encephalopathy.
imaging_findings: Large confluent near symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities are seen in periventricular white matter in the bilateral fronto-parieto-temporal region involving the bilateral corona radiata with sparing of the subcortical U-fibres (Figures 1a and 2a). There are selective supratentorial white matter hyperintensities involving the posterior limb of the bilateral internal capsule and sparing the anterior limb of the internal capsule (Figure 1b). Also, symmetrical cerebellar white matter hyperintensities sparing dentate nuclei on FLAIR (Figure 1d) and on T2-weighted images (Figure 2b). Mild diffusion restriction in the posterior limb of the bilateral internal capsule is observed (Figures 4a and 4b).
discussion: Background Leukoencephalopathy is a term for diseases affecting the white matter of the brain [1]. These can be attributed to various aetiologies, such as autoimmune, genetic, metabolic, or toxin-related conditions. Toxic leukoencephalopathy can be caused by chemotherapeutic drugs, environmental toxins, or substance abuse [1]. Here we have a case of toxic leukoencephalopathy by heroin inhalation. Histologically, it is characterised by spongiform changes in the white matter due to vacuolation of oligodendrocytes and myelin sheaths [2]. Clinical Perspective Heroin inhalation is an important cause of encephalopathy in young patients regardless of the documented history of drug abuse [3]. Patient symptomatology may range from dysarthria and ataxia to flaccid paralysis, depending on the stage (initial, intermediate or terminal stage) at which they presented to the hospital [4]. There could be a possible progression of the disease process for up to 6 months after cessation of heroin use [5]. Imaging Perspective Patients presenting with acute encephalopathic symptoms need MRI evaluation to rule out cerebral haemorrhage, infection or infarct. Heroin induced toxic leukoencephalopathy manifests as confluent, widespread, bilateral, symmetric white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities involving both supra and infratentorial compartments [5]. White matter hyperintensities involve corticospinal tracts and periventricular white matter, often sparing the subcortical U-fibres. There is symmetrical involvement of the posterior limb of the internal capsule, usually sparing the anterior limb [6]. Confluent symmetrical white matter hyperintensities in cerebellar hemispheres with sparing of dentate nuclei, giving a butterfly-wing pattern, are seen. Diffusion restriction may be seen in acute stages [5]. Along with signs and symptoms supportive of heroin induced leukoencephalopathy, positive heroin toxicology, history of heroin abuse by the patient, and neuroimaging findings consistent with this entity help in making a confident diagnosis. Outcome Imaging in cases with acute presentation helps to rule out haemorrhage, infarction or infection and aid in narrowing the differentials to leukoencephalopathy, especially when eliciting history related to drug abuse is a common challenge encountered in the clinical setting. Patient prognosis can be assessed based on clinico-radiological evaluation. If leukoencephalopathy and other toxin-related complications are recognised early, healthcare providers may timely intervene to provide appropriate medical therapy prior to the onset of irreversible white matter damage [3]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points A wide range of toxic and metabolic encephalopathy syndromes affect brain white matter and should be evaluated in the backdrop of appropriate clinical history and laboratory investigations. Prompt radiological investigation in cases of acute presentation is necessary to rule out other possible aetiologies. Written informed patient consent for publication has been obtained. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Fabry cardiomyopathy
clinical_history: A 36-year-old male with heterozygosity for the known pathogenic mutation in the galactosidase alpha ( GLA ) gene, consistent with Fabry disease, presents with shortness of breath on exertion, heart palpitations and fainting.
imaging_findings: Cardiac MRI (CMR), carried out at 1,5T, demonstrated markedly reduced native T1 values (Figures 1a and 1b) consistent with intracellular sphingolipid accumulation. Normal values on the T2* mapping (Figure 2) excluded myocardial iron deposition. There was no evidence of focal myocardial oedema or inflammation based on the T2 maps (Figure 3). There was focal, non-ischemic mid-wall fibrosis in the basal inferolateral left ventricular wall, as evidenced by late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) (Figure 4). In addition, mild concentric left ventricular hypertrophy was present with a maximal wall thickness of 14 mm (Figures 5a and 5b).
discussion: Background Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in the GLA gene, resulting in deficient α-galactosidase A [1]. This results in glycosphingolipid buildup within lysosomes, which disrupts cellular function, especially in endothelial cells, causing hypoperfusion, inflammation, oxidative stress and cell death, eventually leading to fibrosis [2]. The biological diagnosis typically involves two steps: screening for deficient α-galactosidase A (α-gal A) enzyme activity (reliable in males) and measuring the accumulating substrate, globotriaosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb3), in plasma or urine [3]. Due to random X-chromosome inactivation, α-gal A enzyme activity can be normal in female carriers, and lyso-Gb3 levels may also overlap with the normal range in up to two-thirds of affected women [4]. Therefore, molecular genetic testing for GLA gene mutations is essential for a definitive diagnosis in all individuals, but particularly in women, where enzymatic and biomarker assays can be inconclusive [5]. Cardiac involvement is a major determinant of morbidity and mortality. Fabry cardiomyopathy is typically characterised by concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), fibrosis, arrhythmias, and eventual heart failure [1]. Clinical Perspective Patients may present with non-specific symptoms such as exertional dyspnoea, palpitations, syncope or chest pain [1]. Because Fabry cardiomyopathy can mimic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and hypertensive heart disease, early recognition is challenging [1]. CMR with native T1 mapping is crucial in the detection of Fabry disease, prompting genetic testing and enabling timely therapy initiation [1]. Imaging Perspective CMR is the gold standard of imaging. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) typically can show mid-wall fibrosis of the basal inferolateral wall, indicating myocardial inflammation and/or fibrosis [1]. T1 mapping reveals reduced T1 values due to intracellular sphingolipid accumulation [1]. This unique characteristic makes T1 mapping essential in differentiating Fabry disease from other phenocopies of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, as the reduced T1 is highly specific to the storage of sphingolipids. Moreover, there is an evolving clinical perspective that the presence of reduced native T1 time, even in the absence of LVH or LGE, should prompt consideration for timely therapy initiation to prevent progression to irreversible myocardial fibrosis [6,7]. Beyond lipid storage, CMR can detect myocardial inflammation indicated by increased native T2 values, a finding often linked to chronic troponin elevation and suggesting chronic myocardial oedema; specific Fabry disease treatments appear to be effective on this inflammation, as shown by the comparative evolution of T2 values over time [8,9]. Outcome Disease-modifying therapies include enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) [1]. These interventions may prevent progression if started before irreversible fibrosis occurs [1]. Gene therapy and substrate reduction therapy are under investigation [1]. Imaging plays a central role in identifying early myocardial involvement, monitoring treatment response and determining prognosis, as the presence of extensive fibrosis on CMR is associated with worse outcomes and reduced treatment response [1]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Fabry cardiomyopathy should be suspected in patients with unexplained concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, especially when accompanied by systemic features or family history [1]. Cardiac MRI (CMR) with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and T1 mapping provide key imaging and diagnostic clues. Early imaging and recognition enable a timely initiation of disease-specific therapy, which may alter prognosis [2]. title: A metallic mistake: Complications of intravenous mercury poisoning
clinical_history: A 19-year-old female nurse presented with six days of high-grade fever, vomiting, diarrhoea, and dry cough. She had no dyspnoea, abdominal pain, altered sensorium, or seizures. On admission, she was febrile but vitally stable with a normal physical examination. Labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia. Cultures and tropical fever profile were negative.
imaging_findings: The chest radiograph showed multiple pinpoint metallic densities diffusely scattered in both lungs and liver, arranged in a branching, symmetric pattern (Figure 1). High-resolution CT (HRCT) thorax confirmed hyperattenuating bilateral metallic densities with artefacts in the lung parenchyma (Figures 2 and 3). No pleural effusion was initially observed, and the pulmonary arteries appeared normal. Similar high attenuation metallic densities were also identified in the heart, both lobes of the liver, spinal canal, and right kidney (Figures 3 and 4), suggesting widespread systemic distribution, likely via vascular or embolic routes. The branching lung opacities were consistent with deposition in the pulmonary vasculature or airways. The absence of initial pleural or structural abnormalities supported an embolic aetiology. Multiorgan involvement raised suspicion of systemic metallic embolism, possibly from intravenous injection of metallic substances. Follow-up imaging after two weeks (Figure 5) showed no change in the distribution or appearance of metallic densities, but a new moderate right-sided pleural effusion was noted, indicating evolving pathology potentially linked to the underlying embolic process.
discussion: Mercury is a toxic heavy metal that affects multiple organ systems. Elemental mercury is particularly hazardous when inhaled or injected intravenously—a rare occurrence often linked to self-harm or accidental exposure [1]. Once in circulation, it crosses biological membranes, accumulates in cells, and causes dose-dependent toxicity. Acute manifestations include fever and gastrointestinal, respiratory, or neurological symptoms, while chronic effects involve nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, and dermatologic changes [2]. Documented complications also include interstitial pneumonitis, peripheral neuropathy, asthenozoospermia, aplastic anaemia, and cardiac granulomatous inflammation [3]. A prior report described a case involving high fever, lymphadenopathy, rash, dyspnoea, tachycardia, and chest pain after inhalational exposure [4]. Our case similarly presented as pyrexia of unknown origin. Suspicious imaging prompted further history-taking, revealing a history of intravenous mercury injection, possibly self-administered, a day before symptom onset. Serum and urinary mercury levels were elevated. The patient also had leukocytosis with neutrophilia. A systematic review of 69 studies confirmed mercury’s haematotoxic effects, including anaemia, lymphocytosis, lymphopenia, neutrophilia, and basophilia [5]. Cardiac evaluation revealed a few ectopic beats, with a normal ECG and serum electrolytes. Intravenous elemental mercury produces pathognomonic imaging findings central to diagnosis. Chest radiographs show multiple radiopaque, branching metallic densities symmetrically distributed along the pulmonary vasculature, mimicking a “tree-in-bud” pattern—indicative of metallic emboli [6,7]. HRCT refines this, revealing hyperdense foci (> 1000 Hounsfield units) within pulmonary arteries, cardiac chambers, and sometimes systemic organs like the liver and kidneys [6–8,11]. Pooling in the heart and branching vascular opacities reinforce a vascular origin [8,9]. HRCT is the most sensitive modality for detecting intravascular mercury, while chest X-ray is a useful initial screening tool [6,8]. MRI is generally avoided due to susceptibility artefacts. Echocardiography or ultrasound may show echogenic foci in the heart if mercury has accumulated [8,9]. Diagnosis is supported by characteristic imaging, elevated mercury levels, and clinical context, often involving self-harm or accidental injection [7,10]. Imaging is crucial for guiding management. Localised emboli without systemic symptoms may be treated conservatively, while widespread cardiac or systemic involvement can necessitate surgery or chelation therapy [7,9]. Our patient was initiated on oral DMSA and selenium. The patient remained haemodynamically stable, with no worsening breathlessness or oxygen requirement. A follow-up chest radiograph after 2 weeks showed a right-sided pleural effusion and persistent mercury deposits in both lung fields (Figure 5a). Hence, imaging also helps detect complications such as pneumonitis or pulmonary hypertension, and allows monitoring of treatment response. Early imaging ensures accurate risk assessment and timely intervention, improving clinical outcomes [6,9,10].

title: Critical illness-associated cerebral microbleeds mimicking emboli in sepsis
clinical_history: A 79‑year‑old male with right lower limb necrotising fasciitis, post-debridement and fasciotomy, was admitted with confusion, disorientation, and respiratory distress. He developed septic shock, encephalopathy, and acute kidney injury. No meningism was noted, but severe quadriparesis was present.
imaging_findings: MRI brain revealed multiple punctate foci of susceptibility weighted imaging (SWI) blooming in bilateral cerebral (predominant subcortical white matter) and cerebellar hemispheres, corpus callosum, bilateral internal and external capsules, and pons. No diffusion restriction was seen. The classical pattern of SWI blooming and clinical setting favoured critical illness–associated cerebral microbleeds (CIACM) over embolic lesions.
discussion: Background Critical illness–associated cerebral microbleeds (CIACM) represent a distinctive neuroimaging entity increasingly recognised in severely ill patients. These microbleeds diffusely involve the juxtacortical white matter, corpus callosum, and cerebellum, sparing the deep and periventricular white matter, as well as the cerebral cortex. The proposed mechanism centres on hypoxaemia-induced endothelial injury and blood–brain barrier disruption, which cause leakage of erythrocytes into the parenchyma. Oxidative stress and inflammatory mediators during sepsis or respiratory failure further aggravate vascular permeability. This pattern closely resembles microbleeds seen in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) therapy, and high-altitude cerebral oedema, supporting a unifying hypoxic–vascular pathogenesis [1,4,5]. Clinical Perspective Patients with CIACM are typically critically ill, with conditions such as sepsis, respiratory failure, or shock, and often require intensive care or ventilatory support. Neurological manifestations are non-specific, including altered sensorium, encephalopathy, or generalised weakness. In this case, the patient presented with septic shock and quadriparesis in the absence of focal deficits or meningism. Recognition of CIACM is important to avoid overdiagnosis of embolic or haemorrhagic pathology and to guide appropriate clinical management. Imaging Perspective MRI using susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) or T2*-gradient echo sequences is diagnostic, showing numerous punctate hypointense foci with a characteristic distribution. In contrast to hypertensive or amyloid angiopathy microbleeds, CIACM lesions cluster at the grey–white junction and the corpus callosum, while sparing the basal ganglia and thalami. The absence of diffusion restriction or infarction supports a non-embolic origin [1–3]. Outcome Most patients exhibit neurological recovery as systemic illness resolves, although cognitive sequelae may persist. Follow-up MRI often demonstrates partial resolution or stabilisation of lesions without new haemorrhages. Teaching Points Critical illness–associated cerebral microbleeds (CIACM) is a distinct, hypoxaemia-related microvascular phenomenon. Juxtacortical and callosal microbleeds with deep grey sparing are diagnostic clues. Recognition prevents misinterpretation as embolic lesions and avoids unnecessary therapy escalation.

title: Intramuscular myxoma with radiological-pathological correlation
clinical_history: A 46-year-old patient presented with a gradually enlarging, painless swelling in the posterior right thigh, first noticed two years earlier. There was no history of trauma. Discomfort was mainly triggered by sitting or exertion. Examination revealed a soft, mobile, non-adherent mass without neurological deficits.
imaging_findings: MRI of the right thigh (Figure 1) demonstrated a well-circumscribed, ovoid lesion within the proximal semitendinosus muscle, measuring 5.6 cm craniocaudally. The lesion exhibited marked hyperintensity on T2-weighted and fluid-sensitive sequences, with fine internal hypointense septa, and low signal on T1-weighted images. Subtle adjacent muscle oedema and limited fatty infiltration indicated slow growth. No evidence of tendon or neurovascular involvement, haematoma, or bone marrow abnormality was observed. Follow-up MRI at 15 months post-excision (Figure 2) confirmed complete resection, with no residual mass or recurrence and preserved surrounding muscle architecture.
discussion: Background Intramuscular myxoma is a rare mesenchymal tumour and most frequently arises in the deep muscles of the lower extremities, particularly the thigh. Patients are typically middle-aged adults with a slight female predominance [1,2]. Histologically, it is characterised by an abundant extracellular myxoid matrix with absent mitotic activity and necrosis [1]. Multiple myxomas with associated polyostotic fibrous dysplasia represent the rare Mazabraud syndrome, but no imaging or clinical features suggestive of this syndrome were present in our patient. Clinical Perspective Patients often report a slow-growing, deep, painless mass, although mild local discomfort or pressure can be present, especially during physical activity or when sitting. Typically, there is no history of trauma or systemic symptoms. Clinical suspicion is often low, and imaging is essential for lesion characterisation, evaluation of its relationship with adjacent structures, and exclusion of aggressive features. Imaging Perspective The classic MRI features of intramuscular myxoma are a well-defined, ovoid intramuscular lesion with low T1 and marked T2 hyperintensity (reflecting the myxoid matrix’s high-water content). Fine internal hypointense septa are highly characteristic and, when present, strongly support the diagnosis. Mild adjacent muscle oedema and limited fatty infiltration are commonly present, supporting the diagnosis of a slow-growing, expansile benign tumour. Occasionally, a “bright cap” or “bright rim” may be visible on T2-weighted images at the lesion’s poles or periphery. Differentials include myxoid liposarcoma, which presents as a heterogeneous, infiltrative mass with ill-defined margins, areas of haemorrhage and necrosis, as well as prominent enhancement after contrast administration [3,4]. Myxofibrosarcoma, another differential, frequently displays a “tail sign” that represents curvilinear extensions of the tumour along the fascial planes, as well as a more infiltrative growth. Chronic organised haematoma may be considered if there is a history of trauma, especially if the lesion has changed in size or signal over time, or if blood products are seen. Although less common, intramuscular haemangiomas are also a differential, often containing vascular channels, phleboliths, or flow voids [5]. Outcome In this case, histology demonstrated a hypocellular myxoid stroma with scattered bland spindle cells, focal permeation of muscle fibres (“checkerboard” pattern), and no evidence of atypia, mitosis, or necrosis (Figure 3). Surgical margins were free of tumour, confirming complete excision, which is almost always curative [1,5]. Recurrence is exceedingly rare. Imaging follow-up at 15 months post-resection showed no signs of recurrence or complications (Figure 2). Take Home Message / Teaching Points Intramuscular myxoma presents on MRI as a well-circumscribed T1-hypointense and T2-hyperintense lesion with fine septa and mild perilesional oedema. Stable slow growth and an absent history of trauma help differentiate it from a haematoma. Malignant myxoid tumours, such as myxoid liposarcoma, often show heterogeneous signal, infiltrative margins, or aggressive features. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Thrombosed superficial venous aneurysm
clinical_history: A 27-year-old female dentist presents with a small, painful mass in the first interdigital space of the left hand. Ultrasound (US) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were ordered for further characterisation of the mass on the left hand.
imaging_findings: On US, a small subcutaneous mass was visualised with an incomplete hypoechogenic peripheral ring and a central isoechogenic area (Figure 1). Minimal peripheral compressibility was observed (Figure 1b). Adjacent small vessels were noted with colour Doppler (Figures 1c, 1d, 1e, and 1f). On MRI, the lesion showed high T1 signal (Figure 2a), high PD FS signal (Figure 2b), high T2* signal with peripheral blooming artifact (Figure 2c), high DWI signal on b800 images (Figure 2d), low ADC signal (Figure 2e), high signal on the pre-contrast T1 FS sequence (Figure 2f), and no contrast enhancement on the post-contrast T1 FS sequence (Figure 2g). Histopathology (Figure 3) revealed a thrombus with focal signs of organisation and early recanalisation. A vascular structure with venous appearance and a dilated lumen in the adjacent connective tissue was also identified, as well as an artery without alterations.
discussion: Background Venous aneurysms are rare [1]. There is no known gender or age predominance. The pathogenesis is unknown [2]. In our case, repetitive occupational microtrauma (dentist) is the suspected cause of the lesion. The best definition of a venous aneurysm is a solitary area of venous dilatation (more than 1.5 times the diameter of the normal vessel) with a communicating vein and without a communicating artery (arteriovenous malformation, AVF) or a pseudoaneurysm [3,4]. Focal dilatation of a varicose vein is not considered a venous aneurysm. Clinical Perspective Venous aneurysms are usually not of clinical significance [1]. However, they can present as a part of an episode of deep venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism. Symptoms, if present, include pain and extremity oedema due to vascular reflux [1–4]. Diagnosis by physical examination is often straightforward when presenting as a soft compressible mass, but it can mimic inguinal or femoral hernias [3]. Differentiation with imaging (ultrasound, angiography, CT, MRI) from other forms of vascular malformations or soft-tissue masses is necessary, especially if thrombosis in the venous aneurysm simulates a solid mass. Biopsy or surgical excision should be considered for unequivocal lesions. Imaging Perspective On ultrasound, compressibility, blood flow, connection to the venous system, and total or partial thrombosis can be visualised. In cases of thrombosis, a peripheral halo of low echogenicity is indicative of a thickened vessel wall, while internal heterogeneous/high echogenicity signals the thrombus. With MRI, the flow void, connection to the superficial venous system, and additional post-contrast images confirm the diagnosis. With chronic thrombosis, high T1, high/low T2 signal, T2* blooming artefact, and diffusion restriction can be observed. Outcome Symptoms and cosmetic reasons might lead to surgical excision, generally without reconstruction [2]. Establishing localisation and differentiation from AVF and soft-tissue masses is the goal of imaging. Take-Home Message Venous aneurysms, especially when thrombosed, represent an important differential diagnosis in suspected soft-tissue masses.
