title: Peritrochanteric elastofibroma – An unusual cause of snapping hip
clinical_history: A 49-year-old male patient presented with bilateral lateral hip swellings and clicking. On clinical examination, there was a palpable firm bump over the greater trochanter with mild tenderness on pressing. There was an audible click in hip flexion.
imaging_findings: Anteroposterior plain radiograph of the pelvis and both hips (Figure 1) showed bilateral reduced joint space with femoral cam and pincer morphology. No enthesopathy or calcification around the greater trochanter (Figure 1). Hip ultrasound (Figure 2) demonstrated a soft tissue lesion lying superficial to the greater trochanter, hypoechoic with internal echogenic fatty streaks. The appearance is quite similar to that of the more superficial gluteal maximus muscle. No abnormal vascularity at Doppler. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), axial T1-weighted, demonstrated a soft tissue lesion located superficial to the greater trochanter and deep to the iliotibial band, larger on the right side. Both T1 (Figure 3a) and T2-weighted (Figures 3b and 3c) showed the lesions to be isointense to nearby muscles, with intrinsic high-signal fat streaks creating the characteristic striated pattern. Coronal STIR images (Figure 4) redemonstrated the soft tissue lesions lying just deep to the iliotibial band, with the right lesion slightly larger; otherwise, both are of similar heterogeneous internal signal.
discussion: Elastofibroma is in the category of fibroblastic/myofibroblastic benign soft tissue tumours, according to the most updated WHO classification of soft tissue tumours [1]. It usually arises in the subscapular region [2]. A few other locations have been reported in the literature, for example, around the olecranon process, mediastinum, stomach wall, gluteal region and anterior thighs [3–7]. It has been postulated that the lesion arises secondary to friction and repeated microtrauma or perhaps altered fibrogenesis leading to abnormal soft tissue growth [8]. The pathogenesis however remains unclear. Elastofibromas are usually slowly-growing, asymptomatic lesions. We are more familiar with the more common subscapular lesions. These are usually detected incidentally while imaging for other purposes. They may also present as a swelling, which is occasionally painful, or with contour asymmetry. They are often associated with a click or a snap when moving the shoulder [2,8]. Bilateral concomitant gluteal elastofibromas were described in a case report of an adult male who presented with right side swelling, discomfort and pain on walking. The contralateral side lesion was recognised on MRI [7]. Histologically, elastofibromas are composed of a mixture of collagen, elastic fibres and adipose tissue. On imaging, this appears as a soft tissue lesion with a texture quite similar to that of normal muscles on US, CT, and MRI. The most defining appearance is at MRI, where the lesion is isointense to skeletal muscles with a characteristic striated pattern created by internal fat streaks (Lasagna-like appearance) [9]. Malignant transformation has not been reported or described, and hence an aggressive behaviour at imaging should be concerning for an otherwise diagnosis. In the peritrochanteric region, elastofibromas can mimic more common conditions such as trochanteric bursitis. Differentiation relies on imaging, as bursitis typically demonstrates a fluid-filled bursal sac without the internal striated fat pattern seen in elastofibromas [10]. The management of elastofibroma is based on the clinical presentation, mostly conservative for asymptomatic lesions and surgical excision for symptomatic ones. Take Home Message Elastofibroma is a benign soft tissue tumour with a characteristic striated pattern on different imaging modalities that may arise at atypical locations, such as the peritrochanteric gluteal area. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Magnetic resonance imaging features of hereditary spastic paraplegia
clinical_history: A 12-year-old female presented with progressive gait disturbance and lower limb stiffness over 2 years, followed by the development of dysarthria and impaired coordination. Neurological examination revealed lower limb spasticity, brisk deep tendon reflexes, and mild cognitive impairment. Family history was unremarkable.
imaging_findings: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and spine demonstrated hallmark abnormalities. Sagittal and coronal T2-weighted brain sequences (Figures 1a and 1b) revealed diffuse thinning and atrophy of the corpus callosum [1,4]. Axial T2 FLAIR imaging showed the classic “ear of the lynx” sign (Figure 2a), consisting of symmetric periventricular hyperintensities adjacent to the frontal horns [2]. Additionally, sagittal T2-weighted images of the thoracic spine demonstrated diffuse spinal cord atrophy (Figure 2b). Together, these imaging findings strongly supported the clinical suspicion of hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP). Corpus callosum involvement is a well-recognised marker in complicated forms of HSP, particularly in SPG11 and SPG15 subtypes [1,4]. Also, spinal cord findings are consistent with corticospinal tract degeneration reported in autosomal dominant and recessive HSP variants [3].
discussion: Hereditary spastic paraplegias (HSPs) are a heterogeneous group of inherited neurodegenerative disorders characterised by progressive spasticity and weakness of the lower limbs. They are broadly classified as “pure” (spastic paraparesis alone) and “complicated” forms (associated with additional neurological features such as cognitive decline, epilepsy, or ataxia) [4]. MRI plays a pivotal role in diagnosis, especially when clinical features are nonspecific. Atrophy of the corpus callosum is a well-recognised imaging marker in complicated HSP syndromes, particularly SPG11 and SPG15 [1]. The “ear of the lynx” sign, seen as bilateral periventricular frontal white matter hyperintensities, is considered highly suggestive of SPG11-associated HSP [2,5]. Spinal cord atrophy is another supportive imaging feature, reflecting long-tract degeneration [3]. Early recognition of these imaging markers can direct genetic testing, shorten diagnostic delays, and aid family counselling. Differential diagnoses include leukodystrophies, demyelinating disorders and other causes of hereditary leukopathies. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Corpus callosum atrophy and the “ear of the lynx” sign are highly suggestive of complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia. Recognition of these features on MRI helps guide genetic testing and avoid unnecessary work-up. Spinal cord atrophy is a supportive imaging finding reflecting corticospinal tract degeneration. Written informed consent for publication of this case report and accompanying images was obtained from the patient’s father, as the patient is a minor. All identifying information has been removed to ensure anonymity.

title: Persistent lateral knee pain in a 48-year-old patient
clinical_history: A 48-year-old man of African descent presented with persistent lateral knee pain, reduced motion, and difficulty with weight-bearing, nine months after a minor traumatic event. Orthopaedic examination revealed significant tenderness over the lateral femoral condyle, with stable ligaments. He smokes ten cigarettes daily, failed physiotherapy, and laboratory tests showed marked thrombocytosis and microcytic anaemia, with all other blood tests unremarkable.
imaging_findings: MRI of the right knee, performed with proton density with fat saturation (Figure 1) and T1-weighted (Figure 2) sequences, demonstrated bone marrow oedema involving the lateral epicondyle of the femur, extending proximally into the femoral shaft. Within the subchondral region of the lateral femoral condyle, a serpiginous low-signal-intensity line was identified, associated with confluent subarticular cyst formation. No unstable bony fragments were observed. Moderate joint effusion was present, without intra-articular loose bodies. Menisci, cruciate and collateral ligaments, articular cartilage outside the described area, and the patellofemoral joint were preserved. Surrounding soft tissues were unremarkable.
discussion: Background Knee avascular necrosis (AVN), is a progressive degenerative process caused by loss of blood flow to the subchondral bone. This results in bone cell death, progressive structural weakening, and, if untreated, eventual collapse and joint surface destruction [1]. The exact mechanisms remain incompletely understood, but proposed contributors include vascular obstruction, direct injury to bone tissue, and elevated intraosseous pressure [1]. In haemoglobinopathies, such as sickle cell disease, repeated microvascular occlusions caused by abnormally shaped red blood cells and chronic anaemia make the subchondral bone particularly vulnerable to ischaemia [2]. Without early diagnosis and intervention, the disease can advance to chondral damage and severe osteoarthritis, at which point knee arthroplasty is often the only definitive solution [1]. Clinical Perspective Early-stage AVN of the knee can be difficult to recognise clinically, as initial symptoms such as pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility are non-specific [3]. Known risk factors include trauma, corticosteroid exposure, alcohol misuse, and haemoglobinopathies [3]. In sickle cell disease, the knee is a relatively frequent site of AVN, but early lesions are often missed on plain radiographs [2]. For this reason, MRI is crucial, not only for confirming the diagnosis but also for establishing the stage, assessing the subchondral surface, and predicting the likelihood of collapse. From a reporting standpoint, radiologists should describe the lesion’s size, location, stage, and any associated joint changes to guide whether conservative or surgical treatment is the most appropriate [1,2]. Imaging Perspective MRI is both the most sensitive and most specific imaging method for AVN, with reported diagnostic accuracy approaching 100% [3]. Early in the disease, imaging may reveal only subtle marrow oedema in areas where AVN commonly occurs [3]. As the process matures, a serpiginous or ring-shaped low-signal border appears on T1-weighted sequences, marking the interface between necrotic and viable bone. On T2-weighted or fat-suppressed sequences, this often produces the classic “double-line sign”, combining an inner bright line of granulation tissue with an outer dark sclerotic rim [4]. In haemoglobinopathy-related AVN, lesions can show mixed signal patterns depending on chronicity, often with serpiginous high T2 signal [2]. Follow-up MRI may capture the transition from early ill-defined marrow changes to the established infarct rim, the so-called “birth of death” evolution [4]. CT and radiographs have limited sensitivity in the early phase [3]. Outcome Management aims to preserve joint function and delay replacement. Our patient was managed conservatively with a lateral offloading knee brace for daily practice and scheduled for follow-up. In advanced cases, options include core decompression, osteochondral grafting, regenerative techniques pre-collapse, osteotomy and arthroplasty. Informed patient consent for publication has been obtained.

title: Calcified chondroid mesenchymal neoplasm of the mandible: A diagnostic challenge
clinical_history: A 69-year-old male presented to his general practitioner with an 8-month history of a painless left cheek lump. On clinical examination, the lump was approximately 6 cm in size, non-mobile, non-tender and showed no erythematous changes. Initial bloods performed were unremarkable, and the patient was referred for an ultrasound examination of the lump.
imaging_findings: Initial ultrasound showed a well-circumscribed left pre-auricular mass with mixed isoechoic solid and cystic components, and minor peripheral vascularity, raising suspicion for a salivary gland neoplasm (Figure 1). Fine-needle aspiration was inconclusive, prompting an MRI. MRI revealed a large, multilobulated mass centred on a widened temporomandibular joint, hyperintense on T2 (Figure 2a), isointense on T1 (Figure 2b) with a hypointense capsule, and heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement (Figure 3) without diffusion restriction (Figure 4). There was no joint effusion. The lesion caused glenoid fossa attenuation (suggesting bony erosion) and extended into the masticator space, encasing the left mandibular condyle and ramus without direct erosion (Figure 5). Adjacent muscles were displaced but not infiltrated (Figure 6). CT showed an expansile lucent mass with “ring and arc” calcifications, confirming erosion of the glenoid fossa and adjacent middle cranial fossa floor, with surrounding sclerosis (Figure 7). FDG PET/CT demonstrated intense uptake (SUVmax 18.7) (Figure 8). Excisional biopsy identified a benign, locally aggressive calcified chondroid mesenchymal neoplasm.
discussion: Background Benign, locally aggressive calcified chondroid mesenchymal neoplasms (BCCMNs) of the mandible are rare soft-tissue tumours characterised by a mixture of cartilaginous, osseous, and fibrous components [1,2]. Although histologically benign, they exhibit locally invasive behaviour. These tumours are believed to originate from mesenchymal precursors capable of cartilaginous differentiation. The pathophysiology involves proliferation of immature chondroid cells within a calcified matrix, often resulting in expansive growth and cortical disruption without distant metastasis [3,4]. Clinical Perspective Patients typically present with painless mandibular swelling, facial asymmetry, or loosening of teeth. Occasionally, pain or paraesthesia may occur if the lesion encroaches on the inferior alveolar nerve. Imaging is essential due to the lesion’s deceptive benign appearance on clinical evaluation, yet aggressive radiological behaviour. Radiologists must convey the lesion’s size, extent, cortical breach, periosteal reaction, and potential involvement of adjacent structures to aid in surgical planning [5]. Imaging Perspective On imaging, BCCMNs often appear as well-defined, expansile radiolucent lesions with scattered calcifications or chondroid matrix mineralisation. CT is valuable for detecting fine calcifications and assessing cortical destruction. MRI provides superior delineation of soft tissue extension and marrow involvement. A “rings and arcs” calcification pattern is suggestive of chondroid origin. Diagnosis is confirmed via biopsy with histological evaluation, revealing a mix of chondroid tissue, immature bone, and myxoid stroma [6,7]. Outcome Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment due to the tumour’s locally aggressive nature. Curettage alone may lead to recurrence. Long-term follow-up is necessary given the potential for local relapse. Imaging significantly influences the surgical approach, extent of resection, and reconstruction planning [4]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points BCCMNs, while benign, behave aggressively and can mimic malignant lesions. Early and accurate imaging assessment is critical for optimal management. CT and MRI are complementary tools for evaluating calcification and soft tissue extension, respectively. Histopathology is mandatory for definitive diagnosis. Surgical resection with clear margins offers the best prognosis. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Young woman with uterine mass, lung nodules and cysts
clinical_history: A 41-year-old woman presents with thoracic pain and slight dyspnoea after a minor chest-related trauma earlier that day. Her medical history revealed resection of a uterine mass one year ago.
imaging_findings: A CT chest (Figure 1) was performed, which showed a prominent right-sided pneumothorax accompanied by a small haemorrhagic pleural effusion. No rib fractures could be identified. Bilateral cysts were present in both lungs, without a distinct predominant location. The cysts were round and showed a thin, symmetric wall. Some cysts (for example, the one in the left lower lobe in Figure 1b) showed vascular indentations. Two solid nodules of approximately 10 mm were visualised, in the right middle lobe and right lower lobe, respectively. A pelvic MRI approximately one year ago (Figure 2) showed a large, well-circumscribed mass located in the uterus. This lesion was heterogeneous, mostly hypointense on both T1 (not shown) and T2-weighted imaging with focal necrotic areas. Multiple flow voids were present within the mass. There was heterogeneous, intense contrast enhancement. The mass did not invade other nearby structures.
discussion: PEComas are rare mesenchymal tumours, consisting of perivascular epithelioid cells (PECs), of which the precursor cell or normal counterpart is unknown. While most cases are benign, some might have a malignant potential [1–3]. PEComas are most often located in the retroperitoneum, the kidneys, and the genitourinary tract, but can also be found in other organs [3]. Although very rare, multiple PEComas in either one organ or in multiple different organs have been reported [4,5]. On imaging, these tumours do not have specific imaging characteristics to differentiate them from other types of tumours [1,6]. In this case, it is important to realise that lymfangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is considered a low-grade neoplasm, which is classified as a sub-entity within the PEComa family per the WHO 2015 classification [7]. LAM is a rare neoplastic disease, almost exclusively found in women. LAM can be divided into two groups: sporadic (S-LAM) and tuberous sclerosis complex-associated (TSC-LAM) [8]. In this case, there was no history or signs of TSC. LAM is characterised by cystic destruction of the lung parenchyma [9,10]. These cysts are classically uniform, round, thin-walled, and distributed in a diffuse, relatively symmetric pattern. These cysts are commonly around 2–10 mm large. In comparison to other cystic lung diseases, these cysts do not show any predilection site or a region of sparing. Common complications include spontaneous (multiple or bilateral) pneumothorax or chylothorax. Frequent associations, especially in TSC-LAM, include renal angiomyolipomas and multifocal multinodular pneumocyte hyperplasia (MMPH), the latter presenting as small, scattered ground-glass lung opacities [8,11,12]. However, this case showed solid lung nodules, which would have been atypical of MMPH [1,13]. In this case, the mass in the uterus (Figure 2) was resected approximately one year ago due to volume progression. On imaging, the main differential diagnosis was a uterine leiomyoma. However, on histology, this tumour proved to be a PEComa with possible malignant potential. The patient underwent video-assisted thoracic surgery on the right side due to the combination of lung nodules, lung cysts and pneumothorax. The lung nodule located in the right middle lobe was resected during the procedure, which, on histopathology, turned out to be a PEComa. This was believed to be a metastasis from the uterine PEComa or, less likely, a new primary PEComa. The lung cysts were considered to be LAM, but no pathological proof was obtained. Teaching Points Consider the diagnosis of PEComa for new lesions or masses found in patients known to have lymfangioleiomyomatosis (LAM). And consider LAM in patients with PEComa. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: PEComa of the uterus with lung metastasis and associated lymfangioleiomyomatosis Lymfangioleiomyomatosis with associated multifocal multinodular pneumocyte hyperplasia Uterine leiomyosarcoma with lung metastasis Sjögren with associated lymphoid interstitial pneumonia
final_diagnosis: PEComa of the uterus with lung metastasis and associated lymfangioleiomyomatosis

title: From lesion to resolution: Rare case of seronegative Bickerstaff encephalitis
clinical_history: A 45-year-old woman presented with a two-day headache, giddiness, blurred vision, and without weakness, slurred speech and fever. She had a fever with loose stools a week earlier. Lumbar puncture revealed mild pleocytosis (polymorph predominance). All serological testings for anti-GQ1b, ANA, encephalitis panel, anti-MOG, and anti-NMO antibodies were negative. Contrast-enhanced MRI was performed.
imaging_findings: The initial MRI demonstrated an ill-defined confluent FLAIR/T2 hyperintense lesion (Figures 1a and 1b) with mild expansion involving the pons, midbrain, right middle and superior cerebellar peduncles, and adjacent right cerebellar hemisphere (Figure 1c). The lesion was hypointense on T1, showed irregular peripheral contrast enhancement (Figure 1e), and had no diffusion restriction (Figure 1d) or susceptibility blooming on SWI. MR spectroscopy revealed preserved NAA peak without significant Cho:NAA (choline:N-acetylaspartate) ratio alteration (Figure 2), while perfusion imaging showed no increase in rCBV (Figure 3), suggesting a non-neoplastic inflammatory process. MR angiography demonstrated normal flow signals without stenosis or occlusion (Figure 4). Spine screening was normal. Whole-body PET-CT (Figure 5) showed no FDG uptake, ruling out neoplastic or infectious aetiology. Follow-up MRIs at one and three months (Figures 4a and 4b, respectively) demonstrated progressive and near-complete resolution of the lesion, correlating with clinical improvement after high-dose methylprednisolone followed by intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy.
discussion: Background Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis (BBE) is a rare, immune-mediated, often post-infectious demyelinating disorder predominantly involving the brainstem and cerebellar peduncles. It forms, along with Guillain–Barré and Miller Fisher syndromes, part of a clinical-immunologic spectrum often linked to anti-GQ1b antibodies [1,2], although seronegativity does not exclude the diagnosis. The pathophysiology is presumed to be molecular mimicry following respiratory or gastrointestinal infection, leading to autoimmune attack on brainstem myelin [3]. The condition remains underdiagnosed due to overlapping features with infectious and neoplastic brainstem syndromes. Clinical Perspective Clinically, BBE presents subacutely with the triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and altered consciousness [2,4]. Some patients may also exhibit facial palsy, dysarthria or pyramidal signs. In this case, the patient presented with headache, giddiness and blurred vision—an atypical but compatible prodrome. The cerebrospinal fluid may show mild pleocytosis or elevated protein levels; however, antibody positivity is not mandatory for diagnosis [5]. Imaging is crucial to guide early immunotherapy and to reassure the referring neurologist regarding the benign, reversible nature of this disorder. Imaging Perspective Lesions typically involve the pons, midbrain, and cerebellar peduncles, showing T2/FLAIR hyperintensity with or without patchy/peripheral enhancement and minimal mass effect [6,7]. In our case, the absence of diffusion restriction and increased perfusion, with a normal Cho:NAA ratio on spectroscopy, favoured an inflammatory demyelinating aetiology over a neoplasm. PET-CT showing no FDG uptake further excluded malignancy [4]. The progressive resolution on serial MRI confirmed the inflammatory nature. In contrast: Central nervous system lymphoma typically shows diffusion restriction with marked FDG hypermetabolism. Brainstem glioma usually shows progressive mass effect and solid nodular enhancement. CLIPPERS (chronic lymphocytic inflammation with pontine perivascular enhancement responsive to steroids) presents with punctate/curvilinear “peppering” enhancement. I nfectious rhombencephalitis often shows diffusion restriction with leptomeningeal enhancement. ADEM (acute disseminated encephalomyelitis), MOGAD (myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease), and NMOSD (neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder) all commonly display multifocal white-matter involvement rather than isolated brainstem involvement. Serial imaging is pivotal in excluding neoplasms and avoiding unnecessary biopsies. Imaging thus not only aids early diagnosis but also serves as an objective biomarker for treatment response and resolution. Outcome The patient responded dramatically to intravenous methylprednisolone followed by IVIG, achieving both clinical and radiological remission within three months. Literature supports similar outcomes with early immunotherapy, with combined or sequential steroid and IVIG therapy yielding excellent recovery rates [3,8]. Relapses are rare but can occur in anti-GQ1b-positive cases. Teaching Points Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis (BBE) should be suspected in cases of acute or subacute brainstem dysfunction following infection, even when antibody tests are negative. MRI showing reversible T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the pons or in cerebellar peduncles is highly suggestive. Early recognition and immunotherapy lead to near-complete recovery in most cases. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
differential_diagnosis: Brainstem lymphoma Brainstem glioma Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis ADEM (acute disseminated encephalomyelitis) MOGAD (myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease) NMOSD (neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder) CLIPPERS (chronic lymphocytic inflammation with pontine perivascular enhancement responsive to steroids)

title: Imaging spectrum of disseminated nocardiosis post-renal transplantation
clinical_history: A 57-year-old female with post-renal transplantation status presented with cough, fever and back pain for several days.
imaging_findings: Contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) of the chest was performed, revealing mass-like consolidation (Figures 1a and 1b) with an air bronchogram noted in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe. There were surrounding areas with ground glass opacity noted adjacent to this area of consolidation, suggestive of the halo sign. CECT of the abdomen revealed the presence of a peripherally enhancing collection within the left psoas muscle (Figures 2a and 2b). No evidence of spondylodiscitis changes was noted on the adjacent vertebral bodies. The culture of the abscess was positive for nocardiosis. Non-contrast CT (NCCT) of the head, followed by MRI, was done to look for dissemination. NCCT revealed a heterogeneously hypodense conglomerate cystic lesion, noted in the right paraventricular and vermian region of the cerebellum (Figure 4), which is producing mass effect in the form of effacement of the surrounding cerebellar foliae and effacement of the foramen of Luschka and fourth ventricle. However, no upstream hydrocephalus was noted. MRI showed a well-defined lesion in the right cerebellar vermis, which appeared hyperintense on T2WI/FLAIR (Figures 5a and 5b) and hypointense on T1WI (Figure 5c) with a peripheral rim of hypointensity in SWI suggestive of haemosiderin deposition (Figures 7a and 7b). Peripheral restriction of diffusion is noted in DWI (Figures 6a and 6b).
discussion: Background Nocardiosis is a rare infectious disease caused by Nocardia species, a group of aerobic gram-positive filamentous bacilli [1,2]. Nocardia can infect nearly every body part, or it can be a disseminated disease impacting organ systems. Nocardiosis predominantly affects patients with impaired cellular immunity, such as those with solid organ transplants or those receiving corticosteroids, as T-cell-mediated immunity and pulmonary macrophages play a crucial role in controlling Nocardia [3]. Clinical Perspective The presentation of nocardiosis greatly varies depending on the organ system involved. It most commonly presents as pulmonary nocardiosis. In immunocompromised patients, such as solid organ transplant recipients, dissemination to extrapulmonary sites, including the central nervous system, skin, or musculoskeletal system, can occur through haematogenous spread [4]. Early diagnosis is often challenging due to the subacute course and lack of specific clinical features. Imaging plays a crucial role in detecting the extent of disease and identifying disseminated foci. Prompt imaging-guided diagnosis and microbiological confirmation are vital for initiating targeted, often prolonged, antimicrobial therapy and improving outcomes. Imaging Perspective Imaging plays a pivotal role in the diagnosis and assessment of nocardiosis, particularly in identifying dissemination, which significantly impacts management and prognosis. On chest CT, pulmonary nocardiosis typically manifests as irregular nodules, mass-like consolidations, or cavitary lesions, sometimes accompanied by surrounding ground-glass opacity, forming a halo sign suggestive of an angioinvasive infection [5]. In cases of suspected dissemination, brain MRI is the modality of choice. Lesions often appear as ring-enhancing masses with restricted diffusion and a hypointense rim on susceptibility sequences, representing haemorrhagic or proteinaceous content [6]. These imaging features, though nonspecific, should raise suspicion for nocardial abscesses in immunocompromised patients. Definitive diagnosis relies on microbiological confirmation through culture or molecular identification of Nocardia species from clinical specimens. Outcome Given the variable antimicrobial susceptibility profiles among Nocardia species, therapeutic management must be tailored to each case based on species identification and sensitivity results. Optimal management of nocardiosis requires prolonged antimicrobial therapy, typically for a minimum of six months and continued for at least one month after full clinical resolution. Empiric treatment for pulmonary or disseminated disease should include two to three agents, with sulfonamides, particularly sulfadiazine or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, as first-line options due to their effective penetration into the central nervous system. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Nocardiosis should be considered in immunocompromised patients presenting with subacute pulmonary symptoms or multifocal abscesses involving unusual sites. CT and MRI are essential for detecting dissemination and guiding diagnostic sampling. Typical imaging findings include mass-like consolidations with halo sign in the lungs and ring-enhancing abscesses with diffusion restriction in the brain. Microbiological confirmation remains the diagnostic gold standard. Early diagnosis and prolonged, targeted antibiotic therapy significantly improve outcomes.
differential_diagnosis: Disseminated nocardiosis Disseminated tuberculosis

title: Focal splenic lesions: A challenge for the radiologist
clinical_history: A 45-year-old asymptomatic woman, with a history of right nephrectomy 8 years ago for clear cell carcinoma (T2aN0M0, G2), and normal blood tests (biochemistry, haematocrit, and PCR), underwent a follow-up computed tomography (CT).
imaging_findings: The initial contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) showed multiple focal splenic lesions of approximately 1–1.5 cm, diffusely scattered throughout the parenchyma, which were solid, well-defined, hypovascular in the arterial phase, with mild progressive enhancement during the dynamic study, and without associated splenomegaly. Post-surgical changes from right nephrectomy were also observed, with no signs of local recurrence. No other relevant findings were observed in the thorax or the abdomen. Three months later, a close follow-up CT scan was performed, which demonstrated growth of the lesions (Figure 6). For this reason, a splenectomy was finally performed (Figure 7).
discussion: Background Sarcoidosis is a multisystemic disease of unknown origin, which is histologically characterised by the formation of non-caseating granulomas. It is more frequent in the USA, particularly in African American women in the 3rd–5th decades of life [1,2]. It predominantly affects the lungs and the mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes (90%), with possible involvement of extrathoracic locations (skin, lymph nodes, eyes, liver, spleen, etc.), usually in combination with the aforementioned. Infrequently, it may manifest with exclusively extrathoracic symptoms (10%), with isolated splenic involvement being a rare manifestation [1–4]. Clinical Perspective Although it can sometimes be asymptomatic, patients often present systemic symptoms (fever, malaise, weight loss) or symptoms related to the affected target organs. Splenic involvement can produce splenomegaly and/or hypersplenism [1–4]. Since the symptoms are nonspecific, the diagnosis is usually reached by a combination of clinical, radiological, and pathological findings after the exclusion of other entities that potentially cause non-caseating granulomas [1,2,4,5]. Imaging Perspective On imaging, splenic sarcoidosis typically presents as homogeneous splenomegaly or, less frequently, as multiple focal splenic lesions [1,2,4–6]. They are usually small nodules scattered in the splenic parenchyma. On ultrasound, well-defined nodules are usually hypoechoic, whereas smaller, discrete nodules can be difficult to identify, giving a heterogeneous appearance to the splenic parenchyma [1,2,5]. On dynamic CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), they are usually hypoenhancing on the arterial phase, with fading on the equilibrium phase. They are usually hypointense on T1 and T2-weighted images (WI), being more evident on T2-WI with fat suppression [1,2,5,6]. On PET/CT, nodules are usually hypermetabolic [4,6]. When these signs occur in combination with perilymphatic-distributed pulmonary nodules and/or symmetric hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, they are highly suggestive of sarcoidosis [2]. However, when these lesions occur in isolation, imaging findings are nonspecific due to overlap with other granulomatous diseases, splenic lymphoma, or metastases. Therefore, splenic biopsy or even, in some cases, splenectomy, are necessary to reach a diagnosis [1,2,5,6]. Outcome Sometimes, spontaneous regressions can occur in asymptomatic patients, whereas symptomatic patients are usually treated with corticosteroids. In cases of splenic sarcoidosis refractory to medical therapy, a splenectomy may be necessary. Approximately a third of patients may develop chronic sarcoidosis, with mortality related to pulmonary or cardiac involvement [1,2,6]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points The spleen is a potential site of involvement of sarcoidosis, manifesting as homogeneous splenomegaly or multiple focal splenic lesions on imaging. Although typically associated with thoracic manifestations, isolated splenic involvement can occur in rare cases. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Idiopathic lactational atrophy of the unilateral breast – A rare entity
clinical_history: A 27-year-old woman with two live children presented with a gradual decrease in her left breast size over four months (Figure 1). She had no complaints of breast pain, any lump, or discharge. She was lactating at the time of presentation and was amenorrhoeic for ten months post-delivery of a healthy baby. Milk production from the left breast gradually declined over six months and stopped completely in the last three months before presentation. On examination, there was marked asymmetry with a smaller size of the left breast. There were no palpable lumps in the bilateral breast and axilla. The nipple-areolar complex was normal bilaterally. Her hormone profiles, such as thyroid profile, prolactin, serum follicular-stimulating hormone, and luteinising hormone levels, were normal. Her previous pregnancy was seven years back with a normal lactational and breastfeeding history. Her menstrual cycles were regular before the last pregnancy. There was no history of any contraceptive use, previous chest wall trauma, burn injury, radiation, or breast surgery.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound of the right breast (Figure 2) showed hypertrophic breast lobules with mildly enlarged ducts, consistent with lactating breast morphology. The left breast (Figure 3) showed markedly reduced fibroglandular tissue, with a corresponding reduction in parenchymal thickness. A reduced number and size of ducts were noted on the left side. There were no focal lesions in either breast. The bilateral axilla showed no obvious lymphadenopathy. The patient, who was in the lactational period, chose to avoid contrast administration. Thus, non-contrast MRI of the bilateral breast (Figure 4) revealed marked asymmetry, with reduced fibroglandular tissue on the left breast compared to the right breast. The subcutaneous tissue, nipple–areola complex, and chest wall were normal on both sides. There was no architectural distortion or focal lesion in either breast. DWI was not obtained, as the examination had to be terminated early due to patient discomfort within the gantry.
discussion: Background Idiopathic unilateral lactational atrophy of the breast is seldom reported in the literature [1]. No evident cause was found to be linked with this condition. Lactation and pregnancy cause various changes, such as lobular growth, the involution of fibrofatty stroma, and ductular growth, to facilitate milk production and ejection. After lactation, the breast returns to the pre-pregnancy state with the involution of lobular hyperplasia. However, such a marked asymmetry with gradual atrophy of one breast during lactation, as seen in our patient, is rare, and to date, only a few cases have been reported in the literature [1,3,7]. Clinical Perspective Galactocele, mastitis, fibroadenoma, and lactating adenoma are common findings in lactating breasts. Less frequent conditions such as gigantomastia, pregnancy-related cancers, and juvenile papillomatosis of the breast can also occur [4]. Acquired unilateral breast atrophy in the lactating breast is rare [1,3,7]. Breast asymmetry can be due to atrophy of one breast or to the enlargement of the opposite breast, caused by lesions such as breast carcinoma, phyllodes tumour. Breast atrophy can be congenital or acquired, with involvement of either unilateral or bilateral breasts. Developmental unilateral or bilateral atrophy can be in the form of breast aplasia or hypoplasia. Congenital unilateral breast atrophy includes Poland syndrome and can also be associated with chest wall deformities such as pectus excavatum or carinatum [5,6]. Congenital bilateral breast hypoplasia can have syndromic associations such as Turner syndrome. Radiation, chest wall lesions, burn injury, Epstein–Barr virus infection, and iatrogenic aetiologies such as previous tube thoracostomy, thoracotomy, and breast surgery, can impair breast development, leading to unilateral acquired breast atrophy [5,6]. Acquired causes of bilateral breast atrophy are mostly due to hormonal alterations, such as postpartum Sheehan syndrome or hypoestrogenic states [7]. Unilateral breast atrophy during lactation has no identifiable definitive cause. However, the milk production and the breast used during lactation can be potentially related [7]. Imaging Perspective Ultrasound imaging of the breast shows reduced fibroglandular parenchyma in the atrophied breast. The ducts in the nipple–areolar complex are also reduced as compared to the normal breast. Any focal mass lesion in the breast or chest wall causing breast asymmetry will be ruled out. MRI plays a crucial role in assessing the contralateral breast, particularly because mammography and ultrasonography may miss suspicious lesions during lactation due to increased breast size, marked glandular density, and higher echogenicity. The milk-rich fat makes the breast look more echogenic in ultrasound and causes a diffusely increased T2 signal on MRI [2]. In such cases, MRI of the breast provides three-dimensional imaging, which can help confirm the breast findings and exclude any underlying chest wall pathology. An additional advantage of MRI is that it is a radiation-free modality, making it especially suitable for imaging during the lactational period. For optimal sensitivity in detecting occult lesions, contrast-enhanced MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences is recommended. Idiopathic lactational unilateral breast atrophy should be kept as a differential whenever any lactating female presents with complaints of marked breast asymmetry after excluding other aetiologies of breast atrophy with relevant history and imaging. Outcome Treatment includes breast reconstruction, such as augmentation mammoplasty of the reduced breast or surgical breast implants. Counselling and patient education are a must to help them overcome the psychological trauma of sudden gross disfigurement. In our case, along with counselling, augmentation mammoplasty and surgical breast implantation were offered but denied by the patient. On follow-up over two years, and even after the cessation of lactation from the normal right breast, there was marked asymmetry with the reduced left breast. Teaching Points Idiopathic lactational unilateral breast atrophy is a rare entity that should be kept as a differential whenever any lactating female presents with complaints of marked breast asymmetry. Imaging modalities will help in excluding other differentials of breast asymmetry. More cases and research insights are needed to find a definitive aetiology and associations of this condition.

title: Relapsing polychondritis with tracheobronchial involvement
clinical_history: A 52-year-old man with a history of chronic sinusitis presented with low-grade fever and persistent cough. Blood tests showed elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and leukocytosis. Despite five courses of antibiotics over six weeks, symptoms persisted, and he was referred for a CT thorax/abdomen and whole-body FDG PET/CT for further evaluation.
imaging_findings: Initial thoracic and abdominal CT with contrast showed diffuse circumferential wall thickening of the trachea and main bronchi, with subtle peritracheal reaction and a few enlarged lymph nodes (Figure 1). A whole-body FDG PET/CT scan was subsequently performed. It showed intense symmetrical FDG uptake in the laryngeal cartilage, thickened tracheal wall, main bronchi, and bilateral segmental bronchi (Figure 2). Additional mild uptake was seen in the nasal septum and in a few mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes. The pattern of symmetric FDG uptake in cartilaginous structures of the upper airways in combination with wall thickening was interpreted as inflammatory and considered consistent with relapsing polychondritis.
discussion: Background Relapsing polychondritis (RP) is a rare, chronic, autoimmune disease characterised by repeated inflammation of cartilaginous tissues, including those of the auricles, nasal septum, respiratory tract, and joints [1]. The pathophysiology remains unclear but is believed to involve both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses against cartilage-specific proteins, such as type II collagen and matrilin-1 [2]. This results in inflammation, oedema, and progressive cartilage degeneration, which in the respiratory tract can become life-threatening. Typical onset is in mid-adulthood, often presenting with subtle or fluctuating symptoms, causing diagnostic delay [3]. Clinical Perspective RP often presents with non-specific, fluctuating symptoms such as low-grade fever, fatigue, cough, or localised pain, depending on the affected cartilage [1]. Respiratory involvement occurs in up to 50% of patients and can manifest as dyspnoea, stridor, or recurrent respiratory infections [4]. However, in early stages, symptoms may be subtle and transient, leading to significant diagnostic delay [5]. Imaging is essential to evaluate the extent and distribution of cartilaginous inflammation, particularly in the airways, where early detection of wall thickening or collapse is important [6]. Imaging Perspective In RP, contrast-enhanced CT is an essential first-line imaging modality for assessing airway involvement. A hallmark finding is smooth, circumferential thickening of the tracheobronchial wall with sparing of the posterior membranous portion [3], which helps distinguish RP from other causes of airway disease, such as malignancy or granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) [1]. Calcifications in affected cartilage may also be seen in chronic cases [3]. FDG PET/CT provides complementary information by highlighting metabolically active inflammation in cartilage structures, even before morphological changes become apparent on CT. This can be particularly useful in early cases [7]. Increased symmetrical FDG uptake in laryngeal, tracheal, or bronchial cartilage is highly suggestive of RP, and PET/CT can help assess disease extent and monitor treatment response [1]. While there is no single pathognomonic imaging feature, the combination of CT findings (cartilaginous airway thickening with posterior sparing) and PET/CT evidence of inflammatory activity strongly supports the diagnosis in the appropriate clinical context [8]. Biopsy is not always required, but may be considered when imaging and clinical features are inconclusive or to exclude mimics such as neoplasia [3]. Outcome The patient was referred to a rheumatology department for suspected relapsing polychondritis. Biopsy was considered but ultimately deferred due to airway risks. Medical treatment was initiated with high-dose prednisolone, followed by biologic therapy. Treatment response was assessed with follow-up MRI, demonstrating partial regression of the tracheobronchial wall thickening (Figures 3 and 4). Despite treatment, the patient continued to experience recurrent respiratory exacerbations.
differential_diagnosis: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) Tracheobronchial amyloidosis Relapsing polychondritis Sarcoidosis

title: Superinfected retroperitoneal lymphatic malformation draped around the left ovarian vein
clinical_history: A 46-year-old female presented to the emergency department with progressive abdominal pain, initially localised to the left lower quadrant but later diffuse. She reported mild nausea without vomiting. A temperature of 39.6°C was recorded. Laboratory results revealed an elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) of 183.9 mg/L and leukocytosis (18.98 × 10⁹/L). No relevant previous abdominal surgery or known malignancy was reported.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound demonstrated a polycystic mass in the left hemiabdomen, with surrounding fat stranding suggestive of inflammatory changes (Figure 1). CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large (max. craniocaudal length 19 cm), lobulated, hypodense, cystic mass in the left iliac fossa and retroperitoneum, indistinguishable from the left ovary and draped around the left ovarian vein, which remained patent (Figures 2a and 2b). The lesion showed thin walls and no mural contrast-enhancing nodules. There was a small amount of free intraperitoneal fluid, perilesional fat stranding, and focal peritoneal thickening in the left hemiabdomen. MRI confirmed a multiloculated mass that was hyperintense on T2-weighted (Figure 3a) and hypointense on T1-weighted (Figure 3b), without solid enhancing components. The lesion extended along the retroperitoneum adjacent to the left ovarian vein. No evidence of haemorrhage was seen. Multiple uterine leiomyomas were incidentally detected.
discussion: Background Lymphatic malformations (LMs) are congenital vascular anomalies caused by abnormal development of lymphatic channels. They are usually diagnosed in childhood, most commonly in the head, neck, and axillae; retroperitoneal occurrence is rare (< 1% of cases). In adults, they may remain asymptomatic until incidentally discovered or when complicated by infection, haemorrhage, or rapid enlargement [1]. Clinical Perspective While usually asymptomatic, lymphatic malformations can become infected, causing acute pain, fever, and inflammatory markers. This infection can occur because of stasis of lymph within cystic spaces, bacterial translocation, or contiguous spread from adjacent structures. Imaging Perspective On ultrasound, LMs typically appear as thin-walled, multiloculated anechoic cystic masses. CT demonstrates hypodense, non-enhancing lesions with possible surrounding inflammatory changes if complicated. MRI provides optimal tissue characterisation: uncomplicated LMs are usually T1-hypointense, T2-hyperintense, and may have thin septations without solid components. A key feature to differentiate LMs from other cystic lesions is that they are transspatial, involving multiple tissue planes and often moulding themselves around adjacent structures, without mass effect [2,3]. Outcome Our patient received broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy for several days and was able to leave the hospital in good condition. Complete surgical excision or sclerotherapy might be considered to prevent recurrence. Teaching Points Retroperitoneal lymphatic malformations (LMs) are rare in adults and can mimic other cystic masses (e.g., cystic neoplasms, cystic degeneration of tumours, abscess). Infection may lead to atypical features, including wall thickening, surrounding fat stranding, and systemic inflammatory response. Cross-sectional imaging (especially MRI) is crucial for characterisation and for determining the relationship to adjacent structures, including vessels. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Beyond the big toe: Chronic gout presenting as peroneal tendinopathy
clinical_history: A 59-year-old female with diabetes and hypertension presented with left leg and ankle swelling for 3 months. She had no history of known gout. Physical examination showed swelling of the left distal leg and ankle region with no evidence of erythema.
imaging_findings: Dual-energy CT (DECT) images show multiple small monosodium urate (MSU) crystal deposits in bilateral peroneal tendons (R > L), around the base of the first metatarsal in the right foot and periarticular region of the tibiotalar joint (Figures 1 and 2). Peroneal tendinopathy with mild soft tissue thickening is seen in MRI (Figure 3). Based on the imaging findings, a diagnosis of bilateral peroneal tendinopathy secondary to chronic gout was made. The patient was treated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and xanthine oxidase inhibitors.
discussion: Background Gout is the most common crystal arthropathy caused by deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joints and periarticular tissues, most commonly the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint (podagra) [1,3]. Extra-articular involvement is less frequent, and tendon infiltration is rare, usually affecting the Achilles and patellar tendons, with peroneal tendon involvement extremely uncommon [3,4]. Pathophysiology Gout results from hyperuricaemia (> 6.8 mg/dL), due to overproduction or underexcretion of uric acid. At high concentrations, MSU crystals precipitate in joints, cartilage, tendons, bursae, and periarticular tissues, especially in cooler peripheral sites (first MTP, ankle, ear pinna). Neutrophil/macrophage phagocytosis of crystals activates the NLRP3 inflammasome, releasing IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, and chemokines, producing acute gout flares [1,3]. Clinical Perspective Gout typically occurs in people above 40 years of age with a strong male predilection. Disease stages: (1) asymptomatic hyperuricaemia, (2) acute gouty arthritis, (3) intercritical gout, (4) chronic tophaceous gout, and (5) gout-related nephropathy [6]. Patients usually present with pain, swelling and erythema of the affected joint. Sudden painful monoarthritis, classically the first MTP joint is seen, later progressing to oligoarthritis and polyarthritis. Imaging Perspective Radiograph shows punched-out erosions with sclerotic overhanging margins (“rat-bite”), juxta-articular location, soft tissue tophi and swelling. CT and DECT are the modalities of choice. Tophi appear as 160–170 HU soft tissue masses within bones, around joints, tendons, or in the soft tissue planes. DECT can be used to identify MSU deposits in articular and periarticular regions by exploiting the photon energy-dependent attenuation of different materials [2,3,5]. DECT can also be used to assess treatment response [3,6]. Ultrasound detects effusion and synovial thickening. Tophi appear heteroechoic, sometimes with the double contour sign. Inability to visualise intraosseous gout is the main disadvantage of ultrasound. MRI is best for bone marrow oedema. Tophi show low to intermediate T1 and heterogeneous T2 signals, with variable enhancement [2,3]. Thickening of the involved tendons with tophi, adjacent soft tissue thickening and inflammation can be seen. Differential Diagnoses Pseudogout is more common in wrists, metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints with chondrocalcinosis, and hook-like osteophytes. Hydroxyapatite crystal deposition disease is characterised by periarticular and intra-articular calcium deposits. Septic arthritis shows juxta-articular and subchondral bony destruction with joint effusion and synovial enhancement on MRI. Erosive arthritis most common locations are interphalangeal joints and the first MCP joint, with subchondral erosions (gull-wing appearance). Treatment Acute management is done with NSAIDs, colchicine, glucocorticoids, IL-1 inhibitors (anakinra, canakinumab) for refractory flares [7]. Long-term prevention is done with xanthine oxidase inhibitors: allopurinol, febuxostat, uricosurics like probenecid, pegloticase (for refractory tophaceous gout) [7]. Surgical management includes the excision of symptomatic tophi/tendon deposits that cause pain or dysfunction. Teaching Points Tophaceous gout involving peroneal tendons is rare and appears as heterogeneous, lobulated soft-tissue masses along tendon sheaths, often with low to intermediate T1 and variable T2 signals. Dual-energy CT can confirm urate crystal deposition by colour-coding monosodium urate material. Recognising these imaging features helps distinguish gout from other causes, such as calcific tendinopathy.

final_diagnosis: Bilateral peroneal tendinopathy secondary to chronic gout

title: Incidental finding during active surveillance of Gleason 3+3 prostate cancer
clinical_history: A 70-year-old male with a history of bladder cancer (Ta), treated with transurethral resection and periodic instillations of Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG), and a Gleason 3+3 prostate cancer in the right prostatic lobe under active surveillance, underwent a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for prostatic evaluation.
imaging_findings: Follow-up 3 Tesla (T) multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) showed a new 18 mm nodule located in the left posterolateral peripheral zone (PZ) at the prostatic apex. The nodule was homogeneously hypointense on T2-weighted images with a broad contact and bulging of the prostatic capsule (Figure 1). Moreover, it showed marked high signal intensity on diffusion-weighted images (DWI), prominent low signal intensity on apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) (Figure 2), and a peripheral rim enhancement on dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) T1-weighted images (Figure 3). Since the patient was under active surveillance for his Gleason 3+3 prostate carcinoma, a biopsy was scheduled 15 days after the MRI. Finally, the histological analysis confirmed the diagnosis suspected on the MRI.
discussion: Background Granulomatous prostatitis (GP) is a rare inflammatory condition of the prostate, found in 0.6–1.5% of prostate biopsies, histologically characterised by the presence of granulomas. GP has a broad aetiology, and can be idiopathic, infectious (tuberculosis, fungal), iatrogenic (post-biopsy or post-surgery), or related to systemic granulomatous diseases (sarcoidosis, vasculitis). BCG instillation for the treatment of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer is one of the most frequent causes of GP [1–6]. It has been proposed that idiopathic cases result from an autoimmune reaction caused by stasis of prostatic secretions and urinary reflux [1,2]. Clinical Perspective Patients may be asymptomatic or present with lower urinary tract symptoms, such as urinary frequency or dysuria. The PSA (prostate-specific antigen) value is usually raised, and a hardened nodule is often observed on digital rectal examination, which may raise suspicion of prostate cancer. For this reason, mpMRI is necessary to make an accurate differential diagnosis. However, in many cases, there may be an overlap between the imaging findings of both entities, making biopsy necessary [1–6]. Imaging Perspective On mpMRI, GP can be diffuse or nodular and affect the PZ, potentially extending to the transition zone. It is usually hypointense on T2-weighted images, hyperintense on DWI, and markedly hypointense on ADC [2–6]. It can also produce periprostatic fat stranding and bulging of the prostatic capsule, suggesting extraprostatic extension [2,5]. All these findings overlap with prostate cancer, resulting in PI-RADS 4 or PI-RADS 5 lesions [7]. On DCE, although it can show diffuse enhancement, GP usually shows peripheral rim enhancement in cases of caseous necrosis formation [2–6]. This enhancement pattern is rare in prostate cancer, as it usually demonstrates early diffuse enhancement with late washout on DCE [3,4]. Therefore, in a patient in an appropriate clinical setting (such as BCG instillation), the presence of peripheral rim enhancement with a central non-enhancing necrotic area may suggest GP diagnosis, thus avoiding biopsy [3–6]. Outcome Treatment is only necessary in symptomatic GP cases and will vary depending on the aetiology. Most idiopathic cases are self-limiting. Contrarily, symptomatic cases caused by BCG instillations are treated with anti-tuberculous medications and discontinuation of the instillations [1,2]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Granulomatous prostatitis (GP) may be indistinguishable from prostate cancer on imaging, resulting in PI-RADS 4 or PI-RADS 5 lesions. However, in an appropriate clinical setting, the presence of ring enhancement on DCE may suggest the diagnosis. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Visualisation of ischaemic priapism with sickle cell disease on CEUS
clinical_history: A 19-year-old boy diagnosed with homozygous SS sickle cell disease (SCD) 10 years previously, presented with persistent penile erection, without sexual stimulation and lasting more than 4 hours.
imaging_findings: The initial procedure was a non-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure 1). The T2-weighted sagittal plane showed lower signal intensity than expected in the normal erectile state. The scattered and unevenly distributed focal low signal intensity in the central corpus cavernosa indicated areas of small infarction or segmental thrombosis (Figure 1). Later the same day, colour Doppler ultrasound (Figure 2a) and micro-vascular imaging (Figure 2b) only demonstrated the vascular supply outside the corpora cavernosa surrounding the tunica albuginea. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS), 4.8 mLs of SonoVue™, demonstrated the patency of the cavernosal arteries in the late arterial phase, with limited filling of the arterial branches, and a truncated cavernosal artery (Figures 2c and 2d). There was no enhancement in the parenchyma of the penis. Enhanced MRI of the penis at 18 days (Figure 3) showed no enhancement on post-contrast imaging in the corpora cavernosa. A thin rim of peripheral enhancement was present bilaterally, without definite internal septal or trabecular enhancement. Patchy enhancement was seen towards the crura. The MRI features are consistent with the chronic sequelae of ischaemic priapism.
discussion: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is caused by a genetic mutation that results in an abnormal structure of haemoglobin. Homozygous patients with SCD may suffer from intermittent micro-vascular occlusive events that affect the entire body. Priapism is one of the common manifestations of SCD and may affect up to 42% of the male SCD population [1,2]. Priapism caused by SCD is an ischaemic, low-flow type of priapism, secondary to erythrocyte sickling, leading to stasis of the venous and sinusoidal penile vein drainage. On physical examination, a painful and rigid penis is usually seen. This patient underwent insertion of a malleable penile prosthesis (Coloplast Genesis ® ) bilaterally. Intraoperatively, the penis was rigid and fibrotic, with a “woody” consistency. At 10 days post-operation, the dressing was removed without complication. There were no signs of infection, and the patient reported adherence to oral antibiotics. Classical colour Doppler ultrasound findings are little or no cavernosal arterial inflow. Decreased colour Doppler flow also indicates possible thrombosis of the corpus cavernosa [3]. MRI could assess erectile tissue in ischaemic priapism and the extent of necrosis, with necrotic/infarcted tissue manifested as a low T2 signal in the central corpus cavernosa. MRI also plays an important role in differentiating ischaemic priapism from some mimicking penile metastasis, with post-contrast MRI adding further information, determining the degree of infarction for surgical planning [4–6]. Because a significant number of SCD patients have kidney dysfunction, the contrast agents of computed tomography (iodinated contrast) or magnetic resonance (gadolinium) arteriographies are not suitable. The ultrasound contrast agent used in our case is safe in the presence of renal impairment and provides better temporal and spatial resolution compared to MR or CT imaging. Ultrasound contrast agents are purely blood-pool agents that can clearly show very small blood vessels, allowing haemodynamic assessment of the cavernosal arteries. Importantly, ultrasound is radiation-free, portable, and inexpensive, and is particularly suitable for superficial male genital examinations [7]. Take Home Message This case illustrates the usefulness of CEUS to rapidly and accurately, without patient compromise and with patient comfort, establish patent cavernosal arteries, thrombosis of the corpora cavernosa in a SCC patient with low-flow priapism. This enabled early and definitive surgical intervention. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: Dedifferentiated liposarcoma
clinical_history: A 70-year-old male patient with known prostate cancer and bone metastases presented to a surgery consult complaining of a mass in his right thigh. Physical examination revealed a firm, non-mobile mass located within the adductor muscle region of the right thigh, which was painful on palpation.
imaging_findings: MRI of the right thigh revealed a heterogeneous 13 × 9 × 8 cm (longitudinal, transverse, and anteroposterior dimensions) mass involving the right adductor muscles, showing soft-tissue enhancing areas, necrotic and cystic regions, and peripheral fatty components (Figures 1 and 2). This mass also showed significant arterial vascularisation (Figure 3).
discussion: Background Dedifferentiated liposarcoma is an aggressive subtype of liposarcoma with metastatic potential, mainly to the lungs. It occurs most commonly in men over 65 years of age, typically involving the extremities and retroperitoneum [1]. Data from a large population-based registry (NETSARC+, > 11,000 cases) confirmed that dedifferentiated liposarcoma carries a significantly worse prognosis compared to well-differentiated liposarcoma [2]. Most commonly, it has a well-differentiated liposarcoma component and a non-adipose sarcomatous component. Clinical Perspective In the extremities, dedifferentiated liposarcoma typically presents as a rapidly enlarging, sometimes painful soft-tissue mass. Imaging is requested to characterise the lesion, assess its local extension, and guide biopsy and surgical planning. Radiologists must convey the heterogeneous nature of the tumour, identify dedifferentiated areas, and help distinguish it from other soft-tissue sarcomas [3]. Imaging Perspective On MR images, the well-differentiated liposarcomatous component demonstrates fat signal intensity that may be globular or nodular (Figures 1b and 2a). There are often thick (> 2 mm) enhancing septa. The non-adipose sarcomatous component can be as small as a 1 cm nodular area and as large as the totality of the lesion. It is usually iso to hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, remaining hyperintense after fat suppression/saturation. These areas enhance heterogeneously. Some other components may be variably present, namely myxoid areas, cysts, necrosis, haemorrhage, mineralisation, and fibrosis (Figures 1 and 2) [3,4]. Pathology Perspective When dedifferentiated liposarcoma is suspected, biopsy should target a solid, enhancing, non-adipose region of the lesion. Histologically, the transition from well-differentiated to non-lipogenic sarcomatous areas defines the diagnosis. Immunohistochemistry is useful to confirm divergent differentiation and exclude mimics. Diffuse nuclear expression of MDM2 and/or CDK4 strongly supports the diagnosis, and large registry studies have confirmed the consistency of this expression pattern [4,5]. Outcome The patient underwent wide local excision with adductor transposition. Pathology confirmed dedifferentiated liposarcoma, staged as pT4, with a minimum resection margin of 3 mm. Postoperative adjuvant radiotherapy was initiated. Prognosis remains guarded, given the higher risk of recurrence and metastasis compared to well-differentiated liposarcoma [1,5]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Dedifferentiated liposarcoma contains both fatty and non-adipose sarcomatous components. MRI is essential to identify dedifferentiated areas and guide biopsy. Biopsy should target solid, enhancing, non-adipose regions. MDM2 and/or CDK4 positivity supports the diagnosis and helps exclude mimics. Multidisciplinary management is essential; surgery and radiotherapy remain the mainstay of treatment.

title: Multiple intracranial masses and progressive bilateral hearing loss
clinical_history: A 43-year-old woman with a 20-year history of progressive headaches and prior resections of intracranial masses (2014 and 2015) presented for follow-up evaluation. During the preceding year, she had developed severe bilateral hearing loss, seizures, and symptoms of intracranial hypertension, including new, intense headaches.
imaging_findings: The current contrast-enhanced cranial MRI demonstrates multiple bilateral intracranial lesions. Several extra-axial, contrast-enhancing masses were identified along the falx cerebri, consistent with meningiomas (Figures 1a and 1b). Bilateral vestibular schwannomas were also evident, characterised by heterogeneously enhancing lesions arising from both internal auditory canals (Figure 1c). Additionally, a distinct enhancing lesion was noted in the left eyelid. A non-contrast head CT obtained on an emergency basis revealed progressive ventriculomegaly with rounding of the lateral ventricles, consistent with developing hydrocephalus and correlating with the patient’s acute symptoms (Figure 2).
discussion: Background Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) is a rare autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NF2 tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 22 [1]. This gene encodes the merlin protein (also called schwannomin), a protein which regulates Schwann cell growth [2]. The absence of functional merlin leads to the classic triad of tumours: schwannomas, meningiomas, and ependymomas. The presence of bilateral vestibular schwannomas is the diagnostic hallmark of the disease [1]. Clinical Perspective NF2 typically presents in young adulthood, with an average age of diagnosis around 25 [2]. The most common presenting complaint is progressive sensorineural hearing loss, followed by tinnitus and balance issues, related to bilateral vestibular schwannomas (BVS). Our patient’s presentation with severe bilateral hearing loss, seizures, and intracranial hypertension is a classic, though advanced, manifestation. Case severity can be stratified into the mild “Gardner” phenotype or the severe “Wishart” phenotype; this patient’s early onset and multiple tumour burden align with the more severe form [2]. Imaging Perspective Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the imaging modality of choice for both diagnosis and lifelong surveillance [1]. In this case, the current (2025) contrast-enhanced cranial MRI was crucial for demonstrating the constellation of tumours, such as multiple inherited schwannomas and meningiomas. The pathognomonic BVS are seen emerging from the internal auditory canals (IACs), showing typical T2 hyperintensity and heterogeneous enhancement [1]. The multiple meningiomas, the second most common tumour in NF2, are also classic. They appear as dural-based, extra-axial masses that are T1 isointense to grey matter and demonstrate avid, homogeneous enhancement, often with a “dural tail” sign [3]. Longitudinal imaging is critical, not only to monitor tumour growth but to detect life-threatening complications, such as obstructive hydrocephalus. Outcome The management goal in NF2 is often palliative, not curative. Given the patient’s acute presentation with intracranial hypertension, the immediate life-saving intervention was a ventricular shunt followed by a staged surgical plan to resect the most symptomatic tumours. Radiotherapy was specifically contraindicated. Radiation use in NF2 patients must be carefully considered, as it can induce or accelerate new tumours in these patients. It has been reported that nearly 50% of all malignant post-radiation degenerations occur in the context of NF2, which fully justifies the decision to avoid it [2]. Teaching Points Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are pathognomonic for Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2). The presence of multiple intracranial tumour types (schwannomas and meningiomas) should immediately suggest NF2. Lifelong surveillance with high-resolution, thin-cut MRI of the brain and spine is essential for monitoring tumour growth and complications. Radiotherapy should be avoided in NF2 patients due to the high risk of radiation-induced secondary neoplasms. NF2 management is complex and must be handled by an experienced, multidisciplinary team. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.

title: A hit in the target: Baló’s concentric sclerosis
clinical_history: A 54-year-old male with a history of bronchial asthma and ankylosing spondylitis presented to the emergency department with progressive left-sided hemiparesis, primarily of the arm (strength of 4/5) and central left facial pain on examination.
imaging_findings: Magnetic resonance imaging showed pseudotumoural-like lesions affecting the corpus callosum, periventricular and juxtacortical white matter with apparent alternating T2 signal in concentric rings (Figures 1a, 1b and 1c), a peripheral ring of restriction (Figures 2a and 2b), and heterogeneous enhancement with different uptake patterns after intravenous contrast administration (Figures 3a and 3b). No significant mass effect or perilesional oedema were present. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination ruled out the presence of IgG oligoclonal bands and malignant cells.
discussion: Background Baló’s concentric sclerosis (BCS) is a rare demyelinating disease to be considered a subtype within the spectrum of multiple sclerosis [1–4]. This entity usually presents as a single or multiple concentric tumefactive-like lesions, which cause widespread neurologic dysfunction. Clinical Perspective Clinical course of this disease is considered similar to Marburg’s variant of multiple sclerosis, which shows a severe, monophasic course, with rapid and sometimes fulminant progression [1]. Most common symptoms include headache, aphasia, focal seizures or cognitive/behavioural dysfunction [1]. Cerebrospinal fluid analyses also often reveal a mononuclear inflammatory reaction and occasionally oligoclonal bands. Imaging Perspective The most characteristic feature of this condition is the alternating concentric layers of demyelination and preserved myelin, giving rise to the characteristic image seen on MRI of alternating bands or concentric rings appearance on T2-weighted and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images (bull’s-eye sign/onion bulb appearance) [3,4]. Lesions may be solitary or multiple and often mimic intracranial space-occupying lesions [4]. Although diagnosis has historically been made postmortem based on pathological findings, the most recent studies support the fundamental role of brain MRI for early and definitive diagnosis of BCS [3]. It is important to remark that this role may have a significant influence on morbidity and mortality associated with the disease [2]. In our case, diagnosis was based on clinical signs and symptoms consistent with Baló’s concentric sclerosis, the characteristic concentric rings on MR images, and exclusion of other neurologic diseases. Outcome As with other forms of multiple sclerosis, the use of corticosteroids in the acute phase is essential, although this subtype is usually rapidly progressive and responds poorly to treatment. Take Home Message / Teaching Points Although this subtype of multiple sclerosis is infrequent, the role of MRI is fundamental in early diagnosis. Radiological findings can be challenging and may be mistaken for intracranial occupying lesions, and thus, the radiologist’s knowledge of this entity can be the key to interpreting the imaging study correctly.

title: Persistent dorsal forefoot pain in an active adult
clinical_history: A female adult with weeks of progressive forefoot pain was referred by the occupational health department to radiology for a suspected Morton’s neuroma. She had recently increased physical activity. During scanning, the patient localised the maximal tenderness over the dorsal distal second metatarsal. There were no initial radiographs, as the request targeted soft tissue.
imaging_findings: Ultrasound of the left forefoot was initially focused on the third intermetatarsal space, given the patient’s complaints, but it was later extended to the symptomatic dorsal distal second metatarsal. Greyscale ultrasound showed mild periosteal reaction at the metatarsal neck with hyperechogenicity of adjacent fat and soft tissues, compatible with reactive oedema (Figure 1a). Conventional colour Doppler acquisitions were attempted but did not demonstrate visible periosteal hyperaemia, likely due to extremely low velocity flow, and therefore, no image was recorded. A microvascular Doppler mode was subsequently used, which successfully depicted subtle periosteal hypervascularity (Figure 1b). A small third-space Morton’s neuroma (≈ 6 x 5 mm) was also identified (Figure 2). No metatarsophalangeal joint effusion/synovitis or tendon abnormality was seen. MRI performed one month later revealed a stress fracture traversing the neck of the second metatarsal with marked marrow and soft-tissue oedema (Figure 3). No other osseous or articular abnormalities were seen.
discussion: Background Metatarsal stress fractures lie within the bone-stress spectrum from stress reaction to cortical break. The second metatarsal is most frequently involved due to repetitive forefoot loading and relative rigidity within the forefoot lever arm [1]. Early radiographs have low sensitivity and may remain normal for 2–3 weeks [2]. Clinical Perspective This case illustrates a common clinic-imaging discrepancy: the referral asked for a neuroma, yet the patient’s point of maximal tenderness was located over the dorsal distal second metatarsal. The referral from occupational health focused on a suspected Morton’s neuroma, and therefore, no initial radiography was obtained. Directed questioning revealed a recent increase in physical activity, a classical precipitating factor [1]. Proactively scanning where it hurts transformed a soft-tissue work-up into a bone-stress pathway, avoiding diagnostic delay that a normal early radiograph could have introduced. Imaging Perspective In our case, ultrasound raised suspicion and MRI confirmed/staged the lesion. Early radiographs have low sensitivity and may remain normal for 2–3 weeks [2]. Ultrasound findings of periosteal thickening or subtle reaction with adjacent soft-tissue oedema should raise suspicion for stress injury [3]. In our case, conventional Doppler was negative, a recognised limitation when periosteal flow is below the velocity detection threshold of standard Doppler modes. This justified the use of microvascular Doppler, which revealed subtle hyperaemia supporting an early stress response. Ultrasound is therefore considered a triage tool because it cannot evaluate medullary oedema or grade the injury. MRI is the reference standard: fluid-sensitive sequences depict marrow oedema and, when present, a low-signal fracture line at the metatarsal neck. MRI grading correlates with the time to return to activity, guiding prognosis and follow-up [2,4,5]. A small third-space Morton’s neuroma is common and may be incidental; insist on symptom–lesion concordance. Other differentials include extensor tendinopathy, plantar plate tear, Freiberg infraction at the metatarsal head, and osteomyelitis when clinically suspected [6]. Remember that bone marrow oedemas are non-specific; location/morphology (linear peri-cortical pattern, fracture line) separates stress fracture from bone contusion or infection. Outcome Second-metatarsal neck injuries are low-risk and usually respond to conservative treatment: activity modification, protected weight-bearing (stiff-soled shoe/boot), analgesia and optimisation of risk factors (training load, footwear, vitamin D). Routine imaging follow-up is unnecessary if symptoms improve, but persistent pain warrants reassessment [2,4]. Take Home Message / Teaching Points In forefoot pain, scan where it hurts: periosteal hyperaemia and focal peri-metatarsal oedema on US should be better characterised by MRI. Periosteal hyperaemia and soft-tissue oedema on ultrasound should prompt MRI for confirmation and grading. Microvascular Doppler may help detect low-flow periosteal hypervascularity when conventional Doppler is equivocal. MRI confirms and grades bone-stress injuries, which then affect expected recovery. In second-metatarsal neck stress fractures, conservative management is usually enough. All patient data have been completely anonymised throughout the entire manuscript and related files.
